The Wolf of Wall Street is the most disappointing film of the year for me. It is a film with bad people doing terrible things for three butt-numbing hours. It is a film that asks its audience to laugh at gratuitous and dangerous drug use. It is a film that asks its audience to be entertained by the degradation of women. (Every woman in the film is portrayed as an object.) It is a film that asks its audience to take delight in one mans conniving ways that hurt people. I could not accept what the film asked of me. I was repulsed by everything about it, especially its mens locker room tone and humor. 
Unlike filmmaker Martin Scorseses Goodfellasa film with bad characters whom you liked in spite of their badness because they possessed a certain charmnone of the characters in The Wolf of Wall Street are likeable, charming, or have a redeeming feature. For this reason, I had difficulty being interested in the true story of Jordan Belfort (Leonardo Dicaprio) and his rise to and fall from wealth. 
I am not a prude about sex and drugs in film, and I am capable of laughing at dumb, lowbrow jokes and situations however, I could not laugh at the material in The Wolf of Wall Street because it insulted my gender and intelligence, and also because I was aware the situations in the film actually happened, which made it all the worse. It is rare for a film to offend me in every possible way a person may be offended, but The Wolf of Wall Street managed to do so.   
My friend who attended the screening with me said I had a scowl on my face through the entire film. She generally likes every film she sees (she is not highly critical), and she did not like the film either. 
The Wolf of Wall Street will likely appeal only to men who like bro humor. I caution men who see this film with a woman whom they care about to be very careful about what they say to the woman afterwards. 
The only way I could have enjoyed The Wolf of Wall Street is if, before the film, I snorted as much coke and downed as many quaaludes as Dicaprio and Jonah Hill do in the film.

Scorsese glosses over the fact that Belfort served only 22 months of the 4 years he was sentenced to in prison. 
All of the terrible things shown in the film are not shown for the purpose of exposing or critiquing them as wrong they are simply a gratuitous display meant to entertain.

I dont like pantomime.
As it turns out I am also not particularly fond of messed up, Bacchus driven, deprived pantomime in the hands of Scorcese.
I love Scorcese. Even when some of his films dont speak to me there is always the feeling that youre in the hands of a competent and skilled filmmaker with a clear sense of style and a great ability to weave a tale. In that respect the Wolf of Wall Street is an odd beast. Its hard to ignore some of the absolutely brilliant directorial prowess Scorcese puts on display. There are long, beautifully choreographed shots alternated with some frenetic scenes in which he betrays a keen sense of comedic timing. Yet for every good choice he makes, he seems to make a bad one as well, making this an overlong and bloated mess, with a terribly uneven script to match it.
For three hours we get to see Jordan Belfort go from wannabe asshole to complete and utter asshole. Now, for all intents and purposes that is a character arc, its just not one I want to be stuck with for such a long time. The entirety is so over the top that it exceeds any satirical potential it might have and lands smack dab in the middle of farcical comedy, losing any possibility of taking something from it as it gets overshouted by all its own sound and fury.
I cannot get over the ludicrous running time. Im sure that, as it is based on Belforts biography, all the acts of debauchery must be fun to read, but watching them pass by in a showreel for two and a half hours got very tiresome. I cant say that I was bored, I was just numb after a while seeing the narrative slowly get burried under an avalanche of repetitive nonsense. Every time I got the sensation that wed get an inkling of character development or a glimpse of a reality filled with real people I could  connect to, Scorcese pulls the rug from under you and veers off towards yet another drug infused party. I am fully aware that is probably not the point to connect to the characters here, but I want to understand them and that just doesnt happen, unless theyre all one-dimensional, greed driven bastards, in which case you really dont need three hours to relate their antics. I guess that thats where the satire is supposed to lie, but it just isnt dealt with cleverly enough to really say anything about it. 
After all these superficial shenanigans, the final half hour suddenly lands in an out of place tonal shift that, in itself, holds scenes that are excellent and among the best in the film, but in the film makes no sense at all. You cant all of a sudden start to invest in and explore potential drama and characterization after 150 minutes of ignoring them. Exemplary of the frustratingly messy nature of the film.
The acting is excellent, especially from the supporting cast. Hill channels some sort of coked up Jerry Lewis and fits the style of most of the film perfectly. Reiner, McConnaughey, Robbie theyre all fine. Which brings me to DiCaprio. I think hes a great actor and is unbelievably talented. The thing is, with his latest films I always get the feeling Im watching a DiCaprio Performance. This is no exception. He is obviously having fun with it, but he never seems to completely lose himself in his character. He just doesnt seem to be able to take himself out of the equation. Im sure that the brashness of his performance will win many people over, especially come award season, it just didnt do it for me. Should the Academy give him an Oscar for this, that, to me, would feel like a pity fuck (pardon my French).
The weird thing is that I see the appeal. I fully understand why so many people like this. Its crude, brash and over the top. It has, despite its flaws, more quality in it than most films. But in the end it did absolutely nothing for me. Style, plot, narrative, they all missed their mark, making this a very long three hours leaving me with a film that I consider to be one of Scorceses weakest films.

woo boy. i cannot say that i came into letterboxd looking to win friends and influence people today.
yes, i am about seven years and two million think-pieces too late in watching what is commonly considered to be scorseses late career magnum opus. lets get this out of the way- this is by far his funniest, flashiest picture. (i laughed until i cried at certain points thank you leo and jonah hill.) its so devilishly entertaining you almost (almost) forget that gargantuan, foreboding run-time. its bombastic. its excessive. its dizzying. its exhilarating. its fun. so much fun.
im not sure what the point was.
part of my issues are the exact opposite of the issues everyone else seems to have (of course im talking about those who have issues with this- we are a small and lonely group). ive seen a fair amount of complaints about being expected to spend time with reprehensible characters. im wondering where exactly all these people have been all this time scorsese has released movies. jordan belfort is one of his most palatable protagonists! try spending two hours watching jake lamotta hideously abuse yet another well-meaning person in his life and get back to me!
and unfortunately, thats the problem. i never got a sense of what exactly this man was doing that made him deserve the karmic ass-kicking we all knew was coming. sure, we are told that his firm is committing some very illegal, no-good acts and in passing, we get some vague sort of assurance that theyre defrauding innocent people. but were never shown that! instead, were shown yet another scene of leo taking ludes and being filthy rich. the only person jordan actually seems to hurt is himself (and his wife on occasion- the movie doesnt seem that interested in this though.) this man doesnt need jail. he needs rehab and maybe a nice massage after.
look, to make it clear, i dont think this film is glamorizing jordan belfort or his lifestyle (its not exactly not glamorizing it either but well be generous). its (rightfully!) cataloguing, transmitting, piously recording the very real story of a group of men who seized the world and managed to be untethered to any sort of mortal obligations for a few sweet, sweet decades. its a satire. to observe the excess and to be excessive is the point!
its just... not doing much more than that. yes, we get the sense that jordans life is getting increasingly empty as the run-time goes on and yes, theres that patented scorsese fall (tm) that occurs in the last thirty minutes or so. most of this film however is given over to the repetitive rinse-repeat of getting high and fucking blondes and making the same damn sales pitch day in day out while luxuriating in mind-blowing wealth... what is scorsese trying to say here? that outrageous lifestyles consisting of prostitutes and drugs sure are outrageous? that wall street is corrupt? dont take ludes when you havent checked the expiration date? dang, boy, i could have figured those ones out by myself.
im not going to break the wheel here by pointing out that tonally and artistically, this is pretty much the white-collar version of goodfellas (and yes, i did love goodfellas). however, goodfellas was just as much a deconstruction of americas fascination with gangsters as it was a straightforward chronicle of henry hills life. scorsese instinctually understood both the appeal and the danger of the mafia, he seems more out of his depth here.
there are times where the movie almost grabs me however. there are times where i can almost reach onto something genuinely interesting. the interpretation that i like best of this whole thing is that wall street and the fradulent business jordan belfort created represent a twisted ideal of the american dream. the most lasting scene for me personally is the one wherein leo paternalistically praises his underling. kimmie, he bellows has gucci clothes and a vacation home in the bahamas. when i knew her, all those years ago, she was a single-mom who couldnt pay her rent! why not focus on that? more of the very real pain in leos voice when he entreats us to remember that hes been a rich man and a poor man (and hell choose being rich every time), less scenes of men with bad toupees mugging for the camera as they bicker over whether or not they can get away with launching someone at a bulls-eye.
we needed more of the rise, not the plateau of success that this movie stalls in for far too long. give me the hunger, desperation, the twisted means to an end that capitalism forces on far too many people. give me the anguish of those that invested in penny stock, let me see the effects of jordans company. satire only works when it cuts and this slides down my throat far too easily.

Few films are so defined by their final shot. Scorsese turns the camera around on us. Are we what allows a Jordan Belfort to thrive? Are we complicit through our observation? If we didnt watch what came before with total disgust, dont we have little of Jordan Belfort in us?
Maybe its not fair of Scorsese to condemn us. Hes the one making the movie, showing Belfort in all his vibrant, disgusting, glory, as he has numerous times in the past with terrible people. 
Much of Scorseses project seems to be showing evil with a romantic flair, only to subtly condemn it in the last moments. It in this context that, for me, The Irishman hits so hard.

It only gets better and better, and somehow funnier. Scorsese takes the colossal office blocking of The Apartment and amps it up with cocaine energy, sprinting through Stratton Oakmont in flurries of movement that emphasize the frat energy of its dipshit executives. How a single person watched this movie and came away with the idea that it does anything less than relentlessly mock its characters for three hours is truly beyond me. If Howard Hawkss formula that a great movie is three good scenes and no bad ones holds true, what to make a film that is three hours of iconic scenes stacked one after the other with no let-up? I cant pick a favorite scene the Lemmons bit is unreservedly the comic setpiece of the decade, a work of sublime silent comedy set to a soundtrack of slurred, incomprehensible groans, but even smaller-scaled bits like Jordan and Naomis first tryst, with Jordan meekly asking if she climaxed after his 11-second round of pumping, really just nails that character to the wall in less than a minute. 
This time around, though, I was most taken with all of Kyle Chandlers scenes. In a film where everyone else is bouncing off the walls, Chandler barely moves, yet in his few minutes of screen time he absolutely levels Jordan, even in their first meeting where Chandler plays the agents ambiguous openness to palling around with Jordan induce doubt into his friendliness until you can just barely spot him elegantly directing the conversation toward letting the broker incriminate himself. Jordan says the subtext aloud when rallying the troops by screaming I want you to fix your problems by becoming rich, but its in Chandlers by-the-book G-man, whose disgust for Jordan is as much rooted in his own jealousy as Belforts attitude, that really illustrates the pervasive resentment that informs Belfort and his cadre of bullish social climbers who all stepped on their brethrens necks to make it to the top rungs.
Scorsese is often accused by the laziest film viewers alive of repeating himself, but its nonetheless interesting to see how he often echoes earlier films in his work but with subtle revisions. Wolf clearly fits with a loose trilogy of greed with GoodFellas and Casino, recalling the former in Jordans unapologetic confessional and the latter in Aces desperate need for attention, including Jordan putting himself front and center in ads even as the walls close in. Yet the biggest revision here is that Henry and Ace, whose legitimacy is built on a foundation of sand, crumble so totally that they are left shellshocked and abandoned after the universe corrects itself around them. Yet as evidenced by the coda here, Belfort, jailed for a host of crimes but still booking sold out speeches to train the next generation of bullshit artists, destroyed lives in a way not only perfectly legitimate to the system but crucial to the maintenance of its current structure. Its the most simple, devastating critique of the post-2008 American landscape of utterly unchanged predatory capitalism yet made, and as we teeter on yet another implosion, its soft fade-out from Jordan calmly restarting the cycle is utterly nightmarish.

Umpteenth viewing. Not a surprise to learn that Bernie Sanders watches this one on his iPad, because its a ferociously anti-capitalist film. Of Scorseses films, it echoes Casino most closely Both are about low-class outlaws who are eventually arrested for ripping people off in the same way as their more respectable counterparts. Just as corporate-run Las Vegas shakes money from the pockets of everyone who flies into town, snooty Wall Street firms are all about fleecing their investors. (Key scene here is the lunch with Matthew McConaghey.) Anyway, its also an absolute blast to watch, and Leos career-best performance.

Hits a little differently for me than it did in 2013, when the smiling frontmen of our depraved world order were people like George W. Bush, Mitt Romney, and Barack Obama. Back then, just a few years after the financial crash led to exactly zero repercussions for anyone who caused it, it felt a bit like Scorsese and Co. were pulling the curtain open on how this awful world really worked. But nowadays Jordan Belfort is the god damn President of the United States! And hes not waiting til he hangs up the phone to tell you what a fucking slur you are! Everywhere you turn, from every screen and speaker, youre hearing people even worse than Jordan saying even worse things. For a picture of the present, imagine a boot stamping on a human face, forever, telling you to sell me this pen.  So for that reason, it took a little longer for this to get its hooks in me on this viewing than it did in 2013.
That said, I was very sad when this ended and wished it lasted another three hours, so it still passes the five-star test and then some. The quaalude scene is as good as movies get.

Scorsese builds to the final shot. We understand the point of view of Belfort through his actions and the relentless energy of the editing and structure. In voice-over it becomes clear he is a figure who cannot see beyond his own two eyes, and the editing and filmmaking mirror this notion. In a montage of explicit sex at the firm Jordan discusses a girl who gave everyone a blowjob and the man who married her, his voice never falters in rhythm when he says that man killed himself three years later and an image is inserted of the mans bloodied corpse in a bathtub, but then immediately the film moves back to sex uncaring about the aftershock of individuals who are not Jordan Belfort. We, as an audience, understand this is poisonous and while Belfort remains intoxicating the film slowly overruns with this poison. Earlier in the film Jordans wife asks him if it is fair to sell penny stocks to the poor while they became rich, and later Jordan is heard saying their money is better in my pocket. 
When Jordan is eventually whisked off to jail for his crimes on Wall Street hes seen playing tennis, and later in a seminar he is seen once again selling his brand to the poor. Through the entirety of Wolf of Wall Street weve walked alongside Belfort until this moment when the camera turns and points into the audience and they stare slack jawed, in awe of his brilliance and the possibility of getting rich through his gospel. But theyre merely pawns being taken advantage of in the quest for money, fame and power. It would be prescient for the current situation in the United States if this wasnt the narrative of the States to begin with.

notes
-- I still think the idea that the film approves of Belfort is ridiculous the movie opens with him describing all the drugs he needs to function because his life is so miserable, and ends with him beating his wife and crashing a car with his little girl in it while high on coke. Im sure people watch the movie and think that Belfort is to be emulated, but you cant blame a movie for a persons broken moral compass.
But it is true that the movie does not really tell us why exactly the things he was accused of doing were illegal (in fact, the movie makes a point of not explaining this), and so implicitly endorses the defense that Belfort makes what he and his firm were doing wasnt any worse than what larger firms were doing, or indeed, running the perfectly legal scam that constitutes the brokerage business model. 
You could read this as letting Belfort off the hook, or you could read it as making a larger systemic critique of Wall Street. But you probably cant argue that, debauchery and dissoluteness aside, Belfort is a particularly egregious criminal. 
-- I generally dont care about the Academy Awards but Leo and Marty both should have taken home Oscars that year. I love Gravity, but its a glorified theme park ride the less said about Dallas Buyers Club, the better. Egregious.

Based on the biography of Jordan Belfort, and adapted to the screen by Terence Winter, this is ultimately Martin Scorseses entry into the canon of epic sexism. Its a movie which portrays women like nothing more than nonentities, and its unimaginable to discern any emotion other than an intense dislike for Belfort and his entourage.
Its egotism and greed thats primarily on display from the perpetrators here, and while horrendous people can create fascinating viewing, it helps to be at tiny bit sympathetic to what theyre objectives comprise. Belfort evolves into something outrageous and profoundly immoral very quickly in fact, after about his fourth sentence, he reveals himself to be an utterly detestable character. In the end, this is Scorseses three-hour frolic of nineteen-eighties excess, and it makes for a demoralising and infuriating watch.

Scorsese always had one big issue to his work, at least to the second half of his oeuvre he couldnt find the balance between affirmation  critique. Sem se prender a nada, nem a ninguém, sem crises existenciais a todo o tempo, Jordan pensa exclusivamente em prazer imediato, e sem dúvida aproveita como consegue. O Lobo de Wall Street são três horas de palavrões, sexo, nudez, drogas, mulheres, bebida, luxo e todo tipo de fantasia (com anões, carros, animais) que o dinheiro pode pagar. E nada disso é gratuito. Moral e ética, aliás, são valores que aparecem no filme apenas para serem ridicularizados e até questionados a longo prazo. Terence Winter tece seu comentário sobre a imoralidade especulativa de Wall Street testando acima de tudo os limites da realidade. Engana-se quem acha que o longa glorifica o meio de vida de Belfort, embora o filme se divirta bastante com a glória do protagonista, o vemos também em papéis deploráveis e ridículos, sucumbindo ao uso de drogas e mostrando ser um homem sem pudor ou remorso ao delatar seus amigos. Scorsese nos mostra a ascensão e também nos mostra a derrocada. Com um grande time de excelentes atores, temos Leonardo Di Caprio entregando a performance de sua carreira. Matthew McConaughey aparece pouco mais de cinco minutos e deixa sua marca com uma das cenas mais antológicas da década, o canto de guerra cantado de boca fechada e com o punho fechado batendo no peito. Em suma, O Lobo de Wall Street é um verdadeiro sonho paradisíaco desregrado e altamente descontrolado, que ao mesmo tempo que traz uma tonelada de diversos prazeres, abre espaço para a mesma quantidade de problemas.

So whats all this then? Basically Banks of New York, with Leonardo DiCaprio as hedonistic stockbroker Jordan Belfort, the kind of guy who caused the global recession.
Here he is having an awesome time. Look at his wife. Look at his car. Look at the size of his house. Here he is snorting cocaine off a hookers boobs. Here he is doing it another eighteen times. Here he is making money. He has lots of money.
Scorseses admirers will tell you that the directors presenting the facts about Belfort without comment or embellishment, and letting us make up our own minds. I dont buy it. Look at the final shot of the agent assigned to Belforts case (Kyle Chandler), then try to tell me were supposed to be energised on his behalf, rather than gloating on his adversarys. Im not saying Scorsese is on the side of rapacious financiers, more that the films gleeful tone is a botch job.
The film is troubling and immoral, then, but is it any good? Not really, no. Theres an unshakeable confidence about it, DiCaprio gives an assured star turn in the Catch Me If You Can mould, and there are some big laughs and good scenes, particularly near the beginning Leo having lunch with his mentor -  weird, unrepentant über-Gecko, Matthew McConaughey - aceing a penny-share sale, quizzing Jonah Hill about marrying his own cousin, and sparring with FBI agent Kyle Chandler on the deck of his gargantuan yacht. Ive seen the film compared endlessly to Goodfellas, but its more like DePalmas wretched remake of Scarface. Its just deadeningly debauched a three-hour, one-note exercise in coke-fuelled, fleshy excess with almost no narrative impetus, virtually nothing to say, and even a certain desperation in its supposed strong suit of comedy. Given the critical bouquets being flung in its direction, I was expecting something special. Martin Scorsese directs this biographical crime black comedy about the rise and fall of ambitious stockbroker Jordan Belfort (Leonardo DeCaprio), whose hedonistic lifestyle and corrupt practises lead to equal amounts of fame and infamy, with Jonah Hill, Margot Robbie, Kyle Chandler and Rob Reiner in supporting roles. 
Its an engaging look at the American Dream pushed to the very limit, with Scorsese allowing us to see into a world of wild parties, excess and rampant greed. What makes all of so compelling is ambiguous way its all presented, gleefully embracing the unreliable nature of the story and deliberately playing with the way its told. 
The rapid fire editing and frenetic visual style helps to show Belforts increasingly hectic point of view as he becomes more and more successful, with his often skewed point of view helping to give the film a lot of its humour. In execution a lot of this style and structure does feel a bit derivative of Goodfellas, but I think it lacks some of that films weight, never quite leaving the same impact. 
Nevertheless, its probably one of Scorseses funniest, most purely entertaining movies, packed full of energy and a whole host of out there, memorable moments that cement it as an incredibly immersive and engaging experience. A particular highlight are the scenes where Belfort is under the influence of quaaludes, with Scorsese creating a brilliantly heightened and surreal segment that features some of DiCaprios most committed and physical bits of acting. 
Throughout the whole film he really throws himself into the role, getting the brutish charisma and crass swagger of a man whos sold his soul for the materialist, glamorous lifestyle hes long aspired to. Even though Belfort is completely amoral, we cant help but be swept along this journey with him, the films sleight of hand quality playing with our perspective just like the web of deceptions spun by the man himself. 
Its only towards the end where the lifestyle begins to catch up with him that the story really feels like it has some weight, but that allows it to have even more of an impact, as this excessive need for more and more money ultimately proves to be Belforts undoing. 
Even so, I think the film does feel a little too enamoured of all of his antics to really get to what made him tick, remaining on surface level too often. This uncritical outlook causes it to lack the depth needed to really get home a lot of its satire, telling the story in a way that the real Belfort (who has an obnoxious cameo at the end) would have approved of, shying away from the darker side to paint him in a better light.
Despite that, I really enjoyed The Wolf of Wall Street while it doesnt have the power of his best works, and becomes a little repetitive after a while, Scorsese fills the film to the brim with a virtuoso style that perfectly matches the larger-than-life subject at the centre.

Why dont you boys go down to Wall Street and find some real crooks?
This is Tuddy Cicero speaking to the FBI agents as they arrest his brother Paulie near the end of Goodfellas. Its a revealing moment  when even ordinary gangsters admit they cant hold a candle to the Wall Street guys. Twenty-three years later, Martin Scorsese finally did justice to Ciceros words by taking on the bigger players through his adaptation of Jordan Belforts autobiography.
Jordan Belfort is a guy who, as far back as he could remember, always dreamed of making money  and he found an easier way than being a gangster he became a trader. He wasnt more handsome or charismatic than Henry Hill (as portrayed in the films) he just studied and got his passport to Wall Street. He did what Hill did  legally  proving Al Capones quote that Capitalism is the legitimate racket of the ruling class. In fact, he almost made the Goodfellas look like Robin Hood figures  at least they bribed a few working-class men.
Goodfellas was craftsmanship compared to what these wolves in Armani clothing did elevating theft to an industrial level  making millions in a few hours, and generating money out of virtually nothing, which is the essence of finance. It reminded me of those business school courses that teach how to make risk-free money through arbitrage. What Belfort does is more straightforward he sells worthless stock to blue-collar people. Then its the traditional supply-and-demand game  the more people buy, the more others want to buy. The value increases, and when it gets high enough, you sell. What happens to your client after that is none of your concern.
Call it unethical, cynical, or even criminal  but this is the worlds holistic system. And the only skill that can make you rich faster than talent or merit is being a good salesman. Because when you have to sell s, you sell dreams. A good trader sells securities and buys capital he sells promising values and makes real money. And it takes serious communication skills to make that happen. Thats the key to these characters likability, at least by cinematic standards they know how to communicate their appeal.
The screenplay, written by Terence Winter, is full of pep-talk speeches echoing the famous Greed is good tirade. We get similarly motivational lines like Theres no nobility in poverty. Wall Street set the tone for financial-themed films, and theres a reason these films fascinate us we all love money, we all dream of being rich  and if we dream of something else, it likely includes wealth along the way. Theres no dream that doesnt, in one way or another, involve sex, money, or power. These films speak to us on a very personal level.
I often found myself thinking that an average guy has to make money to have sex with a beautiful woman, while a beautiful woman can attract a rich man more easily than an average one. The film helped me understand why essentially, a mans main currency is the money he earns. Even if he doesnt dream of sleeping with hot women, he still wont earn his nagging wifes respect if his pockets are empty.
A womans currency, on the other hand, is her beauty, her body, and her willingness to use them. Margot Robbies frontal nudity isnt shocking  its necessary. When you see these men throwing lobsters, wiping themselves with hundred-dollar bills, or harassing flight attendants, its just the language of money. They get away with it because they can. In that decadent world, full nudity is a woman showing her most valuable asset  its a fair trade.
And only Scorsese could have portrayed such loathsome, amoral characters with that flamboyant, dizzying, and electrifying style. The characters are sleazy, with nicknames as pathetic as their intentions  as if behind every trader, there were a crook waiting to wake up. And yet, they strangely appeal to us. Here we have Scorseses obligatory morally corrupt protagonist someone who rises high only to fall hard  a multiple-time sinner granted fleeting moments of redemption, but who wont go down until the sun truly burns his wings. Leonardo DiCaprio finally delivers a performance that showcases a wide range of emotions  being charismatic and pathetic within the same five minutes. Credit also goes to the films grippingly realistic portrayal of cocaine, crack, and Quaalude use.
No film has ever portrayed drugs and lust  and the combination of both  in such a straightforward way. That was essential, because there has to be a catch behind such a dreamy lifestyle. This ambivalence runs deeper when you realize the title was borrowed from an unflattering portrait of a young yuppie go-getter  yet it gave him the perfect publicity to build his reputation. Did things change much? After cooperating with the FBI, he served a few years in prison and went on to become a motivational speaker. In the films closing scene, you see people looking at him with respect and adoration. The joke is on us.
From Leo to the surprisingly good Jonah Hill as his right-hand man Donnie Azoff, from Matthew McConaughey as his first tutor, to Kyle Chandler as the FBI agent and Jean Dujardin as the suave, crooked Swiss banker  the film features some of the finest performances of these actors careers. That includes Rob Reiner as Leos father and the then-promising Margot Robbie. The Wolf of Wall Street is Scorsese back to his roots  and one of his best.

The Wolf of Wall Street marks the end of Scorseses populist era. Its a big, loud epic, where greed is obnoxious and civility is absent. Scorseses two most recent feature films, The Irishman and Killers of the Flower Moon, are much more sombre and contemplative, but alongside The Wolf of Wall Street they create a reverse trilogy about American capitalism in the twentieth century. Killers of the Flower Moon presents wealth pursued through racial violence. The Irishman presents the entanglements of business and crime with organised labour. Finally The Wolf of Wall Street presents the 80s and 90s as a new era of obscene wealth that sits as numbers in a bank account at the expense of ordinary Americans. Scorseses films have so often examined Americas sins and The Wolf of Wall Street is one of his many masterpieces on the topic.
The Wolf of Wall Street is the most vulgar of Scorseses films, depicting people living the most lavish lifestyle while spending all their time fixated on drugs and sex. The film is about the pursuit of money and the animalistic urges it unleashes. The characters have no decency nor morals, living solely on the belief that more money makes them a better person. The film is clear to emphasise that the wealth here is illegally gained and comes at the expense of others. Yet what makes The Wolf of Wall Street so engaging is how deeply funny it is. The characters are vile and their culture is toxic, but the film depicts their arrogance, immaturity, and vacuity in entertaining ways. The humour often comes at their expense, but especially through narration the film also tries to seduce us into this world before revealing how pathetic the characters are. 
The Wolf of Wall Street is a classic rise and fall story, on the largest level Scorsese has done. Its a huge film, built on excess, and every scene has some excitement and thrill to it. However by the end it is clear that this life is empty of anything meaningful. The Wolf of Wall Street depicts capitalism as distasteful and gross, where the imagination of the wealthy extends no further than their own hedonism. Its a darkly comedic masterpiece and one of cinemas modern classics.

I think George Carlin once said something like theres nothing less impressive than a businessman, and it really is true. They dont really contribute anything of lasting value, no one really loves them, and once they die they are alternately forgotten and despised in a ratio that starts out weighted towards the latter and slides inexorably toward the former. So why do so many people want to do what they do? Besides the obvious material comforts, I imagine that for a lot of people the appeal is very similar to morphines Its fucking awesome. 
Half of the brilliance of this movie is that its not afraid to depict that, in a way thats exciting and hilarious (this is by far Scorseses funniest movie, and I feel like a schmuck now for suggesting American Hustle was different from his stuff because its so funny, I probably laughed 50x more during this). But the other half is just as crucial - the shifts into not fucking around anymore gear are incredibly bracing, as tense and viscerally horrifying as any of the much more (physically, anyway) violent movies of Scorseses career. Punches are not pulled for the sake of laughs, quite the opposite. Just one example The throwaway gag about one of Jordans early recruits marrying the office tramp (I would say thats the films terminology but I dont remember what exact phrase it used to describe her, thats how not sexist I am OK, I respect women so much that I dont even remember what specific words are used to insult them, thats true respect for women right there) is immediately followed up by the reveal that he went on to commit suicide three years later, complete with a shot of his bloody bathtub. I was in the middle of laughing at his awkward wedding photo  and my laughter was caught in my throat - THATS when I started to realize what Scorsese was going for here, and thats when I stopped subconsciously dismissing this as some trifle Marty tossed off in his sleep. El día de hoy Margot Robbie y yo cumplimos años,así que por tercera vez anualmente veo una de sus películas como forma de pasar mi cumpleaños y también por ella.
¿Que mejor forma de pasar mi cumpleaños con ver algo del género que más odio? Biopics 

Pero... Con Wolf of Wall Street fué una buena experiencia. Me agrada ver cuando  hacen un Biopic de una persona cuestionable bajo el humor negro,me parece una excusa inteligente de los guionistas y directores para justificar la representación exagerada de las cosas que vemos como escenarios,hechos, personalidades,etc. (Así debió ser Marty Supreme )
El guión de Terence Winter es una comedia negra sin miedo la locura dentro de la oficina,la película no por nada es bastante explícita,Scorcesse visualmente no deja nada a la imaginación sobre lo cuestionable que son los excesos sexuales y sustanciales de esos hombres bajo la sátiracomedia negra de lo que para ellos es el sueño norteamericano.
La escena en la que Belfort anuncia la venta de acciones de los zapatos Madden,la fotografía del mexicano Rodrigo Prieto es un plano secuencia frenético en la que Scorcesse enfoca el comportamiento de que sus empleados se comportan como animales empujandose,lanzando cosas y gritándose, aparte de dar un enfoque frenético,Martin usa ese juego de cámaras para hacer ver aquella oficina de estafadores como una jungla con hombres desatados sin límites con sed de más,una oficina sin orden que perdió totalmente sus protocolos de seguridad gracias al mandato de Belfort intepretado por el gran Leo DiCaprio.
Martin Scorcesse usa el filtro vertiginoso en ciertas escenas en el tercer acto para simbolizar que Belfort ya estaba perdido en excesos de sustancias ilicitas,perdido como persona. (Dato Jordan Belfort dijo que todos estos excesos realmente eran muchos peores. Y eso que la película ya es muy explícita por si sola)
Quizás lo más negativo que veo de Wolf of Wall Street tiene una edición... Rara. Algunas transiciones de escena porque si,sin significado visualnarrativo por parte de Scorcesse (Si,incluso él comete errores) o esa escena de Jordan retrocediendo su vehículo con un corte de escena bastante adelantado.
Toda esa escena del accidente del yate se me hacía exagerada en su cgi e incluso ridícula pero en el contexto de sus personajes marcaba perfectamente la ambición pero satira exagerada de como desde ahí empieza el declive, ¿Cómo lo escribe Terence Winter? Con Jordan Belfort y Donnie Azoff pidiendo salvar a gritos la cocaína en vez de sus vidas al borde de morir ahogados. 
Hablando de Margot Robbie,sus últimos minutos como Naomi Lapaglia en su ex relación con Jordan Belfort son caóticos como parte de la comedia negra en mostrar las consecuencias,marca la cúspide del caos en la vida de Jordan y con eso una línea que como humano,Jordan no debió alcanzar con ella acabando en una escena atroz. Escena muy bien filmada si me lo preguntan. (Dato Nadine Maculoso confirmó que lamentablemente lo visto en la película es lo más fiel a su relación con Jordan)
Con esto ya debió quedar claro que Wolf of Wall Street relata la cuestionable vida de Jordan Belfort engañando al espectador con una supuesta vida de riquezas sumergido en la comedia negra,Terence Winter se salta el proceso,no va paso a paso en mostrar la evolución de Jordan hasta la cima,se centra en lo que ocurre cuando Jordan estuvo ahí arriba,como los excesos lo llevan a creerse un ser superior,hacer lo que le dá la gana con sus empleados hasta transformarlos en animales eufóricos,como los excesos son todo para empezar lentamente su declive empresarial y como ser humano.

The aging controversial auteur has become fairly docile in the past couple years and I hate to be that guy but I think Wolf of Wall Street is a triumphant, loud, brazen, side splitting, excessive return to form for one of American cinemas most valued treasures. Seeing the hordes flow into the theater for a Martin Scorsese film filled my heart with just a tiny bit of faith in the current general audience. But those thoughts were about to become moot. Soon after we all sat down we were whisked away from our boring Midwestern AMC movie theater and taken to a time and place on Wall Street where excess was a lifestyle and our main character is introduced to us getting head in a Ferrari and soon after that, blowing coke out of a hookers asshole. 
By the end of the film these two scenes become childs play. Over the course of 3 hours, the life of wealthy stock broker Jordan Belfort is examined with lightning quick pacing rarely ever slowing down except for the need to create drama every once in a while. The film, emulating the book of the same name, looks at virtually every faucet of Jordans life both good and bad. But mostly bad. Leonardo DiCaprio brings to life a cinematic badboy the likes of which we rarely see in such a mainstream film. Ive never really been a believer in Leo, but Christ this film has some of the best physical acting from an actor Ive ever seen. I dont know if its content will win it any big awards come Oscar season but fuck if Leo and Hill dont at least get nominations. Ive always admired Hills comedic timing but here its paired with gut bustingly hilarious mannerisms that make his and Leos conversations, both sober and high, an absolute riot. This is by far Scorseses most humorous film to date. Rarely anything is taken seriously and its edited in a way to make it seem like a satirical infomercial take on a biography. Stock footage. Commercial cut-ins. Advertisements. The film is like a raunchy visual guide to being a modern alpha male and it goes to places only a filmmaker like Scorsese could pull off with such confidence. I cant say everything I want to say about the content of this film because it would be ruining some key moments and frankly, Im still remembering certain scenes days later. There is just so much to guzzle down. Each frame is packed with so much visual information and it moves so lightning quick when you walk out you feel like youve lived a whole lifetime flashing before your eyes in x3 speed. When you can get past the gay orgies, public masturbation and something called the Cerebral Palsy Phase you will find one of the most daringly brilliant films of this generation. The fucking stones on Scorsese to release this on such a large scale....
Some of the criticisms for this film revolve around this perception of a thin story and weak character depth. My opinion on that is this 
Scorsese is a man that doesnt just forget those things. The film takes place mostly in the Reagan era, but now is a good time as any to heed the warnings that WoW preaches. Its dressed up like good, fun time, and it is, but the film has a darker side that will sink its claws into you deep. Scorsese turns Jordan Belforts memoir into a three-hour odyssey of greed, addiction, and hedonistic spectacle, that revels in the grotesque without ever losing sight of the cultural rot its portraying.
Leonardo DiCaprios performance is a force of nature. Hes volatile, comedic, and unhinged with a kind of actorly fearlessness few stars ever reach. His physical comedy alone, from the infamous quaalude crawl to the manic motivational speeches, is worthy of a separate award category. 
Scorseses direction is both hyper-stylized and ruthlessly efficient. The relentless pace, Thelma Schoonmakers kinetic editing, and the barrage of fourth-wall breaks create an experience that mimics the highs and crashes of Belforts lifestyle. 
Relentless, vulgar, and shockingly funny, The Wolf of Wall Street is Scorsese at his most provocative. Its not a cautionary tale delivered from a moral high ground its a mirror held up to a society that celebrates the very figures it claims to reject. The result is a modern American epic  furious, energetic, and disturbingly entertaining.

Wolf of Wall Street is definitely in the GoodfellasCasino tier of Martin Scorseses film catalogue. LOTS of similarities in story-telling as well as  quality. I saw Leo lose a job at one firm, rise through a penny stock scheme at another, start and build-up Stratton Oakmont into a major financial player, being crowned Wolf of Wall Street, and descend into a world of drugs and sex. It felt like I had gotten the full Rise portion of a Rise  Fall movie.

The pacing in this movie is absolutely bonkers, and unfortunately it ends up working against it. We got the Rise. Stylishly directed by Scorsese in whats his 5th collaboration with DiCaprio, this is arguably his best film to date and certainly the most enjoyable of them all. Further uplifting the viewing experience is the excellent production design, sharp camerawork, neat editing, breakneck pace, fab costumes, dynamic score  stellar performances. Overall, The Wolf of Wall Street is an endlessly funny  deliberately unrestrained exercise in excess that promises 3 hours of non-stop extravaganza and finds both the master  his protégé delivering on all fronts. O Lobo de Wall Street é a mais eletrizante e explosiva das cinco parcerias entre Leonardo DiCaprio e o diretor Martin Scorsese
Como trainee em Wall Street, Jordan Belfort, 22 anos, casado com uma cabeleireira e recém-chegado a Nova York, fica com os olhos brilhando quando ouve falar dos bônus que os corretores tiraram no último ano  300.000 dólares um, 1 milhão de dólares outro. Então vem o 19 de outubro de 1987 a bolsa de Nova York despenca mais de 500 pontos em um só mergulho, a empresa em que Jordan trabalha vai à falência, e ele perde o emprego que acabou de ganhar. E, no entanto, quatro anos depois ele vai estar jogando dinheiro fora. Sem brincadeira, jogando-o fora amassando notas de 100 e arremessando-as no lixo, atirando-as pela balaustrada do seu iate em cima dos agentes federais que tentou subornar, torrando-as com prostitutas. E também em quantidades de pó, barbitúricos e álcool que derrubariam um cavalo, em uma Ferrari branca, em orgias diárias no escritório (de novo, sem brincadeira orgias mesmo, na acepção da palavra), em uma mansão gigantesca, ou em um diamante de noivado do tamanho de um Polenghinho para a amante, Naomi  nos termos em que Jordan raciocina, uma vida assim veloz requer um modelo mais esportivo de mulher, e Naomi (Margot Robbie), além de loira e estatuesca, tem competências que ele julga notáveis. Não há descrição dos feitos (e incontáveis malfeitos) de Jordan, porém, que dê conta da eletricidade e da potência de O Lobo de Wall Street (The Wolf of Wall Street, Estados Unidos, 2013), que concorre a cinco Oscar.
Esta é a quinta parceria entre Leonardo DiCaprio e o diretor Martin Scorsese, e de longe a mais explosiva, arriscada e infernalmente divertida de todas  uma demonstração de que certas colaborações precisam atravessar uma fase de estabilidade e até de separação temporária para atingir a etapa seguinte, a da absoluta confiança mútua que um filme como esse requer. Durante as três horas que essa adaptação das memórias de Jordan toma, DiCaprio sustenta um nível de energia exaustivo e faz coisas que ninguém sonhou vê-lo fazer antes, muitas delas impublicáveis. Um resumo editado DiCaprio fala barbaridades (no linguajar que usa e na amoralidade do que diz), seja dentro da cena, seja dirigindo-se diretamente ao espectador ou em voice over  um recurso típico de Scorsese. Arrasta-se pelo chão tentando entrar na sua Ferrari, trincado demais com Mandrix para se pôr de pé, levando a plateia às gargalhadas. Faz gestos de obscenidade inacreditável  como na cena em que ensina o pessoal da firma a vender papéis que não valem nada a clientes desavisados. Não tem, enfim, medida nem barreira. E, todo o tempo, Scorsese não só paga a aposta como joga mais fichas na mesa a cada rodada, exibindo vitalidade comparável à de Os Bons Companheiros, de 1990, e que na fase mais recente de sua carreira só em Os Infiltrados (sua terceira parceria com DiCaprio) ele esteve perto de igualar. Essa exuberância já está provocando certa grita para alguns (por exemplo, os coitados que Jordan arruinou com suas tramoias financeiras), há algo de indecente em cativar de tal maneira o público com um personagem tão abjeto.
Personagens abjetos, contudo, são uma das matérias-primas  a mais valiosa, talvez  de que Scorsese fez sua carreira. Do violento e desequilibrado Travis Bickle de Taxi Driver aos mafiosos de Os Bons Companheiros e Cassino, ou os gângsteres e os policiais corruptos de Os Infiltrados, o diretor teve sempre uma atração pelos bottom feeders, como se diz em inglês  os que se alimentam do lodo, do que é sórdido e podre. E Jordan Belfort não é outra coisa senão uma dessas figuras. Depois de perder o emprego em Wall Street, ele foi parar em um estabelecimento de porta dos fundos e práticas duvidosas em Long Island. Em um mecanismo que Scorsese explica muito bem, o que as grandes firmas de Wall Street vendem são as ações blue chip os papeis valorizadíssimos que só gente grande compra, e que rendem ao corretor comissão de 1. Já o que os corretores suados e amarrotados de Long Island estavam vendendo eram as pink sheets papeis de empresas tão obscuras, ou medíocres, ou sem futuro, que nem chegam a entrar na cotação. As pink sheets valem centavos, mas rendem comissão de 50  porque é preciso premiar o corretor que empurre esse bagaço para alguém (em geral gente com pouquinho dinheiro, muita ilusão e zero de informação).
Jordan descobre que nasceu para isso mente com volúpia, convence qualquer um de qualquer coisa e faz chover sobre si o dinheiro que rouba de sua clientela ingênua de carteiros, motoristas de ônibus e operários. E daí imagina e se conseguisse vender essa papelada inútil para os peixes grandes? Inventa uma empresa de nome pomposo  Stratton Oakmont , associa-se a um sujeito sem nenhum caráter (o enlouquecido Donnie Azoff interpretado por Jonah Hill), chama uns amigos escusos para se juntar a ele e, aos 26 anos, já comprou a mansão, o iate, o helicóptero. E já vendeu a alma também, com muito gosto e sem arrependimento.
Graças a um levantamento realizado pela revista Variety, sabe-se que O Lobo de Wall Street é o filme recordista no uso de um certo palavrão são 506 fs em duas horas e 59 minutos de projeção, ou 2,8 por minuto. Parte deles é dita em clima de euforia, quando o dinheiro está entrando a rodo. Outra parte é dita em estado de desespero, quando um agente do FBI (Kyle Chandler, excelente) detecta a vastidão da maracutaia em que está envolvida essa falsa firma de respeito, prende o banqueiro suíço da turma (Jean Dujardin, de O Artista) e encosta Jordan e seus associados na parede. Joel M. Cohen, um dos promotores que durante meses interrogaram Jordan Belfort, escreveu no The New York Times que o personagem que viu no filme é, em certo sentido, exatamente aquele que conheceu mentiroso, mitômano, megalomaníaco, covarde e muito bem-sucedido em vender ao mundo (e, por extensão, a cineastas e atores, insinua Cohen) uma versão épica de sua canalhice.
Há espaço aí para uma dúvida Scorsese se deslumbrou e deixou tapear pelo vigarista  ou tão somente se deslumbrou com o poder de um vigarista de tapear? As evidências favorecem a segunda hipótese grandes fraudadores, da mesma forma que os mafiosos e agentes da lei corruptos que o diretor tantas vezes retratou, moram no lado escuro da terra das oportunidades e são a excrescência que às vezes brota de uma qualidade americana, o empreendedorismo. Se há um filme recente que se alinha com o de melhor que Scorsese fez no passado, portanto, é este aqui, sobre lobos que nem sequer se dão ao trabalho de vestir pele de cordeiro.

Every time Jordan Belfort starts explaining the mechanics of his misdeeds and then abruptly decides those dont matteryou just need to know that he got the money, thats Scorsese withholding a fraud instruction manual from malfeasance-minded viewers and also mirroring big financial institutions that said dont worry how derivatives work, whats in them or how stable they are, just buy them. The array of references is, as usual, staggeringly eclectic the Quaalude car crawl seems clearly modeled on Jerry Lewis inability to simply cross an empty room in the panic-attack-inducing opening of Cracking Up, while the yacht party bit  complete with a helicopter shot cruising over the at-sea revelers  seems to be quoting Notorious B.I.G.s Hypnotize clip (or half a dozen Little X videos, for that matter).

Id think itd be pretty clear where the movie stands about a protagonist who can gloss over a former associates gunshot-suicide (and the bloody corpse photo illustrating it) to go back to talking about his drug habits, and who punches his wife in the stomach, and who has the stones to show up at films end to introduce his fictional self as a badass rather than slinking off into the night. But the back half  especially after his fighting days are over  are a constant catalogue of the same kind of sexdrugsasshole behavior depravity as Wolf, and its pretty obvious that Tysons still tickled by the stories they make for, which is eminently understandable. He also understands that this would be considered a socially unacceptable attitude, so every three paragraphs he throws in an excuse I was just a total prick at the time, I was really out of it, I was so arrogant. Argue with yourselves but this is still one of the all time comedy films, theres not more than a minute that passes where Im not at least giggling at the mayhem unfolding. The story is a classic, the location work is perfect, the chemistry between the group is amazing and the soundtrack is a nostalgia overload. 
Cant begin to tell you how often I watched this, its probably between this and The Dark Knight for my most watched movie. Easily the sole reason Ive ended up visiting Vegas 7 times, I couldnt believe a place like this existed when I first laid eyes on it. Vegas may have changed over the years Ive visited but the feeling I get landing into Vegas will always be partnered with the love I have for this film. 
The Hangover was great upon its release and still holds up today. But just like most classic comedies, the humor and jokes wouldnt cut it today with cancel culture annoyingly. Comedies are a dying breed because of that films are great because we get to escape life for a few hours, to be able to laugh at stupid shit, and ultimately not be babied about something that is offensive to a low percentage of the population.
I love this movie man, so much so that I bought a framed display piece with real Bellagio prop cards used for the Alan Blackjack scene, its been up on my wall for the longest time probably one of the cooler items I own. 
As the years go, I begin to connect with this movie more and more, probably because they all have their own respective lives and things they hate about their lives which we all do. Past that each of the four leads are different personalities with different arcs.. besides Doug who kind of just exists as the fourth member of the group.
But what Im trying to get at is most three act structures usually dictate that there is only one main character. In an ensemble, typically you pick one of the group to be the structural main character and even though the other characters may be involved, everything hangs on that one main character. Thats what makes this film pretty unique once the gang heads to Vegas, our three main guys Phil, Stu and Alan are always together, makes this thing so much fun and brings a unique dynamic we dont see often. 
I love each character for different reasons Ed Helms as Stu has the craziest arc no doubt, marries a fucking stripper and gives up his grandmas holocaust ring before dumping his bitch of a partner back at the wedding. Then theres Bradley Cooper as Phil who seems to be having the finest time out of the group, easily one of my favorite Bradley Cooper roles. Like I said before Doug is just here to help the plot progression, which is a shame as I actually enjoy his character. 
MVP of this whole thing is clearly Alan. Maybe my favorite comedy character oat, literally anything he said would make me laugh. Unhinged in the best of ways and if I was to drop my favorite Alan quotes Id quite honestly be here all day, its relentless. I dont think you guys quite understand.. I was a theatre kid at school loved it, and there was a time we had to perform a movie monologue and I shit you not I memorized Alans wolf pack speech and performed that to my theatre class. 
Theres even a multitude of great cameos Mike Tyson, Bryan Callen, Matt Walsh, Rob Riggle, but no one could compare to the one Ken Jeong who has one of the all time introductions to any character I wont ever forget seeing Mr. Chow leap out the back of that Mercedes with his bushy pubes beating the crap out of Phil, Stu and Alan. This performance only gets me excited to see him return in the sequel, the sequel turns this already ridiculous concept up another notch, Ill probably watch that in the next couple of days also. 
I really enjoy the structure of this film, the fact we dont see the events of the night is a great slice of storytelling having to go back and piece together the night is nothing short of good fun. It couldnt be more effective if it tries, with some great pacing and a really easy going structure its hard not to get lost in this one-day adventure. 
Which in turn makes the ending with all the photo frames so rewarding Ill never forget hearing Flo Ridas Right Round with these iconic and ridiculous photos finally showing the mayhem of the night before. Honestly I wish they made a fourth movie where they actually showed the night from the second they finished that second shot of Jager on Caesars Palace roof.   
Anyway the hangover is nothing short of a slice of cinema that was unfortunately left in the past due to snowflake takes and woke energy. It will always be a classic though, for good reason full of nostalgia, incredibly comedic, really well layered with great pacing and amazing cameos. Todd Phillips birthed one of the great comedy movies, its incredibly entertaining, and a perfect use of the Vegas backdrop.

Buenísima película, no pensé pasarla tan bien viéndola.
The Hangover es una de las comedias más caóticas y entretenidas que vi, con un grandioso elenco que mejora a sus personajes y los vuelve todavía más memorables, dentro de una historia que no es brillante pero sí que la pasas muy bien viéndola.
Sinopsis Dos días antes de su boda, Doug y tres amigos viajan a Las Vegas para una fiesta inolvidable y salvaje. De hecho, cuando los tres acompañantes despiertan la mañana siguiente, no recuerdan nada ni encuentran a Doug. Con poco tiempo por delante, los tres amigos intentan recordar sus pasos y encontrar a Doug para que regrese a Los Ángeles para su boda.
La historia es buenísima, muy caótica y llena de momentos divertidos. Sinceramente no le tenía tanta fe y al ser una comedia podría no haber conectado tanto con ella, pero creo que también es el tipo de película que suelo disfrutar, con una trama muy alocada pero que está bien construida para que te lo pases bien y encima contando con una buena calidad en varios aspectos. Una de las mejores cosas es su humor, muy absurdo por momentos pero funcionando casi siempre, no hubo un chiste o escena que me haya sobrado por parecerme tonta o que está mal implementada, todo tiene su toque de humor perfecto. Además, el ritmo es buenísimo para que no te aburras en ningún momento, creo que es imposible que se te haga pesada ya que en todo momentos están pasando cosas. Por último, destacar la secuencia de las fotos sobre todo lo que pasó en la noche, algo genial y bien implementado para cerrar de buena manera varias cosas que habían quedado en el aire sobre lo sucedido.
Los personajes me encantaron, tres protagonistas bastante icónicos. Alan me pareció el mejor de todos, un personaje con muchísimo carisma y que cae bien desde el primer momento, siendo potenciado por el actor que lo interpreta. Igualmente los otros dos también tienen un gran nivel, tanto Phil como Stu me cayeron muy bien, sobretodo éste último al tener más desarrollo. Por otro lado, Doug es el cuarto integrante del grupo pero lamentablemente no sale tanto como los otros tres y a pesar de ser clave en la historia principal termina sin ser tan memorable como los demás. De los secundarios los que más destacan son Jade y Chow, éste último con pocas escenas pero también resultando algo memorable al ser muy divertido de ver. Además, no puedo pasar por alto la participación de Mike Tyson, también sin tanto tiempo en pantalla pero siendo algo muy agradable de ver.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente el gran elenco con el que cuenta, resaltando Zach Galifianakis, Bradley Cooper y Ed Helms, los tres mejorando a sus personajes de una manera notable. También destacar el trabajo de Todd Phillips, otro responsable de que la película sea tan divertida, contando con secuencias bien realizadas. Por último, la banda sonora original no resalta mucho pero las canciones utilizadas me gustaron y siento que quedaron bien con el tono de la historia.
En conclusión, una gran película que estuvo mucho mejor de lo que esperaba, espero que sus secuelas se me hagan divertidas aunque no creo que al mismo nivel que ésta, por ahora no las veo muy necesarias. La recomiendo.

Surprisingly, though the cast (Bradley Cooper, Ed Helms, Justin Bartha and Zach Galifianakis) have a nice chemistry amongst them and individually performed as needed, it wasnt their acting that shined but the situations involving them.

Fresh, skilfully directed  brilliantly acted, The Hangover is a roller-coaster ride of quality entertainment that simply ranks amongst the finest comedies to come out in the past decade, for the film is full of hilarious moments, crazy characters  an engaging storyline that never goes dull for a moment.
The story follows four friends who travel to Las Vegas to celebrate the bachelor party of one of their own only to wake up the next day with no memory of what happened the previous night and discover that the bachelor himself is missing. So among watching films like The Green Mile, or watching Chainsaw Man for a fourth time in theaters, when I was chilling at home and not watching anime or getting some assignments done in advance, me and the fam were rewatching The Hangovers cause they got em on Netflix again yes, in my house, these are family movies. Even my mom and soon to be 13 year old little brother enjoy them lmaoo.
Surprisingly so Ive yet to even talk about them.
My thoughts on The Hangover can be quite simple, but I promise you my love and actual enjoyment I get outta these movies is beyond maybe what my words I type here can actually provide.
Theres nothing easier to say than that its just a series of films that are hilarious to me and my familys sense of humor, and in regards to the first film, it plays into the comedy extremely well. The concept of a bachelor party gone crazy wrong where theres a clue every couple of minutes leaving a trail as to what exactly happened the night before along with the lingering mystery of the groom to be, the film is able to have this chaotic and engaging structure with both its plot and comedy.
From the very moment the film starts and youre wondering what the heck mustve gone on that these guys are a little beat up, to the set up of the night before, to then the aftermath and picking up the pieces after, it just makes for a wildly entertaining premise with much comedic potential. The morning then after is already chaotic as it is, with a tiger in the bathroom, a baby in the hotel, one of the characters straight up missing a tooth and the missing groom, and then the film only ever elevates it further.
Suddenly youve got the very special and rare Mercedes up and disappeared for a squad car instead, then got the same dentist whos gonna propose to his girlfriend has accidentally married a hooker, whom the baby belongs to, and of all things, the tiger in the bathroom belongs to Mike fucking Tyson!
The film has this constant stacking effect to it where it just continually builds on its comedy and pieces, where one piece of the puzzle or night may be resolved, it leaves another 3 to solve, or comes with bigger problems like an angry flamboyant Chinese gangster whos lead to believe has a ransom on just the guy our trio are searching for.
Not to mention that the setup of the film, that entire first 15 minutes or so brilliantly set up so many things from the actual character journeys like Stu goes through with his shitty relationship and basically growing a pair for himself, or sets up the comedy for the rest of the film between reveals like with Alan and the drinks, or the Holocaust ring Stu had planned to propose with. And thats the best kinda comedy, set up, pay off. Actually, its not just the best kinda comedy, IT IS the standard rule of comedy! And this film plays into that quite well!
Nothing that is said in this film has no reason to get paid off, even the fact that Alan studied up on how to gamble to win big at the casinos, a line of dialogue that makes Alan such a goat in this film in the final act (as opposed to admittedly how insufferable and unlikable he can be at times in the sequels, but more on that when we get to those).
On top of the stacking effect is just the casting and performances here. Be it the over the top characters like Alan played by Zach Galifianakis or Chow played by Ken Jeong, who I still cannot believe was only a doctor when he did this film and then this lead to him being in more roles, I seriously cannot see anyone else ever playing this character and certainly not ever to the degree he does, he is so fucking perfect, or Ed Helms as Stu and his reactions to basically everything that happens in the film. Bradley Coopers pretty fun and charismatic in it too.
Director Todd Philips at this stage in his career (yknow before he decided to troll us with Joker 2) I feel also had quite the keen eye for at least a certain look or style to the film and with its comedy. This absolutely feels like the kinda film that was a product of its time. Came out in 2009, which means I mustve been 4 at the time, and am currently 20, and honestly, having grown up with quite the large number of films from that time this film absolutely feels like the kinda movie you wouldve gotten from that time.
The fun, hilarious, mid-budget comedy with an engaging enough premise and solid casting altogether that seems to be missing entirely nowadays or you just see is the brand new Netflix or Amazon Prime streaming original of the weekmonth. This film isnt that, cause its got its own sense of identity with the comedy and direction. 
Even the way Las Vegas is made to look in the film is quite fun, with the whole look of the town and city during night and day, taking and utilizing several possible Vegas scenarios and stories like getting married in Vegas, a hangover in Vegas, exotic animals, celebrity, and gangster relations in Vegas, like the setting itself is quite the literal perfect backdrop to all the insanity in this film. And when it comes to some of the more desert scenes with the time-lapses, lowkey even feels like something straight outta Breaking Bad.
Ive been to Vegas myself, and honestly, this film does a pretty nice job of capturing the vibe and feeling of being there. Dont worry, it was the family and I was only 12, we def werent doing even half the fucking shit these guys were lol.
Oh and shoutout to the films end credits, back when the credits could be just as fun as the rest of the movie, especially since it was able to basically give us all the pieces of puzzle of the night along with a few hilarious photos! The fact that some of those photos were actually real and authentic between the cast is just insane to me, and goes to show just how much thought was put into films like these back then.
Is it some revolutionary piece of storytelling thatll make you question your life and mentality for better or worse?

Well it might make you think twice before having a bachelor party in Las Vegas.
But besides that, the film is just a really damn fun, completely hilarious, immensely entertaining film for the family and I. Is it just the simple laughs we get out of it? Yeah, sure. But thats the fun and beauty of comedies isnt it? They make you laugh and the best ones are always the ones that you can even remember jokes or gags, you come back to them, and they still have you laughing like if it was your first time seeing or hearing the joke, and thats when you know youve found a comedy that sticks for you.
Simply put, The Hangover is that to me, my dad, my mom, and my little brother. Its a film that never fails to make us laugh, never ceases to entertain us, and that honestly, I dont think we could ever tire of.
For The Hangover, I feel a very high and strong 8.510 on it all in all. Certainly among my most favorite comedies, lowkey I would maybe even give it a 910 just cause of that opinion of mine, since I dont really know what that list would look like lol. I just know Id throw Hangover up there almost immediately. Heck Id even consider it a comfort film lol.
Thank you for reading!

Im about 10 years too old for this. 

The Hangover is essentially a time capsule of what the general public found funny in 2009 (spoiler alert its mostly homophobia and racism). Ultimately I think I laughed once the entire film, which is an incredibly disappointing hit rate for a comedy. 
This is another film that I remember being held in high regard. I was 10 when it came out, and I remember kids in school talking about how hilarious it was, singing the songs from it, and describing the bizarre nature of the film. It was something that held almost mythic origins for me. It was never going to be able to meet the bar set by my pre-teen classmates, and the truth is, I think I saw this film about 10 years too late, as only 15-year-old me wouldve been dumb enough and naive enough to find this funny.
Much of the humor in the film revolves around being edgy, whether thats through slurs, strippers, swearing, drugs, or over-the-top cameos and moments. Needless to say, it has aged like milk. Where a film like Superbad still stands the test of time because there is genuinely good comedy and performances beneath all the vulgarity, The Hangover seems to be phoning it in, with a predictable and boring ending to boot.
So much of what I liked about the film was the mystery of itWhere is Doug, and what really happened? While this is answered and the audience is more or less given a mystery solved, it is far from Knives Out. The reveal is boring and feels as if every other part of the film was added simply to be a red herring. While there are a handful of strong visual moments, like the baby with the blu-blockers, the majority of the film feels forgettable.
The real silver lining of the film, though, is the cast. Bradley Cooper, Zach Galifianakis, Jeffrey Tambor, and Ed Helms are all memorable, but even this brings up another issue with the film. There is not one interesting or well-written female character. Unlike Emma Stone or Martha MacIsaac in Superbad, the film feels expressly written for the bros, and much of the comedy relies on how funny you think it is to get one over on your significant other. While surely the idea of a crazy bachelor party caper in Vegas is the kind of thing teenage boys dream of, in reality, the film is just not funny, clever, or original.
In short, there is not much to like about The Hangover in 2025. It lacks the emotional weight of a film like Planes, Trains and Automobiles, the sheer lightning-in-a-bottle quality of a film like Superbad, and genuinely doesnt stand the test of time.

I think its easy to forget that much of this movies climax hinges on the independent decisions made by female characters, i.e. Jules sobriety and Becca getting shitfaced on her own, both of which spotlight the boys insecurity and the shortsightedness of their plan. Though Superbads premisea Homeric odyssey for booze in part to loosen up objects of affection so theyd consider hooking up with dorksis probably no longer kosher for good reasons, the way that it eventually wraps up scans as broadly progressive, especially for the times. Evan and Beccas failed sexual encounter, in particular, is somehow more gloriously uncomfortable than I remembered not only does it run the emotional gamut, from genuinely sweet (I sooo flirt with you in math! Samesies!) to heartbreaking (Becca imploring Evan to Go get Gabby! after she pukes really makes me wince), it also perfectly captures two kids clumsily trying to act mature by imitating what they think the other wants. I had completely forgotten that the issue of consent was actively discussed, albeit in a realistic 90smid-00s teenage sort of way, and Evan levels the power imbalance by chugging tequila alone in a strangers bathroom so that hes as drunk as Becca, a depressing, yet accurate outcome. Its somewhat notable that when he decides to pull the ripcord at the last second, he does it without embarrassing or shaming her in any way.
With the exception of some homophobic language, this holds up concurrent to 2019 sociocultural standards far better than I ever though it would, but even if it didnt, it would probably still hold a place in my heart anyway. Its a right timeright place sort of thing. During its opening weekend, my friends older brother somehow snuck both of us into the Michigan Ave. AMC (our second attempt after being denied entry at the River East earlier that night) and we had to crouch low as ushers checked the aisles for underage kids, which, in hindsight, seems ridiculous and something I cant remotely imagine ever happening today. (Do multiplexes even pay employees enough to care about stopping teens from seeing R-rated movies?) If I were a little bit older or a little bit younger at the time, this might not have made any impact, but I was in the pocket to adore this crass, gentle movie about kids around my age that was operating entirely on its own wavelength while still working within, and paying homage to, a genre template. 12 years later, its remarkable how much it embodies an adolescent perspective, in all of its unpleasant shades, wholly without judgment. These movies should be juvenile after all.
On this umpteenth viewing, I mostly appreciated the idiosyncrasies. Barring a few exceptions, major studio movies rarely get to have this much personality anymore, no matter how little they cost. But its everywhere here the RBfunk-forward soundtrack, the winning opening credits homage to Foxy Brown, the references to Orson Welles and Richard Pryor that are actually character specific and not examples of writer self-flattery, the emphasis on public transportation (so many bus rides), the flip phones and regional cell reception issues (I get one bar everywhere I fuckin go.). Amid the relentless barrage of 2000s coming-of-age teen comedies, where mediocrity far outweighed laudable merit, Superbad emerged towards the latter half of the decade as a luminous breakthrough a gleaming light at the end of the tunnel that promised a better horizon for a category of commercially resonant guilty pleasures. It arrived less as a generic entry in comparison to other projects conceptually alike to it, being more of a coarsely sophisticated evolution of the genres well-worn tropes and storytelling clichés. And with comedy visionaries such as Bill Hader and Seth Rogen at the helm of its cast, alongside newcomers Michael Cera and Jonah Hill in their breakout performances, the stage was clearly set for a whooping blast of delectably cheap yet inversely alluring humor. 

Within the day-in-the-life of two neurotically vulgar high school seniors, we find a duo of victims in mild-hearted distress from the fallout of their self-imposed circumstances, notoriously driven by the age-old imperatives of adolescence, such as those of intoxication by alcohol and intimacy by the loss of ones virginity. Theres a full buckets worth of lewd antics, amplified by an unapologetically raucous screenplay that is akin to the juvenile wit of its ensemble cast of young adults (save for Christopher Mintz-Plasse, who was 17 years old at the time of shooting). Even if all of these elements may initially threaten to morph themselves into an intolerable viewing experience, the film manages to be unexpectedly rescued by the saving grace of a peculiarly addicting charisma that permeates throughout its whole runtime, such as one that is found in Edgar Wrights very own Cornetto Trilogy, as a palpable, in-your-face charm that follows every onscreen interaction. 

The opening of the story in particular tends to rely more on a nauseatingly overbearing concoction of crude humor, slowly meandering closer to the unwatchable side of it all. But after that flashback scene in the schools cafeteria, the overall comedic tone turns itself down a notch to just the right amount of brazenness, where that breezy appeal of laid-back hedonistic pleasures shines through. However, this doesnt come without its flaws, as the final act suffers from a sudden lurch into tepid sentimentalism, with a handful of derivative tugging-at-your-heartstrings moments that dont feel thematically earned, acting as a conventional nod to the multitude of melodramatic connotations of the genre. Thankfully, this misstep comes at an episode that is ultimately of fleeting length, doing little to diminish the hectic exuberance of everything that precedes it.

As such, Superbad stands tall (that is, if it can stand, with all the alcohol it must have consumed) as an off-the-wall celebration of the blatantly immature debauchery that its so proudly centered on. It wonderfully captures that often wavering euphoria of ones fading teenage years, in such a way that will continue to undoubtedly resonate with generations of impressionable youths around the world, who see their own sexually refracted psyche in the eyes of Evan, Seth, and McLovin, through a final glimpse of liberty before they become unanimously engulfed by the monotonous vacuum of adulthood. And should Lady Fortune truly smile upon their souls, they might just come across an Emma Stone to spend some time with amidst all the chaos.
