I didnt know how to feel about Superbad when I saw it in 2007. I felt like I was supposed to like it, but its hard to force comedy that doesnt really work for you, even in a film thats well directed, as this one was. When it came out there was a buzz around it, mostly among boys, who swore that it was the funniest movie theyd ever seen, but these same people also wore Vote for Pedro shirts a few years earlier, and said the same thing about Napoleon Dynamite, which has thankfully been cannon-blasted into space by the wages of time. Superbad was better, but I was left wondering what I was missing and its maleness was off-putting in a way that I could unconsciously feel. In the months after Superbad was released it didnt leave the public sphere of high school and was still being quoted and talked about. It was a genuine phenomenon that seemed to pick up more steam once it hit DVD, and those who were in grades slightly below me got the chance to watch the movie. It was impossible to escape all the bad McLovin t-shirts and dick jokes, but in a more productive way it was also difficult to elude its anxieties over a looming end to grade school, and the beckoning of college life. I was in the 10th grade when Superbad came out, and it was that particular element that worked for me, made me circle back to it a few more times when I was a teenager, and what stood out strongest when revisiting the movie at thirty years of age.
High school movies have to operate through a lens of discomfort around transformation. This can be hormonal, educational, or through a relationship, and the best examples that exist in the American cinema tend to circle around those elements with a wayward dissonance. Director Greg Mottola is good at these sorts of movies, with his follow-up film Adventureland (2009), hitting all the right notes of frustration when time begins to slip through your fingers without even realizing it. Seth (Jonah Hill) and Evan (Michael Cera) are really aware that their time where they could fuck around wasting days with one another is almost up. Its the elephant in the room that they dont talk about, because to speak it into existence would signal the end of that part of their lives. Theyre both off to different colleges at the end of the semester, and are so co-dependent on their friendship with one another that its a running joke among their classmates. They have a third wheel in Fogell (Christopher Mintz-Plasse), who is none-the-wiser to the dynamics between the trio. Hes going to be dorming with Evan in the fall, but Seth doesnt know it. Its a secret between the two, as if Evan were cheating on Seth with another. In general their relationship is homoerotic, bedding in the same sleeping bag, and playfully flirting with one another, because theyre both in on the bit. This particular element has aged well, and enlivens their relationship as something thats a little more than friendship. Its stranger still for boys to be presented in this way, as it is usually girls who are given the BFF treatment. In 2007 this threw me for a loop and the unique qualities of their relationship made me wonder if they were going to kiss in the final moments. They do not, but their relationship remains captivating all the same. In the years since its release their dynamic has only grown more compelling. There havent been a lot of great movies about teenagers since 2007, and most of those have been about girls. Superbad stands on its own as a portrait of young male adolescence on the edge of a deep transformation of their lives. While there were parts that didnt work for me in 2007, I now have enough time and distance to recognize Superbad for what it does well, instead of ensnaring it around my own hangups with masculinity, which were at a breaking point at the time of its release.
Like a lot of high school movies the thrust of Superbad takes place at a party where Seth has volunteered to bring the booze. The only hitch in his plan is he did this without thinking, because the someone who asked him was a girl he has a major crush on named Jules (a brand new Emma Stone). Also like high school movies, regrettably, Seth thinks if he can get her drunk shell want to sleep with him. Yikes, but Seth and Evan are morons, and Superbad handles the eventual follow-through of their plan with a level of maturity, and decency, that wouldnt have happened a couple of decades earlier. What follows is an odyssey for booze that takes them down many humorous paths that include fake I.D.s, running into the cops, and most impressively, stranded at a party of twenty-somethings where more serious drugs are on the table. Much of the comedy is delivered well, and doesnt have too much of the Judd Apatow house style of riffing for the sake of it to ungodly run-times. This is a more structured affair with a script from Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg that they apparently wanted to get off the ground in the 1990s, but didnt come to fruition until The 40 Year Old Virgin (2005) proved to be a success. The real stars are Jonah Hill and Michael Cera, and it is telling that theyve managed to prolong their careers beyond comedy as actors of some considerable skill. Hill has gone on to work with Martin Scorsese and Cera has popped up with David Lynch. Hills interpretation of horn-dog teenager Seth is petulant, aggressive and has notes of danger, where it wouldnt be totally out of place for the character to commit an act of violence on someone or even himself. Cera is working from a playbook of straight-man discomfort that he developed while working on Arrested Development (2004), and he has a strange, lanky, uncomfortable body language that is perfect for a teenager like Evan. Cera gets the funniest scene in the movie when hes mistaken for a friend of some coke-heads who sang at a funeral, and fumbles through a rendition of The Guess Whos These Eyes. They think he sings beautifully, and its made all the more hilarious by their sincere emotions to Ceras very average singing.
While Seth and Evan end up stuck at this terrifying party, Fogell ends up hand-cuffed to two dumbass police officers (played by Rogen and Bill Hader), after a robbery at a liquor store ends with the teenager being decked in the face. They cant get over the fact that his ID says McLovin, and they carry-on with him like theyre long friends. This part of the movie isnt as funny as I remember it being, and thats probably due to a more generalized awareness of police brutality than I had when I was a teenager. Hader and Rogen are capable, especially Hader, but firing bullets at civilians and blowing things up for the hell of it rings a little differently now. In some ways it is an accurate portrait of police officers being able to get away with anything. While that wasnt the intention of the filmmakers, because the work involving the cops is broad and goofy, it does make things a little sour going down, because it clashes so severely with how were supposed to think of these characters. Its curious viewing now, because in 2007 everyone couldnt get enough of McLovin, but that character and this part of the movie, seems to have disappeared in the cultural memory. When people think of Superbad it isnt necessarily the cops blasting Van Halen and driving drunk, but the exploits of Seth and Evan.
While watching Superbad another element became increasingly obvious, and this one was accidental. This is the last movie about American teenagers before social media became a dominant tool in the lives of future generations. Theres one brief mention of Facebook, but otherwise this movie is unencumbered by the drama of social media, or the need to be on a smart phone throughout the day checking in on your friends. Theres a level of privacy that these characters are afforded, and whose conflicts today would be solved with a text, but in Superbad they have flip phones cursed with bad cell reception. Ive mentioned before to my friends who are my age that we were the last generation who didnt grow up with access to smart phones, and theres an odd feeling that comes in knowing you were the last of a sort. Were just as addicted to the internet now as any generation, but when we were teenagers that wasnt the case for most of us. Theres something a little bit tragic about Superbad being the last movie of its kind, about teenagers in this particular moment, before everything changed. I couldnt help but feel nostalgic for that period, even though it was personally terrible for me. These characters just seem to have more air to breathe. Theres something beautiful about the fact that they can get lost and need to find their own way home. Theyre inconvenienced and dont even know it, but in that inconvenience they live just a little bit more than they would have had they been able to call for an Uber to take them to the right party.
The cat is out of the bag for Seth and Evan at the uncomfortable party. They end up talking about their future, blow-up at one another and release all the pent-up bile theyve been holding in for months. Its a fight that needed to happen for either boy to grow up. Seth feels left behind because he doesnt work hard enough to get into the college where Evan was accepted, and Evan feels like Seth has held him back from being more socially extroverted. Evan slings a particularly nasty barb at Seth that has a nugget of truth in it when he tells him that hes wasted the last three years of his life sitting around talking about bullshit. Seth has no way of responding to that one. Its a fight that friends sometimes have, and performed admirably by both actors. When they do end up at the right party they find one another, drunk off their asses, having failed to have sex with either of the girls they were interested in. A lot can happen in 24 hours when two best-buddy co-dependent outlier HS seniors get an invite to the big party. teaming up with a third-wheel friend getting his fake ID with just one name mclovin starts the ball rolling down a steep slippery slope of chaotic comic events, and rapidly turns into a day and night that will forever be ingrained in their memories. the writing and acting captures the awkwardness of the teenage lifestyle with pinpoint accuracy, at the same time makes it fun and painful to witness. i can think of quite a few films that allow their characters to thrive on ego and self-interest, with no redeeming qualities. here, the characters in superbad just want to fit in and achieve the girl of their dreams, but shallow stereotypes and one stutter too many prevent this goal from happening.
Superbad is truly an evolution of the genre. Its every bit as crass and wacky and full of horseplay as all the others since porkys, but this is the first time one of these mindless comedies dares to make us think and feel on a deeper level. like I said, its largely due to the great casting. michael cena, if youre not familiar, plays his signature role of an awkward deer-in-the-headlights kid but with a strong sense of who he is, even though nobody else seems to understand. jonah hill plays his best friend, sort of the antithesis a loser who thinks he knows what he wants but hes really quite confused. emma stone knocks it out of the park with a great role thats quirky, cool, rebellious and responsible all at the same time. rounding out the troupe are bill hader and seth rogan who play a pair of despicable yet loveable cops whose combined IQ is around the same as their blood alcohol level.

Seth and evans friendship is messy, built on insults, crude jokes, and years of shared hallways and cafeteria tables, obviously its played up for comedy, but its a legitimately terrifying position to be in. when youre a kid, its tempting to want to integrate yourself into adult actions, but the truth is youre still not old enough, and those adult actions can have a lot more consequences than a child could understand. you can get dangerously sick, physically injured, even arrested for doing things or being in places youre not supposed to, it even goes into a speech about how weird it is that guys cant say they love each other, and is just a genuinely heartfelt scene that perfectly ends an otherwise raunchy movie.

Directed by Greg Mottola, the film brought together a talented ensemble cast including Jonah Hill, Michael Cera, and Christopher Mintz-Plasse. The movie follows the misadventures of Seth and Evan, two socially awkward best friends trying to secure alcohol for a party in hopes of impressing their crushes. The story unfolds over the course of one chaotic day as they navigate parties, fake IDs, and unexpected encounters. The plot is reminiscent of classic coming-of-age films and is driven by the boys pursuit of popularity and relationships.
The film excels in character development, with Seth and Evans genuine friendship at its core. Their interactions are both hilarious and heartwarming, capturing the essence of adolescent camaraderie. Their personalities are distinct and relatable, making the audience root for them despite their flaws. The supporting characters, like Fogell and McLovin, add comic relief and depth to the story.
Superbad is known for its raunchy and irreverent humor, often toeing the line between outrageous and endearing. The witty dialogues, awkward situations, and running gags keep the laughs coming. The film successfully balances humor with moments of vulnerability, making the characters feel authentic rather than caricatures.
Greg Mottolas direction provides a fresh take on the teenage comedy genre. The camera work captures the characters emotions and the chaos of their day, while also using visual gags effectively. The pacing is energetic, maintaining the audiences engagement throughout.
Beneath the surface humor, the film touches on themes of friendship, growing up, and the fear of change. It highlights the anxieties teenagers face as they transition to adulthood, exploring the idea of leaving one phase of life behind for the unknown future.
And while primarily its a comedy, it subtly touches on social issues such as peer pressure, self-esteem, and the consequences of trying too hard to fit in. These elements give the film a deeper layer of relatability and provide viewers with moments of reflection amid the laughter.
Superbad has left a lasting impact on pop culture, giving rise to memorable catchphrases and influencing subsequent comedies. Its often regarded as a defining film of its era and a quintessential representation of the coming-of-age comedy genre.
In conclusion, Superbad is a hilarious and heartwarming coming-of-age comedy that expertly captures the essence of teenage friendships and the journey into adulthood. With its witty writing, relatable characters, and cultural impact, it remains a beloved film that continues to resonate with audiences.

Had to revisit this after reading Seth Rogens semi-autobiography, Yearbook. Ive seen this countless times and somehow never realized the main characters of Seth and Evan are based around the writers of Rogen and his longtime friend, Evan Goldberg. It took several years to make after completing the script in their younger years but once everything finally came to fruition, this iconic comedy became the instant classic we all know and love today.
The hilarious interactions between the trio of Jonah Hill, Michael Cera, and Christopher Mintz-Plasse perfectly capture the way high schoolers actually act, talk, and treat each other which makes this coming of age journey feel much more authentic than most of its influences and contemporaries. The premise isnt exactly the most original but Seth Rogen and Bill Hadens inclusion as the carefree cops causing chaos mixed with the treacherous threes desperate attempts at scoring alcohol and impressing chicks make this story based on real life experiences well worth the ride.
Its a pivotal project that came at a transitional time in comedy, serving as a passing of the torch from veterans like Ben Stiller, Will Ferrell, and Owen Wilson to newcomers Seth Rogan, Jonah Hill, James Franco, and Danny McBride. While vulgar and raunchy humor isnt anything new, this pioneering film created a shift in the culture that included the younger generation by giving them a relatable and funny film to claim as their own while paving the way for a whole new class of films like Pineapple Express and This Is the End in the process.
I have newfound appreciation for Seth Rogen and his brainchild after reading his book. Hes a talented writer, actor, and comedian whos responsible for many peoples careers as well as our cultures current climate in comedy. Martin Scorsese had the saying the most personal is the most creative and that proves to be the case here as Rogen incorporated his personal life experiences as a teenager into his own film and the result is one of the most popular, successful, and iconic comedies ever made.

I remember being so psyched for this film when it had just come out and I was all of 17 and in my last year of high school...
This is a filthy, chaotic coming-of-age comedy that somehow ends up being strangely tender. Superbad thrives on its raw, unfiltered portrayal of teenage friendshipthe kind built on insecurity, co-dependence, and saying the worst possible things to each other as a form of love.
The humour still lands hard awkward silences, escalating disasters, and characters who are painfully human in their desperation to be liked. McLovin remains iconic, and the absurdity around him never really ages.
...But watching it now, theres an undeniable shift in how some of the dialogue lands. The casual use of slurs and the way masculinity is performed feels very much of its timeless malicious than careless, but still jarring through a modern lens.
What holds it together is the heart beneath the vulgarity. Beneath all the chaos, its really about two friends on the brink of growing apart, terrified of what comes next and too immature to say it out loud.
It may feel slightly regressive in moments today (this is me being kind), but its emotional corefriendship on the edge of changestill hits exactly where it should.

Superbad feels like the perfect encapsulation of those final months in high school where nothing really mattered, yet everyone thought it did. That mad rush to make it seem like those last 4 years werent wasted, and that you were in on the fun that everyone else was having. If you could just have one night of fun before the ever-approaching graduation date, then it would all be worth it. You might not have been to any parties or social gatherings before this point, and were instead at home, playing video games or watching movies with a few select buddies, but going to just one party would signify that your high school career wasnt wasted. And its times like these that I remember an old adage by one John Lennon
Time you enjoyed wasting wasnt wasted.
This film solidifies that alcohol, sex, and drugs is not the be-allend-all of the high school experience. All night long, Seth and Evan strive to attend that party that will supposedly change everything. And through their trials and tribulations, they still have each other (and Fogel, I guess). Getting the most out of high school doesnt necessarily entail attending ragers after every sports game with a keg just as much enjoyment can be derived from the simpler things, like bonding with a best friend, or going on a crazy adventure with two immature cops. If thats what you enjoyed doing, why would anyone give a shit about popularity or scoring or whatever?
Ok, maybe I am giving this film a bit too much credit in that department, but thats at least what I personally took from it. And hey, even if you dont think this film was trying to make some profound statement on how you should enjoy your high school days, the film works fine enough as off-the-wall comedy that just keeps escalating until its eventual climax. It can be a bit awkward at points, but its sort of that intentional awkwardness that we can all relate to. And, I mean, like  it has McLovin. Do I really need to say anymore?

While known much more for MILF, band camp anecdotes and baked good banging, American Pies greatest contribution to the world was the re-birth of the R rated youth comedy.  The late 80s saw a transition into PG-13 territory for comedies.  Even franchises who began life with a beautiful R like Revenge of the Nerds and Police Academy, had cleaned up their act.  
Dominated by fish-out-of-water films and an almost complete absence of the once dominant high schoolcollege comedy, the 90s chugged along with Robin Williams in drag, doofus humor, TV adaptations, Robin Williams in drag again and save for a couple of indies, no mainstream R comedy.  The 1-2 punch of Theres Something About Mary in 1998 and Pie in 1999 showed that the masses didnt need their comedy castrated, we like them to have a pair.  Granted South Park came out the week before Pie with modest success, but it had fizzled inside of a month, whereas Pie dominated and was the 20th highest grossing film of the year, and the 3rd highest-grossing high schoolcollege film behind Animal House and Porkys.  
Pie isnt high art, but it is well cast and well plotted with a nice mix of sight gags, situational comedy and very funny and quotable lines.  Running gags and setups pay off well and, a couple of stiff performances aside, it acquits itself nicely.  It is actually very accessible, charming  and pretty friendly for a film about young mens quest to shed their virginity, not unlike Last American Virgin, but without the heartbreak at the end. (No hookers or VD either) It is a solid film, all-in-all, rating aside.  
A comedy shouldnt necessarily be R for Rs sake, but sometimes a subject is a subject.  Most young peoples lives especially are quite R rated.  To clean it up is to take away the real context and humor from it.  It would be as ridiculous as a PG-rated Die Hard (hmmmm...).  We have a mix now of good and bad comedies, both R and PG-13, and many of them are about younger people.  The R rated youth comedies in the 80s were never for older people in the first place.  They were for that times young audience.  I would hypothesize that the reason that many young people in the 90s connected with the same films as young people in the 80s is that they didnt have anything like that of their own.  That is certainly not the case anymore, and American Pie can be thanked for that.

I was a goth back then, and the film had big skate-punk energy, which seemed terribly important at the time. More fool me, because I would probably have enjoyed it. Watching it all these years later, Im surprised by how much it feels like a teenage, 1990s version of The Big Chilla hangout movie about a group of familiar types approaching a change in their lives, with a soundtrack carefully curated to supply the feelings they are too immature to express. At best, the boys pact to lose their virginity before graduation seems an unnecessarily stressful deadline to impose on an already awkward business, but I found the cluelessness beneath all their bravado quite endearing.
The trouble for this hangout movie is that there are very few members of the group I would actually want to hang out with. Seann William Scott certainly commits to Stifler, but I found his company exhausting, and the webcam episode is particularly unpleasant, not least because the film seems far more concerned about Jims embarrassment than the girl whose privacy he has invaded. I felt much more sympathetic in the rare moments when the boys bluster gives way to insecurity, and I rather liked Oz discovering that spending time with a girl might be enjoyable in itself, even if it takes him a while to arrive at this fairly modest insight. To my surprise, there is at least some sweetness beneath the competitive stupidity, and enough funny moments to keep things moving. I can certainly imagine having been more entertained at 14, although I suspect I would still have wanted to go home before Stifler arrived.

Doing for the teenage sex comedy what Scream did for the slasher film, Chris and Paul Weitzs American Pie is a turn-of-the-millennium crowd pleaser that reheats a heretofore stale cinematic form. Rowdy, raunchy, and recognizably real, the film is an often-hilarious gem that sports a huge heart.
Reduced to its barest narrative bones, American Pie is about four friends who vow to lose their virginity by the end of the school year. Clumsy sexual chaos ensues, and the gang learns lessons about life, love, and lust.
Those bones do not tell much of story, but, in the Weitzs hands, the tale takes on life as a satire of the male sex drive coupled with a pretty honest observation sexual and romantic energy,
The comedy ranges from over-the-top to down-to-earth, and the high-volume broad beats mesh well with more realistic moments. There is gross-out, there is grace and all of it is delivered with confidence that tempers potential slease with a yeah-but-youve-been-there honesty.
Driven by a better-than-solid cast, the production bounces with an upbeat energy. The characters have chemistry, and every coupling is memorable. The fashions and music are pure 90s, but, somehow, the look and sounds of the film are as much timeless as they are locked in 99.
American Pie starts out by taking its cues from the well-tread notion that boys are horny happily, the film allows that idea to coexist with the suggestion the girls like sex, too. Somewhere along the way, both of these threads becomes couched in genuine affection. The comedy presents these narrative beats with such a combination of bawdiness and truth that the work becomes outstandingly inviting and neatly refreshing. Heartfelt and highly amusing, the film is a treat.

Review In A Nutshell
The 80s was the peak of teenage angst in American cinema, exploring the relationships that drive our high school experience, tackling subjects of drugs, sex and personal growth. The problem that resulted during this abundance of productions is the lack of variation between each one tackling the same problems continuously and delivering little uniqueness to its execution, leaving many films as forgettable and tedious. However there are a notable set that stand out from the pack, even up to now standing high above its contemporary peers examples including The Breakfast Club and The Last American Virgin. American Pie may not deliver its themes as effectively as the films that I have just mentioned, but there is no doubt that this was a film that pushed the boundaries left by its predecessors and coming into a time where the genre was seen as a doomed avenue for contemporary cinema.
American Pie focuses heavily more on the sexual aspects of being a teenager, exploring the difficulties and pressures that come during this time on ones life. American Pie allows its characters sexual predicaments feel believable due to their problems being rooted from within them, there are actually very little external forces that pushes them to making these decisions, and I felt this was an accurate portrayal of a person going through high school. It is usually our own minds that pushes us to areas in life that we are not yet comfortable or competent to handle, leading to mistakes that would define our entire lives or at least that portion of our lives. We are definitely laughing at the characters in this film, but a part of us is doing so because we see a part of ourselves in them who hasnt experimented with sex or at least have thought about it, who hasnt told lies about themselves to their peers in order to make themselves more desireable, or who hasnt changed their entire personality in order to become closer to a certain girl or guy? I certainly have with all of those things, and looking back I no doubt loathe myself but I am not ashamed of it, as everyone goes through it and without those experiences, I would have been a much different person who have learnt nothing in his days of youth.
As I have said before, American Pie pushed the boundaries of the genre, allowing its topics to draw adolescent audiences in, but letting them experience the subject with more raunchiness, exaggerating the situations and its characters for comedic effect. I found myself laughing during only a few of these intense moments because many of what was being served seemed to be present for immediate effect rather than something that would cause resonating impact and most of these moments that worked were found from the character Stifler, who brought a sense unpredictability and surprise in his responses, leaving me stunned in the process. The stronger comedic elements of the film are found in its awkward moments, particularly during the scenes between Jim and his father, as these were the moments that felt real leaving me drawn towards my own personal experiences. Though the film is pegged as a comedy, it still manages to deliver its romantic aspects with such grace, providing a sense of balance to its tone and preventing the film from becoming a complete satire.
American Pie may not be a film that deals with anything unique, but it elevates the execution of its common themes, while still remaining honest, and through that it was like experiencing a fresh of breath air.

Probably more so than in almost any other movie genre, comedy is entirely cyclical
Beginning with the classic silent slapstick era of Chaplin and Keaton, through to the Hawksian screwball comedies of the 1930s and the more optimistic, romantic, post-WWII love stories brought to life by pratfalling goofballs and starring Hollywood royalty such as Doris Day and Audrey Hepburn, for many, the late 1970s and predominantly the 1980s saw the birth of one of the most formative comedy cycles, the teen movie.
Best encapsulated by the oeuvre of one John Hughes, from the likes of Porkys and on to The Breakfast Club, this trenche of films seemed to herald a new generation of both audience and film makers, creating gem after gem that whilst bearing no resemblance to any awkward youths actual life, spoke to them in a way that captured what it felt to be a teenager almost perfectly. And as the 90s encroached and these too began to evolve into something more post-modern, darker and savvier (from Clueless to Heathers), the genre started to feel like it was running out of steam, beginning to eat its own tailtale as the stories and films began to look back for inspiration and delivering the watered down, self-referential and super-bland likes of Shes All That
and then came THAT pie.
Vividly remembering the fevered recommendations of a university friend who had a year abroad back in 1999, its reputation had begun to precede it. This was a film the likes of which we hadnt seen beforewell, certainly not in mainstream cinema. And not in the cinema aimed at younger generations. And thus was born, what became affectionately known as the gross out comedy.
Nothing ages like shock however  what was shocking several decades before is now prime time family friendly entertainment. But American Pie retains its gloriously outrageous shock moments  and of course, delivers some new unintentional ones  easily earning and retaining its place as the genres now grandfather. But what always was so overlooked, and is also thankfully retained a quarter of a century later, is the films sense of heart, of warmth, of character, creating a beautifully balanced and somewhat realistic view of the lives of a teenager, now, then, at any time, in any era its messy, its awkward, its, yes, gross for sure, but also kinda sweet as expectations, friends, inexperience and general misadventure befall everyone, no matter the intention.
Taking a very traditional set-up  four horny high school boys, unlucky in love throughout their short lives, make a pact to lose their virginities at the end of year Prom  it gives us our cast. And whilst interesting that not many have gone onto global superstardom, as an ensemble, they work beautifully from Jason Biggs brilliantly horny and unlucky loser and Seann William Scotts obnoxious frat-bro template, to Alyson Hannigans superbly nerdy and naughty band geek and Eddie Kaye Thomas old-before-his-time sophisticat wannabe, they work fantastically well together. And while its likely no surprise that the most traditional characters  the handsome jock (Chris Klein), the blonde hotty (Tara Reid) and even Shannon Elizabeths exchange studentsex object  are the most dull, theyre absolutely needed to round out arguably the full gamut of the teenage experience wonderfully characterising every element and facet of teen life, their highs and considerable lows seem to come from them as characters that despite being thinly drawn, feel much more rounded than the usual fare seen thanks to its plucky cast.
But writer Adam Herz and director Paul Weitz sensibly dont ignore the adults here, making sure that Eugene Levy as Jims well-meaning father who is every bit as genetically cumbersome as his son, and of course Jennifer Coolidge as Stiflers Mom, not just smoking hot but introducing a term into the cultural lexicon that has remained a part of everyday parlance ever since, further round out these characters and start to bring in just a little of that heart that the film has firmly in the right place.
Because whilst there is sex with baked goods, questionable beer drinkage, awkward parental encounters about lascivious educational reading material and the streaming of a vulnerable young woman without her consent on the internet (yes, today that scene has a very different context and no, it doesnt warrant cancelling the film due to it firmly generating a worthwhile comeuppance), the characters are sweet, theyre charming, theyre funny and most importantly, they have their heart in  absolutely the right place. There could have been darkness and maliciousness behind most of these scenes, there could have been a mean spirit driving most of these characters who after all, only want to get laid and not care a jot about who theyre getting laid withbut Herzs script delightfully counters all that with some genuine warmth. There are arcs that come the films ending are quite delightful  no, not everyone gets to have sex and those that do run the gamut of being joyfully used through to the realisation that even at that tender age, there has to be more to a relationship than just sex.
And of course, theres still Stiflers Mom
With a banging pop-rock soundtrack to boot and some clever nods to teen comedies of generations past (back when nods were just that and not whole, entire story and plot beats), American Pie may now be more fondly remembered for its now oh-so-quaint shock factor, but what it should be more remembered for is its thoroughly modern look at teenagers (of the time of course) that didnt have them acting way beyond their years and that rightly created some of the most memorable genre moments (and even a sub-genre in itself) and characters of the last twenty five years.

One of the seminal teen sex comedies, a runaway summer hit that coined permanent cultural phrases, introduced iconic movie moments, kick-started some big careers, spawned several equally successful sequels, an entire spin-off franchise and influenced a generation of R-rated young adult hijinks-with heart and cringe comedies alike. 
My opinion of it hasnt wavered in the 25 years since I saw it in theaters - its certainly not excellent in any way, unlike some other teen movies of that late 90s resurgence (10 Things I Hate About You, Cant Hardly Wait, Go) (I would even rank it below Varsity Blues, Cruel Intentions, Never Been Kissed, Dead Man on Campus, Detroit Rock City and others) its put together in a rickety manner, with primitivesimplistic writing, acting, editing, directing, even the lighting is noticeably poor in a lot of scenes. The personality types of the core friend group are painfully mild, the boys are all cretins, potentially engaging conversations only ever last about 12 seconds and 2-3 lines at most...
But I laughed nonetheless, then and now, and happily recognize the crowd-pleasing instincts begging for better filmmaking savvy. Its a jolly ensemble cast even if theyre not brilliantly used, and some really clever stuff gets through now and then (pale ale, aged 18 years, just the way I like it), along with a respectable attempt to open up the taboo topic of sexuality to frank(goofy) consideration at a teen level. The raunchy set-pieces of sexual embarrassment (Biggs with Shannon Elizabeth) andor general grossness (Shitbreak getting laxatived) are worthy of a Farrelly Bros. joint, the trending popularity from whence this whole movie was no doubt inspired. 
While the cast is arguably too big, spreading excessive subplots out too thin, combined it all forms a lovable portrait of this world, with everyone getting a minute or two to make a lasting impression, down to (or perhaps especially) the bit players and cameos, like Eugene Levy stealing all scenes as the ultimate understanding dad in a role that would become synonymous with the franchise as its great mascot, or Shannon Elizabeth as every teen boys wet dream come true (troubling objectification here in retrospect, but as a sex symbol she delivers), or future Oscar winner Casey Affleck as the cool older bro, or John Cho getting a laugh in 6 seconds of screen time as the MILF guy, or Jennifer Coolidge sauntering in as said MILF, or Alyson Hannigan throwing a curveball at the end (her and Coolidge provide satisfying payoffs to their male counterparts arcs), or Seann William Scotts breakthrough appearance not as one of the gang, but as their asshole acquaintance whose belligerent jerk energy overshadows every single one of them and made him the other expand-his-screentime must-see fan favorite of the series alongside Levy.
For what its worth, Tara Reid, Mena Suvari, Thomas Ian Nicholas, Chris Klein and Eddie Kay Thomas are all basically fine, just very limp. They dont pop off the screen whatsoever. Natasha Lyonne flashes her trademark saucy spunk for the first time but has no real character to play. Jason Biggs fares best among the leads, when hes playing off outrageous situations, doing some cosmic blend of Michael J. Fox scampish physicality and Michael Cera insecure nebbish.
This loaded soundtrack, meanwhile, is like a direct listing of what we were obsessed with from the radio at the time (at least in my circle) - Barenaked Ladies One Week, Flagpole Sitta (that one was more memorably deployed in Disturbing Behavior though), Blink-182 songs (and them showing up on screen too as fellow teens), Sway this ballad by Bic Runga, Semi-Charmed Life (used in at least half of all movies from 1997-1999), plus not needle-dropped but backgrounded tracks from Semisonics Dan Wilson, Sugar Ray, Foo Fighters, Goldfinger, Tonic. Heavy flashbacks to my scene in 1999. Trivia point Laid by James was the anthem that became associated with the American Pie franchise but its not used at all in this movie. The ensemble cast is a blast, with Jason Biggs nailing the everyman cringe and Chris Klein radiating goofy charm. Seann William Scott steals every scene as the obnoxious yet iconic Steve Stifler, while Eugene Levys turn as Jims painfully sincere dad delivers comedy gold and those amazing eyebrows.
This film isnt just a nostalgia trip its one of the 90s comedy hits that redefined teen movies, blending crude gags with genuine heart. Its not perfect, but its a fun, quotable romp that still holds up.

Fifth viewing tonight this was a rewatch on the big screen at The Revival House Perth on 35mm film, and it was a treat finally watching a film that I had seen so often on DVD at the cinema with a laughing audience in tow. The print jumped at a couple of points but was mostly in great nick with very little damage, and the sound was sharp and clear, which was a major plus given how many great songs are crammed into the soundtrack. The humour in the film is admittedly variable and the most childish parts (Finch on the toilet Sherman at the prom) sadly received the biggest audience reactions, but the best parts of the film are very funny every moment when Jason Biggs and Eugene Levy share the screen is comedy gold with their uncomfortable, candid discussions on things best left unsaid. The best aspect of the film though is how much growth each main character undergoes. While the movie starts off as a raunchy sex pact comedy, it concludes as a tale of four teens realising that sex is not everything.
There is a surprising amount of technical finesse at hand here as well from a shot that whips around from Mena Suvari to Chris Kleins baffled face as she walks out on him, to a shot that pans towards a pivotal pool table towards the end, the camerawork frequently shows thought and consideration. The reaction shot editing during the webcam scene is spot-on too, while the whole webcam subplot evokes nostalgia for a simpler time in which live streaming a video in 144p was the best thing ever. The so-called bible that Kevin finds is also something that would have been on a smartphone these days. In short, this is very much of a film of its time and not necessarily in a bad way. At no point do the filmmakers endorse the sex-crazed behaviours of the teens, much of which would not fly in post-MeToo times. The film is about growth and getting past childish behaviour. It is a very sweet movie overall, and surprisingly so for a film that has a reputation as that movie where a guy puts his dick in a pie.

Good God Almighty, what a fucking trip this was. Where does one even begin to describe such a movie? Its fucking batshit insane. That should do it. But for the sake of making this review way longer, as usual, I think Ill elaborate with bullshit arguments.

Im not familiar with Nima Nourizadehs game, but the guy truly knows. Add Todd Phillips from The Hangover and a cocaine-fueled (probably) Joel Silver as the lead producers, and this is pure unadulterated chaos. 
One complaint I do have while I do get that the obscene raunchiness is a big point in the movie to show the heights the party reached, as well as appropriate to the mindset of a bunch of high-schoolers, I cant say that I really enjoyed it. I enjoy raunchiness, but Ive got some limits. Who knows, maybe Im just the biggest wuss ever. 
Its got some explosive performances, especially by Oliver Cooper as Costa, who pretty much carried most of the film. Hes so goddamn funny. Thomas and JD are also excellent additions, bringing a lot of personality to their characters. Those bodyguards as well, my God, they were a laugh riot. And a brief appearance by Miles Teller just to top it off. 
The technical aspect is also something remarkable. The fact that its a found footage film allows for some incredible POV shots that do an excellent job taking you to the party. Even the shots that clearly were taken with a cellphone do the work. Matter of fact, the production actually gave the extras cellphones to record everything they could, leaving them with an absurd amount of footage. Man, the post-production for this film mustve been a nightmare. I dont know how much did they pay the editing and sound crew, but it wasnt enough. They did a phenomenal job. And also, that soundtrack, just fucking beautiful banger after banger after banger. 
In conclusion, a great teenage comedy, and an excellent time capsule of the early 2010s. Its raunchy, its chaotic, its stupid, its legendary. A new comfort film on my list.

Holy shit, dude. Its Miles Teller.
You know what makes a high school film any good? Its the realism. Superbad, Booksmart, and Easy A have dialogue and humor that feels authentic to the age and situation of the characters. The Perks of Being a Wallflower, The Edge of Seventeen, and Breakfast Club are less upbeat, but feature characters that are more true to parts of ourselves people rarely see. Project X fails at that because it comes off as though its trying too hard to be an iconic high school comedy instead of an actually fun movie. Its unpleasant, but not in the way a film like this should be. Like The Fk It List, it has the unlikable characters, but not the necessary self awareness to recognize how bad they are. And even by the end when it seems to gain that self awareness, it doesnt redeem them enough for you to like them even a bit, or at least thats what its like to me. Its obnoxious, and while it has a few entertaining moments, it feels overly long despite its short runtime.

I thoroughly believe that there is room for recklessness, debauchery and vulgarity in film just as much as there is room for deep introspective art.
People hate this movie, and I can definitely see why, but those very reasons are why I love it. Its rough around the edges, theres next to no nuance, its obscene and its offensive. Its a film with characters that do bad things and were supposed to laugh at it. And while many cant find humour in such tastelessness, I certainly can.
Movies arent supposed to be reality. If I wanted to see real people do real things, Id sit by my window and stare out into the street like a dog whos been left home alone. Project X is gloriously over the top (but also an incredibly authentic portrait of toxic masculinity and party culture) and purposely offensive. I shouldnt laugh at it, but I do, and I feel no guilt because these arent real people. In theory everything that happens in this movie is funny, but in reality its pretty fucked up. But its not reality, and the film doesnt condone their actions. Nobody in their right mind watches this and completely flips their perception of party culture. Watching a movie where people do bad things doesnt make you do the same bad things, unless youre incredibly impressionable. 
Much like Animal House and Jackass, Project X is a movie that would make film snobs recoil in terror due to its lack of depth. But like those movies, the lack of depth becomes depth of sorts. So superficial, so stupid and ridiculous, its mere existence is a raised fist of protest against high art. Its a film that shows something many people really want to see, even if they wont openly admit it. In turn, it feels like a catharsis, like screaming Fuck at the top of your lungs into the empty air. Project X is debauchery incarnate with young, impressionable characters doing stupid things. You can see it as a time capsule of 2010s party culture, a critique of masculinity, a reckless showcase of immoral acts that would probably give Michael Haneke a stroke, but for me its one thing above all else, its a really fun fucking time.
Ps. A much as I loved it, the Superbad ripoffs were shameless. Still love this though.

This might just be the wildest, most chaotic movie Ive ever seen, and I loved every second of it. From the very beginning, Project X throws you into an out of control ride that only gets more insane by the minute. It gave me literal goosebumps. The energy, the madness, the sheer scale of the party, its something you cant look away from.
What makes this film stand out isnt just the crazy moments (though there are plenty of those), but how well it balances everything. Despite all the mayhem, theres still room for a bit of romance, a hint of drama, and even a touch of action. It somehow pulls off the impossible, making you care about the characters while still keeping the party vibe going strong. That balance is what makes it more than just another party movie.
The found-footage style adds to the raw, real feeling, like youre actually there, watching this legendary night unfold. The soundtrack is fire, the visuals are wild, and the pacing never lets up. Every time you think things cant get more insane, they do. Flamethrowers, cops, cars in swimming pools, its a full-blown riot.

Eu estava pensando seriamente se iria voltar a escrever textos grandes, confesso que fiquei bem desanimada com o tempo e também por conta de ter largado a faculdade de cinema em minha defesa, eu recebi oportunidades melhores em que eu teria que escolher entre a faculdade ou a oportunidade. Continuo na área do cinema, mas não na faculdade. Um dos outros motivos do desânimo é que eu assisti a bastante filmes mês passado e, esses dias, eu estava enjoada só de ouvir a palavra filme, mas agora eu quero assistir a todos os filmes do mundo. Mas enfim, voltando para o filme...
Project X  é definitivamente uma das maiores obras sobre desobediência civil da última década, transformando a utopia e a busca pelo êxtase do alpha-adolescente machinho de high school em uma energia bruta, transformadora e puramente niilista, com uma realidade pandemônica de corpos e fluidos que concilia uma lógica invasiva de intimidade através do formato found footage. Embora parta de uma premissa boba derivada de comédias teen pós-Superbad e de fitas de câmera na mão que flertam com o vulgar, o filme exibe uma confiança plena e sem concessões em seu registro cinematográfico, onde o embate final com a polícia articula perfeitamente a dinâmica do dispositivo tecnológico com a tática de combate de rua, gerando uma catarse que serve como um ato manifesto de protesto contra a alta arte e uma legítima repolitização do espaço. A produção e a pós-produção operaram milagres ao transformar a absurda quantidade de filmagens brutas feitas por celulares em tiros de POV incríveis e um design de som primoroso, tudo isso embalado por uma trilha sonora que é um banger atrás do outro, com destaque para A Busca da Felicidade, capaz de fazer qualquer um levitar e que merece ser guardada em um cofre, funcionando quase como um tributo à Charli XCX e à pulsão de morte do ego da nossa geração digital em nome de apenas uma noite.
O filme transmite uma sensação de nos sentirmos lá dentro, construindo um grupo principal de amigos tão autêntico com performances explosivas (especialmente Oliver Cooper como Costa), que nos faz importar com eles e sentir que poderíamos ser seus amigos na vida real, equilibrando com maestria a loucura generalizada com pitadas de romance, drama e ação. Há quem sinta falta de uma transcendência mais profunda ou que critique o retrato da masculinidade tóxica, o humor de mau gosto e a obscenidade do comportamento autodestrutivo desses jovens que arruínam suas vidas na busca por reconhecimento profissional e social, mas o filme não tolera ou finge ser a realidade ele transcende o delírio e o ridículo para funcionar como um verdadeiro filme de terror de festa superior e uma cápsula do tempo memorável do início dos anos 2010. A imersão nesse filme traz um choque de realidade sobre a nossa própria mortalidade e sobre a sorte de estarmos vivos, encapsulando com perfeição o lema de ir duro ou ir para casa em uma escalada ininterrupta de eventos selvagens, agradáveis e bizarros, como um garoto preso no forno ou carros voando em piscinas sob lança-chamas. Resumindo, o filme é uma comédia adolescente descarada, estúpida, lendária e que dá aquela sensação indescritível de gritar FODA-SE no topo dos pulmões mantendo a distância perfeita do perigo, Project X entrega um caos puro e inalterado que se consolida com convicção como um novo filme de conforto.

All things considered, there arent many movie watching experiences that can be described as being as much of a consistent thrill rush as Project X. Even with such a wide array of glaringly obvious flaws (the pseudo-documentary structure, horrible writingconsistency issues), the entertainment value that is inherently imbedded comfortably within the core of the film has no trouble being my main takeaway from the experience as a viewer. That being said this type of story is clearly intended for a specific audience, meaning this will work better for some than it will for others. Had I seen this maybe two or three years ago I wouldve thought it was the coolest thing ever, being that the movie is essentially a projection of every 14 year olds high school fantasy, but watching now I find myself more or less unimpressed by the work as a whole although I certainly had a good time in the moment. You may love Adam Sandler, you may hate him, but you cant deny this being his friendcoworkeremployee (whatever the supporting cast in this movie is supposed to be) has got to be one of the funniest things that could happen to you. 
Its finally Friday, and tomorrow will be the beginning of a rather heavy and unpleasant weekend, so I chose to rewatch one of my favorite comfort films, which I hadnt watched in a very, VERY long while. 
For starters, yeah, it has little to no plot, we know. But sometimes all you need is having a bunch of old pals having a great time so that you yourself can have a great time as well. And I dont think that there was any other person who understood that as well as Adam Sandler. His writing, alongside Fred Wolf, is as barebones as it gets, with your classic emotive moments and half-assed moral lessons, as well as some conflicts to fill in the blanks matter of fact, I think that Sandler and Wolf were pretty much check-listing every single classic narrative aspect while writing this movie. But what makes up for it is how well it shows a bunch of friends just having fun. Sure, it doesnt sound like much, but it certainly makes for a very entertaining movie. The fact that its directed by Dennis Dugan, another one of Sandlers closest friends and most recurrent collaborators, makes it ten times better. As for the comedy, its either lowbrow and slapsticky and in-your-face, or its more lowkey and subtle and offensive. As someone whos very used to Sandlers humor style, I gotta say that I didnt really mind it in fact, I enjoyed it, which might be really blinding me, but what the hell. 
It also features a great ensemble. Sandy, James, Rock, Spade and Schneider are certainly a great team, and you can tell that they were enjoying themselves quite a lot. Salma Hayek did a pretty good job for Sandlers overly-beautiful-and-definitely-undeserved love interest. Maria Bello, Maya Rudolph, Joyce Van Patten, and the rest of the main ensemble were pretty great as well. The kids were also pretty good, amongst them a young Cameron Boyce (RIP). And the smaller roles, such as Colin Quinn, Steve Buscemi, Tim Meadows, Jonathan Loughran and even a rather flashy appearance by Norm Macdonald are also a very fun time. 
And that soundtrack, good fucking Lord. Its a Sandler tradition to have classic bangers as needle drops and thats certainly one thing about his movies youll never hear me complain about. 
In sum, this is, for me, the culmination of a comfort film. Almost pure style, almost no substance just a bunch of old friends having the time of their lives. Its simple and vulgar, yeah, but itll always put a smile on me, particularly now that I need it the most. Thank you, Adam Sandler. Youre the best worst thing thats happened to the industry.

Back in 1978 a group of young friends won their city basketball championship under the tutorage of Coach Buzzer Ferdinando. After the win, Buzzer gives the kids a heartfelt speech about sticking together. Years later the kids are all grown up. Adults with families of their own. Upon learning the news of the passing of Coach Buzzer they all meet again at his funeral and book a weekend getaway together. A getaway that reminds them of how important they are to each other and how that bond can make their familys lives better.
In just a few days my  31 Days of Horror  thing begins, so the entire month of October is horror films. Im going to cram a view non-horror films in until then. I logged on to Netflix and decided to watch the first comedy flick that appeared on my screen. That film is  Grown Ups , a Happy Madison film that came out in 2010 when Adam Sandler movies were still ok....I think. The cast is chock full of heavy hitters so my expectations going in were higher than theyd be for many other Sandler films, especially those in recent time.
I have to say, Im glad  Grown Ups  was the film. I found myself laughing often, especially at the stuff that would be taboo to laugh about nowadays. This film was released at the tail end of when comedy was still funny and at some points its very obvious. Most of the cast had worked together before and the chemistry shows. I dont normally find Kevin James funny, but when he has someone like Adam Sandler to bounce off of it makes a huge difference.
 Grown Ups  isnt one of the best comedies around, its not even one of the best Happy Madison films, but its a solid family chuckle-fest from the end of the heyday of Happy Madison films. Not long after this, the brand was tarnished with a long string of shitty movies and eventually Adam Sandler would sign exclusively with Netflix and continue making even shittier films. That is until A24 got their hands on him and the brilliant  Uncut Gems  brought him back in a big way, minus his worn out comedy schtick.

Providing exactly what an audience would expect from a comedy teaming Adam Sandler, David Spade, Chris Rock, Kevin James, and Rob Schneider, Dennis Dugans Grown Ups is a goofy, good-natured piece of work that will do nothing to sway those in the anti-Sandler camp. Offering low-hanging comic fruit from start to finish, Grown Ups boasts an, at least, moderately pleasing collection of belly-laughs and groaners that allows Sandler to play the semi-straight man against silly, nearly family-friendly set-ups.
When a beloved basketball coach dies, a group of his now grown-up players converge with their families for a Fourth of July weekend celebration of the coachs life. Grown Ups revolves around the comic personality clashes and the facades built in the name looking more successful than they might actually be.
Ending with a reprise of the basketball game that put the coach on the map, the story makes a solid foundation for the films combination of physical comedy and low-brow laughs. Grown Ups drags in spots, but Dugan keeps most of the energy high and his cast is capable of handling what is required of it. 
It may not have artistic value, and it will not change the minds of those predisposed to disliking the Sandler brand. Grown Ups, however, is built to please, and it succeeds in creating a mildy enjoyable experience. It clearly is not a great comedy, but it supplies enough fun to be likable.

In 2010, Happy Madison released a film featuring an all-star cast from the glory days of SNL. A lighthearted reunion of iconic comedians who knew each other since the 1990s. However, theres nothing really special about this one.
Grown Ups is about five lifelong friends who reunite with their families for a Fourth of July weekend after the sudden death of their former basketball coach.
Ive been on somewhat of a mood for Adam Sandler movies during my vacation and I was able to stream a few titles on some of these past nights. Today is my last day in Destin, Florida and I think I had a good vacation. I got to spend precious time with my family, see my son experience the beach, I got to go on a dolphin cruise with my wife for our anniversary, and I got to have a couple of fun drunken nights with my dad. Im not even ready to go home because it all went by so fast and I dont want to be back for work on Monday. So before I have to return to my mundane work life, lets talk about Grown Ups. 
I remember going to the movies with my mom, my cousin and his mom, this is before one of us got to have a drivers license for our 16th birthdays, and it felt nice after knowing I stayed up all night watching the Nightmare on Elm Street movies by myself. My mom woke me up sometime in the afternoon and asked if I wanted to join her to watch Grown Ups at the movies. After my reaction to it, I thought it would be a good enough movie if the comedy wasnt focused on too much goofiness.
The film features an all-star cast. It includes Adam Sandler, Kevin James, Chris Rock, David Spade, Rob Schneider, Selma Hayek, Maria Bello, and Maya Rudolph. Sandler plays Larry Feder, a Hollywood talent agent. James plays Eric Lamonsoff, Larrys friend and former furniture seller. Rock plays Kurt McKenzie, Larrys second friend and is stay-at-home father. Spade plays Marcus Higgins, Larrys third friend and is a slacker. And Schneider plays Rob Hilliard, Larrys fourth and final friend who is a hippie.
On paper, this wouldve been a great idea to have these five cast members together for their own movie. Including Kevin James, whose character was originally written for the late great Chris Farley in its earliest conception in the nineties. Ive always loved James ever since he was in The King of Queens and other Happy Madison films he did on his own, but I sometimes wonder how would Farley turn out after his success in Saturday Night Live and Tommy Boy. Come to think of it, I think Farleys soul is reincarnated into James. Anyway, it seems to me that having these guys together in their own movie and their chemistry makes it worth the effort as a buddy comedy. However, the cast members who play their wives and kids are unimportant. Dont get me wrong, its nice to see them interact with each other during the films runtime and have the sappy moments of how family means everything, but the inclusion of having them didnt feel necessary due to not having enough meat on the bone. It wouldve been better off with the bromance material the more time those five can spend together alone the better.
Grown Ups was directed by Dennis Dugan while the script was written by Adam Sandler and Fred Wolf, and it was produced by Sandler and Jack Giarraputo. This is the sixth collaboration between Sandler and Dugan since their first time together at making Happy Gilmore, and they both have a solid relationship with each other at Happy Madison. I have no quarrel with Dugan, he does what he can do as a director and just lets his cast members improvise with the comedy. But it doesnt really cut it when the script relies on too much goofiness to add in the runtime and not have enough to grasp onto for the characters. Yes, I know its a silly and stupid comedy from Adam Sandler, its going to get really silly and stupid. But a movie that is a buddy comedy could be good if it had some depth, because the movies attempt at blending comedy with heartfelt moments sometimes misses the mark, coming off as more forced than touching. Its like the my way or the highway deal with M. Night Shyamalan and his bland craftsmanship.
In my theatrical experience, I was expecting some more outrageous, inappropriate, and juvenile giggles that for the most part just werent there. Grown Ups is a solid movie for those that love it for what it is, but for me it was a misfire. Of course, I dont hate it, so if some of you among the majority have that opinion, I guess that, even with this film, Im still not 100 with the majority, oddly enough. Some of it was enjoyable, I wasnt that entertained. It is what it is. You cant like them all. Individuality a thing of beauty.
Im giving Grown Ups 3 stars.

For someone whos avatar on this ere Letterboxd (and Twitter actually) is some sort of ZAZ mashup I have to confess I lost track of the comedy genre a little while ago, at least in terms of mainstream comedies that most regular people like to watch. Specifically the art of the traditional spoof movie fell by the wayside some time in the 90s. But its the straight up comedies that failed to resonate through the 00s and I sort of lost track. Well Ive decided to do something about it.
And what else is a guy to do in this situation? I filtered my Letterboxd to comedys Ive never seen. Then I made a list based on the filter. And specifically today I filtered that list down to streaming services (the Just Watch integration is brilliant, isnt it?) And I should say Im talking about straight comedies. Not dram coms or rom coms. Im talking about films whose remit is to make me laugh until my belly aches. Thats the sole emotion Im looking for here. 
There is an irony then that somehow I landed on Grown Ups to begin this journey. The central conceit at least rings true, to a point. Kids spend too much time inside, Dads want them to experience the great outdoors. At first the kids are not receptive. So the Dads lead the way by reliving their childhood by doing a bunch of immature stuff. In the end, everyone learns some valuable life lessons because of a game of basketball. 
Aside from the arrow Rob Schnieder gets through the foot and a few off colour references, this movie is surprisingly pedestrian. Whether thats a good thing or not, Im not sure. I wouldnt have minded feeling a little more on edge. Its a very safe movie that, in my case, failed to raise much of a titter. Having said that, I can see a lot of the Sandler comedies I used to enjoy when I was 18 and 19 in this movie. I have to confess to a little nostalgic kick when some of his old stalwarts from those films dropped in. Having said all that, the humour in this movie largely went over my head. Perhaps Ill save Grown Ups 2 until later on in this particular challenge.

Grown Ups is an Adam Sandler movie that is almost annoyingly funny. It follows a group of childhood friends who get together as adults in honor of their childhood basketball coachs death. Everyone and everything here feels like it is on autopilot, so its actually surprising how funny it is. 
Its a Happy Madison studios production, and is chock full of Adam Sandlers friends, who range from hilarious to annoying. Although it has a ton of eye rolling one liners and 2000s jokes, it is surprisingly funny. Adam Sandler, Chris Rock, Kevin James, and Steve Buscemi are all truly hilarious. About half of the time I was laughing, and the other half of the time was spent rolling my eyes, but the real downfall of the movie is how absolutely incoherent it is. 
It almost feels closer to a Jackass movie rather than a true film. Its as if the plot is a vessel for the different scenes and sketches to come together. So when it tries to have moments of sentimentality, call backs, and tries to tell a heartfelt story it begins to crack at the seams, as its impossible to take almost everything in the film seriously. 
Whether that is a public pool that allows for a death trap zip line, or the entire movie hinging on a point being a 2 pointer or a three pointer, when the actual scene is completely incongruent with the rest of the film. This along with much of the Rob Schneider scenes and David Spade one liners make the movie genuinely bad, no matter how funny it is during its best moments.
Overall it is a loose and poorly thrown together Sandler movie, but as I watched it with my dad it was clear why the film is so popular and why they made a second one. The Sandler and co. formula will always offer a few truly hilarious moments, and for many, that is enough.

Grown Ups has some of the best performances and chemistry I have ever seen. Absolute powerhouse performances from Sandler, James, Rock, Spade, and Schnieder. I am a sucker for incredibly expressive and over-the-top performances, and all 5 leads bring such an animalistic ferocity to their immature, weak, damaged, wild, animalistic characters in ways that are constantly hilarious, scary, and depressing. Despite some occasionally odd pacing, the magnetic performances ensure constant excitement and engagement. Seriously some of the most entertaining and fantastic performancesdynamics I have seen, and anyone who loves this film, I would recommend checking out the 5 lead actors visit on the Jimmy Fallon show, where they brilliantly market the film by playing (or perhaps being themselves?) their same drunk, untameable, childish, off-the-wall characters. Anyone who has a fear of confronting growing up and maturing and flees to some sort of vice or form of escapism, no matter what age, will find a deep and painful emotional resonance here that is super effective. Dugan captures all of this in an incredibly cinema verite style, which makes the film and the characters hedonistic endeavours masking damaged, vulnerable, confused souls all the more beautifully intimate. Overall, its a very powerful film that captures the aspects of the human condition that it is aiming to explore so emotionally potently. The exploration on friendship, masculinity, and existential crises is so affective. Dugans typical verite style and use of intense, and seemingly improvisational performances has never resonated so strongly. Dugan is the king of capturing flawed, damaged, intense, and real human emotion, and this is the most powerful showcase I have seen of it thus far.

I dont think theres been a film that was as hyped up for me as this one. Okay, there are a few, but this has always been near the very top, with so many people calling it one ofif not thegreatest comedies ever put on screen. Of course, I had a feeling it probably wouldnt reach that pedestal for me.
But man, this was a really good time. I never found myself laughing out loud, and Will Ferrells brand of slapstick, physical, over-the-top humor doesnt always land with me, but this is one of those films that makes perfect use of his strengths and comedic sensibilities. Reilly also has terrific comedic timing, and the banter and chemistry between him and Will are pure gold. They had already proven in Talladega Nights that they made a fantastic duo, and McKay takes full advantage of that dynamic by giving them a really strong script packed with memorable jokes and quotable lines, many of which people still reference to this day. Ferrell singing Por Ti Volare was genuinely beautiful. Within the first seven minutes these two lovable man-kids Dale (but you have to call him Dragon) and Brennan (you have to call him Nighthawk) introduce themselves while  LCD Soundsystem - North American Scum  plays and the letters for the title drop in between them as they face each other in a standoff.  Step Brothers  is the simple minded comedy stuff that you would expect from a Will Ferrell flick but its the  BEST EXAMPLE  of it. Make sure to stick around through the credits. Some real assholes get what they deserve and youd never know it if you didnt hang around a bit. Youre welcome.
I know Ill re-watch this film at least a dozen more times before I die and Ill laugh every time.  Step Brothers  is the top of the comedy mountain in my eyes and I recommend it to everyone from your little brother to your grandparents. Its pure dopey excellence on film, and Ill carry that sentiment forever.

Step Brothers es una comedia que no cumple con la función principal que debe tener hacerte reír y divertirte. En general es bastante tonta y los personajes principales se me hicieron insoportables, tienen una personalidad de nenes que no me causó nada de gracia y solo me irritó.
La premisa es sobre Brennan Huff y Dale Doback, quienes tienen una cosa en común ambos son flojos, están desempleados y aún viven con sus padres. Cuando la madre de Brennan y el padre de Dale se casan y empiezan a vivir juntos, el mundo de los chicos se transforma totalmente. Su enfermiza rivalidad y narcisismo amenazan con separar a la nueva familia, lo que obliga a Brennan y a Dale a trabajar juntos para reunir a sus padres.
La historia es mala, nunca pude llegar a conectar con ella. Me esperaba que no sea la gran cosa la verdad, pero la cantidad de buenas reseñas que vi acá me hicieron pensar que al menos la iba a pasar bastante bien viéndola, y al final todo lo contrario. Se me hizo bastante aburrida en su mayoría, teniendo solo un par de momentos donde me pude entretener y se hacía llevadera su trama. Esto me pasó principalmente por la personalidad tan estúpida de los personajes, entiendo que no se tome en serio pero esto es mucho peor que eso. Además, su humor ni siquiera es que tiene una excelente calidad, teniendo solo un par de chistesmomentos que me causaron algo de gracia, pero son muchos más los que me dieron vergüenza ajena.
En cuanto a los personajes, estos no me gustaron para nada. Tanto Brennan como Dale son dos personajes que se me hicieron insoportables, teniendo ambos una personalidad muy parecida por conveniencia de la trama. Ellos son dos inmaduros que hacen todo lo posible para regalarnos momentos de comedia que funcionen, pero muy pocas veces lo logran, haciendo que al no causar nada de gracia en más momentos se vuelvan algo infumables. Los demás personajes son totalmente de relleno, no destaco a nadie y no creo que recuerde a ninguno después de un tiempo de ver la película.
En otros aspectos destaco únicamente la banda sonora, tiene algunas canciones conocidas que dentro de todo son divertidas de escuchar. Por otro lado, la dirección de Adam McKay es normalita, no me parece mala ni tampoco llega a ser buena, ya que creo que tiene más la culpa en el trabajo del guion que hicieron. Por último, las actuaciones no me gustaron, Will Ferrell no me parece un mal actor, pero en esta cinta está algo regular lo mismo me pasó con John C. Reilly, solo que me parece un actor que está un escalón abajo del otro.
En conclusión, una mala película con la que nunca pude llegar a conectar con su humor, seguramente haya mucha gente a la que le funcione porque por algo tiene tantas buenas reseñas. No la recomiendo.

Step Brothers is a top shelf comedy whose leading men and consistent hilarity make the film work. It is an enjoyably goofy yet subtly smart experience whose story beats and comedy gags are impressively rich and consistently memorable.

Step Brothers é um filme dirigido por Adam McKay e roteirizado por Adam McKay junto com Will Ferrell. O longa é estrelado por Will Ferrell, John C. Reily e Richard Jenkins. A história acompanha dois adultos desempregados que ainda moram com seus pais e que são forçados a dividir uma casa depois que eles se casam. E assim, com um orçamento de 65 milhões de dólares, o filme foi lançado em 2008 mas será que é bom? Vem comigo analisar ele.
