Antes de tudo queria agradecer muito os 800 seguidores, eu só tenho agradecer a cada um de vocês, pode até parecer meio repetitivo essa frase, mas é isso o que eu sinto sobre isso pois eu realmente sou grato a vocês por só terem apertado um único botão, amo vocês. Agora falando do filme, eu já tinha uma certa expectativa justamente pela recepção positiva que o longa recebeu muito em seu lançamento especialmente, e ele até teve uma bilherteria positiva, e é de um diretor que eu gosto e que já tinha demonstrado autenticidade para fazer comédias desse tipo, mas vendo hoje o longa percebo que eu gostei de como a narrativa fluiu e como os personagens influenciam muito nesses dilemas propostos, só que confesso que esperava um pouco mais do filme e já vou explicar o por que. Eu já falei por aqui que o gênero Comédia, e até sub-gêneros como comédia romântica ou comédia dramática, são difíceis de fazer especialmente pelo desafio que é trabalhar uma história em cima de piadas e essas piadas se não forem bem encaixadas podem afetar diretamente a experiência do espectador, então eu gostei de como Step Brothers conseguiu equilibrar bem suas situações e dilemas, e tudo isso com uma dose bem válida de humor que encaixa certinho na proposta abordada pelo filme, o que me fez ter uma experiência bem agradável pelo filme justamente saber o que está fazendo dentro da sua trama. Tem momentos bem memoráveis para um filme que não tem grandes ambições, inclusive vários deles estão disponíveis para colocar no banner do longa (não aconselho a comprar hahaha), especialmente no seu desenvolvimento o filme trabalha muito bem suas situações onde nenhum personagem é são de verdade por que todos rendem piadas o tempo todo, que poderia não dar certo se o filme não encaixasse e soubesse utiliza-las mas aqui elas parecem ajeitadinhas e com uma certa diversão envolvida. Não é um filme que eu recomendaria para uma pessoa que se diverte com algo mais explorado e com piadas mais sofisticadas pois, para falar a verdade, esse é um projeto que possui  piadas bem bestas e de fato algumas não conseguem funcionar (um dos motivos para minha nota ser mais baixa), mas pegando o resultado final, o longa consegue ter um ritmo muito decente de acompanhar o que justamente acarreta na minha reação final para o filme que foi positiva. Mas como eu falei, nessa metralhadora de piadas envolvendo especialmente os protagonistas, o longa perde força por apresentar alguns segmentos sem graça e, portanto, desnecessários por justamente duvidar que o espectador tenha uma experiência agradável apenas com poucas piadas, ele bota na cabeça que precisa ter mais e mais piadas o que acaba gerando esses tais segmentos que eu disse, que comigo analisando depois de assistir, percebo que afetou a experiência e até o ritmo geralmente mais pelo segundo para o terceiro ato. Eu sempre penso que quanto mais pessoas voltados especificamente para a história de um filme, mais a chance de ele virar uma sopinhas de ideais misturadas e mal encaixadas, portanto, quando eu vi que os responsáveis pela histótia foram três pessoas (Adam McKay, Will Ferrell e John C. Reily) eu acabei me afastando mais do projeto justamente por ter esse pensamento, mas felizmente, eu até que gostei da vertente que a história quis trabalhar e que ficou divertido mesmo, com ajuda do elenco e direção, só que é uma pena que o roteiro tenha falhas bem descaradas que afeta justamente o sentimento que o espectador sente pelo longa. Já o roteiro é assinado por duas pessoas apenas (Adam McKay e Will Ferrell), mas ele nunca parece avançar de verdade pois fica se repetitindo muitas vezes e enrolando até o seu ato final que não se encaixa bem no longa em geral, ás vezes o roteiro parece até perdido em alguns momentos e distoa da vertente que o filme queria abordar e desenvolver, que até começa de forma interessante e com ums boa apresentação de personagens, mas a medida que vai chegando ao final, fica repetitivo e um pouco cansativo. Felizmente, isso não me faz desgostar do filme, pois ele tem um ritmo muito bom e empolgante, e a direção consegue imergir muito bem o espectador naquela história, especialemente utilizando suas piadas, pois elas são fundamentais para o longa se desenvolver e aprofundar seus temas. Como eu falei, o Adam McKay já estava se consolidando no período por trabalhar uito bem o gênero que ele costumava fazer (hoje ele já faz outro tipo de longa) e aqui eu consigo enxergar bem essa versatibilidade dele, especialmente como ele trabalha em cima da narrativa com essa vertente mais exagerada e cheia de nuances (eu realmente gosto de como ele aplica essa vertente) mas também como ele conduz a trama até o final, que ele faz de uma forma bem agradável, o problema é que o roteiro (também assinado por ele hahaha) nunca aproveite essa direção de verdade, com problemas narrativos e situações genéricas, o que também afetou na minha experiência por apresentar um roteiro superficial a ponto de parecer distoante da direção, mas de novo, isso não me fez desgostar do longa, pois ele consegue subverter isso de forma que fica legal ao espectador. O elenco manda muito bem por aproveitar o que a história quis abordar, então temos aqui um Will Ferrell e um John C. Reily muito mais caricatos do que de costume, mas isso não diminui o resultado deles pois a caricatura não é ruim, o que acontece em outros filme é a caricatura não ser explorada, só que aqui como eu já disse, a direção aproveita muito bem essa implementação por saber como abordar e desenvolver ela de forma divertido pro espectador, e isso o Adam McKay sabe fazer muito bem, o que os atores também aproveitam isso fazendo papéis memoráveis para o público. O elenco coadjuvante não tem muito destaque mas eles também conseguem atuar de forma bem divertida, realmente dá para perceber que eles se divertiram fazendo o projeto, o que é bom, pois dá a ele um tom mais natural e sarcástico. Eu não considero um filme espetacular mas ele consegue entregar muito bem o que ele se propõe que é a diversão, pode até ter piadas comprometedoras só que o importante é que eu me diverti e tembém considero o Adam McKay um diretor para a comédia junto com a sagacidade que os longas deles entregam.

My wife tends to steer away from traditional Christmas films over the holiday period, especially during the last couple of years. She lost her father and stepfather around two years ago and has struggled with the memories that some of these yuletide favourites inspire, so when she suggested the Adam McKay directed Step Brothers, who was I to argue? 
John C. Reilly is one talented actor, hes done everything, every genre,  and excelled in films as diverse as the directors hes worked with over a career thats spawned Nominations across a broad spectrum of the arts. Academy Award Nominations, Golden Globes Nominations, Tony Award Nominations, even a Grammy Nomination, he seems comfortable working in what ever discipline he decides to participate in. Some would argue that drama isnt Reillys forte, but Magnolia, Gangs of New York,  or his debut performance in De Palmas film Casualties Of War would suggest otherwise. Hes genuinely one of the few actors around whos adept at switching genres effortlessly, but comedy seems to be where he lets loose with often his best results. 
When Reilly gets teamed up with Will Ferrell, they usually deliver. Talladega Nights was hilarious, and this second film has moments where the insanity takes over to such an extent that the tears of laughter flowed as the silliness was delivered in spades. As two immature adults living at home with their respective parents, Ferrell and Reilly characters become step brothers following their parents wedding. Instantly hating each other and playing up in ridiculous fashion that sees their parents patience finally snap with them, they form a bond that sees them act even stupider than before. Its juvenile and crass, with Kathryn Hahn bringing her own brand of nuttiness to proceedings as Ferrells sister-in-law and Richard Jenkins playing a blinder as Reillys father on the verge of a breakdown, theres much to love here if you like this sort of humour.

Ive lost count of how many times Ive watched Step Brothers before I got into movies, for Id always come out laughing at the silliness shown inside of a concept that revolves around 40-year-old man children still trying to acquire normal lives for themselves. But I was worried what coming back to Step Brothers for my first time in so long would do to my own opinion for my own taste in films has only grown within the many years, although to my own delight it didnt only hold up. Ive only found myself laughing even more from watching Step Brothers than I could remember having done so years back. And Im not always a fan of Will Ferrell in the meantime, but with watching him in Adam McKay movies he makes this silliness work so perfectly, and thats what Ive always loved about Step Brothers, the manner in which it embraces how silly it is without pretending to be more.
Brennan Huff and Dale Doback are both in their 40s and they still live with their parents, without any sort of job and now they live together because their parents married. They start out like any other rivaling pair of siblings, for they fight constantly over small things and they still behave like children. Its not unusual to see Will Ferrell playing these sorts of roles but with Adam McKay coming behind the camera to write a role for this persona of Ferrells, he allows charm to shine inside of his style of comedy. Its a film thats tailor made for Will Ferrells brand of humour and doesnt keep everything as such on the surface level. We know its a film about man-children at heart, and yet its so open with the sort of comedy that it is it only becomes irresistible. But when one looks at running trends within American comedies, these sorts of protagonists are usually common, so it was only fitting that McKay had went ahead to make a film about such characters where we would not expect so much as a whole from them.
Ferrell and Reilly make a great comedic pair once again after having collaborated in another Adam McKay film, Talladega Nights - once again displaying excellent chemistry all around between the two. But for as much as Ferrells style of comedy has never always appealed to me, there always seemed to be something more coming out when Adam McKay was the one directing him. For as much as Ferrell and Reillys man-child antics drive the films humour towards the more juvenile whether it be within how vulgar it is or fart jokes, yet somehow theres a dramatic balance that elevates Step Brothers above being a simply juvenile comedy. It isnt pretending to pose these people as more than just man-children, its a tale about their own growing up and theres another level to where it only begins to show another level of cleverness.
When we reach a point in our life where we turn into adolescents, sometimes we have it rooted inside of us that we want to remain children because it was a point where we allowed our own sense of self-discovery to flow at its most free. It was only clear from here I found something extremely thoughtful about Step Brothers and how it embraces the ridiculous and sometimes idiotic nature of its comedy, yet another part of me just remembers how much of this wouldnt be nearly half as funny if Dale and Brennan were played by actual children like Ferrell and Reilly are playing them to be. But it doesnt ring solely for comedy films where these man-children are thriving upon the way they are seeing the world around them, and its clear enough from the casting of Ferrell whos always played a man overwhelmed with responsibility in his most common role. It almost feels nostalgic in its delivery, one part of where its charm finds itself working beautifully.
The films humour doesnt always work, but where it does its immensely quotable and its a gag that comes and goes. Perhaps it seems to reach for far too much when it hits the middle for it only begins to find itself slowing down all the more, occasionally going back towards repeating jokes that have already been done perfectly in previous scenes. I still find myself laughing my head off at the drum set fights for theyve brought out where the movie is indeed at some of its most quotable, but when it begins slowing down theres a feeling that certain scenes go on too long for their own good. Upon re-watching OLD SCHOOL -- which I once thought hysterical -- I found it not only unfunny, but pathetic. Its a less edgy version of classics like ANIMAL HOUSE, STRIPES, and REVENGE OF THE NERDS, movies that seem to get better with age (although the rapey vibe of NERDS makes it a little harder to enjoy).
About the only part of OLD SCHOOL that holds up is Will Ferrells performance. As Frank the Tank, Ferrells sensitive man-child character has never been more exciting, whether he is streaking down main street in his birthday suit, falling in a pool after shooting himself with a tranq dart, or catching fire in a mascot outfit.
I just wish the rest of the movie worked better. Luke Wilsons performance is absolutely flaccid, Vince Vaughns smarmy supporting man act feels tired in the face of 14 years worth of the same performance, and the female cast is utterly abused by a script that treats them with the sort of respect Sea World affords orcas. And Jeremy Pivens miscasting as the mean ol dean just puts a big fat cherry on top of this melted sundae of a movie.
Its amazing how the changing times so completely impact the way we watch things. In 2003, I was 27, a father of three, and felt trapped in a marriage. OLD SCHOOL was a catharsis for me. Of course I loved it. This was a movie that totally got me. Now, Im just turning 40, engaged to be married to a special woman, and so much more aware of how the political elements of our movies reflect and influence our culture. Twenty-seven year old me didnt care about the fact that every woman in OLD SCHOOL was a variation on the bitchwhoresaint stereotype I just wanted a movie that could speak for me. I met my ex-wife in college, and I think I blamed her for stealing the high times I was meant to have. There was no one to blame, though I just needed time to grow up. 
Watching OLD SCHOOL now is a reminder that I did grow up, but the 30-40 year old men at the heart of this film never do. They cling to their adolescence like it has religious significance. No one grows -- they all just move into the bigger frat house at the end. Frank works at the campus radio station, spinning the records from his teen years. Beanie inevitably stays faithful in his marriage while looking forward to parties designed for ogling co-eds. And Mitch stays in the right about everything. He even gets the saint with the kid simply because he was right about her boyfriend (never mind he was KY wrestling with other women, banging his boss high school aged daughter, and hosting keggers seemingly every night while hazing the frat recruits). These guys all stay young and righteous and cool.
But reality is that we do have to grow up. The party has to end sometime. People need to move on. Shopping for flooring at Home Depot isnt a fate that should drive one to drink. Enjoying one woman sexually for the rest of your life isnt death -- its an opportunity. OLD SCHOOL is a mid-life crisis movie for white dudes in arrested development. And like that old guy who hangs out at high school parties, dressed like the kids, trying to fit in and be cool, the movie is actually pretty pathetic.

With its solid cast and spry direction, Todd Phillips Old School is an always amusing, sometimes hilarious comedy. Starring Luke Wilson, Will Ferrell, and Vince Vaughn as fraternity-hosting man-children, the film is a crisply goofy party comedy where the jokes fly fast and the personalities are colorful.
After a surprise break-up, Luke Wilsons corporate drone moves into a house adjacent to a college campus. Soon, he and his buddies attempt to recapture their youth by throwing ragers and, more or less, chartering a fraternity. Revolving around the conflict started by stodgy, envious campus power players, and the protagonists own tug-of-war between maturity and the desire for keggers, the story makes an apt foundation college-days frivolity and good-natured raunch.
Phillips imbues the production with inviting energy, allowing his cast to create nearly iconic characters like Ferrells Frank the Tank. The comedy hits the mark and, though the gags may never be smart or deep, all of the films jokes are effectively amusing.
With its cast-driven energy and well-orchestrated comic beats, Old School easily entertains. The comedy may only have superficial punch, but that punch lands with an enjoyable zing.

Before Todd Phillips tapped into his inner Scorsese to do Joker, he had two classic comedies in his filmography. Road Trip and Old School. Will his second film be as timeless as it ever was, or will it be dated?
Old School follows three best friends who cure their depression and boredom by trying to relive their college years by starting a fraternity near their alma mater.
This is a movie that takes me back to my teenage years, although I didnt enjoy it as much as I do now. I remember looking for something to watch on TV one day after doing some work with my grandfather. It was one summer when he came over for a week to see us and we were doing yard work. And after calling it a day, I had a shower and felt so tired, I went into my bedroom and I was going to go to sleep. Two hours later, I wake up to find something to watch. So thats where I landed on Old School. It was a movie that aired on Comedy Central with a cast that promised to make me laugh. The whole plot reminded me of Animal House when I was watching it, but it was just as ridiculously funny as it was. 
The acting from the cast is really funny! You have Luke Wilson, Will Ferrell, Vince Vaughn, Jeremy Piven, Ellen Pompeo, and you have some surprising faces with the likes of Seann William Scott, Simon Helberg, Elisha Cuthbert and Snoop Dogg. Wilson plays Mitch Martin, a man who got out of a relationship with a woman who cheated on him regularly by having orgies while he was away on business. Ferrell plays Frank Ricard, a newly married man who cant seem to conform to the married life. And Vaughn plays Bernard Campbell, another married man with two kids and tries to get Mitch on board with their own fraternity.
I would say Luke Wilson is pretty much like his brother Owen for playing the pretty boy with the distinctive Texan accent in comedies in the 2000s. I prefer Owen Wilson because hes someone Im use to seeing him in movies like Zoolander, Starsky  Hutch, and of course, Wedding Crashers. But thats beside the point. I thought Wilson was good in Old School, hes more of the opposite when it comes to his comedic co-stars. By the opposite, I mean hes more about fun, but hes trying to reconnect with his old crush and better himself. And thats an interesting subplot. 
Will Ferrell and Vince Vaughn are where its at when it comes to their comedic trademarks! Ferrell has his moments of being downright hilarious for his stupidity and being able to play what his character does. He was still in SNL at the time when he was doing this film and this was what got him into more roles in comedies. In Old School, he is freaking hilarious and memorable as John Belushi in Animal House! As for Vaughn, he brings his quirky personality to the film as well as doing what requires him to do.
Todd Phillips is the director of Old School while he did the screenplay with Scot Armstrong and Court Crandall. I believe he was the next guy to make comedic films when people like John Landis and John Hughes were slowly dying off for a new generation. You all know I love Phillips as a director! I love all of his films, excluding the two sequels for The Hangover. He shouldve learned his lesson after what happened in The Hangover Part II. But anyways, this film and Road Trip was what got him more opportunities for making raunchy comedies for the unforgotten era and I thank him for making us laugh!
Old School is a movie that many people in the world can watch and quote from by heart! Its silly, raunchy, juvenile and it will show you a good time! This is one of the golden comedies from the 2000s era that will never disappoint you. If youre a fan of Todd Phillips or a fan of the cast members, I recommend you to look for this on Blu-ray and have fun. Now, lets go streaking!
Im giving Old School 4 stars!

To talk about Old School is to talk about Todd Phillips, the aspirational bro turned multi-hyphenate Oscar nominee who spent his formative years making shallow edgelord travelogues exploring the otherwise fertile grounds of reprehensible men (GG Allin) and groups of reprehensible men (frat boys). Like his later work, these early projects seem rooted in interrogating the adage boys will be boys but fatally eschew the depth that could come from asking do they have to be?. 
Its all about as pat as youd expect for a commercially minded mid-2000s artifact produced and marketed to mobilise the widest possible audience of weed enthusiast.  Luke Wilson stars as Mitch an inoffensive slab of human man designed to make you feel like you too could get the woman of your dreams if you just once paid for a 100 haircut instead of going to Just Cuts, Shane. Rounding out the cast are Vince Vaughn as Friend (character description complete), Will Ferrell as Funnier Friend (character description complete) and Ellen Pompeo as Eventual Romantic Interest (character description, sadly, complete).  Its worth noting that Pompeo and Ferrell are phenomenal in this Ive always thought of the Will Ferrell persona as dumbass Cary Grant and its on full display here.  Likewise, Pompeo injects her small amount of screen time with so much kind Vera Farmiga energy Im left wondering why I havent seen her more (I know, I know, Greys Anatomy).
Interestingly, its when Phillips dips into edgy man 5000 territory that this works.  Theres a 23 minute stretch from the pledging of the fraternity through to the horse tranquilizer thats genuinely hilarious.  Its in this section that Phillips shows comedy is contrast and explores the inherent sadness of his premise men in their 30s using the people around them to retreat from their adult responsibilities.  Sadly, just as hes about to really start punishing them for their cowardice and explore their psychology, we backpeddle to satisfy threads we yawned through being set up in the first act.
Ultimately, Old School amounts to an uneven high jinks fest that, with a few tweaks, could have been a brilliant comedy about men in arrested development learning to level up. Todd Phillips will finally give us the good movie hes capable of (and that we deserve) when he realises that to be populist is not to lower your expectations.

Old School is an awesome party comedy. The film is about three friends named Mitch (Luke Wilson), Frank (Will Ferrell), and Bernard (Vince Vaughn), who attempt to recapture their glory days by opening up a fraternity. Todd Philips direction is fantastic. Todd Philips and Scot Armstrongs screenplay is excellent.
Luke Wilson, Will Ferrell, and Vince Vaughn deliver top-notch comedic performances. The characters are fun, and they all have wonderful chemistry. I love the banter and comradery between the characters. The characters feel like they are actual friends, and you totally believe that they have been friends for years. The film is over-the-top, dirty, wild, raunchy, and hilarious. 
The jokes and gags are hysterical. The script is chalk full of sharp, witty, and quotable lines of dialogue. The soundtrack is outstanding. In my opinion, Old School is one of the best comedies from the early 2000s.

I have not seen Animal House or other fraternity movies that came out after it, but I am 100 sure Old School reused the plotlines from these movie while swapping out college-age kids for the all-ages fraternity found in this film. It has everything I expect from a fraternity movie a no-good dean who wants to shut the fraternity down, wild parties, hazing, binge drinking, and naked college girls. Since Old School is also a comedy from the 2000s, it features a forgettable romance subplot between Luke Wilson  Ellen Pompeo typical of romance plotlines from its time. I will say that this film is well cast, as each of the three main characters are played by actors well within their comfort zone Luke Wilson plays the understated everyman lead character, Will Ferrell plays an out-of-control party animal, and Vince Vaughn plays a jerk. While Old School does have its share of hilarious moments, it ultimately does not do enough to stand out in the crowded space of 2000s raunchy comedies.

I hadnt seen Old School since I was a teenager, when it never quite landed for me. Will Ferrell still wrings out laughs and carries almost the whole of Old School on his back, although Ferrell is relegated mostly to sketch-comedy territory. You can feel Old School trying to push Vince Vaughn as a character type, the same way it does with Ferrell. But it doesnt work with Vaughn, and, while hes fine, he suffers the most from the movies failure to really investigate the main trio and their search for maturity. Luke Wilson is good as the straight man but doesnt stand out. 
Old School is mediocre but with a workable premise and almost prescient themes. Men, having reached their 30s and ostensibly made it, nevertheless feel unfulfilled and chase after satisfaction by starting their own fraternity. But the theme of arrested development and the quest for maturity almost feels accidental here. And theres no real sense of growth among the three main characters. They arrive at an unearned sense of satisfaction that, you have to imagine, is temporary. The movie almost feels like its missing scenes where the character development occurred. Its no surprise that Judd Apatow came along a few years later and more successfully investigated the same ideas.
On the one hand, Old School tries pushing a more absurd style---the characters can get Snoop Dogg to appear at a party at the drop of a hat and their fraternity has a Fight Club-like effect on the community. On the other hand, theres a sense of restraint. But presenting this scenario as too grounded risks revealing the main trio as inherently pathetic. Old School cant thread the needle, and theres not enough laughs to make up for it. Either make Old School dumber and more absurd, or ground it with better writing and actual character development. Or, thread the needle successfully, but Old School doesnt.

This is one of those movies that I didnt realize Ive already seen 3 times until I watched it again and knew everything thats going to happen right before it does. Granted, dudebro apocalypse filmmaker Todd Phillips story could be so remedial that anyone watching for the first time could foresee exactly whats coming. Its the exact type of crass, head-in-the-gutter material with an unfulfilling romantic sublot weve all come to expect from 00s comedies. I actually watched the unrated cut, which Im pretty sure only added more Will Ferrell ass shots.
Not to tap too deep into my douchebag origins, but I have a soft spot for any film depicting fraternities. The house party sequences here are properly raucous, and I cant help but laugh my ass off at an 89-year-old man going through a pledge term.
Perhaps the biggest weakness of Old School is the fact that its lead got taken behind the woodshed by Vince Vaughn and Will Ferrell. Luke Wilson is so deep in look at me, Im just a regular guy, arent I so relatable? acting that I felt like I was watching some random dude who stumbled onto the set helm a studio comedy. Ferrell gets the best gags, but Vaughn is the most naturally funny here for sure. Vince Vaughn is a funny ass dude.
Both a bad omen for my upcoming year and the most hilarious start possible, Old School is another one of the many enjoyable 2000s comedies where leaving your taste at the door is a prerequisite. I have been singing the dirty cover of Total Eclipse of the Heart for years.

   Fight Club es mi segunda película favorita de David Fincher (la primera toca más adelante) y creo que también es la favorita de medio mundo. Pero, como suele pasar, en su momento fue un fracaso tanto en crítica como en taquilla. Puede que el pesimismo que maneja (mismo pesimismo que Se7en) haya sido demasiado para 1999 que estaba siendo marcado por el optimismo de Un Lugar Llamado Notting Hill, Stuart Little, Toy Story 2 o incluso Milagros Inesperados. Estas, junto con Fight Club, anticiparon una década del 2000 más oscura y desesperanzada como fue un poco la vida de El Juani. 
   Muchos años después de nuestra no-pelea se enfrentó a unos pibes de otro barrio y le pegaron un cuchillazo en el abdomen. Según me contaron fue con un cuchillo de oro propiedad del líder de la banda rival. Lo último que supe de El Juani es que sobrevivió a la puñalada y se mudó de barrio. Me gustaría cruzarlo algún día, preguntarle por qué se la agarró conmigo aquella vez y que me responda Me conociste en un momento muy extraño de mi vida 
   Quizás él era mi Tyler Durden.

Fight Club, then, can be seen as an over-correction to Se7ens insidiousness and defeat. While someone like John Doe is scary, murderous, literate, Tyler Durden, the alter-ego of our clumsy narrator, is egotistical, enlightened, brilliant. Or so he thinks. Fight Clubs vision of spliced celluloid cocks, penguin power caves, testicular cancer meetings, and acts of terrorism have been interpreted and misinterpreted for decades now, and its mostly tiring except when watching the film itself. You cant escape Fight Clubs power, as much as its been run into the ground. It has an everlasting pull, a tantalizing slyness that pulls the viewer in and out of seductively living and rejecting its anti-social behavior.

What is it to be a man? What makes someone know they are a man? As the world slowly moves away from rigid notions of gender and patriarchy, there exists a disconnect between our reality and the expectations of manhood. I am a man, but I dont fight to show my strength, and I dont work a tiring job as my familys sole breadwinner, and I definitely couldnt hunt or shoot if I needed to. I just work at a computer, day in day out, eating vegan food, buying pointless crap, and watching movies on the evening. My emotional connections no longer derive from the physical, from other men, from family, from nature. Now it is all abstract, its emails and messages, its products in sterile packages, its movies on a screen. The world has changed. And where there is change, there is unease. Fight Club is about this unease, and the tensions within men as the world changes. Its a satire on masculinity, on people going to extreme lengths to meet some imagined expectation, and burning everything down rather than changing expectations.
Fight Club is one of the densest and most intriguing American films, as well as being so relentlessly entertaining. It is superior to the book, making more sense and pruning back to the essence of the story. What is perfectly captured is the way society has made it difficult to find value. We are enslaved by consumerism and thus feel emasculated as material goods take the place of spiritual needs. We have nothing to fight or overcome in life, just products to buy. Its a meaningless existence, creating a numb society where everyone is out of touch with their own feelings. Were all just passive observers to the world around us. Fight Club looks at men who find no worth in their life and playfully observes what alternative values they could create. They would fight to feel something, to keep themselves in check, to achieve their ideal self. They would have a nostalgia for patriarchy, rejecting the modern society that they feel coddles and restricts them. Yet these values are dangerous, without love or compassion. The film ultimately rejects the fascist parts of the movement it depicts, because while the modern world may leave you unfulfilled, accepting who you are and finding others to care about is a much better cure than dying for hypermasculine ideals. The world needs to improve by moving forward, not just by resetting to zero.
Fight Club is just great. Its provocative and bleakly hilarious, which makes it fun in spite of its extreme approach. As a film of male intimacy, there are plenty of gay undertones and double entendres, which give it an extra layer. The narration is some of the best in cinema, filled with surreal descriptions and quirky wit. It is very unconventional for a large budget Hollywood movie, tackling artfilm topics and yet being large in scale and filled with expensive visual effects. The cinematography has an approach that makes things look both shiny and damp. Its just a really creative movie, thematically and stylistically. Nothing else is like this. Masculinity should be questioned and examined, because it affects all of society. Fight Club remains one of the best satires on modern men, and is still an entertaining and insightful look at the most heightened versions of masculine uncertainty.

Chuck Palahniuks novel Fight Club is a stunning piece of literary fiction. When I first read it I was blown away by the narrative voice present, laden with  fierce and bleak language with an undertone of unchecked rage towards a society focussed on individualism and consumerism.  Capturing all that is one thing, but also managing to mould all this into a plot that is filled with twists and turns and is perfectly paced without getting lost in all its ideas, well, that is something else altogether. 
Now to say I was sceptical when I read that a film was going to be made out of this book is a huge understatement. I was convinced that they would fail, even Fincher whose work Im a big fan of. I was, very, very wrong indeed.
Not only did they manage to bring across everything mentioned above, Fincher also created a visually stunning film and toys with his audience as a cat would with a mouse. But the true star of this film is its screenplay. The raw, visceral language of Palahniuk is handled with the greatest respect and at some points even improves on the novel by showing more guts, especially in the ending. 
Should this film be considered a classic? Most definitely, but I do think it looks at all the other classics with a big fuck you I dont care grin. And it should, because no film like it has been made since.....

Hard to resist the expertly controlled mania and repulsively dilapidated textures here, Fincher is just too kinetic and sophisticated an image-maker for me not to love it. In terms of composition and cutting and lighting and production design, at any given moment its never short of astonishing to look at and man does it move. That said, the smirky, edgy Gen X punk-rock angstoffice drone consumer satire stuff played a lot better for me as a dumb teenager first wading into movies for adults waters. I still think a lot of it works as an extremely dark and gross mentally ill, self-destructive roommate comedy (where said roommate is your juvenile alpha male fantasy imaginary friend), and I think its hilarious so many guys who made this their personality failed to register that its toxic gladiator contestrevolutionary terrorist cell cult stuffeven if occasionally righteously raging against the Corporate America machineis clearly meant to be just as much of an unenlightened, self-sustaining death trap as the material world hes cathartically abandoning. But ultimately there is a self-satisfied, dumb-guy-reads-first-book We Live In A Society misanthropic philosophizing to it that flirts with courting that crowd for a lot of its runtime so I sort of understand the cult phenomenon. And its still an engrossing feat of filmmaking regardless of that, the Where Is My Mind? needle drop altered my brain chemistry as a high schooler.

A PRIMEIRA REGRA DO CLUBE DA LUTA É NÃO FALAR DO CLUBE DA LUTA.
Dirigido por David Fincher e baseado no livro homônimo de Chuck Palahniuk, Clube da Luta é um daqueles longas-metragens que é mais lembrado pelo plot twist no final do que pela crítica a sociedade capitalista. Ainda que inicialmente a premissa pareça banal, quando você se aprofunda no roteiro acaba percebendo as diversas camadas que compõem a trama. Repare como inicialmente o personagem de Edward Norton é apresentado apenas como o narrador, conforme a história avança nós percebemos que ele não é onisciente, tudo é propositalmente feito para que ele relate sobre o mundo violento de Tyler Durden (Brad Pitt) sobe sua perspectiva, mas quando o longa revela que ambos são a mesma pessoa, nós entendemos que Durden na verdade está falando sobre ele mesmo desde o início. Esse homem que ele gostaria de ser é representado pelo seu alter ego em suas infinitas crises dissociativas de personalidades. Um cara disruptivo, corajoso, impulsivo e que não aceita as conformidades de uma vida robótica, sem propósito. O clube da luta não é apenas violência gratuita entre homens, na verdade a briga era uma válvula de escape para extravasar a raiva e as frustrações aquelas pessoas tinham em relação às suas obrigações com a sociedade, como ter um emprego estável e uma casa cheia de utensílios inúteis. Tem uma cena que Tyler aponta uma arma para cabeça do atendente de uma loja de conveniências, quando ameaçado, o atendente conta que não queria trabalhar ali e sim continuar sua faculdade para ser veterinário, Tyler o obriga a voltar a fazer o que gostava. São cenas como essa que expõem de maneira enfática a proposta de anarquia anticonsumista que o personagem busca. Existe o discurso que para destruir o capitalismo é só acabar com as corporações mundiais, algo que o protagonista acredita, obviamente essa idealização não é tão simples como parece, mas pelo menos serviu como base para o final apoteótico. Em suma, Clube da Luta é um filme que se tornou clássico pelas atuações marcantes de Brad Pitt, Edward Norton e Helena Bonham Carter, mas o que o torna emblemático é a sua perspectiva sobre o consumismo e principalmente como nada mudou de 1999 pra cá. Nós ainda somos transformados em meros consumidores, continuamos escravos de um sistema que esgota toda nossa existência a cada minuto.

Her philosophy of life was that she might die at any moment. The tragedy, she said, was that she didnt.
Fight Club may be the best film of the nineties, but Marla Singer is the best character ever created.
The best individuals in film are the ones who would make you cross to the other side of the street if you ever saw them in real life. Marla Singer is that person for me. She seems like shed stub her cigarette on your new dress or spit in your mouth if you got too close to her on the tube, and for that, I respect her. 
There is something that is almost aggressively alluring about her as a character. The way she is portrayed - shrouded in cigarette smoke - seems to immediately allude to an addictive and dependent personality. She hangs around a health risk of a kitchen in a bridesmaid dress, and compares Christmas trees to sex crime victims. Shes like if a manic pixie dream girl turned to meth instead of mixtapes.
Perhaps what I enjoy so violently about Miss Singer is how different she is to the stars of my other most treasured films. Mia Wallace from Pulp Fiction is similar to Marla in that they are both polluted with drugs and easily swayed by alpha males, but beyond these points they contrast completely. Marla has seen the worst parts of the world and let them consume her, while Mia lives among the top one percent and spends her time being wined and died. Mia was a top priority for everybody close to her, while Marla was dumped by anyone she let get too close. After all, the woman who fakes having testicular cancer because its cheaper than the movies cant be swimming in party invites.
Perhaps I cherish Marla so much because of what she represents for me. Ive always felt uneasy about the day I post a review on Fight Club, seeing as it is one of Letterboxds highest rated films of all time with a whopping 4.3 mean score. I fear for the one-sided response towards my rather pessimistic review. Because with all honesty, Fight Club is perfectly fine. Fight Club is a film I believe to be thought a little bit too highly of. Im really not the biggest fan of Fight Club. Theres plenty of reasons, of course. One is the wind-down in the third act not being able to match the manic and zany energy of the first. I dont think Fincher is particularly well-suited for Palahniuks pop-philosophy, but even still, theres a lot I like about it. Its just not that. Fincher thrives on methodologies. The way he processes exposition imitates reality without the need to solely rely on it. In the context of a pseudo pop philosophy-lite ejaculation like Fight Club, hes out of his depth. It just seems off. 
You know the movies when you know exactly what the twist or reveal is going to be about 20 minutes in? Thats me with Fight Club. Maybe the film wasnt really trying to hide it in the first place, maybe not, but Im not usually good at predicting twists, and that one was crazy. When the scene with Tyler Durden appearing on the plane came on, I just couldnt believe it, and I dont mean that in a good mind-blowing way. The entire time I was like Is this mofo actually real?. And for some reason, in that certain situation, I simply didnt buy it for a good minute. Look I think Fight Club is technically impressive but heavily reliant on a lot of smoke and mirrors when it comes to writing. After all, Fight Clubs first act is up there with any of Finchers best work.
But remember, Fight Club is also but an adaptation of a book written by Chuck Palahniuk, a gay man, with the intention of criticizing internalized homophobia and toxic masculinity, which very much serves as an allegory for this manufactured hyper-macho façade parts of society have constructed. All the more reason why the film, to a decent extent, fundamentally misunderstands its own themes. The whole thing is plagued with so much try hard pseudo pop-macho bullshit that it ends up glorifying the very unpleasantries it vowed to combat. And now, amateur cinephiles are out here venerating Tyler Durden, whether ironically or not, without the misguided communications of themes ever crossing their mind. In time, well all hopefully realize that this sigma male and gigachad adulation we throw at all of Fight Clubs poorly crafted caricatures showcase a great deal of disrespect. Or you could just tell me that Im just flat-out wrong and it really does critique everything I just said. But its been years since Ive disagreed and I dont think Ill ever change my thought process on this.
Its a common case of films garnering this special type of cultural impact where good movies become so beloved to the point where it makes me suspect that someones favorite film has been the same since they were sixteen. Now, if they have some solid reasoning, thats fine ... just makes me raise my eyebrow, is all. It falls under the same set of films like Pulp Fiction (which I like btw), The Dark Knight, and Drive. In terms of taking the cinephile culture by storm, Id call Fight Club the 90s Joker. Dont worry, I still think Fight Club is significantly better than Joker. Its just one of this films whose teen philosophy hits hard with a certain generation and it will always, always, and always be overrated. Every movie-going generation has a movie like this, where it really matters the age you were when you saw it, how many other movies youd seen, etc. Theres a lot of great stuff packed in this film with a lot of great and memorable sequences however, I struggle to acknowledge Fight Club as some sort of cinematic breakthrough. We dont talk about Fight Club because its overrated af.

(Now Im currently writing this at 11pm whilst drinking so bare with me!)
Its a shame how criminally underrated Fight Club was upon its release in 1999 with films such as The Matrix and American Beauty gaining far more recognition. It even got to the point where many critics and fans slammed it and labelled it a flop as it failed to meet the studios expectations at the box office! However, in the years that followed its gained an almost cult following with many naming it alongside The Social Network and Alien 3 ) as one of Finchers best films to date and honestly, whilst it doesnt quite reach the heights The Social Network does, I can clearly say that watching Fight Club, especially if its your first time, is a phenomenal experience. 
Now, I loved this film upon my first watch. The twists left me with my jaw on the ground and the storyline, in the most part, is flawless throughout. Now of course this was never going to be the same experience upon rewatch but strangely...it was. I still loved it and even though I already knew the twists, I was still amazed by the execution and just how good the storyline was. Edward Norton, who plays the unnamed narrator, is fantastic and Brad Pitts performance is flawless. Theres a reason his character Tyler Durden often makes it into peoples favourites, hes cut throat, ruthless, intimidating and hot. Very, very hot. With his style being something I was in awe of throughout.  
Yet, unfortunately Fight Club isnt a perfect film. The grainy, gritty cinematography never quite worked for me. Its not smooth or clean cut like modern day films but thats what the film is going for, so I cant judge it too harshly. Whilst it worked for the atmosphere of the film, its not what I love to watch. On top of that, this exercise in mainstream masochism, macho posturing, and designer-grunge fascism is borderline ridiculous to watch but it also happens to be one of David Finchers richest movies. Both main characters exaggerated machismo and youthful bravado is what ultimately defines this movie as the masterpiece that it is for many young people and is what ultimately allowed this film to gain the notoriety it has.

Demorei muito para decidir assistir a Clube da Luta, pois, pelo título, achei que seria mais um filme sobre lutas e uma temática saturada. Felizmente, não é nada disso. E agora me resta uma única pergunta por que demorei tanto tempo para assistir?
Sem dúvida, é o melhor filme que já vi na minha vida. À primeira vista, o longa pode parecer uma apologia ao caos, mas rapidamente revela sua verdadeira essência uma crítica feroz à sociedade moderna. É menos sobre brigas físicas e mais sobre as guerras internas que travamos conosco. Trata-se de um retrato sombrio e fascinante da alienação provocada pelo capitalismo tardio e pela busca incessante por status, poder e pertencimento, e como, ao perseguirmos uma ideia de sucesso imposta, acabamos perdendo nossa identidade.  
Em meio ao caos da vida contemporânea, o filme nos conduz à percepção de que o que realmente importa são nossas emoções mais autênticas  especialmente quando se conectam com as de outra pessoa, que para anestesiar a dor dessa desconexão, muitas vezes nos jogamos em comportamentos extremos. E Clube da Luta retrata isso de maneira fluida, abordando a luta contra o verdadeiro responsável por todos esses sentimentos O ego  essa força interna que alimenta ilusões, repressões e autossabotagens. Ao mesmo tempo, há uma crítica direta à elite econômica e aos valores que sustentam um sistema opressor e insustentável. 
O filme levanta uma provocação instigante será que temos coragem para transformar a realidade? E até onde essa transformação pode nos levar? Talvez o limite dessa mudança esteja, paradoxalmente, em nós mesmos. São muitas as camadas psicológicas. Algumas são explícitas, outras quase imperceptíveis, mas todas estão ali, construídas com inteligência. O roteiro é impecável cada fala, cada cena, cada detalhe tem um propósito. Nada é gratuito. E quando o grande plot twist chega, tudo se encaixa. É simplesmente genial.
Em tempos em que muitos filmes parecem feitos apenas para gerar engajamento e lucro rápido, Clube da Luta nos lembra do verdadeiro poder do cinema provocar, questionar e deixar marcas profundas. Uma obra que não apenas causa impacto, mas também euforia.

I dont care if this is the film that launched ten thousand film bros. Fight Club is meticulously crafted, its satirical as hell, and its based on exceptional source material that had its finger on the pulse of its time. Ive been dreading revisiting this for years for fear of it aging poorly or worse yet becoming a flat out embarrassment. But when I read Chases fantastic blurb on the film, I felt it my duty as a card-carrying Gen Xer to take the proverbial whack at it. 
In 99 anger was in fashion and being misappropriated as something cool. The self-destructive suicidal thoughts of Cobain were a distant memory and being usurped by a brain-dead version of MTV that featured idiotic boy bands on constant rotation. Eddie Vedder was out, way out...and Fred Durst and his neo-Neanderthal species were stomping their way down the throats of Americas youth. This film stands at that crossroads, with Meat Loaf Aday of all people as its crossing guard. The washed up juicer as a warning scarecrow to the wrathful, fuming dipshits who wanted to fight their bosses behind the dumpster after happy hour. 
UFC fighting was about to take hold and render the entirety of white male earth as either tough guys or pussies. Split right down the middle. No more sweet sciences, just a bludgeoning in an octagon or dry-gulched by Kimbo Slice in some dudes back yard. But this was 99, not GW Bush-era 2004. So when bleach blonde Jared Leto gets his face caved in it was still funny to both factions.. the sensitive classic grunge brooders who hated frosted tipped boy band musical robots... AND the neighborhood rednecks who still wanted to beat the shit out of guys like Cobain. It was a combustible fucking environment to say the least (as evidenced by the trash fire that was Woodstock 99). 
Brad Pitt is at his sneering chiseled man hunk peak here, yet still attempts to vainly subvert it out of pure spite using the Zen Koan word salad of Chuck Palahniuk. A young Edward Norton is the perfect Hitchcockian wrong man caught in a deviant farce and drowning in the undercurrent of 90s angst and self-loathing run amok. Men is what we are juxtaposed with Bobs missing balls and oversized bitch tits bouncing forlornly in a sweaty basement. Enter Planet Starbucks with its cornflower blue flight coupons. What kind of dining set defines me as a person? And Seven Years in Tibet on the marquee? Fuck that noise, lets revolt with this rooster-haired grunge icon and his Gen X Cary Grant compadre. Right!!? Right...? Maybe its a little more complicated than that.
One of the main themes that Fincher was attempting to deploy here was the theme of Generation X vs. the advertising world. This all tracks because Fincher once directed Madonna videos and an ad for the American Cancer Society which depicted a fetus smoking a cigarette. He came up in that world and was now gleefully turning on it. His was the first generation that was raised wholeheartedly on television- literally ad makers telling us how to look, how to act and what to feel.
This is Finchers smirking revenge. Its meant to be satire, not reality. These Fincher themes are played to the hilt in the early going, but when the film nose dives into pseudo-terrorism these timely themes are regrettably put on the back burner. Operation Latte Thunder is a riotously witty concept - but then Fincher gut punches us with the death of Robert Paulson. Paulson is the wannabe, the one who is desperately looking for someone or something to belong to. 
When new generations visit this odd entry in Finchers filmography, I think all ironic humor is rendered moot by every unfortunate series of events since the dawn of MAGA. The satire is now our reality and there really is a not-so-secret underground idiot army at the ready. These new generations saw it pop its ugly head out on Jan. 6th and the like. A nameless, faceless project mayhem clothed in red instead of black that seeks to break down imposed societal systems. For someone in their 20s right now I can see why this is scary stuff. They are living it. 
When I was in my 20s this was still just a movie, an unbelievable farce to be laughed at, not taken as gospel. There were no twin towers collapsing, no Jan. 6, no woke vs. unwoke - in that sense this film is scarily prophetic and can never again be watched on the terms in which it was created. 
Fight Club is a cinematic flash point that put a brutal stranglehold on the medulla oblongata of the angry white male, perhaps without them even knowing it. Maybe instead of cancelling it we should study it. It is no different than harrowing 70s potboilers like Taxi Driver and their ilk, wallowing in male dominance and depression at the same time. Commenting on its disgusting nature by releasing steam valves of ominous, centuries-old human cranial decay. This is your brain on television, this is your brain on social media, this is your brain split clear down the middle with a rusty hatchet. Enjoy the ride, but dont you dare turn away when the car wrecks on the highway. 
Being addicted to addiction groups is still funny damn it! Especially in the age of positive group think Instagram memes. Self improvement is still masturbation. Onward and upward you sad bastards. In the 21st century bros be hurtin too. We are all posers in the cave of life. Its ok to be a tourist, but dont you dare share yourself completely. Single serving personalities are all we get.

You should get up and walk out too!

This is your life and its ending one minute at a time. 
I believe it was when I first viewed Fight Club that I realized how awful a regular desk job would be. The anesthetizing routines of corporate life can be so draining that I was afraid of turning into our unnamed Narrator. 
Edward Norton, who plays the Narrator, gives a pitch-perfect performance of a man hollowed out in exactly this way. He cant sleep and he cant feel. He does whatever he can to find some semblance of rest, even if that means going to every A.A. meeting in town. 
Marla Singer, played by Helena Bonham Carter who the Narrator meets at a meeting, floats through the madness with tragic elegance. 
Finally, we meet Tyler Durden, played by Brad Pitt at the peak of his 90s stardom and looking like a Greek God. Hes a soap salesman who has a philosophy of general anarchy and chaos. During one of their get-togethers, they decide to start beating the shit out of each other and lo and behold, Fight Club is born. 
A brutal underground outlet for men to rediscover their primal selves. 
This story has been misread and misunderstood by generations of guys who think Tyler Durden is a role model. 
Fun fact hes not. 
Hes a cautionary tale. Hes a man who creates the very toxic ideal he thought would save him, only to watch it consume everything. 
Fight Club as a film is a grime-fest as only Fincher can bring. It just feels dirty, especially when youre in their house. The cigarette smoke, the moldy basements. Youre living in the diseased brain of the Narrator as youre watching it. This is a film that just feels like the 90s. 
If were talking about Fight Club, we have to talk about the blatant homoeroticism. This isnt an accident or an overreach. Its part of the films dissection of masculinity. These two are shirtless and are trading cryptic philosophies about masculinity. Theres a flirtatious charge between them. 
Tyler isnt just a friend or mentor, but the Narrators fantasy. His ideal body. His freedom. His aggression. His charisma. Hes everything that the Narrator wants to be. 
With that comes a deeply sensual longing embedded in that admiration. They share clothes, a house, a bed, and bodies (quite literally!). 
The most telling moment might be in the Narrators reaction to Tyler sleeping with Marla. Hes furious in that he feels completely betrayed. Its as if Tyler gave a piece of himself away. 
Chuck Palahniuk, the openly gay author of the book, has acknowledged the homoerotic themes, describing the book as being about a man who loves another man so much that he kills him. 
I always say that the straightest acting guys are the gayest. 
Fight Club is a story of desire repressed so forcefully it manifests as a psychotic break. The Narrator cant be or have Tyler. So, he becomes him or invents him or tries to destroy him. 
Anyway, Fight Club isnt flawless, but its very bold and slaps you awake with its editing and performance. Youre not your job or how much money you have in the bank. You are, however, the audience for this film. 
Just dont talk about it.

Edward Norton delivers his best work, albeit I still have a lot of work to do to complete his filmography, but this seems hard to top. The way he portrays a completely broken mind, whilst managing to balance emotional weight and dark humor is genuinely gold. Helena B. Carter is one of my favorites and shes so amazing here, incredibly deep performance and it seems impossible to imagine anyone else in her role. Not just her but Brad Pitt and Edward Norton, feels like the perfect casting for such characters. 
Brad Pitt has some standout performances, but this is perhaps his greatest role. Tyler Durden is a genuine all time character, such a pure chaotic energy and springs the film into masterpiece territory with how he compliments Nortons persona with this rebellious attitude.

What is FIGHT CLUB about?
A reaction against the fascism inherent in consumer culture?
The emasculation of the modern man and his attempt to reclaim his balls?
The need for fascism to blow up our corrupt society and reclaim our intellectual purity?
The duality of man?
How repressed desires lead to violence?
One thing is for certain FIGHT CLUB is not a film that can be pinned down, put under glass, and viewed from only one angle. It is an intentionally ambiguous, shape-shifting film. Like Tyler Durden, it is seen the way you want to see it. Fincher did not want to spell out a message for you or for anyone. This is the perfect film for the postmodern era, for Generation X -- it rejects definition and embraces multiple perspectives.
Take, for example, the Fight Club itself. We are not to talk about it, right? From one point-of-view, this could be a metaphor for how throughout human history, mankind has found it distasteful to discuss the darkness in our nature. Meanwhile, we all bear the scars of our inherent violence. A different point-of-view, on the other hand, might counter that this is just the first step in creating groupthink for a culture of outsiders in search of meaningful connection and community spirit. Keeping secrets and confidences is a sure-fire way to forge loyalty -- and the fact that the way Brad Pitt delivers this message is so cool, so iconic, that its hard not to trust in Tyler Durden.
It is the embracing of multiple points-of-view that drive FIGHT CLUB, though. Even though Nortons nameless narrator is the films center, Pitts Tyler Durden and Bonham Carters Marla make up a three-headed monster of sorts. The narrator and Durden are schizophrenic doppelgangers, but Marla is the narrators female twin as well. She, like the narrator at the beginning, is confronted with an existential mortality crisis and finds solace in empathizing with the pain of others in support groups. Durden, by contrast, chooses to exploit the pain of others to build a revolution against the institutions he sees as responsible for that pain. Neither point-of-view is presented as more right, and both are reflected in that final shot of the film as the Pixies Where is My Mind? assaults the ears with its plaintive, unanswerable question.
Perhaps my response to the film is the ultimate fence riding, but it would seem Fincher and his collaborators want us to consider our own point-of-views about our society before launching into a think piece about theirs.

To me, Fight Club is one of those films that feels too good to be true. I was even at a loss for words on my first watch, overwhelmed by the experience. As I stated in my previous review, this film deserves another watch  and now feels like the perfect time (youll know why), so here it is.
Fight Club is an aggressive, confrontational, often brutal satire, and a brilliant masterpiece. It takes the Choose Life anti-consumerism rant at the beginning of Trainspotting and carries it to its logical  albeit extreme  conclusion. Its undoubtedly one of the most unique films Ive ever seen. In addition to presenting a fresh take on life, it also presents its material in an equally original way.
This is the way films should be made. Why must we always go through the ABC formula? Fight Club openly rejects this tired, clearly outdated structure in favor of a stylized frenzy of jump cuts, freeze frames, slow motion, and every other film technique in the book that only reinforces its anarchistic message. A film like this would never have been greenlit by a major studio if Brad Pitt had not been attached to the project. But once you see the film, it becomes obvious that he was the only choice for Tyler Durden. Pitt grunges himself down and disappears completely into his role to a frighteningly convincing degree. During many of the brutal fight scenes, he is transformed into a bloody, pulpy mess. Its an incredible performance  probably one of his best  for the simple fact that he becomes the character so completely.
If Pitt has the flashy, gonzo role, Edward Norton is his perfect foil as the seemingly meek yet sardonic narrator. Its a deceptively understated performance, as the last third of the film reveals, but Norton nails it perfectly. He is clearly our surrogate, our introduction into this strange world, and his wry observations on our consumer-obsessed culture are right on the money.
Beyond its unique style and stellar performances, what interests me most is that, in my opinion, the film doesnt present characters for us to think about  it gives us actions to reflect on. I will say that I cant recall ever being asked by a film to both suspend my disbelief  as this film does in its third act  and, at the same time, come to terms with an understanding that there is no room, or need, for disbelief.
Perhaps these comments wont make sense to some people who might dismiss this film  and, unfortunately, its premise  as just another Hollywood flick filled with gratuitous violence. Id go as far as to say that this film isnt about violence. Its about choices. Its about action. Its about lethargy. Its about waking up and realizing that, at some point in the past, we went to the toilet and threw up our dreams  without even realizing that society has stuck its fingers down our throat.
I would argue that anyone who has ever found themselves, at some point in life, caught between a rock and a hard place  anyone who has hit rock bottom mentally  anyone who has uttered to themselves, Wait, this isnt right. I wouldnt dosayfeel what it is that I just didsaidfelt... I dont like this. I have to change before Im forever stuck being the person Im not. These people will know what lm talking about. These people will not only recognize the similarities between Edward Nortons character and themselves  they will feel uncomfortably familiar with him. These people will appreciate Fight Club for what it is a wake-up call that we are not alone.
P.S. I decided to rewatch this to celebrate the birthday of this sweet gal, R.A. Plainview, since its her favorite film. Happy birthday, Re!  Wishing you nothing but a life full of good vibes, real smiles, and everything your hearts been hoping for. Thank you for being one of my favorite humans since day one on this app. Follow her, guys! Shes like a long-lost sister to me. Shes the kindest, prettiest woman  with the best taste in movies  youll ever meet (no gun to my head, I swear).

Fight Club de David Fincher, est à première vue un film sur des mecs qui se battent dans des sous-sols. Mais en réalité, cest beaucoup plus que ça. Cest un film sur le vide, sur la frustration, sur une génération perdue dans la consommation et le travail sans but. Il parle de lennui moderne, de cette sensation dêtre coincé dans une vie qui ne nous ressemble pas.
La réalisation de Fincher est nerveuse, sombre, très maîtrisée. Lambiance est sale, froide et oppressante. Les appartements, les bureaux, les parkings, tout semble étouffant. Les scènes de combat sont brutes, intenses et incroyables, elles ne sont pas stylisées comme dans un film daction classique. On sent les coups, la sueur, la douleur. Et plus le film avance, plus la mise en scène devient chaotique, elle suit la perte de contrôle du personnage principal.
Le film est fort grâce à son trio incroyable. Edward Norton joue parfaitement cet homme fatigué, insomniaque, perdu dans une routine absurde. Il est banal, presque invisible au début, et cest justement ça qui rend son évolution intéressante. Brad Pitt, lui, est magnétique. Il incarne Tyler Durden avec un charisme fou. Il représente la liberté totale, le rejet des règles, le refus du système. Il est séduisant, drôle, dangereux. Chaque scène avec lui dégage une énergie particulière. Helena Bonham Carter apporte aussi quelque chose dessentiel avec Marla  elle est instable, fragile, lucide. Elle voit le chaos, elle vit dedans, et elle casse un peu lillusion des deux autres.
Le récit parle clairement de consommation, de masculinité, de colère, mais il ne fait pas un discours compliqué. Il montre des hommes perdus qui cherchent un sens, une identité. Le Fight Club devient une façon de ressentir quelque chose, de reprendre le contrôle, même si cest par la violence. Mais plus ça avance, plus ça dérape. Ce qui commence comme une rébellion contre le système devient quelque chose de plus extrême, presque dangereux.
Et puis il y a ce twist, qui change complètement la lecture du film. Là, tu comprends que tout ce que tu as vu parle surtout didentité, de double personnalité, de fuite. 
Enfin, ça nest pas juste un film sur la révolte, cest un film sur quelquun qui ne sait plus qui il est.

A white-collar worker (Edward Norton) dissatisfied with his conventional lifestyle and suffering from insomnia starts up an underground fight club with the mysterious, charismatic Tyler Durden (Brad Pitt), which gradually develops into something more sinister, in David Finchers psychological thriller based on Chuck Palahniuks novel, with Helena Bonham Carter, Meat Loaf, Jared Leto and Zack Grenier in supporting roles. 
The leads both give some of their best performances, creating layered, compelling characters that illustrate the storys look at the darker impulses that lurk beneath the surface. Pitt is able to make Tyler charming yet unsettling, showing the magnetic pull he has on his followers which becomes increasingly chilling. Norton is a great choice for the Narrator, possessing an Everyman quality as he sardonically relates his inner thoughts, slowly realising the true extent of the situation. 
Its one of the few film adaptations that really manages to capture what it would be like to read the original book, using narration in a stream-of-consciousness way incredibly well to draw us into the protagonists psyche. Fincher gives the film a brilliantly frenetic visual style to compliment this, with a heightened, slightly surreal quality that echoes the rebellious attitude of the story and characters, and their fractured mental states. 
The film gets across the feelings of disenfranchisement and isolation of Generation X, distilling them into the violent rituals the members carry out to take out their anger on each other and society. At the time, it was thought that the film would inspire people to carry out similar actions, and despite it going a little too far in places, I think theres always a sense of ironic detachment from whats going on that stops it from glamourising the events of the story. 
In that way it reminds me of Goodfellas both films draw us into this dangerous and exciting world only to slowly reveal the darker side to it all, and despite Tyler being a fascinating character were never truly aligned with him, always at a distance. It gets a little far-fetched and silly in places, but the films exploration of fractured identities, the rejection of materialism and nihilism make it feel different and original, even though sometimes what its trying to say is a little unclear, as it looks at toxic masculinity yet sidelines its only female character.

Fight Club is an absorbing, disturbing and darkly funny look at rejecting conformity that isnt always consistent, but still draws the audience into its twisty, compelling story thanks to its performances, style and themes.

Filled to the tee with what seems a rapid succession of what seems foibles followed by virtues, before in its last half hour (also, this is overlong) lapsing into maybe one of the most completely irresponsible movies ever.  But its far from unengaging, not least to say uninteresting. Flawed as it may be, Fight Club may very well be the strongest of the pre-Benjamin Button Fincher works, and of the early works points most directly to the strengths of Social Network and Gone Girl in its concern with a generation whose value system was largely dictated by neoliberalism and advertising culture.  But, for better or for worse, also shares with the former the quiet siding with the protagonists jaundiced perspective.  
Yet for the most part, Fight Club can be genuinely insightful - reaction against a simulated and fraudulent idea of consumer-ready happiness, reaction against a sort-of given life of spectatorship, reaction against external signifiers of happiness, reaction against traditional concerns of failure and success as the meaning of ones life.  What is consistently interesting about Fight Club is that Finchers identification of social planks are most often correct, and it moves in a most fascinating direction where in order for these characters desire to feel reality, they resort to violence - first towards each other as sport, before directing it externally.  In this state of reaction only, rather than active improvement of conditions, this desire to feel everything turns these men into little more than Neanderthals testing each other to see whom is the strongest, while this emphasis on reaction over action shields themselves from the fact that they have no direction.  They become little more than a group of anarcho-fascists, where even though the conditions they are reacting against are completely justified, their own reaction is jaundiced and deluded, ironically only worsening things for themselves.  While Im no Zodiac-hater (I think its just a little boring) Fight Club does seem to stand at a crossroads between the thoughtful David Fincher of a mere nine years later and David Fincher, the Gen-X 90s edgelord. 
The films critiques are spot on but its solutions are not, yet those mistaken solutions are in and of itself surprisingly perceptive in the long term.  When this really becomes a real problem, however, is in the films final thirty minutes, because the films reveal of the split personality motif (already somewhat disrespectful) actually undercuts the actual critiques the film has made and the planks which Fincher has identified, which for the most part, are actually correct.  By now revealing that Norton is detached from reality, it reinstates the normal as truth, when the film has spent the last near two hours showing us that this is not the case.  Its a fatal misstep and one that limits ones own goodwill towards the film from beforehand, because it reveals that Fincher is not as critical towards the NarratorDurdens character and their cronies as one might have assumed previously.  As such, its a tremendous shame because the films own missteps ironically mirror those of the characters...yet its almost there.  Its still nevertheless a worthwhile viewing and in a way stands as a testament to how much Fincher has genuinely matured over the years, especially given that he would revisit and rework similar subject matter again and again, particularly in his study and understanding of how images as a consumer product can so easily manipulate and influence masses of people.
Random note As an aside, Ive always found myself preferring Fincher on a screen rather than a theatre (TSW, Dragon Tattoo and Gone Girl only clicked with me upon their respective Blu-ray releases) and there is something unusually fascinating between this and Panic Room - this one a near bomb on release and both released to mixed reception.  Yet Fight Club would become a hit on its now legendary Fox 2000 DVD release, while Panic Room would become a classic staple of cable television.  Who knows.  Maybe Finchers precision actually becomes heightened and more engaging at home, keeping the mind occupied in our rapid information era, while in the theatre, theres more room to dream.

Fight Club begins with a representation of the neural network of a brain, then with a rapid tracking shot backwards you exit the body of the protagonist who - threatened by a pistol pointed in his mouth - looks directly into the camera, while his voiceover kicks off a long flashback (backward movement par excellence) that makes up the rest of the film. The profound meaning of David Finchers work is already revealed in the first few seconds a storytelling fruit of the psyche of the main character, which for this reason certainly cannot meet criteria of objectivity. Resting on a circular structure, typical of the noir films of the 1940s in which the beginning and the end are joined, Fight Club follows the events of an anonymous employee, slave of his own unsatisfactory life and completely subjugated by a consumerist and alienating society. To save him from all this comes the meeting with Tyler Durden, a fascinating and exuberant soap salesman who involves him in his rebellion against the system and with whom he decides to create a sort of clandestine fight clubs, through which trying to redeem the void of its existence. Tyler represents everything the protagonist would like to be, a free and secure man, capable of escaping the prevailing homologation in a commodified world.
The film is an original analysis on the theme of the double, initially intended as a model to follow, an ideal projection to aspire to, then gradually transforming into an alter-ego to be replaced. Around this reflection, the director stages the increasingly confused relationship between reality and fiction, authenticity and copy, truth and perception, up to the surprising final twist. But Finchers masterpiece is also an acute generational film that denounces the evils of a depersonalizing society, devoid of genuine values, that reduces individuals to obscure consumers, and in which all the twilight insecurity of the turn of the century is felt. Faithful transposition of the extraordinary novel by Chuck Palahniuk, Fight Club is a cult movie, visionary and provocative, supported by a swirling direction, with a strong visual impact, and by a cast of excellence on which the unforgettable performances of Brad Pitt and Edward Norton stand out.

god. what a ride. my second david fincher film watched in preparation for mank, and another classic crossed off my watchlist! im always a bit wary when im reviewing classics because so much has already been said and i feel like im not even remotely in the position to throw in my two cents, so bear with me while i dump this review on here, desperately need a break from all the math and physics!
a timeless cult classic and, in some ways, ahead of its time, fight club is as invigorating as it is thought-provoking. under finchers unique vision and direction, we watch the main characters life and subsequent descent into madness unfold, all while, at its core, experiencing film at its best. 
as with every david fincher movie ive seen so far, the direction is absolutely impeccable. finchers ability to hijack the audiences eyes as much as he hijacks the mind is distinctive to his style, and right from the beginning, it can be felt in every frame, every camera movement, every cut and every nuance in the actors performances, creating a world thats hard to look away from (expect for some scenes, which ill get to later).
needless to say, jeff cronenweths cinematography is just as remarkable and crucial to the movie and to the look weve come to associate with finchers work. for me, his lighting and camera movement give so much indescribable character to the film by beautifully combining scarcely lit settings with tense dolly ins, almost comical whip pans and movements precisely following a characters motion, subsequently making the experience as immersive and remarkable as it is. one moment, or rather just a cut that particularly stood out to me was a scene where the camera was moving before the cut and continued to move with the same momentum even after we cut to another character. 
it goes without saying that the editing in fight club is just as precise, and while im normally not the biggest fan of montages, something about finchers montages is so engaging, entertaining and charming and comedic, even, and, as a consequence, theyre probably the only montages i actually enjoy. theyre just so well-made, not by unrealistically rushing through a series of events, but rather by depicting sometimes tiring and frustrating repetition through movement and cleverly edited sequences over a perfectly matching soundtrack. 
the reason im not rating fight club any higher, despite it being, from a technical standpoint, an ingenious coalescence of so many different elements, is solely because of my personal feelings towards the approach of its subject matter. im (as you all probably already know by now hahah) easily repulsed by violence and blood, and even though i wasnt expecting anything rosy from a film called FIGHT CLUB, it did play a little into my personal enjoyment. i had to cover my screen a few times, only to be shocked by a sudden cut back to the graphic scene i was trying to avoid. nevertheless, it wasnt as bad as i thought it would be, partly because i think im becoming, at least a little, less affected by violence in films and because there was no buildup to it (like sudden gunshots after tense moments of silence). the violence itself doesnt feel like the primary focus of the film, and, at least for me, its not the good characters i connect with on a deeper level that get hurt. 
i feel like i focused a lot on technical aspects in this rather vague review, simply because im still too riveted by the psychological and thought-provoking themes of this movie and because its impossible to talk about anything deeper without getting into spoiler territory (even though pretty much everyone has already this). kinda feels like an easy cop-out, but theres just so much to debunk and, given theres a whole wikipedia article on interpretations of fight club, a lot to think and read about. 
a captivating and enthralling ride from start to finish, fight club encapsulates not only a multitude of psychological themes, but also a feeling that we, as humans, inevitably all go through. be it a product of its unmatched direction, eye-catching cinematography, lively screenplay or outstanding performances, fight club is truly timeless and lives up to its hype on both a superficial and deeper level.
