Its been great to revisit Fight Club again. Typically, whenever you rewatch a film for the first time in years, you tend to pick up more details than the first time. In my case, I picked up on the films subtleties with both the character interactions and the films broader themes. I even picked up more clues on Tyler Durdens true nature than I did the first time. 
Im in love with the editing here, as the frenetic pacing and the integration of Edward Nortons imagination give us an excellent overview of the unnamed protagonists state of mind. It conveys the same exact feeling you get from reading a novel told from the perspective of an unreliable narrator. 
Fight Club was part of that wave of films from the late 90s that dealt with the existential crisis relating to the mundanity of a utopia. Think of The Truman Show, The Matrix, Office Space, American Beauty, and so on. Fight Club is no different, as it tackles the masculine resistance to consumerism and how that manifests in nihilism. Men find refuge in fight clubs because its a place where they can embrace their masculinity and find inspiration in a world without any. Its such a multi-layered narrative, and David Fincher knows how to make that complexity both thrilling and coherent. Theres a crazy amount of thematic depth here, and almost everyone has their own readings on the film.

Norton, Pitt, and Bonham Carter were all excellent, the direction and cinematography were stellar, and the world-building of this cult of men taking down society was a very complex and intriguing plot to watch unfold.

I say that yet this made 202m world wide on a 42m budget, and the second went and blew that out the water with 331m earned on a 50m budget. This really could have done a trilogy, I wonder why it never happened. 
The story following two rookie cop partners undercover at a high school searching for the supplier of a new drug is such fun and a great entry point for the series. The run time is just shy of 2 hours, its the perfect length and flows effortlessly to the finish line with moments of comedy, action and story.
The scene where Tatum and Hill take HFS in front of Eric to maintain cover is hysterical, the conversation they have with Mr. Walters played by Rob Riggle is so good, I love when the VFX start to mess with his face and end up putting his eyebrows as a mustache, that shits classic. Buena película, una comedia policial bastante divertida.
21 Jump Street fue mucho mejor de lo que esperaba, me imaginaba una comedia simple y con un humor que no me iba a funcionar tanto, pero presenta un dúo de protagonistas genial que cae muy bien rápidamente y se desenvuelve a la perfección tanto en los momentos de acción como los de comedia.
Sinopsis Cuando los policías Schmidt y Jenko se unen a la unidad secreta Jump Street, ellos usan sus apariencias juveniles para trabajar de forma encubierta como estudiantes de preparatoria. Ellos cambian sus placas y armas por mochilas e intentan eliminar a un grupo narcotraficante. Schmidt y Jenko descubren que la preparatoria ya no es lo mismo y deben enfrentarse al terror y la ansiedad de la adolescencia que creían haber superado.
La historia es buena, maneja un gran humor y lo que cuenta es muy entretenido. Es una trama con el desarrollo de un buddy film pero con toques muy originales, sobretodo por lo que tienen que hacer los protagonistas y las situaciones en las que se ven envueltos, haciendo que se generen varias escenas buenísimas. Mezcla muy bien la acción y la comedia, resultando buena en ambos aspectos, pero sobretodo el humor es lo que más destaca, encima contando con varios actores ya conocidos en éste género que aportan bastante. También tiene sus momentos demasiado absurdos, algunos funcionan pero a veces ya se pasan un poco. Por último, algo que es genial es que es muy entretenida, dura lo que tiene que durar y el ritmo que tiene es bueno para no aburrirte en ningún momento.
Los personajes me gustaron, sobretodo los dos protagonistas. Schmidt y Jenko son una pareja de policías realmente icónica, ambos actores potencian a sus personajes y los vuelven muy divertidos, además de que su relación tiene un buen desarrollo, teniendo algunos altibajos en el medio pero formando un gran vínculo. Por otro lado, de los secundarios destacan el Capitán Dickson por el lado de los policías, mientras que por parte de los adolescentes resaltan Molly y Eric, ambos también formando una relación importante con los protagonistas y siendo divertidos en las situaciones que les tocan.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente las actuaciones de Jonah Hill y Channing Tatum, ambos los mejores del elenco aunque en general están todo muy bien también me gustó el cameo de Johnny Depp haciendo referencia a la serie en la que se basa. Por otro lado, la dirección de Phil Lord y Chris Miller es buena, me parece que son dos directores que saben cómo llevar a cabo una comedia y encima darle un grandísimo ritmo como para entretenerte. Por último, la banda sonora estuvo decente pero podría haber sido un poco mejor, cuenta con algunas canciones conocidas que no quedan mal.
En conclusión, una buena película que está más que bien para pasar el rato y no es el típico buddy film genérico, suma mucho la gran dupla de protagonistas y lo entretenida que es. La recomiendo.

21 Jump Street has no business working as well as it does. A comic reimagining of a television series from the Fox networks formative years, the film, at face value, inspires little confidence. In the hands of Phil Lord and Chris Miller, 21 Jump Street, however, is turned into a smart, hilarious, and slightly meta take on high school, film remakes, and undercover cops.
The premise of the film and television series finds undercover police officers placed, undercover, in high schools. Where the series was serious toned, the film is a raucous comedy. The undercover cops, played by a surprisingly unwooden Channing Tatum and the always game Jonah Hill, are of the bumbling misfit ilk, and their undercover adventure is commensurately bumbling.
Michael Bacalls script is consistently funny and treats the films premise with restrained reverence. It does not make fun of the televsion series it simply allows the source materials comedic potentialities and possiblities to shine through. The jokes and gags come fast and furiously. There is raunch and cleverness, physical comedy and verbal wit. The films comic beats are placed evenly throughout the film with very little downtime between the gags.
Quick and self-aware, sincere and unceasingly funny, 21 Jump Street may be 2012s best comedy. The cast works well, and Channing Tatum treads new territory, playing a role with actual personality. The production is solid, and the direction focuses on keeping the film tight. The resulting experience is sometimes sidesplitting and always entertaining.

The story is well-written and very well-directed by Lord and Miller, along with Jonah Hill and Michael Bacall, all whom bring us a film adaptation of the 1987-1991 TV series 21 Jump Street. The plot follows two former high school rivals who become good police partners, and are soon assigned to a high school undercover as students to stop a new synthetic drug from being released. Its a pretty fun concept for a plot, and the film executes that plot very well! This is a very fun movie, all thanks to Lord and Miller applying their style of self-aware humor, fast-paced humor blended with a solid emotional core, and their interesting own spin on the buddy cop genre by bringing us likeable characters, thrilling action, and clever wit!
The performances of the cast are very good, starting with the two leads, Jonah Hill and Channing Tatum! The two play police officers Morton Schmidt and Greg Jenko, both whom have great chemistry with each other! Hill does a great job channeling his awkwardness into Schmidts personality, while also being smart as an officer. Tatum is very charming as Jenko, who is Schmidts stupid but strong and attractive partner. Their opposing traits bounce off each other very well, making them such an effective duo! And they grow as characters, too, in how Schmidt becomes a badass shooter while Jenko learns science and how to use it to benefit the mission.
I really liked the supporting cast, too. Ice Cube is in this, and he plays Captain Dickson, a crude police captain. He is HILARIOUS in this, as he gets some of the best lines and scenes here! I needed this after seeing Ice Cube star in that godawful War of the Worlds film months ago, lol. Brie Larson is also in this, and she does a surprisingly good job as Schmidts love interest Molly Tracey. Dave Franco is charming as Eric Molson, as is Rob Riggle (Mr. OHare from The Lorax) as Mr. Walters, DeRay Davis as Domingo, Nick Offerman as Deputy Chief Hardy, and the rest of the cast.
The action sequences are really fun to watch! This film starts off having smaller scale type setpieces, that being Schmidt and Jenko starting off as rookie cops with their arrest of Domingo while on bicycle patrol. And then, we start to see more exciting stuff, like that highway chase (So the chicken truck blew up but not the oil truck?! Lmao.)! I also got a kick out of the party brawl with Party Rock Anthem playing in the background, that hotel room shootout with... Johnny Depp (I didnt know he was in this!), and that epic final chase in the last act leading to the villains defeat of getting shot in the dick. Hey, wait a minute, I thought that was considered weak?! Eric Cartman said so.  
21 Jump Street is full-on comedy gold. So many jokes in this that caught me by surprise and had me laughing hard, such as Schmidt and Jenkos first arrest, Captain Dickson going on a tirade about being stereotyped as an angry black man, Jenko writing on the whiteboard while high on HFS (Holy Fucking Shit), Johnny Depp as the biker, and just all the playful antics between Schmidt and Jenko. Truth be told, I found Ice Cubes character to be the funniest part of this whole movie! This film also has a nice heart to it, as shown by the strong bromance between Schmidt and Jenko, as well as the subplot of Schmidt and Molly.
This film is really well-made for an action comedy, as it has nice cinematography and editing that suits the fast-paced nature of the films buddy cop genre, the setting of the high school and the outfits the characters wear are solid, and everything else is well-done. As for the visual effects, theyre not as flashy as other blockbusters, but they come into play during all the action sequences, with all the gunplay, blood and gore, and that explosion on the bridge all being nicely done. Definitely not the biggest spectacle out there, but it doesnt have to be. )
The music is also good. Mark Mothersbaugh composes a solid score that captures the fast-paced and comedic tone of the film well, and were also treated to plenty of bangers on the films soundtrack! Theres hits like The Real Slim Shady by Eminem, Police and Thieves by The Clash, Helena Beat by Foster the People, Party Rock Anthem by LMFAO, Straight Outta Compton by N.W.A., and the 21 Jump Street (Main Theme). Lots of catchy tunes right here, and its especially funny how Ice Cube was a part of that group that sang Straight Outta Compton. I take it they were being meta right there, lmao.
As for flaws, I only have a couple. One of which is how despite being engaged with the subplot between Schmidt and Molly, I wasnt a huge fan of how it had the typical Liar Revealed trope that ended with the girl being upset, only for them to make amends later on. Pretty predictable, lol. Also, Im not 100 about the running gag of the chemistry teacher being sexually attracted to Jenko, who from her point of view is of high school age. On one hand, its funny how hes actually a cop in his mid-20s, but on the other hand, it made me a little uncomfortable in reminding me of that one Adam Sandler movie where the main character gets his teacher pregnant in middle school...
Shudders
Overall, 21 Jump Street is a surprisingly excellent action comedy from Lord and Miller that I had an absolute blast watching! I feel bad for not checking this out before since Im an outspoken fan of Lord and Millers work, but Im glad I now finally got the chance to see it! Its not quite perfect in its plot, but the story, Lord and Millers direction, screenplay, performances, characters, action sequences, humor, heart, production values, and music all make this one of the best comedies Ive seen from the 2010s! Im eager to check out the sequel now, since Ive also heard good things about it as well! )
Thank you for the recommendation, Justin Luis Encarnacion!

21 Jump Street is a broad but fun comedy, which updates old high school stereotypes for the 2010s.
Young police officers Morton and Greg spectacularly screw up their first arrest and are kicked over to a program revived from the 1980s. Their mission is to infiltrate a high school and find the source of a new designer drug. 
The twist is that culture has changed since the mid-2000s and former nerd Morton is one of the more popular kids in school, whilst Gregs macho behaviour now makes him the lowest on the totem pole.
Most of the charm comes from the Channing Tatum-Jonah Hill double act, and it turns out they are both excellent comedy actors and good at ab libbing. Some of the movies best moments are obviously improvised, like Tatum attacking Hill with a fluffy giraffe during a phone call. 
Hill could actually could pass for a teenager, and its hard to believe that he was 28 when making the film. On the flip side, its genuinely amusing to see Tatums hulk of a character Greg hanging around with nerdy high school kids. 
Ice Cube is also funny in a supporting role as a hard-assed police chief who is highly self-aware about being a hard-assed police chief. In general the best jokes in the story are minor details, like the hilarious cameo from the original TV show actors.  
There are a couple of meta jokes at the expense of the movie, with one character highlighting the fact that the film is a remake of a 1980s tv series all they do now is recycle shit from the past and expect us all not to notice. The characters are also repeatedly surprised when their jobs involve fewer explosions and far more incontinent homeless people than theyd been led to believe.
In a story about how culture changes over time, the differences between 2012 and 2020 are also obvious. Scenes of Hill and Tatum taunting a handcuffed black suspect come off as much darker than they would have in the 2010s, and Ice Cube spouting antisemitic slurs is also an awkward moment. Whether or not its still ok to produce a wacky comedy movie about police misconduct, it certainly makes watching it a different experience. 
This is a fun film which filled the gap in teenage comedies between the Harold and Kumars of the 2000s and the Booksmarts of the late 2010s. Whilst it isnt very original, its nice to see that the Zoomers also had something funny to watch in high school.

And I finally managed to watch the film that was so unglamorously recommended to me, or rather both films of the 21 Jump Street franchise. Because it was often recommended to me as similar and as a combination of police comedy and Superbad. To be completely honest, I knew I would have fun at 21 Jump Street, but I really didnt expect to have so much fun beforehand. The film is in a way half based on an old series that I havent seen, but I had a really good time watching it. As Ive mentioned several times before, films in this genre have the risk and potential to totally flop and become horrible, but here everything goes really well and Ill go into more detail in a moment, but what is this film actually about? Well the plot is quite simple a drug is circulating in a high school and one person comes to harm and dies directly, somehow the police logically try to stop the distribution of the drug and how better to do that than to get 2 cops into this high school to stop the source and prevent more deaths. The two friends are bike cops Schmidt played by Jonah Hill and Jenko played by Channing Tatum, they are fresh, new, young looking or something? And so the story takes its course and logically a lot happens in between, from fights, love, friendship, hate and all sorts of things. These five stars will only make sense to you if you, like me, have at some point in your life crossed paths with Wolverine on those drawn pages of escapist, youthful fantasy.
If you havent, youll get this A well acted, extremely violent, gritty superhero movie with a poorly paced final act, but with enough conviction to be a break from the norm.
So if youre not ready for some fanboy rambling you can stop reading right there, bub.
The trilogy of solo movies about Wolverine actually present an interesting arc. We start with a very comic booky opening film, very much following the patterns laid out by other films. It is followed by a film that feels more like a character study with superhero bits thrown in. And it concludes with the hero looking back at those chapters in his life, treating them as flights of fancy or distorted memories, stuff to be forgotten and hidden in a bottle.
Mangolds Logan is not an easy film. Its extremely course in every single aspect. It is the most tangible a super hero has ever become on film. Logan literally distances himself from his comic book past, making him, his actions and struggles very human. And as it turns out, this is exactly what the genre needed as I consider this to be not a benchmark but a source of inspiration for what a film like this can be if youre willing to take some risk and to show your passion for the source material.
Because that is what Mangold puts on display most here. His total dedication to this character, to show what these claws can really do, to show the man behind the beast, the beast behind the man and to show just how deep a connection he has to his past and the people in it. The shared weight of the past between Xavier and Logan is palpable and rings so very true, especially because of the truly outstanding performances by Stewart and Jackman. The rest of the cast is excellent as well, with Dafne Keen giving a really impressive performance as the young girl ending up in Logans care. She channels a certain ferociousness that was rather unsettling at points. 
The bleakness of this futuristic setting so often hinted at in the old X-men comics is beautifully crafted. It is stripped of all the shiny frills and what remains is a barren wasteland of violence and inequality. It is the perfect backdrop for this heros last confrontation with his past, with hope and with himself. I was truly moved by the inescapable fate Logan is speeding towards. There is a certain endearing humanity to him that is only strengthened by the way Mangold visualizes the extreme violence he is capable of.
Apart from the fact that this is, without the fanboy goggles clouding my judgement, a very solid film, Im also inclined to conclude that I simply cannot think of a better send-off for one of my favourite characters portrayed by an actor that fit the part perfectly.

Its been 17 years since Hugh Jackman first starred in Bryan Singers X-Men and became synonymous with the character Wolverine, the violent, rage-filled Canadian alcoholic drifter. Though hes brought the role to life nine times, since then theres only really been two films to test him in interesting ways one being Singers own sequel X2, which saw him try and reconcile his savage instincts and origins (the lab experiment of a scientist turned hawkish bureaucrat) with the sense of purpose he could have if he only chose to be a team player, the other was returning filmmaker James Mangolds The Wolverine, which put his immortality to the test, revealing all the horror and pain a man thats wandered for centuries is bound to witness and carry with him, illustrating the melancholy that lingers even within what were told to perceive as the characters strengths. So its fitting that Logan, perhaps one of, if not the best film the modern superhero climate has brought us, is the logical and emotional endpoint of those two ideas packaged in a rugged, hardboiled neo-western milieu.
Mangold is the kind of filmmaker that wears his influences on his sleeve so its easy to see throughout Logan the hints of Badlands, The Road Warrior,  Unforgiven, The Searchers, theres an even a direct, perhaps too cued, reference to George Stevens Shane, a film about a lone gunslinger whose chosen path of killing floods every other facet of his life, forcing him into isolation, but the films closest relative for me was actually Sylvester Stallones Rambo series, another story of a manmade killing machine created and abandoned by the banal evil of bureaucratic administration, using the only tools at his disposal to reckon with a world that no longer hasor maybe never did havea real place for him (theres no going back), and its in these concerns that Logan comes to life.
Not wasting any time getting to its R-ratinga development that initially worried me as upping violence and language may imply but doesnt necessarily result in maturitythe film opens with a drunk and weary Logan brutally dispatching a crew trying to steal the hubcaps off of his town car limo, and though the altercation is gruesomely thrilling its the moment immediately after that is the most revealing, the deeply exhausted Logan clumsily making his way back to the car while the camera hovers over the dismembered corpses, unable to shake the carnage he leaves in his wake.
Logans day-to-day life includes balancing his job as a driverescort of city nightlife, his proclivity for boozing and self-pity, and taking care of Professor Xavier, whose dementia is deteriorating the most powerful brain on the planet. A scary thought. No superhero film since Sam Raimis Spider-Man films has so effectively captured the way even the superhuman are susceptible to the crushing, horrifying mundanity of the human condition and economic disenfranchisement. Gone are the struggles of world-ending CGI portals in the sky, here we see characters trying to simply find basic care and safety, afford medicine and retirement dreamstheres a lot of driving and motels and cheap gas stations. And that intimate scale is vital as the film ultimately transitions into deeply emotional story of how we collectively have the power to shape our fantasies into reality Heaven is a place on Earth etc.
Though an optimistic sentiment, what makes Logan even more powerful is how it isnt afraid to horrify us along the way. Wolverines abilities have always been exceptionally savage, his claws force the fighting to be particularly personal and messy, but the R-rating allows the action the weight the character has always neededevery slice, every tear of flesh, every crack of bone is vividly rendered to maximum revulsion and as a result we see the one of the central dichotomies of Wolverine that previously was only ever explored in comic form the deeply traumatized inflicting deep, deep trauma. But Logan isnt the only one to benefit from the horror, perhaps the films most moving scene is Xavier reflecting on the violent past of mutantkind and its lack of a future as a resulthis dreams, his happiness, both fleeting, infected by regret.
Its an essential moment of quiet deconstruction, using the past to consider the future, something Mangold and screenwriter Scott Frank try to do as well with the inclusion of Laura, played with a uniquely compelling ferocity by newcomer Dafne Keen. Unlike Logan and Xavier who are already broken, who already had their chance, shes still in the process of being shaped by the terrifying world around her, and shes been left nothing by the previous generation. Logan sees himself in her for very obvious reasons, her powers, her flashes of rage (one of Mangolds most brilliant gestures is literalizing how terrifying kids can be), but he also sees that shes been forced down a path similar to the one he already took, one he knows leads to nothing but pain and death, he sees one last chance to leave something better than the way he found it, so the claws come out and he starts cutting a new path, one perhaps he mightve taken if he wasnt so jaded.
Most fascinating however, is that this intimately-scaled story of a weary killer in search of purpose, of a teacher with one last lesson to teach, of a child whose future hinges on hope given to her from a comic book, all these moments of sudden, troubling violence followed by quiet melancholy, none of it prepares you for the films finale, a raging howl of an action sequence that climaxes on the petrifying implication that the most disturbing atrocities, the things we are unconsciously reckoning with and reacting to in every facet of our life, have already been done in secret, in government offices, in corporate boardrooms. Not that every piece of art needs to reflect the current zeitgeist, but that such an iconic character takes his bow in a story about violently defying our corporate overlords and handing the keys over to immigrant children doesnt feel like an accident. As soon as genocide enters the dialogue, its over, end the dialogue.

Every time I see Logan go full berserker I burst into tears, a three-minute salute to 17 years of watching a character personify your childhood wonder. Its Shane with claws, Joel and Ellie with superpowers, and goddamn good way to send off a hero. 
Thank goodness they never brought him back for anything silly.

A rumbling, raging action epic, James Mangolds Logan is soulful farewell to one of this centurys most revered cinematic heroes. A powerful and moving meditation on heroism, aging, and family, Mangolds film transcends to tropes of the superhero film to become one of that subgenres most striking exemplars.
Beginning in 2029, a year that finds mutantkind widely exterminated, Logan revolves around the last remaining mutants attempt to live under the dangerous eye of those who could do them harm. When a young girl comes to those men in need of protection, a journey begins that will lead to both a vital hope and a weary end.
Logan is as much about the end as it is the future. Its titular hero is sick and worn down, but there is a new heart beating in the distance. He is dying but has not lost the spark that turned him from a feral assassin into a teacher, friend, and hero.
The narrative serves as a deconstruction and humanization of the superhero myth where its characters face an end unforeseen in their comic book source material. Painting the superhero story as a Western, however, the hero rises even as he rushes headlong into his demise hope and family turn antihero toward a fitting sunset where a human beings heroic truth is writ large.
Mangold eschews comic book color for an action outing that is nearly plaintive. Cameras stare into tired eyes and furrowed brows delivered in close, unblinking shots. This is dusty, gritty, sepia world where the sun has bleached joyful shades out of the landscape, leaving only rust and refuse.
The tone is heavy, but shadows of happiness flutter forth. Character and characters are at the fore of the production, but the work is rife with action spectacle. Violence is stinging, and the film does not shy away from the impact of claw and bullet. Action beats race, creating spectacular and exhilarating stretches that juxtapose stirring, emotionally rich character moments.
Those character are portrayed gloriously by actors who have filled their respective roles for nearly 20 years. Hugh Jackman concludes a 17-year run as Wolverine with a glowering anger and lament that can not conceal a muscular, inviting charisma while Patrick Stewart presents a Charles Xavier that is a broken, empty husk of the man he once was.
Haunting, bold, and riveting, Logan combines melancholy notes with inspiring passages for a film that sends off its titular hero in unforgettably potent fashion. It is a sad goodbye communicated by excellent and invigorating cinema.

Blending the gritty, violent  bleak ruggedness of westerns with the silent rumination of a hard-hitting, powerfully captivating  emotionally involving drama, Hugh Jackmans swan song to his most famous role delivers a finale so fitting  memorable that fans couldnt have asked for a better conclusion, for this final instalment in the Wolverine saga isnt just the best X-Men film to date but is impressive enough to garner a spot amongst the greatest works of its genre.
Set in a dystopian future where mutants are on verge of extinction, Logan follows the eponymous mutant who is now way past his prime and spends his days working as a chauffeur while caring for the ailing Charles Xavier in an abandoned place across the border. Things are set in motion when a mysterious young girl who is being chased by an evil corporation arrives on his doorstep and, after being coerced by Xavier, Logan eventually agrees to embark on one final adventure to take her to safety.
Co-written  directed by James Mangold, the story is envisioned from a new perspective and carries a very human, personal  contemplative feel. Also admirable is the shift in tonality, pace  setting, for Logan bears more resemblance to a western, and its funeral-like quality is further enhanced by its R-rated savagery. And although Logans own cathartic journey is undeniably compelling, it is his exquisitely handled bonding with Xavier  Laura that turns the film into a deftly layered but highly rewarding meditation on life, death  family.
Production design team contribute to its post-apocalyptic setting by keeping the set pieces  sci-fi props to its bare minimum, while the sensibly chosen locations provide more authenticity to its western iconography. Cinematography encapsulates the entire picture with a gritty ambience and methodically employs the camera as per the requirements of the scene. Editing allows the plot to unravel at its own pace  gives each character their own space to breathe freely. And last but not the least, Marco Beltramis evocative score simply fits.
Coming to the performances, Logan finds Hugh Jackman  Patrick Stewart reprising their iconic roles of LoganWolverine  Charles XavierProfessor X, respectively while Dafne Keen plays the young mutant whose arrival puts this story into motion. Jackman, in his last appearance as Logan, delivers his career-best performance and bids a perfect farewell to his signature character. Stewart chips in with a nuanced portrait of the original X-Man in what could be his final outing as well. And Keen renders her part with such ferocity that she steals all her moments with remarkable ease.
On an overall scale, Logan is an absolute rarity in modern superhero filmmaking that subverts the existing tropes  defies all conventions to deliver a finale so fresh, unique  groundbreaking that it effortlessly transcends its genre. Pitched at the very divide between poetry  entertainment, it is a thoughtful, melancholic  artfully constructed cinema that exceeds all hype  expectations. To summarise it all, Logan is what a great comic book film looks like. You should take a moment. Feel it. Cherish it. Because a cinematic experience as fulfilling as this is too rare for its genre. A perfect finale. A fitting farewell. An irrefutable masterpiece. Do not miss it.

Im not whatever it is you think I am...
Every story has a its natural 3 act structure  a beginning, a middle and an end. Very rarely is the the final act the one that audiences love the most. Its very difficult to please everyone.
The X-Men franchise is not one that I immediately think as of being associated with masterclass filmmaking, great acting or storytelling, nor do I think many feel as strongly about when it comes to other superhero franchises, like Spider-Man or Batman, mainly because its comic books and animated tv shows have done a much greater job at adapting this now iconic superhero team. I for one thought they were okay movies that exceded in nailing the castings of Charles Xavier, Magneto and of course Wolverine, who absolutetly nailed his role and has come to make it his own. 
Then in October 2016 while I was laying around in my college room not having much to do, I came across a trailer. You might think a trailer is nothing new in this day an age, but this one was special. I clicked play and I immediatetly understood what this was a superherocomic book movie that seemingly stood out amongst the rest. Seeing those images of Old Man Logan violently clawing into his enemies while trying to protect a young girl immediately piqued my interest and my curiosity. The fact that it was called Logan and not X-Men or Wolverine also made me take notice. It seemed to imply that this entry would be a more character-oriented approach, while its title stressed the humanity of its central character.
Logan follows an aged Wolverine and an extremely ill Charles Xavier who must defend a young mutant named Laura from sinister forces.  
Logan is the single parent struggling to raise his adopted daughter Laura while trying not to show emotion and opting for a much stricter parentage. Wolverines character arc in this movie is so well-written, multilayered and complex. The writers truly nailed everything that makes this character so appealing, iconic and tragic in the span of over 2 hours. You get the sense that Wolverine has been weighed down by a lot of suffering, trauma and loss. Hes looking for a good death and has lost any interest in partaking in the simple little things that make life worth living. His meeting with Laura brings him the opportunity to redeem himself and find some much needed closure to his existence. Its truly a heart-wrenching performance that is very rarely seen in these kinds of movies and I find it very bold of James Mangold and Hugh Jackman to have the balls to not just make another audience pleasing superhero action movie, but to take the time to explore these characters in a new light to reveal different sides to these legendary characters, while also trusting that the audience will welcome this fresh change of pace. Plus who doesnt wanna watch Logan shove his claws into some thugs skull in a gorey R-rated fashion to Johnny Cashs Hurt?
But Hugh Jackman is just one side of the coin that makes this such a great movie, as without the revelation that is the young Dafne Keen this film simply wouldnt work. If you are going to take Logan from the rude, arrogant, selfish, depressing drunk he is at the beginning of this film to a hero who gladly lays down his life to protect the innocent just at the exact moment he finally learns how to live a good life, you need someone or something that will provoke this change. A character like Wolverine is not like to want to change his behaviour after everything hes lived through. Dafne Keens  LauraX-23 is the key to his redemption and purpose. Laura is the much needed source of light that Logan needed to find in this dark, futuristic world in order to give his life meaning. At the start of the film he seemingly acts distant towards her, probably wishing not to get too attached to this kid so as to stave off any potential grief he may experience as a result of her loss. Most of Lauras interactions are mainly between her and Charles Xavier now in his nineties and suffering from dementia. Throughout the film Xavier constantly tells Logan how alike the two are and is constantly pushing him to open up to her more and to enjoy every second of time he has left, to leave his pain behind and move on. Charles ultimate death is the inciting act that promotes the flowering of the relationship of this unlikely father-daughter duo. Much of the second act is devoted to this repressed relationship that only seemingly emerges in bouts during moments of great emotion. They always cared deeply for each other, they just never expressed it as much as they should have.
Logan is the best example of indie movie filmmaking in the superhero genre. Instead of going for grand bombastic scale and cool action sequences everything is scaled down to service this heartbreaking story and its tortured characters. But most of all it delivers one of the best movies of the 21st century and a perfect ending to one of the most iconic characters in comic book movie history.

The end of an era has come upon us with Logan, James Mangolds second film for the X-Men series to star Hugh Jackman as The Wolverine together with the final intended performance from Jackman in the role. Ive grown up watching the X-Men films but now a heartbreaking end must come for a character whom Ive grown up watching all the years and with the Wolverine standalone films not particularly being above average (X-Men Origins Wolverine being rather dire), its only pleasing to see that Logan was as wonderful as it was but at the same time, it packs the emotional gut punch not only supported by knowledge this is going to be Jackmans final appearance, rather instead from the journey weve taken and how far weve gone.
Taking its inspiration from the Old Man Logan graphic novel, we are now watching the X-Men universe where mutants are now on the brink of extinction - as it is the year 2029. Logan, now in a rather weary state, is watching over an ailing Charles Xavier at the Mexican border. One last job swings by and Logan, reluctant at first, now finds himself out of hiding in order to protect a young mutant who may have ties with him more personal than ever. If anything at least had arisen from the knowledge that this is indeed Hugh Jackmans final appearance as Wolverine, we now have a potential for something greater with the younger stars but one last blow only was signaling a journeys end. But the sort of atmosphere that were working around here isnt exactly something weve seen prior for any of the X-Men films and for journeys end it was the only fitting way of telling such a story.
Logan works against the typical superhero structure by having the Western background come aboard. But in a sense theres a greater wonder coming about because James Mangold has a perfect understanding of what made Logan whom he was and now that the character is past his prime, the gritty, pessimistic atmosphere surrounding the nature of Wolverine is the only way to suit this character arc. Everything is now placed within a western environment but whats so much more satisfying is how Mangolds aesthetic never feels restrained in the slightest. In order to give Wolverine a proper farewell, it was only fitting that something near half as gritty or as unhappy could have come about and it was one amongst only a few reasons that makes Logan one of, if not, the best superhero film to have been released within this decade and the most mature film to carry the Marvel name.
When speaking of the maturity to a piece like Logan, whats offered in here feels as if it plays at opposite ends with the idea of maturity that was shown in the previous years Deadpool. For those who have grown up watching the X-Men films as they have run their course will have grown a greater connection with Wolverines journey on the count that he always carried a big part of their soul but now to see a superhero weary and exhausted from what he has been living all of this works to create a great sense of dedication on Hugh Jackmans end as Wolverine, and the very best that one would ever expect to see from any performance from him as the character. Mangolds film humanizes Old Man Logan to the very best effect, even with the sorts of powers he has carried through the years he now finds himself in a state he wants to leave everything behind almost in the manner that Hugh Jackman himself knows this will be his last time playing Wolverine.
Its worth noting that the whole film is so bleak which isnt a particularly familiar route for most superhero films these days, and the sort that best suits everything that Old Man Logan had been heading out for within the years we have grown connected with him. To think that with the gritty action scenes it almost seems as if it could play out like a western picture because Mangold doesnt want to head down that route for a film like Logan and it also reminisces towards memories of the Coen brotherss No Country for Old Men. But to see how Mangold handles the relationship between Wolverine and Xavier only shows a greater dedication on his part, noting the weight they carry upon their shoulders as a result of their past. Yet for how impressive Patrick Stewart and Hugh Jackman are, theres a new star arising from Dafne Keen in a truly unsettling performance from a young actress her age.
I could be speaking merely as one who grew up on the X-Men franchise but to see where Wolverines journey has been taking him this whole time only made sense for why Logan would ever have played upon such a note contrasting what we traditionally would expect from such a film. For those who have grown up on the franchise, it was nothing more than a fitting, if rather saddening goodbye to an era that we have loved. For outsiders to the franchise, the best joy about Logan is that it still works even as a standalone effort and what is presented finds a greater effectiveness as a modern deconstruction of the pathos created by any superhero movie. After all these years of having watched Wolverine on the screen, it was beyond satisfying to see him get the film that he deserved, but at the same time, the fitting farewell that bids the start of a new era. We have only gone so far enough, now a new journey awaits.

Theres no denying it. Im the ultimate mark when it comes to taking a grounded, gritty swing at adapting graphic novels to film. Beyond that distinction, James Mangolds work has almost always spoken to me on an existential level, regardless of subject matter. I mean, Im a Dad, so basically Ford vs. Ferrari is a requirement for me to adore, but even memories of my cool older sister showing me GirlInterrupted as a preteen, in hindsight, subconsciously started to shape my understanding on mental health and how layered these things truly are. To summarize more succinctly, for my personal tastes, Mangolds emotional anvil of a finale to Foxs X-Men saga, Logan, feels destined to be an all-time favorite. And its just so fkn badass, regardless of personal context. 
The final entry into Foxs X-Men franchise abandons the glossy, CGI-heavy look of its predecessors for a sun-bleached, dusty aesthetic, riddled with a hopeless despair. More Neo-Noir-Western with a touch of post-apocalypticism than scrappy comic book in tone, the world we find the X-Mens most Hope-inducing leader is a bleak, grittily tactile and irremediably broken one. And Ive gotta say, its just a perfect setting to bring the X-Men universe to a heart-wrenching conclusion, while still offering another gorgeous layer of Hugh Jackmans series-spanning character. 
Beyond its brilliantly woven narrative which is propped up incredibly by Sir Patrick Stewart, Boyd Holbrook and Dafne Keens nuanced performances, it is behind its action choreography which brings things to another level entirely for me. Quite simply, Mangold crafts some of the best action sequencing and blocking that any film could offer. Logan is a piece of art that can easily be viewed with as much reverence and respect by Comic-Con enthusiasts as it can full on film bros, and I cant think of many other works that can so surely navigate through so many fandoms. And dammit, it still holds up just as strongly. 
Im not crying, you are.

My expectations for Logan werent that high at first. Im not much of a fan of the X-Men franchise and I do find the first two Wolverine solo outings particularly bad. What got me on board were the trailers. They left me with the impression that this actually could be an interesting film. Also I like Hugh Jackman and Patrick Stewart, and director James Mangold made Identity and Cop Land (where he managed to get a genuinely good performance out of Sylvester Stallone), two movies I like quite a lot.
Jackmans last appearance as Wolverine very well may be one of the best comic book films ever made. I purposely avoided the term superhero film because in the end it is as much a superhero film as Nolans The Dark Knight trilogy was. For those of you who are about to go into cardiac arrest, rest assured this is the only aspect they have in common. Logan would be best described as the old Johnny Cash meets the original Mad Max. A noirish western set in a world gone to shit where hardly any mutants are left. Our hero has grown old and weary of life. His self-healing powers are dwindling away, he is depressed, self-doubt gnaws on his mind. Seeking solace in booze only makes matters worse. On top of his own problems he has to take care of a senile Charles Xavier, who is no longer able to control his mental powers. So when he encounters the young mutant girl Laura who is chased by a company that attempts to create super soldiers, he is more than only a bit reluctant to get involved.
Its a grim, remorseless scenario the filmmakers set up, fully confiding in Jackmans ability to get the audience to care for their abrasive protagonist. And it works beautifully, Jackman turned in a possibly career-best performance. Patrick Stewart also brought his A game but the real highlight is Dafne Keen as Laura. She has hardly any dialogue, yet she commands almost every scene she is in.
And in case you wondered if Logan earned its R-rating, it most definitely did. While it is batshit violent it never crosses the line to become self-indulgent and gratuitous. Unlike Deadpool, which used its violence only as a gimmick, Logan is clearly targeted at a mature audience. Its bleak, hopeless tone often reminds me of Watchmen. Thanks to Jackmans gut-wrenching, nuanced performance the film possesses the emotional weight to provide the bleakness with a solid foundation. Its a small scale film in regard to the world it shows and the action scenes never get near the bloated spectacle of so many other comic book movies. Yet the emotional impact is far greater than any CG crapfest could ever deliver.
Logan may not be a perfect film, but it certainly is a worthy and suprisingly thoughtful swan song for Hugh Jackmans Wolverine and Patrick Stewarts incarnation of Charles Xavier.

Logan  James Mangolds Masterpiece of Grit, Emotion, and Brutal Elegance. 
Logan by James Mangold, is a near-perfect film that transcends the superhero genre with its raw emotional depth, intense action, and beautifully grounded storytelling. Set in a bleak future, the film follows an aging, battle-worn Logan as he cares for a frail Charles Xavier while reluctantly becoming the protector of a young mutant, Laura. 
Mangold strips away the larger-than-life elements typical of the X-Men films, delivering a gritty, intimate character study. Every aspect of the film excels from the stunning cinematography capturing the desolate landscapes, to the impeccable performances that anchor the film in emotional realism. Jackman delivers his finest portrayal of Wolverine, showing a man broken by years of suffering, while Keens ferocious yet vulnerable Laura offers a fresh, powerful dynamic.
The films R-rating allows for brutal, visceral action, but its never gratuitous each scene is grounded in character-driven stakes. The score by Marco Beltrami adds a haunting, understated layer to the films mood. 
Logan stands as a masterclass in how to close a character arc with grace and impact. Mangolds direction ensures that every frame, every line, and every action resonates, making Logan one of the most remarkable films in the superhero genre.

The Western frontier was once a dystopia to those who settled it. The Wild West as it were. In the waning minutes of Logan, a group of children make a mad dash for their safe haven across the border, running through pine groves and mountainsides with gorgeous plateaus and rock-faces decorating the chaos. Wolverines last foray into the spotlight highlights the mesmerizing American landscape as a place of opportunity and hopea place that has always been this beacon for people since its inception. 
The reverie of the farmhouse scene induces a calm before the storm, showing that even through dystopia the heart of America still exists. This heart, is the kind people that take a stranger in their home and give them food. This scene is also a callback to the homestead and the gunslingers that came riding up from the horizon.
James Mangolds brilliance is found within his revived take of the western genre, breathing into it an understanding I have not seen so well handled since my recent watch of Shane. It is not only appropriate that Mangold pays homage to the landmark film, but it is altogether the greatest example of genre convergence to meet the 21st century. This is perhaps why I rate Logan higher than its predecessor. While we are being buried by the superhero joint by the minute, its easy to get lost and wonder why so many folks are either fascinated by the phenomenon or dont take to it at all. But what Logan has and deeply understands (versus other films of its ilk and while still paying tribute to its forebears), is it demonstrates the value of legacy. The Wolverine reluctantly finds himself in the middle of a battle of traditions he never wanted to be a part of even with Xavier whispering hints ever along the way. 
Logan does not push for any sort of overt tradition, per sethe film is clearly boilerplate in its bones and character driven in its heart, yet Lauras eulogy to her father gives us all the answers we need. The finale manages to be cutthroat and exhilarating, while also making us glossy-eyed for a particular end. The greatest character trait of the western hero resides in Logan Howlett. Like Shane he is a branded man, one that has killed and done wrong, yet he is the man that was needed to save and push forward the newest generation to salvation while simultaneously ending his own kind. People maybe dont believe in tradition and all its connotations, but it is these values that give life meaning (as well as this film) and provide a glimmer of hope when the next dystopia comes a knockin. Here, the western lives.

Almost all stories and characters need an ending. It is an essential part of the process. You can have a great start, a great middle, but its incomplete without the great ending.
(a few exceptions to this - Bond, Dr Who are two right off the top of my head. And even Dr Who has quasi endings with the regeneration)
I wasnt really into comic books growing up. I enjoyed a couple of the X-Men movies  especially X2  but I never had any strong attachment to Wolverine. When Logan came out and it was positioned as the final chapter for both the character and the entire 20002015 X-Men universe, I didnt really care all that much.
I was genuinely surprised by how much I loved Logan. It felt like a truly fantastic ending. Seeing a down and out Wolverine putting together one last run was an excellent way to finish things off. Having Picard in there as well really helped give the necessary finality to the long-running X-Men story (without Picard, I dont think it would have worked  in the bigger X-Men picture). 
Essentially, Logan nailed the ending. Which was a major reason why I loved it so much. 
Now that we are almost ten years later and we have learned it was NOT the ending (I dont care about multi-verse workarounds, Hugh Jackman, Patrick Stewart, and more, are back on screen. Thats all that matters) I honestly have lost a significant amount of love I had for this film. Without that great hook of being the final ride, now it just comes across as a good (at times very good) movie. 
I know the studios are going to want their money, and many of the Marvel fans can appreciate the movie Logan while still happy getting more from the charactersactorsuniverse. But in a world of remakes, reboots and IP, I just really miss the ending part of stories. I too hate saying goodbye, but to me, a good ending is what takes a story to the next level.
So Logan was borderline 4.5 when I thought it was the last run for the X-Men, but now, its a solid 3.5.

Director James Mangold and star Hugh Jackman gave us the ultimate WolverineLogan and a near perfect send-off to the beloved character. 
Its not all great though. The movie is slow at times and I could feel the runtime. The darkness of the story can feels a little depressing at times and slightly loser the entertainment value. I also wasnt a big fan of the Wolverine clone idea. But the good largely outweighs the bad here. The story is gripping and timely, the performances, especially by Hugh Jackman and Patrick Stewart are very strong, the emotional beats hit hard, the character moments are well-written and performed and I really like the Western style and Shane inspired themes. 
I am glad the studio had the balls and vision to green light an R-rated film like this. The bloodiness and brutality of it gives the story weight and makes the stakes feel higher and more personal than before. Logan has never been more vulnerable and humanmortal. Hugh Jackman drags himself through the movie and one can feel the weight of every step he takes. His final moments are both touching and poignant. Makes you hope he finally found some peace. 
Logan may not be a perfect film but I am incredibly grateful that this was the Swansong my favorite X-Men character got. It is a emotional, dark and personal story that brings the character to a bittersweet but fitting end. Lets just hope that the Deadpool and Wolverine movie doesnt fuck it up.

Envelhecido, cansado de violência e sem vontade de viver, Wolverine é o centro trágico de Logan, um drama que só por acaso é também um filme de super-herói
O cabelo e a barba cheios de fios brancos, o rosto vincado, as olheiras arroxeadas, a respiração ofegante, o andar trôpego este não é o Wolverine das sete aparições anteriores do personagem no cinema. Ameaçado por uma gangue que tenta roubar as rodas da limusine com a qual ele ganha a vida na texana El Paso, na fronteira com o México, Wolverine toma socos e cambaleia. Com dificuldade, faz as garras letais de adamantium projetar-se por entre os dedos. Mas elas nem saem mais em toda a sua extensão. As articulações de Wolverine estão inflamadas, e uma tosse seca interrompe os seus esforços. Expulsar da carne as balas que os inimigos disparam contra ele, antes tão fácil, agora é um sofrimento. O próprio adamantium, o metal indestrutível que substituiu seus ossos, o está intoxicando. Mais venenoso ainda é o cansaço de Wolverine com a vida. Depois de 180 anos sobre a Terra, o mutante de vigor inesgotável, ferocidade mal e mal controlável e capacidade de se curar de qualquer ferimento é uma sombra do que foi, e quer entregar os pontos. Até já planejou o modo como o fará, e só não o fez ainda porque ele e o albino Caliban (Stephen Merchant) têm sob seus cuidados outro mutante, ainda mais frágil do que eles o professor Xavier (Patrick Stewart), cujo cérebro poderoso está sob ataque da demência. É tristíssimo o crepúsculo dos mutantes em Logan (Estados Unidos, 2017)  triste como toda doença, velhice e degeneração humanas. Da decrepitude e da necessidade de vencê-la mais uma vez que seja, o diretor e roteirista James Mangold tira uma tragédia pungente, à qual Hugh Jackman se entrega por inteiro. Até notícia em contrário, esta é a sua despedida do personagem. E ele a faz valer a pena.
Logan é o nome verdadeiro de Wolverine, o que ele tinha antes de sua mutação se manifestar por completo, durante a carnificina da Guerra Civil americana de 1861-1865. É o nome do filme, também, porque as glórias de Wolverine estão diminuídas ao ponto de quase não passarem de lembrança. E porque, contemplando a possibilidade do fim, ele tem de acertar contas com o homem que há dentro dele. Não será um processo simples a trajetória de LoganWolverine é de uma violência indizível, e ele não está desejoso de um reencontro consigo mesmo.
Está-se em 2029, mas pouca coisa anuncia o futuro na paisagem concebida por Mangold e Jackman. A única mudança relevante é a ausência de mutantes quase todos que havia pereceram num acidente provocado pela demência de Xavier, e há mais de vinte anos não se tem notícia de um novo nascimento. Logan acha, portanto, que Xavier delira quando lhe diz que está em comunicação telepática com uma menina portadora do gene X. Mas ela existe de fato Laura (a impressionante Dafne Keen), de 11 anos, tem o esqueleto e as lâminas de adamantium de Wolverine, e o mesmo poder de cura. Não fala e, quando acuada, exibe uma selvageria inocente de si mesma, mas cujo rastro de corpos e mutilações é assustadoramente real. Laura é uma criança que precisa com urgência de limites  e de salvação. Logan, Caliban e Xavier são sua última chance contra o exército particular que a persegue (e cujos financiadores permanecem durante bom tempo um mistério). Mas a fuga árdua, prolongada, repleta de sangue, não faz muito por promover os afetos familiares ou reconciliar Logan com a ideia de paternidade, que o repugna e o consome em igual medida.
Mangold e Jackman já trabalharam outra duas vezes juntos antes de Logan (na comédia romântica Kate  Leopold e em Wolverine Imortal), e aqui a parceria chega à fruição plena. De maneira explícita, Logan traça um paralelo com Os Brutos Também Amam, de 1953, em que um pistoleiro tenta reconstruir a vida na paz, perto de um menino que o idolatra (Xavier e Laura assistem ao filme juntos na TV). E de maneira implícita, mas nítida, ele referencia Os Imperdoáveis, de 1992. No western revisionista que deu os Oscar de filme e direção a Clint Eastwood, o protagonista é um matador que sai de uma aposentadoria tão miserável quanto a de Wolverine para um último trabalho. A causa é justa, até necessária, mas o veneno de matar tem o gosto de sempre  intolerável. Só na definição mais circunstancial Logan pode ser chamado de um filme de super-herói. O que diretor e ator fazem, aqui, é lançar seu herói entre as tragédias humanas das quais não se pode escapar o ocaso, a mortalidade e a constatação tardia de que, mesmo quando a vida é longa, tanta coisa pode faltar a ela.

Logan - Dark, Emotional and Action Packed!
Logan (2017) is a superhero drama movie directed by James Mangold, who also co-wrote the screenplay with Michael Green and Scott Frank. The movie features Hugh Jackman, Patrick Stewart, Dafne Keen, Richard E. Grant, Stephen Merchant, and Boyd Holbrook.
Serving as the third movie in the Wolverine trilogy and inspired by the Old Man Logan comic book storyline by Marvel Comics, Wolverine, an aging mutant (Hugh Jackman), must protect a young mutant called Laura (Dafoe Keen) from a team of evil cyborgs named the Reavers. With the support of an unwell Professor Xiaver (Patrick Stewart), will Wolverine help Laura find a way to protect herself by fighting back against the Reavers?
For a superhero movie, the story was unique compared to other Marvel movies. This is because it has a dark and dramatic tone in the style of The Dark Knight (2008) rather the usual superhero movie that has comedy and action elements. With its great slow pacing, the story has fantastic character development, breathtaking battle sequences, and an emotional weight to make the viewers heartbroken in some scenes. The movie explores the strong themes of family, Good vs. Evil, loss, violence, and death. These have been handled perfectly by James Mangolds directing skills because he wanted to make the movie a great send off to Wolverine.
The performances were stunning since the cast have used serious emotive language and strong body language to convey the movies depressing and thrilling atmosphere. This makes the audience feel excited and emotional as they witness the life threatening acts come alive in a strong execution. Hugh Jackman has delivered the best performance in the movie because of how strong his emotions and energy were to capture the old Wolverines strong characteristics.
The costume designs were incredible since they remain faithful to the source material and that the viewers can visually understand what role and personality each character has.
Unlike Hellboy (2019), the gore and swearing were well executed because they were not overused as the story spends more time exploring its powerful themes.
The special effects were outstanding as it makes the additional features on the characters appear realistically, which also applies to the graphic content as Wolverine kills the enemies. For instance, Wolverines beard was actually digital rather than having Hugh Jackman grow a larger beard. This is an incredible feature of the film as it moves realistically.
John Mathiesons cinematography skills were marvellous because there were some brilliant and memorable camera shots that draw the viewers attention. For example, one scene displays a scene of Wolverine in front of window during the sunset. Mathieson has done this because he wants to catch the viewers attention to the main subject (Wolverine) as the sunset makes him appear intimidating.
Marco Beltramis soundtrack was magnificent and beautiful. This is because it changes the mood of the exciting tone of the overall X Men franchise into a more serious and emotional mood. This makes the viewers upset as they see Wolverine, Professor X, and Dafne Keen go through an intense journey to stop the Reavers.
The movies target audience are people who enjoy watching superhero movies with drama elements. This is because the movie has a dark and serious tone, strong language, and graphic content that is unsettling for younger viewers. This also appeals to older fans of the X Men franchise as they want to see how the movie will end the character arc of their two favourite characters, in addition to recommending the franchises best films to a new generation of superhero fans.
Overall, Logan (2017) has been an emotional revisit because of its intense story full of engaging characters, thrilling battle scenes, and a heartbreaking weight. In my opinion, this is worth the watch! This is The Dark Knight of the X Men franchise! This must inspire future dark and graphic superhero movies! This is one of the greatest superhero movies of all time!

Back in the summer of 2000, 20th Century Fox brought the X-Men film to the big screen, back in the day when comic booksuperhero films werent taken as serious as they are now (to a certain degree) by major studios. It also launched the career of then well known stage actor Hugh Jackman to a worldwide audience playing the role of Wolverine. Fast forward to seventeen years later and Hugh Jackman makes his ninth and final outing as the iconic character in Logan. The film is obviously inspired by the Old Man Logan comic and with the studio allowing James Mangold and Co. to make an X-Men film Rated-R and it feels like thats due to the box office success of Deadpool last year. Were taken to the near future where mutants are all but extinct as no new mutants have been born in two decades. Logan is making a living (sort of) as a limo driver in a town on the Mexican border, where he lives in a remote makeshift home where he looks after Charles Xavier. However for Logan, hes pulled into a new mission as a young mutant being pursued by dark forces, he is drawn back into action despite his hopelessness.




Ill admit that its taken me a few hours after the screening (so its now 4a.m as I write this review) to digest my thoughts overall and I have to say this film floored me. Its a comic book film that plays more into the genre of a western and grounds superhero antics to a minimum compared to what weve seen in comic book films before it (The Dark Knight comparisons are being made for a reason here). Its also one of the most bleak films in the X-Men franchise whilst also feeling distinct in tone to what came before. There is bursts of humour placed in the films two hour and fifteen minutes runtime, but its kept to a bare minimum as the film relies on character interactions and arcs. The Wolverine that weve grown up watching has now become a shadow of his former self, hes old and with his healing abilities not being what they used to be, he has to numb the constant chronic pain he gets by hitting the bottle. Not only is he physically beaten up, mentally hes broken as well as everyone he knew has died all for the exception of Charles Xavier, who he has to take care of as the most powerful mind is now suffering from dementia and also has seizures which can be dangerous to everyone around him. Its sad to see these characters weve followed for seventeen years now become broken shells of themselves and it makes the moments where they have moments of old gory resurfacing, briefly, can be beautiful to watch unfold. The action sequences are more condensed than your average comic book film, focusing primarily on claw-to-hand combat sequences and also with the R rating, Logan is the most graphically violent comic book film since Zack Snyders Watchmen. You would also think that seeing Wolverine slashing bad guys for the five-hundredth time would be dull.....its not. Hugh Jackman has been playing the role for a long time and yet he manages to bring something new to the table as we see Logan at his most vulnerable and broken. Ive always liked Jackman in the role and I think here hes puts everything he got into his swan song, I thought he was absolutely terrific. Patrick Stewart is great as elderly Charles Xavier, playing a different side of the character weve never seen before yet maintaining a few traits that we know and love about him. Making her big screen debut alongside them is eleven-year-old Dafne Keen playing the role of Laura Kinney, a young mutant that is being hunted by a military group lands into Logans life. Dafne Keen almost steals the show from everyone involved here as she doesnt talk and does so much with so little in conveying emotional from her facial expressions when she interacts with other characters. The military group in question is led by Donald Pierce, played with charismatic charm by Boyd Holbrook, who is relentless in his pursuit in capturing Laura Kinney by any method necessary. The direction from James Mangold is terrific here as is John Mathieson cinematography. 




Logan is so tonally and violently different from the X-Men films that came before it, I think (and know) a few casual film viewers of the franchise will be bored by the purposely slow burn pace of the film, as well as feeling that the violence could be too much for some. I mean if youre taking kids to this film expect legs, hands and heads to be rolling around the place when the claws come out to play, as well as including blood and open that rare siting of boobs that pop up just to let you know, incase you forgot, youre watching an R rated film. Theres also quite a bit of swearing thrown into the mix, mostly from Xavier himself, but Ill admit that in the first act it did feel like it was being thrown around too much. As for the films villain, I get why they went with that villain of choice for this film as it fit with the overall narrative, but it falls with the recent X-Men films that the villain is one of the weakest aspects. For me personally, I wasnt that much of a fan of Marco Beltramis score here but that may change on repeated viewing. 



Logan is a sombre swan song for Hugh Jackman as the title character, going out with a bang in a western-vibe setting, soaked up in bloody violence and bleak tone throughout. Sometimes touching, sometimes funny and sometimes heartbreaking, James Mangold has managed to create an absolutely terrific film that feels like the most important comic book film since Christopher Nolans The Dark Knight.

Un solo nome. Quello con cui abbiamo imparato a conoscere il personaggio a partire dalla sua prima apparizione cinematografica nel 2000 con il primo film della saga di Bryan Singer.
Un titolo che ne richiama altri contenenti nomi propri dei propri eroi infatti vengono in mente Gunny, Dirty Harry (o Shane di George Stevens, citato tra laltro in una scena). Non a caso vengono in mente i prodotti degli anni 70 e 80 a cui il film di James Mangold sembra guardare (in particolare a Clint Eastwood, ispirazione principale per il Wolverine fumettistico).
Il terzo capitolo delle avventure del mutante con gli artigli di adamantio é quello che si prende i rischi maggiori e che, allo stesso tempo, resta fedele alla tradizione. Ambientato in un futuro prossimo in cui la razza mutante é sullorlo dellestinzione e un incontro inaspettato porterà un Logan malato e invecchiato per avvelenamento da adamantio e un professor Xavier affetto da demenza senile a iniziare un viaggio fondamentale (il trio mal assortito che si formerà richiama quello de Un Mondo Perfetto. Ancora una volta Eastwood) per la sopravvivenza dei loro simili. 
Quello di Mangold é un cinecomic crepuscolare, ma chiamarlo cinecomic sarebbe un azzardo (può essere considerato un vero e proprio western, un viaggio on the road in cerca di una vaga terra promessa). I protagonisti rimangono gli stessi, ma ormai si può dire addio ai combattimenti tuonanti e sfrenati a base di effetti speciali. A regnare sono la crudezza e la spietatezza (non solo nei combattimenti, più crudi e realistici che mai) dellambiente secco e polveroso che non sembra risparmiare alcun essere vivente, tranne quelli più geneticamente predisposti.
Logan appare come un guerriero stanco, burbero, relitto e ombra delleroe di un tempo. Resta soprattutto un individuo disilluso con rancori e profonde perdite alle spalle. Il suo ritorno allazione sembra richiamare lennesimo eroe eastwoodiano, il William Munny de Gli Spietati, e la relazione che si viene a creare con la giovane Laura, figlia indesiderata e inizialmente malvoluta, si avvicina a quella tra Ryan ONeal e sua figlia Tatum (protagonisti occasionali di un altro viaggio in unAmerica arida e depressa).
Questo resta comunque uno dei cinecomics più drammatici, coinvolgenti e commoventi degli ultimi anni in cui la parte più umana, misericordiosa e in apparenza più debole delleroe colpisce più di qualunque altra sua versione ultra-potenziata e con pieno controllo dei poteri, resa famosa dalla cultura popolare. Just one name. The one with which we have learned to know the character since his first film appearance in 2000 with the first film of the Bryan Singer saga.
A title that recalls others containing the proper names of its heroes in fact, Gunny, Dirty Harry (or Shane by George Stevens, mentioned among other things in one scene) comes to mind. It is no coincidence that the products of the 70s and 80s that James Mangolds film seems to look to come to mind (in particular Clint Eastwood, the main inspiration for the Wolverine from the comic books).
The third chapter of the adventures of the mutant with the adamantium claws is the one that takes the greatest risks and which, at the same time, remains faithful to tradition. Set in a near future where the mutant race is on the brink of extinction and an unexpected encounter will lead a sick and aged Logan from adamantium poisoning and a Professor Xavier suffering from senile dementia to begin a fundamental journey (the ill-matched trio that will be formed recalls the one from A Perfect World. Once again Eastwood) for the survival of their peers.
Mangolds one is a twilight cinecomic, but calling it cinecomic would be a gamble (it can be considered a real western, a road trip in search of a vague promised land). The protagonists remain the same, but now we can say goodbye to the thunderous and unbridled fights based on special effects. What reigns are the crudeness and ruthlessness (not only in the fights, more raw and realistic than ever) of the dry and dusty environment which does not seem to spare any living being, except those most genetically predisposed.
Logan appears as a tired, gruff warrior, a wreck and shadow of the hero of the past. Above all, he remains a disillusioned individual with resentments and deep losses behind him. His return to action seems to recall yet another Eastwood hero, William Munny from Unforgiven, and the relationship which is created with the young Laura, an initially unwanted daughter, is similar to that between Ryan O Neal and his daughter Tatum (occasional protagonists of another trip to a dry and depressed America).
However, this remains one of the most dramatic, engaging and moving comics of recent years in which the most human, merciful and apparently weakest part of the hero strikes more than any other ultra-enhanced version of him with full control of his powers, made famous from popular culture. You shouldnt expect a spectacular and impressive death like in most blockbusters (in this sense the film, the second product linked to the X-Men forbidden to minors, is a product that goes against the conventions of the genre itself) here the warriors leave in the least dignified way possible and the end of their journey is accompanied only by looks that slowly abandon themselves to the pain and the flow of tears without having the possibility of exchanging definitive farewell words. So, down with WolverineLong live Logan, the legend, the lone warrior who finds and accepts his humanity until the end.

Logan (2017)
Every once in a while, there comes a movie that leaves me so speechless, that I just dont think anything I can type up will do it justice. Having gone through all the other X-Men movies, its easy for me to say that Logan was worth the wait. Its a powerful, tragic and much more grounded tale than past entries. It will thrill, upset, shock, and even amuse you.
As of here, Logan is one of the few of his kind remaining, now trying to live a normal life as a limo driver while he and albino mutant Caliban take care of a heavily aged Professor Xavier in the outskirts of the Texas desert. Id rather not go into too much detail, but lets just say that a younger mutant named Laura appears in his life, an escapee on the run from Transigen (a corporation dedicated to breeding young mutant experiments).
Here, we see a Logan more complex and human than ever before. Hes a shadow of his former self, a gruff and aged alcoholic who has lost almost everyone he ever considered family. Charles is just the same, withering away in his chair just waiting for his inevitable death, knowing that his goal to help human and mutant-kind co-exist has all been for nothing. Once Laura comes on the scene though, it becomes a battle for survival as the two of them try to get her to safety, all while a vicious group of mercenaries and agents pursue them.
To put it short, everyone gave it their best, the cast especially. Jackman, a young but brilliant Dafne Keen as Laura, and a practically mean and effective performance from Boyd Holbrook as Donald Pierce, a villain so sadistic that youll hate his very guts. Lets not forget Patrick Stewart, whose depiction of Charles from a once wise and knowledgable professor to a foul-mouthed old grump (with less control over his powers) is hilarious as it is upsetting. 
The really great thing here though is that for the first time, were actually presented a Wolverine film that gives us the raw grittiness other instalments were lacking. Its unapologetically gory from start to finish, blood is spilled, limbs are hacked off, and people are decapitated. You think you can be prepared for the onslaught, but believe me that you simply cant. Theres just so many unexpected moments that make the action and battle scenes as hard-hitting as they are.
Even though its undoubtedly the most intense and emotional of the series, it still has a sense of humour from time to time (even if it gets lost within the bloody carnage). Its very big on atmosphere as well. The beautiful desert landscapes (accompanied by the hauntingly brilliant themes of Marco Beltrami who I previously underappreciated) really emphasise the loneliness and isolation that Logan feels from the outside world.
Am I overpraising? Maybe, but I dont care. I thought Mangold did a respectable enough job with The Wolverine, but not only did he outdo himself here, but probably every other director who has worked on the series. This is quite simply a brilliant send off for a character thats been through absolute hell and back. Jackman has perfectly nailed the role for over 15 years, but now couldnt be a better time to move on. 
All I can say is, great job everyone.

Third time is definitely the charm for Wolverine films. I will stop myself from talking about the first one and I thought the second one was average, so I think they shouldve went with this approach to the character right from the start instead of waiting for the very last film to go full-on violence. However, it does make Logan stand out more as the amazing film that it is. Its a film that is built in a way that it feels complete in every sense of the word, a film that isnt afraid of going the extra mile and successfully reaches it.
As expected when taking into account the rating of the film, Logan doesnt refrain from showing violence. The harsh action sequences are wonderfully choreographed and very entertaining to watch, and some of that is due to the great camerawork that follows and captures Laura and Logan as they fight as the iconic duo they prove to be. The film has a story and it makes sure it takes the time to tell it in a clear way to the audience. Some characters, like the villain, couldve been given more screen time and scenes for us to get to know them better but this is Logan, Professor X and Lauras film, a film that wants to be entertaining but at the same time realistic and emotional, so Im not even the tiniest bit bothered by it. 
In exploring that trio and the connections they all have with each other, Logan builds a core, a heart for itself. It establishes a connection between the fictional characters and the real people that accompany them through a two-hour film. That is not only supported by the script that is tightly-written and deservedly Oscar-nominated, but also to the score that gives the final touch without being overwhelming and, of course, the excellent cast. Hugh Jackman and Patrick Stewart are definitely the standouts with memorable performances and one could argue they, especially Patrick, were snubbed by the Academy from a nomination in acting categories.
All of these elements set the tragic and powerful goodbye that serves as the perfect ending to these characters and their journeys. Together they make a violent, harsh, real, human and heartfelt film that completely stands out in its genre and that is a reminder that superhero films can indeed be adult and satisfy the audience with its story in every way a film should and could.
