Now this is a comic book movie I can dig. It manages to avoid some of the pitfalls that I find tedious in other such films. Thankfully, there is no hour long origin story, which many comic book movies insist on. Just like the comic book medium itself, Logan leaves it up to the audience to either go and explore the history and the world of the characters further or to just enjoy the slice of the story they have right in front of them. In this instance, the fact fact that this particular slice of story works mighty fine on its own certainly does help.
Another pet hate of mine is when a comic book movie devolves into a CGI wank-fest of barely intelligible action sequences that bang on for an impenetrable and mindless hour before the never-can-it-come-too-soon end. For me, the more these manufactured images become stupendously fantastic and subsequently fractured from reality, the more they start to seem like a frenzy of fast moving dancing storm clouds Pretty maybe, but of no consequence at all. Not so in Logan, this film has some real rip-snorting chase sequences, shoot-em-ups, hand-to-hand combat and lots of vicious slashing and stabbing. It is is visceral, up close and personal.
I just realised that James Mangold directed Walk the Line, and that kind of makes a lot of sense. In that film, we see Johnny Cash struggle to deal with the hurt that he has done unto others, especially those that he loves. Logan faces similar issues of guilt, self-punishment and redemption. Albeit, for Johnny Cash it was substance abuse rather than adamantine claws that caused all the damage. Unfortunately, Logan is played by Hugh Jackman. He tries really hard to bring Clint Eastwoods stoic and taciturn persona to the screen, but all his efforts just betray themselves in a performance that seems as protracted and agonised as his characters deteriorating condition.
On the other hand, what a treasure is unearthed in Dafne Keen! As Laura, she looks so cute, like a self-professed and pissed off little pixie. But you sure dont want to piss this little girl off and see her chuck a tantrum. She has the coolest most bad-ass fightin moves in the whole film. She could totally whip my butt. And there is something strangely affecting about watching a small child brutally destroying hordes of grown-up assholes. I hope that Dafne is able to graduate from the MCU when she grows up and become a fascinating force of her own in cinema one day.
Surprisingly, one of the people I just came out of the cinema with said that they thought this movie was bleak and depressing. Personally, I found it uplifting and full of hope. Sure, the mutants are on the brink of extinction and everyone is kind of miserable and dying for most of the film. But even when everything looks so  bleak and the world appears to have turned to shit, we can always look to the children for a greater sense of meaning and purpose beyond ourselves.
Even if those children are freaks made accidentally by an abortive and out of control evil experiment.

A world where Logan is no longer a five star film for me? I guess that exists now. Man, 2017 Noah would absolutely strangle current me to death. Make no mistake, as you can see from my new rating, I still think that this is a fantastic movie. Incredibly easy for me to still call this one of the best superhero films of all-time, and still a miracle that a movie like it exists at all. I continue to love how dark, violent, and very heartfelt this film is. Its so clear that the love and care this was given from everyone involved is something you dont see in much of anything at its budget level, and its about as perfect as a send-off to an iconic figure of this genre as you can imagine. Pretty much every performance here sings, Jackman goes without saying, but I somehow feel like Dafne Keen still doesnt get the level of praise she deserves for this movie. This version of Laura is so haunting and frankly scary, and Keen through her presence mixed with her just being a great actress, you never lose the child side to her being a manufactured machine for death. Of course, Logan as a film and Logan as a character within this film is all about trying to abandon that being the only thing that someone with blades in their hands can be. Being The Wolverine is something you pay the price for, which Logan does, but then theres the hope, the hands holding with blood sill smeared everywhere, that Laura and the other Mutants can be something more. Something better. Its of course not something that this film is hiding, another one of the best aspects about this movie is how its as much of a neo-western as it is a superhero film. Since thats said so much, I then also want to add what I dont think gets mentioned often where, although this is fashioned through a far darker lens than this material often gets, it feels like theres no shame felt about its source material. Logan is not just taking it seriously, its taking it sincerely, and theres a difference. This isnt drab, this isnt trying to ground things so much as its facing how tragic and relentless an uncensored X-Men story of a hopeless future would be. People face pain, others just get sliced into chunks, but somehow through sheer will and care, this is centered around hope and a continued dream for a better tomorrow. I dont even know how, but the ending didnt make me cry this time. However, the final shot especially remains one of my favorite images to come from a superhero film. Its the end of an era, the end of a legacy thats a core reason for why these damned super-powered are so popular in cinema in the first place. Still so grateful this exists, and that even if I no longer feel like its a masterpiece, its still an incredible work that deserves little else than admiration and awe. If I had to think about why its fallen for me, I dont know, it just doesnt quite coalesce and feel as devastatingly potent as it used to be. I dont really want to make it too dramatic because, again, I still love it. Last note, some shots have a noticeable digital shakiness that reminded me of late-career Michael Mann, and you can bet your ass I ate that up.

Nossa, que filme lindo. A maneira como ele trata a questão da mutação, com essa constante dúvida entre ser uma dádiva ou uma maldição, é provavelmente uma das coisas que mais gostei nele. Durante quase todo o universo X-Men, a mutação foi tratada de maneira muito abstrata identidade, preconceito, evolução etc. Logan pega tudo isso e transforma em algo muito mais íntimo. Aqui, ser mutante também significa envelhecer, perder pessoas e até questionar se sua existência trouxe mais sofrimento do que felicidade. E o papel do Charles é fundamental nisso. Acho muito bonita a imagem dele literalmente no fim da vida enquanto a Laura está começando a descobrir o mundo. Os dois são extremos diferentes da mesma história Charles representa uma geração que está desaparecendo, enquanto a Laura representa aquilo que vem depois. Mesmo tendo tão pouco tempo juntos, ela cria um vínculo muito forte com ele, como se percebesse não apenas quem ele é, mas também tudo o que ele representa.
E aí entra o Logan, que está preso exatamente entre essas duas gerações. Ele não consegue enxergar um futuro para si e está simplesmente sobrevivendo, até que sua relação com a Laura começa a mudar isso. A dinâmica entre os dois me remeteu muito a The Last of Us, na melhor maneira possível duas pessoas que inicialmente estão juntas por necessidade, uma criança que obriga um adulto emocionalmente destruído a continuar andando e, aos poucos, aquilo que era apenas uma missão se transforma em uma relação familiar. Só que o mais bonito é como o filme consegue fazer isso conversar diretamente com toda a trajetória do personagem. Logan passou décadas acreditando que era um monstro, machucando pessoas, afastando quem amava e tentando controlar aquilo que existia dentro dele. A Laura acaba sendo uma oportunidade de descobrir que aquilo que fazia dele um monstro também poderia fazer dele um pai.
Também gostei muito do uso de gore, porque seria muito fácil fazer um filme melancólico e transformar o Logan em uma versão domesticada. Porém, o filme não faz isso a violência fica ainda mais brutal, as garras atravessam corpos, cabeças são decepadas, mas agora tudo isso está em constante contraste com a humanidade que ele está recuperando. É uma dualidade que acompanha o personagem até seu último instante, o homem e o animal existindo simultaneamente. E é isso que torna sua despedida tão emocionante. Depois de passar a vida inteira tentando entender o que ele é, Logan finalmente encontra um lugar onde pode ser visto não apenas como uma arma ou um monstro, mas como alguém capaz de amar e ser amado.

Something gives me a feeling that Im only going to be all the more frustrated by what Dead Poets Society has left out as I think of it more. A part of me that loves Peter Weir and Robin Williams is begging for myself to love it, but in turn my experiences with Dead Poets Society become all the more frustrating. There are many good intentions to be found within such a film but in turn I cant help but say this is possibly, if not, the one Peter Weir film that I like the least. For how wonderful films like The Truman Show or Picnic at Hanging Rock are, this and Master and Commander The Far Side of the World stuck out to me as the most underwhelming entries from his body of work. As it stands, Dead Poets Society is a film that only managed to accomplish half of its goal.
The energy that Robin Williams puts into his performance as Professor John Keating is the most commendable aspect of the film. He sets a tone for the film while he lets his own energy define the very best moments of Dead Poets Society, and this is where Im finding that the film is suffering greatly. Williamss performance, especially from how one would recognize his energy with comedy, gives the film one tone that does not fit in so well with what else comes along. Im not trying to say this is a bad thing, because in films like The Fisher King, it most certainly works so well, but I cannot help but feel as if in Dead Poets Society it is placed for the wrong reasons.
It seems as if where Dead Poets Society falters is arising from the message it wants to send out. Im certainly not denying the inspirational tone which it wants to send out, but theres a feeling that the film is more undermining said message than actually sending it out properly. The film relies way too much on Robin Williamss performance to carry out how students indeed can be so heavily inspired by their own teachers, but to that extent it ends up forgetting to detail other important aspects that should have made such a message as relatable as it wants to be, in turn lessening the impact it wishes to create. For how inspirational it wishes to play out, what Dead Poets Society is offering is only half of that message.
Although Robin Williamss John Keating is undeniably a great character to set the tone for the film, the students on the other hand are never given so much of a distinctive personality that should have left a note to which audiences should relate to them. Many serious notes that the film should have been hitting especially within the middle segment ended up leaving me rather cold, because the students seemed to come off more as arrogant and unlikable. It certainly does not help that their motivations seem so random especially with the surprising refusal from Peter Weir to show what sort of impact John Keating has laid upon them. Its especially baffling when you remember what Peter Weir is capable of if one watches films like Picnic at Hanging Rock or The Truman Show (both of which stand as my favourites from the director at the moment).
More troublesome is the screenplay, which never fully establishes the many subplots it introduces. For how intelligent some of the dialogue sounds, theres an annoying tendency left by the screenplay to introduce subplots from the students which in turn are as underdeveloped as the students they are about. This is especially the most troublesome aspect to the film because of how it never tries to go beyond the predictable narrative arc which it presents. For how it is aspiring to touch upon more serious issues, the overall execution which we are left with by the film is heavily uninspired and thus the final product is both a jumbled mess and only half of a film (which I will get to sooner).
One aspect that somewhat saves the film from all the cloying sentimentality is the tragic ending. The ending is where Dead Poets Society indeed manages to reach the dramatic heights which it had been aspiring to achieve in the first place especially since it was within this moment Robin Williamss performance fits the tone it had wanted to accomplish the whole time. While I will not deny the fact that he is an unorthodox teacher, the over-reliance upon his comedy in order to show that Keating is a teacher unlike any ordinary, feels so blatant much to the point of emotional manipulation. Its a bit shameful that when the ending hits, we are only left with half of a film especially because many subplots which it introduces within the middle are left without any real sense of resolution.
Dead Poets Society is a highly frustrating film that certainly wants to carry an inspirational tone, but instead suffers to a predictable arc and an over-reliance on sentimentality that bogs everything down so heavily. In spite of excellent performances coming from Robin Williams together with Ethan Hawke amidst all of the students, none of Dead Poets Society rang a note that felt so inspiring as opposed to giving off the sickening feeling of superficiality. When one comes to consider what Peter Weir is capable of bringing out, what he presents in Dead Poets Society disappointingly tries too hard to latch onto the emotions but in turn, never fully realizes what it could have been and leaves on a note of incompletion.

OH CAPTAIN, MY CAPTAIN
Quando paramos para pensar em quem nos molda para a vida, geralmente os nossos pais é a primeira coisa que vem à mente, mas quem possui uma grande influência no nosso futuro é a escola. Um lugar de autodescoberta, onde criamos laços de amizade e aprendemos a primeira noção de responsabilidade social e afetiva. Os professores são os verdadeiros responsáveis pelos ensinamentos que levamos para o resto da vida. Em Sociedade dos Poetas Mortos, Robin Williams conseguiu o papel onde ele faz o que sempre fez bem inspirar à vida. É basicamente isso que o personagem dele, o professor de literatura Jonh Keating, faz com seus alunos, ele não somente ensina o grupo de garotos a ler e amar poesia, como também os ensina a buscarem seus desejos e viverem a liberdade de fazer suas própias escolhas, contrariando a estrutra educacional inglesa que prepara seus estudantes para ingressarem em Havard e se tornarem futuros advogados e médicos. Seguindo os costumes dos quatro pilares da Academia Welton, honra, tradição, excelência e disciplina, os garotos não são apenas vítimas do sistema autoritário e rígido, mas também dos seus pais e das expectativas que despejam em cima dos filhos. É justamente em meio a atividades excêntricas e nos poemas de autores famosos, que Keating faz com que os seus alunos passem a buscar o conhecimento, ao invés de simplesmente absorvê-lo, entrando em rota de colisão com a pedagogia inflexiva do internato, o que ajuda no entendimento dos meninos como indivíduos. É justamente ai que o filme acerta. Explorando o conflito entre romantismo e realismo, nós acompanhamos a jornada de amadurecimento dos jovens enquanto buscam se libertar das amarras que foram impostas a eles, motivados por essa nova perspectiva eles são conduzidos a descobrirem suas verdadeiras aspirações. Ainda que as vezes o longa-metragem seja excessivamente melodramático, todos os temas abordados são representados perfeitamente, discutindo desde repressão parental até os perigos de uma sociedade conformista, servindo de metáfora para criticar a censura a arte e nos ilustrar que devemos fazer o que queremos, ao invés de apenas aceitarmos um destino imposto pela sociedade.

Popularíssimo na comédia, prestigiado no drama com seu gênio às vezes atordoante, Robin Williams tornou irrelevante a distinção entre uma coisa e outra
          Quem nunca viu Robin Williams fazer stand-up não tem ideia do que ele era capaz. Na forma mais classicamente americana e desafiadora de comédia, aquela em que o comediante fica sozinho no palco, de microfone na mão, sem cenário, efeito sonoro nem nada que o possa amparar, e enfrenta a plateia, Robin Williams era, sem tirar nem pôr, um gênio. A maioria dos comediantes se lança nesse abismo munida de pelo menos um paraquedas  o texto cuidadosamente preparado, testado, lapidado, afiado de tal maneira que os espaços para o improviso vão sendo criados pela reação da audiência mas nunca se transformam em vácuo letal. Williams preferia a queda livre. Com uma rapidez de raciocínio inigualável, um repertório descomunal de referências, um dom singular para a imitação e paixão cega pelo risco, Williams ia de zero a cem em segundos qualquer ocasião  uma entrevista, uma participação num talk-show, um depoimento num documentário, um mergulho com golfinhos para um programa de natureza  podia virar (geralmente virava) um stand-up antológico simplesmente ao sabor do momento.
          A porção cômica de sua imensamente bem-sucedida carreira no cinema é, nesse sentido, uma amostra não raro brilhante, mas ainda assim incompleta e imperfeita, de seu talento monstruoso. Williams, porém, teve êxito comparável, ou até maior, no drama se filmes como Uma Babá Quase Perfeita o tornaram um ícone do humor-família (e quando ele fazia humor nada familiar os resultados eram ainda melhores), foi no papel do professor de Sociedade dos Poetas Mortos, aquele que incita seus jovens alunos a aproveitar o dia  carpe diem , ou ainda no do mentor de Matt Damon em Gênio Indomável (pelo qual ganhou o Oscar de coadjuvante) que ele se consagrou. A comédia dá popularidade, mas não confere prestígio. Como se ela fosse uma arte menor, ou mais fácil, ou menos sofrida do que o drama. Por transitar livremente entre uma e outro, Williams  que se suicidou por enforcamento, aos 63 anos, na segunda-feira 11, em sua casa na Califórnia  indignava-se em dobro com esse menosprezo.
          A comédia é a tragédia mais o tempo, disse o comediante (além de escritor, compositor etc.) Steve Allen nos anos 50. A formulação, de notável simplicidade e portanto elegância, é também de uma precisão indiscutível. Consta que existem, sim, comediantes ou humoristas felizes, serenos, satisfeitos. Os grandes raramente o são Groucho Marx, Lenny Bruce, Richard Pryor, Woody Allen, Steve Martin, Jim Carrey  a lista segue  têm todos biografia em que sentimentos como a insegurança, a neurose, a angústia, a raiva, o medo, a compulsão, a autodestruição, desempenham papel saliente. Robin Williams, tataraneto de senador, filho de executivo da indústria de automóveis, estudante por um breve período de ciências sociais e egresso da prestigiosíssima escola de artes Juilliard, foi assombrado por demônios persistentes álcool, drogas, depressão. Os dois primeiros, ele conseguiu conter desde 1983, quando nasceu Zak, o mais velho de seus três filhos (ele deixa ainda Zelda e Cody), estava sóbrio (A cocaína é o jeito de Deus dizer que você está ganhando dinheiro demais, observou). O terceiro demônio, a depressão, nunca deixou de rondá-lo seu humor de altíssima velocidade era, de certa forma, ao mesmo tempo uma expressão da mania que se opõe aos vales mais profundos do ânimo e uma libertação deles. Nunca se saberá o que empurrou Williams à sua decisão trágica, mas especula-se que o diagnóstico de Parkinson que ele recebera havia pouco  informação revelada por Susan Schneider, sua terceira mulher, alguns dias após sua morte  tenha contribuído para ela.
          Com seu estouro no seriado de TV Mork  Mindy, em 1978, Williams inaugurou uma carreira profícua e duradoura. Foram mais de sessenta filmes e inúmeras participações em humorísticos e episódios de seriados, além de dublagens para desenhos animados  como para o Gênio de Aladdin. Entre o ano passado e este, ele estrelara uma série, The Crazy Ones, cancelada após a primeira temporada. Deixa três filmes inéditos, sendo um deles uma animação. Seria uma desonra para com um homem de tal inteligência, porém, omitir as várias ocasiões em que seus excessos não resultaram positivos. Williams podia ser constrangedor (em Jack), piegas (Patch Adams), equivocado (Amor Além da Vida). Mas, entre uma coisa e outra, provava-se também assustador (Insônia), anárquico (Morra, Smoochy, Morra), ácido (Candidato Aloprado), hilariante (A Gaiola das Loucas), encantador (Bom Dia, Vietnã). Provava-se, enfim, uma criatura rara um homem com um talento que não apenas era imenso, como não se parecia com o de mais ninguém. O que Williams fazia, só ele sabia fazer.
Fazer comédia é fingir otimismo.

Robin Williams teaches a bunch of 1950s private school boys to reject conformity by all doing the same thing. Dead Poets Society is a shallow attempt at saying something profound - and even then the seemingly profound things its trying to say are just truisms. The film conducts itself with all the self-satisfaction of a freshman liberal arts major. It can only be cliche. 
This is a movie obsessed with self-important posturing. Is there anything less inspirational than a bunch of privileged white boys reciting poetry in a cave? The fact that that its so highly regarded says more about us, as a society seeking easy answers, than it does about the actual questions good education can teach us to ask.

There are movies that entertain, movies that move, and then there are movies that leave an imprint on your soul. Dead Poets Society belongs to that rarest category, a story that dares you to live. With every verse of Walt Whitman, every unorthodox lesson, and every whispered carpe diem, the movie challenges you to break free from the mundane and embrace lifes fleeting beauty. At the heart of it all is Robin Williams, not just acting but embodying inspiration itself. John Keating is more than a teacher hes a force of nature, a reminder that words and ideas can change the world.
Williams performance is nothing short of transcendent. He moves between humor and heartbreak effortlessly, making wisdom feel like an act of defiance. Theres a kindness in his eyes, a weight behind his words, as if he knows exactly how fragile dreams can be in a world so eager to crush them. His presence electrifies the movie, lifting the boys out of their rigid traditions and into something greater the realization that life is theirs to seize, not simply endure. His lessons arent just about poetry theyre about freedom, about daring to live fully, regardless of the consequences.
Then, those final 30 minutes. Oh, those devastating final 30 minutes. My heart was in my throat, my eyes blurred with tears, overwhelmed by the crushing weight of hope and tragedy woven together. Its a slow, aching build, a reminder that the pursuit of passion and individuality is not without cost. Yet even in the heartbreak, even in the pain, Keatings voice echoes Seize the day. Stand up. Live boldly. As the movie finished, with my face still wet with tears, I realized I would never watch Dead Poets Society the same way again.

sociedade dos poetas mortos, de peter weir, não é apenas um filme. é um lamento. um sussurro profundo vindo de jovens que mal começaram a existir e já sentem o peso de uma vida desenhada por mãos que não são as deles. não se trata apenas de ensino, ou poesia, ou rebeldia adolescente. é sobre o embate entre liberdade e obediência, entre o desejo de ser e a obrigação de parecer.
à primeira vista, a academia welton representa excelência tradição, disciplina, hierarquia. mas por trás de seus muros rígidos, há corpos frágeis sendo moldados à força para caber num molde que exige sucesso, não autenticidade. a chegada do professor keating é a faísca que toca esse terreno seco. ele não ensina literatura. ele evoca o espírito adormecido da liberdade em cada aluno. e por isso, se torna perigoso.
a atuação de robin williams é cheia de uma ternura inquieta. há algo no olhar do personagem que parece saber, desde o início, que está acendendo tochas em um túnel que talvez não possa percorrer até o fim. keating não promete salvação. não diz que será fácil. ele apenas aponta uma outra possibilidade de existir mais viva, mais honesta, mais dolorosa. seu carpe diem não é uma exortação ao prazer, mas um chamado à coragem de escutar a própria voz.
neil, talvez o mais trágico dos alunos, encarna esse conflito em sua forma mais devastadora. o palco, para ele, é mais do que arte. é o único lugar onde pode ser inteiro. mas a peça que encena diante do pai não é shakespeare é a performance contínua de um filho ideal sufocado por um papel que nunca quis. seu destino não é um ponto final, mas uma vírgula violenta num texto que nunca lhe permitiram escrever.
a escola tenta enterrar keating como se extinguir a fonte fosse apagar a sede. mas a última cena, com os alunos em pé sobre as carteiras, é um gesto silencioso de resistência. não há gritos. não há revolução. apenas a presença irreversível de algo que já foi despertado a consciência. keating foi afastado, mas a dúvida ficou. e uma vez que ela entra, nada mais é seguro.
terminei o filme com um nó na garganta e a mente em espiral. me peguei refletindo se estou realmente vivendo a vida que quero viver ou apenas a vida que esperam que eu viva. se minhas escolhas são de fato minhas ou apenas ecos das vozes que aprendi a obedecer.
peter weir não oferece respostas. apenas nos empurra para dentro das mesmas perguntas que assombram os personagens. o que é viver de verdade? para quem vivemos? até onde vai o preço da obediência?
sociedade dos poetas mortos permanece como um espelho incômodo para pais, escolas, e qualquer estrutura que tenta sufocar o desejo em nome da ordem. não há vilões caricatos. há apenas uma máquina que gira, triturando singularidades em nome de um futuro que ninguém parou para perguntar se vale mesmo a pena.
o filme não termina com um triunfo. termina com uma ausência. a ausência de neil. a ausência de uma geração que poderia ter florescido, mas foi podada antes de brotar. a ausência de liberdade em um mundo que tem medo do que não pode controlar.
talvez seja isso que mais doa perceber que viver exige coragem. e que, em muitos lugares, ainda se ensina mais o medo do que a coragem. carpe diem, afinal, não é uma frase bonita pra se tatuar. é um risco. um salto. uma escolha solitária num mundo que prefere robôs a poetas.

Dead Poets Society is a touching film about teenagers finding their own identity, or at least being given the opportunity to do so. Set at an elite school with strict discipline, it is a film about learning to seize the day and not just conform to expectations. That said, the film is ironically quite rote in its dramatics, with the central arc clearly spelled out and predictable. There are some unexpected darker moments, but even these are well worn storytelling tropes. Dead Poets Society is very well made though. Peter Weir is a fantastic director and each scene is expertly paced. Robin Williams does a great job as the teacher encouraging his students to think for themselves. And despite all the platitudes and mediocre story, in the end the final scene easily brings tears. In that sense Dead Poets Society is a success, an emotional journey that stays with you, even if the film itself isnt very inspired.

All-Time Favourites 
Given my graduation from school is on Tuesday, I figured there would be no greater opportunity to rewatch this masterpiece. 
It is only after rewatching it having completed school that I come to appreciate all of the nuances that flesh out each individual action from every character, the camaraderie, the memories, legacies, insecurities, passions, pressures and successes of adolescence. It is as intimate as any film ever made, and, as someone that has adored school more than almost anyone, one that will always represent what school meant to both me and my life.

Carpe diem, seize the day!
A film that teaches us to be creative, pursue our dreams, appreciate the beauty of art, appreciate the beauty of life, and to be passionate in our endeavors. This is what we stay alive for. Dead Poets Society will always be a phenomenal masterpiece in my eyes.

Quem é vivo sempre aparece. E quem some, volta gripada, debaixo do cobertor, fingindo que não tem compromissos da universidade acumulando. Eu, no caso. Fazia tempo que não escrevia nada por aqui, mas achei que essa sinusite dramática merecia um mínimo de proveito assistir Dead Poets Society, um dos filmes favoritos da minha lettermiga Sarah. Foi a melhor pior escolha da semana  e olha que a concorrência é alta. Um filme que me dilacerou por dentro, me fez chorar sem pudor e me marcou de uma forma inesperada.
O drama do filme é, à primeira vista, quase óbvio. Adolescentes perdidos, à procura de voz e propósito, encontram em Keating, um professor substituto, um sopro de liberdade que contrasta com a rigidez sufocante da escola onde estudam  um padrão que já vimos inúmeras vezes em outras histórias. E, ainda assim, Dead Poets Society consegue ser dolorosamente eficaz. Mesmo adulta, é impossível não se identificar com aquele medo constante de errar, de decepcionar, de se encaixar onde não se quer. A conformidade é fácil, confortável e muitas vezes premiada com boas notas  mas não dá a vida que realmente importa. É justamente essa impossibilidade de viver plenamente sob regras alheias que faz o filme doer tanto ele celebra o pensamento livre, a inconformidade e nos lembra que cada dia é uma oportunidade única de buscar o que realmente amamos.
No começo, confesso que foi difícil entender por que adolescentes ficariam tão fascinados por poesia, mas logo ficou claro qualquer forma de expressão que escapasse das amarras da escola parecia irresistível. Reunir-se à noite para ler, escrever e recitar versos se tornava um ato de coragem e liberdade, uma pequena revolução silenciosa dentro de paredes que tentavam moldar tudo ao mesmo padrão. No fim, não era exatamente sobre a poesia, mas sobre a brecha de liberdade, a chance rara de respirar sem pressões. Talvez seja por isso que, mesmo adulta, ainda me sinto tão próxima dessa história  ainda espero, no fundo, encontrar coragem para subir na carteira e enxergar o mundo de outro ângulo.

Ive always been a dreamer. My dreams are big, artistic, shooting for the moon kind of dreams. I want to be an actor. Throughout junior high and high school, I would always have at least one teacher tell me that I couldnt do what I wanted to do. One teacher in particular told me I couldnt get a real job if I didnt pursue science. Dont you want to be a doctor?, she said. The thing is, knowledge isnt only scientific. Knowledge is also art, entertainment, and music. Knowledge can be anything and everything when you know what to do with it. 
It wasnt until senior year, when my theatre teacher had us sit in a circle on the final day of class to talk face to face with one another, that I ever felt like I could truly do something with my artistic knowledge. I had this specific teacher for two years of my high school career and had developed an incredibly close and mutually respectful relationship with him. He was a mentor to me. On this day, he told the whole class spoke to each other from the heart, and say one thing we loved about each of our classmates. It was an incredibly moving activity that he ended by sharing something he loved about each of us. When he got to me, my teacher looked me in the eyes and told me tearfully that I could do anything I set my mind to, that he admired my passion and to never give up on my dreams, cause I could do something truly great with it one day. I weeped at this of course, because if he believed in me, I knew I should believe in myself. 
Dead Poets Society has such an emphasis on the dreamers. The way Mr. Keating talks about poetry so beautifully, as if they were words dripping from the tongue like honey, moved me to my core. The film feels like a crisp autumn afternoon, a warm, long overdue hug, and a punch in the gut all rolled into one. I see so much of myself in some of these characters, especially Neil, and so much of my teacher in Mr. Keating. I truly loved every second of it, even the ones that made me cry a whole lot. A masterpiece.

Let it be stated for the record that Robin Williams is the only celebrity death that I have shed tears over. This was the first film that I saw of his and I now watch it whenever I feel lost or silenced in any way. 
John Keating is the unconventional English teacher at the rigid Welton Academy. Williams, famously known for his comedy, shows no manic energy here. He just shows a man with the fire of art in his chest. 
Keating is the kind of teacher we all dreamed of having. The one who lets you do unconventional things, not simply for rebellions sake, but to see the world differently. 
When he tells his students that words and ideas change the world, you believe him. Because he says it like someone who has seen the alternative of a life unlived. 
The true protagonists, however, are the boys that he inspires. Robert Sean Leonard as Neil is heartbreaking. In A Midsummer Nights Dream, he finds his voice. However, in this world, conformity is more important than courage. His final silence is devastating. 
Each of these boys brings something real and fragile to the story. They are idealists, jokers, dreamers, lovers, humans. Some with privilege, others with pain. Grappling with the suffocating expectations of authority, be they parents, headmasters, or society itself. All bearing down with a crushing finality. 
Ethan Hawk as Todd is the painfully shy boy with a stammered voice and slumped posture. Under Keatings guidance, we see his transformation. Possibly my favorite scene in this film is where Keating pushes Todd to create a spontaneous poem in class. Its a birth, not of a writer, but of a self. 
The backdrop of Dead Poets Society is a love letter to New Englands brooding winters and golden woods. Having traveled through Boston, Maine, Connecticut, and more, its just naturally gorgeous. 
John Seales cinematography helps put into perspective the cage that these boys are in and how close (or far) salvation is. The brick walls of Welton surrounded by wild, untouched nature just outside. 
Dead Poets Society is a battle cry against institutional inertia and against the killing of curiosity in the name of tradition. Keating uses Whitman and Thoreau as shields. Shakespeare and Frost as swords. 
Art, for these boys, becomes a path to freedom and as someone who dabbles in many forms of art, its a sentiment that resonates profoundly. 
However, its not naive. It doesnt pretend that passion alone can topple the world. Neils fate is proof of that. Instead, it challenges us to recognize the cost of silence and of not speaking up when it matters most. 
O Captain My Captain! has become one of the most iconic film scenes in history. Even in loss, inspiration survives. We see that Keatings seed took root. 
5 out of 5. Carpe that fucking diem.

Seize the day. Make your lives extraordinary.
This phrase, which so many tattoo as a sun-drenched mantra, is, in truth, a terrifying imperative. Observing the hallways of Welton, I realize that Keating does not deliver freedom he delivers the anguish of choice. If life must be extraordinary, the common becomes an ontological failure. I see myself there, among those boys, feeling the weight that beauty is not a consolation, but a crushing responsibility that biology did not prepare us to carry.
Im certain as the sun rising in the east that this would be Belles favorite movie. Not for the aesthetic of the books, but for the affinity with the monster. Belle is the only one who understands that erudition is a form of isolation she inhabits the same non-place as Neil Perry. Both suffer from the same pathology the inability to adjust to a reality that demands utility instead of transcendence. For her, the film would not be an inspiration it would be a tragic mirror of one who knows that, to live poetry, one must first betray the village.
Many attempt to separate the utility of mathematics from the futility of art, but this is a shallow dichotomy. Art is as fundamental as mathematics because both are human attempts to domesticate chaos. Mathematics is the attempt to measure the infinite. Art is the attempt to survive it. To say one is superior to the other is like saying oxygen is more important than blood. Mathematics builds the stage, but art is the only reason the actors do not abandon the theater in the first act.
What we call Dark Academia today finds its rawest expression in this film intellectual necrophilia. It is not about loving books, but about loving the dead who wrote them. The philosophy here is that knowledge is only true if there is blood involvedbe it the sweat of discipline or the sacrifice of life itself.
The film and the aesthetic share Eros and Thanatos the burning desire to know and the fatal attraction to the end. No matter what anybody tells you, words and ideas can change the world.
There is something so painfully beautiful about being young, about having an entire life ahead of you and slowly realizing that the world may never let you live it the way you imagined. Dead Poets Society feels like a love letter to youth, to rebellion, to the terrifying and exhilarating experience of discovering who you are before the world starts telling you who you should be. Peter Weir captures the beauty of those fleeting moments of freedom so effortlessly, making every laugh, every whispered conversation, and every stolen moment feel precious precisely because they cannot last forever. Robin Williams is extraordinary, bringing so much warmth and sincerity to a man who simply wants his students to experience the beauty of being alive, while the young cast makes every dream, every act of defiance, and every heartbreak feel achingly real. And that score is absolutely beautiful, quietly carrying so much emotion beneath the surface until the tragedy becomes almost unbearable. What makes this film so devastating is that the rebellion at its heart is never really about disobedience. It is about wanting to live a life that belongs to you. About wanting to be remembered for who you were rather than who you were expected to become. And sometimes, the most heartbreaking tragedies are the ones that remind us just how precious the freedom to live, love, create, and simply be ourselves really is. A beautiful, bittersweet reminder that youth is fleeting, life is fragile, and we should never wait for permission to truly live.

Sim, são ditos com sinceridade, e a performance de Robin Williams dá vida a eles, mas ainda assim soam superficiais.

Directed by Peter Weir, with an Oscar-winning screenplay by Tom Schulman, the film tells the story of John Keating, an inspired and nonconformist literature teacher who, in the late 1950s, revolutionized the traditional teaching methods of a strict all male boarding school in Vermont. Keating encourages his students to set themselves apart from the crowd, following their inclinations regardless of the judgment of others. He urges them to live every moment intensely and express their emotions without fear, rebelling against the oppressive environment around them, completely inadequate for their authentic personal growth. Above all, poetry - seen as the purest manifestation of human sensitivity - is the useful tool to bring to light the unexpressed energy enclosed in each of them.
Dead Poets Society is a hymn to freedom of thought, to the supreme importance of remaining oneself in a world that tends to homologate and regiment, but also a reflection on the dangers of going against the rules and expectations imposed by society. In the role of the professor who teaches how culture, literature, and art are not something stale and dusty to be relegated to the past, but rather represent an absolutely disruptive life force, Robin Williams is unreachable. Under the careful direction of Weir, the actor wipes his interpretation from the typical histrionics and illuminates Keating with the charisma, empathy, depth and passion that the character requires. Excelente película, no creí que me iba a encantar tanto.
Dead Poets Society es una cinta con muchísimo corazón que te transmite demasiado con lo que cuenta, teniendo un guion magnífico que nos regala frases y personajes memorables, los cuales también están interpretados a la perfección.
Sinopsis Un maestro en un colegio privado emplea métodos poco convencionales para inspirar las vidas de sus estudiantes.
La historia es excelente, una trama que juega mucho con tus emociones. Sinceramente nunca creí que me fuese a gustar tanto, sabía un poco sobre lo que trataba pero no pensé que podía llegar a conectar tanto con ella, cosa que por suerte terminé haciendo muy rápidamente. Si me costó un poco conectar con ella, sus primeros 1520 minutos se me hicieron un poco lentos y lo que estaba contando no me atrapaba tanto, pero con la aparición de Keating todo cambió, al igual que la vida de los personajes con su llegada. Luego de esto la trama mejora mucho y se vuelve muy entretenida durante sus dos horas, haciéndote sentir muchas cosas durante el visionado. Funciona tanto como drama y también como comedia, ya que tiene algunos momentos divertidos y otros que directamente te parten al medio, incluso hubo escenas que me pusieron la piel de gallina, siendo el final una de ellas, emocionante y memorable. Por último, la crítica que hace hacia el sistema educativo me parece formidable, creo que por esto y muchas otras cosas es una película que debería ver todo el mundo.
Los personajes son fantásticos, realmente entrañables. El profesor John Keating es uno de los mejores personajes de la cinta (aunque es difícil decidir uno), como dije me parece que su aparición cambia la película y la vida de sus alumnos, comenzando una relación muy linda en la que les va a enseñar mucho sobre la vida mediante clases diferentes a lo que establece el sistema educativo. Es un personaje muy carismático potenciado por la excelente actuación de Robin Williams, quien, en parte, vuelve tan icónico a su personaje, es muy difícil que otro actor haga lo mismo que él. Por otro lado, de sus alumnos el que más destaca es Neil, otro de los personajes que más me gustó, un chico que no puede hacer lo que le gusta por culpa de que está bajo el mando de sus padres, quienes lo obligan a hacer lo que ellos creen que es lo mejor para él, cosa que no lo deja ser él mismo hasta que Keating le cambia la forma de ver las cosas. Otro al que también afecta su vida logrando un enorme desarrollo es Todd, con un papel más secundario pero clave para la historia. Después también hay otros personajes interesantes como Knox o Charlie, con un papel todavía más secundario a los anteriormente mencionados, pero cumpliendo con lo suyo.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente las actuaciones, sobretodo las de Robin Williams y Robert Sean Leonard, ambos en uno de los mejores papeles de sus carreras sin lugar a dudas, una parte fundamental para que la película sea tan buena también menciono a Ethan Hawke que está excelente en su papel. Por otro lado, la dirección de Peter Weir es sensacional, solo me vi dos películas de él y ambas me encantaron, ahora se me hace difícil elegir una de ellas porque ambas me parecen obras maestras. También destaco la fotografía y la ambientación que crea, es muy linda visualmente y toda la escuela se ve de maravilla, tanto los interiores como los exteriores. Por último, la banda sonora de Maurice Jarre es bastante buena pero no de lo mejor del film, destaca en algunos momentos como el final (donde juega un papel muy importante) pero podría haber sido más memorable como muchos otros aspectos.
En conclusión, una excelente película que es tan encantadora como todos dicen, ahora entiendo por qué es tan aclamada, creo que todos deberían verla por lo menos una vez, yo estoy seguro que voy a volver a verla en algún momento. Muy recomendada.

Every movie has the capacity to captivate, inspire, and empower however, the extent of a movies impact is definitely variable.
Dead Poets Society is a movie with this undeniable capacity. It might not be a movie that would make people exclaim with excitement when talking about it to their friends, but for me, its a treasure. Its a movie that I just want to keep to myself. Its not cynical, but I wouldnt categorize it as visionary either. I first watched the movie when I was 15, and I was so in love with it that I kept a small pocket notebook filled with its quotes. To say the least, this movie has taught me lessons that continue to provoke my thinking. Like a symphony, it has soothing melodies and melancholic harmonies. It evokes emotion from deep within, and it is haunting and stirring.
Below I have listed some aspects of the movie that impacted me greatly.
 Carpé Diem
Gather your rosebuds while you may. The Latin term for that sentence is Carpé Diem. Carpé Diem. Thats seize the day. Why does the author use this line? Because we are food for worms, lads. Because believe it or not, each and every one of us in this room is one day, going to stop breathing, turn cold, and die.
This is probably one of the most famous quotes from the movie. Professor Keating says this to his students on the first day of school at Welton Academy. This quote leaves the students, as well as the audience, in awe Keatings beliefs are exactly the unorthodox approaches to education that neither Welton nor the students parents support. Yet, it is this quote that rings true to his students.
At Welton, the students are programmed into following the same, old, boring, and predictable lifestyle that their fathers, their fathers fathers have lived. Therefore, Keatings way of life immediately shoots down the one size fits all belief that is held at the academy. We are all going to die, no matter what kind of person we become. Because of that, we should live life to its fullest. While Welton sees sameness as what is needed to sustain life, Keating sees it as what is needed to die. Through this, we are able to see Keatings aspiration as an educator to inspire his students to follow their dreams and think for themselves.
However, a downfall of this teaching is the way many students misunderstood the idea of the end of the road. They believe that a meaningless life is one without creativity when they are supposed to believe that a meaningless life is one where they arent able to pursue their passions. Neil Perry, one of the main characters in the movie, dreams of becoming an actor but is oppressed by his father to go to Harvard and become a doctor. Neil takes his teachers advice, to seize the day, to heart and takes up the role of Puck in the school play. However, when Mr. Perry finds out that his son had been neglecting his studies for some theater bogus, he furiously pulls Neil out from the play and threatens to send the latter to Braden Military School. This is where Neil makes the mistake of twisting Keatons words  while Keating says live life to the fullest because we will all die, Neil hears we should die if we cant live life to the fullest.
 Standing on desks

I stand upon my desk to remind myself that we should constantly look at things in a different way. See, the world looks very different from up here Just when you think you know something, you have to look at it in another way. Even if it may seem silly, or wrong, you must try.

The idea of standing atop their desks is another recurring motif in the movie and holds great meaning. It originally serves to represent open-mindedness it encourages thinking from different perspectives and thoughtfulness from outside the box. And Keatings teaching methods were cynical. He teaches them to look at things from different points of view by literally making them look from a different point of view. He also makes his students tear out the pages of their textbook to shut down the assumptions that you should just accept what is told to you, but rather you should think for your own self and make your own ideas.
Now, when you read, dont just consider what the author thinks, consider what you think. You must strive to find your own voice. Because the longer you wait to begin, the less likely you are to find it at all. Faroes said most men lead lives of quiet desperation. Dont be resigned to that. Breakout. Dont just walk off the edge like lemmings. Look around you. Dare to strike out and find new ground.

In the first and last scenes where Keating makes his appearance, characters are directed to stand on desks  he stands on his desk in his first scene, and his students stand on their desks in the last. The last scene is also when the movie takes a turn (after the sacking of Mr. Keating), and the action serves to represent unity, togetherness, as well as rebellion against an unjust system. At the end of the movie, as Mr. Keating is shown to collect his belongings and leave his teaching position, his students, one by one, rise up and stand on their desks, saying O Captain, my Captain
 O Captain, my Captain

Its also interesting to note that the line O Captain, my Captain appears twice along with the standing-on-desks action, and its also an allusion to Walt Whitmans poem about Abraham Lincoln who, as claimed by Whitman, died an unfair death despite sacrificing and working tirelessly to help his people. By appearing in Keatings first scene (and by being said by Keating himself), it may possible foreshadow the cruel sacking of Keating despite all that hes done for his fellow students and by appearing in Keatings last scene (being said by Todd, one of the students), the line demonstrates the nonconformist that Keating has taught his students to be. This proves the immense influence that Keating had on his students despite only being around for less than a year  he has passed on to his students his enthusiasm, his passion, his love, and his freedom of mind.

My first time watching the movie was also my last. And I finally revisited it after so many years. Its just that special to me, like an old CD that I only take out to look at and appreciate but not to listen to. Maybe another time maybe a time when I am stuck or when I really need the comfort and empowerment, will I watch it again. But until then, I would just like to reminisce on and appreciate the lessons that the 15-year-old had learnt. Until then, just the comfort of knowing I have such a beautiful thing to turn to in times of trouble is good enough for me. Continue to rest in peace, Captain.

Before my parents married, my father was studying to be a concert pianist at the Canadian Royal Conservatory of Music in Toronto the upper echelon of musical academies up here in the Great White North.  Before that, while still at home in New Brunswick, he would spend his weekends playing in a swing dance band This is where he met my mum.  He spent his weekday evenings practicing at home.  
My grandfather, a colonel in the Canadian army, advocated his 7 children play instruments violin or piano strongly encouraged.  A well rounded individual required musical training.  A proper career, in his view, consisted of military, medicine, or theology tracts.  My Uncles Paul, Emery, and Ernie became Medical Doctors.  My Aunt Alice, an RN.  Oscar followed his fathers footsteps into Canadian Armed Forces.  My Aunt Evelyn, a Catholic Nun.  My Uncle Omer, an accountant.  From what I understand that choice was tolerated barely.  Needless to say, my fathers choice of music as a vocation, even the lofty goal of a classically trained concert pianist, did not meet my grandfathers exacting expectations and resulted in a rift between my father and his that was never mended.
My father never spoke to me about my grandfather.  Hed passed away before I was born.  What I did learn of him was from my mother, and that he was very demanding of all of his children.  You were to be hard working and earnest.  You were to get good grades.  You were to practice social skills.  You werent supposed to have fun.  Although she never spoke ill of him, I could tell that my mum was not a huge fan of her father in law especially as her own large family was so completely the opposite  they loved having fun, and didnt care much about social status or lofty careers.  They loved my dad.  He fit right in.
Whiplash painted a picture of my fathers life growing up, but from a distorted perspective.  He had the pressure to perform, the constant demands, and the harsh discipline but not about the music.  Music was the escape.  
Whiplash also took my breath away.  Both Teller and especially Simmons give electrifying performances with nothing being held back.  I think I bonded with both characters so well because their combination of strengths and flaws made them honestly relatable.   Simmons demanding perfection scarred by the accompanying pettiness.  The first scene with the two of them together where Simmons simply turns away and walks out, only to come back for his coat.  Did he really forget his coat, or did he just want to further drive the spike into Tellers Andrew.   Ive always loved Simmons particularly for his brilliantly droll comedic delivery.  This is a whole new level, though.  The intensity of his performance is something I would never have expected.  Teller gets points for simply not being blown off the screen by Simmons wattage.
You also have to admire a film that achieve so much dramatic tension with only the slightest narrative.  Theres no huge arc, theres no big event.  Even the music festival is rather downplayed, and seemed more like an evolution in the plot rather than a point of dramatic crescendo.   No, Whiplash is a series of connected scenes.  Those scenes evolve the drama, escalating it ever higher.
And the music I felt swept back to my childhood and my fathers record player.
My father graduated from the conservatory and married my mother.  He was a brilliant player, but he realized not quite brilliant enough to be the best.  Only the best can make a living at being a concert pianist.  He did the sensible thing and got a job to support his wife, and somewhat later, me.  He went back to University, taking night classes while working a day job, and received his degree in business.
My father passed away many many years ago.  My most vivid memory of him was him practicing the piano.  Usually two hours a day, after he came home from work, and pretty much all day Saturday and Sunday.  He would hardly ever play a complete piece he would just go over and over a section, maybe playing the entire piece once before finishing for the day, but more often  than not he didnt.  I always wondered if it was because of my grandfather that all my father really did was practice.  It was easy to tell he loved to play, but just as easy to tell that he was still striving for perfection, even though there was no longer anything at stake.
Although I took classical piano, and had to suffer through Royal Conservatory Exams, there was really no huge amount of pressure from my Dad.  I quit just after barely passing my Grade 5.  I dont think it bothered him when I quit.  He knew I didnt have the gift, and in music, you cant excel without it.
Musical ability passed me by, but it only skipped me.  My son has the gift.  Hes a drummer.

A rapid, unforgettable, and absolutely stupefying work of romanticism, invigoration, and exquisite character development Whiplash is a prodigious study of the quest of greatness. Anchored by two marvelous and dueling performances by Miles Teller and J.K. Simmons, the film starts by taking your breath away and holding it just out of arms reach until the credits roll. The piercing flow of the editing, the knockout quality of the dialogue, the tinged and textural flavor of the cinematography, the fucking direction Goddamn this was good. I really cant overpraise Whiplash enough, Its a triumph of vitalization, both visually and dynamically. 
Lets start with Miles Teller and J.K. Simmons, both of which give some of the best performances of 2014. Ive been a champion of Teller for awhile now, and Im happy to see hes grown even more in regards to his acting. He unleashes here, bringing both physicality and likability that is essential to connecting with the story as a whole. J.K. Simmons however is on some different plane of existence or something, because his work here is some of the best Ive seen period. The rage, the facinating quirks, the endless depths and angles that Fletcher showcases is just remarkable and here I thought he was mean to Peter Parker in Spider-Man 2. If Peter Parker was in this film, hed probably die from crying too hard. 
Theres something about simple stories that connect in regards to character and theme rather than twisty plot that works so much better if its executed well. The tapestry of Whiplash is very simple, but thats what gives the film its striking character development and its frenetic energy. Damien Chazelles story is given room to breathe, flow, and evolve without feeling cheap or tacked on. The feeling that you get when everything in a film is going exactly how you want it to is really something special, and thats how I felt about Whiplash.
However, the simple story would be nothing without Damien Chazelles direction. It is quite simply, bewildering in every possible way. Its got this trance-like quality to it where youre just forced to pay attention and feel the film. I know that may sound silly, but with every single aspect working so fucking well, Youre just kinda required to scoot a little bit further in your theater seat as the images and sounds are so vibrant and alive. The way the camera moves, the way it follows characters, and the way closeups are used all culminate in a work that already feels timeless. 
Sharone Meirs cinematography is wonderful, highlighting flashes of colors and making a musical stage come alive in both its hypnotic qualities and its fascinating intimidation. The lights, the darkened faces in the audience I felt like I was there with Andrew, and Meirs work really exemplifies that. Colors such as yellow and brown play a significant role, strikingly pushing the audience deeper into the story by providing a spellbinding look to the material. 
Tom Cross (Oscar-nominated) editing is potent and fast beyond words. The cuts are plentiful, but always in time with the incredible musical score by Justin Hurwitz. It adds up to a visual sense of music, always flowing with the drumming or the many moments of studio band nirvana. The cinematic quality that results from all these elements is SO GOOD.  I was basically thinking the whole time, this is why I love movies. 
An immaculate amalgamation of flawless technical flourishes, faultless performances, and story that is as emotionally resonant as it is gleefully deranged and seductive Whiplash cast a spell on me that has yet to wear off, and Im happy for that. 
Whiplash. I think I love you.

Whiplash misses a tad too many beats to reach perfection.
Lets face it, the two main reasons why this film works as well as it does are the two leads and the incredible music. Both Teller and Simmons are fantastic, with Simmons really pushing the envelope with a vitriolic performance filled with bitter passion. He truly gets under your skin and poor Miles Teller makes a great victim. Shrugging off his usual smirkiness, Teller gives a sometimes understated and sometimes forceful performance that betrays a range he definitely has within him when working with great material.
I cant say that Im a huge jazz fan, but the music in Whiplash is just phenomenal. It accompanies just about every scene, sometimes like a soft breeze, sometimes like a relentless tormentor, but always as an addition that enhances. There are a couple of scenes that provide an aural and visual ballet, so in tune with each other they are simply breathtaking to watch.
The plot is where it loses me somewhat. When you have great characters who have fantastic dialogue you shouldnt waste them on a dime a dozen plot. I was hoping for an exploration of ambition, drive, the limits of pride, but I didnt get that. What I got was a collection  of (very good) conflict driven scenes, held together by the flimsiest of threads that holds no surprises. It lacked a depth that I wish had been there. I guess it has a lot to do with Tellers character arch that was a bit too condensed. He goes from shy kid to the pinnacle of arrogance in a heartbeat only to reinvent himself at the next beat. Its a very predictable arch, which is fine, but it just didnt flesh out the guy Im supposed to root for enough.
What makes up for a lot though is not so much the conclusion of Tellers story, but the way it was filmed. It is a riveting scene, filled with stunning editing, once again that gorgeous music and finally a non-verbal standoff between the two leads. Whiplash most definitely goes out with a bang.
There is a lot to love and admire in Whiplash and even though it has its faults, there is no denying the sheer quality of all the talent involved in creating this infernal drum solo.

This is it! This is where the search for the best picture of 2014 ends for me. And although there are few films from last year that I still need to check out, I highly doubt that watching them is going to make any difference because after sitting through what is undeniably a goosebumps-inducing cinematic experience from start to finish, I can say with absolute certainty that Whiplash is my Movie of the Year.
Whiplash tells the story of Andrew Neiman a 19-year-old Jazz drummer who aspires to become one of the great drummers like Buddy Rich  finds himself under the wing of the schools most respected but fearsome teacher, Terence Fletcher. Determined to impress the instructor after getting the grilling of his life on his very first day, Neiman completely dedicates himself to his craft but Fletcher aims to push him beyond what hes capable of.
Fabulously written  meticulously directed by Damien Chazelle, Whiplash is a work of blazing originality that takes over the screen like an invading horde  from its opening moments to the spectacular finale, Chazelles kinetic direction in what is his sophomore effort controls the films charged atmosphere with sublime precision while also keeping the rest of its elements perfectly in rhythm with each other.
Coming to the technical aspects, the entire picture is a work of astounding production  every aspect only contributes in further enriching the overall experience. Sets are refined to smallest of details, Cinematography makes near-perfect use of colour palettes, hues  lighting, Editing is one of its strongest aspects that makes its viciously paced story all the more engaging while its jazz-heavy soundtrack keeps the premise on the verge of explosion at all times.
As far as acting goes, this is easily Miles Tellers best performance to date for the actor gives his all in what is a physically demanding role to completely reinvent himself  hes an absolute revelation as Andrew Neiman. And yet, he is completely overshadowed by J.K. Simmons who is in as Terence Fletcher and with his intimidating screen presence, he manages to deliver the most impressive, memorable  dominating performance weve ever seen from the veteran actor.

Whiplash, Damien Chazelles 107-minute-long ode to mentors, musicians, and motivation, is a taut and mesmerizing piece of filmmaking. A quick-moving and engrossing drama that explores the roles of teacher and learner, parent and child, Chazelle builds a film that brims with energy and emotion, bursts with authentic character beats, and soars with a percussive and narrative brilliance. 
With its powerful performances, crackling direction, and riveting story, Whiplash is a truly great piece of work.
Chazelles story is built around Miles Tellers Andrew, a young music student at the prestigious Shaffer Music Conservatory. Andy is a drummer whose ambitions find him falling under the demanding eye and ear of Fletcher, J.K. Simmons searingly realized conductor. The narrative focuses on the relationship between the two men as Fletcher pushes Andrew, violently and angrily, to reach heights of musicianship. The drama is potent, the dialogue is spry, and the themes are classic. It is a teacher-student tale, with notes of danger and exuberance. 
The film is small-scale, even intimate, but it pulses with electric vibrance. Chazelles cameras float and fly, flinging themselves between their subjects. The mix of character, composition, and story create a wire-tight tension that powers the film. From its bourbon-colored practice rooms, to its high-contrast performance stages, the films aesthetic generates a warmth that rebukes the martinet-chill of Fletcher. The production is quietly dazzling. All of its elements are subtle, smart, and satisfying.
Elevating Whiplash beyond its already-excellent direction and narrative are the films performances, both human and musical. Simmons creates a near-Machiavellian monster whose wisdom and soul seethe under a slave-driving surface. He is a volcano, a puppet-master, and a father whose methods of nurturing are both damaging and effective. He is a frightening creation.
Tellers Andrew is just as fully-rendered. A student learning his craft, Andrew is given an impish sense of humor, steadfast sense of drive, and a triumphant, if ill-thought-out, ability to spar with his mentor by Teller. It is a performance grounded in literal blood, sweat, and tears.
Chazelle casts jazzy musical standards and an ever-present percussive drive as a character just as important as Simmons Fletcher and Tellers Andrew. The bold and boisterous musical pieces flow through character arcs and energize the entire affair. The music is there through failure and victory and it punctuates the films thematic subtext, enlivening and tying together ideas of relationships, lessons learned, and forcefully finding fulfilled potential.
Ending with a climax that is breathlessly exhilarating, Whiplash uses its 107-minute running time to paint a cinematic portrait that is economical, ferocious, and utterly enveloping. Its story, themes, performances, and direction are things of beauty. Rich, gripping, and inspiring, Chazelle and company create one of 2014s best films and one of the decades best films about music.

There are no two words in the English language more harmful than good job.
Lucky for you, youre here for rock bottom. You absolute horror of a human being. So says Simon Bishop (Greg Kinnear) to Melvin Udall (Jack Nicholson) in James L. Brooks As Good as It Gets. It is a rare moment of outspokenness for the usually meek and conciliatory Simon, but in ones darkest hour politesse has a way of evaporating like so many spilled tears. And though it may be an uncommonly direct and pungent statement from poor Simon, it possesses the virtue of truth. Whatever problems there are with As Good as It Gets, one of its great strengths is its commitment to following a truly terrible, off-putting manan unusual choice for a romantic comedy. Melvin is given his share of excuses (OCD and other possible disorders) and is quasi-redeemed by a womans lovea smug and insufferable woman significantly less acerbic but only slightly less obnoxious than Melvin himself, but a relationship develops as it must under the dictates of the romantic-comedic impulse. But notwithstanding his slight softening and his broadened social circle, Melvin is and (mostly) remains an absolute horror of a human being. He is a monster wandered away from his usual monster-movie environs.
Andrew Neiman (Miles Teller) and Terence Fletcher (J.K. Simmons) are also walking monstrosities, absolute horrors of human beings, but they have not drifted into uncommon generic territory. While at first glance writer-director Damien Chazelles Whiplash presents itself as a take on the inspiring teacher or mentor-protégé drama, as it evolves, it reveals itself to be just as much informed by the sports movie and the horror film. Chazelle wisely avoids clichés (or perhaps more accurately, he draws them from disparate sources), making his story unpredictable and lending a sheen of complexity to his characters by virtue of their contradictions. Like all of us, Andrew and Fletcher are multifaceted but with a constant core. Andrew may be capable of winsomely awkward flirtation and Fletcher may possess an unexpected ability to chat sweetly with a former students little girl, but at their centers they are beasts.
Like Melvin and most other people consumed by insecurity and anger, Andrew and Fletcher seek to level the world through hostility and cruelty, creating the illusion of an even surface through incessant demolition. But unlike Melvin, whose sweeter generic climes deprive him of a partner of comparable causticity, Andrew and Fletcher have each other. While on its own such extreme abrasiveness leads to isolation and resentment, when paired it creates a powerful chemical reactionthe corrosiveness burns and burns until all that is left is scorched earth. It is a symbiosis in which each party is both host and parasite.
But it does not reveal itself as such immediately. Chazelle first positions Andrew as a clumsy, socially maladroit 19-year-old, struggling through New Yorks prestigious Shaffer Conservatory and dreaming of becoming a great jazz drummer. As Andrew watches Rififi at a repertory theater with his father, Jim (Paul Reiser), and hesitantly talks to the concessionaire, Nicole (Melissa Benoist), it seems he is a decentalbeit introverted and interpersonally ineptkid. This conception is reinforced in Andrews early interactions with FletcherAndrew stammers and flounders when Fletcher confronts the boy practicing alone late one night, then is reduced to tears at the shock of Fletchers first abusive tirade. Poor Andrew, we think. Poor sweet Andrew.
A more cookie-cutter film would then follow one of two approaches either Fletcher would be evil and Andrew would eventually seek revenge upon and destroy his adversary, or Fletcher would be revealed to possess a heart o gold beneath his gruff exterior and his ways, while unorthodox, would lead Andrew to realize his full potential. Whiplash, instead, has something more complex on its mind What happens when the mentor truly is evil, but also possibly inspiring? And what happens when the student is every bit as villainous as his elder counterpoint? Its an interesting take on a standard setup that sometimes goes over the top, but never loses its sense of suspense or tension or dramatic flair. What at first appears to be Dead Poets Society-cum-Raging Bull becomes a psychotic roundelay. Were this a true cousin to Melvin Udall and As Good as It Gets, it would be The War of the Roses, but with the romance excised it becomes something even bleaker.
The revelation that Andrew is as hubristic and heartless as his professor comes at first as something of a surprise, but Chazelle lays the groundwork for this descent in smaller early moments Andrew treating his father with exasperated rudeness at the theater Andrews obvious and unvarnished contempt for Nicoles lack of concrete lifeplan Andrews lack not only of friends but of competent friendly interaction with his fellow students. It is as though a little hatemonger has been hiding somewhere deep within young Andrew, unsure of when and how to unleash itself until shown the dark way by Fletcher. And once unleashed, it does not look back.
Chazelles camera and Tom Cross editing keep things crisp and surprising, mixing fluid movement and staccato cuts in an appropriately rhythmic and musical way. (The decision to cast skilled musicians is critical, avoiding the common pitfall of having to edit around the actors musical shortcomings.) And Chazelles script contains several surprising turns. Elements that in other films would be intended to humanize a characterAndrews budding romance with Nicole or Fletchers teary-eyed speech about a deceased former pupilare revealed to have far different implications for their characters than at first suspected. Every turn, even when outlandish (one particular bloody moment stands out as shocking despite having been copied from numerous other films), serves the characters and the storys underlying themes. 
And what are those themes? The most obvious one, the one hammered most insistently, is what price greatness? Is any amount of degradation and abuse acceptable if the end result is sublime art? Are such degradation and abuse necessary for the production of sublime art? The film waffles on these questions, unwilling to firmly answer them one way or the otheran approach that could be maddeningly noncommittal but somehow feels right. There is no sense that the means are anything less than heinous, Whiplash seems to say, but the importance of transcendent ends cannot be fully discounted. Yet tied up in this question are Whiplashs other, broader concerns, about the ways in which people abuse each other, the ways in which they justify that abuse while fulfilling darker needs, and the cyclonic pull of that abuse, the ways in which it creates a whirlpool from which escape is exceedingly hardnot that either Andrew or Fletcher have any desire for escape.
Teller and Simmons are both as brilliant as advertised. Teller invests Andrew with a wealth of detail, fully persuasive as the asshole convinced that life is a concerted act of persecution against him and of his need to transcend the worlds banality by hectoring it into, if not submission, at least cowed hesitance. But Teller also lets glimmers of a better Andrew sneak through, keeping hope alive that all of his humanity is not lost. Simmons, meanwhile, plays Fletcher as a man of such bottomless rage that every interaction, no matter how still or quiet, seems to possess a dreadful potential energy. As much as any villainous mastermind of horror or suspense, Fletcher always seems the smartest person in the room, always with an eye on multiple angles to any situation and ready to exploit them with a vocabulary to rival the Malcolm Tuckers of the world. So commanding is Simmons presence that he need not scream constantlyhe is as often soft-spoken or even silent as he is brayingbecause of his overwhelming sense of control. (Chazelles frequent framing of Fletcher from beneath, giving him a Mephistophelean vibe, enhances this sense of omnipotence.) Even hanging up his hat and jacket becomes a latent threat. Simmons also cleverly plays the glimpses into Fletchers non-studio lifea conversation with a former student a performance at a jazz clubas equally suggestive of a richer, kinder man than the one who berates his students or of a ruse designed to lull the onlooker into a false sense of security. (The fact that Fletcher always seems to suspect an onlooker suggests the likelihood of the latter explanation and the depth of his depravity.)
But to what do all the tremendous acting, the propulsive editing, the memorably profane dialogue amount? It depends, I suppose, on how one reads the ending, which is utterly captivating while leaving an ambiguous impression. (Spoilers, naturally, follow.) Andrew, having been dismissed from Shaffer and surreptitiously gotten Fletcher fired for his conduct, stumbles across his former teacher several months later at a jazz club, where Fletcher strokes Andrews ego and invites him to join an ensemble performing at the JVC Jazz Festival. Andrew jumps at the chance to bathe once more in the limelight while feeling the upper hand over Fletcher, only to find out at the performance that it was a setup Fletcher knew it was Andrew who had him dismissed, and as payback Fletcher has failed to give Andrew the correct sheet music, guaranteeing his crash-and-burn in front of the assembled jazz-industry literati. Andrew flails and fails spectacularly, just as Fletcher knew he would, and storms off the stage in embarrassment. And then....
Then Andrew storms back onto the stage and begins playing Caravan, a notoriously difficult piece that he and his fellow drumming students had struggled with before.
