Whiplash poses the question what does it take to be like Charlie Parker, the greatest musician of the 20th century? Im not the kind of person who wants to find out, but I bet Damien Chazelle is.
Jazz music requires dazzling technical skill, and you may end up with bloody blisters, but is Andrew a great musician because of the tough teacher or despite him? I believe Andrews greatness comes from within, evident from the start of the movie.
The nicest guy in the movie is Andrews dad, a failed writer turned schoolteacher. In the last sequence, Andrew has crashed and burned on the first song of the concert. His dad puts a loving arm around him, showing him he doesnt need to become the next Charlie Parker to be loved. 
A weight is lifted from Andrews schoulders and he finally plays the drums for the love of jazz music and not to please Fletcher. The scene features rhythmic cuts between different angles of the instruments and Andrew, as the tension builds. Chazelle effectively conveys how masterful Andrews drumming is through Fletchers approving reaction shots. 
Earlier, we see Fletcher playing piano in a jazz bar with his eyes closed, fanning the flame of his pure love of the music. We later learn that this enlightened version of Fletcher is just a facade and he still resents Andrew. But hes let go of his obsession to mould the next Charlie Parker. It took getting fired and a car crash to break the obsessive spell and downward spiral of both these characters. 
In the jazz bar, Fletcher recounts his theory that Good Job are the two most harmful words in the English language. Im not convinced. I believe the encouragement of great teachers had a lasting impact on me. Its interesting to contrast Fletchers approach with Robin Williams teacher in Dead Poets Society. Which rang more true for you? One things for sure both exist in the real world and I cant speak for anyone elses reaction to negative encouragement. It numbs me.
The best scene in the movie is when Fletcher recounts the death of his former pupil, a trumpet player. He plays a mournful trumpet solo on a CD player while expressing his love for the deceased boy. He takes out his grief (and guilt) on the three drummers competing for first chair in the band. 
The tension mounts as each drummer fails to match quite his tempo. Its a performance that showcases acrobatics and endurance of pain more than it tests musical skill. While super fast drumming may not be particularly musical, it sure is spectacular as a movie scene.
Miles Teller portrays a character who exhibits traits that could be interpreted as autism. He struggles with maintaining eye contact and is intensely focused on his drumming, neglecting his budding romance and behaving rudely towards his fathers dinner guests. 
The love story isnt very well-developed, which makes the heartbreaking phone call where he tries to patch things up less effective. However, I still think Teller portrays it well, attempting to save some dignity but failing to appear aloof.
Teller possesses the nervy, neurotic intelligence reminiscent of Dustin Hoffman. I cant say he has fulfilled the promise of this performance in the ten years that followed, except for Only The Brave. His performance was overlooked by the Academy. Its puzzling to me what the Academy considers when evaluating a Best Picture contender if not the lead performance. 
The film is so rewatchable because of its fast-paced editing. Once you start watching Whiplash, its like going down a waterslide  you cant stop. The soundtrack is so good that its hard to believe some of the songs were specifically composed for the movie. The quality of the big band jazz music plays a crucial role in selling us on why the characters in the movie are so obsessed with it.
 Chazelle questions whether the teacher is a necessary evil or a malicious demon, ultimately presenting a parable about the extraordinary skill required to play jazz. Chazelle may be suggesting that we need to be pushed, but perhaps being encouraged would be better than the method of our teacher. Maybe becoming a jazz great shouldnt literally cost blood, sweat and tears. What do I know? I cant even carry a tune.
P.S. I love the poster in the rehearsal room If you dont have ability you wind up playing in a rock band. Ill stick with rock music, but theyve got a point when it comes to pure skill. There are a lot of lousy drummers in prominent rock bands getting away with murder.

Whiplash  Em Busca da Perfeição, dirigido por Damien Chazzelle, o filme retrata a história de Andrew Neyman (Miles Teller), um jovem baterista que sonha em engrandecer o seu nome no jazz americano, como fez Buddy Rich, seu maior ídolo. Após chamar a atenção do impiedoso mestre Terence Fletcher (J.K Simmons), Andrew entra para a orquestra principal do conservatório de Shaffer, a melhor escola de música dos Estados Unidos. No entanto, pelo rígido e abusivo jeito de ensino do regente, o rapaz transforma sua paixão em obsessão, com o objetivo de chegar ao nível de gênio, sem se importar com os relacionamentos dos outros e, principalmente, os sentimentos. Whiplash vai muito além de um filme sobre o jazz trata-se de um olhar intenso e perturbador sobre o que o subtítulo já deixa claro a busca pela perfeição. Este plot poderia facilmente ser ligado a algum trabalho de Darren Aronofsky, pela personalidade obsessiva que busca constantemente a perfeição, como já visto em Black Swan, porém o longa-metragem não se concentra somente nesse quesito   apesar de explorá-lo com maestria. O cineasta Chazelle demonstra atenção no tema debatido e nunca deixa a música como plano de fundo. A trilha sonora assinada por Justin Hurwitz é o cerne que move toda narrativa, pois não só embala e empolga com canções fenomenais, como também dá o tom a vários momentos da película. A montagem de Tom Cross também é fundamental na criação de raccords energéticos e inspiradores, utilizando uma linguagem de videoclipe para unir a música à imagem. Com cortes habilidosamente sincronizados ao jazz somos fluidamente jogados de plano em plano, de cena em cena, acompanhando a crescente dedicação e loucura de Andrew, que cada vez mais se vê ansioso pelo sucesso. Sharone Meir dá o retoque final e com suas paletas de cores intensas fazendo uso de tonalidades estéticas mais clássicas na fotografia. A direção é muito boa. A utilização de closes para mostrar momentos mais tensos, dando enfoque na bateria, nos pingos de suor, nas lágrimas e no sangue que escorre pelas mãos traz veracidade e aproxima ainda mais o telespectador do personagem central. Você sente o desconfortante grau de dedicação, esforço e o cansaço de Andrew. Assim como quando Fletcher levanta a mão ao alto, já sabemos que algo deu errado e esperamos por um grito, ou, até mesmo calculamos que ele vai acabar obrigando Andrew a repetir e repetir, por horas a fio, o mesmo trecho da música até conseguir a total e perfeita sincronia. Outro ponto importantíssimo em Whiplash é o casting, o longa é recheado de grandes atuações. O veterano J. K. Simmons faz o seu papel com exata perfeição, como seu personagem exige. Miles Teller não fica atrás e impressiona na construção do protagonista que transforma a dedicação em fanatismo, ao passo que é deixado clara a mudança em sua personalidade, que vai do jovem músico de natureza sonhadora até um homem ambicioso e arrogante, totalmente obcecado pela perfeição, à imagem de seu tutor. Ambos entregam a nós uma explosiva relação de aluno e mestre que surpreende ao falar abertamente sobre como a grandeza só pode florescer com esforço - e que muitas vezes os empurrões se fazem mais necessários que tapinhas nas costas. Ao final, Whiplash traz um debate sobre perfeição, objetivo, genialidade, talento, conflito psicológico e determinação, elementos pontuais que causam  um evidente desconforto, entretanto, consegue deixar o público ligado do início ao fim, e ao terminar, queremos , imediatamente, assisti-lo novamente.

Simmons is so committed that his character feels too unnervingly real and demonic, and he deserves the attention that he gets right now. Overall, it is certainly one of the best films of the year. Its merciless direction, bravura performances, and terrific writing makes this truly intense, unforgettable experience.

Whiplash is about a drummer (Im a drummer) who joins an ensemble (I joined an ensemble) so when I first read about the film, it had me at drummer joins ensemble.  Luckily (or unluckily) thats where the similarities end. Whereas my band-leader uses words like Good Job, J.K. Simmons character believes no two words are more harmful.
Its tough being a drummer in an ensemble (boo hoo Graham) but the film goes someway to explaining why. You are essentially the backbone to a whole piece. The rhythmic spine as it were. Youre also most likely the loudest and so more exposed to mistakes. Multiple brass and wind instruments cloak their errors, but with only one drummer it can feel lonely there at the back.
I keep good time though but over the years have sometimes rushed or dragged and faced the glares of the all mighty one in charge. Ive never had a chair thrown at my head though and for that, I am thankful.
Almost immediately in Whiplash, you get a sense of who this kid is. Hes much more handsome than I ever was (imagine Miles Teller in a room with Old Schools Frank the Tank) and hes instantly relatable he goes to the Cinema with his Dad, he likes the girl behind the counter but is too shy to say anything and he practices his instrument every day. You know, the normal things. Theres a softness to Andrews face but a desire in his eyes. He yearns for something.
Its an incredible opening, not just with introducing the hero but also the villain. Within only a few words and actions, the aforementioned leader of the band Terence Fletcher (played by Oscar Winner J.K. Simmons  youll see!) establishes his intimidating, no shit taking self. Dramatic and compelling off the bat - it gets better!. Director Damien Chazelle cuts the film as if it were a jazz piece itself. Was there a moment toward the middle where I thought it was pushing too many dramatic buttons? Yes, but the moment passes as quickly as a mis-hit of the snare. Chazelle deftly skits into an interesting final third thats equally wonderful and again, full of that taut, seething tension. 
I wont comment much on the finale other than to say its breath-taking. To musicians and otherwise, it satisfies in ways most dramas could only dream of, leaving you thrilled, exhausted AND looking forward to that next viewing.
Whiplash is a resounding success both in performance and execution and its ambiguity is a blessing. Make no bones about it, Director Chazelle is a force to be reckoned with.

in english The brutality of perfectionism has never sounded this visceral. Whiplash beats with the pulse of obsession, conducted with the precision of a metronome and the ferocity of a drum solo on the verge of collapse. What could have been a simple story about a young musician becomes an almost mythological psychological duel, where every snare hit feels like a punch and every pause carries the weight of emotional torture.
Damien Chazelle demonstrates astonishing technical and narrative mastery, turning confined spaces  rehearsal rooms, narrow hallways, dimly lit stages  into battlegrounds. His direction is relentless, denying the audience any moment of rest. The camerawork is meticulously crafted sharp cuts and aggressive close-ups capture sweat, strained muscles, and the smallest flickers of pain or arrogance, creating a rhythm that blends with the pounding drums. The final scene, in particular, is a tour de force of pure cinematic language the camera moves like a dance partner to the music, oscillating between suffocating close-ups and sweeping movements that amplify the grandeur of that silent duel between student and master. Its cinema stripped to its raw essence  where image and sound become one, beating like a single, desperate heartbeat.
Beneath this impeccable technique lies a disturbing study of talent and sacrifice  how much one must bleed to achieve greatness, and whether its worth the cost. Chazelle offers no comforting answers, and thats precisely why the film lingers its cruel, ambiguous, and brutally honest.
In the end, Whiplash isnt just about jazz its about destruction and glory, about pushing harder, faster, louder  until genius finally emerges or you fall apart trying. And Chazelle, with the same discipline he demands of his characters, proves that cinema, like music, can be an act of pure emotional exhaustion.

Em Whiplash, um diretor estreante consegue fazer com que tudo  atores, roteiro, música  atinja ao mesmo tempo o máximo de potência e de precisão
Durou 27 anos o recorde de abuso psicológico e verbal estabelecido por R. Lee Ermey em Nascido para Matar, de Stanley Kubrick. Mas ele é estrondosamente  quebrado por J.K. Simmons em Whiplash  Em Busca da Perfeição (Whiplash, Estados Unidos, 2014). No papel de Terence Fletcher, professor do mais prestigiado conservatório musical americano, Simmons não é capaz só de torrentes paralisantes de insultos, como o sargento de Nascido para Matar ele opera também nos modos sedutor e perverso. Cria ocasionais zonas de conforto para seus alunos que logo serão arrasadas em bombardeios obliterantes e garimpa informações íntimas sobre eles com as quais causar o máximo de dano em bombardeios cirúrgicos. Não existe terreno firme em torno de Fletcher  e, graças à performance de J.K. Simmons, composta não só com grande inteligência mas também com um jogo intrincado de gestos mínimos e detonações imprevistas, mergulhar nas duas horas do filme é compartilhar com o jovem protagonista Andrew Neiman (o também ele excepcional Miles Teller) a sensação de nunca ter onde pisar.
Atrair a atenção de Fletcher, bandleader do principal conjunto de jazz do Conservatório Shaffer, uma versão ficcional da Juilliard School, é o objetivo de cada um dos alunos da escola. E, pela amostra que se tem na cena inicial, na qual Andrew detona a bateria ao estilo do lendário Buddy Rich, ele é plenamente merecedor da vaga que Fletcher lhe oferece no grupo  e que então a todo instante ameaça tirar-lhe.
Entre todas as excelentes escolhas como diretor e roteirista do estreante Damien Chazelle, de 29 anos, a mais decisiva e consagradora é colocar a bateria no centro do filme, em vez dos mais sedutores metais na onda fabulosamente inovadora que varreu o jazz dos anos 30 aos 70 ela não é um mero instrumento de acompanhamento ou de base. É o motor de propulsão verdadeiro das bandas, ao mesmo tempo um metrônomo, uma usina de força e uma catalisadora  ou, dependendo da peça que se toca, uma tirana. Como nas duas canções mais executadas no filme, Caravan, o standard celebrizado por Duke Ellington, e a Whiplash de Hank Levy, um estudo em tempos virtualmente inexecutáveis. A glória na bateria jazzística é para conhecedores, não a glória mais chamativa do trompete ou do saxofone  e o desprezo pela opinião de qualquer um que considere desqualificado para julgá-lo é uma parte fundamental da obsessão de Andrew. Na lógica do filme, portanto, a bateria é de fato o único instrumento que Chazelle poderia ter dado ao seu protagonista.
A combinação singular de fúria e precisão do instrumento dita ainda, em Whiplash, toda a estrutura do filme e o seu alcance dramático. A bateria é tanto mais empolgante quanto mais lógico e definido (e também mais surpreendente) for o contraste entre os momentos de explosão e os de concentração, ou entre as etapas de variação e retomada de seus tempos. O ritmo imposto por Chazelle mimetiza essas oposições à perfeição e empurra a narrativa com um ímpeto irresistível da mesma forma, essa potência e essa exatidão são a matéria-prima de que J.K. Simmons e Miles Teller moldam Fletcher e Andrew (Teller, aliás, treinou bateria até ficar com os dedos e a palma das mãos em carne viva, o que, se não foi suficiente para fazer dele um músico do calibre de seu personagem, o torna ao menos perfeitamente crível como instrumentista). E, a cada cena de Andrew em ação com suas baquetas, o diretor vai também alargando os conceitos da plateia  por que, afinal, é tão importante o padrão impossível de ortodoxia musical que Fletcher cobra de Andrew, se ele não parece deixar espaço para nenhuma expressão pessoal? Na vulcânica sequência final do filme, Chazelle responde a essa pergunta  e expande para muito além do molde habitual a narrativa clássica do protagonista que persegue a excelência a qualquer custo. Para certos talentos, essa é mesmo a única alternativa ou se alcança absolutamente tudo, ou não se terá conquistado rigorosamente nada.

Whiplash, which presents us how far a person can go to achieve success and what they are willing to lose, manages to make us think while giving us a musical feast by putting us among multi-layered characters. In the film, which once again touches upon the fact that people who are ready to sell their souls to get somewhere in life seek happiness under the name of being the best, the ambition of Andrew, a music student, brings with it many questions. In the film, where we constantly think about how right the violence and verbal abuse-heavy education of the character Fletcher is, the question of whether human life has any value also comes to light. Whiplash, which doesnt hesitate to confront the audience with the fact that success is necessary to live in this world, is really perfect in the way it follows to constantly make the audience fall into disagreements. As I said above, it is simply incredible that director Chazelle turns a different narrative, perhaps a cliché, ambition story into a life marathon. It wasnt hard for me to empathize with Andrew, as I was a little psychopathic girl who was obsessed with academic success and being the best throughout my life, and who didnt hesitate to harm myself and those around me when I couldnt, just like Andrew. When you watch the film from this perspective, its not hard to see that Fletcher is actually trying to make Andrew his own Charlie Parker from the beginning to the end.
When Andrew wounds himself by playing the drums, he wounds himself in order for his mind and soul to reach a superego because these wounds are also a symbol of heroism for him. With the flow of blood, he shatters the insurmountable boundary between his body and his standards. Thus, the weakness that moves away from the body also moves away from the soul. In this context, the trilogy of blood, sweat and tears becomes an expression of the holy trinity for Andrew. While watching Andrew, I sweated as much as he did, ruined my nails, and couldnt sit still. Even though it was my second time watching it and I remembered all the scenes. Whiplash makes us question the first question above in general terms of the ethics of success due to Fletchers attitude towards music, success, teacher-student, conductor-musician and even father-son issues, as his understanding of education leaves no room for error but leaves too much room for play. The relationship between Fletcher and Andrew displays one of the best examples of the double bind. The theory is based on the fact that a person is conditioned with the fact that no matter what he does, he cannot please the other party with whom he is in a mutual relationship. This conditioning creates a situation that paves the way for the fragmentation of the self if the condition is not eliminated. Fletchers relentless continuation of doing this brings with it another challenging test for Andrew in terms of his self, his music, his mental and physical health. When Andrew tries to prove himself to Flatcher, we are also afraid of what he can do. A tired and unhappy young man who can put his life aside in order to break the dilemma and pursue the feeling of success for his musicianship is growing up before our eyes. This state of being left in a dilemma that continues until the end of the film facilitates the fragmentation of Andrews self, while the final game that Fletcher performs at the festival at the end of the film, which we can call Upswingin, brings with it a magnificent finale where Andrew breaks this conditioning and brings the film and Caravan to an end. Andrew breaking this actually works in a process that goes parallel to his search for an answer to the second question mentioned above. While he has included music in his life as an indispensable rather than a goal and has chosen to be alone in pursuit of this Andrew becomes so desperate that he will do anything to be the best, the most valuable. When he realizes that this road leads nowhere, when he realizes that he can advance towards his goal by making the talent he has accepted as already valuable, that magnificent Caravan solo comes along. This scene is what turns Andrew and Fletcher into Charlie Parker and Jo Jones.
In addition to all this psychological foundation of the film, Damien Chazelle approaches directing like a musician, offering a spectacle that further strengthens the purpose of the film. Chazelle has made the film his own instrument and approached each scene with Andrews meticulousness. The fact that blood, sweat, shouts and spit are not missing from the jazz pieces turns both the pieces and the instruments into a living entity. The blood spilled on the drums, the cymbals soaked in sweat and the drumsticks whose speed we cannot follow come to life by integrating with the musician playing them. Chazelle proves that the instrument has become a part of the body not only verbally but also visually, and he also brings the drums into a third leading role. Miles Teller, who integrates it with his body, also gives a performance that does justice to this film that has jazz in it. I love jazz music. Whether its bebop, hard bop, modal jazz, free jazz, cool jazz, smooth jazz or jazz rap, its some of the most interesting and exciting music for me. Its also one of the few genres that my dad and I can bond over, as he enjoys playing drums. In fact, hes even doing that right as Im writing this review. It was only natural that we decided to finally watch this movie together today.
Now, some of you may wonder why I gave the movie such a low rating (compared to the average score) if I love jazz so much. To put it simply This is not a jazz movie. Its essentially a sports film decorated with cheap jazz attire. That doesnt automatically make it bad, but for being the only representation of jazz education in popular media, it felt so grossly exaggerated and misleading that it started to distract from the amazing cinematography and decent acting. If youre trying to engage your audience in a setting taken directly from real-life, at least have some level of consistency.
A lot of the directions taken story-wise were predictable, and of course theres also the issue of inaccuracies, though I cant personally comment on that since I havent attended jazz school, but hearing about it from people who have felt strange considering the director was a student himself. Granted, its only natural for a movie to take creative liberties with its concept and not strive for complete realism, but even if you have basic knowledge of music, wasnt it odd for Andrew to practice playing as fast as possible to the point of bleeding when the songs themselves didnt necessarily need that? Im pretty sure jazz is more about steady time keeping, but I guess that would be too subtle for this film since its about as subtle as a punch to the snare drum with all the swearing, yelling and macho attitude going on.
The movie was so busy emphasising the aspects of competition and struggle that it came across as soulless and utterly cynical, especially towards the idea of music making. According to this film, its not about having fun or forming a friendly community, just mean-spirited competition and hierarchy. Like, do people find the abusive learning methods inspirational for some reason? Cause I can only imagine this will discourage most people to even step foot inside a jazz school. Also, how ironic that Fletcher condescendingly called modern jazz Starbucks jazz even though the piece he performed at the club had none of the energy that hip-hop infused jazz bands express in current day New York.
I could go on about all that or the ridiculously vulgar dialogue that served little to no purpose from what I could tell, but at the end of the day, Im not here to tell people theyre not allowed to enjoy this movie because of how it misrepresents jazz education or music. Nonetheless, it perplexes me how it managed to reach such level of acclaim.

I told you that story about how Charlie Parker became Charlie Parker, right? ... Jo Jones threw a cymbal at his head.
It amazes me how this quote so perfectly sums up the thrill ride that is  Writer and Director Damien Chazelle masterpiece Whiplash. 
Not quite my tempo.
Spoilers....
This was my third time seeing it, and I still find this film to be so immersive and powerful, with each of the major dramatic moments still having such a fierce impact. This movie almost seems tailor made for me since I was a serious trumpet player in High School, that went on to march two years of Drum Corps, and play casually in college. While I was never instructed by someone as violent as Fletcher, I definitely had a few that were as intense and intimidating. During the out of tune sequence during the group ensemble, I can totally envision myself being that poor trombone player whose mind blanks when being questioned by the force of nature that is Fletcher. It has to be noted that J.K. Simmons was spectacular in that Oscar winning role, that was so reminiscent of Sgt. Hartman from Full Metal Jacket. 
I never really had a Charlie Parker. But I tried. I actually fucking tried. And thats more than most people ever do.
Miles Teller is equally amazing as the main character Andrew, especially in those wild drumming scenes where he is pushing his body to the limit by trying to play faster and faster. I love all the close up shots in these sequences with beads of sweat dripping off his face, and him jamming his bleeding hand into that pitcher of ice water. 
His journey is such a roller coaster as Fletcher messes with his mind by giving him confidence, but then stripping it away. That scene where he is trying to get to the competition but everything seems to go wrong is basically a musicians worst nightmare. The moment where he rushes back to get his sticks, gets blindsided by a truck, but then still runs to the performance despite being a bloody mess is simply devastating. Then how can you not feel so moved when we see his dream coming to an end, and he watches that video of him drumming as a kid, when he had such pure passion while having so much fun learning to play a drum set. While I am proud trumpet player, I would be lying if I did not admit that I always thought playing the drums would have been way cooler.
Then HOLY SHIT, how about that ending. Once again we are given that nightmare scenario where he is sitting in front a packed audience without any music, and ends up looking like a fool. Then in one of the most adrenaline packed climaxes I have ever seen, he throws down so hard and somehow manages to finally gain Fletchers respect and bring it home with a heart pounding drum solo for the ages.
I was there to push people beyond whats expected of them. I believe thats an absolute necessity.
Chazelles direction is so on point and you can absolutely tell that he has musical experience, especially in that scene where Andrew has to sight read a piece of music, and we quickly get shots of everything on the page a musician would look at in order to quickly prepare to play it. While I love the cursing and intensity, it almost seems a bit too much at times and would put off a musically minded person that would otherwise love this movie. I think they made it so extreme, in order to hook in non musical people, and show them this not some lame movie about college jazz band.       
I am not sure if it was the Bluray or my TV, but I often noticed these yellow and purple hues of light on some of the characters faces at times which was really distracting. 
One of the great over looked elements of the film is the supporting cast with Paul Reiser as Andrews dad and Melissa Benoist as his girl friend. Reisers performance is so perfect with how he shows that he supports Andrew, but really has no idea what makes him tick. And that comes off beautifully in the scene at the movie theater, when his dad puts Rasinets on their popcorn thinking thats what they both like. But then he cant grasp Andrews courtesy with just allowing his Dad to do this ritual, while he eats around the candy.
Then I just love that chemistry Andrew has with Benoists character during their first date. She comes of so genuine with how much fun she is having with him despite how awkward he is. Then it is a shame to later witness him being a total ass to her by being so condescending, becasue Fletchers manipulation has pushed him to work even harder, and feel that he needs to break up with her in order to fully commit to his music.         
Whiplash is simply a tour de force, and it if does not get your heart racing by the end I would encourage you to check your pulse!
Thanks for reading!

The exhilarating impression imparted on me from a first-time screening of Damien Chazelles Whiplash was hard to ignore. The virtuoso features were seemingly endless an impeccable set decoration and use of heightened interior lighting a razor-sharp script with passages that coupled the highs and lows in the music room to personal life peaks and troughs, and an intensity in the leading acting performances. The coda also happened to leave me breathless in spite of my righteous take on the immorality of the screen figures. I watched the movie at the end of 2019 in preparation for a best of the decade appreciative piece, and was slightly concerned that it would not hold up. My knowledge of jazz music had progressed from the dilettantish perspective of how the film presents its version of a jazz conservatory as factually accurate, and I could comprehend with deeper reasoning as to why the disparagers of Whiplash would not analyse it beyond the tendentious view that artists must literally put themselves through obsessive hell to achieve the pinnacle of their potential greatness. The narrative can be defined as rather limited in scope, the heavy-handed antagonist flirts with caricature, and there are a few moments of suspended disbelief. Such minor flaws represented trivialities when attached alongside much of the perfection produced in this riveting and audacious triumph. Whiplash is a palpable adrenaline rush lean, visceral, and impassioned. A sure sign of a competent director and screenwriters successful output is in highlighting a niche subject (jazz drumming) to mass audiences, and finding the correct notes to make everyone care about each strike of the snare or cymbal like their life depended on it.
Recent appreciative essays on great movie selections have brought me additional context to answer such anxious uncertainties on the level of adversity one must endure to reach that standard. In John Cassavetess Opening Night the actress Myrtle Gordon professes a comprehensive dedication and drive for the art, even sacrificing her biological clock to prioritise a lifes legacy in theatre. In Powell and Pressburgers The Red Shoes the ballet impresario Boris Lermontov gives authoritative testament to his protégé Vicky that a great dancer cannot ascend from a reliance on doubtful human love, which brings distractions and a diluted focus to the core effort. Even playwright Wally in My Dinner with André helpfully quotes from Ingmar Bergmans Autumn Sonata on how someone can live (and die) in their art, but never feel anything in their life. These examples, among others, tend to present an artist challenged and encouraged by a shape-shifting mentor, and often the climax builds to a crescendo wherein the artist seizes control to give a radical, in some cases possessed, performance bordering on a semi-divine presence (yes, even Wally finally injects himself into the dinner conversation). Whiplash might not be an accurate portrayal of the ways in which a jazz fraternity, here represented by the fictional Shaffer orchestra, utilises teamwork and helpful tips to improve their synergy, but rest assured there is a healthy cutthroat rivalry to compensate for benign jam sessions. As a deliberation on the incessant, ugly hunger to be the best in a given field, however, it is arguably peerless through its beautiful execution of competitiveness. Like Myrtle and Vicky, the coveted public adoration for our leading player is a temptation that justifies leading a private life in lieu of applause.
The movie begins with an enthralling image and sound dichotomy to instantly grab the spectators complete attention. The sound of a snare drum being hit and growing louder, complemented by a long shot of our perspiring protagonist Andrew (Miles Teller) playing the kit from a narrow corridor vantage point, drenched in harsh fluorescent light and harsher green-coloured walls. Slowly the camera tracks closer and, as writer Chris Norris perceptively notes, here is the hero of a coming-of-age tale just waiting for his mentor. Chazelle blindsides us with the reveal that this camera movement is a subjective point-of-view gaze from that very mentors introduction, Terence Fletcher (J.K. Simmons), who leaves an indelible, albeit perplexing, mark on the rookies psyche. I went back to sample the opening sequence and unconsciously ended up persisting in viewing the entire feature, which I suspect is a common occurrence for others. The director Chazelle struggled to get funding based on the concept, but after completing a namesake short to showcase the proposed style and substance, investors began to understand the filmmakers approach beyond their preconceived notions of a dull jazz presentation. As film critic Emma Myers articulates, the feature-length Whiplash contains the kind of physicality one might expect from a sports movie but rarely finds in films about musicians. A.A. Dowd picks up the conversation on this topic, insisting that Chazelle has captured the rare music movie to focus not on the liberating joys of playing, but on the sheer, punishing hardship of the craft. Chazelle meticulously implemented storyboards in preparation for filming. This is evident in the result, as his editing style leans towards incorporating lots of cuts, primarily close-ups of the tools (the spit valve insertion is a wonderful visual cue for a musicians perennial pressure). Dowd expresses how much of the editing is an expression of internal anxiety, as Chazelle syncs his editing rhythms to the quickened pulse of his hero. The analogy of a sports movie is perceptive as we witness the resolute resolve to overcome the metaphorical losing position against the clock.
Most movies of the musical genre prefer to handpick either an artist who is naturally gifted, or conversely an imposter for comedy value purposes, although Inside Llewyn Davis is a notable exception with its reasonably talented journeyman musician. Since he was accepted into Shaffer, the top American university conservatory, Andrew is the former. It is difficult for the uninitiated to grasp whether the aspiring drummer in Whiplash is a true prodigy or a much of a muchness falling just short of greatness. On repeated viewings I have studied his play in comparison to his two alternate candidates, who are also vying to be the permanent core drum member of this elite New York studio band, and the difference initially appears incremental. Teller has experience of musical participation from his youth upbringing, and performs admirably on the drums in one of the few onscreen roles not filled by a trained musician, adding to its authenticity. In a scathing assessment of the films idea of jazz, the esteemed critic Richard Brody is adamant that theres nothing in the film to indicate that Andrew has any originality in his music. What he has, and what he ultimately expresses, is chutzpah. At a point in the film Fletcher confronts Andrew for being self-righteous and it is difficult to disagree with this despicable mans comment. Andrew has the air of superiority and self-entitlement, resenting the fact that he must earn the part and crassly dismissing the farcical level of his opponents. His arrogance spills over into the domestic sphere when he emasculates some family relations at the dinner table for playing football at a level well below the acceptable breeding grounds for the NFL. His attitude stems from the fact that the adults around the table find football a more attractive proposition to drumming, but it also insinuates his lack of teammate camaraderie because Andrew believes he is the centrepiece of the band. He idolises Buddy Rich, and that might account for some of his mimicked egotistical demeanour. Rich was one of the best drummers of all time with speed and precision, and he was not afraid to tell a fellow colleague when they were not keeping up with his rhythm or tempo.
Andrew fully intends to become one of the great drummers as he practices in the opening scene, but he has not yet pushed himself to the point where he practices so hard to move his hands at break-neck speed, in order to meet the commanded tempo demanded by his abrasive teacherconductor (Chazelles hiccup editing mirrors the abrasiveness). Resembling the side effects of a ballerinas feet as a reminder of their bodys punishment from repetitive motion, Andrews digits will resemble a fleshy collection of open sores, manifesting as tangible evidence to his self-destruction as he ups the ante to seek approval out of sheer desperation. His rivals Ryan (Austin Stowell) and Carl (Nate Long) are unlikely to bleed for their craft during after-hours prep, because they have friends, a social life and other interests. Andrews repression fuels a complete fixation to mastering his technique. It is true that Andrew regularly accompanies his dad Jim (Paul Reiser) to the cinema, but one can easily glean that the hermits highlight is exploiting a brief interaction with the attractive kiosk employee Nicole (Melissa Benoist). It is no shock to discover that once Andrew is given a confidence boost and promotion by a judging Fletcher for his drumming ability, he feels like a new man who is now also worthy of asking a woman on a date. Nor is it a surprise on the flip-side, that when humiliated by Fletchers sadism Andrew feels undeserving of love until he can once again prove himself with dedicated resilience, before seeking pleasures in other avenues. There are no two words in the English language more harmful than good job.
The obvious temptation with Whiplash is to either tear it to shreds on its own principle that criticism makes you stronger, or to (sarcastically) praise it, thereby spelling the directors doom. (Sadly I have the ability neither to seriously criticize it nor to ironically eulogize it.) The central question of the film revolves around the cost of success, asking whether genius can be achieved without sacrifice and perseverance (and what your life is worth if you have neither).
Andrew (Miles Teller) is constantly being pushed to (and past) his breaking point by his teacher Mr. Fletcher (J.K. Simmons), and all of the narrative turning points pivot on his decision to keep trying or give up and take the easy way out. These are the elementary psychological coordinates for (death) drive, as Andrews proximity to his own destruction makes clear whether this ethical standpoint ought to apply to jazz (does practice really make perfect in a profession where passion takes precedence?) is a question the film never really asks, for better or for worse.
Where writerdirector Damien Chazelles love for music comes into play is the films unique rhythm. It builds tension quickly to a small peak just after the halfway point, then drops back down and slowly builds back up to a higher peak for its climactic ending. In terms of Vonneguts famous Shapes of Stories, this approximately represents the Cinderella story that fascinated him so much, but with the princesss happiness replaced with Andrews success as a drummer (something which doesnt necessarily entail being happy). The overall structure of the story might not be anything new (its basically a sports movie in the mold of Miracle), but this distinct narrative tempo gives it a musical ebb and flow that makes it stand out from the rest of the years more mainstream releases. 
Since its that time of the year, the most obvious thing to note is that Miles Teller and J.K. Simmons both give outstanding performances (Teller is great not merely for a young actor but in general). More interesting for me, however, were the editing and sound mixing. The former is a large part of what I liked about the films rhythm (and there are some great montages particularly during the performances) the latter is easy to forget about but absolutely integral to the success of a movie where music plays a central role (the drums are a character created by the sound department). The cinematography is fairly strong as well, and for the first time in a long time I felt the use of handheld was actually quite tasteful.
The films not without its problems. Beyond the question of whether its philosophy ought to actually apply to the world of jazz, Im not at all convinced the girlfriend worked for the story (not because of anything Melissa Benoist does or doesnt do, her character just wasnt written in well enoughthe final phone call is particularly perplexing).
Every year I have a difficult time around awards season because of the inevitable gap between what are considered good movies and what I actually enjoy watching. A lot of attention is paid to big performances, and I often feel this comes at the expense of other aspects of film I personally find more interesting. In this sense, Whiplash is a case of the best of both worlds. Its a well made film about the struggles of a young man to maintain his drive, and thats exactly the kind of Oscar-bait Im willing to put my weight behind. A late comer to my favorites of 2014, this movie has now sneaked into my top 10 for the year.

Why do we strive for greatness? What pushes someone to practice something over and over, until his hands bleed, until he perfects it? Can this intensity be brought out in all of us? Whiplash is a portrait of a young jazz drummer, Andrew Neiman, who possesses this drive to such a degree that everything else in his life is just background noise. The film contains superb acting performances, stylish but effective cinematography, and an upbeat, unpredictable nature that resembles the very essence of jazz itself. Blood, sweat and a hideous use of the term faggot flow amid rolling abuse that is homophobic, sexist and all shades of offensive. It spills out of the mouth of Terence Fletcher and infects the ears of his young proteges  fearful, sad-eyed obsessives. This verbal ugliness  off-putting though it may be  is intentional and just one note of the multi-instrumental jazz-band that makes up Whiplash. Damien Chazelles film feeds off his experience as a student drummer. It asks questions like Where is the line between motivation and abuse?, What would you sacrifice to be creatively great? and Who cares what you do when youve set out your stall as a revolting human being? It does so within a tightly told, euphorically shot tale of an ambitious drummers relationship with a psychopathic teacher. Andrew and Fletcher share an intensity that is unmatched by most people. It causes them to alienate themselves and harm the ones they care about as they pursue perfection. Whiplash does not idolize them for this, nor does it vilify them, Damien Chazelle paints a picture into their world and how the pursuit of success tramples most other qualities of life.
Whiplash moves to comic beats, just one of its many shape-shifting skills. Simmons is a beloved comic actor and he spits out lines at the right tempo to front them as hilarious. For a short spell he could be the loveable rogue, just as Andrew could be an introverted hero destined to flower and be redeemed through musical recognition. Chazelle plays with our presumptions. When Andrew shyly asks out Nicole, he seems to be headed down that exact path. What if success doesnt suit a person? is another question the film asks amid intense practice sessions, there are sufficient reminders along the way that one mans dream is anothers grotesque isolation. After all, at its core Whiplash is not only about jazz its about who you want to be. For then the last ten minutes of the film plays out, a virtually dialogue-free psychological battle of wills between Andrew and Fletcher. A piece of cinema that has me utterly holding my breath each time I watch it, my body tensing, my nails bitten to shreds. Its daft I know whats coming. Ive seen the film a few times. Yet each time I get so invested in it, that its like watching it afresh. I cant remember in recent times being invested so much in a finale featuring characters I really wasnt fond of. But the intensity, focus and brilliance of Whiplash had me willing the two of them on. Every single time. Its an ending that sticks. The film leaves moral questions,  Do the ends justify the means, after all? No answers are given, no side is taken. Thats left to us afterwards. Damien Chazelle has made a film that entertains as it interrogates. One final question is when the abuser wants from you exactly what you want out of yourself, can you still call it abuse?

Watching Whiplash in theaters was nothing short of a religious experience. This masterpiece has all of the cinematic elements that make it ripe for the big screen. The crisp cinematography, beautiful deep yellows and greens, the coked-up camera movements and of course an iconic soundtrack that elevates this already perfect film. 
This movie balances between a character study and a psychological thriller. Choosing to display complex character traits and other times heightening the tension with a symphony of brass instruments. This movie is mythological in how it showcases Niemans pursuit of perfection. Never for a moment are his intentions unknown, his obsession bleeds into every aspect of his life. I think Teller gives a career performance and deservedly put him on the map. However, the real star of this movie is J.K. Simmons. He absolutely shines in his role of a sadistic instructor. Its hard 10 years later to fully understand how meaningful this performance was for Simmons career, even I dont fully understand. Simmons was well respected in the industry prior to this movie, but never an actor you thought would have an Oscar winning performance. Drawing from his personal experiences as a jazz drummer, Damien Chazelle (La La Land, Babylon) intensely explores the toxic relationship between Andrew (Miles Teller), an ambitious young musician obsessed with greatness, and Terence Fletcher (J.K. Simmons), the tyrannical instructor at a Manhattan conservatory.
The direction is as precise as a metronome, turning each rehearsal into a battlefield. Chazelle captures sweating bodies, bloodied drumsticks, and piercing gazes with an energy reminiscent of war films. The opening scene, where the camera advances like a predator toward Andrew before Fletchers sudden interruption, immediately establishes the psychological duel. Tight editing, oppressive close-ups, and a dark palette create unrelenting tension.
Yet the film is not without flaws. An early second-act segment, where Andrew questions his pursuit, lacks subtlety. More troublingly, two major issues persist Fletchers racist and homophobic tirades go unchallenged, normalizing abuse, while Andrew, equally unlikable, scorns his girlfriend after courting her.
Despite these reservations, Whiplash remains a fascinating work, elevated by extraordinary performances. Simmons embodies a mentor who is both monstrous and captivating, while Teller portrays a student willing to endure anything for perfection. The climactic sequence, of rare intensity, transforms this musical drama into an epic battle where every note becomes a weapon. Chazelle achieves the remarkable feat of making jazz accessible, even thrilling, while probing the moral limits of artistic ambition.

La mise en scène, aussi précise quun métronome, transforme chaque répétition en champ de bataille. Chazelle filme les corps en sueur, les baguettes ensanglantées et les regards percutants avec une énergie proche du film de guerre. Pourtant, le film nest pas exempt de défauts. Un passage en début de deuxième heure, où Andrew doute de sa quête, manque de subtilité. Surtout, deux problèmes majeurs à mon sens subsistent  Fletcher, sous couvert dexigence, déverse des insultes racistes et homophobes sans que le film les questionne, banalisant le harcèlement  Andrew, quant à lui, peu sympathique, méprise sa compagne après lavoir séduite.
Malgré ces réserves, Whiplash simpose comme une œuvre fascinante. Simmons incarne un mentor à la fois monstrueux et captivant, Teller un élève prêt à tout pour la perfection. The tension here not only between Finchers direction and Sorkins script but Sorkins own internal war between his worship of institutions and Great Men and his disdain for everything Zuckerberg represents produces a film that reckons with technocracy as the new empire. For something that came out well before the truly dire potential of Facebook manifested itself, The Social Network is surprisingly far-seeing, extrapolating a horror show from a site founded by an unfeeling, envious nerd with a superiority complex, tacitly identifying in Zuckerbergs willingness to cheat and steal from rivals and friends alike the seeds for an entire outlook that would see Facebook eventually steal everyones ad revenue and sell metadata, not to mention the capacity of social networking to scramble everyones relationship to the world and remake socializing in the image of an antisocial sociopath. Finchers gliding shots over Harvards campus take on a Visconti vibe as he surveys one of the old markers of power and status as it is rendered irrelevant by sharks like Zuck and Sean Parker, who recognize they can ascend the ladder not by kowtowing to societys betters but completely reorienting society itself.
It is hard to ignore how, in classic Sorkin fashion, the film can open with a woman righteously shutting down Mark for being exactly the megalomaniacal misogynist that he is only for every subsequent female character to be some combination of starstruck groupie, total klutz or clingy psycho, but for once this is at least somewhat balanced by Sorkins jaundiced view of the new masters of society who are all emotionally stunted, greedy monsters. Even Eduardo doesnt get out of this clean, coming across as naive and so interested in his own bottom line that he doesnt realize hes been cheated until its too late. Finchers love of shadows and sickly color grading are oddly perfect for the seemingly low stakes of the film, capturing the shut-in, wired-in focus of these programmers and pushing stereotypes of basement dwelling nerds into unsettling visual language. The final scene, of Mark dead-eyed refreshing his feed to see if Erica will accept his friend request on the world-changing site he developed in part out of resentment for her criticism of him is so much more unnerving in 2020 than it was in 2010, not a cry for help but a harbinger of a completely broken relationship to other people that has become the norm.

I was excluded from Facebook!
Back in 2004 (maybe early 2005), I was living with three guys who were students at the University of Texas, and I remember when The Facebook showed up on the UT campus. I couldnt get an account because I wasnt a UT student and didnt have a UT .edu email address. I remember being like, oh man, I want to be a part of that. 
So a movie about a guy driven by his desire not to be excluded hits a little different for me.
The opening scene is a date, and his girlfriend tells him hes going to go through life thinking girls dont like him because hes a nerd, and that its not that, its because hes a jerk. Then the whole movie plays that out. 
This version of Mark Zuckerberg is such an unlikable human, and you cant take your eyes off of him. Jesse Eisenberg is so good at playing these neurotic characters that are socially awkward, talk too fast, sort of clueless, but somehow sympathetic at the same time, because you feel bad for him while hes saying such rude and awful things. Add the Aaron Sorkin zingers, and Im sitting there going, dude, back off. Stop talking. Why are you being so mean to someone that helped you out so much? How can you not see where this is headed?
He so desperately wants to connect with people and be accepted, but hes so bad at it, and he pushes away anyone whose approval hes actually wanted. He achieves so much, but he cant overcome his own character defects. By the end hes burned all the bridges, he has 500 million friends on Facebook, and hes lost all of his real friends. Its an underdog story while being a tragedy at the same time, and when a movie can have both of those going at once, you know you have something special.
Everyone is written to perfection and played to perfection. When I first saw it, I didnt know who Armie Hammer was, and I just assumed they got actual twins. Weirdo Armie Hammer is so seamless as both of them. Andrew Garfield is the one character without that duality. Hes just a good guy trying to do whats best for his friend, and assuming the best of people is his weakness.
Fincher and Sorkin dont seem like an obvious pairing. Sorkin left to his own devices can get a little too over the top (Sorkin on top of Sorkin), but here hes contained just enough in the box that is Fincher, and they turn a story about coding and court depositions into something funny and fascinating, with characters probably a lot more interesting than their real life counterparts. Then theres the Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross score. Their modern and unique style brings a lively energy to whatever they work on, and a synthesized score in a grounded drama fits perfectly with something so computer based.
Mark Zuckerberg was 26 when this came out. and it still feels like a fraction of the story.

A principios de los años dos mil, yo era muy fanático de Alejandro Dolina. Casi todas las noches me quedaba despierto hasta muy tarde escuchando La Venganza Será Terrible, su programa de radio que se emitía de lunes a viernes a la medianoche. Aunque Telefe prometía su inicio a las once de la noche, en realidad, solían empezar mucho más tarde, desafiando mi voluntad y capacidad de permanecer despierto. El cansancio siempre ganaba y solo veía la primera mitad del capítulo. La otra se me entremezclaba con lo que soñaba, y una noche soñé con Milazzo infiltrado en Irak matando iraquíes.     Retomando lo que venía diciendo. Por unos amigos, también fanáticos de Dolina, me entero que en 1998 escribió (y protagonizó) una opereta llamada Lo Que Me Costó El Amor De Laura. Me prestaron los dos CDs y la escuché. Quedé enloquecido con toda la obra, especialmente con un temazo que se llama Tango De La Muerte, cantado increíblemente por Juan Carlos Baglietto, y que lo pueden escuchar ACÁ AHORA MISMO. 
    No escribo todo esto porque quiero hablar de Lo Que Me Costó El Amor De Laura, mi intención es destacar la poderosa primera frase con la que comienza la opereta Se ha dicho que los hombres hacen todo lo que hacen con el único fin de enamorar mujeres.

Mark dice Esto es lo que impulsa la vida. Es por eso que la gente toma ciertas clases, se sienta donde se sienta y hace lo que hace Para conocer a alguien 
    Tanto Mark Zuckerberg como Alejandro Dolina, personas extremadamente opuestas la una de la otra y que jamás pensé verlas juntas en un mismo texto, tienen razón. Especialmente en el contexto del mundo digital e internet, lo que dijo Dolina adquiere más relevancia. Cada cosa que uno hace, cada palabra que escribe o publicación que comparte en las redes sociales tiene como objetivo (en la mayoría de los casos) llamar la atención de alguien en particular. 
    Es cierto que esta dinámica existe desde la era del MSN, cuando incluíamos frases de canciones en nuestro nickname que solo esa persona entendería, o nos conectábamos y desconectábamos repetidamente para que recibiera la notificación y se percatara de nuestra presencia. Y esta tendencia persiste en plataformas como Instagram, donde compartimos historias públicas que en realidad están dirigidas a una persona específica, o likeamos alguna publicación como una señal para dar pie a una conversación. Sin embargo, generalmente nos encontramos en un impasse eterno, donde ambos esperamos que el otro dé el siguiente paso. Todos estamos dando indicios para que nos hablen, pero al final, nadie lo hace.

    En fin En el medio apareció Facebook, y me acuerdo perfectamente el día que lo conocí. Con una interfaz muy simple podías subir una foto por día, acompañada opcionalmente de algún texto, y comentar las fotos de los demás. Listo. Así de simple. 
    Una noche nos juntamos en la casa de Sofía, una amiga y compañera de cursada. Su departamento siempre era el punto de reunión porque era la única que vivía sola. Whats kind of most immediately striking upon revisiting this is how much this is a push-pull between Sorkin and Fincher - as opposed to Sorkins later Steve Jobs, clearly written for Fincher, the director came to this project as a virtual for-hire job for Sorkins immensely industry-popular script, and part of what makes this film so entertaining is its core contradictions Sorkin critiques Zuckerberg and turns him into a Horatio Alger myth crossed with a Faustian bargain.  Fincher, on the other hand, relates to him.  Its even more obvious now too look at how he left Steve Jobs after Scott Rudin wouldnt raise the budget  give Fincher control over advertising, or both Utopia and Video Synchronicity falling apart at HBO - the latter after having already shot six episodes shot, or the recent collapse of World War Z 2.  Sorkin despises Zuckerberg, an arrogant proto-millenial who cant stand anyones voice but his own and who is willing to sell out his closest relationships to get what he wants.  And almost perversely, the director admires that Zuckerberg thinks outside the terms of the defined, knows the value of his ideas and thus will pursue them independently, ultimately changing the digital landscape, perhaps permanently - and maybe even regardless of the consequences to boot.  The film itself however, sits somewhere in between - Sorkins moralism and Finchers ambiguity colliding make the film as interesting as it is.  And sometimes Sorkin is right, and sometimes Fincher is right.  And the rest of it is a Wikipedia page on steroids.  Far from a problem - in fact, pretty suitable for the information age.
This turns The Social Network into a kind of best of both worlds scenario, and where Sorkin and Finchers perspectives converge is in the films early section, where unambiguous misogyny is fundamental to one of Zuckerbergs inventions and furthermore grabs the attention of the Winklevoss twins, who are absolutely willing to have Zuckerberg join their team as his talent and skill is of more potential market-value than any moral perspective or any consequence of Zuckerbergs actions - which ultimately get erased.  There is a problem here misogyny is only part of this films setup.  Beyond that, its rarely part of the films basic functions, and only is subject in further interactions with Erica Albright (also rare) and this seems like the subject is only part of the film as a kind of safety-net rather than any serious quandary or investigation.  Its odd, because misogyny becomes a core subject of Finchers following three works (including Mindhunter) but here seems like, even though the sequences are strong in themselves, very much like somewhat insincere window dressing - perhaps as its well known how the corporation began.  As the film progresses, Sorkin is more interested in classic themes like friendship, power and betrayal, while Fincher is more invested in Zuckerbergs superceding of old structures a la Ivy League culture and Harvard itself by his skill level in digital media.  
This surprisingly makes The Social Network resemble Fight Club more than it does any of Finchers following works in its investment towards a totally male-dominated business model, at least in this chapter of the businesss existence.  But this is also where it gets a bit confusing - confusing nevertheless only in retrospect, its an absolute thrill to watch.  The film sets itself up as ostensible critique of this boys-club dynamic yet Fincher is completely enthralled in Zuckerbergs ability - its obvious by the way Fincher edits Zuckerbergs breakthrough montages and the blinking lightbulb scoring which accompanies them.  In this regard, The Social Networks overnight success and becoming a borderline cultural phenomenon is kind of perplexing - theres something mildly evil about this movie.  In a way, Finchers willingness to overlook the misogyny of Zuckerbergs initial motivation mirrors that of the Winklevosses - an aspect to this film which is only tempered by Sorkins moral judgement of Zuckerberg.  
Its this push-pull between the two creatively which makes this film so unusual - a collision of Sorkins moralisms and Finchers energy from being in awe of Zuckerberg.  And as mentioned before, there are sections where Fincher isnt necessarily off-mark in that admiration Zuckerberg overrides the entire Harvard social structure so much to the point which it is no longer even the barest consideration.  The class structure of the society becomes completely meaningless and at the same time he is unwilling to let anyone else take advantage of his ideas or talent.  He absolutely nabbed the idea for Facebook from the Winklevosses, and hes also not wrong when he exclaims If you had invented Facebook, you would have invented Facebook.  But this is also much more clever than it looks - see how Fincher subtly undermines Saverin.  
Sorkin sides with Saverin - Zuckerberg is a ruthless asshole and Saverins complaints are justified on a moral level.  But Fincher is more devious - while we intuitively grasp Saverins position, Fincher makes him out to be almost completely incompetent to the point of him having not accomplished a thing throughout the films entire runtime, going to parties and fraternity entrance exams while Zuckerberg stays in writing code, being part of the world that Zuckerberg is deftly overriding.  Furthermore, Zuck only cracks once in the entire runtime while Saverin is having an emotional meltdown in what feels like every other scene, pointing fingers and blame at everyone but himself.  Saverin lives in the moment, Zuckerberg works for the long-term.  Note especially how Zuckerberg points out that he had actually defended him, while Saverin believes (for no real reason) that Zuckerberg planted a story about him.  Sorkin believes Saverin Zuckerbergs momentum was created by jealousy towards him and not getting into the clubs, so Zuckerberg destroyed them.  Finchers with Zuckerberg no, he just hit the game really hard.
Its only the ending which seems a bit heavy-handed now, though the recall to Albright is welcomed (and probably necessary) - otherwise this feels like wrapping things up way too quickly, something which I thought at the time and am surprised to see that I feel the same way.  Suddenly, Timberlakes Parker seems like a comical parody of a cocaine addict, while Zuckerberg sits at the computer, alone, refreshing Albrights page.  But that Alger-esque ending seems too easy nine years later - because we know that Zuckerberg is quite comfortable and only got bigger.  But maybe its a case of having it both ways again on one hand it seems a bit moralistic - the way I took it when it first came out, but on another hand it reminds me of the ending of Rossellinis Louis XIV - the king alone in his room, refreshing the page that he created.

There are many things I like about this movie but the bit that always impresses me the most is the sound mixing in the club scene where Zuckerberg is being indoctrinated by Sean Parker.
In every other scene ever made where characters are having a conversation against loud noise, the background sound gets pulled down to a level that centers the dialogue while preserving the desired atmosphere. Thats the obvious and sensible approach. But Fincher and his mixer have the music blasting at max volume through the entire scene  not just louder than the dialogue, but louder than anything else in the entire movie. And through some kind of dark EQ magic, they have the vocal frequencies sitting against the music in exactly the right way to replicate the experience of actually being in a loud club and mentally focusing on the sound of another persons voice. Every line is perfectly audible even though you feel yourself straining to listen.
Its a neat way to make an audience lean in, and its also a clever reflection of what it feels like to live in the social media attention economy Zuckerberg and his cohort are about to create. The Feed blares at us day and night and we hone in on the signals we choose to listen to.
Its also interesting that Fincher, a legendarily insane stickler for detail, nailed everything about the look and vibe of an SF douchebag night spot, but instead of using period-accurate music, he chose a then-new progressive house track with a sound thats distinctly 2010s instead of early-2000s. It makes perfect sense  it was a scene about right now, and it still is.
 This is partly due to stagnation in the field of big room house music, which I will examine in a future review.

We lived on farms, then we lived in cities, and now were going to live on the internet.
Ten Years, Ten Films Revisiting 2010
The Social Network isnt just about Mark Zuckerberg creating Facebook, its about the birth of social media and the beginning of a new era. Sure, social media existed before Facebook, and it certainly exists now outside of Facebook, but Facebook marked a turning point, the point where it blew up and infiltrated every aspect of our social lives. As Sean Parker astutely points out, Private behavior is a relic of a time gone by.
David Fincher foregrounds the central issue to this turning point in social media toxic masculine competitiveness. The film opens on a conversation between Mark Zuckerberg and then-girlfriend Erica Albright about Final Clubs, exclusive all-male college groups built around hazing rituals and other forms of social competition. Mark wants to be recognized by the clubs hes looking for validation from his male peers, and the film directly connects this search for recognition with his invention of Facebook. 
But this vision of masculinity also comes with a healthy dose of misogyny. We initially see this in the way Mark disrespects Erica throughout the opening scene, berating her for the unintended implications of the things she says (Which club is the easiest to get into?) while simultaneously making all the same sorts of backhanded, passive-aggressive comments with intentional malice (You go to BU.). This is eventually developed into the blatant objectification of FaceMash (literally rating girls based on their physical attractiveness), which itself serves as the foundation of Facebook. The invention of Facebook was rooted in sexism.
While this explicit misogyny may be more hidden in todays mainstream iteration of Facebook, the same roots remain. It still reproduces the unhealthy social dynamics it was inspired by as Mark frantically hacks into different school databases of student photos, Fincher cross-cuts to the social clubs Mark desperately wants to accept him. Theyre out partying while hes inside on his computer. This is both Marks motivation for what hes creating (he wants to party) and a visual representation of what hes creating (a permanent digital party). Facebook isnt just the future of social clubs, it is the very essence of social clubs distilled down to its purest form. Through parallel editing, Mark writes the social clubs into code.
And whats so wrong with that? Theyre just college parties theyre stupid, but the students will eventually grow out of them, right? But precisely by inscribing them into the most popular social media network on the planet, people now no longer have to grow out of them. Mark takes a business call from his backyard pool while implicitly underage girls take rips out of a ten-foot bong in their underwear. He throws away the only positive relationship in his life in order to get closer to Sean Parker. Why? Because Sean is cool, the same way Final Clubs and frat parties are cool. Mark idolizes cool hes not an asshole, hes just trying so hard to be. 
Writing about something thats become such a massive part of our everyday lives is a daunting task. How do we talk about the way that Facebook has become an integral part of our cultural and political landscape? That brings me to Eisenbergs performance. His rapid and confident delivery of his lines enhance and enlarge the character he is portraying, in essence a disturbed, socially inept whiner. Rewatched this mostly to check in on how the RED ONE footage has aged, and Im pleased to say that this is now unquestionably no-doubt-about-it dated in an era when even Fincher cant seem to resist the urge to emulate aesthetic tics associated with older mediums, the specific combination of high contrast, heavily sharpened, stridently denoised shallow-focus imagery, extremely fussily-composed spherical scope frames, sickly lighting and sicklier skintones, moderately limited dynamic range and monochromatic color washes that this film exemplifies so well feels like a hugely interesting aesthetic road that has largely not been taken by anyone since.  
Its a real shame because its wildly effective here in a film about the dawn of a new, dehumanized world in which a bunch of the worlds worst guys work to supplant tactile reality with the sterile negative space of textureless pixels on a screen. Rarely has a radical aesthetic been so perfectly-matched to its subject, and it feels like a profound loss that in the wake of this type of innovation the bulk of popular cinema has reverted to fetishisation of older formats or complete apathy towards image texture. 
 My suspicions that Cronenweths visuals here work significantly better for me than any of Finchers subsequent films were confirmed on this viewing, and the colour rhythm is a significant contributor. The use of bold monochromatic washes here is completely fearless and inspired every scene is color-coded, and so in a nonlinear film like this with constant intercutting Fincher and Cronenweth are able to create a fantastically propulsive visual rhythm by simply letting the green of one sickly office smash right into the overbearing tungsten lighting of an wood-paneled musky Harvard interior before letting that smash into a pale blue scene in the dead of winter and so on and so forth.

In preparation I just got done rewatching The Social Network on my 4K copy, which  my thoughs have not changed, I have watched this films so many time, and every single time I love it more and more, and its a film that I think is timeless to this day. Directed by David Fincher ( side note he is in my top ten maybe top five favorite filmmakers of all time) the film charts the founding of Facebook by Harvard student Mark Zuckerberg and the ensuing legal and personal fallout. 
When it comes to the film The Social Network it is a cinematic tour de force that transcends the biographical drame genre, it delivers a reveting as well as masterfully crafted exploration of ambition, betrayal, and the complexities of human relationships in the digital age. Aaron Sorkins razor-sharp screenplay is a marvel of structure as well as dialogue, he weaves in timelines together with precision to unravel the dramatic genesis of Facebook and the personal rivalries that defined its early days. What I love so much about the films is its ability to balance dense legal and technical subject matter with deeply engaging character drama that it makes it nonthing but extraordinary.
David Fincher direction is nonthing short but masterful, he employs his signature visual style to create a film that is both sleek and atmospheric. The cinematography is just incredible, it enhances the films tone really well, using mood lighting and dynamic compositions to mirror the tension simmering beneath the surface. But the score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Rosss is my favorite craft of the film, it won a Oscar for a good reason it is a perfect complement, it manges to blend electronic snd orchestral elements to heighten the films intensity and underscore its themes of isolation and ambition. It really is that damn good.
The performances here are just incredible. Jesse Eisenberg is one of my personal favorite actors which here he delivers a career-defining performance as Mark Zuckerberg, he potrays the Facebook founder with this fascinating blend of intelligence, social awkwardness, and ruthless determination. Eisenbergs nuanced potrayal makes Zuckerberg both compelling as well as enigmatic, capturing the relentless drive for success at the expense of personal relationships. But Andrew Garfield deserves credit too as Eduardo Saverin, he brings the emotional heart of the story, whose friendship with Zuckerberg forms the films tragic core, now Justin Timberlake as Sean Parker he dont belong or deserve to be in the same category as Eisenberg  Garfield, I also  dont like him like at all as a person but I will say this he is charismatic here, and he brings a layer of seductive ambition as well as calculated chaos to the narrative that honestly suits him for the type of person he is. There chemistry elevates every scene, it makes the tension and betrayal feel palpably real.
But what makes The Social Network so damn good and honestly so timeless, is that it was never really about Facebook. Underneath all the technology, money, lawsuits, and business deals is something incredibly human wanting to belong. Mark acts like he doesnt care about popularity, exclusive, clubs, status, or what anybody thinks about him, but almost everything he does suggests otherwise. He wants respect, he wants acceptance, and most importantly he wants the people who rejected him to eventually realize how important he is. Thats why Ericas words at the beginning basically hang over the entire film, Mark can spend his life convincing himself people dont like him because hes different when the real problem might simply be how he treats them. His relationship with Eduardo makes that especially painful because Eduardo believes in him BEFORE Facebook becomes Facebook, yet the bigger the company gets, the smaller their friendship becomes. Then Sean Parker arrives representing everything Mark seems fascinated by confidence, success, rebellion, and the appearance of being completely untouchable. 
I also love how this film somehow turns creating a website into a damn good thriller. Every success creates another opportunity, every opportunity changes another relationship, and we already know these people end up sitting across from each other in deposition rooms. Were not waiting to see if everything falls apart, were watching how, and Facebook itself becomes the perfect contradiction at the center of everything. Mark creates something capable of connecting millions of people while becoming increasingly disconnected from the people directly in front of him. Technology has changed dramatically since 2010, but insecurity, jealous, status, validation, and our desperate need for acceptance havent gone anywhere. Thats why that ending is still damn perfect. After all the money, power, betrayal, and success Mark is sitting alone refreshing a screen hoping one person accepts him. He changed the way millions of people connect without ever figuring out how to connect himself. 
Overall The Social Network  is not just a film about the birth of Facebook it is a profound and unflinching look at the cost of innovation and the fragility of relationships in the pursuit of greatness. This in my opinion is a top three David Fincher film and to this day it remains one of the most defining films of the 21st century and a testament to the power of storytelling at its finest.
