It is extremely rare to come across a film that defines perfection from the first frame to the last. One that exhibits precision craftsmanship in even the minutest of aspects. One that takes its viewers on an unforgettable journey and leaves them absolutely speechless in the end. And for me, Paul Thomas Andersons There Will Be Blood is one of those rare gems that fits those attributes with unfailing accuracy.
A jaw-dropping work of originality, an immensely captivating vignette of greed  obsession, and a thoroughly intriguing character study that still remains in a league of its own, There Will Be Blood is a haunting portrait of family, religion, hatred, oil  madness that not only marks an artistic high for its writer-director but is the very pinnacle of 21st century American cinema and deserves to be ranked amongst the greatest films ever made.
Set during the times when America was just discovering oil, the story concerns a ruthless  cunning oilman Daniel Plainview who tries to buy the Sunday familys ranch after being informed about oil deposits in the area but the familys younger son Eli sees through his plot and demands more money. The rest of the film covers Plainview  Sunday clashing over matters of business  religion which eventually culminates on a devastating note.
Written  directed by Paul Thomas Anderson, There Will Be Blood presents the writer-director in sublime form and is a marvel of period filmmaking that I have no hesitation in calling his best work to date. The script comes packed with interesting characters and is driven by their actions but where Anderson impresses most is in turning those pages into imagery in a way that exhibits his precise control over each aspect.
Coming to the technical aspects, every single element here works in harmony with the other and is expertly executed under the directors supervision. The desolate locations are reminiscent of the timeline it is set in. Cinematography employs slow zooms, steady manoeuvres, wide tracking or panning shots  long unbroken takes in ways that make this drama more immersive. Editing lets the plot unravel at its own pace. And Jonny Greenwoods score is as fitting as it is unsettling  unconventional.
Coming to the performances, Anderson had already done an excellent job in carving out  refining the personality of Daniel Plainview but the sheer intensity  passion with which Daniel Day-Lewis brings him to life transcends all expectations, for it is a truly maddening, extraordinary  career-best performance from the revered actor which single-handedly elevates an already great film to an even higher level of greatness. Also contributing with strong support is Paul Dano who manages to hold his own against Day-Lewis imposing act.
On an overall scale, There Will Be Blood is one of the all-round perfect films in existence and is certainly amongst the most flawless works of 21st century cinema. Addressing the themes of greed, lies, manipulation, obsession  power, it is an aesthetic, artistic  influential film that pushes the cinematic artform into newer realms, marks a massive leap for both its director  lead actor when compared to their previous works, and is filmmaking at its most perfect, genuine, complete, crystalline  pure. Strongly recommended. Multiple viewings advised.

There are only a handful of artists that have it in them to comment through their medium on the nature of humanity. In cinema there havent been that many that do or have done this as consistently impressively as Paul Thomas Anderson has. 
There Will Be Blood is Shakespearean in nature and like The Bards great tragedies, it offers no easy exits and no redemption. We are presented with a protagonist representing our species most problematic possession, the ego. Daniel Plainview is a rotten man, only concerned with his own growth and personal gain, with one goal, to get away from people because he doesnt like them. Throughout the film we are shown how he manipulates, bullies and murders. Whether because he wants people to do things for him or because he is deceived in some way, he has to be the one in control, the one with the power. He is also a self made man. We can admire him for his drive and for his enterprising demeanour. But in the end, he most definitely isnt a good man. Id even go so far as to say that he is evil.
When filmmakers or storytellers want to comment on the nature of evil, they often forget that for someone to be evil they first have to be human. Daniel Plainview is a thoroughly evil man, but Anderson never loses sight of his humanity. Even when, later in his life, he becomes more beast than man, we are always fully aware of who he is, where he came from and that in his road to where he is now, he has made poor decisions and felt the pain of the loneliness he so sought after. And that is what makes him a tragic character instead of just the villain of the piece. Daniel Plainview is one of the most intriguing and frighteningly human characters ever created.
In most stories there has to be balance, but in Andersons tale there isnt. The force countering Plainview is good at the surface, but deep underneath Eli Sundays character lies the same ego that drives Plainview. With a façade of religious goodness, he is as manipulative as his counterpart with him betraying his true nature in that phenomenal final scene. Plainview is never intimidated by Eli in the film because he sees him for what he is, he recognises himself and thus knows how to deal with him. 
With these different sides of the same coin it seems Anderson wants to highlight the duality of man. From ambition can come great things but we need a connection, a moral compass to guide us along the way. Plainview has convinced himself he doesnt need that connection, but we are also shown his regrets and his eagerness when a possible connection shows up out of the blue. Eli seeks this guidance in, what Plainview considers, a fabrication. It most certainly seems that Eli doesnt do what he does out of faith and conviction but out of doubt and a need for validation. Slowly but surely Anderson allows his characters to regress into a more basic state of being, almost primal in their archetypical roles, bound on an inescapable collision course, much like where we are now as a society. It runs deeper than capitalism versus religion, it is man versus himself which always seems to be the source of any conflict in history and current affairs. Im glad I am a bit more hopeful than Anderson but his grim depiction and condemnation of what we are and can be is frighteningly accurate and recognisable.
Daniel Day Lewiss total immersion in his character and Andersons choice to place him in practically every shot, mostly in close up is what makes this film so mesmerizing. Studying Lewiss face is fantastic, the nuance he puts into his character, the command of his voice, everything is breathtaking. This is probably one of the best performances I have ever seen by any actor. As distant as the character is, the performance sucked me in and made it impossible to look away. Paul Dano is great as well, giving strong competition in the scenes they share, but it does feel that happens because of the generosity of Lewis. He commands and dominates when he needs, but is fully aware when he has to give room to his fellow actors.
The music is absolutely amazing. It enhances every single shot it is put under, sometimes striking a nerve because of its discordant nature. It is simply a perfect companion to the amazing images, be they epic or small.
Anderson has with There Will Be Blood produced a film that is a technical marvel, a soul searching comment, an example of pure craftsmanship and a cinematic milestone. He pushes the boundaries of existential storytelling and film making so hard with this film that it most deservedly should get all the accolades it has been given. On all levels, this is an important film.

Paul Thomas Andersons There Will Be Blood deals with epic themes and settings the emergence of modern American capitalism and religion on the wide-open California oil fields of the early twentieth century. Whats remarkable about the films approach is that these issues are largely pushed to the periphery of the frame. At the center of the frame, for nearly every shot in the this two and a half hour film are Daniel Day-Lewiss piercing, fiery eyes. The film is monomanically focused on the character of oil baron Daniel Plainview.
This is a radical departure for Anderson. His films tend to feature large casts of characters, all struggling to overcome their personal weaknesses and traumatic pasts and forge real connections with each other. There Will Be Blood never takes the focus off of Plainview, and his character arc is one of raging misanthropy and a repeated turning away from human trust and companionship. The viewer gets a long and harrowing view of the rocky outcroppings of Plainviews burning mind. Although larger issues of class, capitalism and culture are kept in the background, the film does offer a critique of capitalism that comes from a unique angle. While a character like Charles Foster Kane begins Citizen Kane as a young idealist who has his humanity sapped from him by his isolating wealth and growing power, Plainview starts out the film as an isolated, vengeful misanthrope, and it becomes apparent throughout the course of the film that he has sought out wealth and power explicitly to allow him to dominate those around him. Also, we see that his world-encompassing mistrust and contempt serve him very well in his frantic grasp for wealth.
The result is one of the most vivid and terrifying depictions of human misanthropy in film history. Jonny Greenwoods dissonant score suggests the demonic, and Andersons camera captures stark shots of desolate California brush and an oil fire belching forth from the earth like a portal to hell with a grace and restraint his previous films have lacked. In the end, though, the film is mesmerizing because Day-Lewis is mesmerizing it might be the most sustained, powerful performance Ive ever seen. He is in almost every shot, and your eyes are drawn inexorably towards him, but at the same time the character is so closed off that he seems almost alien his bizarre, mid-Atlantic accent certainly adds to that perception. What sense of the character the viewer does come away from is to be found in Plainviews relationship with his adopted son H.W. and his long-lost brother Henry. In these relationships, we see the constant battle within Plainview between his accumulated hatred of humanity and his real yearning for human connection. Now, whether that yearning is born out of an authentic desire for compansionship or a need to conform to the expectations of civil society is never made clear. Its just one of the many quandaries of the character that are left unanswered. After all, Daniel Plainview is a man who doesnt care to explain himself.
For all of Day-Lewiss bravura mastery of his role and Andersons elegant set piece direction the film would not be nearly as haunting or powerful were it not for the brilliant, audacious and perfectly over-the-top final scene, in which the full flower of Plainviews rage and hatred come to bloom. In this scene, the damage that he has carelessly wrought on those around him, until now only hinted at, is made chillingly manifest. Plainview, rich and old and retired from the field of capitalist combat, has just disowned the son who provides him with his only tether to the human family. He is lying unconscious before a half eaten meal on the beautiful parquet floor of his mansions personal bowling alley. He is in every respect a broken, deracinated husk of his former leonine self. Then, Eli Sunday, his old nemesis, comes into the room with a business proposition. What follows is a cinematic transformation as vivid, riveting and illuminating as any Ive ever witnessed. As Plainview reveals himself to be the master of the situation and Eli realizesthe vulnerability of his position, Plainview grows monstrous before us, filling with vigor, rage and sadistic joy as the will to live drains out of Eli. Here we find Plainview in his moment of ultimate triumph destroying another human being emotionally, spiritually and, in a act that is surely the happiest moment of Plainviews life, physically. This is where we find the only real use that Plainview has for the human race they are his fuel. To vanquish people, to destroy them, to grind them beneath his heel is what sustains Daniel Plainview. Its the real reason behind his obsession with accumulating wealth and power the better to eat you with, my dear. And, as befits a gentlemen of leasure, he calls for his butler to take away the remants of his meal when hes finished.

The dawn of so many elemental components of what manufactures and systematically confronts our base desires. Capital is the only truth we are afforded. PT Anderson returns to the primordial well to mine much of that evidence. Why we weasel up and cry in the face of power, why we root for a man to earn, and not to respect. Why the spark of a pickaxe, the soft glow of a fire near a dead body, the morning light of men stumbling towards the job-site, are all so very enticing and intriguing. For we are him, and until we are finished, we will never be satisfied.

In my PTA book I tried to write at least a little about Daniels protective, affectionate relationship with Mary Sunday (shes the smaller one?) and each time I see (and think about) the film, I realize I should have written more. The conventional wisdom on TWBB is that - for better and for worse, but mostly for better - its a broad, direct, bombastic movie a full frontal assault, a bonk on the nose, a bowling pin to the skull, the analogy is up to you. Its not wrong, either. But the film is also so much (so much!) about things happening on the margins, things that point up how the kind of single-minded megalomania that defines our antihero(es) and their prophetprofit motivations also blind them to the periphery even as the mise en scene carefully emphasizes it, especially in the way the blocking keeps occluding and then revealing hushed onlookers.  Depending on how you read the overwhelmingly masculine thrust of Andersons narrative - I.e as satire, sociology, or a symptom of its makers historically faulty gender politics - Mary is either a minor supporting character or the source of the storys most tragic and devastating emotional schism its her leap that triggers the ellipsis between 1911 and 1927, and her steadfast, empathetic loyalty to HW after his accident (in contrast to his adopted Dads performative and erratic devotion in the same timeframe) that leads him to sever ties with Daniel once and for all (when the adult HW forces himself to speak out loud despite his deafness, its to pledge his loyalty to his wife and  choose a life with her over a nightmare version of filial piety). The  metaphysics of childhood sweethearts (and their discontents) would later  loom larger in THE MASTER and LICORICE PIZZA but the ideas are still beguiling here in embryonic form Mary is a cipher and potential skeleton key at the same time, always quiet, always watchful, always hovering. On this viewing I was moved, almost to tears, by her gesture at the end of the church baptism scene, where, in contrast to the patronizing, mortifying laying on of hands by Daniels new brothers, Mary(a child of abuse with no feeling at all for her pathetic father) embraces him quietly, from behind, with what looks like real concern - a proxy, maybe, for the absent HW (Ive abandoned my boy!) but nevertheless a moment of genuine connection in a film that brutally and systematically stifles the possibility of reciprocal, unconditional love under Christ or capitalism. Shes also present in the swift, wordless flashback towards the end of Daniel instigating and then ceasing some sweet natured horseplay and walking away from HW, back to the derrick and towards the isolation that is his not so secret desire - this time I was aware of how its directed so that both of his adopted children are being left behind. All of which is one small but real reason why the only thing I trust less the overbearing consensus view of TWBB as a flawless epochal masterpiece is the idea (hatched variably in good and bad faith and articulated to greater and lesser degrees of persuasiveness) that its all just huffing and puffing hot air, and that Anderson finally doesnt know what hes doing as a dramatist. The latter criticism is especially annoying to me because I used to believe it - and repeat it - myself.

I regard this as probably the finest work of Paul Thomas Anderson, undoubtedly. However, I think that after watching the film after all these years and coming back to it, thinking of how painful the truth really is, its clear enough that capitalism has rarely looked this monstrous, this divine, this biblical. There Will Be Blood is less a movie and more a prophecy. A film that starts in total silence, no dialogue, just the sound of industry being born in dirt and pain, and ends in complete collapse, spiritual and physical. Its about America. About men. About the rot beneath progress. And yet, despite all that has already been said about it, it still feels like something that resists containment. Daniel begins in a pit, almost dies in it, and spends the rest of his life dragging everyone else into it. And Daniel Day-Lewis doesnt act him, but in fact, he becomes him. The performance is beyond legendary. You look at this man, and you see greed with a limp and a thousand-yard stare. You see a soul thats been traded away for power, long before the first line is spoken. So of course, Paul Thomas Anderson captures it all with complete control, and thats where he balances grandeur with rot, ambition with madness. Every frame is gorgeous, almost too gorgeous. The open landscapes feel like theyre mourning whats about to be taken from them. Oil rigs rise like churches, and by the end, they collapse like gods struck down everything about this movie is mythic, patient but furious. You feel the weight of time, of inevitability.
But thats where the genius of There Will Be Blood isnt just in its technical perfection. Its all in how every element - writing, performance, sound, image, feeds into this singular idea that greed, once internalized, devours everything. Plainview alienates everyone. Partners, family, even the illusion of love. Its not that he loses its that he wins, and it means absolutely nothing. The relationship between Daniel and Eli Sunday is one of the best metaphors Ive ever seen on film. Business vs. religion. Greed vs. faith. Two con men pretending theyre different. And as the movie progresses, you realize neither believes in anything but power. Both want the other to submit, and this is where their final confrontation is horrifying and hilarious, like watching the gods wrestle in a bowling alley. Ive seen this film in theatres many times and witnessed people actually walk out during the final confrontation, specifically when Daniel forces Eli to denounce his own faith. Still, considering the intensity, Im not surprised. What else can you say? This is it. This is the American epic. Its a film about oil, blood, and power, but even that feels too simple. Its a film about us, the world weve inherited, and the hunger that built it. There Will Be Blood is a promise. And by the end, you realize it was always a warning.

Once, I was visiting the Uffizi Museum in Florence with my best friend Alex. I was 20, so I didnt think to spend five minutes reading about what was actually housed in the Uffizi. I just thought it might be a nice way to spend an afternoon. (I dont know why I said my age, as if to imply being seven years older has made me the slightest bit more proactive. It hasnt.)
Anyway, two of the most famous paintings in the world are staged in the same room of this museum, both by Sandro Botticelli. Theyre called Primavera and Birth of Venus. These are all remedial facts about both renaissance art and Italy. Theyre meant to be. Some things in life are so famous, the only way to speak about them is as if youre writing their Wikipedia page. 
When we stumbled into this room, we were rendered speechless. The paintings are good, but you probably knew that. We this is sick, bro-ed each other for about 10 minutes, before pausing to take a time-stamped selfie with Birth of Venus (it was 420). In general, I think this is one of the most profound experiences Ive ever had with art.
I say all this not because I want to self-flagellate for the embarrassment of a) not knowing Id see these two paintings, b) not knowing what to say about them besides this is sick, bro or c) making a weed joke at the expense of one of the finest works of art man has ever created (no apology necessary as far as Im concerned), but instead to say that expressing ones feelings about this film feels a little like posting a selfie with a Botticelli painting. 
This film is titanic. 
I was 11 when it came out. I was 22 when I finally watched it for the first time. I have nothing to add that isnt already canonized in books, or the archives of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, or the forever ink of the internet (I seem to remember someone I know going long on this). Talking about There Will Be Blood as a 27 year old who is ostensibly in the film world and supposed to have good opinions is like observing that yes, water is vital to human life and it would be uphill sledding to keep society going without it. Its a black hole.
In so many ways, professional and personal, it feels like this movie was meant to scratch my brain. I cant think of a piece of art so subjective and soright? There Will Be Blood isnt a film of literal blood, but one of pain and suffering, of family blood, of the blood of the poor, and of the blood of Christ. Daniel Day-Lewis plays Daniel Plainview in one of the all-time great performances, a performance that completes this perfect, slow-burning character study. This is a masterpiece from the first second, when the opening scenes play as just a wall of noise, a soundscape of silence and just the sounds of hard work. Theres no words, just darkness and beautiful images within that. This is likely the best made film of the 21st century, every creative decision just seems right. The old-school storytelling in entrapped by an amazing score, loud and ancient and primal, filled with classical pieces that draw attention to themselves. The music is ominous, slow and unforgiving. It creates dread in a lonely landscape, creating ever-rising tension out of nowhere. The production design is sticky and tactile, and splashes and objects fall onto the lens frequently. This is a film of music and visuals and sound effects, not an adventure in dialogue or storytelling.
Intentional or not, There Will Be Blood is an important treatise on capitalism. Its about a turning point, frontier capitalism turning into nationwide exploitation. A train with black smoke arrives at the limits of civilisation, industrialisation has conquered America. Daniel gives a speech to the community, promising education, prosperity, hope. This is what capitalism revolutionised a long time ago it grew the world. Communities innovated and took risks, profits rose, living standards increased. But theres a tension between the oppressor and the man who provides (the same person), why make profit for everyone instead of just yourself? From communal capitalism, where everyone worked for the same business and cause, we eventually get to today, where were all individuals trapped in a series of different corporate operations. Daniel is ahead of the curve, an individual without a need for people (except to make him more money). Capitalism was reaching the edge of the world, and now collectivist mindsets were been inverted into individualistic ones. As the world grew closer, communities became further apart. There Will Be Blood is a film of unfettered capitalism, filled with montages of hard work, the meritocracy in action. When Daniel opens the oil well, we hear celebratory music. The camera lingers on the well as if its a thing of beauty, a source of happiness. But heres what we never see if Daniel kept his promises to the community he built.
Daniel Plainview is a villain, an evil who pursues money over all else. Or rather, the power that comes with that money. Or rather, the freedom capitalism supposedly allows, which is only reached through power and not love. Daniel doesnt like people who dont understand money, which, in his mind, is most people. Daniel talks of hating people and not wanting others to success, the crux of the hierarchical economic system he endorses. He looks at people and sees nothing worth liking, a perfect cover for exploitation. Daniel is an individualist to the extreme, believing only he can do what he can do, and once Daniel sees the oil he has access to, he becomes even more ruthless in his exploits. The only person Daniel might love is his fake son, but even then how much is that just a ploy to seem more respectable. When his son becomes deaf, that becomes perfect for Daniel. Now theres an excuse for the boy to never hear his father say I love you. 
Tension in There Will Be Built is built through Daniels animosity towards Eli, played by Paul Dano. Eli is religious and that stands against what Daniel values. Daniel doesnt see God as having power over him, he rejects religion because he believes nothing is greater than the power man wields. Daniel is a businessman and hates unearned power, even if its Gods. Religion is also the only thing that goes beyond money, or so the poor are convinced (opium of the masses etc) and Daniel hates the power that religion yields. Luckily for Daniel, money is becoming dominant and belief, especially in the case of Eli, is emasculating. Eli wants power as much as Daniel does, and uses religion to get people to listen to him, but belief is weaker than the human desire for greed. Theres two sets of brothers in There Will Be Blood (Elis and Daniels) and in both instances one brother is smart and ruthless whilst the other is dumb and clambering for unearned power. Daniel is a smart brother, Eli is less fortunate. Eli foolishly assumes everyone believes like he does, and he provokes Daniel with his ignorance and arrogance. Yet, strangely enough, Eli is the only person to get one over on Daniel. He baptises Daniel in a passive-aggressive, scolding manner. In a way, he won. And thats why Daniel hates him. 
SPOILERS AHEAD
Daniel gets more unhinged as There Will Be Blood goes on, leading to a final half hour set fifteen years after the main story. Daniel is no longer working for his wealth, his money is now making money. He doesnt want competition, even from his own son. At this point God does not run the world anymore, capitalism does. Daniels fancy house is a miracle, something achieved only through the grace of capitalism. The world of Daniel is now starting to reach the world of today. We see bowling alleys, hear mentions of radio and Hollywood, entertainment has arrived and now theres a product for consumer capitalism to thrive upon. Religion is no longer the opium of the masses, entertainment and the media has replaced it. This is why Eli begs for help, his choice to pursue power through religion was a lost cause. Daniels revenge on Eli is brutal and harsh, his words cuttingly evil. Daniel destroys what little remains of his morality in order to crush the weak. All opponents are vanquished, all the hard work is over, Im finished. Truly transcendent cinema.

The score by Radioheads Jonny Greenwood will be the first thing that coats you with the thickness of the films black atmosphere. 
Greenwoods compositional skills have developed over the arc of Radioheads career, pushed forward after the group dropped their guitars post OK Computer. His haunting use of strings since then have become a prominent feature of some of their most memorable songs which comes into its own for this soundtrack. As a confrontation between the dual forces of religion and commerce for Americas soul, the film doesnt quite make the case for these as oppositional forces, yet the deeper story it presents, of those two powers as Cain and Abel brothers spawned from the same source of greed and power, it is a raging tour de force that, in retrospect, launched Andersons mature period. This, The Master and Inherent Vice form a loose trilogy of spiritual wanderings at the desert edges of Americas frontier spirit, and all three undermine the western mythology of rugged individualism by suggesting that people headed west not in search of freedom but of people to whom they might belong. The townsfolk of Little Boston seem quaint and self-sufficient, but they are entranced by the possibility of wealth they couldnt possibly spend and give their entire homesteads over to Daniels false promises.
Of course, all of this bubbles up on the surface (perhaps it would be right to call it seepage) of what is fundamentally, like The Master, a compelling two-hander of a collision of wills. In this case, there is no obvious subordinate but instead two manipulative forces hitting each other at top speed, each issuing commands to the other and acquiescing in ways that air passive-aggressive defiance. 
There are plenty of vistas here, but the films most bravura moments of direction come in the use of close-ups and reaction shots to convey power in any given conversation. At first, the consistent focus on Daniels face as he speaks and even is spoken to is thrown into chaos in the face of Elis own head games. Anderson wrings so much tension from who he decides to frame when someone is speaking, saying much about who is in control in any given moment by whether we see the person talking or the one listening.
Both performances are, of course, phenomenal, and the contrast between Danos eerily wizened baby face and DDLs hunched, angry frame. As ever, so much talk revolved around DDLs commitment and research ignores that his actual performance excels precisely in its subjective richness over ostensible realism. This is American gothic writ large, with its strange, vast moral reckonings in well explosions and maiming, and DDL is almost expressionistic as his initial slouch and oozy charm curdles ever more into the full contempt that his wealth can afford him to display. So much of the films violence comes from the moments where Daniel realizes that he genuinely wanted to love the people he shoves away to maintain his Self, the one true western individual who must kill and repel to keep control of his hollow empire.

Paul Thomas Andersons There Will Be Blood is a symphony wherein every note sounds clearly the destruction of greed, and every movement observes characters torn apart by lust for ownership, wealth, and fame. Both operatic and quiet, blaring and meditative, There Will Be Blood chronicles lives built up and undone by a thirst for goods both worldly and ephemeral.
Based on Upton Sinclairs novel, Oil! Andersons film observes his protagonist, Daniel Day-Lewiss Daniel Plainview, beginning the story as a rough and tumble prospector whose life is changed by an oil strike. A character study that tracks Plainview as he collects more, buys more, and reaches for more, the film is a cautionary tale.  Marked by the classically told irony that as one possesses more, he loses more, the story ties Plainview to characters that are both analogous and disparate.
As the film is more about character and human nature than plot, it only makes sense to cast actors who can carry the tragic, dramatic, and all-too-human load. Daniel Day-Lewis is astounding as Plainview. With his glowering voice and unflinching glare, Day-Lewis imbues Plainview with a sound and physicality that are both dangerous and honest. He is a calculating man of business whose lusts drive out his humanity. Day-Lewis makes Plainview both larger-than-life and menacingly real.
The film gives Plainview two foils. One is his son, HW, played by Dillon Freasier the other is Paul Danos Eli Sunday. If anything, HW is Plainviews conscience, guiding Plainviews vacillating sense of humanity through life. He is also a symbol of Plainviews greed, an object collected and then thrown away by the prospector. Freasier presents young HW with wide-eyed control and maturity.
Danos Sunday is simply another version of Plainview. He is a man with his own lusts. Though they may be spiritual in nature, he is as much a collector of followers and souls as Plainview is a hoarder of land and oil. When faced with each other, the actors create explosively electric scenes of anger and passion. Dano deftly stands toe-to-toe with Day-Lewis.
As with its casting, There Will Be Blood is masterfully crafted in all other cinematic areas. Cinematography is clear and steeped in a beauty of nature made unclean by human hands. Production design is handsome, and editing moves the film at a steady pace. Cameras observe the character beats and plot threads at an unobtrusive distance. They watch the action but never add to it the fiery displays of character creating scenic energy. The films score cements a tone that is deadly serious and brooding.
There Will Be Blood is archetypal, cinematic, literate and wholly excellent. It is a film that presents humanity and human beings as dangerous, destructive forces whose passions can be the undoing of  themselves and those who share familial space with them. It illustrates the dangers of shrugging off salvation and argues that salvation is not always given by those who claim to offer it. It is an already iconic, fully engrossing, and masterfully rendered piece of film.

For me there will be blood is just a perfect film which is widely regarded as a masterpiece of modern cinema. Themes like the pursuit of wealth, the clash between capitalism and religion. This entire layered narrative makes it a complex and thought-provoking work. 
The film is an intense character study of Plainviews descent into greed, isolation, and obsession. And the tour de force of a performance by Sir Daniel-Day Lewis made the character come to life in the big screen. So happy that he has made the decision to return back into acting. He fully embodies the character of Daniel Plainview, both physically and emotionally. His voice work is equally impressive. He employs a unique accent that reflects the characters origins and status as an oilman. His vocal delivery ranges from calm and persuasive to explosive and authoritative. His role is certainly one of the defining performances of his career and a landmark in film history.
Alongside him we cant forget about the brilliant performance of Paul dano His portrayal of the ambitious and manipulative preacher showcases his range and depth as an actor the rivalry between Eli and Daniel is central to the film, and Danos performance enhances this conflict. 
Paul Thomas Anderson crafts a narrative that explores the rise of Daniel Plainview, an oilman whose pursuit of wealth leads to personal and moral conflicts.His ability to build tension, utilize symbolism, and collaborate closely with actors results in a powerful and thought-provoking film which stands as testament to contemporary cinema. Alongside the brilliant direction comes the cinematography by Robert Elswit which is stunning, featuring breathtaking landscapes, the use of natural light and wide shots creates a sense of scale and isolation. Additionally, Jonny Greenwoods haunting score adds a layer of intensity and unease, enhancing the films overall impact. Below are some of the core observations and overview of the entire film with some key directorial choices  character development overview.
OPENING SILENCE FOR 20 MINUTES
This silence is a bold narrative choice by director Paul Thomas Anderson and leans heavily on visual storytelling during this time, showcasing the grueling work of drilling, the natural sounds such as clinking of his tools, creaking wooden structures, and distant wind create an atmospheric realism that emphasizes the isolation of the deserts and hardships of the setting.
OIL CONGLOMERATE  GREED FOR OIL
As we see a time jump straight into the early 20th century. Daniels transition from a struggling miner to an influential oil tycoon demonstrates how the chase for oil drives not only financial success but also a hunger for power. The discovery of oil becomes a means for Daniel Plainview to gain immense wealth and influence. As he builds his oil empire, he exploits landowners, manipulates communities, and breaks apart his own relationships. Plainviews obsession with oil not only brings him financial success but also leads to his emotional collapse.
POWER STRUGGLE BETWEEN DANIEL PLAINVIEW  ELI SUNDAY
One of the films most compelling dynamics, marked by a constant power struggle between capitalism (Plainview) and religion (Eli). Both men strictly belief in their ideals and motives but for the sake of profit and their wants can even act as hypocrites in their respective pursuits. Plainview pretends to engage with religion when it suits his business, while Eli is shown to be as greedy and power-hungry as the man he opposes.
OIL RIG EXPLOSION
The oil rig scene is a pivotal moment in the film from this point onwards the film complete and drastic change. The visual spectacle of the oil spraying uncontrollably is both awe-inspiring and haunting at the same time. H.W., is knocked unconscious by the blast and seems to have lost his hearing from the blast, daniel is seen almost ignoring his sons pain and instead, he watches the burning oil rig with a mixture of pride and obsession.
RE-UNITING WITH HIS LONG LOST BROTHER
On a random day out of the blue a man appeared in front of the Plainviews house and introduced himself as Daniels half brother. Daniel, though initially suspicious, accepts him, largely out of a desire for connection. For a short while, Daniel seems to find happiness in Henrys presence, discussing their past and future plans. The audience sees Daniel in a rare, vulnerable light, as someone who longs for trust and a bond. As time passes, Daniel becomes increasingly suspicious of Henrys true identity. Daniel confronts him demanding the truth. Under pressure, Henry confesses that he is not really Daniels brother but a man who knew Daniels real brother, who had died. Henry had hoped to take advantage of Daniels wealth and success by posing as his brother. Seeing the absolute betrayal and deceit Daniel violently kills Henry in a fit of rage. His brief hope for a familial connection with Henry is shattered by deception, leaving him even more disconnected from the world around him.
ABANDONED HIS SON
H.W. is injured during the oil rig explosion, which makes him deaf. Daniel seems emotionally detached from his sons condition and instead of addressing his sons trauma, Daniel decides to send H.W. to a school for the deaf in San Francisco as Daniel only sees him as a liability. Which is heartbreaking for H.W. who is not only coping with his new disability but also with the rejection from the man he considered his father.
BAPTISM SCENE
Daniel Plainview agrees to undergo a public baptism in the Church of the Third Revelation in exchange for access to a important piece of land owned by the Bandy family. Eli take this opportunity to humiliate Daniel in front of the entire congregation. As the Eli has Plainview kneeled and confess his sins. He pushes Daniel to say, Ive abandoned my child! referring to Daniels earlier decision to send H.W. away after his hearing loss. Daniel throughout the entire baptism has a cold, detached demeanor perfectly potrayed by Sir Daniel Day Lewis. Though Eli has power over him in this moment, Daniels compliance is purely transactional. Daniel may be physically bowing and shouting his repentance, but emotionally, he is merely playing along to get what he want. The scene also exposes Elis hypocrisy. While Eli appears to be a man of faith, his true motivation is power and control, not spiritual redemption. He uses the baptism as a tool to assert dominance over Daniel, seeking to humiliate him publicly.
REALITY TO HIS CHILD
As H.W. grows older, he begins to recognize the reality of his relationship with Daniel that he was never truly seen as a son but rather as a business tool. Daniel adopts H.W. after his real father, one of Daniels workers, dies in the drilling accident at the start of the film. By the end of the film, H.W. now an adult decides to leave Daniel to start his own business. This decision marks the final break between father and son. Daniel bitterly declaring that H.W. was never truly his son but merely a bastard in a basket.
BOWLING ALLEY SCENE
This climactic moment just took place after the confrontation with his son, Daniel bottling down bottles of alcohol to make up with the fight he had with his son prior. Eli enters the bowling alley to confront Daniel Plainview for negotiation and confrontation over the land that Daniel had acquired. Eli attempts to leverage his position as a preacher to manipulate Daniel. During their conversation, Daniel reveals his hatred for people and his belief that everyone is ultimately self-serving. He expresses his distaste for Elis religious pretensions and manipulations, showing that both men are motivated by greed and a desire for power. The power dynamics between Daniel and Eli have shifted. Earlier in the film, Eli had the upper hand when he forced Daniel to undergo a baptism to secure land rights. However, at the bowling alley Daniel is now in a position of dominance. Films most memorable line I drink your milkshake took place in this scene, which adds a layer of dark humor to the scene, Daniels tone is mocking and condescending, emphasizing his contempt for Eli. The imagery of drinking his milkshake suggests that Daniel has taken everything Eli has his religion, his authority, and ultimately his life.

PTA is making it look easy at this point its almost absurd how many near perfect scores Ive given his filmography, but he genuinely delivers every single time. A few years ago, a film of this scale and intensity might have missed the mark for me, but having adapted as a cinema head, I feel Im finally watching his work at the perfect moment. This is an undeniable masterpiece that, for me, sits just behind Phantom Thread as his absolute best, thats despite me having four of his films at a 97.. I think Id knock OBAA down on a rewatch purely because these two feel a slight level above.
That first fifteen minutes of no dialogue and pure storytelling through nothing but a hypnotic tension inducing score and the craftsmanship of PTA, is as good as it gets. From that moment you are thrust into the world of Daniel Plainview and it doesnt let you go for a second you realize the sort of film you are getting yourself into, and youll know if its time to embark on a journey of this magnitude almost instantly. 
The narrative is incredibly compelling, built on a rock solid foundation, with a structure that heightens the stakes at every turn. Theres a visceral intensity to the storytelling that kept me on edge, particularly as the evolving power dynamics were implemented, the temperature is always rising, and even past the oil well fire.. the film is relentless. Its a fascinating and dark character study to see how far Plainview can expand his reach and what hes willing to sacrifice to ensure his empires growth is exceptional cinema, especially when employing an actor like Daniel Day-Lewis.
The collaboration between PTA and Daniel Day-Lewis is a gift to cinema and should be revisited as often as possible. So finding out he retired after making Phantom Thread in 2017 makes me a little sad, Id kill for another PTADDL film, Ill be revisiting their collaborative work for the rest of the year though
I think I log both films at least once more each. I dont want to throw words out there.. but its the sort of partnership that feels as essential as Scorsese and DiCaprio, just outstanding cinema at every turn.
Day-Lewis possesses a rare 100 commitment to his craft, and in this decade spanning narrative, he delivers a transformative performance that the years of character growth feel so raw and authentic. Its a privilege to watch an actor of this caliber work, and this film serves as a definitive justification for his record breaking three Oscars.
The performance is so dominant that his Best Actor win feels like an inevitability from the jump. The structure of the film allows him to showcase every facet of his craft the physical intensity of the oil well disaster, the emotional weight of H.W.s accident, and the theatrical power of the final sequence. Perhaps most impressive is the silent opening act, where he carries the entire narrative through expression alone. It is the work of a genius at the absolute height of his powers.
Then you partner someone of the level of Day-Lewiss caliber with someone like Paul Dano the screen practically crackles whenever theyre together. Its remarkable how Dano holds his own against a titan, frequently stealing scenes with that frantic, maddening religious fervor. Watching this back in 2007 would have been crystal clear that Dano was a generational talent destined for a long career. His energy is electric, and its fascinating to look back now and see the seeds of the intensity he has brought to roles like the Riddler.
The technical achievement here is staggering. The grain and structural composition of each shot contain a powerful and tactile quality. PTA has this unrivaled ability to blend atmospheric realism with hauntingly beautiful imagery, creating a world that feels both historical and in your face. I dont say this lightly, but the oil well sequence may be the most striking imagery of the century a perfect storm of visual depth and flawless practical execution that is almost peerless in modern cinema. Its a sequence that makes you stand up and applaud, its not often we get cinema at this level. 
Johnny Greenwoods score is a masterclass in cinematic tension, instantly gripped me from minute one and pushed the films pacing forward with a relentless energy. Its deeply woven into the narrative structure, serving as the films pulse that shifts seamlessly from quiet dread to explosive hostility. The way the music builds venom alongside Plainviews descent is a just another component of why the film works so well, the balance of elements is clear and precise.
The authenticity of TWBB stems from PTAs refusal to use digital shortcuts theres a mix of historical engineering, old school pyrotechnics and some incredibly mundane materials to create whats one of the most grounded and realistic pictures of the century the film looks plucked from the very era it was set in. I mean weve got production lead Fisk using 1914 blueprints from a museum to ensure the 80 foot wooden cable tool derrick was historically accurate, even having 50 carpenters building the structure over a four week span! 
Things like the mine shafts were real the scenes where Plainview is digging by hand utilized actual abandoned silver mine shafts near Marfa, Texas, some of which were 60 to 70 feet deep, fucking cool. The thick oil is made from the same thickening agent used in fast food milkshakes, it looks insane fair play to the cast and crew because Ive heard it stained things permanently! 
Then you have the oil well fire a scene that sits at the peak of the industry, and it warms my heart knowing it was made with almost zero CGI. So it was shot in one take because who has multiple full size Derricks to set ablaze.. so its incredible how it turned out honestly everything had to be perfect, it was. The heat was so intense that the crew were wearing fire retardant suits, poor actors just stood there in the sweltering heat at least they aura farmed to the maximum though, holy cinema!!
Its all shot through Robert Elswits use of vintage Panavision lenses from the 1960s. They purposefully removed the anti-reflective coatings on some lenses so they would flare more easily, giving the desert sunlight that harsh, washed out feeling, its a striking sight and a masterful combination of PTAs steady hand and Robert Elswits eye.
PTA delivers an ending for the ages, anchored by a swell of torment that makes the eventual blow feel both shocking and inevitable. The chemistry between Day-Lewis and Dano is phenomenal they both give 1010 performances capping off a 1010 film. The milkshake monologue is iconic for a reason, and the way PTA utilizes the bowling alley and props creates an atmosphere that is as legendary as the acting itself. For me its the definition of a perfect ending, what a film, I sensed this review being a long one the film deserved as much though, watchlist this asap.

Quite possibly one of the greatest films ever made. Loosely based on the 1927 novel Oil! by Upton Sinclair, There Will Be Blood is a sprawling American epic that barely conceals its parallels between oil tycoon Daniel Plainview and the devil himself. As Plainview embarks on his ruthless quest for wealth and land during the Californian oil boom, he brings the promise of prosperity to those who allow him in. But this prosperity is never really shown to trickle down to those who believe him, as he seems to be draining the wealth and life out from beneath their feet. 
In one of my favorite scenes, when an oil well has caught fire at night and Plainview gazes upon it, his face covered in the dark liquid gold, and only his red eyes are illuminated by the burning fire. It then cuts to the local preacher who allowed him to build there, looking on in horror, like he were seeing the fires of hell spewing out from the depths below. Its such a brilliant scene, showing Plainviews burning desire to control all, even at the cost of his own son, his neighbors, and himself. His insatiable greed swallowing up all those around him, until he is left with everything and nobody. 
There Will Be Blood is a masterpiece. Thematically its such a powerful statement on capitalism and the pitfalls of American individualism, but it also contains some of the greatest performances, cinematography, and music as well. Daniel Day-Lewis and Paul Dano are simply on another level here, in this toxic rivalry over a scrap of land neither really needs. Visually its breathtaking, with so many scenes just embedded in my mind, the entire burning oil well especially. And the score by Jonny Greenwood is this horrifyingly beautiful blend of strings. 
Really, this is absolute cinema. Goes beyond the 55 score.

Many believe this is wholly an anti-capitalism film. This is not the case. It is an anti-greed film. Yes, capitalism can provide a means for exercising greed, in many cases quite easily, but it is the vehicle for this films condemning message, not the target. The oil industry was extremely domineering in the decades leading to the publishing of the novel on which this is based, making it an effective example of greed, but greed can exist without capitalism.
In the same vein, many believe this is wholly an anti-religion film. This is not the case either. It is an anti-pride film. Yes, religious popularity can inflate ones ego drastically, but it is another vehicle for this films condemning message, not the target. Showy religious presentations were exceptionally common and popular in the time when this is set, making Elis authority an example of pride, but pride exists without religion.
Watching this film and leaving it with a shallow capitalism bad or religion bad takeaway is a little close-minded, as There Will Be Blood could better be identified as a diptych of cautionary tales that put on full display the corruption of the human heart. This masterpiece enforces the importance of contentment, humility, family, and love, by forcing us to take a gruesome look at their tragic absence... as greed, pride, hatred, stubbornness, and other agents of destruction all too naturally take their place.
Does this film prove itself worthy, credible enough to share these messages? Absolutely. The epic scale unfolds with masterful detail and personality. All the pieces fall so expertly into place for an experience as impressive as it is disturbing. From the sound design to the camerawork to the incredible acting and haunting score, this is a more than phenomenal piece of art. Also, talk about movies that transport you to their time periods. This is the golden standard for period pieces... and frankly the golden standard for American film.

There Will Be Blood is a masterful film about deep American founding values and the intersection of the individual maximalist contrasted with community leaders. The story follows the rise of Daniel Plainview as he builds his oil empire one rural drill at a time.
I must mention the all-time performance delivered by Day-Lewis. His seething rage boils just beneath the surface while appearing as a family man to potential shareholders. He is great in these subtle moments but its the bombastic outbursts that will continue to live on in my head. Dano is amazing as Eli as his smugness seeps through every word until his desperate finale.
The relationship of Daniel and his son is a constant boomerang between family structure and his career pursuits. We see him repeatedly choose his empire over his son in key moments but still hold hope that he will turn. His final conversation with his son is both heartbreaking and electric, as Daniels last remaining piece of goodwill is shredded right in front of us.
The plot is somewhat simple but thought-provoking in the societal themes being explored. Daniel represents capitalism and individualism in that he seeks to build to the detriment of any one around him. Eli represents both organized religion and thought leaders. Both men are exposed for their largest weakness, Daniels abandonment and Elis false sermon. Both men are fueled by expansion of their empires, but also the petty humiliation they both inflicted on each other.
These two dichotomies are (literally) at odds, and both men are taking advantage of rural homesteaders that trust their position in the societal hierarchy. The comparison  competition of capitalism and religion still resonates with me 18 years after its release.

The score slowly creeps up from nothing to soothing to menacing as Plainview turns from gold-digger to oil-driller to monster. All that coupled with detailed costume work and set designs that all come together to drops you straight into the early days of the 20th century.
Now for the story, is there a name for the genre where the protagonist rises from nothing, turns friends into enemies, alienates their family and dies alone? Citizen Kane, The Godfather saga, The Social Network... what do we call this genre? American Dream or American Greed? Or its all the same since it requires greed to achieve the dream?
These movies are different than The Wolf of Wall Street where the protagonist suffers from an eventual fall from the top. Plainview never gets humbled, he just keeps on rising and rising until he has everything he wanted, or at least he thought he got all he wanted.
The ending is Michael dying alone in Sicily, Kane drawing his last breath in a big empty manor, Zuck and his billions compulsively refreshing his exs Facebook page as his soul slowly rots away. The American Dream is a hollow idea, its a myth.
There Will Be Blood portrays the most psychopathic protagonist in this genre and I am left wondering what it says about me when I find the ending with Plainview bludgeoning Eli to death both tragic and cathartic.
Im finished.

Um novo clássico
Com o poderoso Sangue Negro, Paul Thomas Anderson se torna mais do que um diretor talentoso ele agora já é um dos grandes do cinema americano
           	É 1898, e Daniel Plainview, trabalhando sozinho no poço estreito e profundo de sua pequena mina de prata, escorrega num degrau da escadaria tosca, despenca até o chão, quebra uma perna  e, antes de começar o que será uma longa e penosa ascensão até a superfície, pára para admirar as pepitas que conseguiu desencavar. Plainview vai ainda se arrastar da boca da mina até o escritório poeirento onde venderá sua prata. Enquanto ela é pesada, ele pode ser visto, deitado no chão, com a perna esticada em uma tala rústica e um sorriso beatífico no rosto. Com essa abertura estranha, que sublinha com a música dissonante e extraordinariamente perturbadora composta por Jonny Greenwood, guitarrista da banda Radiohead, o diretor Paul Thomas Anderson estabelece o tema dominante de Sangue Negro (There Will Be Blood, Estados Unidos, 2007), que estréia nesta sexta-feira no país durante toda a sua trajetória, de garimpeiro paupérrimo a magnata do petróleo, Daniel Plainview (Daniel Day-Lewis) nunca deixará de brigar, corpo a corpo, com um solo que reluta até em deixar crescer um ou outro arbusto retorcido. Tudo o que ele guarda de valioso está em suas entranhas, e tem de ser arrancado de lá pela força da vontade. É uma vida brutal, que molda homens também eles brutais  como Plainview.
           	Sangue Negro é baseado no romance Oil!, publicado em 1927 por Upton Sinclair. Mas o que Paul Thomas Anderson faz, em sua adaptação muito livre, é engrandecê-lo o que era uma história da conquista da segunda fronteira do Oeste  a de seu subsolo  passa a ser um épico de dimensão espiritual. Ou, na verdade, de uma dimensão que, na alma americana, é ainda mais forte o empreendedorismo. Quatro anos depois daquele início, Plainview pode ser encontrado à beira de um poço de petróleo rudimentar, com seus empregados. Um deles beija o seu bebê, desce e morre empalado por uma estaca solta. Plainview adota o menino por afeição (a qual, à semelhança do solo com que trabalha, ele esconde nos seus estratos mais profundos), e também porque uma criança pode ser um trunfo para um negociante. Na etapa seguinte, situada em 1911, Plainview vai comprar uma porção significativa da Califórnia de rancheiros que não conseguem plantar nada, mas estão sentados sobre um oceano de petróleo. Sempre com o menino ao seu lado  o qual chama de H.W., como se este já fosse um pequeno magnata , ele se apresenta como um homem de família, e portanto mais atento ao bem-estar da comunidade do que os outros aventureiros do ramo. Há ali um rapaz, contudo, que compreende que isso não passa de retórica Eli Sunday (Paul Dano), pregador messiânico e fundador de uma certa Igreja da Terceira Revelação. Insinuante e extremamente ambicioso, Eli vai iniciar com Plainview uma rivalidade mortal, que não visa a definir apenas qual dos dois é o homem mais forte visa, principalmente, a decidir qual deles tem o meio mais eficaz de controlar outros homens  se a promessa de enriquecimento ou de salvação.
           	Upton Sinclair era um socialista e um romântico Paul Thomas Anderson tem oito décadas de história de vantagem sobre ele, e nada do idealismo do escritor sobreviveu em seu filme. Ele é, ao contrário, apocalíptico na maneira como retrata as duas forças motrizes do desenvolvimento dos Estados Unidos  a riqueza e a religião , e na forma como identifica nelas apenas manifestações diversas de uma mesma obsessão por domínio, controle e conquista. Filmado em planos longos, de vistas imensas, Sangue Negro reproduz em toda a sua potência a mitologia do Oeste modelada nos faroestes de John Ford. Mas é como se ela fosse vista aqui pela lente de Stanley Kubrick, em que a simetria e o formalismo anunciam não a ordem, mas o caos latente sob ela. Como em toda a ficção e o folclore americanos, porém, são os indivíduos que encarnam as grandes forças. O diretor desenha, assim, o pano de fundo, mas entrega aos seus atores a tarefa de se pôr em primeiro plano e concentrar a ação  e Day-Lewis e Dano se enfrentam e se sobrepujam cena após cena, dobrando um ao outro em combates de uma violência moral e física que ao mesmo tempo choca e eletriza. Dessa combinação entre a intensidade de seus atores e a maestria com que evoca o mundo que eles habitam, Anderson tira algo poderoso o equivalente cinematográfico do grande romance americano, como, na tradição literária, são chamadas as obras capazes de encapsular de maneira definitiva os estados de alma do país. Desde Boogie Nights e Magnólia, Anderson se revelara um cineasta de talento incomum. Agora, aos 37 anos, ele acaba de se tornar algo maior  um clássico.

Paul Thomas Andersons filmography is one of the most accomplished of any director working today and this is the culmination of his brilliance. There Will Be Blood is his magnum opus and has whats among the conversation for the greatest acting performance in the history of cinema. Daniel Day-Lewis method acting dedication to his character is easily the greatest performance of the 21st century that Ive seen. And the story is an almost inconceivably complex commentary on religion, greed, megalomania, capitalism, and the American Dream as a whole. 
Daniel Plainview (Daniel Day-Lewis) is an oil prospector who moves to California as the state is full of oil. He uses his adopted son, H.W. Plainview (Dillon Freasier), to help him appear trustworthy while trying to purchase up land. Upon his success, one young preacher, Eli Sunday (Paul Dano) suspects his dishonesty and pressures him to help his church. 
This is a two and a half hour slow burn styled epic. However, its paced in a manner that never lets you escape from your immersion. The two main performances are enthralling in every way and refuse to allow you to ever get bored. Day-Lewis, as Ive already mentioned, is beyond incredible in the role. He embodies every aspect of what makes the very concept of acting great. Everything from his eyes being laser focused when he speaks (he barely even blinks in some scenes) to his unique cadence are simply superb. 
Paul Dano also has a fantastic performance as both brothers, Paul and Eli Sunday. His irritating nature was a product of Danos commitment to such a mentally taxing role. His monologues in the church have considerable energy to them. And the final sequence in Daniels house has Dano portraying a broken soul with such precision. I truly felt his fear with his deeply terrified tone.  
The two characters of Eli and Daniel are tragic in more similar ways than Eli initially thinks. In the end, theyve both obsessed over power and greed. And having Eli verbally announce hes a fraud is the final blow to solidify the idea that both are full of sin. I interpreted the ending as showing Daniel is the future (capitalism) and Eli is the past (religion) in this transitionary period for the U.S. The conclusion is profound and worthy of many rewatches to fully grasp what it all means to you though. 
PTA brought on a new composer for his filmography in this and its one of my personal favorite composers, Jonny Greenwood. To no surprise, the duo are like bread and butter. PTA encourages uncomfortable music to linger on in his thrilling sequences. And Greenwoods main shtick is those discomforting and oddball pieces so I couldnt have imagined someone better to become PTAs regular composer. From this film on, Greenwood has composed every one of PTAs film scores and I look forward to hearing them. Reference the oil derrick explosion scene to hear an example of Greenwoods tremendously unsettling music. 
The scenery was gorgeously captured by Robert Elswit. The shots in the desert plains were taken at a ranch in Marfa, Texas and some of the other interior shots were in L.A. Watching the oil explosion scene is so tense thanks to his talented camera work. The wide shots are a sight to behold. Another example of a shot I admire was the much quieter final shot of the movie, being framed in a way that was almost like having the old phrase the end at the end of a movie. It was a clear reference to Stanley Kubricks work with how he framed the shots in his movies. 
When people try to tell you they dont make movies like they used to, this is probably the first film I would recommend suggesting to them. There Will Be Blood feels like an old time epic and is compelling on every level. Everyone interested in cinema should see it at least once for the Daniel Day-Lewis performance alone. It has instantly found a place in my all time favorites.

There Will Be Blood de Paul Thomas Anderson est un véritable chef-dœuvre. Une fresque fascinante sur la naissance du capitalisme américain entre la fin du XIXe et le début du XXe siècle. Tous cela de manière intime et humaine, à travers le parcours dun mineur dargent devenu prospecteur de pétrole et prêt à tout pour réussir. À la fois intense et réfléchi, le film mêle drame, critique sociale et réflexion sur la religion et lavidité. Il nest pas démonstratif, il montre simplement comment une ambition peut devenir une obsession, et comment celle-ci finit par détruire tout ce qui lentoure.
La réalisation de PTA est sobre, maîtrisée et puissante. Les paysages désertiques, les puits de pétrole, le silence des grandes plaines donnent au film une dimension presque biblique. Il y a très peu de musique au début, beaucoup de silence, ce qui renforce la tension. Elle se développe au fil du film. Chaque scène est posée, construite avec précision. La violence nest pas spectaculaire, elle est morale, progressive. On voit un homme sélever socialement, mais se vider humainement. Paul Thomas Anderson livre lun de ses meilleurs films. Il explore la solitude, lobsession et la corruption morale avec une grande précision. Plus Daniel Plainview réussit financièrement, plus il sisole. Il devient incapable daimer, incapable de partager, incapable même déprouver autre chose que de la rivalité. La richesse ne lui apporte aucune paix intérieure. Au contraire, elle renforce son vide.
Coté performances, Daniel Day-Lewis est magistral, certainement son meilleur rôle. Son interprétation de Daniel Plainview est impressionnante. Il incarne un homme intelligent, ambitieux, charismatique, mais profondément solitaire. On sent dès le début quil ne fait confiance à personne. Son rapport avec son fils est particulièrement marquant. Il lutilise au départ presque comme un outil pour rassurer les investisseurs, mais il y a malgré tout une forme dattachement réel. Pourtant, au long du film, lobsession prend le dessus, et labandon de son fils devient lun des moments les plus durs du récit. Cest là que le film montre clairement que le capitalisme, dans sa forme la plus brutale, détruit même les liens familiaux. En face de lui, Paul Dano est tout aussi impressionnant, peut-être dans son meilleur rôle également. Son personnage dEli Sunday, incarne la foi, mais une foi ambiguë, parfois sincère, parfois manipulatrice. La confrontation entre lui et Daniel Plainview est le cœur du film. 
Liconique scène dans léglise est lun des moments les plus forts  voir Plainview se faire baptiser et obligé de shumilier, de reconnaître ses péchés, crée une tension incroyable. Ce moment montre que la religion, comme le pétrole, peut devenir un outil de pouvoir. Daniel accepte uniquement pour son projet pétrolier  cest un calcul stratégique, pas une conversion sincère. Ceci montre jusquoù il est prêt à aller pour gagner et garder le contrôle. Le film ne critique pas la foi en elle-même, mais la manière dont elle peut être utilisée pour contrôler, manipuler ou dominer. De même, dans la scène finale, quand Plainview fait subir un retour de bâton à Sunday et loblige à shumilier à son tour. 
Enfin, There Will Be Blood offre ainsi un portrait sombre et fascinant dune Amérique en construction, portée par lambition mais rongée par lavidité, la foi et la quête de pouvoir. Une œuvre toujours aussi intense et marquante.

Excelente película, la obra maestra de Paul Thomas Anderson.
There Will Be Blood superó mis expectativas, no creí que me iba a gustar tanto por lo poco interesante que me resultaba su premisa, pero al final fue un viaje increíble en el que vemos el rotundo cambio que sufre el protagonista, acompañado de interpretaciones magistrales y de un apartado técnico magnífico.
Sinopsis La historia de un buscador de petróleo de Texas y los problemas que enfrenta en el negocio al comienzo del nuevo siglo.
La historia es espectacular, pero hay que tenerle paciencia, no es para todo el mundo. Su inicio me sorprendió, quince minutos en los que no se dice un solo diálogo pero se entiende fácilmente todo lo que está pasando. Luego su ritmo continúa siendo lento, por eso digo que no es para todo el mundo, pero sinceramente nunca llegué a aburrirme por lo atrapante que se me hizo su historia y el desarrollo del protagonista. Además, sus actos son diferentes a pesar de estar conectados por la misma ambición que tiene en todo momento Daniel, pero comienza más tranquila, con una búsqueda urgente de petróleo para comenzar a meterse en el negocio. La segunda mitad sigue siendo buenísima por el constante cambio que comenzamos a ver en Daniel, quien ya deja de importarle hasta la vida de su hijo con tal de convertirse en el dios del petróleo. Encima cierra de una manera perfecta, su acto final es brillante y de lo mejor que tiene la historia, es donde el protagonista más toca fondo y lo vemos completamente desatado. Además, va transcurriendo en años diferentes, para el final ya estamos casi 30 años después de lo que vimos en el inicio, algo interesante y arriesgado pero que está bien llevado ya que nos deja ver perfectamente la transformación de Daniel lo único que me chocó un poco de esto es que no noté más avejentado al personaje que está interpretado por Paul Dano. Por último, la ambientación es sublime, me encanta que se grabe todo en locaciones reales y se sienta tan real todo, tranquilamente podrían haber grabado todo en esa época.
En cuanto a los personajes, estos son increíbles. Daniel Plainview es un protagonista memorable, un hombre ambicioso y narcisista que busca éxito y riqueza en la industria petrolera, sufriendo un fuerte cambio a lo largo de la historia. Me encanta que al inicio lo vemos trabajando humildemente y solo, para poco a poco irse adentrando en un negocio que le terminará arruinando la mente. Además, comienza a cometer actos despiadados y destructivos, protagonizando escenas que le dan mucho carisma al personaje por la locura que maneja. Por otro lado, la relación con su hijo adoptivo tiene un buen desarrollo, al principio podemos notar como a Daniel le importa la vida que tiene H.W., pero su fuerte ambición termina cortando la relación que tenía con su hijo, volviéndose más hostil a medida que pasan los años y terminándolo viendo como un sólido rival. El desarrollo individual de H.W. es genial, al inicio lo vemos como un chico inocente que termina en el medio de los negocios turbios de su padre, teniendo una infancia arruinada por los diversos problemas en los que termina estando entrometido. Por último, Eli es un fanático religioso que termina siendo un perfecto adversario para Daniel, formando una relación fascinante e icónica por lo opuestos que son uno del otro. También tiene un hermano idéntico a él llamado Paul, quien tiene mucha importancia en la historia pero sale muy poco, me hubiera gustado verlo más.
En otros aspectos destaco las actuaciones, principalmente la de Daniel Day-Lewis, impresionante lo de éste actor, primera vez que veo una película donde actúa y la verdad es que es increíble su interpretación, podría decir que es una de las mejores que vi en una película, un actor de método que, con solo ésta actuación, ya me compró para ver más de su filmografía, merecidísimo su Oscar las demás actuaciones están muy bien también, Paul Dano es otro a destacar, tiene escenas buenísimas que están muy bien interpretadas. Por otro lado, el trabajo de Paul Thomas Anderson en guion y dirección es sensacional, es la segunda película que veo de él y va a ser difícil que alguna la supere, muy bella visualmente, con planos memorables. Además, me sorprende lo bien que está hecha, todo se siente demasiado real y eso le suma demasiado, debe haber sido una locura la producción. Por último, la banda sonora de Jonny Greenwood es genial, acompaña de una manera perfecta los sentimientos del protagonista en muchos momentos.
En conclusión, una excelente película que me parece completa en todo sentido, difícil encontrarle alguna falencia más que su ritmo lento que puede generar aburrimiento en algunas personas, por suerte no me pasó así a mi y pude disfrutar de la tremenda obra maestra que es. Muy recomendada.

This is the story of a great and terrible Destroyer. Retched from the earth, he is a devil in the flesh, with organs of stone and flame. His tongue is gold his stare, cold steel. Through his veins courses the blackest oil, and he is a vampire both of the literal and figurative meaning. His one purpose in life is to feed - to feed until there is nothing left, until he stands alone atop the empty corpses of man and earth alike. He is a monster who abhors existence, most of all his own.
As we watch his unrelenting march towards this goal, we are witness to his three most heinous acts. The first act is the consumption of his hands. His most beloved tools, broken in the path of his destruction, are discarded. It pains him greatly, but as they are of no more use to his purpose, he must lay them aside and soldier on. The second act is the consumption of his heart. He knows his humanity is a weakness it always has been. When the suggestion of kin reaches his heart and kindles pity, he knows he can no longer afford his emotions, and both destroys the pretender and preempts the breach from happening again.
At last, the Destroyer has one task left the consumption of his own body and soul. Stood proxy by a man who is but a faint shadow of himself - a false shepherd whose spirit matches his own, but without the fortitude to see their shared goal to the natural end (yet surprisingly, the only enemy who ever truly hurt him by twisting his aims to force him to momentarily renounce himself) - he delights in the endgame. He savors every morsel of himself, and revels in his ascent to self-styled godhood. He has become nothingness incarnate, and having reached his fill, finally, is finished.

Das Schichtwerk Toastbrot 

(Paul Thomas) Anderson und (Jonny) Greenwood sahen bzw. einigen sich, das Publikum durch Unstimmigkeiten, Zögern, Unvollkommenheit zu verstören, eine Musik und ihre Stücke zu erschaffen, darin etwas nicht stimmt, die andeutet, Dunkelheit an diesem OrtFilm suggeriert. Passend dazu und es voll und gänzlich auf den Punkt bringend eine Musik als ein giftiges Motiv, wo Dissonanz vorherrscht, lange, anhaltende Töne Schmerzen bereiten, eine (auf) heulende Musik gleich dem einer Sirene im Ankündigen von Gefahr bedeutet. 
(Quelle Wikipedia)   

Film-dienst bezeichnete den Score als wütend, zum Wiederspruch reizend, dabei aber gleichzeitig anrührend, eigentlich unhörbar. 
(O-Ton Wikipedia)

Der Score, viel mehr das in Worte fassen von Jimmy Greenwoods Arbeit, gibt beängstigend klar und deutlich, meine Meinung zu There Will Be Blood wieder, zu mal Mr. Greenwood selbst, federführend für meine Dissonanz mit besagtem Film wiedergibt.
Seine Musikstücke haben alle Adjektive verdient, dich ich aufgezählt habe. Er ist kaum näher einer Alarmsirene wie der den Schall weitertragende Trichter um das Gehäuse dessen. Besticht mit einer Konsequenz an Misstönen, für dessen Einsatz und Aufrechterhalten beiden Anerkennung gezollt werden muss, was sich da Anderson und Greenwood auch immer dabei gedacht haben, genau diese bekommende Aneinanderreihung von (Miss)Tönen auf die Zuschauer loszulassen, hätte weniger verzerrendes, giftiges wie ein sich langsam ausbreitendes Toxin von Musikstücken selbige Unbequemheit hervorgerufen wie gewollt. Es ist ihr beidiges (Klang)Werk, was mich auch nach dem dritten, vierten Mal, völlig zwiegespalten zurücklässt, eben wie das im Supermarkt gekaufte Toastbrot.
Der Score von Jimmy Greenwood fordert mich auf, There Will Be Blood wie das Schichtwerk einer Toastbrotpackung anzupacken. Sind Filme oft ein einziger, harmonischer und homogener runder Brotlaib, in verschiedenen Stadien von steinhart wie mach ein Holzkopf auf der Straße, bröcklig wie die zusammengeklebten Brotkrummen von Hänsel und Gretel, wiederum andere mehlig wie die über das Mehl fahrende Zunge, andere wiederum verführerisch in weich wie außen kross, gibt es immer die wenigen perfekten eines fluffigen, geschmackintensiven Inneren mit einer kross gebackenen Kruste in goldig braun, haben wir es hier mit dem maschinell geformten, relativ neutralen Toastbrot zu tun. 
Kann ein Toastbrot wahrlich gut sein, vielseitig in seinen Verwendungszwecken als einen warmen Toast bestrichen mit Butter oder Marmelade, zu einem Spiegelei gegessen werden, wie als ein kulinarischer Gaumenschmaus mit etwas Butter, Pfeffer oder Chiliflocken und einer Prise Salz mit dem im Namen beinhaltenden Toastschinken, und je nach Gaumen mit Käse und später mit Salatblättern oder anderem Grünzeug, ist Paul Thomas Anderson fünfte Regiearbeit, die Toastbrotpackung mit der eigentlich einzigen, oftmals recht schnell alt werdenden obersten Scheibe, die hier jedoch sich zwischen den schmackhaften guten Scheiben vermehrt und niedergelegt hat.  
So ist jede einhergehende und nachfolgende Sichtung, mit Arbeit verbunden um an diese schmackhaften, wahrlich vielseitigen Brotscheiben heranzukommen, die an den Rändern beginnenden harten, sich in ihre Bestandteile auflösenden Störenfriede, auszusortieren ihres vollumfassenden Fremdkörpers wie der eine faule Apfel, der den ganzen Most ungenießbar macht.  
Die Guten von den Schlechten Scheibend getrennt, die Waagschalle sich knapp zu Gunsten der mit stolzgeschwellter Brust als Sieger hervorgegangenen fluffigen Toastscheiben, erlebe ich das Phänomen Daniel Day-Lewis in beängstigend gewohnt brachialer Qualität, wie sie sich selten so wiederholt Paul Dano am Rande des Wahnsinns unter dem Deckmantel Gottes wie die hingehaltene Wange Dillon Freasier in einer würdigen Ein-Film-Karriere und Paul Thomas Anderson zum klassischen Drama in der Größenordnung von Spiel mir das Lied vom Tod.
