To die is to witness the end of the world. What is a bullet if not a meteor, rocketing into your orbit and shattering the hard bone that protects your universe from collapse. How does it feel to be shot in the brain? Do you disappear all at once, like an ice cube dropped into boiling water? Or do you slowly feel yourself shed your identity piece by piece? Is there a split second where all of a sudden you cannot remember any of your childhood? The faces of your loved ones? Your ambitions? Your fears? Do you feel  trapped in that moment, agonizingly watching yourself revert to mindless meat without any way to stop it? 
Uncut Gems exists in that space. After the universe is created in a Big Bang of greed and racial exploitation the viewer is birthed like a shit-soaked Athena out of the ass of Howard Ratner, an NYC Diamond District jeweler who we have the honor of watching writhe and scream and fight and spit and bleed and die. If Howard ever does experience peace, we are not allowed to see it. We are only allowed on the stage to watch his death throes, his final struggles as the earth crumbles around him and the few moments of grace that makes the loss worth mourning. 
The Safdies frequently populate their films with grotesques, monstrous individuals who want love but can only seem to communicate in destruction and excess, and they have gifted their Vaporwave Gothic tale with their strongest serotonin-chasing-monster yet. He is Victor Frankenstein and The Creature rolled up in one, prevented from achieving meaning by his own hand instead of by the hand of a capricious creator. Like a shark he pushes forward, always talking, always hustling. Whenever he is forced to stop he seethes, grinding his teeth watching the Weeknd perform or made to take out the trash by his soon to be ex-wife, becoming painfully aware in these quiet moments of his profound lack of that eternal Thing that he pursues but can never seem to find. Maybe Julia, his devoted mistress, is The Thing. Maybe watching the History Channel is The Thing. Maybe the Opal is the Thing. Maybe that big bet hitting is the Thing, the Thing that will make him important and worth something in the world. The Thing that will open doors. The Thing that will bring respect. The Thing that will let him see what Kevin Garnett can see when he looks into the Opal. The Thing that finally lets Howard into the universe. 
So he continues to push forward, shedding pieces of himself along the way. He gives up his assistant Yussie. He gives up his apartment in the city. He gives up his prized Knicks ring. He gives up his Opal. And then, finally, his life. Howards death is shocking in spite of its inevitability (a bullet in the brain is the only kind of justice a parable deals in after all). It is shocking because preceding it we are allowed into a moment of unparalleled ecstasy. The bet hits, and it feels like the entire world spins. Julia jumps and screams in celebration and the camera cannot even keep up with her excitement, dancing through the air desperately trying to get even a partial glimpse of her. The music surges and pulses and then, all at once, with a single piercing shot, the moment is broken. All at once, the world finally crumbles. But as Howards ambitions and love and dreams and struggle leak out of his face and are lost forever on the floor of his shop, it finally happens. Howard can see the universe. And its so beautiful.

Remember growing up, the kid in the class who was the loudest, the one that would remind you that he was listening to Loft Music before House of Balloons even dropped, the one that liked Adam Sandler ironically, the one that came into class with the Air Jordans XX2s that their dad bought them but boasted how he stole them from the back of a truck?
Uncut Gems is kind of like that kid. Its relentlessness makes sure you know just how cool, funny and badass it is. There are no moments of quiet contemplation because if there were you might stop to think about just how dumb everything is. Instead, Gems plays like a fastest Badminton rally youtube video with sneaker squeaking and everything. The Safdies aggressive style has become their trademark. Its a generational grab-bag style of direction, one that throws out things that once mattered like nuance of performance, framing, thematic quality and holds onto the other stuff like overlapping dialogue, treaties on greed and Adam Sandler.
They describe their film in interview after interview as Goodfellas for this generation, which despite its arrogance, could be the most incorrect statement of the decade. Schoonmaker once recalled how film students came up to her and asked why Scorsese didnt cut every film like the climax of Goodfellas to which she replied, the story doesnt call for that. It has an arc, it builds up to that tension so that you can feel it whole-heartedly. The Safdies dont build up to anything, its pace exceeds itself and renders everything numbing. Other viewers relish in this rush of kinetic anxiety and confuse it for good filmmaking. Though sensorial extremity is a skill, it is not a quotient for the whole sum. Rather, it attempts to deafen your thoughts of discernment.
And if its bad - well, its ironic. Yes, the Safdies have kind of bulletproofed their approach, a trend Ive noticed amongst some of the new generation of filmmakers. An approach that both admonishes sincerity and lives in the safe confines of ironic badness with heightened aestheticism. You see, when Garnett is shown the Furby necklace, were supposed to laugh at its ironic hideousness, but also perhaps laugh so that people know were in on the joke too. Wearing it, thus, becomes a badge of ironic honour. The worst kind.
The film opens with Howards colonoscopy. We zoom in on the Oplaine crystal from Ethiopia only to come out of the ass of Howard. The brief bloody injury thats inflicted from it is classic exploitation Safdies. The suffering of the African person is handled with as much distance and lack of grace as it was in Good Time when an Ethiopian security guard suffers a forced drugging. The intro in Gems is a lazy and redundant scene that attempts to convince the viewer that the narrative has some kind of social conscience. Even more lazily spelled out by KG when he confronts Howards exploitation in the third act. Or worse, the tragedy leading up has cast some ancient, ethnic curse upon the Opal. I think either reading is equally troubling.
But the Safdies dont care about being troubling. Because its cool, remember? They cast actual addicts and convicts because theyre real! In Gems they cast the charming KG and the Weeknd as themselves. This is where the venture into reality stops though.
The two directors are obsessed with neo-realism (as stated in interviews) and everything about their characters seem real. And yet its all a paper tiger. Dig a bit under the characters and theyre all one dimensional. KG as an athlete obsessed by Jewelryriches, the Weeknd with drugssex, Lakeith Stanfield as the uncooked muscle for KG, Adam Sandler as the pathetic dealer, Julie Fox as the whoremadonna, Judd Hirsch as the father with the heart of gold. Theres nothing particularly real about anything or anyone and the former examples lend themselves to racist tropes. But again - the ironclad defense with this particular kind of creation is well, its not supposed to be real. Its an ironic b-movie thriller. See the John Carpenter titles tell you so. Great. But then Im left feeling stalemated. I dont ever get the intelligence of a Carpenter thriller, nor the emotion of a personal drama.
So what do you get? Well take away the novelty of KG, the Weeknd, and Adam Sandler as the cast and youre left with 130 minutes of wall-to-wall music, overlapping dialogue and a portrait of a pathological liar and gambler. You want to see Howard succeed but none of it makes sense. During the first half, you want to make sure Howard gets his Gem back from the African-Americans who stole it...think about how that sounds. The other half, you wanna see him win because hes Adam Sandler. And for the record, when dont you want to see a gambler win? Weve seen this film, a million billion times.
And as far as gambling goes, its weak sauce. Listen, I love gambling. So this is a little aside but sports gamblers know the deal. He makes his first bet through a bookie - who apparently can cancel bets by proxy? (Ive never heard of this happening. Even if you owe money to someone, that owed person could never cancel your wager. It would mean lost business for the bookie.) But then bets with a casino? What? Everyone knows you shouldnt wager through casinos because theres records and you end up losing net 30 in the U.S. on any winnings. So Spoiler he decides to fly Julie out to Connecticut to the Mohagen Sun Casino. Again, gamblers you know the deal.Anytime before 2018 you couldnt walk into any casino outside of Nevada to place a sports bet. Are you kidding me? And Connecticut of all places?! They just legalized sportsbooks in CT maybe as of last year. This is set in 2012 right? OK, so you lost me there. But on top of that, you fly to CT instead of NY? I thought at first it was a tax thing, maybe you dont pay as much off the top in CT, but no its all the same. Makes no sense. I think they chose that specific casino because they just literally implemented a sportsbook there and Im almost 100 percent certain they got funding from that Casino. Because what better advertisement exists than the woman-as-desired-object walking out of your casino with a million dollars? Poor taste.
So it doesnt get into the psychology of a gambler whatsoever. Because as anyone knows, a gambler wants to protect their bets like crazy. They would never place a parlay with a bookie that cancels bets, let alone a casino that doesnt take them. But its a moral tale about the corruption of greed, right? I think?...I dont know. Again, we can chalk this up to none of this is real man. Get it? Its all a fever dreamnightmare with a new age soundtrack to make it hyper-surreal?
This is a moral aside, but I kinda take issue with the way this treats gambling. You get the rush of betting in the first half, but the only valley of the gambler thats explored is when he doesnt lock in his wager. This is not under any circumstances the low of any pathological gambler. The rest of the film hes just jacked to get his wager in for the finals. You never, ever feel the downtrodden loss of gambling. It tries to stilt your expectations but effectively omits the Big Lose, the one where your wife leaves you, you take the second mortgage out on the house, you kidnap your kids best friend for ransom money. Instead it deals with the cartoon-ish slapstick thugs that are chasing Howard down for owed money. Nothing could be further removed from the experience of a real gambling addict. An addict wagers on how many bids therell be at the auction of his Opal or on how long the standing ovation is at his kids play. And when they dont have money, they dont get comically de-robed or pushed into public fountains. They make them do heinous, heinous things. Its a slap in the face of gambling addicts. This is more a casual gambler whos addicted to...ancient Ethiopian uncut Opal?
What youre left with is a film with zero reality, zero depth, zero soul. But big stars and big style. Fitting then that it will be coveted among cinephiles the way KG and Adam Sandler covet the uncut Opal. Its an unfortunate metaphor. But perhaps more fitting is this unknowing metaphor from a distance, Gems looks precious and valuable but the further you dive in, the further up the asses of the Safdies you truly get.

Writing on Uncut Gems at this point almost seems completely pointless, as its become possibly the most overwritten film of the year within critical communities, and has ended up being the most overrated and underrated movie of the year.  At the end of the day though, the only annoyance with the Safdies with me is that theyre not really confident filmmakers, theyre filmmakers of anxiety.  But at the same time its something theyre highly aware of.  Still, its hard to not find myself agreeing with many of the criticisms littered throughout Letterboxd - until the movies final moments (which in complete fairness, I think is some of the best filmmaking youll see all year) its essentially like watching the climax of Goodfellas for an entire film, except without any of the buildup, any of the specificity, and any of the arcs.  So were supposed to what - assume Howard Ratner has really bad anxiety?  In a way its the first real dip for the Safdies, who have otherwise gotten better with each film - theres nothing wrong with kinetic anxiety as a formal device, but here its not just leaned on entirely to drive the film, but it also plays out as something completely telegraphed rather than organic note for example Kevin Garnett and crews first sequence in Howards jewel shop, how they get locked in the door, and everybody yells unintelligible things, and eventually they get in, and how it serves completely no purpose.  And more than any of the Safdies other films, this completely leans into that old Robert Altman trick - constant unintelligible overlapping dialogue to mask how vacuous the endeavor actually is.  Safdies have made their first film with unfathomable rich kid energy, and as another fine write-up on this film noted, theres not one moment of contemplation in this film, because if there were you would notice how dumb the entire movie is.
This is ultimately a disappointment coming after Heaven Knows What and the fantastic Good Time  - and its still rather annoying how much of this is a grab bag of 70s American character pieces, as another astute write-up noted.  The 70s American character study is a genre I never had much affinity for, and if the Safdies have ultimately become the NYC Indie version of JJ Abrams I still have to admit that I think Uncut Gems is a far better film than many of those.  Gems is still a rather likeable movie about seeing classic American individualism in crisis, even if the racial politics never go much beyond Well, we both like capitalism and even though the film is perhaps too empathetic towards Ratner, a mysterious mashing of Homer Simpson and Carlito Brigante that makes you wonder how he ever got to where he did.  And still there are touching moments, like Howard at Weeknds show, watching while feeling inferior.  Buts its still this sense of crisis (also Ratners obvious Gen X mid-life crisis) which propel the film through even the generic family sequences, which without it would be obvious how poorly written this movie can, and these scenes in particular are.  One tweet I saw recently noted how the films black opal is about challenging the energy of oppression which makes sense perhaps given the pull ins and outs of the gem into some kind of colorful version of the Big Bang, which - sure - but at the same time that tries to make the film into a bigger statement than what its actually good at doing (and this isnt helped by conforming the Ethopian section to the prologue, in a sort of attempt for the rest of the film socio-politically to play out via implication) and furthermore comes down to a nihilism which Im ultimately not privy too.
The unfortunate part about writing this was lowering my rating - I liked the movie more until I actually wrote on it and got to this point!  Its just annoying to see filmmakers you like level down rather than up, but theres something overblown about the movie given how small the scale and stakes actually are here, but perhaps with those imperfections, the Safdies wouldnt have it any other way - especially given that theyre a good representation of Howards character himself.  That being said the last 25 minutes or so of this film is a complete joy, with some of the most skilled crosscutting in modern cinema.  If this is where the Safdies end up going I wouldnt complain!  One of the most interesting this about Uncut Gems on a formal level is how it basically expands their filmmaking apparatus into big (or reasonably sized) budget filmmaking - which is fun because this movie doesnt have much to really do so you can just lean into the form.  Without Sean Price Williams its very clear how much of their formal strengths are on them, and with Darius Khondji, they visually achieve subtleties that Good Time and Heaven Knows What couldnt approach - the lighting is far more focused and nuanced, and especially within the films middle-section we get a window into Howard internally that the film might not have been able to do on the basis of Sandlers performance alone.  Its also honestly jaw-dropping how alive the film becomes within the sheer skill of the final 25 minutes, these big lights and a movie star pared down to the most elemental basics of cross-cutting.  The rush must be something like seeing The Girl  His Trust in 1912 for the first time - especially since the film doesnt really set up these structural delineations other than the fact that it separates the previously established characters.   But it works and Id be the last person to try to debate how engrossing the film becomes, and the sheer energy on display is delightful. Wenn man Kohlenstoff enormen Druck aussetzt, dann wird ein Diamant daraus. Wenn man einen Menschen enormen Druck aussetzt, dann wird Howard Ratner in Uncut Gems daraus Wie ein moderner Hans im Glück steht er ständig unter Strom, vollgepumpt mit Adrenalin und getrieben von der (Sehn)sucht nach Anerkennung.
Ratner hat unverwüstliche Überlebensinstinkte und ist nervtötend wie ein unablässig kläffender Chihuahua. Sein Leben ist ein einziges Telefonklingeln, eine unablässige Kaskade an gebrochenen Versprechen, eine erdrückende Menge an Problemen und Verantwortlichkeiten - vor denen Ratner aber nicht wegläuft, sondern sich ihnen stellt. Seine Faszination zieht Uncut Gems auch daraus, dass immer unklar ist, ob Ratner in den nächsten Sekunden implodiert oder explodiert. Für jedes gelöste Problem tauchen zwei weitere auf, sodass ihm gar keine andere Wahl zu bleiben scheint, als mit einem noch verzweifelteren Versprechen versuchen, Zeit zu schinden. 
In Ratners Existenz spiegelt sich das gesamte Weltwirtschaftssystem wider eine einzige Wette mit fremden Geld in der Hoffnung auf noch mehr Geld unter enormen Zeitdruck und die wahren Verlierer dieser Wette sind nur eine Randnotiz, denn Geschichte wird von Gewinnern geschrieben. Für die Minenarbeiter in Afrika hat Uncut Gems deshalb nur wenig Zeit von seiner üppigen Lauflänge übrig, bevor er in den Diamond District von Manhattan abtaucht und die Nutznießer ihrer Arbeit bei ihrem schäbigen Tagewerk verfolgt. 
Äußerst faszinierend ist auch, wie beiläufig es Uncut Gems gelingt, unsere Fetischisierung mit Gegenständen zu beleuchten, denen wir einen Wert bzw. eine Eigenschaft zuordnen, den sie per se gar nicht besitzen Geld besitzt nur deshalb einen Wert, weil wir als Gesellschaft uns darauf geeignet haben. Ein Opal besitzt aus den gleichen Gründen einen Wert und wenn er für einen Basketballspieler sogar noch einen übergeordneten Wert als Glücksbringer besitzt, dann wird der Warenfetisch unserer Zeit endgültig offenbar. Denn ein Edelstein allein lässt uns keine Körbe werfen - erst unser Glaube daran führt dazu. Einen kleinen Exkurs in die Theorien von Marx gibt es also zwischen all den überlappenden Gesprächen, Beschimpfungen und Drohungen noch gratis dazu.
Zwischendurch blitzen auch immer wieder kurze Momente der Stille und Rührung auf, wenn etwa Ratner seiner Geliebten exakt das gleiche Geschenk machen will, wie sich selbst bereits gekauft hat - aber diese Momente werden vom gnadenlosen Takt des Sekundenzeigers zermalmt, denn Ratner muss immer weiter und weiter und weiter, schließlich er in seiner ganz eigenen Wahrnehmung der Welt ein Gewinnertyp. Wie sehr ihn das zum Loser macht, ist erschreckend lustig und bitter zugleich anzuschauen und auf allen Ebenen absolut beeindruckend. Zugleich deutlich zugänglicher als Good Time, der durch den Hype um Uncut Gems hoffentlich (wieder)entdeckt wird.

Uncut Gems is a film that explores the endless pursuit of satisfaction and how people can become addicted to the dopamine rush of getting what they want. Gambling becomes his biggest obsession, to the point where hes willing to risk everything, even his relationships and principles, just to feel that excitement again. What I found interesting is how the film shows that sometimes the pursuit of happiness becomes the very thing that destroys us.
Adam Sandler did a really good job as Howard. His character is far from perfect, and watching him struggle with his debts, humiliation, and the consequences of his own decisions makes you understand how trapped he is in this endless cycle. I also liked how the film shows his problems with his family and relationships, especially how his selfishness and dishonesty affect the people around him. The Safdie brothers direction felt familiar to me after watching Marty Supreme, with a similar chaotic and stressful style, even though the films are very different. Overall, Uncut Gems is an intense film about addiction, greed, and the idea that sometimes we become so obsessed with chasing satisfaction that we forget how to be satisfied with anything at all.

Joias Brutas tem uma proposta arriscada. O filme mantém, em toda a sua duração, uma mesma frequência alucinada que não apresenta muitas variações. 
Tanto a abordagem formal dos diretores como a performance de Adam Sandler possuem uma descontinuidade que é caótica, mas é também constante. Howard passa o filme inteiro com o mesmo temperamento. Os irmãos Safdie estão sempre atrás de estímulos visuais e sonoros. Mesmo dentro desse princípio caótico, existe uma previsibilidade.
O elemento que faz o filme progredir não é, exatamente, essa desordem, mas a maneira como os cineastas tiram forças peculiares - forças místicas, em última análise - de elementos banais que constituem essa experiência caótica.
A forma como cada sequência vai recompondo toda a estrutura do longa a partir de uma ideia comum - a ambiguidade entre a banalidade e o sagrado - traz uma inegável unidade ao trabalho.
Se por um lado a instabilidade dos acontecimentos parece refletir a instabilidade de um ideal capitalista. Um busca por mais dinheiro que é também uma busca pela sobrevivência - a própria construção claustrofóbica dos espaços de riqueza  (a joalheria fechada, o escritório de Howard, a boate, os apartamentos de luxo escuros e apertados) dá a impressão de ambientes de sobrevivência, como se fossem bunkers.
Por outro, a presença da pedra - de algum modo o símbolo bruto e essencial do capitalismo, a sua essência ainda não lapidada - seria o único objeto que traz uma certa ordem mística para quem a detém. Um senso de vitalidade contínua. O objeto de desejo ideal que motiva todo o caos. 
O que gera o movimento, o crescimento e a desgraça é a própria busca desmedida por esse ideal. O filme serve como um registro esquizofrênico dessa jornada, desse livre mercado da sobrevivência.
Essa talvez seja uma das chaves mais interessantes de Joias Brutas. A forma como, através de uma abordagem relativamente crua (a câmera instável, o trato realista com os espaços, a atmosfera evidentemente urbana), os diretores articulam elementos que beiram o fantasioso. 
Por meio de uma combinação de identidades étnicas, valores culturais, dogmas religiosos e até superstição envolvendo esportes, o filme propõe um amálgama esotérico que coordena - ou descoordena, não faz diferença - a imprevisibilidade dos acontecimentos. 
O mundo é um lugar caótico justamente por abrigar todas essas energias. As montagens envolvendo cores abstratas reforçam essa ideia. A primeira, que abre o filme, é das mais significativas um ideal místico que vai do que é mais sagrado e, teoricamente, valorizado (a joia misteriosa) ao que é mais mais sujo e científico (uma colonoscopia em Adam Sandler).
O filme constantemente joga com esses dois valores - o banal e o sagrado - em seus acontecimentos.  Além do evidente poder da pedra (o objeto mais sagrado justamente porque é, também, o mais valioso), não existe uma disposição específica desses valores. 
Mesmo que o mundo, em todos os seus contextos, lide com esses símbolos (até mesmo a criança na peça representa um milagre ao cuspir ouro), não existe um caminho correto para a salvação. 
Quando Howard parece certo do seu destino e faz a aposta final vencedora, atingindo assim uma possível redenção que finalmente assimila o aspecto sagrado (a natureza aleatória dos detalhes da aposta, a confiança na pedra) com o ideal capitalista (o prêmio em dinheiro), ele é morto com um tiro na cabeça por um oportunamente imprevisível agente do caos.
Carl Jung já disse que Deus é tudo aquilo que acontece e eu não posso controlar. Uma definição que, definitivamente, resume bem essa constante ambiguidade de Joias Brutas. 
Ao construir toda a sua dramaturgia e sua abordagem audiovisual sobre ideias de aleatoriedade e esoterismo, os cineastas articulam uma das experiências cinematográficas mais intensas e misteriosas da década. Um filme que, como poucos, assimila com riqueza a dúvida eterna sobre o determinismo das situações da vida.

The Safdie Brothers direction is frenetic yet meticulous, employing a gritty aesthetic that immerses the audience in Howards high-stakes world. The films pacing is frenetic, matching the pulse of Howards desperate decisions as he navigates a series of increasingly perilous bets. Every ticking second feels charged with tension, a testament to the Safdies skill in building suspense. The use of overlapping dialogue and ambient noise creates a sense of claustrophobia, enhancing the viewers anxiety as Howard spirals deeper into his self-destructive behaviours. Furthermore, the films visual and auditory elementsranging from its vibrant cinematography to its pulsating score by Daniel Lopatincontribute to an atmosphere that is both intoxicating and oppressive. Uncut Gems is not just a film its an experience that demands your full attention and emotional investment. Uncut Gems is a masterfully crafted exploration of greed, risk, and the human condition, anchored by a stellar performance from Adam Sandler. The films relentless pace and brutal honesty leave a lasting impression, making it a standout entry in contemporary cinema. Its a gripping watch for anyone who appreciates a well-executed narrative that challenges the viewer while delivering an unforgettable cinematic experience.

The film is an absolute chaotic joyride the Safdies are a talented duo and after watching both Marty Supreme and Uncut Gems, they certainly have a specific style(I know Benny didnt work on Marty Supreme). 
Both Howard Ratner and Marty Mauser are built from the same blueprint the obsessive New York Jewish hustler. Hugely different paths of destruction and journeys, but the feeling is the same and the films flow with similar chaos, honestly it makes me want to revisit Marty Supreme and I should be checking out Good Time soon too. I think on a revisit Marty Supreme would push up to a 4.5 star. 
Anyway, at the center of this hurricane is Adam Sandler, probably delivers what is easily a career best performance. He completely transforms into Howard Ratner, the frantic jeweler and loser family man who slowly loses his marbles over the 140-minute runtime. I love how Howard borrows money to bet money to pay back money, such a slippery slope. Sandler plays Howard with a desperate, contemporary slickness, curated in iconic costume design that feels both clean and memorable. 
The cinematography uses highly claustrophobic, long-lens zooms. This technique never allows us viewers to see the whole picture trapped in the sweaty, tight-knit orbit of the protagonists panic. Its engaging and unique filmmaking, the way chaos is portrayed on screen the overlapping phone call scene is a prime example that comes to mind, so chaotic but the meticulous screenplay allows it to flourish in majestic ways. 
Why am I seeing TraxNYC taking Uncut Gems to the streets, that video floating around X right now is hilarious, TraxNYC is doing this shit fr, talk about a poetic film. 
Plus, despite the constant noise, the film is incredibly well-paced. The narrative is gripped by the opal from the jump and never lets go. The Safdies carefully balance a dozen different subplots the gambling debts, the collapsing family life, and the professional risks. All without ever losing touch with the main plot, flowing effortlessly toward a finale that is as shocking as it is fulfilling. To put it simply the film doesnt leave a single stone(or opal) unturned.
The technical elements elevate the entire piece the score, the setting and the supporting cast all increase the stakes and raise the atmospheric boiling pot of high stakes tension. The music and score is incredibly fresh, it almost feels like a Tangerine Dream score, the vibe is both clutch and enduring, provides the perfect electronic heartbeat to Howards panic. The setting is captured by the raw authentic hustle and bustle of NYC, the Diamond District is explored and I love the Safdies approach to explore niche subcultures by treating them like high-stakes battlegrounds. 
Julia Fox delivers her finest work. While her screen presence is undeniable(almost started barking at the screen during one particular scene), her acting is nearly as strong, providing a vital anchor to Howards chaotic world. Whatever happened since is a disaster, she could have had a future as a solid B lister, I mean the talent was there. 
Uncut Gems is a relentless story that manages to be both a character study and an adrenaline-fueled thriller. It is a meticulous piece of filmmaking that finds a balance in the chaos and anxiety to deliver an illustrious film that lets Adam Sandlers acting shine like the opal he is, really enjoyed this one and almost contemplating picking up the criterion, Ill probably wait till the next sale.

Uncut Gems.2019. Directed by Bennie Safdie and Josh Safdie.
Arguably, Adam Sandler delivers one of the best performances of his career in Uncut Gems (2019). He is channeling a bit of his Punch Drunk Love character Barry Egan but, Howard Ratner is the levo stereo isomer of Barry Egan. The Safdie brothers made a dizzying, disturbing, yet highly engaging show of addiction at its pinnacle in this character study. The narrative has a pace that leaves one feeling a sense of hopelessness for Howard Ratner. The diamond district has blood on its hands as miners in Ethiopia are mining uncut gems (opals) and selling them for scraps while they are sold for millions in the United States. How will Ratner make it out of his bets that have literally put him in a choke hold? 
The chaos of Uncut Gems benefits from Daniel Lopatins (David Byrnes American Utopia and The Bling Ring) score. As the music breathes inspiration from eighties heist films (Heat, 1995 by Michael Mann) with synths, Ratner is betting his life, family, business, and mistress as he cannot take another breath without making a bet. His addiction to gambling is so deep it is genetic. The cut throat world of New Yorks loan sharks, bookies, and goons are showcased in a dream like race car pace that never leaves one asking if the film can give more. From the gaseous beginnings of the planet, to the mines of Ethiopia, and into a deadly wound the colors of the uncut gem (opal) never stop mesmerizing the audience.

A blistering, full throttle descent into madness that manages to make a bunch of terrible men yelling over each other extremely entertaining. Sandler is a force in this film - you can see every one of this characters impulses eating away at him from the inside, driving his every thought and action. Its an incredible performance, especially from a body language perspective, its own high wire pressure cooker imbued with just the right amount of tragic comedy. Julia Fox holds her own and then some opposite him, clearly understanding both the ridiculous and brutally sad sides of the story in tandem. Daniel Lopatins score is brilliant, per usual. 
For all the talk about how this is an anxiety-inducing, nonstop thriller , the Safdies also seem intent on painting a sobering picture of a life and family in chaos. The general theme behind it is something weve seen time and time again, but from the beginning, theres such a clear disdain for Howard coming from all fronts - especially within his family - that it manages to work. This is not to say that the story wouldnt have been tighter had it clocked in at under 2 hours, because it drags a bit in the middle theres only so much the performers can do, and only so many scenarios they can get themselves into. Some scenes seem less driven by character and more by a general dictionary definition of intense scene. 
But thankfully, the film finds new legs in its final stretch, delivering a series of impeccably crafted scenes that kicks off with Sandler and (a wonderful) Garnett sitting across from each other at a table. This scene is the film in a nutshell, and it sets into motion a crescendo that is thrilling in a way unlike anything else Ive seen this year. It is one of the most memorable final acts Ive seen ever. Where the film thrives is in a state of being unpredictable, yet also driven by a sense of inevitability - its an ambitious, imperfect, strange, and yet wholly compelling piece of entertainment that is in a perpetual state of careening off a cliff.
GRADE A-

this loses some of the immediacy that carried the last 2 Safdie films, but their switch in dp to Darius Khondji both pulls them closer to the new hollywood style theyre often compared to while creating more of a dissonance between their hyper-contemporary point of view and their obsession with the past (whether the cultural details of 6 years ago, or the film style of 40 years ago). their eye for composition has vastly improved with the help of Khondji, and the editing taking a step down from Good Times fully breakneck pace allows more time to absorb all the moving parts in these very dense frames. 
the period recreation is incredibly precise, and show that the Safdies wereare keeping an eye on all of the cultural shifts around them. the archival footage of that playoff series with its already-vintage espn graphics, KGs classic pregame scream, and Mike Francesa as a high-powered bookie who uses his angry radio voice for every line delivery. from Sandlers iPhone (never thought id see the sandman text r u wet?) to the rap scene, (Amen by the pre-beef combo of drakemeek, early weeknd, trinidad james, Swimming Pools) it truly does feel like i logged into seven years ago. 
theres no pepe the frog on an acid tab to stamp this as a film of the Current Moment, but the way that the Safdies are able to look back at such a recent period and use it as a cultural playground as well as a launching pad for both drama and cultural critique earns them the spot of the most contemporary american filmmakers.

I think you are the most annoying person I have ever met. I hate being with you, I hate looking at you, and, if I had my way, I would never see you again.
Ill admit it. I am, in mind and soul, the farthest from an Adam Sandler fan that I could possibly be and that bias cast a shadow over this film from the moment I learned of his casting. Sandlers single-brain-cell frathouse brand, while enjoyable in the early running (Im not going to pretend Billy Madison wasnt a guilty pleasure for years), has now become a dirge of cinema. He embodies everything thats wrong with modern filmmaking. And, yet, with Uncut Gems, he gives not only the best performance of his career by a generous mile, but one of the finest of 2019. 
Going into this, I couldnt fathom why the incredibly talented siblings behind the fantastic Good Time elected to place him at the center of their highly anticipated newest outing. But whether he deserved it or not, Sandler was gifted with the artistic integrity equivalent of a genuine lifeline and he went all the way with it.
Gems is a blunt force shockwave of a feature, pulsing with even more of the electric immediacy they made a name for themselves with in their last flick. Its a frenzied, nerve-frying masterwork parable set to one of the raddest scores Ive heard all year. I was left--and to be honest, still am--more than a bit physically shaken by this. 
The way the Safdies play with tension, twisting and unleashing it as if it were a game of Russian Roulette verges on panic-inducing. I cant stress this enough, if you suffer from any sort of stress-based anxiety, please know that itll feel like this thing is almost feeding off of yours.
The extent to which we feel this seemingly limitless dread is amplified by Sandlers stellar get-out-of-shitty-paycheck-movie-jail card performance as a sleazy motormouth opportunist. One of the best compliments I can give this film is that traditional Sandler fans are bound to hate it. The films supporting players are all outstanding as well with the likes of Lakeith Stanfield (expanding his versatility yet again), Idina Menzel (reminding us just how much she can do beyond her musical prowess), Judd Hirsch (its heartening to see him in fine form), and Eric Bogosian (fresh off his second stint on the phenomenal Succession) matching Sandler beat for beat.
If anyone thought the Safdies were only capable of generating cinematic lightning once, Gems is the indisputable renunciation of such an idea. They are without a doubt, two of the most exciting filmmakers around and their work here is a crystallized testament to their singular vision. I seriously need to go lie down and watch some puppies running through a field now. 
What a trip.

CODA is zero pretension and 100 percent heart and soul. Its a dazzling, heartfelt representation of coda experience that never strives to be something its not, and it succeeds gloriously in building an inviting, dazzling world where familial bonds eventually trump everything.
Chronicling a hearing teenagers struggles to balance her singing dream and the responsibility of her deaf family who depends on her, CODA is first and foremost an effective comedy that relies on the off the charts chemistry between the cast members to work. Troy Kotsur and Marlee Matlin, two deaf veterans, executed their characters with abundant personal charms and understanding of the deaf issues, and provided most of the gags throughout the movie. This is the film Ive been waiting for after two admittedly slightly disappointing Sundance premieres. CODA follows Ruby, who is the only hearing member of her deaf family, as she navigates through her life. Over the course of the film, writer and director Sîan Heder carefully explores her struggles and emotions, creating not only a wonderfully moving, but also an eye-opening filmand hopefully setting a precedent for even more representation of the deaf community on screen.
There are movies that move me, and then there are movies that make me smile, sob, and laugh, only to find myself unable to focus on anything other than how deeply Im affected by the story playing out in front of me CODA, needless to say, has become one of these films, leaving me with hurting cheeks and a headache, but in the best way possible. 
Masterfully interweaving humor and dramatic elements into a stirring flow of dialogues, Heders brilliant screenplay bursts with character right from the beginning. CODA treats its characters with care, never once rushing them and subsequently allowing each individual to feel and express their emotions. The scriptalthough reliant on some crowd-pleasing cliches, but again, not necessarily in a bad waydevelops each character with depth and subtlety, most of all Ruby, our protagonist. 
As a result, this film turns into a powerfully human symphony of emotions because once we got to know the characters and their motivations, every second of their interactions are bound to affect us as well, be it Ruby expressing her passion for singing, or a shot of the family hugging each other tightly. A few extremely impactful moments (mainly the ones that made me sob the most) still linger in my mind, but I wont be getting into them since I believe theyre most powerful in the context of the narrative, and no words would do them justice.
Much of this films impact comes from Heders script and direction, but just as much is attributed to the actors both spellbinding and moving performances, namely Emilia Joness. She plays Ruby with determination, wit, and charm, masterfully expressing her feelings not only through Heders words, but also through her nuanced expressions. Since Rubys conflicts are central to the story, her emotions are essentially what guide us through the film, and Joness does a phenomenal job at doing so. 
For me, the best films are the ones that understand human emotion, the ones that dont only make me think or appreciate some technicality, but the ones that stir me emotionally. Tender, heartwarming, uplifting and utterly human, CODA touches on many things struggles experienced in the deaf community, coming-of-age as a child of deaf adults, finding your voice. In the end, however, CODA is a story about family, and the incomparable love and bond that can exist within it. And thats everything I needed today.

As a deaf person, its been nice to see an explosion of our presence throughout various media, whether it be articles or television, but sometimes it does come at a price. While I really enjoyed the deaf talent here as they are Marlee Matlin, Daniel Durant and Troy Kotsur, I found their framing to be frequently eye-rolling, manipulative and its all the more obvious that some of the drama was created to heighten tension or to gain sympathy. 
Of course, movies are supposed to accomplish these objectives, but to me, it failed as I found myself being annoyed as to how theyre often portrayed as helpless. I dont doubt that CODAs (Child of Deaf Adults) do each possess an unique life experience in which theyre literally in between two worlds. In fact, I was sold on the premise and wanted to see what they would do with that unique perspective, but it should be known that I am not a CODA, just as an only deaf child. I cant claim that Im knowledgeable of their experiences, but Ive met a fair number of them and I can attempt to convey my interpretation if this felt authentic to me, as I recall their stories. Though there are long ways to go as far as accessibility goes, sign language interpreters are readily available in a lot of places if you know where to look. Yet it is here that they are completely absent, even going as far as to a courtroom hearing which would make anyone scream their heads off knowing that there was a landmark law signed by President Bush in 1990 to prevent these very things to happen in the first place. Which brings me to my point here, is that the trio of Matlin, Durant, and Kotsur are frequently portrayed as helpless, though I doubt its maliciously intentional, but it feels incredibly detached from reality in which the script fails to deliver a suspension of disbelief, and I could not bring myself to really believe in what I was watching. It also doesnt help that the script is painfully average, though it does have its moments which I really think was in no doubt delivered by the deaf actors here. While we may coexist in the same world, we the deaf people do have our cultural language and unique experiences in this world which are hearing-centric, and I think this film does deliver on the idea that we do live in a fundamentally incompatible world, and we do experience frequent frustrations everyday. I know all about that. 
But I do think this movie is barely passable, just I would say this isnt entirely reflective of deaf people nor does it live in the same reality most of us live in. Its a feel-good movie that does accomplish its objectives as a coming-of-age movie from the perspective of a child of deaf adults, and it does get its message, however messy, across. I just wish there was more authenticity to this not just in the front of the camera but behind it too, as I felt some parts were painfully done for either sympathy or hearing gaze. But one cant get it all right, and despite some cons I listed in this review, I wont lie as I did laugh at some parts and generally enjoyed myself, but this isnt the feel-good movie of the year at all. But I know the rest of the world probably will disagree, and thats fine by me. Nothing new about that sort of thing, though. 
PS. Troy Kotsur probably is at least two stars worth of a movie. His performance felt the most authentic out of them all, but Durant and Matlin shouldnt be ignored either for they do a good job. An all too familiar coming-of-age family drama, from the unique perspective of a Child of Deaf Adults (CODA).
I was worried that we wouldnt connect. Like me and my mom, were not close. I thought I would fail you. That being deaf would make me a bad mom ... Dont worry. You are a bad mom for so many other reasons.
Although I was not pulling for CODA on Oscar night, I cant be all that bummed about such a sweet and funny film winning Best Picture. Plus it would not be the first time the Academy decided to honor a smaller drama, with movies like Ordinary People, and Terms of Endearment coming to mind. While watching I could not help but think how this felt like a combo of Lady Bird and Sound of Metal, but thankfully by the end CODA does feature some powerful moments to help it stand on its own.
(Quick Hits) ... Spoilers
- I thought it was fascinating to see this story where a teen girl basically becomes trapped by her parents, since they depend on her to interpret for them
- We get a bunch of complexity from the characters as they try and embrace that Ruby has discovered a new passion for singing, and wants to go to music school. For instance, Marlee Matlin who plays the Mom suggests Ruby has chosen this hobby because she can not easily share it with her family. We see that she is a loving Mom, that does not want things to change. And it is brave of her to admit that even she struggled with the fact that Ruby was not deaf
- Troy Kotsur who plays the Dad is a whole other story since he is more of a lighthearted, stubborn, and pretty raunchy fisherman. It is hilarious to see how far he will go with his signing for some laughs
- Rubys brother played Daniel Durant might be the most intriguing since his feelings are more bottled up. We can tell he wants to take more of a leadership role in the family business, but somewhat resents his sisters abilities and wishes she would let him prove himself
- I cant even imagine having to go fishing every day before school. Plenty of time is spent watching Ruby getting worn down by this aggressive routine of trying to prep for her college audition, all while supporting her familys business and patching up things with her boyfriend
- Factors of being a CODA that I had never considered included how loud her family was since they are not self-conscious about noise and being heard, the family admitting that they are getting their daughters interpretive services for free, and how being raised in a deaf family would make it more of a challenge to speak properly at first ... and the bullying that would come with that difference
- The whole first part of the movie we are getting to see Rubys strained perspective, and it is not until close to the end when we are finally brought into the headspace of her father. As he experiences not being able to hear his daughters concert. I liked the natural buildup of him seeing others enjoy her music, which then leads to the tender moment of him wanting to feel the beautiful vibrations of his daughters voice for himself
- The whole time I was wanting to see her sign to the songs so badly. But that was saved for the audition scene, which did get my waterworks flowing   
CODA is much better than just being a Lifetime original deaf family movie. The drama is cliche, but despite some of the characters not being able to speak, it is amazing to see how much unique personality flows from this story. Then the ending brings things together in the typical coming of age story way, while still managing to leave an impact by taking its time to get us invested in the human drama of what a deaf family with a child who can hear experiences. I prefer the more artsy style of Sound of Metal, but I can see general audiences more easily relating with and enjoying CODA.
Thanks for reading.

Despite being a remake of a French film, Coda knows how to find its own specificity thanks to director and screenwriter Sian Heder who fought to have deaf actors in the cast, managing in this way to break away from the original and give her work a strong dose of spontaneity and realism. A sincere and honest bittersweet comedy, Coda takes what could be an unpretentious story and turns it into a heartfelt exploration of family and the benefits of inclusion. Ruby is 17 years old and the only hearing person among her relatives, who rely on her as a interpreter and for her role in the family business. While her brother and parents are about to start a new fishing business, the girl is torn between her loyalty to them and her desire to leave to attend a prestigious music school. Thus begins a tale of sentimental and artistic coming-of-age, full of grace and measure, which entertains a lot, makes you think and moves without ever being sappy. A work with an extremely classic structure, but thanks to a cast of interpreters extremely credible and a gaze that can always be very close to the characters, is able to distinguish itself from many other films of this genre. In a difficult and complicated historical period like the present, a small film that knows how to speak to the heart and reminds us that every voice is essential, even if it expresses itself in a different way, can only be welcome. Perhaps also for this reason the Academy Awards jury decided to award it three Oscars Best Picture, Supporting Actor and Adapted Screenplay.

Gefeiert, preisgekrönt und wirklich nichts Besonderes. Ein Child Of Deaf Adults kann gut singen und will sich, auf Anraten des Musiklehrers, vom Fischkutter-Familienbetrieb lösen, um die Begabung weiter auszubauen. Klingt wie die typische Coming-of-age-Story, ist auch eine typische Coming-of-age-Story und dazu sogar noch das Remake einer französischen Erfolgsdramödie. Die Unterschiede es geht eben um Fischer in Amerika, nicht um Käseverkäufer in Frankreich und im Gegensatz zum Original besteht die Familie der eher selten strahlenden, aber schön singenden Emilia Jones dann aus echten gehörlosen Darstellern, zu denen auch Oscar-Preisträgerin Marlee (Gottes vergessene Kinder) Matlin gehört. Was folgt, sind die Dinge, die folgen müssen. Peinliche Proben, unbeholfene Turteleien, der schwere Schicksalsschlag, der zeigt, wie instabil das Leben von tauben Fischern sein kann und natürlich ein Vorsingen, von dem alles abhängt. Das lag unter anderem am Umgang mit dem Thema Gehörlosigkeit. Er fühlt sich so selbstbewusst wie selbstverständlich an. Nie zu überdramatisch, nie zu bitter, nie zu arg kitschig (und kitschig wird es), aber auch nicht zu platt oder billig in seiner Leichtigkeit und stets respektvoll. Es lag auch ein wenig am Setting, das sehr hell und clean, aber auch so Postkarten-freundlich und warm eingefangen wird. Es lag aber vor allem an den Familienmitgliedern und ihrer kauzigen Einheit. Sie haben es nicht leicht, nehmen es aber alles andere als schwer. Sie sind offenherzig, aber haben auch ihre Vorurteile. Sie leben Rausch und Sex aus, können aber auch nachvollziehbar scheiße sein. Und das alles ist so sympathisch und einfühlsam gespielt, wie es auch von Regisseurin Sian Heder inszeniert wird. Obwohl man so gut wie alles auch mühelos als gefällig, sicher und eben konventionell bezeichnen kann. 
Aber es gibt Tage da reicht so was dann auch, um mitlachen, mitgehen oder mitweinen zu können. Gerade, wenn es dann noch ein paar Momente gibt, die wegen ihrer Idee doch etwas hervorstechen. Zum Beispiel ein Konzert, das zur Tonspur von Vater, Mutter und Bruder wechselt und somit anders ergreift. Oder die Szene, in der Papa Frank (reizend Troy Kotsur) den Klang seiner Tochter erfühlt. Und dann ist da auch immer noch Eugenio Derbez, bei dem nie so ganz klar ist, ob er eine Figur spielt, für die in Glee kein Platz mehr war, oder eben einen sehr spleenigen Typen, der Musik nur lehren, aber nicht wie mal geplant leben darf. Kann anstrengen, kann aber auch erheitern. Also ähnlich wie der Film an sich. Keine Frage, Sound of Metal ist die härtere, intensivere, etwas smartere und meditativere Erfahrung gewesen, mehr the terrifying power of silence. CODA ist dagegen eher ein stabiler, schnucklig-rostiger Bootsausflug, der auch mal mühsam ist, aber Zeit zum Lieder singen und Sonne genießen lässt. In einer mir fremden Welt, die doch so normal wie dieser Crowdpleaser ist.

Equally corny and uplifting, this Sundance-style bowl of cinematic clam chowder nourishes the soul with a hearty serving of feel-good ingredients. Not enough use of sound design for the material (there is one effective scene of silence at the school choir concert), but this is not after Sound of Metal level artistry. It is content being a gooey coming-of-age tale about a child of deaf parents (CODA) and her difficulties navigating high school life and familial responsibility. So much better than the bazillion half-baked teen melodramas Netflix has been cranking out in recent years. Emilio Jones is endearing as the lead, but Eugenio Derbez steals the show  playing the finicky, exacting choirmaster Mr. V, he is the unsung hero of the entire film.

Its incredible how little we are starting to expect from our movies as movies. Beyond lacking for almost any visual eloquence or aesthetic finesse, CODA barely acts as if these are goals to which a film might aspire. Theres exactly one scene where you might detect some audiovisual shaping a key concert where a sudden rack focus, in cahoots with a drastic change in the soundtrack, communicates something essential about the story and its characters experience of the world. Even so, its a point that has already been made in more typically pedestrian ways earlier in the same sequence. Soon afterward, a nighttime exchange between Ruby (Emilia Jones) and her dad Frank (Troy Kotsur) offers a similarly qualified peak in the film. Its a moving moment of earnest vulnerability and disclosure between these characters, but its a mystery why nothing like it has transpired any earlier in CODAs plot. Plus, having wrung some honest feeling from its audience via this delicate moment, CODA immediately proceeds toward a more elaborate, clunky, and dishonest riff on whats fundamentally the same scene. This reprise, styled as a big, tearjerking climax, no longer conveys a unique, private bond between two characters in the central family but instead sells the audience hard on a bedrock of warmth, intimacy, and mutual recognition that allegedly unites the whole foursomea sweet idea that CODA has spent almost two hours demonstrating as untrue.
Despite its inexplicable bounty of awards from Sundance (not a festival from which I necessarily expect more discernment), CODA cannot be chalked up as one of those occasions where a sturdy script receives disappointingly flat treatment at the level of image and style. CODAs screenplay is itself a mess, as beholden to Hallmark Channel templates as are its bland, overbright, indifferently framed shots. (Regarding the Hallmark Channel, I know wherefrom I speak just trust me on this.) Behavior within the family is an incoherent mishmash of fondness and alienation, just as their public-facing life combines reckless outspokenness with timid insecurity in bewildering ways. Of course I understand that people are complicated (!), and I know well that inhabiting a minoritized identity can easily lead to all kinds of behavioral and temperamental inconsistencies in public and even in private life, varying by the circumstance and the moment. What CODA offers, though, is not a dispatch on human complexity. It just feels like a piece of simple-enough pegboard furniture in which someone has nonetheless managed to misassemble the crude, unambiguously labeled parts. 
For an inordinately long time, Ruby conceals from her family a passion for singing (even though its literally the first thing we see and hear her do, in their company!) and then is shocked, shocked when they dont understand that her nascent musicianship is the single thing around which they must reorganize their own shifting priorities, or else emerge as The Bad People in a borderline-bratty coming-of-age flick. Rubys connections to a music teacher, overplayed by Eugenio Derbez, and an I-guess-boyfriend, underplayed by Ferdia Walsh-Peelo, never resolve or convince in relation to the generous amounts of screen time they receive from writer-director Siân Heder. Rubys mother Jackie (Marlee Matlin), seems markedly more selfish, more fearful, and less empathetic than either her husband or her son Leo (Daniel Durant), but CODA itself feels fearful of etching distinct characters or holding each accountable to the implications of their specific choices and plotlines. Frank, Leo, and Jackie are often written and framed as a nondistinct unit, either as Rubys consolidated support system or her monolithic problem, which feels artistically and ideologically dubious. Leo, in particular, feels narratively short-changed despite the repeated suggestions that he understands things about this family and its reflexes that other members dont see or wont admit. 
Ruby, conversely, feels over-lavished with attention by a film that places wild pressure on her modest vocal gift and compulsively absolves her of responsibility in scenes where shes definitely the asshole. I wish the performances were stronger, but these problems are all baked into the script, as are whole forcefields of incoherence about the familys longterm standing in its community and a flat, anachronistic sense of deaf people as totally cut off from the worlds of sound, of music, of rights and accommodations, of political life, of communication with hearing people.
I guess the last thing Ill say (my coda about CODA) is that Heder is way too wedded to scapegoats and potshots as means to facilitate conflict or construct narrative and tone. Why portray deafness as a complicated experience unto itself and in deaf peoples relations to hearing peopleeven when everyone is trying to work together or understand each otherwhen you can take the shortcuts of summoning the single-scene bigots you need in school cafeterias, in bars, in audition spaces, etc., to embody adversity as an individualized problem? Why explore the layered necessities and problems of government regulation of an industry like fishing, especially as its felt in working peoples lives, when you can just take a reckless and reactionary anti-regulation stance, get your audience cheering for some utterly out-of-character and unrealistic behavior from your leads, and present the woman assigned to monitor your boat as a cruel and incapable caricature? Why present the Berklee College of Music as a high-caliber institution with a justly formidable bar to entry when you could just make the arbiters of admission look like snooty dicksjust because you showed up late and without sheet music for your own big moment with them? And why explore with any texture or specificity the verbal and emotional lingua franca among your main characters when you can just lard their exchanges with sex gags and sophomoric profanities, as if this makes them Real People? I guess thats where I land on CODA its no more interested in engaging reality, even a consistent fictional construction of reality, than it is in engaging the unique expressive resources of cinema.

NOTE I am not deaf nor hard of hearing. That said, I also encourage you to read reviews, articles, and comments that come from deafhard of hearing writers or any actual CODAs, especially in light of this films Best Picture win.
If you are looking for a good source on pieces that cover this film which were written by deaf writers, me and my friend Jakob Sanchez have searched high and low in order to compile this thread on Twitter.
There are a few questions that I think are worth asking about CODA the first of which is, if this movie is supposedly a win for the deaf community, how come I havent seen deaf writers being treated on the same playing field as hearing critics? This was something I figure was worth asking as a hearing viewer because it doesnt feel right to me that the conversation about this film is dominated by hearing viewers. Did we just suddenly think that because deaf actors are playing deaf characters, we didnt need to ask them any further about what this film means for them?
Another one I wanted to ask how many times have we seen this story being done before? I know this is something we say about a lot of coming-of-age narratives, but this is one case where I feel like you could easily take away the key aspect defining it, about being a child in a deaf family, and this film wouldnt be getting the same raves that Ive seen it receiving back and forth. I assume theres so much more that can go into the life of being a hearing child in a deaf family, but in this case, her perspective is definitely the less interesting one.
Lastly, how much research about the deaf community was done by Siân Heder if she had absolutely no connections to them whatsoever? Because so much of what happens in this film, whether it be the familiar trope of deaf characters being unable to experience music or the fact that the reliance on the hearing child to be an interpreter in large settings would not fly well with the Americans with Disabilities Act.
Im sorry, but I just cannot get on board whatsoever with the framing of this movie as wholesome because it definitely does more to reinforce ableist beliefs that weve only been accustomed to over the years. The deaf actors are good though Troy Kotsur especially is incredible. But it cant be shaken off that this movie is far more harmful than people realize it could be.

Siân Heders coming of age music drama is so simple, yet astonishingly moving.
Ruby (Emilia Jones) is a 17 year old girl who is a child of deaf adults (CODA). Her entire family is deaf and work in the fishing business, yet she is hearing. She has a passion for music that she must attempt to balance with her important role in the family business. 
Hearing negatively impacts Rubys life, as her family is overly dependent on her to help them with their business (as their interpreter). I enjoyed seeing a different perspective from the typical hearing focused film. It shows the unavoidable impact that being deaf has on those around you. When it comes time for Ruby to try to create her own life, complications arise. She joins a chorus at her school and is motivated by her teacher to try to get into a music university. Yet, she doesnt get the full support of her family as she wont be able to help in the business if she left for university. 
I connected with the film quite a bit as I was a member of chorus all throughout my life in school. The nervousness of being heard by others was very relatable and I loved to see Rubys passion for music. It also didnt hurt that Emilia Jones has a lovely voice, that I hope to see utilized in other music movies musicals. And although this film isnt a comedy, I have to point out that it was really funny. The effective humor made me like the cast even more. 
Most of the performances were notable. Emilia Jones acting felt genuine as this nervous teenage girl, which was helped by the fact that she was an actual teenager casted for the role (Hollywood, take notes). She handled the emotional moments with ease and had wonderful chemistry with her parents. Marlee Matlin and Troy Kotsur as her mom and dad were so lovable and deeply impactful in their heartfelt moments. Kotsur had more moments to shine though and needs to be nominated for best supporting actor. The scene with him watching the concert and then asking Ruby to sing the song again for him was exceptional. He has mastered non verbal acting and conveys some of the most genuine emotion Ive seen this year without a single spoken word. 
What works so well in CODA is with the hard hitting emotional sequences with its characters. The coast guard scene with the observer is eye opening and effectively crafted. Being deaf is even more limiting than many may ever realize. The audition, concert and final goodbye scenes are equally as notable with their ability to capture the effect of a familys love on a child. Ruby learns to move on from them through their help and encouragement and its very touching. 
I think the film has some unfortunate missteps though. Even though rather minor, Rubys experiences with Miles (Ferdia Walsh-Peelo) are a little more basic for coming of age stories than I wanted. But the main problem in the film is with her teacher. Although Eugenio Derbezs acting was solid, the character wasnt written very deeply. He doesnt need to be Terence Fletcher but he shouldnt be as overly cliche as he is. It is strange considering how well written almost every other character is and how genuine they all feel compared to him.
But I loved CODA and it reminded me of my affection and appreciation for the simple construct of being able to listen to music and singing. Siân Heder deserves every bit of buzz shes receiving and I hope to see more movies centered around this topic in the future.

Coming-of-age movies are often effective, but their stories tend to travel the exact same route. A young person who doubts him or herself finds someone who believes in them or inspires them, comes out of their shell, and finds a way to succeed in the short term, thus starting their dream. The formula has been done so many times because it works, but for a film to rise above the clichés, it needs to have a great hook. CODA is the type of film that has that extra something special. The title is not the word coda but rather an acronym for Child of Deaf Adults. The child is Ruby (Emilia Jones), the only hearing member in her deaf family. CODA tells the story of Ruby, a teen who doesnt want to go into the family fishing business. Instead, she wants to go to college to pursue her dreams of singing, but feels pressure as the interpreter for her mom, dad and brother, who are deaf.
This film is incredibly moving because of its authenticity. The film works to provide a message of inclusion all throughout the story, and, for the most part, it does a very good job. Though the central plot revolves around the one hearing member of the family, the film deftly represents the Deaf community without the usual disability tropes and reflects the depth of their experiences without making deafness an all-defining feature. Unlike many films, the deaf characters in CODA are not portrayed as helpless, sympathetic, or defined by their disability, but rather possess a depth of character that transcends any one aspect of them. But Heder is careful to not let the audience forget the characters deafness. This is not a story of people overcoming a disability to have normal lives, but rather a story of people not defined by their disability and who do not see their disability as an obstacle to overcome. Heder has crafted a story that goes in many directions, but intertwines all of them into the delicate fabric of Rubys life. Lively and surprisingly funny dialogue permeates the film, warming the heart and balancing the more serious events portrayed. Emilia Jones shines as Ruby, bringing subtle humor and powerful emotion to the starring role. In a story like this that is so character driven, any one performance could have shattered the illusion created in the film, but no one did.
While the cinematography in the film is beautiful, it is carefully crafted so as not to be noticed. Subtle camera movements and the juxtaposition between Steadicam and handheld camera positions give small glimpses into the mental state of characters. The director and cinematographer used rather simple techniques to draw the audience in and allow us to pay attention to more important things the life-affirming narrative, and the incredible sound design. Through the sound design, Heder balances the audience alongside Ruby between an intricate world of sounds and one of silence. My only gripe is When CODA strays away from the family at its center, it gets a little too cluttered with side plots that feel inconsequential at times but otherwise, CODA is confident and proud filmmaking that transcends familiarity by further layering the family dynamics as the story goes on. In a year when plenty of movies (including major blockbusters) are pushing the importance of family, CODA does it most potently with a stellar ensemble examining the positives and negatives of a complex, life-changing family situation. Recommended!

With a cast of all but unknown actors, Marlee Matlin being the only identifiable name, the film proved to be a triumph for everyone involved, but most especially writer-director Sian Heder and actor Troy Kotsur. He is warm, witty, and deeply moving on screen.
One of the things that made CODA so successful and likely what pushed it to its win is the manner in which it brings people together. Just dont belly flop, says Ruby as she braces her cute choral classmate for the dive they are about to take into a tranquil lagoon theyve retreated to. Between the trials of high school and the tribulations of her family, Ruby finds herself in the throws of this familiar virginal romance. Two teens too timid to touch teeter on the brink of burgeoning newness. They leap. Their descent is modest, straightforward, and streamline. They land without a splash or a flourish. Undaunted by the depths below them, they seem blissfully content buoyant upon the surface. 
Coda resigns itself to a similarly cautious ambition. Deaf and hard-of-hearing characters have rarely been given the dimensionality and depth which Siân Heder seems to be striving towards with this project. Reckoning with the historic marginalisation of disability onscreen by redressing the balance is an important and admirable ambition this film pursues by representation alone. Subtly drawing upon the lived experiences of deaf actors who play Rubys family lends the film a stronger sense of authenticity. Crucial scenes are all the more emotional thanks to the core cast. 
Yet representation alone proves insufficient in distinguishing Coda as the remarkable film its unprecedented acquisition suggested to many. Apples strident Sundance purchase sent audience expectations soaring to heights this film was never made to meet. Albeit sincerely told, Coda suffers from a severe case of being disarmingly simple which for many will be severely disappointing. By hitting every clichéd beat of any coming-of-age drama, Ruby succumbs to a tediously conventional arc. 
Even Emilia Jones commendable performance as Ruby cant escape the banality of the film she shoulders. Initially, we glimpse discontent in the quiet struggle behind her eyes or the muted frustrations she refrains from articulating. Oppositely Marlee Matlins presence is one of forthright displeasure and overbearing maternity. Jones exhibits the mannered finesse weve come to expect from Oscar winners like Matlin. Eventually, as Rubys arc plateaus into a comfortable cliché, Matlin builds to a heartfelt scene the likes of which we all anticipated and of which I wouldnt begrudge a supporting nomination at next years Oscars. 
The tragedy with which Coda aims to tackle is an endearingly uncomplicated one. To hold a passion which your family cant understand or access easily. To a great extent, the filmmakers squeeze some pertinent albeit predictable predicaments from their premise. Yet their ambition is tempered by an almighty caution without sizeable risk or reward. If met with middling expectations then Coda will likely satiate most, but those who saw a 25m price tag as quality assurance may feel swindled by a perfectly pleasant film doomed by misplaced expectations.

CODA, writer-director Sian Heders second feature and a big awards winner at the 2021 Sundance Film Festival, is a coming of age story told with genuine, crowd-pleasing heart, buckets of empathy and zero pretentiousness. It does at times lean on cliché and sentimentality, and the character arcs and story beats are recognisable a mile off, but this is one of those rare indie dramas where  everything aligns perfectly the acting is top notch, the writing consistently sharp and frequently very funny, and the emotional wallops of the final 30 minutes feel completely earned. What a truly lovely, warm hug of a film this is from beginning to end.
And that isnt even mentioning CODAs primary hook.  The films protagonist, Ruby (played wonderfully by Emilia Jones, who gives a perfect portrayal of an introvert with a growing rebellious streak), is a CODA child of deaf adults. Her parents, Frank and Jackie (Troy Kotsur and Marlee Matlin in standout peeformances) and her older brother Leo (Daniel Durant) are all deaf, and have come to rely upon Ruby to interpret for them in their interactions with hearing persons. However, Ruby is starting to find her own identity encouraged by her teacher, Mr. Villalobos (a spry, charismatic performance by Eugenio Derbez) she joins the school choir and, when it becomes clear that she has a talent for singing, is forced to confront a difficult decision between on the one hand her family who rely upon her and on the other her dreams of going to study music at college.
The films strongest card is in its approach to its deaf characters. Crucially, all of the deaf characters in the film are played by deaf actors- a positive statement of inclusivity and representation in and of itself this and the extensive use of ASL in the script lends real authenticity to the narrative and helps create a world in which these characters feel fully three-dimensional and not defined by their condition (the first time we meet Frank and Jackie is at the doctors office, where Ruby is required to tell her parents that they have contracted STIs and, to their horror, wont be able to have sex for two weeks). In turn, this allows a sensitive exploration of themes such as identity, the isolation of deaf people and the difficulty of fitting in- for example, there is a scene where Leo, angry at being in his view babied by his younger sister, attempts to go out for a beer with the lads that goes horribly wrong.
The deafness angle provides a freshness to the film, even when it falls into well-worn coming-of-age film tropes. The school choir scenes feel ripped right out of an episode of Glee, whilst Mr Villalobos is a classic Inspirational Teacher, cranky but big-hearted. Meanwhile, Rubys tentative romance with the similarly shy Miles (Sing Streets Ferdia Walsh-Peelo) ticks all the usual boxes a meet-cute, a forced pairing (they are selected by Mr Villalobos to perform a Joni Mitchell duet together for no apparent reason), a misunderstanding followed by a falling out, etc.
And yet, by the time the film gets to its barnstorming final 30 minutes, these issues fall away into insignificance. Yes, the final act comes close to floating away into a land of fantasy, and yes it is perhaps a little corny, but there is no doubt that CODA, like its characters, wears its heart on its sleeve and absolutely goes for broke in showing the world not as it is, but as we would like it to be.  Every character gets an emotional moment (some big, some small), and the cast nail every single one of them.  Two scenes in particular stand out (although I could really cite at least five) firstly, in the school choir performance, where Ruby and Miles duet is portrayed from the point of view of Rubys parents and secondly, my personal favourite, the absolutely beautiful scene with Ruby and her father sitting under the stars. Even the stuff that your head tells you that shouldnt work - it somehow does, completely earning a truly lovely ending that is both predictable and yet at the same time the perfect way for this story to end.  If this is schmaltzy sentimentality, sign me up for more schmaltzy sentimentality please! 
In short CODA is wonderful and definitely worth signing up to Apple TV for.

CODA might be the best family movie Ive seen in years. It breaks no ground, it tells a story you can map out beat for beat in your head, and its message is one reverberating throughout the entire canon of modern pop culture - but crucially, its put together so, so damn well. Every element that composes this sweet and savory confection has been polished to a sheen, with everyone in front and behind the camera bringing their full energy to play. There are none of the typical missteps or lazy cliches that derail standard Hollywood family fare, no emotional shortcuts to rob the audience of real catharsis. This movie puts the work in to make you care about these people in their predicament, rendering their feelings and relationships with a high degree of fidelity end empathy. The conflicts feel authentic and relatable because theyre actual meat-and-potatoes problems faced by working class folks around the world. Loyalty to family vs pursuing your own future. Difficult communication in a largely indifferent world. An entire communitys economic survival hanging by a thread. When the big climax arrives exactly on time as you knew it would, it absolutely works because theyve laid the foundation for a genuinely heartfelt experience. The only surprise is a pleasant one, that the movie ends up more thoughtful, more honest, and more flat-out enjoyable than I imagined possible.
