A young girl from Massachusetts tries to balance her life between going to school and helping her family of deaf fishermen who struggle to make ends meet. Her decision to enrol at the school choir makes things even more complicated.
I dont know if CODA is one of the better Best Picture winners in recent history but it definitely is one of the most earnest and most sincere. While it doesnt try to hide its Oscar bait-y credentials, the presence of real-life deaf actors and the small scale of the story result in a drama that lacks the artificiality that is ubiquitous in most Hollywood productions of this pedigree. Regrettably, that doesnt mean that this is a perfect or even excellent feature. There are moments when it looks ready to achieve greatness but in every single one of them instead of doing something daring to surprise the viewer it falls back into the safety net of familiar tropes. It does so skilfully but still, there are more than a few lost opportunities. That said, I must mention that the last 20 minutes are the best part of the movie and will warm the heart of even the most cynical cinephile. 
Emilia Jones might not have the charisma of a megastar but she carries the film with a performance that belies her young age. Her rendition of Both Sides Now is a simply magical moment. Troy Kotsur, Marlee Matlin, and Daniel Durant make us perceive them not as deaf actors but as actors who happen to be deaf. A truly magnificent cast.
Leaving aside its accolades, CODA is a heartwarming picture that despite its seemingly niche story has in fact a universal message to impart, as long as anyone is willing to hear it.

A coming-of-age comedy drama thats crafted with sincerity  brims with authenticity, CODA covers the journey of the only hearing person in a culturally deaf family who finds herself torn between following her dreams  fear of abandoning her parents in pursuit of her passion. A simple, heartfelt  crowd-pleasing delight, the film is further bolstered by its welcome inclusivity  emotional purity.
Written  directed by Siân Heder, the premise is nothing new and the route it takes is also a familiar one but the emotional beats do strike the right chord with the heart and makes it an endearing, arresting  heartwarming roller-coaster. Its portrait of deaf community in typical, day-to-day settings is carried out with care  understanding, and the family dynamic is both relatable  thoroughly captivating.
The small-town setting, radiant camerawork, intelligent wit, breezy pace  silent interplays add more exuberance to the experience but its the performances from its entire cast  the spot-on chemistry they share with one another that strengthens the picture from inside out. Emilia Jones is impressive as our protagonist struggling to juggle her familys interests with her own, and she is brilliantly supported by the rest.
Overall, CODA (Child of Deaf Adults) takes an existing coming-of-age template, doesnt try to subvert any of the genre tropes, and even features an ending thats predictable from afar yet it is rendered on screen with so much heart, warmth  affection that the films honesty  humanity not only stands out but shines through. In addition to that, it also serves as a powerful reminder of why representation matters and the difference it can make when done correctly.

CODA winning Best Picture would feel like a victory for a certain kind of cultural movement.
Its a symbol of the embrace of comfort food art, an extension of that which praises Ted Lasso or Paddington 2. Its endorsed by the kinds of people who say that, in such dark and difficult times, the last thing we want is movies about darkness and difficult things that make you feel bad. What we all (and its always presumed everyone is onboard) crave right now is lighter and more uplifting stories.
CODA, like so many of these other stories, is good because it is nice.
CODA centres on Ruby Rossi, the lone hearing member of a deaf family. Another film might observe that, as the lone majority group member in a mainly minority-group family, Ruby in fact enjoys certain privileges in society that her parents and brother do not. CODA is not that film. Instead, it emphasises Rubys isolation as someone unable to belong entirely to her sign-language home life or her hearing school life. To double down on this disconnect in the most obvious way possible, CODA employs what TV critic Daniel Fienberg calls a vocational irony narrative, as Ruby is the daughter of deaf parents who just loves to sing. If that sounds just a little bit too cutesy for you then I would not advise watching this film.
The film joins a long tradition of art priding itself on representing a minority group despite being entirely filtered through the lens of its majority group protagonist. It wants to hold our hand all the way through as were invited to see how deaf people behave through the only person the audience might reasonably relate to, their hearing daughter. The truth is I dont think a movie that actually centred entirely on deaf people and the deaf perspective would ever become a Best Picture frontrunner, because that might make us as hearing viewers feel uncomfortable. CODA never makes anyone uncomfortable. While it spends time showing us the difficulties deaf people face, it never for a single second makes us as viewers feel an ounce of guilt as people who can hear in a society built for us. This is a feel good film, and no one will feel bad about anything.
But what really gets me about CODA is the insufferable blandness of the craft. There isnt a jot of imagination in its visuals. I certainly dont need showy direction to think a film is worthy. Ryusuke Hamaguchi was remarkably restrained with Drive My Car, but thats a very deliberate choice on his part to emphasise the stripped down and sparse nature of the film. I couldnt tell you why Sian Heder and her cinematographer Paula Huidobro decided to shoot CODA like its an ABC Family pilot from 2012. Its simply not a film that feels like it has patience for craft.
(Im definitely not someone who thinks brilliant filmic visuals cant be achieved shooting on digital the way they can on 35mm. Weve seen enough beautiful work on digital to disprove this now. But I do think celluloid provided a baseline of competence that even the blandest films felt solid. When something as unambitious as CODA shoots on digital, theres nothing even a tiny bit cinematic in its 24 frames per second.)
The script has the same problem. Theres nothing here you havent seen over and over. Again, this would be fine if it had a deliberate purpose or was exceptionally well done. I cant really see either in this. Im fine with a good trope done really well, but none of this is executed with any real panache beyond some of the performances. CODAs every choice is one on autopilot.
But thats not what CODA cares about. It doesnt want to do anything other than make you, the viewer, feel good about yourself. Im a noted cynic who never feels good about myself on any occasion, so I was never likely to enjoy this. And the Oscars have long had a soft spot for this sort of thing. But still, theres something depressing about seeing that formula reworked for the nicecore era. Fans will tell you how achingly sincere it is, but all I see is a cynical calling card movie somehow elevated to awards bait.

I believe I borrowed that turn of phrase from my friend Graham, so credit where credits due.

CODA is a charming US indie movie, though it remains formulaic more than anything. Its a coming-of-age story with all of the usual tropes. However what makes CODA stand out a little is the focus on deaf culture and people with deaf family members. To CODAs credit, it treats its deaf characters with the utmost respect, showing them as normal people rather than stereotypes. The deaf parents are very endearing characters, even if they are stubborn. Troy Kotsur and Marlee Matlin give great performances too. The film is also funny, having some fun with sign language and plenty of sex talk. What makes CODA rather flat however is the central story. The leads journey to move away from her family by nurturing her talent at singing is very cheesy. Its a pleasant enough plot, but it remains so predictable and thus ends up rather emotionally inert. There are some very wholesome moments, but CODA doesnt deliver much more. Its a well-executed movie, but only has a few features of interest.

Ruby is the only hearing member of an entirely deaf family. She works early mornings with her father and brother as a fisher to help support them. She is drawn to music and is encouraged by her choir teacher to pursue music school. Ruby battles choosing between her dreams and the reality of leaving her family.

The entire cast of Rubys family (Marlee Matlin, Troy Kotsur, Daniel Durant) does a phenomenal job. Troy Kotsur as Rubys dad is easily the stand out for me. His performance is equal parts endearing and emotionally cutting. Emilia Jones can sing her ass off and carries every musical number in this thing. 
The screenplay hits a lot of familiar notes, mainly the high school mean girl and the aspirational teacher being over zealous, but the ASL conversations are wildly engaging. Its nice that deaf actors got to play deaf characters. 
Theres one scene towards the end of the movie where they play with the sound of the movie that was spectacular (youll know it when you see it).
Cute little inspirational movie with a lot of soul. Definitely worth a watch.

Normally, I dont really like the sentimental tearjerker type drama that CODA is going for but thanks to its sincerity and amazing performances, this film really managed to surpass its fairly formulaic story to deliver a very heartwarming coming-of-age dramedy. Narratively, this is far from being a unique story and it has definitely been told in different forms in various other movies but I never minded that because of how earnestly made it is and because it is told through some very unique eyes. CODAs characterization and writing of a main character torn between her family and her dreams is very effective and always touching since writer-director Siân Heder does such an excellent job at making the characters feel both realistic and charming. A lot of that undoubtedly has to do with a spectacular cast that imbue their roles with lots of warmth and depth, with Emilia Jones giving a magnificent performance as the lead and she is definitely backed up very well by a supporting cast full of terrific actors in every part. All of this comes together to make CODA the cinematic equivalent of a warm hug that I just adored every second of, easily overcoming its conventional story to make this one of my favourite films of the year with its exquisite performances, writing, and deaf representation.

This is a warm-hearted, beautifully put together coming of age film in which we see teenager Ruby (played by English actress Emilia Jones) confront her family over her ambition to become a singer.  This is complicated by the fact all the other members of her family are deaf (CODA being an acronym for Child of Deaf Adults).   
In many ways its a fairly predictable story - hurdles are overcome, doubters are converted and problems solved, but its executed in such a confident and inclusive way that you are drawn in and cant help but root for a happy ending.  
Email Jones is terrific as the talented teen, but the films real success comes from the casting of deaf actors in the key family roles and the sub-titled sign language sequences are equally as dramatic as any voiced scenes.   Writer and director Siân Heder has done a great job here in ensuring the deaf community were properly represented.
Ultimately, this is a great feel-good movie that gets a little too sentimental at times, so have the tissues ready.

In many ways, this was quite good - excellent acting, good representation of the conflicts faced by the hearing children of deaf parents, good fishing village setting.  And yes, I cried at the ending which was very moving.  
But the story is overly familiar - a young adult separating from a family that needs her - and often it over-relied on set-ups from similar films centered on immigrant andor working class families.  Also, there was a  strong Glee element in the school choir storyline that was pretty obvious. So yes, I liked it but couldnt shake my awareness of the filmmakers intent to provide a feel good experience.
Cant fault the acting though (with one exception).  Emilia Jones who plays Ruby, the daughter, is a young actor to watch out for and quite a singer.  I knew Marlee Martin (the mom) from earlier films and shes great, especially in a later scene with Ruby.  I was also impressed with Troy Kotsur (the dad) and Daniel Durant (Rubys deaf brother).  All are deaf actors and brought authenticity to their roles.  The problematic role is Eugenio Derbez as Rubys choir director and voice teacher.  The part is stereotypically broad - intense and caustic mentor but with his heart in the right place.  But Derbez overplays the diva element. And hes such a drama queen that its a bit of a shock when his wife and child show up at the school concert.
The story did resonate for me in a particular way, though.  As a young social worker in NYC in the 1980s, I learned American Sign Language (ASL) and found myself being the only worker in a small foster care agency with this skill.  As a result, I wound up being assigned all the cases with either deaf foster kids and deaf birth parents.  So I became very familiar with the deaf community and the challenges it faces.  The filmmaker certainly did his homework here, and all thats portrayed is accurate, even though a few of the situations are contrived.  The issues of children of deaf parents (CODA) are not well-known.  Lon Chaney and Louise Fletcher both had deaf parents.
So all told, a good film and commendable but in many ways an old story with a new twist.  I anticipate this will be Oscar bait.  But I cant really see this as the best film of the year, something which it (and its producer Apple TV) is clearly aiming for.

What a way to kick off 2022 with a viewing of Siân Heders CODA. I have been hesitant on the Apple TV subscription service, but after watching both CODA and Swan Song, the service seems to be worth the price. CODA is a coming-of-age flick that focuses on Ruby, the only hearing person in a deaf family. Throughout the film, we are presented with the internal turmoil that Ruby is going through pursuing her dream of becoming a singer, or staying home and helping her parents with their fishing business. As someone who works for his parents business, it was very easy to relate to Ruby and the emotions she was going through. 
In both 2020 and 2021, some of my favorite films are those that focus on the deaf community and ASL, those films being The Sound of Metal and CODA. It is amazing that this community that doesnt get too much recognization has gotten big-screen exposure. Emilia Jones is fantastic as the leading actress, but its Troy Kotsur who steals the show for me. Troy plays Rubys father, and the most emotional scenes come from the interactions between these two. One particular scene towards the end of the film had me tearing up, something most films fail to do. 
CODA is the type of extremely touching film that makes you want to hug your family after watching. It also opened my eyes to how simple a thing such as hearing can be taken for granted, from listening to your favorite music or an I love you from a loved one. The movie shows how hard it can be to not be able to hear these sounds, but it also shows how one thing that can never be taken is love.

I am so absolutely torn on this film. This is the first time in a long time where Im both amazed at how genuinely well crafted this film is and absolutely disgusted and full of hatred over how propagandist of picking yourself up from your bootstraps this film is.
Its a film that understands poverty, the sadness and struggles that poverty induces in a system that keeps people down in it and tries to guilt and trick them into it being exclusively their fault. The fact that so many people live on a constant edge of total collapse, poverty and losing every single thing is something this film gets totally right. It nails that feeling of hopelessness and the pain, paranoia, anxiety and absolute anguish that sets within a person who felt deep inside that they did EVERYTHING right and correctly. Only for the film to then make it a story about how no matter how poor you get if you struggle and suffer enough then anything is possible. Its all about hope when its just not that simplistic. Its not just solving some rubicks cube for some rich dickhead in a cab long enough to get an interview that magically gets you on your way to money. There are systems in place which keep you down and keep you from ascending at all especially for Black men in America. You can do everything that Chris did, work your way to a better tomorrow and still get absolutely fucked for completely no reason. And Im not saying depictions of success itself are bad, but I hate how almost dishonest this film is and the way it manipulates you as an audience member to play its game. 
It makes the suffering this weird kind of justification for capitalist systems that it basically excuses. It shines a light on poverty and condemns it while also doing all that it can to show that Chris is the best dad ever for dragging his son into complete poverty with him and blames him for it. Its a film where you do genuinely feel bad for the characters but Chriss victories feel overshadowed by capitalism, the smiling white faces contrasted with he and his sons misery to the point where the victories feel incredibly hollow, totally undercut by what has caused them to suffer again and again. Its a complete dystopian nightmare where someone is allowed to fall this much for essentially trying to survive, everyone turns them away, theyre completely blamed, and theyre FORCED to hold on as best as they can for any gasp of breath.
Also just wanna say the way this film treats women is fucking abhorrent. Chriss girlfriend is treated as a quitter who left her son behind even though she had EVERY right to leave and deserved to take her son with her. (And given the real story she did so why the fuck would they leave that super important detail out. The answer is that they need to put Chris in the right in basically every single situation.)
The Chinese daycare runner is the other female character in the movie and shes also not treated greatly. Shes chewed out by Chris for being a daycare runner who just lets the kids play and watch TV. Which like who even gives a shit? Its a daycare not a Kindergarten? 
Its a film that wants to be something like Heaven Knows What, Killing Them Softly, Grave of the Fireflies. It wants to wear the mask of coming to understand what films like these do but then it crosses the finish line with a giant lie that people cant realistically live up to. Not that all of them need to be bitter, Heaven Knows What specifically is about being stuck in those conditions, showing the pain and misery of it, how being a drug addict is this self fulfilling prophecy of pain that can be broken but it doesnt fucking lie about it or give it some clear happy ending. It doesnt pretend that systems dont actively keep you down and out.
This movie is propoganda to tell you Its okay if youre suffering! The American Dream totally works and wont just fuck you any chance it can! You just need to work harder! 
Genuinely just a disgusting film that ignores the racialdespairing realities of poverty and how giving some white guy 5 dollars wont do shit for you actually like fuck you.

I figured out why this movie left me depressedyay! 
Throughout the film, Will Smiths character signs up for an internship program and studies hard. But in doing so, he sacrifices his marriage, his mental health, and his home in the pursuit of (not) promised financial stability. Yet, none of these decisions or strengths save him from his sticky situations. When he needs money, he happens to find his bone scanners, then sells them. When he wants the job, he suddenly gets it in the end. He didnt need to learn how to work hard, and he didnt dedicate himself to finding the scanners. He just worked hard because he knew how to do so, got the scanners because they appeared and got the job because he was lucky.
Even if the other interns didnt work as hard as him, there is no self-revelation or character change. So its unsatisfying because the movie tells us you will find success by sacrificing, working hard, suffering, and relying on dumb luck. And I say he finds success instead of happiness because when he gets the job and is happy for 10 seconds, the movie cuts to him walking with his kidthe end. We dont see his new life, how he mends any relationships or gets a better home and all that. We watch him cry when he gets the job for ten seconds, and it ends with some text. For a movie called The Pursuit of Happyness, why not show us some more happiness?
So what is the problem? Well, after it builds all this conflict and empathy, the movie doesnt know how to turn these emotions into genuine, meaningful catharsis. The reality? We just sat through an hour and a half of depressive crap and received 10 seconds of reliefwow, very cathartic. So I sat there, anxious and depressed, went to bed, and constantly worried for 3-4 hoursI did not have sweet dreams. Even if this is exactly how it happened (which I doubt), the story is still unsatisfying. Will Smiths character does not learn or change. He relies on dumb luck to solve his problems. Its not empowering. Fiction has melodrama, plot holes, and manipulation because real life is boring and doesnt always make good stories. Why do you think writers cut all the uhs... and likes... in the dialogue out? Thats because real life isnt the best source for storytelling.

The American dream, from rags to riches, suggests anyone can make it, if only you try hard enough, if you make a proper effort. You may end up, for example, like the homeless man shown at the beginning, lying belly-down on the street in San Francisco, in the gutter. Will Smith plays Chris Gardner, a simple salesman. He has gone into business for himself, peddling a medical device that does nothing more than an x-ray machine. He fails to get rid of it, hes burdened himself with a slow seller, its an absolute bad investment, he still must sell this equipment to doctors who dont need it. He must talk them into it, representing a talent he may apply elsewhere. One could, for example, also work as an investment banker and talk people into any kind of investment model. The plot has two strands that converge into one question Will he make it?
First, will he manage to sell the remaining equipment after all, and will Chris Gardner manage to become an investment banker. Ideology also appears here in persona, embodied by Ronald Reagan. We see him in a televised speech, outlining a difficult economic situation and telling the American people, we can turn it around, even though the national budget is out of whack and the debt is at record levels. We witness the neoliberal narrative judging government debt, promoting austerity politics and an urgent need to curb government spending.
Of course, we find that in politics today, too, for example with politicians like Liz Truss or Olaf Scholz. But Reagan, along with Thatcher, was one of the first movers, inspired by Hayek and Friedman. Ironically, Ronald Reagan did cut social spending and did save a lot of money, but the mountain of debt continued to grow to astronomical heights. Why? At the same time, Reagan increased arms spending enormously. Thats another common theme among conservatives Theres no money left over for anything, not for theater, not for culture, not for social issues, but for armaments. At the same time, Ronald Reagan also disguised his social cuts policy as conservatism, as austerity rarely proves to be popular.
Coupled with a reactionary attitude however, Reagan appealed to a diffuse feeling in people. He directed it at the time willingly against emancipatory left-wing movements. This ressentiment is represented in the movie by a hippie woman, for example, called the hippie aunt here, who steals one of Chris Gardners devices. The film thus manifests the cliché of the antisocial left.
And look, how the film shows the mother of Chris Gardners Child, his wife from whom he separates. This mother is irresponsible, she does not take care of her son properly, she cannot understand her husband. The film paints the picture of the bad mother. Thats been a case of Margaret Thatcher as she condemned single mothers as irresponsible women. The whole German conservatism warned of a motherless society in the 80s. The film picks up on these themes. It reproduces this ideology. Part of this ideology passes down pressure.
The kindergarten for the man is low paid, not good enough and the employees are reprimanded. Chris Gardner beats up the cab driver, when he cant afford the fair. The ideology of conservatives resonates here, treating government debt just as private debt. Chris Gardner cant pay the bill he has accumulated endless parking tickets and he fails to pay those as well. Thus, the film merges private debts and the debts of the state which Ronald Reagan addresses. Nonsense. Of course, national debts are something completely different.
To a well-economically developed progressive nation, it is quite possible to simply print more money. Chris is later thrown out from its housing, he and his son even become homeless and eventually camp out in a subway toilet. How can this be, one wonders, in one of the richest countries in the world? Shouldnt we immediately call for revolution, overthrow the ruling class and radically redistribute?
Everything is alright
You cant pack more injustice and exploitation in a movie. It is unbelievable. But there is no revolution. On the contrary - the conditions are not only accepted, but they are also propagated. A man collapses into the bottomless pit with his son, because the man took a wrong turn. He thought these devices would be a good idea, believed that this is an important medical device delivering progress, I will invest in it, I will earn money with it. That turned out to be a bad investment. Capitalism in its purest form One mistake and you end up in the subway toilet. But as weve learnt from capitalism, each problem carries opportunity.
By chance, Gardner meets a very successful investment banker, and wonders if he could do the same thing, you dont need a degree for that, but he must do an internship there first. Gardner applies for this internship, performing a little differently than everyone else. First and foremost, this internship means unpaid work. It is also clear that out of the 20 interns, only one will be hired in the end. These interns contractually guarantee that they will not be allowed to go to a competitor afterwards.
Even when Chris Gardner is hit by a car, he is still at work on time and runs there without shoes if necessary. He accepts humiliation from his superiors without complaint. It amazes me on the one hand, we have a whole new economic world here at the stock exchange, and on the other hand, however, we also have an old way of working in which diligence and discipline count. We dont have the idea of a stockbroker here, as American Psycho shows, for example, no, here we find a very strong appeal to the Protestant work ethic. Taylorism also plays a role again, but now intrinsically motivated.
Chris Gardner calculates that he can save 8 minutes a day if he doesnt hang up the phone at all but continues dialing right away. He also doesnt drink anything at work to eliminate trips to the restroom. Remember the toilet scandal at Amazon, there were rumors, that the warehouse workers had to pee in bottles. In short, he is the ideal employee. In the process, a contradiction arises He advertises products where one says, let your money work for you. In truth, however, it is perfectly clear that this money does not work for itself but must be earned. Financialization has put him and many of his comrades in their precarious position.
Chris now wants to join those who are responsible for his fate. However, the film sells this contradiction as him taking his fate into his own hands. The film has dramaturgical flaws, but they are very telling. Chris is supposed to sell these devices discipline and diligence are of the essence. On the other hand, the financialized world of work, quite an invisible one, with cold calling on the phone, leading to commission profits. There is not too much difference between the two. The low point for Chris Gardner is finally symbolized by tax debts he cannot pay. If he really cant keep up, hes in free fall.
Here, once again, the film depicts the state as the big problem. Unsurprisingly, the film doesnt pose any systemic questions when it comes to homelessness, for example, which remains, after all, a big problem in San Francisco. The film only shows it through an individuals fate. Chris and his son have trouble finding a place to stay because they are all overcrowded. Again and again, hundreds of homeless people are turned away. Why are there so few homeless shelters? The film does not ask this question. The answer is obvious. Touching, inspiring  emotionally uplifting but also overly sentimental at times, The Pursuit of Happyness is a tenderly crafted, expertly narrated  brilliantly performed biographical drama thats brought to life with utmost care  sincerity, and is also notable for featuring one of Will Smiths most memorable performances to date.
The film tells the story of Chris Gardner, a struggling salesman who loses his wife, his house, his bank accounts  is forced to live out in the streets with his son when the device he invested his entire life savings into does not produce the results he was hoping for. Desperate for a steady job, he takes an unpaid internship to compete for the paid position of a stockbroker.
Directed by Gabriele Muccino, the story unfolds at a steady pace and is able to keep the interest alive throughout its runtime. The struggles, disappointments  desperation that our protagonist undergoes is highlighted in a grounded manner and is relatable to quite an extent. Its character-driven plot  deftly written script provides sufficient depth to our lead guys arc that effortlessly allows the viewers to invest in his journey.
Coming to the performances, this is a one-man show that finds Will Smith at the top of his game as he delivers an emotionally dense, wonderfully balanced  surprisingly down-to-earth input and it remains one of the finest works of his acting career. Jaden Smith also provides a heartfelt support in the role of Gardner Jr. and the moments between this father  son duo are beautifully captured.
There are times when it goes slightly overboard with its melodramatic elements but for the most part, the emotional response it garners from its viewers is well-earned. The technical aspects are finely executed, Editing is smoothly carried out and keeps its plot moving ahead at a consistent pace, while its background score silently enhances the overall experience with its mesmerising tracks and nicely compliments the whole narrative.
On an overall scale, The Pursuit of Happyness is a fascinating illustration of the American dream that also serves as an engrossing portrait of father-son bonding, and is amongst the best films of its year. Powered by a strong lead show by one of Hollywoods most bankable stars and delighting its audience with a real-life story thats heartwarming, heartbreaking  gratifying on more levels than one, this biopic comes thoroughly recommended.

Sometimes we grow up thinking were born special, that we already know everything, that our talent, intelligence, or uniqueness will set us apart from the rest of the world. In childhood, theres this deep, almost naive certainty that we are destined for greatness. But as we grow older, life quickly teaches us how different it really is. Its not about grades, its not about school or university, its not about being recognized or celebrated its about grinding every single day, pushing forward even when the world seems stacked against you.
This movie is about struggle, disappointment, and betrayal. Its about family, about people who let you down, about arrogance, and about the moments when life seems to tell you that you are nothing. And yet, its also about hope a hope that feels fragile but persistent. Its a story about proving to yourself, and the world, that giving up is never an option, that effort matters more than luck, and that perseverance can shape even the bleakest circumstances into something meaningful.
Will Smith delivers what I believe is his greatest performance, capturing the full weight of human struggle, exhaustion, and resilience. Every member of the cast, including Jaden Smith, brings authenticity and heart to the story, making the lessons feel lived-in, not told. Watching this film reminds you that life doesnt come with guarantees, but that doesnt mean you stop trying. You may face years of hardship, moments of despair, and times when everything feels lost,but if you keep grinding, if you keep believing, its never too late to start building your life from the ground up.
What makes this film so remarkable is its honesty. It doesnt sugarcoat reality or give you easy answers. Life is hard, unfair, and sometimes cruel but its also full of moments where courage, resilience, and dedication can make all the difference. The Pursuit of Happyness is not just a movie about success its about the relentless pursuit of meaning, dignity, and the chance to prove to yourself that you can overcome. Its about the everyday grind that defines who we are, the hope that refuses to die, and the small victories that ultimately shape our lives.
Ever time I watch it, Im reminded that life is a puzzle, and we must start assembling it piece by piece. It may take minutes, years, or decades. You may have children, you may feel too old, you may think your chance has passedbut if you keep grinding, if you keep believing, if you make your own luck, everything will be okay. This movie is a lesson, a reflection, and, above all, a reminder that hope and perseverance are the most powerful forces we have.

The story of a man desperately trying to be happy. Life is tough for him. He and his son have to fend for themselves. He struggles with paying taxes. He has to fight hard to make sure he and his son get through all their hardships. You have to fight for happiness. It doesnt always just come to you. Some people are not as lucky as others but it you really fight for it, maybe you can find it. We give the right to have the pursuit of happiness. Not meaning that happiness is guaranteed but that we have the right to find it. Will Smith gives easily that best performance Ive seen from him hands down as a man who really just wants to make life easy for him and his son. He does whatever it takes to achieve that. The movie is about his journey. The end destination is pretty predictable but the film really is about the journey. This man is able to make something out of nothing. You want him in his son, who is surprisingly really well played by Jaden Smith, to find a way to have a happy life. A film that gave me a reality check, just the right one I needed today. I was in the mood to watch some serious drama about lifes struggles. I had always known about this film but was never in the mood to watch it. 
This film is not just about struggling to make ends meet. Its about giving your all when you have nothingabsolutely nothing but the will to fight, to win, and to break the cycle of fear of failure. Nobody could have acted better than Will Smith in this role. Watching him didnt feel like watching a movie it felt like I was working, sleeping, and living with him throughout the runtime. It made me feel grateful for what I have and inspired me to strive for greater success. As Chris said,Dont ever let someone tell you you cant do something. Not even me. You gotta dream, protect it. When people cant do something themselves, theyre gonna tell you that you cant do it. YOU WANT SOMETHING, GO GET IT. PERIOD. This was reminiscent of another quote from Chris in Into The Wild,If you want something in life, reach out and grab it.
After The Pursuit of Happyness ended, I reflected on what I had seen and realized that success was just around the corner for Chris. Every time he lost his scanner machine, he found it on the streets, in a subway, or in a park. It felt like God wanted him to win too. As someone said, God helps those who help themselves. This film awakened the philosopher in me, buried deep under a woman who was also chasing happiness and always complained about not having enough.
Honestly, I believe almost all of us know what the right thing to do is. Yet we are often scared to make the first move because of the fear of failure. However, when life threw lemons at Chris, he made lemonade. He walked on eggshells, went out of his way to make connections, and never gave up despite multiple setbacks. Thats the kind of person God wants to helpthe one who never quits. There is always light at the end of a dark tunnel. You have to keep walking, whether for hours or days. Your patience and willpower will be tested along the way, but nothing is impossible. Everything is possible for those who never quit.

FUCK THIS MOVIE!
Seriously, this movie can fuck right off!
Ill start with the positives.
The lead performance from Will Smith is good and certainly acceptable...BUT its far from deserving that Oscar nomination that he received.
The cinematography is great. I liked how they deliberately changed the way the movie was shot for specific scenes such as the ones inside Wall Street, even if the change was too drastic and obvious.
The Pursuit of Happyness also has an effective pace to it. At no time did I feel anything was rushing or dragging (but then, I could be just like that fat kid in Whiplash, not knowing if it was or not).
Thandie Newton is also in this, so thats an obvious positive!
There are just too many negatives though, and I cant believe how many people love this film.
Firstly, this film has some of the worst editing I have seen in some while. They were just too many annoying cuts at times and I almost wanted to scream at the TV. Why couldnt they just have shot a two-person conversation in one frame. What was the point in them endless close-ups on Will and Jadens faces. Not only were they meaningless but it also would have been better to watch the conversation where both actors are in the shot.
The film also suffers from awful writing at times. There are things in this movie that I couldnt help but squirm at. OKAY, WE GET IT! WERE MEANT TO FEEL SYMPATHY FOR THEM. So many characters were just being mean towards the protagonist for no reason and that just wouldnt happen. I understand that its Wall Street and many people are like that but this was going overboard. It entered the zone that no biopic should enter the zone where the character becomes so sympathetic that it overflows and the audience loses this sympathy. Its exactly why writers should avoid sentimentality. If its an upsetting and sympathetic story, then leave it to show that for itself. Dont just add lazy lines of dialogue or stupid unrealistic plot points that almost admit how lazy the film really is.
The music was so offputting too. I hated the score. It had that annoyingly childish fantasy feel to it. It just wasnt the right score for the movie in my opinion.
I also had a problem with the casting. This one may come off as slightly harsh to those that like the movie but if youre going to tell a story about homelessness and lack of hope, then dont cast one of the most well-known and richest actors working today and dont cast his son either, who has never experienced anything even near the lifestyle of his character. Now, I thought Will Smith did a good job (Jaden, not so much) but that also irritated me.

--- SPOILERS START HERE ---
BUT MOST OF ALL, the message is horrific and very worrying. Now, I am a strong believer in too much money ruining happiness for the most part - it takes knowledge and discipline to not be manipulated by capitalisms God...and the whole plot of the movie is the character trying to get a job at Wall Street. Now, I really thought the ending would be something along the lines of the protagonist coming to a realisation that chasing money would not be the pursuit of happiness and I had an idea in my head from the start that it would end with him changing career goals and ending up happy because of it but NOPE. It literally ends with him getting a job at Wall Street with Will Smith narrating how happy he is now. He then proceeds to become a multi-millionaire and the film expected me to let that slide?! BULLSHIT!
--- SPOILERS END HERE ---
Theres a couple of great scenes in there but as a whole, its just an overly sentimental script visualised with good cinematography, which is unfortunately ruined by the terrible editing.
Will Smith has never starred in a film that I loved. Men in Black comes the closest but wow, for such a huge star, I find his undeniably poor filmography baffling. He shouldve stuck to what hes best at comedy.
Its pretty hilarious to see American Psycho and The Pursuit of Happyness within the same week. The way Wall Street is protrayed in the two movies are on the complete opposite sides of the spectrum.
Even Chris Gardner himself admits that this film dramatizes the story way too much!

If I had a nickel for every time Ive watched a Will Smith character impress an interviewer by spontaneously solving a Rubiks Cube in front of him, Id have two nickels. Which doesnt sound like much. But its an oddly specific thing for an actor to have done in more than one role. Dont you think?
If I had a nickel for every time Ive seen Dan Castellaneta playvoice a character who loves eating donuts at work, Id also have two nickels. But honestly, I dont think its that weird in this case. Because who doesnt love eating donuts at work?
If I had a nickel for every time I watched Will Smiths character in The Pursuit of Happyness get screwed over for cab fare by one of his superiors at his job, I would, once again, have just two nickels. Which I suppose really isnt that much if you think about it. You show up for work every day in a suit and tie, people naturally assume youve got some cash in your pocket. No sense quibbling over a few bucks here or there, am I right? You add in the entitlement that comes with being the boss and situations like that are bound to arise from time to time. It sucks, but its not shocking. 
If I had a nickel for every time I watched Will Smiths character in The Pursuit of Happyness chase somebody through the streets of San Francisco after they stole one of his bone density scanners, plot twist, I would have four whole nickels this time! Which, admittedly, aint even gonna buy you twenty pennies anymorenow that theyre phasing them out of circulation. But holy fuck is that a lot of times to be chasing somebody around for a friggin bone density scanner.
Anyway, on a human interest level, this is a very moving story. I wont deny that there are momentspretty much all of them centered around Will Smiths lead performancethat hit me in the feels quite effectively. 
Im not buying what the movie is sellingphilosophically, politically, or inspirationally. But I dont want to get into how it falsely equates the concept of happiness with the achievement of wealth right now. 
I really just wanted to make that stupid joke about the nickels as many times as I could in one review. And Ive done that. So Im out.

when i tell you i was not ready for how much this movie hits, i mean it. its one of those that sneaks up on you with this quiet emotional punch that leaves you sitting there, questioning life, crying a little, maybe rethinking all your choices. like, its just a dude and his kid trying to survive, but somehow that simplicity makes it feel even more real. and thats what makes it work. it doesnt try to glamorize the struggleit just is. raw, painful, and messy
will smith and jaden smith together were such a gut-wrenching combo. you can tell will poured his whole soul into this role, and honestly, it shows in every scene. hes broke, hes desperate, hes tired, but he never gives up. and jaden, being like, this tiny little kid with the saddest eyes, just made me want to wrap him up in a blanket. that scene in the bathroom? you know the one. i had to pause
theres also something so relatable about the way it captures failure. like, life knocking you down over and over, but you keep getting back up because what else can you do? even when everything seems impossible, theres this flicker of hope that keeps pushing you forward. and yeah, sometimes it felt a little too heavy-handed with the whole never give up message, but it kinda earns that cheesiness because its so sincere

A prova que a resiliência é a força mais poderosa da alma humana. Will Smith entrega a atuação de sua vida como Chris Gardner, um pai que se recusa a deixar que a escassez de recursos apague a abundância de seu amor.
Ao lado de seu filho, ele enfrenta uma jornada brutal, onde a direção sensível de Gabriele Muccino transforma bancos de metrô e abrigos em palcos de pura dignidade.
O filme brilha ao mostrar que a felicidade não é um destino final, mas o esforço incansável de quem se nega a desistir diante de um não. Sob o comando de Muccino, a técnica e o sentimento se equilibram para criar um estudo emocionante sobre a perseverança, mergulhando na mente de quem descobriu que, para proteger um sonho, é preciso primeiro ter a coragem de suportar o pesadelo.

É uma lição visualmente poderosa de que o valor de um homem não é medido pelo que ele tem no bolso, mas pela promessa que ele mantém viva no coração de quem depende dele. Uma obra indispensável que redefine o que realmente significa ter sucesso.

Эмоциональная часть фильма строится на мотивах отцовства и любви. И именно этим он и цепляет. Главный герой делает всё возможное, чтобы обеспечить сыну достойную жизнь и сохранить его доверие и счастье. К тому же лента В погоне за счастьем показывает американскую мечту одновременно и как иллюзию, и как реальность. С одной стороны история показывает, что успех возможен даже с нуля. Im very glad to have those Oscars. Theyre lovely things. But you shouldnt ask me what the best film of the year was, because I wouldnt be voting for Crash.
-Paul Haggis, Director
Unintentionally (maybe?) the single most nihilistic take on racism Ive ever seen... maybe any piece of media have, actually - Crash seems to suggest that not only is racial hatred the original sin which every single person on earth is burdened with, but most of the time, it turns out to be justified, and even if it werent, nobodys ever gonna learn anyway, and itll just keep happening over and over again, so why bother talking about it? This is a movie interested exclusively in friction, one which doesnt know how to have any conversation that comes after the initial conflict. On one hand, this approach is horribly offensive - every character is simultaneously an outsized stereotype of both their race and the hatred they project on others (its as if Haggis  Moresco assumed systemic racism means every person is racist in every way always) with no subtlety whatsoever - but on the other, it makes this so fun to watch. The films everything is connected structure (plenty of precedents, but I would like to point to Magnolia, a movie which has less San Fernando Valley character than this one despite claiming the SFV as an integral part of it) means that where a typically plotted film might offer a moment or two of downtime somewhere, Crash has absolutely none. Every single scene is two white dudes who think theyre woke sitting at a typewriter figuring out new ways for one ethnic group to insult another while acting like they get it. I read the (Oscar-winning) script earlier this afternoon, and theres one big thing that doesnt come across in the movie (or, well, if it does, a viewer probably doesnt think about it) - all of the stereotypical accents are written out. The Korean ladys dialogue swaps Rs with Ls. Cmon. Cannot imagine someone learning anything valuable about bigotry from this, much less what that lesson could even be other than, like, full on blackpill racial separatism cuz nobody will ever get along. There are jokes in this movie.

(The Average Joes Movie Club Cast)
A hyper dramatized large cast film that exposes the cultural collisions that can happen within the melting pot of American society.
Something else funny? ... Oh, yeah ... Yeah? Whats that? ... People, man. People.
I am well aware that Crash is one of the most hated Oscar winners of all time. But allow me to make the argument, why I feel this is a powerful and misunderstood statement on race relations.
(Quick Hits)
- I really enjoyed Crash when it came out because of how emotionally impactful it was. And watching it again now, I feel that much of the film does work, but there are also some hamfisted aspects that dont fully come together
- If you are looking for subtle commentary on race relations, this is not the movie for you. Everything about Crash is aggressively in your face on the topic, and it is often uncomfortable to watch. But the reality is that racism is an ugly topic, and I think it makes sense for it to be examined in this way
- The most common complaint I have heard is that people dont act this way. And for the most part I think that is correct. But Crash does not aim to show reality, but rather a hyper-dramatization of the raw emotions that can come out of people for better or for worst in moments of crisis   
- So this approach essentially rips the civilized band-aid of politeness from these people, to show that anyone is capable of prejudice. Hopefully, the take away is that people are imperfect, and we should strive to do better in both our actions and our thoughts towards one another           
- This is one of those large cast films that is comprised of several interconnected stories. I will briefly touch on a few of these, and for more check out the link to my podcast were we discussed Crash in more detail
Spoilers
- Matt Dillions character is shown to be a truly awful racist cop. The scene where he harasses a black couple he has pulled over is truly awful. Then after getting upset about his fathers healthcare situation, he is very rude to a black lady at the insurance company, when he starts talking about affirmative action. Later in the film, we see him spring into action when the same woman played by Thandie Newton that he humiliated during the traffic stop, becomes involved in a life-threatening car accident. I have heard this scene interpreted as a moment of redemption for him, but I disagree. This cop is totally past being able to be redeemed. But we do see how a person that is as awful as he is, can step up and take action during someones time of need, regardless of who they are. Unfortunately, a big missed opportunity here is that we dont get any additional character development from the woman following this incident
- One of the characters I found most sympathetic is played by Terrence Howard. He is the husband in the traffic stop scenario I briefly described. It is heartbreaking to see him have to keep his cool during this tense situation, as his wife is being sexually harassed by an asshole cop. Then following a string of encounters, including his wife accusing him of not stepping up as a man, he cant take it anymore and ends up in a very tense standoff with the police after he is car-jacked. I think the story does a great job of showing what leads up to him reaching his breaking point in this moment
- The story also takes this direction with a good-intentioned cop that was also at the traffic stop, played by Ryan Phillippe. Despite his good intentions, none of his actions are accepted warmly. This eventually leads to him picking up a black man off the clock, and then shooting him to death during a very bizarre misunderstanding. This is one of the key examples where I dont think the high emotional drama comes together and feels forced ... since it strays so far from the character that is established for him, especially since he tries to cover it up
- The other point of high emotional drama that I felt was hamfisted is when a dispute between a Persian man and a Latino locksmith leads to the Persian man confronting the locksmith with a gun, and then he accidentally fires it at the mans daughter who is in his arms. I will admit that I did get very emotional in this moment, as the score builds to this dramatic crescendo. Plus the man and his daughters relationship is built up so nicely, with a very tender moment earlier on. But after taking in the gunshot scene for a moment, it did feel overly manipulative. Plus, I did not care for how the film felt the need to provide a shot where it says blanks on the box of bullets, like that aspect was not obvious
There is so much more that could be said about all the nuances of the interconnected stories in Crash. There is Sandra Bullocks character who gets held up at gunpoint, which leads to her making a series of racist remarks. Also, Ludacris character who has plenty to say about a variety of racial stereotypes. There is so much context in each of these situations, that I dont feel I would do justice to their complexity by trying to briefly describe them here.
Instead, I hope this review may lead you to check out this film again and consider looking at it with some new perspective. So often Crash is just dismissed as being awful, and while it does have its flaws, I think it is more provocative than many people give it credit for.
I think we miss that touch so much, that we crash into each other, just so we can feel something.
Thanks for reading.
Happy movie watching ... and please be kind to each other!

Paul Haggiss Crash is a movie that I despise with every fiber of my being. Its not for the sheer fact that it won the Academy Award for Best Picture, but with that having been said, Ive no doubt in it being the absolute worst film that Ive ever seen to win the award. Ive known Best Picture winners that Ive downright disliked whether it be trite like Forrest Gump, Titanic, or Gladiator but Crash from every last one of them in particular makes my blood boil. A movie so self-satisfied to such a condescending degree, pretending to say something important yet youll get more subtle deliveries of the same message on a television commercial, it is just so despicable on many levels.
The first thirty minutes alone establish one thing, Los Angeles is full of many racist and unlikable individuals but whats really off-putting about how these people are never really characters we care about. Hey, theyre all interlinked somehow, in the same manner that we have a good chunk of Robert Altman films given to us but at the very least Altman knows how to give these people enough character for us to be interested, whereas you can doze off at any point watching Crash and youre not missing much details. Everyone is a racist one-dimensional being, thats what I can pick up.
Heres another thing that bothers me. Considering how heavy-handed the film is with its approach, it also comes off as insanely condescending to the very degree it just aspires to preach in front of your face RACISM IS BAD! RACISM IS BAD!. We get it already, theres no need to keep on repeating a message weve heard in a more subtle fashion as opposed to having every word shoved in your face like this. Spike Lees Do the Right Thing was never preachy, but it was angry, and thats why that film works better at handling such a topic - its also a much more realistic depiction of such a subject.
Whether it also come from the atrociously generic score consisting of a lot of chanting or just how utterly deplorable the movies delivery of its message comes out, its absolutely insulting. When the two mixed together, I was actually laughing within my seat at just how heavily Paul Haggis relies on sentimentality (theres a scene I can note with Matt Dillon rescuing Thandie Newton from a car crash that provided a laughing riot) because its evident he does not know how to properly treat his viewers, by dumbing down their mentality to that of a five-year-old.
In all honesty, Crash is without a doubt one of my least favourite films of this century. A movie so hateful with its approach to just about everything and just downright insulting considering the preachy handling of such a serious topic, filled with characters whom no one gave any interest within, Ill never even understand why the Academy chose to award such a revolting experience the Best Picture Oscar. If All Lives Matter was a movie, this would be it.

I considered rating this a half-star for a while, but I decided that half-stars should be for films that are truly worthless, and this film is anything but. I know some of you think star ratings are silly, and they are, but for me the difference between a half-star and a full star is simply that I enjoyed hating the latter and not the former. I dont have any fun hating Sausage Party or Epic Movie I had a delightful time hating this.
This film has been a punchline for all of my adult life (and most of my pre-adult life, too) so I think its due for a more even-handed autopsy. This films immense evil and hilariously contrived writing has been pretty thoroughly picked apart, so I think Ill instead try and get into the mindset of its fans and the Oscar committee that chose it as the best film of 2004. In that respect honestly, I get it.
The great evil of hyperlink films is that theyre almost impossible to make boring. By virtue of necessity, every story is stripped to the bone, leaving only 100 incident, and the structure allows for every story, now matter how stupid or tedious they may be, a level of excitement due to novelty. These films almost get to reset themselves every five minutes, allowing us to get re-invested with every baton pass. And if any of the stories are bad, no fear! Just wait a few minutes and there will be a new one. And if all the stories are bad, who cares? Its not like theyre wasting your time. I found Traffic wildly entertaining despite its many, many failings and when this format is done well, like Short Cuts, it feels genuinely transcendent. As much as Innaritu may have tried to prove otherwise, this format is almost foolproof. Easy to understand why the Academy lapped it up.
And despite this films, well, interesting melodramatic choices, I would like to posit that this has something that the Academy values levity. This film isnt funny, at least to me, but it does have a very respectable sprinkling of jokes throughoutthe middlebrow audience does not want a Comedy, but it does want to laugh, and shoehorning comic bits into your city symphony is objectively very savvy. We think of Oscarbait as being ponderous and leaden, but the dinosaurs that vote in the Academy dont have a generous attention span they want to be entertained too. As such, look at the past twenty years of Oscar noms and tell me how many dont have an at least theoretical sense of humor. Hell, I still remember Argo fuck yourself eleven years later.
And maybe if I can play devils advocate a little more, I think that for the liberal audience of this film in 2004, its portrayal of racism might have felt genuinely challenging. Its the type of challenging that still at the end of the day comforts you, but it does situate racism in the present-day rather than the past, and it at least hints that racism exists in all of us, not just the bad people like Matt Dillons hilariously evil cop. The Academy at least somewhat wants to have their thoughts (very superficially) provoked if you can thread the needle of offering both reassurance and provocation, which this film does (in a certain way, to a certain audience), youve won.
So yes, I get why this won, aside from the obvious reasons. I also do think that aside from all of that, there are a handful of genuine virtues here the LA photography looks nice (might just be lingering Collateral love though), and only a handful of the performers embarass themselves. And hell, I was moved a little bit by the stuff with Dillons dad, though thats probably just because I have a UTI-like chronic pain condition. I think this films main virtue, though, is that is a work of evil. And not just in the classical liberal films are evil way, this is genuinely one of the most reprehensible and racist films I have ever seen. Watching it, you can almost touch the moral void in its center. Does that have value? I dont feel comfortable answering that with a yes or a no, but I do think it makes it a worthwhile historical artifact. Ive long since maintained, to the annoyance of many of my friends, that a film being interesting does not make it good. I care about craft, I care about form, I care about thematic resonance. Crash is not good, but you could scarcely ask for a more interesting film. And for that have an extra-half star. You earned it.

Before I say anything about what I thought of Crash, I will state that in terms of people that are out there in the world to dislike, people that think this is a good movie is pretty low. If you have seen Crash and genuinely like it or even love it, cool. Im glad you got a worthwhile experience out of it. Some people had to like it in order for it to do you-know-what. To talk about Crash, you cant really just talk about the movie itself. It has garnered feelings that go beyond itself. You can talk about the Academy. You can talk about the scattered reactions it gets now. You can talk about Paul Haggis. You can talk about how racism is portrayed in movies, and moreso how it should be portrayed in movies. For being a film that, yes, I thought was pretty shitty, it isnt a movie that leaves you with empty thoughts. Love it or hate it, just about anyone could realistically have a long conversation about Crash. Ill even say I didnt think it was all terrible. I think its mostly well-directed and shot, I enjoyed the music of the film (Currently listening to the song from the end as I type this out.), and the performances from Don Cheadle and Michael Peña I thought were good. Also being honest, I think the editing of the movie is damn good. Thats the one thing about it where I wholly get why it got awards.
There are components you can look at with Crash and think to yourself Okay, yeah, thats worth something. Just a shame theres so many other things about it you can look at and just want to implode on yourself based on second-hand embarrassment. This is one of the most overly dramatic, sappy films Ive seen in a while. Every actor is trying, but their material they have to work with, oh boy. Whatever grievances people had with Sam Rockwells character in Three Billboards, thats actually here in Matt Dillons character. What the fuck was that all about? If youre looking for how not to do a redemption arc, that might be the most significant example you have out there in modern cinema. I cannot pretend to be an all-knowledgeable mind on how to portray racism or xenophobia in fiction, but I think I know at least one thing that matters.
Especially with films that deal with dramatic issues, you want to get empathy wherever possible. And not just the understanding that comes from empathy, but the feeling that the characters you are with extend beyond the screen. They become people instead of characters. When I think of great films about race, I think of films like Do the Right Thing and Get Out. Those two movies have one thing in common Levity. Despite being films that are heavy in subject matter and are absolutely dramas over comedies, they have parts in them that are light and even hilarious. You enjoy certain moments, and this enjoyment sucks you into the world and gets you invested in the characters. Levity is a word Crash has never heard of. Its a big-budget Lifetime movie, a soap opera, a slimy, smelly mess of yelling, tears, and expletives. It leaves next to no room for anything other than the most dramatic elements, the lives that are portrayed in its runtime a gross over-dramatization, a Frankensteins monster of what normal people are. Its watching paper dolls rub against each other. The first scene we get with Peña and his daughter and the moment with Dillon and his father are the closest things we get to levity, and theyre fine moments, but they get squandered with whatever melodramatic thing has to follow it up.
I will admit that I was going to give Crash two stars for most of its runtime. Its a bad movie, thats for certain, but I wasnt even going to say it was terrible. Taking the positives I stated earlier, there are worse movies you can spend your time with. But, then, we get a moment. Ill just say its the moment thats on that poster right there. Fuck. That. Moment. It feels like it has been a while since I have seen a movie with a scene that feels so forced, so silly, so goddamn stupid. When it happened, I was flabbergasted. After the movie badgering me with Are you sad? Are you sad yet? How about now?, then it goes Check this shit out! Its so proud of itself, wanting so desperately for you to go slack-jawed, which I did, but not in the way it wanted me to. Then comes the fake-out, and the anger just morphed into something to laugh at. Something to roll my eyes at. When you put something like that in a movie, you lose me. Thats taking whatever trust I could give it, and tossing it into the garbage, then lighting the trash can on fire. I would want to say we as a moviegoing collective have moved past elevating features like this, but then we get Viridescent Publication, and I doubt myself.
I think by now in this review that I have proven my point. I do not like Crash, putting it lightly. But, to give credit where you can reasonably do so, it can be a movie thats interesting to talk about, as well as to bring whatever other subjects into the conversation. The worst kind of movie you can see is the movie that you watch and then forget about the next day. Thanks to the special kind of mess that Crash is, I know I will not be forgetting about it anytime soon. We human beings a weird, funny bunch of flesh monsters. What we can like, and what we can find ourselves getting livid about with just the passing of time. Then again, beyond further exposure to the world, time is a key ingredient in maturity and evolution.

A deeply uncomfortable watch. I remember when Paul Haggis Crash came out. It was critically acclaimed and everyone (including myself) loved it. Fast forward two decades later and the consensus has gone way far in the opposite direction. With that I was curious where Id stand with a film I liked so much I bought it back in the day (in fullscreen like a moron). Well, I dont see what others see because I find this to be a riveting, necessary watch.
Its hard to do what I normally do with film with this, in that the technical details fade way into the background against the narrative. Performances, direction and cinematography disappear in exchange for a harsh truth thats hard to digest. The racism, stereotyping and discrimination run rampant in this film. The politics are corrupt, the police are profilers, and the people are mostly unlikable. There are some scenes that truly disturbed me. In 2005, it was Thandiwe Newtons storyline that hit me hardest. A woman sexually assaulted by a cop (Matt Dillon) has to come face to face with that man in a later scene and dire situation, and I could feel her absolute (and understandable) disgust. Its important to note that Newton gives the best performance in this film, I still feel her anguish but it was Laras (Ashlyn Sanchez) scene, trying to protect her father (Michael Peña) with her invisibility cloak that had tears rolling down my eyes. So much terrible stuff happens in this world, and so much of it could be resolved if people would look at others exactly as they are, other humans just trying to get by. Instead we are swallowed by fear and some, not all, but one too many turn to bigotry instead of embracing the universal truth we are all human, and if you believe in a divine being, we all come from it.
This won 3 Oscars the year it came out, and while I cant say it deserved Best Picture (I need to rewatch Brokeback Mountain), I do think it deserved best screenplay. Im not sure why people have turned on this film all these years later, and I guess I need to do a little homework to better understand but I think this film, as result of its script, is eye-opening, a reminder of who not to be. The only thing that saddens me is the realism of the ending. These characters go through so much, most of them having learned a hard lesson. Then we end with another crash, and the cycle starts all over again.
Yeah, this hit me hard. Definitely one Ill visit again down the line, but I have a weak stomach for injustice, so it wont be one Ill be revisiting anytime soon.

Racism is very bad. I-I really hope thats clear and obvious to the handful of readers that stumble onto my ramblings about movies, but holding onto racist beliefs is a fundamentally unhealthy choice that feeds into negative stereotypes, perceptions, and feedback loops that can be easily passed down from generation to generation in subtle, unsuspecting ways. The solution to racism is not very simple, sure the cause to prevent and take action against racial inequalities are noble steps forward, but the real actions that can bring an end to racism require major societal shifts in how institutionalized and systemic racist views have been unconsciously passed down and manifest in subtle ways, requiring conversations about biased practices against non-white individuals, students of color being sent to underfunded schools, or media distortion of POC lives that pass down to the public what their first gut instinct of a non-white person should be. Mind you, the people who need to have these conversations the most are far more likely to be dismissive and uncaring enough to dismiss these subtle attitudes as overblown cockamamie insinuations, and the amount of people who muddle the mature responses with juvenile finger-pointing and flagrant desperation to walk around every sliver of an eggshell is a bit more than necessary, but it is a social issue that does exist and warrants a thoughtful, measured response to really impart a message on others beyond the most obvious summation I listed as my first sentence, and that something as entrenched in media as structural racism warrants a counterpoint within art to really question and tackle these wrongheaded beliefs.
....I dont think a pat on the back is gonna leave much of a lesson for people to reflect on.
Crash has gone on as one of the biggest blunders in the Academy Awards long and extensive history of fuck-ups and ceremonial missteps, at least once a decade the Oscars have a habit of picking out the most trite and jejune nomination from all their potential winners of their most prestigious award and the sting of its win has only worsened over time, especially in regards to films such as Capote or Brokeback Mountain (when homophobia was still a more powerful prejudice to take a stand on than racism, like both are bad but it was a ballsy move to support Ang Lees movie at a time where the most common adjective was a derogatory gay) that have far more supporters nowadays than this flick. The reasons towards why Paul Haggis message movie is so bad has become apocrypha at this point, mostly because those who saw it back in the day can only utilize generic monikers as brave and daring without being able to actually discern what content actually makes it earn those descriptions, and also because nobody is gonna sit down and watch it nowadays except for schmucks like myself (theres a thrift shop I tend to frequent and I swear they have like 10 DVD copies of this film just scattered around, its like a family where all the kids are the red-headed step-children that get left behind as a collective person non grata), its developmental backwater to the topic of modern racism and likely only one as successful as it was because it tried to teach post-911 fears and paranoia as a personality issue that just needs a little bit of fixing, which we all know goddamn well isnt the case, and part of this films biggest failings is that it presents racism as only overt hatred or bigotry, which is undeniably true in some circles but thats not the only form it takes, thats the most effective and damaging way in which racism can mold a person to hate others for no reason, it instead is a pretentious way of handling the topic and is riddled with fake-deep moments of a few people with equal blame and judgement on their hands that simply doesnt come close to an equivalent of how complex, rooted, unyielding, and confrontational modern racism is.
But thats the very basics in terms of why people dislike this that you can glean from the general atmosphere of its discussion, whats actually INSIDE the film to warrant a person like me to call it an interminable two-hour glurgefest?
I cant fault its ambition too much, Haggis employs a hyperlink story to reach across a diverse and varied set of characters, with multiple races including African-Americans, Hispanics, Iranian-Americans, Asians, and Caucasians rounding out each scene so that it more accurately reflects the wider range of racial profiles that exist within its L.A., but what I can fault is how hollow and generalized it turns racial tensions into, often speaking about stereotypes (including Ludacris character whos so intent on being the angry Negro that hates stereotypes that it ends up reading as a proto-Uncle Ruckus, but without the satire) and propping up familiar arguments into limp puppets all destined to collide and meet the same fate of realizing the error of their ways, no matter how contrived or how dumb as shit (the reason in which Sandra Bullocks character turns her back on being a racist Karen probably being the most infamous) and often even falling into the lazy white savior trope simply because Haggis attempt to create an interwoven narrative requires things to be de-escalated as quickly and garishly as possible. Theres nothing that would make an audience member think about the state of racism, nothing that would be confrontational or challenging, it just presents unrelatable, unsubtle, unsympathetic characters putting on a show about the dangers of racism without the gall to put anything that requires a modicum of question or thoughtfulness since every conversation is required to enter some form of showdown against races with all the slurs, insults, and rhetoric one can expect from a movie that starts with an Asians cant drive bit (and it doesnt exactly get any more nuanced than lightly wagging its finger at how wrong that line of thinking is which, yeah, I already know that mentality is bad, I dont need two hours to reinforce and restate it).
Being hollow about good intentions is one thing, being pretentious and thinking youve cracked some profound puzzle about how racism works is a whole nother ballpark, as the film opens with jibber-jabber about how such dense populations as LA pass by each other so often until moments of intense tensions cause people to collide, a heavy-handed starting point that talks down to its audience and continues indulging in heavy melodrama that escapes any border of realism in favor of peddling out and recognizing stereotypes and then doing nothing to unpackage them, instead luxuriating on the thrill and drama of it all whilst becoming overwrought as it spams its sappy score and songs constantly in order to force you to feel emotions rather than trying to convince you it has anything of merit to say besides that a racist cop can just spontaneously change his mind about race after saving a black woman from a fire (its amazing how the movie of the same name from 8 years ago about car crash fetishists is far more realistic and nuanced than this trite). It presents the illusion of having more to say that just the bare minimum, and to its credit that illusion allows its cast to shine even with how limiting their roles are, Terence Howard questioning and eventually living up to the toughness of his racial stereotypes at the worst time possible, Matt Dillon playing an asshole cop pretty well even is his narrative arc is weak as shit, and Michael Peña balancing his locksmith career, his temper at being constantly mistaken as a gangster, and a family man in the films single genuine, authentic moment as he talks with his daughter about the severity of the world in a heartfelt, warm moment (bell by Peñas best acting since.ever), but talented acting can only hold up a weak and terrible script for so long, and it ends up failing to communicate cultural disharmony as anything more than easy and able to be resolved in the span of two days, which understates like hell the nature of cultural discomfort in large cities at hand.
I do think Haggis had good intentions when writing and directing Crash, Ill take someone who just fucks up with goodwill more than someone who directs and makes a film out of hatred and contempt for a race, but Haggis attempt at being antiracist only ends up being kinda racist as hell in that it has very little good to say beyond reiterating the hellscape of racial discrimination we exist in and how easily it assumes we can be progressive about the matter even when much of the burden rests on the non-white individuals that make up the majority of the cast and presents evolutionresolution only to white characters while making most of the POC just trash people and living no better, and in several cases worse, than where they started (it also doesnt help that even with the variety it claims to have on life, the two Asian characters are either angry and volitile or genuinely scummy and used as a prop to help guide another character towards redemption. Oops). Its damn close to being the worst, I wasnt necessarily angry or bored enough to let it truly rival against the two I do consider worse than this, but man does it live up to its shitty reputation and Im relived to have marked off this completionist checkmark for good.
