- I had to get it back. Before an apocalypse or an alien invasion, before the end of days, I had to get this worry out of my system did the 2006 Best Picture Oscar deserve it, or did it rightfully belong to Brokeback Mountain? That was the dilemma I had to resolve.
- So its that kind of ensemble piece, with different stories that somehow intertwine, over the course of 48 hours, in a collage of connected themes racism, xenophobia, bigotry, abuse of power, destiny, and morality. And all this in Los Angeles. So the film is convoluted and divisive, because although it intelligently tackles sensitive topics, the screenplay (by the director himself and also an Oscar winner) seems paradoxically to shine but also to crumple in on itself. The first part is excessively didactic.  Any reason, whether trivial or important, can make every, and I repeat, EVERY character take offense, sparking racial arguments and endless rants about the subject, all of it stilted and overly descriptive. Then the second half is peppered with intense moments and twists that, as the story unfolds, unravel the entire story. And the point is, I found the connections and related coincidences predictable, mechanical, and bordering on the implausible, all in favor of the plot, at any cost, losing a bit of spontaneity with moments meant to touch the viewer (and while some came close, others seemed forced). What I did like, however, was the psychological and moral reversal of the protagonists neither black nor white. A truthful and bitter analysis of a rotten society cloaked in hypocrisy everyone has their own mask, but anyone can change it depending on the situation. 
So what do I think of Crash? That
- Its not worthy of the most important film award in history. 
- Its definitely not the Best Film of 2005 according to many.
- There are other films that address the topic better.
- There are other similar ensemble films that are better (PTAs Magnolia or Iñárritus Babel).
- Brokeback Mountain clearly should have won, but the Academy would have even let SpongeBob win rather than let the most famous and iconic LGBT film of all time triumph. After twenty years, Ang Lees film is now a cult classic, which has now disappeared. Its pompous didacticism and forced sugariness largely undermine it, but its still worth seeing because it has interesting things to say, packaged with its captivating perspective that, despite everything, makes you reflect and question how much we suck as humanity.

CRASH absolutely blew me away.
   
Prior to my watching this today, the news had been full of expected mass protests of Joe Bidens pending Inauguration at the nations capitol and at Statehouses across the country.  This would follow the Insurrection that threatened Congress last Wednesday.  Such incredible hate is difficult to understand.
   
CRASH taps into hatred.  In this case, it is not about a political Insurrection, but it is about racial stereotyping, insensitivity, and painting entire cultures with a very broad brush of biased opinion.  Its greatest achievement is its recognition that characterizing others as all good or all bad says a great deal about ourselves.  Even people who try to be open and caring have their blindspots ... just as those whose actions denote a bad person probably have positive qualities, too.
   
I especially appreciated the deep dives into the lives of the characters.  For example, Officer Ryan (Matt Dillon) is presented as one of the most odious people I would probably ever know.  Overtly sexist and racist at the same time, he appears to have no redeeming qualities.  Then, we learn what influences his choices ... and, ultimately, we witness a heroic moment.  None of this forgives what he has done to others.  It just makes his actions more understandable.
   
Curiously, the films story structure reminded me of one of my favorite films, LOVE ACTUALLY.  That show, exploring romantic relationships in an often comical manner, had many illustrations of its main theme.  The same style is used in CRASH ... albeit with less emphasis on comedy!  And, once again, I was completely engaged with the stories.  (Indeed, if anyone had been watching this with me, I would have undoubtedly embarrassed myself with my loud, vocal expression of shock during the scene outside of the locksmiths house.)
   
CRASH features ensemble performances from an excellent cast.  I was impressed with all of them, but several really stood out for me Don Cheadle, Keith David, Loretta Devine, Matt Dillon, Chris Ludacris Bridges, Thandie Newton, Ryan Phillippe, Bahar Soomekh, Lorenz Tate, Shaun Toub, and an absolutely winning sequence with Ashlyn Sanchez.
   
Director Paul Haggis keeps all the action moving with surprising clarity considering the number of stories being told within a bit under 2-hours.  And his screenplay (written with Bobby Moresco) is, if anything, possibly a much needed reminder that we cant hate others without diminishing ourselves in the process.
   
CRASH is definitely a show I will be watching again.

What the fuck was that, dawg?
I can honestly, wholeheartedly say that Crash is one of the worst cinematic travesties I have ever had the displeasure of sitting through.
Now, bear in mind I went into this film with low expectations. I had heard all about it before going in the oscars fiasco, the horribly off-base ideas of what racism is, the generally bad script, editing, and acting, Id heard it all. Going in, though, I still tried to give this film a fair shot. I mean I really tried, I pushed all these things aside, and tried to put myself in the mindset of someone who just casually found this film and decided to put it on knowing nothing about it. Despite my efforts, though, I found absolutely nothing worthwhile in this film. I mean nothing at all.
You cant talk about crash without talking about its infamous Best Picture win. Though I do definitely disagree with this choice, I understand that this discussion has been long tired-out. If you want to know more about how Crash managed to win, I recommend this article from The Vulture (thanks Grant for sharing). Instead, Id rather focus on the two other awards that Crash won that night Best Editing and Best Original Screenplay. It is absolutely mind-boggling to me that Crash was even nominated for these awards, let alone taking home the prize. The editing, for one thing, alternates from bland to messy. Its unengaging, so much so that you can feel the pull, you get the sense that the editors were rushed into a messy final product that is. paint-by-numbers Movie-Maker mush.
The screenplay win, though, thats what most catches me off-guard. Crash has maybe the worst screenplay of any film Ive seen. I cant imagine what the writers were thinking while writing this screenplay. It is entirely unrealistic, offensive, and in general superbly annoying. Every other line is a racist comment. Seriously, every other line. Its as if the writers thought that if they simply created a story about a group of racist characters being racist, it would somehow turn out to be an interesting commentary about race. Seriously, the first half of the film is spent simply showing that everyone in the film is racist (except for the moments it spends validating racial stereotypes), and the second half of the film is just these racist people having bad things happen to them, which somehow makes them all no longer racist. Its nonsense, it honestly feels like the director was playing some kind of joke on the audience, but he forgot the punchline.
Every character in this film is personality-less, each being their own one-note, one-faced, emotionless pawn that feels entirely estranged from even being human. Im sure this is largely due to the abhorrently written screenplay, but it is at least accentuated by the poor acting and direction. Its clear that Paul Haggis has no idea what hes doing here. Coming from a TV background, Crash was his feature debut, and you can feel it. The film feels scattered and mindless, Haggis was learning as he went and you could feel it in the constant shifts of tone. The acting was equally bad, though. Its not that the cast was weak, Don Cheadle and Michael Pena can be stellar when given the right role, but it feels like nobody is trying in this one. Its as if the actors were taking it as a joke (and if you saw their pay, I can see why they would). The acting is unrealistic, awkward, and pays a large part in the reason I found this film to be so annoying.
In an interview on Crash, director Paul Haggis labels this film as a fable. He says that the dialogue and events of this film are not meant to be realistic, but its rather meant to be viewed as a cautionary tale. But to me, thats absurd. To take a concept such as this and make it a modern fairy tale is impossible, and Haggis only proves that point with this film. To even call this film a fable seems almost like a cop-out. Its a deflection to any criticism that the way that the film deals with racism is offensive and unrealistic. Its an excuse as to why unredeemable, disgusting characters are given heroic lightbulb moments. In truth, this film is a substanceless, ignorant take on the modern world through the eyes of someone who has clearly never experienced it.

Similar to how I forced myself to watch Emilia Pérez (2024) in the wake of its Golden Globes sweep (and now has 13 Oscar nominations??????), I knew I had to watch this as well to have an accurate frame of reference of the Oscar bait trend where they just throw together a bunch of hot social issues to appear righteous despite relying on regressive stereotypes to make it palatable to middlebrow award voters who actually dont want an authentic depiction of said issues.
But yeah, yikes, yall arent kidding with this shit. Just like with Emilia, its a cartoonishly shallow melodrama, with on-the-nose dialogue that exists purely to hammer in exploitive talking points with little to no momentum or consistent moral compass, in this case how everyone is equally racist and for justifiable reasons, because its apparently just an inherent quality of humans, but that maybe things would be better if we were just a bit nicer to each other.
So any moment thats meant to tug at your heartstrings just ends up being so bombastic and superficial that it makes you laugh. On the other hand, the film is loaded with these lame quips where youre SUPPOSED to laugh, but does so through racist and one-dimensional caricatures that only further downplay any dramatic or progressive weight there might have been up to that point. In other words, when it tries to be funny, its just regressive trash, and when it tries to be symbolic and profound, its hilarious in all the wrong ways.
Defenders of Emilia love to pull the argument of its good, people are just hating because theyre offended, but for both of these films, being offensive isnt really the main issue. If anything, the offensive qualities are more a result of lazy writing and tacky performances from the likes of Sandra Bullock and Brendan Fraser (like how is anyone supposed to take him seriously here?) that you would expect to come from an amateur student film instead.
The Academy thinks theyre doing a service to society by elevating works like this that pretend to shine a light on the struggles of minorities, but in the same breath, the Academy outright dismisses art created by said minorities who do a better job at depicting their struggles from lived experience. Because authenticity has to be sacrificed for the approval of middlebrow voters who dont want to have their pre-conceived biases challenged.
Not to get all sappy, but thats the beauty of Letterboxd. Mainstream awards dont determine our taste or interest in film. The films we love and celebrate on this site most likely have never gotten to that level of widespread recognition or award buzz, yet that doesnt make them any less valuable, because we all have our own film canon to shape.
But at the end of the day, the Academy has the power, influence, and responsibility to get films platformed on a worldwide scale and not just to us in the loop of online film discourse, otherwise no one would be talking about Crash to this day. So if this and Emilia are what works of art they think deserve to stay in public consciousness for decades to come, theyre only saying that out of personal gain and fake woke points to pat themselves on their backs - not for the love of cinema, the minority groups being exploited to feed their egos, or even artistic authenticity in general.
For those who truly love cinema, you know the art form has so much more to offer than this. We deserve better, so its up to us to make cinema blossom, not crash and burn into homogenized stagnation to appease corporate power.

The first time I watched this film was in my AP Psychology class because our teacher thought it was an important message about racism. Even then I could recognize it as the hollow, soulless film it was, but rewatching it now I realized that its also one of the worst edited movies Ive seen. Shots are placed next to each other which arent supposed to be related but give the viewer the false understanding that they are taking place in a single space.
This movie is a perfect time capsule of the era it came from, when the generally accepted view on racism was that we all just need to get along. However it goes way beyond that in the climactic scene where a racist white cop saves a Black woman from a burning car whom he had previously pulled over and sexually assaulted. Whatever lesson this is supposed to impart, it only comes across as a perverted fantasy of someone who cant imagine racism as anything except ones own personal moral character. Wouldnt it be fucked up if it turned out that the person he was saving was the woman he hatecrimed? I think if theres a lesson to be taken from this movie, its that for the American liberal film is a place to stage these kinds of fantasies, which always reveal the sick, disgusting fixation on difference that lies beneath their well-meaning facade. The story assumes that this whole experience has been enlightening and uplifting for its characters, but none of them act like humans, just props which spout timely commentary on race relations (or, when the time calls for it, racist tirades which are so specific that they fail to come across as spontaneous).
I could go on, but my point is that I dont think liberals cannot intentionally make political films that are good, because they can only ever explore reality as it is. They fixate on the things that they hate, but in reality they are only fetishizing it (see the Handmaids Tale). Every film of this nature will immediately become outdated because it can only speak to the moment in which it was made and its accepted ideology. There is no bravery and no risk, only thoughtless repetition. Even if there was a film made in response to this one which attempted to correct its faults, it would still suffer the same problems if it followed this ethos. I dont want to sound like a class reductionist, but I believe a film about race needs to start with the concern of making good artand that isnt a compromise in any way. It simply means beginning from the humanity (as experienced) of the Other you are depicting, not treating their difference as already natural, which even most self-proclaimed progressive art does.

Cinema of relief.
Crash assembles a mosaic of overlapping storylines reminiscent of Altman or Iñárritu. On the surface, this appears to be narrative complexity many characters, time jumps, unexpected collisions. But each episode ultimately serves the same function it demonstrates that prejudices shatter on a personal level as soon as people encounter each other in extreme situations. The interweaving of storylines creates the illusion of ambiguity, but it is schematically constructed
encounter  crisis  cathartic turn. 
This results in narrative redundancy, not genuine complexity.
The film presents racism as a fundamentally evenly distributed character flaw. Police officer Ryan harasses Christine, but later becomes the heroic saviour of the same woman. Through such pendulum swings, the film levels out structural asymmetries police violence, economic precariousness  migration become background noise, while the narrative focuses on individual catharsis. Everyone is a little bit guilty, so everyone can be redeemed. The system remains invisible because guilt and absolution are locked into the cycle of characters.
The title suggests physical impact, and the film takes this literally cars, bullets  bodies collide. However, this metaphorical surface logic obscures the invisible, long-term forces (red line politics, the housing market, institutional whiteness) that have historically been at work in LA. A truly systemic view would ask questions such as
Who benefits economically from segregated neighbourhoods?
Or what role do urban planning, financing  media representation play?
Instead, Crash ends with the warm certainty that a single real encounter is enough to dispel mistrust, a simplification that transforms complex power structures into a feel-good narrative.
Through the emotional shockwave dramaturgy (outrage  tension  relief), viewers experience a cleansing process without having to deal with uncomfortable questions of complicity or political action. This also explains the films Oscar success it delivers engagement without imposition, told in a complicated, but not complex way.
Crash simulates polyphony, but ultimately emphasises a simple message of salvation if we only truly encounter each other, prejudices melt away. In doing so, the film shifts racism from the public sphere to private emotional worlds and offers a convenient, individualistic solution that obscures the harsh reality of structural inequality.

It takes a special kind of genius to so meticulously craft a film like Crash. I find it genuinely fascinating what goes through the minds of individuals such as Paul Haggis when it comes to constructing one of the most didactic examples of moral altruism in a narrative form. I find Crash to be somewhat sickeningly brilliant as a film thats able to reduce such a hot-button topic as racial injustice and discrimination into basic stereotypes and manage to get awarded for his efforts. Im genuinely impressed by how well Haggis is able to play the system and profit from it like some robber baron of the film industry. The effort it likely took to write Crash was probably less than that of a fourth grade Social Studies assignment on racism in America, and yet he still managed to rake in fifteen times the amount of money that was invested in the creation of the film. To call Crash a bad film is giving insult to all the hard-working screenwriters that are able to churn out films such as the likes of Rob Reiners North or James Wongs Dragonball Evolution. Haggis was not ignorant in writing the script of Crash like the aforementioned examples, he had a meticulous intent to get this film made in the way that it was. By doing so, he managed to trick millions of average Americans into believing that his film had something important to say.
Its truly comedic, the sheer audacity that Haggis has in getting his actors to scream all of the most generic racist stereotypes they can at other ethnicities in the film. We can debate on whether or not Quentin Tarantinos common usage of having himself or other white actors in his films say the n-word constitutes racism on his behalf, but its clear that he has a clear vision as to why he uses such words in Pulp Fiction or Django Unchained. Haggis has no real vision other than to showcase that racial slurs are bad, without it being transformative or perspicacious. And it happens so regularly on a consistent basis throughout the film that you wonder if the film is trying to deliberately paint every American as a racist bigot. The 2010s had a big issue with writers using one-line zingers for characters to point out how racist a statement is (most prevalent in comedy films or sequences) but its done so often and with such seriousness in Crash that eventually, I became numb to all of them.
Beyond that though, is Haggiss poor imitation of Paul Thomas Andersons Magnolia, which I am certain is what inspired him to make this film they he did. The idea of a grand story of interconnecting characters who are all connected together by tragedy or happenstance could make for a great film that delves into racial injustices in White America. However, no character in the film undergoes any sense of meaningful development or growth. You have to wonder why Sandra Bullock is in this movie, when all she does is be racist to Latinos and complain to her husband. She technically does go through a change by the end of the film, but it is done in such a half-ass and rushed manner, that it ends up giving you whiplash. Like, in the previous sequence of the film, she was bitching about her maid, and now in this scene, shes all about admiring the work that the help does for her. Meanwhile, Brendan Fraser, her husband, goes through no change at all. Many of the other characters just go through a bizarre character arc andor the wrong change entirely. Matt Dillons character especially is so racist and vile, and yet the film never delivers on any sort of meaningful change-of-heart moment or comeuppance for him, because it is not bold enough to do so. At most, his character arc ends ambiguously, but he shows as so hateful throughout the film that such a finish to his character feels condescending to the audience.
Any sort of social commentary is blown by the wayside, and much of the dialogue feels so obviously disingenuous that it becomes insulting to anyone with a modicum of social awareness. Two scenes, in particular, come off as a white writer creating dialogue for a black character to speak for me. They both feature Ludacriss character and in both instances, I felt like Ludacris the actor shouldve known better. The first revolves around a dialogue surrounding hip-hop music as being a form of white oppression of blacks, because of how often rappers use the n-word in their lyrics. Anyone who even remotely respects rap as a form of musical expression (which Haggis obviously doesnt given those lines) knows how important hip-hop was in developing black culture and black thought in deconstructing White Americas means of repression, far better than what this movie could do. And for Ludacris to be the one to say this line, signalizes how the film needed him to say it because its fine to say because hes a rapper himself. For shame, Luda. The second scene I have in mind is a bit of a plot spoiler so skip over the rest of this paragraph if you dont want to get spoiled. But essentially, what happens is Terrence Howards character tells Ludacris, that by engaging in criminal acts (a stick-up in this instance) he embarrasses Howards character, and also himself. This is sheer arrogance on behalf of Haggis, as he debases African Americans who struggle to keep themselves alive as nothing more than thugs that shame the entire race of black people, which is sheer cynicism.
That is all that Crash amounts to. Its cynicism that disguises itself as social commentary when all it really is is inane preachiness directed toward Bush-era America. Haggis had no intention of creating a film that challenges the social institutions or hierarchies that allow for racial prejudice to fester. Rather, he offers oversimplified individual accounts of why racism bad or twas all a misunderstanding that are morally bankrupt in nature. There is no empathy, just tropes. No deconstructions, just empty platitudes. No narrative depth, just bait for the Oscars. Of course the Academy ate this up instead of choosing a genuinely challenging film of real social injustices like Brokeback Mountain because they didnt want to go against the grain too much. After all, people still used the f-slur to regard gay people back in 2004, no reason to oppose that. 
Im reminded of another scene revolving around Terrence Howard and Tony Danza, so slight spoilers for that see as well here. Danza tells Howards character that a character doesnt act black enough for a scene in the show that theyre shooting and so Howard has to acquiesce to his bosss orders because a black character like that cant be shown to act as smart as that on the show. The irony of the scene is clear that Tony Danzaa character is obviously a stand-in for Paul Haggis himself, and Terrence Howard is every actor in this God-forsaken piece of trite film. It was the only scene of the film that rang true to me, and only because of this analogy I created.

A black-and-white cine-memoir thats remembered through rose-colored glasses, Kenneth Branaghs cutesy and broadly unaffecting Belfast is every bit the contradiction in terms that it sounds like. Some of that seems by design Inspired by the writer-directors bittersweet impressions of being a nine-year-old boy in Northern Ireland as the Troubles first spread to his street (which was still integrated between Protestants and Catholics in the summer of 1969), Branaghs film is the portrait of a fading Shangri-La.
His Belfast is the story of a little kid experiencing his first crush as molotov cocktails explode onto the cobblestones outside his bedroom window of falling in love with the fantasy of the movies as his parents marriage begins to strain under the pressure of deciding whether the family should stay in the only home theyve ever known or flee to another country in the commonwealth. It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, and this scattershot crowd-pleaser renders them both in such broad strokes that it seems as if Branagh can only imagine the Belfast of his youth as a brogue-accented blend of other movies like it.

It has been nearly a week since I watched this at  the London film festival and the stench it has left in my mind has still not abated. I have to articulate this, perhaps Im shouting into the void, but I see this film get so much praise and as someone from Belfast I feel that I at least must make some attempt to intercede. Belfast is increasingly becoming a volatile place and I feel that it is important that popular art should accurately reflect its history, or else it might contribute towards reigniting the powder keg through fueling the ignorance many British people have towards us.
Kenneth Branagh has been lauded for making a personal film, despite the flaws and it makes it hard to criticise, particularly as people come to perceive Branagh as having wartime trauma etc. So it lies on those of us from Belfast to point out just how offensive and damaging this film is to the mythology that has come to surround the Troubles. Even the narrative conceit of the film being seen through a childs eyes makes it somewhat immune to criticism in this regard. In my opinion it is not nearly enough to justify just how false this film appears to me.
First and foremost there is the myth of the Troubles as being a sectarian conflict above all else. Where one side would come to irrationally hate and dehumanise the other side based only on religion. With the troubles this is protestantism vs catholicism, and yes this is a factor, but in reality it is more of a symptom than a cause. It is the same as boiling down Palestinian conflicts to a difference in opinion between Islam and Judaism in other words, complete nonsense. The Troubles was caused by colonialism pure and simple and no amount of empty sentiment that this film loves to trade in would fix this. It was a conflict started by nationalists who happened to be catholics, who fought to establish themselves on the island and were crushed by unionistsbritishprotestants who evicted them and denied them democracy. The native Irish were discriminated against for many jobs and gradually alienated in their homeland over hundreds of years.  
Belfast opens with a scene of Catholics being purged from the street in which our protagonist, Buddy lives. The protestant family at the centre of this film is safe from this purge, the film bloodlessly depicts the forced eviction of families from their homes, with little commentary on its significance. Unless the viewer is already previously familiar with the history they will not know the seriousness or meaning of what is happening.  We come to see any sense of danger in this scenario through the unionist mobs irritation that Buddys father is not participating in this purge. The loyalists set up a barricade on Buddys street and even though they are portrayed as villains to a certain extent there is little doubt that it depicts their actions with a light and toothless touch. They are cartoon characters. It appears that they are simply some people having a lark. The violence is never depicted or contextualised. We never see violence in the form of the British vs the Irish, the main form this violence took. 
Throughout the film Branagh goes to great pains to depict his father as played by Jamie Dornan as someone above the conflict. He sees Catholics as people and makes sure his children do as well. However he is also completely apolitical, he stays out of the conflict to his own self interest, while also standing on the sideline as his neighbours are being forcefully evicted for the crime of being native Irish. This is posited by the film as a heroic action. 
Again I cannot stress this enough. At no point does Branagh ever make an attempt to contextualise the troubles. The audience comes to see it merely as irrational hatred between two ethnic groups. Why does this annoy me so much? Quite simply because the troubles are so poorly understood by the masses while still being so fresh. By putting the blame for the conflict on an irrationality of the Other, instead of on the British it is letting the true perpetrator off the hook. Since this film takes a moral high ground in depicting it in this way many people will swallow it as gospel. Many of those people being the British themselves who are all too keen to live in ignorance. 
Besides these political issues the film is also rife with poor filmmaking. First there is no sense of place whatsoever for a film that has been titled after a place. No real locations are used and it has been shot on a lifeless backlot. The dialogue is largely dull and worse poorly delivered. This is an issue with direction for sure. So many scenes are rushed with no beats taken between lines, scenes have no room to breathe at all. We move from scene to scene with very little through line. I get a strong sense while watching this that the actors have no sense of trust in the filmmaking and apart from perhaps Ciaran Hinds and occasional moments from Catriona Balfe the performances are simply lazy
Finally for a film set in a war zone it feels like there are no stakes or danger whatsoever. We bounce between the families debt crisis and them being intimidated by protestant mobs, each plot has no flesh or urgency. The intimidation in particular feels almost comedic in its lack of threat, a moustache twirling bad guy practically only being held back from not making good on his threats because the script hasnt let him yet. Furthermore though protestant on protestant intimidation definitely happened I would put good money on Branagh having invented this subplot to make it feel more of a time. In reality the family being in debt seems to be the truth of why they left Ireland. This feels exceptionally narcissistic to me especially considering the film practically ignoring loyalist on catholic violence. 
Another bug bear is the use of Van Morrison music. He even gets a credit as music by. Its embarrassing that this guy might get to represent Northern Ireland on the world stage during this awards season, Van Morrison has been a staunch covid denier and is by all accounts a class A dickhead. A lot of people in the North would rather not be so closely associated with him
I spoke to my Dad about this film and he said something that made me truly sad. Theres only ever going to be one film called Belfast. Hes unfortunately correct. Since this film has garnered so much success already it will become inseparable from the title and therefore from the city itself. Even as Im sure most people from Belfast will see little in this film that they truly recognise.

Belfast ist nun zum ersten Mal ein sehr persönlicher Film mit autobiographischen Bezügen und ich merke wieder, was ich schon häufiger dachte - es liegt nicht am Stoff, den er wählt, es ist Branagh selbst, der einfach kein guter Regisseur ist.
Es hat tatsächlich etwas seltsam faszinierendes dabei zuzusehen, wie Branagh zwar eigentlich eine Geschichte erzählen möchte, die zu Herzen gehen soll, dabei aber keine einzige menschliche Emotion transportiert. A young boy and his working class family experience the tumultuous late 1960s.
While I admittedly expected this to be one of the better films of the year after festival reception, Belfast does a rock solid job of delivering a story that almost everyone will be able to see the beauty in. Home is indeed where the heart is, and Jude Hills Buddy leads us on a journey that tackles life, love, complacency, fear, but most importantly, the desire to escape this colorless life and find a passion in the unknown. Speaking on that, I am just a massive fan of what Branagh does here, as he uses that splash of color within certain scenes that show our family watching something on screen (or stage). Movies are the ultimate form of escaping reality, and this being a personal film for Branagh is evident because we are most likely getting direct looks into what turned him into the filmmaker we (mostly) love today. Is it my personal Best Picture? Im not sure if I would be thrilled to see it win over a few others, but I would completely understand why.
A lot of the beauty comes from his direction, as he delivers his best outing in years (other than Artemis Fowl of course). Whether it be the idea of making this mostly black and white, or telling it through a childs perspective, almost every decision made here is one that amplifies the narrative. The story of Belfast is one that will hit and sit with many because of the passion and soul it displays, but seeing someone pour their heart and soul into a narrative is enough for me. Sometimes that heart is difficult to latch onto, as a few of these deep and intimate moments never resonate as intended. The simplistic aspects like impressing the girl or chatting with his grandparents are enough for me to fall in love with. What never hits as hard are the moments with his parents where they are trying to figure things out. That being said, performances themselves are nomination worthy. There is also one plot point that hits every emotion it needs to, but it plays out in the exact way you expect seeing it coming ended up hurting the overall impact. Overall, Belfast is a beautiful look at a time and place worth exploring, and Jude Hill makes for a wonderful lead.

Belfast is Kenneth Branaghs Roma tryout, and its every bit as dazzling, sincere and heartbreaking. Chronicling Branaghs own experiences growing up in a conflict-filled Belfast in the 60s, Belfast is as faithful as it should be, presenting a story purely from a childs perspective, where the cruelty of life never seemed to penetrate the little protagonist Buddys mind, while his parents are at the same time torn about the prospect of leaving Belfast for a better future. like Cuaróns Roma, Belfasts also a black-and-white time piece that takes on a mournful, retrospective tone, except for the slightly playful touch to it due to the nature of the story. Where language fails, art fills in the gaps. Still, its the variances of each unique language that create the most essential art. 
Kenneth Branaghs biographical Belfast is less a roman a clef about the makings of one of Britains most famous living cultural figures than it is a treatise about how he shaped the art around him because of how he, himself, was made. 
In the tradition of Cinema Paradiso, Roma, and many many others, Belfast sees Branagh interweave the tender sentimentality of his childhood and his art. Also in the vein of these predecessors, Belfast has the benefit of being born beautifully from its authors own most precious memories. And if there is anyone most fit to render the images from their own past - it is a proficient film director. 
Belfast adds little to the realm of biopics or self memoirs, but it is without a doubt one of the years most gorgeous movies to look at. 
Shooting on a camera model that (appropriately) first came into the world around the year of Belfasts unfolding, Branagh and Cypriot cinematographer Haris Zambarloukos use its depth of lens to escape the apathetic flatness of so much modern film. With references to John Fords The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, its a straight line across the horizon between the Western legends frames within frames to how Belfast sublimely traps its characters within the suddenly stifling intimacy of their familiar environs. 
Environs, though, without which Branagh would have been born a much different artist. Perhaps not a lesser one, but one without the singular language which he has brought to the world.

Kenneth Branagh directs this pleasant little drama through a very personal lens, having witnessed the rioting in 1969 Northern Ireland as a child, which lead to The Troubles, an ethno-nationalist conflict. 
Being told through the eyes of a young boy named Buddy (Jude Hill), Belfast provides an around the corner experience of the uproar. 
The audience only ever feels the harsh nature of the riots to the extent of how much Buddy feels them. We only see, for the most part, what Buddy witnesses (and we dont see what he misses). He is a boy that loves his family and his home. He desperately wants to stay in Belfast but his parents have disagreements on whether its safe enough or economically feasible to do so.
The family connection was lovely. Especially with Buddy and his grandparents. Judi Dench and Ciarán Hinds as Buddys grandparents have some excellent moments of wholesome dialogue with consistently great delivery. Every time either spoke, my heart was melting. Buddys mom and dad (Caitriona Balfe and Jamie Dornan) have a lot of solid emotional acting during their conflicts as well. But the star of the movie was clearly Buddy with Jude Hills very memorable acting debut. He brought so much joyful energy to the hard times the family was experiencing. 
I also really liked the message that Branagh went for. Belfast will forever be Buddys home and he will likely mostly remember his best moments there. A part of him will be forever attached to his hometown, even with the mess it was. Our childhood experiences will never fully escape us and its an integral aspect that goes into becoming an adult. I also enjoyed some other themes that were explored, such as the fear of change and loving ones community, regardless of differences in viewpoints. 
I think the black and white works pretty well for the themes of the film, and it certainly looks gorgeous. This is helped by the fantastic cinematography by Haris Zambarloukos. There was always something interesting happening in the shots, especially with how often the camera would follow along with the characters in long takes. The music was effectively done by the Northern Irish singer, Van Morrison. I thought it was a nice choice, considering his similarly personal connection to the story as Branagh. 
While I enjoyed most of it, there were some faults. Telling the story through the childs lens does sometimes encourage too light hearted of a tone for how serious the conflict is. And the shift between the parents and Buddys perspective occurs quite often, which made that tone feel fairly uneven as a whole. I also never deeply connected with any of the characters on the emotional level that I wanted to. They were all well acted and likable characters but more depth for nearly every character could have helped a lot. 
In its entirety though, Belfast is a sweet story of the overwhelming love a child has for their family and their home, even in tumultuous times. It reminds us of the importance of our past, even as we try to push it behind as adults.

A subset of Oscar season is Oscar backlash season. There have been many vitriolic and negative takes on Belfast lately. People are entitled to their opinion, but I personally found Belfast to be perfectly fine. It has issues and Branagh is not a daring director, but he has crafted a film which is absolutely charming and engaging to watch. 
Cinema can be many things, but one of the best things it can be is a personal expression. Belfast is so obviously personal to Kenneth Branagh. To some extent the film feels too generic to be a personal statement, but that isnt really a problem, since the setting and characters are distinctive enough. The film is clearly a collection of memories, which is why the film is not totally realistic or accurate. Memories become stories become Hollywood-ised. This is a view of childhood filtered through decades of life. Often the film succeeds when it captures the parts of youth which are small and irrelevant, like playing football, stealing chocolate, watching movies, and reading comics (its a nice touch that the film contains a Thor comic). Belfast may not necessarily be about much, but it doesnt have to be. Branagh has clearly put a lot of his heart and soul into Belfast, and I appreciate the story it is trying to tell.
People often forget that Northern Ireland was in a state of irregular war for many years. We dont usually think about civil war as something that happens in the modern era in the Western world. Belfast deals with this from a childs point of view and it does not go into the wider situation. I dont think it has any obligation to do so, especially given the sectarian nature of the war, which did not always make a good side easy to find. But Belfast is mildly political, and it does firmly oppose violence against civilians, especially on purely religious or tribal grounds. Belfast is about living in war, and ultimately about fleeing from war. It deals with difficult decisions that real people had to make, since they feared discrimination or injury, but also did not want to leave their home. The film is a bit too cheesy in resolution, but there are also other cheesy scenes, in particular a final act musical number, that really work on an emotional level. Belfast is not a film to learn about The Troubles, but it does give a perspective which is interesting and different.
On a technical level I have many criticisms of Belfast. The cinematography is honestly terrible. It looks so flat, bland, and textureless. Black-and-white is my favourite aesthetic, but the execution here is a digital mess. The editing is also a bit strange at times, and the use of music is a mixed bag. Sometimes the soundtrack fits a scene well, other times it seems out of place. Parts of Belfast have been done in a lazy way, and it suffers in the detail. Branagh is a very talented actor and storyteller, but he tries something slightly formally adventurous in Belfast and doesnt succeed.
Belfast has a very promising premise, given it is such a personal movie. Yet it doesnt deliver in the way that something comparable like Roma did. However it does create a mythical take on Belfast, derived from personal memories to create a tribute to a city and a time. The film is funny and moving, so it works as a real crowd-pleaser. By the standards of mainstream awards contenders, Belfast is pretty solid. It certainly has more value than most, because whatever happens this awards season it will be seen as a very personal work that transcends punditry and discussion. Branagh has made the film he wants, and it doesnt really matter what the rest of us say. He hasnt made some box-ticking biopic or big budget sprawl. Hes made a low-key movie that reflects his own experiences. It is mightily flawed, but I cannot find it within my soul to dislike Belfast.

Kenneth Branaghs semi-autobiographical coming of age drama explores a working class Ulster Protestant family during the rising tensions of the Troubles, framed through the eyes of youngest son Buddy (Jude Hill) as he tries to make sense of the turbulent situation, with Caitríona Balfe, Jamie Dornan, Judi Dench and Ciarán Hinds making up the ensemble cast. 
This is one of Branaghs most personal films, shedding some of his usual mannered sensibility for a deeply nostalgic and affectionate portrait of his childhood. He never downplays the severity of the situation, but fills the story with a real warmth that adds to a bittersweet quality that runs throughout, exploring the past as it was versus how we remember it. This comes across best in the relationships within the family, told with a keen eye and sharp sense of detail that helps to bring the rich cast of characters to life. 
Newcomer Hill is so natural at the centre of it all, finding the right balance between naivety and awareness thats quite hard to pull off. Its all told through Buddys eyes, and Branagh explores how a childs perspective can effect the way they see the world, finding humour and a wonder in the everyday that slowly builds over the course of the vignettes. 
Each member of the cast is given a moment to shine, with Hinds probably the standout as the grandfather. He gives a performance full of an understated sweetness and wisdom, showing a man still full of life despite his ailing health and giving some of the best moments in the film. The scenes he has with Hill are the definite highlights, with the heartfelt relationship between grandfather and grandson providing a lot of the storys emotional core. 
I found the film moving, though scenes like the climactic Western-style gunfight do tip into overly twee territory at times. Its in moments like this where Branaghs more indulgent qualities rise to the surface, but his deep connection to the story helps to balance some of this out, giving the film an intimacy that helps it to rise above some of the more cliched aspects. 
Theres a scene where Buddys cousin tries to explain how to spot the differences between Protestants and Catholics, and through Buddy the film shows just how arbitrary these prejudices and casual hatreds are, poisoning the community and becoming exploited by opportunists out to profit from the violence.
I dont think Branagh can ever quite mix the feelgood elements with the darker moments, though, as the opposing tones often feel at odds with one another. This does hold the film back a little, shying away from some of the harder questions it raises for a more conventional upbeat coming of age tale. 
Belfast does verge on being overly sentimental, and could have gone further into some of the themes it explores, but Branagh fills every frame with an poignant wistfulness thats incredibly affecting, leading into a quietly heartbreaking final scene that perfectly ties the sweet message about family together.

Wait, that was Belfast? The film that is currently a front runner for best picture at the Oscars? Nah, I dont believe it. I hated nearly everything about Belfast, and no, Im not exaggerating. Every creative decision Branagh made, from shot placement, to music choices, only seemed to make the film progressively more out of touch and ineffective, which is more than enough proof of the fact that Branagh cannot direct. It is supposed to be an autobiographical story, but the details in this film are so unconvincing, that this could honestly be about anyone, and anywhere. I was surprised to see the titular city of the film did not play a larger role, in fact Belfast itself almost played no role in the film, apart from accents. Branagh doesnt build up the character of this city at all, which confuses me, since he did grow up there himself. This is a film that could have taken place in any city, which was surely not part of Branaghs intentions. 
There are many low points in this movie where a scene becomes laughable, with Branaghs choices in music feeling so ridiculously out of touch with the emotion the film is supposed to be portraying, it almost feels purposefully comedic. But I can assure you it is not. There are multiple moments where the filmmaking is so noticeably awful, that I had to keep reminding myself that this film is somehow critically praised. I mean, some of the angles taken here in very key scenes completely throw off the focus of a shot and command attention to other areas besides our characters. This is quite literally a high school film class level skill to master, and somehow Branagh still cant properly frame a shot. And dont even get me started on how the film takes absolutely no stance on the politics of the time, talk about playing it safe. This is an extremely bland portrayal of Branaghs own life, which really makes this a pointless film. I hated everything about this movie other than the fact that Balfes performance was really good in a few scenes. But still, the acting for the most part, and the film in general is subpar in almost every way imaginable.

There is a disconnect here the inability to convey both visually and it in written form what seems like it should be so readily translatable at the forefront of his mind. Brannagh, in an honest and understandable  desire to tell his story - and Belfasts - is simply not able bring the ideas of war and the innocence of his childhood together in the way so many (both real and fictional) films have before. What were left with unfortunately is a lovely, yet generic dud.

None of them smoke.
You cant recreate Belfast of the 1960s, the community and struggle and hope and despair, the cold and grey, if nobody smokes. Everybody should be enveloped in thick cigarette clouds, the stench of tobacco should be radiating off the screen, through the bw I should be able to see the yellow of the teeth and the nails. But none of them smoke. This is a film in which a man coughs to signify he will become ill and die later in the film. Imagine trying to pull that in a film set in checks notes working class Northern Ireland.
Smoking is cinematic. Its dramatic. It gives the actors something to do. It adds character, it adds texture, it adds movement. It adds puffy white plumes to transform even the most sterile frame into something alive. But none of them smoke. And I do not believe what I see.
Just a complete failure on every front. As both a portrait of a specific timeplace that provides any kind of detail, and the broadly cloying charmer it tries to be - no tension, no passion, no development (you could literally shuffle every scene around and you might not notice). Every disjointed scene, every flaccid moment and every tepid emotional beat feels barely sketched. Either Branagh is totally incompetent at capturing the emotions of his youth or he just lived the most bland fucking childhood a boy in 1969 Belfast could have. My hot parents used to take me to the movies, also I saw a tank once. Everything about this is so dull its embarrassing, even the distracting overcomposition of almost every shot just serves to highlight how hollow it all is. Honestly its quite baffling to me that anyone has responded to this with any passion at all. I saw someone call this the best movie of the year according to people who see 4-5 movies a year or something like that, and thats pretty apt. Shout out to my parents (who I would have thought mightve fallen for this thing) for recognising it as the shite that it is. Nice to see Merlin again I guess.

So seeing him embrace such a 100 personal and authorial project already comes as a guaranteed freshness, too bad is in the form of a pretty standard by the numbers Oscar-tailored drama, with some genuine heart present here, but tripping in its failed attempts of being this pseudo-cult drama about historical grief and nostalgic escape found only in the childhood days. Achieved through a by the numbers execution trying to be cute and adorably funny while following some of the characters small relationships, and glimpse away from all the historical weight behind the material that are shown in the brief horrors of war usual scenario of emotion manipulation. 
Trying very hard to deliver this mix between Life is Beautiful, Germany, Year Zero, How Green Was My Valley, Cinema Paradiso  and not hitting a resounding note in neither. From the war forming generations the escape from reality through the love of parents and relatives the nostalgic revisitation dipped in melancholy of a piece of time founded on both love and sadness life gradually becoming less idyllic, and cinema is the last resort of hope. 
All elements that are definitely played in the film, but treated mechanically to cause specific affective emotions and beaming reactions, and you feeling that they are designed for such just immediately takes away any amount of effect that they could have! Some people just tend to take an exaggerated bite out of that, like a personal offense was inflicted on them. But personal is the key word in here huh?! Coming from the directors own experiences and testimonies, so how far the questions of legitimacy can be extract from that if the very film is not making any political statements?! Just trying to mourn the pain and recover what used to be good and pure still left to be remembered.
Maybe its because to be trying to soften this period from this perspective of a childs innocence, that for those still wounded by Taika Waititis Jojo Rabbits may still feel the scars itching. Belfast is about as straightforward as a coming-of-age movie gets these days. If it were a real person rather than a film, it would be a man who would put on two condoms during a bout of intercourse to prevent his partner from becoming pregnant.
Kenneth Branaghs latest film is a mash-up of numerous personal vanity projects focusing on an auteurs childhood adolescence. 
Movies with a semi-autobiographical nature to them in the likes of Spike Lees Crooklyn, Cameron Crowes Almost Famous, Barry Levinsons Diner, Louis Malles Au revoir les enfants, François Truffauts The 400 Blows, Federico Fellinis Amarcord, and John Boormans Hope and Glory, and so on.
Furthermore, and perhaps most visibly, Branaghs picture follows in the recent footsteps of Alfonso Cuaróns Roma, another black-and-white drama depicting its own directors formative childhood upbringing. Though Cuaróns film, on the other hand, ended up being significantly different from Branaghs. As Cuarón framed his picture entirely around a fictitious adult protagonist deliberately developed for the film, instead of Branaghs approach here, the films central protagonist is patterned after his early adolescent self in his upbringing.
In this film, newcomer Jude Hill plays Branaghs supercharged adolescent alter ego young self, who reads Thor comics (wink wink) and watches films like High Noon and Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, both of which appear to have had a significant impact on Branaghs insane personal ego as the auteur nutball filmmaker with a hard-on for William Shakespeare that we all know and love today.
All of the other significant actors in the film, including Caitriona Balf and Jamie Dornan, who play his parents, and Judi Dench and Ciarán Hinds, who play his grandparents, are all outstanding in their roles here. 
Although I must say that I found it amusing that Branagh had to be coaxed into enabling Judi Dench to sit throughout all of her scenes in the movie, I mean, shes 86 years old and still recuperating from Cats, so Ill excuse her.
Lastly, I should mention that the films soundtrack is entirely composed of Van Morrisons songs. Which, now that you think of it, really wasnt the wisest of decisions, given that Northern Irelands health minister just recently sued him over his criticism of COVID-19 lockdowns because they interfered with one of his shows in Belfast recently, prompting him to cancel his entire performance forcibly cause of it.
Like ouch...
Overall, the picture is a lot of fun to watch. And with everything said and done, the shit leaves you feeling all oozy and gooey on the inside, like any good coming-of-age film really ought to do nowadays.  
Check it out. You still have some time until everyone begins shunning it once it wins Best Picture at this years Oscars.

Thats what made it easy for me to connect with. Different place, different time, but childhood always centers around grandparents as heroes, parents as giants, and the backyard as the whole universe. Theres a universality to that, no matter where youre from.
The film achieves an intimacy to the struggle of the family, especially against the context of riots and sectarian violence. You can tell that its personal to Branagh, its half-autobiography in gravity and in love. Visually, its stunning with that luminous black-and-white cinematography wraps the story in a nostalgic glow, as if were flipping through a memory were trying not to forget. Belfast may be a deeply personal film for Branagh, but its emotional core is universal.

Belfast is a refreshing return to form for writer and director Kenneth Branagh, an adoring love letter that churns chaotic brutality into a fairy tale. Chronicling the existence of a working-class Northern Irish Protestant family from the perspective of their nine-year-old son Buddy in the turbulent late 1960s, the film belongs to the same strain of sparkling cinema-as-memoir as Amarcord and Roma. Its as personal a film as they come, with Branagh penning dozens of everyday moments, comments and simple glances with fervent zeal after his years in the relatively anonymous work-for-hire wasteland. The autobiographical story delivers some genuine surprises from the frequent exchanges between family members and others, which jump wonderfully from the gorgeous black and white cinematography. Branagh includes numerous pop culture references, although it has to be said that some song selections are a little too on the nail. He reveals himself to be an enormous Van Morrison enthusiast, with seven ballads of the Irish musician getting cued up throughout the film. Belfast is beautifully shot and is comprehensively amplified by its protagonists childlike perspective.

A brightly lit, colorful montage of aerial shots capture present-day Belfast mostly the shipping yards where the Titanic was built. The array of images play with the uniqueness of a Chromecast screensaver before a harsh transition takes us back in time to a black and white 1969-set residential corner of Belfast. Buddy (Jude Hill) skips down the street, waving to his cheerful, salt-of-earth working class neighbors. Its an idyllic scene of an apparent, tight-knit neighborhood, that is blown asunder by an approaching mob. The rioters are the first sign of The Troubles, and are composed of Protestants. They want the local Catholics out. 
In this destruction-laden scene, director Kenneth Branagh relies on every visual cliche in the book the soundscape of explosions is overcooked, flattening the intended heart-stopping effect to a permanent flatline. The camera does an obnoxious 720 rotation around Buddy as he stands in the middle of a melee composed of punishing wooden clubs and smashed windows. Branaghs Belfast, a personal story for the writer-director, contains little dramatic momentum, and even less of a coherent visual language. full review via RogerEbert

Não chega a ser tão impessoal como um ROMA (2018), mas passa bem perto. Nada da contextualização política convence - é uma abordagem que quer evidenciar uma brutalidade daquele entorno, mas é bem higiênica e simplista em tudo - e o que salva o filme são alguns momentos das relações entre a família (os avós são uma carta na manga que funciona).
Até gosto de alguns elementos que envolvem o cotidiano do garoto, principalmente quando o filme lida com isso de modo isolado e não tenta impor relações com a questão política ou com os conflitos familiares óbvios. Então talvez exista um bom coming of age à Lasse Hallström (da época que ele sabia o que estava fazendo) perdido em algum lugar.
Pelo menos, de modo geral, o Branagh assume mais as suas limitações do que o Cuarón. Não tenta fazer um filme denso e faz o que pode pra se encaixar nessa fórmula drama histórico pseudo pessoal, porém good vibes e fofo.
Ele tenta centrar toda a sua abordagem no contraste entre a hostilidade daquela realidade e a intimidade do núcleo familiar e da vizinhança, mas nunca se coloca em uma posição de alguém que realmente deseja se aprofundar nesses aspectos.
O fato das cenas serem bem curtas reforça essa ideia. Como se ele quisesse explorar o drama somente até um ponto, sem correr o risco de tornar a narrativa enfadonha. O que poderia ficar bom se fosse estruturada em uma base de lampejos familiares mais espontâneos (como o Kore-eda faz). 
O problema é que tudo precisa se encaixar nessa fórmula perfeita de um filme artístico e leve. Tudo precisa se expressar através desse meio-termo aprazível.

Belfast is the story of Kenneth Branagh and the search for balance. It shows the director floundering between dramatic and comedic exposition, an unclean dichotomy for fatiguable end of year fare. Belfast almost certainly exists as a bridge between less serious projects. A would-be awards contender that might contend anyway in a year with not enough movies that everyone has seen. Its a dreadfully dull and politically pointless aside from the perspective of a child, covering The Troubles, a heightened moment of unrest in the modern history of Northern Ireland. Mr. Branagh even refuses to take a side here. The message of the film is that sectarian violence is bad and division is divisive, and through slick cinematography, perhaps there is some emotionally manipulative potential to wring out of a dark history of events, but without any distinct vision, it also seems squarely improbable. There are moments of comedy but there is no joy. The film is full of stagey drama but there is no point.
What the film wants to say but never successfully gets across in its text is that everyone is brave. Those who stayed. Those who left. Those who did anything. Theyre all brave and this movie is for them. It does not offer any breadth for the multiple decades of turmoil touched by The Troubles. It misunderstands, even from an outsiders perspective, what either side effectively stands for, or what motivates their positions. As unionists and loyalists banter and fight over territory, it never actually feels like anything is at stake. The dramatic scenes land with less impact than the comedic ones. Somehow the conflict on the street is never believable. Nothing is particularly believable, or nearly as engaging, as Buddys nascent love of cinema from other places. Belfast sings when it offers an escape from itself. When Buddy goes with the family to the cinema or watches cowboy films on television and the landscape begins to transform like the pictures hes watching, its the rare moment where the film carries a unique and standalone beauty. Its never about Belfast. Its about escaping it, even if you choose to stay.
The cynical take is that someone saw Alfonso Cuaróns Roma and made Kenneth Branaghs Belfast in response. That also feels like the accurate take. The difference is vast. In Roma, the film is inseparable from the setting. Roma is an honest and unflinching look at childhood living within the soundscape of its sense of place. These thing are not totally alike. In Roma, the aesthetic is analytically attached to the land. It means something and is derived naturalistically from a classical sense of place. The black and white is not simply nostalgically reaching but seems to expose something vital and new about how we frame Mexico. Its a clear and definable statement, where Cuaróns direction and cinematography make a hearty handshake deal and trade well in tandem. The way Belfast is framed is with a saccharine rose-colored simplicity wherein the city always feels like a movie set and never a tangible place. It is, instead, a stage for the actors to perform on.
The good news, perhaps the only good news, is that Kenneth Branagh is an actors director. His years of deep immersion in the craft is evident when he works with good, capable actors. The stars of the show are Buddys Ma (Caitriona Balfe) and Pa (Jamie Dornan). They are both very good and save the scenes they are in from the bog-standard child acting that is the norm here. Buddys Jude Hill has to carry more dramatic weight than he is quite ready for. Its awfully hard to center a film around a child who isnt ready to uphold the entirety of a movie. Its a big responsibility. And it feels bad. But the performance is bad next to the deeper understanding shown by his cast of relatives. Such is the risk of child actors. Also of note is the surprisingly unremarkable Judi Dench as Granny and the markedly better Ciarán Hinds as Pop. Yes, all the characters are named this way, and yes, its annoying.
Holistically Belfast is a two-dimensional film. Kenneth Branagh is a simple and unfussy director. He never finds the proper mode of expression for this particular story. It is more bogged down by its place in history than enhanced or especially willing to dig in and explore why any of this matters. Despite being named Belfast, it is not anchored by any remarkable sense of place, and feels more theatrical than cinematic, and yet, is not engaging on either front. There are moments of light comedy that do a good job of alleviating any tension, but then, maybe there should be a little more feeling. What we end up believing, most of all, is that the authors perspective has been shaped by some really lovely movies. There is a sliver of cinematic imagination, of a place being lifted onto a stage that is enhanced by having a camera on it, but it never truly cashes that check. Belfast is a slight awards contender that feels out of place in any conversation of that type.

Watching Belfast felt more personal than just experiencing a film. Having chosen to make Belfast my home, trading the warmth of the Philippines for its cold, rainy charm, it became a way of understanding the citys history, its people, and the stories that shaped the place I now belong to.
The film immediately establishes its tone with that rotating opening shot, which feels deeply intentional. It places us in the perspective of a young boy, grounding the story in both innocence and conflict. From the very beginning, we see how quickly normal life can be disrupted, setting the emotional foundation for everything that follows.
What stands out is how the film balances this tension with warmth. The opening, paired with a lively, almost playful song, reflects the spirit of the city full of humour and life despite the unrest beneath the surface. There are a lot of funny banters that genuinely made me laugh, but theyre carefully balanced with emotional scenes that ground the film and give those lighter moments real weight. This duality continues throughout, most memorably in the scene where neighbours gather, dancing and drinking in a barricaded street. Its a striking image even in the midst of division, people hold on to connection and joy.
Narratively, the film resists a conventional structure. It doesnt force a clear direction but instead unfolds naturally, allowing us to sit with the rhythms of everyday life. By focusing on family and community, it creates a sense of intimacy that makes the story feel lived-in rather than constructed.
This is why moments of dialogue carry such weight. Lines like, That wee girl can be a practicing Hindu, or a Southern Baptist but if shes kind she and her people are welcome in our house, cut through the surrounding tension with something simple yet profound. In a story shaped by division, the film quietly insists on kindness and respect as guiding principles, giving these words a resonance that lingers.
The use of contrast is one of the films most powerful tools. Visually, the black-and-white cinematography captures the harshness of its setting, while the bursts of colour in cinema scenes feel like a deliberate escapea glimpse into a brighter, more hopeful world. This contrast extends beyond imagery the backdrop of the Troubles is undeniably heavy, yet the people remain vibrant, finding moments of laughter and joy amid uncertainty.
Ultimately, Belfast succeeds because of this balance. It doesnt shy away from the weight of history, but it also doesnt let it define everything. Instead, it highlights the resilience, warmth, and humanity of its people making it not just a story about conflict, but about the everyday lives that continue in spite of it.

Its hard to feel charitable towards Belfast when its such obvious awards bait. Clearly positioned as Branaghs Roma, this autobiographically inspired portrait of Belfast in the late 60s feels every inch a pale imitation. It says a lot about a film when its most resonant moment is the final moment, one that only hits at all because of extra-textual details our knowledge of the history around these characters and what the final plot point means. This is also telling as so much of the film aims at emotion, with dramatic events happening each scene and never really impacting.
It is tempting to fall back on Belfasts heart being in the right place. It is a look back at a very complicated time that doesnt really point fingers and focuses on the familial, on the human, rather than the political. This doesnt work though, partly because it never achieves these aims (the whole thing rings too false to be a convincing human portrait) and because the entire film has the feel of no politics at the dinner table, please. It is the cinema of avoidance, where The Troubles exists as a backdrop and is addressed only in generalisations and platitudes. It is a reductive approach and feels disingenuous.
Of course, you can make films in which a serious backdrop is used as a device for the foreground. Films like Pans Labyrinth expertly do what Belfast thinks it does promoting a childs eye view of the world and thusly only showing the harshness of the world in broad strokes. Though, that film feels deeply aware of the entire context, even if its protagonist does not. In Belfast, a childs eye view is not as deftly evoked, neither is reality, and the film just seems simplistic. A lot of this comes down to direction overall, Branagh approaches the production like a play. The sets have the feel of stage setups and the acting has a theatricality to it. It is a dialogue first production full of vignetted conversations. The cinematic language has a surface level artistry but does very little. Its a collection of interesting shots, prioritising atypical angles and framing, but none of it speaks cinematically. A lot of it also just doesnt look very nice interesting and atypical dont mean attractive. The camera work is also constricting, with inconsistent usage of establishing shots and too many narrow perspectives. It isnt in line with any character, and often doesnt seem to be communicating much, and rarely feels like it is in the right place, or a place of purpose. The black and white aesthetic also doesnt appeal. The contrast doesnt look quite right, with a washed out falsity that further hinders an already artificial feeling film.
So much of this artifice is down to the scripting. It is an episodic retelling of a childhood (in which the cinematography could be equated to looking through a photobook, trawling through memories But that doesnt make it good, nor effective) and one that just feels overly incidental. We jump from moment to moment and it all rests on an attachment to characters. Unfortunately, this isnt evoked. The central child is annoying, written as a rose-tinged remembrance of a former self, full of wisdom from the mouths of babes moments. Characters talk in theatrical platitudes and theres no semblance of naturalism. If this was more based around being a portrait of a time and place, this wouldnt harm the piece (as much). However, time and place is evoked vaguely and, as mentioned before, in a reductive fashion. All is built around foregrounding the family and the family are not that interesting. Branagh may be pulling from memory and the film may chronicle an important moment in history, but that doesnt mean hes gleaned anything cinematic or interesting from this.
The whole thing is just fine. Some moments work, more dont. The Van Morrison music is annoyingly good, because Van Morrison is an arse (and one does have to question the ethics of commissioning Morrison at this point). Occasionally a composition hits, mostly the visual language is subpar but the piece as a whole is so purposefully inoffensive. And this is perhaps the biggest issue. It is all a supreme push for warm, fuzzy relevance with a melancholic centre. Something to cosy up with with your family. All sentiments antithetical to the setting of the film, and indicative of how it engages (or more appropriately, doesnt) with all of this. There is an interesting film here about how a childs perspective is ignorant to the specificities of conflict, and what that can mean for an audience. This is not that film. This is an awards campaign.

I wasnt too taken with Belfast, but I feel genuine compassion for it, partly because it gives every sign of meaning an enormous amount to writer-director Kenneth Branagh, and partly because the worst possible thing is starting to happen to it, which is becoming an Oscar front-runner. Im glad its moving and delighting people, even if the film is not for me. Belfast commits no important ills and I dont wish it any. But I dont see any argument that this shakily constructed, nostalgic-despite-itself wisp of a thing is remotely built to withstand the years of scrutiny that a projected Best Picture Oscar will impose on it. Why cant it just be the near-and-dear, one for me mediocrity that Branagh got to make after all his lucrative brand service for Marvel and Disney and Christie, and with his hefty paycheck for so egregiously acting the villain in Tenet?
In a just world, this would be one of the movies I forget when I try to jog my memories of everything I saw last year (or even last week). I appreciate its impulse to stage the sentimental minutiae of childhood side-by-side with major public clashes and era-defining crises. I dont think the movie handles either half of that equation very confidently, much less the ways they affect or refract each other. But some of that asymmetry is surely intended, and at least Branagh doesnt allow the weight of History to make his movie too big. Caitríona Balfe and Jamie Dornan have underwritten roles, but better ones nonetheless than either has reaped elsewhere on the big screen. Both actors are good enough to nudge casting directors to keep them in mind. Jude Hill, the young lead, seems like a sweet kid. Faint praise would be a blessing in this case its the hype machine thats about to invite damnation.
So, before the movies modest virtues get further blown out of all proportion, and before the critiques proportionally intensify into unmerited odium (and get waved away as backlash), Ill just file my brief against shoddy filmmaking and slink back out of the claims office. Haris Zambarloukos, whose CV has too few Enduring Loves by now and too many Mamma Mia!s, shows no real photographic eye here, despite the surface sheen of his black-and-white lensing. You wouldnt divine anything interesting about character or circumstance from looking at any still-frame from Belfast, even the logistically complicated ones. (Look, we caught Moms reflection in a mirror!) The lack of grain, texture, or visual depthagain, even in shots that are technically deep-space compositionscomes across as weirdly synthetic, mitigating any sense of actuality or of period. The movie was shot on location but doesnt really feel like it. Sometimes the compositions have the pixelated feeling of VR. Sometimes they have the flatness of a click-through slideshow. They dont often evoke life, much less in 1969, though some of the sets and props are endearing.
The editing is bewildering. Branagh has achieved a compact 98-minute runtime by seeming to omit about half the scenes that would explain the others or fulfill their promises. Subplots and supporting characters drop away willy-nilly and resurface at random, like dolphins coming up for air before they return to the deep. (Something about a tax man? Something about a collaborative school project? How long has grandpa been gone? Is he...still with us? Oh, he is? Oops, maybe not?) I genuinely believe you could remix most of Belfasts scenes in almost any order without shifting the experience very much, a clear sign of weakness in a script thats got plenty of other problems. Heres one among many based on the nearly 90 minutes preceding, I defy you to convince me why that mom elected to teach that lesson to that kid in that store, at that moment.
And Im not sure why Branagh hasnt settled on a point of view, which admittedly is seldom his strength, even in good films. (The controlling POV in Henry V and Much Ado is Shakespeare the camera is there to capture mood and performance, the soundtrack to record language and score.) Belfast has all the trappings of a Hope and Glory-style childs eye view on public and private jaunts and travails. However, we depart quite often from Buddys rather nonspecific vantagedarting often into all-adult worlds without, it must be said, any palpable boost in maturity, clarity, or sophistication. Thus, Belfast comes across less as a childs movie than a childish one.
I feel bad for even belaboring the flaws in this determinedly small film. Would that dozens more movies each year, whatever their limitations, felt as personal as this one! I promise I was rooting for it. Sometimes Oscar buzz does a lot of good work for a tiny movies fortunes, and I wish this were one of those cases. But sometimes that golden statue, even before its been handed out, feels like a magnifying glass, focusing all the solar energy of the worlds attention on a beetle just going about its businessor on a poor kid with nothing but a tin shield and a cardboard sword to defend himself. Good luck in that Coliseum, Buddy.
(Landmark Century Cinema, Chicago)
