Kenneth Branagh is a big-hearted guy, and if anyone was going to make a workable coming-of-age film set amid the sectarian violence and gangsterism of the early convulsions of the Troubles, it was always going to be him. And with a likeable child star, eye-catching performances from Caitríona Balfe, Jamie Dornan, Judi Dench and Ciarán Hinds as his resilient and loving family, and the ubiquitous songs of Van Morrisonwho else?to hold our hand, Belfast largely succeeds in making the very specific feel universal. I am not surprised that it won a lot of awards.
The problem is that Branaghs heart might be too big. Several pivotal moments, presumably meant to be tense or emotional, are so over the top as to be unintentionally hilarious. Whoever decided to set Pa confronting the gangster who is holding his family hostage to Do Not Forsake Me, Oh My Darlin and then resolve the standoff in the silliest way imaginable deserves some sort of comedy prize, although Im pretty sure it wasnt meant to be funny.
Belfast is more hit than miss, though, and never more so than when it focuses on its characters, rather than the set pieces. From a distance, it is easy to wonder why people didnt just leave Belfast during those difficult times, and the film perfectly captures the sense of belonging and community that made the choice to leave for an uncertain future abroad so difficult for so many people. Some of the religious commentary might be comically reductive, but the message about love and friendship across the literal community divide is certainly powerful.
Belfast is a visually impressive film, but its episodic structure struggles to differentiate itself from countless other jaunts down memory laneTerence Davies, for one, does this stuff a lot better. The choice that faces Buddys parents, however, is movingly handled, as is the final dedication to those who stayed, those who left and all those who were lost.

A wee bit twee for me but theres some tender moments, particularly between Pop and Buddy, that tugged at the heartstrings. The Belfast streets looked both stunning and sterile  shot crisply in BW, yet ruined by the glossy veneer of backlot facsimile. When Branagh leans into Roma400 Blows territory, as in the quotidian scenes where Buddy does maths homework, the results are marvelous. When he tries to magnify the stakes with riot scenes and sectarian violence a la 71, it feels grandiose and cartoonish. This is truly a case where the fear of letting an autobiography remain intimately isolated and microscopic got in the way of greatness. Retreating to broader historical contexts felt like cheap pandering to narrative gravitas, and frankly, it made the film feel smaller than it would have been had it simply catered to the kid-like concerns and whims of Buddy.
I dont give a damn what other critics have to say about this film. Ive always had a soft spot for films with a strong family theme, which is why I adored Belfast.

The film also had some great cinematography too as it is a beautiful film to look at with some beautiful shots of Belfast and just overall nice scenery. Im glad more and more films are black and white too as I just think that it fits certain films very well and this is a good example of that. The ending will probably hit hard too for many people as its honestly a pretty short movie for this kind of story. It did feel a bit slow in parts but honestly I didnt mind it as it was short sweet and to the point as it was more effective this way for an autobiographical film like this. 
Conclusion I enjoyed this film more than I thought I would. Is it Oscar bait? Absolutely. However I still was very charmed by it and thought everyone did a great job with the story being very simple but very effective as well with small details thrown in too for a better experience. Is it anything fantastic? Not really but I still think its a good time and I think Kenneth Branagh did a great job at bringing his childhood to life here. Id say check this one out as I see this winning many awards in the future and if youre into stories like this, youll probably have a good time with this film. A welcome pleasant surprise for sure.

Under a charming childrens gaze, Belfast tells an intimate and genuine story that sadly forgets to embrace its historical narrative and just passes through it.
It is obvious that Branagh decided to focus the film on little Buddy to avoid confronting the reality of 1969 Belfast while getting empathy from the audience. And although focusing on a child is not a mistake as it is (many great films have done it successfully), it is easier to forget about the purpose of doing so. 
I get that he was trying to depict accurately the events he lived and the way he experienced them, but that isnt an excuse to be as naive as you were when 8.
To his credit, the screenplay is really funny and the performances are perfectly charming. Grown ups play the heavy part and absorb everything that is happening around them, but are limited to transmit their full emotions. We only see parts of Pa and Ma, but we dont really see their internal struggles and their full character, although we can imagine it. 
Throughout the film, many important themes about the situation of Belfast at the time are suppressed rather than elevated, themes that would be relevant in todays world and are worth reflecting on, specially from a person who lived that situation personally.
Leaving your home due to political, social, religious or economic issues is a situation no human should ever face. I can only imagine the anxiety and fear of making a decision like that. It means giving up everything that you and generations before you worked for in search of something better, something safe. It is a huge decision, yet the screenplay decides to fast forward through it, I personally would have loved to pause a bit and get a more personal look into the decision makers, specially with Dornan and Balfe giving two phenomenal performances.
It may seem that I hated the movie, but not at all. As I previously stated, the charm is undeniable and is able to capture the feeling of a child that the director was aiming for.
In the end, Belfast does work as a perfectly fine family story, but stays at that.
And yes, I did have a huge problem with the cinematography...
It felt unmotivated, gimmicky, and worst of it all, it didnt even look good.
Ill just stop, it isnt as bad as my review makes it out to be.

Considering all the hype surrounding it, I was taken aback by just how humble and quaint Belfast feels. The narrative is rather simple as far as award contenders go, but Branagh and cinematographer Haris Zambarloukos compositions are masterful. 
Much like the rest of the film, the shots never come off as showy, but the precise framing is the work of a master craftsman. In fact, Belfast feels like a lost cousin to Orson Welles style of filmmaking A solid feature on the surface thats just brimming with movie magic if you dig a little.
Oh and Judi Dench better start preparing her acceptance speech because shes got Best Supporting Actress in the bag!

Kenneth Branagh throws his hat into the arena of directors making a nostalgic film recapturing their childhood. The approach, seeing the broader historical conflict through the eyes of a child, works fairly well here. It gives us a perspective that allows for a reset on what we think of the events when we experience them alongside someone who is unchallengeable in their innocence, and also allows us to infer a gravitas through what we know about the conflict in hindsight. 
Branagh coaxes excellent performances out of the cast, particularly the children. I always hold my breath waiting for a bad performance from a kid to derail things but, if youre like me you can breath easy. Theyre all really good here. Jamie Dornan has real screen presence as well. Without saying much he projects a quiet desperation and determination to get his family out of Belfast and away from danger while still being aware of what will be lost by leaving their community. The real MVP performances here are from Ciaran Hinds and Judi Dench as the grandparents. 
With all that being said, this didnt entirely resonate with me. It was clearly made with love and artistry, but strays into the territory of distractingly showy in a way that took me out of things and felt a little artificial at points. This one feels like its getting a little unfairly targeted because its up for best picture. Though its not outstanding by any means its an enjoyable enough watch. 
Final thought - Jamie Dornans Everlasting Love song is fantastic stuff

Despite the societal anxieties of Belfast in the late 1960s, and the looming bleakness that swept over the Northern Ireland capital, Kenneth Branagh manages to avoid such human depravity, instead capturing the beauty within the poverty, through a wonderfully youthful lense.
This story is first and foremost a love letter to family, to community, and to Belfast. Instead of using the troubling times families faced all across Belfast to drive the narrative, Branagh only used them as a backdrop to aid the growth of the semi-fictional characters. This isnt a film about hardships, politics and war, its a film about love, growth, experiences, and the way family get through shit... together.
Jude Hills performance will warm the heart! He is charming, and absolutely wonderful. You wouldnt think this was his feature film debut. Caitriona Balfe is marvellous, her performance offers a spotlight to all the incredible mothers that held their families together during the riots while the men worked. Jamie Dornan is as remarkable and handsome as ever, and I must say, monochrome really works wonders on his chiselled jaw.
Belfast is a beautiful personal gesture, from one man, to all his idols, role models, family, dreams, his home... and the moon! Must see!

Wonder was very disappointing. I was looking forward to this, actually. I remember the trailers being pretty good, and the director also did The Perks of Being a Wallflower, which is a really flawed film I love nonetheless.
 Going into this, I was expecting a film about Auggie. What I got instead, was a film not only about Auggie, but also about Auggies mom, Auggies dad, Auggies sister, Auggies sisters friend, Auggies sisters boyfriend, Auggies bully, Auggies bullys friends, Auggies friend, Auggies other friend, hell, even Auggies dog. In many ways, it feels as if Chbosky was trying to make a coming of age epic telling the intertwined stories of multiple people, and he really failed. Some of these stories work, some dont.
 At first, the film takes a somewhat Rashomon-esque approach to this, and shows the same day at school through different characters POVs, but then the film suddenly gives up on that concept and just starts sloppily telling 50000 different stories at once. As a result, most subplots end up feeling extremely underdeveloped and useless.
  The pacing in this film is really bad and the film has a severe lack of focus. And there are no character arcs. The only character arcs that do happen are barely noticeable. I mean, the biggest character arc in this movie happens to Auggies bullys thugs, and that character arc is so abrupt and jarring and cheesy and comes out of nowhere and ultimately is completely meaningless to the story.
 And the film has some really awkward ways of telling its story, raging from one hell of a lot of cheesy and extremely exposition-heavy narrating to a scene that literally entirely takes place in Minecraft.
 And the film is cheesier than a Cheese soufflé. This movie is so cliched and predictable and emotionally manipulative. So many scenes made me roll my eyes or cringe.
 Now besides that, there are still plenty of good things about it. The acting is pretty great, despite some inconsistent supporting child performances, and Owen Wilson is just the best human being ever. The film has its moments, and plenty of the jokesdrama hits. It has a lot of charming moments. The make-up is also pretty good. And the film does have some great messages and stuff
 So yeah. Wonder probably works well as a family film but it doesnt work as well as a film. I didnt despise it, I liked many aspects of it, but I had many problems, which mostly had to do with the films messy, jumbled, cheesy, unfocused, underdeveloped, cliche and predictable script.

Have you ever just watched a film and felt this sense of joy that feels like a rarity today? Only so many films can give me the emotions that Wonder manages to give, and only so many films can make me cry in the theater. Wonder was the second time in 2017 that I got this emotional in the theater. The first time was Logan. It was a strange year because I rarely get all that emotional during movies. There is something about bringing everyone together in the way this film does that I absolutely love. Wonder delivers a message that people (straight-up) need today. I have a feeling those who need to hear it may watch the movie and scoff, but I implore you to listen. Why in the world would someone judge another person who has an issue like what August has to deal with?
This poor kid gets ridiculed for the way he looks on the outside, but hes a genuinely incredible human on the inside. Seeing Jacob Tremblay take on this role is a win in itself (because he is top-notch), but everyone is amazing. There are so many elements to praise, and movies I have seen that attempt to do what Wonder did end up failing. There is a proper balance of tone that many films never achieve. Sometimes theyre too cheesy, sometimes theyre over-acted, and sometimes the script flat-out sucks. While we have seen similar stories before, the real change-of-pace here is the structure. The concept of moving from character to character, and telling each of their perspectives on the overall situation is brilliant. It has been done but never in a film dealing with something like this.
When a child looks forward to dressing up on Halloween so others cannot see his face, thats when we need to re-evaluate the way we are treating others. These kids slowly manage to do this throughout Wonder, and we see character arcs (good or bad) for almost every notable character we encounter. How often do we get a genuine and good-hearted film like this? Wonder includes no cursing, its family-centric, the film is full of incredible talent, and (best of all) it is extremely well-directed. Stephen Chbosky went from The Perks of being a Wallflower to this. How has this man not been talked about more? We need another project now. While there are plenty of heartbreaking moments that feel real, there are nothing but happy tears at the end. This movie ends on the highest of highs, and its all handled so well in the process.

Sons pick for family movie night.  
Back before my son was cognizant, the rest of the family watched and enjoyed Wonder.
We enjoyed it so much that I took the book out of the library and read the whole thing with my daughter.
Returning to the movie years later, a lot has happened.  My daughter is a teenager now and has a life eerily similar to the eldest daughter in the movie.  And although my son doesnt have a facial deformity, he does have a hard time making close friends.  Once school starts up again his one close friend is going to a different school than he is.  And just like the mom did in this movie, we will need to put on a brave face and send our son into the wilds of elementary school, hoping he is not eaten alive.
My wife cried a lot during this movie.
In fact, all of us shed a tear or two during this family movie night.
Parenting is hard and wonderful.  And if we can all help our kids to be a little kinder to their classmates maybe we can help sustain that wonderful in our children just a bit longer.

One of the most emotionally manipulative films of the year, Wonder manages to make it work thanks to a good performance by Jacob Tremblay, some good direction by The Perks of Being A Wallflowers Stephen Chbosky, and a character-centric storyline. It doesnt break any new ground or attempt to do anything different from normal, but at the same time, its inspiring and well-done, having a powerful message about bullying and kindness to say which hopefully will affect its target audience in a good way.
Julia Roberts is great here and the whole cast is pretty much spot on. Most of the pre-teen actors arent that bad and the film handles their development well. Its not going to blow everyone away, but it should be just what its target audience will love. Its a film that follows Tremblays Auggie Pullman who is a home-schooled kid with facial differences that have prevented him from going to school up to this point. Some of the kids are nice and others arent when he ends up going to school, and the movie plays out like youd expect. I did like the fact that it was able to focus on characters other than Auggie and explore how they were affected by him, and the performances from the actors playing them helped sell their parts well.
For the right audience, this will be a 45 star film or even higher. Its rare to find a kids movie aimed at kids that doesnt insult their intelligence these days, but Wonder fits that category nicely.

Jacob Tremblay as Auggie is outstanding too how this kid didnt secure a major acting award is unbelievable.
Having lesser subplots couldve helmed Wonder more, as the stories of Miranda and Jack Will - while helping Noah Jupe shine - bloats the script unnecessarily. 
The extremely woke crowd may be angry why Auggie wasnt played by someone who underwent a real facial reconstruction, but for me, Wonder is a gentle, anti-bully movie that utilized its strengths for an inspiring watch.

A young dreamer who has been sheltered his whole life due to a facial deformity must take on his most daunting challenge yet ... Middle School.
When given the choice between being right or being kind, choose kind.
My oldest son read Wonder in his 5th grade class this year, so he insisted the family gather around to meet the very special August Pullman together. It is your typical sappy coming-of-age story, but I thought the film did a good job of enduring us to Auggies struggle while also giving the perspective of those around him experiencing their own hardships.     
You cant blend in when you were born to stand out.
(Quick Hits)
- Is it a good or bad thing I could not tell that Jacob Tremblay had a prosthetic mask or CGI ... since it had a softer look. Regardless I thought the mast was effective and Tremblay was great in the role
- Owen Wilson is around, but dont get too excited since he mostly just says uplifting Dad stuff
- Meanwhile I enjoyed Julia Roberts performance more as she does her best to help her son, while avoiding putting the rest of her life on hold
- The part I appreciated most was his sister Vias story, who has been very mature about taking a back seat to her brother when it comes to her parents attention. But her situation becomes even harder to deal with when her best friend suddenly ghosts her following Summer break
- We do get to see her friend Mirandas side of this, with her dealing with her parents divorce. But her gaining popularity from claiming that Auggie was her brother was a bit odd. But it was sweet to see them all together in those flashbacks
- That was a great moment when Via finally breaks through to Auggie, that it is not always just about him all the time
- The additional perspective that I did think was insightful was Auggies friend Jack Will who he has a big time fall out with ... which drags on for a long time. But this inside perspective lets us see how Jack actually comes to prefer being friends with Auggie, but just got caught up with going along with the bullies since he did not realize Auggie was right there
- That bully kid was another level of cruel with him actually devoting his Darth Sidious Halloween costume toward picking on Auggie
- The bullys mother actually justifies all those hate notes ... yikes
- Just imagine Halloween being your favorite holiday, since it is the only time Auggie can go out in a mask and feel totally normal
- The blooming relationship between Via and Justin was written really well with them both being involved with theater, and him encouraging her to come out of her shell 
- Well that was pretty obvious we were going to get the Mr. Hollands Opus styled standing ovation and award for Auggie at the end
I am a softie so ofcourse this movie had me smiling and tearing up at points. It has some cliche elements to it, but overall the depiction of the character struggles in Wonder was exceptional.

Wonder was released in 2017 and was directed by Steven Chbosky, and has a fantastic cast of Julia Roberts, Owen Wilson, Daveed Diggs, Mandy Patinkin. But the most impressive stars from the cast was the fantastic performances from the children Jacob Trembley and Isabela Vidovic in particular. 
The film is all about this young boy with a face disorder and he attends a new public school as we see all the troubles along the way of his first year at school. The child is clearly seen as different compared too the other children at school, which creates so much uncomfortability, emotion, and sadness for the young boy. We also see the struggles that this bullying has on his family, mainly his sister and how her life is affected since the birth of the boy, as well as the different mindsets and views from all of the children in the boys class. 
I love the music in this film as well it brings so much too each scene, and really helps with the tone of the film. The script is also fantastic in this film with so many heartwarming, great messages which can be used too teach everyone of all ages about treating others nicely. The film highlights how the real world is, with different people being nasty but then showing there is people out there willing to help, no matter the circumstances. The affects of bullying and even judging people can have huge effects on the self esteem of people therefore this message should be shown to everyone. The film feels so relatable as everyone goes through the school periods in their younger ages and these scenarios that occur are all relatable and occur regularly. 
I love the ending of the film as it truely brings all the plots together with such a powerful emotional impact. Once those kids see the friend within the boy, they soon have a relationship with him and he finally enjoys being confident too show his face and be himself. The only criticism of the film is the sisters story is a little rushed at the end with her gaining a friendship within one scene.  
Overall Id rate this movie a 5  it is truely an exceptional film and everyone should watch this. The cast is excellent and all delivery outstanding performances, the script, music and messages in the film is so emotional.

I finished the book Wonder in April this year. Ive already written about how the beginning of this year was one of the best times of my life. The book moved me so much, I just laid in my bed for a long time and thought about it for a while and then wrote an entire essay over it for class. I should find that and post it sometime because the book really did give me a lot to say.
The reason I picked it up was because it quotes one of my all time favorite songs, Light and Day, and I wanted to see how it came up in context, and it ended up being one of the most beautifully profound books and best writing about inclusion and acceptance Ive ever read.
In the current world we live in, we are divided. We judge eachother based off our believes constantly, forcing our own beliefs. Since its been a year since the ugliest election in the US, it was a perfect time for the movie Wonder to come out and be a hit- because its message is simple, Always be kind.
Thats all there is. Even if a kids face scares you, even if that kid is gay, or bisexual, or black, or muslim, or whatever- ALWAYS. BE. KIND.
This is the perfect film that shows the life of Wonder through a lot of different peoples eyes, much like the book. We dont only walk through Auggies shoes and sees how he feels about his face (with the help of Star Wars characters) we see also how it effects his sister and his best friend. I was afraid if the movie tried to tackle this it would feel disjointed, but, its directed and written in the smoothest and most natural way possible. I was really impressed with what they were able to accomplish here. This is maybe the best book to film adaptation Ive ever seen in the sense that yeah- it goes beat for beat like the book. Theres hardly a thing missing and it keeps the same tone of the book as well. The spirited and the overwhelming emotion I felt reading it came flooding back when I watched this. 
The double feature with this and The Florida Project was amazing. Kinda secured my hope in the future of making sincere and honest films again.
I just relate so much to this story- even if Ive always looked normal. Ive felt isolated sometimes, and its a scary thing. I love how they show Auggies sister also has to deal with a lot of emotions even if she turned out normal, because of the stigma revolved around her situation. Thats such a great subplot because it shows one thing- everyone has problems that are important to talk about and its a good idea to be there with everyone.
I love the fact that schools are really promoting this book and movie- because this existing just in my opinion is important- its actively making the world a better place.
Conan O Brian once said after leaving The Tonight Show, Cynicism is my least favorite thing, and I agree with him. After seeing so many movies that are so cynical and so self indulgent, its good to see a film just wanna be good and wanna do the right thing- that is filled with people who are good and kinda hearted and are trying their best. Films that take people that are self important and says, this isnt the way you should act. I love that. Weve needed this movie for a long time.
The film also looks amazing. I was really impressed with the shots here. It feels like just a normal town but theres something so intimate and inviting about it too. Just the chill of fall and the whimsy of winter as the time passes by throughout the year is so well felt here. The passage of time is very well felt here- I felt like I spent a year with Auggie in this film, like I did in the book. 
The fact that we have a family movie out right now all ages can enjoy that doesnt talk down to kids and is able to make 5th graders talk and act the way 5th graders do instead of talking down to them or mugging the camera like in every Hallmark movie is so refreshing to see. It just shows that all age entertainment can also be taken seriously and not just jokes about farts and butts (cough The Star cough).
Some of my all time favorite movies, like Where the Wild Things Are and Fantastic Mr. Fox, are family movies that dont talk down to everyone and is able to be artistically pleasing and poignant to all ages. I truly believe Wonder is in the same boat. I adore this film. I was worried about it because the trailers look so bad- like a generic Nickelodeon movie thats trying as hard as possible to get kids to see it- when in all reality its essentially its just the book brought to life in the most effective way possible.
Is it a little too ham fisted or schmaltzy at times? Yeah, of course. I like a little schmaltz though and the movie handles it so well, I really dont care. Its good to leave a movie again and feel clean, like I have some hope for the future of America. Please, go out and see this film- its an important watch in my opinion but its also just a wonderful time at the movies.

A strong family drama with a good message. Wonder is a well-made film with a clear purpose. To help people understand that being different doesnt mean being less.

2nd Stephen Chbosky (after The Perks of Being a Wallflower)
As someone who spends most of his time thinking about minority experience on film, theres always a tendency to give the side-eye to anything made by the Hollywood system as fundamentally dishonest pandering to a bunch of milksops who want to feel better about themselves. So I avoided Wonder because I, cynically, believed it would be little more than another Forrest Gump. But I was pleasantly surprised. Wonder is a film drowning in treacly sentiment and contains too many plot strands for its own good, but credit should be given for the multifaceted approach to Augusts existence with a facial deformity and how it impacts those around him, especially his sister and his friends. Doing so, the film sidesteps the traditional approach to disability that stresses the disabled as some sort of innocent above reproach. The familys relentless focus on August is to the detriment of his older sisters sense of self and August himself is depicted as fundamentally quite self-centred and unable to see the problems of others. Though when youve had something in the region of twenty surgeries simply to keep you alive, a tunnel vision is understandable. 
And indeed August would be a thoroughly dislikable character were it not for Jacob Tremblays excellent performance. He manages to give Augusts somewhat perfunctory narration a cheeky charm and energy that endears him to an audience, and theres one wonderful moment where he runs his hand through his hair in a mocking manner that is simply priceless. Actually, the whole young cast is very good here, though Id like to have seen more of Summer, whose warmth was worth far more than one single scene. Speaking of shafted characters, Owen Wilsons father spends most of his time on the sidelines as some sort of all-knowing hipster dad with no other plot development. How he managed to bag a babe like Julia Roberts is beyond me, he just Vibes. Credit to Patinkin for giving a tiny role so much warmth too, amazing actor that he is. 
But despite these good performances and good intentions, Wonder is let down by an excess of fantasy sequences and a pat ending that feels like it wants to desperately make August the centre of attention when the entire film has been about him being Just One of the Kids. It feels too schmaltzy for me to ever really give it a seal of approval, but Im weirdly glad to say that its for filmic reasons and not the result of being patronised for two hours. 
Also, lovely to hear Were Going to be Friends again, thats a lovely song.
Chbosky in Order
1. Wonder
2. The Perks of Being a Wallflower

Wonder is a emotional filming experience made in 2017, directed by Steven Chbosky. This film is treated to a wonderful cast of Julia Roberts, Owen Wilson, Daveed Diggs, Mandy Patinkin. But the stand out performers in this film was the children, who gave brilliant emotional performances. Jacob Trembley and Isabela Vidovic was special to see in this film. 
This film is all about this young boy with a face disorder and he is attending a new public school as we can see all the problems and troubles along the way his first year at school. As this child is clearly seen differently to other kids at school, which creates so much heart ache, emotion and sadness for the young boy and for us as viewers. We also see how brilliantly the film has shown the affects on the family of the bullying of the young boy has on them. Particular the young boys sister, and how her life is affected since the birth of her younger brother, as well as the different mindsets and perspectives of all the children in his school class. Which is brilliantly written. 
I love the music in this film as well it enhances the emotion in every scene, and really helps the tone of the film. The script is also incredible in this film with so many heartwarming, great messages which can be used to teach of everyone of all ages about treating each other nicely and fairly. The film highlights how the real world can be, with different people being nasty but then showing there are some people out there willing to help and have a good heart, no matter what the circumstances. This message is brilliantly done. As this story really brings to life how people can be affected by bullying and even judging people can have a massive negative impact on peoples self esteem this is a very important message and this message is delivered with high quality and with brilliant emotion to it too. The film feels so relatable as everyone goes through the school period in younger ages and these situations are realistic and can happen regularly. 
I feel that the ending of this film is perfect, as it truly brings all the plots together neatly, in a clever and smoothly written way. As the plots coming together brings such a powerful and emotional impact onto the audience. Once these kids see the friendly side to the boy after seeing his face, they soon gain a friendship, and Auggie finally enjoys being confident to show his face and be himself and be happy. This is such a satisfying ending for me, it just works and really makes you as an audience member want to smile after all Auggie has gone through. 
The only criticism I have for this film is that I think they rushed the ending to Auggies sister storyline with her gain her friendship back within only one scene. Didnt feel as powerful or emotional as the other stories and I thought they could of done that better. 
Overall, I would review this film 5, it is truly a phenomenal film and everyone must watch this film. The cast is amazing and all produce fantastic performances, the script, the music and music is this film is so emotional and heart warming and the ending is incredibly satisfying and powerful to see.

One day a film like this will kill me. Thats not a statement on the quality of Wonder, just a comment on how this type of overly sentimental movie is not for me and draws out my ire at the disparity between reality and the happy fictional world depicted. Im still able to judge Wonder on its own merits but the lies inherent in the world-building of Wonder are the sort of thing that make me overanalyse the world to a point where my eventual death becomes exciting. Its just not my type of film.
In all honesty, I expected the worst from Wonder. I do absolutely love The Perks of Being a Wallflower by the same director so perhaps I should have known this would be okay. But the trailers for Wonder made it look like the most cringe-inducing, cloying claptrap. Reviews talked about how inspiring it was which informed me that this was ultimately a happy movie about how great we can all be (and my eternal pessimism makes that unwatchable). Then it got an Academy Award nomination in some minor category and my completist attitude eventually got me to watch it. I did save it till last though (the only nominated feature films Im yet to see havent had a UK release yet). So imagine my surprise when I realised early on that Wonder is actually a pretty good film.
So lets talk positives. Wonder is most definitely a well put together movie that shows competency in almost all areas. Its never particularly boring and I found it an easy watch (beyond my internal grappling). The characters are broad, but they are all likeable and relatable. The cast are generally good, especially for a film with many child actors, although Owen Wilson, Jacob Tremblay, and Izabela Vidovic are the standouts. Theres also a partial Rashomon-like structure which isnt utilised well but it is at least interesting. I imagine someone with less cynicism, self-loathing, and pessimism will likely get a lot out of Wonder.
Wonder however has a significant problem. Its unable to tell a genuinely human story. Every few scenes contains a super cheesy moment. Theres also a lot of cringey dialogue. Random Star Wars characters also appear in the film and that did nothing for me either. The films cheapest ploy involves the death of a dog, a tug at the heartstrings that I gave zero fucks about. This a lazy trope that I really wish goes away, especially as society is so hypocritical on animal rights. In general, Wonders only real problem is that its unable to genuinely earn its emotional moments and thats a real shame.
It makes me sad to think that people might find Wonder in some way representative of real life, as if people actually learn to be as accepting and as good as they do in Wonder. My life (and school) experience was certainly very different. I dont remember people randomly talking to and trying to be friends with introverts. I dont remember kids being nice to you if youre nice to them. I didnt realise that people dont care if the crux of their friendship turns out to be a lie. I didnt realise that bullies come around to respecting their victims (and the implication is that the bullies are absolved of their sins). Then again, my school was nothing like the one in Wonder. It wasnt privileged, rich, and well-equipped and my teachers werent all young, attractive, totally understanding people. I also love how brazenly Wonder depicts the school standing up against corruption and rich donors. Its like the film is actively trying to lie about the world. Its a film which tells us that the system works well when it demonstrably doesnt. A really nice teacher literally makes a point of previously having worked on Wall Street just to re-enforce the attitude that the system works well (or it does for these fictional children at a rich school). The entire film is based on a lie about how fundamentally great everyone is. Theres a lot that arent and its just disingenuous nonsense to suggest otherwise. This is the equivalent of a cinematic safe space, comforting the audience by telling them that whatever bad exists can be solved because people will do the right thing. Bullies will turn good, those ostracised will be approached by others, the rich wont have any advantage in life. Hahaha, nope. Yet people buy into these movies and that makes me sad because either so many have fallen for these lies or Im among a minority of people who dont find everything around them fundamentally good. This is why I need to stop watching this kind of movie.
Wonder is a decent film that never really messes up. However its not for me because I cant stand its viewpoint. I didnt exactly enjoy Wonder either but I did find it relatively endearing. I dont like it and I dont respect it but I know its an okay film outside of that. Id recommend it to others but Im not interested in ever seeing it again.

This movie stars Jacob Tremblay portraying a boy named August (Auggie),
A 10 year old boy with Treacher Collins Syndrome that at this point has had 25 surgeries in order to see, smell, speak, and hear without a hearing aid.
Auggies parents (played by Owen Wilson and Julia Roberts) make the decision to enroll him in public school for the first time, and much of this movie is about Auggies attempt to fit in despite being....well, different.
This film is great for a variety of reasons. Perhaps most of all, the concept of fitting in and finding ones place in the world is a universal theme it doesnt matter who you watch this film with - their age, their ethnicity, etc - it is sure to provoke emotions that other people find incredibly easy to relate to despite the subject of this film being ostracized for reasons that are particular to his specific situation.
Secondly, this film has pretty heavy subject matter when you get down to the bits of it, but its presented in a way that (again) is easily understood by its intended audience. The parents are relatable. The children are relatable. The reaction to Auggies condition by compete strangers is again - relatable. This film doesnt attempt to sugarcoat the cruelty people like Auggie are subjected to on a daily basis and tells it EXACTLY like it is.
Lastly, the nature in which this movie flows is just the icing on the cake. It isnt all happiness. It isnt all sadness. It isnt all shock. It isnt all disgust. But the emotions move through the film so sporadically and methodically - like they would, naturally - that it lends to the authentic nature of its contents. You almost feel like you are in the movie doing exactly what the characters are doing - and thats going through life and dealing with all the nuances that come with doing so.
This film will make you cry, but the tears will be from joy and inspiration you arent unexpecting when the film begins. It doesnt matter what kind of day you are having. Wonder will lift your spirits, if even only for a little bit.
Just thinking about this movie and typing this up has filled we with an immense amount of joy - it REALLY is that good of a movie. So, here it is.
Please watch this movie, if none of the other ones Ive posted here have drawn your attention. I promise that you wont be disappointed.

Stephen Chboskys Wonder is one of those rare family movies that seems to hit all the right notes by moving its audience without ever feeling overly manipulative. Each time I felt the film was going to fall into a typical Hollywood trope, it managed to turn the corner and skip all predictable outcomes. I kept on waiting for the film to fail because there is a sense of familiarity with the narrative, but it manages to avoid all those common expectations and present something truly honest and unique. Audiences found themselves moved and emotional, but when you think of it, the film isnt a sad story at all and it avoids the most common conflicts we tend to find in these genre family films. Chbosky did a very similar thing in the coming of age film The Perks of Being a Wallflower, another delighftul and engaging movie that feels familiar but isnt at the same time. Chbosky seems to play with the familiar genre conventions in these movies, but at the same time avoid the most common tropes and create something fresh out of it.
In Wonder we have one of the brightest child actors working today, Jacob Tremblay, playing Auggie, a young boy born with a facial diformity who must face the consequences of having to go to school for the first time in his life. Up until now Auggie has been homeschooled by his dedicated mother, played by Julia Roberts. She has put her own ambitious career goals and dreams aside to raise Auggie and make him feel loved. Owen Wilson plays the loving father, while Isabela Vidovic plays the understanding and supportive sister. The family dynamics here have all revolved around Auggie and making him feel loved, but now that he is about to face the real world and school bullying that dynamic has been completly shattered. The conflicts in the film arise from how this affects Auggie at school and back home as well. Noah Jupe also delivers a great role as one of Auggies classmates who seems to take a liking for Auggie. The narrative is told through the view point of some of these characters and through them we learn how each one is shaped by their interaction with Auggie. In a way it turns out to be a film of understanding and putting ourselves in the place of the other person, because not everything is what it seems to be.
I was pleasantly surprised at how well this film seemed to work for me. it was moving and uplifting at the same time. I was struck by some of these child performances, but most importanty by how well the story was constructed and how it avoided to fall into manipulative territory. The film is sweet, charming, and funny. The audience can sense the fear and agony that Auggie is feeling as he has to walk into school for the first time. Its an emotion the audience can identify because in a way weve all feared the start of something new like the first day of classes. We easily identify ourselves with Auggie and want him to succeed. The film may not be intended for cold hearts, but if you dont mind feeling warm inside than this is one family drama you wont want to miss because it is directed in a very crafty way. The secret lies in that even though the central message of the film is the most common cliche (being accepted for who you are on the inside and not based on your looks) it still manages to deliver it in a fresh and original way.

Based upon R.J. Palacios 2012 novel, this is Stephen Chboskys sophomore effort in the directors chair. The film takes place in Upper Manhattan, where August Auggie Pullman (Jacob Tremblay) is a ten-year-old boy being home-schooled in North River Heights. Because he was born with a number of physical defects, his youth has been a series of operations to correct his eyesight, hearing and facial features, which make him look like hes been an auto accident or a fire. But the boy is intelligent and excels at subjects like English and science.
Auggies mother Isabel (Julia Roberts) decides it is time for him to attend classes with other children. She enrolls him at a mainstream school called Beecher Prep, where the principal Mr. Tushman (Mandy Patinkin) is quite friendly. He has three students show Auggie around. Theres the budding child actress Charlotte Cody (Elle McKinnon), the snobbish trust-fund kid Julian Albans (Bryce Gheisar), and the rather average boy on scholarship, Jack Will (Noah Jupe), who will later become Auggies best friend. The first day of fifth grade is a challenge, with teasing to endure, but Auggie makes it through and starts to become determined to fit in.
At the 25-minute mark, a section begins entitled Via. Thats the nickname for Auggies high-school-aged sister Olivia (Izabela Vidovic). Although Via loves her brother, mother and father Nate (Owen Wilson), shes felt very alone since her grandmother Grans Minel (Sônia Braga) died a while back. Adding to her feelings of isolation, her best friend Miranda Navas (Danielle Rose Russell) returns from summer break changed and seems to want nothing to do with Via. Fortunately, the lonely girl meets a drama club member named Justin Hollander (Nadji Jeter), who invites her to sign up for the Theatre Arts elective.
At 50 minutes in, theres a section called Jack Will. It flashes back to his mother (Nicole Oliver) convincing Jack to help give Auggie the school tour. We learn how Jack develops a true friendship with the newcomer, but they have a falling out when Auggie overhears Jack telling Julian hes only being nice because Mr. Tushman asked him to. The good news, the split creates an opening for a girl named Summer Dawson (Millie Davis) to approach Auggie at lunch and become friends.  
The section called Miranda begins at 61 minutes. We learn of her past BFF relationship with Via, how her parents split and home life turned depressing. Lies she tells while working at a summer camp, pretending Vias family is her family, makes her ashamed to face Via in the fall, which explains their split. But as Via becomes closer to Justin, Miranda feels she is missing out, so she calls Major Tom (aka Auggie) to try and bridge the gap shes created. We learn also it was Miranda who bought Auggie his NASA space helmet one Christmas. 
The film jerks tears, to be sure, as the sentimental situations and heartstring tugging predominate. Themes of bullying, discrimination and compassion are front and center. The Grand Budapest Hotel is the film with which Wes Anderson finally answers his critics, and the message could not be clearer or more immaculately embossed in Futura on an insert shot of the most delicate stationary Go fuck yourselves. Anderson has been contemporary American cinemas most hostile aesthete for well over a decade, and ever since 2003s The Life Aquatic made it obvious that the filmmaker has exactly zero interest in apologizing for his affectations, each of his subsequent projects has been met with the kind of ecclesiastical rapture and blind derision typically reserved for racist politicians and superhero movie casting.
Rather than trying to show the naysayers that hes capable of more than they think, Anderson has instead devoted himself to proving the value of what they think he is  rather than broadening his film universe, Anderson has narrowed, deepened and dimensionalized it, the difference between The Royal Tenenbaums and Moonrise Kingdom being similar to that between a mural and a diorama. The framing device of The Grand Budapest Hotel would be enough in and of itself to continue Andersons inward trajectory, the story unfolding via a simple nesting doll structure that allows the filmmaker to practically incept himself. But The Grand Budapest Hotel isnt the most Wes Anderson film because of how densely it delivers all of the familiar tropes and fetishes (Miniatures! Orphans! Characters dangling from high places!), no, his eighth feature is a logical leap further down the rabbit hole of his own imagination because its the first Wes Anderson movie thats about Wes Anderson movies.
A four-tiered confection that moves with the wild energy of Fantastic Mr. Fox but lingers with a more brutal, weaponized version of the wistfulness that haunted Moonrise Kingdom, The Grand Budapest Hotel is a caper comedy about how the rise of fascism in the 1930s robbed an entire continent of its civility. More literally, its about Ralph Fiennes providing an 84-year-old Tilda Swinton with such regular and divine sexual satisfaction that several people meet their gruesome deaths as a direct result of her octogenarian pleasure. Its Wes Andersons third consecutive home run, but more importantly its the only one of his films to make all of them better.

Wes Andersons vertical movie, in which narrative, theme, and visual style all cohere to vertical principles. The film literally launches us into vertical territory by emphasizing the height of characters (Tall Gustave to short Zero), the use of vertical travel in elevators through hotels, trollies through mountains, and ladders through prisons. More than that, the frame itself becomes more interesting for its vertical properties in the 43 aspect ratio, where we see the height of these characters (Andersons makes a clever joke out of this with the giant prisoner), but also the space between them (how many other films use wide angle lenses for 43 compositions?). Then there is the idea of vertical history, of passing down from one generation to the next (take over), and the items we use to keep those who have departed alive - the shock cut to the final image of a girl reading a book while the statue monuments a small history in a world that few remember perhaps one of the directors most devastating gestures. Even as the world changes around us, perhaps we can keep our little bubbles safe, or sustain the illusion with marvelous grace. Andersons changing aspect ratios reflect this, as even as the world literally widens, the central composition remains the same, the negative space perfectly composed. Anderson always draws us into the central vertical - the space between two people and how they become one (Author and Zero begin in some of the films most distanced spaces as the exchange in the bath tub puts them on opposite fields of the 2.35 frame their final exchange is a pair of center framed one shots).
Anderson used to tell quite simple narratives in very idiosyncratic ways, but his last three films have become more metaphysical in a way that reflects the central questions of his aesthetics.

I think his world had been slowly shrinking, but in the end, it was all he had.
The Grand Budapest Hotel is visually stunning, with every frame pulling you deeper into its world.
Each shot feels like a work of art, and Wes Andersons signature style is evident throughout, creating a unique and immersive atmosphere.
The comedy is fantastic and perfectly executed, adding a distinct flavor to the film. Anderson is undoubtedly one of the directors with a unique and exceptional approach, and this film is a brilliant example of his talent. The attention to detail, the quirky characters, and the perfect blend of humor and storytelling make for an amazing experience.

Along side Fantastic Mr Fox, I believe this is the very peak of Wes Andersons powers. I actually think this could turn into another Sinners and be my next film to reach 13 revisits, theres just something so satisfying and special about the whole film. From the process of filmmaking to the actual application, its perfect in every sense and I cant imagine anyone else capable of creating such a masterpiece. 
Anderson employs a relentlessly beautiful commitment to symmetrical composition and meticulous staging that turns EVERY frame into a piece of art, and me being such a sucker for symmetrical composition and immeasurably pleasing staging.. well I was always going to love this, it was just a question of how much the answer is a lot. 
I could live in this world forever, I mean who wouldnt want to eat Mendls three-tiered Courtesan au Chocolat or listen to historic tales about The Grand Hotel all day.. probably very few. 
The use of color palette is a masterclass in visual storytelling, effectively segmenting the narratives different timelines and moods. The 1930s Golden Age of the Grand Budapest is curated by the iconic fuchsia, purple, and rich red uniforms, evoking a sense of decadent European luxury. Then theres the later years the Soviet-era timelines shift to drab oranges and browns, mirroring the hotels physical and spiritual decline. 
I love the clever use of aspect ratio shifts. It enhances the narratives distinct timelines with the main 1930 story presented in the classic 1.371 ratio, a deliberate nod to the cinema of that era, making the film feel like a crisply preserved relic. The 60s and 80s also get formats that mimic the popular cinematic formats of their respective eras, I cant speak highly of how flawless these ratio changes occur, its a testament to how well the narrative is layered. 
The ridiculously authentic and deadpan performances are the motor that drives the films unique humor. Andersons known for those ensemble casts that feel like a revolving door of cinematic royalty, its kind of amazing how many a-list actors want to be apart of Andersons stylized vision, showing just how regarded he is in this space. 
It was great seeing all these familiar faces turn up Willem Dafoe appearing made my day.. I went in without much knowledge of the narrative or cast, so this whole film was a gift that kept on giving. Faces like Harvey Keitel, Owen Wilson, Bill Murray, Jeff Goldblum, Adrien Broly, I mean you guys know how many names sign on, it was a joyous event to say the least. 
But its Ralph Fiennes as M. Gustave who is unequivocally the films centerpiece. He manages the challenging feat of delivering a highly poetic, often blasphemous language, all whilst operating with a completely straight face, making his character a sublime contradiction a refined, attentive, deeply sentimental lover of art and blonde women, yet a man capable of genuine courage and loyalty. To say its Fiennes best performance wouldnt be out of reason, its in the hat. 
The chemistry between Gustave and his loyal lobby boy, Zero Moustafa, is the emotional core and the cog that keeps this engine spinning. Zeros wide-eyed, committed deadpan contrasts beautifully with Gustaves theatrics, creating a comedic duo that nails the humor and drama work perfectly. Tony Revolori delivers his best work to date, honestly surprising considering Ive only seen him in the Spider-Man series.. which honestly doesnt do much for his acting chops, he deserves better than whatever arc Flash Thompson has been on in the MCU. 
The ending of the film is one of the best i can remember from recent memory, it doesnt just wrap up the adventure it provides a quiet, moving reflection on the nature of memory, loss, and the preservation of beautiful things. It shows that even the most perfect things, like the Grand Budapest Hotel at its height are fleeting, yet their memory is cherished through story in a way that can survive any political storm or harsh reality of change.
The Grand Budapest Hotel is a triumph of design, performance, and heart a singular work that confirms Wes Anderson as one of the most distinctive cinematic voices of his generation. Ill be watching this again by Sunday evening, I cant get enough of this world. Plus the fact it utilizes snowy conditions so perfectly makes it a must for the winter season, youd be foolish not to watch this in the next few weeks!
Happy to own this Blu-ray criterion, I can only imagine the level of excellence a 4k transfer of this would be.

For many years, Wes Anderson has been celebrated as an offbeat American auteur, with a narrative and visual style all his own - a colourful, melancholic whimsy riven with a biting, black comedic undercurrent. At times its worked well, others it misses the mark, but with The Grand Budapest Hotel he has created something truly wonderful. Inspired by the writings of Stefan Zweig, Andersons film is light, fun, thoughtful, cheeky, rude, farcical and emotional all in one rip roaring stew, never stopping for breath to tell a sumptuously filmed story about the passing of time, of friendship, of codes of honour, as well as commenting on a memorable slice of history, backed up by a galaxy of fantastic character actors. Its a joy from start to finish.
If youre new to Anderson in the cinema, prepare to be swept away, because The Grand Budapest Hotel looks utterly gorgeous. Set in the fictional Eastern European republic of Zubrowka, we are immediately presented with a landscape filled with colour, be it mountains of white snow or the classical elegance of the hotel, riven with reds and purples its a feast for the senses, a Wonka factory for the eyes, and his choice to shoot in three aspect ratios to represent the three time periods he plays in (the 1930s, 1960s  1980s) allows for the texture to change, representing one of the key themes in the piece. One might think this means Anderson has made a different kind of film with the period setting and time shifting narrative, but from the off this has all of his trademarks - oddball characters, hyper-real, stylised locations  careful camerawork capturing mood and expression, yet with a penchant for the comedic. That filters too into his script, which is an absolute triumph - touching, clever, frequently hilarious, with a story that neatly manages to weave a tapestry across three separate decades and even satirise the rise of Nazism without ever becoming too stodgy, or heavy, or forgetting were here to have fun with our plucky, debonair hero  literal moustache twirling villains. It often feels like a classic caper, left over from a bygone movie age, like a gem we forgot, yet one unafraid to be rude and sting you with a real darkly comic bite that other filmmakers would shy away from.
Though if Anderson deserves lashings of praise for such work, credit too must be shared with the phenomenal cast he assembles to tell his story - beyond frequent collaborators such as Owen Wilson, Jason Schwartzmann or Bill Murray, the list is breathtaking Jude Law, Tom Wilkinson, F. Murray Abraham, Mathieu Amalric, Adrien Brody, Tilda Swinton, Willem Dafoe, Jeff Goldblum, Harvey Keitel, Edward Norton, Saorise Ronan... some of whom have tiny or minor roles, yet all feel connected and part of the patchwork, memorably bringing to life Andersons offbeat creations. The whole piece belongs, however, to the leads Ralph Fiennes  newcomer Tony Revolori. Fiennes once again gets to play with his unexpected gift for comedy as Gustave, the suave hotel concierge whose peculiar proclivities drag him into a tale of murder, wealth  art, and hes effortlessly brilliant in the role - cheeky, charming, devilish, crafty yet touching  sweet, the kind of role you see rarely these days  one Fiennes eats up with relish. If anything though, Revolori is the revelation as Zero, the lobby boy whos story this all truly is, a naive young immigrant who becomes Gustaves partner in misadventure. Its their friendship that drives the picture, a double act thats often hilarious, more than not touching, and one Anderson wonderfully constructs with two gifted actors who work superbly together. Both deserve awards down the road and hopefully well see much more of Revolori to come.
It shouldnt come as much of a surprise, but The Grand Budapest Hotel is possibly a masterpiece. Wes Anderson is well known for his sense of whimsical style, though his work doesnt always properly connect beyond the senses. This does, in spades. Its a sweet black comic farce, masterfully put together with an amazing ensemble of performances, a beautiful score by Alexandre Desplat, peerlessly edited, gloriously shot by regular Anderson collaborator, cinematographer Robert Yeoman, working from terrific writing and direction. Honestly, you wont see many better films this year, and its quite possibly Andersons zenith so far.

O mundo perdido
No delicioso O Grande Hotel Budapeste, o diretor Wes Anderson retorna à Europa de sonho das primeiras décadas do século XX, que logo o fascismo iria desfigurar
Em 1987, nos exaustos anos finais do bloco soviético, um escritor, ensimesmado, toma de um exemplar de sua obra-prima, o romance Grande Hotel Budapeste. O que se verá, porém, é que o escritor é menos um romancista que um cronista de memórias  tanto das suas quanto das lembranças de um homem deveras curioso que ele conheceu no estabelecimento do título muitos anos antes. Corta para 1964. Por fora, o Grande Hotel Budapeste é ainda uma edificação grandiosa, pousada num topo e cercada pelos picos nevados da fictícia República de Zubrowka. Por dentro, porém, tudo já sucumbiu à desenxabidez do décor socialista a recepção de lambri e fórmica, os horrendos laranjas e marrons dos móveis e tapetes, as mesas cobertas com as toalhas brancas puídas que sobraram dos bons tempos, os uniformes de tecido sintético barato. Só uns poucos hóspedes ainda frequentam o decadente Budapeste. Entre eles está o escritor, aí ainda quarentão (Jude Law), que, durante um banho no spa de azulejos desbeiçados, trava amizade com o misterioso Zero Moustafa (F. Murray Abraham). Embora seja o homem mais rico de Zubrowka e o dono do hotel, quando se hospeda lá Zero dorme sempre em um mesmo quartinho acanhado da antiga ala dos empregados. Explica ele ao escritor foi ali que sua vida verdadeiramente começou. Corta, então, para o início dos anos 1930, a partir dos quais se adentra de vez o mundo excêntrico, particularíssimo e prodigioso do diretor Wes Anderson e seu O Grande Hotel Budapeste (The Grand Budapest Hotel, Estados UnidosAlemanha, 2014).
Todo filme de Wes Anderson  Três É Demais, Os Excêntricos Tenenbaums, Moonrise Kingdom  é de fato um mundo inteiro em si mesmo eles têm cada um seu próprio tempo, seu relevo, sua história pregressa, seus ambientes distintíssimos, tudo disposto com uma deliberação e uma simetria que os tornam imediatamente identificáveis como criação de Anderson. Tal rigor, perfeição e autossuficiência são, claro, contrários às leis da existência. Não resistem ao assédio da realidade (mesmo que uma realidade tão fantasiosa quanto a do diretor), e por isso seus personagens são flagrados sempre em momentos de transe ou crise. No mundo de O Grande Hotel Budapeste, o despontar do fascismo dos anos 30 começa já a ameaçar aquela velha Europa que ele logo mais vai arrasar. E, de modos diretos ou oblíquos, vai tocar todos os personagens.
Nas primeiras décadas do século XX, o Budapeste é ainda suntuoso um reino de cristais, pratas, veludos e linhos que Monsieur Gustave, o concierge, supervisiona com olhar implacável para a perfeição dos detalhes, como não tarda a descobrir o recém-contratado mensageiro Zero. O rapaz, que ainda nem saiu da adolescência (e é nessa fase vivido pelo ótimo Tony Revolori), é um refugiado de uma ou outra das numerosas tragédias étnicas eou fronteiriças que desde sempre afligiram o Leste Europeu, e cujos sinais já começam a se manifestar também em Zubrowka. Zero transborda admiração por Monsieur Gustave. E Gustave, que na interpretação inspiradíssima de Ralph Fiennes é ao mesmo tempo profundamente superficial e dedicadamente inconsequente, ama o Budapeste e seus hóspedes  especialmente suas hóspedes, e mais ainda se elas forem bem velhas, bem ricas e bem carentes.
Gustave é um caçador de tesouros, mas nem por isso suas atenções para com suas milionárias caquéticas são menos sinceras. Quando uma de suas preferidas, Madame D (Tilda Swinton), morre, ele se abala sem pensar duas vezes para a capital para prestar suas homenagens à falecida. Na mansão cavernosa de madame, porém, a briga pela herança já começou. E, na confusão, o filho mais velho e caviloso (Adrien Brody) põe seu temível capanga (Willem Dafoe) no encalço de Gustave, que fugiu carregando debaixo do braço um quadro de valor inestimável.
O Grande Hotel Budapeste não apenas retoma as várias idiossincrasias de Wes Anderson, como prossegue na bela curva ascendente que começou com a animação O Fantástico Sr. Raposo e há dois anos rendeu o que era seu melhor trabalho até aqui, Moonrise Kingdom. Além dos atores recém-chegados ao mundo do diretor, como Ralph Fiennes, Jude Law, F. Murray Abraham, Tony Revolori e Saoirse Ronan (adorável como a confeiteira por quem Zero se apaixona), batem ponto aqui, em papéis de maior ou menor monta, os seus companheiros habituais. In English Wes Anderson created in The Grand Budapest Hotel a nostalgic microcosm where formal rigor conceals an irreversible melancholy. More than an eccentric fable about rocambolesque adventures, the film unfolds as a lament for a world that no longer exists. Inspired by the literature of Stefan Zweig, its fragmented narrative structure, with layers within layers, reinforces the idea that history is always reconstructed with loss  of time, memory, and humanity.
The meticulously crafted mise-en-scène, with perfect symmetry and a saturated palette, is not just a stylistic device but a mechanism of preservation. M. Gustave, with his anachronistic elegance and almost farcical refinement, is a living reliquary of an ideal of civility. The dry humor and artificial framing contrast with the brutality surrounding him  the rise of fascism, the inevitability of decline, the loss of splendor. A tragic weight lurks beneath the playful surface, and that is what makes the film more than just a display of sophisticated aesthetics.
In the end, only the memory of a time when beauty and kindness could still exist remains. But even that memory is fragile, distorted by retelling and forgetfulness. The Grand Budapest, once majestic, becomes a ghost of itself. Like the stories we tell, the places we love, and the people who leave a mark on us

As we reach our halfway point for the year, Ive been revisiting the films which stuck with me most. Grand Budapest Hotel is still my favorite of the year so far, and since my first review was a bit of a cop-out (even if a rather successful one by my standards) Ive decided to write out the two central reasons why I love this movie.
Surface. Its often unpopular to claim that a movie is worth watching simply because it has a unique visual style, but Grand Budapest is really a tour de force of a single stylistic idea. The comparison between the movie and the Mendls boxes which it contains has been made before, but its not only the textures that are similar. The space of the movie itself is cubic and boxy.
The camera exclusively moves in 90- or 180-degree turns. There are a plethora of 90-degree pans, and the 180-degree rule is violated constantly. This makes sense navigating the halls of the titular hotel as it is quite boxy itself, but even outside the hotel the camera restricts itself to sharp-angled movements. There are a few exceptions to this, like the 45-degree upward pan when Gustave is talking to the man that hired Zero and the (relatively) unsettlingly odd-angled pans during the scene when Adrien Brody discovers the absence of Boy With Apple, but for the most part its surprisingly consistent. Even the aspect ratio for the majority of the film is trimmed down to 1.371, giving it a distinctly square feeling (despite obviously not being quite square).
Theres also a visual motif of people talking inside of, into, or out of boxes or other frames. This sounds excessively mundane until you realize how much of the screen is taken up by inert framing devices. During the prison escape theres a great shot where the escapees are looking through a hole in the ground, with the surrounding ground taking up 50 of the screen. People are shown through windows with the surrounding wall occupying the majority of the screen. This builds on the composition of the images which are for the most part perfectly centered. Its really quite spectacular in how un-spectacular it is, in how much it minimizes the spectacle on screen. This minimalism (both here and above in terms of camera movements) is interestingly ironic given how excessive everything else about the style is. These aspects are almost imperceptible next to the grand immensity of the color palette, and are a surprising example of restraint among excess.
Substance. With obviously stylized movies like this it can be easy to either be overwhelmed by the visuals or emotionally check out thinking its style without substance, but here Wes Anderson draws one of his more mature dramas to date. The film opens with the death of the author and from there continues on to contemplate issues surrounding the passage of time. 
The movie begins in present day and shifts gradually back to 1932. On the way, however, it moves through the 80s and 60s in order to get there. Then at the end of the movie we slide back upwards through these time frames. M. Gustave constantly laments the changing times and the fact that civilization is disappearing with the Grand Budapest being the last bastion against societys degredation. The hotel itself however also falls into disuse and fails in its role as the final wall against change. The central artwork Boy With Apple is described as a boy on the cusp of manhood, someone for whom times are about to change. 
This provides a framework for understanding the intrusion of the war which begins in the background and ends up taking a large portion of the story. The war is first introduced immediately after we learn that Mme. D. is dead, the sign of a transition to more serious times. Toward the end of the film Zero reveals that the war is the reason hes at the hotel to begin with, that he was displaced and has become a refugee. The army gradually becomes a larger and more influential part of the drama until they end up essentially taking over the hotel itself. The hotel and the story of the film is an allegory for the way life and the world around us is changing, and how it might not be for the better.

 Too Much Wes Anderson? No Such Thing.
Im a huge Wes Anderson fan. His films are events for me.
Too symmetrical. Too artificial. Too whimsical. Too much Wes Anderson.
You hear that criticism all the time.
I understand it.
In theory.
In practice, my answer is
GIVE ME MORE!
Give me the colors. The miniatures. The absurd camera moves. The dollhouse sets. The changing aspect ratios. Give me a hotel that looks like someone crossed a Sachertorte with an old picture book and a dollhouse.
Ill take the room key.
And as a Viennese, I feel disturbingly at home here anyway.
Of course Zubrowka never existed. Of course this hotel never existed. And yet I look at this world and somehow feel like I know it.
The grand hotels. The uniforms. The etiquette. The coffeehouses. The confectioners.
And when I see Mendls, I dont think
What a fantastic invention.
I think
Yeah. Basically Demel on LSD.
And I absolutely mean that as a compliment. 

 Monsieur Gustave H.
And there he is at last.
Our concierge.
What Ralph Fiennes does here is simply magnificent.
Gustave is cultured, vain, meticulous, romantic, utterly convinced of his own importance, and a man who apparently considers good manners one of humanitys greatest achievements.
At least until someone gets on his nerves.
Then his vocabulary can go from grand hotel to train-station toilet remarkably quickly.
I love this man. 
He recites poetry. He douses himself in perfume. He charms elderly hotel guests with a level of dedication that occasionally makes you wonder whether this is actually still part of a concierges job description.
And when the police show up at the hotel?
Naturally, he greets them politely.
And then runs away.
Monsieur Gustave H., ladies and gentlemen.
Ralph Fiennes plays him with such complete conviction that I believe every single second of this utterly absurd human being.
And then theres Zero.
Zero enters this world and gets to accompany Gustave through it.
And frankly
If Monsieur Gustave had asked me to become his new Lobby Boy, I probably wouldnt even have asked about the salary.
Give me the uniform.
Where are the suitcases?
IM IN.

 Everyone Gets to Join In
And apparently I wouldnt be alone.
Because at some point during casting, someone clearly decided that EVERYONE was allowed to be in this movie.
Ralph Fiennes. Tony Revolori. Adrien Brody. Willem Dafoe. F. Murray Abraham. Jude Law. Tilda Swinton. Jeff Goldblum. Edward Norton. Harvey Keitel. Saoirse Ronan. Bill Murray 
You half expect Marlon Brando to climb out of a cupboard somewhere and ask if theres a small part left for him.
And everyone looks like theyre having an absolute blast.
Im certainly no card-carrying member of the Adrien Brody fan club, but hes perfect here.
And Willem Dafoe?
Willem Dafoe is always an event.
Then theres Alexandre Desplats score, which for me belongs to the Grand Budapest just as much as Gustave himself. A few notes are all it takes and Im right back there.
I dont just hear this music.
I enter the hotel.

 My Favorite Scene
Thats roughly like standing me in front of the display case at Demel and saying
You may choose ONE thing.
Inhumane.
But fine.
The chase through the snow.
I love it.
Its completely over the top, gloriously artificial and so ridiculously cartoonish that the only thing missing is an ACME sign somewhere in the snow.
And I laugh every damn time.
Then again, I laugh an astonishing amount during this film anyway.
Gustaves way of dealing with his elderly ladies would be enough on its own.

 Where Does It Rank Among Wes Andersons Films?
Number 1.
Any questions?
EXACTLY!!!

I could actually hand in my room key and check out right here.
Five stars.
My favorite Anderson.
I laughed.
I enjoyed my stay.
What more could I possibly want?
And yet thats only half the truth.
Because somewhere between all the pastries, chases, poems, colors and perfectly symmetrical compositions, something happens.
The film becomes sad.
Not suddenly.
Almost without you noticing.
This beautiful little world begins to disappear.

 A World That Is Disappearing
Maybe it hits me especially hard because Ive read quite a bit of Stefan Zweig and Im from Vienna. That longing for a vanished Central European world is something you encounter again and again in Zweig.
And Wes Anderson takes that memory and turns it into his own fairy tale.
A world of grand hotels and coffeehouses. Confectioners and concierges. Uniforms, titles and manners.
A world in which even the utterly unhinged Gustave still believes that civilization might begin with the way one human being greets another.
And outside, another era is already waiting at the door.
A more brutal one.
Gustave holds on to his world anyway.
To his poetry.
To his perfume.
To his manners.
Maybe thats why, to me, he becomes so much more than just an incredibly funny character.
He is the last concierge of a world that is disappearing.
And the strangest thing is
That world never really existed.
At least not like this.
Not in these colors. Not with these people. Not with Mendls pastries and Monsieur Gustave H.
And yet I miss it.

Maybe thats why I really do want to be Zero.
At the beginning of the film, the answer would be simple
Because I want to have adventures with Gustave.
Because I want to run through the Grand Budapest with him, smuggle Mendls pastries and flee from the police.
But by the end, Zero is the one who does something far more important.
He remembers.
Gustave.
Agatha.
The hotel.
That completely insane, beautiful world.
A time that is gone.
A time that will never return.
And maybe thats a good thing.
But a little wistfulness is allowed to remain.
Maybe even a lot.


Five stars.
