Since the dawn of cinema, many filmmakers have left an indelible mark in the film industry for they employed a number of tricks or styles that made their motion pictures stand out from the rest. And in their attempt to do the same thing differently, they didnt only influence a wide range of filmmakers who followed them or were inspired by their works but those directors signatures  trademarks also pushed the art of filmmaking forward with time. Every director has his or her own way of shooting a film some employ unedited long single takes, others use swiftly edited sequences. Some present a certain theme in all their films, others present a discrete visual look. Some make heavy use of non-linear narration, others prefer a streamlined, simple version of a story. And the list just goes on.
And so when it comes to director Wes Anderson, there is only one thing thats present in every single filmmaking aspect of his works that makes it all unique the quirkiness. But more on that later. Set in the fictional Republic of Zubrowska, an alpine state situated somewhere in Europe, The Grand Budapest Hotel recounts the final years of the hotels glory days and tells the story of Monsieur Gustave H. the charming  devoted concierge who is highly responsible for the exceptional service  hospitality the hotel is famous for and who also takes great pleasure in courting the elderly blonde women whenever they visit the place. But when Madame D, one of his ladies, dies under mysterious circumstances and he is wrongfully framed for her murder, Gustave teams up with the hotels newly recruited lobby boy in order to get out of prison and prove his innocence.
Wes Anderson is one of the very few directors in the industry who has managed to stay true to his cinematic vision and never tried to compromise with his craft. All his films present an immensely distinct visual flair thats seamlessly blended with quirky wit, eclectic dialogues  idiosyncratic characters to give its viewers a bizarre cinematic experience. And on that scale, The Grand Budapest Hotel is no different for it is very emblematic of Andersons style and also has a tremendous charm to it. The production design is absolutely wonderful as the symmetrical sets  miniatures are wonderfully structured  meticulously detailed. Cinematography captures the film in three different aspect ratios to signify the timelines of the stories, and adds more lushness to its visual presentation. And lastly, the background score by Alexandre Desplat is another impressive feature in the composers bag that continues his rise in the film music industry.
Coming to the acting department, The Grand Budapest Hotel features a stellar cast in Ralph Fiennes, Tony Revolori, F. Murray Abraham, Edward Norton, Adrien Brody, Jeff Goldblum, Willem Dafoe, Jude Law, Saoirse Ronan, Mathieu Amalric, Tilda Swinton, Tom Wilkilson, Léa Seydoux  many more. Each actor is assigned an odd character to play on the screen and is introduced to the viewers in Andersons usually unusual style. Ralph Fiennes stars as Gustave H. and delivers the most impressive performance of them all as his stylish appearance  rapid-fire dialogues delivered with poker-faced expressions keeps the film moving with a cheerful vibe throughout its runtime. Tony Revolori plays the lobby boy Zero Moustafa with fine balance and does an excellent job at it while F. Murray Abraham gets to play the older version of this character who is narrating the story to The Author played by Jude Law. And we also have Edward Norton here in the role of Inspector Henckels the states cop.
The performance by the rest of the cast is no slouch either. Tilda Swinton plays Madame D and the story mainly revolves around her death as well as her will. Adrien Brody is in as Dmitri Madame Ds son, who is enraged with Gustave after the deceased lady bequeathed him with a very valuable painting in her will. Willem Dafoe plays Dmitris henchman, J.G. Jopling, and delivers an absolutely cold-blooded performance which was equally hilarious. Jeff Goldblum is in as the lawyer of Dmitris family and even his character has an interesting resolution. Saoirse Ronan plays Agatha Zeros fiancé  the baker at the Grand Budapest. And finally we have Mathieu Amalric who plays Serge X Madame Ds butler who had to forcefully testify against Gustave for the murder but later plays an important part in helping the concierge prove his innocence. The remaining cast also chipped in with valuable contributions in their little cameos and overall, there isnt much to complain about in the acting department.
I havent seen much of Wes Andersons films except for his last feature, Moonrise Kingdom, which was my first venture into this directors peculiar works and while it was no doubt oddly impressive but purely from the story perspective, I found it a little overrated. The ornate visual environments that so beautifully encapsulate his movies also end up overshadowing whatever little substance is present in those stories and this film is no exception. Still, there is no denying that Andersons latest is one of his finest films even if it may not qualify as a genre masterpiece. On an overall scale, The Grand Budapest Hotel bears all the signatures of a Wes Andersons feature and maybe even more. Its arguably his most accessible work to date thats exquisitely designed, gorgeously photographed, elegantly composed  is bolstered by some lively performances from its ensemble cast. Its like a delicious dessert course that is delicately served to its viewers and is one of its years sweetest, quirkiest, funniest  most enjoyable films. If you still havent seen it then just leave your doubts behind  check into The Grand Budapest Hotel as soon as possible to savour its high-quality hospitality. You certainly wont regret it.

Wes Andersons The Grand Budapest Hotel is far more than just a film it is a unique cinematic experience, a mesmerizing blend of sophisticated comedy, mystery, and nostalgic tale. Ralph Fiennes stars as M. Gustave H., a concierge of unparalleled elegance, whose charm, dry wit, and sense of honor make him one of the most memorable characters in contemporary cinema. His story, filled with twists and misunderstandings, unfolds in a luxurious hotel nestled in the mountains of Zubrowka, a fictional Central European country, where every visual detail is meticulously orchestrated.
As a true architect of the film, Anderson achieves a technical and aesthetic marvel. The pastel colors, symmetrical framing, and shifts in aspect ratios create an atmosphere that is both dreamlike and precise, as if each frame were a living painting. Alexandre Desplats Oscar-winning score, blending yodeling, flamenco, and church organ, enhances this playful yet deeply melancholic mood, while underscoring the underlying emotions.
Beneath this elegant surface lies a poetic and humanist fable. The shadow of fascism and war looms over a disappearing world, where luxury hospitality symbolizes a bygone era of refined and carefree Europe. Cultural references enrich the narrative with historical depth. The film explores universal themes friendship, loyalty, resistance in the face of barbarism, and nostalgia for a world that already seems like a thing of the past.
The cast, packed with stars, is simply exceptional.
A film that is both funny and poignant, The Grand Budapest Hotel celebrates the beauty of small things, the resistance of art against barbarism, and the power of human connections. It is a work where style never sacrifices substance, where every frame looks like it belongs in a painting, and where every detail tells a story. A timeless masterpiece, awarded Oscars for its costumes, production design, makeup, and original score, it continues to captivate with its narrative audacity and subtle emotion. A true treat.

Bill Murray as a style of film and as an added bonus .. usually starring Bill Murray.  I gave Rushmore several attempts, but could never finish. Maybe Id been misjudging Mr. Anderson all along.  Then, after expressing my love, I heard the grumblings.  Moonrise wasnt real Anderson.  He was off his game.  It was childish.  Oh oh.
Well, to start off I must say that I think I embrace his style more lovingly now.  The quirks, the beats, and the musical cues all seem to flow in a way that transports you into Wess world.  I loved the opening act, and how we were drawn into the story by Jude Laws Young Writers tale, then only to be transported into that story.  I love bedtime stories, and this was exactly the device that Anderson was using.  The aspect ratio switch when we move the sixties was kind of cute, but, well worn enough to be contrasting with Andersons original cinematographic style, but thats a minor quibble.
The Young Writer and Z Moustafas dinner, where the owner tells him his story, is gripping me even more.  This is exactly what I like, and its told in such a kindly way that I cant help but be enamored.    I also love the sixties signage that adorns the Grand Budapest today .. an encroachment of modernism on the grand ol dame.
Another aspect ratio change, and were back in the 30th.  Ray Fines M. Gustave winning manner is sweeping me off my feet. He certainly is commanding, and the camera follows him lovingly.  Dialogue is razor sharp, and Im completely charmed by his witty repartee as obviously is Tilda Swintons Madam D. is.  The staccato switches from gentle eloquence to Sailors mouth and back provides a smile.  So far so good, maybe Ive really come to like this Mr. Anderson.  
As the thin plot arc is revealed, and our protagonists follow, Im still captivated by great character renditions from Adrien Brody, William Dafoe, Harvey Keitel Jeff Goldblum, and Anderson regulars Edward Norton and, of course, Bill Murray.  But then it started to happen.  In or around the escape scene I began to get board.  While Id considered the events up to this point inventive and charming , they were now devolving to quirky, repetitive, and almost slapstick.  I really didnt want another twist, or another clever repartee.  I just wanted it to end.  I suddenly had echoes of Rushmore.
I think thats a bit too harsh.  I wanted to turn Rushmore off within the first 10 or 15 minutes.  This time, it was a good 80 minutes.  Maybe thats progress.  Maybe Ill love Life Aquatic or Bottle Rocket.  Im not counting on it, though.

Like any movie by Wes Anderson, Asteroid City is the epitome of a Wes Anderson movie. A film about a television program about a play within a play about infinity and I dont know what else (as one character describes it), this delightfully profound desert charmer  by far the directors best effort since The Grand Budapest Hotel, and in some respects the most poignant thing hes ever made  boasts all of his usual hallmarks and then some. A multi-tiered framing device, diorama-esque shot design, and Tilda Swinton affectlessly saying things like I never had children, but sometimes I wonder if I wish I should have are just some of the many signature flourishes that you might recognize from Andersons previous work andor the endless parade of A.I.-generated TikToks that imitate his style.
As expected, the world of Asteroid City is meticulously arranged with clockwork precision, and  as expected  that world is then populated with memorable characters who try to assert the same degree of control over their own lives. Characters like Augie Steenbeck (Jason Schwartzman), a quietly grieving war photographer waiting for the perfect moment to tell his four young kids that their mom just died, as if there were a correct way to drop that kind of bomb on someone. The time is never right, he laments to the father-in-law who never liked him (a wonderfully sour Tom Hanks as Stanley Zak, a pistol always jammed down the front of his shorts). The time is always wrong, Stanley replies.
The good news for Augie is that his teenage son Woodrow (Eighth Grade standout Jake Ryan) is probably smart enough to figure it out on his own after all, the science prodigy is one of four Space Cadets whos been invited to the 1955 Junior Stargazer Convention in the tiny Southwestern outpost of Asteroid City, where theyll get to show off their latest inventions to a government delegation that includes five-star general Grif Gribson (Jeffrey Wright) and famed astronomer Dr. Hickenlooper (Swinton). 
Perhaps the most notable of the many other figures in town for the weekend is famous movie star Midge Campbell (a Scarlett Johansson, in full control of her own star power), who looks like Liz Taylor, takes after Marilyn Monroe, and materializes in the window opposite Augies motel room with the cosmic alignment of a solar eclipse. Shes always rehearsing for something, and never misses her cue. Her daughter Dinah, also being fêted in Asteroid City, will inspire a similar awe from Woodrow par for the course in a film where love and loss orbit around each other in an endless chase, bound together by the gravity shared between them.
So far, so typical, even if Asteroid City itself is as vibrant and elaborate a location as Anderson has ever conceived. Home to exactly 87 people, this one-pump town is split along either side of a long desert highway and criss-crossed by a set of train tracks the government uses to transport everything from pecans to nuclear warheads. Theres a luncheonette with 12 stools, a motor-court with 10 cabins, and a vending machine where you can buy tiny plots of real estate as if they were candy bars. Theres an unfinished off-ramp that strands cars about 15 feet in the air, and  in the distance  a massive crater formed by a meteorite thats been waiting at the bottom of it for who knows how many years. 
Soaking up the clean light of the desert sun, Robert Yeomans camera reveals most of these sights to us in the span of a single 360-degree swivel, a flex that underlines Andersons absolute command over the films Chinchón set where his characters will soon be trapped against their will, thus forcing them to surrender the delusion of control that has defined so many of Andersons characters over the course of his career. Its maybe the most radical thing that has ever happened in one of his movies  the sort of transformative moment that A.I. could never dream up no matter how much data it ingested  and it spins Asteroid City in a cosmic new direction. What until then was just another immaculate Wes Anderson film suddenly becomes one of a kind.

In the midst of the cringiest and off-base TikTok trends youve ever seen, Wes Anderson just so happens to release his most meta and layered film of his career.
Asteroid City is Wes Anderson on hyper-drive. The setting, the dialogue, the play within a movie style, the cue cards dictating scene changes, on top of all the stylistic flare Wes Anderson already naturally possesses all come to fruition in Asteroid City.
A nuanced look at grief and trauma through the eyes of Augie and Midge, a beautiful back and forth on love and loss between Schwartzmann and Robbie, and the vast uncertainties of the universe and our place in it are just a few of the many themes tackled in this neatly packaged 100 minute film.
Brainiac and the fellow stargazers at the convention seemingly know everything vast engineering knowledge, the ability to remember and retain almost any and all information, and an almost arrogant confidence in their level of intelligence. We then realize just how little they actually know, how little we all know, and how things being uncertain in life is okay.
This is a movie that takes time to grasp, and I surely need a rewatch, but I was blown away by now meta Wes Anderson went here. A likely frustrating film for many due to the overarching realization that there is no answer, no justification, and no knowing for what is happening, what is next, and how to process it all.
What a picture. Andersons most complex film to date by miles, and it couldnt have come at a better time.

Wes Anderson films are best when they focus on young peoples emotions because theres no additional construct to get to their feelings when it comes to adult emotions, Anderson (almost) always has to add extra narrative structure that keeps distance from the adults. In Budapest and City its a meta-text nesting doll on the creative process that complicates the intimacy but feels more like safety for the director to not let us too close. 
Asteroid City is perhaps his most frustrating film for me because there are moments of such clarity that involve barriers between characters  such as Jason Schwartzman interacting with Scarlett Johansson between windowed bungalows and Margot Robbie on a fire escape  which perfectly encapsulate and illuminate his spatial distance from the audience hes trying to touch. These scenes are so strong that the whimsy beside them feel separate and tangled and ultimately what works the best Im not sure what it amounts to in the end because the whimsy of stargazing and alien spotting carries the story. 
Ill admit after much reflection that Im not exactly sure what Asteroid City adds up to. The creative process lets people go and confuses those involved because its impenetrable by its creator? But I love the look of it so much that it kept me interested throughout even if my head was spinning from trying to figure out why the meta text was inserted. Andersons films always have impeccable design qualities with certain colors that lead but he lets his Loony Toon landscaped desert lend a delicious color palette here of oranges and teal. Unreal and enhanced colors. I havent loved an Anderson movie since Moonrise Kingdom but I have loved how his camera use has evolved. Just gorgeous vistas, negative space, and fluid movements.
Aside from the black-and-white play within a play bits, there is a deeper meta text in the vending machines. Behind the hotel row of bungalows in this small community, a plot of land can be purchased though you dont own it really. This feels more in the realm of artistry that isnt being spelled out. If you enjoy the sights of a film you can purchase it and build upon it, but existed before you saw it and you dont know its history, roots, its layers of soil below. You only know the surface. But with Anderson, often, thats mostly what he gives us. With Asteroid City hes letting us know theres more but in such an elusive way it frustrates as much as it excites. But Tom Hanks and Johansson understand the sadness that is inherent in this work. They never get cute and you wish their wounds were given more landscape. Id buy those plots to explore.
Nihilistically, Asteroid City feels a lot like our place in the universe  its dotted with so many people, so much beauty, but it doesnt add up to some touchable truth, just a lot of noise. And in the end, as much as you think there should be some statement, its easier to just broadcast our initials plus someone elses cuz fuck it.

The French Dispatch was an ode to the writers and now Wes Andersons Asteroid City stands tall as an ode to the actors. The inner musings of purpose, the hunger for lasting effect, the drumming of a heartbeat frantically explained away by pain over existentialism because one is easier than the other to stomach. The era of storytelling Anderson has moved into is one particularly rich and auspicious. A love letter to cinema and stories and art and the artists who keep humanity eternal through their works. Particularly timely, isnt it? 
Andersons latest reminds that its not just symmetry or visual quirk that makes his work sparkle, nor is it AI smashing scraped bits and bobs together that makes art in general. Its the people, their stories, their perspectives, their emotions, the reflections of their lives that make life a worthwhile experience.

Anderson has been experimenting considerably since The Grand Budapest Hotel (maybe he realized that movie was a culminating magnum opus for his career to that point), and the decidedly mixed response to his recent work may account for this. Isle of Dogs played games with its language and translation gimmick that make total conceptual sense on paper but in execution played perhaps a bit too fast and loose with what we call The Discourse. The French Dispatch upped Andersons literary ambitions with its interwoven short stories that was easily his headiest and most philosophical work since The Life Aquatic. Yet this is his biggest departure yet, one that uses a prologue to painstakingly erect its set dressing and multiple levels of reality just so it can immediately induce a chaos that is normally conveyed only subliminally in Andersons work, and usually only at the climax.
We see a playwright come up with the idea for the story and struggle immediately with everything from a good title to a resolution to a theme. Actors wander into frame and realize theyve stepped into the wrong scene. The story is wildly upended just as soon as you think you know what its leading toward and leads toward a collapse unlike anything Anderson has attempted before. And yet, this leads to some of the most emotionally direct work of his career Schwartzman portrays the inside-the-story character with so many twee tics that it pushes Anderson to the point of parody, only to reveal they are the result of the outside-the-play actor admitting he is struggling to understand Augies mindset and motivation and is having a performative crisis. Augie himself radiates grief in a way that other Anderson characters do a better job of hiding, and slowly the films structural ruptures come to reflect the protagonists broken attempts to reconstruct the facades of Wesland to comfort himself. There may not be a moment as ragged as bits of The Royal Tenenbaums or Moonrise Kingdom, but thats only because the sadness is there from the outset.
Anderson captures all of this with work that is exceptional even by his standards. The Looney Tunes pastels of the cinematography and production design the actors all consciously drawing on both Old Hollywood poses and the stirrings of method that were on the rise in the 50s setting props are both janky and elaborate and show just how much Wes has developed his stop-motion in the years since The Life Aquatic by making entire features out of it. This is easily his best work in a decade, even for those of us who have delighted in his post-Grand Budapest material.

Similar to The French Dispatch, Asteroid City feels very much like Wes Anderson at his most idiosyncratic and free, exploring the construction of stories with his singular wit and distinct style. Asteroid City has a fascinating layer of artifice, functioning as a story within a story. The silly intricacies of such an approach are very endearing. For me Wes Anderson films are at their best when they are funny and set within an entirely constructed fiction. Therefore it shouldnt be too surprising that I find Asteroid City to be one of my favourites. Its very charming and funny. The narrative seems aimless and emotionally distant, but all the scattershot scenes form a story that delivers an arc across multiple levels of reality. Theres something refreshing about seeing a film which follows its own rhythm and structure without any compromise, especially since part of Asteroid City is an examination of the way stories are told, felt, and lived. There are so many characters here, most of them existing as amusing oddities that wander in and out of the narrative rather than following a dramatic arc. Asteroid City works best on those terms, as a fleeting blip of a film that exists in each moment as an unpredictable piece of fun that plays with form and structure. Its a top tier Anderson work and a fantastic encapsulation of his strengths.

Following a writer on his world famous fictional play about a grieving father who travels with his tech-obsessed family to small rural Asteroid City to compete in a junior stargazing event, only to have his world view disrupted forever.
As always with Wes Anderson, the question of whether this movie will be style over substance or not comes to mind. The majority of his outings work well, but will occasionally bring a story that doesnt quite work on the level he intends. It was evident that the film would look spectacular, and it absolutely does, but does this come together? Asteroid City begins in a compelling way, and the intrigue is evident from the opening sequence. Even though there is an overly complicated behind-the-scenes aspect to this story, the events that take place in Asteroid City always manage to reel it back in. When the focus is on this stylistic 50s setting that features a magnificent cast of characters, the narrative proves to be just as interesting as its trailers. Jason Schwartzmans Augie (and his family) is the highlight. Their dynamic is lighthearted and often hilarious, but arriving to this city seems to throw everything off. Augies relationship that he strikes with Scarlett Johanssons Midge may be the best aspect of the film, and Tom Hanks plays a down-to-earth grandfather who has some incredibly hilarious moments with the kids.
The town is spiraling out of control in the calmest sense imaginable, and as always with Andersons unique touch, we approach this madness in a stylish way. The shots are intricate, the cinematography is fluid, and the color palette is stunning. His approach to the 1950s is slightly different than I imagined, but the way he captures the elegance is fantastic. As subtle as what is happening at the forefront is, the madness of the background is what stands out here. Everything outlandish comes to a head in a scene later on in the film, and while it may be a divisive one due to its odd style, the moment works extremely well in and out of context. The humor that spawns from that key scene is fantastic. Where this film begins to wear you down is within its commitment to trying to be more than it should have been. The black and white scenes are filled with a few fantastic performances, notably Bryan Cranston, but this behind-the-scenes element is unnecessary. It is later upon layer, and I always found myself breathing a sigh of relief when we would return to Asteroid City that definitely isnt what Anderson wants here.
The resolution to this portion of the story also falls flat. Anderson has something absolutely fascinating to say somewhere within the confines of this sequence, but general audiences are going to get nothing from it. There is also a missed opportunity to move further into the exploration of the phenomena that our characters witness. A few of these intriguing plot threads created for us to soak in never fully get the care that they deserve. What does work hits hard, and the dialogue is so compelling at times. I expect a nomination or two, specially with production design. It is incredible what a visually authentic set can do, but there is some heavy lifting being done here by the visuals. Combining beautiful backgrounds with impressive use of lighting makes for a nice big screen experience. Anderson may be a bit in over his head when it comes to finding a narrative focus for Asteroid City, but a few of the characters and relationships will rank among his best to date. It will be interesting to see how this plays upon rewatch, but there is so much to like about this experience, even if I expected more overall.

It just takes you into this world and instead of progressing linearly just decides to tell you fun facts and go around the margins a bit. This world isnt merely a script bought to life. It exists somewhere that well never find. 
The performances are stellar all around, Johansson is great, Schwartzman is great, that big Margot Robbie scene was nice. Wes Andersons becoming less and less interested in being conventional and seems to aim for deconstructing his artifice. Wes Andersons style cant be replicated in a TikTok or even completely understood from his current line of work. Im not really a fan of Wes Anderson, from what Ive seen of his work. As you can tell I didnt like this film, nor did I like The French Dispatch, and I HATED Rushmore. I didnt mind Fantastic Mr Fox or The Grand Budapest Hotel but I didnt go crazy for them like a lot of people do and still came out a bit cold after watching them.
Honestly the only Anderson films I got genuinely into were Isle of Dogs and Moonrise Kingdom, but Im not even sure how theyd hold up upon re-watch. I should probably watch his other films but to be honest I lack any real motivation to do so. On average I just do not get on with his films.
I cant deny that it does bother me a little bit. Wes Anderson is an auteur with a very distinct style, and I think its great studios are willing to constantly throw money at this weirdo filmmaker. I definitely respect him, but I just generally dont like his films, and for a while I couldnt figure out why. 
Watching Asteroid City I came to an epiphany I prefer to look at a Wes Anderson film a lot more than I like to watch a Wes Anderson film.
Wes Anderson visual style is unparalleled. Every scene in a Wes Anderson scene is immaculate and brimming with detail. The sets are like meticulously detailed models brought to life and the colour palettes are striking. Every Wes Anderson LOOKS like the best film youre about to see, and its why despite my feelings towards his actual films Im always suckered in by the trailers. Without context his films look amazing.
So I can look at a Wes Anderson film absolutely fine. But when it comes to actually investing in whats going onscreen? Most times Im left incredibly numb and really uninvested in any of these characters, and I think a big part of it is how Anderson directs his actors.
Im not saying EVERY character in a Wes Anderson film is like this, but most characters in his film are made to act in a very monotone, static manner where their expressions dont change and they often just stare with void expressions at the camera usually TELLING us how they feel rather than SHOWING us how he feels.
That last point is a mild sticking point for me because I really dont get why Anderson doesnt seem to get shit for it. I honestly think the way Wes Anderson directs his actors is terrible, and even if its a stylish choice on his part I do think people should be harder on him about it. What adds salt to the wound is that he always attracts great actors to his films and directs them poorly. Seriously the cast for this film is insane!
Now because I cant invest in the characters, I cant invest in the story. In most of his films I just do not care or emotionally invest in whats going on, and its a shame because he does often try to deal with heavy subjects like the dealing with trauma and loss of innocence, but if Im being honest when I watch Wes Anderson try to talk about these things I feel like its being made by a robot, trying and failing to understand human emotion.
Sorry if this seems like a review of Wes Anderson in general and not this specific film, but truthfully everything I say above is what I think of this film. I love the set designs and how everything looks, and again the cast for this film is epic...but outside of admiring the visuals, I do not give a shit about almost anything I watched in this film.
I say almost because the alien scene is fucking great. Best first contact scene ever.

Its been a long time since I can say a filmmaker made me reconsider every notion Ive had about this medium yet its so tied to every single thing I hold so dear about it. Steeped deeply in the tradition of the theater, of cinematic language with a knowing acknowledgement of its place within the story but these elements exist for their own means and ends. Wes is taking an active refusal to adhere to any proper narrative function, a severing of the divide between theater and cinema, that when the form spills we see how far this can really go. Art is a play thing done by amateurs navigating the moment by moment growing pains of performance, telegraphing each of their lines and actions in a series of uncomfortable decisions and emotional breakthroughs. The troupe becomes the shining star, every off the cuff thought is entertained, all those first draft ideas you thought had no value are given credence and its passionate, intimate, has all the heart in the world and it wants to show it to you. 
Thats why Augie is the center of all this, hes the one actively trying to understand the production in real time and when he cant he lets it speak to him. Its a discovery that can only come through opening yourself up to the work and coming into it on your own (I do think this is extended to the entire cast, when the author leaves it was always them that were the creators). The rehearsal was the production, film is a young medium that deserves to be opened, inferring as much as you can and I have yet to learn so many things (all these mediums are much more free flowing and interchangeable than I ever realized). 
Right now I have lots to think about, I dont have to rush this just letting it simmer for a bit is the right call but I know Ill never have an experience like that again. Sometimes you really arent ready to have your fucking mind blown.

With Asteroid City Wes Anderson creates an incredibly vivid little world onscreen he gives his small town retro-with-a-twist 50s environment a level of care and craft thats really enjoyable just to get drawn into, filled with great little details that help compliment the understated quirky humour threaded in here. 
Within this setting Anderson adds lots of interesting layers, a variety of framing devices used to express some big themes (especially grief and artifice vs reality) in inventive ways. All the different flourishes added here can feel a little like theyre done for the sake of it at first, but eventually factor in really well, playing around with the story to add some extra weight to it. 
Theres a lot going on under the surface here, but it somehow never feels heavy, telling a charming collection of little character-based stories centred around an eclectic group of outsiders thrown together. This is brought to life by the all-star ensemble cast, all fitting the style here like a glove (Anderson newcomers Scarlet Johansson and Tom Hanks matching the vibe here especially well, while regular Jason Schwartzmans sensitive performance holds it all together).
Its sweet to see these different closed-off people gradually connecting with one another, leading to some endearingly offbeat moments. Each little thread developed here works well in its own right, brilliantly deadpan while also managing to pack in a lot of genuine emotion underneath.
Asteroid City can feel a bit too much like a writing exercise at times (maybe slightly stronger in theory than in execution), but I think theres ultimately enough substance there to back those ideas up and weave everything together, a charmingly low-key story with a unique feel all its own.

Amerikan bağımsız sinemasının nevi şahsına münhasır ustalarından Wes Andersonın kariyerinin başlarında yarattığı heyecan ve filmlerine karşı seyircilerin hissettiği merak ve çekim duyguları zamanla yön değiştirmiş ve Andersonı bir sinemacı değil simetri hastası bir tasarımcı ilan edenlerin sayısı hayli artmıştı. 
Kariyerinin özellikle son döneminde çektiği filmlerinde, bir araya getirdiği geniş oyuncu kadrolarının ihtişamına fazla kapılıp, iki boyutlu karakterler yaratmaya başlayan dolayısıyla izleyicilerin de bu karakterlerle bağ kurmasını güçleştiren, informatif yanı dramatik yanından ağır basan senaryolara imza atma tuzağına düşen yönetmenin son işi Asteroid City de bu eğilimden nasibini alıyor.
Kurgu içinde kurgu şeklinde bir anlatıya sahip film, tıpkı bir önceki Wes Anderson filmi The French Dispatchte olduğu gibi odağına yerleştirdiği malzemenin oluş aşamasını da senaryo kurgusuna dâhil ediyor. 1955 yılında hayalî bir Amerikan kasabasındaki bilim fuarına katılan çocuklar ve onların ebeveynlerini merkez alan bir bilim kurgu hikâyesini canlandıran oyuncular, bu hikâyenin yazarı ve yönetmeninin üretim süreci Asteroid Citynin esas anlatısına dönüşüyor. Bu anlamda Asteroid City, oyuncularına oyunun içindeki oyunda rol veren bir meta film aslında.
Film içinde filmin mantığını kavrayabilmek Wes Andersonın bu filmde karşımıza çıkardığı tek zorluk değil. Asteroid City aynı zamanda yönetmenin Isle of Dogs ve The French Dispatchteki gibi karmaşık yan hikâye ve karakter detaylarıyla dolu bir örüntüyü takip edebilmeyi de filmden alınacak seyir zevki için şart koşuyor. Açıkçası bu takibi yorulmadan gerçekleştirebilmenin bir yolu yok gibi. 
Zira Wes Anderson kadrajın her yerini simetrik bir düzen ve onlarca ufak ayrıntıyla bezediğinde aynı zamanda hem çerçevenin kendisine hem merkezde yer alan oyuna ya da oyunculara hem de kimi zaman bu tabloda yazan yazıya bakmak gerekiyor ki bunu tek bir seyir zamanı üzerinden gerçekleştirebilmek imkânsız. Bu noktada yaklaşık iki saat boyunca eksik hissetmeye gönüllü bir izleyici olmaya ve yönetmene gönülden bağlı bir kabulle hareket etmeye zorlanıyoruz. 
Başta sözünü ettiğim ayrışma ve Wes Anderson sevmek ya da sevmemek de tam bu noktada devreye giriyor. Anderson rüştünü çoktan ispat etmiş bir yazar  yönetmen olarak müdanasızlıkta bir beis görmüyor ve dışarıda bırakılanlar Wes Anderson sinemasını, suratlarına yapıştırılan süslü bir pasta olarak nitelendirmekten kaçamıyor.
Tüm bunların yanında Asteroid City, anne kaybıyla baş etmeye çalışan bir çekirdek ailenin yasla yüzleşme sürecinin de hikâyesi. Film içindeki filmde her duygu büyük büyük sahnelenirken, bir yandan da içinden çıkılamaz bir duygu, aynı işin yazarı tarafından tanımlanmaya çalışılıyor. Kendi özel hayatında da sevgilisi tarafından terk edilen yazar, meta filmde eşine veda etmeyi becerip bir başka kadına yeniden bir şey hissedebilme ihtimalinin varlığına kapı aralıyor. Çocuklar da kendi yaslarıyla farklı şekillerde hesaplaşmaya çalışıyor ve fondaki bilim fuarı, devletin uzaylı politikaları ve diğer detaylar yasın evrelerinde verdiğimiz tepkileri aynalıyor. 
Asteroid City bir oturuşta sindirilebilecek ve tüm detaylarına hâkim olunabilecek bir film değil kesinlikle. Hatta ilk seyir biraz sahneler boyunca karşımıza çıkan oyuncuları fark edip eğlenme, bazı görsel esprileri keşfedip gülme gibi davranışlara yönelik bir tecrübe gibi ilerliyor. Ancak özellikle Jason Schwartzman ile Margot Robbienin benzersiz bir etkiye sahip karşılıklı sahnesinden sonra filmin esas meselesi nihayet gün yüzüne çıkıyor. 
Hemen ardından tüm oyuncuların hep bir ağızdan tekrar tekrar Uyuyakalmazsan uyanamazsın diye haykırmasının da anlamı iyice belirginleşiyor. Wes Anderson kaybın içinden çıkabilmenin mağrur ve sarkastik bir umuda tutunmakla, bu kâbustan tam manasıyla uyanabilmenin en az bir kez uykuya dalabilmekle mümkün olabileceğini nazikçe fısıldıyor Asteroid Cityde.

Movies are meant to be fun visually and narratively. Wes Anderson understands it and Wes Anderson has no problem delivering his famous signature style time after time. To characterize Asteroid City it would be reasonable to call it a piece of meta-textual storytelling in its weirdest form. 
What I dont get is the meaning of Asteroid City. I feel dumb, and I probably am, but its the case where style over substance is prioritized over giving the audience a chance to have some coherent meaning. An over ones head experience. 
Yes, its a play within a play, but what else? And because of that, even if I found enjoying myself the entire thing, it was hard to engage with the characters that were -for the most part- underexploited. In terms of scoresoundtrack, a step-down compared to The French Dispatch. 
In terms of visuals, I think its his most organized, rich, and gorgeous. A disciplined art. A bold symmetrical cinematic triumph. Ingeniously evoking charming ideas and incorporating them within the rhythm of the film. Every frame is, in my estimation, compelling and smart. Monopolizing my attention wasnt too hard. 
All things considered, arm yourself with patience, it could be classified as boring and blurring and I dont think anyone would blame you. Definitely one that I will NEED (caps lock intended) to rewatch.

Better than French Pisspatch but thats not saying much. Andersons dedication to his style has quickly and efficiently become his biggest detractor, as his cold and overwhelmingly quirky tone often undermines his measly attempts at emotional or connective resonance.
Andersons work, especially as of late, presents itself at arms length, constantly reminding you of its own artifice and layers to a point where characters arent characters but rather two dimensional figures in a painting. Andersons best work, such as Fantastic Mr. Fox or Grand Budapest Hotel or even Rushmore are built on emotive connective tissue, emotions and messages drive the style, and in these works Andersons style is the substance. However through the years, this has changed, and all were left with is an auteur in crises, helplessly caught in the (false) dichotomy of style and substance. False is in parenthesis because this dichotomy has been self imposed by Anderson himself.
Theres a beauty to Asteroid City beyond its visuals but its a fleeting feeling, intangible and always out of grasp and out of focus. Like a handful of Andersons work, there is a melancholy present, but its presence is weak, often not felt or seen but desperately pushed by Anderson and his characters to communicate some non-existent complexity or sincerity. 
Perhaps its rather reductive to say this but Asteroid City feels like a Wes Anderson parody, yet this isnt the insult you think it is. The film is not without its impressive and intriguing moments of whimsy and marvel, and in the moment they feel feverishly fresh and exciting, but when considered in the grand scope of the film, feel like afterthoughts. 
Obviously this is a lot of critiquing and negatives but I still admired it because of Andersons quirks as well. Its beautifully shot, the set design is immaculate, the cast of characters are impressive and interesting. All of these aspects are done better in other Anderson films, but without comparison theyre great. 
Im not sure Wes Anderson is for me, I think as he furthers along in his career and gets more self-indulgent and dependent on his style, hell lose even more of the humanity he seems desperate to cling to, and then all well have is a bunch of pretty frames and fast talking quirky monologues about trinkets. Were nearly there as is.

This is my favorite Wes Anderson, the best movie of 2023, and the best movie Ive seen period since  I dont know when.
Any movie, even one that practically screams pay attention to the themes and subtext! like this one does, succeeds or fails based on how engaging its story and characters are. And Asteroid City succeeds wonderfully. Its a medley of interconnected storylines, three main ones and a collection of smaller ones, presented in two nested settings. Theres plenty of Anderson-esque humor to be found in all of them, but many of them also deliver some powerful emotional beats. And by the time we get to that devastating Margot Robbie monologue near the end, it hits like a ton of bricks.
The language used by the characters is delightfully awkward and wrong, mostly because they all redundantly over-hedge every statement. (I never had children, but sometimes I wonder if I wish I shouldve. Just a fantastic line.) It gets us laughing and amused while were listening to it, but after a while we begin to realize that it also lets us know how lost and uncertain they all are about everything.
But as great as the text of the movie is, its the subtext underneath the dialogue and characters and story that really sets Asteroid City apart. So, what is that subtext  whats it really about? Ask 20 moviegoers that question and youll probably get at least 15 different answers Its a meditation on grief. Its about theater and the relationship between performers and playwright. Its about the nature of art. Its about religionbelief and its relationship with science. And on and on.
Im in the camp that says its about the search for meaning. Specifically, its about how people have an instinctual need to look for deeper meaning in almost everything  in traumatic events, in peoples behavior, in art, in phenomena we dont understand, in life itself  and how we use (grasp at?) art, science, religion, etc. to satisfy that need for meaning. 
I read once that Anderson said that Close Encounters of the Third Kind was the movie that influenced this one the most, and my first reaction was yeah, of course, the spaceship and alien visuals. But I realize now its much more than that. The bulk of Close Encounters is focused on two people who are nearly driven mad by an all-consuming drive to understand what they witnessed and how it affected them. And you see that same sort of drive (minus the madness) in Asteroid City. Nearly every character is diligently trying to understand the hidden meaning behind something. Why did my motherwifedaughter have to die? What is that aliens purpose? Why does Augie burn his hand? Why doesnt the Celestial Flirtation math work? Whats behind my sons quirky habit? Anderson is saying here that you dont need extraterrestrials to artificially implant that craving for meaning, as they apparently did in Close Encounters thats just part of who we are as people.
I love that midway through the movie Liev Schreibers character emphatically says Whats the meaning? when confronting his son about his odd You dare me? fetish, rather than something more natural like Why do you always do that?. I also love that after the alien visit all the children quickly start doing unassigned art projects in an attempt to make sense of it all (again, echoes of Close Encounters).
Ive also seen this take on the movies subtext yes, its clearly about the search for meaning, but the movies answer is that its all meaningless, making the movie an unsatisfying exercise in nihilism. I think its telling us pretty much the opposite of that. The movies answer, spelled out metaphorically in the Willem Dafoe workshop scenes, is that there is meaning in life, and in art, but in order to find it you have to abandon your need to look for meaning in every little detail. You have to surrender yourself to the fact that a lot of the individual pieces of life (or art) are random and chaotic, and not driven by some larger purpose. You cant wake up if you dont fall asleep.
Its intelligent, its funny, its moving, its gorgeous, its thought-provoking, and it delivers a powerful and optimistic message. I think Ive seen it five times now, and Ive discovered new things in it with each watch. For me, its worthy of the word masterpiece.

Asteroid City follows a writer and his famous fictional play about a grieving widower who travels with his hyper intelligent, tech savvy family to the small town of Asteroid City to compete in a junior stargazing event, only to have their perceptions of the world changed forever.
Ever since I saw the first trailers for Wes Andersons Asteroid City, I slowly have built up anticipation for the films release, waiting to see what the director has cooked up. Asteroid City delves into grief, parenthood, and human connection in  Andersons own quirky way and for the most part, really connected with me. So many aspects of Asteroid City are the best or among the best of the year for me, with the star studded cast delivering the best acting from a cast, top to bottom, all year, Wess direction and cinematography being the best Ive seen all year, and the production and set design being my favorite of the year. All of these ingredients and more blend together to reel you in the small town of Asteroid City and its current inhabitants. While the ending was lackluster and left me confused and wanting more, I think Asteroid City is a film that is required to be seen twice, due in large part to Andersons uniquely distinct style and the rapid pacing, in order to get the full picture. 
None of the cast wouldve signed on and none of us would be in the theaters watching if it wasnt for the man behind the camera, Wes Anderson. Truly a master of his craft, Anderson continues to impress me with what I think is the best directed film of the year so far. Moving at such a rapid pace and bouncing between so many characters would make almost any director lose focus of the story and how to interweave everything you are trying to tell, but Anderson pulls it off nicely. Im a big fan of the symmetrical look Wes Anderson has become synonymous with and I think it may have worked the best in here out of all his films that Ive seen (Having only seen three of his works prior). This symmetrical technique mixed with the changing of aspect ratios helped to capture the feeling of watching a stage play come to life. While his direction and camera work were fantastic, Andersons writing left room for improvement. The film ends at a weird point and leaves me feeling like thats the end?. The films pacing was breakneck, resulting in a lot of characters speaking super quickly for no reason. Regardless of this speech pattern being utilized brilliantly for certain characters, like Jeffrey Wrights, there were also plenty of times that they were spewing out words far too quickly for my comprehension. Maybe that was a product of a late night showing or one of Wes Andersons stylistic staples, but I dont find that a reasonable enough excuse to not give more time in between some dialogue to give the audience time to retain everything being thrown their way. With the writing not being on par with the rest of what Anderson brought to this film, Id call it a flawed masterclass in filmmaking.
A Wes Anderson film isnt complete without its colorful cast of quirky characters played by Hollywoods A-List of actors and actresses and Asteroid City more than delivers in that department. Jason Schwartzman and Scarlett Johansson, as Augie Steenbeck and Midge Campbell, were the biggest standouts in a cast of excellent performances. I loved how they slowly formed a connection with one another through their shared life experiences and had great chemistry bouncing off one another through their neighboring windows. I was definitely the most invested in the Steenbecks family journey through grief and life in Asteroid City the most of all the plot threads. Tom Hanks plays another grumpy old man this year, as he plays Schwatzmans late wifes father, and nails the Wes Anderson look in here. Margot Robbie plays the late wife of Augie in a small cameo that later comes back into play at the end of the film in one of my favorite scenes of the film. Out of the four Steenbeck children, Jake Ryan was far and away my favorite. I loved the shy demeanor of his character and I couldnt help but smile when he finally kissed Grace Edwards character, Dinah, in the end. Out of the subplots and side characters in Asteroid City, I enjoyed Maya Hawke and her class the most. Hawkes personality fits like a shoe into June and I loved watching her character try to teach her class normally when theyve all just witnessed something that fundamentally changes everything they previously understood. Montana, played charmingly by Rupert Friend, is so likable and earnest that despite getting off on the wrong foot with June, due to her ongoing beef with one of her pupils, she cant help but fall for him. Jeffrey Wright, Liev Schreiber, Ethan Josh Lee, Steve Carell, and Sophia Lillis make up the other standouts in the supporting cast and delivered the best laughs in a film littered with great humor. Despite being the least engaging of all the parts of the film, I really loved Edward Nortons performance as the writer of the play. He is one of those actors that is perfectly made to be in a Wes Anderson film, so he cant do much wrong. I loved the cast of this film and its exciting to see so many talented actors and actresses line up out the door to be in a Wes Anderson project.  
I wouldnt have been as lost in the world of Asteroid City without the absolutely stunning production and set design. I dont think Ive seen this level of beauty and vibrancy in the set design of any other Wes Anderson film, and thats saying something. Filling the screen with bright colors and backdrops that look like a painting adds even more to the assetic of the film being a stage play coming to life. Production designer Adam Stockhausen better be up for the Academy Awards when this year is all said and done because the work he did on this film is nothing short of amazing. Asteroid City and Rye Lane stand alone as far and away the most visually appealing films Ive seen this year, both through their use of vibrant color palettes.
So many amazing technical elements are on full display in Asteroid City, which makes it easier to notice when certain elements are not up to par. Not only are the visual effects used for the alien worse than the atrociously bad visual effects in The Flash, but it makes absolutely no sense as to why they would do it the way they did in the first place. Wes Anderson is known for his love of stop motion and I think that couldve been a much better way of animating the alien touching down to earth and wouldve given it that feeling of truly not being of this world. review_text:
100
Gosh, this is about as good as it gets, isnt it? Wes Anderson, around the making of The Darjeeling Limited, maybe even before that with Life Aquatic, began to dive into the haunted rooms and melancholy nostalgia of his own fussy dollhouse aesthetic. His early films functioned as messy mannered displays of human absurdity, often chiseled with a quick line or grace note, the creative flower that allowed everything else to bloom into meaning. Gut punches like Ive had a rough year, Dad. or I know, she was mine too. soon fell into a form of precise flowery scripting that held the weight of the world in its balance the first time I heard I wonder if it remembers me and In the end, they shot him. could be on a personal shortlist of memorable movie moments. Wes Anderson, over the course of his career, has found a method of so outwardly and vibrantly sculpting his own universe that it seems to be a secret challenge of his to bury traditional schemes of emotion deep within the earths crust. The delight isnt merely in the mile-a-minute sight gags, the luminescent pastels, the harsh contrasts of vulgarity and sweet candy styling. Its also that one line, or that simple gesture, which wraps the entire production in a soft silky bow. All you need to do is think of that one moment, and the movie in every detail rushes back, a sudden flicker of memory. 
The Grand Budapest Hotel played with this effectiveness, tumbling down a rabbit-hole of stories within stories, observing how the façade of pre-war opulence is contrasted with the toils of history and the evils of fascism, and concluding with a harsh dose of reality that was often mistaken upon release as cold or sudden. If you felt that way, itll only take a second viewing to realize its devastating as fuck, and Wes Anderson hides his cards until the very last minute, depending on his lavish crime caper exterior to illuminate the anguish within. The French Dispatch isnt as politically-minded in spite of a partial May 68 inspiration, but it is fully an evolution of GBH (Isle of Dogs, which at release felt like a side-step, is even more so now) in terms of structure. Wes Anderson may not have a firm grasp of elaborating on the political context of his playhouse dioramas (and beyond aesthetic showmanship, Id argue theres no reason for him to, I dont need him to give us that), but he knows how to let these characters loose. 
His latest film is a joy of inventive sights and finnicky wonder. Taking on the format of The French Dispatch, a magazine that is basically The New Yorker in all but name, there is a great beauty in observing the ebb and flow of Wes Anderson freed from the constraints of a central focus. He leads us to that gut-punch in a tantalizing non-linear fashion. As an anthology movie, he dismantles and toys with ideas of city history, art culture, revolution, hostage situations, food, even the forbidden taste of poison. This is less of an ode to journalism as a concept and a practice, which is understandably how Searchlight has been selling it, than yet another tribute to Andersons appreciation of the collective. How our personal triumphs and failures, and the intertwining destinies of individual histories, can be organized into a single issue of a magazine. Our own stories guided along by an editor, maybe not exactly how they happened, but how they were meant to be known. Its an astonishing vision, and an absurd flex of filmmaking. 
Whats most obviously impressive is the length Wes Anderson goes to construct details that are almost immediately tossed aside. Its practically impossible to find your way into this movie. The shifts from BW to color, live-action to animation, not to mention the delicate balance of multiple aspect ratios. It starts and it rarely stops for a breath. But if youve been keeping up, itll knock the wind out of you, or whatever you might have left. Every actor is in pure Wes mode, drunk on that snappy, modulated serum he mustve concocted in a lab. DP Robert Yeoman continues to create images that will linger in my head (and one perfect shot instagram pages) for the rest of time. And Alexandre Desplat is still quietly filling the auditorium with the prettiest soundtracks of the modern era. Its so WES that the claims of it being self-parody arent fully off-base. 
But theres something here that I havent found in any other Wes Anderson film, except maybe Life Aquatic a genuine sense that hes searching for something beyond the structure of his own intricate design, or delving into the mechanisms of a great story. Not even focusing solely on narrative, but pushing towards the boundaries of his style, diving into sheer pleasantries for the sake of it. Hes really exploring his brand of iconography, self-aware and yet fully embracing his usual characteristics and quirks. But all the while, it becomes clear that hes painstakingly building up these tableaux, these scattered caricatures and stories, not just for a line, or even a moment, but one of his strongest conclusions yet. A final scene that is one crushing blow after another, moving and hysterical in equal measure. A band of workers mourning the loss of a man who believed in each and every one of them. No crying.

review_text:
Outlaw Vern had a viral tweet this week in which he said The Wes Anderson negativity Ive noticed lately is so goofy. Were people ever like, Oh great. Here comes Jacques Tati with another one of his fucking Jacques Tati movies? Putting aside the fact that, yes, people absolutely did feel this way about Tati, I am somewhat sympathetic to his broader point. Wes Anderson is a supremely talented filmmaker who has created a style uniquely his own, and thats not nothing. Hes also somehow managed to build a career in which he gets to hone further and further in on that style with each new movie. Thats not nothing either. In the current cinematic landscape, hes one of the only people whos able to work this way at this level, and I suppose I should be grateful.
However.
By the third of The French Dispatchs three stories, my stamina was flagging. Im trying to figure out why this very skilful movie has left me a little cold. I do think that Andersons cinema has started to be afflicted with a certain If everything is awesome, nothing is awesome syndrome. Again, I hate to sound ungrateful, because this movie is funny and entertaining and offers one perfectly manicured frame after another... but wow, these frames sure are perfectly manicured. It can feel exhausting. It would be nice to let a little air in there. Are we ever going to have another performance in a Wes Anderson movie like the one Gene Hackman gave?
I dont have this problem with Jacques Tati, whose cinema is every bit as fussed-over as Andersons. I think the difference is, movies like Mon Oncle and Playtime are about issues that meant the world to Tati, and about which he had complex emotions, whereas I felt a certain hollowness in The French Dispatch. Take its second story, which features Timothee Chalamet as a young would-be revolutionary during what appears to be May 1968. This segment depicts the student protestors as charmingly immature, and their cause as vague and ill-defined. Its funny, but its also the glibbest and easiest take you could have on this subject, and I kinda resented it. Anderson likes May 1968 as an aesthetic, but he also wants to stand above it, and frankly I dont think Wes Anderson has ever had a political thought in his life. Obviously hes seen Breathless and Masculine-Feminine and La Chinoise and he likes their style, but how much does he really care about them? For Godard, this political stuff wasnt a joke, and it still isnt.
The Anderson films that I find the most resonant, The Royal Tenenbaums and The Grand Budapest Hotel, are deeply melancholy films that foreground characters who embody the passing of an old world. This is clearly an idea that Anderson cares about, and which he gestures towards here, but which simply doesnt come across. Am I really supposed to feel anything when this films titular newspaper finally closes? As with Isle of Dogs, Anderson is playing in a foreign culture but is interested mostly in its surface, and thats a problem. One of the best scenes in Tatis Playtime comes when, in the middle of all this glass and steel, we catch a quick reflection of the Eiffel Tower. Its a powerful moment because Tati laments the loss of an old Paris that he loves, but he clearly also kinda likes the glass and steel. Is there any moment like that here?

NO CRYING.
Anderson goes back to his early love of cinema with this perfectly-crafted little pastel, new-wave dollhouse that is filled with so much obvious passion and joy in its construction and yet is populated with really sad characters experiencing these equally funny and painful vignettes around feelings of loneliness, aging, mortality, the death of politics and art. Some I think might find the lack of narrative focus distancing but for me, the winding formal tricks and strangely-detailed detours were the most moving part. They felt like an artist looking for a reason to put up with all those messy, painful feelings and stick around in a timeplace they may no longer belong in because who knows when or how you might discover that new flavor that reignites your passion.

Ich kann mir nicht helfen, ich bin verliebt! Andersons erster Anthology-Film, erzählt durch die Leitartikel verschiedener Autoren des fiktiven French Dispatch-Magazins, ist pure Kinomagie. So wundersam und schräg, wie man es vom Meister erwartet, so verkopft und sperrig wie schon eine ganze Weile nicht mehr. Anderson tischt vier Geschichten auf, die irgendwie ganz viel und irgendwie auch nichts zu sagen haben. Die Dritte, um Klein-Revoluzer Timothy Chalamet und Frances McDormands Polit-Journalistin, ist noch am Schwächsten, weil der narrative Unterbau zusagen wir luftig ist. Die restlichen Geschichten sind aber pure Andersonsche Quirk-ophonie. Vor allem aber visuell ist das einfach nur noch bezaubernd. Es mag Zuschauer geben, die werden in all den beweglichen Set-Elementen, ComicStrip-Einschüben und Hintergrund-Gimmicks dieselbe Oberflächlichkeit erkennen, die zum Beispiel Superhelden-Blockbustern vorgeworfen wird, Style over Substance, um von den dünnen Geschichtchen dahinter abzulenken und - ja gut, Unrecht will man ihnen nicht unterstellen. Aber ach, ich kann mich an diesen Bildern nicht sattsehen. Überall dreht und windet sich etwas, die Kamera spielt mit Sehgewohnheiten und Andersons Gespür für Timing und Schnitttempo erzeugen immer noch mehr Comedy alsechte Comedy.
The French Dispatch ist eine Ode an den Journalismus, eine Ode an Geschichten und Egos und Menschen. Viel zu lang und objektiv betrachtet sicherlich nicht Andersons Bester - aber guck, da dreht sich schon wieder das Bühnenbild auf den Kopf

review_text:
Usually, its easy to review a Wes Anderson film. Really, its as simple as employing a flow-chart do you like Wes Anderson films? If yes, you will like this one, now read on for a breakdown of what flavour of Wes this is if no, you will not like this movie. This time, it is not so simple. You see, I love Wes Anderson films. Ive seen them all and have found things to love in each film (even the lesser ones), a whole host of them I completely adore. So, it is with a heavy heart that I admit I hated The French Dispatch.
Here, Anderson takes us to a fictional French town where an American magazine is written, The French Dispatch. It is a portmanteau film, the bookends being the death of the editor-in-chief of the magazine (played by Bill Murray). Hes a man that loved his writers, but treated the rest of his staff horribly, and through this uneven indulgence ran his magazine into the ground  though this is sidestepped. There is a parable about the death of print here, a medium based on love, craft and obsession that will never be economically viable, but it seems forced and is prey to the overall artifice of this empty film. Really, this framing device is just an excuse to tie together some disparate short films. Each is themed after a section of the magazine and supposedly covers an article in an edition. We have a cycling piece (a travel piece, really) an arts piece a political piece (chronicling a youth uprising) and finally a gastronomical piece, that is actually a true crime piece. Each section is partly narrated by the fictional writer of the article, characters in their own right in the film, and is presented as an eclectic mix of colour palettes, aspect ratios and directorial decisions. It is all very, very fancy.
Frustratingly, the film is nothing but pastiche. It hides behind a veneer of homage but is too obsessed with its own craft, and its own fictional world, that it never resonates externally. On paper, it is an ode to the New Yorker, journalism, French cinema and a whole host of famous writers (theres even a dedication to them at the end). Theres even something pleasing about the idea of a New Yorker style editorial magazine writing from a French town for a Kansas audience. It is a titter-worthy juxtaposition but is endearing, reflecting what the film thinks it is a love letter to a country known through foreign eyes, and through cinema, from an American. This would put it of a piece with a lot of Andersons work, which often manages to glean real emotion and humanity by building towards, or around, tender cores. Yes, Moonrise Kingdom (2012) is an arch production of his trademark symmetry, but it is also an achingly beautiful film about what it is like to be a child in a world of adults. Even The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014), though a delightful romp, is built around melancholy. The French Dispatch has no human core. It is a hollow thing, a filmic machine made with upmost precision that just tells you a few hyperbolic stories in flashy fashion.
It is completely scattershot though, and tiresomely formal. This focus on stories in stories pushes the viewer further and further away. Each narrative is stylised and hyperbolic, an ode perhaps to the art of poetic and imaginative writing, but this approach fails massively. Wes Anderson films already exist in hyperrealities, the office of The French Dispatch itself already feels like a toy, a quaint thing, and from there we dive into further layers of fictionality and artifice. The already hyperbolised becomes exaggerated to the point of apathy, with no central core or emotional aspect to keep a viewer in tow. Really, it is all just too much. We keep switching aspect ratios, we go from colour, to black and white, to animation, to extended pastiche, to stage-shows, to lectures. It is a precisely made Russian Doll but it is assembled and disassembled with abandon. There is craft here, everything is meticulous and formally beautiful, but the craft is doing nothing. Our first story is a fictionalised cycle tour around the town full of kitsch and uncomfortably handled allusions to sex-work and a mortality rate. We are being introduced to our town and already it is nonsense, and overly affected nonsense at that. The narration is so consciously overwritten (this is true throughout the film), so relentlessly verbose, that it becomes numbing. This is combined with busy visuals where things go into split screen, or different text is appearing on the frame, or we have some overly complex visual setup. It is all too much.
This opening story is brief, thankfully, and has a few nice visual gags. There are some open homages to Jacques Tati, which establish an ongoing motif of alluding to a golden age of French Cinema. The problem is, as Anderson borrows from Melville, Truffaut, Godard (to an extent) and more, he doesnt capture the soul of those works. This is most apparent in the youth in rebellion segment, one with clear connection points to the work of Truffaut and Godard. It is a politicised sequence about an educated, intellectual youth realising their disaffection, and refining their anti-imperialist sentiments, so they can overthrow a bourgeoise system. It is in line with French cinema of the 60s and often filmed in a way that references that style, with production design that plays into this. But, those films meant something. They came out of an actual want for change. They were human or at least heartfelt. Even when overly polemical and annoying, there was an intent. This Wes Anderson sequence means nothing. It is framed via a reporter, Frances McDormand, and adopts her supposed journalistic neutrality. It is also all constructed as a sardonic joke. Rebellion is the punchline here, accentuated by playful gags and consistent irony. It doesnt capture anything human or meaningful, it is protest as aesthetic and also wants to mock the thing it is presenting. It also codes its characters, though they are often acted by adults, as teenagers (as children) and then sexualises them. We also have a referenced sexual relationship between McDormand and Timothée Chalamets revolutionary teen that causes more discomfort.
Another segment is about modern art, and it plays just like old person makes jokes about modern art for its runtime, interspersed with suspect representation of prisoners and those suffering due to mental ill-health. It is built around tropes of tortured artists and muses and madness as inspiration it is all hollow and irritating. The whole sequence goes on for far too long, has no real meaning and is a nice microcosm for the films overall issues. Yes, it looks nice, but nothing resonates and nothing fits together. This story has no relevance to the film as a whole and is not independently engaging. And were not even at the films nadir, yet. That would be an extended homage to James Baldwin that is completely tone deaf. In it, Jeffrey Wright plays the jouranlist, told through yet another framing device of him being on a talk show telling his story. The setup is like the iconic James Baldwin interview shows you will have seen and Wright, who is very good in the role, is telling a story that would become a famous article. This story is nominally a food piece, but is actually a true crime tale about a kidnapping that Wrights character happened to get caught up in. So, we follow him and the story, while we also follow him telling the story. It is structurally clever, in a technical sense, but yet another overwhelming affectation in a film full of these stylisations. The issue here is the content itself. The character is written as a crude caricature of Baldwin, saying things that you cant imagine Baldwin saying and even including a couple of homophobic moments. In this sequence we have clear cinematic references to Melville, perhaps Bresson too, but, as always in this film, the problem is Wes Andersons style and direction.
The film is just quaint. His films are always quaint. This quaintness is usually in concert with the subject matter, but here the chosen stories do not fit. This quaint take on Baldwin is reductive and part way through it we have a quaint presentation of police brutality. The film keeps on taking on bleak and politicised subject matters but does so with consistent, insufferable irony. This film is purely an aesthetic thing, it exists only to be affected and arch. It is fascinating as something based around journalism as the obsession seems to be about the form of this medium, not the content. Here, Wes Anderson is the editor not the writer. He is the curator of stories, the one that makes them sellable and that wrangles them into a homogenous thing. He is interested in the magazine as a physical object, as ephemera, not in the human stories contained within. It is an homage to the presentation of the written word, to the way stories are packaged and sold, but not to the stories themselves and the resonance they have. It is allusion, inside allusion, inside allusion, but, really, it is perpetual emptiness. It is an off-putting, gratingly ironic portrait of falsity that offers nothing outside of empty aesthetic pleasure.

review_text: A love letter to journalists, yes, and a love letter to newspapers, yes, but more than that is this a love letter to the world at large. If you really think about newspapers, theyre filled with wild stories that, front-to-back, would have enough material for several books. Interesting things happen all the time and the papers are a way of consolidating such events, bringing the world closer together while simultaneously expanding our perception of it. The French Dispatchs anthological nature is thus a perfect fit not just in representing the diverse set of stories that newspapers contain, nor the many personalities that write such stories, but also because it conveys the increasingly-chaotic nature of information that comes with globalization. The world is, and has always been, a fascinating place.

review_text:
To the surprise of no one, Wes demonstrates complete aesthetic mastery here. All of his typical bells  whistles are present and, to my surprise, The French Dispatch is chock full of new ideas and experimentation as well. The Grand Budapest Hotel felt like Wes taking his core style to a logical extreme, The French Dispatch feels like him finally building on that core and expanding his repertoire. Constant play with aspect ratio, black and white and text on screen feels genuinely fresh and exciting even for Wes, a filmmaker who has always stood out. If for nothing else, a Wes movie is always worth seeing to see an artist with a singular vision continue to push said vision to the next level.
With all of this said, I still had many of my fears going into the film confirmed. In his doubling and then tripling down on his aesthetics, Wes has all but left behind the heart and grounded characters of his earlier work. Its hard to describe, but the characters in French Dispatch feel not unlike Wess stop motion characters. They feel robotic, controlled to the T to spout Wes Anderson dialogue on perfect cue. No character felt like they had a life outside of their immediate scenes, they felt like actors pretending to be Wes Anderson characters who will then return to being themselves as soon as the camera stops rolling. Which is obviously what they are, but for the first time in his filmography Im unable to suspend my disbelief, they are too puppeteered, I cant ignore the strings.
Ive said it once and Ill say it again. Wess strongest skill was always his writing. In his best films, the style exists purely to uplift an already great story. The French Dispatch runs opposite, its desperately searching for a great story to uplift its already expected style.

I could just live in his pastel, organized, eclectic world for the rest of my life, and I got to for another two hours. People sometimes insult his work by calling it style over substance, but when the style is this stylish, I cant say I have so much of a problem with it. This was like having a big bowl of candy. I enjoyed every minute of it and was laughing throughout. From cameos, to bold story structure choices, this movie is going a mile a minute, throwing stuff at you from the beginning to end. I wanted to pause it sometimes just to enjoy how much effort he put into each frame, its simply astounding.
This is simultaneously his most beautiful film, and possibly the weakest story wise. His dialogue is superb, his staging is excellent, yet when this many characters are crammed into one little movie, its hard to feel strongly about any which one or their role. Wes Andersons best work involves unconventional relationships. While his movies are quite Instagrammable, its Suzy and Sam in Moonrise Kingdom, Zissou and Ned in Life Aquatic, and the Tenenbaum family that keep me coming back. There were characters in this movie that I really wanted to get to know more, and some that just existed as a hey, thats that person!
Even if this isnt a chef doeuvre, its impossible not to love and FUCKING FINALLY WE GET TO SEE IT!

review_text:
The French Dispatch is something you admire more than you actually enjoy. Overpacked with information, metaphors and details, The French Dispatch is not Wes Andersons most crowd-pleasing output, but it has all the potentials to become his most revered one in the future.
An uneven three-parter fantasy anthology, The French Dispatch shares some of Andersons trademarks and past glories, evidenced by its star-studded cast, quirky style, and exquisite designs. Yet its also unlike anything Anderson has put out, in that it sacrifices tons of entertainment values for artistic expressions, so much so it can be a hardship to fully immerse oneself into some segments of the storytelling, most notably in its first story of an incarcerated artists creative process. The stories do find their familiar grooves back at they go, as we witness the cutesy political ode of the second story and the cat-and-mouse crime thriller of the third. Overall The French Dispatch is not my favorite experience watching a Wes Anderson movie, but it has an air of maturity and warmth to it that eventually wins you over and pushes you to rate it higher than you normally would. Recommended for Anderson fans with patience.

review_text: I read a review of Amelie once that said it presented a fascist dream of France as scrubbed of any troubling social antagonism. The charming exterior was a whitewash of modern Paris for a twee cash-in. I never really agreed with that but I felt it a lot while watching The French Dispatch. Wes Anderson has become perfect at making references that are slightly off-center in a way that is both infuriating but ultimately makes me laugh. The jumble of bourgeois affectations and filmmaking techniques felt a bit like Annie Hall, but theres something similar with the later Woody Allen as well - relentless quirky self-comparisons to famous old styles. It made me want to scream at the screen a bunch of times, and to rage about how its middle class narcissism systematically avoids the ambiguous politics that informed the originals. Thats too easy, though, because there is a lot of ambiguity here. Every time I thought oh, thats so stupid I felt like Wes was whispering yeah, I know.
