review_text: As often with Anderson movies it is a fantasy that suggests both an utopia of craft and a sort of nightmarish escape. Some very creative minds imagining alternative worlds and what isnt on screen haunts what is. It is lovely made and for all the talk about its reinterative quality as usual Anderson tableaux are for more varied in feeling and strategy than given credit. Of course it also happens to be pretty much Andersons utopia and as such as revealing of the man as limiting for anyone who doesnt connect at least a bit with his imagination. It is about  an alternate New Yorker alright, but it is very much about the idea of idiosyncratic American auteur cinema done with large resources as a dying species. It is as morbid as celebratory, It is self-serving for sure, but very moving for me more often than not. Murray hangs over the film as a kind and attentive editorbenefactor while his death informs the action. The magazine closing with his death both a power display and a fair recognization the thing would likely be turned into crap by investors anyway. He allows creation, gives good counsel and ultimate owns it and can take it away. Every one of the major stories are about art and storytelling in a form or another and it is telling that they progress as they do (Swinton is a point of view over the Del Toro tale, the second is about McdormandChalamet relationship and the final one finally becomes Wrights own story). I like how the opening Wilson vignette offers a formal energy that help sustain the movie throughout. The DelToroSeydouxBrody triangle of artistic creation has such a great balace between energy, power and cruelty. The May 68 section is indeed by far the weaker although I think the main failure of imagination is how it set as a limited profile from the outset, the distance the story subject in a manner that isnt productive.  The Wright one is so encompassing and keeps find good detours and it has a couple of Anderson very best scenes (the one with Ronan and the final grace note), It moves from the overdetermined foreign perspective to specific in rewarding ways. Theres some mediocre jokes and like all Andersons work for the past 15 years one wishes he didnt overdo thing on post production. It can feel very tight conceived in spots and just take a turn into possibility in the next. The three tales have been clearly written for its stars and Anderson love for actors and how much they give it back to him shines through, I cant really get why anyone calls something with so much attention to minor bits of human behavior lifeless, a lot of what so good about it can be traced back to people who are in it for a  scene or two that are allowed to make such lively impression.

review_text:
A film about depth beyond the surface. Andersons films almost always appear in two dimensions to us, so what is apparent throughout is how often the film seems to push further in or out within the frame.  Layered surfaces are literally pulled back to reveal something in and out. Temporal strategies are employed throughout to contextualize art in ways otherwise inexpressible. An aside of (violent?) sexual rapture requires moving closer in to the audience to break the spell of presentation. The use of deep focus frames (evocative of Welless European work in particular) put faces in the context of horror disguised as whimsey (The most violent depiction of the police state just happens to come through a James Baldwin stand in whose only honest remark on the similarities of the US and Foreign lives shared by another POC is considered a passé remark by him but beloved by his white editor).  Often a staid frame is suddenly lit up through bullets and tear gas.  The pictorial here often becomes dimensionalwhat irony that in its literal animated sequence, it is the lack of a three dimension plane that leads to the villains demise.
The shallowness of art and its context has always peppered under the surface of Andersons films but now becomes the text of all three stories. Not that art is shallow, but its existence within historycapitalism, revolution, and the state as told by each storyoften blur its potential for appreciation.  A great meal cannot but be sidelined to a  smaller frame by the greater stakes of police violence. And thus Anderson holds color for moments when beauty might actually break through (the lights coloring a painting, a getaway by motorcycle, a pair of blue eyes). Why write about food?  Wasnt this supposed to be about a chef? once again demonstrates how Anderson more and more pushes the aesthetics of his films as his form of politics. What might be dismissed as a whimsical doll house of the past becomes a vehicle to reassess what it might mean to live in the chaotic present of history.

A letter on a film made by an American who moved to Europe, as written by a fellow American who moved to Europe
My dear Wes Anderson, 
your works have so eloquently collected the fragments of spiritual un-belonging, since the time when this letters author tried to make the characters of your early entires into mirrors of herself. 
Your first films lavished more so in character than they did in style. Your visual distinction existed through the aggregate portraits that you manifested of misfits and miscreants. You made a type of delicate symphony out of the sharp edges that come from fitting in nowhere in the world. 
As you aged, and, this author along with you, your films became more perfect, although, the individuals in them, perhaps - less singular. Style and character grew to live as equals in service to each others significance of existence. It is as if you have come to better know your own self and your own art, and so have less need to displace the search for both in the creation of other personas within it. 
If your initial films were generally on the theme of delinquent fathers, you have reached a point where you are, instead, a sort of father to your own invention. So, you now have less of a need to search for a parent who would rather not be found. 
Your portraits of absentee figures have instead become multi-faceted mosaics. 
Every piece is chosen with the care that you sought to find in the love of your former characters. They are made from the materials of Godard, Fitzgerald, Renoir and colored with longing. Not from lack of belonging, but now - from the recognition that even your having arrived at an intricate artistic perfection cannot -  on its own -  make a new wave out of one long ago crashed into foam upon a foreign shore. 
And so, you resurrect it as you are best able
As a stranger who has become at home in a foreign land ceaselessly enchanted by the  ability of its past to influence your own particular vision of the future. 
In place, you have finally created your greatest of characters.

Sincerely,

TRJ

review_text:
All great beauties withhold their deepest secrets.
A love letter (or perhaps a love newspaper?) to the artistic process in its holistic entirety. All about art, its inspiration, its medium, its subject, its object, its creation, its revision, its consumption, its meaning, its interpretation, its distribution, its reception, and, finally, its induction into culture at large, its presentation via Tilda Swinton lecture hall, its birth not only as an artistic object but as a cultural one as well. 
The moment I finally felt like I understood what was going on here was when, after much anticipation, Benicio Del Toro unveils his great masterpiece, and Adrien Brody flips out because he painted it into the walls of the prison gymnasium. But this is precisely the point he couldnt have painted it any other way or it would have been an entirely different painting. The medium is the message, and here the medium is the wall of a jail. Its not incidental that Benicio happened to paint his masterpiece straight into the concrete as Bill Murray says later, Thats the entire reason for it to be written. 
Likewise, The French Dispatch itself meets this function with its own form. Try to make it sound like you wrote it that way on purpose, Bill Murray says, and Wes Anderson does precisely that  and he does that with all of his films, of course, but most significantly here, where style is not only part of the substance, it is the entire substance, it is the meta-substance, it is both the text and the subtext. 
The medium is the entire message, whether its a fresco painted onto the concrete wall of a prison gymnasium, or its a political manifesto scribbled into a pocket-sized notebook, or its a meal cooked in the kitchen of a police station, or its a series of fictional newspaper articles inscribed onto celluloid. Its all about context. The beauty of art lies in finding different flavors, and some of those flavors might come attached to poisonous compounds, but they wouldnt taste the same if they didnt. The physical nature of art is inextricable from its artistry, its meaning is eternally bound up in its existential essence, form and function forever in a delicate dialectical dance.
2021  Wes Anderson

Damn you Wes Anderson ... you modern auteur visual genius of a quirky art-house filmmaker! Somehow you keep getting better!!! 
It began as a holiday. Eager to escape a great future on the Great Plains, Arthur Howitzer Jr. transformed a series of travelogue columns into the French Dispatch ... A factual report on the subjects of world politics, the arts, high and low, and diverse stories of human interest.
For me Wes Anderson has to be the most fun art house Writer and Director in the game today. I am just obsessed with how he can transform a live-action film into a cinematic storybook. And this time he went a step further by managing to incorporate the look and feel of his masterful animation into the film as well. There is so much dazzling Wes Anderson storytelling going on here, that it demands multiple viewings!     
(Quick Hits)
- Damn I am kicking myself for missing the one chance I had to go see this in the theater
- What a treat it was to get an all-new Wes Anderson experience drenched in his signature style. As much as the visuals are fantastic, so is the brilliant script that ties it all together
- We get the return of so many of Andersons favorite cast of characters. But then it was great to see new talents brought into the mix as well like Benicio Del Toro, Henry Winkler, Jeffrey Wright, Léa Seydoux, and Timothée Chalamet
- The film is this grand quirky but heartwarming salute to France, artistry, journalism, the writing process, and storytelling  
- There is so much packed into this film that I would need to go back through it bit by bit, and take notes in order to fully capture the interconnective flow of this narrative that still manages to be broken into a couple of sections
- In the past Anderson has gotten criticism about diversity in his films. And you can tell he has been listening to the comments since he included political elements like strong feminist and minority central story beats
It is strange to say that I love a film that I barely was able to take in. But the visual experience and wonderful characters alone of The French Dispatch had me not only thinking this is the most amazing film I have seen this year ... but this is Wes Anderson at his best!

I couldnt care. I just couldnt bring myself to care for anything that happens in this movie or for any character who inhabits this story or for any actor who is part of the ensemble or for any stylistic choices the director makes. A Wes Anderson film at first looked wonderfully quaint  quirky to me and Ive given them the benefit of doubt over the years but I cant do this anymore. This is it. His films are not for me.
The French Dispatch is a Wes Anderson film through n through. And I dont mean it in a good way. Like most of his works that Ive seen so far, the visual aesthetic is no doubt appealing to the eye, it is beautifully shot, comes decorated with exquisite set pieces, and is steered by a big roster of Hollywood A-listers. But just like most of his films, it is also emotionally disconnected, tediously paced, and devoid of any flavours.
The story finds the American filmmaker in self-indulgent mode and he makes the most of it in ways that only makes it all the more insufferable, not to mention that it also feels twice as long. Add to that, the oddball characters remain cold  distant, the nonsensical ramblings go on forever yet never create any intrigue or interest, the laughs in store are few n far between, and Alexandre Desplats score only adds to the eccentricity.
Overall, The French Dispatch is one of the blandest films Ive ever sat through and is arguably the worst film of the year for me, and easily the most disappointing. Fans of the filmmaker will have a better time with it than I did and may even find it delightful  amusing. But for me, this was an eyesore from start to finish that also affirmed what Ive known for a while now. Wes Anderson films are simply not to my taste and Im perfectly okay with that.

I like Fantastic Mr. Fox (I think - need to revisit it) but Im generally not a fan of Wes Anderson. Hes a meticulous craftsman, theres no denying that, and theres a kind of orderliness in his images that are nice to look at. Think folks are naturally drawn to eccentric, geometric, or symmetrical compositions, but its not like anyone can easily replicate what Andersons working with here. Yet to me, most of his films arent entirely satisfying (tbph they can be really annoying). He treats his aesthetic model as confectionary artifice - his illustrations may be alluring, but they come off more quirky than rapturous, consuming, or meaningful, perpetually resistant to any aesthetic or directorial invention. Basically if youve seen one Wes Anderson film youve seen them all cuz he rarely reimagines the very possibilities of cinema as comprehensively as his aforementioned model demands. Theres no point in making your films pretty if they dont offer any semblance of inner portraiture or some form of radical stylization. The French Dispatch is obviously more of the annoying shit that Im used to but theres something especially reductive in what it was trying to accomplish (reminded me of how I felt about Isle of Dogs), and I think its because its one of those films where its supposed to be a love letter to journalism  French cinema to some capacity (I see Godard, Vigo, Truffaut, Tati, Clouzot, and several other French cinema influences). Thing is Anderson conflates the cinematic penmanship of a love letter with this annoying kind of (cultural) nostalgia, and this lover letter is specifically addressed to The New Yorker (its not surprising at all that they gave the film a positive review). Their articles and essays can be good but Im not particularly fond of the magazine cuz they tend to be very highbrow and esoteric, so its basically for cosmopolitan readers who want to be intellectual and upwardly mobile. Essentially its aimed at an elite readership by providing intellectual delight to those capable of intellectual pleasure. Nothing wrong with wanting to be intellectual (Im a teacher after all), but its clear to me that their writing is primarily for these annoying bougie dorks who dont really care about the working class. And this attitude defines the way the film reductively treats its characters. 
Barely remember the first vignette in this anthology tho I remember the tortured artist rescuing the elites and the prison guards from the prisoners rioting? That was weird. But its the second and third segments that especially annoyed me. The second centers around this youth rebellion (May 68 reference?), which is obviously influenced by the highly political works of French New Wave filmmakers. review_text:
This is so beautiful that it reminded me why I love movies. The French Dispatch is easily, by a long shot, Wes Andersons most unique movie and unquestionably one of his best. Its a grand story about a magazine called The French Dispatch and its editor who recently passed. The story we follow is both about the magazine and the articles in it. Its a love letter to journalists and each of the three main stories is written by a character inspired by real-life people. 
There are three separate stories shown. The first is about an artist in prison, the second about a student revolution, and the third is about a kidnapping. The first story is a homage to the art dealer Lord Duveen. 
The story about student riots is inspired by Mavis Gallant and one of her articles about the May 68 student protests. The last story is very clearly a homage to James Baldwin. Anderson has stated that his source of inspiration for this film is his love of The New Yorker. Baldwin and Gallant were both frequent contributors and Lord Duveen is notable for having a huge six-part article about him published in the paper. And not just the writers, but most of the main characters are based on real people involved with the newspaper in some way. 
Each story has a distinctive visual style and tone. Scenes will switch aspect ratio and from being in color or not erratically. I consider this Wes Andersons most unique movie not only for those reasons but because there are shots in this that are completely unlike anything else hes done. Theres an intimate level of emotion in many shots here, on the same level with a handful of my favorite shots throughout the rest of Andersons filmography. 
I am in love with how this movie looks. It has a sense of movement that I think is much greater than most other of Andersons films. Its constantly moving from story to story but lets each moment breathe for as long as it needs. There are so many tender moments that even though there are dozens of characters I still felt like I got to know each one. 
Its amazing how large the cast is and how great is cast is. Just now looking at the list, there are a little more than 20 actors that I recognize by name. Its an awesome cast and there are even roles that are on screen for less than a minute and yet Anderson still filled that with a great actor. I think my favorite performances were from Léa Seydoux and Jeffrey Wright, I also really loved Christoph Waltzs cameo. 
Another thing I loved is how much this feels like reading a book. The film is about writers and pays homage to many real-life writers, so it makes sense that a huge focus is on the passion of writing. For this and for a few other of Anderons movies they give me an intense desire to read a book, and that feeling is awesome. I think that urge comes from how perfectly written his dialogue is and how often his characters feel like accomplished and passionate people. Its a strange mix that makes me want to both be productive and consume art in the most focused manner. 
This film inspires me and fills me with an overwhelming feeling of wanderlust. Its the kind of movie that makes you want to create art and consume art devotedly. Ive just seen it but I already feel like every scene is etched into my mind. Its a movie that I can tell will stick with me and that I will only grow to love more and more over time. I cant wait to watch this again and it has the potential to become my favorite Wes Anderson movie.

review_text:
Wes Anderson making an anthology movie seemed inevitable, since his films are often about moment-to-moment cinematic quirks rather than fully fleshed out stories. I was personally very excited for The French Dispatch, anticipating a Wes Anderson film more to my tastes. I find his comedy side fun and exciting, whereas the dramatic portions of his films generally feel insubstantial and dull. So an anthology of comedic short stories and sketches seems ideal for what I consider to be Andersons strengths. Sadly however, it ends up like most anthology films, being very inconsistent, with some stories working better than others.
There are three main stories, with various odds and ends crammed around them. The first story, The Concrete Masterpiece, is a long but funny segment about an imprisoned artist. Benicio del Toro and Léa Seydoux are clearly having a lot of fun, and their characters have a perverse relationship which is quite amusing to watch. It drags on a bit though and ends up unwieldy as a story, with so many time jumps and needless asides.
The middle story is Revisions to a Manifesto and it is easily the weakest. It isnt as funny as the other stories and the central characters are not very interesting, especially Frances McDormands drab journalist character. There are allusions to deeper meanings, as the story parallels student revolutions in the 1960s and theres a lot of pondering about journalistic neutrality, but these themes are reduced to surface level lip service and little more.
By far the best part of The French Dispatch is the final story, The Private Dining Room of the Police Commissioner. Jeffrey Wright is absolutely stellar as the central character, with his wonderfully expressive voice perfect for the narration. Its a ridiculous plot, but delightfully nimble and absurd, and leaner than the other stories, with the main action taking place over hours and days rather than months or years. Plus this is the silliest segment and so I had the most fun with it.
At this point Wes Anderson has really honed his craft, and The French Dispatch showcases fantastic technical detail, in the production design and cinematography. Though his stylistic flourishes seem arbitrary here, with the colour to black-and-white switches almost random, and the same goes for the aspect ratio changes and mid-sentence shifts from English to French dialogue. The huge cast of recognisable names clearly enjoy his style though and it looks like they all had fun making this movie.
The French Dispatch is presented as some kind of tribute to journalism, similar to how The Darjeeling Limited was presented as a tribute to India, but really this is just an excuse for quirky stories to be thrown together. The French Dispatch is wordy work, that makes you admire the beauty and humour of language, but its not a lot more than that. It is the weakest Wes Anderson film in a while, and personally I think it is just the final segment that elevates it beyond some of his others. The French Dispatch is both fun and insubstantial, but nevertheless its charming enough to entertain more than bore.

i read somewhere - its likely to be on this app somewhere - that what was so alluring about Wes Andersons films is that he makes gorgeous people, well strangely ordinary. although, after seeing and hugging Saoirse Ronan the other day, i can say that she is far from ordinary. 
what is most fascinating about these, the characters of Wes Andersons The French Dispatch, is that, despite what we may feel, they remain nothing more than acquaintances to us. 
so why do they feel so warmly familiar? why do their movements and awkward gestures all seem to point in the direction of home? its an enigma that is so truly hard to understand, yet in understanding it would likely lose much of its beauty. so, lets stay unknowing - at least for the most part. 
Wes breaks that boundary, destroying the convention we are all so used to expecting, that we are meant to deeply and truly feel for the characters of a film on a wholly emotional level. 
rather than mourning the way they mourn, laughing the way they do, or crying over their same woes, we feel indebted to them and all they are offering us, all that is being served to us purely as a piece of entertainment designed to consume us. 
and that couldnt more perfectly encapsulate the essence of this film as a masterful exhibition of what art truly is. 
despite being abstractly cynical throughout its entire runtime - and would it be a Wes Anderson film if it wasnt - it retains the almost childlike like view of the world and fascination of the unknown that he has within his grasp.
beyond the enjoyment of breathing pure fresh air of Wes Anderson, the film is otherwise a show of the pure power that a few words scrawled down upon a plain piece of paper can have, and perhaps this is also why.  
its so easy to fall in love with the films and their vibrant colour palettes, plotted out to be even bolder than ever with Wes only now offering them to us as a slice before taking away the rest of the pizza. you cant help but be left wanting more of his eye-popping, mind-lulling, heartwarming sets in your eye view on that cinema screen. 
as much as that made for the cinema Dune marketing trick is likely true, you cant help but feel that this film is also made for such a comforting place. 
the true heart of it shines out, glowing over every face in the either large, airy space bringing everyone together, or small, cosy room drifting all into their own worlds from the comfort of their seats. all while their popcorn sits perfectly on their lap, almost full from the lack of time given to even think of such a thing. 
Wes Andersons The French Dispatch is a beautiful meditation on life, art, journalism, and the heart of the individual - no matter how coldly he presents it - and is simply one of his best works to date.

Theres always that one line in Wes Anderson movies that just knocks me sideways. He knows the moment in this one. He acts coy and he toys with it, but it stills hits as hard. Its the line from Jeffrey Wright where he says, with good luck, maybe well find what eluded us in the places we used to call home.
Im a big believer in the idea that we can learn so much from other places. Not everywhere has it completely right or wrong, but nationalism and isolationism are toxic ideologies under any circumstances. In the case of The French Dispatch Liberty in Kansas is richer for its cultural gifts from the city of Ennui. 
This is a line that makes me think about the way Wes might feel about his new Parisian home and his connections to his Houston roots. He may have escaped to a world that better suits his own kind, but he continues to think about where he came from, and what he can give back, focusing on crafting work primarily designed to be distributed in US markets. 
As an immigrant myself, I often think about what eluded me in England and whether or not Im finding it here. I feel like I do when I get the opportunity to participate in experiencing films like these. This is a line that reveals the heart of The French Dispatch and how its one of Wess most personal exports yet.

Maybe with good luck well find what eluded us in the places we once called home.
Like I said in my Marty Supreme review, passion can turn into religion when the sin of obsession drips like blood onto a page, a free-flow of ink and consciousness you into a piece of art against Gods will. Its an illumination of the things we love the most away from the devotion of God and the angels above, an illusion well defend till we die, and in Wes case, he wholeheartedly does.
I wanna buy it.
Why?
Because I like it.
Its not for sale.
Yes, it is.
No, it isnt.
Yes, it is.
No, it isnt.
Yes, it is.
No, it isnt.
It is. All artists sell their work. Its what makes you an artist. If you dont wish to sell it, dont paint it. Question is, what is your price?
50 cigarettes. Actually, 75.
Sometimes the greatest of artists are the loneliest of people, giving up a life of religion, joy and socialisation to form their own lives on a typewriter or screen, they forget the horrors of a world not built for them, a world they must survive in all the same. A prison cell can turn into a church where the bars crystallise to stained glass, a product of the mind of a genius mistaken as a murderer. The prisoners, (Moses), brain doesnt think in the same way as the obeying and committing hive mind the rest of France does, therefore he MUST be somewhat of a threat. His work catches the attention of Julien Cadazio, an art dealer adamant on turning his work into something of commercial or economic value. Theres a sense of the tortured artist and the artist and his muse as themes in the first act of the film, both of which eventually become the fuel to Moses limited and unique creativity in which his modern art isnt understood by most, but thats what makes it so intriguing. Often the most broken people find their medicine in painting away their pain, smearing a bloody red over the camera lens or stressing a melancholic yellow on the bland wall behind them. As an artist Moses is unhinged, romantic, and flailing, just like his mental state. His internal, yet loud, work is vigorously brought out into the open world by the art dealer Julien, becoming an enormous hit globally to the public and critics alike. Hes asked to have a second piece made soon, in which he struggles to create without his muse Simone, who he also has possible slight romantic connection with (I mean who wouldnt with Lea Seydoux). His final piece, a mural of amber carved into the wall like insects in sap, is a warm piece of genuine art thats presented inappropriately to a cold world that isnt there for admiration, but for their own gain, not appreciators of art like they claim for the cameras, but exploiters of talent as known to their clients.
He is not an invincible comet, speeding on its guided arc toward the outer reaches of the galaxy in cosmic space-time. Rather, he is a boy who will die young. He will drown on this planet in the steady current of the deep, dirty, magnificent river that flows night and day through the veins and arteries of his own ancient city. His parents will receive a telephone call at midnight, dress briskly, mechanically, and hold hands in the silent taxi as they go to identify the body of their cold son. His likeness, mass-produced and shrink-wrap packaged, will be sold like bubblegum to the hero-inspired who hope to see themselves like this. The touching narcissism of the young.
The entirety of the film faces a miserable world of black-and-white mixed with a flourishing mentality of an artist in pastel, chaotic French revolutions and handheld camera movements, all while remaining symmetrical and intricate in its design. Its an expression of the true form of all art in general, raw yet careful, free but controlled in a manner that differs based on the artist or writer. The controlled protests that happen on the streets of Ennui, using chess as a metaphor for a stylish movement over a violent one, using the blunt cutlery of the checkerboard chess board over the sharpest knives of the block. The conflict becomes a performance, a dark blue and yellow dance with the local police over differing beliefs and ideologies. Theres a naivety to the youth of the protestors, because when challenged on what theyre actually fighting for, the barricades of their defenses fall quicker than a depressed man off a roof.
There is a particular sad beauty... well-known to the companionless foreigner as he walks the streets of his adopted preferably moonlit, city. In my case, Ennui, France. I have so often... I have so often shared the days glittering discoveries with no one at all. But always, somewhere along the avenue or boulevard there was a table set for me. A cook, a waiter, a bottle, a glass, a fire. I chose this life. It is the solitary feast that has been very much like a comrade... my great comfort and fortification.
As presented with food and meals, the hidden flavour of life can be found in art, too, it isnt always just an excuse to create a delicate violence or an escape for the mentally insane. Because just like a magazine, art tells a story. Any passion can fill the field of loneliness once it becomes a routine, a sensory overload of joy and abundance of depression that can give life and energy to even the least motivated writer on the planet. This entire film is a homage to art, in particular journalism and writing, a three-part anthology that comes together to form a beautifully tedious yet never boring tale that says a lot more than meets your eye.

A love letter to journalists set in an outpost of an American newspaper in a fictional twentieth century French city that brings to life a collection of stories published in The French Dispatch Magazine.
This may be the most Wes Anderson that Wes Anderson has ever Wes Andersond. Did that make sense? Basically, this is a combination of all of the things that we think of when he comes to mind, but each element is turned up to an 1110. There is a lot to The French Dispatch, as the overarching plot is composed of three distinct stories. Beyond these stories, you have the editing room that we cut back to and the mini Owen Wilson adventure at the beginning. Wilsons role is integral because he describes this fictional town in the best way possible, and he gives us some insight into the type of tone we are in for. Everything that happens here is being told to us through the perspective of a few individuals trying to collect these stories for this magazine, and we are dealing with the fallout of the death of the editor (the film starts with this). As you can see, it is a lot to take in and this collection of tales can be overwhelming at times.
The story never feels jumbled, but it is difficult to get attached to a few of these characters when we spend so little time with them. The middle tale is probably the least effective, even when the performances are just so good. The entire cast is top-notch throughout, but the standouts include Del Toro. Seydoux, and Wright. Jeffrey Wrights performance is a 2021 highlight, as he delivers so much through his delivery. Each story brings something different to the table in terms aesthetic, atmosphere and even tone. We even get an animated portion that adds a distinct feel to that final story. Judging by visuals alone, The French Dispatch is truly outstanding. Part of me thought it could get overlooked for production design, but there is just no way it doesnt get a nomination. Each story is interesting enough, but I didnt quite with them on the level I should have. A more focused narrative seems to be Andersons strength, so I hope his next film gets back to that, as opposed to an anthology.

review_text:
Wes Anderson fazendo um filme sobre o seu próprio método. Não no sentido de uma mera punheta vaidosa e autoconsciente (ainda que, definitivamente, flerte com isso), mas no sentido de explorar os limites do seu próprio processo de um modo maníaco.
Enquanto que em vários dos seus outros filmes a natureza literária das narrações e dos diálogos é bem evidente, mas nunca, exatamente, o tema central, aqui ele assume os textos da revista como uma espécie de partitura que irá ditar a construção visual de cada capítulo.
Literalmente se utiliza de um arsenal histórico do cinema e do audiovisual - Jacques Tati, Rouben Mamoulian, cinema moderno francês dos anos 60, talk shows, cine reportagens, animação, etc - para encenar esses textos-partituras. 
Remete até mesmo a uma dicotomia entre um cinema de atrações (as ilusões, os efeitos de montagem) e a potência dramática que os textos sugerem. Usa esses formatos audiovisuais tanto a partir da sua fascinação mais direta e primária como também explora as suas potencialidades narrativas. 
Mesmo algumas relações mais básicas com a decupagem tendem a ser subvertidas. Principalmente em como trabalha com a variação entre a cor e o preto branco, e como faz planos com enquadramentos exatamente iguais que apenas vão alternando de eixo pelo cenário (já na reunião na sala do editor no início faz isso muito bem).
É um filme muito rigoroso no modo em que trabalha com essa variedade de formatos, mas também muito aberto na forma em que mescla tudo isso em apenas uma cena. 
Tudo isso poderia virar um carnaval pseudo hipster com muita facilidade, mas ele nunca se deslumbra com nada e tá em busca mais de uma agilidade que dita a métrica poética do que uma fascinação barata ou meramente sentimental. 
Inclusive dá tudo tão certo porque o sentimental brota dessa lógica cumulativa, dessa dinâmica de acontecimentos e imagens que vão se acumulando, e não de uma imagem ou situação final que integra tudo isso em uma última e derradeira mensagem. A moral da história está mais no processo do que na história.

review_text:
Wes Andersons The French Dispatch is a flood of descriptors and details you can be overwhelmed or just go with it and get swept away. It has an avalanche of actors, but the largest parts in the anthology ensemble are allotted to Benicio Del Toro, Adrien Brody, Leá Seydoux, Tilda Swinton, Timothée Chalamet, Frances McDormand, and Jeffrey Wright. It concerns ex-pat American journalists covering culture, politics, and food in France but done in the style that The New Yorker trailblazed early on, through portraits of individuals not privy to be profiled before. Andersons film is essentially one issue of a magazine, with each section not so much acted out but rather blown out. This is a pretty big statement but I think its the best-looking film Wes Anderson has ever made mixing black-and-white photography, Tin-Tin animation, bright pastels, miniatures, and frank (not shy) sexuality. Sometimes theres so much packed into every frame youre not even sure what the story is anymore. But it doesnt matter because every detail is so meticulous, and our awareness of the type of film it is, makes the brisk and impersonal pacing permissible. 
The black-and-white and use of negative space is such a welcome look for Anderson, who often stuffs so much into every scene. While it retains the heightened design quality, this frequent New Wave framing approach does mix in lots of new looks for the auteur. After a few stumbled introductions that work like a table of contents, including an Owen Wilson bike tour of Andersons made-up French town of Ennui-sur-Blasé, Anderson sinks into a pleasure dome groove for the lengthier stories. Theres the story of prison artist, his art dealer and his muse (Del Toro, Brody, and Seydoux) told by Swinton as the article writer then a very Wes Anderson appraisal of the 1968 student rebellion with fewer politics outside of access to the girls dorms and desire for perfect manifesto language (this is Chalamets section) told by McDormand as the author. And then theres a kidnapping story thats supposed to be about food. The latter, featuring Wright, one of the most criminally under-used actors for decades is an absolutely PERFECT actor for Andersons pastiche. Del Toro is also a welcome addition who would make a great regular in Andersons massive ensemble of regulars. His story is the best of the three. In fact, I wouldnt have minded if that was the entire movie.
With a jaunty score, Alexandre Desplat outdoes himself, too, because he, like the camera and production design, gets to play with multiple genres and appearances to match Andersons ode.
Structurally, its somewhere in between the Coen brothers Hail, Caesar! than The Ballad of Buster Scruggs because the film affords Anderson many different styles he wants to replicate from film noir, to a stage production, to Tin-Tin. And as opposed to not being linked to anything except location, the story he has made is done by writers reporting to Bill Murrays editor and publisher. For me, its a little overwhelming, but its a complete joy to watch, though emotionally more distant than Anderson has ever been (due to the anthology structure). Theres no ability for Anderson to slow down here, he just sets down the track and puts the train on full steam. The rare movie I would want to rewatch at a slower frame rate than intended. But even though that would let me see more of the details it would not let me locate a heart.
More on day 7 of Cannes.

review_text: Like The Grand Budapest Hotel, The French Dispatch is a celebration of humanity amidst decidedly inhumane circumstances. Frames within frames spin narratives within narratives, each segment a unique depiction of authoritarianism running rampant, with only a select few dedicated to preventing art, culture, romance, and compassion from being blotted out entirely. Latter-day Anderson films tend to double as pseudo-documentaries about their own worlds, and this is the most complex example yet, dense in its storytelling and visual detail, and reminiscent of a trailer in how rapidly it barrels through each painstaking beat. The actors do the heavy lifting when the script cannot, and although its pacing threatens to suffocate the otherwise thoughtful character work, its still light enough on its feet to facilitate moments of rambunctious humor or disarming emotion. Jeffrey Wrights journalist explaining his Why immediately ranks as one of the directors most breathtaking scenes.

SILENCE. WRITERS WRITING. 
Its in the tenderness hidden amidst the sternness of Bill Murrays voice. Its in the furrow of Timothée Chalamets brow. Its in the cracks sounding up and down Léa Seydouxs back as she stretches. Its in the way Jeffrey Wright crosses his legs as he sits. Its in the widening of Frances McDormands eyes. Its in the way Saoirse Ronan pulls the trigger.
Its in the promptness of Mathieu Amalrics movements. Its in the way Adrien Brody embraces those around him. Its in the way Tilda Swinton adds inflection to her words. Its in the way Lyna Khourdri snaps a compact shut. Its in the way Owen Wilson leans into his words, as though they are their own actions. Its in the way Steve Park maneuvers up a set of spiral stairs.  Its in the deafening emotion permeating from Benicio del Toros gaze. 
Its in the details. In Wes Andersons worlds, its always in the details. 
What comes next? 
Everything. Nothing. Anything in between.

All great beauties withhold their deepest secrets.
Here we find Wes Anderson at his creative aesthetic zenith. Unending quirk delivered with all the unbridled energy of a sugar-starved child let loose in a sweet shop. Endlessly playful, ceaselessly so. A million morsels of art. Fragments collide and fall like a flurry of flecked paint upon a triptych of canvases. Not every element of this ever-changing symphony sounds as sweet as it first seems. Often the quantity overwhelms the quality. Any hope of harmony is betrayed by sheer chaos unfolding onscreen. Albeit incohesive, The French Dispatch does function as a hectic collage of heightened madness. This is a barrage upon the senses of a certain sensibility not suited for all. It can be as dazzling as it is dizzying. What more can be said that it is doubtlessly the most Wes Anderson film to ever have Wes Andersoned.

At once the most and least of Wes Andersons recent films. Most because his stylistic and organizational acumen is in overdrivestories within stories, sets within sets. Least because it all seems even more flat and diorama-ish than usual. Certain of the characters and scenarios were memorable, particularly Del Toro and Adrian Brody. Jeffrey Wrights riff about dining and restaurants being a comforting port-in-the-storm was truly moving, even tearful (I know, NO CRYING). But thats pretty much it.
McDormand MUGS. And her story is bad not just because of its condescending, parent culture politics (its probably wrong to assume that a director who dresses like a ventriloquist dummy is anything other than a bourgeois caricature, politically). Because even its basic beats feel so conventional. The student radicals just wanted to look pretty and fuck? Yawn. This is what everyone thought at the time. I know Anderson is solely interested in that impression, and not the underlying action. But I think it still behooves a filmmaker operating 60 years after the fact to muster something about May 68 that might qualify as an insight. 
And he is capable of such insight he does it in the modern art sequence, which frames the emergence of that movement in ways that dont give it the obvious short shrift. Teenage leftists arent so lucky I guess. As Anderson ages, I worry hes becoming one of those people who pins pretty butterflies inside of glass boxes doomed to be admired more than pondered. Its too bad, because his films used to muster real affect more capably.
Some nice wallpapers, though. And I enjoyed the tableau vivant bits especially.

This is an ode to magazine feature writers told through three short stories connected by scenes from the editors office. If nothing else though, this will be the most stylish film youll see this year  every frame is beautifully composed, and it will need a couple more views before Ill be happy Ive picked up on all the details.  
Theres no attempt at realism - this is the Wes Anderson cinematic universe so theres a combination of models, moving scenery and animation pulled in to drive the stories forward.  The whole film is bursting with creativity and ambition, and while it may occasionally over-reach itself its a fun, fun ride.    
Not everyone is going to appreciate this though  the lack of a single narrative arc will frustrate some and it will just be too Wes A. for others, but I had a big smile on my face throughout.

review_text: Something Im not sure has been remarked on this is Andersons first film where the young are completely at the periphery. The only other film of his I could see working in that mode is Fantastic Mr. Fox, my favorite of his, and thats somewhat mitigated by the use of animation. Saying Bottle Rocket counts hinges on referring to the central characters as adults, which I am not comfortable doing. The French Dispatch is grounded entirely with adults in comparison, and Anderson takes the chance to deploy arguably his most dense and ecstatic collection of compositions to underline a myriad of ethical considerations in the world of arts, politics, journalism, and food preparation. Its as eruptive in its humor as his other films, but it no longer feels like Anderson is convinced that adulthood is just a more tormented, less ethical, and passionless progression of childhood. Fatherhood might have very well made him more hopeful. Absolute god-tier stuff from Benicio and Wright.

Nonetheless, I think it still has a charm to it even if it doesnt quite have the same heart to it that a film like Moonrise Kingdom or The Grand Budapest Hotel had. The cast is often wonderful, also as expected.
Pretty decent, but like most anthologies some stories really worked for me (Timothée Chalamets in particular is incredibly funny) and others dont always hit the landing. Not going to do much to change what you think of Wes Andersons movies, whether you like or hate him.

A showcase of skill, passion, and untamed love of the craft, The French Dispatch is a wild, beautiful, chaotic (yet somehow still mindblowingly organized) mess of a film. The movie is sectioned into 3 chapters, and each chapter is great (although the third is for sure my favorite). The insane scope of cast members is dizzying at times, and the film goes at breakneck speeds. Its hard to maintain any real semblance of meaning of a scene until the next one has already started. And I get thats kind of the point, how these publications are set in this fast changing environments by necessity. But just from an audience standpoint, I would have taken more away from each moment, if it were paced slightly slower. Wes films are often criticized for being style over substance, but this is a film where Id argue the style IS the substance. So much hard work obviously went into the technical aspects of this, itd be unfair to rate it low just because it has less character or story strengths. Its just a bit more of an abstract piece, is all.
Wes is a great filmmaker. But remember that so many other artists work go into the realization of these films as well. The style of Wes Anderson is just as much the style of the production  set  costume designer, or the cinematographer, composer, editor, and even gaffers. This film is a huge flex on every technical front, so if you praise it, do praise the whole effort, and not just the big name up top!

review_text:
Es war einmal ein kleiner Junge, der rückte alles und jenes zurecht. Er rückte Bilder wie Möbel, Häuser wie Autos, Menschen wie Tiere und ganze Stadt- und Landschaftsbilder zurecht. Macht aus Kurven Ecken, aus Kreise Vierecke, aus Wellenlinien Linien. 
Warum er dies tat, einem inneren Trieb entsprechend, seiner viereckigen Brille geschuldet, seiner pedantischen Ordnung zu verdankend, es war einerlei, den das Rätsel um seine Vorliebe für die Symmetrie, den auf alles niedergeworfene Bilderrahmen, es blieb ihm zeit seines Lebens verschlossen. Er wuchs damit auf. Seit er denken konnte, war dies so. Und so akzeptierte er es, als eine Grundfeste seines Lebens. 
Was viele Probleme hervorrief, lebte der kleine Junge in einer Welt aus den Fugen, in seinem Fall, aus der Symmetrie. Bilder blieben, geschuldet ihrer schludrigen Verankerung, Möbel durch ihren Designer, Häuser im Aussetzen der Zeit, Autos im selbigen und der Witterung, der Mensch aus Gottesebenbild, die Tiere als ein Gedankeneinfall dessen, und Stadt- und Landschaftsbilder dem Wandel Untertan aus der Symmetrie. Schließlich waren sie eine Grundfeste in der Welt in der er geboren und aufwuchs.
Die er gedachte für sich zu gewinnen, sich als ihr Herr über sie zu stellen, sie unter seine Grundfesten zu ordnen. Und damit begann seine Lebensaufgabe, die er mit dem Kindergartenalter erstmals der Weltöffentlichkeit zeigte, eben in seinem Kindergarten. Es waren die Bauklötze, die er symmetrisch ordnete, ob er sie aufeinanderstapelte oder sie verräumte. Als der sprichwörtliche Stein dazu angestoßen wurde, ordnete er die Buntstifte in seine Symmetrie, Spielsachen wurden Quadratisch in ihre Regale eingeordnet, selbst die Tascheninhalte seiner Kindergartentanten fanden sich im Rahmen seiner Wahrnehmung wieder.
Verdiente er hier seine Sporen, die er mit einem anerkennenden Nicken der in die Hüften gestemmten Armen seiner vierundzwanzigstündigen Arbeit die er selbst dann fortsetzte, wenn er schlief und somit anstelle Schäfchen zählte sie versuchte in viereckige Formen zu treiben, kam er in der Schule erstmals zu Atem. Hier fand er Unterstützung, passten sich die Kindergartentanten ihren Kindern an, ordneten die Lehrer ihren Schülern die Symmetrie ein, mit dabei die Werkzeuge das Heft und das Lineal. 
Wurde die Schulzeit für den kleinen Jungen zur Erholungsfahrt die hier und da einen kleinen Motivationsschub brauchten, für das er sich nie zu Schade war, bröckelte es, so ehrlich musste er zu sich selbst sein, von Schulstufe zu Schulstufe und von Schule zu Schule auf, da er erkannte, sie bauten am Erdgeschoss, wobei er längst Wolkenkratzer erschloss. Wollte er nicht verkommen, musste er aus dem Schultag ausbrechen, es gab zu viel aus der Symmetrie auf der Welt, die er entdecken und in seinen Rahmen pressen wollte. 
Somit lernte er das viereckige Kamerabild kennen, ein Bild hervorgerufen aus einem Kreis. Besser noch, konnte er seine Symmetrie wie er sie sehen wollte und er dafür alles tat, dass er es tat, festhalten  für die Ewigkeit. Sein größter, unbezwingbarer Gegner blieb die Welt in der er lebte selbst, sie tat alles Gegenteilige wogegen er so viel Zeit und Mühe auf sich nahm, es richtig zu machen. Mit der Kamera konnte er die Zeit selbst einfangen, was er tat, probierend, testend, experimentierend, sich und seine Arbeit entwickelnd und vielleicht eines Tages perfektionierend. 
Sein erstes richtiges Werk war unzufrieden, mehr Überforderung und aus der Symmetrie abweichend, als sie zu fangen. Sein zweites Werk dagegen, war eher nach seinem Erstreben, zeigte es wie es sein könnte, in welche Richtung es hieß hinzugehen, der niedergeworfenen Rahmen seiner Wahrnehmung nicht nur einzufangen, sondern sie hervorrufen, wie er es mit seinem dritten Werk tat. Hier rückte er Möbel zu Recht, die Menschen darin, das einhergehende Leben darin, seine Kamera darin und erkannte, halte die Kamera still, und der Rahmen wird niedergeworfen.
Mit fortlaufender Dauer seines Schaffens, fing er die von ihm selbst erschaffene Symmetrie ein, in U-Booten, in ihrem Mobiliar, ihrem Leben, nicht minder in und auf Frachtschiffen, der Unterwassernatur, der Inselnatur, ebenso in Bahnhöfen, Zugabteilen, Zügen und das Fortbewegungsmittel und das Konstrukt an sich, das Gerne wechselnd in einer Kinderbilderbuchwelt aufrechtgehender Tiere ob Fuchs, Dachs, Ratte oder Opossum, seine ganz eigene unverkennbare Optik ideal wiedergegeben unter der Order eines Pfadfinderlagers. Sein Turnaround brachte ihn auf Inseln im Doppelpack ausgesetzter sprechender Haushunde, zuvor lernten wir ein Hotel kennen, ein symmetrisches durch und durch wo selbst das Denken symmetrisch wurde was uns schließlich zu seinem letzten Werk führt, die auf die Leinwand projizierte und somit wiedergegebene Zeitung und ihren Schlagzeilen. 
Und abermals und wohl wie selten zuvor, packte er alles und jenes in seinen niedergeworfenen Rahmen. Ob im Gefängnis, auf der Straße und ihren Cafés, in Talk-Studios oder im Esszimmer, der kleine Junge der längst erwachsen wurde, lebte sich aus. Viel mehr als das, denn innerhalb seiner Symmetrie, wurde er unverhoffter Dinge verspielt wie der stets zielstrebige, vergessen nach links und rechts blickende Geschäftsmann. So baute und fing er 360-Grad weite Kamerafahrten mit ein, wechselte vom stillstehenden Kamerarahmen auf die Egoperspektive, und, wie er früh erkannte und insgeheim auch aufgezwungen bekam, tollten sich seine Menschen und Tiere darin wie sie wollten herum, zogen sich seltsam bunt und seltsam eintönig an, trugen absonderliche Friseuren, absonderliche Bärte, alte und längst vergessene Klamotten, Frisuren und natürlich wiederum Bärte. Wo ihr Äußeres der Anfang ihres Herumtollens war, wurde er eigentlich das Ende ihres verinnerlichten Herumtollens festgefahrener Ansichten, verrückter Ansichten, exzentrischen Ansichten, kontroversen Ansichten, und jegliche Ansicht zu der der Mensch fähig ist. 
Ansichten die der kleine Junge von einst der zum Manne wurde, akzeptiert, hier, in seinen Filmen, hervorruft, sie an seinen Figuren auslebt, gesteckt in seinem niedergeworfenen Rahmen der Symmetrie.

review_text:
Three months after first seeing The French Dispatch at Cannes Film Festival, I was finally able to watch it at my favorite movie theater with friends who had previously never heard of Wes Anderson. Needless to say, they were stunned and walked out of the theater laughing and vowing to check out more of his work.
Wes Anderson returns with a fiery movie devoted not only to a lengthy list of influential writers, but to writing itself. In 103 minutes, he conceives up stories composed by a slate of writers at a local magazine, the eponymous French Dispatch. The film opens with a lively introduction to the magazines office set in the fictional city of Ennui. A narrator reads an article from the French Dispatchs final edition the nostalgic obituary for its creator, and, at the same time, for the magazine itself. Soon, we dive into the articles published in this last issueranging from a detailed travel log set in a French city with an average snowfall of 190.000 flakes a year to a story about an artistic genius who just so happens to be a convicted murderer.
As expected, the film is engulfed in distinctive Wes Anderson features Symmetrical shots follow witty whip pans, smart cuts link comical monologues, and ingenious compositions reveal a background rich with details, all while vivid colors fill the screen. Compared to The Grand Budapest HotelAndersons last live-action filmthis film takes his obsession with tracking shots, black-and-white cinematography and comical editing one step further. The French Dispatch is Wes Anderson, but make it even more Wes Anderson. Different aspect ratios and black-and-white cinematography guide us through the films layers of unique stories, effortlessly transitioning from color to black-and-white withliterallythe flip of a switch, and earning quite a few chuckles in return. 
This film once again showcases Wes Andersons unparalleled ability to convey humor exclusively through cinematic techniques. While his writing is brilliant in its own way, he doesnt need words to carry the movies comedic narrative. Instead, The French Dispatch gets a majority of its laughs from its witty editing, static camera movements and, above all, its composition andcompared to previous Anderson filmsunusual dividing of the screen. This movie often splits its frame in two to compare different perspectives and to depict events in relation to each other, like contrasting past with present, cause with effect. Anderson takes two related shots each amusing on their own and puts them next to each other, thus adding another dimension of comedy to an already funny world filled with bemusing characters. 
While this particular set of personalities lives in its own, almost dreamy world, not one of them shies away from breaking the fourth wall As usual, Wes Andersons heroes seem very aware of the camera or speak directly to it. Much of the films charm traces back to the rich personalities living in its world, and the ensemble cast does a phenomenal job at bringing them to life. Having previously worked with Anderson, Owen Wilson, Adrien Brody, and Tilda Swinton embody their characters with ease, delivering their lines at just the right speed and, most of all, with deadpan humor. Although Ive been a bit of a fan of Timothée Chalamets work (who am I kidding, my username is 12angrychalamet), his acting in The French Dispatch misses the blunt and dry delivery needed for Andersons writingrather, this specific performance tends to be slightly too dramatic for my taste. Overall, however, the ensemble cast fits perfectly into the marvelous world of its director.
When I first watched The French Dispatch, I was unsure of what to make of it. On one hand, as a passionate Wes Anderson enthusiast, I had no choice but to love it (albeit in a more biased manner). On the other hand, I was missing something essential from this film the warmth and comfort I feel after seeing any Wes Anderson movie. Because of its structurearticles as short filmsThe French Dispatch struggles to build enough momentum to keep the audience fully engaged from start to finish. The film introduces a variety of characters within an arguably convoluted narrativemaking it not only difficult to build a storyline within the classical narrative arc but also to create characters the viewers can get to know and root for. As a result, especially after the first watch, The French Dispatch can feel like a collection of pieces each very strong, but altogether lacking an equally strong glue. 
Nonethelessand probably obvious because this is my fourth watchthis film is easily one of the most rewatchable movies Ive seen in the past year (and this is coming from someone whos seen Tenet six times in theaters). Even better, The French Dispatch gets more entertaining and amusing with every rewatch BECAUSE of its unusual structure and rich details. Every frame is carefully composed, inviting the audience to marvel at its countless embellishments. This film takes many of the techniques Wes Anderson used in previous films and welds them together Isle of Dogs tracking shots spanning multiple halls are now tracking characters through full-size rooms, and the smoke in fight scenes paused mid-action are reminiscent of dust clouds used in his stop motion movies. 
Charming, fun, ingenious, and amusing, The French Dispatch is, simply put, pure magic, and Wes Anderson conjures up another delightful feast for the eyes and the heart. Its a wonderful tale dedicated to writing and journalism, but above all, its made with an audience in mind. Like the authors write for their readers, The French Dispatch is filmed for its viewersranging from the colorful production design to its quirky soundtrack and absurdly comical characters. This film needs to be experienced in a (preferably packed) movie theaterand in the end, were once again reminded of the reason why cinema exists the feeling of belonging, the collective emotions, and most of all, the shared laughs.

review_text: Idiosyncratic, unceasingly detailed and crammed with the type of humour thats now familiar from Wes Anderson, The French Dispatch paints an affectionate and adventurous portrait of the publishing business as well as French arts and culture. Centred around an American magazine based in France, it constitutes three shorts that re-enact republished articles for the final farewell edition after its editor Arthur Howitzer Jr. (Bill Murray) dies abruptly of a heart attack. It is populated by a star-studded cast full of Anderson regulars such as Bill Murray and Owen Wilson alongside newcomers that include Elisabeth Moss and Liev Schreiber. The tales experiment with a blend of black and white and colour cinematography, together with animation, and unfurl with numerous bizarre and humourous moments. Theres a concentrated focus assigned to the films inventively stunning visuals its lavishly decorated sets and costume designs are positively overflowing with details that delight the eye. The French Dispatch is both an ambitious project and a love letter to journalism, and its essentially like watching three thoroughly unfettered shorts from the mind of the remarkable auteur.

review_text:
A 108-minute glimpse into Wes Andersons rich, lushly packed, delicately served inner world. The most rewatchable film Ive seen so far!!

The French Dispatch (of the Liberty, Kansas Evening Sun) is a captivating array of three newspaper stories, each one of them outlandish and stunning, yet heartwarming in their own ways. Theres love, despair, impulsiveness, longing, detachment and wonder expressed by intricate, effectively written characters who stand out through either their a) complicated personal history, b) eccentric appearance, or c) their little personal quirks, à la Wes Anderson. 
I had gone into The French Dispatch without watching (or remembering??) the trailer and I would highly recommend everyone to do the same!! The film had a distinct rhythm to it, but it took me a while to catch it, so having any preconceptions wouldve been distracting. 
I found the film to be SO BEAUTIFUL. Because the stories did not drag on for too long, I found myself facing a lot of different themes expressed by the wide range of stories and characters in the film. Each frame was also so finely crafted, especially the lighting, particularly in the black-and-white scenes. They were at times flat and storybook-like, other times angular and theatrical. I had gone to the cinema with a few friends from my theatre class and we came out with so many new ideas for staging!! Overall, the refined intensity and the general ARTSINESS of The French Dispatch made me realise how many ways there were to present a theme, mood or relationship, whether in terms of production, writing or acting. Everyone involved did such a beautiful job it gives me such JOY to see such a masterpiece on the big screen. 

Heres where I will be breaking down my favourite scenes so if you dont want your impression of the film to be tainted look away!! 
You have been warned!!

- The prisoner scene with Benicio Del Toro and Lea Seydoux. Omg. Their relationship is so fascinating and the scene where young Rosenthal gets replaced with old Rosenthal was so simple yet cool. Also, the changes in camera angles and colours added so much to the story. I couldnt stop laughing in the shaky shot where Rosenthal chased those people down with his wheelchair. And all the tableaux were so funny too!! Visual humour is generally so respectable. 
- The scene where Timothee Chalamet hops on the moped while his voice reads out his letter. That was so atmospheric. The slowed-down movements and the obscured but highlighted figures on the bike aligned with the feeling of being indestructible and immortal that was expressed in the narration. Note that this was only a minute in runtime (?) but it effectively created that infinite feeling, which was recalled in the form of infinite dread when Timothees parents were riding the taxi.
- The animation in the last story!!! I think it was introduced so seamlessly but it made a lot of the action and chasing possible. I also couldnt stop laughing when the strongman was thrown off the windshield of the car and jumped back onto it  
- The narrator of the last storys monologue about always finding acceptance and hospitality at a restaurant. I found it so impactful because Ive recently realised that Im not a very mindful eater. This film will change that. Also, the conversation between him and the chef about immigration and finding a place to belong was quite relatable! 
- Somehow I dont like the scenes in colour that much perhaps there was too much to take in? I really believe this will change upon rewatch though!!
If youre still reading here I assume youve either watched the film or youre spoiling it for yourself (insert sad face) or youre leaving a like (insert happy face). If youre the former you are SO WELCOME to start a conversation in the comments!! And if youre the latter two, well, please put down your phone and watch The French Dispatch already!!!!
Thank you for reading 


P.S. My friends and I dressed up in suits and robes to watch it in the cinema in Freiburg. It was such a wholesome experience and a memory I will cherish. Go on, be extra and show up in full costume to a Wes Anderson screening!!

such a brilliantly executed concept for a film. its also a subtle flex by wes anderson showing off how many insanely talented people he can get for his movie, even if theyre only on-screen for 30 seconds.
i know this is par for the course when it comes to wes anderson films, but every frame of this film feels like its own piece of art. every performance is wonderful, and andersons unique direction is so fun to watch. i love how characters move and act in his films.
because of its kinda unorthodox structure, i just wanted to give some quick thoughts on each segment of the film (minor spoilers)
The Cycling Reporter
although its extremely short, owen wilsons bike tour was wonderfully presented, and the way wilson delivers his lines is perfect. old people old people who have failed.
The Concrete Masterpiece
love love love this segment. benicio del toros reserved performance as this tortured murder-y artist was so engaging, and léa seydoux as his muse is perfect. theyre complicated relationship is kinda sad to watch, in a way. the scene where del toro chases adrien brody around in a wheelchair and throwing shit at him is peak comedy. side note this is like the 5th movie ive seen this year where henry winkler randomly pops up, and i just think he needs to have a cameo in every movie.
Revisions to a Manifesto
definitely the weakest, in my opinion. the first half of this segment took a while to catch my interest, but it picked up around the time juliettes character gets more involved. loved the costume design in this one, tho.
The Private Dining Room of the Commissioner
definitely my favorite segment of the film. jeffrey wright has the voice of a god. saoirse ronans eyes gave me chills. steve park as the cook was great with the little screen time he had. the entire animated scene felt like it was ripped right out of the comic section of a newspaper.
Obituary
bill murrays character is initially shown to be kind of a hard-ass, but you see little glimpses of his respect for the writers of his magazine throughout the film. the last scene really shows the impact his character had on all of them as they mourn him. this part really just made wish that owen wilson had a bigger role.
just a beautiful, perfectly crafted film. the visuals, performances, music, editing, dialogue, all amazing. cant wait to watch it again.

review_text:
The French Dispatch is so stylised that it feels as though anything could break the tension and bring it crashing down. Its the film equivalent of an occasionally x-rated poem.
The story begins with the cantankerous editor of The French Dispatch magazine Arthur Howitzer (Bill Murray) dying suddenly, leaving his writers to release one last edition in his memory. The film takes us through each section of the paper on a whimsical but bittersweet journey featuring an insane artist, a student revolution created by sexual frustration, a superlative chef and the kidnapping of a police commissioners son.
The film has a typically Wes Anderson-esque exaggerated style which complements its bizarre subject matter. The third sequence devolves into a cartoon chase scene involving a wrestler, a firefight between a horde of police and gangsters and a radish pie. The other anthology segments feature rabid packs of drunken choirboys, Benecio Del Toro as a patient in an asylum who shows an unexpected talent for painting, and a revolution where a battle at the barricades also revolves around a literal chess game between the leaders and the mayor of the city.
The dialogue goes past like a flood of consciousness which barely allows the audience to keep pace. At times it sounds like they had the script for a film an hour longer and didnt want to cut anything out, so they just had the characters talk twice as quickly. Quick jokes streak by as sight gags or quips an early one which got a laugh from me was the name of the town being Ennui-sur-Blasé.
On the dramatic side loneliness is the key theme of the movie, with the journalist narrators distanced from the rest of society by their personalities or the demands of their job. Frances Dormand is terrific as Lucinda Krementz, a woman who seemingly embodies the ideal of an aromantic and detached journalist with no connection to anything but her writing. Even her editing of a revolutionary manifesto feels more like a case of perfectionism than an actual relationship.
Tilda Swinton gives the most restrained performance as J.K.L. Berensen, an impeccably groomed academic with a drinking problem and a romantic streak, whilst Jeffrey Wright is excellent as Roebuck, a baritone-voiced scribbler whose hyper-articulacy conceals a past of pain and discrimination. All three journalists have to balance between being too disconnected and too involved with their subject and the world in general. One of the main characters in the second section, Lt. Nescaffier, tellingly reveals that as a foreigner to France he struggles with some of the same issues.
Wes Anderson shows a fascination with depicting processes, from the painting technique of the conceptual artist, to the exact cooking style of master chef Lt. Nescaffier. While The French Dispatch wont be everyones cup of wine, its a unique viewing experience which balances whimsy with lingering sadness.

review_text:
Even Wes Andersons weakest film is still pretty good! 
The fact this was an anthology movie is its biggest weakness for me personally. Wes Anderson is one of my favorite directors and I love to get immersed into all of the creative worlds within each of his films. Since this is 3 short films in one movie I really wasnt able to immerse myself into the worlds Anderson creates as much as I would have liked because all 3 stories are separate and unrelated to each other. New settings, actors, and stories for each short.
MVPs Benicio Del Toro, Lea Seydoux, and Adrien Brody. All 3 stared in the same short film, which was by far my favorite.
Going in I had no idea this was an anthology movie. Im not the biggest fan of that type of format when it comes to a film. So from that standpoint I found The French Dispatch to be a little disappointing. Again, that just boils down to a personal preference. Everything looks great and is a real treat to your eyes. Performances were all very good. Id rank the short films in the exact order they were shown. 1 being my favorite and 3 being my least. Loved a lot moments all throughout the film. It just didnt totally work for me as a whole. Still overall quite enjoyable nonetheless!

I loved every single second of this film, and I wish it couldve been three hours longer. This is probably Wes Andersons funniest movie to date, but its also filled with so much love, and passion, and tenderness. 
Every character is so well thought out that it seems almost unfair how easy it is for Anderson to create these people that are so outlandish and yet so relatable with an ease that most filmmakers never seem to achieve.
Perhaps my judgement is a bit clouded for the love I have for journalism as a profession, but I think this movie will resonate with everyone who has the privilege to watch it, in one way or another.

review_text:
An abundance of nothing earnest to say about anything at all.
The references to Monsieur Hulots Parisian house in Jacques Tatis Mon Oncle (at the beginning of the film) and to the shootout at the end of 1934s The Man Who Knew Too Much (in the last story here) only served to remind me of how much more humanist Tati and Hitchcock are than Anderson.
I too love Tati and Karel Zeman. I too am a lifelong subscriber to the New Yorker and read bandes dessinées. I too love neo-surrealist  world building and bold mise-en-scène forward flicks. Its not that I dont love the things this movie slaves over, its that I wonder if this movie actually loves those things too, or loves anything. Wes Anderson seems to care more about wallpaper than he does people. I know this is the standard criticism of Anderson at this point, but for me, it stands.
The story featuring Benicio del Toro as a murderous painter comes the closest to having a human heart. Benicio emotes in a way that legitimizes the artifice all around him. A weariness that has unspoken meaning. Theres a haze of genuine pathos settled over the story. Léa Seydouxs stern, uniformed beauty is absolutely worth painting and so theres a light of truth to it all, unusual for Anderson in this, his late masterbatory stage.
After that... things got real hollow, real inauthentic, and real boring real fast for me. 
Next we get the most cynical bougie smug bullshit take on youth revolts imaginable, reminding me that Wes Andersons aestheticism is inherently materialistic, that he does not give a shit about the working class, and is Woody Allen-esque in his disregard for anyone but elite intellectuals. These are cartoon lives without the cartoon joys. Though his characters sometimes talk about money, they have no actual bills to pay. I dont mind an apolitical work, but for fuck sake, as an artist shouldnt you believe in something other than your own snark and obsessive sense of style? 
All people in jaunty Anderson World are the same. Characterization is only as varied as the need to impact filmic progression and tone. A character is either young or old, man or woman, meant to carry the plot forward or cause it to make a sharp turn. Thats the extent of them as people. Some of his actors work very hard to be unique and interesting inside his snow globe stories, but most of this effort is lost. All are puppets to the dance. Nothing is an active, dangerous, or bold ingredient, and so the soup is bland.
However, when an actor in this is given just a little space to work outside of the strict staging and affected dialogue, it has a profound impact. Its like the movie has relaxed and accidentally let in something honest. But its never long before the movie moves to kill any spark of life that had awakened inside of it. Pressing its oppressive formalist jackboot down on it. Outside of del Toro and Seydoux in the first story, Saoirse Ronan does a little magic with her 30 seconds, as do a few others throughout. Part of the distance I feel here is that the cast is stacked with hugely talented people, yet very few players get any real screen time because Anderson hardly lets anything breath. This gives a lot of the roles the vibe of stunt casting. Im sure it was fun to get all of those amazing personalities into a room for the last scene of writing the obituary, but its rewards for me as a viewer were minimal.
Also, Anderson is a list maker, thats his dominant writing schtick. Listing clever things, items, and ideas. Personally, I love making lists in my writing too. Its very satisfying to list things. Its indulgent, of course, because you dont have to settle on a single idea or build a complex observation. You can just tick off all your concepts and call it a day.
I did like the Gwenn Germain animations, but they didnt quite feel like the visual comps I would have set in this world. Theyre, only slightly, too modern for the throwback era and source materials. The still illustrations were fantastic, though. And really, it goes without saying that the production design throughout is immaculate. Every single image has aesthetic value on its own, even if, when taken all together, it felt tedious and empty hearted. Little more than a series of set pieces with low emotional resonance and a disregard for any sense of narrative or charactological curiosity.
Because I make comic books theres still a lot here to adore, or maybe just learn from (like homework). So often in this a single image represents a sentiment thats also being narrated over. Almost entirely the narrator is someone reading something written by someone else. Its all very much captions on top of panels to me. But its in service to a grifty, bunco attitude towards everything from love to politics to creativity.
What we really need next is Andersons Straight Story.
One other thing though, as a person who makes a living writing words down, I really do so love editors. Thats one profoundly misunderstood and beautiful profession. I am most grateful in my career to all the editors I have worked with. If you edit the written word in any form, prose, comics, journalism, poetry... go with God, my heart is with you.
Signed, 
The Foreign Chef

review_text:
In einer Zeit, in der es hier auf Letterboxd nur so vor Anthology-Filmen wimmelt, kommt also auch Wes Anderson mit seinem ersten Beitrag für dieses Sub-Gerne zu uns daher und wie erwartet, ist dies ein ganz besonderer Eintrag in die Analen der Anthology-Filmgeschichte geworden. 
Einen Film von Wes Anderson würde wahrscheinlich sogar ein Blinder mit Krückstock sofort erkennen. Mit seinen symmetrischen Bildkompositionen, der speziellen Art Farben zu verwenden, einem Ensemble von Top-Schauspielern und extrem detaillierten Sets, die mich teilweise immer an die Bilderbücher von meinem Sohn erinnern, erweckt Anderson auf komische Art und Weise, leicht melancholische Geschichten zum Leben. 
Dies ist in The French Dispatch genau so, außer, dass er diesmal noch viel detailverliebter, ein äußerst unterhaltsames Labyrinth aus Geschichten, Sets und bizarren Figuren, zu einem Gesamtkunstwerk verwoben hat. Mit The French Dispatch schafft es Wes Anderson, in weniger als zwei Stunden mindestens drei abendfüllende Spielfilme abzuliefern. Der Film enthält eine beispiellose Fülle an Referenzen, Stilen, Orten, Details und Spaß.
Aber vor allem hat der Film all das zu bieten, was ich an der Kunstform Film so liebe eine komplexe Handlung, einen einzigartigen visuellen Stil und ein ständiges Spiel mit Licht, Farbe, Bewegung und Ton. 
The French Dispatch ist ein absolutes Highlight in Wes Andersons ohnehin schon beeindruckendem Oeuvre und ein herausragendes und sehr unterhaltsames Kinoerlebnis. 
Mein Ranking der Filme von Wes Anderson
