review_text:
La crónica Francesa es, sin dudas, la obra al más puro estilo Anderson (para bien y para mal). 
Esta, puede ser interpretada por muchos (y me incluyo) como una carta de amor al periodismo y todo lo que conlleva. 
La película se divide en 3 partes, un tipo de prólogo, aunque no funciona como tal, y un desenlace. 
Un aspecto que me ha gustado muchísimo de la película es la forma que tiene de ser contada. Durante todo el film el director nos abraza y nos invita a disfrutar de su mundo, esta vez en forma de revista, y nos deleita, una vez más, con personajes maravillosos. 
Comenzando con la primera historia, recalcar el magnífico trabajo del trío protagonista, Léa, Del Toro y Adrien, siendo este último mi favorito. Esta historia, personalmente, ha sido la que más me ha gustado. Gracias a su despanapnante y extravagante forma de ser contada, esta logra enamorarnos con cada escena. 
El segundo relato, a diferencia del primero, es el que menos me ha gustado y el que, a la vez, tenia más ganas de ver. La historia está un poco desdibujada y hay veces que se estanca o simplemente no sabe cómo resolverse. Aun así, esta nos brinda unos muy entregados Thimotee y Frances. 
Y para acabar, nos encontramos con la historia de Wright. Siendo perteneciente de la sección de gastronomía y comida, el articulo nos relata la historia de un secuestro un tanto peculiar con un cocinero de por medio que de bien seguro nadie olvidara. 
Aun que la he sentido un poco menos personal (a diferencia de las otras), recalcar la sensacional persecución en animación y, como no, las actuaciones. Eso si, mejor no hablar del personajes tan soso y desaprovechado de Dafoe. 
En aspectos generales, recalcar la fotografía y ese juego de colores y negros que hay durante toda la película. Como no, el diseño de producción es implacable y se nota que hay un gran trabajo detrás de esos decorados al estilo barroco. 
En conclusión, La cronica Feancesa (al igual que el resto de película de wes) acaba enamorándome y logra hacerme olvidar, al menos las casi dos horas que dura la película, de mis preocupaciones y simplemente disfrutar de su peculiar mundo. 
Wes Anderson nos recuerda lo bello que puede llegar a ser el cine y lo mucho que este nos puede hacer sentir. gracias.

Weird, whacky  wicked but equally dull, sterile  vapid, The Lobster is a strange delight that starts quite well but tumbles down the road after the halfway mark to conclude on a rather uninteresting note. The concept is no doubt interesting and it takes its time to make us familiar to the society inhabiting its story but all of it doesnt amount for much in the end and fails to leave a lasting impression.
Set in a dystopian future, the story presents a world in which single folks are arrested  taken to a hotel where they are obliged to find a matching partner within 45 days or they are transformed into animals and released into the woods. The plot follows a man who arrives at the hotel for same reason but his endeavours of finding a mate before his time is over ends far more tragically than he expected.
Co-written  directed by Yorgos Lanthimos (Dogtooth  Alps), the film marks his English-language debut and the idea  inspiration behind it is both intriguing  clever. The sequences taking place in the hotel are neatly carried out but the second half lacks the same level of creativity thats present in the first half. The excitement goes missing once our protagonist leaves the hotel and from thereon, it just limps towards the finish line.
The hotel is neatly maintained but it also has a creepy vibe about it. Camera movements are fluid, colour hues wonderfully complement its overcast ambience and lighting seems natural for the most part. Editing allows the plot to unfold at an unhurried pace but the whole story feels twice as long coz of that, with no idea of where its headed. Lastly, the background score is just as odd as the storys content and is wickedly utilised.
Coming to the performances, the film features a fab cast in Colin Farrell, Rachel Weisz, Léa Seydoux, Ben Whishaw  John C. Reilly but their input is mostly bland  lifeless. It can be argued that the spiritless rendition of these characters is deliberate but it doesnt entirely help in enriching the experience. The deadpan humour is occasionally amusing but then, it is also too easy to get frustrated by whats unfolding.
On an overall scale, The Lobster is an uncanny mix of bizarre ideas that, in its effort to play with multiple things at once, may end up drifting many of its viewers. While there is nothing laudable about it, its parody of the society that gives way too much credit to companionship, in addition to the dig this film takes at those match-making algorithms which rely on similar traits  likeness factor is one aspect I liked. But in all honesty, this sci-fi comedy is too mediocre to be of any significance.

Relationships are consistently seen as some kind of societal requirement for one to appear as normal nowadays. You cant just be content by yourself without someone else having to antagonize you about when youre going to meet the perfect person in your life, or pass along some unrequested suggestion or preconception about yourself. The Lobsters farcical, Anderson-esque dialogue delivers the dry, monotonous feeling that relationship traditionalism tends to emulate to people such as myself- whilst the idea of having a relationship is wonderful in its theory, and the notion of love itself is something I experience at a very real and personal level, I dont have very much use for relationships at all. Theres a strict mindset that dominates society (at least the one I find myself surrounded in) that Ive felt compelled all my life to follow, and yet I havent found any satisfaction within its normativity. In fact, its almost repulsive in the sense that its mandatory nature feels practically forced onto me by those who declare they know exactly what is best for me. Its the time-constrained pressure of finding the perfect match or face what others perceive as an eternal fate worse than death that I find most relatable in The Lobster.
It took me three viewings, but Ive finally grasped onto the ending and why it fits so perfectly with the rest of this absurdist piece of perfection. The climax of Davids constant pressure to find the perfect match and to have commonality with them. The heart-wrenching feeling that if you dont find the perfect match to be with for the rest of your life, you could face social ostracization. How does one even begin to describe the enigma that is Yorgos Lanthimos The Lobster? Since reading a brief description of its bizarre narrative months ago, it has been one of my most anticipated films of the year, and those familiar with Lanthimos previous work (most notably his 2009 Academy Award nominated film, Dogtooth) are probably aware of how strange his work can be - but never without justification. The Lobster tells the story of David (Colin Farrell), a man who has recently been left by his partner and decides to check into The Hotel, where he has a month and a half to meet a new, suitable partner otherwise he will be transformed into the animal of his choice.
The film functions as part absurdist comedy, part dark romance and part social satire. The comedy is sharp and the romantic elements provide it with a sense of lightness which would have otherwise been absent the execution of its societal commentary, however, is what sends it into uncharted territory, and the main reason why it comes across as such a deeply original work. Lanthimos pokes fun at certain commonalities of the modern romantic relationship, such as the notion that birds of a feather flock together, by utilizing the element of exaggeration. For instance, each character in the film has their singular unique characteristic. David is nearsighted, and thus is only interested in finding a woman who is nearsighted as well. The Limping Man (Ben Whishaw) pursues a woman who suffers from frequent nosebleeds, and so in order to capture her attention and fool her into thinking that they are a match, he begins inflicting trauma upon his nose, causing it to bleed when in her presence.
When I first saw Dogtooth, I praised it for its technical mastery its carefully framed static shots, sharp editing and claustrophobic production design. Still, something held me back from fully embracing it, and looking back on the viewing experience now, Im certain it was that I had a difficult time trying to figure out what it was saying about civilization. Its surreal and otherworldly, for sure, but what sort of comment is it trying to make about the human condition? It is indeed a tough egg to crack. The Lobster, on the other hand, is much more coherent (and dare I say accessible) in its satire. I dont want to get ahead of myself, as I never thought I would be describing a Lanthimos film as accessible, but I definitely think people will have an easier time figuring out the meaning behind all of the madness here.
The technical elements of The Lobster are just as sound as those of Dogtooth, and aesthetically similar. The cinematography is almost perpetually static and much attention is paid to the framing of certain shots, which is interesting because it allows the director to isolate aural elements such as off-screen noises that, though they cannot be seen, having a significant bearing on specific scenes. The musical score is jarring, but not in a negative way I imagine it will be one of the first technical aspects that viewers take notice of, as its a loud and powerful score which makes itself known within the first few minutes of the films runtime. There isnt much that I would change about The Lobster. If I was to suggest anything to the editors, it would be to pick out and remove certain scenes which might not seem as pertinent as others, for the film does exhaust a bit in its third act. Aside from that though, it is a hilarious and biting critique of interpersonal relationships that is sure to appeal to a wider audience than Lanthimos previous works, and may bring him back into the limelight when award season rolls around.

Another of those movies I watched so long ago that I barely remember a lot of itwell, actually, I was surprised at how much I did remember. Which shouldnt come as such considering this film is one of those that manages to leave an impression on you, for better or for worse.
But yeah, this film really represents the point at which Yorgos finally came into his own. Its all been building up to this. Dogtooth more or less, was, if we were to use architectural language, the building already built. We got the skeleton with the blocks, bricks, or woods and we get to see the house in its true form. However, theres no windows, a door, etc. Its just the house. With this film we finally get the painting, the doors, the windows installed and even a lot of the furniture. A lot of the traits, trademarks and brand of absurd humor made their debut or were fully honed in here. The stunning cinematography paired with the strident score creates this sense of gloom and heightens the themes of detachment and unease, and it visually conveys that this is as much of an absurd comedy as it is a psychological horror that, to some extent, feels kind of relatable. Not the animal conversion but the pressure to find a couple, marry, etc. I am sure its something you may relate to. Though were also living in a generation that doesnt have the same level of pressure upon themselves as those in the past, but still. The script is engrossing in that Lanthimos way. As I pointed out in my last review, he knows how to come up with these interesting ideas, some quite familiar, but he spins them with his own twists and turns that make them his own.
The performances once again are all really great, with everyone capturing the absurdity and offbeat tone of the movie, some with such a seriousness that, just like Leslie Nielsen in Airplane, the contrast really works well with the more subtle self-awareness. Farrell is great as this depressed, pathetic man whos just at the border of breaking down. As with many of the characters here, the urgency in his (and everyone elses) quest for a loved one is not a matter of pursuing happiness or finding that special someone but survival.
All in all, whether you dig this world and the script as a whole or not, theres no denying this is just peak creative writing. The direction and performances do a great job, if anything, elevating the material, whereas, as I noted before, it would leave a lasting impression.

Thanks to Siegel, Ive been getting used to watching weird films in 2020. The Lobster is no exception. This is easily one of the weirdest films of 2015, and it felt like I was watching a 2-hour long episode of Black Mirror. Director Yorgos Lanthimos creates a film that is a dark-humored, satiric, and mocking parallel of society reflecting on humans obsession to fit in certain rules of society, despite how ridiculous they are. The main message of the film is so interesting to me. Its a commentary on the social construct of relationships in our society. We step on our feelings and ignore our instincts just to play by the rules, to belong. 
A great example of this is exploring the common traits idea. The guests in the hotel (including David) try to find a common trait with another person so they can feel they are a match with one another. Limping man pretends to get nosebleeds, and David pretends to be cruel. Sure, these common traits are exaggerated in the film, but its a good comment on what we play up to in our society, too. 
After the main character, David, runs into the woods, where he finds rebels of coupling, its clear that they are as extreme as the people in the hotel. The hotel is obsessed with the rules of finding a couple within the first 45 days of one persons stay, or else they will be turned into animals and be set off into the woods for a second chance at love. The forest people are obsessed with independence and not showing affection. The setting fits quite well as in a hotel, you are usually there with a significant other, whereas in the wilderness, you are free and independent to roam wild. Yet there are still rules in both settings. The first half of the film has taken place in the hotel perfectly mirrors the second half of the film has taken place mostly in the woods.  In the woods and the hotel, it looks like its shown that people have to belong to survive, but options are limited, and you have to obey, pretend, or risk to be destroyed. 
Many examples of dysfunctional relationships are shown in the film, which looks so familiar, pretending to have something in common, and pretending that you understand that you are the same. Desperation, rejection, cruelty in the relationships are things we have seen and know it all. Still, the director finds a way to remind us with a lighter tone, with the possibility to laugh at ourselves and society. We see these themes and tropes of relationships shown many different times, almost as if they are repetitive. 
I would like to point out the repetitiveness of the music as well. Two pieces of music continuously play throughout the film, one somber and depressing piece by Beethoven and another piece by Shostakovich (sounds like the Wii Mii Theme). Furthermore, the repetitiveness of these songs signify the repetitiveness of both halves of the film. Even though they seem different, they parallel each other. The only difference is David, as he is an outlier here. These pieces distinguish David from the rest of the world with its rules. He was forced to find a partner in the hotel and could not deliver. When he ran away and found the loner forest people, he fell in love when he wasnt supposed to. 
The obsession with having something in common with your partner reached the peek at the end. It looked like even David and blind women are still in love, but a realization that in societal norms, they dont have anything real in common drives to an extreme decision. It shows that we sacrifice so much if we love someone different, and all just to be more acceptable in the society, but in the end, society doesnt care, so do we just have to be braver? If David chooses to blind himself, hes taking the bullet for his partner, therefore sacrificing himself for her. But if he doesnt blind himself, hes turning the gun on her, saving himself for his benefit. This scene was foreshadowed when the forest people attack the hotel managers and give them an ultimatum with the weapon. 
Yorgos leaves it up to the viewer to determine whether David blinds himself or not. I would also like to point out that a Lobster has terrible vision and are blind in brought light. He says he wants to be transformed into a lobster at the beginning of the film, but I wonder if that changed towards the end when he finds his person. Yorgos used so many metaphors and parallels. Its so hard not to love this film, and I cant wait to catch more after more rewatches. This film makes more think than feel. Its not a feel-good film its a smart and innovative reminder.

Love, when reduced to rules, feels less like a miracle and more like a contract. Thats what The Lobster wrestles with the paradox of intimacy in a world obsessed with categorization, pairing, and the illusion of order. Watching it, I kept thinking about how much pressure society places on the idea of love as a requirement and not as a lived experience. Whether its through dating apps, romantic comedies, or the weight of cultural expectation, were constantly told that fulfillment depends on coupling. Yet love, in its truest form, resists these structures. Its irrational, messy, even brutal at times. It cant be organized into checkboxes or measured against surface-level compatibility. The Lobster magnifies this absurdity by pushing the logic of a couple-fixated society to its breaking point, revealing how fragile and even cruel our notions of partnership can become when enforced by systems rather than choice.
For me, the movie worked as both a dark satire and a strange meditation on what it means to connect. In todays world, where so much of romance is mediated by screens and algorithms, Lanthimos asks is love genuine when its filtered through these systems, or does it only come alive when it slips past them? Ive thought about that question after the movie had finished and I realized how close to home this critique really is.
Now, if youve been following me for a while, then youll know that I didnt love Poor Things. It didnt quite click with me, but after watching Dogtooth and now The Lobster, Im starting to think I may have judged Yorgos Lanthimos too quickly. His dry, clinical, and deeply absurd style isnt easy to warm up to. Yet the more I sit with it, the more I see the strange wisdom lurking beneath the deadpan delivery. The Lobster surprised me with how much it resonated, how it balanced biting satire with genuine commentary.
All in all, The Lobster is a sharp, clever, and beautifully bizarre movie that made me pause and reflect on my own views of love in a world that treats romance as both a marketplace and a mandate. As for Lanthimos, I still have more of his work to explore, but I can say this much his movies are slowly growing on me, and The Lobster just might be the one that unlocked that door.

Im already eager for another look at The Lobster, the latest absurdist whatsit from Greeces Yorgos Lanthimos (whose third feature, Dogtooth, was the best film I saw at Cannes 2009). Is there an actual literal lobster in it? I asked my roommate, Blake, a couple of days ago. (Hed read the synopsis, I deliberately hadnt.) Answering that would probably tell you more than you want to know, he replied. As it turns out, though, the films bizarre premise, which involves the possibility that protagonist David (an overweight Colin Farrell) may be surgically transformed into a lobsteris something of a red herring. In a dystopian near-future, single people are considered unfit to live as humans once a relationship ends, the uncoupled get 45 days to find new partners, with those who fail getting turned into the animals of their choice. Most become cats or dogs, but David fancies being a lobster, because they live a long time and he likes the sea. Singles can extend their mate-seeking windows beyond 45 days by hunting down Lonerssingle rebels fighting their repressive society from the woodswith tranquilizer guns.
Lanthimos and his regular co-writer, Efthymis Filippou, mine some sharply black humor from the animal-fate concept, but they could replace it with euthanasia without materially changing the movie. Whats central hereand not fully clear to me, at least a few hours after seeing itis the films allegorical take on romance and its societal codification. If I squint hard, I guess I can see (speaking as a currently single person) how some folks might feel like people who arent in long-term relationships are treated like second-class citizens. But there isnt a lot of real-world resonance in The Lobsters notion that we pair off with those who share our defining characteristic, exaggerated here as a dictum that, for example, someone who suffers from nosebleeds must find someone else who suffers from nosebleeds. Most characters apart from David are named for their must-match attribute Rachel Weisz plays The Short-Sighted Woman, John C. Reilly plays The Lisping Man, etc. What about opposites attracting? Or the more scholarly notion that people seek out mates with complementary attributes? And when David eventually joins the Loners (led by Léa Seydoux), their own strictly enforced rules against sex, romance, and even flirting make even less allegorical sense. Personally, I wanted an entire movie about David feigning heartlessness in order to get paired with The Heartless Woman (Dogtooths Angeliki Papoulia), a desperate move he makes as he runs out of time. That felt familiar to me. I am 47 years old.

There was no way that honest to goodness movie stars ( or their agents for that matter ) would put up with the extreme weirdness and violence that has sprung from the Greek auteur in past foreign language films.  No way  it would have to be a kinder, gentler Lanthimos  a watered down Lanthimos.
I was wrong.  Im happy to report this is full octane Lanthimos.
In this outing, he sets his mischievous ( and some might argue twisted ) absurdist sights on relationships and their influences in society, and societies influences and pressures on them.  Like his past films its best not to know any specifics, just like our hapless characters as they enter his special world.  At the TIFF QA Rachel Weiss ( who confessed to being an absolute Lanthimos film lover ) was asked how she prepared for her role, to which she replied there is no way to prepare, you just have to trust that hell guide you.  And guide you, the audience, he does through his twisted mazes of societal observational critique and shockingly absurd truisms that are only amped up a fraction from the real life world we live in.
The cast is uniformly excellent.  Colin Farrell as our gentle, nebbish, protagonist David turns in his finest performance since In Bruges.   Rachel Weisz convinces as a loner looking for connection  and rabbits.  Lea Seydoux as the calculating Loner Leader and Olivia Coleman and the deliciously domineering Hotel Manager are a delight watch ( we get a treat seeing Coleman do a little Lanthimos Dance).  The biggest treat, though was to see Angeliki Papoulia, star of Dogtooth and Alps render a phenomenally dark and scary, and mercurially droll turn as Heartless Woman, as well as a small part by Alps co-star Ariane Labed as The Maid.  I secretly think that these two actresses may have been a grounding force for Lanthimos, and a beacon that the movie stars could follow.
My worries about Lanthimos biting absurd humor losing its bite were unfounded as well.  The wordplay from him and his long time co-conspirator writer Efthymis Filippou is still as sharp as tacks.  The audience, I think mainly comprised of first timers, laughed openly and often  and sometimes rather nervously.  Those laughs were tempered by quite a few gasps, as well, as those familiar with the auteur would expect.
Im also happy to report that theres plenty of crazy dancing, classical guitar solos, and ultra-violence that could cause unwellness.  My only complaint is that the third act could use some tightening up, but other than that small grouse I think it joins Dogtooth and Alps as modern dystopian absurdist masterpieces.
I wish The Lobster the greatest success, because I want to see Yorgos Lanthimos keep doing what hes doing, exactly the way hes been doing it.

A very weird one, as expected because its a Yorgos Lanthimos film. My first impression is always the same with him, you walk in knowing youll be confronted with metaphors stacked on metaphors, a strange but deliberate absurdity, and a sharp dissection of the bizarre ways we construct society. Every time, he gives us a world that feels completely insane and almost unfathomable, yet oddly coherent, filled with rules and rituals that mirror our own reality in unsettling ways.
The Lobster is no exception. Its a dystopian narrative, but one that feels eerily close to the way our world actually functions. The idea of people being given 45 days to find a partner before being transformed into an animal felt like its a reflection of how institutions, traditions, and cultural norms attempt to control something as intimate and unpredictable as human relationships. That deadline is absurd, yes, but its also a brutally clever metaphor for the pressures society imposes on us, the pressure to couple up, to meet milestones, to fit into frameworks no matter how ridiculous they are when looked at in the abstract. The brilliance is in how convincing this world becomes. No matter how bizarre, it feels internally consistent, and thats what makes the satire hit so hard.
One thing that I do love the most about The Lobster is how fully realized its concept is. Its not just a thought experiment, but a living, breathing film where every detail builds into this cynical portrait of conformity and human desperation. Its mocking, yes, but also sobering because behind the absurdity, theres always that sting of recognition. You cant help but see yourself, your society, and the way relationships are measured, evaluated, and judged. Thats what makes it captivating, it pulls you into an insane story but never lets you dismiss it as pure fantasy. Instead, it forces you to sit with the discomfort of its allegory.
To me, the film reads as Lanthimos most biting critique of societal structure and conformity, and how weve let those structures seep even into the way we love. Its funny in the darkest way, absurd in all the right ways, and cynical enough to leave you unsettled long after it ends.

This film, like Lanthimos other films, takes place in a bizarre world. While the first half hour of the movie is spent trying to understand whats going on, you immediately imagine yourself in such a situation. Escape routes, theories, psychological analyses, reasons, purposes. Lanthimos invites us to one of his dystopias by tearing us away from the utopia we have created in our minds while walking down a street or listening to music on the subway or doing anything anywhere.
Throughout the film, all characters stand out with their emotionlessness. The robotic acting of the actors in the film supports the emotionless lives of the characters, and this deliberately makes the audience bored. The universe depicted by The Lobster is so devoid of emotion that people do not laugh, do not cry, and almost never get angry. They voice empty topics with dialogues that sound very artificial and always with the same emphasis. This indicates that society no longer has emotions, and the film satirizes exactly this and expresses it through the acting. As in the movie, David doesnt even know when he should cry. This reminds the audience once again how callous human beings have become. In this respect, I think casting is very important. I think the casting was very successful. Lea Seydoux jumpscare! When I see her, I get stunned, she is extraordinary.
The callousness and superficiality we see throughout the film, combined with the narrative of the film, makes us question todays relationships Do we currently have relationships with people based only on concrete things (beauty, career, money, etc.) instead of superficial, human-like connection? When establishing a relationship, what is important is the bond or the characteristics we have in common or the characteristics we want to share? Thanks to this dystopian narrative, all of this becomes conceivable for todays reality.
Also, my favorite part of the movie was Lanthimos dragging us from a world where being a couple is mandatory to a world where being alone is mandatory. By creating worlds that are completely opposite to each other, he has simply conveyed the modern understanding of relationships with two different extreme examples. The well-chosen music, character expressions, and color choices convey a tense mood to the audience throughout the film. Taken as a whole, it seems that the director wants to show the audience a dilemma and problematizes this by sometimes using irony. We come across many sociological and philosophical issues that are discussed and questioned in the subtext of the film. Those who choose partners to avoid turning into animals when they are not in love, and those who act as if they are not in love when they are in love with each other among those who walk alone. Its like wanting to go there when you say dont go there. Its like wanting to eat the forbidden fruit. Human beings and their desire to break prohibitions never ends.

The Lobster. 2015. Directed by Yorgos Lanthimos.
The Lobster (2015) is a unique multi-genre spanning love story. Lanthimos used suspense, comedy, and a sci-fi scenario to build a unique screenplay that was so dynamic that it was nominated for Best Original Screenplay. In addition, it was the Cannes Queer Palm Special Mention, Jury Prize Winner, and Palm Dog Winner. In this dystopian world, single men and women are in danger everywhere. If one is single they are taken to The Hotel where they have very bizarre rules and 45 days to find a partner. If they do not succeed at The Hotel they are transformed into animals. However, there are Loners that live in The Woods and they have their own rules and culture. The Hotel and The Woods are well written sociologic experiments. 
The actors have a rich deeply mined script to work with. As such, they can showcase their brightly tuned talents. David (Colin Farrell) and Rachel Weiss (Short Sighted Woman) have an arch that is inspiring and tragic. Lanthimoss films are inspired by Greek tragedy. I have not found a direct reference for The Lobster but, there are instances in mythology where people are punished and turned into animals. In The Killing of a Sacred Deer (2017), Lanthimos used Euripides for inspiration. Nevertheless, this film was shot in Ireland making for a great landscape and hotel environment to breath life into his brilliant screenplay. Thimios Bakatakis (Attenberg, The Lobster, and Dogtooth) captures the A list actors while acting transformed in this surreal, riveting story. Each of Lanthimoss films is singular in its own way while still staying in a niche world. His films have garnered awards. The Favourite (2018) won Oscars, BAFTAs, and AFI movie of the year. Despite all of the awards, Lanthimos is stubbornly independent and this is what attracts us to his films. He brings arthouse to Hollywood and wins.

If you encounter any problems you cannot resolve yourselves, you will be assigned children, that usually helps.
The Lobster is something strange and seems to be made by some sort of alien. Its tonally boundless and yet feels exactly as it was intended--as if made by someone with a grand vocabulary in every language ever created. The film is set in a city in which being in a relationship is a necessity. Without being in a relationship one is forced to stay at a hotel to find a partner or, after forty-five days, be turned into an animal--luckily one gets to choose which animal. David (Colin Farrell) has been taken to the hotel to find his new partner. 
The film features a completely committed cast from greats like Colin Farrell and Rachel Weisz to the recognizable and always good supporting cast of Ben Whishaw, John C. Reilly, Léa Seydoux, Angeliki Papoulia (of Dogtooth fame), Ariane Labed and the delightful Olivia Coleman. They all seem to fit this world like a group of character actors in a Christopher Guest film. They are asked to accept this unimaginable world and to commit to its uncategorizable tone. Its a feat most would not accomplish and one just as much in Lanthimoss hands as theirs. Luckily they all step up their game whether theyre stomping a dog to death or dancing in the woods to electronica.
The film has all the fashionings of a dystopic as much as The Hunger Games or Never Let Me Go. However, he paints the film in dazzling colors which, though highly contrasted, do more to highlight the suffocated possibilities of the world around them as opposed to most dystopics, which seek to suppress all color. Lanthimos does not attempt to hide the similarities, but instead reminds us in every frame the same potential parallel of each preposterous scene can be noticed in the coloring of our own world. Yet there is almost always this sickly green hue over the frame to remind us--to comfort us--that this is not explicitly our reality, but perhaps our near future.
Unlike common dystopics The Lobster approaches the circumstances more as a common trait than as a freedom that has been lost. Yet the question remains Will David be able to find that one person that he is meant for? That one person, based on one silly characteristic, which they share? The Lobster, like Lanthimoss other films, is a social satire on monogamy, sexuality, domesticity, and relationships in general. Lanthimos communicates these notions intelligently, humorously, and violently with utter discomfort. He allows a world to exist where we are confronted with the question what if no one ever loves you? Thats not funny and yet he is able to build an entire rom-com out of it. I am almost thankful for the violence in that it felt more appropriate to the themes. Like Wes Andersons films, the violence is done quickly and almost out of nowhere. Its incredibly hard to accomplish this in a film with a discomfort level that breeds violence in its nonchalant dialogue and its every frame. Yet the possibility to live without an assurance of love can drive people to more gruesome things than violence. Psychological deterioration. Complete emptiness. Essentially the Heartless Woman--a sociopath.
The difference between this and Lanthimoss other well-known film Dogtooth is that there can be no empathy in Dogtooth, only sympathy. A majority of audience members--hopefully--would not feel subjected to the behavior and psychological treatment of the children in Dogtooth but viewers of The Lobster will, almost certainly, understand what it feels like to feel as though no one in the world is meant for them and that they may ultimately end up alone. Both feature a satirical world satirizing the home in different aspects. Dogtooth highlights the psychological trauma of family but with The Lobster he takes a more particular look at domesticity and monogamy, the bread and butter of family. Theres no surprise that the disgust and violence of Dogtooth ultimately stems from the psychological trauma enacted by the parents.
In The Lobster Colin Farrells David is very Twombly-esque and much like the Her character, he conveys a loneliness which is common but still just as moving. What is uncommon about his character is how he attempts to deal with his loneliness. There are lonely people all around him who have been forced into the same isolation. They are told to capture the loners, the people they want desperately not to be, in order to give themselves more time to find their partner. Ben Whishaws Limping Man lies and pretends in order to ascend from this place. John C. Reillys Lisping Man catches loner after loner to secure his time. David attempts both and can do neither. Does he really want love that badly and is what he striving for love at all?
The introduction of the loners demonstrates just how oppressive societal expectations on relationships are. The couples want you to be a couple and the loners want you to be a loner. You cannot escape one without being the other. You get shoved in box after box. It reveals that some of the couples are not really happy, perhaps not even made for each other. However, the loners are without comfort and affection. They are bound by nothing other than their hatred of the couples. Being a loner means being independent but in this film it means being independent of society--not of thought. The punishments doled out by the loners appear just as bad as the couples. They promise mutilation--eventually an act of blindness. The couples literally dehumanize them  as if they were animals but ultimately feel more humane than the loners. They cut off any connection one could have towards another human being.
As much as the film turns into a sort of dystopian love story it really doesnt promise all that much love. In this world love is based on a common characteristic. David and Short-Sighted Woman are both short-sighted. However, once Short-Sighted Woman is blinded, her and David are no longer a match. This means that, in order for them to technically be a match and be able to live freely, David must too be blind. Its a ridiculous premise but one the film sees as commonplace. Is David making himself blind as silly as Limping Man pretending he gets nosebleeds? Is their love anymore truthful since Short-Sighted Woman used to be short-sighted? Even in real life relationships can evolve but we forget sometimes that only people do. Sometimes it is hard to catch up to ones partner and sometimes its hard deciding whether or not its worth it. Thats what this film ends on--is it worth it? Is it worth it--in a society drastically more oppressive and controlling of its relationships--to love? Is love worth literally stabbing ones eyes out? Lanthimos doesnt give us an answer yet the audience is reminded that in our relationships they are either David with a blade to their eye or the Short-Sighted Woman alone at a table. Which is better? Which one are you?
The Lobster has been highly anticipated all around and, after seeing it, has been well worth the wait. The worlds Lanthimos creates feature violence and extreme discomfort and yet they are sights audiences cannot wait to sit and bear. Like any good filmmaker he is able to show the audience a different world than their own, as if looking through a telescope aimed high above somewhere, but all the while actually holding up a mirror which, though distorted, has all the same shapes and features of the world around us, of you and me.

Its the kind of idea that immediately sticks with you because there really isnt anything else quite like it.
Yorgos Lanthimos has such a distinct voice, and thats easily one of the films greatest strengths. Every frame feels carefully composed, the deadpan humor works effortlessly, and the unsettling atmosphere is present from beginning to end. Even though I dont always click with his films, I cant help but admire how uncompromising his vision is.
That being said, I dont think this one is entirely for me. I usually enjoy unconventional, offbeat films, but The Lobster sometimes dragged a little too much. As fascinating as the ideas are, I never felt fully invested in what was happening, and by the end I was left admiring it more than loving it. Theres an emotional distance to the whole film that feels completely intentional, but it also made the experience feel a bit empty for me.
Even so, its a beautifully crafted film that fully commits to its strange world without ever second guessing itself. Its the kind of movie that stays in your head after the credits roll, whether you connected with it or not. It didnt completely land for me, but I still liked it a lot and I wouldnt be surprised if I appreciated it even more on a rewatch.

Gracias por existir Yorgos
Que mejor manera de llegar a las mil películas en Letterboxd que viendo alguna cinta de mi director favorito, había escuchando tanto de esta cinta que llegue con el hype mega alto y aún así no me decepciono en lo absoluto.
The lobster fácilmente podría ser la obra mas apegada a la ciencia ficción de toda la filmografía de Yorgos Lanthimos, y aún así puede mantener la esencia de su cine y su sátira atemporal que se puede asemejar a las conductas sociales contemporáneas. En esta ocasión se presenta un futuro distópico en donde la humanidad ha sido afectada por una importante reducción en su población al grado en que la mayoría de la sociedad y las autoridades han optado por tomar políticas extremas para impulsar el brote de la tasa de natalidad mediante el emparejamiento forzoso de sus habitantes. En este universo futurista parece presentarse una regla sencilla, como ser humano el único fin es encontrar una pareja, en caso no se logre o se rompa el vínculo matrimonial el propio estado se encargará de emparejar a los solteros en campos de concentración ubicados a las afueras de las ciudades (donde habitan las parejas ya consolidadas) con un plazo máximo para lógralo de 45 días. Del mismo modo y al presentarse un agravado problema de escasez de recursos naturales aquellas personas que no aporten a la repoblación significan un gasto de reservas innecesario por lo que deberán ser transformadas en el animal que ellos deseen.
Así como se presenta al bando en pro de la repoblación también se presenta al grupo rebelde, los solteros, quienes son constantemente buscados y casados por los reclutados de los campos para obtener un beneficio temporal, estos también se ubican en una postura extremista al limitar la libertad y las relaciones interpersonales entre sus miembros.
Esa previa sinopsis podría resultar en algo muy ambiguo en tanto que el cine de Yorgos suele desempeñarse en torno a varias capas, por un lado se tiene la narración de la vida de David, un hombre recientemente abandonado por su esposa quien se ofrece ante un campo de concentración para emprender la búsqueda de su nueva media naranja y de su lugar en esa agitada sociedad, sin embargo, ello es solo la superficie de los subtemas que se van sacando a flote a medida que la historia se desarrolla. En un inicio el prota luce evidentemente afectado por la ruptura con quien compartió más de una década de su vida por lo que adopta una posición de indiferencia frente a conocer a alguien nuevo, es en esta etapa en la que se suelta la primera clave para entender la cinta el animal seleccionado de David es una langosta, la cual en sus palabras es una criatura que poco común de ser elegida, siendo lo usual los perros, del mismo modo es una criatura muy longeva, fiel a una sola pareja y lo relaciona con su atracción por la vida marina. Esas razones parecen ser el motor de su elección pero se puede llegar a presentar otras razones no explicitas que la justificarían, por ejemplo se tiene el hecho que ante las políticas de transformación de las personas en animales el consumo de alimentos de origen animal se halla limitado, siendo uno de los sectores más restringidos la pesca, en consecuencia la langosta por su alto precio sería una criatura casi exonerada de la dieta común de ese mundo. 
Posterior a su ingreso al hotel se van presentando con más claridad las comparativas y críticas que componen el comportamiento humano al momento de cimentar nuevas relaciones, se da una brillante exposición de los prejuicios, del encasillamiento de las personas en base al físico o a cualidades muy específicas, la superficialidad en torno a la elección de parejas siempre que se comparta similitudes que pueden resultar muy banales, y la enfermiza necesidad de encajar en el prototipo de pareja perfecta o de no quedarse solo.
Por otro lado si se habla de características fidedignas del cine de Lanthimos no se puede dejar de mencionar la monotonía y frialdad en torno a la expresividad de su cast, casi como fingiendo conductas, no hay momentos eufóricos, los diálogos son frívolos, los colores y los planos son hasta deprimentes, la propia música aunque imponente se usa de forma muy repetitiva lo cual podría suponer en algo negativo, sin embargo consideró que esa sensación de hartazgo tienen un objetivo el plasmar la simpleza con la que muchas relaciones empiezan y terminan, el como las apariencias y la monotonía generan que el egoísmo humano en su afán de progresar deje en el camino a las otras personas que formaron parte de su vida. 
Los personajes que hacen aparición en el viaje de David tampoco sobran en su afán de dejar lamentables lecciones, se tiene por ejemplo la interacción que se genera entre el prota y la mujer que le ofrece acostarse con tal de obtener una mejor ubicación para arrojarse por la ventana y evitar el otro fatídico destino, ya que por sus características físicas y su desesperación se ve con pocas posibilidades de conseguir emparejarse. Se presentan dos amigos con quienes compartirá su estadía, uno muy a la expectativa de cambiar su forma de ser con tal de agradar a la mayor cantidad de candidatas y otro quien en su afán de conquistar a una de las jóvenes reclusas optará por la mentira. También aparece en la historia el personaje de la frívola mujer quien constantemente se jacta de su habilidad para evadir a las relaciones serias, a pesar de esa descripción el prota intenta seducirla pero ella logrará de forma cruel revelar su mentira, la cual sería castigada con la brutal muerte de su hermano y la probable transformación, sin embargo David siempre se muestra temeroso respecto de su seguridad así que huye del recinto.
Ya la última etapa de la cinta se presenta la otra cara de la moneda, logra encontrar en los bosques a un grupo de opositores solteros quienes le ofrecen seguridad a cambio de seguir sus estrictas reglas. A pesar de las advertencias opta por enamorarse del personaje de Rachel Weisz, con quien sostendrá un romance secreto y prohibido que podría ser castigado de la forma más cruda y simbólica posible.
Lo que me pareció sorprendente es como cada escena puede resultar tan relevante al punto que deja poco margen para vacíos en la trama a pesar del complejo universo que se presenta, y a pesar de darle mil vueltas a los sucesos que se van presentando casi no encontré incoherencias, aún así hay situaciones que quizás se podrían inferir pero no resultan ser del todo claras, como puede ser el rol de las personas homosexuales, asexuales y las personas infértiles al ser en teoría inservibles a este modelo de repoblación, sobre este punto en un diálogo introductorio a la llegada de David al hotel se llega a mencionar que tiene la posibilidad de elegir su orientación sexual pero solo a ser heterosexual u homosexual, pero en el desarrollo de la cinta no se llega a apreciar ninguna pareja homosexual. También llegada cierta parte de sugiere que la adopción es una alternativa, esto cuando hace aparición una niña que acompaña a la joven pareja que reside en el yate, no me quedo muy claro si se les asignó solo durante su convivencia o si es que será temporalmente su hija, o es que acaso alguno de los dos cónyuges tuvo a dicha niña previo a llegar al hotel, insisto que quizás se me pasó la explicación de ese vacío y quizás con una revisión de la cinta pueda hallar la respuesta.
Llegando a su final que amerita una advertencia de SPOILERS este podría aparentar ser muy ambiguo y la verdad me dejó pensando demasiado, aún así da cabida a dos posibles desenlaces la pareja de prófugos al entrar al restaurante de muestran convencidos de una decisión irreversible, a continuación David ingresa con un cuchillo a solas en los baños con el fin de ponerse en las mismas condiciones que su amada. La interrogante es si lo llega a hacer o no. Si es que lo hizo esto se podría justificar en la constante necesidad del prota de encajar en un cualidad muy específica de su pareja a elegir, ya que en un inicio el eligió a Rachel por su misma condición de miopía, ahora con la ceguera requiere estar a mano con ella. Del mismo modo la elección clave de la langosta como animal de transformación es un símil de la condición final del prota al ser este ser acuático un animal ciego.
Por otro lado se presenta un elemento qué pasa desapercibido pero que resulta ser muy concluyente posterior al cierre de la última escena se llega a presentar acompañada de los créditos finales una composición musical que parece sugerir el ruido del mar y de las olas, esto sugeriría que David perseguido por la duda y por su constante búsqueda del libre albedrío no llego a producirse la ceguera y abandono a su pareja con el fin de entregarse y transformarse en su mayor propósito de vida ser la langosta.
Esta cinta lejos de ser solo una cinta compleja de sci-fi es todo una retorcida y original exploración del amor y de las relaciones superficiales, a su vez me pareció un bello ensayo sobre el amor propio, la autoestima, lo ridículo que resulta ciertas imposiciones sociales y la libertad personal como generador de la felicidad, para mi lo tiene todo como para ser considerada de las mejores obras cinematográficas de este siglo.
Btw me quede con ganas de ver un rol más protagónico de Olivia Colman.
PD Gracias por leer y por seguirme por todo este tipo que llevo en esta bella comunidad.

If you havent guessed it already by now, I love Yorgos Lanthimos, just in general. I love that he exists. He has probably, what I believe to be, the best film streak of the last 20 years. The man released Dogtooth, Alps, The Lobster, The Killing of a Sacred Deer, The Favorite, and not a single one was a miss. His unsettling atmosphere and sterile dialogue always works wonders in his favor, crafting films that questions societal norms, and shed light on issues many people refuse to believe exist or either deliberately try to ignore. This man is a genius, and I will find it a hard time to trust anyone that believes otherwise. Im addicted to his aesthetic in which he chooses to make his film appear, and the way he chooses to tell his stories. With that being said, I decided to revisit The Lobster
When talking about Yorgos The Lobster, we almost never fail to discuss about the absurdity of the premise, a premise which some people deem to be as silly. Talks can go on and on about what this premise means, but not enough questions are thrown as to why Yorgos decided to go through with such an intriguing yet weird story foundation. Its simple. Yorgos wants to ask the basic question of is love REAL or just another social construct the sheep of society mindlessly follow? And in my opinion, The Lobster explores this idea really well.
The foolish rule of needing commonalities between a couple is something were all aware of as a myth. Its ridiculous how this is something taken as a normality. The film does a really impressive satirical take to showcase the desperation of people just to be able to attain this so called love. The satirization of societal authorities and rulings on something as fascinatingly complex as love is straight up childish. Faking nosebleeds by banging their head, hitting a little child with no hesitation, and sitting quietly in a jacuzzi while witnessing another person seem to drown with no remorse whatsoever, are some excellent examples in the film. The 1st act consists of most of the films set-up, world-building, and incredible attention to detail, which I argue to be some of Yorgos best work. However, I do believe the film does lose its way nearing the end. Dont get me wrong, the ending including the final shot are phenomenal, but everything that lead up to it doesnt compare to everything that came before it.
One of the most notable key factors to what make Yorgos films stand out are the somewhat dead-inside, monotone way of line delivery. This is something that takes place in every Lanthimos movie, we know this. But I really believe it works the best for The Lobster. The way society and authoritarian rule have systemized and forcefully crafted what love SHOULD be has stripped the normal everyday-men of basic emotions, to the point where all of this is taken as natural. Its disturbing and unsettling because it IS disturbing and unsettling. It enforces a mood onto the viewers to subtly showcase the twisted preposterousness of it all without being overly blunt. Its amazing, if you ask me.
The final shot really stuck me with me even after waking up the next day. This is ambiguity done right. This is the answer to Yorgos question. In order to remain a couple in the city, a similar attribute must exist. Will Farrell blind himself to persevere this love of theirs and continue to play with societys ridiculous rules, or will he choose to remain with sight and risk both their lives as humans. Its an ending we will never be able to truly answer. However, if you do watch till the credits, youll be able to hear the waves of the sea. People have suggested that this is a call back to Farrell wanting to be a lobster, not because he ends up being a beast, but because he is at peace at sea. If you hadnt gotten it already. The evidence points to Farrell successfully blinding himself, playing by the rules of society, but continuing, what we all hope to be, a healthy relationship with the woman he loves.

Shot in controlled static frames, Lanthimos puts all of his effort into static construction, leaving nothing to chance. His playful references to Jean Renoir feel ill-advised Renoir showed a world in which society is brimming with rules, but leaving them always to the abstract. Lanthimos never has the imagination to trust his audience. Ferrel and his co-star Rachael Weisz make good of their playful attitude, but its hard to find interest in a comedy that rarely challenges beyond its initial setup, lulling into comfortable platitudes.

In a future dystopian (and arguably utilitarian) society people are not allowed to be single. Whoever doesnt have a partner is sent to a hotel where he must find one in 45 days or else he will be transformed into an animal. There is also some kind of resistance movement, bands of Loners that roam the nearby forest and occasionally try to disrupt the process of match-making.
Weird doesnt even begin to describe this absurdist dramedy that satirizes modern social conventions and sexual politics. Even the most outlandish situations are played straight and the humor is more often than not of the gallows variety. The film has its flaws, for example some bits seem to have been included for no other reason other than their shock value and the ending is a predictable cop-out. But to Lanthimos credit while his movie is very ambitious artistically and demands full commitment from the viewer, it never becomes pretentious, abstruse or boring. Its easily accessible and the social commentary is clever and insightful.
The actors are all very good, successfully immersing themselves into their roles and becoming an integral part of the directors universe. A low-key Collin Farrell, almost unrecognizable as a slob loser, is excellent as the protagonist. His chemistry with Rachel Weisz is very good and we believe their relationship despite the absence of any of the usual romantic tropes. They are supported by a no-nonsense Lea Seydoux (considerably less glamorous here than in Spectre), Ben Whisaw and John C. Reilly.
Perhaps the biggest achievement of The Lobster is that it manages to present an old and overused premise in a way that is original, fresh and thought-provoking. If you feel adventurous enough to enter into Lanthimos world then I can guarantee you that you wont regret it a bit.

What a beautiful weirdness Im always searching for. Yorgos Lanthimos turns dating into a surreal nightmare, and I love how its weird, sad, and oddly hopeful all at once. His films make you question everything about human connection while keeping you uncomfortably entertained.
This film is my spirit animal... except Im pretty sure Im just gonna stay human and lonely.

For a generation terrified of sex, or even companionship, romcom can only be processed as a horror movie now. Otherwise its problematically normative or abusive (meaning they dont like watching funny, lively people - its too threatening to their misanthropic self-regard). Torture, trauma and mutilation are a big laugh for subverting gender or half-assed girlboss class-war, but the idea of two people living happily ever after makes them sick. One day they may even get the option of sentencing Cary Grant or Doris Day to jail at the end of every movie (not Rock Hudson or Marilyn Monroe though, suffering in itself makes you radical and iconic). They watch old romcoms as if theyre having to meet mum or dads new partner again. The eternal recurrence of adolescent resentment. 
Yorgos Lanthimos knows how to pander to both his audience and industry peers, who are equally as misanthropic. Maybe apart from Dogtooth, his satires are toothless, pandering and old hat. They look very ugly and have ugly attitudes, but threaten nothing except aesthetic sense. No global northerner in 2015 felt under pressure to marry. This isnt 1955. If anything, the leading motivation for rushed marriage is buying a house - a financial anxiety Lanthimos would wave away as irrelevant. Once again he wastes an excellent cast on geekshow schtick, this time talking like Dr. Who aliens instead of toddlers in adult bodies. As ever, his sloppy timing and pacing makes this already overlong film feel even longer. Once we get the joke theres nowhere left to go. Its a 00s comedy sketch that should have lasted about five minutes. His brand of surrealism is no more radical - and definitely no more original - than that of Spike Milligan or Monty Python. His recurring motifs of weird dancing and attractive women mutilating themselves is a dead giveaway of what he pays sex workers to do for him. He might be selling pain to people who prefer watching that to joy, but hes as much the sadistic John as his biggest fans are.

Maybe Im projecting, but at times it felt like a parody of how society fetishizes romantic relationships.
Like its making fun of people who have that if I dont find my soulmate I am doomed mentality. And the corollary of that I found my soulmate I am so much better than you now!
Probably one of the strangest film Ive ever watched.

The first hour threatens to be a high concept drama set against the backdrop of this strange but compelling dystopian society that is interwoven with intrigue and dehumanising dating politics. 
The second hour is a passable romantic comedy that lacks genuine substance.

Very cute in a very weird way. I love the underlying message of truly loving someone for who they are instead of matching up because of certain traits. I think its a really important look at how superficial people can sometimes be when looking for a relationship, and how all that leads to is loneliness. I also found a lot of the way they acted as kind of endearing in this odd almost love on the spectrum type of style.
That isnt to say it doesnt have its flaws. I know its based on a book but I wish we could have seen more of the hotel storyline because I was really interested in the things that were going on at the actual hotel itself. Once it got to the woods the pacing slowed down very quickly and felt a bit sluggish for the rest of the movie. It also was excessively weird at certain points to the degree where it took me out of the movie a little bit, but overall it was still not as aggressively absurd as other Yorgos films can be. However the ending is a really interesting ambiguous type thing that definitely has you thinking once its over.
Colin Farrell gives a great performance and has so much likability and depth in his character and the ensemble cast does great as well.

This might be one of not only Yorgos Lanthimos best movie, but also one of Colin Farrells best movie role in his career. Very bizarre at best,  a fantastic cast. What a perfection from Yorgos Lanthimos!

Its a time-honored truth the couple that develops their own language and likes to dance to a Nick Cave and Kylie Minogue duet about bloody murder is a couple thats bound to stay together.
We build relationships and societies on habits, rules and rituals. Could any of those shared qualities be more or less ridiculous than another? Maybe all true love is that twisted condition, a folie à deux - you make your various preposterous agreements, for better and for worse.
Im reminded of the ending to another film that I admire now, Great Freedom for love, some people would be ready to make any sacrifice. It only matters that the choice makes sense to them.
Are you sure youre prepared to do that?
Yes, of course Im sure. I wouldnt propose it otherwise.

So following the critical and commercial failure of Transformers The Last Knight, Michael Bay has since decided to step away from directing the Transformers movies and make his next feature a very expensive Netflix original called 6 Underground. Even then, I wasnt aware of this films existence until one day a few months ago, my dad puts this film on and watches it with Mom, and they didnt like it for how crude and graphic it was. I wasnt even paying attention because I was on my phone doing my own thing, so just recently was my first time seeing 6 Underground. And I hated it. Its not the 1 worst Michael Bay film, but its definitely in the bottom 3 for me...
6 Underground has an admittingly fun premise, being about a team of vigilantes trying to overthrow a ruthless leader. Sadly, the execution of the storytelling is pathetic! I dont hold much high standards for Netflix originals, but some of them have managed to be pretty good. This, however, is a textbook example of a bad Netflix original. Despite having an expensive budget, the writing for 6 Underground is so subpar, and Michael Bay just doesnt have the right sauce for this one like he had with The Rock, Armageddon, and the first Transformers. Instead, its another piece of bottom-of-the-barrel Bayhem, not much different from his other low efforts. Its boring, its obnoxious, its loud, its poorly shot, and its not funny.
I was hoping the cast would be the saving grace for this otherwise standard plot, since it has a few stars that I enjoy seeing, but they werent very enjoyable. Contrary to all of the vocal film bros on the internet, I dont hate Ryan Reynolds. I actually really like him as a comedian, even if his wise-cracking shtick that he perfected with Deadpool got kinda repetitive after a while. With that said, I didnt like him at all here! Reynolds tries his best as Magnet S. Johnson a.k.a. One, but hes at his most obnoxious here. Just a much weaker version of Deadpool as this billionaire turned vigilante leader and not much else. Mélanie Laurent got wasted badly here as Two  Camille, and so are Manuel Garcia-Tulfo, Ben Hardy, Adria Arjona, Dave Franco, and even Corey Hawkins. Theyre all a bunch of lame vigilante characters who dont have any special arcs. You only know them by their numbers, and that just doesnt cut it for me!
A lot of the action in this film isnt that good. Im sure some of the stunt work was alright, but my goodness its so hard to enjoy when this film has such awful editing! This whole movie felt like an action movie trailer drawn out for two hours, the cuts were so annoying! I cant think of that many action sequences that were truly cool to watch, and its no help the editing makes it hard to keep up with all the fight choreography and chase scenes here. I guess the opening chase was kinda cool, and one particular scene Ill address very soon worked pretty well for me, haha.
As for the comedy, 6 Underground really doesnt work with its comedic moments. For one, Ryan Reynolds usual snarky persona outside of Deadpool is pretty annoying here. Whenever he interrupted a serious moment with his wise-cracking attitude, I just rolled my eyes. It worked for Deadpool because it was meant to be a parody of superhero flicks, but here is a regular action movie, and undercutting serious dramatic scenes with that in-your-face Ryan Reynolds comedy feels so forced and try-hard, on top of all the bloody over-the-top violence. Like, for gosh sake, quit trying to be an MCU knockoff and just let the comedy come naturally! Smh. I didnt feel anything during the so-called emotional scenes, either, since everything about the political subject matter was only surface level at best.
As for the audiovisual experience, this film falls extremely flat on its face! Sure, I liked a few of the stunts and the city locations the characters drive around in, but the editing is what makes this film look much worse than it wouldve been. I dont think Ive ever seen a Michael Bay movie with editing this bad aside from maybe The Last Knight, but that films issue was the aspect ratios, lol. I also didnt like the soundtrack that much, which is a first for a Michael Bay movie besides Bayformers 4  5. Most of the song choices felt oddly distracting, like why the hell did they think it was a good idea to play a techno-remixed version of O Fortuna from Carmina Burana? Why does that remix even exist in the first place?! It sounds so amateur compared to how simple the original recording was!
Ok, those are pretty much all my major gripes with 6 Underground. There are a couple of things I liked about this that save it from being the worst Bay film, one of those being how the film has its fun moments. Like I said, I kinda enjoyed the opening car chase, which more or less set the tone for the fast-paced action I was in for. I maybe laughed once or twice, and theres one specific setpiece that I got a kick out of the one where they shatter glass with sound waves using the THX Deep Note. I miss THX, so that was a joy to hear. Not since Over the Hedge have I seen the Deep Note used in such a clever fashion, lol.
Also, I did enjoy some of the visuals. Shitty editing aside, I dig the vibes this films going for in its locations. They went to Italy, LA, Budapest, and several cities in the United Arab Emirates for this, and I heard how they got the UAE military to help out by having their soldiers and aircraft show up in the film. Also, generally speaking, the sound design, visual effects, and stunt work are decently solid for a Netflix original. I could tell Michael Bay and crew took advantage of the 150 million budget and made it look as cool as possible for whats only available on streaming. If only other certain Netflix originals wouldve thought to do the same, smh.
Overall, 6 Underground is an awful Netflix original action flick from Michael Bay that I just couldnt stand watching. I barely knew anything about it before seeing it, and it looks like wasnt missing out on anything! Its so, so bad, having shitty storytelling, bad direction from Michael Bay, annoying characters with try-hard performances, subpar thrills, cringe comedy, lackluster depth, choppy editing, and a disposable soundtrack. Granted, it has its few fun scenes and some cool visuals, but theyre not worth being in what is ultimately another terrible Michael Bay film that Im slowly forgetting about right now. The whole film lurid, crass, borderline reprehensible in its revelling of violence, and goddamn if you can get on its wavelength it is some of the most fun youll have with a film. The final set-piece on the yacht in particular is some of Bays most creative filmmaking to date.
Better yet Bay addresses one of the biggest complaints with his films theyre too damn long and often excessive and plodding. Not 6 Underground, being just over two hours its one of Bays shortest films, but it is paced almost perfectly. Theres always something going on, but it works because unlike The Last Knight its not trying to juggle a dozen plots at once.
For as crass and tasteless as the whole film can be, theres a surprising sincerity behind the film, and what I mean by that is that Michael Bay is taking the concept of the film quite seriously. Most directors would take the idea of a group of individuals becoming vigilantes to overthrow evil dictators and completely deconstruct the very idea of it, but not Bay. Bay treats the very idea with complete wide-eyed sincerity and makes the protagonists look like the most badass motherfuckers alive. Its child-like power fantasy, but Michael Bay himself once said he made films for teenagers, and with films like 6 Underground he shows that he can do it better than most. 
Its safe to say that I like more Michael Bay films than I dont, and with being one film away from completion I feel like 6 Underground completes an unofficial trilogy of sorts. None of these are my personal favourite Bay film, but I think this film, Bad Boy 2  Pain  Gain are Michael Bay at his Purest. While it seems like his movies speak the language of normal blockbuster cinema, their absolute insanity results in viewing experiences like nothing else. Theyre not good, but any film experience where you never look away and the film stays on your mind constantly afterwards is a worthwhile one, whether good or bad. Bad Boys II was Bay unleashed at a level where it seemed impossible for any studio to let him go that hard again. I didnt have huge expectations for his latest Netflix release, but it surprised me by being Bayhem on nightmare mode, unleashed for the second time (maybe third? I still need to see Pain  Gain). This still doesnt reach the lurid heights of Bad Boys II, but what does? 
The film opens on a 20 minute car chase that is lit like a student film but contains enough destruction to fulfill the 150 million dollar budget. The overcutting is so exaggerated that it becomes borderline experimental, especially in the beginning. Any other blockbuster would have it as the climax, but this is only the beginning of 6 Undergrounds non-stop Bayhem. I was worried that the plot would be white noise to fulfill the space between the setpieces, but 6 Undergrounds plot is the most absolutely nutty libertarian bullshit Ive ever seen. Ryan Reynolds plays a billionaire ancap who makes on Oceans Eleven-style mission to lead a coup for a Middle Eastern country because the American government doesnt do anything to stop the cartoonishly evil dictator. The story structure turns this ludicrous plotline into an incoherent one. Nothing makes any fucking sense. Scenes are just abruptly strung together with no regard for pacing or timing. Flashbacks are thrown in seemingly at random. It gives the movie an unintentional fever dream quality which only adds to the absolutely amazing experience of viewing Micheal Bay hell. Im sorry to say that I was way more engaged in this stupid bullshit than actually good movies from this year because of how baffled I was by just about every scene. While Bay will never truly make another Bad Boys II, this is as close as well get in the modern era. A must-see for anyone whos into vulgar auteurism or cinematic trainwrecks. I would still rank it as better than Midsommar.

Cineaste trigger warning the following review contains unrepentant praise of Michael Bay.
Too few directors have a truly distinct visual style. Cinema is, after all, a medium reliant on the stimuli of imagery. I suspect part of the reason is that even legendary, accomplished, and excellent directors can achieve tremendous artistry with a merely functional eye for imagery. Woody Allen is a perfect example. Before he was cancelled and banned from discourse, Allen was a masterful writer who tended to wring excellent performances from his actor. And yet throughout his career he remained a staid visual stylist content with bland camera movement and functional editing. Even his most visually compelling films like Midnight in Paris feel like the imprint of his artistic collaborators rather than real evolution in Allens eye. Michael Bay is not Woody Allen, but Michael Bay has one hell of an eye for an image.
If youre saying to yourself But Bernard, he wastes those keen visuals gifts on steroidal action heroes and bimbo call girls filtered through a lens of a strangely expansionist, yet resoundingly Libertarian, America Fuck Yea! ideology, I dont really have a comeback. He does! His politics are nonsensical and basal. For someone with 45 production credits and 57 directing credits, its remarkable that he has not one writing credit. 
And yet...
Any film fan can pick out a Michael Bay movie with just one second of footage. His visual voice is as instantly recognizable as the true masters of the craft, a Scorsese or a Fincher. Many have attempted to emulate his style, and most of the pretenders are now folks like McG making low budget Netflix schlock. I do think this matters. Bay, too, is a kinetic and stylish action filmmaker. His older films like The Rock and Armageddon have aged reasonably well in large part because the action is so competently staged. And, I say this with love, Bay remains true to himself.
So whats to be said about this. Its certainly not Bays best film, but I dont think the experience is all that different from transition from snorting Bayhem to inserting it directly into your blood stream. This movie is fucking bonkers. Its percussive, concussive, propulsive in the action beats, and startlingly violent. The film houses three main action set pieces each more extreme than the one before (though each feels like a diminished return because of some screen writing issues). Chasing cars end up flying through the air at a rate of approximately two every 10 seconds. Whats new here is the way Bay seems to relish in making sure we see the additional carnage of bodies ejected from each vehicle causing their own cascading crashes. It almost feels like the influence of Angry Birds on cinematic vehicular mayhem. I cannot recall another movie to embrace that sort of violence with such aplomb.
The screenplay is structurally broken. As is their wont, writers Paul Wernick and Rhett Reese cant help themselves but to rely on flashbacks to explain the characters. While none of these bland archetypal characters really need explanations, the flashback structure absolutely crucifies the films momentum time and again. The actors are fine enough. Ryan Reynolds does his usual Ryan Reynolds thing. Melanie Laurent gets to collect a paycheck and look bad ass. Iranian actor Payman Maadi (of A Separation) and Israeli actor Lior Raz (of Fauda) are for some reason cast as the feuding brothers of a terrorist sympathetic fake country that emulates the United Arab Emirates. They too were likely happy with their paychecks. The overall story about heroic sorts who fake their deaths so they can assassinate evildoers doesnt even really merit a breakdown of the bonkers politics or human cost it necessarily encompasses. The story is dumb and bad, and manages to get in the way of the action.
But, fuck it, I like Michael Bay. The action is fun. The visuals are stellar. The initial car chase delighted me as did the hilariously stupid climatic magnet fight. 
I totally get it if you cant turn your thinking mind off for this sort of thing, but Im glad I still can.

Transformers Revenge of the Fallen es una secuela que logra entretener y presentar una buena acción con efectos más que decentes, pero no va más allá de eso, su guion es muy pobre y tiene cosas muy absurdas en su desarrollo.
Sinopsis Han pasado dos años desde que los Transformers irrumpieran en la vida de Sam Witwicky. Ahora, el objetivo de Sam es ingresar en la universidad y llevar una vida tranquila, pero se ve otra vez involucrado en la guerra entre Autobots y Decepticons.
La historia es regular, el guion es más pobre que el de la primera cinta (lo cual ya dice mucho). Para empezar hay que destacar lo mejor que tiene la acción, la cual me parece que está muy bien lograda y nos otorga secuencias y momentos muy frenéticos que me gustaron por más exagerados que son. Sin embargo, cómo se complementa esto con el humor me parece patético, los chistes son horribles y encima hay muchos sexuales que no tienen nada de sentido y ni siquiera logran funcionar, una lástima la verdad. Por otro lado, la forma en la que expandieron el universo me parece que no estuvo mal, quizás es lo mejor que tiene el guion, ya que sacando eso me parece que tiene muchas inconsistencias y momentos convenientes para el desarrollo de la trama, además de que tampoco me gusta que no se tome en serio en cuanto a muertes de personajes, ya que hay algunos que aparecen o vuelven a aparecer sin sentido alguno, si entendí bien hay algunos que habían muerto en la primera que acá reviven por que sí. Por último, la duración acá si que se sintió, dura más de dos horas y media y tiene varias escenas innecesarias que no aportan nada a la trama, una lástima porque todas las películas de la saga tienen éstas duraciones y me da miedo que cada vez se ponga peor.
Los personajes son más de lo mismo, pero no estuvieron del todo mal. Sam sigue siendo mi favorito de los humanos, por más momentos tontos que tenga me parece que acá le dan un poco más de desarrollo y podemos ver esa faceta de líder que esperaba. Mikaela sigue sin ser mucho de mi agrado sinceramente, la relación con Sam es un poco peor que la que vimos en la anterior entrega, la llevan hacia un lado muy genérico. Por otro lado, de los Autobots los que más destacan son Optimus Prime y Bumblebee, me alegra que le hayan dado más desarrollo a éste último ya que en la anterior entrega se me quedó muy corto. Por último, de los Decepticons los que más destacan son Megatron y Fallen, ambos algo normalitos y hasta olvidables por sus motivaciones más que nada, me gustó que éste último tenga la voz de Tony Todd, lo hacía bastante imponente.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente los efectos, por lejos una de las mejores cosas de la película, para el año en el que salió no están nada mal y supieron aprovechar el gran presupuesto que tenían. Además, Michael Bay repite el rol como director y sigue siendo más de lo mismo, sigo manteniendo que es un director que no me agrada mucho, pero sabe cómo llevar a cabo las escenas de acción más que nada. Por otro lado, las actuaciones son normalitas, Shia LaBeouf es el que más destaca de los actores que salen en pantalla, ya que en las voces resaltan Peter Cullen, Mark Ryan, Tony Todd y Hugo Weaving. Por último, la banda sonora de Steve Jablonsky es algo olvidable, los temas de Linkin Park siguen siendo lo mejor.
En conclusión, una regular película que por lo menos sigue entreteniendo y expandiendo éste universo, pero es una lástima que el guion siga siendo flojo y ahora hasta tenga varias escenas de relleno. La recomiendo igualmente.
