So here I am, about to explain to you why I not only liked Revenge of the Fallen, but why its genuinely a better film than the first, generally better thought of, Transformers 2007.
......Well, this isnt how I expected to spend my Tuesday.
Thinking back on Transformers 2007, it really did feel like Bay was half-heartedly trying to emulate Steven Spielberg to some extent. Theres the boy and his car set-up, the attempts at making the Transformers feel awe inspiring, the many speeches from Optimus Prime about how humans are actually wonderful (even if quite a few of them are portrayed as assholes in the film). It really does make me realise what my disconnect was with that film because once again it was Bay trying to be something hes not.
Revenge of the Fallen is 100 Michael Bay, and yes, I think that makes for a better experience. The film moves at a far faster pace than Transformers 2007 and feels far more varied in scope. This particularly feels prominent in the big action set-pieces. 
Optimus Prime battling the Decepticons in the forest is probably the best action scene in the franchise, not only because the green surrounding helps for the grey, metallic Transformers to stand out, but because theres a feeling of actual choreography to it seeing Optimus pretty much getting his ass handed to him trying to fight off multiple Decepticons as once.
Similarly the final battle in Egypt feels like a better set pieces to Transformers 2007, again for its contrast in scenery, but theres also a great variety in Transformers. Giant testicles aside that huge Decepticon that climbs the pyramid looks cool. The Egypt set-piece does become impossible to follow as it goes on, and the final fight between Optimus and the Fallen is lacking, but its improvement over the first film.
Of course going full-Bay means that the juvenile humour gets ramped up, and I can see why it got so many people angry in 2009, but thats Michael Bay for ya. I can see why the depiction of those two Transformers felt racist to some, but to be perfectly blunt thats how Bay present almost all non-white people in this series. I dont think theyre the worst example of this in the franchise. 
Funnily enough despite the film being more eventful and on the rails than Transformers 2007, from the characterisation point I think Revenge of the Fallen was an improvement. Most noticeably were Megatron and Starscream, who actually get a few scenes together and have characterisation befitting their origins. With the Autobots meanwhile having Optimus taken out for much of the film was a wise choice because it gave importance behind the films McGuffin. 
Megan Foxs Mikaela is still the best character in the film and shouldve been the main lead once again, but to be fair Shia Lebeoufs Sam is actually improved from the first film. I wouldnt call him likeable, but hes not insufferable anymore. His defining trait isnt being horny and is actually quite dedicated to his relationship with Mikaela. God its so fucking great that that will be gone in Dark of the Moon.
Probably the best improved characterisation though is John Turturro, who goes from one dimensional bureaucrat to brave, if cranky, hero. From a character point of view the only regression was Sams parents, who were annoying in the first film and almost tank the first 30 minutes of this film.
On a final note, I actually think Bay toned himself down in one way this film feels a lot less liking its giving the US Military a hand-job. Hes still glorifying it to an extent, but it actually feels like he was more interested in selling us on the actual Transformers this time. Honestly Id call that an improvement.
I keep thinking back on my experience watching this film, thinking how I should hate it, but I cant deny how much of a better experience it was than Transformers 2007, where I had to keep pausing the film because it struggled to keep my attention. Revenge of the Fallen is a dumb, loud, probably straight up offensive film...
...But the film is fun with a capital F. It rarely sags or takes forever to get to the next part. Its surface level as fuck but if surface level entertainment can keep me pre-occupied for 150 minutes? Ive got to give the film credit.
So yea, I legit enjoyed Revenge of the Fallen. Genuinely makes me glad Im doing this Michael Bay marathon. You discover feelings about stuff you wouldnt ever have imagined having

Transformers Revenge of the Fallen. Now, Ive got some relatively unique thoughts about this one. This is the highly anticipated sequel to the crowd pleaser Transformers from 2007, and upon its release, its reception wasnt pretty. Revenge of the Fallen has been widely panned by critics and most TF fans as a very disappointing and terrible sequel, even going as far as winning the Razzie Award for Worst Picture. Like, wow. All it took was one sequel for most who were onboard with Michael Bays Transformers to change their minds and say his TF adaptations suck. As for me, I knew all about this films horrible reputation, and when I first saw it, I basically forced myself to despise it since I was aggressively Anti-Michael Bay as an edgy teenager. 
But, after growing out of that phase, I gave this sequel a real chance, and honestly, I dont know how many out there are with me on this, but I kinda have an ironic soft spot for it. Oh, its bad, dont get me wrong, but compared many other bad sequels Ive seen, I find this one a lot more fascinating and entertaining in its shortcomings, on top of it being so tonally unhinged and insane. In that event, ROTF is essentially to me what Cars 2 is to several of my moots, only I admit that the movie blows instead of glazing it as a misunderstood masterpiece like the latter films fans do, but I digress, lmao. (Wait, didnt I already make that comparison to Space Jam 2 last year? Uhhhhhhhh, scratch that, it applies to this film now).
Theres actually several redeeming qualities Revenge of the Fallen has for me even going beyond my ironic enjoyment for it, and the first one of those is that it has a few legit fun moments in it. The most obvious one is the forest battle between Optimus vs. Megatron and the other Decepticons, since even most of the films haters admit thats a cool fight. I also liked the climax where Optimus was given Jetfires armor and weapons to fight off the Fallen, and Bumblebee gets a few cool fight shots, too. Theres also one joke here that gets a genuine laugh out of me, that being the humorous exchange between Sam Witwicky and the two college frat guys about Bumblebee illegally parking on the campus.
Sam No, uh, this is a friend of mines. He just... went to go get you a tighter shirt.
Frat Guy There isnt a tighter shirt! We checked! (fist bumps other frat guy)
The visual effects are also still pretty great. Im not as big a fan of some of the designs for certain Transformers as I was for the first film, but setting that aside, the effects still deliver on providing a spectacle (to an extent, that is)! The CGI and designs for Optimus Prime, Megatron, Bumblebee, Jetfire, the Fallen, and several other Transformers look damn good, the effects for all the chaotic action sequences are admittingly well-done, and other things like the abundance of explosions and the Matrix of Leadership are solid, too. The sound designs still great as well, for the Transformers transforming, their various weapons, and other things. All flaws aside, this film kicked ass with the sound design, haha.
The musics also a highlight once again. Steve Jablonskys score isnt quite as solid as his for the first film, but it still has a few noteworthy moments, mainly the scoring for the climax where Sam revives Optimus for him to defeat the Fallen. Also, I really liked the soundtrack! The song choices are pretty neat, including the likes of Green Day, Cavo, Taking Back Sunday, and Nickelback, as well as a few brief needledrops like Im So Excited by The Pointer Sisters and Super Freak by Rick James, lol. My absolute favorite is definitely Linkin Parks song New Divide. Not just one of my favorite end credits songs, but one of my favorite songs in general! Youve done it again, Chester Bennington (R.I.P.)!
Ok, Ive done enough praising. Time to rip on this shitshow, haha.
I should first address the elephant in the room about this movie Revenge of the Fallen was made during the Writers Strike. This was a time when it was rough for producers and directors to get finished scripts written for their films, and while some films managed to work in spite of that (like Iron Man), this Transformers sequel absolutely didnt work. This is literally a glorified repeat of the first film, where the humans and the Transformers have to find this lost artifact to stop the Big Bad from taking over the world, the military gets involved in the chaotic action climax, and it has the same plot beats of comedic scenes with the humans and all the typical Bayhem of the action sequences. The only difference here is that this is done SO much worse. All those problems I had with the first Bayformers are present here, and the story is much messier in its writing and direction!
I liked the human characters in the first Transformers, but here, theyre not as fun or interesting. I guess Shia LeBeouf is trying his best as Sam Witwicky, clearly trying to carry this messy narrative with his performance, but his arc is much more nonsensical than before. He touches a piece of the Allspark and then he starts acting like a hyperactive imbecile in college, then has to find what the messages inside his head mean. Ok, how am I supposed to take that arc seriously? Ill say that Megan Foxs acting as Mikaela Banes has improved here, but her role isnt as engaging as it was before, no thanks to the typical romance drama between them. Lennox and Robert are back, but theyre kinda wasted, and Seymour Simmons is especially given a downgrade here. What a waste of John Turturros talents!
Were also treated to some truly irritating supporting human characters. Sams college roommate Leo is a fucking nuisance, usually either screamingcrying during the action scenes or having his mind on sex even when being chased by a female pretender on campus! And for those of you who didnt like Sams annoying parents in the previous film? Not to worry, theyre given even more screentime here! Boy, do I just love seeing Sams mother get high on pot brownies and his father as an even bigger punchline than before instead of, you know, seeing more of the Transformers! On that topic, as cool as the Transformers are, theyre not given as much focus. Optimus gets killed off most of the movie, Bumblebee doesnt do much, Megatron mostly just talks, and the Fallen doesnt show up until in the climax for a few minutes!
But you know who IS given a lot of focus? Skids and Mudflap. Those two obnoxious Autobot twins who follow Sam, Mikaela, and Leo in their journey for the Matrix of Leadership. Theyre annoying, unfunny, and racist. They talk in a stereotypical fashion, and they say they dont read, despite being advanced alien robot beings. Just why?! And then theres Tom Kenny as Wheelie, whos this miniature Decepticon whos incredibly horny for Mikaela, even humping her leg at one point. And that leads me into another critique of mine the juvenile humor. So many crude sex jokes that dont land well, and make this pretty inappropriate for a film based on a franchise meant for kids. But, there were some jokes that I found ironically funny, like Sam rapidly flipping through book pages and making silly noises, on top of his priceless girly screaming.
All of the drama in this is hilariously pathetic, like Sam and Mikaelas arguments about their relationship being over after Sam literally gets violated by a female pretender, Optimus getting killed only to be brought back later, and Sam dying and going to Autobot heaven before coming back to bring back Optimus. Most of the action is much more over-the-top than the first film and not as easy to enjoy for how poorly shot and edited the setpieces are, the so-called story overstays its welcome with its long-winded 2½ hour runtime, and theres even some questionable character designs like the giant Decepticon having wrecking balls as... well, its balls. What is this films obsession with sex, wtf?!   
Overall, Transformers Revenge of the Fallen is a massive downgrade of a sequel to its fun predecessor, but not exactly what I view as the cinematic abomination that everyone else does. This films technically awful by sequel standards, but subjectively, I really cant say that I hate it. Sure, it falls flat with its poor writing  direction, weaker performances and characters, terrible humor, half-assed drama, and subpar cinematography  editing, but it has a few fun moments, good effects, and a solid soundtrack, on top of being what I find a hilarious disaster of a Transformers sequel. This won the Razzie for Worst Picture, but to be honest, Im not sure I fully agree with that. This came out the same year as Dragonball Evolution and Birdemic, so theres definitely worse from 2009 than this. Its not even the worst Transformers movie to me. The worse ones Ill be discussing later...

Review In A Nutshell
Another visit has shown that I was too over-critical of my previous review.
Behind all of its critical backlash and shallow-minded viewers, Transformers Revenge of the Fallen is a gem that pushes the capabilities of its audience providing a storyline that demands intense concentration due to its remarkable depth and swift, but precise editing. Bay puts it all on screen in an almost kind-of barrage to the senses, but if one simply lets themselves go, a sense of euphoria could be felt, one that taps into our childish imaginations and desperation for hard-hitting adrenaline. Sure there are instances where the characters themselves are taken too seriously, distracting us from the intense carnage that surrounds them, but Bay makes the transition from humans to robots with smooth-like camera movements and appropriately timed music cues that connects to the character in focus. No doubt Age of Extinction is still awful, and the other two films from the franchise remain competent, but none could ever emotionally charge me the way that Revenge of the Fallen does.

A hideous piece of corporate cinema, Transformers Revenge of the Fallen is just ugly film-making. It doubles down on the worst aspects of the garbage original (the totally unfunny humour, the objectification of the female characters, the unappealing military aesthetic) and adds even more tacky emotional moments and useless subplots (any scene involving Sams parents is unwatchable). Beyond all those hideous features, Transformers Revenge of the Fallen fills itself with both incoherent action and storytelling. In all seriousness, is the plot explainable in any way which makes sense and justifies the endless plot holes and contrivances? I would be embarrassed to put my name on a script like this yet Ehren Kruger, Roberto Orci and Alex Kurtzman not only turned out this turd but continue to have successful careers in writing hack movies of the lowest quality Hollywood offers (Transformers 3  4, Star Trek Into Darkness, The Amazing Spider-Man 2, Ghost in the Shell, The Mummy). They deserve to be named and shamed for their net negative contributions to current cinema. However, considering the trio were paid 8 million dollars for this shit, I suppose they havent got to work hard for their money. As for Michael Bay, a director who actually has a clear visual style, its beyond insulting that he clearly makes Transformers movies without passion for nothing but a pay check (notice he keeps on quitting the franchise then re-surfacing for some reason). Overall, Transformers Revenge of the Fallen is just despicable and the epitome of lazy Hollywood film-making.

I believe in my review for Quantum of Solace, I talked about how one of the most fascinating times for movies in the industrys current history is during the WGA strike from 07 to 08. Massive projects get canceled, others get significantly affected on the creative side, and movies come out during this era that completely shift the trajectory of specifically blockbuster filmmaking for at least a decade if not onward. Here we have, from its year, the highest grossing and likely the biggest-budgeted film affected by this era. Transformers Revenge of the Fallen to me in a single sentence is a movie thats a candidate for the most engaging movie thats also maybe one of the worst ever made. I view it as an antithesis yet in the same discussion of spectacle as a film like Avatar The Way of Water. You see Camerons new feature, and its like you are submerged in wonderment and total awe for the art of visual effects and pristine yet bold world-building. Youre there for the light show. Revenge of the Fallen, youre also there for the light show, but its garish, its shrill, its a little goopy, it kind of smells, and youre either uncomfortable or overwhelmed. Akin to a more recent Bay, 6 Underground, this is his mind on full display in a digital area not brought down by pesky plot competency or that silly thing called taste. Hes going to throw you the most crass and stupid humor imaginable, film explosions and clanking mechanical monstrosities in a way where you cant tell which ones on which side during any climactic fight scene, and if you dont like it, turn the other way. So, theres the thing. It is in fact hard if not impossible to turn the other way during this. This movie is many things. Boring or uninteresting is not one of them. I think 21 Guns ends up being played like four different times. Theres posters for other Bay films in the dorm room of the excruciatingly annoying college roommate of Sam who I think is meant to be like a parody of Facemash-era Mark Zuckerberg. LaBeouf has seizures and shrieks like a banshee, and Fox looks as much like a special effect as any of the eponymous Transformers. (Both of those things I find to be at least somewhat compliments.) A case to be made that Skids and Mudflap are the worst attempts at comedic relief in a blockbuster from the twenty-first century, made even worse by how much the film seems to so eagerly insist on their dynamic and voices. Turturro returns, and he both gets to show ass, hang out underneath a fifty foot alien robots balls, and I frankly think its really sweet and touching that he apparently in real-life cried when he got to climb the steps of an Egyptian pyramid through the magic of working on a Michael Bay film. Optimus Prime doesnt want to go to war, but he doesnt just kill every Decepticon he interacts with, he fucking mutilates them and rips them apart, organs and fluids staining the ground below him. Oh yeah, on top of voicing one of the twin racist Autobots, Tom Kenny gets to voice a robot that humps Megan Foxs leg in a prolonged comedic beat. Bumblebee either like pisses or cums on a woman who ends up being like a siren Decepticon, because now not only can Decepticons make mock humans inside themselves as vehicles, they can now just perfectly mimic humans walking and talking on their own? I could be wrong, but I dont think that happens again in any of the future sequels? What is this movie? I am flabbergasted, yet not feeling like I wasted my time. Instead, Bay let me inside of his unfiltered mind for about two and a half hours, in the process melting some of my own mind. A film thats hazardous for your health more likely than not, but one that can clearly and has been picked apart piece by piece, perhaps because it is like Devastator jagged pieces masquerading as a whole. I am actually technically raising this a half star higher from what I used to have it rated lol. As far as origin stories go, the first Transformers was very muddled. Michael Bay did a fine enough job adapting some plastic toys into an explosive blockbuster, but it was super unfocused and was visually very lackluster. Now Transformers Revenge of the Fallen on the other hand...is pretty much more of the same. But it is even louder, more explosive, makes less sense, and six minutes longer! Might I be as bold to say this is the best Bay Transformers movie too.
Turning these plastic toys into the latest and greatest arm of the U.S. military was the only sensible path forward for our robots with Bay at the helm. Their tenuous relationship with the United States government is strained further when misguided foreign policy interruptsso pretty much par for the course in American history. But the story in Revenge of the Fallen is messy fun at its best, incoherent at its worst. There was a looming Writers Guild strike when this film was set to begin production, so Bay locked his team of writers in a hotel and had them bang out the entire thing in only a couple of months. It shows.
Michael really doubles down on his maximalist style with this sequel. There are way more robotic characters this time around, both Autobots and Decepticons get a fleshed out entourage  somehow there is even more action, the climax is like 45 minutes long and the humor stays in line with the trends of the late 2000s aka a light sprinkling of racism, sexism, misogyny, the works.  
The writing wasnt a strong suit in the first film, so I find it interesting when people blame the writers strike happening on making the writers rush a script. Would this movie have been even marginally better if there wasnt a strike? My guess is not even a little. The plot is one macguffin after another. The sun harvesting machine hidden in the pyramids wont turn on without a special dagger, and we cant get the dagger until we decipher the glyphs, oh and we cant decipher the glyphs until we find an expert on alien language. The story is allllllll over the place it is a 149 minute film after all, so we gotta keep busy.
Pretty much everything apart from the big dumb CGI robot alien fights  is atrocious. That seems like the one constant the franchise maintains. The visual effects still look great, with even more intricate and exciting transformations. Plus, we get a scene with a Power Rangers style combination of Decepticons, turning construction equipment into a towering evil alien named Devastator. I definitely had that toy as a kid. Scratch thatI had a lot of these toys as a kid. So yeah, Revenge of the Fallen still fails to be a good movie, but it does improve on the boring plot of the first and expands the roster to an exciting size.
In closing, Id like to point out that this movie has way too much religious subtext. Was it deliberate? Im not sure, but theres too much for it to have been an accident, right? The villain is literally called The Fallen...anyone ever hear of that fallen angel from heaven? What about Optimus being the only one who can stop him-wait hes dead-wait hes been resurrected! Not only did Optimus triumph over death, he defeated The Fallen!! Yay?!

Michael Bay returns with a second helping of his raucous, violent science-fiction action romp. Shia LaBeouf and Megan Fox must prevent the Decepticon robots from destroying Earth. 
This is the first sequel and the second entry in the Transformers series, following the success of the first film released two years earlier. However, with the description of what this first sequel is about, it is virtually the same story as the first. 
Shia LaBeouf reprises his role from the first film as Sam Witwicky, who is now facing a new battle on his hands  going to college. On the other side, Optimus Prime and the Autobots and trying to make it feel like home on Earth, but a decepticon called The Fallen has other ideas and tries to cause chaos. Sam and his new lover must prevent The Fallen from creating disaster and try to stop him once and for all. 
This time, Shia LaBeouf offers very little in his role as Sam, while Megan Fox also offers very little in her role as Mikaela, Sams new girlfriend. 
The direction from Michael Bay is awful because he creates no tense atmosphere in the film whatsoever, while the script is written to a lacklustre standard as the film ends up going nowhere for the majority of the duration. 
The duration itself did not need to be anywhere near 2-and-a-half-hours long as there are scenes that did not need to be in the final edit. 
Also  normally action sequences in a science-fiction film would keep you on the edge-of-your-seat  but on this particular occasion, they dont, which does not surprise me. 
The films visual effects, however, do dazzle enough. The visual effects won an Academy Award nomination, which it didnt win. 
But it dominated the nominations for the Golden Raspberry awards that year, winning a total of seven nominations  Worst Picture, Worst Director (Michael Bay), Worst Actress (Megan Fox), Worst Screenplay, Worst Screen Couple (Shia LaBeouf and either Megan Fox or any Transformer), Worst Remake, Rip-Off or Sequel and Worst Supporting Actress (Julie White). 
It won the awards for Worst Picture, Worst Director and Worst Screenplay. 
Overall, the second entry in the Transformers series is one to completely forget about, due to the poor performances, direction, lacklustre script, slow pace and lack of tension, action and character determination.

Revenge of the Fallen is no doubt weaker than its predecessor, but I still enjoyed it, especially more than I did the first time I watched it. But, there are some things that really bugged me.
Now, Ill probably be the first person to admit this, but I actually found Ramón Rodríguez to be quite funny and I didnt mind the Twins at all. Yeah, the Twins are a bit racist and the humor that Rodríguez and the rest of the cast has might be dumb and immature, but I found myself chuckling quite a few times. But, I will admit that some of the sex jokes go too far in this one (that scene with the dogs and the robot humping Megan Foxs leg immediately come to mind).
As for the rest of the human characters though, I just couldnt connect with most of them like I could in the first one. Shia LaBeoufs character was actually likable and I found myself rooting for him in the first one, but here, hes just unbearable. Hes cocky beyond belief and is almost an entirely different character. Same goes for John Turturro, whos been changed from the serious, but semi-idiotic agent in the first one to a complete buffoon this time around.
As for the actual plot, I honestly believe that the filmmakers forgot that they actually had to have one of those (who knew?) until the last hour, where they try to cram soo much information into our heads that it hurt to even attempt to understand any of it. But, I will cut them some slack because of the writers strike and its affect on the movie. But, I will not forgive the movie for giving The Fallen, a character whos name is in the god-damn title of the movie, only around five minutes of screen-time. Thats just unacceptable.
Overall, Revenge of the Fallen fails by trying to give its audience too much and too little at the same time. Not much progress story-wise is made in the first two-thirds of the movie, but the last half tries to make up for that by giving us soo much exposition that it just feels rushed and doesnt make much sense at all. The film is actually a lesser in pretty much every way compared to the original. The action is not as exhilarating or fresh as it was the first time around, the story is much harder to follow, and characters start becoming parodies of themselves or even worse, make complete personality changes to the point where they could be entirely different characters.
Theres some enjoyment to be found throughout, though, as the film has many humorous moments and its always fun to watch Michael Bay blow shit up, but following the first film, its hard to deny that Revenge of the Fallen is a disappointment. But, its nowhere near as bad as most people claim. Thats for sure.

I was never interested in comic-books, cartoons, or most television shows that featured robots or superheroes, and U.S. shows for kids werent really shown here before the mid-1980s when I was already a teenager. Well, with most people seeming to agree this is one of, if not the worst movie in the franchise, I was really expecting to hate this one. Im not gonna lie here and say I enjoyed it, as it is worse than its predecessor in nearly every way, but they still manage to get the Transformers part of the Transformers movies right. For starters, the effect still hold up remarkably well. If you were to show me clips of this, and I didnt know otherwise, I would think this were something released in the last few years. Sure, theres some occasional jank here and there, but it mostly works and the new designs for the Transformers look pretty cool. I also still like the voice work. Peter Cullens voice as Optimus Prime is legendary and he is the sole character who is able to elevate this dreadful script. I still think Hugo Weaving is completely wasted here as Megatron, I dont care for their treatment of Bumblebee here, and I really did not care for the newcomers, Mudflap and Skids, but pretty much everything else with the Transformers themselves works for me.
Now for what doesnt work pretty much everything else. For starters, the plot here is a complete non-event. The first hour or so of this movie is just Sam heading off to college. Sure, there are a couple of decent action set pieces and plot points set within that first hour, but much of the padding could have been cut. Even once they leave the college, theres still like a 20-30 minute section where Sam and co. try to find someone who can translate these symbols Sam keeps seeing. So nearly an hour and a half in to this movie does the plot well and truly kick off. Then theres the Fallen himself. This is one of the most pointless baddies I have ever seen in a movie. Hes barely here and just acts as an exposition machine. I am not lying to you when I say that the bulk of his screentime has him sitting in a chair, explaining plot points and then hes in a 10 minute action scene in the final 15 minutes. Just a plain, boring bad guy.
Then there are the usual suspects of a Bay film that Im pretty tempted to just copypaste over from my review of the first from last week, but I wont be as lazy as Bay and his writing team. The script is obviously pretty terrible, filled to the brim with annoying (and in some cases, racist) humor. Theres the objectification of the films one actual female character (a Transformer literally humps Makaelas leg for a good minute in one scene). Bays usual brand of over the top action is here as well, but this time slightly more clunky than before (some of it is fun, some of it, not so much). So yeah, Bayisms in full force here.
In the end, this wasnt as bad as I had expected. Age of Extinction was so bad that I completely skipped The Last Knight, so in comparison to that its not terrible. At least the next one is, if my memory serves, a bit better than this.

In Bays world, the wrong people are in charge and the good guys ought to torch the system in slo-mo! Meanwhile the Transformers source material are about gender fluidity and resource allocation heady themes for what was supposedly Reagan-era deregulation plastic toys for kids!

I find that most people who defend the Bayformers are only tangentially aware of the Transformers as big robots that fight. But if you watched the cartoons and read the comics, you know these are deeply political with leftist sensibilities and rich lore - you probably screamed in horror at the thought of Michael Bay being the one to adapt these. Bay cannot do mythological he can certainly do Americana iconography to appeal to flyover States. 

The first 2007 movie worked cause it was an alien invasiondisaster movie that treated the Decepticons like an existential threat. Bays Decepticons are cold, heavy, emotionless military hardware that speak Cybertronian to each other. The good guys descend like fiery angels, clumsily acclimatizing themselves to this human world while their leader waxes poetic about freedom. The evil guys, though? Theyve been here all along, hiding, sleeper cells caring for nothing more than the signal to finally come out and destroy. These guys were Megatrons homeboys. They had their own look and attitude an overwhelming authoritarian presence. What Bay lacked in characterization, he made up for by taking robots in disguise to its ultimate horrifying conclusion. 

There is also the Spielberg of it all. For all of Spielbergs predictability, he can boil a high concept into an understandable human relationship. The script at least has setups and payoffs. You can tell Spielberg was the producer keeping Bay at bay (wink). Transformers 07 was Independence Day for the Bush era! Cue the Linkin Park alt rock banger What Ive Done!

Everyone agrees that the Writers Strike fucked this sequel up, right? But what if the Strike excuse was just that, an excuse? What if Unionised Labour didnt outright cause this particular movie to drop the ball so hard?
Successful Hollywood movies shooting without a functional script is nothing new (see Gladiator and Iron Man). Bay and his writers Roberto Orci and Alex Kurtzman had ideas for where the story should go long before the strike began. They made specific decisions in this movie because they wanted to, in terms of action and humour. Bays oeuvre is mean-spirited, coked-up, assholic humanity. You cannot mesh that tone with the uplifting Transformers universe. So ROTF was never gonna be some Michelin Star dining regardless of the Writers Strike! The Bayhems of the first film only worsen in this sequel.

The first film had a mythology where the Allspark fell down to earth. The sequels invents Decepticons hiding Mcguffins in the pyramids of Giza, moon landings conspiracies with Buzz Aldridge, Harriet Tubman and King Arthur?!  Everything just resets in each film. Theres no consistency to anything. Its just whatever excuse Bay can come up with to blow stuff up. In a sense, Bays m.o is more similar to a toyline.....no different than HasBro!

ROTF has no real hook its just the movie hopping from idea to idea! At the risk of sounding like some purist geek, the actual lore is basically the Primes being Godly angels. Before Optimus time, the Primes agreed to only harvest energy in planets devoid of life. Then the Fallen goes after planets with life on em. Like Paradise Losts Lucifer, he is cast out by the Primes for breaking this pact. I dont understand why BayOrciKurtzman didnt just stick to this simple yet effective template. Everyone understands a Judas archetype. Just keep it simple. We can do better than a shard of Allspark stuck to Sam Witwickys shirt. I mean, the very reason that the Decepticons know about the surviving Allspark is because some government bureaucrat exposits the Mcguffin at the NEST headquarters - and the satellite Decepticon known as Soundwave overhears this scoop! It happens that fast and randomly!

And I havent even brought up the Skids and Mudflap of it all! Theres something so insulting about their names atop of their racist caricatures. The filmmakers were so gung-ho about these 2 that they released a whole strawberried peanut butter MMs with Skids and Mudflap having blinggolden tooth on the wrapper! Really think about it there was an entire marketing apparatus that believed America was gonna love Skids and Mudflap! And you thought Jazz in the first movie being the only Black-coded autobot to be brutally dismembered was bad enough?! 

Is ROTF the worst movie ever made? Not as long as Age of Extinction exists. It wasnt even the worst movie of 2009 - that honour goes to X-Men Origins! There are ancillary elements that keep ROTF from falling down the bottom of the barrel IMO. Linkin Parks New Divide Green Days 21 Guns and a surprisingly steller Burning Down The House cover by The Used are among many of the bangers in this soundtrack. Im no kooky Billy Corgan crybaby, but I do miss when rock music informed the monoculture!

Sams college stuff by and large works for me. It grounds the movie in some reality. I even laugh at some of the Frat boys stuff. Theres an unspoken tension re Mikaelas insecurities about her relationship with Sam now that hes in college and shes a mechanic who didnt get past high school. Hell, they coulda expanded on the class commentary with Sam being the first Witwicky to enter college! If 07 was a boy and his car, the next logical step for 09 was to be a boy goes to college, learns how to be a man, until hes attacked by a Terminator girl story. Instead, the filmmakers drop the college section after they get Sams mum high and suddenly a constantly farting Jetfire teleports everyone to Egypt for some reason!

John Turturro is to these movies what JK Simmons is to Raimis Spider-Man a character actor with a New York background who knows the exact tone to strike in a cartoonish movie. Turturro is a Three Stooges guy. He just lives in goofball Island. Bay lets him off the chain by making him run a butchers shop - and he gives us nutrients when he chews the scenery!

Thats why Peter Cullens passing hits for many of us. Hes the one constant throughout this misanthropic design. In spite of Bays numerous sins, he at least knew to cast no one else to voice Optimus besides Cullen. The death of Optimus reminds me of the many failed attempts to adapt X-Mens Dark Phoenix saga. If I told a non-comic reader whos only seen FOXs X-Men films that Dark Phoenix is one of the greatest storylines in comics, they wouldnt believe me. Likewise, ROTFs blunt execution of Optimus Death and the Matrix of Leadership deserved better. These storylines mean more in the animated movies its about who steps up to be a leader. The best he could give us was Shia LaBeouf in autobot heaven!

Paul Thomas Anderson making Dirk Diggler sing the Stan Bush song Optimus Prime dies to in Transformers 86, instantly makes Boogie Nights a better Transformers movie than this one!

Transformers was sometimes tone deaf, sometimes brain dead and sometimes just plain deafening, but it was also fun and didnt take itself too seriously. With Revenge of the Fallen, instead of taking the conventional approach and doing more of the good stuff, Michael Bay decides to double down on all his worst impulses, of which he famously has many. The first films relatively gentle high-school comedy has become a full on Animal House frat partythe idea of explaining this stuff to my kids gives me palpitations. The insufferable comedy sidekicks now have their own even more insufferable comedy sidekicks and, of course, the battles are bigger, louder and even less intelligible.
The big problem is that the plot is so opaque and the stakes so cosmically vast that it is hard to know who to root for. Never mind the Decepticons, it felt like the world, and particularly its cultural heritage and infrastructure, would be better off without the Autobots, the military and that self-centred arse Sam Witwicky, too. No amount of alleged comic relief, in the form of Transformer genitals and stoned parents, no less, can make up for the fact that not only could I not tell what on Cybertron the robots were doing to each other, but I didnt much care.
I think the biggest disappointment of the Transformers films, and of Revenge of the Fallen in particular, is the involvement of Steven Spielberg. We could have had a child-friendly Amblin production that captures the majesty, wonder and infinite possibilities that I felt watching the G1 Transformers as a child, but instead we have Michael Bay shagging the frame like an annoying puppy.

A work of tacky ecstasy, ahead of its time in approximating the cultural overload of the high-speed internet era. Its the Limewire musical, just ahead of its time in capturing the post-mp3 explosion of musical possibilities and the attention-deficient surfing between wildly unconnected songs that resulted. No other musical of the modern era has so perfectly captured the sense of spinning an iPod wheel every 45 seconds to play something else. That it approximates this visually with majority in-camera effects, using CGI for backdrops while otherwise communicating impossible movement through editing and frame-rate chicanery, makes it an overwhelming experience, a barrage of cheesiness so relentless that one must either flee or succumb to it. In so many ways it feels like the celluloid equivalent of what the Wachowskis would later accomplish digitally with Speed Racer.
And through it all, the overwhelming sappiness of it just works. Musicals take basic human emotions and rev them up to jet engine decibels and youd be hard-pressed to find another as outlandishly Too Much as Moulin Rouge. Ewan McGregor never half-asses anything, but he is so thoroughly committed here that its impossible not to feel along with him, his buoyant joys and shattered lows. Even Kidman here gives a performance so unlike her usual persona, trading smoldering intensity for expressionistic teasing and head-over-heels love. Its the sort of completely un-self-conscious work youd never expect from her, and she throws herself into it as passionately as McGregor. Combined with a musical format that mashes up all of the most animal-brain-triggering snippets of a song for maximum emotional efficiency, the story steamrolls you before you can protest it, and when McGregor is left howling in grief after two hours of sublime energy it still feels like my heart is being torn out.
Its one of the great 21st century films. Baz Luhrmann is only good when figuring out how to make historical periods of excess into contemporary displays of grotesquerie, somehow turning great films (French Cancan) or great literature (Great Gatsby) into tacky Technicolor vomit that somehow understands the underlying sorrow of the material better than any serious-minded adaptation.

When love turns tales into memories. Welcome! To a rollercoaster of colors and stimuli, where conflicts, colors, and exaggerated aesthetics blend into a full-blown circus. Dreams and attire from both the modern and the past intertwine, creating one hell of a chaotic mess that I cant quite graspbut perhaps I dont need to. This is theater and a visual celebration. This is a film that broke rules, a musical turned into a product meant to sell itself to us. Whether it succeeds is entirely a matter of taste. For me, this is a amazing musical, but something feels missing.
And perhaps thats exactly the point. The film is madness, a fever dream that leaves me asking, What the hell is happening? yet it dazzles with entertainment spinning wildly on its own eccentric carousel. It bursts out of the gate with fast pace, brimming with joy, jealousy, desire, love, and chaos, it almost feels overwhelming. But then, gradually, the frenzy begins to settle. It softens, weaving a bittersweet undertone that aches and, in its unique way, creates something extraordinary. It doesnt hand us a neatly told story, instead, it immerses us in raw emotions.
A timeless tragedy, an experimental expression. A passionate manifestation. The film is the pulse of modern music, sung in its own voice. The music, to me, is nothing short of magnificent, it sweeps me away completely. It halts me but also sets me free. It anchors my eyes to the screen, where my gaze dissolves into a cascade of colors, reflecting the essence of love. This musical feels like a perfect, dreamlike love story, floating above the clouds, drenched in freedom. Yet, beneath it all, it remains a heartbreaking tale of love.
The film also has a comedic undertone that takes me in an unusual direction. It works, but at the same time, it feels a bit off. Everyone gives a fantastic performance, but, surprise, surprise, Kidman steals all the attention completely. Okay Im lying Mcgregor is the real deal. And the films caricatured nature is clear and it doesnt try to hide it at all. This is an intense experience and i loved it.
But in the end never fall in love. But imagine a world without it? The musical lets love soar, carried by the familiar rhythm of its songs its like breathing, a hope for whats yet to come. Its the one feeling that drives a person to do anything, no matter the cost. All the films flaws dissolve for me, because love is never perfect, and neither is this film. Its a billboard, a billboard for that eternal feeling that slices through you even as you stand at the pinnacle of your life. The musical doesnt offer simple solutions or a flawless narrative. Instead, it embodies that raw emotion. After the credits rolled, I was, at least, a different man and that, at its core, is what the magic of cinema is all about

Moulin Rouge! is a kaleidoscope explosion of colours and music and passion - its no wonder that most of the songs are mash-ups since everything here is so mashed up, turned up, thrown in your face. The visual style is unrelenting Moulin Rouge! is energetic to the point of frenzy - each frame is filled to the brim with detail, the world of the film spins like youve been drinking too much champagne. Everything feels like its so much. 
I wondered, for the first hour of this, how Baz Luhrmann had managed to balance such in-your-face stylistic audacity while maintaining a genuine feeling of care for the characters and their struggles - is it all down to Ewan McGregors wonderfully earnest face, or the way Nicole Kidmans smouldering temptress persona is worn down by one of the most charming cinematic uses of Elton Johns Your Song? But as the Elephant Love Medley transformed into David Bowies Heroes, I stopped caring, I just swooned. 
Its so easy to make fun of Moulin Rouge!, and as someone who has never really liked Baz Luhrmanns films, Im familiar with the adjectives used to describe him pretentious obnoxious annoying and theres many things in Moulin Rouge! that couldve annoyed me, if I wasnt so completely delighted by them. Richard Roxburghs Duke is ridiculous, a parodic villain, the songs (notably Jim Broadbents rendition of Like A Virgin) are often silly, the plot contains absolutely no surprises. And at the same time, Moulin Rouge! delivers true pathos, through the bohemian values that Christian wants to embody freedom,  beauty, truth, and above all, love. Moulin Rouge! makes me grin, forces my mouth open with glee, but mostly it makes me cry it works as a film because its so overwhelming. You get drunk on that flamboyant, frenetic visual style and soundscape, and suddenly youre crying in the bathroom about Satine and Christian and love. 
(also, the Indian themed play seems misjudged at best, even if it does speak to a certain cultural fascination of the French at the time - but Moulin Rouge! takes enough liberties with history that it feels, to me at least, that it couldve taken another one here)

Moulin Rouge! is so excitingly bizarre, but I think Bazs style, specifically his use of intense over-editing, both simultaneously highlights and minimizes the vastness of the overarching epic production. Rapid cuts and energetic camera movements dazzle, obliterating a whirlwind of visual and auditory stimuli. The aesthetic at play is incredibly proactive and hyperactive, an approach that inherently enhances the films sense of grandiosity and excess.
This same vigor can sometimes overshadow the intricate pieces of the production design and the depth of the story. The rapid pace and constant barrage of unorthodox visual language make it challenging for me to fully appreciate the completely out-of-touch, bonkers fantasy world. The overall heightened sense of excitement and spectacle correspondingly dilutes its scale.

O musical Moulin Rouge é mesmo inovador. Mas só na histeria
           	O australiano Baz Luhrmann, de 38 anos, só rodou três filmes desde sua estreia como diretor. Mas é do tipo que sabe fazer barulho a cada passo que dá. Seu primeiro trabalho, o simpático Vem Dançar Comigo, de 1992, passava-se no mundo brega dos concursos de dança e rapidamente virou um favorito no circuito de festivais. Romeu  Julieta combinava Shakespeare à linguagem dos videoclipes (para alguns, uma coisa nova) e pavimentou o caminho da adoração juvenil para Leonardo DiCaprio. E Moulin Rouge - Amor em Vermelho (Moulin Rouge, Estados UnidosAustrália, 2001) vem sendo vendido, com surpreendente sucesso, como o musical mais singular e inovador de todos os tempos.
           	O motivo para tal entusiasmo é que o filme se passa no final do século XIX, mas os protagonistas entoam canções que só seriam escritas muitas décadas mais tarde, de The Sound of Music (da trilha de A Noviça Rebelde) a Like a Virgin, de Madonna. Até para I Will Always Love You, com que Whitney Houston azucrinava a pobre plateia de O Guarda-Costas, o diretor achou uma brechinha, já que o objetivo é que as letras das músicas façam as vezes de diálogos entre os atores. Luhrmann se pretende radical também no visual corta a cada milissegundo, usa todo tipo de truque e película conhecido no universo e cria cenários tão apinhados que dariam para pelo menos uma dúzia de filmes. Moulin Rouge, é certo, já tem uma legião de defensores fervorosos. Mas é realmente insuportável.
           	O título é uma referência ao famoso cabarébordel que animava as noites parisienses. Lá, o escritor pobretão interpretado por Ewan McGregor conhece a cortesã Satine (Nicole Kidman), por quem se apaixona perdidamente e para quem decide compor um espetáculo espetacular (sim, é isso mesmo). Satine, porém, está prometida a um duque rico, untuoso e vingativo. Para completar o amontoado de clichês, a cortesã padece com uma tosse insistente. Vez por outra, suja de sangue um lencinho ou desmaia. A vacuidade desse roteiro não é obstáculo para a histeria de Luhrmann, que empilha músicas e imagens de forma atordoante e incoerente. Daria para compará-lo ao pai de todos os frenéticos, o inglês Ken Russell. Mas seria injusto, já que filmes como Mulheres Apaixonadas e Tommy provam que Russell era acometido não só de desvarios, mas também de ideias (e mesmo assim anda esquecido). De Moulin Rouge salvam-se só a beleza de Nicole Kidman e a atuação de Ewan McGregor - que, além de ser a única presença razoavelmente humana do filme, tem uma voz muito agradável.

I think while watching Moulin Rouge!, youre seeing how a world built on artifice and neon might not be what its cracked up to be, especially when the sadder realities of mortality hit so closely. Yet thats where Luhrmann finds a greater hook for all of them, using a brave, energy-driven pace so that you cant help but surrender yourself to exactly what hes presenting here. Specifically, that El Tango de Roxanne scene is just phenomenal art, acknowledging the innate jealousy and sadness present in such an impossible romance.
Much like Ken Russell or even Michael Powell, Luhrmanns melodrama doesnt come just from a heightened awareness of circumstance, but its all about those difficulties that define the human hearts struggle against time. Step into Baz Luhrmanns Moulin Rouge!  and leave reality at the door. This masterpiece reimagines the musical as a sensory revolution, where the boundaries between dream and reality blur in a dazzling explosion of color, movement, and raw emotion. The story unfolds in a Paris where the Moulin Rouge isnt just a nightclub  its a living, breathing entity, a place where art, love, and ambition collide in a symphony of excess.
At the heart of this visual and auditory feast is Satine (beautiful Nicole Kidman), the clubs radiant star, whose path intertwines with that of Christian (Ewan McGregor), a young writer drawn into the intoxicating world of bohemian Paris. Their love story, set against the backdrop of the clubs opulence, is as tragic as it is exhilarating. Luhrmanns direction (Australian with opera background), transforms every frame into a painting, with reds and golds dominating the palette, symbolizing the passion and decadence of the era. The soundtrack, a bold fusion of modern pop and classic musical influences, pulses through the narrative like a heartbeat, with standout moments like Satines electrifying performance of Diamonds Are a Girls Best Friend.
Yet Moulin Rouge! is more than just a visual and auditory spectacle. Beneath its glittering surface lies a deeply emotional core. The Dukes (Richard Roxburgh) obsession with Satine adds a layer of tension and danger, while her own struggles, caught between artistic integrity and survival, lend the film its emotional weight. Kidman delivers a performance that is both glamorous and heartbreaking, embodying the tragic beauty of a woman torn between love and duty. McGregor, as the idealistic Christian, brings a touch of wide-eyed innocence to the chaos, making their chemistry all the more compelling.
What truly sets Moulin Rouge! apart is its unbridled creativity. Luhrmanns signature rapid-fire editing and extravagant visuals create a rhythm thats as exhilarating as it is immersive. The film doesnt just tell a story, it sweeps you into its world, blending spectacle with heart in a way that feels both timeless and fresh. Its a celebration of love, art, and the power of imagination, a testament to the idea that the most unforgettable stories are those that dare to defy convention. Spectacular !

Plongez dans Moulin Rouge! de Baz Luhrmann et laissez la réalité à la porte. Ce chef-dœuvre réinvente la comédie musicale comme une révolution sensorielle, où les frontières entre rêve et réalité sestompent dans une explosion éblouissante de couleurs, de mouvements et démotions brutes. Lhistoire se déroule dans un Paris où le Moulin Rouge nest pas seulement un cabaret, mais une entité vivante, un lieu où lart, lamour et lambition sentrechoquent en une symphonie dexcès.
Au cœur de ce festin visuel et auditif se trouve Satine (sublime Nicole Kidman), létoile radieuse du club, dont le destin sentremêle avec celui de Christian (Ewan McGregor), un jeune écrivain attiré dans lunivers enivrant du Paris bohème. Leur histoire damour, sur fond dopulence du cabaret, est à la fois tragique et exaltante. La réalisation de Luhrmann (habitué de mises en scène dopéras en Australie) transforme chaque plan en un tableau, avec des rouges et des ors dominants, symbolisant la passion et la décadence de lépoque. La bande-son, fusion audacieuse de pop moderne et dinfluences musicales classiques, pulse à travers le récit comme un battement de cœur, avec des moments marquants comme linterprétation électrisante par Satine de Diamonds Are a Girls Best Friend.
Pourtant, Moulin Rouge! est bien plus quun simple spectacle visuel et auditif. Sous sa surface étincelante se cache un cœur émotionnel profond. Lobsession du Duc (Richard Roxburgh) pour Satine ajoute une couche de tension et de danger, tandis que ses propres combats, déchirée entre intégrité artistique et survie, donnent au film son poids émotionnel. Kidman offre une performance à la fois glamour et déchirante, incarnant la beauté tragique dune femme partagée entre lamour et le devoir. McGregor, en Christian idéaliste, apporte une touche dinnocence désarmante au chaos, rendant leur alchimie dautant plus captivante.
Ce qui distingue vraiment Moulin Rouge!, cest sa créativité débridée. Le montage rapide et les visuels extravagants de Luhrmann créent un rythme à la fois grisant et immersif. Le film ne se contente pas de raconter une histoire, il vous emporte dans son univers, mêlant spectacle et émotion dune manière qui semble à la fois intemporelle et nouvelle. Cest une célébration de lamour, de lart et du pouvoir de limagination, une preuve que les histoires les plus inoubliables sont celles qui osent défier les conventions.

Movies, more or less, are made up of sound and a quick succession of streams of color reflected off of a blank screen. It really only becomes an art form when its determining what the sounds ought to be, how to get the sounds, how the color should look, and obtaining the color exactly how you wnt it, and matching it up with the sound. 
In other words, movies are an art form of artifice. 
Movies arent real. 
Movies are fake.
Movies are the burlesque of sight and sound.
But sometimes, somewhere beneath all the trickery and the gloss, movies get us to feel something real, something authentic, something ecstatic.
Its a reality from artifice. 
Its Moulin Rouge.
Bursting with life, giddy stupid humor, melodrama, tragedy, farce, cheeky sensuality, and more sweeping shots and cuts than you can count or even sometimes register, Moulin Rouge is a masterpiece of trash in the best way. Its trash in the sense that its nowhere near anything like a Godard movie - unless you think hes gonna put Lady Marmalade in Goodbye to Language - and its beyond silly, and it has pretty much no subtext. Its a masterpiece in the sense that it is profoundly moving, bizarrely genuine, expertly directed, a visual spectacle with real purpose, and incredibly enthusiastic and oddly intelligent about the meaning and purpose of art. Its also wickedly, senselessly, intensely fun. It is, essentially, a dream of a movie in every sense.
Theres a strange, horrible complaint lodged against this movie that its characters arent well developed and that the story is thin. What I find so fascinating about this is that they seem to be missing the point off having such simplicity. It is a story of brutal manipulation of the audience and of the characters. You laugh and love and then the movie breaks you heart, not through any sense of earned characterization, but because of the sheer thrill of emotional catharsis. It evokes emotions through pure, carefully orchestrated cinema. Its the same thing Baz Luhrman is trying to do in every one of his films, but, especially in his adaptations, it ends up draining his films of any wit. Because Luhrman has never been a particularly deep filmmaker. But hes a masterful visual storyteller. This movie works without dialogue, and the emotions still resonate. Thought the music, thats essential, and actually is the key that pulls the film from a gret cinematic experience to a great work of art. Because most of the music is, well, 70s to 90s pop music. Its a musical of recycled parts. Its story which beat for beat has been told for centuries. Its a staged show drawn from the lives of the characters themselves. All of a sudden, Moulin Rouge takes on an entirely new dimension this is a film which is bold enough not just to say that all art is about finding your own meanings behind someone elses ideas, and that all art is just copying and stealing, but that this can be totally valid and authentic. When Nicole Kidman sings Your Song to the Duke, shes stealing from the writer, and Luhrman is stealing from Elton John. But when Ewan Mcgegor is singing to Kidman, its the most magical moment you could possibly imagine. 
Thats what makes Moulin Rouge a true masterpiece. Cinema has never been more fake, and cinema has rarely been more real.

It had been years since Id last seen Moulin Rouge!, and in my head it had somehow become an absolutely badass masterpiece.
Well...
Lets just say...
My memory and reality werent exactly on the same page this time.
I still admire Baz Luhrmann for his seemingly limitless imagination. But at the same time, I also found the film unbelievably exhausting in places.
Anyway...
Lets go through it point by point.
 Story  Screenplay
Moulin Rouge! is basically what youd get if you threw La Traviata, La Bohème, and an industrial-sized line of cocaine had a baby.
Then handed the whole thing over to Baz Luhrmann.
Love.
Jealousy.
Passion.
Sacrifice.
Death.
Every single emotion is turned up to maximum volume.
And thats both the films greatest strength and its biggest weakness. 
Sometimes this emotional overload works brilliantly. Other times it feels as though the film mistakes sheer intensity for emotional depth.
 Characters
I genuinely like everyone in the cast.
I like Ewan McGregor.
I like Nicole Kidman.
I like the supporting cast.
The only issue  The singing.
Compared to whatever Russell Crowe was doing in Les Misérables, theyre basically vocal legends.
But if were being honest, neither McGregor nor Kidman are exceptional singers.
They absolutely get the job done.
But you can also hear the limitations.
 Style  Direction
If someone asked me to define Baz Luhrmann in one film
Id probably show them this.
The editing never stops.
The camera never stops.
The colours never stop.
The film constantly throws images, music, movement and ideas at you.
Sometimes its exhilarating.
Sometimes its simply overwhelming.
Whether thats brilliant or exhausting probably depends on your tolerance for sensory overload.
 Music
This is, of course, a jukebox musical.
The film raids several decades of pop music and stitches everything together into one gigantic musical collage.
Sometimes those songs fit surprisingly well.
Sometimes they feel a little forced.
Overall Id say it works
until it doesnt.
 Atmosphere  Impact
There isnt a single quiet moment in this film.
Everything is bigger.
Louder.
Faster.
More colourful.
That creates an incredibly unique atmosphere.
But after a while, I honestly wished the film would simply breathe for a minute.
 How Well Has It Aged?
Surprisingly well from a visual standpoint.
The style is so deliberately exaggerated that it never really feels dated.
Whether you enjoy that style
Thats another question entirely.
 Favorite Moment
Oddly enough, its the very beginning.
That wonderfully unhinged little conductor introducing the film immediately made me laugh.
 Final Thoughts
Sometimes, style over substance just isnt enough for me.
If someone had told me yesterday that I would one day write a sentence like this, I probably wouldve punched them right in their filthy fucking mouth.
Well...
Apparently the heat has burned away the very last bit of common sense I had left.
Anyway...
Im off to completely reorganize my worldview.
 Would I Watch It Again?
Not anytime soon.

Moulin Rouge was so wonderful! I adored the songs and the vibes and the costumes and the characters. I liked how it started out loud and playful, then slowly became more serious and emotional. That change in tone made the story feel deeper, like it was reflecting the characters emotions as everything around them started to fall apart.
The music was one of my favorite parts. I loved how it used modern pop songs in a 19th-century setting. It could have been cheesy, but instead it made the story feel familiar and alive. The mix of different songs added a fun rhythm and also helped tell the story in a way that dialogue couldnt. The Elephant Love Medley was especially fun to watch, and later songs carried more emotional weight as the tone of the movie shifted. The music felt like a language the characters used to say what they couldnt say directly.
The visuals were incredible. The sets, lighting, and costumes were so detailed and creative. Every scene felt carefully planned to show the chaos and excitement of the Moulin Rouge, and then later to show the more personal, painful moments. The direction and cinematography reminded me a bit of Amélie with how colorful and dreamlike it was, especially in the way it made ordinary moments feel magical.
What stood out most to me was how layered the characters were. At first, they seem simple, like types youve seen before, but the film slowly gives them more depth. Satine and Christian both felt real by the end. Satines mix of confidence and fear made her story really moving. I cared about what happened to her and to their relationship. Even the side characters had small details that made them feel alive in their own ways.
I liked how the film explored the idea of performance and illusion. The Moulin Rouge is a place built on fantasy, and the movie keeps reminding us that what we see is both real and not real. The characters are performing for the audience and for each other, which makes the story about more than just romance. It becomes about how people use art, love, and stories to make sense of their lives.
The editing style was also really interesting. In the beginning, the quick cuts and movement make the world feel wild and overwhelming. As the story becomes more serious, the pacing slows down and gives you time to focus on the characters and their emotions. That contrast helped show how the excitement of the dream eventually turns into something more real and fragile.
Overall, Moulin Rouge felt joyful, sad, and beautiful all at once. It had moments of pure fun and others that were genuinely emotional. I would absolutely rewatch it, and Id recommend it to anyone who likes musicals with heart and style.

Let me put this out there, I dont like Baz Luhrmann as a filmmaker. Im pretty sure hes a fine guy and all, its just that his films are not my particular taste. Moulin Rouge is no exception to this and despite most everyone else praising it, I think its a loud, obnoxious, pretentious and downright bad film. 
The plot takes place in Bohemian era France and focuses on Christian, a writer who decides to write about the past year he had. At the center of these events is the Moulin Rouge, an extravagant nightclub where many upperclassman go. While posing as a duke Christian meets Satine (comment when you get it), the main star of the nightclub. Her ultimate goal is to be an actress and she takes an interest in Christian. Along with many supporting characters, the Moulin Rouge puts on a play. This film mostly focuses on the behind the scenes of the production as well as the struggles of putting on this play. I didnt like the plot of this film at all. Despite everything that happens, it always goes back to the words love. Everything is centered on that one word. Christian and Satine love each other, Ziddler loves his theater and the duke loves Satine as well. This concept of everything relating to love has been done many times and it felt to me like nothing was new. The film makes it out to be that the most important thing in the film is love.  Another thing I wasnt sold on was the use of pop songs as dialogue, let alone them being in the film at all. Just like one of Luhrmanns other films Romeo  Juliet which uses most of the original Shakespearian dialogue in a modern setting, it just doesnt fit. While I was liking the atmosphere in the film at first, once the pop songs started I lost interest quick. I wouldve preferred it to stick with the atmosphere of the film. I wouldnt say that the plot of this film was genetic, but you know the ending at the beginning of the film. In voiceover, Christian EXPLICITLY TELLS YOU THE ENDING OF THIS FILM! You see it coming from many miles away and once it happens you feel no emotion for these characters. Speaking of the characters, theyre are extremely over the top, with the exception of Christian. He was the only one I could tolerate out of all of them. Even Satine, Christians love interest, disinterested me at points because of his eccentric behavior. Thats how Id characterize all the characters, eccentric. Ziddler is way over the top, but I have to admit I liked the Like a Virgin scene. The Duke was a villain straight out of a cartoon, mustache and all. And speaking of character, theyre given little development. The most developed by far are Christian and Satine, but not enough for you to get emotionally attached to them. All the other characters like Ziddler and the Duke you cant get behind because theyre so poorly developed. 
The cast does alright with their performances. Ewan McGregor was the standout for me as Christian, a writer recounting his past year at the Moulin Rouge. He does the best out of everyone and seems the most sane out of the cast. Hes not given much in terms of development, but does his best with what hes given. I almost liked Nicole Kidman as Satine, the nightclub performer who wants to become an actress. Sure shes beautiful and all, but her character is very unlikeable as well as eccentric at points. All this made it hard for me to get behind her character, especially in the more emotional scenes. Jim Broadbent is over the top and unlikeable as Harold Ziddler, the owner of the titular Moulin Rouge. While I normally like Broadbent with him being great in Cloud Atlas, I wasnt too fond of him in this film. That being said, I did get a few chuckles In during the Like a Virgin scene. Dont even get me started on Richard Roxburgh as the duke. I absolutely despised him in this film. His performance is straight out of a Saturday morning cartoon. Hes extremely unlikeable as a character and as a villain. 
Ive said it before and Ill say it again, I dont like Baz Luhrmann as a filmmaker. His films are just not my style and this is no exception. While I do commend him for his vision, I dont think it was executed all that well. The film is very grandiose in scope that it was destined to fail at some points. I was on board with this film in the beginning, but after the 5 minute mark when the Unconscious Argentinian was introduced I was slightly less on board until I wanted to turn it off. Some scenes felt like a live action cartoon, sound effects and all. The editing of this film is so hyperactive that you dont get to appreciate some of the cinematography, especially with big party scenes in the Moulin Rouge. During the CanCan scene in particular I was disappointed because all of this skilled choreography and cinematography was absolutely Butchered in the editing room. This film, for the most part, holds up well for 2016 which was a good thing. 
The music by Craig Armstrong was my favorite part about the film. If its one thing this film got right, it was the score and Im not talking about the covers of pop songs. Its so mysterious and melodic that it complimented the film very well. As for the covers of pop songs, I was less thrilled. Any movie that butchers Smells Like Teen Spirit has done a disservice. The Elephant Love Medley in particular takes snippets from great songs and tries to force them into one song in which the only good thing was the singing by Kidman and McGregor. 
Overall, Moulin Rouge is a bad film with annoying Characters, a generic plot and an ending you see from a mile away. I would stay away from this film at all costs.

A feast for the eyes is undoubtedly what director Baz Luhrmann has created with Moulin Rouge. Nominated for eight Oscars at the 74th Academy Awards, it is recognised as the third part of the Australian filmmakers Red Curtain Trilogy (following Strictly Ballroom and Romeo  Juliet). Nicole Kidman and Ewan MacGregor demonstrate themselves surprisingly well. They make terrific leads and possess some fair to middling singing talents as cabaret entertainers and courtesan Satine and English poet Christian.
Luhrmann throws everything but the kitchen sink to graft together medleys of pop songs from Nat King Cole, David Bowie, Elton John, The Police and a host of others. However, the approach regrettably is not always used in ways that encompass a great deal of imagination. More often than not, the musical jukebox approach is merely employed in the name of audience-pandering and to underline specific plot points and serve as an unnecessary leitmotif. 
Even when the film quietens down for occasional moments as the tale bends and twists into a romantic drama, theres no great deal of sentiment thats felt or even a dramatic gesture thats genuinely earned. Still, theres a particular pleasure to be had as Luhrman handles the visual splendour of every scene with the subtlety of an LSD trip that seems preoccupied with producing the results of hybridisation between Timothy Leary and Pat Boone.

Moulin Rouge! is a visual and auditory feast, pushing the boundaries of both cinema and the musical genre. It is a dazzling spectacle, combining tragedy, romance, and frenetic energy, all wrapped up in a whirlwind of color and sound. The film manages to strike an impeccable balance between over-the-top theatricality and deep emotional resonance. I cant believe it took me this long to watch it, and now it has firmly landed in my top 4 favorite movies of all time, a testament to how special and unexpected the experience was.
Baz Luhrmanns direction is nothing short of extraordinary. His distinct visual style is characterized by rapid cuts, vibrant colors, and the merging of historical periods with contemporary influences. He takes a 19th-century Parisian setting and infuses it with a modern soundtrack and sensibility, creating a timeless atmosphere that is both nostalgic and fresh. Every scene is meticulously crafted to evoke a visceral reaction from the audience, pulling them into the chaotic world of the Moulin Rouge, where everything feels heightened, love, desire, and heartbreak. Luhrmanns keen attention to detail and his unrelenting pace make it impossible to look away.
The performances are a key reason why this film transcends the musical genre and becomes an emotional experience. Ewan McGregor, as the idealistic poet Christian, gives a heartfelt and passionate portrayal, making the audience believe in his overwhelming love for Satine, played brilliantly by Nicole Kidman. Her portrayal of Satine is layered she is vulnerable, strong, and tragic, embodying a woman torn between her dreams and her reality. The chemistry between McGregor and Kidman is palpable, grounding the otherwise flamboyant and exaggerated world in something profoundly human. Even the supporting cast, including the whimsical John Leguizamo as Toulouse-Lautrec and Jim Broadbent as the exuberant Harold Zidler, offer performances that are both comedic and touching.
Cinematography plays a massive role in the immersive experience that the movie offers. Every frame is like a painting, rich with detail, color, and symbolism. Cinematographer Donald McAlpine uses lighting and camera movements to accentuate the emotional highs and lows. The use of quick zooms and dynamic shots during musical numbers creates a kinetic energy that mirrors the chaotic and intoxicating atmosphere of the Moulin Rouge itself. At the same time, moments of tenderness are often captured in soft, intimate close-ups, providing a stark contrast to the dazzling sequences of excess.
The music is where the film truly shines, and perhaps why it resonated so deeply with me. The way Luhrmann and his team re-imagined contemporary pop songs in the context of a period musical was revolutionary. From the energetic rendition of Lady Marmalade to the heart-wrenching medley of love songs in Elephant Love Medley, the soundtrack acts as an emotional conduit, connecting the audience to the characters inner worlds. The musical numbers are not just performances they are extensions of the characters emotions, dreams, and desires, enhancing the storytelling rather than interrupting it.
Themes of love, art, and sacrifice dominate the movie, and these are explored through rich symbolism. The Moulin Rouge itself is a metaphor for the world of art, glamorous, intoxicating, but also fleeting and destructive. Satine represents the tragic artist who is consumed by her pursuit of dreams, a reflection on the sacrifices one makes for love and art. The overarching theme of truth, beauty, freedom, and love is constantly challenged and tested throughout the film, offering a poignant commentary on the cost of idealism.
Symbolism extends even further with the use of color. Red, the dominant hue, represents passion and danger, enveloping the film in a sense of urgency and desire. Blue, often used in Christians scenes, symbolizes innocence and purity, contrasting the more corrupt and decadent world of the Moulin Rouge. The interplay of colors subtly tells the story of Christian and Satines doomed love, highlighting the emotional stakes without needing overt exposition.
The films editing deserves special recognition. Jill Bilcocks work is frenetic and rhythmic, especially during the musical sequences, where cuts often match the beat of the music. This quick pacing creates a visceral energy that mirrors the pulse of the nightclub itself. However, during more intimate moments, the editing slows, allowing the audience to breathe and absorb the emotions. This careful control of pacing enhances the emotional rollercoaster the audience experiences.
Another fascinating aspect is its commentary on the nature of storytelling. The film is, after all, Christians recounting of his love affair with Satine. There is a self-awareness to the narrative structure, where the film constantly reminds us that it is, in essence, a melodramatic tragedy. The larger-than-life emotions and theatrical flourishes work because they are part of Christians romanticized retelling. This storytelling device adds an extra layer of depth, as we realize that the films events are shaped by his grief and idealism.
Its hard to pin down why I hadnt watched Moulin Rouge! earlier. Perhaps it was the reputation of musicals as lighthearted or superficial entertainment. But this film completely shattered that misconception for me. It is as emotionally rich and deeply affecting as any great drama, but with the added dimension of music amplifying every feeling. It made me realize that musicals can explore profound themes while still being unabashedly entertaining.
By the end of the film, I was left with a bittersweet feeling, having been swept up in the epic romance and the heartbreak that followed. Its a rare cinematic experience where every element from direction, performance, cinematography, music, and themes work in harmony to create something truly magical. Its not just a film its an experience that leaves a lasting impact long after the final credits roll.
In conclusion, Moulin Rouge! is a masterpiece of modern cinema, redefining the musical genre while telling a timeless story of love and loss. The fact that it now sits comfortably in my top 4 films is a testament to its emotional power and artistry. I only regret that it took me so long to discover its brilliance, but like the best art, it arrived in my life at the perfect moment.
