Musicals are, when you think about it, really absurd. People break into song in the middle of dialogue, emotions swell up into grand-full-orchestra tunes, and life collapses inward around a lovely staged scene. But maybe thats the whole point of it, musicals take the messy, frequently bedraggled human experience and make it bigger than life, unapologetically theatrical. Theyre meant to knock you out. Thats the notion. Theyre not understated theyre designed to make you feel, in all caps.
And Moulin Rouge lives that mantra like a glitter-sensitized fever dream.
Baz Luhrmann sets it ablaze with confetti, delirium, and a head-reeling sensory barrage. He performs a pretty straightforward romance and overlays it with a visual and sonic montage so hyper-intense that it shouldnt exactly work and by some magic, somehow it does. Hes a maximalist director in all ways, and Moulin Rouge is perhaps his most unapologetically over-the-top film. The camera whorls, snaps, twirls, swoops, and near-dances with the characters, and that relentless motion becomes a kind of music.
But whats great is that beneath all the color and craziness, theres heart. The film isnt trying to outsmart us, its busier observing its characters discover each other and themselves, in the moment, in this hotbox of doomed romance. The films feeling is unapologetic even when its rhinestoned up, and that honest heart is what holds the madness together.
Moulin Rouge is cinema as spectacle while Luhrmann refusing to let you forget that visual language in the cinema can be just as emotionally potent as dialogue or score. Its not subtlety but its sensation. Youre whirled round in a kaleidoscope. And when youre done, you stumble out bemused, blinded, and somehow affected, already drooling for another hit of that theatrical high.

Babylon is already a misunderstood gem, in my opinion. Weirdly called a mess, even though its plotting and character arcs are tightly interwoven and classically structured (you could almost accuse it of being a tad too simple rather than chaotic). 
Its a fascinating critique of the ways the white capitalistic greed of Hollywood forced (and still forces) assimilation onto the dreams of the marginalized and then forces them to turn on each other. It spotlights who cannot live without the business as opposed to who must leave, if they hope to keep their creative integrity (Im thinking about writing more on this subject in the future). 
So many reviews have missed how funny this movie is, so many reviews have missed how this is clearly a fable, so many reviews have missed how each actor imbues further depth into these characters through the tiniest and subtlest of beats, and so few reviews have actually tried to understand Mannys character in the milieu of this world in lieu of dissecting Chazelles bonafides for making sweatier, grimier material. 
But most of all, the misunderstanding of the final montage by many is confounding. How could such a bleak movie, one totally aware of the real seediness of Hollywood still end on such a hopeful note? Well, what tensions do you think are always at play in Tinseltown? This film is very aware of tensions talent and luck, identity and assimilation, apocryphal myth making and the lesser-known truths, moral incongruity and creative spunk, and the hate of the business, the clawing shit-stained antics required to remain in its good graces and the love of the medium. 
Its a well-acted, sonically and visually bombastic film which does what we beg of films  to take big swings  yet never loses its common touch. It is unequivocally Chazelles best, most truthful film.

A dorky Caligulan ode to the early days of Hollywood, Damien Chazelles sprawling Babylon may begin in 1926, but the movie is soon burdened with a clairvoyance that allows it to become unstuck in time. Several of the epics characters are haunted by glimpses of a future theyre powerless to prevent, a curse that its director brings to bear by drawing inspiration from across the entire spectrum of film history.
Burdened with the knowledge that this 80 million studio project could be the last of its kind, Babylon refracts Hollywoods first major identity crisis through the prism of its latest one. It reminds us the movies have been dying for more than 100 years, and then  through its heart-bursting, endearingly galaxy-brained prayer of a finale  interprets that as uplifting proof theyll actually live forever. It just doesnt have any idea how the movies will do it, or where the hell they might go from here.
Singin in the Rain naturally casts a long shadow, as the classic Stanley Donen musical created the template for telling emotionally Technicolor stories about the birth of the sound era (and the silent icons that it left on the cutting room floor). So does D.W. Griffiths Intolerance, which Babylon alludes to in title, scope, and structure alike. There are whiffs of La Dolce Vita, which Chazelles film evokes through its manufactured glamour and melancholy sex appeal, and also The Wolf of Wall Street, which Babylon channels throughout its go-for-broke first hour (while also borrowing half of its cast).
Thats just a tiny sample of the films that Babylon references, borrows from, or alludes to over the course of its 188-minute running time, as Chazelles anachronistic touchstones eventually become so vast and overt that they threaten to spill out across the screen. But as the hyper-focused ecstasy of the movies first half gives way to the meandering death march of its second, its hard not to wonder what Babylon is giving back to its medium in return.
Of all the people lost and gone to whom Babylon pays its own form of tribute, Jean-Luc Godard  an unavoidable touchstone for any film so concerned with the fin de cinéma  is perhaps the most instructive. Thats not because Chazelles end times Hollywood spectacle channels the free-wheeling anarchy of the French New Wave, but rather because it doesnt.
If The Jazz Singer is the kind of movie that the cast of Babylon cant see coming, Breathless is the kind of movie they cant even begin to imagine. More to the point, its the kind of movie that Chazelle reveres but, endearingly, cant quite bring himself to make, even with a bottomless reservoir of talent at his disposal, and a blank check to rewrite history.

In Kenneth Angers Hollywood Babylon, the myth of Hollywood sweeps in like a sandstorm out of the desert. Before long, the director is God and Movie Stars rise and fall. They marry and divorce and die and are reborn, again and again. It was practically pre-packaged a destiny of consumption. For our Tinseltown icons, the silver-screen is both their graveyard and their afterlife. A key component of cinemas appeal is that it is another world beyond our own, a space far past the limits of our mortal coil. 
Damien Chazelle utilizes Angers seminal hot gossip as a basis for his own Babylon, but he doesnt quite match the absurdity of its ecstasy or the horrific details of its half-truths. Right from the jump, Babylon feels sanitized, sparkly, as if the extravagance was initially written for a PG-13 rating. No matter the golden showers or casual nudity or incessant language or Chazelles tightly-wound signature whip-pans - this 3-hour exercise in reckoning with 1920s Hollywood cant help but feel squeaky-clean. It dances around in delirium, but it is sober, sexless, cartoonish. 
Part of this creates a dialectic in how Damien Chazelle himself views the time-period. Especially towards the end, this is less of a narrative and more of an essay-film, in which the audience is given a whirl-wind tour of cinemas progression, from Lillian Schwartz to Jim Cameron. Hollywood is initially conceived here as an amusement park of drugs and exploitation, all in pursuit of a great sunset and the perfect image. We go from the death of various extras on monumental epics to scheduled lunch-time. Elephants shit on the screen in the opening minutes and the discussion around the arrival of sound is punctuated with a nasty fart. Babylon has Things To Say on what the characters are experiencing in their present moment, but the script falters when they are allowed self-awareness for the space they exist within. 
Chazelle cant quite choose between archetypical distance and more complex character portraits, so the film is at a constant imbalance. It struggles to provide any genuine spark or danger to its plotting. Even a third-act descent into hellish kinks and alligator hijinks (carried by a demonic turn by Tobey Maguire) is warmed-up material. Babylon wants to be a crock-pot of big ideas and set-pieces and showstopping craft, and it does succeed on that level, but it ends up feeling like a bit of a trifle.

Babylon comes off like Chazelle wanted to copy a formula he knew would work, established by the likes of the aforementioned PTA and Scorcese but he never once took the time to ponder on what makes their maximalist excess films actual works of art.
This film asks the industry, the audience and the filmmaker itself How many pointless scenes can you cram into 3 hours? and then challenges itself constantly to outdo itself. He really thought the film would spark enough controversy with that vile first 45 minutes or the dungeon scene but its hilarious how no one cares lol.
Look, if you like this film, thats fully fine. Im happy for you. I loathe it and I loathe Chazelle more and more as time goes on and he reveals how little he actually has to offer. We can agree to disagree but theres also something to be said that we live in a world of Chazelle apologists who have basically loved everything hes done and even they are having severe issues with this film.
Okay, Im going to mention some of the positives so its not all shit-talk and we can get them out of the way.
Diego Calva is an absolute star. He was exactly how I pictured Manny and he brought that character to life. His transformation was only believable due to his performance because the narrative never really fully explores his rise in status in a realistic way.
The music was phenomenally written (as expected from Hurwitz) and a lot of the the moments remind me of the same classy and purposeful filmmaker who made Whiplash with an absolute love and respect for showing the dark side of the world while honoring the same aspects of the world he adores. Id listen to some songs off this soundtrack 100 outside of this movie. No doubt.
The visuals were insanely good. I didnt expect any less but I was also pleasantly surprised. The camera moves gracefully in some scenes and the compositions are pretty solid. It also has a frenetic chaotic energy in some other scenes which can really add to the vibes here.
The editing was definitely enjoyable.
I just cant say there were any scenes where an image is elevated a step above what it is actually showing. No nuance or artistry behind anything at all. It is what it is and no more.
The comedy was fine. There were a couple of funny moments, no doubt. I laughed out loud in an empty theater a couple times but for every time I laughed the film would remind me that what Im laughing at is just crude ridiculous over-the-top attempts at being the loudest clown in the room.
Its a shame the rest of the film is an atrocious piece of garbage and none of those positives make it a good film or even warrant giving it any extra stars.
Back to the issues.
Sitting in a FULLY empty theater watching this was an odd experience lol. After the first hour or so, I honestly was just squirming in my seat and felt like I was a prisoner. I somehow convinced myself to keep giving this a chance to win me over but I started looking at the time way too often. At one point I looked at the time and realized there were 2 hours left, and it dragged on for what seemed like an eternity, and I looked again and only 20 minutes had passed. Jesus.
This film is shallower than an inflatable kiddie pool. Its just pathetic and gross too.
The sequence in Tobey Mcguires dungeon? It came off ridiculous in the script and I had then compared it to the gimp scene in Pulp Fiction. Its somehow turned out to one of the worst things Ive ever seen. How does anyone watch this and find anything of value in this? A film that wants to shock and appal and succeeds, but there is no purpose here. I was more shocked and appalled by Tobeys ridiculous performance. What a terrible actor.
In fact everything in the last hour was just a string of illogical character decisions, ridiculous push your buttons moments, or silly screenwriting conveniences that take away any of the momentum that is shoe-strung here by a director so in over his head that he fails to see the forest for the trees. The plot armor? LOL RIDICULOUS. 
That ending?! Has to be one of the most laughable pieces of wink-wink-nudge-nudge tomfoolery Ive ever sat through. It came off bad in the script and it warranted even more eye-rolls as I watched it. Like we get it bro, you love singing in the rain, you made that clear to us in la la land. You love how movies have developed over time? Okay sure but this was a piss poor way at showing the audience. Im again so concerned about the state of film and what people seem to like and get out of the films they watch. It may have held even an ounce of weight if this was based on a real person.  WHAT THE FUCK WAS THAT MONTAGE?!?!?! Why did it go THERE of all places? Jesus Christ. The irony of me seeing clips and bits from films that are insanely better than this, like Persona and The matrix. It even showed a clip from Avatar?! Like What?
Its crazy how you can make a 3 hour film that doesnt have a single purposeful and meaningful moment. You could literally miss solid 30-40 minute chunks out of this film and you wouldnt miss anything important at all. Maybe a joke or a zany silly goofy moment but nothing that serves the story and nothing that acts like a profound commentary on cinema, the industry, or even the people who got truly affected by the introduction of talkies. You could literally scrap so much of this movie and nothing would be truly lost. 
If the film was 90 minutes shorter, this could have probably been salvaged.
Look, Ive made it pretty clear I read the screenplay around 6 months ago and I had my hopes crushed with this script. I then heard they were doing rewrites to clean it up and make it less vile and repulsive.  So I was truly hoping they would salvage this project from the depths of the abyss. There was undoubtedly potential here, especially if the story would have focused more on Manny and on the transition to talkies instead of all the obscene scenes that are sprinkled throughout, the random side characters and the constant meandering. Unfortunately, this is like 95 close to the script I read and I can truly say this film deserves to bomb. Chazelle made one of my all time favorite films but every single project since then has gotten progressively worse and shown that he basically has nothing else up his sleeve. I called this months ago, people didnt believe me, and thats fine. But a terrible script can NEVER somehow turn into a magically great movie, so I dont really know how I was expecting it to pivot and somehow maybe possibly turn it into gold.
Babylon is no more a loving ode to cinema as any of us taking a dump, watching Singin in the Rain on our phone and immediately writing a letterboxd review while still sitting on the toilet.
I have some heavy schadenfreude watching this film flop. Chazelle doesnt deserve to get blank checks or have creative liberties. He shouldnt be surrounded by YES MEN just because he made 1 (maybe) 2 good films. He should in fact be surrounded by as many people who would call him out on his shit as possible. The marketing team did this film no favors and I think the studio knew the product they had wasnt worth investing any more money into. It shows.
Not just one of the worst films of the year, one of the most pointless pieces of garbage Ive ever seen.
2022 is literally a joke. People were cooped up during the pandemic for so long they forgot how real films are made, they forgot how real people interact and are now just trolling audiences with garbage films.
This piece of filth was not my tempo.

Babylon is a big fucking mess. There are so many bad and clumsy edits. The cinematography, with its frequently out-of-focus backgrounds, is garish and irritating. The opening five minutes has an elephant shit on the lens and the ending is a corny montage filled with questionable choices. But my god I fucking loved the experience of watching Babylon. Its three-hour, hyperactive sprawl is so much fun. Every frame of this behemoth is alive and energised. Montage after montage, accompanied by the most addictive score of the year, it all works as a breathless piece of cinematic ecstasy. There are large stretches of Babylon, particularly in the first two hours, which are mini-masterpieces.
Say what you want about Chazelles scattershot execution, at least Babylon has a soul, a pulse, a passion. His film is little more than a silent era Boogie Nights, coupled with the excess of The Wolf of Wall Street, but theres an ambition here which few films achieve. Not just technical ambition, but a desire to keep a movie dancing in the mind for such a long runtime. No pauses, no recovery, no forgiveness, Babylon goes all in on debauchery and mayhem. Yet its also about a culture changing, about the finite and fleeting moments that define our lives. Nothing lasts forever, but film, as art, can immortalise us. It preserves memories. Few people get to work on something that truly mattered, and that desire to live, not in a passive way, but to truly live and make an impact, that desire runs deep in so many people. Live a good fucking life, climb the social ladder, and drop out before you fall to the bottom and splatter.
Babylon is imperfect in so many ways, but watching it reminded me just how stunning cinema can be. Its a filthy, outrageous ode to filmmaking, made to remind you of so many other movies and yet not overshadowed by them. Its a buzz, its a high, its a drug of a movie a high tempo flash that never seems to end. Eras come and go, but memories remain. Babylon brings the past to life and throws us into it. Few films achieve the highs of Babylon and for that alone it should be sought out. Its cinematic masturbation, a self-pleasuring fever edging itself towards disappointment. But you dont regret pleasure as it happens. Embrace the collapse of culture, take another shot and keep on living. Immerse yourself in Babylon and come out dazed.

Rolled out to see this - the biggest flop of the year - projected on beautiful 70mm film. It had been a few years since Id seen something in 70mm (Im pretty sure the last time was... wait for it... Joker), and whatever else is wrong with this movie, it was a pleasure to live in those deep, rich colors for three hours. If this is playing in 70mm in your area, youd better act fast and see it so you can understand what theyve taken from you.
This is a collection of received wisdom about Tinseltown, much of it contradictory, rendered through borrowed aesthetics that underscore the distance between Chazelle and his influences. Theres no coherent statement or vision here - its a pastiche of tones and myths that might seem good in the moment but dont fit together. It seeks to rip the veil off the Dream Factory by scandalizing us with wild parties full of drugs and explicit sex, but then later has a scene where Margot Robbie tells off the bluenoses at a high-society party for sitting atop their moral high horses. Tobey Maguire takes us on a tour of a depraved sex dungeon, Jovan Adepo becomes a saintly martyr for institutional racism, and Robbie gets in deep trouble with Hollywood gangsters, but despite all this, Chazelle ends with Diego Calva (a star is not born) dreaming a montage of film history (capped off with a clip from, I swear to god, Avatar) and realizing with tears streaming down his face that hes been part of something greater than himself - thats right, folks, the movies! Imagine if Scorsese had ended Wolf of Wall Street with a montage about the magic of Wall Street. Chazelle undoubtedly drew a lot of inspiration from Wolf, but that movie depicted its world as both totally evil and extremely sexy and desirable - both feelings seamlessly integrated. Scorsese hates Wall Street, but Chazelle loves the movies, and his approach to film history is paternalistic - he wants to use his art to fix historic wrongs rather than live with the discomfort.
Also, Chazelle ending a movie with clips from all the scenes from Singin in the Rain he ripped off is not the mic-drop moment he thinks it is. That said, great to see Eric Roberts back on the big screen.
(The scene where Adepo silently fumes while a bunch of condescending white liberals shower him with clumsy praise... could somebody have told Chazelle that hes no better than these people?)

BABYLON (2022) popped on Prime and I gave it a second look. Id so anticipated the film four years ago and was so dissappointed. Its even worse than I remembered. Everything that should have been easy to do right was wrong. All because of excess. Was there ever a party as debauched in the Twenties as the one which opens the film? Was the ever a so debauched party ever? Similarly difficulties with early sound shooting. Every aspect overplayed. What a missed opportunity--an opportunity which wont come again.

Babylon seems to have a sincere reverence for the lawlessness of the 1920s and a strong distaste for the barbarism disguised as lawfulness that followed. If you dive into a lions cage and get eaten you knew the risk, if youre torn apart in a cat cafe perhaps the cafe is to blame. 
Not unlike the irony of La La Lands dare to dream message led by A-list celebrities and millions upon millions of dollars, there is a strange irony underneath all of Babylon.
The fact of the matter is that we arent any more dignified, any more gentle with peoples dreams now. Your worth to the machine is decided solely by your usefulness and that can run out and that can be replaced. The anointed few get the gift of making their own Hollywood movies and the extras, the crew and the audience alike all have nothing to go home to but a dream. The very same dream that makes them come back the next day to the same settheater. The machine relies on this.
With this in mind, how do you make a movie criticizing the Hollywood of the past within that same unchanging, cold system? Are we so much better now because of unions and safety protocols and social awareness or have the fates of the casualties remained the same? If one is killed gently and quietly are they not still killed? Lord knows there are still vapid parties where everyones head is up each others asses, as well as orgies with similarly stuffed orifices. There are still stars burning the brightest and cockroaches merely surviving in the shadows. There are still headshots on a bloody table that belonged to no one in particular.
This is the story of the movies. From Muybridges Horse in Motion to James Camerons Avatar. Its suffering in the name of progress, in the name of art, in the name of leaving something behind other than a body.

Babylon seems acutely aware of this and yet it still exists. With the advent of digital technology and the internet the form has finally been democratized, we are all filmmakers, our dreams are held hostage by no one and this will only become more apparent in time. Is Hollywood a necessary evil? Perhaps at one point it was. The ultimate smile here tells me Chazelle would argue it still is. He has to believe that or else his movie is a dejected shrug.

Chazelle es Dios. Entiende absolutamente todo técnicamente. Sabe manejar cada travelling, cada barrido, cada montaje rítmico, cada profundidad de campo... Sabe filmar en espacios cerrados y abiertos. Sabe hacer escenas de comedia, de aventura, de drama, de acción y hasta de terror. Sabe rodar conversaciones de dos personas y dotarlas de cine. Sabe alejar al cine del teatro, del vídeoclip, del videojuego y de la literatura, para ser solo cine, cómo si las herramientas las hubiera inventado el cine. Sabe manejar a 500 actores corriendo, aún mientras el foco esté en otro lugar. Sabe en qué momentos específicos prestarse a la cámara en mano, y cuándo amerita un zoom.
Como si fuera poco, al ser músico posee una virtud descomunal. Entiende de tempos, de ritmos, tiene gusto, tiene estilo. Sabe qué le gusta y qué no, qué corresponde y qué no.
Además, es cautivante porque pone a los actores del momento, aquellos que más amamos, haciendo cosas divertidísimas y que siempre soñamos ver y que, por supuesto, ellos saben hacer a la perfección. 
Sabe que hay algo de todo ese desborde que invita a quedarse viendo hasta el final sin importar tanto qué suceda en sí, sólo por el placer de ver a la orquesta tocar, más allá de que los personajes no sean los más queribles del mundo. 
Todo esto no es menor porque es lo que compone al cine como lenguaje y también lo que hace que uno vaya a ver una película en pantalla grande, es el diferencial de la pantalla grande, por eso despierta estas sensaciones generales de cine total, porque en ese aspecto lo es. En resumen, es un virtuoso como pocos en el mundo. Esta es su mejor película en ese campo, o al menos en la que mejor lo demuestra. Y que es abismal lo que filma no es ni siquiera una opinión, ya es algo indiscutible.
Algunos ejemplos el fundido a negro después de la muerte de Greg, por la muerte en sí, pero también porque finaliza una etapa en la vida de Jack Conrad y en la vida de todos. A partir de ahí, todo irá en bajada y se da a lugar a una nueva instancia.
Las muertes también son, en efecto, grandes decisiones. Por un lado, Nellie La Roy, quien hace su primera aparición por la noche luego de bajarse del auto para ingresar a una fiesta en la que no estaba invitada, tiene su escena final, bajándose nuevamente del auto cuando no corresponde, y en este caso, para esfumarse en la oscuridad como si de un noir se tratara, más siendo su personaje una especie de femme fatale.
Por otro lado, Jack Conrad quiere romper el círculo. Tras hacer mención que su esposa no sabe que todo volverá a repetirse, abandona la conversación con Lady Fay Zhu (con quién había conversado también en la fiesta inicial, una muy distinta a esta última) para finalmente suicidarse en una habitación en solitario. El plano final permite ver la puerta entreabierta, emulando el formato del cine mudo, etapa en la que Jack era amo y señor hasta la llegada del sonido. Por esto mismo no vemos su muerte, sólo podemos escuchar el sonido del disparo, en sintonía con la idea de que el cine sonoro asesinó su carrera. Es una resolución magnífica.
Pero Chazelle no es solo Dios, también es el diablo, porque todas estas herramientas terminan siendo puestas en disposición de una idea más grande, la de ir en oposición de la idea primera del cine de Hollywood que, quierase o no, guste más o menos, es la responsable de hacer nacer y mantener al cine con vida. 
Aquí no solo se despliega una cinefilia de posters (Singing in The Rain termina quedando como una película hipócrita si vemos que Chazelle dice que, detrás de esa película, estuvo todo esto, y se eligió contar algo lindo), si no también una réplica de situaciones de la historia negra de Hollywood, extraídas del libro de chismes Hollywood Babylon, que ya fue, no una, cien mil veces desmentido, y hasta tuvo delirios tales como cambiarles el destino a personajes históricos.
No conforme con esto, lo que termina retratando Chazelle es un grupo de productores que no tenían idea (cuando se sabe que la época de Hollywood triunfó porque los productores sabían tanto como los directores, a veces más, a diferencia de la actualidad), un cúmulo de actores borrachos, cocainómanos y actríces promiscuas, un compilado de tanto hombres importantes como ejecutivos que son pedófilos (se dice no menos de cinco veces que hay pedofilia, como si uno fuera torpe y no hubiera quedado claro literalmente a los primeros cinco minutos de película cuando encuentran a un productor con una menor muerta), sumado a que los negros eran discriminados, las asiáticas tenían que estar puestas a un costado, todas las películas están manchadas con sangre porque la gente se moría, los castings eran un circo donde se elegían a los talentos de pedo, las películas no contaban nada más que espectáculo, y los grandes planos salían bien de casualidad. 
No hay absolutamente nada bueno en el Hollywood que retrata Chazelle, su étapa brillante en el cine fue por esas cosas de la vida, son todos malos, cínicos, corruptos yo pedófilos. No por nada abundan películas como Babylon, Mank o Blonde, que se apoyan en historias ficticias para retratar miserias de los tiempos de oro, en sentido falsamente revisionista, todas financiadas por productores actuales que quieren manchar aquel Hollywood para limpiar al actual. is the intimacy, and the concoction of the two is thrilling. there will be many more thoughts on this film from me, as it sits with me longer and when I inevitably rewatch it. but for now, I would like to leave on the fact that the final montage felt like a re-invention of the cinematic form in that moment, a re-contextualisation of everything thats come before in all its hybrids and Ich hätte gewarnt sein sollen, als in der fünften Minute ein Elefant frontal in die Kamera kotet. Zwei Männer werden komplett besudelt, die braune Suppe spritzt auf die Kameralinse, bleibt dort kleben und es sprudelt und sprudelt. Keine 10 Minuten später wird dann einem nackten, schwer adipösen Mann der Oberkörper bepinkelt. Später wird ausgiebig gekotzt. Man wähnt sich kurz im falschen Film - ist das hier Babylon oder doch schon Jackass 5?
Es muss so sein, zumindest wurde ich lange im Kino nicht mehr so oft angebrüllt, sind Darsteller panisch übereinander gestolpert, ständig passieren kleine und große Pannen an Sets und in den Leben der Figuren, alles schraubt sich hoch, bis zur finalen Pointe der jeweiligen Szene, die selten bis nie zündet. Mich hat das an Monthy Pythons Sinn des Lebens erinnert, minus deren feinen Sinn für bissige Satire. Die Schmuddeleien der Briten oder etwa ganz aktuell in Ruben Östlunds Triangle of Sadness sind als überzeichnete Metapher auf die Gier der Reichen inszeniert. Bei Damien Chazelles wirken die endlosen Exzesse jedoch unmotiviert, weil es an Biss und satirischer Klasse fehlt.
Und dann beginnt der nächste Sketch jemand hastet von links nach rechts ins Bild, weil wieder irgendwer ins Drogenkoma gefallen ist, mal ist der Gag, dass der Wechsel vom Stumm- zum Tonfilm zu tumultartigen Zuständen am Set führt, was hier passend zu den forcierten Extremen des Films natürlich mit einem Todesfall enden muss. Damien Chazelle zitiert irgendwann ironischerweise noch Singing in the Rain, bei dem er sich überdeutlich bedient. Wo Gene Kellys Meisterwerk noch heute betört, weil sein Blick auf Hollywood zwar durchaus kritisch, aber sympathisch und geistreich war, hat Chazelle nur Zynismus entgegen zu setzen.
In den seltenen Momenten, in denen Babylon mal still hält und tatsächlich vom Filmemachen erzählt, von der Amoral Hollywoods, ist der Film noch am Besten, aber davon gibt es zu wenige. Irgendwann wird dann ein halber Horrorfilm aus der Nummer und weil Chazelle wirklich so gar nichts über das Medium zu sagen hat, fällt ihm am Ende nichts Besseres ein, als wahllos Filmszenen aneinander zu schneiden. Denn nichts feiert den Film mehr als ein Supercut auf Trailerlänge.

Welcome to the asshole of Los Angeles. Its LAs last real party.
-James McKay-
Ok. So. First off all, can you imagine how the writing process and the the subsequent pitch for Babylon must have looked like? I can. I just watched it on the screen. Youll never convince me that Damien Chazelle and his crew didnt ingest copious amounts of uppers before each step of the making of this film. Results? Pure, beautiful, movie-making chaos. 
Babylon is a blisteringly deranged and frenetic chronicling of love, loss, and overt debauchery  of the otherwise revered Golden Era of Hollywood. Babylon doesnt give us the ritzy, glamorous, and posh backdrops that are oft associated with 1920s Hollywood. No. Rather we are subjected to a perverse, drug fueled frenzy that plunges us deep into the bowels of Hollywoods underbelly. Babylon is as ambitious as it us unhinged, managing to be both controlled and chaotic. Chazelle crafted a new epic here with Babylon. Its rich and stylistic world has a numbing effect, rendering you in a trance-like state, barring you from looking away. Or that could be the drugs. Probably the drugs. Regardless, Babylon is a bold and daring fever dream that is a raucous good time. 
Many films today dont take a ton of risks, studios are scared of it because theyre afraid it wont profit. I get it. Its a harsh reality but reality nonetheless. I just love that Damien Chazelle who is riding on a multi-movie high said eff it. Did a line of coke, popped a xan and made Babylon, which he knew no one would turn down. Thankfully he was right. Chazelle took us to the asshole of LA, and gave us one the best cinematic parties of the year. Just make sure to watch your drink at all times.
What a stunner Babylon is. The cinematography is gorgeous. The range and diversity of its sprawling and evolving sets was a wonder, a true touch of genuine artistry. Babylon felt like a MOVIE. A grand and fantastical descent into a sin-laced Bazar of longing and desire. It was sharp and full of life, colors dripping from every corner of the screen both in bright over-the-top ways and in hushed, depressive tones. There is so much happening on the screen at all times, almost to an overwhelming extent. But. Chazelle never gets lost amidst his own storm, instead he managed to make every detail (even when there are 100s of people on screen at once) come to life. There was no static, no dead space, no lull. In a way, Babylon felt like Uncut Gems solely from a whiplashed cinematography perspective. My eyes were shifting all across the screen in a futile attempt to fully absorb the insanity before me. My senses were accosted by the brilliant dissonance of the boisterous trumpet brigades that drive Babylon in its entirety. Justin Hurwitz really flexed on us with this score. A big band orgy of cocainic sound (yes I just made up that word, but hey, it works). Babylon is a visual feast. A true cinematic achievement in every technical aspect. Its almost hard to even put into words. Just see it. Youll understand.
I would like to go ahead and put this on record. This is one of the best assemblies of talent in a cast that Ive seen in recent memory. Each actor used to their strengths and then dialed to ten. Each performance was impactful, each performance mattered. And with such a large cast, thats no small feat. So kudos to Chazelle for the masterful direction. 
Lets start with Margot Robbie. If you have listened to our Mostly Film podcast (which you totally should) youll know that I think Robbie is a little overrated and overused. However, I couldnt be happier to report that Babylon has changed my tune. Margot Robbie was an absolute powerhouse here, delivering her greatest and most nuanced performance to date. Robbie put forth a exaggerated but grounded performance that was entrancing and heartbreaking. Robbie delivered a well rounded and Oscar worthy performance that will for me, be a litmus test for all future outings. Two of my favorite scenes of the whole year came via Robbie in Babylon. The sound set fiasco scene, and poolside rattlesnake romp both were just mesmerizing and full of surprises that Robbie effortlessly carried. Brad Pitt. For this role you couldnt have cast anybody better. In my opinion Pitt was Babylon, he made this film palatable. Pitt was the reprieve from the unending onslaught of dicks, tits, and elephants shits (lol could be a new Babylon inspired kids book). Pitt is synonymous in present day as a bona fide movie star, and he slid into this role so seamlessly. Pitt had the most impactful story arc of Babylon, one that that left me shellshocked and mouth agape, even though it was predictable, but thats what also made it so harrowing and tragic. Pitt was phenomenal, restrained and explosive. A quiet expository performance that was carried with the gravitas that only someone of his caliber could deliver. Diego Calva. Listen, Calva was good, but I didnt think he was great. Babylon is obviously his big mainstream, breakout-role, and while he was the titular star, I feel like he was lost amongst the swells that were Margot Robbie and Brad Pitt. Calva did have a few scenes that showcased what he could really do, specifically towards the end of the film. Maybe this was purposely designed, Im unsure, but as a whole, I felt like Calvas performance was lacking just a little bit. Tobey Maguire, what a fun little creep he was. His brief role was most assuredly one of the most memorable and detestable of the year. I want more of this from Maguire. Hes almost ready to go full Norman Osborn. Babylon was phase one. 
Babylon is a sensually grotesque and alluring tale of passion and despair, of dreams crashing into nightmares. Babylon tells a shockingly coherent story despite its bewildering and breakneck desensitization style of storytelling. Babylon kept me fully engaged and wholly absorbed from beginning to end. To me, Babylon is the most artistic blockbuster Ive ever seen. Divisive? Certainly. Im just afraid after seeing the box office numbers that people have forgotten that film is an outlet for creativity and art. Babylon is art. Babylon is creativity. Babylon is beauty. Unorthodox and uncomfortable sure. But a masterpiece nonetheless. Stop what youre doing and go see Babylon right now. If you love film, you will love this movie. 
Seriously Tom Cross, Babylons editor deserves every accolade possible. I can imagine the daunting task of piecing this hot mess juggernaut together. Shewwww couldnt be me.
Did anyone else see the dwarf with the giant cock bouncing on the pogo stick? Wow. High class. 
The Count deserved better, and probably the alligator too.
Also, Im glad to know that Sloth from The Goonies is still finding work. Albeit chained in a underground sex club. But hey, times are tough. 
Unless I missed it, I didnt get to see Brad Pitt dance on a table and Im mad about it. 
Olivia Wilde was a nice touch, and so was Flea.

Babylon is easily one of the best movies of 2022. Its bonkers yet sincere, cynical yet sympathetic, and has one of the best ensemble performances of the year.
A tragedy wrapped in glitters is how I would describe Babylon, a three-hour odyssey that never feels bogged down by its whooping runtime. Focusing on a group of Hollywood silent era stars during the industrial update to sound pictures, Babylon provides quite an intriguing entry point into an era long gone from the point of view of a Mexican immigrant who rises and falls with the industry. 
From the long opening sequence of the orgy scene, the anti-Hollywood stance of Babylon is clear from the get-go, as well as its technical supremacy, and it never lets up showing the hypocrisy and cruelty of the industry and how it chews up and spits out its stars as a tradition, which is why the scarce moments of sincerity and soul-baring feel so refreshingly powerful from Margot Robbie and Diego Calva, whose all-consuming love story simply goes beyond languages and time. Highly recommended.

This film has stuck in my mind more than any other awards-season movie, including the ones that are wildly superior to it. It is often simultaneously too vulgar and too reserved, offering a travelogue of hedonism that is a bit too precisely ordered to truly convey chaos. Its recreations of the silent era are so wildly inaccurate that the mourning it expresses for that periods end rings hollow, and its cynicism is a bit rich coming from one of the precious few filmmakers of his generation who has enjoyed total carte blanche in the industrys current deeply restrictive and artistically compromised state.
But beneath all of this is, I think, a much more multivalent, thoughtful movie than its outward sheer would indicate. Chazelle may filter silent techniques through modern methods that warp them beyond recognition, but there is a real underlying emotional logic in watching the mass abandon of the first act slam suddenly and coldly into the static, aesthetically simplified rigors of early talkies with their lugubrious soundproofing blimps and curbed room for spontaneity. Despite being an ensemble piece of committed actors giving mostly excellent performances (from breakout Diego Calva as the slowly corrupted moral POV to Tobey Maguires leprotic gangster), Margot Robbie seizes the reins early in this, and the sight of her untrammeled sexual wildness abruptly put in a cage in the scene of her first talkie is some of the best print the legend material about the pitfalls of shifting to sound.
This is, in unlikely fashion, maybe Chazelles most character-driven movie to date, one that reveals a real care for his characters once you move past the poison pen letter to Hollywood. These are all cheats and hustlers and nobodies who have latched onto the movies as their only way to make it. Is it any coincidence that the two American cities most renowned as mirages of false promises of prosperity, Los Angeles and Las Vegas, literally sprang out of the desert? The films (admittedly slow and overemphasized) descent into doldrums and despair in the second and third acts is a grim reminder of how easily the public can move on from their idols, and also how much of that transition is openly shepherded by the moguls in charge.
There are many blatant connections here to Singin in the Rain as the most classic Hollywood movie about moving to talkies. But the subtext of Singin in the Rain was one of celebration, that the rough birth pains of the talkie era ultimately made possible the movie musical and with it new forms of innovative splendor. Here, though, the tacit argument is that sound was the opening salvo in cinemas fraught relationship with technological gimmickry, the first and longest lasting special effect. (You think thats footsteps that youre hearing? Morpheus might ask of us Neos as we listen to a character walking down a street as their sound of their feet was created in a Foley booth by someone hand-stomping pumps on a wooden board.) Its also a reminder that the money men will always, always throw everything into the new gizmo at the expense of what it might mean for the artists who have mastered things as they are. 
But there is ambivalence here instead of pure doomsaying The ending of the film cannot really be spoiled because it leaves behind the story entirely, instead giving over to a psychic vision of the next century of gimmicks from physical models to CGI to glimpses of emerging digital-age AI and post-cinema techniques. That this dream belongs to someone who completely gave up his identity multiple times to be in and escape from the Dream Factory is telling, but he, like Chazelle, is left at a muted peace with it.

Damien Chazelles epic of debauchery amidst the start of the Hollywood system is his most ambitious film to date. This bombastic and in your face depiction of the 1920s is the biggest gut punch to your preconceived notions as to how this era of society went about life. It really was this crazy and wild where drugs ran rampant and the parties were unhinged at an unsettling level. Babylon feels like a demented cousin of La La Land in a sense that it is about the Hollywood Dream Factory but instead of showing an ideal version of it we get the underbelly of such a vile society who were actually looked upon as trash of the earth. The film industry was new and the world looked down on it as unworthy art. Both of Chazelles Hollywood pictures contain both versions of the city where dreamers either make it until they fade into obscurity or never make it at all.
Chazelle is adamant about showing us this huge canvas of characters chase after this dream and how the Hollywood system chews them up and spits them out into the black depths of obscurity. In all of his doom and gloom I couldnt believe how funny this film was. Its the hardest Ive laughed at the movies all year and the comedy works so well with the cocaine paced editing of the film. Babylon literally starts with one of the greatest (and obscene) parties scenes in all of film and ends with one of the most ambitious endings Ive seen to date. This doesnt feel like Chazelles most nuanced and controlled piece of art hes ever made, but it definitely feels like his most ambitious and admirable. 
Epics that follow a vast array of characters are very tricky to do and we dont see many of them anymore. Chazelle does it with as many surprises as possible and doesnt let the viewer off the hook. The period detail is immaculate and I couldnt stop smiling at all of the silent movie era elements being displayed to me. Im incredibly interested in silent filmmaking (Chazelle obviously is also) and to see a whole movie dedicated to it and how it birthed this massive art movement for humanity through its wild and chaotic birth is something I will forever cherish. Hearing Charlie Chaplin, Harold Lloyd, and Buster Keatons names in the film was a treat! It is obvious Chazelle did a decades worth of research for this movie (he did!) and it all paid off in a fantastic way. The score for this movie by frequent Chazelle collaborator Justin Hurwitz is my favorite score since his previous score for La La Land back in 2016. 
Margot Robbie gives one of her best performances as Nellie LaRoy, a Clara Bow stand in whose career is on the rise and fall trajectory. Brad Pitt brings his movie star charisma to such an endearing and heartbreaking character. Diego Calva is a newcomer and he portrays Manny with the dreamer spirit that allows the audience to follow him into this world of Fd up excess and glamour. The ensemble cast is excellent with Tobey Maguire, Li Jun Li, Jean Smart, P.J. Byrne, and Carson Higgins. Chazelle painted a massive mural of Hollywood personalities among a disgusting and harsh world where hard work, blood, sweat, and tears will torturously only get you so far before the system decides it is done with you. Its done so in such a broad, energetic, brassy, sensual, and hilarious odyssey into the journey of the life of what we call the movies. These people paved the way and all of their sacrifices were not in vain. Manny wanted to be a part of something bigger than himself, something that will change the world. 
The movies were built by people like Manny, Nellie, and Jack who gave everything to this art form that decided when they werent good enough for it. Manny found what he was looking for, but it was years later when he realized just how big of a thing he was a part of. Chazelle drives this home with the most breathtaking and ambitious ending Ive seen this year with the most massive fourth wall break you could ever imagine. Manny, Nellie, and Jack paved the way for a huge art form that continues to push boundaries 100 years after they were birthing it. Essentially confirms all the most cynical readings of La La Land and then expands and doubles down on those elements to the tune of an Avengers Endgame-size runtime. You could write for a year about how catastrophically misguided this entire enterprise was from the beginning, but the thing that struck me most is how similar this is to Infinity War and Endgame. The MCU has utilized the trappings of dozens of genres, as well as countless mirror scenes of set pieces and memorable bits from major action, adventure, science-fiction, and comedy films and repackages them as their own original products that just happen to be really homage-crazy. This movie does the same thing but with slightly snobbier tastes. There are Coppola scenes, there are Griffith scenes, there are Cassavetes scenes, there are Aznor scenes, there are P.T. Anderson scenes, and my good holy christ half-naked on the cross are there Scorsese scenes, all funneled through the image-sensation machine that is Damien Chazelle but to no emotional, philosophical, or even spectacular end. Nothing lands. Its all pomp. Talent and beauty for miles and none of it works, even for a second, unless you completely give up on caring about whats going on in the film. Even then, you have to watch all the sumptuous light and color, all the seductive and mesmerizing faces and bodies, get slathered on by the bucket to cover up the fact that Chazelle probably does think all the violence, exploitation, trauma, abandonment, and death were worth it for us to get to see X-Men Origins Wolverine or three-plus hours of him feverishly jerking off to a Kenneth Anger paperback.

Lets start with the elephant in the room. (Strictly speaking, its initially the elephant in the truck.) In Damien Chazelles Babylon, this animal is part of the entertainment at a party thrown by a Hollywood mogul in 1926. The elephant does eventually make it to the party where it becomes a literal elephant in the room. Now an elephant shitting may or may not be a metaphor, an elephant in a room is never not a metaphor. In Babylon, it represents the long-forgotten seamy side of this era in Hollywood history.

About 15 minutes after Margot Robbie and Diego Calva thanked me for watching the movie the way it was meant to be seen, just as their characters are discussing the magic of the movies, the movie shut off for five minutes and somehow turning it back on caused the curtains to close up to 1.85, where they stayed the whole rest of the movie. Lol.
Anyway, something feels off about the profanity and nudity here. On paper there should be no problem how else would you convey the level of primal lawlessness and sexual depravity of these parties and the silent era? And its not like Damien Chazelle even has a squeaky clean track record considering the language in Whiplash, but here it feels like a PG-13 filmmaker went in and carroted swear words and other explicit material into his script to punch things up. It honestly reminded me of when I decided I was finally old enough to say fuck in fifth grade and started excessively using it in sentences it had no place being in. Damn ass rock type beat.
My real theory is that Chazelle included all these bits of vanilla depravity (ooh golden showers! dead hookers! Isnt this seedy? Perhaps stock is the better word here  what he assumes general audiences ie humans want from this bacchanal movie, even if theres specific historical precedent) to distract us from the fact that his real fetish is 1920s period design, silent film eyeliner and flapper haircuts and what have you. And in that department hes a total sicko, fully one of the guys awooga-ing over Marias dance in Metropolis. And I love him for that  Im all for filmmakers subconsciously realizing their perversions on screen, especially when theyre this backwards. But that sense of explicit box-ticking is hard to swallow at times. I genuinely think a thorough investigation of the way this movie executes shit jokes and vomit as opposed to, say, Triangle of Sadness would reveal some fundamental insights about the respective artists. As it stands, off-screen explosive diarrhea during a conversation about sound in movies is not the formal fuck-you Chazelle clearly thinks it is.
The irony is that most of that verbal wonkiness happens earlier in the movie, when its at its best. Three really great set pieces more or less in a row with Hurwitz and Sandgren expectedly delivering (the bari sax brings a much-needed horniness to the typical fare), and though the following two hours are about decline so it makes sense that the same energy doesnt persist, Chazelle is still borrowing from other movies and seeing diminishing returns in execution. And that leads me to the end of the movie, which commits two crimes. One is the montage of movies to come, which celebrates these form-evolving works while failing to do so itself, that very montage striving for experiment and abstraction but playing it generally very safe (I wouldnt knock the movie for not redefining the form if there werent so much assertion about it). The other is Diego Calvas knowing smile, suggesting that all the exploitation and suffering was worth it.
This isnt dissimilar to his other endings, but the characters in Whiplash and La La Land are destroying their own lives in their pursuits and only really have to reckon with themselves. When Fletcher and Andrew smile at each other, Andrew knows what hes signed himself up for. With First Man and now Babylon, Chazelle is starting to hint at (to put it lightly) grander systemic collateral damage, but he still ends on beats deciding it was worth it for the main characters personal journeys. And in this particular case, he ends on Avatar as the signifier that were still making forward progress, a movie that came out 13 years before this one. How many movies from the 60s were in that montage, by comparison? Maybe hes hoping Babylon is itself the next piece of the puzzle. Tbh it wouldve been a big dick play if he threw all his movies into the mix.
Ill be honest this was still frequently an engaging watch, it could even be a 4 one day, but every fun bit was met with some qualifier that made it hard for me to fully lay into, and on a thematic level its more confused than ever, which is probably an accurate translation of Damien Chazelles psychosexual relationship with old Hollywood. And to me, thats the real value here.

A tale of outsized ambition and outrageous excess, it traces the rise and fall of multiple characters during an era of unbridled decadence and depravity in early Hollywood.
Babylon is as hectic and chaotic as one could imagine from that first trailer. Calva and Robbie are spectacular in this ambitious explosion of fast-paced madness. Chazelles darker take on Hollywood in this era is fascinating, but he isnt always able to balance so many storylines happening at once. It is a complete 180 compared to La La Land, less from a filmmaking standpoint and more within its approach to to the ins and outs of Hollywood. The era is obviously impactful here, as everything was so different during this time. The transition from the silent era to talkies brought about chaos and madness, and this is obviously a big factor within Chazelles decision-making. The idea of making the movie feel just as hectic as the era itself will work for so many, but it also causes the story to lose focus more than a few times while watching. Unlike his other films, Babylon feels sloppy in its presentation, whether this is intentional or not.
There are several scenes that stand out as some of the more well-constructed and satisfying movie moments in recent memory, one specifically that will have audiences cracking up. So it isnt a film without its highlights. The score is ridiculously memorable, as Justin Hurwitz once again proves that he is one of the better composers in the business. Every moment is amplified by the music behind it, and there is so much range within the score the best example is how it conpliments the finale. The cinematography is great (as expected), there is so much to adore about the costumes and production design, and there is this dark comedy feeling to a few scenes that will have cinema lovers laughing. My biggest issue may be attempting to stuff this story with so much, even considering the three-hour run-time. Im not sure if the overarching plot hits as it intends to because of the chaotic nature of the storytelling, and even though it is clear why Chazelle makes these decisions, they may not sit well with someone who isnt as interested in the behind-the-scenes look that we get.
The movie is attempting to balance so much, and there is a ton to admire within that balance, but it left me somewhat unfulfilled until the finale. The finale is mesmerizing, and cinema-lovers will rejoice after seeing it, so it leaves you on the highest of highs. Babylon has all of the ingredients to make a masterpiece, and the most impressive part (beyond the technical elements) may be how Chazelle himself has changed. His perspective has obviously shifted over the last several years because this is not a pleasant approach to how Hollywood works. We see the darkness and slimy nature of some of the individuals who will do whatever it takes to make their way to the top. We also see those stars and producers who whither away over time, and as the industry they know changes, they find themselves no longer having a role in the madness. It isnt all bleak, as the best scene in the film surrounds a hilarious sequence of events involving a shoot indoors. The film is also elevated by the brilliant performances, specifically with Calva and Robbie. Robbie gets a few Oscar moments here that will have viewers locked in. The final result is a messy and chaotic story that embodies what cinema is all about yet lacks the proper structure to tell a cohesive story. Nevertheless, the standout moments are worth it alone.

The aptly titled Babylon is cinema at its most exhilarating and outrageous. A filmmaker given the freedom to indulge in all of his wants and desires, fashioning a cocaine-fuelled fantasy of excess and extravagance. It was inevitable that this film would prove divisive, especially considering its runtime, but I was completely wrapped up in the unabashed exuberance of each wild sequence. 
Piecing Babylon together was clearly a mammoth undertaking for Damien Chazelle and his crew. At no point does the acclaimed director choose the simple path. Each scene is filled with technical filmmaking of the most elaborate nature, illustrating the decadent allure of early Hollywood, as well as its venomous underbelly.
Babylon isnt a sycophantic love letter to cinema in quite the same way as La La Land, though it is a tribute of a sorts. While brimming with passion for the silver screen, the talented filmmaker is also committed to outlining the industrys knack for emotional devastation. Our protagonists, each representing a different perspective on the period despite the pictures anachronistic style, are both elevated and diminished by its fickle and callous world. 
Delivered through a series of lavish set-pieces, the film mimics the manic energy of a drug-riddled party. And, like those parties as they near their natural end, the film becomes discomforting and exhausting, a fact that doesnt feel entirely unintentional. 
Mileage has varied on Babylons unrelenting style - for some it is a somewhat bludgeoning experience. I happened to find it completely intoxicating and deliriously joyful.

Id expected self-indulgent woAh HoLLyWooD iS wiLd glorification of dysfunction but its a whole lot more meditative and melancholic than that. it wouldve been easy for a movie like this to either fall into a worshipful reverence of cinema or an everything is corrupt cynicism, but I think Chazelle manages to find a fascinatingly enigmatic balance between the two, almost overwhelming and spirit-breaking in its sheer irreconcilability. thats two for two with The Fabelmans making me question if movies are such a great thing or maybe the worst thing ever. you get the sense that even Chazelle doesnt quite know how to reconcile the depravity and the glory. hes just trying to tell it like it is and make up his mind in the process.
anyway, despite the many thoughts swirling in the films periphery (and there are...a lot of thoughts) its also just really watchable from scene to scene, and utterly fascinating as a portrait of a particularly tumultuous era even as that era also represents a universally constant change within the industry. this couldve been made in the 60s, 70s, 80s, 90s, or 2020s and read as a parable for the industry during any of those eras.  so many brilliant little sequence setups and punchlines, too. there are at least a dozen moments where Chazelle drops a bomb of information or an impossible objective halfway through the scene that makes you go oh, thats too good and not want to look away, even if maybe you should. 
lots of legitimately haunting stuff, though. that shot of Nellie slipping away into the dark toward the end is sticking with me. even the final montage feels less to me like woah, arent movies great and more like an existential crisis in the same way of seeing NASA photos of the seemingly uncaring-but-beautiful expanse of the cosmos. more than any other movie about Hollywood, the whole thing reminds me a bit of Nightmare Alley, in both the monkeyorgan-grinder dichotomy and the impersonal melancholy of the slow march of time and progress.

Babylon is a love letter to the art of film and filmmaking, but its also a brutal reminder of how Hollywood will chew you up and spit you out.
In Babylon, the spiritual evil twin of La La Land.
Hollywood doesnt care about the individual. It will elevate you, consume you, and move on without a second thought. The memory of you may disappear stars fade, eras come to an end. Babylon understands the tragedy of that, but it also understands the beauty of what remains.
Your time today is through, but youll spend eternity with angels and ghosts.
That sentiment essentially captures the entire heart of the film. Nothing lasts forever, but film does. The people who made it may pass on, but their art becomes immortal.
Babylon is imperfect, sometimes wildly so, but experiencing it speaks to the raw, chaotic nature of artistic expression in film. It feels like being on drugs an elevation of emotions that keeps escalating, refusing to come down until it has completely exhausted itself. Its messy, emotional, excessive, beautiful, and occasionally ridiculous. But most importantly, this film is alive.
Babylon is a film that appreciates and celebrates every technical aspect of filmmaking and the harmonious nature of all its elements when they come together. Film is the ultimate art form because it unites every facet of artistic expression into something greater than the sum of its parts, reaching into the deepest, almost divine depths of the human soul and consciousness in a way no other medium can. 
Damien Chazelle refuses to play it safe, and thats exactly what I love about Babylon and cinema in general. Film is supposed to take risks. Its supposed to swing big. Sometimes those swings will fail, but the courage to take them in the first place is the true mark of a visionary genius like Chazelle.
Babylon may be chaotic, but it has soul, a beating heart centered on the personal risk and reward of chasing immortality through cinema. So take that gamble. Dont regret the fun. Keep on living. Embrace the pleasure and take that risk. You never know when it may be your last chance.

Ambientado na década de 1920, período de transição entre o cinema mudo e o falado, o longa acompanha um grupo diverso de personagens cujas vidas são transformadas pelo universo cinematográfico. Nellie LaRoy (Margot Robbie) é uma mulher ousada e confiante, que se considera uma estrela em ascensão à espera de sua grande descoberta. Manny (Diego Calva), um jovem mexicano, sonha em fazer parte da indústria cinematográfica, desejando trabalhar nos sets de filmagem e estar perto da ação. Já Jack Conrad (Brad Pitt) é um astro decadente, preso ao alcoolismo e incapaz de aceitar que sua era de glória pode estar chegando ao fim. Os destinos desses três personagens se entrelaçam durante uma extravagante festa organizada por um influente executivo de Hollywood. A partir daí, suas trajetórias se desenrolam em meio às mudanças turbulentas da indústria, refletindo as transformações culturais e sociais da época. Com carreiras marcadas por momentos de glória e quedas abruptas, eles enfrentam os desafios de uma indústria moldada pela ambição, vaidade e instabilidade.
O início é vibrante e divertido, deixando claro que será uma obra sobre aproveitar a vida ao máximo e explorar figuras autodestrutivas, até que algo surge para interromper a festa  ironicamente e de forma proposital, é a chegada do cinema falado que dá início a esse processo, acompanhado por um moralismo social que confronta a libertinagem. Após a aparição do título, porém, a diversão se torna mais escassa, e o desenvolvimento narrativo apresenta tropeços. A intercalação das histórias merece críticas, tanto pela edição, que não consegue criar fluidez entre os núcleos, quanto pelo foco insuficiente dado a Sidney e Lady Fay Zhu, que, ao lado de Manny, são os personagens mais interessantes na representação de figuras marginalizadas na indústria.
Ainda assim, encontro problemas narrativos mais profundos. Há várias cenas excessivamente didáticas sobre o destino cruel de artistas descartados pela indústria cinematográfica, como o monólogo arrastado de Jack Conrad, o previsível arco de LaRoy e até mesmo o simbolismo do título. A obra transborda de lições morais e tentativas de mea culpa para personagens de caráter questionável. O desfecho (aberto a interpretações) e sua montagem experimental da história do Cinema sugerem que todos os excessos foram justificados pela criação da Arte, como se o progresso do Cinema estivesse intrinsecamente ligado a uma espécie de sacrifício humano contínuo. Essa visão, embora provocativa, carrega uma inquietante justificativa de abusos e uma romantização perigosa das tragédias individuais, sem o mesmo senso de ponderação que obras como Whiplash ou La La Land conseguem transmitir em seus finais. O filme parece propor uma reflexão sobre o custo da imortalidade artística, mas sem a delicadeza necessária para escapar de um tom condescendente e fatalista.
O que realmente eleva a experiência é o estilo com que tudo é feito, os maneirismos de câmera e dos personagens, e as diversas cenas icônicas, sensuais e malucas, embora o filme como um todo acabe sendo um pouco exagerado e com várias sequências que parecem arbitrárias. A cena da cobra, por exemplo, é completamente desnecessária para mim, enquanto o evento com participação de um insano Tobey Maguire é perturbador e aterrorizante da melhor maneira possível. Em vez de cenas como pessoas vomitando umas nas outras, fezes de elefante sendo despejadas sobre os personagens ou mortes durante performances, o declínio moral da Velha Hollywood se torna mais evidente em momentos como quando Manny pede uma oportunidade a um executivo do estúdio, e a resposta que recebe é que ele está exatamente onde merece estar. Assim como Manny, um imigrante latino, todos os outros personagens centrais enfrentam esse tipo de opressão, presos às limitações que a sociedade da época lhes impõe. Ao recorrer a expedientes exagerados e simplistas, como a exploração de repulsa a fluidos corporais, o filme parece negligenciar o fato de que vomitar em uma festa é nada perto de ter que renunciar à própria identidade para se encaixar em um sistema.
O filme se encaminhava para um desfecho excelente. Após começar a assistir Cantando na Chuva, Manny se emociona. A câmera se afasta dele, mostra o cinema lotado e, em seguida, desce para a fileira inferior da plateia. Um travelling percorre a sequência de espectadores maravilhados com o musical. A câmera retorna à plateia de cima e foca em Manny, que está chorando. Este deveria ser o último plano de Babilônia. No entanto, o longa perde completamente o rumo e inicia uma série de flashes de obras cultuadas da história do cinema, em meio a um excessivo espetáculo visual. Além de ser uma manobra forçada, pois a mensagem já estava clara com Cantando na Chuva (que, por si só, é altamente representativo), o diretor parece estar forçando uma identificação do público, além de tentar inserir seu próprio filme nesse grupo.
O sorriso final de Manny, após a sequência de vinhetas, parece suspender toda a melancolia do final e colocar a arte em primeiro plano. Fico em dúvida sobre qual discurso esse encerramento endossa uma romantização que não se encaixa com o tom do filme, ou uma resignada sensação de pertencimento e realização por finalmente ter feito parte da indústria. 
Babilônia é, sem dúvida, um filme impactante. Com uma fotografia impressionante, edição precisa e direção competente na maior parte do tempo, a obra conta com Margot Robbie entregando uma performance marcante, explorando bem seu potencial. Ao lado dela, Brad Pitt e Diego Calva também se destacam, com atuações que dão uma boa dinâmica à narrativa. Assim como a Babilônia antiga e a Velha Hollywood, o filme atinge momentos grandiosos. No entanto, sua principal falha é a falta de definição de limites. O exagero excessivo se torna um fardo, e Damien Chazelle, ao tentar criar um espetáculo monumental, esquece que o poder do cinema muitas vezes reside em momentos mais sutis, misteriosos e autênticos, que falam por si mesmos.

Rewatching Babylon at the Egyptian Theatre in Hollywood felt very fitting. Theres something surreal about watching this feverish, chaotic, and romantic ode to cinema in the very city its trying to eulogize and resurrect. Its been two years since I last watched it, and I finally get it now. I understand why some people were blown away, and I also see why others were repelled. Make no mistake, though this movie is overly hated and, in my opinion, completely misunderstood.
There were moments during this rewatch that reminded me so much of Boogie Nights, like the sprawling ensemble, the rollercoaster tone shifts, and the way it captures the thrill of entering an industry built on dreams, only for those dreams to turn to dust. Both movies depict the rise and fall of people swept up in a cultural wave, caught between the euphoria of creation and the crushing weight of change.
In the Bible, Babylon was a city of grandeur and sin, pride and punishment. It was powerful and seductive, but ultimately fell because of its decadence and arrogance. Damien Chazelle mirrors this exactly in his movie. Hollywood becomes the new Babylon, which is a city of dreamers and monsters, where the divine beauty of storytelling collides with the grotesque machinery of fame. The movie shows the rise and fall of characters, but it also becomes a lament for a dying world and a celebration of its burning beauty. Just as the biblical Babylon collapsed under its own weight, the same thing happens with this version of Hollywood.
There are so many moments that I love here, but the ending is probably my favorite of all. It captures everything I love about movies. Its as if Chazelle stepped into my soul, took all the heartbreak and magic that cinema has given me, and projected it onto the screen. I honestly teared up and sat in awe. Its the kind of finale that reminds you why you fell in love with movies in the first place and why theyll never die, even if the industry burns to the ground.
I felt so many emotions the second time I watched Babylon. I experienced joy, sadness, nostalgia, discomfort, and inspiration. Its unfortunate that this movie flopped at the box office, and I hope Damien Chazelle gets another shot. It was a massive swing for the fences, but in the end, its a messy, glorious piece of work and one that deserves to be called a masterpiece.

Reflecting back on Babylon, I still am not entirely sure if it is an ode to films in general or a dissection of the chaotic ecosystem of which Hollywood is so famous. Its probably a mix of the two, but Chazelle really leans into this churning aspect from actors and elites alike. The debauchery and hedonism are a lot starting off and my interpretation of what is represented here shifted dramatically between the start and end. 
Prostitutes arent simply peeing on fat guys just because. In this world of instability, everything becomes excess. The people in the mansion gorging themselves on everything in sight have no idea what their future in the industry holds, so they just get as much as they can in their systems in the moment. Yet, everyone is on different wavelengths. 
Manny is on one end, not having the biggest personality in the room. Hes absorbing everything around him in real time. Calva gives Mannys initial belief in the power that film holds an earnest charm. Manny is willing to do most anything to simply be involved in whatever way he can, even if it means shooting a gun in the air to get extras to stop striking. One of the funnier scenes in my book. 
On the other end is Nellie LaRoy. My head canon now is that when Nellie dies, she is reborn in BarbieLand as Stereotypical Barbie. But, I digress. As with everything Robbie does, Im increasingly impressed at how fully she commits. In particular, to this characters appetite for fame and sensation. Shes already a star the world just doesnt know it yet. However, there is no fitting in for Nellie.
She doesnt care about becoming one of the pompous bluebloods that she cannot stand. Shes just trying to overwhelm all that is in the industry. Her dance sequence is electric and serves as a great start to this descending arc. Those same qualities that made her the best of the best begin to work against her. Nellie doubles down in her anarchy whereas Manny keeps going up, playing the game. And, the game can be terrible. 
One of the most questionable scenes is with that burnt cork that Manny gives to Sidney. I could see that he didnt want to, but he also is now deep in the machine. Its this adaptation that Nellie refuses. Shes incapable of adapting because adapting would mean becoming someone else entirely, which is why she runs off without Manny at the end. The settled-down life is not for her and whats more is she knows it. 
In the middle of these forces is Mr. Jack Conrad who gives us a peak into the time that one has and how fleeting it can be. One of the big points in Babylon is depicting the transition from silent films to talkies. It actually made me think about something I hadnt before. What must that have been like? If you have a not-likeable voice, are you just done? The answer, at least here, is yes. 
Jack is comfortable and Brad Pitt plays this comfortability in a way that makes his downfall hit even harder. He tries to adjust time and time again to what is new and what is now, but despite his best efforts, it doesnt work. What I love about Pitts performance though is that he never makes Jack into this pathetic caricature. He may be outdated, but hes certainly not insignificant. 
After watching this, Im not sure if La La Land is Chazelles best work anymore. Its incredible, but Babylon is just volatile in all of the right ways. The camera surges and crashes through rooms. Everything is overwhelming. I adored the shots in the theatre where he lets that stillness creep in after huge sequences of chaos. Without them, I think I would just have sensory overload the entire time. 
But, how he portrays the evolution of Hollywood, in both the highs and lows (way, way lows) is to be applauded. Chazelle made this film about how uncontrollable everything is and at the same time gives us a monologue of how cinema is something that outlives the very people who create it. He indulges in his feelings often and I question the over three-hour runtime in some sections. 
Ultimately, Babylon works. The final montage is beautiful and captivating. Its a shame that more people havent seen this.
