Não acho que funciona quando tenta compor esse retrato escandalizador dos bastidores de Hollywood. Mas, em compensação, funciona muito bem como um retrato melancólico sobre o que foi, talvez, a curva de aprendizado mais impiedosa de Hollywood o advento do som.
Tudo o que envolve esse contexto imoral e excessivo daquela elite me parece meio forçado e sem tom. É uma abordagem que possui a intenção de ser crua e grotesca, mas o Chazelle nunca consegue se segurar e acaba estilizando ou higienizando tudo. Até os momentos com vômitos ou planos que mostram pessoas depois de uma overdose são bonitos.
Existe ali uma intenção bem interessante em integrar tudo aquilo a um aspecto absurdo e grandioso, como se os bastidores fossem um reflexo sombrio e invertido daquele imaginário dos sonhos, como se aquelas pessoas que encenam os sonhos dos filmes vivessem um pesadelo de deturpação moral, porém, ironicamente, nada soa realmente pesado. 
Tudo parece uma brincadeira ou uma sketch bem montada. E o virtuosismo técnico obsessivo do Chazelle também não ajuda. Aquela primeira sequência da festa na mansão, além de não funcionar nesse sentido grotesco, é cheia de planos-sequências que soam mais vaidosos do que propriamente eficientes ou com algum objetivo dramático e expressivo mais forte.
Mas de resto, quando o filme mostra os aspectos práticos da produção dos filmes e localiza esse contexto do advento do som, praticamente tudo funcionou comigo.
Até o virtuosismo técnico, que sai daquela contemplação besta e vai pra um lado mais caótico com toques de comédia, funciona bem.  E, de modo geral, o trabalho ganha muito por seguir uma estrutura narrativa descentralizada que remete diretamente ao PTA e ao Altman.
Como ele não se centraliza em apenas um drama, e até faz dessa alternância obsessiva entre sequências o seu grande apelo convidativo e dinâmico, consegue propor algo que é mais sobre aquele entorno do que sobre aquelas pessoas. Não fica naquela punheta obsessiva, sentimental e autocentrada que rolava com os personagens dos filmes anteriores do Chazelle.
Os personagens desse filme, inclusive, são colocados mais como uma consequência daquele ambiente do que como criadores ativos de algum grande e novo significado - a trajetória do personagem do Brad Pitt, principalmente, dialoga diretamente com essa efemeridade, com esse aspecto cíclico de que, como diz a personagem da Jean Smart, ele é apenas mais um em meio a tantos outros atores que chegaram a um fim.
Além de que todo o arco da personagem da Margot Robbie também possui esse curso padrão de uma estrela em ascensão e depois em queda. Enquanto que o Diego Calva, ainda que possua um papel ativo, é tratado como um observador daqueles percursos e transformações. 
Então, de modo geral, as relações dramáticas funcionam mais como uma consequência daquele ambiente e contexto e menos como a vontade de personagens que são impostos por um roteiro sentimental. A boa sacada aqui foi tratar a nostalgia não como uma imposição emotiva, mas como parte de uma história muito prática sobre o cinema. 
A melancolia vem mais das consequências desse contexto do que de um diretor que quer parecer sensível. Claro que ele tem os seus momentinhos de piá de prédio que amou demais o cinema, mas dá pra engolir. O modo como tudo evolui não depende dessa paixão e, no geral, remete muito a uma força destrutiva do tempo. O que inclui  referências bem diretas ao Boogie Nights, principalmente em como os os personagens vão se perdendo a partir daquele sonho inicial.
Esse método de montagem alternada periga se tornar previsível em alguns momentos, já que diferente do PTA que se baseia muito mais numa certa temperatura dramática para cortar, o Chazelle baseia os seus cortes em ações práticas e aspectos concretos das ações em cena, e aí  tudo pode soar um pouco impessoal ou meramente videoclíptico vez ou outra, mas são problemas bem pontuais que ele parece ter certa noção. Quando as coisas começam a soar mecânicas, ele passa pra outra dinâmica dramática ou faz cenas que funcionam de modo isolado.
Inclusive, existem ótimas cenas longas isoladas. Todo aquele momento  da Nellie LaRoy no set gravando com o microfone pela primeira vez segue essa dinâmica de uma montagem que vai se acelerando de acordo com as ações práticas da cena ao mesmo tempo que constrói uma tensão em prol desse objetivo final da filmagem dar certo. Ele centraliza tudo em um só ambiente sem perder o aspecto dinâmico.
E também trabalha muito bem com um senso de comédia e drama nesses momentos. Até o modo como ele alterna entre planos fixos e câmera na mão, sem nunca bagunçar a decupagem, enfatiza essa alternância e mistura de tons. Algo bem presente nessa cena deles se debatendo com o microfone.
Talvez a principal e mais positiva diferença desse filme com o La La Land é que, devido a essa descentralização, os personagens nunca agem isolados e apenas baseados numa crença romantizada do que é o mundo. Eles agem, como essa cena com o microfone mostra, juntos e de modo muito mais prático. Eles trabalham para uma meta comum (para que os filmes sejam realizados) e não se alienam (pelo menos não totalmente) na própria busca.
Claro que cada um possui o seu ego, seu lado vaidoso e objetivos pessoais, mas eles sabem que pra qualquer coisa ser concretizada deve existir esse equilíbrio não somente entre as pessoas no set, mas mesmo um equilíbrio milagroso do acaso pra que tudo dê certo.
Nesse ponto o filme representa muito bem esses momentos de milagre de um set. Momentos em que tudo parece perdido e depois tudo se encaixa sabe-se lá como. É um êxtase coletivo próprio desse ato criativo em conjunto de uma gravação. Ainda que, simultaneamente, também mostra o contexto precário pra se atingir isso.
Eu acho até que a possível legitimidade artística envolvendo esse cinema mainstream é bem debatida pelo filme. Ele usa bem o personagem do Brad Pitt pra pensar nessas origens marginais do cinema, de como era visto (e naquela época ainda era) como uma arte menor que as artes tradicionais justamente por manter um diálogo mais direto com pessoas que não fazem parte de uma elite. O monólogo do Pitt sobre isso com sua terceira esposa é bem revelador.
Mesmo que sejam atos criativos pouco romantizados e postos com certa ironia (como a relação da personagem da Margot Robbie com sua diretora, interpretada pela Olivia Hamilton), existe um impulso criativo que se mistura com uma fúria por tudo dar certo.
É um filme que tenta fazer justiça aos esforços dessa geração que, em partes, foi perdida devido ao advento do som. Não porque não tinham talento, mas porque tiveram que ser a geração a se adaptar a todo uma nova possibilidade de linguagem e novas convenções. É um filme sobre esse sacrifício. 
Aquele epílogo com o Manny indo ao cinema talvez tenha como objetivo mostrar essa evolução da linguagem como uma espécie de recompensa final. Algo que a montagem que o próprio Chazelle insere depois, com cenas de filmes antigos e contemporâneos, também vai atestar e dar continuidade.
É interessante como é uma montagem que não tenta intelectualizar nada. Ela segue uma vibe ingênua de supercut de youtube que se limita a aspectos fascinantes mais superficiais na sua relação com os trechos que mostra. Filmes experimentais e industrias, independentes do seu contexto, fazem parte dessa mesma força expressiva do cinema.
Claro que não é uma montagem simples, já que  junta planos de obras diferentes de modo muito natural, mas é uma montagem quase infantil pela maneira que  evidencia um certo fascínio primordial e uma relação afetiva com o cinema. Lembra até a sensação daquelas montagens antigas da Globo de quando o canal apresentava os filmes que iria exibir na temporada e, mesmo que anunciando obras muito diferentes, todas as imagens se mesclavam num amálgama de novidade e êxtase.

Babylon was my most anticipated movie of the year, so clearly I was head-over-heels ecstatic when I got to be in the first ever Audience to see the movie at a test screening back in March. And the experience was a memorable one. 
I arrived three hours before the screening, since seating wasnt guaranteed (and I was the first one to arrive). It was smart that I arrived early though because the line quickly formed and eventually grew to over 200 people (only about 80-90 of us were let in). The three hours flew by and soon after being seated in the small theater, Damien Chazelle and his executives walked in and Chazelle sat in my row, 5 seats from me. This excited me because Damien Chazelle is one of my favorite directors and getting the opportunity to watch him experience watching his own movie he created was thrilling. 
The runtime was over three hours, but it made the experience all the more worth it. At the time there were no trailers or even on set photos of the movie, so the entire audience went in completely blind. Early on there was about a 30 minute scenemontage that I consider some of the most entertaining and impeccably well edited scenes Ive seen in years. Its a fast paced cocaine laced energy entertainment. Really set a good tone for the majority of the movie. And one of the more fun scenes was the 20 min scene with Toby Maguire who really gives 150 dedication to his role.
BABYLON was a lot to process after seeing it. I gave my initial thoughts in the focus group afterwards but I still didnt fully grasp what I thought of it til days later. As a couple days went on, the movie kept sitting the back of my mind and I realized that there was a lot that I really liked. I found myself continuously thinking about the movie and its performances and the beautiful production that was put into it. Justin Hurwitzs score was amazing, creating high energy throughout the movie. Chazelle directed the hell out of this. I still dont think its better than his other movies, but he had already set the bar really high because his other three movies are near perfect to me.
Its risky, bold, daring, sexy, and a whole lotta fun. Babylon is if Singin in the Rain did 100 lines of coke, and I loved it for that. Chazelle directed the movie with extreme doses of confidence and it pays off. There were moments I felt was a bit over the top (the whole snake scene, some of Margot Robbies acting) but the overall theme of the movie made me look past all that. Cant wait to watch it again so I can digest it further.

First off, let me tell you something. Ive lost count of how many times Dan recommended me this film. I kept putting off watching it due to its runtime, but thank god, he finally pushed me over the edge. So, let me start this review by saying thank you for your relentless effort, Dan.  I finally got to witness what I consider the real love letter to cinema.
Babylon is a cinematic experience like no other. Its a lightning bolt of a filma hectic, chaotic, yet still poignant escapade that grabs me by the wrist and firmly holds on until the final frame. Its brave, audacious, and hugely provocative, but ultimately, its the film cinema needs now more than ever.
On a technical level, theres not much even the films most passionate detractors can take away from it. Beautifully shot, supremely scored, whilst also featuring amazing costume and set design. Its hard not to become completely immersed in Babylons blazingly unique take on the 1920s-1930s film industry. On a performance level, the three-piece dramatic core of Diego Calva, Margot Robbie, and Brad Pitt outdo themselvesespecially Robbie who, in my eyes, gives the performance of her career thus far (and excuse me, where tf is Robbies Oscars for this performance?!).
The one word Id use to describe Babylon crescendo. The characters journeys and the number of spectacular sequences in the film are like a flame on a stick of dynamite burning, burning, burning, until the inevitable bang, the climax, the resolve... whether that resolve is the flame suddenly burning out or the flame torching everything around it. It wasnt a film I expected to keep me on the edge of my seat, but for 3 hours and 10 minutes, there I sat.
Babylon is, at its core, a story of ugliness and beauty coexisting in the same space. Damien Chazelle called Babylon a hate letter to Hollywood and a love letter to movies. Its a scathing critique of the culture and system of Hollywood, but one of the most poignant and honest love letters to the art form of cinema Ive ever seen.
A far cry from the magical and glamorous look at the industry seen in most films about the subject, Babylon knocks Hollywood off its gold pedestal and exposes the seedy underbelly of its sparkly covering. No scene personifies this idea better than the absolutely terrifying and riveting sequence where mob boss James McKay (played with absolutely scene-chewing perfection by the excellent Tobey Maguire) leads Calvas Manny into what he calls the asshole of L.A. a nightmare-inducing underground Hollywood party that acts as a metaphor for the darkness of the industry itself.
In this party is depravity, hedonism, exploitation, and immorality to the furthest extent. Maguires McKay simply sees it as fun and a good time. Each floor Manny descends reveals even more debauchery, until they reach the main act at the bottom a large man who is chained up and exploitednotably, he will do anything for money. Is this underground hellhole beginning to sound like the dark version of Hollywood that Babylon presents to us? A world full of exploitation, bigotry, and a chilling disregard for basic moral decency.
I read that some critics have complained that the films view of cinema is far too cynical, but I think that, in its own way, its kind of hopeful. Its not always pretty, but its honest. The film simply knocks the industry off its pedestal while simultaneously bolsters the art form of cinema upwards. Thematically, despite the coarse and unflinching narrative of the film, Babylon has the purest message about filmmaking lve ever seen on screen.

Its on you now, kid. The future is yours
The birth of the talking picture. The death of cinema. 
To quote my good friend on here, reibureibu, in his recent review of Godards The Joy of Learning, Cinema is dead. Long live cinema! 
The last theatrical experience of 2022 for me is probably the most divisive of the big films released here in late 2022 and for good damn reason. Academy Award winner Damien Chazelle throws every single thing he can, including every bodily fluid and function, at the screen for us to gawk at and laugh about and marvel over here in his first film in four years and oh boy is it a doozy of a picture and like nothing else we saw in 2022 or have seen in quite in some time. And, honestly, Im still not sure how I feel about it. 
Crafted to the hilt with excellent work across every one of its facets (that Hurwitz score in particular is fire from start to finish), Babylon is everything I would want out of gloriously over the top big swing of a picture dedicated to the enduring power of cinema... Except that its not that kind of picture. Im a sucker for big swing pictures and also there is just something about movies about movies and Chazelle knows this and uses this oh so well here (the extended sequence of the making of their first sound film is a certified banger). But,  this is no love letter to cinema. 
This may be wrapped up in its nostalgia and curiously saccharine ending, but its actually a bitter pill of nostalgia that has a nihilistic coating to it.  This is Friedkin doing The Exorcist this is Russell doing The Devils. This is someone coming off critical successes and Oscar wins and saying Fuck it!, Im gonna do this picture right here the way I want to and go down swinging with the camera still firmly in hand and what an audacious, magnificent mess it ends up being a result maximalst cinema by way of vulgar autuerism. Its everything we love about cinema and so many things we dont. Chazelle is putting himself on the line, while giving exactly not one fuck and that is admirable in and of itself. I dare say hes earned that carte blanche, but I feel like none of us were ready for it. 
As I write this, the film is dying a quick death at the box office, proving that the films thesis will continue to be an ever-present omen in this still constantly changing medium cinema as we know it is indeed dead, and its been dying since it was created. But, 100 years from now someone will turn this film on and see Margot Robbie dancing in the opening party sequence and have that same reaction that Manny and the rest of the movie theatre does to Singin in the Rain and that is The Magic of the Movies that somehow keeps this constantly dying art alive and well no matter what.

Babylon. 2022. Directed by Damien Chazelle. 

Damien Chazelles Babylon (2022) is a highly engaging and entertaining period piece that is an homage, biopic, and poison pen letter to HollywoodlandHollywood from 1920 to 1952. The dream factory is home to broken dreams even for the famous. Babylon had a budget of approximately eighty million dollars and covered the rise and fall of silver screen stars that were based on real life actors, directors,  producers (e.g. Anna May Wong, Clara Bow, Irving Thalberg, Marion Davies, William Randolph Hearst and John Gilbert). Film history, story telling, and the machine that delivers these movies to audiences is at the heart and soul of Chazelles passion project. In addition, Chazelle put the spotlight on immigrants and their treatment in early HollywoodlandHollywood and how  if they survived? The transition from silent films to talkies created jobs for some and destroyed the careers of other stars. The transition from silent to talkies is shown in astutely crafted scenes that never disappoint. The early years of Hollywoodland was built on actors from the heartland of America who were wild at heart and lacked refined etiquette. Furthermore, drug use (at parties, on sets,  from producers) and gambling were rampant and this made conditions optimal for gangsters, mobs, and the exploited lower socioeconomic class. 
A great deal of scenes involving animal welfare and their treatment (e.g. an elephant, a snake,an alligator, and rats) were crass and unnecessary as this was not cgi. The bear in the trailer for Cocaine Bear was clearly cgi and this left room for laughs. However, when Babylon began in earnest, we sighed at the elephant that was literally terrified and defecated on several actors and a camera. Again, this could have been visual effects and cgi. I just verified that visual effects and cgi was not used in an  Entertainment Weekly Round Table Interview with the lead cast members. The rattlesnake and rat that were terminated could have been real. At the very least, they were terrified. The rat eater was real. I am sure Babylon had wranglers for all of the aforementioned fauna but for a vegan couple, this was hard to view.
The story of Babylon reminded us of Van Guylders Hollywood Babylon (1971) with a much better budget and cast. Kenneth Anger wrote the book Hollywood Babylon that Van Guylder utilized for his screenplay. Furthermore, Babylon had a comedic The Wolf of Wall Street (2013) vibe that collided with the carnal nature showcased in The Day of the Locust (1975) starring Karen Black and Donald Sutherland. Without the comedic elements, Babylon would have been difficult to view for 3 hours and eight minutes. Damien Chazelle put a treatment on the aforementioned works and refined the material so each chapter of his screenplay was packed with tension, melodrama, history, and comedy. A great deal of viewers complain about the Eyes Wide Shut (1999) nudity levels. Kubricks cinematographer (Larry Smith) lingered on the orgy nude scenes whereas, Chazelles cinematographer (Linus Sandgren) made use of kinetic sweeping shots leaving one thinking did I just see two shriveled penises, an alligator, and a series of non-simulated sex acts in one tracking shot. This cinematography technique kept Chazelle from getting the NC-17 rating that Blonde (2022) received. The nudity and hedonism were a blast to watch as they were creative and integral to the story. This was pre Hays Code HollywoodlandHollywood and the after parties and parties in general were bacchanal beyond outrageous excess. The most difficult aspect of the film was animal abuse and a tunnel referred to as the asshole of L.A. where hardcore SM, violent bloody human abuse, and disgusting (literal) underground partying that involved fights to the death. In other words, it was UFC fighting with no medics before UFC was even a thing. The other component of Babylon that was challenging, were young and middle age suicides due to excess drug use, gambling, or losing a career. The aforementioned thoughts regarding deaths is the poison pen letter from Chazelles brilliant original screenplay. Babylon has an incredible ensemble cast, outstanding lead performances, and an original screenplay that deserves accolades. 
Overall, we had a blast watching the history of Hollywoodland transition from silents films to talkies. Brad Pitt (Jack Conrad) and Margot Robbie (Nellie LaRoy) gave phenomenal performances that are definitely award worthy. Jean Smart (at the top of her game) portrayed a Hedda Hopper styled journalist who helped make or break careers just as The Hollywood Reporter and Variety do in contemporary society. Diego Calva (Manny Torres), in our opinion, gave the knockout award worthy performance as an immigrant who moves from Butler to Studio executive. Jovan Adepo (Sidney Palmer) gave another standout performance that we will never forget as he was the Louis Armstrong like character brimming with talent. Moreover, Li Jun Li (Lady Fay Zhu) portrayed the Anna May Wong based character who made our jaws drop. Wow! She was sexy, talented, and needed more screen time. Chazelles original screenplay was executively produced by Tobey Maguire and Maguire also gave a stomach turning portrayal of the mob leader James McKay who killed many characters and lead them to the hedonistic multi-tiered tunnel of hell in Los Angeles. Fortunately, Manny escaped. 
For all the bad publicity, Babylon was highly enjoyable and filled with characters that cinephiles of Classic Hollywood will recognize and enjoy. Moreover, watch this film on the largest screen available and with a large audience. There are lots of detailed sets, set pieces, elaborate costumes, and a montage of film history. In fact, the film history montage after Singing in the Rain (1952) is extraordinary and chronicles silent films to talkies to high fidelity to Dolby sound in films such as Avatar (2009). Actual footage from Avatar, Jurassic Park, 2001 A Space Odyssey and more are flashed one after the other as the film winds to a color coded screen test countdown. Then the credits roll. We clapped along with the other five to eight audience members. At any rate, your money will not be wasted this is an exhilarating roller coaster of ride movie that will give one an enormous endorphin rush. Cheers! Happy Holidays. Happy New Years. We love our LB friends and family.  This is a five star film worthy of multiple viewings. Enjoy Chazelles masterpiece.

Babylon follows silent film star Jack Conroy (Brad Pitt), young go getter with aspirations Manny Torres (Diego Calva) and aspiring actress Nellie LaRoy (Margot Robbie). Life is good and getting better for all three as they find more and more success in the silent film era. The wild parties seem like theyll never end. Fame, renown and power seems anything but fleeting. However, things are about to take a turn with the advent of talkies, which will change the industry, and their fortunes, forever. 
Babylon is one hell of a film! It raises some interesting questions about art and cinema and asks what happens when chaotic creative energy gets constrained. The shift from the unrestrained, Dionysian revelry of the silent era to the endless rules and codes of studio talkies is a great way to frame things. The mad improvisations of directors and actors go up like a puff of smoke. There are a million new ways to blow a take with sound and less room for experimentation. Chazelle does a phenomenal job using the struggle of the characters to adapt to the new era and their varying degrees of success to illustrate his point. 
The first act is pure relentless turbo charged frenetic energy. Chazelle never lets his foot off the gas pedal for even a moment, smashing the more polished veneer of some of his more proper work like La La Land and First Man to bits. The movie has more in common with the energy of Whiplash and comes out of the gate hard and is a complete blast. Even when that energy gets tempered by the second act, its always there, pent up and waiting to explode. The moments where it boils over and manages to escape are as glorious as they are sad. Completely satisfying but a primal scream lost in the wind to a new age they no longer belong to. And that third act...wow. Tobey Maguires section has a chunk that was freakier than most horror movies Ive seen. 
Jack and Nellie in particular have problems making the shift to sound pictures. If it sounds familiar that an actress is mocked for her voice and struggling to reinvent herself dont worry. Chazelle shows his work clearly and pays homage explicitly to  Singin in the Rain in a wonderful way. In fact, he pays homage to cinema in general in a moving way that allows him to embrace it fully, not glossing over the place debaucherous excesses that would make Caligula proud have in film history. Theres such force to the films argument about a form of immortality acquired by being captured in frames (no small irony when applied to Pitt who played Achilles). Its as though Chazelle rediscovered a way to speak the language of film that allows for the ever rarer modern reconciliation of silent film magic and the power of spoken dialogue that few directors manage to pull off. Justin Hurwitz score here is, much like with First Man, fantastic and a major selling point as well.

Película hermana de La La Land. En una dos jóvenes soñadores queriendo triunfar en L.A, que hacen lo posible por cumplir sus sueños en una ciudad idealizada, pero sin querer traicionarse a sí mismos y a sus ideales, dos jóvenes inocentes, en última instancia, que creen que el amor y la pasión lo pueden todo.
En Babylon tenemos a dos jóvenes soñadores que no durarán en hacer todo lo posible por formar parte de un Hollywood totalmente corrupto por la droga, el alcohol y los placeres mundanos. Uno puede estar de acuerdo o no con esta visión, pero Chazelle no duda ni un instante de lo que quiere mostrar en pantalla y lo hace a la perfección.
En La La Land, Mia decide abandonar su sueño y L.A al ser rechazada de incontables castings, hasta que Seb va a buscarla por una llamada telefónica milagrosa de una productora que vio su pequeña obra independiente (su último manotazo de ahogado) y decide darle un casting super respetuoso y ameno donde finalmente se le da la oportunidad de ingresar en ese Hollywood idealizado.
En Babylon tiene 2 respuestas con 2 personajes en el paso del cine mudo al sonoro
1) Jack Conrad es incapaz de adaptarse al sonoro, su voz y entonación es la burla de todos los espectadores y él es incapaz de cambiar dar un paso atrás e ir al teatro para aprender a actuar y entonar, no quiere aceptar ni sacrificar nada. Tras la muerte de su mejor amigo y el único que creyó en él (si se quiere puede equipararse a la muerte en la relación de Mia y Seb) recibe una última llamada, esta vez no será como la de Mia, ya que solo se lo solicita como reemplazo, un ultimo baile antes de su retiro para salvar financieramente una mala película de un famoso productor. Ni siquiera en el final de su carrera le permiten conservar su dignidad. 
2) Nellie LaRoy es vista como una mujer vulgar tras su paso por el mudo y no consigue papeles serios, además sus problemas con las drogas y las apuestas la llevan a ser acechada por mafiosos del bajo mundo de L.A, por ser incapaz de rehabilitarse, pese a que su mejor amigo le de una nueva oportunidad tras otra y ella seguir desperdiciando todas, incapaz de abandonar su ego. Una joven que quería atropellar a Hollywood y vengarse termina consumida por eso que creyó que podía domar pero como le dice una periodista a Jack, todo esto es más importante que ustedes, que sus nombres, toda esta maquinaria seguirá funcionando aún cuando estén muertos. Finalmente, en el intento con Manny por intentar escapar de esta demoníaca ciudad (idealizada en La La Land), Nellie baja del auto en que iban y completamente drogada desaparece entre la oscuridad. Lejos de preocuparse por buscarla, Mannie no duda en salvarse sólo pese a haber dicho que la amaba minutos atrás. 
Ambos personajes mueren, uno en cámara y otro en fuera de campo. 
Mannie es el personaje fundamental de esto, un joven que es capaz de traicionar sus principios y adaptarse a lo que venga, con tal de lograr sus objetivos, lo que Seb no logro con su banda de Jazz electrónica (irónicamente está misma decisión de Seb es lo que mantiene la dignidad y la vida de Sydney Palmer en Babylon). Mannie no duda en hacer lo necesario, de fingir ser alguien más, de cambiar su nombre y nacionalidad con tal de seguir perteneciendo a esa maquinaria, a eso más grande que él.
Esta es la primera película de Chazelle que no termina con su clásica devolución de miradas, también es la película donde Chazelle entiende, desde su punto de vista, que para cumplir tus sueños no basta con abandonar al amor de tu vida, hay que abandonarlo todo (aún más que en Whiplash), aunque eso incluya tu dignidad, aunque eso implique la soledad porque la trascendia que consigue Mannie en esa sonrisa final al entender que lo logró que todo sacrificio valió la pena es el dictamen final de Chazelle como el mayor egoísta de Hollywood. Saber que lo lograste aunque no haya nadie que te recuerde puntualmente, aunque tu nombre no esté en ninguna marquesina, porque tu historia, o al menos el significado de ella permanecerá por los siglos de los siglos. 
La muerte de un Chazelle promesa y el nacimiento de un Chazelle realidad, a costa de las críticas por sus excesos, a costa de la crítica por su visión de la vida y de los sueños pero así como Mannie, Chazelle lo logra, es parte de Hollywood, ¿por cuánto tiempo? Para siempre.

Absolutely one of the best classics. Its strange to describe a film taking place almost entirely in one room as thrilling, but 12 Angry Men was. As was it gripping and terrifically acted. Im rarely so engrossed in classic, all-dialogue, black and white films, but 12 Angry Men is an exception, and an exceptional one.
Its always difficult to keep personal prejudice out of a thing like this. And wherever you run into it, prejudice always obscures the truth.

One room. Twelve men. Debating for ninety minutes. Thats it. Thats all there is to this story. And yet, despite such minimal setup, what 12 Angry Men accomplishes is something that many films despite their lavish productions  sumptuous set pieces never manage to. It expertly demonstrates what all can happen when a flawless script, an intelligent director and a committed ensemble come under one roof and function in harmony, for this courtroom drama is one of the greatest films ever made.
The story unfolds inside a jury room where a group of twelve folks from different backgrounds gather to decide the fate of an 18-year old boy whos accused of stabbing his father to death. With the preliminary vote indicating that most have already made up their minds and consider the defendant guilty, one juror sets into motion more discussions regarding the case by voting not guilty. The rest of the plot covers their attempts to reach a unanimous verdict.
Directed by Sidney Lumet in whats his directorial debut, the film setups its premise swiftly and once the discussion starts, it makes for a riveting, absorbing  thought-provoking drama that maintains a firm grip on the viewers attention and doesnt let it waver until the very end. Written by Reginald Rose who also scripted the teleplay this film is based on, the screenplay features a lean story that offers all characters their fair share of screen time while simultaneously moving the plot forward.
Production design team does well with the limited space, for much of the film unfolds in a single location. Cinematography is expertly employed as the camera slowly n steadily brings each character closer as plot unfolds and photographs the events  emotions in crisp detail. The black n white imagery also adds a timeless touch to the story. Editing keeps things taut and methodically paces the tightly-knitted narrative from start to finish. Music is intermittently used and has a muted presence in the final print.
Coming to the performances, the film features a talented powerhouse in Henry Fonda, Lee J. Cobb, Ed Begley, E.G. Marshall, Jack Warden  more, and all of them play their roles with utmost sincerity. All the twelve jury members are relevant here, each is given a distinct personality, and the actors breathe life into these scripted people with effortless naturalness. Fonda  Cobb are easy standouts but that doesnt mean the rest dont contribute with strong enough inputs, for every performance is deftly measured here.
On an overall scale, 12 Angry Men begins Lumets now-celebrated filmmaking career on an astonishingly high note and for me is the single greatest directorial debut in cinema history. Original, accomplished in every aspect and packed with dramatic twists n turns, this right here is the best courtroom drama of all time, one of the finest films ever made, and one of the most engrossing, entertaining  emotionally rewarding experiences you could ask for. Thanks to its universal appeal  timeless story, it has stood the test of time for nearly six decades and is destined to do so for a foreseeable future. In short, masterpieces dont get any more simpler than Lumets magnum opus. One hundred percent recommended.

I recommend checking this out if you havent seen it, most of all if you enjoy character-driven stories that make you think. 12 Angry Men, directed by Sidney Lumet, may be the most radical courtroom drama in cinema history. A behind-closed-doors look at the American legal system that is as riveting as it is spare, this iconic adaptation of Reginald Roses teleplay stars Henry Fonda as the dissenting member on a jury of white men ready to pass judgment on a Puerto Rican teenager charged with murdering his father. The result is a saga of epic proportions that plays out over a tense afternoon in one sweltering room. Lumets electrifying snapshot of 1950s America on the verge of change is one of the great feature-film debuts.

There is a certain predictable inevitability when watching a classic when youre a bit older than the first time you watched it. You up the rating to reflect its classic status. Im glad to say that this is also the case for 12 Angry Men.
The always underwatched Sidney Lumets first feature film proves to be the first promise he made for all the marvellous films he has made after it. 12 Angry Men is a dialogue driven cross section of male America in the fifties and it is unflinching in how it dares portray the pettiness and weaker sides of us humans. Weaknesses that are still present some 50 years after this was made.
The premise is brilliant. 12 jurors, one murder case and one vote of not guilty. It is astounding how Lumet manages to pace his film and keeps his audience completely enthralled for its entire running time. The way he switches from heated debate to mesmerising monologues, swaying from wide shots to perfectly placed close-ups is a thing of beauty to behold. This film has a certain cadence to it that makes it simply impossible to look away.
The performances are, without exception, stunning. These twelve men depict their archetypical characters with refreshing realism, never overreaching and always convincing. Fonda is perhaps the star in this film as he has the most important role and I have to say the way he verbally plants seeds of doubt, questions everything and reiterates his theories is very impressive, but most (especially Cobb) match him every step of the way.
With all these intrinsic qualities of such a high level, what puts the icing on the cake is the fact that this film has something to say. It gives an intriguing insight in the American Justice systems and poses some strong moral questions. How do you decide on a mans life? What do you base your decisions on? But, most importantly, what if youre wrong? And thats what struck me most about the film. This is essentially about manipulation. We are inclined to root for Fondas character as he is the one pleading Not Guilty. He is intent to make his case and wants to debate everything. What he, in fact, does is plant seeds of doubt in the other jurors. Slowly but surely, they start to see his point and join him, mainly because he is civilized and eloquent. There is a turning point when they are split down the middle. What Lumet does then is to show close ups of Fondas face whenever another juror changes his vote. There is triumph in his eyes. He becomes almost as fanatic as Cobbs character, who is clearly set away as the crude bad guy, a polar opposite of Fonda. What this film left me was this question What if Fonda was wrong? The film cleverly does not provide an answer. It does show us that within the proceedings and decision making process, people will often act out of their own best interests and will always look for leadership and people telling them what to do.
This without a question of a doubt one of the best films ever made. On all levels.

12 Angry Men is not so much about seeking justice as it is about avoiding injustice. It is a film which questions who truly has the right to send someone to their death. It is a movie of liberal values, of finding morality in democratic and civil processes. It is also about the value of life and the responsibility we each bear to not condemn others hastily. Obviously the story is so contrived and the legal framework faulty, but as an exercise in pursuing supposedly noble values it is beautiful and humbling.
By focusing on anonymous characters who are reduced to just their juror numbers, 12 Angry Men tries to create a sense that these men could be any of us. Anyone could be the hero who stands against the mob and holds out against hysteria. McCarthyism was a powerful force in 1950s America and the upcoming 1960s would become a watershed in the fight for civil liberties. 12 Angry Men is sat at a place in history where American notions of freedom and justice were being challenged. It is incredibly forward-looking, as the jurors struggle with biases and intolerance. One of the films finest scenes has a bigoted character slowly silenced as all the others turn their back on him and ostracise his views.
The premise of 12 Angry Men is brilliantly concise, following a seemingly simple jury deliberation that takes all kinds of twists and turns. It is one of the most compelling and exciting movies ever made, with a precise script that never bores as each discussion becomes more intense. It has one of the most inspiring, against-the-odds stories in cinema, with a single juror fighting against 11 men with strong personalities about an open and shut case. Yet the script and performances so naturally moves each character gradually towards acquittal. They dont all reach that decision for good reason, some are merely lazy or uncertain or forced to swallow their pride, but it all emphasises how complex it is to decide the fate of someone else, to be given such power of life and death.
From the credits onwards 12 Angry Men stays in one room until the final scene, yet Sidney Lumets direction doesnt falter. The camera slowly descends over the movie, placing greater emphasis on the importance of the jurors decisions as the film begins to look up at them with reverence. The camera moves around the room so openly initially and yet by the end the film is intimate and close-up with the characters, intercutting between them. Like the script, everything is so detailed and precise. The film builds up an unseen crime from words rather than actions. It makes discussion so incredibly cinematic and compelling. As the jurors sit there, sweating on a hot day, the tension grows and all the explosions of 1950s masculinity reveals so much about both society and the characters.
12 Angry Men remains a masterpiece. It is still my favourite American film from the 1950s. While it may seem simple, it is absolutely stunning in technical execution, storytelling, and ethical confrontation. It represents a form of socially conscious New York cinema detached from Hollywood glamour. It deals with ordinary people faced with a duty that requires them to fight against social judgments and intergenerational conflict. It presents with care the ideas of being a good citizen and seeking fairness. As far as modern day morality tales go, 12 Angry Men is still unbeaten and one of the greatest works in all cinema.

The film follows twelve jurors who enter a single room to make a decision about a young man accused of murder. The decision is supposed to be clear based on the evidence they have heard, but from the very beginning, the film puts us in front of a much more complicated question what does it really mean to be certain about something? And is our belief in the truth actually based on evidence, or sometimes on our desire for things to be a certain way?
The film is not simply a story about a murder or about figuring out whether the accused is guilty or innocent. It is about the way people judge others. Each of these men enters the room carrying his own thoughts, experiences, anger, biases, and beliefs. Some of them are eager to reach a decision and leave without truly thinking about the weight of what they are deciding. And this is where the real issue of the film begins to emerge how much can our judgments be influenced by personal things within us without us even realizing it?
The film explores bias in a very intelligent way. Not just obvious and direct prejudice, but the kind of bias that hides inside the things we consider logical. Sometimes we do not tell ourselves, I hate this person. Instead, we look for reasons that make our position seem rational. We choose the evidence that fits what we already believe and interpret things in a way that confirms our assumptions. That is exactly what makes the film feel timeless, because this is not a problem limited to a certain era or society, but a part of human nature that continues to appear in different forms.
The film does not rely on major events to create tension. The tension comes entirely from the dialogue, from the differences in perspective, and from the small details that slowly make the characters question what they once felt certain about. As the discussion continues, the room itself begins to feel like a space where their personalities are being tested, not just a place where they are supposed to make a decision about the case. Every word reveals something about the person saying it, and every reaction shows that, for some of them, the case is no longer simply a case in front of them, but something connected to their own experiences and their view of the world.
In the end, to me, this film is less about reaching a verdict and more about the responsibility that comes with judgment itself. It is about the difference between being convinced of something and actually having a reason to be convinced, and about how fragile the truth can become when it passes through human emotions, personal experiences, and biases.

12 Angry Mens biggest advantage is its agelessness. It could have been filmed last year and it still wouldnt be any more modern than it already is. It never once seems constrained by the time period it was filmed in. Its issues are as pertinent today as they have always been. And its lack of theatricality makes it completely timeless.
The film has a simple premise a jury of twelve gets together to decide whether or not to send an accused youth to the electric chair. It seems like an open and shut case - all the evidence is against the boy, and nobody feels otherwise. Except for the one man who votes not guilty. Its never quite clear why he does so does he really believe in giving the boy full justice, or is it a personal matter, if the increasingly triumphant look in his eyes is anything to go by?
Thats the other ingenuity of 12 Angry Men it never passes judgment on anybody. Even by the end, we arent sure if the accused is innocent or guilty. In fact, some of the evidence against him lines up pretty well, and some of the arguments that the first dissenting juror brings forward are quite weak.
The accuseds ethnicity is cleverly never named. The kid could be Hispanic or Italian or anything in between. The only thing we know is this he isnt white, but his fate will be decided by white men regardless of the prejudices they may have against him.
The characterization is absolutely brilliant. Right from the beginning each of the jurors has something to set him apart from the other jurors, and as the film progresses we feel as though were in that room getting to know them as well. Each juror brings some facet of his personal life to the table, and it affects their judgement in complex ways.
12 Angry Men has a brilliant ensemble cast. Each actor has his moment to shine, but its their group dynamics that are even more interesting. They play off each other in such a genuine and spontaneous manner that I kept forgetting that I was watching a group of actors rather than an actual jury.
Henry Fonda pulls off a tough role with ease, but its Lee J Cobb whos absolutely marvelous here. He starts out as an impartial, rational businessman, but by the end, when he breaks down completely, its an intensely pitiful moment. Several of the other jurors are excellent as well, inhabiting their characters so well that it feels as though theyve been these people all their lives.
The cinematography is pristine in its minimalism. The atmosphere is terrific you can almost smell the sweat. The film feels more and more claustrophobic as it progresses, and hearing the director talk about the way he accomplished it is nothing short of marvelous. If this was Sidney Lumets debut, I cant wait to see the rest of his filmography.
12 Angry Men defies categorization. Is it a talky thriller? Or perhaps a court procedural mystery without an outcome? Whatever it is, 12 Angry Men is one of the best films Ive ever seen. Its going to be just as relevant and ageless in fifty years as it is today. And if that isnt an indicator of a true classic, I dont know what is.

12 Angry Men is the cinematic version of Reginald Roses television drama, centered on a jury debating a case of patricide on a hot New York summer day. One of the members tries to persuade the other eleven jurors to suspend the guilty verdict. During the discussion - which takes place in the courtroom - prejudices and respectability emerge on the one hand and the exercise of reason on the other, the American judicial system is analyzed and the rights of the individual opposed to the majority are affirmed. The film is an unparalleled example of the results that can be obtained with an intelligent distribution of roles a remarkable cast - on which Henry Fonda and Lee J. Cobb excel - helps to create a compelling portrait of the middle-class mentality of America of 1950s. Each character has their own counterpart, so a clash of personalities and ideologies is inevitable when it comes to deciding the fate of a Hispanic boy who may or may not have killed his father. Around the theme of the ethical implications connected to the exercise of justice, Sidney Lumet realizes an exemplary work in terms of compactness and rigor, with a strong social commitment, but without moralistic intentions. The writing and the staging are highly calibrated and do not hide the theatrical structure, but rather exploit its claustrophobic and suffocating potential.

How do you ever begin to top a directorial debut such as this? Well Sidney Lumet certainly gave it is best shot over the years that followed creating an enviable filmography packed with cinematic gems. That he can turn a simplistic set-up of twelve men stuck together in a steaming hot room, into such a in-depth social, intellectual and thrilling 90 minutes speaks volumes for the man. 
What does remain a mystery is how the creator of the screenplay Reginald Rose never even came close to this sort of standard again. His next project was 1957s Dino and then it was mostly back to the food and drink of TV scripts for the rest of his career. Whilst Lumet deserves the credit he receives for the film, it is the script that provides the ammunition for such compelling performances by the cast.
A group of men can be reinterpreted into a bunch of silly boys at the best of times, falling into a pecking order through will, personality and juvenile bullying. The peer pressure in this condensed courthouse room traps together the egos and moral baggage from their personal lives, already convinced of the verdict.
We never get to find out what really happened in that apartment, whether the boy actually killed his father or if it was simply a case of mistaken identity. That isnt the central concern of the film. 12 Angry Men is about the legal system, how nothing other than absolute certainty can send a man to his death. Right and wrong. Beyond reasonable doubt.
To not pass judgement on someone can be hard thing to do, first impressions associate themselves with our personal experiences, information we have acquired over time. We summarise what we think we know about someone in a matter of minutes, sometimes even seconds. The film questions our social responsibilities, the fairness we sometimes refuse to extend to others even in life and death situations such as this. 
With such a small space to work with the use of the camera in the room is nothing short of amazing. It avoids the most obvious choices such as head-on monologues as each man says their piece, making us feel like an observer to the ongoing discussion in the room. Somehow the room never feels too overbearing due to the use of angles that let the men breathe where they can in the thick air.
There are times when a play is transferred to the screen and never quite manages to escape the idea it should remain on stage. 12 Angry Men never once encounters that problem, seeming for all the world as if it was meant for the film hall of fame status it has since achieved.

Was always more about prejudice, subjective truth and the human capacity for rationalization and denial than it was our legal system or America, which is why, oh brother, does it feel timely as hell 60 years later. That timeliness also accounts for how rushed and, I suppose, convenientfalsely optimistic, the ending felt to me this time. 
We know all of these men. We really know some of these men, and Lumet and co. is too quick to have them not only acknowledge the error of their original perspectives but to reverse them. 12 ANGRY MEN (2017) ends with a hung jury and at least four bloody men being hauled away by the cops.

A film that is literally just dudes shouting at each other in a room for 90 minutes, yet it holds so many insanely powerful moments, and is one of the most captivating, intense, and engaging narratives ive ever seen. The big reveals are undoubtedly great, but im just a sucker for the smaller ones, like how the sweat-less man started sweating, or how we slowly see the mind state of each character shift in subtle ways.
12 Angry Men is the pinnacle of character study, and showcases 12 unique mindsets of men we dont even know the names of, yet we learn almost everything about them. 12 Angry Men. 1957. Directed by Sidney Lumet.
Sidney Lumets (Murder on the Orient Express, 1974 Network, 1976 Critical Care, 1997) 12 Angry Men (1957) is like a male version of Women Talking (2022). Instead of the setting being in a barn in Canada, it is a jury room in a court room. We are given a behind the scenes view of a jury of 12 peers. Moreover, their decision can destroy or liberate a sentient beings life. Lumets film is shot mostly in one room where the jury members are sequestered. The films succeeds because of the tension, democratic process, anger, speculations, and pseudo-scientific forensics that push Juror 8 (Henry Fonda) to challenge the other eleven jurors. Justice is supposed to be blind but often our subjective feelings can occlude our objective, rationale mind. Lumet focuses on this aspect but also has a laser focus on the power of discussion. 
The A-list ensemble cast of Henry Fonda, Lee J. Cobb, John Fiedler, Jack Warden, Jack Klugman, Ed Biegler, and Robert Webber to name a few was made for this film. On IMDBs list of Top 250 Narrative films this lands at number 5. However, on LB it lands at number 7. This is not a statistically significant difference. This film deserves to be in the top ten as it deals with the wheels of justice and everyone should watch this film at least once. Free will and the ability to control our own lives rests not in the scales but within a labyrinthine justice system of which 12 Angry Men depicts very well.

12 angry men (1957) throws us right into the jury deliberations after the trial has ended. we see 12 white men in a jury room, a reflection of the time period in which the film was made, and watch them decide the fate of a young defendant. its an anti-mccarthyism film, coming out of an era defined by blacklisting, paranoia, selling people out, and people refusing to take a stand if it meant going against the mob.
the film also does such a great job of setting up its environment and ambience from the beginning. they say its the hottest day of the year, the room is stifling, the fans wont turn on, and the men are opening windows just to get some air. the heat, tension, and claustrophobia gradually ratchet up throughout the film, and you can practically feel how the atmosphere adds to everyones anger and emotional outbursts. it sets up the tension so well that you just know its going to be fucking amazing.
were introduced to different kinds of jurors  some couldnt care less, some are easily persuaded, some just want to get it over with, and some care deeply about the case and the responsibility that comes with deciding another persons fate. and thats what makes this so compelling! everyone enters that room with their own personal backgrounds, experiences, biases, and prejudices, whether theyre aware of them or not.
that powerful scene where the other jurors turn their backs on the one who keeps ranting and spewing his prejudices was absolute cinema. his racism is so blatantly on display, and it becomes impossible to separate his personal biases from the way he views the defendant. then theres juror 3, whose own prejudice comes from a different place his pride, his anger, and his unresolved relationship with his estranged son. he projects all that baggage onto the defendant, and it says so much about how our personal experiences can cloud our judgment. there are so many personal and systemic biases and inequalities already at play before jury deliberations even begin. theres no such thing as perfectly objective justice when the people responsible for it bring all of themselves into the room. prejudice always obscures the truth.
love that little detail with juror 4, the redditor-coded juror who insists he doesnt sweat. when hes asked about his whereabouts and the movies he recently went to, one bead of sweat starts rolling down the side of his face hahahaha
and to think that this film was made almost three decades before dna profiling was first used in a criminal investigation. it really reminds us how much can be at stake when a jury is asked to decide someones fate based on evidence that can be questioned, witnesses who can be mistaken, and assumptions that can go unchallenged. overall, this was so well-written and well-shot that it made me a bit emotional  the acting performances, mise-en-scène, and out-of-order continuity just make me fall in love with the art of filmmaking. the staging is incredible and reminds me so much of akira kurosawas works. the way the camera gradually makes the jury room feel smaller as the tension builds is especially brilliant. and that ending scene in the jury room is a class act 
a classic, a masterpiece. its powerful to see filmmakers inject a political sense into their work, reflecting the mccarthy era and the people who werent comfortable with what was happening but werent necessarily brave enough to go against it. the films message about independent thought and questioning authority still feels relevant today

12 Angry Men is about a jury trying to decipher the facts they just heard and their personal prejudices that may sway their decision. The backstories of these characters are covered during small talk breaks and by the end we know the archetype for each juror.
The script is fantastic, using juror arguments as exposition to inform the facts of the case and which facts weigh heavily on each juror. The film starts with a vote of 11-1 guilty and the viewers perception is supposed to mimic the current vote of the jury.
Each fact of guilt is slowly torn down by small details that could go unnoticed originally, but when further analyzed, introduce doubt. When doubts pile on top of each other, it threatens the entire guilty argument.
Fonda is meant to be the arbiter for a fair penal system. He doesnt let his prejudices overtake him and instead asks the jury to place the burden of proof on the prosecution. Begley offers the opposite, as his personal history with his son colors his judgement of the similar aged boy on trial.
The cinematography and blocking was incredible, but especially for 1957. The acting was also spectacular, as these men using subtle movements to display large feelings. The jurors walking away from the table when Juror 10 conveyed his racism was powerful.
This film would be a star film in any era, but when stacking up against its counterparts, its incomparable. The Wilt Chamberlain of this era.

A dinâmica da ação é bastante simples o grupo permanecerá insistindo na interrogação das convicções, das impressões, dos prejuízos (isto quer dizer do particular, do individual) até que cada jurado baixe a sua guarda (através de outras convicções, outras impressões, e em alguns casos até mesmo de outros prejuízos). Esse é o interesse e também o limite do filme, um interesse e um limite que são brilhantemente explorados por Lumet (e por Boris Kaufman, Carl Lerner, Robert Markel etc.).
O que eu não lembrava é que a dinâmica de interação das personagens não é tão simples, ao contrário do que ocorre na refilmagem pavorosa do Friedkin o filme não é realmente sobre cada personagem baixando a sua guarda, mas sobre cada personagem que já baixou a sua esperando que a próxima baixe a dela. Não é no início que existe um grupo, um grupo que seria desfeito ao longo do filme para dar lugar a cada indivíduo o grupo só existe realmente no final, e é por isso que ao final, na rua, sob o arejamento que vem depois da tempestade, o grupo poderá se dispersar em indivíduos.
Trata-se, portanto, de um processo, e por isso a escolha de encerrar essas personagens em uma sala por praticamente todo o filme é congruente com o projeto. Um processo que é detonado no momento em que a personagem de Fonda, ainda nos primeiros minutos do filme, faz o gesto com a mão sobre o rosto no exato instante em que o juiz fala its now your duty to sit down and try and separate the facts from the fancy. É por isso que é aberrante comparar este filme ao do Friedkin para dizer que o de 1957 peca pela falta de definição das personagens é exatamente isso, essa definição (isso e um trabalho de encenação que consegue ser ao mesmo tempo hiperbólico e flácido), que faz o filme do Friedkin ser completamente estático, do início ao fim, formalmente e filosoficamente, enquanto o do Lumet é do início ao fim dinâmico, evolutivo, pulsante e crispado. Impressão, ao fim do filme do Friedkin, reforçada pela péssima escolha de fazer com que a cena final se passe em um corredor de um palácio da justiça, de que as coisas permaneceram rigorosamente as mesmas ao longo do filme e apenas saíram reforçadas, ao passo que no do Lumet há como que um alento ao término de um longo sufoco, que se dá sob a forma de uma ampliação no cosmos, isto quer dizer na sociedade (e é justo nesse momento que o filme se assemelha a Losey), da dinâmica que foi se desencadeando naquela sala fechada, quase irrespirável.
O que quero dizer é que neste filme a questão não é a personagem ser de classe média ou pobre, racista ou negligente, idosa ou sisuda, estrangeira ou simplória, hipócrita ou cínica, ainda que tudo isso importe a questão é o momento não da revelação (de si), mas da superação (de si), esse momento em que a personagem de E. G. Marshall, quase sem expressão, diz I did see it, strange but I didnt think about it before, o fato de que diz isso sem a carga de uma expressão, desarmado, esgotado, ou quando Lee J. Cobb por uma vez sepulta o histrionismo a que deu curso ininterruptamente e diz, escondendo o rosto por trás do antebraço, com a voz baixa e soluçante, not guilty. A passagem para uma outra coisa, e não o reforço desta. Esse processo pode ser questionado (a assertividade da câmera de Lumet, que pena para acompanhar no ritmo e no rigor dos seus percursos pelo espaço a trepidação das vacilações das personagens, aquilo que vemos no  suor, nas expressões e nas reações fragmentadas de cada ator), já seus resultados muito menos.
O que quero dizer, também, é que pensando no que parece ter sido o ensejo de um cinema que nasce de uma ambição crítica em relação aos anos Eisenhower, o qual durou mais ou menos de 1957 (12 Angry Men, Edge of the City) a 1964 (Fail Safe, Seven Days in May), e que constituiu talvez o único projeto consequente de um cinema de espetáculo de viés liberal-democrata no interior do cinema americano, o que há de mais interessante em 12 Angry Men ainda é mais o que o liga a filmes de clausura como Crime of Passion e The Killer Is Loose (contemporâneos do filme do Lumet mas realizados por diretores de uma outra geração) do que o que o ligará mais tarde a filmes como Murder on the Orient Express ou a refilmagem do Friedkin. Talvez porque o filme de estreia do Lumet também faça parte de um grupo atrelado a um determinado corpo, a um determinado pacto social do qual o cinema americanohollywoodiano foi por algum tempo o reflexo.

12 Angry Men is a seemingly impossible example of a film where everything comes together perfectly. The film is an intense sweaty potboiler, as a jury of twelve strangers deliberate over a seemingly open and shut murder case. Its almost all set in a single room - fantastically captured by director Sidney Lumet. The drama is well paced and constantly feels fresh and captivating. The writing and performances are superb. We get to know each juror quickly their individual personalities and experiences colouring their interpretation of the case. This is a very serious business, gentlemen
The film is considered a classic because of the films great direction of keeping such a small space visually fresh and because well its a darn good story, i think a lot of people think the film is about an innocent man being freed by a jury that was initially hobbled by prejudice and vindictiveness. ie. juror 10 is a bigot, juror 3 was trying to convict because of personal demons around his son. that is the first impression the film gives. but the film is a lot more nuanced than that. instead, the film is about a man-who probably did commit the crime-being freed because the state failed to met its evidential burden. the first take on the film is a moral polemic, the second take is compelling legal drama, its the hottest day of the year, and these twelve men must decide the fate of an accused killer. but twelve men means twelve personalities, twelve temperaments, twelve political views, twelve religious opinions and twelve preconceived notions. As the temperature swells, so does the temperament.
What strikes me most about this film is how progressive it is for its day. Indeed the issues this film makes about american society of the 1950s, still rings true for western society today. this film concerns twelve jurors debating the sentence of an 18 year old puerto rican boy who on the face of it, has no real alibi. however one man, played brilliantly by henry fonda, is ill-at ease putting a young boy to death without even debating his case, much to the despair of the other jurors. what follows is a brilliant piece of film making, slowly revealing many of the jurors complex characters to the audience as they react to fondas concerns with their own mix of metal scars, prejudices and insecurities. what especially struck me about this film is how ordinary most of the characters are, none of the jurors are shown to be especially bad men, indeed most are portrayed as honest everyman type people. the use of ordinary characters is the films master-stroke because as one by one they begin to question their initial instincts, the flaws of society that have let this puerto rican boy down are presented to the audience. tragically it appears that many of the issues that were beginning to be discussed in the 1950s have only got worse. for me there is one immortal comment in this film one of the jurors, a man in his 50s says that the youths of today have no respect and have changed so much for the worse since his day. How ironic is it that some grumpy old men of today who may not even have been born when this film was made, still say exactly the same thing? everyone can identify with at least ONE of those characters. whether or not he may WANT to is a different matter. The thinker, the sensitive man, the arrogant bully, the opportunist, the mentally challenged loudmouth, the slimeball, the emotionally withdrawn, the sheep etc - theyre all here! welcome to the society folks! 
While juries have changed in 60 years (allowing women to serve being the most obvious change), what hasnt changed in the conflict of trying to understand the truth and to agree with 11 other people about it. fonda goes against what would be allowed today by acting on his own and visiting the neighborhood of the crime, but his passion in figuring out the truth is very admirable. he is quiet in his determination, making this typical fonda but one that fills his soul with humility and integrity.
The writing is snappy too, you can tell it worked and worked and worried, going through several generations, it is easy to be mesmerized by this writing and acting, and miss the rare accomplishment of the camera-work. This camera is so fluid, you forget you are in one room, it moves from being a human observer, to being omniscient, to being a target, it is smart enough to seldom center on the element of most importance, so expands the field to all men, this is very hard. very hard, to make the camera human. so much easier to do what we see today -- acknowledge the machinery and jigger with it. rarer still is the ability to poke a finger at ones own pre-conceived notions of guilt or innocence, forcing us to take a seat at the jury table and examine the facts from all sides before voting guilty or not guilty.

Twelve men, one verdict, justice at skate- a jurys room heat, where truth would awake- prejudice and doubt, a delicate dance- as reason and empathy take a second chance.

The suffering of man is everlasting and entirely a result of chance. Loyalty is cheap amongst a pair of human beings, at least, the vast majority of the time. Love is but a fools errand if it is not reciprocated in full by the other person. Dogs are loyal, yet even they can turn on each other if corrupted by the greed and brutality of man.
This is the philosophy of Amores Perros a bleak and downtrodden work that pulls no punches in its blunt depictions of violence both emotional and physical. Until we reach the end of the film, when Iñárritu decides to shed the nihilistically dismal mindset of the last two hours and fifteen minutes, much like El Chivo sheds away years of pain and anguish to try and salvage what he can of the pieces that together make what used to be his life. Chivo almost resembles a divine force he observes the suffering of both man and beast, but unlike God, he intervenes when he sees the opportunity to rescue Cofi, while at the same time attempting to help Octavio, but not without robbing him first. So, he isnt a God in the sense that we recognize the Holy Divine, but he no less human or saintly prone to lend a helping hand, while also allowing his humanity to get the best of him. He is a poor man, and he doesnt know these two men he has stumbled uponwhy shouldnt he take the money? Is it morally wrong? Maybe, but he takes Cofi and nurses him back to health, so we cannot say he is immoral. The irony of his good deed is the result of him taking in Cofi and reviving him, which could be seen as a punishment for his own transgressions.
Cofi is a dog, therefore he is in many ways at the mercy of mans will. A double edged sword at best, we see how Cofi has been conditioned by said will to be a killer, and consequently this proves to be deleterious to Chivos other loyal canines. And this is what fascinates me most about Amores Perros the subject of destiny vs. conditioning. What is it that makes us feel so certain that we are in control, and what does it matter if we are (when something, anything can go wrong either by no fault of our own, or at the hands of another) powerless to stop fate? Although it is easy to say we have some kind of say in the way our lives will play outand it is an indisputable fact that the decisions we make in life will directly effect the overall outcome of our existenceat the end of the day, what can we really do to ensure that our road is paved with success and prosperity when it could all come crashing down at any given time?
The closing moments of this film provide us not with answers, but hope and in a world where any and everything is both totally dependent upon fate while simultaneously the result of every decision, big or small, that we make along the way, hope is all we can reasonably ask for.

QA w Alejandro González Iñárritu
Amores Perros thrives on a straightforward yet brutal concept love is a bitch. Love can wound, humiliate, corrupt, and still refuse to let you go. Alejandro González Iñárritu doesnt present love as salvation here. He presents it as an instinctual, messy, and desperate act. Sometimes noble, often selfish, love drives people to cling harder, lie deeper, and hurt themselves in ways they cant undo, as seen in the three interconnected stories.
In the first story, love is portrayed as reckless and obsessive. It exudes an urgent, almost adolescent intensity, convincing you that running away will resolve everything. Its driven by impulse and fantasy, and you can feel how fragile it is from the start. Theres something tragic about how badly these characters want escape, how convinced they are that love will redeem the chaos around them. Instead, it exposes their immaturity and desperation. Love here isnt tender its combustible.
The second story shifts the lens to vanity and dependency. Love becomes transactional, tied to beauty, status, and control. When that foundation cracks, whats left is insecurity and resentment. This section struck me in a quieter, more suffocating manner. It raises the question of what happens when the very thing that made you lovable, or what you believed made you lovable, vanishes. Is love still there, or was it only ever conditional? The unraveling feels intimate and cruel, like watching someone slowly realize they built their life on something unstable.
The final story is the most reflective, almost mournful. Love here is regret. Its the weight of past choices. Its the kind of love that haunts you long after youve ruined it. Theres a tenderness buried beneath the grime in this section, a sense that redemption might be possible, even if it comes too late or costs more than you expected. If the first story is impulsive and the second is corrosive, the third feels like someone staring at the wreckage and finally understanding what they lost.
Beyond the narrative structure, what ties all of it together is how raw it feels. The movie is chaotic, handheld, and alive with sweat and panic. Mexico City pulses in the background like a living organism, indifferent to everyones private catastrophes. Iñárritu doesnt romanticize pain, but he doesnt look away from it either. The performances feel unfiltered, almost invasive at times, like youre intruding on moments that are too real to be staged. That emotional volatility is what makes the movie hit so hard. Love, in this context, isnt poetic its territorial, prideful, and irrational. Despite these flaws, its the only thing these characters possess.
That said, this movie wont be for everyone. Its bleak, violent, and there are scenes involving dogs that are difficult to watch. The movie doesnt take that element lightly its a crucial part of the metaphor of instinct and loyalty. However, it can be disturbing. If youre sensitive to that kind of imagery, this will be a tough experience. For me, however, thats part of why it works so powerfully. Amores Perros offers honesty rather than comfort. It comprehends that love can be both devotion and destruction simultaneously. It can embolden you, but it can also make you monstrous. It can make you believe youre doing the right thing while everything around you burns.

I watched this several days ago now, and its still pretty fresh in my mind. Having watched Digger and realizing Ive only just scratched the surface of Iñárritu I knew this 52 week criteria would be Amores Perros a film set in Mexico. Amores Perros follows a fatal car crash in Mexico City that sets off a chain reaction of three different individuals lives, really thriving on the idea that every action carries consequences and one mistake can create a severe ripple effect that impacts lives forever. 
Its a masterclass in the triptych structure, elite storytelling so brilliantly layered and exceptionally written that its 150 minute runtime flies by without a single lulled moment. Love that we get introduced in the middle of the action, Iñárritu opens the film with a high octane car chase that ends in a horrific crash. This exact car accident serves as the narrative axis that pushes this narrative in several directions. Each story bleeding into the next in fantastic fashion whether its briefly tracking the homeless man or watching the supermodel on tv through the eyes of Octavio, its so well worked. 
All driven by immaculate pacing, the film effortlessly weaves together these three interconnected lives in Mexico City its gritty, guerrilla-style camera work grounds the sprawling narrative, Iñárritu keeps the lens intimate and intensely human amidst the chaotic backdrop of urban struggle. I really took a liking to the first story, Octavio and the dog fighting ring was raw as you like the dog fights were vicious and brutal, and I really got into the story around Octavio, his brother and the lady in their life, the dynamics were crazy and the ramifications of the story were heartbreaking. 
The film thrives on the emotional resonance of its characters theres stellar performances all around, but particularly from Gael García Bernal as the desperate Octavio and Emilio Echevarría as El Chivo, the older homeless hitman devoted to his pack of stray dogs. Both actors bring a raw, vulnerable authenticity to their characters, bound by hardship and love. The supermodel and her issues were definitely strong, but for me it was the weakest part of the film. 
Far from being brash, the music is restrained and minimal, opting instead for ambient noise and long periods of silence, its very effective and adds a weight of real world atmosphere to an already tense and visceral film. This minimalist approach allows us to fully absorb the characters internal worlds, placing their raw emotional states front and center. It is this powerful synergy of storytelling, cinematography, acting, and subtle soundscapes that makes Amores Perros such a visceral and unforgettable piece of cinema.
