You and your plans. You know what my grandmother used to say? If you want to make God laugh... tell Him your plans.
Director Alejandro Iñárritus debut feature is both poetic and brutal in its depiction of love gone wrong for its three main characters in Mexico City. I suppose if I wanted to be cheeky I could say Amores Perros is like Must Love Dogs gone horribly wrong ... just remember no dogs were actually harmed in the making of this film.
If not now, then when?
(Quick Hits) ... Spoilers
- The first story which ended up being my favorite follows Octavio who attempts to win the heart of his sister-in-law, who is seriously mistreated by his asshole brother. So to get money in order for them to run away together he gets involved in the seedy world of dogfighting, and finds out his dog is a remarkably strong fighter
- But things go wrong when the sister-in-law takes off with the money he gave her and leaves with his brother one day. And then Octavio must flee from a dog fight when his rival shoots his dog, which prompts Octavio to put a knife in his rivals gut
- Octavios car chase ends abruptly when they crash into the second main character Valeria, which is also the moment that opens the movie
- Prior to the crash Valeria is living large off her successful career as a headline model, and has just moved into a new apartment with a man she got to leave his family for her
- She is seriously injured in the accident forcing her into a wheelchair. Her boyfriend tries to be supportive, but their relationship becomes strained when her lap dog gets lost after jumping into a hole in their floor
- Things go from bad to worse for her as she slowly comes to the realization that her career as a model is over, and all the moving around she does on her injured leg to try and find her dog ends up causing her to have to get it amputated
- In the third and final chapter we begin to follow the story of an older homeless hitman we have seen from time to time leading up to this point more closely. The man named El Chivo just happened to be walking by the accident when it happened, and he takes Octavios injured dog with him
- El Chivo is by far the most complex character who deeply regrets losing contact with his daughter when he went to prison. He agrees to take on one last hit where he is paid to kill a businessman whose partner claims he is cheating him
- El Chivo seemingly nurses Octavios dog back into good health, but him being a good steward is betrayed when this new dog in his home savagely kills all his other canine companions when he is not there
- The reason I say he seemingly nursed this new dog back to health, is based on how quickly the dog seems to recover after being shot. In my mind I came up with the theory that Octavios dog actually died, and came back as an angel of death to punish El Chivo for his wicked way of life
- This results in El Chivo not carrying out the last hit, but instead bringing the two business partners together, who are actually half brothers to let them settle their dispute between the two of them Cain and Abel style
- El Chivo then reaches out to his daughter to let her know about his deep regret that he was not a part of her life, before walking off into the horizon with Octavios dog
- In several ways this film reminded me of a more gritty version of the Three Colors Trilogy condensed down into one movie. For example, a crash brings all the characters together, there is a huge advertisement of one of the main characters who is a model, and a dog is used as an emotional plot device
While I did get really invested in the stories of these three main characters, I think the story did not fully resonate with me since I am not much of a pet person so I did not get as emotionally invested in these dog relationships as the film wanted me to be. But overall Amores Perros is an intensely visceral thrill ride that shows what happens to these characters when their fates collide in this one life-changing moment.

Ive always heard over the years that Amores Perros is like a Mexican version of Crash.  That would be inaccurate because Amores Perros was released several years before Crash so it would be more accurate to say Crash is like an American version of Amores Perros.  Theyre similar due to their interlocking stories and a car crash at the center of it but honestly thats where the similarities end.  The overall story arc is completely different in each film so my mentioning of Crash ends in this paragraph.  Director Alejandro González Iñárritu has crafted an intriguing thriller with excellent performances by a talented cast.
A horrific car crash connects the stories of three men.  Octavio, Daniel, and El Chivo.  Each of which is dealing with loss, regret, and the harsh realities of life.  Octavio (Gael García Bernal) has an obsessive crush on his sister-in-law, and makes money fighting dogs in hopes he can convince her to run away with him.  Daniel (Álvaro Guerrero) dumps his wife and kids for a disturbed supermodel whos connection to the car crash further complicates their lives.  The third man in this story is El Chivo (Emilio Echeverría).  He lives in poverty, has a daughter he hasnt seen in years, loves dogs, and makes money based on skills acquired in his past life.  The similarities between these three men are often subtle but also painfully obvious.
Man what a good fucking movie!  Each segment of this interlocking story is rich with content and well thought out characters.  Three men dealing with their own personal baggage in different yet similar ways all connected by a car crash and believe it or not dogs.  I read a review somewhere that called this film Of Dogs and Men.  Thats actually pretty damn accurate.  
I think the best thing about Amores Perros is how good each part of the story is.  Each character has depth and a full slate of problems making the time we spend with each one feel full and satisfying.  Octavios blind obsession with his sister-in-law, and complete disregard for his own brother is riveting stuff.  El Chivo who I felt was the most interesting of the characters wears a lifetime of pain and regret right on his face, and we see how one big mistake in life can completely alter who we are.  Daniels part in all of this was my least favorite but it was still really, really good.  His willingness to drop his wife and two kids for a supermodel girlfriend shows hes a flawed man just like Octavio and El Chivo.  What happens to his girlfriend Valeria (Goya Toledo) could be seen as a bit of karma for both him and her.  I think all three tow the line of being good or bad people.  None of them are particularly likable, but I think all three have redeemable qualities.  Essentially I felt there was good inside each man, but that they were in a difficult place in their lives.
In a film like this that uses a single event to connect the lives of multiple people I think its important for that event to be a strong one and it has to make sense.  Alejandro González Iñárritu does a fantastic job of making the connections even the loose ones to the car crash work.  I didnt notice any holes in the connections, and felt the overall story played out very well.  He got the most from a talented cast, and a wonderful script from Guillermo Arriaga making Amores Perros must see in my opinion.

Amores Perros surprisingly impressed the hell out of me. Its a difficult film to watchone that continuously challenges its audiencebut a reward in itself for those who can withstand its brutality. It puts a magnifying glass to the pain of love and those who are destroyed by it, giving new meaning to the films literal title translation love is a bitch.
In a single moment, several lives in Mexico City are changed forever by a devastating car crash. The film is divided into three separate segments, representing the past, present, and future. Octavio is searching for recognition and love but looks in the wrong placesa desire that drives him to make choices that will soon haunt him. Valeria, whose life is most impacted by the accident, finds herself trapped in a crumbling, self-destructive relationship. El Chivo must confront the absence of his daughter and the void it has left in his life. He finds companionship in the stray dogs he takes in, who become the only living beings he can truly connect with. The lives of these individuals collide in more ways than one, bound by a single thread loveand the hell it can unleash.
Its a visceral and gritty filmraw, intense, and unflinching. You may think youve seen it all, but Amores Perros will challenge even those rarely fazed by cinema. At times, it may be hard not to look away. The films sheer violence is penetrating and disturbing, packing a mighty punch. And while its definitely not for the squeamish or faint of heart, theres no question that Amores Perros carries a tender heart and a message worth hearing. Iñárritu crafts a compelling story from start to finish, stripping it down to the bare essentials. His ability to capture a piece of the human spirit is remarkableeven if it doesnt always show us at our best. Its dark, fierce, and relentlessbut nothing short of greatness.
The film features an array of actors and actresses, all of whom work wonders in their respective roles. Gael García Bernal is brilliantits a more restrained and less quirky role than Im used to seeing him in, but he nonetheless has the rare ability to capture and hold my attention with ease. Emilio Echevarría stars as El Chivo and delivers a haunting performance as a man who finds himself alone and broken. Goya Toledo brilliantly plays Valeria, a celebrity crippled by the accident around which the film revolves. I found her part of the story the most compellingif only for the opportunity to witness the fall of someone who goes from having it all to nothing at all. There are numerous other performancestoo many to coverbut each actor brings something vital, contributing to something truly extraordinary.
Amores Perros is an adrenaline rush for its entire two-and-a-half-hour runtime. Combining a multi-faceted story with electric performances, it operates on many layers to deeply satisfying effect. An original and bold step in filmmaking, this nearly perfect picture takes you through a collage of emotions and invites you to invest in flawed charactersall for the sake of love.

Melancholia and tragedy has always been the heart of Alejandro Gonzalez Inarritus work, or so I have been told. I say this due to the fact that as far as experiences go with his filmography, it only extends to the range of his last two films, the hilariously self-critical and satirical Birdman, and the persistent danger and urgency of nature in The Revenant. Both films were pieces that I adored, the latter in particular from the get-go, exploring upon thoughtful concepts in its narrative while viscerally tingling its audience through Inarritus partnership with cinematographer, Emmanuel Lubezki.
Innaritus debut, Amores Perros (translated in english as Loves a Bitch), is one that brims with confidence and passion for its characters. It compromisingly allows them to be endured with weight upon weight of failed expectations and familial or social detachment. Though the films narrative intersection lies in a depicted car-crash, an event that collides the world of each involved character, and with it demonstrating the ripples that it causes or in the films first acts case, the catalysts that has led to it, each one can be viewed as a seperate entity, an opportunity of individual analysis that deconstructs the essence of each character. Not one of the characters that Inarritu and his writers presents for us are neglected, given ample time to convey the relationships that provides the momentum of their lives, validating their significance to the narrative and the strength of their reflection upon realitys most tragic of circumstances.
Speaking of reflecting reality, Inarritu wanted to expressively demonstrate the crushing nature of lifes pitfalls, how we are placed upon such unfortunate circumstances, a feeling of defeat and disappointment that is fed through our place of comfort and expectations, and how we must somehow learn to adapt to the new circumstances that is presented to us, forced to rebuild our lives in order to either learn our lessons and stimulate change or to once again reassemble ourselves to recreate that optimum state of comfort and content that previously existed. Touching upon aspects of unrequited love, regretful decisions, and personal loss, it fuels the films emotion through and through, shaping its characters in a manner that manages to stray from repetitiveness, with each storyline providing a fresh perspective and earn unique rewards despite coherently linked by Inarritus central theme.
Though I cannot find myself personally attached to its characters to an empathetic level, as but as a cinematic feat, I highly appreciated its capabilities of dwelling such passionate emotion, even if it leans more towards pessimism, as it manages to keep me curious and intrigued by the progression of its characters, to see how far they would exert themselves given their circumstances, how much they choose to fall as the victim of life, or how much they feel helpless of the ethereal fabric that pulls their lives along. Amores Perros is not a fully realised masterpiece, but it is a significant breakthrough for Inarritu, in that he manages to instil his personal voice early in his career, in a manner that is confident and impacting, a quality in ones filmmaking that would be the point of envy for many his peers, Amores Perros is the testament to the beauty and power of his own filmography.

I wanted to set the world right, and then share it with you. I failed, as you can see.
The title, just two words long, is actually a little summary of the entire film. Loves, dogs, and all the ugly and beautiful things that connect them. The Spanish title carries this wonderful ambiguity. Amores Perros is something between dog loves and rottenbad loves, and the more I thought about it while watching, the more perfect it became. 
I went into this not really knowing what to expect, and I cant remember the last time I watched something that felt this different from anything I had seen before. It is three stories that seem completely separate at first, but slowly start breathing the same air. Three kinds of love, three kinds of pain, three lives that are changed by one moment. And in all of them, in one way or another, there are dogs. Dogs are both a link between the stories and an emotional extension of the people. Loyalty, violence, despair, attachment, fear, love... everything experienced between the characters seems to exist in some way between them and their dogs as well. 
The first story completely pulled me in. And of course, Gael García Bernal. In any film hes in, theres no chance of anyone else stealing the spotlight. Hes gradually becoming one of my favorite actors, and I want to see him in every film hes in. Octavio, especially since hes so young and emotionally vulnerable, I could see the terrible decisions he was making. Selfish, desperate and reckless, but also defenseless, and Bernal embodies all of that simultaneously. And then the film keeps shifting. Just when I think I understand what kind of film Im watching, it moves somewhere else.
The other stories are similar although they all tell completely different things, they all connect at one point. But my absolute favorite was the part of the film that delved deep into El Chivos story. The films physical atmosphere also stuck with me the city, the noise, the blood, the cars, the dogs, the confined spaces, the heat. Also the film never tries to tell you who deserves sympathy. Everyone is flawed, everyone hurts someone, everyone wants something they probably shouldnt want. That made the film much more interesting to me than if it had simply divided everyone into good and bad people. By the end, I was left thinking about how little it sometimes takes to completely change a persons life. Just one accident, one decision, one person you love, one thing you refuse to let go of. 
We like to imagine that our lives are built from big, deliberate choices, but actually theyre not. Maybe that is what it means to me in the end sometimes love is the thing that saves you, sometimes it is the thing that ruins you and sometimes you dont know which one it is until everything has already changed.

Según Alejandro González Iñárritu, Amores Perros refleja el caos de la ciudad de México con realismo y crudeza. El director utiliza la metrópoli gigantesca de México DF como una experiencia de antropología para destacar la vulnerabilidad del ser humano en un entorno sofocante y demasiado grande para él. El tema de la sobrepoblación y sus consecuencias aparece varias veces en la película. Ante todo, el embarazo involuntario de la joven Susana es un ejemplo de la falta de educación de la clase proletaria en lo que concierne los métodos anticonceptivos, que es una de las causas de la fuerte demografía. Además, tenemos ilustraciones de la violencia, de la delincuencia y de la corrupción, muy a menudo relacionadas con una fuerte densidad de población, en las actividades del Chivo y de Ramiro. Se puede añadir que el ambiente urbano ocasiona una pérdida de valores. No hay una familia en Amores Perros que presenta un esquema tradicional con el padre, la madre y los hijos. Octavio y Ramiro viven sólo con su madre, Susana engaña a Ramiro con su cuñado, El Chivo y Daniel dejaron a sus familias, y tampoco Valeria parece tener buenas relaciones con sus padres puesto que no quiere decirles que tuvo un accidente. Se puede ver también la pérdida de los ideales revolucionarios en la historia del Chivo, que es un hombre desilusionado.  No obstante, a la pérdida de valores se añade la pérdida de la identidad en la inmensidad anónima de la ciudad. Por ejemplo, al Chivo le queda sólo un apodo y su hija cree que está muerto  Valeria, al perder su pierna, tiene que definirse una nueva identidad, diferente de la imagen que puede observar desde su ventana en la valla publicitaria. Este sentimiento de pérdida de identidad en la muchedumbre tiene eco en las letras de la canción Lucha de Gigantes de Nacha Pop, que se oye en la película
En un mundo descomunal Siento mi fragilidad  ... Me da miedo la enormidad  Donde nadie oye mi voz .
Sin embargo, no sólo las grandes aglomeraciones hacen perder los valores y la identidad, sino también hacen resaltar la parte bestial y el instinto primitivo del ser humano. Para protegerse contra el desconocido en el ambiente hostil de la gran ciudad, el hombre tiende a ser individualista. La ley de la selva parece ser la única ley que importa. Esta comparación del ser humano con el animal se destaca en la película gracias a la presencia de perros. Mejor amigo del hombre y símbolo de la amistad, cada perro refleja a su dueño. Primero, Octavio cuenta con las victorias de Cofi en las peleas para ganar dinero. Ambos luchan para sobrevivir. Como Cofi, que descubre que puede matar, Octavio encuentra también el odio y la osadía necesarios para apuñalar a alguien. En segundo lugar, la incapacidad de Valeria para volver a su imagen de modelo famosa se refleja en la imposibilidad de encontrar a Richie, perdido bajo el suelo. Ambos pierden su belleza en experiencias dolorosas después del accidente, Valeria resulta amputada de la pierna, y Richie sale del hueco completamente estropeado por las ratas. Sin embargo, eso va a permitirles construir una nueva vida que no se basa en la superficialidad. En tercer lugar, El Chivo ve en Cofi su propia situación de asesino. Perdonando a Cofi después de que éste ha matado los demás perros, El Chivo entiende sus errores y decide que ya no matará a otro hombre. Gracias al perro, empieza a seguir el camino de la redención.
Para concluir, se puede decir que los protagonistas de Amores Perros, a veces conducidos por un instinto animal, resultan muy humanos, con sus cualidades y faltas. Todos están luchando para sobrevivir en un ambiente que los supera, y al final, descubren el valor inestimable de la vida.

Aside from watching lots of Tom Cruise movies in prep of Digger (such controversy around that ), I also wanted to check out some works from our fellow Latino filmmaker Alejandro Iñárritu, so here we are )
Such a fascinating debut from Iñárritu, a film that explores just how far human nature can descend under the influence of that beautiful yet destructive feeling we call love, portraying it all with remarkable brutality and technical precision.
I adore its presentation and tone, built around three interconnected stories that eventually fit together with admirable precision. Its a filthy, violent, deeply uncomfortable portrait of a reality that, despite its extremity, never stops feeling intimate and familiar abuse, poverty, crime, infidelity, exploitation, and survival all exist within a world where hardly anyone is completely good or evil. They are simply broken people trying to survive, move upward, or obtain what they desire, even when doing so means getting their hands dirty.
The title is particularly brilliant, the double meaning of perro in Mexican Spanish evokes both the misery these relationships can create and the dog-eat-dog nature of life, while the dogs themselves become reflections of their owners. Ironically, the humans often prove to be far more savage than the animals.
Narratively, I love that Iñárritu trusts the audience and never feels the need to explain everything. The accident connecting the three stories becomes the heart of the film a single moment can alter entire lives, reminding us how small and unpredictable our world can be, and how one persons misfortune can become anothers fortune. Amidst all this cruelty, there is even room for an unexpected and deeply moving possibility of redemption.
Visually, it is extraordinary, the cinematography captures both chaotic energy and moments of intimacy, while Mexico City becomes a character of its own, inseparable from the films identity. There is an almost documentary-like harshness to its imagery that makes everything feel dangerously real.
Of the three stories, I consider the middle one the weakest and most redundant, although it remains quite solid. The first and third, however, essentially split the crown one stands out for its narrative complexity, dramatic tension, and depiction of youthful corruption, while the other is more contemplative and profound, reaching the heart from a different angle and making El Chivo its most memorable figure.
At the end, though, they are all pieces of the same organism. What I find most admirable is how Iñárritu uses a specifically Mexican reality to explore universal themes with such visceral force, leaving enough room for every viewer to take something different from it.
I completely understand why its depictions of animal abuse may be unbearable for some, especially because they feel so disturbingly real. Precisely because of that, I think its brutality serves a purpose it does not glorify cruelty, but confronts us with it.
Perhaps the best way to describe Iñárritu here is a sheep in wolfs clothing, covered in blood.
A difficult experience, yes, but also an extraordinarily powerful one. If you can stomach its harshest edges, there is an incredible amount to appreciate here. A genuine triumph of Latin American cinema.

Amores Perros is director Alejandro Iñárritu at his most trendy, straightforward, and ultimately - uninteresting. 
Perros is peak late-90s and early 2000s multiple perspective cinema. Mastered by PTA in 1999s Magnolia and eventually murdered in 2004 by Paul Haggis Crash, Iñárritu employs it to messy effect midway through its life in Perros. 
In (long awaited) hindsight, the multi-story technique was over-used to the point that it renders a great deal of decent movies from that era unwatchable in their repetitiveness. But even excusing Perros being very much of its own time, there is no pardoning its sloppiness. 
There is no clear overarching thread between the three primary pairs, other than, maybe... be nice to dogs? Dont be a violent or deceptive asshole? At least Crash, had - you know - racism. 
The worst insult and the best compliment that can be applied to Iñárritus oeuvre is gimmicky. Sometimes, like in Birdman, (and I am a solid Birdman defender) he deviates enough from the expected tricks to make a compellingly unique creation. 
Perros does not deviate. Despite a charismatic performance by Gael García Bernal anchoring its solid first third, Perros falls, in a splatter of blood and guts, into a messy, extremely early 2000s example of a trend old before its time.

As someone who loves movies split up into multiple chapters based on shifting POVs (think Weapons, Magnolia, Pulp Fiction), Amores Perros skillfully weaves together this dark story as these characters lives intertwine around a brutal car accident. Its hard to predict where this film is going next, and each of the three chapters has such a distinct and contrasting tone. With chapter one feeling like a dread-inducing forbidden romance, chapter two reminding me of a twisted Edgar Allan Poe short story, and chapter three ending with a hitman experiencing an existential crisis.
I watched this last night and to be honest Im still not sure what it all means. But it certainly made an impact, and had me locked in for its 2.5hr runtime. Definitely leaves you with a lot to think about, and probably upset lol.  Also the second I heard the music for this film I was like the Leo meme pointing at the TV saying this gotta be Gustavo Santaolalla, it sounds exactly like The Last Of Us theme!!

Amores Perros finds something painfully human in the ways people love, possess and hurt one another. Across its three stories, the longing for a better life keeps running into the circumstances that shape it, with people often passing their own pain on to others. The dogs embody this contradiction, loved deeply but also exploited to serve human needs. Inarritus restless editing and raw energy give Mexico City a life of its own, with private worlds constantly colliding. Theres also an uneasy thrill to the way he films violence, even when it makes the suffering harder to separate from the spectacle. The men get room to reckon with their failures, while the women often bear their consequences. Still, beneath all its brutality, the film leaves space for tenderness and the possibility of change, however incomplete. Its characters cant undo the damage theyve caused, or the conditions that shaped them, but they arent entirely beyond reach.

When it comes to directorial debuts, Im always wowed whenever they hit it out of the park, especially if the film is as ambitious as Amores Perros. Alejandro González Iñárritu, right from the beginning, displays his skills in directing a film with a gritty and heartbreaking touch. Amores Perros is set up as a triptych where three characters a teenager involved in dog fighting, a supermodel, and a vagrant hitman, have their lives greatly affected by a car crash that briefly links them together. Its not your typical gangster film, it touches on humanist themes like inequality and animal cruelty. The film has many amendable qualities, but the momentum slows down after the first story. When the novelty of hyperlink cinema wears off, the narratives arent engaging enough to sustain the film. Really, the only thing connecting these three stories besides the car crash is the involvement of dogs. Despite the regrettable inconsistencies, its still an admirable effort from Iñárritu.

Amores Perros is a tragic Spanish language anthology about searching for love in dire conditions and the directorial debut for Inarritu. It covers three separate storylines that only intersect with one fatal car crash.
Its a unique plot structure that I can only compare as a Mexican version of Magnolia, or interweaving interpersonal dramas with loosely connected themes but recurring imagery. That imagery would be dogs, which are integral to all 3 stories even if little else is in common. The plot is very bloated in this way, and you feel all 150 minutes of runtime, but asks some very thoughtful sociological questions in the aggregate. 
For thematic messaging, you have to look at the dogs role in each story. The first story uses dogfighting as a way to elevate economic status, but similar to crime, is hurting others to selfishly elevate yourself. Octavio thinks hes better than his brother because he doesnt beat women or rob, but dogfighting and subsequent treatment of Susanna shows their overall similarities.
Just like the dog under the floorboard, Daniel is being trapped within walls of his own creation, but I found him and Valerias fights to be uninspiring and repetitive. The homeless narrative contains the best acting of the film, but doesnt quite have the necessary resolution to its elongated search for family. The scene of Chico discovering his dogs and his response solidifies the core themes of the project.
In the end, Octavios dog is a product of his violent environment and just continues doing what those around him have taught. While that same message applies to all the characters in this story, its message is complicated with non-likable characters with bad decision-making (especially Octavio). The characters are not blameless, but its clear they were nudged into these decisions by the imagery around them.

Much like Iñárritus filmography as a whole, Amores Perros left me gravely divided. Iñárritus major theme throughout the film (which can be roughly linked back to its title Loves a bitch) is that somehow, no matter how much love we can put into an action, no matter how much goodwill can be behind a thought or a prayer, it can all be whisked away by the unpredictability of our world which in some way still feels constructed by some sort of order. It makes for a somewhat determinist work. The three stories in which the main theme is conveyed are linked by one big event thats either the cause of the following story or the consequence of it. Iñárritu has made somewhat of a habit of dissecting this determinist worldview in his films and to his fault, it either completely works or it hardly does anything. Where Babel makes a much more universal and (dare I say) beautiful statement on this causality through a story about miscommunication around the world, Amores Perros stays frightfully empty.
We follow the characters. Theyre trying to find love in one way or another. They act foolishly and their plans turn sour (and thats a serious understatement) after which they end up with less than they had before. As far as their character arcs go, theres really not much to it. After 2,5 hours of film, theres not much of a lesson theyve learned. Theyve failed to obtain their goal and are now... nowhere. If that lengthy running time and those harrowingly stretched out stories only end up to service the titles vacant quote, love is a bitch, the label of misery porn isnt too far off. I dont like to put that stamp on films too often because even in some of the examples that tend to lean towards that genre (think of Irreversible, mother! or even American Honey) theres still an abundance of artistic merit to be found. They arent just soulless pictures made to show how bad things can get they offer renewing views on such situations. Amores Perros does not. We really already knew by then how harrowing the suburbs of any town in the world could be. The exploration of the stories within Amores Perros thereby becomes quite insignificant. Their meaning almost ceases to exist because of the plots ineptitude to convey their importance. Shit happens but then what? What does it amount to?
This film leaves quite a lot to beg for and if it wasnt for the powerful performances, this couldve easily become a full-on 2,5-hour drag. Theres something to get from this film. It isnt a complete debacle, but its most inventive, noteworthy moments are hidden behind a whole load of mindless misery and empty cinema.

La opera prima de Alejandro González Iñárritu.
Está película nos cuenta tres historias de tres parejas en la ciudad de México, conectadas por un trágico accidente de tránsito y con un elemento en común, los perros.
Desafortunadamente ayer no pude ver la nueva peli de Superman, así que aproveche para ver el DVD de esta película, la caja venía con un disco adicional con un documental sobre la producción, comentarios de Iñárritu, etcétera y también tiene un pequeño librito que la verdad no le he podido leer aún. Esto fue un regalo de madre por mi cumpleaños, un poco tarde pero aún así estaré eternamente agradecido con ella (más de lo que ya estoy) por permitirme ver está obra maestra de mi México.
El título Amores Perros se refiere a amores imposibles, rotos, caóticos, y esto se ve representado en las tres historias que nos presenta la película.
La película arranca con una frenética persecución de coches, con una dirrección errática por parte de Iñárritu nos pone dentro del auto que de un momento a otro... Choca, y ahí, ahora sí comienzan las historias.
La primera se títula Octavio y Susana, Octavio es un chico que se enamora de Susana, la cuál está casada con su hermano Ramiro el cual es un tipo bastante prepotente y violento. Aquí vemos uno de los principales conceptos de la película, la conexión entre un perro y un dueño ya que como se dirá en la última historia, todo dueño se parece a su perro. En éste caso, Octavio usará a su perro Cofi como un perro de pelea para ganar dinero e irse de la ciudad con Susana y su hijo bebé, es la avaricia y la creciente violencia de Octavio lo que transforma a Cofi de un Rottweiler amigable en una máquina de matar perros, siendo un oscuro reflejo de la psique de Octavio. Todo su viaje lo lleva a un punto de no retorno que culmina con el choque que vimos en el inicio y donde ahora nos daremos cuenta que las tres historias están conectadas por ese mismo choque.
La siguiente historia es la de Valeria y Daniel, una modelo española la cual se irá a vivir junto su perrito Richie con su novio el cual es editor de revistas en un apartamento lujoso en la Ciudad de México, hasta que Valeria choca con nada más ni nada menos que Octavio, dejando como resultado a una Valeria en silla de ruedas por un buen tiempo y es aquí donde sucede otra cosa, el perrito Richie se escabulle debajo del apartamento para no salir por un muy largo rato. Es toda esta sucesión de eventos desafortunados que hace que la relación entre Valeria y Daniel empiece a estancarse en peleas y discusiones, tal como Richie siendo otra vez un reflejo de la relación de estos dos y cuando por fin parce que sus problemas se resolverán, solo se vuelven peores. También está historia tiene un poco de crítica social hacia el mundo del modelaje y como las estrellas son fácilmente desechables por no cumplir estándares de belleza estúpidos y saben que es lo peor, que esto ni siquiera fue culpa de Valeria.
La última historia y mi favorita es la de El Chivo y Maru. El es un ex Guerrillero convertido en sicario que fue contratado por un hombre de negocios para asesinar a su socio, a su vez que intenta reconectar con su hija la cual no sabe que el está vivo. A diferencia de las otras historias aquí se nos presenta otro tipo de amor, el de un padre a su hija. El Chivo es un hombre solitario e insensible, vaya su trabajo es asesinar a otros seres humanos sin un motivo personal hasta que el presencia el choque del inicio, donde rescata a Cofi salvandole la vida, ya que el rescata a perros de la calle y los vuelve parte de su familia, es su forma de escapar de su realidad hasta que Cofi, el nuevo perro que el rescato, sede a sus instintos asesinos previamente adquiridos gracias a Octavio para asesinar de forma brutal y sin ningún motivo a otros perros, esto obviamente emputa a El Chivo lo que lo lleva a considerar matar a el perro, pero este se ve reflejado en el, un ser roto que lo único que hace es matar porque aparentemente no sabe hacer nada más. Es ahí donde El Chivo empieza a aceptar su realidad decidiendo dejar su vida de sicario atrás (cumpliendo su último trabajo de forma peculiar) e intentar reconcilarse con su hija.
Ya por último, el choque que conecta las tres historias puede ser interpretado como un choque vaya la redundancia de tres distintas clases sociales de la Ciudad de México que aunque parecen distintes, un evento no importa si es simple o catastrófico, puede cambiar el rumbo de cualquier persona de cualquier clase social.
Con una asombrosa y errática dirección de Iñárritu, un guión súper pulido con potentes mensajes, actuaciones sobresalientes, Amores Perros es y seguirá siendo una obra maestra del cine contemporáneo de México además de ser la película que catapultó a la fama a uno de los mejores directores mexicanos de la historia.
Eso sí, si son muuuuy sensibles con el tema de violencia hacia los perritos, no se las recomendaría ya que la película retrata escenas muy crudas pero importantes para la narrativa a través del sufrimiento de muchos perros, así que están advertidos.

The title Amores Perros (which loosely translates to Loves a Bitch) refers to impossible, broken, chaotic loves, a theme clearly reflected in each of the three stories presented in the film.
The movie begins with a frantic car chase, and with Iñárritus erratic direction, we feel like were right inside the vehicle, until, in a sudden moment, it crashes. And thats when the stories begin.
The first one is titled Octavio and Susana. Octavio is a young man who falls in love with Susana, who is married to his brother Ramiro, a violent and arrogant man. Here, were introduced to one of the films main ideas the bond between a dog and its owner, which is later echoed in the final story, every owner ends up resembling their dog. In this case, Octavio uses his dog Cofi in underground dog fights to earn money and escape the city with Susana and her baby. Its Octavios greed and growing violence that transform Cofi from a friendly Rottweiler into a ruthless killer, a dark mirror of Octavios own psyche. His journey leads to a point of no return, culminating in the crash we saw at the start, the event that ties all three stories together.
The second story is about Valeria and Daniel. Valeria is a Spanish model who moves in with her little dog Richie and her boyfriend, a magazine editor, in a luxurious Mexico City apartment. But everything changes when Valeria crashes, with none other than Octavio. The accident leaves her in a wheelchair for an extended period. On top of that, Richie disappears under the floorboards of the apartment and doesnt come out for a long time. This chain of unfortunate events causes Valeria and Daniels relationship to unravel, with constant fights and tension. Richie, again, reflects their relationship, lost, isolated, and slowly deteriorating. Just when things seem like they might get better, they only get worse. This story also offers subtle social commentary on the modeling industry and how stars are quickly discarded for failing to meet absurd beauty standards, and whats worse is that none of this was even Valerias fault.
The final and my personal favorite story is El Chivo and Maru. El Chivo is a former guerrilla fighter turned hitman, hired by a businessman to kill his partner while trying to reconnect with the daughter who believes hes dead. Unlike the previous stories, this one focuses on a different kind of love, the love of a father for his daughter. El Chivo is a lonely and emotionally detached man, after all, his job is to kill strangers without personal motive. But everything changes when he witnesses the accident and rescues Cofi, saving his life. El Chivo is known for rescuing stray dogs and making them part of his family, his way of coping with reality. But Cofi, still carrying the violent instincts instilled by Octavio, ends up slaughtering the other dogs, brutally and without cause. This enrages El Chivo, and he considers killing the dog. But then he sees himself in Cofi, a broken creature who only knows how to kill because its the only thing hes ever learned. Thats when El Chivo begins to face his own reality and decides to leave his life as a hitman behind (carrying out his final job in an unusual way) and try to reconcile with his daughter.
Lastly, the crash that connects the three stories can also be interpreted as a symbolic collision of Mexico Citys distinct social classes. Though they seem separate, a single event, whether minor or catastrophic, can alter the course of anyones life, regardless of their class.
With Iñárritus bold and erratic direction, a razor-sharp script full of powerful messages, and outstanding performances, Amores Perros is, and will remain, a masterpiece of contemporary Mexican cinema. Its also the film that launched one of Mexicos greatest directors into international fame.
That said, if youre extremely sensitive to depictions of violence against dogs, I wouldnt recommend this film. It features several intense scenes that, while crucial to the narrative, may be too distressing for some viewers. So consider yourself warned.

Just a few days ago, Amores perros failed to win this years Oscar for Best Foreign-Language Film, having had the misfortune to compete against Crouching Tiger, Foregone Conclusion. Still, its something of a miracle that the movie was nominated in the first placenot because its undeserving, but because its graphic violence, amoral sensibility and complicated structure set it miles apart from the Mediterraneos and Belle Epoques that tend to warm the hearts of AMPAS voters. The untranslatable title suggests a vicious, dog-eat-dog take on love and romance, and Amores perros fulfills that promise not just figuratively but literally Never before have I seen a movie that opens with a no-animals-were-harmed disclaimer. Sensitive caninophiles should proceed with caution.
Set in Mexico Cityenvisioned here as a grime-encrusted wasteland where even the luxury apartments sport gaping holes in the floorGonzález Iñárritus arresting debut tells three separate but interrelated stories, with the same horrific traffic accident playing a decisive role in each. In the first and most impressive tale, a love-struck teenager (Gael García Bernal), hoping to flee town with his brothers wife, raises money by entering the family mutt in a series of brutal dogfights. Story number two, which could function as a terrific stand-alone short (it runs about half an hour), finds an injured fashion model (Goya Toledo) and her new lover distressed when her beloved pooch disappears for days beneath the floorboards. Only in the final segment, an alternately smug and maudlin account of a half-crazed assassin (Emilio Echevarría) seeking forgiveness from the daughter he abandoned years before, does González Iñárritus touch falter.
While the films tripartite, dislinear structure makes comparisons to Pulp Fiction inevitable, the tone of Amores perros has virtually nothing in common with Tarantinos trademark juxtaposition of offbeat humor and shocking cruelty. Ultimately, it feels closer to Buñuel (who worked for years in Mexico)especially in the second part, where the dog beneath the floor serves as a surprisingly poignant metaphor for the relationship between the model and her lover something vulnerable thats trapped and stifled and just barely audible, mostly very late at night. Had screenwriter Guillermo Arriaga succeeded in weaving all three parts into a seamless whole with a clear, overarching theme, wed be talking about a minor classic. But while the films bark (style) may be more impressive than its bite (content), sometimes a really loud bark will suffice.

Excellently acted and paced by a mostly-on-target musical score, Amores Perros, the feature film debut from Alejandro González Iñárritu, richly deserved all of the many accolades it received, which included the Critics Prize at the 2000 Cannes Film Festival. It comprises three interlocking stories that work towards one coherent tale circling a nightmare of a car crash in the otherwise unrelated lives of a penniless assassin, a young dissatisfied underground dogfighter and a spoilt supermodel. Each of the balanced stories shares a variety of common elements, one of them being the presence of dogs. The lines that bring together the three groups, all from varied walks of existence, shape like the strands of a spiders web with the emotional elements dialled up to significant effect by a visual flair thats proportional parts gut-wrenching, blood-soaked and beautiful. The brutal car crash opens the narrative compellingly and effectively, and Iñárritu repeatedly displays the accident while divulging new things each time. While its true that Amores Perros works predominantly on a purely visceral level, in that regard, its truly masterful.

La primer película de Alejandro González Iñárritu, un hombre que sabe hacerte sentir raro después de cualquiera de sus películas, y no es su única antología (también hizo Babel que la recomiendo un montón), pero demuestra de una forma tan desgarradora y confusamente realista las desgracias de estos personajes que la hace mi segunda película favorita de este genial director (aunque con el tiempo he escuchado cosas que no lo hacen ver una muy buena persona, pero tiene talento para sacar muy grandes cosas de sus actores e historias en general). No soy mexicano, asi que no he visto muchas películas de este país (pero creo tampoco he visto tantas de mi propio país), y esta es la más fuerte que he visto de ese país y una de las mejores películas en español que he visto en mi vida, es simplemente increíble el retrato de estas tres historias tan salvajes como si tuvieran rabia, sucias con pulgas, muy fiel al estilo de Iñárritu observando distintos tipos de crueldad en estas vidas, y cada una deja una mordida (capaz alguna más grande que otra, pero las tres me dejaron algo). Es impresionante que Iñárritu haya empezado con una película así. Perfecta no me parece, y a veces si se siente un poco demasiado dramática o no destaca tanto tanto en cosas más técnicas (aunque para no tener tanto presupuesto es increíble lo que lograron, por ejemplo la escena del choque es excelente, y la sinceramente me encanta esa ambientación y atmósfera que entrega, y no solo en México hay barrios así), pero el punto seguramente es sofocarte y lo logra muy bien, y cosas como el guion o su elección en el elenco son espectaculares. 
Primero hablaré de cada historia por separado o primero por las tres en conjunto y luego cada una por separado? O mejor, las tres en general entre medio de las tres por separado, o mejor me dejo de decir estas estupideces y me pongo a escribir aunque igual estoy escribiendo, no estoy seguro cual elegir, pero de lo que si estoy seguro es que me encantan los perros, y debo decir que esas escenas, ESAS ESCENAS duelen. 
Esta es una película que se basa mucho en la emoción y crudeza que tiene el amor y las diferentes adversidades en estas tres diferentes clases sociales, es un drama en donde la intensidad es constante a pesar de que el ritmo va cambiando bastante, pero nunca me aburrió. Es interesante como la conexión de estas historias solo por un accidente sea tan natural, como esto le da pie a tramas tan distintas, pero con el mismo espíritu, y que en las tres los perros sean factores considerablemente importantes teniendo en cuenta de que en lugares como en mi país hay muchísimos perros callejeros, lo cual puede reforzar más esta mirada del instinto humano parecido al de los caninos, estamos perdidos pero al menos queremos ser buenos compañeros, es absolutamente brillante. Cada historia tiene un peso diferente, pero en especial la primera y la última me pegaron feo.
La primera historiatrama, Octavio y Susana, es seguramente la más memorable y mi segunda favorita, es simple, es la que más energía tiene y encapsula fabulosamente una gran incomodidad y pasión y obsesión, o mejor dicho avaricia, o mejor dicho el deseo de algo más sacrificando integridad para conseguir ese algo más. Aquí vemos al amor como una neblina a la brutalidad que se adentra Octavio, quien se mete en este mundo no solo por casualidad, si no que para tener un futuro asegurado con un alguien que ya parecía imposible mantenerse. El como podemos conectar con este protagonista y lo triste que se siente ese final es digno de un aplauso. Gael García Bernal es fenomenal, una de sus mejores actuaciones y los secundarios son excelentes. Es la historia más violenta hacia los sentimientos y moral del protagonista, aunque haya sido un protagonista que lo dio todo para poder conseguir su sueño.
A mí me sorprende cuanto me atrapó esta película, se llega a sentir tan cercano que a veces quieres que les vaya bien a estos protagonistas o a los perros, y elegir la tragedia para los tres funciona muy bien, en ningún momento me perdió y no se me ocurre otra forma de que podrían haber terminado. Es una película que no será del todo inolvidable para mi, pero es una gran película y es sorprendentemente recomendable. Y antes de que se me olvide, el soundtrack es impecable. 
La segunda historia, la que he visto que se lleva menos cariño, Daniel y Valeria, y es cierto que es mi menos favorita, pero igual me parece muy muy buena. En esta el accidente es el punto de partida y no el climax, y me gustó, si estoy de acuerdo que rompe un poco con el ritmo que llevó la anterior, pero me gusta mucho como muestra que la gente con dinero no sufrirá más, y sus preocupaciones no son muy grandes, pero aún se mantiene esa actitud más desprevenida y más inocente que la anterior trama, y cuando esta gente cae, la caída es mucho más fuerte. Es una desesperanzada muestra de que la fama no te libra de la desgracia, e incluso la puede incrementar. Esas dos actuaciones principales son excelentes, y me gusta un montón el concepto de todo esto, solo me parece que la fotografía no tuvo tanto peso, a pesar de que es seguramente la más historia más trágica de las tres, ya que la primera es la más cruda y la tercera es la más dolorosa. Es seguramente la que emocionalmente se vea más sencilla y para varios no es tan fácil de conectar, pero para mi sirve muy bien y no es para nada innecesaria. Aquí no hay mucho amor, lo que más hay es fragilidad tanto en sus personajes como en su relación, como ya se pierde la ilusión de felicidad y ya no hay superación por culpa de una falta de ayuda mutua.
Cuando la película termina yo me quede como wow, que triste que esto, pero después de un corto tiempo pensando dije el punto de esto es mostrarme la realidad de distintos tipos de vida o quiere advertirme de que mi vida puede tomar uno de estos caminos? y me quedé pensando, y ahora la veo como una película más positiva de lo que parece, eso me pasa mucho con las películas de Iñárritu (excepto con Bardo), y la veo como que en las situaciones más oscuras o duras, las personas siempre tienen algo de esperanza de cambiar, y la película está llena de momentos tensos o de directa violencia, pero al final me da una sonrisa lagrimienta (creo que se entiende, espero que se entienda).
Y la tercera historia y mi favorita, El Chivo, la trama que me rompió más el corazón y que me hizo ver de una forma más positiva los mensajes de esta película. Es el personaje claramente más misterioso de todos y como parece no haber redención para él, ya no tiene forma de volver y arreglar su pasado y como la vida ya le dio la espalda para nunca perdonarlo, pero es esto cierto, acaso eso significa que ya no le queda nada más que hacer, o tal vez solo se convirtió en uno de los propios perros que pelean con otros sin verdadero motivo sin que se diera cuenta. No se si sea la más lenta de las tres, pero para mi eso la hace más cruel, y como vemos este cambio de un personaje de un viejo que mata por dinero a disculparse a si mismo, a querer ser visto como una persona otra vez, a buscar de una forma sincera y firme, no un regreso, si no un cambio o un rumbo nuevo a su vida, uno que no será peor y no sabemos si mejor, pero será uno importante, en donde ahora no estará solo. Emilio Echevarría es extraordinario, dio al personaje más intrigante y al que sentí más real de los tres, y ese plano final es una maravilla. Terminar con esta historia fue una decisión perfecta, es tan cautivante y fascinante que estoy pensando en demasiadas cosas, me encantó. Una historia poderosamente impactante con un personaje quebrado pero esperanzador. 
La primer historia es la más angustiosa y la más entretenida, la segunda no me esperaba que fuese así y es la única que no tiene optimismo, y la tercera es la obra maestra para mi, el como la forma en la que respondemos a esas cosas difíciles muestran lo que en verdad somos, eso une a estas historias. Y mezclar todo esto se ejecuta de una forma magnífica. Nada de lo que hacemos es por nada. 
No es una película que haya disfrutado ni me dan ganas de volver a verla en un tiempo, pero si pueden véanla. 
Mientras películas veo más me doy cuenta de lo común que es ver hablar mal de nuestra moralidad, y es porque es verdad, estamos terribles en ese tema, y me gusta como juegan con eso en los personajes como Octavio o El Chivo y con el propio expectador de si apoyar a Octavio o como sentirnos con la historia del medio. Es una película interesante e intensamente difícil de ver a veces, es una experiencia novedosa a pesar de sentirse como algo un poco nostálgico de algún modo. 
Me encanta como la cámara se mueve y la película se siente muy humana, no se como describirlo, pero hay algo en todo que me hace sentir que esto pasó. Hay un balance tan alineado como imperfecto en estas tramas que me enamora, el guion es completamente bellísimo. 
Esta película tiene exactamente el reconocimiento que se merece y eso me hace sentir muy bien para una película que te deja bastantes cosas que reflexionar sin descansar casi ni un segundo. Emoción desgastada, triste y realista. Ouch. 
Una película hermosa.

Amores perros se prevodi kao Pasja ljubav. Naslov se, međutim, može čitati  u meksičkom žargonu i kao Okrutna ljubav, što mnogo više odgovara tematici filma. Sami autori poigravali su se i izrazom, pa su isticali da film može da se zove i amor es perros  ljubav su psi.
U samom naslovu krije se toliko značenja, toliko različitih tumačenja ljubavi, da se čini kako bi se o njemu mogla napisati zasebna studija. A sam film? Njegovi slojevi kao da nemaju kraja.
Ovo je remek-delo, i to bez ikakve sumnje.
Injaritu u svom debitantskom filmu pripoveda tri naizgled nepovezane priče, koje spaja saobraćajna nesreća. Sve tri priče savršeno prenose punokrvnost i gorčinu ljubavi, ali i brutalnost, surovost i beznađe meksičkog društva.
Moram priznati da me je posebno iznenadio njegov rediteljski pristup. Kako bi dočarao tu brutalnost, Injaritu često pribegava izrazito širokim kadrovima, čak i u skučenim prostorijama. Na taj način stvara osećaj da smo i sami postali deo sveta filma, da više ne možemo da se sakrijemo iza bezbedne distance između posmatrača i onoga što se odigrava na ekranu. Kao da nas je uvukao u jedan trenutak vremena i zauvek ga tu zaledio, zajedno sa svim njegovim nasiljem, očajem i neizgovorenom tugom.
Sve tri priče govore o ljubavi kroz motiv pasa. 
Zašto baš psi? 
Moje tumačenje je da oni predstavljaju jedan od poslednjih izvora bezuslovne ljubavi u svetu u kojem su ljudi gotovo zaboravili šta ona znači. 
Zato nas psi, i na svesnom i na podsvesnom nivou, neprestano podsećaju na ono što nedostaje likovima u sve tri priče. Dok ljudi svoju ljubav uslovljavaju, izneveravaju, psi ostaju vezani za njih čak i onda kada za tu odanost bivaju kažnjeni. 
I u tome leži najokrutniji paradoks filma oni koji su sposobni za najčistiju ljubav najčešće stradaju zbog ljudske prljavštine.
Pored toga, kroz tri priče Injaritu gradi izuzetno slojevitu sociološku studiju meksičkog društva. U prvoj se spušta u svet siromaštva, u kojem nasilje postaje gotovo svakodnevni jezik preživljavanja u drugoj ulazi u život imućnijeg, naizgled zaštićenog sloja, čiji se savršeno uređeni svet raspada pred jednom nesrećom dok trećom prati čoveka koji je ostao na samoj margini društva, odbačen i od drugih i od sopstvenog nekadašnjeg života. Tri različita društvena položaja, tri različita oblika nesreće, a ista praznina koju ljubav, ma koliko joj se približili, ne uspeva sasvim da ispuni.
U prvoj priči pratimo mladalačku, neostvarenu ljubav. Međutim, Injaritu tu ljubav smešta u okruženje u kojem siromaštvo i nasilje nisu tek pozadina priče, nego pre svega sile koje određuju njene granice. Kada je budućnost neizvesna, a izlaz iz sopstvene stvarnosti gotovo nezamisliv, nasilje postaje prečica do novca, moći ili privida slobode. Ljubav se tada ne doživljava kao utočište, već kao još jedan razlog za sukob, posesivnost i očaj. Film pritom ne tvrdi da siromaštvo nužno rađa nasilje, već pokazuje koliko lako ono može da postane njegov plodno tlo, naročito tamo gde su mogućnosti za drugačiji život gotovo sasvim iščezle.
U drugoj priči, na prvi pogled, suočavamo se sa idealizacijom ljubavi. Međutim, kako se priča odvija i nesreća za nesrećom nadolazi, taj idealizam postepeno ustupa mesto surovoj stvarnosti. Ljubav više nije romantična predstava o zajedničkoj sreći, već svakodnevica u kojoj se želje, strpljenje i odanost suočavaju sa sopstvenim granicama.
U toj priči posebno mi je značajan Ričijev lik (Valerijin pas). Dok se Valerijin svet zasnivao na lepoti, izgledu i pažnji koju joj je takav izgled donosio, Ričiju je bila važna ona sama. 
Njegova privrženost nije zavisila od toga kako Valerija izgleda, niti se promenila onda kada joj se život iz korena preokrenuo. U svetu u kojem se ljudska vrednost tako lako poistovećuje sa spoljašnjim sjajem, Ričijeva odanost predstavlja bolno čist oblik ljubavi.
Treća priča je, za mene, žal za propuštenom ljubavlju.
U El Čivovom odnosu sa psima nazire se poslednji ostatak čoveka kakav je nekada mogao da bude. Prema njima pokazuje nežnost koju više ne ume da iskaže ljudima, kao da je lakše voleti bića koja od njega ne traže objašnjenja, oproštaj ili suočavanje sa prošlošću. Ali ni tu ne može da pronađe potpuno utočište. Nasilje koje je godinama nosio u sebi ne nestaje samim tim što je okružen bićima koja ga vole. Naprotiv, ono se uvlači i u jedini prostor u kojem je još sposoban da oseti privrženost.
U tome vidim i najdublju tragediju El Čivovog lika čovek može da provede čitav život donoseći odluke koje ga udaljavaju od ljubavi, a da tek onda kada ostane bez svega shvati koliko mu je ona bila potrebna. Njegova priča ne nudi jednostavan oproštaj niti briše ono što je učinio. Ona samo ostavlja mogućnost da se čovek, čak i nakon svega, suoči sa sopstvenim zlom i pokuša da prekine krug u kojem je godinama živeo  to je možda jedini oblik iskupljenja koji mu je preostao.

Amores Perros has to be among the best debut films ever made.
After watching Digger, I was really looking forward to seeing more of Iñárritus work, and wow. This might be his best film from what Ive seen so far. Its between this and Digger for me, which is kind of crazy considering how different they are. But even here, in his first feature film, you can already see just how much control he has over his craft.
What makes Amores Perros so incredible is how it takes three very different stories and connects them through one moment that changes everything. Every story introduces different people, different problems and different ways of looking at life, yet the more time you spend with these characters, the more you start to see the connections between them.
And at the centre of all of it is love.
But not the beautiful, romantic version of love we usually see in films. Here, love is selfish, obsessive, destructive and sometimes downright ugly. People hurt each other because they love each other. They make terrible decisions because they convince themselves that things will somehow be better if they can just get what they want. Some are desperately trying to escape their lives, others are trying to hold on to something they have already lost, and some are carrying so much regret that they barely know what to do with themselves anymore.
The film never turns these people into heroes. They can be difficult to sympathize with, and some of the things they do are genuinely horrible, but they are still human. They have their own reasons, their own desperation and their own idea of what love is supposed to mean. And watching those ideas collide is what makes the film so compelling.
The first part is incredible. Octavios story immediately pulls you in, and the whole situation surrounding him, Susana and Ramiro gets more and more intense as it goes on. There is so much desperation here. Octavio sees running away with Susana as a way to start a new life, but the further he gets pulled into dogfighting, the more destructive his decisions become. He thinks he is doing all of this for love, but there is also so much selfishness and recklessness behind it. He wants to escape his life so badly that he barely stops to think about what he is doing to everyone around him.
The dogfighting scenes are difficult to watch, and not just because of the violence. There is something so uncomfortable about seeing how easily affection, loyalty and cruelty can exist alongside each other. Cofi becomes such an important part of Octavios life, but the way the dogs are treated also reflects the behaviour of the people around them. Everyone is fighting for something, and so much of that fighting comes from desperation, pride and the need to survive.
Then there is the second part, which I still think is very good, but definitely the weakest of the three for me.
I liked what Iñárritu was doing with Daniel and Valeria, especially the way their relationship starts falling apart after the accident. Valerias career and appearance have been such a big part of her life, and suddenly everything she has built her identity around is taken away from her. Meanwhile, Daniel has to watch the woman he left his family for suffer, while their relationship becomes increasingly difficult to hold together.
Richie being trapped underneath the floorboards is such a simple but effective idea. Something as small as a dog disappearing beneath the floor slowly becomes this constant source of frustration, desperation and helplessness. It mirrors what is happening between Daniel and Valeria, who are trapped in their own situation and seem increasingly unable to reach each other.
There is a lot to like about this storyline, and I think it adds something important to the film. But compared to the first and third parts, it just didnt hit me on the same level. The ideas are interesting, and everything is executed well, but I found it less compelling overall. It also fits a little less naturally between the other two stories for me. I never disliked it, but I was always waiting to return to the other characters.
And then we get to El Chivo.
At first, he seems like this mysterious, almost ghostlike figure moving through the streets of Mexico City, but gradually you start to understand who he is and what he has lost. There is so much sadness behind him. He has spent years living with the consequences of his choices, and now he is left trying to figure out whether there is anything he can still do to make things right.
Emilio Echevarría is incredible in this role. There is something about his performance that makes El Chivo so difficult to forget. He looks like a man who has completely abandoned himself, someone who has spent so long living outside the world that he barely knows how to return to it. But underneath all of that, there is still a person who wants something more, even if he has no idea whether he deserves it.
His relationship with the dogs is also one of the most affecting parts of the film. They become a connection to something he has almost completely lost in himself, and watching that relationship develop adds so much humanity to his story. I found myself thinking about him long after the film ended, especially because of the way his past continues to follow him.
What I really appreciate about this final part is that it doesnt offer some easy redemption. El Chivo cannot simply undo what he has done or return to the life he abandoned. He has to live with it. But there is still the possibility of making a different choice, of finally trying to move forward instead of remaining trapped in the same cycle. That gives his story a kind of hope that I really liked, especially after everything we have seen.
And the way all three stories connect is just fantastic. The car accident is the moment that brings these people together, but the film never makes it feel as if their lives exist only to serve one big puzzle. They have their own worlds, and those worlds continue beyond what we get to see. The accident simply reveals how close people can be to each other without ever knowing it.
I also have to talk about the filmmaking, because this is an incredible debut on that level alone.
The cinematography is superb. The handheld camera, the close ups, the way Iñárritu follows his characters through crowded streets and cramped interiors, all of it gives the film this raw, restless energy. Mexico City is not just a backdrop. You can feel the chaos of the place in almost every scene, with people constantly moving around each other while dealing with their own private struggles. There is so much life in the way everything is filmed, but there is also a constant sense of danger and uncertainty.
I love how the visual style changes between the three parts, too. Each story has its own atmosphere, yet the film never loses its identity. The editing is just as impressive, especially when it revisits events from different perspectives. You begin to understand how much can be happening around you without you ever really knowing it. Two people can experience the same moment and carry completely different versions of it for the rest of their lives.
The music is another highlight. Gustavo Santaolallas score has this haunting quality that works so well with the images, and the use of songs throughout the film adds so much to its atmosphere. The montage set to Lucha de Gigantes is a particular highlight for me. It captures so much emotion without needing to explain everything, and it is one of those moments that really shows how much power cinema can have when the music, editing and images come together.
For a first feature, the level of ambition here is remarkable. You can already see Iñárritus interest in human suffering, the way people are connected, and how one moment can change the course of several lives. But what I appreciate most is that he doesnt lose sight of the people at the centre of it all. The film can be brutal and chaotic, but there is so much humanity underneath that.
I do think the film is a little uneven, mainly because the second part didnt work as well for me as the other two. But that is a relatively small criticism when the rest is this good. The first part is incredible, the third is fantastic, and even the weaker section still has plenty to offer.
Amores Perros is a brutal, emotional and beautifully made film about love, regret, loyalty and the things people do when they are desperate to change their lives. It is also an amazing introduction to Iñárritu as a filmmaker, and I can already see why this is considered one of the great debut films.
A must watch. I cant wait to see more of his work, even if I already have a feeling that this one is going to be hard to top.

Horrible movie that, apart from a pretty major case of animal violence (dogs were tranquilized which is questionable), is thoroughly exciting thanks to Inarritus skill at balancing narratives and wielding time and consequences like a madman. Its horrible because the people are horrible and the paths theyre pushed onto gives them only bad options. Plans never go right, misunderstandings, communication breakdowns and near-misanthropy, rugs pulled from under your feet, pursuing something only to make a bad decision at the finish line. Santaolallas score full of wrong notes almost ironically enforces that anxious, erroneous atmosphere yet it also creates airiness that Inarritu and Prieto command visually. 
Formally theres no real weak links and I sort of expected that going in. I knew even though I was a little tired that I was going to enjoy this more than some 90 minute film. Maybe its also that watching horrible people in a horrible social setting is too tangible to fall asleep to, but you have to give credit to how Amores Perros is put together with every available technique on display. High speed chase, rapid cutting, and video camera quality is abandoned in favor of a lingering wide shot from across the street. Nothing is left unseen but we have time to process previous events during the calmer sequences. Low angle long take or neutral eye-level tracking and then again more chaotic handheld or a montage in order to connect the violent, sex-fueled battle of brothers. Its a masculine movie for sure. Straight from the Cain-Abel Bible references and unfortunate use of F-slurs to diminish someones manhood to the female characters shown as mothers, daughters or models. 
Obviously the women are given agency too, most notably Valeria, and they arent just vehicles which the stories revolve around. For example Susannas arc develops in the background and is left deliciously open as are most of the characters journeys. Theres probably a lot more subtext than I could pick up too, although sometimes I feel like Inarritus stylistic capabilities overcame the essence of the content. Not that it was the case the whole time but ccasionally it seemed like Amores Perros was more about lifes incoherence and wrong decisions than anything else. Which is fine but the rats under the floorboards or the different types of dogs that connected each story made the idea of conditioning under any kind of leadership, whether related to relationships, class or ownership, unnecessarily confused. But there was plenty of viewpoints to get the ideas across and most importantly it manufactured the grounds for gritty, cultural drama.

Alejandro Gonzáles Iñárittu is known for genre-bending films that blend reality and fantasy with interconnected lives -- see Babel, Birdman, or 21 Grams -- and dramas where a man is something more than human at times -- see Biutiful and The Revenant -- but many claim that his first feature movie Amores Perros loosely, Loves a Bitch may be his best of all, nearly 20 years and many accolades later. It remained the only film of this acclaimed Mexican director I had yet to see, until tonight.
The Oscar-nominated and Golden Globe-nominated Spanish-language film from 2000 weaves three narratives about Mexico City in a dramatic crime story that came to be the first of Iñárittus Trilogy of Death, followed by 21 Grams and Babel. In Amores Perros, longtime veteran Mexican actors Emilio Echevarría and Vanessa Bauche -- and newcomer Gael García Bernal in his breakout role -- are just three of the multiple characters whose lives connect in mysterious, ironic, and sometimes disturbing ways. At various moments, the film is wildly ambitious and tightly constricts what the audience is allowed to know and see at other moments its simply a stirring and occasionally brutal crime thriller.
Using the common themes of dogs (i.e. the bitch pun in the title), class inequity, and violence, its ultimately uniting in a treatise about loyalty and honor. Through three segments, life in Mexico City is given a harsh look, until these very different people are connected by a car crash. Now now, dont you go making a poor comparison to the film I think youre thinking of theres no heavy-handed metaphor here thats simplified into stupidity. We see the before, during, and after in the three coequal narratives about very different people.
This is a challenging film to digest. The triptych of tales -- one of a street punk who is pulled into dog fighting, one of an injured model and her lost dog, and one of a hit man rescuing a wounded Rottweiler -- revolve around two unshakable truths these are all flawed if downright unlikeable people, and many dogs appear to be abused through the story. There is much more under the surface though.
Please be assured though, animal lovers no dogs were harmed in the film. At times, its frankly hard to believe, because the apparent brutality of the dogfighting and abuse is astounding -- as well as a later scene thats horrifically sad, where a dog is only doing what hes been taught. Through some effects and clever editing, though, Iñárittu and crew filmed it all ethically and brutal as it may be, dogfighting was (and remains) an integral part of Mexican street culture. However, much like other trigger warnings, it may be fair to highlight how real it all looks to viewers. So, be forewarned. Promise though, its all just film tricks. Id never watch a film that knowingly participated in animal abuse.
The script, written by Guillermo Arriaga, skillfully grounds the characters lives while also pushing them to the brink. The music and songs which complement the film are wide-ranging and perfect from the aforequoted gangster rap Si Señor by Control Machete to the electro punk Corazón by Titán, the soundtrack is a double album of hits from all sides of Mexican life and culture at the turn of the century. And the cinematography and camerawork are fitting for the grittiness of the film (and its moments of human drama) with handheld shots and low angles looking up at the events as they collide. I couldnt help but assume the perspective is literally that off the dogs vantage point.
There is just so much to love about Amores Perros, a richly layered and deeply thematic film. I try not to quote him too often because its just too easy, but as usual Roger Ebert said it way better than I ever could
It is the work of a born filmmaker, and you can sense Iñárittus passion as he plunges into melodrama, coincidence, sensation and violence. His characters are not the bland, amoral totems of so much modern Hollywood violence, but people with feelings and motives. They want love, money and revenge. They not only love their dogs but desperately depend on them. And it is clear that the lower classes are better at survival than the wealthy, whose confidence comes from their possessions, not their mettle.

Amores Perros can be a very difficult watch for some people. Animal violence is a recurring element throughout the film, with dogfighting playing a major role in the story, so its important to keep that in mind. There were several moments that made me incredibly uncomfortable.
I think the brilliance of this film lies in its screenplay. The story follows three different storylines that become intertwined through a single event. The film is divided into three chapters, but the storytelling itself feels remarkably fluid. Rather than constantly jumping back to recap events or restarting each storyline to bring it to the point where everything connects, the film allows all three stories to develop naturally alongside one another. 
I can only imagine how difficult it must be to pull off something like this, and Im so impressed by how seamlessly everything comes together. The pacing never feels compromised by the structure, it keeps you engaged throughout, and the film manages to avoid unnecessary repetition while giving each storyline enough room to develop. Everything feels carefully positioned.
Despite following such different characters and circumstances, the stories are connected by the pain that love can bring, the consequences of our decisions, and the more violent aspects of human nature. Love is often what drives these characters, but it doesnt necessarily make them better people or lead them towards better choices. Actually, its precisely what brings out the worst in them.

This film is a silent killer. It sneaks up on you, and you cant really see it coming, until its all too late and youre in too deep. 
At first, the way everything just sort of happens can feel jarring and can cause a disconnect, but then everything starts to merge together in a meticulous fashion and the viewer finds themselves not even realizing how hard they had been hit. 
This film has a plethora of hard hitting, beautiful, and effective scenes, all of which are of course driven forward with the great writing, pacing, and performances. Its insane to think that this was a debut, Ive been going a backwards through Iñárritus films up until this point, and its been very interesting to see how similar his style still is, and how nobody really makes films like he does. There have been comparisons made about this film with many others, but to me, this is truly something that stands on its own. 
I also have to commend the use of animals as supporting characters that mean just as much to the plot as the humans do. In fact, without the dogs, there would be truly something missing. They cant speak, but without them this film truly wouldnt be what it is. None of these characters would be who they are, when you think about it. Its a fascinating aspect of this film, and it broke my heart to see these poor animals get affected by this cruel world just as much as their human counterparts. Worst part is, theyre innocent. They dont know exactly what is going on, what the people around them are doing, they rely simply on their instincts. They trust the people around them, that have always cared about them, having no idea what goes on behind the scenes. And they still pay the price. Thats probably what hurts the most. 
Its not an easy watch by any means, but its so quietly beautiful and devastating in a way that makes me feel like it should certainly be talked about more, why is it always left out of the conversation of great debuts? It definitely shouldnt be.
