Oh man, where to begin? This is the one film on the list that I had been eager to rewatch, mostly because I just picked up the Criterion Collection of the film, but also to see how my opinions have changed since I first watched it about a year ago. Set against the chaotic backdrop of Mexico City, this psychological drama weaves together three separate lives connected by a single catastrophic event. The film opens with Octavio (played by Gael García Bernal), a lower-middle-class teenager who falls in love with his abusive brothers wife, Susana. In a desperate scheme to secure enough money to run away with her, he enters his dog Cofi into the dangerous underground world of illegal dogfighting. His path quite literally collides with the two other narratives of the film Valeria, a supermodel navigating the upper class of Mexico, and El Chivo, a mysterious homeless man drifting through the slums of Mexico with a pack of stray dogs. By using a sudden and violent crash to bridge these contrasting worlds, the film sets off a brilliant chain-like reaction that forces each character to confront the raw inescapable consequences of tragedy.
All these overlapping segments are structured beautifully, using each narrative to portray a completely different social class in Mexico, alongside a totally different depiction of love. Octavio and Susanas chapter is all about a naive, fairytale look at love, where desperation blinds them to the harsh reality that things dont always work out the way you hope. Daniel and Valerias upper-class segment shifts the focus towards disloyalty and lust, following the intense fragility of a relationship that is forced to find resilience through the hardest physical and psychological trauma imaginable. Finally, El Chivos narrative displays the rock-bottom of society, showing us a deeply broken man plagued with regret for his self-destructive past, leaving him longing for a chance at redemption with the family he took away from himself.
This intersection of passion and heartbreak among the plots is precisely what drives the films brilliant butterfly-effect plot even further, with each tragedy just as depressing as the next, all occurring from one central accident. The most entertaining of the three is arguably Octavios dogfighting plot, where I will completely admit that the dogfights are incredibly brutal and hard to watch at times, which is why I didnt enjoy this film quite as much the first time around. However, if you can stomach through those sequences, you are rewarded with some of the best storytelling ever put to a Mexican film. The realism behind those fights is extremely impressive to the point where its concerning at times. The production relied on a mix of highly trained dogsprofessional handlers, hyper-realistic mechanical puppets, and clever makeup to make the execution beyond fascinating, even if the scenes are tough to visually process.
The movie is packed with impressive performances across the board. For this to serve as Gael García Bernals film debut is insane, especially considering the legendary status he hss achieved in Mexican and global cinema ever since. The inclusion of legendary Mexican actor Emilio Echevarría also delivers a standout performance as El Chivo. Its awesome to see that these two actors would share the screen again just a year later in the iconic Y Tu Mamá También. 
Im beyond glad to have checked this out again and have it in my collection now, as it stands as one of the most revolutionary films that helped reshape a lot of Mexican and Latin cinema as whole. Its a brilliant and an unforgiving look at tragedies that has you hooked from the beginning, all the way to the final shot.

Given this was his first feature, its probably no surprise, but Amores Perros is very much in keeping with the early films of Iñárritu.
By that I mean ensemble, episodic stories centred around a select few characters whose lives intertwine throughout the narrative.
Honestly, it never really works for me. Just as is the case with both 21 Grams and Babel, I find the incredibly convoluted  and convenient  contrivances end up serving nobody, and whilst the idea these characters all continually cross paths might imply clever construction, it actually just serves to make the universe of the film feel far smaller.
When Robert Altman  the master of this kind of cinema  explores similar narrative structures and storytelling devices, its always in service of the characters. We dont watch Short Cuts to figure out how and why it all comes together in the end its about the journey we take with each of the characters before that moment arrives.
Iñárritu doesnt understand that at this point in his career. Instead, he labours every motif and thematic connection to the point of exhaustion, as if terrified the audience might miss what hes trying to say. The fact he compensates for these shortcomings by reaching for the controversy of dog fighting doesnt do the film any favours either.
For a film that should feel so incendiary, these heavy-handed touches end up making it incredibly fucking dull.

An abrasive, disturbing, and gritty take on hyperlink cinema, somehow even more unpolished than that of Pulp Fiction. Three distinct stories find themselves meeting in the middle of an incredibly idiosyncratic Mexican intersection, both literally and figuratively, and it does a phenomenal job at exploring what it truly means to be a product of your environment. Its uneasy and relentlessly harsh tone catches the audience off guard, but never gratuitously so. Instead, they serve to amplify the films searing commentary on socioeconomic inequality, class division, and survival. The handheld camera technique intensifies the raw atmosphere, drawing the audience uncomfortably close to the action and forcing them to sit with the chaos rather than escape it. Its the kind of film that grabs you by the collar and doesnt let go. By the time the credits roll, youre left with nothing but a sense of nausea.

Una buena manera de empezar el mes es mirando una de las obras mas importantes del cine latinoamericano del siglo, especificamente una que cambió el de México e impulsó tanto la carrera de un gran director asi como de Gael Garcia Bernal, que bueno que faltaba a sus clases de estudio y le dedicó tiempo a esto.
Primero que nada, creo que si esto es tu opera prima ya te podes retirar bastante tranquilo, creando una de las mejores -y seguro que para muchos la mejor- peliculas de historias interconectadas.
Me encanta el uso de cámara durante las dos horas y media, transmitiendote el caos, haciendote sentir cercano y, por ejemplo, en un robo a un banco utilizando los cortes y movimientos rapidos para que el frenetismo sea total. 
Claro que Amores Perros es una película dura de ver, como la vida misma, y es fuerte en lo visual. La crudeza que muestra desde el lente es impresionante, haciendo parecer reales los incidentes que involucran animales por lo gráfico que se muestra.
No buscaría compararla con otras que utilicen la misma composición narrativa ya que creo que esta tiene alma propia como para perder tiempo en eso Es una obra sobre el destino, la venganza, las complicadas relaciones humanas.
Hablando de lo primero, la manera en la que se conectan las tres historias me fascinó mas que en otras similares porque no tiene la necesidad de hacerlo de manera directa, dándonos tres crónicas con su encanto particular que comparten, obviamente, a los perros.
Las típicas composiciones y los sonidos de mi compatriota Santaolalla le dan ese sentimiento de desolación y tristeza, pero que al mismo tiempo en algún momento puede ser tranquilidad. Me encanta como es tan fácil reconocer que el está ahi atrás con sus instrumentos confort.
Lo que es Gael Garcia Bernal en la primera historia me gusta mucho, y también detalles como la decoración en su cuarto stickercitos de autos, poster de Kiss, aparece usando la remera de Scream. Y esa epoca donde usaba esa vestimenta deportiva le sentaba muy bien, envidia.
En el medio, la caída a la locura de Goya Toledo es desesperante de ver. ¿Como podria alguien seguir con su dia a dia con una situación como la de Richie? I could never. No dormiría, no comería, rompería todo el piso y llamaria por ayuda. 
Pero, el desarrollo del personaje de Emilio Echeverria es de lo mejor que vi en un buen tiempito, sin palabras. ¿Vieron como una renovacion de look te cambia la vida?
Creo que es la manera para introducir a alguien de manera misteriosa y generar la necesidad de descubrir mas pero sin apuro porque todo lo que sucede en medio es importante.
Es muy gratificante la sensación de terminar peliculas de esta duración y sentir que no sobró ni faltó nada, cada segundo justificado y solo quedan los aplausos.
Disfruten del arte, abracen y cuiden mucho a sus mascotas, y aprecien cada segundo que nunca se sabe que es lo siguiente, aunque no necesariamente de manera negativa.
Que viva el cine latinoamericano, cabrones.

En ese momento, pensé que había cosas más importantes que estar contigo y tu mamá. Quería componer el mundo para después compartirlo contigo. Como podrás ver, fracasé.
Algunas relaciones están destinadas a salir mal por la naturaleza de muchas personas el egoísmo y el materialismo es algo que a la mayoría les puede más que el amor hacia otra persona, y esta película muestra tres ejemplos de eso mismo. Por medio de tres historias muy duras de ver por su carácter emocional, Iñárritu juega con una dualidad algunas personas son iguales a los perros, o viceversa. Ellos se acompañan mutuamente y son un espejo mutuo en el que los protagonistas se sostienen cuando todo se les va al carajo, cosa que pasa seguido porque en total habré contado dos decisiones inteligentes en las dos horas y media de película. No es una crítica, creo que justamente muchos tomamos pésimas decisiones cuando las cosas se complican.
Las tres historias me gustaron, una en concreto sobresale, pero a su manera cada historia muestra algunas de las formas mas destructivas del amor.
Octavio es la fantasía del marginal que quiere un amor imposible en un lugar mejor, la esperanza de ascender socialmente, iniciando de una forma mas o menos inocente para caer en un lugar aún peor y mas violento que en el que empieza.
Valeria podría ser su opuesto una mujer exitosa y egoísta que vive en una nube de pedos que le impide ver lo frágil que fue su ascenso, y que inevitablemente acabó en una relación tóxica que la lleva a un espiral loco que desesperaría a cualquiera 
Y El Chivo, para mi el mejor personaje, es la cara de el fracaso y la cobardía de reconocerlo, prefiriendo vivir borracho y matando gente antes que dar la cara con sus seres queridos, pero con un final que a su manera logra ser esperanzador, ya que hasta alguien en su situación parece haber encontrado una forma de redimirse sin buscar un perdón que parece inalcanzable.
Como la película une las tres historias en el mismo ambiente es espectacular, y también como cada una se siente como una película independiente por sus cambios narrativos. En concreto el cambio en los puntos de vista de Octavio y Valeria es tremendo.
Difícilmente se puede debutar mejor como director, el cine de Iñárritu es uno al que me costó darle una oportunidad pero sin duda el primer contacto fue muy bueno.

Jarring, moving, confrontational, emotive and deeply sincere. Any great piece of art should possess one or more of these qualities and Hanekes film simply possesses them all. And for me personally, Id like to add soul searing.
I am not that familiar with Hanekes work and the films I have seen by his hand range from brilliant to boring for me. But they all have one thing in common, they are relentless to their audience and their themes. It is therefore intriguing by default when someone like Haneke decides to explore love. 
This is a story that excels in its simplicity. What happens when life long lovers face the inevitable, death? How do they cope? In many a writers hand, this notion would have turned into a shallow, melodramatic affair. Not so here. Hanekes film and script allow no room for romanticism, no free pass for cheap manipulation and certainly no breathing space for the audiences hearts. Make absolutely no mistake, this film is absolutely devastating to watch.
One could argue that this film is boring as not that much happens for a long time. Hanekes way of filming makes us observers, silent ghosts that happen to pass through the final stages of a couples life. We see everything from the mundane to the life altering, we are allowed glimpses of their past and, most importantly, we get to know them. There are moments where I wished I could look away, but Haneke doesnt allow that. There were moments where I wished I could intervene, offer comfort, do something. If you, like me, embrace this couples plight wholeheartedly, this is what this film will do to you.
The two central performances are, simply put, transcendent. They surpass that realm of performers performing. They simply are, its as simple as that. The main reason this film works is because they completely immersethemselves in the roles. Their performances are sincere, genuine and daring. And they kind of wrecked me.
Love is a word with the shallowest connotations. It has been commercialised and for the better part lost all its meaning. It is therefore that in film it often gets the same treatment. It is also, however, the basest of human emotions in all its guises. It is something that should fuel life, be it familial or romantic. What makes this film so beautiful is that it shows love in its fully developed beauty. This is old love, almost a natural symbiosis. And seeing that bond being slowly ripped to shreds by the frailty of the human body is absolutely heartbreaking. Haneke does not shy away from the ugliness of such a union. He dares show the selfish nature of the fear of being alone as well. This is perhaps best shown in a scene I feel every filmmaker should watch to learn something about conveying drama. It is the scene where the husband tries to make the wife drink something. Everything beautiful and ugly about human nature is present in that one short scene. If youve seen the film, you know what I mean. 
I love the fact that we really get to know these people. We get to see snippets of their past life through conversations with friends and family. These are gentle, erudite, dare I say, realistic characters. They share a passion for music that, throughout the film, provides a window out of their misery. Their story is one I am glad I witnessed, even if it made me feel miserable to my bones.
I am hesitant to say this, but I am going to do it anyway. This is an important film. It explores what we are, it doesnt condone or condemn, it relates human nature. It is as beautiful as it is ugly, showing the elated to the mundane and everything in between. It is deserving of a place in cinemas canon as it is a startling depiction of what makes us human.

Georges Laurent does not shed a tear. Age is the greatest sculptor of all. When young, we are afraid, but we pretend not, of what punches life might throw at us. We are afraid of the future, we are afraid of Death, not of our own but of our beloved ones. Age, apart from wilting the physicality and deteriorating the health, infuses great determination and gives humans the solidity to face the pains of life and death unlike any other. Age cleanses us of rashness and enlightens our life with equanimity. Age makes us lose our physical beauty, only to give rise to the truest form of soulful love. Aging is always seen as a one of the greatest enigmas of human life. It is mostly blamed for the superficial miseries it causes. But the way it changes a human being and gives him strength to accept the inevitability of life on earth is always underwhelmed. How aging is the most under-appreciated gift of all is described with great realism and subtlety in Michael Hanekes lifetime achievement.
This is Hanekes love letter to love itself and to the beauty and essentiality of human aging. This is a matured and explicitly honest look at the life of an aging couple. How they deal with the ineluctability of their future with calmness and composure gave me a sense of great admiration towards them and gave a greater sense of imperturbability within myself. Hanekes method of using rigid camera positions and static shots are put to full use here as I was felt locked up with Georges and Anne and the twilight events of their love filled lives. Their lives are shown in full detail. Even the minute parts of everyday life are highlighted here. There is no back ground music at all, none, zilch. And there is a reason to it all. By showing all these seemingly inessential activities without any music, the story unnoticeably creeps up on our subconscious and gives us a feeling of experiencing real life events and not mere actors performing on screen. His cinematography is like a candid camera placed in their house and making us watch their happiness, memories, sorrow, frustration, pain and their lives unfold before us. Such was the beautiful weaving of it with the characters and place such were the performances of the Trintignant and Riva. This method of story-telling became most effective and hit me real hard when I got to experience the shocking event later in the film.
Another thing which I like about Amour is that there are absolutely no diversions. Like his camera, his storyline too focuses all its concentration on a singular plot without any meandering sub plots introduced for the sake of melodrama. This works brilliantly here as we see the couple and we see only them for the entire length. We see other people too but Haneke makes us see those appendages from the view point of Georges and Anne and hence we never move away from them. He never lets us to move away from them. There is absolutely no wavering. I reinstate that this is the reason why I shed tears during the finale even though Georges never flinched and remained resolute. He had age on his side. I am 50 years younger than him. That is why I cried and he did not.
The ending is one of the most superiorly poetic I have ever witnessed. It shows how one can be true to his love even after death. How a person can live with his loved one even after their death. It also gave me hope that age and life experience would definitely make me a person like Georges Laurent. The man is one of the strongest and truest persons I have ever seen. He never winced when The Light of His Life was disappearing. He never forgot her even when he was in the dark.
Death for Georges is just like a photograph. It is just a moment. It can capture his life for just a moment and cannot make him grieve all his remaining life. That moment passes. He lets it pass. The love and soul of his beloved wife will always remain with him. He knows and has always known that Death can never deprive him of that. That is what the miracle of aging has done to him. That is what true love has done to him. He remains true to his love whatever comes.
This, in my opinion, is Hanekes best work and the culmination of a persons admiration for life and love. It would be solemnly poetic if this remains his best work, because it deserves to be. Amour is one of the most realistic, sincerest and extremely honest tributes to love I have ever seen.

When I was seventeen, my father was diagnosed with Alzheimers. Suddenly, this indomitable figure in my life was becoming increasingly infantilized and dependent. I would sometimes have to drive around our neighborhood and find him we could take away his car keys, but we couldnt keep him trapped in our house. Most of the time he seemed blissfully unaware of his circumstances, but at other times I could see in his eyes that he knew he was losing control.
My fathers whole life had revolved around art. He was always eccentric, but now things were at a whole new level. He would start a sentence in 1993 and end it in 1953. If I said new school, he would randomly say that he was a guest lecturer at the New School. If I brought up a baseball game, he would jump to a memory about Ebbets Field in 1950s Brooklyn.
The thing that resonated most about Amour was how stroke, dementia, or any debilitating affliction can transform the dynamics of relationships. The adult becomes a child, and it can be both humiliating and profound. There were small moments when it felt like my father was my son. Long past the time when he recognized me, I would just sit with him and read whatever book I was in the middle of. It didnt matter if it was Hunter S. Thompson, D. H. Lawrence, or Judy Blume he would have the same placid smile on his face, nodding at some moments and nodding off at others. 
The first time I saw my father in a diaper was shocking. This man had gone west in his 20s to be a cowboy. He had run museums in New York City and Paris. He had published books on sculpture, ceramics, and graphic art. And now he was a small child again. These were some of the most disorienting yet profound moments of my life, and somehow it wasnt all heaviness. At some moments certain rough edges of his personality actually seemed smoothed out by the disease. Despite his fragmented and fractured mind, his sense of humor somehow seemed to have improved.
A discussion of Michael Hanekes work always seems to begin and end with his endless provocations and ability to shock. Its clearly a component of his work, but Amour proves how humane and compassionate he is as a filmmaker.  Jean-Luis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva are both fantastic Georges feels a fierce need to close ranks and protect his wife as her condition deteriorates, and Anns feelings of humiliation make it difficult for her to keep fighting. 
My step-mothers role as primary caretaker was just as if not more painful and draining than having the disease itself. I was in high school and college, so while I had a couple responsibilities, I did not experience the relentless stress and anxiety of consistently living with Alzheimers. That kind of love, dedication, and sacrifice is something Ill never forget.

What does love actually become when life strips away dignity, independence, and the version of the person you once knew? Its easy to talk about love when everything is beautiful and stable, but Michael Haneke is interested in something much harsher than that. He looks at love as endurance, obligation, patience, and sacrifice. Georges and Anne are not young lovers caught in passion or fantasy. Theyre two people who have already lived full lives together, and now theyre forced into a stage of existence where love is no longer romantic in the traditional sense. It becomes physical labor, emotional exhaustion, routine, and helplessness. Amour understands that growing old with someone is not just about sharing happiness together, but also about witnessing each other slowly decline in ways neither person can truly prepare for. Theres something deeply unsettling about that because it forces you to confront how fragile the human body really is and how powerless love can sometimes feel against time itself.
What I found most interesting is how the movie tests the limits of devotion. Society romanticizes the idea of unconditional love, but Amour asks what unconditional love actually looks like in practice. At what point does caring for someone stop feeling like affection and start feeling like survival? How much emotional weight can one person carry before exhaustion and resentment begin creeping in? The movie never sensationalizes these questions. In fact, Hanekes direction is so restrained and emotionally cold at times that it almost feels observational, like youre watching life unfold with no dramatic manipulation guiding your feelings. That realism is probably what makes the movie so devastating for many people. It refuses escapism. Its just the slow reality of aging and the emotional isolation that can come with it. You can feel how love here is being stretched to its absolute limit, tested not by betrayal or conflict, but simply by the unbearable reality of watching someone suffer.
At the same time, Ill admit this movie didnt emotionally destroy me in the way I expected it to. I really wanted it to hit me the way The Father did, and unfortunately it never reached that level for me. The Father completely shattered my sense of stability because it immersed me directly into confusion and deterioration from a subjective perspective. Amour, by comparison, feels much more distant and restrained. That isnt necessarily a flaw, because I think Haneke intentionally keeps the audience at arms length to avoid sentimentality, but it did stop the movie from emotionally overwhelming me the way I hoped it would. Even so, I can still appreciate what the movie is trying to say about love and mortality. Its about staying beside someone even when theres nothing beautiful left in the situation except the fact that youre still there. Honestly, that may be the most frightening and honest portrayal of love there is.

A shattering experience. They truly made the most devastating movies in 2012. The Master, The Hunt, Amour.
Pretty much every scene was terribly powerful but I found the penultimate scene to be the most harrowing, even though visually it was nowhere near the most distressing. I guess it all piled up for me right there and seeing the husband as wrecked as his wife had been in her last days was more than I could take.
Amour is comprised of scenes that Hollywood movies would omit for being too boring or uninteresting but this picture focuses on exactly those scenes. In this respect, it resembles life more than it does a movie.  A nearly 10-minute scene of the wife learning to walk again after her stroke with the help of her husband. Just her limping, her right side paralyzed, struggling to progress step by small step, taking heavy breaths, scrunching her eyes shut from the pain, but persevering and managing to walk an almost full circle, all the while her husband calmly beside her, holding her upright, supporting her... Ladies and gentlemen, this is filmmaking at its most vulnerable. Filmmaking at its most powerful.
Amour is the type of movie you appreciate more than you enjoy. You appreciate its absolutely wonderful title choice, its organic artistry with the static camera approach, its timeless message and its leaden gloom whose demolition is magnified by the double nature of love, the everlasting devotion which, in turn, is even more soul-crushing as you see your loved one reduced to a primitive being capable of only screaming Hurts! Hurts! Hurts!, as you stand there, hopeless and helpless, unable to ease her pain... Love, the strongest, the most enduring, the only meaningful emotion in this world of meanness, breaking free of the confines of the movie and devouring everything with its sweeping power, the last bit being mans sanity itself. As I said. Powerful. With all its best and worst qualities walking hand in hand.

Quando se pensa em romance, a imagem mais comum é a de dois jovens descobrindo o amor, enfrentando obstáculos para ficarem juntos. Mas quem estaria disposto a acompanhar a história de um casal já envelhecido, que divide décadas de vida e agora precisa lidar com os desafios trazidos pela velhice e pela doença? O filme é sobre o casamento. Sobre a vida a dois em sua forma mais crua. A relação que já conheceu o entusiasmo da juventude, que superou crises, e que hoje vive no espaço da rotina e da serenidade. A paixão deu lugar ao amor, à parceria e ao cuidado. É interessante perceber que, em Amor, a palavra que dá nome ao filme não é mencionada uma única vez ao longo das duas horas de projeção. Conforme a narrativa avança, entendemos que se trata de uma trama simples, mas de enorme carga emocional, onde os pequenos gestos carregam mais significado do que a própria palavra amor.
Georges e Anne ocupam o tempo frequentando concertos, lendo bons livros e ouvindo música clássica. Certa manhã, algo inesperado acontece. Enquanto tomam café juntos, Anne fica subitamente imóvel, com o olhar fixo e ausente, como se estivesse em transe. Georges tenta chamá-la, mas não obtém resposta. Ele umedece um pano e coloca sobre a cabeça dela, sem sucesso. Desesperado, sai da cozinha em busca de ajuda, deixando a torneira aberta. Ao retornar, encontra Anne falando normalmente e reclamando da água desperdiçada. Georges explica o que viu, mas ela não se recorda de nada. Ele acredita que seja uma brincadeira até perceber que não é, e que Anne está tão assustada quanto ele. Procuram o médico da família, que indica uma cirurgia para desobstruir a carótida, mas o procedimento traz complicações. Anne sofre um derrame e perde os movimentos do lado direito do corpo. A partir desse momento, tudo se agrava e a relação dos dois é levada ao limite.
A solidão é o eixo central em Amor. O apartamento permanece quase sempre mergulhado na penumbra, sustentado por uma fotografia fria que intensifica os longos silêncios. As noites parecem intermináveis, preenchidas apenas pelo som da respiração cansada do casal. Michael Haneke, fiel à sua estética rigorosa, opta por cortes abruptos e pela câmera fixa, que observa os cômodos como uma testemunha muda. Anne e Georges atravessam o ocaso de suas vidas. A filha os visita de forma esporádica. No entanto, o vínculo que mantém com os pais se enfraquece à medida que a saúde da mãe, debilitada por dois derrames, se agrava, e o pai precisa encarar escolhas dolorosas. Haneke retrata a velhice como um exílio silencioso, em um presente que perdeu a reverência pela memória e pelas histórias.
Outro ponto central do filme é a forma com que ele retrata as perdas do final da vida. Uma cena que se destaca nesse sentido mostra Anne chamando Georges para ajudá-la a se levantar do vaso sanitário após urinar. Haneke mantém sua câmera fixa, marca registrada de sua direção, em um plano frontal longo o suficiente para que o espectador sinta quase a obrigação de encarar a situação. O cineasta nos faz partilhar do constrangimento profundo que envolve tanto a esposa fragilizada quanto o marido que a assiste. A imobilidade de Anne, sua demência crescente e a fala lenta e gemida na segunda metade do filme tornam a rotina do casal ainda mais pesada e dolorosa.
O amor e o carinho se manifestam quando ele a ajuda a se mover da cadeira de rodas para a cama ou para outro assento, e também nas memórias que compartilham sobre a vida, os anos passados e o esforço constante de cuidar, mesmo diante do sofrimento e da iminência da morte. Esse afeto se revela na presença ininterrupta que ambos oferecem um ao outro. No entanto, ele desaparece no momento em que ele tira a vida dela, um gesto carregado de desespero frente à solidão, à monotonia e à dor de uma existência esgotada. O amor ressurge em sua própria morte, numa busca de reencontro com a pessoa amada. As duas cenas com o pombo, uma no meio da narrativa e outra no final, têm grande carga simbólica e refletem o estado emocional do protagonista. Depois de cometer o ato, ele se depara novamente com a ave no corredor e, desta vez, a acolhe, compreendendo que ali se encerra o ciclo de ambos, um instante de aceitação da morte e do que foi feito.

Hanekes use of technique is perfection in Amour, but the themes he draws on get lost in a film so transparent and simple that little extra can found after a cursory analysis. Yet simplicity is the greatest virtue of Amour, its strengths coming from its lack of pretension and deep humanity, despite its cold arthouse exterior. This is pretty shallow stuff for Haneke, but that just means hes being less cynical. Theres a couple of aspects that hint at more, notably a pigeon metaphor that I just dont understand, but Amour is pretty much what it appears at face value.
One of the greatest fears that we have is our own loss of identity, or alternatively having to watch someone else lose theirs. With that loss, with our soul burned away, comes a loss of dignity, a humiliation to be endured or be witnessed. Amour is, to an extent, the story of being a burden, of not wanting to go on, perhaps even of not wanting love. Hanekes cold perversity in calling this film Amour reminds us that hes the master of ironic detachment. This is a film of death above all else, and love is only secondary.
The male lead tells a story in an early scene, recounting not the events but the emotional imprint they left on his life. Reality doesnt remain with us, just the shape of our emotional sprawl. That may well be the greatest success of Amour, not that it is a memorable film, but that it leaves an emotional imprint that will linger for a while.

Amour es una obra maestra y la mejor película de Michael Haneke, una cinta sin ningún defecto más allá de que el ritmo pueda ser algo que moleste a algún que otro espectador, pero se me hace muy redonda en todos los aspectos, contando una historia muy emotiva con personajes entrañables y muy reales.
Sinopsis Los maestros de música retirados Georges y Anne han pasado sus vidas dedicados a sus carreras y ellos mismos. Su relación enfrenta el desafío más grande cuando Anne sufre un derrame cerebral. A pesar de que Georges sufre los dolores y achaques de la vejez, valientemente ignora sus incomodidades para cuidar a su esposa, y está decidido a mantener su promesa para que ella no regrese al hospital.
La historia es excelente, puede resultar un poco pesada pero es muy interesante. Es una trama que se desarrolla muy lentamente, pero es un ritmo muy adecuado para lo que quiere contar, siendo algo que puede resultar un poco difícil de ver al tener en cuenta que es algo que pasa en la vida real y es bastante triste que sea así. En general el ritmo es lento y puede hacer que a algunas personas no les atrape tanto, pero creo que arranca excelente y te engancha muy bien, recién en la última media hora es donde se me hizo un poquito larga, justo en los momentos más fuertes es cuando se termina haciendo más pesada. Por otro lado, cuenta con algunas escenas dramáticas brillantes que logran pegar bastante fuerte, es de esas películas que al terminar te dejan reflexionando sobre todo lo que acabaste de ver y sobre la vida en general. Además, el romance es sensacional, me imaginaba que iba a conectar porque es una historia sobre dos personas mayores que pasaron toda su vida juntos y se siguen amando hasta el último día, construyéndose de una manera maravillosa para lograr emocionarte siempre que pueda. Por último, algo que me encantó es que casi toda la historia se desarrolla en un mismo lugar, lo que también se complementa con varios planos secuencias donde nos presentan la casa y el entorno de una manera perfecta para que ya tengamos en la cabeza toda la estructura del departamento.
Los personajes son maravillosos, dos protagonistas memorables. Georges y Anne son una pareja que tras una vida juntos afrontan su mayor problema cuando ella sufre un derrame cerebral, algo que cambia la vida de ambos y lo lleva a él a tener que hacer todo lo posible para mantener su promesa de no llevarla al hospital. La historia nos muestra a lo que puede llegar una persona por amor, ya que el hombre hace todo lo posible para cuidar a su esposa incluso cuando él también tiene que confrontar todas las consecuencias de esto, causándole mucho cansancio o dolor. El romance entre ambos está perfectamente desarrollado, creo que vemos lo suficiente de ellos antes de que el conflicto comience, lo que nos hace darnos cuenta todavía más de lo que cambió su vida y también su relación. Por último, de los demás personajes la única que destaca es su hija Eva, quien hace algunas intervenciones en la historia pero tampoco me parece tan buen personaje como los dos protagonistas, simplemente hace lo que se debe durante la trama.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente las actuaciones de Jean-Louis Trintignant y Emmanuelle Riva dos actores increíbles que quizás hicieron el mejor papel de su carrera, demostrando que sin importar la edad todavía podes lucirte y hacer una interpretación digna de varios premios. Por otro lado, el trabajo de Michael Haneke en guion y dirección es espectacular, acá me parece que destaca más por el guion que por las visuales, aunque el trabajo detrás de los planos secuencia que vemos también es para destacar.
En conclusión, una excelente película fantásticamente interpretada y con una dirección espectacular por parte de Haneke, un director que cada vez me gusta más y me demuestra que hasta puede hacer obras maestras que pueden perdurar con el tiempo. Muy recomendada.

our minds were nowhere near anything serious, we were on vacation, just enjoying ourselves with absolutely nothing on our minds beyond having a good time. eventually the man left the conversation ended, and everything went back to normal
but today, while rewatching Amour that same sentence came back to me.
love isnt what you do with your wife in bed.
and i started thinking. id watch the film, get lost in my thoughts return to the screen, then start thinking again, as the story unfolded, images and meanings id never really considered before slowly began to make sense.
i started thinking about georges and anne, about the life theyd shared the years theyd spent together before we ever meet them at that stage of their lives, and all the little details we never get to see but that must have made up their world.
how many ordinary days had they spent together? how many casual conversations, laughs, and quiet mornings had passed between them without either of them imagining that one day, they might wish they could return to them?
i thought about how differently we understand love when were young compared to what we might come to understand after decades of living.
when youre young, love can feel like waiting for someones text, hoping a phone call wont end, or counting down the days until you see someone again. you worry about who loves the other more, whos waiting for a reply, or what to buy for a birthday.
just like us, sitting in that café in rome, laughing and talking about our little lives without having the slightest idea how much life can change, or how many meanings love can take on that we havent even begun to imagine.
when you watch two people who have grown old together, and one of them begins to lose their health and the ability to live the way they once did you start to understand that all those years they shared werent just time passing. they were an entire life.

i began to understand why that sentence had come back to me, why i couldnt get it out of my head while watching the film, maybe that man was talking about a kind of love we simply hadnt experienced yet. a love that stretches far beyond the beautiful beginnings, into the days when caring for someone becomes part of your everyday life and into the years when words and promises no longer seem enough to express what having someone beside you really means.
i dont know if that was what he actually meant, but i couldnt stop wondering about his life and what he might have experienced to say something like that so casually, maybe hed spent decades with his wife. maybe theyd been through things a stranger could never imagine maybe he had an entire story he wanted to share with us, while we sat there laughing, completely unaware of everything his words might have carried beneath the surface.

god, we were so stupid that day, we were laughing at a man we knew absolutely nothing about. we didnt know how much life hed lived, what hed been through, or whether those words carried a story of his own, maybe maybee he was trying to tell us something we wouldnt understand until years later. or maybe he didnt mean any of it that way. ill never know.

i wish i could go back to that day, not to change anything significant but simply to listen to him this time, to give him the few minutes of genuine attention we never gave him and ask what he meant by that sentence we laughed at for so long.
maybe he wouldve told me his story maybe he wouldve just smiled and walked away without saying anything else.

Amour is a film about the disappearance of a human beingof what one man does in the face of losing the woman he has loved his whole life, every day, little by little. Amour tells the story of George  Anne an elderly couple well into their eighties who are living a life of retired piano teachers in Paris. I have been putting of watching Amour for a long, long time.  I knew it would be a great film.  I knew it would be somber.  I knew it would be soul crushing.  It was check, check, check.
Director Michael Haneke does not shy away from the uncomfortable and unavoidable dark moments of the human experience.  Aging and elder care is something that will challenge nearly everyone at some point during their life. Amour looks at these issues with a stark, unblinking eye.  His film does not rush to move from one plot point to another.  Instead, it lingers, painfully, and makes us feel the desperation and anguish of Georges (the husband) and he tries to care for and love his failing wife (Anne).  The long shots of Anne trying to read a book, or simply stand and move, or taking a shower with a nurses help, or feeding, or having her adult diaper changed seem to just go on and on.  You dont just get a quick jolt of the sadness and pain, you are forced to  wallow in it.
Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva, both French actors with  long and accomplished cinematic careers, give performances that may be their greatest.  The emotions, love, and empathy conveyed with simple gestures and expressions is great acting.
One of the best classes I ever took in college was called Death and Dying.  The class examined customs and cultural beliefs from many religions and societies around the world the and across time.  Nearly everyone struggles with finding a dignified way to address those moments towards then when a loved one is no longer themselves and is suffering.  Euthanasia is accepted as a viable option in some cultures and a mortal sin in others.  One Cherokee tradition address the situation by allowing those near the end to choose (not be forced) to just walk away from the village, lie down, and return to nature.  Other cultures make it the norm for the failing elderly to return to the family to be cared for by many, rather than just one.
Watching this movie will make you reflect on your personal beliefs on these issues.  Perhaps psychedelic journalist Hunter S Thompson (Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas) had the best take on end of life times Life should not be a journey to the grave with the intention of arriving safely in a pretty and well preserved body, but rather to skid in broadside in a cloud of smoke, thoroughly used up, totally worn out, and loudly proclaiming, Wow! What a ride!

Amour is an intricate and subtly crafted film that addresses love in the face of sickness and death. Starring Emmanuelle Riva, who appeared in Alain Resnais first feature-length work, Hiroshima mon amour, the film sees her delivering an incredible performance as Anne Laurent, a retired music teacher.
One morning while she is eating breakfast with her husband Georges (Jean-Louis Trintignant), she silently suffers a stroke that paralyses her bodys right side. Riva gets to play her character as fully healthy, partially paralysed, and then utterly dependent on others for her care. Alongside Trintignant, who also delivers an accomplished performance, they extract heartrending power from their tiniest moments together within their claustrophobic apartment.
Haneke, who is never voyeuristic through the film, wholeheartedly rejects the idea of death as a communal experience, presenting the slow act of dying as an intensely isolating experience. Theres meticulous staging from the Austrian film director and screenwriter of Annes physical degeneration through gestures from which neither she nor her husband can escape.
Haneke furthermore creates the couples apartments setting to be a meaningful character theres a heavy significance given to portals such as doorways and windows, constantly being closed, opened or locked. The central hallway seemingly represents the passage of life. The various rooms leading off from it being the now compartmentalised chapters of Anne and Georges life together with the camera becoming fixated increasingly on empty spaces.
Love takes shape as a largely abstract concept as the film shows Georges mechanics trying to care for all of Annes needs, from wheeling her around the apartment to helping her to the toilet. Its both subtle and well balanced in its combined elements of psychological horror and drama while also avoiding melodrama. It deservingly saw Riva become, at 85, the oldest nominee for an Academy Awards for Best Actress in a Leading Role.

Das Altern, ein Gerüst wie das eigene Heim. Es wird erbaut, Stein auf Stein auf Stein, sein Mörtel, das eigene vergossene Blut und der eigene von einem abtropfenden Schweiß mühseliger und langwieriger Arbeiten, investierter Zeit, geraubter Kraft in Aufopferung des eigenen Wohlseins und das Vernachlässigen der Liebsten. 
Ob Zeuge oder Täter bei der Verrichtung von Wundern binnen Wochen und Monaten, ein aus dem Boden gestampfter Kelch unzähliger Hände und unzähliger Zeit multipliziert zu hunderten zum Wohle komprimiert für einige wenige als das eigene Wohl ein Heim erbaut zu haben. Das Fundament ach so wallender Fruchtbarkeit steht und will den Samen Leben empfangen, ihn in seinem Schoss betten und ausbrüten. 
So wird das Heim mit Leben und Existenzen gefüllt, aus den Fenstern der Freiheit wird die Geborgenheit einer eingekuschelten Wolldecke, aus der Leere wird die Wärme aus Schränken, Kommoden, Tischen und Stühlen, Sofas und dem eigenen Bett ob in natura, bemalt oder behangen. 
Als dann gehen die Jahre und Jahrzehnte glücklicher Augenblicke gedehnt auf Stunden und Tage dahin, der Mörtel aus Blut und Schweiß verliert seine Haftung, Risse entstehen die sich ausdehnen, ein Wurzelgeflecht wie der Stammbaum und dessen Verästelung zu Millionen. 
Der Kelch unzähliger Hände erbaut zum Wohl des anderen als das eigene Wohl, wird plötzlich zum Fänger der undichten Stellen der Tropfen und ihr plopp, plopp, plopp. 
Er füllt sich schließlich, Tropfen auf Tropfen auf Tropfen bis er überschwappt, das Heim unterwandernd des Sklaventreibers und zu dessen umfänglichen Sklaven werdend und die Liebsten gefangen ihres eigenen Lebens eingefangen in den eigenen Vierwänden. 

In Michael Hanekes Werk Liebe ist der Tropfen Alzheimer der Klangkörper der sich ausdehnt, an den Wänden abprallt und wiederhalt. Der überschwappende Kelch ist die eigene Hilflosigkeit mit ansehen zu müssen, wie er sich unaufhörlich füllt, wogegen jedes Abschöpfen ein Kampf gegen Windmühlen ist. 
Wie eben das unstetige Wetter, tropft die undichte Stelle am Dach einmal langsamer und einmal schneller, folgt nach einem Gewitter und einem Schwall auf den Fußboden klatschenden Wassers eine Besserung des Betroffenen, ein Hoffnungsschimmer wie das hinter dem Rücken gezückte und begierige Messer. 
Alzheimer ist ein schleichender Prozess, ein über Jahre vorausgehender Krankheitsverlauf, so lässt sich Liebe beschreiben er ist gemächlich, schlurft anstellte zu sprinten oder im Laufschritt zu gehen wo Hecheln und Krämpfe einen niederzwingen als Folge dessen, bleibt Hanekes Werk ein rhythmisches Atmen und wie hier, ein Atmen im Beisammensein seiner großen einen Liebe.

Daqui tô vendo o amor irritado, desapontado... Mas também vejo outras coisas vejo beijos que se beijam, ouço mãos que se conversam e que viajam sem mapa. Vejo também muitas outras coisas que não ouso compreender..., O Amor Bate na Aorta, de Carlos Drummond de Andrade.
Imagine amar tanto alguém a ponto de matar essa pessoa? Essa seria uma questão conflitante dentro de distintos níveis interpretativos, e minha visão quanto ao filme não se esquivaria dessa contradição. Antes, quero dizer que Anne, uma senhora de idade avançada, parece definhar conforme os dias passam. Primeiro, é o lado esquerdo de seu corpo que se paralisa e, antes que já nem tivesse controle sobre as próprias escolhas, faz o marido prometer algo não leve-me ao hospital novamente. Acho lindo a forma de como, mesmo hesitante, ele acata seu desejo. O amor, dentro dessa obra, se expande para o conjunto de nós, porque, antes de pensar em sua relação com Anne, presta respeito e admiração por ela enquanto ser individual e isso é algo raro, quase inexistente dentro de filmes sobre amor romântico e, naturalmente, idealizado. Mas a questão é que a rotina junto à esposa doente vira um estado sólido, sinônimo de fadiga, desgaste e cansaço. Isso só se intensifica quando, mesmo esgotado, ele precisa manter a promessa. E, por mais que cumpra exatamente isso, acaba a matando por sufocamento no final. Amor nunca extinguiu impulsos de medo, raiva ou desespero ele segue, enfim, como um sentimento diluído sobre todos os demais.
Antes de tentar refletir sobre qualquer outra coisa, fui sequestrado por revolta. Como ele pode ter sido tão egoísta? E por que tratou a filha como sem o direito de discutir sobre a condição da própria mãe?, eu pensava. Tentei observar brechas que me fizessem compreender mais a fundo sem, é claro, tentar justificar. Não há uma só resposta, mas existe a indiscutível razão de que, sobretudo, também havia amor naquela ação. Em minha visão, George a amou tanto que sacrificou a presença de Anne, e essa é a coisa mais potente que já vi.
Há uma cena dentro de tudo isso que me marcou bastante. Anne estava comendo com o marido quando pede a ele o álbum de fotografias. Enquanto passa as folhas, ela deixa escapar algo abstrato olha.... George pergunta o que exatamente, e a senhora responde A vida. Isso se torna ainda mais alarmante no momento em que percebemos que a própria já não se sentia daquela forma. Já não se podia fazer qualquer outra coisa que a revigorava, bem como tocar instrumentos ou ler certos livros. Essa reflexão me fez pensar como George pode ter matado um corpo que já estava morto?. 
O símbolo da pomba intensifica-se quando o casal aparece junto no final. Para mim, é a representação do amor como algo que transcende uma mera presença física. Anne e George vivem nas paredes, nas pinturas, no chão e na cama onde dormiam.
Antes de assistir ao filme, julguei o título. Na minha opinião, era um tanto genérico, o tipo de nome que poderia ser facilmente confundido diante de outras obras com uma temática semelhante a essa. Mas hoje eu sei que não haveria título melhor senão Amour. Porque, nessa produção, há várias esferas do tal sentimento o amor romântico, o afetivo e, como dito no verso inicial, outros que vão além de nossa compreensão.
Confesso que, até a escrita desta review, o filme era um 3,5. O ritmo lento me causava irritação, e não que eu deteste obras contemplativas a questão é que elas excediam um limite de espaço. Eram paradas, mas nos davam noção de diversos lugares, o que causava dinamismo. Essa obra não ela acontece quase que completamente dentro da casa, algo que sufoca. É uma escolha artística consciente, um retrato do cotidiano que passa a abafar, a adoecer. Não posso ignorar toda a complexidade do filme em detrimento do ritmo que, por sua vez, também é essencial no que se diz respeito ao entendimento de outros fatores.

Amour is very difficult to review.  It is a near perfect film, but kind of boring. It is essential viewing but too slow and subtle to recommend to anyone.
Henekes film is about an older couple who face illness, degeneration and death. Told with no sentimentality, it is the perfect look at the reality of living with someone who is ill and taking care of them. The scenes are slow paced and I mean slow paced, and some scenes are Tarkovsky long. It would not take much to fall asleep in this film. And yet there is no other way to tell this story. This is what love looks like behind closed doors. This is what it looks like when caring from someone. It is a deeply personal experience, where any  knock on the door is an invasion of privacy, any kind of pretense to previous normality is unwelcome. Caring for the love of your life, losing the love of your life is not to be shared.  It is slow, it is painful, and it is practical. And when all interaction with the love of your life is impossible, when the person you love is no longer there to share your life in any meaningful way, all that is left is to love them, care for them and ensure they get the dignity and respect they deserve. 
This may sound easy it may sound obvious, but it isnt.  Too may people associate loving someone with how that person makes them feel. They love someone because of something. When that because is no longer a possiblity, the wayside seems like a pretty decent option. 
This film portrays love with no conditions, and what that love looks like when two people in love are being transformed by illness.  My initial reaction was that it was a masterpiece, even though I never want to see it again. Now I wonder if perhaps the film was a little too slow and subtle to raise the questions in us that we will all have to answer.  I hope not.

En el cine de Michael Haneke el amor no es una promesa ni una caricia, es resistencia. No se mide en besos, sino en la forma en que alguien permanece cuando todo lo demás se derrumba. En Amour, ese sentimiento se desnuda hasta los huesos. 
Haneke arranca las palabras, los gestos y hasta la dignidad, para mostrarnos lo que queda cuando el cuerpo se rinde y solo persiste el vínculo. Anne y Georges viven su vejez como un pacto silencioso. En su apartamento enfrentan la lenta descomposición de una vida compartida. La película encierra la cámara con ellos, sin escapes ni consuelos. El amor aquí no es redención, es carga. Es el dolor de sostener al otro cuando ya no queda nada que sostener. Haneke filma la degradación física con frialdad, pero detrás de esa distancia late una ternura feroz. La crueldad del director nunca es gratuita, su rigor es una forma de respeto.

Im not sure why, but this little ditty from a certain Elvis A Presley came to mind as I was watching Amour.  A film about connection, love, pain and lifelong commitment.
Considering the simplicity of the story, the level of detail in this film is astonishing.  A film about two eighty-somethings caring Georges and gentle ex teacher Anne who suffers a debilitating stroke.
When you spend decades with someone, things can become routine. In younger life that might be considered as stale or boring, but as you get older routine can equate more to stability, and safety.  The small, seemingly inconsequential moments in the partnership between these two characters following Annes stroke are what makes this stand out as a recent top-tier French drama.  Feeding each other, the washing of hair when your partner cant reach, providing an interesting book to stimulate their mind when they cant get out of bed.
We do this for our partners not because we feel obliged to, or we feel bad about the situation.  We do it instinctively as part of the deeply connected partnership formed over decades on this crazy little ball we call home.  The prospect of dealing with life without our other half after all the years is, well, terrifying.
So, the movie takes us through the mundanities of life while cleverly forming a bond between the viewer and each of the main characters.  Weve seen Michael Haneke do this over and over in Cache, Funny Games and the Piano Teacher for example. Genius direction.
It all adds up to a wonderfully drawn picture of the two halves of this relationship making a whole.  This couple have truly become one and it is beautiful to watch, through the steady and devastating decline in Annes health.  There is a natural arc to the film and though I instinctively knew where it was heading, the journey was still emotionally traumatic.  Im not crying.  Nope, its hayfever.  Stoopid eyes.
Gorgeous filmcraft and wonderful performances from Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva make it all quite real, and a film that Im sure will leave a mark on me for some time.

In 2011, an underrated Icelandic jewel was released. It was called Eldfjall (Volcano), a film centered around an aged man that has been distanced from his family and wants to make ammends while confronting his past. This transformation is greatly influenced by his wife, who gets considerably ill and, against the opposition of many, including his own distanced family which grows suspicious because of his suddenly benign behavior, decides to take care of her instead of putting her wife in a home for the deceased.
The conclusion the film offered was considered extremely realistic, but proportionally shocking, finding a memorable place in the minds of the audiences.
With enough time, Haneke literally remakes the film, sharing a surprising amount of similarities, including key plot scenes, for unfolding his new amour testament, making an interesting mix between his signature style that predominated in his early essays about views on violence, and the hauntingly passive and peaceful style that abounded in his immaculate The White Ribbon (2009). Some cinephile entity within me is screaming loudly to call Haneke a ripoff, but another objective side is struggling against that exaggeration, forcing me to pay attention to how Haneke, even if he copies the most basic concepts of another film (he seriously did that), has enough capacity to add a strong substance of his own and consolidate his currently justified auteur status like a true boss does.
This substance is the one that matters the most in this review. Haneke has always been concerned with elevating the audiences status as authentic spectators. Every scene, gesture, stare, silence and shot is carefully designed to make the situations as tangible to the viewer as possible, creating some authentic sense of realism and dredd, in both the beautiful and in the menacing situations. Everything is there for a reason, and the even the smallest details communicate things of significant human value. The characteristic pace proves these intentions. This effect is just accentuated by two extraordinary leading performances of two well renowned French cinematic legends in acting Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva.
Looking back at the overall reception Amour had, my perception about the still respectable Cannes Film Festival having a bias favoring French films is strengthened, but at least their selection of French contestants remains exquisite. Few times can the modern forces of celluloid reunite such significant acting figures, including the amazing Huppert, and deliver an impactful powerhouse of reflection about the repercussions of love and the consequences of impotence, especially when the harsh circumstances are affecting the ones closest to you.
Floating around the 10th spot of Hanekes best films, Amour is a memorable event that, despite my small complaints, I strongly recommend.

The quiet contentment of two retired music teachers (Emmanuelle Riva and Jean-Louis Trintignant) is turned upside down when Riva suffers a stroke. It paralyzes her entire right side. Her condition worsens when medical treatment fails. Riva extracts a promise from Trintignant not to send her back to the hospital, but that promise gets increasingly difficult to keep. Apart from the expense of hiring part-time nurses to help him take care of her, the caretaking process itself takes a physical and emotional toll on Trintignant, who is elderly, too, and is often stiff if not actually frail. It soon becomes clear that Rivas progressive deterioration is inevitable and irreversible. At what point does extending her life serve a meaningful purpose? Shes constantly in pain or a mental fog, and Trintignant is grappling with his own sorrow and growing resentment. Is it kinder to hold on or let go?
Watching this at a time when my 90-year-old father is struggling to recover from a recent bout of pneumonia and my 82-year-old mother is showing signs of cognitive decline was both unnerving and cathartic. Writer-director Michael Haneke, whose films I sometimes find overly cold and even cruel, uses his detached, unsentimental style in a deeply humane way here. Like other of his films, Amour confronts its characters and viewers with unwelcome violence, but that violence  the simple fact that life ends  is universal and mundane, not sensational. The problems Trintignant and Riva face (watching a loved one fade and die or, eventually, confronting our mortality) are problems we, too, are going to face if we havent already. Amours hard look at the reality of cognitive and physical decline is empathetic in a way I rarely find Hanekes other work, which occasionally strikes me as smug. A warm grace infuses this film.
A lot of the credit for that warmth comes from its leads. Riva, who received an Oscar nomination (the oldest nominee ever in that category), and Trintignant are excellent. Rivas characters physical decline is so believable that we begin to pity her. When she becomes petulant, spitting the water Trintignant tries to get her to drink in his face, we understand the anger, exhaustion, and helplessness that motivate it. When Trintignant responds by slapping her, we understand his frustration, especially his frustration with himself. He loves Riva and never breaks his promise to take care of her so that she can stay in their home. But at what point might he begin to hate her for putting him through this and making these his last memories of her? Even when he takes drastic action late in the film  this is a Haneke film after all  it makes sense. 
What makes this film a minor masterpiece, in my opinion, is its transcendent climax. Without giving too much away, Haneke gives Riva and Trintignant a final moment together. The implication is that death offers us a chance to wake up from the dream of life  a dream that can turn into a nightmare under certain circumstances. As I said above, I found it genuinely cathartic. Then again, Amours topic has been on my mind lately, and I saw a bit too much of myself in the couples middle-aged daughter (Isabelle Huppert), who lives so far away from them that she really has no idea what theyre going through and is shocked when she catches glimpses of it. Shes in for an even bigger shock, and the films final shot is of her, the survivor who is still (for now) in the prime of life, processing it all. 
Amour reminded me a lot of Simone de Beauvoirs classic account of her mothers final illness and death, A Very Easy Death. I doubt the parallels between the film and the book are accidental the (relatively) healthy family members perspective, the sense of irony, and the existential questions about how people want to die and how the rest of us let them. I suspect Hanekes also familiar with Leo Tolstoys short novel The Death of Ivan Ilyich, which popped into my head, too (though much less frequently). But with the presence of Riva and Trintignant  two icons of French cinema  its hard not to read the film as a contemplation of the passing into history of a particular era of arthouse cinema, to which Haneke and Huppert are heir. That impression was particularly strong for me this time around, now that Riva and Trintignant are gone.

A solemn and sullen slowburn that soaks in the various challenges one elderly couple faces as Father Time begins to creep up. Michael Haneke is a bold director known for his cold, calculated, and callous style of filmmaking yet the emotional provocation hes able to evoke through even the bleakest of subject matter is unmatched and on full display here.
Death is a terrifying thought on its own but the idea of our bodies drastically decaying as we age to the point of disease and disability is downright depressing. We experience this vicious and visceral sensation from the perspectives of both victim and caretaker here with neither one offering much catharsis other than the fact that were all in this together. Its a haunting examination of what it means to reach the end of your life and be forced to patiently await you and your partners demise, doing all you can to help ease the pain and the burden.
Having witnessed my grandparents deal with this in a similar manner, I cant help but view this as more exploitative rather than profound at times. I understand the nature of Haneke is to create a thoughtful and melancholic watch about unconditional love in the face of death but my personal relationship to the story hit a little too close to home for me to properly immerse myself in it.
Nonetheless, its a spiritual study of the human condition in its most raw and vulnerable form as it acknowledges the elderly and the inevitable waiting for us all in a way that few films ever have. Haneke can be a difficult director to connect to depending on your taste but this is undoubtedly one of his finest works for all the truth, pain, love, and life it has to offer.

It doesnt happen gradually, it happens in one quick moment. In the opening minutes of Amour, we see the final night before Georges and Anne hit the wall  their lives soon after will no longer be about leisure or enjoyment, but about maintaining a routine just to stay alive a little bit longer and make the pain of dying more bearable. The film isnt necessarily presenting reflections on the finality of life as much as it asks us what the point of living is if life is already over. Anne can sit in front of the piano and pretend to play for as long as she wants, but the song will never come back to her.

A masterpiece, one that has you shaken while it is going on. Amour (Austrian, French language in English subtitles) is about the final days of an elderly couple together. Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva are the long-married octogenarian couple facing the unwanted final stages of old age. Director Michael Haneke (The Piano Teacher, Caché) shoots with an unyielding directness and crispness, capturing long gazes as the wife Anna goes from active and alert in an introductory scene, to carotid malfunction, to paralysis on the right side of her body, to dementia. She at one point takes a conscious rejection of her husband Georges care, a half-spoken uttering of desire to die.
People from the outside, including their daughter (Isabelle Huppert), visit for a few minutes to offer their opinion of how Georges is doing his caretaker job. If they were only there hour after hour to see what he goes through. He is the only one that has spent 24 straight hours with her, and beyond. He momentarily brings aboard a licensed caregiver that he must fire. The caregiver is found to be mistreating the wife, but according to her, Georges must be old and senile. Nobody knows of his dedication. Nobody knows either that after decades of marriage, only Georges would know how to interpret Annas unspoken communication.
In some of the more touching passages, Georges opens up with stories from inside himself that have been locked up his entire lifetime. They were too embarrassing to share, but now he does with his wife while she is hurtling to the end. He can share with his wife not just the stories, but the humility. Trintignant (age 82) has acted for decades but has been missing from the screen for years. In the 1994 Polish masterpiece Red he played a judge who was discovered by others that he had been a longtime voyeur, tapping in on peoples conversations. These are the two best pieces of his career, both performances embodying long dormant shame.
For Riva, she has a career that goes back even longer. Most famously for Riva is Hiroshima, Mon Amour (France, 1959), which dealt with mass deaths and survival in the aftermath of the WWII Tokyo bombings. A film about aging and the end of a natural lifespan is almost innately subversive, when we consider all Hollywood has done to spearhead the general worship of youth in Western culture. Early in Amour, Anne has Georges promise never to take her back to the hospital, out of concern for her comfort and dignity, on the face of it, but also in defiance of the out of sight, out of mind philosophy toward aging that seems to inform such innovations as Botox and assisted living. Her resolution not to go on if she can help it is only secondarily motivated by the feeling shes become a burden to Georges she says, rather, its for my own sake. Here shes violating another social norm religions decline has yet to dispel from society the traditionally Christian assumption that our lives are not our own to take.
Michael Haneke shows a fair bit of audacity in titling a film Love. After meeting Georges and Anne, though, Ill admit that he earns it. Love (as I see it), being oriented toward the good of the other person, requires a certain amount of self-sacrifice. Having honored Annes request to stay in their apartment, Georges proves his devotion time after time, from morning speech exercises to spoon-feeding to bedtime stories about his own early life, and, most heartrendingly, by helping her walk while holding her to him and guiding her feeble steps in rhythm across the floor, just as though the two lovers were engaged in a slow dance.
As was the case in Hanekes first Palme dOr winner The White Ribbon, non-diegetic music is absent from Amour. Instead he goes the opposite direction, allowing drawn-out silences to fill the interstices of the scenes. In these moments, which often show Anne supine in bed and staring into the middle distance, the reflective tendency of an individual on the verge of eternity is transmitted to the viewer, so that we imagine Anne looking back on all shed done on Earth, scarcely sure whether Emmanuelle Rivas expression betrays regret or simply physical agony. Narratively Haneke has already shown his hand in the opening scene weve seen her head encircled with petals on the pillow all that remains to be discovered, then, is whether Georges, in a last self-sacrifice, has followed her out the door.

Though Jean-Louis Trintignants Georges and Emmanuelle Rivas Anne, Michael Haneke crafts a masterful display of real world, universal struggles. Cracking open and laying bare a future bound for almost all of us at one point in our lives, caring for a dying loved one. Its something that is impossible to grasp and fully comprehend unless youve experienced it, no amount of love and patience you have for someone can prepare you for the pain and torment as you watch the them melt away. Their once exuberant life force, memories and experiences slowly slip away day by day like sand through clutched hands. The carer is often left with just the fragments of their once grand existence, dreaming of even just a few weeks earlier when they were more lucid. Early in Amour, even before her stroke, Anne has a bout of paranoia about an invader within her home. 
But its only as the film kicks into its second act that we realise that invasion was taking place within her own body all along. Internally she is fighting a battle. Her brain is attacking her. That bout of paranoia was almost a premonition of what was to come. Nothing is going to invade the house from outside. The real danger, transforming it into a quasi horror film, is within her own flesh. With the delicate flashbacks of their earlier happiness, Haneke really shows the quintessential life of these two people. The harmonious existence that theyve led together, which makes their suffering all the more unbearable. Their apartment, once a beautiful safe-place of content happiness and understanding, steadily transforms into a space of sadness, pain, decay and eventually death. In the end, it becomes their tomb.
Things will go on, and then one day it will all be over.

After watching Vortex recently, I had to see where Gaspar got his obvious inspiration for the film. And Amour is certainly the powerful force that pushed him towards another work about old age and love. Amour has  much different qualities as it goes on further down the road. It is uncomfortable, unsettling, heartbreaking, and bitter sweet in the strangest way possible. Haneke and Gaspar certainly share similarities  in their obviously sadistic manners , but they get a little soft on us in both of their films about dying. Haneke still seems to provide scenes of heavily emotional matter , but he combines it with a cruel yet sweet wisdom. His message is a tough one to take in, clearly displaying what love becomes at old age and what you do for the person that you love. But also the way in which this love gives death meaning. And our little pieces of wisdom or touching memories that also build more on this meaning of love. Theres so much to analyze in a film like this without going off into another direction. Superbly acted and so well written I think that older actors seem to carry such a  meaningful presence and sprit. Their obvious wisdom to the job as an actor is shown in the best way throughout Amour. Certainly , an almost perfect film , to me at least. And definitely one of Hanekes best. Michael Haneke virou sem dúvida um dos meus cineastas preferidos por causa da maneira como ele retrata os seus temas de forma brutal e intransigente. The Piano Teacher foi minha porta de entrada para a sua filmografia e eu já pude ver logo de cara a sua visão profunda acerca das complexidades que envolvem repressão sexual e psicologia Isabelle Huppert dando uma das melhores atuações da história do cinema. Em Funny Games, o diretor despertava nossa indignação pela forma como ele nos provocava a olhar para aquela família sendo feita de refém por dois jovens inconsequentes aquela sequência de 10 minutos foi uma das coisas mais aterrorizantes e perturbadoras que eu já presenciei. Agora, nesta review, eu falarei sobre Amour, um dos filmes talvez mais acessíveis de Haneke, mas que consegue com muita eficiência dilacerar totalmente o seu coração do começo ao fim. Acompanhamos um casal de idosos, Georges e Anne, ambos ex-professores de piano, morando no lindo apartamento deles. Percebemos desde o início que os dois se amam profundamente eles se comunicam perfeitamente um com o outro e parecem se entender em todos os aspectos. Só que, quando Anne tem um derrame silencioso durante uma manhã, as coisas parecem se complicar. O que vemos a partir daí é Georges tomando conta de sua esposa com o maior cuidado e paciência do mundo, enquanto ela definha cada vez mais aos poucos. 
Gostei muito da forma como esse filme começa o serviço de emergência arromba a porta do apartamento dos protagonistas, encontra o quarto do casal totalmente vedado por fita isolante e mais tarde descobre o cadáver de Anne em perfeita posição e adornada com flores. Por que ela estava naquele estado de decomposição dentro daquela casa? Onde está o marido àquelas horas? Será que ela se matou? Quem era ela? São as diversas perguntas que acabam brotando na nossa mente naquele momento. E é logo após essa primeira cena que a gente vai acompanhando cronologicamente os acontecimentos para descobrir o que houve de fato naquele lugar e desvendar os segredos por trás dessa tragédia. 
Esta obra me fez notar bastante os típicos artifícios técnicos que o Haneke utiliza para construir as suas histórias. Ele gosta de cenas bem longas e planos médios e abertos, que trazem realismo e uma naturalidade nas interações entre os personagens é como se a gente estivesse flagrando um pouco do cotidiano deles, observando as nuances, o equilíbrio e a harmonia desse relacionamento. Os cortes abruptos das cenas são outro detalhe importante que faz uma enorme diferença na forma como a gente enxerga esse filme. A sensação que nos traz é que não estamos vendo um drama ficcional, mas uma história real com pessoais reais sendo retratadas. A ausência de trilha sonora em praticamente toda a extensão da narrativa também intensifica a nossa conexão com Georges e Anne, que estão presenciando momentos delicados em suas vidas. E, assim como os outros trabalhos de Haneke, esta trama se sustenta principalmente através dos silêncios entre os diálogos, como um convite a mergulhar profundamente no difícil e complicado estado emocional do casal. 
Eu simplesmente amei as interpretações avassaladoras dos atores principais. Se a Emmanuelle Riva já tinha brilhado com sua atuação maravilhosa em Hiroshima Mon Amour, aqui ela realmente transcende tudo! Foi doloroso e triste ver como a sua personagem vai enfrentando o declínio físico e mental não há nenhuma rede de segurança ao qual se apoiar nesse filme e a atriz, de forma destemida e sem medo, nos presenteia com uma interpretação fortíssima e muito íntima que carrega absolutamente tudo. O mérito também deve ser dado ao Jean-Louis Trintignant, que eu o vi pela primeira vez em O Conformista e que aqui consegue uma atuação mais refinada, trazendo mais camadas ao seu personagem e trabalhando de maneira fenomenal o aspecto dramático da história. 
Com relação à temática do filme, eu senti que Haneke quis explorar igualmente a situação complicada em que Georges acaba ficando. Ele dedica todo o seu tempo e esforço no cuidado de sua esposa, e isso acaba consumindo drasticamente sua energia conforme o tempo vai passando. O que o diretor parece querer desenvolver com maior necessidade dessa forma não é o enfraquecimento de Anne, mas o amor mais puro e genuíno que Georges sente por ela, que lhe dá força e resistência para todo dia acordar cedo e cuidar da sua companheira. Tanto que a dor e a compaixão sentida por ele ao vê-la cada vez mais fraca é tamanha que culmina naquela cena muito pesada envolvendo um travesseiro. Para mim foi um baque instantâneo, foi tão rápido e inesperado que eu nem sabia o que pensar direito porém, ao mesmo tempo, eu senti no fundo que talvez essa solução drástica tivesse sido o melhor a ser feito em nome da dignidade de Anne. É um sofrimento indescritível que eu não desejaria isso nem para o meu pior inimigo! 
O final deixa em aberto o destino do protagonista, o que foi uma decisão muito interessante para que aquele sentimento que nós tínhamos presenciado anteriormente continuasse ressoando com intensidade dentro dos nossos corações. Os créditos começaram a passar na tela em um silêncio absoluto, o que acentuou ainda mais o que eu estava sentindo não pude acreditar no tanto que esta história tinha me impactado. Enfim, Michael Haneke novamente nos destruindo por dentro e expondo a nossa vulnerabilidade e fraqueza graças aos temas delicados que ele discute.

Michael Haneke drops his unrelenting sadism found in the likes of CACHÉ and THE PIANO TEACHER for something much more empathetic, and in doing so creates a work that is meditative and melancholic, in part thanks to tremendous performances from Jean-Louis Trintignant, Emmanuelle Riva, and Isabelle Huppert, as well as reliably stellar work from cinematographer Darius Khondji. Simultaneously grim yet full of warmth, Amour is my favorite work Ive seen from Haneke thus far. An absolute masterpiece.
