amar é cuidar, proteger, enfrentar desafios e obstáculos impostos pelo destino. Amour retrata isso da forma mais linda e dolorosa possível, e é através de um casal de idosos que tudo isso é posto à prova. Jean-Louis Trintignant e Emmanuelle Riva são atores bastante renomados na França e aqui eles reforçam suas reputações dando um show de perfomances devastadoras e descomunais, tanto que rendeu a atriz a nomeação ao Oscar. Ambos interpretam dois músicos aposentados e admiradores da cultura erudita que tem sua relação interrompida, entretanto que não se esvaecem de amor e reciprocidade, característica que os uniu durante uma longa vida conjugal até aquele determinado ponto. Sentimos na pele o que amoroso Georges passa com sua esposa Anne, que de uma hora pra outra, se deparam com sua vida conjugal se despedaçar por causa de um derrame que torna a senhora debilitada e incapaz, tendo apenas seu querido marido para cuidar dela. O drama de Michael Haneke se ambienta quase que inteiramente no apartamento do casal, cuja a mobília denota uma vida de bom agrado e bastante realizadora, onde conhecemos gostos peculiares dos idosos, exemplo bastante presente disso é a música. Outrossim, logo após a ruptura inesperada, o cenário gradualmente vai perdendo seu brilhantismo quando equipamentos hospitalares e medicamentos ocupam espaços enormes do aconchego as artes e pinturas antes bastante notáveis em meio ao ambiente, agora não passam de uma decoração a parte. O que antes era uma residência de pessoas experientes e cultas, não passava mais de um mausoléu. Amour é uma jornada cheia de idas e vindas, que nos mostra como podemos estar desfrutando da vida ao lado daqueles que amamos hoje, e de repente, num piscar de olhos, tudo isso pode sumir. Quando nos damos conta, o impacto final pode destruir completamente o que está à beira do colapso. Esta é uma dádiva escondida entre muitos, ademais, sua preciosidade convém de uma das histórias mais bem construídas e conduzidas por possuir aspectos tão imersivos e didáticos em toda a história do cinema francês.

An artful and deeply affecting exploration of aging and long-term companionship. It moves with a methodical slowness that feels mundane, to the point of being quietly immersive. Like youre not just watching these lives unfold, but living in them. And when the central incident strikes, its absolutely devastating in its inevitability.
Becoming old and fragile is one of my greatest fears, as it probably is for many, but theres something strangely beautiful about it, too. Its a marker of having lived, of having experienced love, pain, and everything in between. I think Haneke deeply understands that duality, and it comes through in every frame of this film.
Watching Amour isnt exactly pleasant, in fact, it feels like a bit of a burden at times, not unlike Jeanne Dielman. But thats part of the point. It embeds you in the routine, in the emotional and physical weight of being near the end. And in retrospect, thats where its greatest strength lies not necessarily in what it shows, but in what it evokes and allows you to think about even after it ends.

Anne and Georges Paris apartment has the humble look of two long lives taken root. But Haneke gives it a wintry feel dark with warm lamps reaching out from the edges casting a feeble glow. Its symbolic of their stage of life, now slipping into the shadows of old age. Their familiar ease is shaken one day when Anne freezes mid conversation, vacant like a statue, only to return to normal again a minute later, with no memory of what happened. Except things will never be normal again. Its the first slip in a savage decline that robs her of her freedom and dignity and robs Georges of the love of his life. 
After a series of strokes and a failed operation, Anne is paralysed down one side and her immobility leads to insecurity and her helplessness to hopelessness. Georges does everything he can to nurse her in their apartment but his own slow decline cant support her rapid deterioration. He starts to suffer anxiety dreams, and his relationship with their daughter suffers.
Most of us are desperate to keep living for as long as we can, but everyone who lives to be old must suffer, and every old person who loses a lover must suffer again. As you get old the physical dysfunction and pain you feel, and the things you took for granted that made you who you were are lost, slowly and inexorably, or else suddenly and irreversibly. And the loss exposes you to the limits of State care, and the insensitivities of youth. My decline has begun, and while I can still run a half marathon, there are bits of me that are not so vital. I worry that one day I will be a burden to my wife. Shes a lot younger than me and so if we last the distance Ill likely fail first. I hope we can afford care so that I dont drag her down, and I hope that if I am too much of a burden, and my quality of life poor, then I will still have the wits and guts about me to choose euthanasia. 
Anne only has Georges. She says she doesnt want to live, but he cant accept it. His love is too strong, and where there is love there is hope, but Anne is not getting better, and instead gets worse in frightening lurches. Considering this is the fate of many people, it is remarkable how unrepresented this reality is in film. Often death in old age is sentimentalised - the graceful drawing of the curtains on a life full of light. But in reality, death is often cruel and agonising. 
Haneke is famous for making films that are cruel and agonising, and that is what makes Amour such a distinctively Hanekeian film. But in other respects it breaks new ground for the Austrian auteur. Here his direction is characteristically precise, but his hand is far less visible. Its a chamber work, set mostly inside the couples apartment, and he keeps things very quiet. The soundtrack captures the noises of lifes scrapes and squeaks as a chair is moved or a door closed, and the noise of the outside world recedes to the occasional coo of a pigeon. And theres music too, mostly in the form of Schubert, that great chronicler of death. Georges and Anne are both musicians, and the way she loses her ability to play and even enjoy music is crushing. 
I had two old friends who I used to live next door to for a year when I was a child and see regularly thereafter. They were great music aficionados with enormous speakers that resembled the monoliths in 2001, and they were part of the reason I fell in love with classical music. Geoff died just over a year ago, nearing 90 years of age, while Gretel struggles on. She still listens to music every night which gives me hope that despite its capacity to imprint memories that inevitably become tainted with loss and sadness, she still prefers that over silence. For Anne and Georges though, it is too much. Even while she is still mobile in a wheelchair, Anne struggles to listen to her student prodigy performing one of Beethovens Bagatelles. The youthful passion embodied in the music is now lost to her forever. 
The musician who performs for her is the real life French concert pianist Alexandre Tharaud. His cameo is an interesting one for showing a young virtuoso with the technical skills to dazzle, but at a loss to know how to deal with real tragedy. It is a subtle commentary on the need to experience life if you are to really understand the tragedy of its music. 
I dont usually focus my reviews on the acting, but I greatly appreciated seeing two actors who were famous in their youth, now in their twilight, giving such astonishing performances. My memories of their youthful potency is still fresh, having seen Emmanuelle Riva recently in Leon Morin, Priest, and Jean-Louis Trintignant in Il Sorpasso and My Night with Maud. Seeing them now, in such intimate proximity, and in such distress, with their bodies shocked into frailty, is a sobering experience that really helps me feel the cruelty of old age. Haneke does well to tone down his direction and let the characters speak for themselves. He doesnt allow any sentimentality to sweeten the blows, but the brilliance of the acting ensures the blows hit hard and hurt bad.

My girlfriends guide me to watch Haneke 
Its a very tender film about a pair of elderly people who, after one suffers an accident, are forced to take care of the other. In part, the film seems like a combination of Leo McCareys great work, Make Way for Tomorrow, and Peter Docters Up, of course, with Michael Hanekes cold, cruel, and human style characteristic of the film.
It may be ironic, but here Haneke captures his most tender and beautiful view of love overall, its a love letter to affection. Its warm in its simplicity, human in all its actions, and the performances are impressive, both from Emmanuelle Riva and Jean-Louis Trintignant, who capture the most tender love in their eyes, looks, and gestures. I would even say that, above the script and Hanekes always brilliant direction, they are the driving force of the film. They carry the weight of something Haneke knows isnt his strong suit tenderness.
Its beautiful how love is portrayed here, always with care, always concerned for her, whether she knows it or not.  Its one of the most beautiful testaments to the tenderness of love, that beautiful thing we have, and when we lose it, well miss it forever.
Deep down, I wish I was like that, had something like that, achieved something like that. To have that love with which I could be tender and care for it until its final days and miss it. It would be beautiful to miss it after having cared for it, after having done whatever it asked of me to make it well. I already have it, now. I want to get to that point, and its not a short road...
It may be strange to see Haneke directing this film, but he probably needed to direct his love letter to love.

My mom died in 2024 after several years of battling Parkinsons. She stayed at home until the end, and my dad took care of her, feeding her, bathing her, and helping her in the bathroom, and doing almost nothing but take care of her, despite also working full time. When she went into hospice he never left her side for 2 weeks.
When I say this film reminds me of that experience, what I really mean is that this is so accurate, comprehensive, and true, that I felt re-traumatized. The moaning, the mood swings, the inability to speak or think or walk, the sippy cups, the refusal to eat or drink, the ignominious bathing of a shrinking body, the sundowning, the empty horrified baby-like stares, thats all a very real walking nightmare for many. Emmanuelle Rivas performance was horrifyingly, spectacularly accurate. All the details and specifics of this felt eerily familiar--my mom was also a former pianist (among many other thingsthat was just one of her many degrees), and they live in a home full of books and wingback chairs. The sound of my childhood memory is my mom playing Chopin. Like the husband in this film, my dad also stopped sleeping in their communal bed, and slept in a little bed in a room next door to my mom. He still sleeps in that little bed. He too, went through a period of magical thinking, equating the birds that he and my mom would watch at the bird-feeder as some sort of messenger spirits or psychopomps. And like Jean-Louis Trintignants character, he keeps the door to her bedroom closed, and goes to bed every night hoping he would wake (or not) to a different world, where shes still around.
The criticism for this film, and Haneke in general, is that he is cold, and distant. Ive found most of his films unpleasant, cruel, or at the very least aggressively challenging. I went into this with my dukes up, ready to sneer at his slow cinema and icy European intellectualism. You know when people get married and they say
From this day forward, for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, until parted by death. This is my solemn vow
Amour encapsulates this vow and puts it forth on screen. This is a heartbreaking portrayal of growing old. An inevitability that most people face in life. Amour is a heartbreaking study on growing old with your spouse and caring for them when they can no longer care for themselves.
Following this old man care for his slowly dying wife is tragic and painful. You feel these sentiments transcend the screen through the fantastic performances from Jean-Louis Trintignant (Georges) and Emmanuelle Riva (Anne). Seeing their arc as a a fading pair feels so genuine on screen. Seeing Anne slowly lose herself to illness is tough to watch. More tragically Id argue, seeing Georges not only lose his wife to illness but lose himself through the process of caring for her is tragic to watch.
I credit Director Michael Haneke as a filmmaker who shoots scenes in static long takes with minimal cuts, only cutting when the scene deems necessary and never has this style of his been more effective than in this film. This fly on the wall, observational esque cinematography is powerful. It sets the stage for this tragic story to unfold properly and without barriers.
Amour is a heartbreakingly meditative film that had a profound impact on me by the films end. A film that really puts life into perspective and makes you think about your future and those that you love now and those that youll love in the future.

De una simplicidad que se torna su mayor virtud y una honestidad demoledora, la película completa es una crónica de amor, vejez, compasión y lealtad donde el guión te rompe el corazón y las performances te lo trituran.

An engrossing and harrowing experience, Amour chronicles the end stage of Annes life after she suffers a stroke. Her devoted husband Georges attempts to take care of her even though he is physically compromised by old age himself.  Ive seen a few of Hanekes other films, so I expected it to be extremely dark, unsentimental, and bleak.  Instead, I think its incredibly human and warm, like he wants to make Georges the most lovable villain you could ever imagine.  He doesnt want to romanticize the love story weve all seen in other films.  Instead, I feel like he wants to ground it in the hardest-to-watch variety of realism that seems to suit his incisive view of human nature. 
Emmanuelle Rivas performance is an absolute revelation.  Shes able to convince you from the very beginning that Anne has a history and flaws that inform her decision to guilt Georges into keeping her out of the hospital.  The film is much more focused on how Georges is dealing with Annes illness.  He becomes the main decision maker and is forced to defend and explain his actions to those who know little of what he deals with on a daily basis.  His exchange with a nurse cuts you right to your core as you come to realize he has very few people he can trust to aid him.  The way Jean-louis Trintignant portrays the loneliness pervading every look he gives to Anne is mesmerizing and heartbreaking.  A powerhouse performance that is best when he gives tiny hints to his frustration and inner struggle.
I was hoping for more flashbacks than the very few Haneke peppered in, because being able to imagine them younger and happier wouldve helped clarify some of Georges actions.  The fact that he murders Anne and then lovingly surrounds her body with flowers suggests that he was trying to put her out of her misery.  The way I read it was that he had grown tired of being without the Anne he once knew.  To the outside world, he was stoically handling the situation, like he was noble for honoring Annes wishes to stay out of the hospital at all costs.  In my opinion, it was cowardly of him to take her life without letting her illness run its course.  I could also see the situation as a sort of implied assisted suicide, in which a healthy Anne would condone Georges final act.  I can see her taking that as the ultimate act of love.  The ending also leaves it open to the fact that he may have killed himself at the end.  Then it really becomes about you hoping that theyre together and happy on the other side.
I went in expecting an extremely depressing story about two aging lovebirds slowly drifting away from each other due to a fatal illness.  What I came away with was a story of how selfish people can be when faced with soul-crushing loss.  I didnt become as emotionally invested as I thought I would, but I found myself thinking of the film for hours and days after it ended.  Haneke deserves an Academy Award because hes able to successfully mask the fact that Amour, one of the most devastatingly beautiful love stories ever put to film, is really about a murder.  Well-played, Haneke. Well-played.

When I saw this film, written and directed by Michael Haneke, at MIFF2012, I was working as the Projects Manager at Palliative Care Victoria where one of my projects was developing an awareness campaign to promote discussions about Advance Directives and substitute decision-making.  Part of that campaign had a focus on the importance with Alzheimers of planning ahead so that your wishes could be set out clearly for when you were no longer able to make your own decisions.
Haneke begins the film at its end point, then tells several months of the story as a flashback.  We see retired Parisian piano teachers, Anne (Emmanuelle Riva) and Georges (Jean-Louis Trintignant) Laurent, both in their 80s, at a piano recital by one of Annes former pupils.  Next morning, at the breakfast table, Anne has a stroke, and from that point on the film becomes a chamber work as Annes world shrinks from the couples apartment to her bedroom as Haneke chronicles, often in excruciating detail, Annes physical and  psychological decline and its impact on Georges.  
Riva and Trintignant work off each other intuitively, but this time it was Trintignant who really impressed me - his use of his physical skills rather than dialogue, to convey Georges pain and retreat into his own fantasy world as he watches, more or less helplessly, as the love of his life disappears in front of him, is a master class in non-verbal acting.  
One of the early clients (1988) that I took care of as a homecare volunteer at the Queensland AIDS Council was an American anthropologist, Eric Michaels. The title of Erics AIDS memoir, Unbecoming (Empress Publishing, 1990), worked on two levels - the unbecoming physical indignities involved in a long process of decline into death and the multiple changes involved in your position in the world as you un-become.  The scene in which Annes naked body is manipulated by a homecare nurse who is bathing her in a way that seems to ignore her personhood, even as she is carrying out an intensely personal task, ties together both of Erics meanings in the way he would have recognised immediately.
Watched an Umbrella DCP as part of Melbourne Cinémathèques season Continental Divide The Unflinching Vision of Michael Haneke.  Alex Williams film notes are available online at Senses of Cinema.

Amour begins as the movie ends with residents from an apartment building in Paris, France complaining of a smell.  When they open the door, they find the body of Anne (Emmanuelle Riva) lying in bed.
Anne and her husband Georges (Jean-Louis Trintigant) are retired piano teachers who are coming home after attending the recital of one of Annes former students.  The next morning during breakfast, Anne has a stroke which leaves her in a brief catatonic state.  Georges does everything he can to communicate with her and gets nothing.  When she finally comes back, she does not recall the situation at all and Georges is unable to get Anne to receive medical attention.
Anne has a failed surgery to unblock her carotid artery, and as a result, she is left paralyzed down her right side and wheelchair bound.  Georges and Anne must learn to live their day-to-day lives all over again with Georges being trained on how to keep Anne fed, clean, and exercised. Anne makes Georges promise not to hospitalize her no matter how tough her situation gets and Georges agrees. Day by day, the situation gets tougher and tougher for Georges, their children, and all who knew Anne to see her deteriorate.  Finally, Georges decides to end both of their struggles by suffocating Anne with a pillow. Georges dolls Anne up and tapes the door shut. The movie ends with their daughter, Eva, sitting in the now empty home.
I rarely give movies 5 stars, but Amour absolutely deserves the rating.  The film takes you on the highs, lows, and everything in between of living with a medical issue as well as the impact it has on those around you. I myself dealt with this as I watched my grandparents who I once saw as such strong individuals wither away over the years.  The movie touched me in ways I never knew a film could. The film is so honest and open and the acting performances were for the ages.  Emmanuelle Riva not winning Best Actress for this timeless performance is a snub of the ages. Amour will stick with me for a while.

Witnessing stories like this always evokes a deep sense of empathy and concern for the future that lies ahead for me.
In sickness and in health is really tested here.
This movie had a lot going against it. The slow pacing. No music to move it along. Static camera shots. Not based on a true story. Not much of a plot. Finding the right time to watch such a heavy movie.
The prospect of transitioning from our daily routines to a life governed by stringent medical oversight in our last years in itself is daunting and the mere thought of facing unforeseen illnesses or unexpected tragedies without any of our loved ones nearby is even scarier.
I extend my heartfelt admiration to all those elderly couples who, despite confronting significant challenges, remain steadfast in their commitment to each others safety and well-being.
Their willingness to be each others unwavering support embodies the profound love that many of us yearn for but few are fortunate enough to behold.
The opportunity to have a beloved companion by your side, unconditionally, amidst trying times is a true blessing. If you find yourself surrounded by the love and warmth of those dear to you in your moments of need, consider yourself incredibly lucky.
Haneke, as the director, poignantly illustrates this very sentiment through the narrative of Georges and Anne, albeit with his characteristic bleak and nihilistic conclusion that leaves a sour aftertaste.

Im about to violate my own rule about giving away too much personal information online. If youre not interested in that, please feel free to skip this, but I feel its necessary to describe where Im at with Amour.
My mom died on January 4th, 2018. Cancer sucks. It had metastasized, and she had chosen to not undergo treatment once it was found to be as aggressive as it was. Everyone informed understood her perspective the treatment was set to take quite a lot out of her, and the potential benefit was minimal. She also chose not to enter hospice, and lived out her final few months at home with her husband. 
Her birthday was on Christmas Eve, so I brought my daughters, then aged 5 and 11, over for a few hours both that day and the next. I had seen my mom just the week before, and we talked every day, as we always did. But on her birthday, something was noticeably wrong. While most of what she said was fine, she was starting to stumble over words. I asked if she was okay, and she said she was just tired. All good, I took her at her word.
When we returned the next day for Christmas, she was unable to articulate a coherent thought together for more than a few words, much like what happens in this movie with Anne (Emmanuelle Riva). The speech patterns were stilted, unusual, the words were all English but didnt make sense as a string of thought. The only lucid thought she got out that day was when she pulled me aside privately and said, Dont bring the girls back here.
This is not a terribly unique experience. Plenty of people have had loved ones pass, and under very similar circumstances. Im also not looking for any expressions of sympathy or empathy by bringing any of this up, as you have gone through something similar, as well, Im sure. And, as far as the movie tells us, Annes body fails her after a stroke, so the parallel isnt perfect.
But Im always going to remember that sinking feeling when my moms speech wasnt right. And I point it out because I was left pretty cold seeing it again. Ive already been through this, so there was nothing for me to glean from this film. There is no deeper understanding for me to get from this. I already got that experience, just like so many others have.
Is it a well-made film? Sure. My moms death didnt have a controversial final act, so I guess thats something, but I also found that so alien to my own way of thinking that I just blew it off. Im sure the movie is an effective portraiture of processing change and grief to many, and I hope that everyone else who watched it got something from it. I didnt. It didnt put me in an emotional place, it didnt jog up sniffles or anything like that, it just  left me flat entirely. Thats possibly a very strange reaction, but we all carry our own weird baggage, and mine didnt let me connect with any of this material.

Ingeniously balancing beauty with horror from start to finish, Black Swan is a harrowing depiction of a passion turning into an obsession which ultimately sets in motion a chain of events that results in complete self-destruction. Apart from being one of the best offerings of its year, this psychosexual thriller is also Darren Aronofskys finest work since his 2000 manic Requiem for a Dream.
The story concerns Nina Seyers, a highly skilled ballet dancer who is chosen as the ballerina for her ballet companys next play Swan Lake. Perfect in the role of the delicate  innocent White Swan character, Nina fails to convincingly pull off the personality that is required for the sly  sensual Black Swan. And in her desperate attempt to get into the psych of this dark character, she begins to lose all grips on her sanity  eventually ends up discovering a dark side of herself.
After starting his filmmaking journey with Pi, Aronofsky has managed to stand out with films that deal with a central theme of obsession and at times leave a scar. And this time, he brings the same destructive theme of obsession into the world of ballet dancing and delivers the goods yet again by recreating the winning magic of his previous feature, except that this time around his direction feels much more refined  complete.
Crafted with meticulous care, beautifully scripted and executed with precision, this insane cinematic piece is as much a winner in technical aspects as it is in narration. Art direction  cinematography create  capture the ballet environment in an eerie yet delightful fashion. Editing is finely executed. Clint Mansell delivers an intensely strong  haunting score which, despite being based on an existing ballet score, stays very original  faithful to the films plot.
Coming to the performances, the picture features a dependable cast in Natalie Portman, Mila Kunis, Vincent Cassel, Barbara Hershey  Winona Ryder and under Aronofskys supervision, every one a fantastic job, especially Portman who delivers an immensely mystifying performance as Nina which easily goes down as her career-best work so far. Mila Kunis also deserves a mention for an incredibly seductive rendition of her role.
On an overall scale, Black Swan is a bizarre, beautiful  bewildering study of madness and a thrilling piece of aesthetic filmmaking. It is a tragic tale of striving for perfection and how at times it backfires, often resulting in terrible consequences. A must for fans of Aronofsky, a must for fans of psychological thrillers and a must for anyone who appreciates good cinema, this psychosexual horror comes strongly recommended.

Natalie Portman stars as Nina, the lead dancer for Swan Lake. In order to achieve artistic perfection, this also means it will cost her own sanity and even turn her own role much like that of Odile, the Black Swan - just as she finds her own life beginning to parallel that of Swan Lake while not being a literal follow beat by beat. To try my best to avoid comparing Black Swan to films that have already handled similar stories better (The Red Shoes and Perfect Blue, the latter of which Aronofsky himself had purchased the rights for in order to recreate a scene in Requiem for a Dream), Ill get it out of the way that Black Swan is already telling a story that has been done before, which is the least of my own problems with it. Rather instead, my immense dislike of Black Swan lies within how it tells what weve already seen before as it only comes off as needlessly exploitative of her own misery in favour of artistic perfection.
This sort of pessimism was one thing that has always stuck out most from my own viewing of Requiem for a Dream. Darren Aronofsky relishes in it by placing so much on the surface, and the most aggravating aspect of said film came from how it further pushes down upon an agreeable message without expanding on it by growing increasingly worse on the surface. In Black Swans scenario, it seems to be the same for presenting Ninas misery of working within the world of dancing, where shes forced to grow into the sort of person that she is in order to achieve artistic perfection, which is where Aronofsky loses subtlety with the narrative, for hes always played upon melodrama like a sledgehammer - something that Id also find myself appreciating more if this film werent taking itself as seriously as it was. By Aronofskys lens, it only believes in misery and its an extremely oppressive one at that.
Among many more of its own exploits, Ninas forced sexual growth as a result of her own instructor as played by Vincent Cassel also brings up another one of its biggest faults. Theres an uncomfortable male gaze coming in with every minute of the interactions between Lily and Nina, for their own homosexuality feels portrayed as a fantasy for the outside as opposed to a part of themselves. But how Black Swan goes away with handling its idea of duality is perhaps the most troubling aspect, because it revels in another overused trope from horror movies split personalities. But considering how many times it shifts between identities without setting a distinguished tone for each, it all feels like worthless meandering. Everything that the film wants to be feels present on the surface, tossed out in favour of another idea, then brought back at the last minute theres no thought coming forth as opposed to broad self-indulgence.
If Natalie Portman were even any good in Black Swan, then Id be convinced that a film destroying artistic perfection truly is baked out to be the way it is, but coming back to the artificiality of the films narrative, most of the cast only strikes me as mechanical. Perhaps part of this comes from me not being a fan of Natalie Portman, but her hallucinatory performance only strikes me as overdone - like a bad mix of melodrama and horror tropes. The whole cast feels so mechanical, almost as much as the dancing itself, but that adds more to why I find Black Swan so ingenuine - it just seems to pride itself on aggressiveness in the same manner that Aronofsky had went on to pride himself on appearing more intelligent than it actually is, for its all just bare bones we see. Aronofsky doesnt blur the line between a hallucination and reality, and as a result the final reveal only feels anticlimactic.
Sometimes I wish I was able to appreciate Darren Aronofsky the way I know many of my peers do, but other than The Wrestler and The Fountain hes only seemed to let me down with every film after another. I wont deny that hes good at what he does, and I see why these films carry the appeal they do - but I just find Black Swan so unpleasant an experience even to think about. Theres no subtlety present in Black Swan, but at the same time I dont see much point when I know already I recognize so much of it as derivative of many other films that have handled a similar outlining better - for they dont indulge in the needless exploitation that Black Swan does. It all feels so sleazy in the sense that Brian De Palma was, although without being any bit as fun or as interesting - because the lack of subtlety only shows an evident lack of self-reflexivity on Darren Aronofskys part, for its all kept on the surface. I suppose this indulgence would have its appeal for some, but clearly not me.

The story of Nina, a ballerina in a New York City ballet company whose life is completely consumed by dance, is incredible. Capsulating me from the very first minute, to the last utterly breathtaking sequence. 
This is, without a doubt, a tour de force, a work that fully lives up to its directors ambitions, creating 103 minutes of pure anxiety inducing beauty. Director Darren Aronofsky captures everything beautifully in frame, his movement of the camera is almost as fluent as the very dancers on the screen, his use of behind the head vantage shots allow us to transport into the mind of the characters, experiencing their thoughts as if our own, and his use of lighting is nothing short of extraordinary. She absolutely dominates the screen, exhibiting a controlled screen presence against the backdrop of her characters ever-fluctuating mind. Alongside Mila Kunis and Vincent Cassel, who are both fantastic as the sly rival and suspicious teacher, Portman delivers one of the best performances of the decade, truly deserving the Academy Award. 
Part thriller, part drama and heavily swaying into the psychological horror territory, Black Swan perfectly captures the anxiety some performers battle with when trying to perfect their dream role. By the end, Ninas quest for perfection-and Portmans remarkable performance-will leave you breathless and that, for me, is what instantaneously dazzled me. A truly brilliant film indeed.

No fascinante Cisne Negro, Natalie Portman brilha como uma bailarina que, a um passo de se consagrar, começa também a se desintegrar psicologicamente
           	A bailarina, vestida como o cisne branco de O Lago dos Cisnes, rodopia no palco quase sem luzes  mas é vista do que seriam as coxias, e não da plateia, por uma câmera que, despercebida da dançarina, gira junto com ela. E então uma figura sinistra, coberta de penas negras, acossa-a por trás segundo o libreto do balé, seria Von Rothbart, o feiticeiro que transformou a princesa Odette em cisne. Mas, no tumulto da cena, tem-se a sensação de que ele é mais do que isso  é um íncubo. Nina Sayers (Natalie Portman) então acorda. Mas seu pesadelo vai continuar esse íncubo não é um demônio que veio de um inferno exterior para atormentar seus sonhos. É uma criatura feroz e exigente que assoma do fundo de Nina para apoderar-se dela e confundi-la. São, enfim, os recalques guardados no inconsciente de uma jovem que vive de recalcar-se  de reprimir a fome, as dores nas articulações, a solidão, o medo de fracassar e de ter êxito  para, assim, metamorfosear seu corpo em uma criação etérea que, livre dos constrangimentos da gravidade e dos limites humanos, possa tudo. Nessa busca, porém, Nina reprimiu algo mais selvagem do que fome ou dor é uma mulher adulta que se congelou numa infância grotesca, cuja pureza é estreitamente vigiada por uma mãe que projeta na filha tanto as ambições frustradas quanto seu pânico sexual. Virginal e intocada, sempre trêmula de dúvida e aflição, Nina é talhada para interpretar o Cisne Branco. E por isso mesmo, provoca o coreógrafo Thomas (Vincent Cassel), dificilmente ela será capaz de encarnar a versão anárquica e sensual da personagem. Ou Nina encontra dentro de si o Cisne Negro, então, ou perde a chance que perseguiu durante toda a vida. E dizer que ele vai, sim, aflorar não dá a medida dos delírios angustiantes que Nina atravessa em Cisne Negro (Black Swan, Estados Unidos, 2010), o novo filme do diretor Darren Aronofsky.
           	Cisne Negro surgiu da mesma matriz da qual se originaram outros dois filmes notáveis de Aronofsky, Réquiem para um Sonho e O Lutador quando aquele primeiro filme foi lançado, há uma década, ele já trabalhava também com as ideias de O Lutador e Cisne Negro. Os três filmes, assim, inseminaram uns aos outros e constituem algo como vertentes de um mesmo projeto. Em O Lutador, Mickey Rourke, magnificamente exposto em sua monstruosidade, era um astro decadente da luta livre que aceitava todo tipo de martírio físico para recuperar um momento de glória. Em Cisne Negro, Natalie Portman, magnificamente retratada em sua perfeição, é uma estrela em ascensão do balé que aceita todo tipo de martírio físico e psicológico para ter seu primeiro instante de glória. Mas, se a narrativa de O Lutador era brutalmente naturalista, a de Cisne Negro é aparentada da de Réquiem para um Sonho, em que a plateia se via aprisionada junto com os personagens nas suas horríveis viagens de drogas. Distinguir o que é real do que é imaginário no mundo de Nina é uma tarefa à qual o espectador se entrega com gosto  mas sem grande chance de sucesso. O que é uma das razões, aliás, pelas quais esse filme lúrido e hiperbólico é também tão instigante. Como a música ora pungente, ora tenebrosa que Tchaikovsky compôs para O Lago dos Cisnes e com a qual o diretor brilhantemente pontua a ação, tudo aqui é inseguro e cambiante.
           	Não que a veia naturalista de Aronofsky não sobressaia também poucas vezes o esforço que antecede uma apresentação de balé foi mostrado de maneira tão incisiva. Nas coreografias propriamente ditas, o diretor não está tão interessado assim. O que desperta sua curiosidade (e um de seus talentos é saber despertá-la também no público) são os ensaios e, mais ainda, os preparativos. A truculência a que são submetidas as sapatilhas, por exemplo, é ilustrativa do seu enfoque quase lisérgico nos detalhes numa sequência, veem-se as bailairinas martelando raivosamente as pontas contra o piso, para quebrar o gesso e torná-lo mais obediente à flexão dos seus dedos cortando como assassinas ranhuras no solado, para aumentar sua aderência arrancando como selvagens as palmilhas, para reposicioná-las enrolando os dedos em carne viva em esparadrapo e, com eles dentro dos calçados já assim torturados, jogando todo o peso de seus voos sobre aquela área minúscula de contato com o solo. No palco, o balé é um espetáculo de beleza incorpórea. No quadro de Aronofsky, é um rito de violência, sangue e humilhação contínua, torrencialmente administrada por coreógrafos e maîtres e maîtresses de ballet. Não é de admirar que, entre esses dois polos, o do sublime e o do sofrimento, personalidades instáveis como a de Nina em algum momento soçobrem.
           	Como Nina, Natalie Portman é uma revelação, se é que se pode dizer isso de alguém que trabalha sem parar desde os 14 anos. Uma atriz sempre associada à fragilidade, Natalie carrega para suas interpretações, também, um componente de recato  ou reserva, ou inibição. Até em Closer, como uma stripper, esse resguardo era parte preponderante de seu apelo. Em Cisne Negro, ela pela primeira vez abandona essa cautela. Da mesma forma que Aronofsky tirou Mickey Rourke da sua complacência em O Lutador e o fez ser mais extraordinário até do que em seus melhores dias, ele aqui priva Natalie dos mecanismos com que ela aprendeu a se proteger da curiosidade excessiva, e algo lasciva, que provoca espontaneamente. Desde os vários meses treinando balé oito horas por dia  aos 29 anos, não é fácil  até o regime brutal para perder 10 quilos não se sabe de onde, o diretor fez a atriz doer e se frustrar até o limite. Obriga-a também a enfrentar, em cena, as dimensões ameaçadoras de outros atores a sensualidade agressiva de Vincent Cassel, a radiância sexual de Mila Kunis (excelente como uma bailarina rival, mas também muuuito íntima de Nina) e a mutação cirúrgica da outrora exoticamente bela Barbara Hershey. No papel da mãe devoradora de Nina, ela como de hábito é uma atriz soberba. Mas é improvável que um diretor tão sensível à delicadeza de Natalie e ao calor de Mila ignore o choque de ver o rosto de Barbara tornado quase irreconhecível pelas intervenções. Pode-se especular, então, que ela foi escolhida também pela aparência Nina preserva a beleza, e sua mãe espelha as deformidades psicológicas em que ela incorre na sua tentativa obsessiva de ser perfeita. É cruel. E é assustadoramente eloquente.

the white swan inside of nina has a fully apollonian psyche, a self organized entirely around form, restraint and the ideal image. its what shes made of. her mother built her an identity out of discipline and infantilization, the stuffed animals, the music box, a small glass world where nothing is allowed to grow. all that remains is a girls body attached to a blind desperation to be perfect.
the black swan inside of her has the dionysian psyche, everything she repressed to become the white swan. anger, sexuality, appetite, the capacity to take up space, all of it cut away and gathering in her body like feathers pushing up beneath the skin. thomas telling her to let go of herself is about as dionysian as a phrase gets, but hes not a liberator. his idea of release is another kind of control, like her mothers protection. neither of them is offering her freedom.
the transformation arrives as a symptom. the repressed returns through the only channel left open, the body. the scratch on her shoulder that keeps reopening as if someone other than her is doing it, the skin she tears at her fingertips until it bleeds, the toes that fuse, the legs that bend backward like a birds. each one is staged as a small violation of the apollonian surface, the clean line interrupted by something unwilling to stay hidden. dionysus is the god of dissolved boundaries, and ninas transformation tracks him through her boundaries failing one by one, the skin, joint, bone, and finally the border between self and reflection.
the reflection in the mirror is the half of her she buried, the hand that moves half a second early as if waiting for her to catch up. the double was always there, nina simply stops being able to look away from it. it is the shadow cast by her desperation for perfection, the version of her that is allowed everything she denied. she fears lily because lily is the closest thing to her own black swan. lily is easy, hungry and unashamed, and nina experiences her as an enemy because the alternative is admitting she is looking at herself. 
when she drives the glass into lily, she believes she is removing a rival. it is her own abdomen. the apollonian self is being killed from the inside, by repressed material that has finally grown stronger than the structure holding it.
then the black swan emerges, wings unfolding, red eyes, a body that no longer obeys proportion, dancing as though possessed, the self stepping aside to let something larger move through the flesh. in the birth of tragedy, nietzsche argues that greek tragedy was born from the union of apollo and dionysus, form giving shape to frenzy and frenzy breaking open form. for a few minutes nina is that complete thing, form and freedom fused for the first time, order and frenzy occupying the same body.
in the final act of swan lake the white swan kills herself, and the only way for nina to achieve that with perfection was to live it. the old self bleeds out beneath the new one. she gets exactly what she desired, for the first and last time. it was perfect is the most apollonian phrase said at the dionysian moment.

Well, today I accidentally had a crazy idea and then did it. After noticing that Vincent Cassel was in both Black Swan and Irréversible, I thought maybe lets watch them both in a row. Then halfway through Irréversible I figured might as well add Antichrist. So I present to you The Swanychrist Challenge. At least half of the point was the name.
These films are not actually picked to shockthey are three very different films, and the choices each film makes is clearer in the context of the others. Using cinematography as an example, in Black Swan, during the dance sequences, the camera moves with the dancers in frame, twirling with some chaos but staying focused in well composed (if dizzying) shots that suit the scene and follow the person. Irréversible starts with dizzying rotation through darkened space, twirling against brick buildings and when focused on a person, still displacing and decentering them. All of the shots are disorientating through the first half of the film, only stabilizing to center directly on the eight minute rape scene. Every scene is a single take. And Antichrist could not be more different from either of these two. Where Irréversible is warm and flesh toned and stroby and scattered, and Black Swan is cool and kinetic and moves with the dancers, Antichrist starts with a series of nearly frozen images, where nearly every shot is perfect, but the faces are blurred out on all characters but the two protagonists. These are each stories of human tragedy and they are told very differently, but the pain and loss (or anticipation and fear of it) is similar in each. 
Black Swan was unrelentingly tense for me. Watching it was enjoyable but very socially painful, transferring the feeling of a slow breakdown of reality under pressure with a total lack of social support and antagonism from ones family and peers. Here the quest for perfection executed totally alone and the fear of failure and replacement is the thing that slowly destroys. 
Its got a lot of body horror in a surprising way, and I think its a daring and clever film. The pinfeathers prickling out of the skin and vanishing, the wing wound, and all of the other imagined harms that, in case somehow youre reading this and have not seen it, I will not spoilall of these along with the social interactions with peers filled me with genuine dread. It was hard to breathe throughout, and I felt anger at and fear for the harm that accrued to Nina.
The ending is cathartic in representations of both triumph and tragedy. In retrospect, the scale of the drama compared to the intensity of my experience interests me. Im not sure it was easier to watch than either of the subsequent films. It was a different type of difficulty, horror, and tension. My sense is that it perfectly conveys Aronofskys vision of a horror that is not less because it is human-scale and subtle. Cracking under mental strain happens in each film here, but very differently. Here the horror closely resembles All About Eve, and combined with the other horrors above, it is potent and worth experiencing. Most people have probably experienced these fears to some degree.
What I appreciated after watching these in sequence was that they exercised three different forms of horror with three aesthetics and three different scales of drama. Black Swan is not less for being more grounded in daily experience.
I am, I suppose, pitching this challenge, but Im also pitching Black Swan. I held off on watching it for a long time and Im glad I finally have gotten to it now. Its a beautiful, playful, dreadful film, and you can probably guess that I thought Natalie Portman and Vincent Cassels performances were inspired. If you havent watched it yet, now is the time. Then please watch Irréversible and Antichrist and tell me how it goes.
Enthusiastically recommended.

When I was a kid, I used to play a game called Kingdom Hearts. 
You play as a kid named Sora who fights black demon monsters with a giant key. It was actually a Disney property too. Sora was friends with Mickey, Donald, and Goofy. You fought across multiple worlds inspired by Disney movies and met Disney characters. It should be obvious by now that this game was meant for kids, and while it felt more like Game of Thrones to me as a kid, the handling of themes was textbook for childrens media. I would spend hours engaged in this world-spanning epic and involved in this huge-feeling storyline, and when it came time for the theme to be delivered, it would be some shit like through friendship, anything is possible.
This is how Aronofsky feels to me.
Black Swan is my third Aronofsky feature after seeing mother! and Requiem for a Dream. From those films, it seems to me that his basic ethos boils down to be as dramatic as humanly possible. And I can see the appeal in that, but for me, it just makes it hard for me to take anything he has to say seriously. Him taking everything to its highest possible extreme just distances me from the story being told instead of roping me in tighter. 
Its common to look at directors as craftspeople and at filmmaking as a craft. Aronofsky seems like hes not equipped with an entire toolbox, but instead, he has only a hammer. A hammer is a tool you have to be careful about using. You have to know when to use it and how much force to apply. Aronofsky hammers away with reckless abandon. Without any regard for subtlety.
It doesnt help that I saw Perfect Blue before I saw Black Swan. A film that has a heavy influence on Black Swan and Aronofsky in general. A film that is widely praised for its sharpness. A sharpness that makes Black Swan look unwieldy in comparison.
Im being harsh, but I didnt hate the film. I actually like what it had to say, if not liking the execution. Portman gives a great performance. Some of the horror elements are super effective, and the film is extremely technically proficient. I just think that every once in awhile Aronofsky might need to just smoke some weed, light some candles, have a nice cup of chamomile tea, take a bubble bath, and play some Kingdom Hearts.

Well I dont know what I was expecting but it certainly wasnt that. From the cast to the psychologically thrilling narrative, its a twisted and stunning film that masterfully blurs the lines between reality and delusion, and the fact this was released on IMAX just last month.. pisses me off so much. I messed up big time, as not even 3 weeks later Im watching it for the first time at home, still though what an incredible experience and a breathtaking slice of cinema. 
I really dig the cinematography, rather than a polished high-budget look, its got a home-film sort of vibe, and with it primarily shot on Super 16mm film, its easy to see why it looks that way having a coarser, grainier texture than standard 35mm film. Its a visually claustrophobic world that mirrors the protagonists fragile state, with cinematographer Matthew Libatique often placing us right in arms way we see the sweat, the strain on her face, and the subtle twitches of her anxiety, we share every moment of stress Nina experiences. 
Natalie Portman delivers what is undoubtedly one of the best female performances ever, completely embodying the complex and troubled character of Nina Sayers. Her portrayal is a mesmerizing deep dive into the psyche of an artist on the brink of collapse.. or perfection? Easily my favorite role of hers, still yet to watch V for Vendetta but I loved her work with this deep character study, and the rest of the ensemble are quite magnificent also. 
Vincent Cassel plays the Director, Ive only recently seen his powerful performance in La Haine, so it was an amazing realization to see him here. Now at a completely different point in his acting career, you can tell, hes a veteran actor now with extraordinary depth who expertly helms this nightmarish vision, guiding the film with a sharp and unyielding hand.
Mila Kunis probably puts in her career best performance as Lily, providing a perfect foil to Portmans Nina. The pair of them represent the White and Black Swan(and then, you know.. the thing happens), brilliant embodiment of both sides of the coin, with the core of their dynamics instantly becoming a harsh and unsettlingly rivalry that goes much deeper than artistic passion.
The film itself is a fascinating concept, really made me question a plethora of uncomfortable truths whether it be art, identity, or reality itself. Its a film that explores profound themes, with the pursuit of greatness being as central as Ninas painful and unsettling change from a girl to a woman. This change is not one of graceful maturity but a horrifying unraveling, and the twisted combination of the pursuit of greatness and the chilling coming of age tale works effectively in its powerful storyboarding. 
The films aesthetic is impeccable, an elegant visual style that complements the dark narrative and the score is a chilling but beautiful adaptation of Tchaikovskys Swan Lake. Both are integral to the films success with the score building a sense of dread and tension that never lets up. The visuals paired with the music creates an incredible sensory experience that pierces the beauty and horror of Ninas internal struggle right into the soul of oneself. 
I definitely felt some Whiplash vibes, especially with Black Swan exploring a very similar core theme the destructive nature of the pursuit of perfection. Both with an overly assertive instructor, and leave us with an ambiguous ending, they are two different tales of the same side of the coin. I prefer Whiplash out of the two but my word is Black Swan one of my favorite first time viewings of the year. 
That moment where we finally see her letting go, is a film scene that will stand the test of time shes soaring in her final leap of pure, transcendent artistic expression. Throughout the film we see Ninas grip on reality slip the mirrors, the scratches on her back, the doppelgänger, all of these elements blur the line between whats real and whats a manifestation of her psyche. So by the time we see her take the stage one last time, we are no longer sure what to trust making the revelation all the more visceral and for some cases confusing. 
For me this can only be described as a modern day classic its brilliance works on every level, and that comes from the seamless fusion of its components. Aronofskys direction is the engine that drives the films unforgiving descent, and then theres the fine tuned performance from Natalie Portman one of my favorite performances of the year and up there with my favorite female performances oat, she steers the ship of this relentless pursuit of artistic perfection. Its a beast of a film and in a way it leaves you with more questions than answers a powerful juxtaposition in many senses and Ill be thinking of this film for some time.

in english Darren Aronofsky doesnt direct a film about ballet  he dissects a body that dances itself to the brink of insanity. Black Swan is about Nina, yes, but Nina isnt a character shes a prison. What we witness is the trapped body of a ballerina raised to please, to obey, to be perfect  and perfection here is pathology. The film follows her implosion the way one might watch a flower bloom in raw flesh.
From the very first frames, Aronofskys camera clings to Nina like a shadow  or a parasite. Theres something almost documentary-like in its claustrophobic closeness, but it soon becomes clear we are not watching reality, we are seeing a mind unraveling from within. Every mirrored frame, every distorted sound, every physical or psychological crack contributes to the sensation of a mirror breaking from the inside out. Nina sees doubles everywhere, but her greatest double is herself  or the part of her that shes repressed.
Her obsession with the role of the Black Swan isnt merely professional its existential. Its a scream muffled by repression, by imposed purity, by a mother who infantilizes and molds her into a porcelain doll. Ballet, as an art form, demands absolute control of the body  but what Aronofsky reveals is the toll of that control when there is no room for desire, for chaos, for imperfection. Ninas transformation is both bodily and symbolic she bleeds, scratches, transforms  and ultimately flies. But her flight is terminal.
The interplay between reality and hallucination is never closed off by easy explanation. Aronofsky knows that what matters is not what is true, but what is felt. The rising paranoia, the repressed sexuality bursting into delusion, the physical horror that flirts with Cronenbergian body terror  all of it serves to make the intimate feel tactile. Black Swan is a character study, but also a study of disintegration. And the most disturbing thing is that, in the end, Nina finally feels whole. Because for her, perfection is worth the price of existence itself.
It was perfect, she whispers  and that final breath isnt a triumph. Its an epitaph.

Darren Aronofskys filmography ranges from the sublime to the ridiculous, encompassing genres as diverse as kitchen-sink melodrama (The Wrestler) to hallucinatory sci-fi (The Fountain). The connective tissue between all of these films is an obsession on the part of the filmmaker with the massive psychic toll suffered by self-conscious beings bound by decaying physical vessels. Our glories are fleeting, our decline is assured, even our greatest moments are bound by physical and mental limitations. Aronosky explicates these themes more painfully and insightfully than most directors, but every one of his films to this point have been wildly uneven. Requiem for a Dream is a visual tour de force, but its manic singularity proves exhausting and somewhat hollow. The Fountain is the rare film to confront the issue of mortality without resort to metaphysics, and its also sometimes embarrassing to watch. The Wrestler introduced a new strain of effective naturalism to Aronofskys repertoire, but it also hewed too closely to familiar genre beats. Black Swan is the culmination of Aronofskys inquires into human fragility he brings together every element that worked in his previous films while doing away with anything clunky or unconvincing. Theres something deeply enthralling about watching a film director hone his craft to a point of absolute incisiveness.
Black Swan and The Wrestler were originally conceived of by Aronofsky as parallel stories in a single film. At first glance, it seems like a terrible idea, and its clear that breaking them up was the right call, but the two stories make for a striking mirror image. Randy the Ram Robinson and Nina Sayers share a central dilemma they are both characters defined, both to themselves and to the world around them, by their physical bodies. Randy the Ram is only alive to the degree that his leathery hide dishes out and absorb punishment in the wrestling ring. Ninas only means of self-expression is the voiceless grace of her body. Both of them are haunted by the specter of their inevitable physical decline Randy is smack in the middle of his own, while Nina sees her future all too clearly in the person of Winona Ryders fading star ballerina. Both characters are driven to self destruction by their insatiable demand for perfection and adulation. Black Swan distinguishes itself as an altogether more penetrating and brilliant piece of work by burrowing so deeply into Ninas warped psyche and by expertly dissecting the specifically feminine dilemma she faces.
Natalie Portmans Nina lives an absurdly proscribed existence her daily routine, her life goals, her values, her self-esteem, are defined by dance. Her mother, a failed ballerina living vicariously through her daughter, uses a complex system of passive-aggressive conditioning to keep Nina focused on presenting herself as a symbol of purity and aesthetic perfection. When the film starts, Nina is somewhat comfortably cocooned in her frigid little world (although there are signs that the prospect of playing the lead in her companys production of Swan Lake has already put some cracks in the veneer). The real trouble begins when she wins the part of Odette and her director, played by Vincent Cassel, demands that she get in touch with her sexuality in order to channel the Black Swan, Odettes seductive alter ego. The tug-of-war for Ninas soul waged between her Mother and her Director places Nina in an impossible situation. She must simultaneously embody Mona Lisa and Mata Hari. Its the classic VirginWhore dichotomy all women have to navigate in some way, heightened to psyche-shattering heights by Ninas preternatural focus and artistic devotion. Her mechanisms for coping with the uncertainty and peril of depending on her intensely vulnerable human body (just listen to the knuckles of her toes crack as she gets out of bed!) are all based on a mechanized rigidity that cannot process paradox. Shes like a cartoon robot sent into sputtering meltdown by a logic puzzle.
Aronofsky documents Ninas mental breakdown by deftly synthesizing every effective gimmick in his directorial bag of tricks. He utilizes the over-the-shoulder shots and overall sense of docu-drama realism first displayed in The Wrestler to wed the viewer to Ninas point of view, making the films lurch into Requiem for a Dream-style hysteria credibly disorienting. While Requiems all-out visual assault created a fatal distance between the audience and the character, Black Swans hybrid approach draws the viewer inside Ninas head so effectively that her descent into madness is heartbreaking, terrifying and mercilessly logical. The performances are universally excellent, with Natalie Portman finding the role that her icy, repressed screen presence was made for. The dance sequences recall the fight scenes in The Wrestler in their emphasis on awesome grace and grim physical punishment. The films themes sex, decay, artistic obsession, radiate from every frame. Black Swan is the work of an artist at the peak of his power someone who has clearly wrestled with his defining subject matter for years and has learned through grueling trial and error the most effective application of his gifts.

Black Swan, aka Flight Club (Get it? Because swans can fly? Oh shut up), is the story of a performer literally losing herself in a role. I saw it back in its original run and thought it was great then, and Im happy to report that it still is today, 15 years later in its IMAX rerelease.
Its a delightfully deranged and surreal tale of an obsessed artist and her drive for perfection  which in turn drives her decaying grip on reality. The technical and effects work Aronofsky and his team do to create the illusion that Portman is dancing at a world class level is astonishing. (And thats not to take away from the work Portman did toward that herself.) And Aronofskys imaginative and trippy visuals heighten the tension, mystery, and utter insanity.
I tried to pay super-close attention to the Mila Kunis character on this watch. Despite her considerable screentime, she almost never speaks directly to any characters other than Portman, and on the one or two instances she seems to, its mumbled or unintelligible dialogue. Same with other characters speaking to her  almost never, and at best mumbled. Other characters do seem to acknowledge her presence a couple of times, but usually obliquely and always in Portmans presence. And thats not to mention all the clear(?) hallucinations where Portman and Kunis get mixed up or one transforms into the other. 
I do think the movies small budget weaken it in a few places. Particularly at the end, with a production of Swan Lake whose staging looks like something youd find in a high school play. No way Manhattanites are paying Lincoln Center prices for that. And Vincent Cassel is another sore spot  Ive never thought much of him as an English-language actor, and the writing for his character is extremely one-note.
In the end, Aronofsky seems to be telling us that that the key to achieving perfection as a performer is to find our inner dark side, turn it into Mila Kunis, and let her go to town on us. And who can argue with that? Just be careful around mirrors.

Its absurdly campy and intensely bleak at the same time. it refuses to give in to the ridiculous notion that a story about a woman must be of interest only to women, as so many films do by avoiding acknowledging that the authorities and madnesses of women are human, instead of somehow indicative of a peculiar female malady and so black swan becomes that rarity, a story about a woman that is  or should be  universal in appeal and power.
Was Nina on the edge even before she wins the role, and must learn how to exude evil as effortlessly as she does good? probably. ninas ambition has already been expressing itself in ways she wouldnt intend shes so single-minded that shes lost herself in the process of becoming perfect and shes losing what she needs to be a compelling dancer. beautiful as always, nina, a coach tells her during a group warmup session, but then relax. leroy keeps insisting she has to lose herself and let go and not fake it, but she doesnt know how. nina is stunted in many ways her abusive mother treats her like a child, and nina lives as one, surrounded by pink stuffed animals and ballerina music boxes in her bedroom, she lives with the denial of sensual pleasures, from purging to keep thin to being shocked when leroy tells her to go home and masturbate as a way of cutting loose not shocked that he would say such a thing but shocked that she might do such a thing.
Much of where nina goes when she does begin to do such things may well be nothing more than her own fantasizing about cutting loose. we know that her horrific visions of her own body transforming  growing webbed toes, spouting wings  are nothing more than hallucinations. what else may be as well? in the thoroughly gripping climax, does she even actually ever dances either the white swan or the black or is it all merely her nightmare of perfection coming to pass? portman so completely lives the performance that were inside her head looking out, and can never know for certain whats real and what isnt. that sort of delicious ambiguity  it works on many different levels, and works whether 10 percent is real, or 50 percent, or 100 percent  is an uncommon treat.
Some might consider leroys comment and other of his actions sexual harassment, while others just the sort of shoves niina needs to break free and its possible theyre both at the same time. aronofsky finds fascinating visual ways to draw us deeply into ninas troubled passion. the scene in which she mutilates a brand-new pair of ballet slippers, with the camera close in on her hands ripping the shoes apart, is provocative and riveting for what it says about both nina and ballet she isnt destroying them out of anger or frustration, but merely breaking them in so theyll be flexible enough to dance in and hence its a perfect metaphor for what Nina does to herself.

It also deals with the perils of getting too absorbed into a role to the point of obsession, having that line that separates reality and fantasy get really blurred, to the detriment of the self-absorbed thespian, and here we observe ninas horrific metamorphosis from all things good to a mean, and psychotic even, streak. the backstabbing, the trash talking, and the two faced nature of that world is portrayed with a deft and brilliant touch. there is a constant fear that you are one mistake away from losing not only your part, but your future parts as well. you feel like you are a part of this world, that the pressure of it is part of your world.
Portmans performance, which I noted above was anxiously anorexic, is slightly more subtle than that, especially with regards to her repression, shes holding back her happiness because she thinks that she shouldnt show her mother anything but a professional demeanor. the smiles she offers in the first few minutes evaporate for the rest of the movie she even looks uncomfortable when shes given the lead part in the ballet, i think we can all relate to the discomfort we go through trying to appear stoic to our parents, as if showing pleasure would be somehow cheating and acknowledging them as our friends who only want to see us happy.
While ms. portman carries the entire film on her little dancing feet, the stellar supporting cast includes mila kunis, who gives possibly her best performance to date as ninas free-spirit rival. kunis is gorgeous, of course, but it is her characters sexy, wild personality that is the perfect counterpoint to portmans frigid beauty. they greatly complement each other. vincent cassel is perfect as company director thomas. hes passionate, brutal, demanding, caring, sexual, artistic his impeccable performance gives us a three-dimensional character for us to love to hate and hate to love. the most impressive aspect of the story is the character development. we get three-dimensional characters who are neither saints or devils, just human beings trying to find their places in this world but also transcend their mortality. the relationship between nina and her mother is particularly complex and multilayered. the sexual tension between thomas and nina is just as palpable as that between nina and lily, which gives the story a dark, unconventional sexual energy that is the antithesis of ninas control and quest for perfection.
I felt with nina throughout the entire film experiencing very punishing routine, stretched muscle and tight joint.from when we first see her, it already looks like shes on the verge of burnout. a little girl trapped inside the body of a woman. a compelling performance due portmans ability to balance ninas drive with her immaturity. throughout portman holds a fearful, childlike gaze to everyone she encounters. answers back are mumbled while childish outbursts slip out by outside stimulus. this encapsulated world is clearly created by a domineering mother and ninas newly gained promotion installs a fight against her, she never felt she had. the relationship between the two to me, feels very reminiscent and aronofskys direction carefully teases the psychosexual aspects in many scenes. portman is also spot on with the films later scenes as psychical pain breaks down into psychological. a good performance becomes a great one as the melding of sexual awakening, social isolation and grueling routine explode into a dazzling, liberating, final display as swan lake is performed.
It is the films final, unbelievably tense third where everything comes together brilliantly. the sound design ramps up and the music becomes thunderous,  the visuals that only tricked you slightly in earlier sections come at you in full force to assault you. there are horror tropes that have been used throughout that would come across as cliche in lesser films, but are extraordinarily manipulated here. aronofsky understands that the best horror comes from very simple and primal things, breaking ninas natural order with exhaustion, further isolation and of course fear of the other. he allows us to construct our own narrative and piece together how nina sayers became who she is. he accomplishes this through both natalie portmans performance and the films visual choices for instance, we only get short glimpses of horror theres never a moment to seriously linger on what were seeing.In truth, the most effective horror is oftentimes achieved by withholding, not by revealing.
One doesnt often think of ballet, with its graceful moves and untouchable sensuality, as a blood sport, but aronofskys perspective argues that rasslin may not be that far removed from dancing. black swan is presented as a psychological thriller with a twist the viewers perspective is that of the lead character and her sanity is in doubt. as a result, the films sense of reality is warped. sorting fantasy, nightmare, and hallucination from what is real is likely to require multiple viewings and careful conjecture. aronofsky has created a twisted piece of art - the kind of things that lovers of the mind fuck subgenre will delight in.
Its about control and the loss of that control. what happens when a perfectionist control freak is in a position where she has to let go of that control? what takes over when she does let go? in typical fashion, aronofsky shows us that sometimes in striving to get what we want, we risk losing a part of us that we may never be able to get back, and dont realize how desperately we need, black swan is a film that examines the journey with an emphasis on the shadowy corners that encompass it. when trekking towards notability, sometimes you must traverse dark passages. this is when the real inquisition takes place. what is the price of perfection? would you sacrifice relationships? would you compromise your morality? would you risk your sanity?
Contention can fuel our motivations, test our wills, and catapult us to greater heights. when the mind overcomes the body, we all possess the potential for greatness. within

Never underestimate the power of rewatching. I saw Black Swan for the first time a little over a year ago and I remember liking it, but not thinking it was anything extraordinary. Now that Im binging Isabela Boscovs list of the 100 best films of the century, and with a little more cinematic baggage, I decided to revisit it, and it simply became one of my favorites. This is a true masterpiece.
Black Swan, directed by Darren Aronofsky, portrays in a poetic psychological thriller the relentless and destructive pursuit of an impossible perfection. Nina, a ballerina, achieves the great feat of being chosen to star in Swan Lake, but she doesnt expect that, in order to embody both Odette and the Black Swan, shell have to let go of what she has always clung to and chased obsessively perfection.
Natalie Portman deserved every single vote for Best Actress. She delivers a spectacular performance not only as Nina, capturing all the purity and insecurity of the White Swan, but also in portraying the gradual transformation into the Black Swan. Her gestures and expressions throughout the dance sequences translate Ninas internal conflicts with astonishing precision. Its also clear how desperately the character struggles to free herself from the perfectionism that has dictated her every move, to the point that she tries to achieve perfection in the act of being imperfect. Portman is undoubtedly one of the films best choice.
I was so invested in the movie that I barely wrote anything while watching. If youve been following my reviews for a while, you already know Im obsessed with descent into madness arcs, and Black Swan elevates that to a spectacular level. The film uses every audiovisual resource at its disposal to portray Ninas deteriorating mental state, giving a true lesson in symbolism and metaphor as she begins to live out, in her own reality, the story of the ballet shes about to star in. 
The score and cinematography tell the story just as powerfully as the script. Constantly contrasting white and black, light and shadow, not only referencing the dual roles Nina plays but also her internal conflict, the artistic choices are impeccable and translate her inner world majestically. Alongside the breathtaking music, the sound effects of wings flapping that we sometimes hear faintly in the background show the meticulousness of this sound design. This exceptional direction makes the dance scenes, especially the final one, striking and absolutely mesmerizing.
Finally, something I find perfect is how the film tackles so many themes like excessive self-pressure, self-harm, abuse of hierarchy, sexuality, self-esteem, maternal narcissism, aesthetic expectations placed on women, and of course, perfectionism, and manages to develop each of them not only satisfyingly, but in a way that ties directly into Ninas core conflict.
Well, thats all for Black Swan! I definitely want to watch more of Aronofskys work.
See you in the next review, and always remember take a break from chasing perfection every now and then and just live a little (and you dont need drugs for that, ok?)

Black Swan managed to do one of the things I value most when watching a film  it pulled me into its tension. Its not just something you watch its something you start to feel, scene after scene.
What struck me most was Ninas transformation throughout the film. She is extremely gentle, almost too fragile for the world she lives in. Everything about her is restrained  the way she speaks, moves, and feels. It creates a certain unease.
That transformation is the heart of the experience. It isnt something beautiful or inspiring  its uncomfortable. Gradually, that delicacy is worn away by insecurity, paranoia, and an unhealthy need to be perfect. The films atmosphere adds a lot to this. Everything feels slightly suffocating, slightly unsettling, as if reality is always just a bit off. You never feel entirely sure about what youre seeing, which fits perfectly with Ninas state of mind.
The mirrors play a very clever role in this. They appear constantly, but never feel neutral  its as if they show different versions of her, or even something she doesnt want to face. This reinforces the sense of losing control and identity over the course of the story. Its a simple detail, but used in a very effective way to heighten the unsettling tone.
In the end, it felt like a heavy film, but very well made  the kind that isnt exactly pleasant, but is well worth watching.
