One of the most popular foreign language films ever made City of God is indeed an impressive work.
Adapted from the novel of the same name by Paulo Lins this is an undeniably gritty feature. Writer Bráulio Mantovani and Director Fernando Meirelles do terrific work here. What I find most impressive is that unlike many American made films about gangsters City of God goes to great lengths to portray this lifestyle as the farthest possible thing from glamorous. Indeed much of the time it looks pretty grim. What City of God presents to us is the shocking reality of gangland life as we see regular brutal murders and even the phenomenon of child murderers and children murdering other children which is something Hollywood productions often shy away from showing. Some really violent moments are shown here almost casually which highlights the normality of such horrific events in the city and also the sadistic nature of them. 
Fernando Meirelles does a brilliant job here in visually presenting the horrendous squalor and poverty the characters here live in. The slums are always shown as overcrowded, dirty, depressing places that are usually sickeningly bright in colour that underscore the violence that occurs within them and through seeing the characters all moving about with shirts off we can almost feel the heat and the tension of these claustrophobic conditions. Although there are some really stylish visual touches from the Director this is always a thoroughly realistic drama that never skirts around its dark subject matter. Meirelles does a brilliant job in ensuring his subject matter always has an edge that makes it remain fresh and tonally different to other pictures within the genre.
A bold decision is also made in the casting of City of God to allow an entirely non-professional cast to play the characters. Although at times this backfires and we have some awkward moments of poor acting it does mean that the action remains realistic and unpredictable. We never feel safe watching this as there are no familiar faces to reassure us that everything will be ok which further increases our insecurity at this world of poverty that really is alien to most of those watching in the wider western world. This means it is a truly frightening watch at times.
To conclude, City of God is a gritty, punchy and surprising crime drama that brings to light the true horrors contained within its subject matter that many pictures examining the same types of material fail to show probably due to censorship. This means that City of God is a far more fascinating, visceral and at times downright ugly feature that remains fresh no matter how many times you see it.

Muy buena película, de las más inversivas que vi en mi vida.
Cidade de Deus es una de las mejores obras del cine latinoamericano, contando una historia muy cruda que no tiene miedo de mostrar varias de las cosas que pasan en las favelas brasileñas, todo a través de un relato muy bien dirigido y hermoso visualmente.
La premisa es sobre un joven y su mejor amigo que, después de formar una pandilla en Río de Janeiro, pasan de los robos, al narcotráfico y a los asesinatos.
La historia me encantó, es tan buena como me la esperaba. Desde el primer momento te engancha por lo interesante que resulta su historia y por la belleza de sus visuales. Sin embargo, por momentos maneja un ritmo lento que puede llegar a aburrir a algunos, aunque no fue en mi caso. Si tuve problema con la gran cantidad de personajes que se nos presentan, ya que llegaba un punto donde había demasiados y no me podía acordar de quien era cada uno además, los diferentes cambios de bando que tienen algunos hacían que esto sea peor. Por otro lado, una de las cosas mas positivas que tiene la película es su ambientación y la representación de las favelas de Brasil, todo se siente tan real que podría ser tranquilamente un documental. Esto nos regala algunas escenas bastante crudas, donde la cinta no se guarda nada y muestra muchas de las cosas que pasan en estos lugares. Por último, destaco la manera en la que esta contada la historia, teniendo diversos saltos temporales que quedan bastante bien y no se sienten mal ejecutados.
En cuanto a los personajes, estos son bastante buenos. Buscapé es el narrador y protagonista de la historia, el cual me gustó ya que es de los pocos con los que se puede empatizar fácilmente al ser una de las personas más buenas que conocemos en la trama, teniendo un gran desarrollo donde vamos a ver cómo intenta alejarse del mundo oscuro y callejero de su país. Otro personaje que también es rescatable por esto mismo es Bené, a quien lo presentan como la persona que todos quieren. Por otro lado, con Zé Pequeno pasa todo lo contrario, a quien conocemos desde que era un simple nene, pero ya veíamos desde ese momento lo psicópata que era. Este es otro personaje que tiene un excelente desarrollo y que me encantó por la locura que maneja, de los más locos que conocí en el cine.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente la dirección de Fernando Meirelles, quien hace un excelente trabajo y logra que la película se vea fenomenal. Además, también destaco el montaje, la edición y la fotografía, que son cosas que potencian a que la cinta sea visualmente una maravilla. Por otro lado, las actuaciones son brillantes, y tienen mucho más merito al ser actores que no eran profesionales y terminaron haciendo este increíble trabajo. Por último, la banda sonora de Ed Cortês y Antonio Pinto me pareció genial, cumple con lo que esperaba de una película con este tono y situada en Brasil.
En conclusión, una muy buena película que tiene ideas muy interesantes en la manera que tiene de contar su historia, siendo potenciada por una gran calidad visual y actoral que hace que sus personajes sean tan recordados. La recomiendo.

City of God tells the story of two completely different people who grow up in one of the poorest neighborhoods in Rio de Janeiro, called City of God. As a young boy, Locke dreams of a career as a gangster and gradually rises to become the undisputed boss of the drug scene. Buscapé really wants to be a photographer. Although both pursue their own goals, their paths cross more than once in the midst of bloody gang wars and corruption.
With City of God director Fernando Meirelles created an incredibly intense portrait of the hard life in the favelas of Rio de Janeiro. His staging is very immediate and close to the action. You can literally feel the city of God with all its facets. The focus is not so much on the individual figures, but rather on the vicious circle of violence and power that none of the residents can escape. Anyone who tries to legally earn their money fails. This becomes clear in the story of Mane, who actually wants nothing more than peace, but ultimately became one of the main characters in the bloody drug war.
Buscapé itself tells the story of the City of God from off-screen, with skilful cross-fades always switching between the past and the present. 
It was shot almost exclusively with amateur actors from the real favelas, who manage to give the characters on the screen a deep authenticity through their own experiences.

City of God was one of my favorites to watch and show friends in middle and high school, back when I thought the confluence of high style and realistic violence was everything films could and should be. I can still see why its formalism is studied in film classes a synesthetic barrage of seemingly every flourish in the proverbial book. One that remarkably doesnt clash with the setting and (non-)actors but harmonizes in a radically singular verisimilitude. See it for that, but not for the story.
Its narrative is by no means badthere are a lot of engrossing, moving partsbut some of its beats too convenient, some of its dialogue too theatrical. And under its coming-of-age story, its surprisingly one-note cyclical poverty, gang violence, and mostly futile attempts to escape it. Over. And over. And over. A reality of systems the film doesnt concern itself with. A reality shared with its actors.
Obviously everyone cant be a star, everyone wont get paid fairly, but I struggled to parse the exploitation versus representation debateespecially after watching the documentary City of God 10 Years Later, which I have no intention of logging. Its crushing and damning that these underpaid non-actors were used for their authenticity only to be left in those very favelas to this dayfavelas that were mostly depicted as brutal, almost animalistic. Frames of humanity exposed, but rarely any warmth. 
Im reminded of that scene in La Haine where Hubert tells the reporter, This isnt Thoiry. These are homes, not a playground. Workplaces, where some of the cast still make a living. In the documentary, Felipe Paulino visits Seu Jorge at a hotelPaulino works there, Jorge often stays. Look, I love Seu Jorge and Im glad for his success as an actor and musician, but its Paulinos utterly harrowing, realistic pain that lingersa pain that was scared out of him as a child. How bitterly ironic that he ends his segment by saying, I just need a break. Again, equity is never guaranteedIn the last ten years, every day I asked myself, Can a work of art change someones life? What do you say?
Returning to City of God was challenging, but sometimes nostalgia is best viewed through a clearer lens.

Virtuosic pop cinema at its most visceral and at its most entertaining! An unsentimental and unflinching look at crime and poverty that punches you in the mouth and takes the top of your skull off!

You enter the City of God with quick cuts of a knife being sharpened on a black slab an anxious hen desperate to escape its slaughter a bunch of street kids recklessly firing pistols in pursuit of this one hen and then a standoff between the street kids and the local cops.....You are knocked off your feet, not sure of what to make of this chaotic intro! And then the movie takes you back to the 1960s to a bunch of kids playing street soccer! Its a promise to the audience that if you hang on for dear life in this wild ride, you will have your hunger satisfied and your thirst quenched!

The camera hangs, whizzes, rolls, sprints, and flies like were looking through the last visions of a decapitated head! The camera is the true tour guide to the City our narrator is merely a commentator on things unfolding. It is shot like how a hood would shoot their own film it can freeze the frame or fracture the narrative or split the screen or go back in time! The camera has a personality, overwhelming the audience with this overwhelming world!

I get the sense that directors Kátia Lund and Fernando Meirelles plan meticulously what goes into a shot but will allow these non-actors to breathe life into the frame. No one person is more important than each other in any one scene - this keeps things vibrant and highlights how one character decision affects others. The characters are always inhabiting the open world and interacting with the Citys other denizens - thats why the script can have chance encounters without feeling like contrivances. Its the kind of film that makes you question, Wait was that angle planned? Was that blocking following the script? Effortless performances that looks like they werent even trying! 

Our narrator is never safe in this film. You the audience are never safe in this film. Theres constant dread at least every two minutes. Its strange to call violence hard earned, but it is in this film. Theres never a time when someone is killed and you dont ultimately know why they died! Either they ran and the beast caught them, or they stayed and the beast caught them!

The City of God is always alive the environment is a character as well as a reflection of the plot. The characters grow as the City grows. There is no obvious beginning or end. The plot is snowball-like and expands across different city locations and decades. Its like a constant in media res. This is objectively one of the best paced and edited movies ever! The audience is so familiarized with the setting and its characters, so we are immersed in whatever is happening. 

City of God is the finest kind of literature that sticks with you long after the credits roll. Even as the initial shock of the events in the movie wears off, you realize you have just been giving a lecture on how inequality creates a lawless environment that set entire generations back in Brazil.

And yes City of God outgoodfellas Goodfellas as my favourite crime drama of all time! Now if youll excuse me, Im gonna go on a lam hiding from Joe Pesci after that sacrilege, lest he whacks me!

It isnt so much that if youre going to throw stones that you have to be without sin. Its just that if youre going to throw stones while in a state of sin, you have to accept when someone throws stones at you. If youre going to make a film with an agenda, a commentary, an idea to it, you open those ideas up to examination. Sometimes, in examination, your agenda falls apart. Sometimes, other ideas are found, good or bad. Sometimes they affect your original idea, and sometimes they dont. Though its beyond the control of the filmmakers to some degree, the film also gains a new context as audiences interact with it after initial viewing, the film is no longer in the hands of its creators. That context surrounds any film, feeding the experiences of those who come after. For Clueless, this means a lot of things nostalgia from 90s kids, skepticism or embrace from Austen fans, the death of one of its stars and the right wing career of another, dated humor and product placement, and, of course, its reputation as popular feminist art.
I dont know much about Emma, so I cant comment on the adaptation (lou can, though). Jane Austens work has a place in feminist history, defined both by its own value, in its own context, and its adaptability in later generations. Given that so many of Austens works qualify in film adaptations as period pieces, its appropriate that Clueless serves as its own sort of time capsule. From the instantly dated Mentos commercial sing-along to the cartoon references, from the slang (which it propagated as much as appropriated) to the aesthetics (called out quickly as a Noxema commercial), the film is specific to its moment. I have no remove from that moment late high school pop culture is ingrained in me. From the response this film has from people younger than me, I assume it works outside this context, but I cant see it without it. Regardless, it is a rare positive relic from that time for me. 
I had no understanding of feminism the last time I watched this. Seeing it from the other side of a basic understanding, its arc of female friendship stands out (not just to me), and the critique of the perception of teenage girls neatly woven into the characters and dialogue is impressive. The joke is almost always about the absurdity of how they are perceived or how their ideas are presented. From the opening monologue where the way normal life Cher supposedly leads is put to the lie visually to the mockery of the idea that she might be getting married at 16, the film mines humor from the often ridiculous sexist tropes and stereotypes in media and (wearyingly) in real life. Much of this is done through the films exploration of the superficial.
Josh is an easy example. Hes shown to be more than the stereotype of a philosophy undergrad (encapsulating his era by playing insipid, then-alternative cool music constantly), but the film mines that type for humor in two different ways. The first is simply making the character a punchline with simple jokes like the Nietzsche book or his beliefs about make up the second is by mocking the view of these stereotypes, such as the contrast shown with the girl he takes home with Cher and his apparent pleasure at her being proven wrong. Cher, however, is the masterpiece, her role as central character giving the film plenty of time to explore everything about her. Her repeated flashes of insight (including her absurd but not so absurd debate about Haitian refugees) show an understanding of concepts a a bimbo (apologies for the slur) would not normally be depicted as understanding. Whats more, her understanding isnt treated as a punchline as other movies (Romy and Michele, for instance) would, but the manner of her understanding is instead used as the source of humor. She gets it, but through pop culture and her own experiences. The film quietly shows that someone can not be traditionally educated but still be intelligent, wise, or perceptive. 
This theme is hit upon over and over again. Almost every joke seems to stem from this idea, this insistent statement that women--people in general, but here especially women--are not stupid just because they are teenage girls with an interest in what most people would deem as shallow. My favorite writer has said more than once that, not seeing herself represented in media, she picked her own stories out of other peoples, finding resonance amidst fragments of things intended for others. Though undoubtedly there wasis media for Cher that perhaps would have more eloquently connected to, but in an MTV world inundated by blockbusters, music videos, and commercials aimed toward her own demographic that is intentionally lacking in depth, she plucked out hidden gems of compassion and complexity. Its not that the film is suggesting there is real value to mindless pop culture, but that those who consume are not defined by it. Its a direct refutation of the scorn heaped on teenage girls.
It should be noted, too, that the film looks and sounds good. Its soundtrack (other than, blech, Radiohead) is a fantastic slice of poprock 90s atmosphere, mixing unlikely bits that only make sense at the time (the Mighty Mighty Bosstones?!) with bigger hits and older cuts. Its fun and silly and bouncy, and it matches what were seeing perfectly, almost always fueling moments (and sometimes in on the jokes) with the right energy. It fuzzes in the background even when it wouldnt seem likely to, filling spaces and flavoring characterizations. Meanwhile, visually, it takes advantage of the disgustingly wealthy setting by indulging in building porn and drawing from the lavish scenery, and (I feel like I am belaboring this point) using its visuals for humor in fun ways. Brightly lit fountains erupting at the right moment and smash cuts to the mall are just the start of it.
If that were the extent of the film, it would likely be a masterpiece. Instead, it stumbles. The most significant is that it relegates the black characters to diminished sidekick roles, reinforcing white supremacist ideas of subservience. It tries to include in their depiction a smaller arc showing that their own performances (the characters performances, not the actors) to show that, say, Turkletons use of street slang is as much a shallow distraction from who he really is, but (a) the sidelining prevents any meaningful exploration of race, class, and gender, which is necessary when trying to do a story like that and (b) it comes off as apologia for how badly he treats Dionne. It makes clear that their conflict is real, and though it suggests that it only occurs when theyre being watched by others, that doesnt make Dionnes discomfort any less valid in those moments--indeed, the idea is disturbingly close to defending outright abusive behavior by suggesting tender moments from an otherwise abusive person invalidate the abuse. Its not quite that extreme, perhaps, but it has that stench about it. Certainly the comparison to Ike and Tina Turner didnt help.
The second problem is Christian, the gay (?) character, who is subjected behind his back to a string of homophobic slurs and depicted mostly with a string of stereotypical attributes (shopping, dancing, etc.). To the films credit, he is shown to be more than that, but again, as a side character, he doesnt get the exploratory treatment needed to expose the shallow treatment as absurd. The PE coach is similarly relegated to a punchline, and unlike most of the straight characters, neither is coupled off at the end (though coupling off as a default happy ending is problematic in and of itself fuck you yes I said problematic). The third issue that stands out is the use of ableistsaneistneurotypicalist (?) slurs, something most people will handwave as realistic, but again, you know, I repeat that you can use realistic dialogue and show visually, verbally, or tonally that its wrong. This film did not do that, so it gets its cookie smashed up and thrown away just to make it cry.
Like so many pieces of intelligent pop cinema, it aims higher than it reaches, but the veil of nostalgia still tinges it with warm memories. This is a rare piece of girl-centric media that didnt drive me away in dysphoric-fear or feel threatening to my tenuous hold on perceived masculinity, allowing it to lodge itself both in my teenagehood as a cool little film and in my awakened state as some anchor of femininity in my past. Its a node in the network of gender exploration, a rare successful navigation on my part, and revisiting it is still pleasurable in that regard.

I can confidently say that Clueless is, without a doubt, one of the best and most intelligent adaptations of Jane Austen ever made.  Yes, you heard that right. While other films strive for period accuracy, Clueless brilliantly captures the spirit of Emmathe comedy of manners, the well-meaning but misguided matchmaker, and the light, insightful social commentaryand transports it to the hallowed halls of 90s Beverly Hills high school.
I simply love how Cher is constructed. She is the embodiment of the spoiled American rich girl stereotype pampered, frivolous, obsessed with fashion and social status. But what makes Cher unforgettable and the movie so lovable is that she is so much more than that. Beneath the Chanel jacket and the concern over footwear, there is a genuinely good heart. She cares deeply about the people around her, from the new student Tai to the mismatched teachers. Her intention is always to make them happy and improve their lives, even if her matchmaking or makeover tactics are totally misguided, condescending, or even disastrous. Its this purity of intention that makes her a captivating heroine, just like Emma Woodhouse.
I was exactly 18 years old when I first watched this masterpiece. My teenage mind immediately identified with the exaggerated drama, the existential concerns about grades, cars, and who was going to which party. It was a hilarious mirror of an era. Today, at 26, already a grown man, its funny how I can still relate. Of course, Im not crying over a stained Ralph Lauren, but the journey of self-discovery, the innocent mistakes made in trying to do good, and the search for purpose beyond the superficial still resonate. Its proof that the film deals with timeless themes.
And speaking of timelessness... Paul Rudd. To be honest, I dont remember liking any other movie with him, but as the cynical (and eventual love interest) Josh, he is totally adorable, handsome, with that aura of the smart, irritable older stepbrother who, deep down, cares. His charm here is undeniable, and the chemistry with Alicia Silverstone is perfect. To be honest, I would also date my stepbrother if he were like that.
Clueless is the cinematic equivalent of a tutti-frutti bubblegum sweet, with a deliciously nostalgic flavor, and you cant stop chewing it. You shouldnt expect grand existential developments or Shakespearean dramas. Here, the great disasters are elite micro-tragedies.
We dont have time to cry over real-world problems. Here, we cry because red wine was spilled on a pair of suede shoes. And thats exactly how it should be. Ugh, as if!

Amy Heckerling was able to define two very different high school experiences with this and Fast Times in the 80s. Its pretty amazing to capture the cultural zeitgeist of your time 15 years apart, especially when it comes to teen movies. Clueless affected the way people talked, dressed, and acted for at least 10 years.

If John Hughes high school films carry a good amount of what I dislike watching in the sort, then Clueless is what I would cite as a perfect example of the high school movie done right. Amy Heckerlings loose adaptation of Jane Austens Emma works on a count that not only is it one of these teen films by appearance, but also at how its poking fun at the sort of ideas that they present on the screen. It took me a second viewing to realize what it was about Clueless that I absolutely loved about it, for it had been years since I last came around to watching it. Amy Heckerling leaves behind not only a fun teen comedy, but a cultural staple for the 1990s going down from both the fashion and the soundtrack, and an entertaining time capsule from start to finish. It can be referred to as a chick flick all you want it to be, but that doesnt take the clever aspects of it away.
Emma Woodhouse in this take on the story is a valley girl-type teenager by the name of Cherilyn Horowitz. Updating the setting to 1990s Beverly Hills, its interesting to at least watch where Amy Heckerling is taking the story and tell it to another set of audience members, but its also fascinating to see how she is playing around with everything that forms a teen comedy. While it carries many of the elements that build a teen comedy, it still presents a great understanding of its source material and it transfers that sort of elegance which a Jane Austen story would suggest into a different period of time. Soon enough, it becomes clear that Cluelesss use of the source material also becomes its greatest asset, for it also subverts the image it carries and turns it into something else entirely.
Theres no dispute to how Cher Horowitz is the valley girl stereotype, but the way that Amy Heckerling writes a character like her is why she stands out from the clique which she would fall under, taking what is already misguided inside of a John Hughes movie and being more self-aware about it.  Amy Heckerling sets her up to be a personality we should dislike, but theres a specific charm that comes from Alicia Silverstones performance that makes her immensely lovable. Cher, a mirror of Emma Woodhouse in the 20th century is a girl who does have good intentions for the people around her, but given the shell of what her character is supposed to be, it is also made all the better when Amy Heckerlings writing puts her character in on the joke that was created by Clueless. As the title would suggest, it is common to refer to a valley girl as clueless about the world around herself, but Cher differs in the sense that she is a somewhat more knowledgeable figure in comparison to the many tropes of the stereotype, she is also unselfish, even with all the wealth she flaunts at others, and an independent figure, for she describes searching for a boyfriend as searching for meaning in a Pauly Shore movie.
Alicia Silverstone has never been better than she ever has been while she played Cher Horowitz, but also notable are the performances of the late Brittany Murphy and a young Paul Rudd. Brittany Murphy is yet another clueless figure that defines the film, as she starts out clearly unfitting into a new environment, then after meeting Cher who brings her in, gains a sense of identity. A young Paul Rudd appears in the film as Chers ex-stepbrother, and its nice watching how a young talent has started and eventually grown inside of his future - showcasing Amy Heckerlings talent for discovering new stars and providing a good future for them as she had already done with Fast Times at Ridgemont High, a vastly different sort of high school film from this.
While Clueless certainly does follow a pathos that is not anything unfamiliar to the sort of comedy which it appears to be, its wonderful to see how Amy Heckerlings writing is also very self-aware about these sorts of films, which is the key to its own effectiveness. The dialogue is only a small factor to Cluelesss own wonder for it deconstructs the tropes that are already familiar for the stereotypes which it is portraying, but Heckerlings own directorial eye gives the film a look of a regular high school comedy, only a small part of what makes it more fun to watch compared to many of the rest. She knows already how such characters are meant to act and behave, but Heckerling also gives these people a sense of development away from their stereotypes, giving them all such a lively feel.
Clueless is a girly film, no doubt about that, but when does a film being girly detract from its merits? Amy Heckerling takes what could easily appear as any ordinary high school comedy and turns everything around to show how misguided some of the most iconic examples can be (take Ferris Buellers Day Off for example, which I view as John Hughess best film of these sorts). Its a time capsule that is very much reflective of the time period in which it came out, but if I were going to say that it is never entertaining to watch, Id certainly be lying as Clueless always manages to get a smile out of me. But as Cher shouts, As if! As if theres supposed to be any shame in me, a male, finding great enjoyment out of a film that would be deemed girly in some circles. Its proof that high school movies can go beyond what they usually set out for.

Cher (Alicia Silverstone) and her best friend, Dionne (Stacey Dash) notice that two of their teachers, Mr. Hall (Wallace Shawn) and Mrs. Geist (Twink Caplan) are both single and unhappy. Cher sets up a fake love letter to trick them into dating. The plan works, making the teachers happy.
Emboldened by her success, Cher befriends an insecure new transfer student named Tai Frazier (Brittany Murphy). Cher and Dionne give Tai a complete makeover, trying to mold her into a popular High School girl. 
Tai falls for a stoner kid named Travis (Breckin Meyer) but Cher pushes Tai toward a rich, popular boy named Elton (Jeremy Sisto). Elton rejects Tai and goes after Cher, leaving Cher confused.
Chers perfect world starts to crack when Tai suddenly becomes more popular and confident than Cher herself. Tai even shows an interest in Josh (Paul Rudd), Chers college-age stepbrother, who lives watcher and their father (Dan Hedaya). This causes a new emotion in Cher, jealousy, as she realizes she has feelings for Josh.
Clueless is a brilliant, modern, loose adaptation of Jane Austins, Emma. The writing is smart and funny. Silverstones performance as Cher is a defining, iconic, comedic, turn. She is charming and deeply endearing. Instead of playing Cher as a spoiled and vapid mean girl, Silverstone injects a sweet-natured innocence that makes her lovable.
I would be remiss if I didnt mention the late Brittany Murphy. She was only seventeen years old during filming and this was her breakout role. Her performance as Tai was bubbly and genuinely funny. She easily provides a clumsy yet lovable contrast to Silverstones protagonist.
Clueless is one of the best comedies from the 1990s and is effortlessly entertaining.

Sinopsis Cher y Dionne son dos de las chicas más populares de una escuela secundaria de Beverly Hills. Su máxima preocupación es llevar la ropa más atractiva y ser tan populares como sea posible. Pero a pesar de su apariencia, Cher tiene un gran corazón.
La historia es buena, no creo que presente algo muy original dentro del género pero es disfrutable. Como ya dije, me parece que es una película que tiene mucho estilo, es más que nada por eso que me parece algo memorable, no tanto en cuanto a trama, pero si tiene algunos momentos geniales por culpa de lo buenos que son sus personajes, teniendo diálogos muy buenos en el medio. El romance no es malo, pero si es un poco polémico lo que se muestra, es por eso que me quedo más con la comedia, me parece que éstos momentos están mejor logrados. Por otro lado, la duración de poco más de hora y media es perfecta ya que se complementa bien con el buen ritmo que tiene, haciendo que se pase bastante rápido.
Los personajes son geniales, de lo mejor de la película. Cher es una protagonista icónica, con una personalidad genial y una actuación por parte de su actriz que mejora su personaje. Cae mucho mejor de lo que pensaba y el desarrollo que tiene me gustó, como ya dije el romance que le presentan es un poco polémico pero tampoco me parece algo mal planteado dentro de la cinta. Después tenemos a Dionne y Tai como personajes un poco más secundarios que también me gustaron, ésta última como un gran alivio cómico en algunos momentos. Por último, Josh es el que menos me gustó de los que mencione, me parece que para lo importante que termina siendo en la historia no tuvo tanta participación antes, al menos no la suficiente para que su personaje me gustara.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente las actuaciones, Alicia Silverstone, Brittany Murphy y Stacey Dash están muy bien, nada de otro mundo pero es un sólido trabajo para que sus personajes resulten entrañables. Por otro lado, la dirección de Amy Heckerling es buena, en general visualmente me gustó la película y me parece que tiene un tono muy original que la diferencia un poco de otras cintas parecidas. Lo mismo digo de la banda sonora, la original es buena pero tiene temas conocidos que utilizan de una gran manera.
En conclusión, una buena película que entiendo por qué es un clásico y tanta gente le encanta, yo no soy muy fan de éste tipo de películas pero así y todo la pude disfrutar. La recomiendo.

Clueless came out the year I graduated high school, and while I could pretend that I was watching Pulp Fiction on a loop and playing in a Guided by Voices cover band, that wasnt the case. I liked Nirvana, but I actually preferred Pearl Jam. Yeah, I grew up listening to Princes Purple Rain, Guns N Roses Appetite for Destruction, and Wu Tangs Enter the 36 Chambers, but I also grew up on Poisons Open Up and Say Aaah, Lives Throwing Copper, and The Crash Test Dummies hit single, Hmmmm Hmmmm Hmmmmm Hmmmm. (sic) Im not saying I should be ashamed of that music, but, respectively, those bands were freebasing hairspray, subtly evangelizing (though I had no idea what the hell sorry they were talking about), and writing incisive lyrics about a kid that had birthmarks all over her body. (erm, wut?)
At that point in my life, I loved movies, but I was not an According to Hoyle cinephile. Of the thirty super high brow films Ive tagged on here from 94 and 95, I had seen Casino, Natural Born Killers, In the Mouth of Madness, and yes, Clueless. And while the other films not named Natural Born Killers (which of course I loved at the time BEEP BEEP L7) are really great, Clueless is right there with them. 
-Alicia Silverstones performance is not good, its not great, its borderline perfect (even if the Hate-ians part wasnt acting!) 
-the writing is amazing. Its so funny, but in this really benevolent way
 Brittany Murphy is frumpy, but instead of making fun of her, Cher and Dionne give her a makeover and befriend her. 
 the teachers are (unsurprisingly) characterized as nebbish and awkward, but, again, Cher and Dionne feel for them, and melt when the clumsy sparks start flying. 
 even the rivalry between Cher and her half-brother Josh (Paul Rudd), while comprised primarily of trading insults for the majority of the film, is light-hearted and innocuous. (and Im with Cher. I worship Radiohead, but Fake Plastic Trees has always sounded like a noodle left in boiling water ten minutes too long)
Finally, theres Amy Heckerling. A buncha lame people bristled at Fast Times at Ridgemont High being added to the Criterion Collection, but thats ridiculous. Clueless and Fast Times compliment each other so well. Clueless seems light and breezy, and, for the most part it is, but while Fast Times can also seem like that with Spicoli, etc., issues like teen pregnancy, misappropriation of pizza slices, abortion, and having to wear a fugly outfit at a high school job are empathetically portrayed. 
Most importantly, though, is that Heckerling portrays high school emotions like they matter, and have stakes, instead of condescendingly portraying them like a certain movie where an idealized sociopath takes advantage of his anxiety-ridden best friend to enjoy a carefree day that will probably result in said friend getting beaten by a domineering parental figure. 
You dont name your movie Clueless if it actually is. Clueless is a classic thats sometimes treated as a trifle, but as with much of Amy Heckerlings work, theres more to it if youre paying attention.

Theres an excellent series of Wallace Shawn movies currently showing at Metrograph. I wrote about some of the films for Screen Slate. My words cant do justice to his achievement, but I hope the piece at least entices some of you in New York to attend these screenings. Its a really stacked line-up, with many wonderful guests.
Clueless is not among the movies discussed at length in that piece, partially because I wanted to focus hard on Wally-as-auteur, and partially because it such is a towering masterpiece in its own right that it deserves more space than I could there afford to give it. I honestly view it as being totally in sync with the pop mythmaking Gregg Araki was forging in his movies around the same time (albeit within a radically different context) an attempt to render the culture of the nineties as a kind of period piece while it was actively unfolding. That degree of distanciation is immediately signaled within the narrative itself (Cher is a hyper-modern girl who lives in a 1950s-style mansion straight out of Sirk), and continually resurfaces in different configurations as the blinkered characters attempt to litigate their environment. Heckerlings exaggeration of the contemporary is blissfully comic without ever devolving into the demeaning cynicism so many teen movies capitulate to. Her gaze on these characters remains curious and humane even as she delicately skewers the ironies of their existence. Just look at the soft, effulgent light cast on everyones faces, without judgement or distinction, always bringing out the charisma of each actor no matter their role. Its beautiful to behold. And Alicia Silverstone really does give a performance for the ages. I love these track-in shots on her intensely contemplating the dilemmas of her life. Silverstones expressions somehow manage to communicate, simultaneously, her comic naïveté and her underlying, if underdeveloped, moral sense. It is the subtlety poignantly expressed by Heckerling herself in the QA the difference between stupid and clueless. This belongs not merely in the canon of the greatest teen movies, but in the greatest films of its decade, bar none.

It does not say RSVP on the Statue of Liberty!
I knew that for my 500th review I had to go big or go home. It had to be a really good, maybe even great movie. But then I thought, why stop at great? Why not watch a perfect movie? Why not watch... Clueless? Seriously, does this have any flaws? As if!
Lets start with the production design. The bright colors and impossibly fashionable high school students immediately tell us were in a fantastic version of the real world, a fact  commented on in the opening narration, in which Alicia Silverstones Cher says sarcastically What is this, a Noxzema commercial? over too-perfect footage of her and her friends hanging out set to Kim Wildes Kids in America. Normally this kind of self-aware joke would introduce a shift into the less-than-perfect world of the characters (the TV show Freaks and Geeks does exactly this in its opening scene as it pans down from the cheerleader and football player to the real students under the bleachers). But when Chers way normal teenage life is revealed, its no less an idealized fantasy than that initial montage.
A major component of this fantasy is the dizzying array of fashions on display. Forget about high school studentsare there any celebrities that dress as well as Cher? I could write a couple of thousand words on her outfits aloneprobably no one in the history of cinema has done more for plaid. Of course, the yellow number that she starts the movie in is the most iconic, but I want to shout out another outfit, only glimpsed for a second, that combines a pin-striped jacket and a grayblack tartan sweater vestcombining multiple patterns like that is not for the faint-hearted. Unbelievably, Mona May wasnt even nominated for her costume design. 
Then theres the writing. Amy Heckerlings script successfully transplants Emma into a Beverly Hills high school, substituting teenagers hypersensitivity to microscopically varying degrees of coolness and clique affiliation for the stratified class system of Austens nineteenth-century England. Together with Fast Times at Ridgemont High, this cemented Heckerlings position as Americas poet laureate of teenage life. Of course the jokes are nearly all bangers (There goes your social life), but maybe the greatest trick the screenplay pulls off is making Cher both a parody of a clueless rich girl and someone we instantly like and root for. Were somehow both laughing at her and with her. Wicked tries to do something like this with the Glinda character, but not half as well. Heckerlings framing of the story asks the question what if you had been rich and attractive in high school, but instead of indulging in the cruelty that these privileges entitled you to, you were instead kind and unflaggingly positive? 
That brings us to the element that makes this balancing act work Alicia Silverstones performance. It would be so easy to get this wrong, to make the audience either hate the character for being so unaware of her own privilege, or find her constant enthusiasm cloying and obnoxious. Most of this is of course thanks to Silverstones natural charisma, but I think another crucial component is the voiceover narration. One reason this device is so often derided by cinephiles is that actors often deliver it in a flat, newscaster voice that doesnt carry the same emotion that their conversational voice does (this may have to do with the difficulty of delivering a performance while sitting alone in a sound booth). Here, Silverstone talks to us as if were characters in the movie, sitting next to her at the lunch table. It pulls us into the world and makes us accomplices in the act of fantasy the movie is engaged in. On this rewatch I also noticed her many reaction shots, which are often just as funny as the actual jokes. And although Silverstone is the linchpin, all the young actors are good at finding the real human being underneath the caricature. 
All of the needle drops are pitch perfect as well, and have you wanting to get up off your couch and dance in your living room, culminating in General Publics Tenderness (go ahead and listen to it nowits guaranteed to make your day better). In context, the three descending notes that start the song sound like wedding bellslike all good romantic comedies, this one ends with a wedding, and the the movie finds a clever way to pull this off in a story about high school students. Despite what you may be seeing on the news lately, Americas greatest export has always been optimism, and nowhere is that clearer than in Cluelessmore than a movie, its a device for manufacturing joy.

Somebody made a comment to me on Twitter a while back that I dont watch many comedies, and from that I deduced that most people think Im a humourless turd and was very sad for the most of the day afterwards.
But its not untrue to suggest that I dont watch many of them. Unless I can be absolutely sure they are going to be funny, Im very reluctant to watch them. I treat them differently than, say, horror films. I dont steer clear of horror films if I dont think theyll scare me because I have almost never been scared by any horror films. With comedies, however, Im not so forgiving. So yeah, perhaps the humourless turd presumption was a sound one on my part.
That said, when I do find a comedy I like I am very super-supportive of that comedy and I will often watch and rewatch it until I know all the dialogue, and then get on the tits of everyone on Twitter and Letterboxd doing quotes and posting gifs from it. I make up for it, see? And with Clueless, I think it is easily going to slip into that category. In fact, I think I knew about 10 minutes in that this was going to be the case.
I had never been massively arsed about seeing this film and, truth be told, I might not have watched it for a further very long time if it wasnt about to expire on Mubi today. I always thought Id seen all the best lines over the last 21 years (!) in commercials and clips shows and stuff but it turns out that I hadnt at all. This has got so many fantastic one-liners, turns of phrase and just outright funny stuff in it that if youre of a similar mindset then believe me when I say that youre way off.
Of course, everyone else has seen this film and youre all rolling your eyes that I only just got round to this anyway. But you never know.
I think that perhaps the most impressive thing about Clueless is that these characters are all so likeable when, initially, theyre set up as being instantly dislikeable. Yet thanks to a whole load of sweetness that never turns to saccharine, a far bigger dash of self deprecation than I was expecting, the fact that everyone is pretty much as daft as each other, and some brilliant direction and performances, practically nobody here is really all that bad.
There are a few occasions where Clueless could easily float off into some crapper and more compromised areas - in fact, I think it actually does a couple of times. But again, the sheer charm and humour on show just erases all that in much the same way The Breakfast Club is routinely able to put a very thick papering over some pretty sizeable cracks. Its just got the same unshakeable spirit and quality of humour.
Everyone is so great here and I do finally get why everyone ponders why Alicia Silverstones career never hit the heights that were expected of her. Ive always liked Paul Rudd and now, finally, Ive seen him in a film thats actually really good, although little in this film is a match for Stacey Dash and Donald Faisons sublimely written and performed relationship. My howls with laughter at the head shaving scene caused worried looks on the faces of my two eldest daughters.
Throw in the always awesome Dan Hedaya, showing again what an under-appreciated ability he has for comedy, and it was like that extra cherry on the cake with Amy Heckerling putting one of my favourite actors in this. Persistently funny, clever and sharp, Im sure Ill be making up for not having seen this until now many times in the near future. 
I do want to save the last word for Brittany Murphy though. I almost slightly wish she wasnt so wonderful in this because it just makes me even sadder that shes not with us any more, and indeed makes miss her all the more. We didnt deserve her but we should all be thankful that we got her at all.

I could drum up some phony reason not to give Amy Heckerlings Clueless a perfect score. Of everything Ive given 5 stars to, its likely the only one that does nothing original aesthetically. But I feel like a focus on aesthetics might draw attention away from what works in this movie. I could pretend that I was offended by the portrayal of Christian, the only gay character. But its not so much how the film portrays him as much as it is how the other characters see them, which, especially in 1995, speaks to the invisibility of LGBQT lifestyles in mainstream film. I would even go so far as to say Chers initial confusion over Christians sexuality is a pointed comment on heteronormativity and that even though he tries to signal her multiple times, she remains oblivious because the assumption, of course, is that everyone is straight.
But I wont pretend that I did anything but love this movie from cover to cover on this most recent rewatch. I laughed, so hard, at this film, especially all the parts that I didnt catch as a naive teenager (most specifically, no shit you got coke here? yeah this is America). Everyone is unbelievably perfectly cast Im not sure anyone here has been better than they are here besides perhaps Wallace Shawn. In particular, Brittany Murphy and Breckin Meyers chemistry is off the charts.
In a world mostly bereft of films about female friendship, Clueless is a paean to it. More than that, it calls out the vast difference in expectations between men and women, what Cher and Tai and Dionne go through to look presentable compared to the men of the film. In another telling moment, Chers sexual assault and mugging scene are swept under the rug because they dont fit the narrative. People would rather listen to Tais damsel in distress at the mall story because of the clarity of its herovictimvillain characters.
While the main thrust of this film is Cher unlearning her selfishness, learning that she cant get everything she wants through arguing, that turning Tai into a clone has its backlash, I think my favorite part is actually that Mr. Hall and Ms. Geist work out, that the film ends with their wedding, implying that even good deeds done selfishly arent completely erased by their initial selfishness. Theres something beautifully sweet about that that I can really embrace.

50 Shades of Ideology
by Slavoj Zizek
50 Shades of Grey is most assuredly a fantasy. But it is not, as those who flocked to theaters this weekend to bask in its spectacle believe, a sex fantasy. Rather, it is a fantasy enactment of the relationship between the neoliberal subject and Capital. All of the misery and exploitation that are caused by Capital are justified by the idea of consent. We all, as individuals, enter into bilateral relationships with capital as consumers and workers, that are ostensibly consensual and thus ethically permissible. Such is the case of Anastasia Steele, a virginal college senior who enters into a sado-masochistic engagement with billionaire telecommunications mogul Christian Grey. The main plot point of the film is the duos negotiation of a contract that will set the boundaries for what sort sex acts Steele will be asked to perform. These negotiations are framed as an expression of consensual actions between equals, but of course this is ridiculous. One of the parties involved is a twenty-year-old virgin on the cusp of entering a presumably debt-ridden, uncertain post collegiate career and the other is a sexually-experienced member of the global financial elite. During this negotiation, Grey seeks to control and seduce Steele with the trappings of his wealth, all while pushing her sexual boundaries and inflicting greater and greater degrees of physical discomfort on her in the pursuit of his pleasure. The real fantasy that 50 Shades of Grey sells is that such a negotiation could ever be truly consensual. Such a fantasy allows us to go about our days in the absolute thralldom of late capitalism with an illusion of agency.

Of course, I had to see this movie. I wont read the book, because there are limits to my curiosity, but a big budget Hollywood romance with riding crops was too much for me to ignore. I read before that the lead actors hated each other and that the writer of the book hated the director of the film, so I was prepared for an unwatchable mess, a train wreck of glorious misery. Instead, what i got was an awkward, misguided attempt at exploring the mind and heart of a sadist that perhaps rang true for someone but for me just felt hollow and dull.
I wrote previously about how bad dialogue rendered Lying Lips meaningless and weak here, it renders the tension between the leads nonexistent. In part, yes, the charactersperformers had no chemistry, but only the best of actors could have turned the cliche-ridden, unnatural, and irritatingly repetitive dialogue into anything resembling passion or romance. This films best moments are contract negotiation, because at least then, theres some excuse for the stiffness (and honestly, they have some decent moments in there even in the writing, but its fairly juvenile humor that breaks through). 
The other piece of the bad performance puzzle is that the characters these actors were asked to portray were... stupid. I mean, they were not intelligent people. Nor realistic (Christian Grey is a fairly awful fantasy figure, rich and hiding a heart beneath a supposedly cold exterior--a cold exterior we never see). But mostly, this film portrays sad romantic cliches of uncommunicative partners behaving stupidly for the sake of cheap drama, which is one of my biggest pet peeves. Notably, 
Anastasia (you can really feel the roots of this as fan fiction) demands at the end to feel the worst punishment Christian can dole out, then has the gall to be outraged at what it turns out to be meanwhile, Christian has been showing signs throughout the movie of being dishonest with his claims that he would do nothing without her consent. He literally breaks into her apartment, sells her car, and stalks her when she flies 3000 miles away. But its only when he belts her at her request that she has the gall to be outraged? It seems as if the writer has no concept of what consent is, nor the emotional content of submission or dominance.
Visually, the film is fairly slick, and there are moments where it has an impressive look to it. Christians piano room (no idea what its supposed to be) is framed and trifurcated in a striking way, and the contract negotiation took place in a room my friend called the Michael Mann room for a reason. But at other times, the slickness came off as trite and dull--its clear they are avoiding showing anything actually risque during the sex scenes in a way that is almost offensively vanilla--or blatantly commercial. The latter is most evident as Christians car pulls up in a forest highway and the camera pauses on the car in a manner that is right out of a car commercial. Other moments are defeated as the camera shakes and bobs its way up and down, awkwardly, for no discernible reason. 
Overall, this is a film made for its hype alone, it feels like. No one seems much interested in making more it than that, going so far as to avoid any depth of emotion or imagery beyond a few cold cityscapes and clinically austere offices (how fittingly empty). Its a story of two emotionally stunted people bouncing off each other boringly, while the dialogue heavy handedly points you to the obvious conclusions, which are then never reached due to this films being nothing more than an ephemeral pep rally for later installments and more money. it is loud spectacle courting bored milquetoasts for easy profits.

90 of my problems with the film relate back to the book, but even those problems Taylor-Johnson manages to skew or even overcome. My main peeve with the book was Anas asinine inner voice. Sweet Jesus. Shes vapid, repetitive, spineless - the film is already infinitely better than the book because it doesnt dwell on Anas inner musings. It also gives Ana more of her agency back - in the book whenever Christian suggest something, theres pretty much an immediate internal NO, which makes the trepidation feel much more definite, and then when she succumbs to his pestering, it feels forced and insincere, as if she has no will of her own (or worse, it fuels the abusive aspect to their relationship). Here, we see Anas trepidation but, yknow, sometimes you need to get used to an idea first. Theres much less of a problem with consent than in the book. 
Christian is still kind of a douche, but he gets off lighter than in the book. Its still endlessly annoying that hes completely unwilling to tell Ana anything, and so the whole power distribution is off (something I find more unappealing than any bedroom attributes, but I guess in the case of the those its a dont knock it til youve tried it-situation), but Jamie Dornans mischievous grin makes it seem a lot more playful, and less manipulative. Perhaps this is bad (depends on where the second film will go), but it seemed a lot lighter than in the book. 
Anas still overly meek, and I wish Dakota Johnson didnt look up through her bangs endearingly and Diana-like all of the time, but Johnson makes her sassier than in the book. In the book Ana sometimes taunts out of provocation, which I found uncomfortable, but here it adds a playful element. 
The second film, if they make it, will prove if this playfulness is what Taylor-Johnson had in mind, or if theyre the seed of undermining consent. The second is the creepiest of the books, and the real test to see if the issue with consent is the same. All I can hope is that Sam Taylor-Johnson will be on board again (although I highly doubt it), because I think its incredibly powerful that such a worldwide phenomenon can make people think about female sexuality, sexual preferences, and what constitutes consent, domestic violence and healthy relationships, and Taylor-Johnson manages to make mindless, badly-written drivel relevant and valuable. Half a star extra, just for you, Sam.

Young English literature major Anastasia Ana Steele (Dakota Johnson) is asked by a sick friend to interview billionaire entrepeneur Christian Grey (Jamie Dornan) for her. Ana feels an immediate attraction to the handsome Christian, who seems to be interested in her as well. Fifty Shades of Grey is an erotic romantic drama film directed by Sam Taylor-Johnson, based on the novel of the same name by E. L. James. Its the 1st installment in the Fifty Shades of Grey film series.
I usually dont talk much about a movies source material, but in this case, I cant avoid it. James novel begann as Twilight fan fiction which was then self-published and became a global bestseller, oftentimes called Mommy porn, a more harmless form of nonetheless kinky erotica.
Normally, I would applaud a success story like that - but not when its the most atrociously written novel Ive ever read (but not until the end, it was impossible). Its even worse if youre a writer yourself, making it a truly painful experience. I oftentimes thought James had mistaken a list of Things Not to Do When Writing Your Novel as a to-do-list.
It also misrepresents what BDSM really is about, proving the author didnt actually do any research. While Im not an expert, BDSM is based in trust, safety and informed consent. What Fifty Shades of Grey romanticizes and sells to its readers, however, is an abusive and controlling relationship.
A film adaptation can change that, at least to a degree, and the filmmakers actually managed to improve upon the source material, by cutting many controversial or bizarre moments. So, the Ana from the novel who never used a computer or sent an email in her life, as well as the Inner Goddess living in her head, are, luckily, gone.
However, we still get lots of silly dialogue and shallow characters. And while much of it is toned down, the films depiction of BDSM and the relationship Ana enters in - or, more correctly, is manipulated into entering - are nonetheless highly problematic.
And yet, theres good here. Fifty Shades of Grey is a big-budget movie which put that money to excellent use. It looks great, with terrific art direction, production design and cinematography - Christians apartment and the contract scene are among the highlights. Danny Elfmans film score is beautiful as well, and so is the soundtrack, which includes the Oscar-nominated Earned It by The Weeknd.
And theres Dakota Johnson, of course, in her breakthrough role. While I wish this wouldve happened in another movie, she nonetheless very much shows her acting chops. Unfortunately, theres not even a hint of chemistry between her and co-star Jamie Dornan.
The movie, despite receiving negative reviews and five Golden Raspberry Awards, became a huge commercial hit, and both follow-up novels were adapted for the big screen as well, with similar results.
In conclusion, while Fifty Shades of Grey at least tones down its highly problematic themes, what it takes away isnt replaced with anything truly intriguing or of substance, making it a hollow experience, despite excellent production values, great music, and a committed performance by Dakota Johnson.

50 Shades is catnip for the undersexed middle-aged woman whose fantasies involve sex toys and clunky dialogue. 
Christian Grey is a man borne out of her dreary imagination. Hes overtly successful while radiating a soft but masculine mystique. Hes a clean freak (naturally) and his quirks (like his evasiveness and weakness for whips) only serve to make him more desirable. In the first forty minutes he smiles before taking Annas call, pulls her from the path of a speeding vehicle, rushes to her aid at a club, holds her hair back while she vomits, flies her to Seattle on a whim and deflowers her in semi-darkness over romantic pop strings. 
Hes not only fictional, hes inconceivable a celluloid antibiotic for a woman who now believes the best man for her would be one shed invented herself. She despises and longs for Mr. Grey, having known men herself who make romantic gestures while insisting its a casual arrangement (in the movie there is literally a contract signed). 
I have to assume that novelist E. L. James has either never met a man or wasnt paying much attention when she did. If Grey is meant to be fantastic and cartoonish I dont know to what end, except perhaps as a sad consolation prize to women who cant see past their libidos. I wish someone had mentioned to James that good sex is in the real immediate world - its about imperfection the little you-isms and them-isms that perfume it with specifics that ring in our memory. Women know this more naturally than men, so why have so many women given their attention to an insipid white-washed fantasist like E. L. James who writes as sensually as a vulgarian paints with faecal matter? 
The film adaptation does what it can to improve the source material. Theres an even tempo to the images and the pop tunes are nicely integrated. The screenplay takes much of its dialogue from the book (the director apparently fought to rewrite it but was overruled), which means the simplest exchanges between characters sound like aliens mimicking human behaviour from old TV transmissions. The principle actors are fresh and convey a ripening desire in the gaps between the dialogue, but ultimately we are forever pulled back down into the artless swamp of its moist-shrew-fantasy constraints. 
I made it through two chapters of the book and forty solid minutes of the film before deciding to leave and go shopping. I had the impression I was annoying the enraptured women sitting around me. Skimming through the reviews for Fifty Shades of Grey it becomes clear that this is a film many people went in with preconceived notions, and Im no different. Out of nowhere, a few weeks ago, I suddenly wanted to see it. You know, as a movie I would watch ironically, like some people sing along to Britney Spears ironically. What I usually do in that situation is I google a particularly stupid ex-boyfriend, look at his stupid face for a minute or two, tell him right to his stupid face just how stupid he is, and then I feel so pumped up on anger that I feel I can face any challenge that will come my way in the next couple of days. Anger can be paralyzing, sure, but it can also be a fuel. I was certain I was gonna hate this film, and I was going to have fun doing so.
Now, I dont want to say that Fifty Shades of Grey completely surprised me or that my expectations were totally off. They werent. A large part of it was exactly how I expected it to be. It was just nowhere near as bad as I thought it was gonna be, and neither did it make me angry. Maybe its because I had such incredibly low expectations, but I feel I kind of owe Fifty Shades of Grey an apology. Because believe it or not, it made me think. It made me question myself. Expectations can be a funny thing. If youd asked me not a even a week ago if I was going to see Fifty Shades of Grey, I would have laughed at the notion and would have claimed that Id never watch the movie. Well, today I did, and Im surprised to say that I actually liked the film. Mainstream porn and or laughable camp this is not, despite what you perceptions about the source material might be.
For starters, I must congratulate Sam Taylor-Johnson on her work here. For a source whose story (or lack of) has become the butt of many jokes, she handles the material with such care and caution that I was initially thrown off. I went in expecting a trashy erotic flick and while there are some trashy aspects of the film (mostly the dialogue when its trying to be sexy), the film is very careful and almost calm in its approach to something that is considered taboo in mainstream movies today.
Giving the novel a Fincher-esque spin (never thought Id say that), Taylor-Johnson tackles the controversial subject matter head-on, but gives it a high-class, professional gloss. The sex scenes have a restrained, if almost tasteful approach to them, which was an admirable choice, given the audience the film is ultimately aimed towards. This in turn gives the film a sense of importance and confidence, which is much more than a film based on this source material should have ever gotten. And from what Ive heard, the book is pure shit, so this has got to be a massive upgrade.
Taylor-Johnson also creates a surprisingly sturdy character study for Anastasia Steele (played by Dakota Johnson). Not only does this relationship between her and Christian Grey fuel and expand her sexual awakening (duh), but it also develops Anastasia into a well-rounded character as well. Their relationship shows how the mentality of true love that she reads and learns in the classic literature isnt real. And that sometimes, love can be strange.  Granted, it isnt the strongest message, but its better than abusive sex for the sake of abusive sex. In other words, at least the filmmakers tried here. It also shows her strong side, not always doing whatever the dominant partner wishes. She grows from a shy and quiet woman to one with much more authority and power. 
Now, the character building that Taylor-Johnson and screenwriter Kelly Marcel try to set up doesnt always work. For example, the plot never gets the time to explain while Grey likes those chains and whips, leaving us with a sexist, confused man who is very, very mysterious. It leads to some good conflict in an otherwise uneventful movie, sure, but it leaves you hanging when it really shouldnt.
And like mentioned, there isnt much of a story to talk about here. But, going in expecting pure crap, its still more of a story than I was expecting and theres still a lot of elements on display that make up for flaws in the plotting. The greatest aspect of the film is definitely the cinematography from Seamus McGarvey, which is strikingly beautiful, only adding to the fact that Taylor-Johnson wanted to elevate the source material to more than trashy erotica. Also, I must comment on the score. Danny Elfman is on point here, matching the visuals with somber tunes to go with it. And even though some of the musical tracks in the film are clearly added to gain more audience appeal, they work in the context of the film.
The fact that the general public is either avoiding the film because they expected it to be shit or trashing it because they expected it to have more sex or it was too boring is a little shocking to me. Granted, I was avoiding the film for the first reason, but Im glad that I gave it a shot. Sam Taylor-Johnson delivers a utterly impressive film based on material that is better left in a dollar bin, and the fact that people are just shrugging it off anyway is concerning. It isnt a great movie, sure. But compared to my expectations and the expectations of many others, its much, much better than it had any right to be. Its just a shame that Taylor-Johnson wont return for the sequel, as she showed of some impressive skills here in terms of setting a distinct tone, striking imagery, and working with a plot that wasnt necessarily there in the first place.
Grade B

I guess the obvious irony is that, even though Grey is the one in ripped denim and clutching a riding crop, the power equilibrium is firmly tipped towards Ana. The film seemed to be addressing (although never proselytising from either corner) the issue of whether these two forms of romantic interaction can ever be comparable. The assessment that people are essentially boring, unexpressive and seek familiarity in a mate came across as extremely radical. And yet, the material is delivered in a way which is pure enough  in the way its shot, scripted, paced, ordered  to warrent multiple readings. I caught Naruses Scattered Clouds recently which asks whether a woman can ever truly love and accept a man who accidentally killed her husband (who she adored), even though she is physically and emotionally attracted to him and he has gone to extreme lengths to demonstrate his regret. The beauty (and miraculousness) of that film is in the way it takes that central theme and, in a scrupulously analytical way, offers examples of how and why that dynamic could work and how why it could fail. The suggestion, also, is that, you could never know me, despite the fact that I can know you, and youre going to have to accept that, mainly from Grey. Just as a lot of the detail here is transferable, you could easily tell the same story with Ana swapped for a Chinese business envoy. Despite one guy who has a mild crush on her, Ana has no outside influences that might effect the trajectory of her relationship, to the point where the film even avoids those romance fiction perennials of having the housemate plant seeds of doubt or the conservative parents wagging fingers disapprovingly. Greys business activities remain so vague that they could never have any actual bearing on the plot, force a decision or create an unbelievable juncture.

Thats right Academy Award Nominee Fifty Shades of Grey gets five stars from me. Shes among my favorite characters in film history right beside Disneys Snow White, The Wind Risess Jiro, Howls Moving Castles Sophie, Eighth Grades Kayla, and Punch-Drunk Loves Lena, because of how little personality they all seem to possess. She, like those mentioned above, is kind of a vanilla character, but one who the writer respects enough to place at the center of their story, which is something I dont really get to see much of in movies. I always find it rather difficult to relate to movies that star characters with huge personalities (which might explain my initial dislike for Lady Bird) because, quite simply, I dont have a very strong personality. Mostly, I just kind of adapt to whoever Im with. Like, sure, Id sign that contract Mr Grey, if only because theres not really enough Michael in here to resist it. Like Sophie, Id just kinda stumble into a house and start cleaning just cause... Im not really a person unless Im doing something. Like Lena Id absolutely pursue Barry because I need somebody to fill that void that is me. I just need someone or something so I can, I dont know... be an interesting person? Like I do and say interesting things sometimes, but mostly just as a response to whoevers in front of me? And Anastasia makes me feel so seen because of how awkwardly non-human she is. Shes obviously got some agency, but shes mostly just along for the ride. AND with the incredible awkwardness that Dakota Johnson brings to the role, it just hits so so close to home.
and gang... Ive finally found that person. That special guy that fills the void and makes me feel more like a person than anyone ever has before. I felt like I had to watch one of those blank-page-for-a-character movies bc theyre the reason that Ive had faith that Im worthy of being loved. In a world full of Bridges of Madison Countys and I Am Loves, where the boring characters are there simply to be disliked and cheated on, these are the movies that have told me that, uninteresting as I may be, Im worthy of love. The most anticipated piece of erotica ever made, Fifty Shades of Grey is far from a good film but probably acceptable to an audience wanting a safe, slick and sexy flick. The films problems are (in increasing order of bad) simply that the leads lack chemistry, the source material is terrible, the studio played it too conservatively and the relationship depicted is problematic. On the bright side, however, Fifty Shades of Grey is an engaging piece of pulp thats very well directed and perfectly watchable for what it is.
Fifty Shades of Grey has a bad premise. The story is hung together by sex scenes which E.L. James - who is a terrible (see later), talentless person - failed to make into a cohesive story. The film adaptation cleverly attempts to correct James inability to write dialogue, set up plot points or create compelling characters by actually using a scriptwriter who isnt a fucking moron. Unfortunately for Fifty Shades of Grey, E.L. James demanded almost total control over the production and so the film became unstuck before filming even began. The dialogue is laughably bad, the scenes forced and the writing both unromantic and unsexy. It certainly doesnt help that whilst Dakota Johnson and Jamie Dornan are competent actors when dealing with the material in a vacuum, whenever they interact together the spark disappears entirely.
However, despite these massive problems, Fifty Shades of Grey is perfectly fine as a lowbrow sex film. Its predictable, dumb and badly written but so is most garbage erotica and the audience for Fifty Shades of Grey probably werent expecting more. There appears to be a strong level of self-awareness by the actors and director Sam Taylor-Johnson and it almost feels satirical in its tone. When the actors are required to spout ridiculous lines, they seem genuinely aware of their stupidity but perform them knowingly deadpan. The romance is not great, nor is the sex, but for those wanting a love story to get invested in, theres plenty worse. The book, dubbed mommy porn, was aimed at the ignorant. Those aware of erotic literature or online fan-fiction or highly sexual films always knew that Fifty Shades of Grey isnt amongst the best, most substantial or even the most erotic. If you were a fan of these things Fifty Shades of Grey was the bastardised commercial sell-out. But thats why the book attracted an audience of fairly open-minded, middle-aged women. It was different, wildly erotic and very explicit. If people knew better erotica existed, theyd surely not be reading shit like Fifty Shades of Grey. This is not to attack people for ignorance (I am no expert on the subject myself but Ive done a fair amount of reading about it), but just to highlight the cultural expectation upon the film. It needed to be sexy and relatively romantic and that was all. Depth and character are irrelevant to the films purpose and on these limited terms, Fifty Shades of Grey is generally a success.
One problem with the film that should be disappointing to most is that the sex and nudity is all too safe and not very explicit. Hollywood has a sex problem and Fifty Shades of Grey suffers from it more than most movies. For some reason, the good ol US of A seems to be contrarian to many other parts of the world because in film-making, it deems violence more acceptable than nudity. Graphic depictions of limbs being cut off and guts spilling everywhere are perfectly accepted in R-rated films but show too much dick or feature cunnilingus and you get slapped with the far more restrictive NC-17 rating. This is batshit insane as nudity and sex are natural parts of being human which children should be taught to accept and not feel awkward about. Yet plenty of torture porn is considered more suitable. Seriously, how the fuck is this the system? Its even worse when one considers that the majority of theatre owners are so overly conservative they refuse to play any film rated NC-17 regardless of artistic quality or intent. Fifty Shades of Grey could have been the film to change the system for the better. It was a guaranteed hit and if itd had an NC-17 rating, itd force some of these theatres to change their policies which would allow more films in the future to be made without having to self-censor for commercial reasons. Because of selfish reasons, the studio toned the film down and pandered to these genophobic fuckwits who would willingly censor art for their own backward ideology. If you want a reason to despise Fifty Shades of Grey, the profit-motivated censorship of nudity is one of the most reasonable attacks one could launch at it.
Besides the censorship, the chief problem with the nudity presented in the film is that the constrained, conservative approach makes the film seem sexist and less sexy. We see endless shots of Dakota Johnsons naked body but very little of Jamie Dornan even though one presumes the target audience is far more interested in his physique. We see loads of breast but no genitals (from either person) and it feels as though the film is too timid to acknowledge anybody actually has sex organs. The lack of male nudity seems particularly egregious considering how much the film focuses on the female body in various compromising positions. If you want titillation, theres much smuttier and filthier versions of this type of the story that arent just hardcore porn. Sam Taylor-Johnson does at least manage to film the majority of sex scenes in a way which looks classy and not exploitative but why bother hiring an arthouse director who filmed this (WARNING  link leads to a porn site) if youre going to limit the amount of sex and nudity so arbitrarily anyway. Its a real opportunity missed for the studio to push the bounds of how much sex and nudity could be present in a Hollywood blockbuster.
One aspect of Fifty Shades of Grey that is actually problematic is the shitty depiction of BDSM. It is misleading, inaccurate and dangerous.
