The effect that bestseller adaptations have had on Hollywood over the better part of the last decade has led to some rather extraordinary productions, in both the best and the worst senses. Fifty Shades of Grey was always going to be a tough one not only is the source material derived from glorified Twilight fanfiction, but on top of that this is also a studio production thats goal is to become as big a success as possible. This is already an issue as the book itself is pretty smutty to such an extent that much of it would have to be toned down to both cater to the MPAA guidelines and the tastes of the general public.
Fifty Shades of Grey follows the story of English literature student Anastasia Steele (Johnson), a young and naive college graduate who finds herself entangled in the life of the eligible billionaire Batchelor Christian Grey (Dornan).  They enter into a rocky relationship in which Christian introduces her to the world of BDSM, and a majority of the film focuses heavily on the nature of this consensual relationship and the dynamic that evolves between them.
The plot dwells on this design and the contract that Grey wishes her to sign, predominantly focused on their relationship and the way they handle and cater to each others desires. Its more of a peruse into the essence of romance as opposed to the explicit pleasure stimulus of the original novel, and this is already one of the films stronger stances outside of adaptation. Kelly Marcels screenplay works around the gender politics of the situation by constantly reinforcing that this is a consensual relationship they are entering into without feeling too heavy-handed.
The design and reveal of Christians Playroom is fairly frightening in its medieval arrangement, and its all embedded with the notion that you should be as leery towards Greys outlook as Ana is. Greys idea of buying her into his life is inherently uncomfortable and Ana is fully aware of this, treading down the path with much trepidation. The film exemplifies his lifestyle, from cars to luxury penthouses through set pieces and scenes. He is a man whose prowess is extended through monetary capital, and theres some discussion to be made of this that is not fully utilised  such as him treating their relationship with the same cold temperament of a businessman, through emails, meetings and contractual obligation. Even Greys employment may too be purposefully ambiguous, but Ana proves herself by being above the allure of such cynical gestures. Christians struggle to connect could stem from his ridged formality, but his box ticking backstory disarms this.
These kinds of shortcomings and missed opportunities are what brings the film down the most, and the dominantsubmissive context is something better explored in other pictures such as Steven Shainbergs excellent 2002 film, Secretary.
Speaking of which, the sex scenes are not all that they should be. Although shot well, every scene is overlaid with pop music that builds from instrumental to vocal invasion. Its all very tame in presentation, like soft-core pornography that titillates but rarely feels genuine or even sexy. Its quite something that this is this first major studio release in years to be essentially erotica, but theres little to enjoy here on that front. Besides the sexual politics, the film is probably branching into new realms of sexism all on its own, as there is plenty exhibited of the female body while the male member is mysteriously absent from the frame.
The opening act is actually sturdily written and competent at getting across the character of Ana and empathising with her situation. Ana is played with shocking ease and lightness by Dakota Johnson who really helps to make even some of Anas more bothersome decisions and frailty quite believable through raw likability and presence. Dornan certainly gets the brooding quality of the character down through stoic expression and physical demeanour, and while a tad more lifeless he also gets some light humility out of such a role.
The screenplay borders on self-awareness at times, toying with some of the more absurd comedy surrounding the fanciful sincerity of the story and carrying with it an airy sense of amusement. Sadly, this doesnt hold up fully as there are many lines sour enough to bring tears of frustration. Many of the side characters are weakly handled and incorporated, while the last third stoops into soap opera territory with weak dialogue and an awful ending  the botched compromise of a studio trying to capitalise on its status as a series with the dramatic close of a tune in next week cut to black without any proper feeling of resolution. Its aggravating to watch what is almost an autopsy unravelling on screen a salvage job that is being fought by Marcel to make something acceptable out of the bootless errand that is E.L. James cureless input and insistence on sticking to the text.
What makes Fifty Shades of Grey underwhelming, is that just out of reach is the possibility of a far better film being composed by Taylor-Johnson. What has come to pass isnt too arduous an effort to stick with thanks to its pace and direction, not to mention the fact that it is occasionally beautiful looking. Its not that the film ever feels sterile in its approach as Taylor-Johnson does her best to nail down a tone particularly early, but this is the product of a studio and creative team treading lightly around a production that really needed a lot more risks to be taken with it than would probably be necessary. As an adaptation, its better than it probably deserves to be, but as a film alone, although technically well-made, there is little new here to be seen thats not already been done better elsewhere.

My mostly white audience breathed a collective sigh of relief, but the switcheroo on Peeles part is of greater agency than a thrill (although it undoubtedly succeeds). It provides an empathetic meeting place where common ground can be felt across a silver screen and a packed genre crowd in this moment, Get Out teaches. 
And it doesnt only teach about the idea of what we perceive and how such a notion may be constructed due to staggering systemic racial divisions in 2017s America, but that the thought is shared. We continue to live in a society where the combination of a police car and a black citizen inherently alludes to confrontation, violence, arrest, oppression, and yet, the real, and sad, truth is found in how Peele can grasp a situational example of ethnic tension and multipurpose it into a thrill which anyone can comprehend. Starting with this moment, a culmination of dubious cogency, feels like the only logical way to write about such a waking nightmare of a film - feverish, witty, sharp as a deers antlers - because it both begins and ends with us, the public, the American people. 
It begins with us as detached constructing a premise where the white liberal racist tendencies and lingering, stuffy quirks are subtle in their conversational awareness. Youve probably heard age-old generational stories showcasing long-term familial connection with other ethnicities or persisting political issues which only seem to be mentioned for a nod by the receiving party. Maybe youve even been on the suffering end, maybe youve even said such things, but the specificity ends there. Get Out is here to probe these memories - whether personal or collective or cultural - out of you and say look, its all around you, and its in Everywhere, USA, no less. 
But it ends with us having experienced something divided in a divided time yet the audience has been sharing an examination of the Black Experience. Everyone, in every theater in every city and town, is on the same page, witnessing commodification based around racial Myth and devious, harrowing ignorance found under the living rooms of the rich only to fester in the hearts of communities. Get Out is not a film which ends with America metaphorically holding hands, but it is representative of the divide which still casts a shadow across this land and how whiteness continues to own the prospects and attributes of the black body. Rose being left for dead by Chris, deciding not to kill her - an ingenious, unspoken visual image of black command - isnt the only aspect that sets a volatile message aflame. Its that Chris did nothing wrong. 
All for now. Probably more after a rewatch. Formally, structurally, conceptually a masterpiece of American horror.

So much has been written about the perspective this has on race that I hardly think I could add to it. Instead I will simply note the parts that I especially liked (and the one thing I hated)
The moment Chris is told that what the man who bought him at slave auction wants from him is his eyes drives home the intention to capture as many facets of the way capitalism and racism treats black people as commodities. The film flashes (heavy-handedly, sigh) to the objectifying actions of each of the prospective buyers, but the one who bought him is the one who wants his eyes, driving home yet another metaphor (white capitalist consumption of black talent) that seems especially apt in a film that made over 250 million selling tickets mostly to white people it quietly asserts that even if youre enjoying, appreciating, paying for this film, you are still part of the exploitative process. (Unless, of course, you arent.)
The overall plot also addresses a fundamental fact race is not about skin color. Its not biological. Its a social construct, and white is a derived of white supremacist capitalism. White (usually pettybourgeois) minds appropriating black bodies is very directly shown here in insidious science fiction, a metaphor that encapsulates white supremacy on multiple levels, but woven into the story are a thousand references to institutional discriminations and the very real state violence against black people. Disbelief, gaslighting, experimentation, manipulation, and literal harvesting happens to black people. In the film, this is done on a direct, personal level, and it reflects--as I have read many times--real personal experiences, but it also reflects a larger, systemic oppression wherein all of those things are done to black people on a mass scale. Its part of history, part of the fuel of capitalism.
Theres a scene where Georgina apologizes for unplugging Chriss phone, and the camera keeps switching back and forth between Chris and Georgina. Chris is filmed from a medium close up, his neck and face visible, full expressions, mostly confusion, fear, frustration. Georgina is filmed very close up, Demme-close-up, and her facial expressions are that rigid, uncanny blankness that characterizes the assimilated black people of this film. The camera is just slightly beneath her face, the lighting making her skin seem perfectly smooth. A single tear streams down her face and some emotion struggles to come through, but its locked behind this mask that we later learn is the dominance of racism. Its the one moment in the film that was thoroughly unnerving, pitching the viewer outside of reality entirely, a potent illustration of the horror of being locked in ones own body. Removing even the racial implications, this is a moment of horror, but with them, its devastating.
The part I hated, though, is the theatrical ending. Making the ending a moment of comedy and giving a heroic rescue to a member of TSA, even if thats part of the humor to the moment, is a glaring disconnection from the role of TSA in U.S. racist violence, an oblivious copout that undermines the films themes. The alternative ending (which I had to find online because the DVD didnt work right?) was much stronger and eerier, more tonally in keeping with the film, and its more realistic nature a stronger concluding statement. The feelgood ending smacks of studio interference, no matter what theyre saying in the interviews.

Enjoyable, but in the end unremarkable.
This may seem as a harsh criticism for film so universally praised, but for me Peeles ambitious film suffers from an identity crisis that muddles the effect of what it set out to do.
When the first act was drawing to a close I was really into Get Out. It felt like a superbly handled satire on race relations set against a bizarre and sometimes unnerving backdrop. I felt Peele had a clear vision of how he wanted to bend the very topical theme of strained connections between races in his country and snugly fit it into the horror genre. And for a while he really managed just that.
But once the plot starts to kick in he lost me as Get Out seemed to loosen its grip on its own identity and thus becoming neither fish nor fowl. It takes a lot of courage (unfortunately) to actually tackle the subject Peele wants to tackle, but attack it he does, its just that he doesnt seem to be sure what his weapon of choice is supposed to be. 
From the second act onward he foregoes satire for horror for straightforward comedy for thriller for gore etc. He hops and skips from one idea to the next, never really exploring their potential. The bizarre effect this had on me was that I went from admiration for something really clever or well executed (for example the creepy hypnosis scenes)  to raised eyebrows when we are treated to a poorly executed stereotype character (for example, the heros best friend). This unbalance stole away any potential menace or any concern I felt for the protagonist. 
Apart from the uneven tone, the plot is a bit too pedestrian to support its anything but pedestrian intentions. Even though it never really surprised and it is not that difficult to connect all the dots, Peele certainly shows a creative flair on many an occasion, finding cohesion is, unfortunately, not part of his arsenal yet. Really good separate parts do not always make a great whole.
I really appreciate what Get Out set out to accomplish and Im glad it has clicked with so many people. I wish it had had the same effect on me.

George Orwell, it is widely acknowledged, is one of the finest writers the English language has known. In his 1946 essay, Politics and the English Language, Orwell decried the sorry state of English writingmostly political writing, though other types as welland offered by way of corrective a set of six rules, including the following (1) Never use a long word where a short one will do and (2) If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out.
It is hard to be as good a writer as Orwell. Indeed, it is hard even for Orwell, as the second rule contains at least one, if not two, extraneous outs, thereby violating itself. Perhaps Orwell was suffering from something akin to a condition whose name he would never deign to use Anosognosia. What, pray tell, is anosognosia? In a technical sense, it is a neurological disorder by which the sufferer of some disability is unaware of the existence or extent of that disability it commonly follows strokes and other brain injuries. It might be said to be correlative to the Dunning-Kruger effect, the phenomenon whereby one suffering from inadequacy in a given arena is likely to suffer illusions of superiority in that very arena. These are all fancy terms whose deployment is like breaking a dam, releasing a torrent of metacognition and receptive aphasia and proprioception and all sorts of sesquipedalian terms (like, for example, sesquipedalian). But at base these all reduce to some form of the same thinga lack of self-awareness. Everyone overestimates her own abilities and knowledge, both absolutely and relatively, constantly playing the fool and seldom realizing it. It is a cosmic joke told by, as H.L. Mencken might say, a comedian whose audience is afraid to laugh.
A reference to Mencken is strangely appropriate in discussing Get Out, Jordan Peeles terrific writing-directing debut. For one, Mencken, the bon vivant and influential critic and scholar of American life during the first half of the 20th century, showed no trace of self-doubt in his writinga sure sign of some deficit of self-perception. More than that, though, Menckenan often brilliant mind, wittily skewering those on all sides with clarity and incisivenesswas an avowed racist. The educated Negro of today is a failure, not because he meets insuperable difficulties in life, but because he is a Negro, wrote Mencken. Advancement might be possible, he conceded, but it would always and inevitably occur on a delay.
Todays polite society would not tolerate statements as bald-faced as Menckens, but the sentiments havent vanished so much as camouflaged themselves behind all manner of obfuscation and coded terminology, discussions of work ethic and cultural differences and the like. That movement is probably progress, however insufficientthings do not change overnight, but as long as the change is relatively constant and maintains some sense of forward momentum, it is something. But what is truly frighteningwhat Get Out makes central to its horroris that no amount of progress can make people stop being people. No amount of legislative or electoral victory, no quota of social interaction, no scrim of politesse can cure the overarching disease of obliviousness endemic to the human condition. If the Dunning-Kruger effect is realand anyone who has dealt with a precocious child or discussed her vocation with a layperson who once read the headline of an article about said vocation can tell you it isthen the less racist we think we are, the more freely our racism will flow by virtue of our failure to put up any obstacles to stop it. In the moment, Get Out is thrilling, frightening and funny in the manner of so many good horror films. But its implications, rattling around for weeks after the credits roll, are much less thrilling and much, much more frightening.
On first glance, Get Out seems to work best in its opening half, before it has to begin explaining what is really happening and resolving the conflicts it has set in motion. This is unsurprisingit is true not just of many debut films, but also of many mystery or horror films, whose setups are almost always more compelling than their conclusions, which necessarily close doors that anticipation had left open. Peeles script is sharp and perceptive, skewering a particular brand of seemingly well-intentioned but often clueless liberal racism. As Rose (Allison Williams) notes that her parents, Dean (Bradley Whitford) and Missy (Catherine Keener), would have voted for Obama a third time if they could have, or as Dean notes with pride his ancestors accomplishment of losing to Jesse Owens at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, Chris (Daniel Kaluuya) responds with bits of bemusement and self-control and irritation and exasperation. Kaluuya is brilliant, his eyes and face conveying multitudes while his surface strives to convey equanimity. He is a model of sangfroid, and Peeles decision to cast the indignities he suffers against the background of meeting the parentsan already fraught situation no matter the participantsis a stroke of genius.
But then the explanation must come. Peele has been open about his inspirations for Get Out, chief among them Rosemarys Baby and The Stepford Wives, with the malevolent forces facing women in America replaced by those facing black people in America. Thus, although Get Out toys for quite some time with the possibility that nothing is really amissthat Chris is just a person of particularly high situational intelligence surrounded by those of lesser capabilitybecause we know we are watching a horror movie, we know this not to be so. Rosemary Woodhouse might have been paranoid, but she was notthe cultic neighbors and her husband really were using her body to bring the Antichrist to power. Joanna Eberhart might have been paranoid, but she was nother new neighbors really were being replaced by robotic counterfeits full of the submission and soullessness their flesh-and-blood counterparts lacked. And Chris might be paranoid, but he is notas his best friend, TSA agent Rod (LilRel Howery), is happy to remind him, there really is something awry in this exurban enclave. (Spoilers yon.)
It is easy to pick apart a schemes explanation, especially the more convoluted it becomescrafting a satisfactory answer is exceedingly difficult, which is why the lack of an answer is often the most satisfying outcome. It is why Peeles choice not to over-explain the medical procedure that Deans father developed is such a wise one. We can accept that transplanting an older, ailing white persons brain into a younger, healthy black persons body, combined with some of Missys patented teacup hypnosis, results in a black body controlled by a white consciousness, with the former black consciousness relegated to the so-called sunken place. Any attempts to further elaborate would be counterproductive, making the inherently implausible seem less plausible by straining to convince of its plausibility. What is bedeviling upon initial consideration is that, in a movie about race, Get Outs explanation seems to sidestep racial considerations. That the old or enfeebled would want renewed youth and vigor is a universally applicable concernmany attest to a preference for the knowledge and experience they have gained with age over the foolishness and ignorance of their youth, but few would argue that their deteriorating bodies work as well as they once did. And that one might use his resources to acquire eternal or returned youth is universally understandable. It is why the story of Ponce de Leóns search for the Fountain of Youth continues to hold sway despite likely being a mythit seems only too plausible that the royal and rich would expend time and money looking for immortality.
And so Get Outs revelation, while unsettlingbeing trapped as a cave dweller in your own body is horrifying indeedat first seems somewhat lackluster. After such a pitch-perfect satire of post-racial race relations, to have a solution that renders race an afterthought is...peculiar. Yet the more Peeles resolution reverberates, the more its brilliance becomes apparent. Chris asks, Why black people?, and the answer pretends that blackness has little to do with it. But the answer is given by those with sociological anosognosiaof course blackness has everything to do with it otherwise the chosen ones would not be exclusively black. And of course that choice would reside in perceptions of a post-racial America that never existed, in blackness having a moment or being cool, in persistent stereotypes of athleticism and sexual prowessendowment, in covetousness of others artistic impulses and abilities, and in the self-serving lie that one is accepting of all comers. That a rich white person should subject herself to the systemic indignities and difficulties facing a black person in America seems ludicrousunless, of course, that rich white person has convinced herself that those difficulties have been mostly solved (no doubt in large part thanks to her efforts), or that she can solve them once she is operating from the inside, so to speak. Were race truly to have nothing to do with Get Outs twists and turns, it would undoubtedly be a failingbut that its villains claim, or even truly believe, that to be the case undoubtedly is not.
Which leaves only the matter of Get Outs other big revelations Whether Rose is an innocent pawn in her parents scheme or a willing participant and whether that police car arriving at the final moment will be Chris salvation or his undoing. As uniformly excellent as Get Outs cast isKaluuya in particular stands out, and is unlikely to receive the awards consideration he richly deservesWilliams occupies a trickier role than Keener, Whitford, and their friends and family. Dean and Missy need never come across as fully innocenteven before the full scale of their treachery is reveale

I think what makes it work is how personal it feels. Its not just horror for the sake of it. Theres a real-world weight behind everything, and you can feel that this isnt just a story, its saying something about how people see, judge, and reduce others without ever being direct about it.

When photographer Chris (Daniel Kaluuya) is invited to the house of his white girlfriend to meet her parents, what seems fairly innocuous on the surface soon reveals itself to be far more sinister, in Jordan Peeles horror co-starring Alison Williams, Bradley Whitford, Catherine Keener, Caleb Landry Jones, Lil Rel Howery, Lakeith Stanfield and Stephen Root. 
Peele deftly weaves a number of different genres together, gradually building up the tension in a way that slowly lets the darkness at the heart of the plot reveal itself without being immediately apparent from the outset. Theres a good amount of humour mixed into the story (especially through Howerys incredibly likeable character), which helps to give the creepier moments more emphasis, as the tone masterfully shifts and twists thoughout. 
There are some incredibly creepy moments, especially any scene with Betty Gabriel, who gives a memorable and unsettling performance as Georgina, the blank-eyed housekeeper, and both she and Stanfield do an excellent job of showing the deadness behind the eyes of their characters, conveying a sense that something is missing. 
The lurking, prowling camera also adds a great deal to the suspense, with the opening scene in the nighttime suburb setting the tone immediately and creating a palpable sense of dread that permeates more or less over the course of the film. 
Peele manages to get some potent commentary about modern racism into the story, looking at the casual, seemingly unthinking everyday prejudice Chris faces from the family, looking into the reactionary undercurrent beneath their apparently open-minded surface. While it does sometimes get a little on the nose in its allegory, the use of horror tropes to explore these themes of control and privilege stops the messages from being heavy-handed, using a seemingly out-there premise to delve into these issues. 
Kaluuya was nominated for an Oscar for his breakout role, and its a fantastic performance, effortlessly conveying a range of conflicting emotions and thoughts with just an expression or a gesture, and he really makes it all work. Chris has to be a spectator in whats going on as well as an active participant as it goes on, and Kaluuya gives the role a charm and sense of mounting discomfort that allows the audience to feel all of this too. 
The film is full of superb performances, from Keeners quietly unsettling mother to Roots blind art dealer, and each actor gives a lot to the film, making the most of their roles. Its very tightly written, with seemingly insignificant moments and symbols resurfacing later on with new significance, which in turn adds extra meaning to the earlier scenes.
I really enjoyed the film its really well done, and avoids most of the pitfalls and cliches of the horror genre, or if they are used its in a fresh and subversive way. While the comparatively over-the-top finale did wrap everything up well, it did lose some of the earlier understated menace, which I thought worked best, as the shift into more overt horror territory seemed a bit jarring in comparison. 
While some parts arent quite as strong as others, Get Out is an excellent horror, making the most of its surprising and original central premise in a witty, creepy and extremely effective way.

One of the most original, unique  thought-provoking concepts to surface on the silver screen, Get Out is a cleverly structured, masterly told  brilliantly performed satire that offers a cinematic ride so effective, thrilling  entertaining that the fact that it is actually a directorial debut makes it all the more commendable.
The story follows Chris Washington, a black photographer who takes a trip with his white girlfriend to meet her parents, and spend the weekend at their secluded estate. Everyone in the family tries to make him feel welcome at first but as weekend progresses, a series of increasingly disturbing discoveries lead him to a nightmarish revelation.
Written  directed by Jordan Peele, Get Out is a stellar start to his filmmaking career and presents him in total control of his craft. Every moment plays a role in the final outcome, every little detail is vital to the plot, and every twist adds to the mystery. Also, Peeles ability to keep things amusing  infused with biting critique of modern society speaks volumes about his talents as a storyteller.
Its low budget is efficiently handled and all the technical aspects work in harmony to heighten the films foreboding atmosphere  mysterious aura, whether its the plantation-like setting or the fluid but immaculate use of the camera or the steady pace or tight editing or its mystifying score. From its calm opening to its violent finale, it effortlessly manages to keep everyone on the edge of their seats.
Coming to the performances, Daniel Kaluuya chips in with a deftly measured input in the role of Chris but Allison Williams isnt far behind as his girlfriend, Rose, and their input only gets stronger as the plot moves forward. Bradley Whitford  Catherine Keener play Roses parents and theres an enigmatic quality in their work. Lil Rel Howery is mostly used as a comic relief, and the rest of the supporting cast is just as good, if not better.
On an overall scale, Get Out is an exquisite blend of horror  dark comedy that interweaves its ingeniously layered narrative with timely social commentary to deliver a thrilling experience thats accomplished on all scales. Fresh, funny  frightening in equal doses, packed with savvy ideas  bold decisions, and pushing the boundaries of its genre(s) in its own bizarre fashion, Jordan Peeles debut feature is a smart, subversive  sardonic delight thats neither overt nor covert. One of the best all-round films of the year.

A large part of the reason that  Get Out is an instant classic is that it is far more open-ended than it appears to be during the time of viewing. Much like The Matrix, it is obviously allegorical. But it can actually support a multitude of allegorical readings, which will make it a movie of enduring appeal. 
Is it about the so-called Obama Effect, wherein the two-time election of a black president supposedly revealed a new, post-racial America? (Clearly white people have always had the prerogative to be post-racial, and now we have the ability to co-opt African-American culture as well.) Is it about the prison-industrial complex, the fact that America runs on black labor power that is controlled and directed by whites? (The Armitages have certainly found a new way to extract bio-power from African-Americans while simultaneously making their bodies disappear.) It could be largely about what it seems to be about, right on its surface -- the vicious racism lurking beneath white liberalism, the fetishization of the black body as the flipside to conservative fear of same. (In this regard, it speaks metaphorically to the way the Democratic Party makes demands of African-American voters, mobilizing them this way and that, while expecting them to capitulate to a rich, white power structure.) It could also be a paranoid fantasy regarding interracial relationships, which have become so normalized by millennials as to be virtually invisible. (If the threat of love is the basic unknowability of the other, than the acknowledgment of a cross-cultural divide can just as easily occlude understanding as initiate it.)
What is certain is that Jordan Peeles crisp, visually adept direction marks the arrival of a major new talent. (Not new, of course, but scoring handily in a second area of endeavor. He should be able to write his own ticket now. Unless, you know, racism.) Clearly the work of a cinephile and horror aficionado, Get Out bears traces of classics too numerous to mention, although Invasion of the Body Snatchers and The Stepford Wives are clear touchstones, along with John Frankenheimers masterpiece Seconds. 
But the insight into contemporary race relations is all Peele, and I hope that audiences will take it seriously as more than just a clever premise. The opening sequence, in which Andre (LaKeith Stanfield) is lost in a white suburb, should speak to anyone who remembers the name Trayvon Martin. That is, the very things that make white Americans feel safe are justifiably terrifying to most African-Americans. 
This is reiterated in the final scene, when Chris (Daniel Kaluuya) is trying to kill Rose (Allison Williams) in self-defense, and we suddenly see the flashing red and blue lights of the police cruiser. Peele is playing with our fears and prejudices here, but for a moment, it looked like we were witnessing an arrival of the white cavalry, a horrific callback to the Klan on horseback in Birth of a Nation. Alas, Peele uses the power of imagination to give us the horror-genre payoff that has been delayed for as long as the movies have existed the final black man.

Jordan Peele is a director that I have heard about, but for some reason, I have not watched his films. That is most definitely going to change after viewing Get Out. 
This is a film that actually is genuinely terrifying. Throughout the entire film, I was feeling this deep sense of dread (wow David!) and it stressed me out. A young couple, Chris and Rose, are packing for a weekend getaway to meet her parents in a cozy, upper-class suburban enclave. Okay. Chris is Black which makes him feel a bit uneasy while Roses family is of the whitest whites. But, hey! Her dad wouldve voted for Obama a third time, so all good, right?
NOPE. Theres something very off about literally everyone. Smiles are creepy as fuck and the Black servants seem to be programmed in the 1950s. The genius of Peele is that nothing is being rushed. He wants you to sit and marinate in the discomfort. Its extremely effective. 
Daniel Kaluuya, who plays Chris, is the beating heart of this film. I completely understand why his eyes are the poster. He absorbs every strange encounter and his transformation from polite boyfriend to desperate survivor is masterclass-level. 
Also, I fucking LOVE Bradley Whitford to death! He plays the same character in everything that he is in, or at least gives them his certain light flair. chefs kiss Gotta take a moment too for Rod, Chris best friend and MVPTSA of the film. He fucking calls the entire thing after one phone call and it really helped having that comic relief in an otherwise unsettling environment. 
The Sunken Place is incredible. And by incredible, I mean utterly horrifying. Chris is hypnotized (without even knowing it) by Roses Mom and becomes completely powerless while still being physically present. Chris falling backwards into silent darkness haunted me more than any jump scare ever could. 
This is a very forward-thinking film, but at the same time, not really. Its socially conscious without shoving it in your face. Peele completely renovates all of the horror tropes that weve come to know. No gore or jump scares or anything. Just genuinely terrifying in its own way.

Eventually I am going to get around to writing an in depth review of a film that has impacted me in a heavy wayhopefullywhen one comes.  Considering the deep admiration and glorification of this debut effort from Jordan Peele, I felt that a random ejaculation of thoughts was in order at the very least.  It should be said that I arrived late to the party on this one and my judgment was undoubtedly affected by the incredible hype surrounding this film.  I liked it yet I didnt love it.  
It starts out with a clever concept for a horror film.  The subject of interracial dating is still uncomfortable for a lot of folks and I find it a wonderful concept to attack this taboo with one of cinemas genre most suited for a forum of social commentary.  The interactions in this film hit close to home for every black person or any person who has ever been around one.  That ever so particular misstep of white patronization of black people is something that is excruciatingly  grating and uncomfortable to be around, though arguably harmless and full of good intentions, it is its own form of incidental  racism.  Get Out features exchange after exchange of  such condescension maybe most perfectly illustrated in the party scene.  White people who are uncomfortable around minorities seem to always have the instinct to immediately point out their difference in skin tone by complimenting the person, almost congratulating them on being black.  It is always the elephant in the room and white people are always quick to try diffuse their unease by overcompensating with disingenuous kindness and tenacious resolve to prove, Hey, Im one of the good ones.  What they never realize is that they are creating an awkward situation because of their own mental confinements.  The more you try and beat people over the head with your awakening of self-righteous tolerance, the more you single yourself out as having to all but admitted to being fixated on your hangups.  These social blunders are every bit as skin crawling as any scene of gratuitous violence.  It is on this point that Peele hits the nail on the fucking head.  White people can be ridiculous, and he has filmed a bit of redemption to out this behavior and for that, he should be fully commended.
However, my problem with the film is that it becomes its own negative stereotype.  In the words of Michelle Obama opportunistically co-opted by the aggressively Caucasian Hillary Clinton, When they go low, we go high,  a statement that should be the cornerstone when confronted with any unwarranted persecution, Jordan Peele has not done this but rather fallen into his own pitfalls.  There is not a single redeemable white character in this film.  For all intents and purposes to the universe this world creates, white people are evil.  You  know, I can actually live with that.  Weve had our way for..ever, so Im fine eating a fuck you of this nature.  Thats not my problem with the film.  It is that it operates under the guise of furthering a forward momentum of bringing us together to a more unified and harmonious state of being but accomplishes just the opposite.  It suffers from the usual tropes.  Our main character is not representative of any sort of person I have ever met and therefore not a flattering voice for which to root on.  An affluent, self-employed photographer sounds a bit like they highly specific lifestyle of one Jordan Peele than it does to serve as any sort of surrogate for the vast majority of people encountering this friction.  His friend, the TSA agent is a carbon copy of every token black comic relief voice that I have ever seen.   His lines might as well have included, I gotta get me one of these, or you fill in the blanks.  Admittedly he was a funny character but also a staple of some of the stereotyping I would have liked to see Peele move away from.  
Or does it go deeper than all of this?  The plot of the film realizes black men and women being lured into white culture AKA opulent suburbia and being brainwashed into subservient automatons, a new and more camouflaged era of slavery.  Is Peele trying to say  that black peoples ingratiation into a predominantly white environment changes them, erasing their true and black identity.  It certainly seems so to me and If so, that is a nasty message.  In fact, a message that  contradicts what many people think this film is about, the absurdity of modern day prejudices.  This film seems to argue keep it in the family rather than bringing anyone together. 
Dont get me wrong, I enjoyed the movie and as a horror installment, it is certainly above average.  It is beautifully filmed, expertly paced and the performances are amazing across the board.  There are some plot loopholes and the climax felt very ill-conceived, but on the whole, as a debut effort.how in the hell?  Someones been doing his homework.  Again these are only a couple reasons holding this one back from being truly great for me.  I think if you dig deeper,  this film is mean spirited and misses the mark of being the cultural milestone that this generation so desperately wants.  On its surface it seems to be saying a great deal of how much work is left to be done extinguishing the rancor imbedded in our country but underneath it is in fact disobeying the Golden Rule with a malicious and sardonic taunt to the very source of hostility it so deeply resents.   Does Get Out (its very tile) address a problem in a positive way or does it only further widen the schism.  I am not so sure.

Did not need hypnosis to give it that score after keeping my eyes glued to the screen, because Get Out is fantastic. In terms of telling a horror story, on paper its nothing too new, but Peele is able to build upon the off-kilter clues that something is seriously wrong until the ending barrels like a freight train to the finish, keep the dialogue interesting and get the most from his actors, and add some interesting everyday social commentary to make it interesting. This movie really owes it to the actors, especially Daniel Kaluuya who always look on edge and constantly thinking behind his awkward smile, this is a film where every part is played perfectly and I cant imagine a single line delivered in any other way by anyone else. The movie plays up the social awkwardness between people of different backgrounds who dont see eye to eye for both comedic effect and for creating tense scenes. Nothing beats those awkward encounters as Chris tries to find brothers he can relate to better and have his expectations dashed by their strange mannerisms. Things always feel off thanks to the dialogue  the delivery, the framing of shots, and the effective score, which only build to the frighteningly surreal Sunken Place and the eventual reveal of the master plan. I really wish I went into this film without any idea of where it would go, but it is fun to fit together the pieces and the film must be incredibly rewatchable. Peele plays with imagery and themes of slavery (and LilRel Howerys hilarious rants about sex slaves) to lure the audience towards one place, only to go to another that is even more terrifying the ability to wipe away ones identity completely and how devastating it would be if the Coagula treatment was utilized by much more discriminatory groups to homogenize a culture. Its a film that reinforces how important identity is to individuals and to cultures, and how actions that may not be racially motivated can devastate identity. All coming from a movie with a bonkers brainwashing premise.
And holy shit that ending is tight. Peele is not afraid to make Chris Washington into a no-nonsense badass who will fight his way against the villains. That final confrontation between Rose and Chris is so layered and devastating with a smile that says a thousand words reinforced by centuries of racial violence and a subversion of a culturally significant trope that luckily leads to a crowd-pleasing ending (Seriously, William is the man. One of the best comic relief characters Ive seen in a while.). Get Out is a phenomenal, deceptively simple and effective horror movie that plays with every element to offer a biting social wake-up call. Trim down a few of Williams scenes after he cant get in touch with Chris and take out that stupid-ass exposition VHS, and its a perfect movie.

Smart, fresh, hilarious, and dripping with tension and atmosphere, Get Out makes for a rock-solid directorial debut from Jordan Peele, with great performances, excellent writing and direction, and a bold, perfectly handled balance between chilling, effective horror and balls to the wall social satire on liberal racism.

Get Out is wild. At first, you think its a romance about an interracial couple, Chris and Rose. But then it turns into a full on nightmare disguised as a sweet love story.
The movie opens with a random Black guy getting kidnapped in the middle of a white neighborhood. No context, no explanation. That early scene hits harder once you realize who he really is. Its weird, but it hooks you right away. From there, Jordan Peele slowly builds tension through Chriss point of view. You feel every awkward and uneasy moment as he realizes somethings off with Roses family.
The guests at the family party seem friendly, but the way they talk to Chris feels off. They comment on his body, skin, and lifestyle like hes a product, not a person. Even the Black house workers act strange, almost like theyre trapped inside someone elses body.
Then the truth drops, and its insane. Roses family has been kidnapping Black people and transplanting old white folks brains into their bodies. Every bit of kindness and charm turns out to be a setup for something disturbing.
What makes it stand out is how Peele mixes horror with social commentary. The horror doesnt come from blood or jump scares. It comes from that uncomfortable feeling of being watched, judged, and controlled in subtle ways.
Get Out isnt just a horror movie. Its a sharp, psychological ride that makes you think about privilege, control, and how racism hides behind politeness.

Had to give the new Blu-ray (from a 4K scan!) a spin, and its as impossibly gorgeous as can be, enriching the murky, glorified details and cranking all the exhilaration and eventual paranoia up to 11. Even though Ive seen this around 20-30 times at this point, I still get dizzy from all the detail an entire world built up and thriving through soda pop nostalgia and the eventual nervousness of violence. Scorseses attuned style commits fully to every aspect of the production, but it is in the strange, banal moments where his genius fully shines. Although it may be glorification in terms of technique, Goodfellas never romanticizes its band of characters or its almost Herculean setting, instead exposing vapid transactions and customs through their overvalued and savage culture. 
In a sense, purchasing fir coats and brand new cars is the ultimate prize, even more so than the dirty cash. Its an opportunity to gloat and let the neighborhood know who they are, utilizing their level of success as a cushion for their internal securities. When Henry Hill confesses at the films conclusion, it isnt a shock to the audience, but an apathetic cry for help. Scorsese rapidly cuts when any sort of connection is attempted. Tommy DeVito unloading a clip of ammo right through the screen is a shattering revelation. Cinema as a true trance, pinpointing all the right details while the rug is pulled out from under the audiences feet and all the jewelry is stolen. 
Scorseses mode as movie-magician makes the vibrant, holy fuck I cant move sequences and edits appear larger than life an opening scene with a throat-grabbing 80s horror feel, a sudden made-man beating with Donovans ATLANTIS gaining speed and subsequently blaring all its soul when the anger and fury starts flying with visual and aural glory, freeze-frames while Liottas voiceover continues to run like a feature commentary, the entire helicopter section where its as if the celluloid itself took a hit etc. Thelma Schoonmaker gives and takes away the life of Goodfellas at will through impeccable editing. Paranoiac fevers begin to affect the film grain, needle-drops feed the pace of the images, and the vulnerable static shots take in all the drama like a watchful spirit.   
Its also, especially on this rewatch oddly enough, really fucking funny, with Karens nail-biting in the helicopter sequence after Henrys gun dealer labels him as paranoid being a classic moment of physical comedy and expression. Scorsese goes all in on the ticks and units that make up the frame, both through image and sound (a highlight has to be the random individual yelling wheres OUR table?!?! while Henry and Karen get their celebrity treatment), while peppering it across the characters. 
As young Hill looks out at the hang-out spot for wise-guys in the middle of the night, its evident that these Mythical beings all move like ghostly presences, carrying weight yet light and mysterious on their feet. Scorsese aims his camera towards hands, car sides, and whispering lips, desperately trying to capture the unknown secrets and plans dissipating into the summer night. For when LAYLA starts to sing in the air, humming alongside the unflinching carnage captured through Scorseses eye, I just cant help but ponder their wrongdoings and if they stayed to haunt the world. Theyd sure have a lot to say. Its a sharp contrast when compared to the most cold-blooded of them all a monster who, after putting a screwdriver through the back of someones neck, blurts out thought hed never shut the fuck up. 
A masterpiece of American Cinema.

A great film that I admire more than love (as opposed to, say, After Hours, a good film that I love more than admire gave them almost the same rating, 80 vs. 81), though the day of Henrys arrest may well constitute the single most galvanizing sequence in cinema history, for which I credit Schoonmaker every bit as much as I do Scorsese. Had never consciously noticed before that while GoodFellas is wall-to-wall needle drops, we dont hear any true rock n roll until Henry starts dealing and using cocaineits all e.g. Bobby Darin and the Shangri-Las prior to that, even well after the timeline moves into the 70s. So  Jump Into the Fires opening bass riff packs a real wallop. (Mad Men would later use rock music in a similarly judicious way.) I was gonna start listing all the small touches from those 11 minutes that still leave me awestruck, like the camera tilting from a distorted reflection of Henry in his Cadillacs chrome tail fin to a closeup of his hands placing a bag of guns into the trunk to a closeup of his face as he again checks the sky for helicopters, with Ry Cooders steel guitar lick in Memo From Turner accompanying the second move, but quickly realized it would turn into a novel. (Though Ill add that Schoonmaker then cuts from movement upward and left to movement downward and right, as we bounce from a strip-mall sign to find Henrys car on the road, and that this pleasing symmetry is repeated throughout, while also occasionally being ruptured by paranoid flurries of cuts that deliberately cross the axis.) You could conceivably teach an entire course in basic film grammar using just this one sequence. Its all there. (Though Id also throw in the Sunshine of Your Love shot of De Niro. This isnt generally one of his strongest performances, but the almost microscopic, slightly crazed look Jimmy shoots Tommy at one point, and the way De Niro narrows only his left eye at the endwhatever happened to that guy?)
In any case, dont think I recognized in the early 90s (hadnt seen it since) just how conceptually radical this film is. In essence, its a talking-head documentary in which the interview subjects reminiscences are delivered by professional actors, supplemented by onscreen re-enactments, à la Wormwood, that just happen to take up 100 of the films running time. (Casino would push this concept even further, focusing on procedural detail at the expense of character.) Conventional dramatic scenes are rare, and usually brief instead, the story is relentlessly, almost obsessively narratedannotated, which creates some necessary distance, even as were encouraged to share the entitled thrill of just brutalizing anyone unwilling to ignore societys so-called rules. Still found the first hour or so harder to enjoy than I once did, and was grateful when Karens voiceover kicked inunlike Henry, she hadnt wanted to be a gangster (or a gangsters mollwife) for as far back as she could remember, and its useful to observe someone getting more gradually seduced by this world. But Karen also frankly admits that most of her friends would have fled at the first opportunity, thereby taking a tiny measure of personal responsibility that the film pointedly denies Henry the Schnook, via a happy ending daring to equate his living hell with our own mundane daily existence. Crime doesnt pay, but neither does honest hard work. Nothing pays.

To like or even care about a character is by no means an essential component within a film. Give them dimension, make them intriguing, so we can indulge in our darker side or those traits we would rather not own up to, which can more than compensate. When they offer neither of the above, then there is very little to latch onto, no entry point into wanting to spend time with them. Ray Liottas Henry Hill fits that bill.
It is through his eyes that we get to see the inner circle of the mafia across thirty years. He is the straight man set against the more expansive DeNiro and Pesci, two charismatic guys with larger than life personalities. The three key elements that most people remember about Goodfellas is firstly the technical skill employed by Scorsese, secondly Joe Pescis manic performance and thirdly DeNiros alluring presence on-screen. 
So what of Henry Hill? What is there to recall, or to particularly keep you involved with the recollection of his glory years? The problem is that his two closest friends are far more interesting but are not the ones telling their stories. Henry himself has little redeeming features. He came from a good home and decided to spend a life chasing money by whatever means necessary. He stays out all night, neglects his marriage, turns to violence and sells drugs.
All of which is fine if he just had a personality. Something about himself to make his story resonate. To spend two and a half hours with somebody who cannot entice or continue to sell the idea of his lifestyle affects the strength of the elements around him. Wolf of Wall Street is accused of being style over substance, the difference being that is driven by an actor in full throttle, who manages to charm you where Liotta begins to stall.
The effect is that the telling of the story runs out of steam at least thirty minutes before leaving Henry on the doorstep of his witness protection home. An exploration of any of the relationships in that world would have been more involving than the marriage which took too much focus with little in return. That relationship really offers nothing to the narrative as Henry would have ended up where he did either way.
Im only focusing on criticisms here because the strengths of the film have been written in any number of ways you care to mention. At one point I was a huge admirer of this film, in awe of the skill on show from behind and infront of the camera. After my first watch in over a decade, its safe to say that Goodfellas is no longer the film I used to think it was.

Martin Scorsese, the gangster king. No one could have directed this film better than him. Its hard to admit that I had never seen Goodfellas before today. Its arguably one of the greatest films ever made, transforming audiences outlook on extensive narration, an aspect thats often been something I enjoy the most in a film and showcasing an incredible cast and storyline that kept my attention for its entirety. 
From the soundtrack to the dialogue to the brutal violence, everything is coated in humour, making you laugh at times you know you shouldnt and wince at others. Its an uncommon but wry style to impart on a movie with such serious themes. Its one of Scorseses most brutal but stunning films, an incredible, relentless experience about the single-minded pursuit of crime. As soon as you see the title card Based on a true story, appears in a Scorsese film, you know you are in for a treat. I had no idea going in that this was true, the story of Henry Hill, a half-Irish, half-Sicilian Brooklyn kid who is adopted by the neighbourhood gangsters at an early age and climbs the ranks of a Mafia under the guidance of Jimmy Conway was one I adored. Showcasing his life perfectly, capturing the period feeling to a tee, bringing out just enough of the colours and styles of the setting without it feeling like a pastiche while exposing the misguided loyalties and greed that often inhabits organised crime.
Now if the premise didnt already have me interested, the cast alone would have. The central performances in Goodfellas are all first-class, with each of the three leading men being given a chance to shine. Ray Liotta is terrific as Henry you can see and appreciate the amount of research and preparation which he put in, and yet its not artificial or restrained in any way, he lets loose when he can and is just guarded enough when he needs to be to fully stand out alongside the best. Robert De Niro is great as Jimmy Conway, bringing all his familiar skills to the party but working hard in every scene to be true to the character, what an incredible decade he had. And Joe Pesci, who won an Oscar for his performance, is a firecracker, managing to be impulsive and dangerous without seeming over-the-top. He stands out in every scene and truly deserved the acclaim he garnered. Similarly, the supporting cast is also excellent, particularly Paul Sorvino as Paulie and the smashing Lorraine Bracco, who beautifully balances Karens desperation, jealousy and feeling of being in slightly over her head perfectly. Theres no one that felt like the weak link. Everyone gives it their all and enhances every single aspect of the film.
The film is nigh-on perfect, with great performances being matched by a tight script, fixating sets and masterful direction from the master himself, creating a compelling cinematic experience that more than merits repeat viewing. Its been a long time since a film has garnered my respect as much as this has, its an epic, its powerful, funny, tough, and hell is it cool. Goodfellas truly is one of Scorseses best and one of, if not the best gangster film ever made.

Why I think Goodfellas still resonates today.
1. Scorsese has managed to very effectively capture and explore the Mafia lifestyle (based on the actual story of Henry Hill), giving it an incredibly authentic rendering on the big screen without sanitizing it. 
2. Its realistic storytelling content makes it different from other gangster films. 
3. The stylistic techniques (use of date and time, kinetic camera shots) really enhanced the story with a genuine narrative feel.
4. The use of voiceovers to heighten the documentary feel and autobiographical point of view, as well as the freeze frames and fast-cut editing, were brilliant.
5. The soundtracks use of classic rock gems from the late 1950s- early 1970s infused into his shots (my favorite - Layla) gives it an authentic period vibe.
6. The famous character lines that became iconic.
7. Its influence on modern culture even writer David Chase admitted that Goodfellas was his Koran in the creation of The Sopranos series.
 8. It inspired directors in the 90s to make films like Reservoir Dogs, Pulp Fiction, and Fight Club. 
 9. Anyone watching this will see a front-row view of why gangsters chose their risky lifestyle, trading poverty for a life of easy money, wealth and glamour. Its an honest movie, and it is a reality that no one can deny.In other words, no sugarcoating.

Goodfellas has been praised as one of the greatest films ever made, and it deserves every bit of its critical acclaim. Directed by Martin Scorsese, this classic mobster movie takes you on a wild ride from the 1950s to the late 80s as we follow three buddies as they embark on a life of organised crime. 
Robert DeNiro, Joe Pesci and Ray Liotta are perfectly cast as the trio at the heart of the movie. DeNiro is a master of his craft, quietly captivating as he conveys an almost Shakespearean sense of power and solemnity. Joe Pesci is utterly terrifying as the volatile mobster, his intensity completely gripping. This is matched by Liottas performance as the ambitious young associate who soon finds himself out of his depth.
At its heart, Goodfellas is a modern retelling of the classic gangster film, with gunfights, double crossings and booty-snatching. But what makes it great is its authentic look and feel due to the incredible attention to detail that Scorsese has applied to his direction. Nothing feels contrived, and its easy to believe that youre experiencing the true gangster lifestyle. The level of craft and artistry present in the film is quite astonishing. Goodfellas is a masterpiece, and it stands out as one of the greatest cinematic achievements of all time. If you havent seen it yet, its a must-watch.

Scorseses four major gangster movies (this, Casino, The Wolf of Wall Street, and The Irishman) are about the accumulation and management of capital, although Goodfellas is the only one that keeps this point implicit, which is also one of the reasons it is probably the most popular. Like Wolf, its most obvious double on Scorseses body of work, this is an effective a Dionysian comedy of sin very much predicted in voraciously consuming all the perks its main ideological promises offer its main character, and like it is very much animated by a deep contempt for the normalcy going on off-screen, a point much better articulated in this one (although the differences in the forms of resentment involved in that are also very telling). The movie gets a lot of mileage out of its occasional pit stops, suggesting the different lives going out of the gangster world, and of course, much more than Wolf, it does feel like Henry Hill does get his comeuppance by the end because of hoe much the movie leans on this on-screenoff-screen dichotomy . The endorsement discussion is of course a bore, although Goodfellas defenders will probably also never win it unless they accept that, like Hawks Scarface, to get a different anarchic action comedy, it does make being an outlaw very thrilling (which I shall add is Michael Ballhaus doing most of the time). If one wants to question Scorsese, it would probably be more useful to observe how the HenryTommy duality has a very safe logic that makes our main character usually come slight off the hook (the two Michael Imperioli scenes, which are the movies moral point of no return, for instance, are blocked and acted, so we understand that Liotta is at least a little troubled if not as outright horrified as us). The movie hedges its bets a little too often about not coming out as monstrous as possible (so Id argue Goodfellas critics are often wrong this movie could use to be as amoral as the original Scarface), but then thats the price of making something on this scale on Hollywood money. Of course none of this would be possible without some truly outstanding work by Ballhaus (who really shoots this for all its excitement worth), Liotta (who, as great as the deep supporting cast is, does hold it together), and probably above all else, Thelma Schoonmaker, her best job for Scorsese, just a terrific holding half a dozen tall tales together with perfect forward flow.

If Scorseses career were a cathedral, Goodfellas would be the stained-glass window. I think this is his most effortlessly rewatchable film. He has this ability to take stories of moral decay and make them feel exhilarating without ever losing sight of their cost. I know that he has a lot of mob movies and I understand the sentiment that many of his films can feel like the same thing. 
With all due respect, youre wrong. 
As far back as anyone can remember, Henry Hill wanted to be a gangster. Ray Liotta, to me, fits so well between De Niros cool menace and Pescis feral volatility. Henry isnt the toughest guy or the craziest or, quite frankly, the most ambitious. He is the most relatable guy and his eyes tell us exactly what hes thinking constantly. I love his eyes. 
Behind all of the excited bravado that he has in this life, his eyes are always saying, I hope I dont die today. His arc is so organic too. He goes from this confident young man to someone more grounded in the world to finally detonating in a coked-out panic. 
Scorsese follows the rhythm of Henrys heartbeat with his signature kinetic camerawork. It looks so good and its further developed by the unforgettable editing. Thelma and Scorsese dont really transition between scenes. More glide or snap depending on where Henry is psychologically. 
The cocaine sequence is just fucking magnificent. I feel this building anxiety every time I watch it, even though I know whats coming. The helicopter overhead, the time jumps, the switches between drugs, cooking sauce, paranoia. 
Opposite that anxiety is Robert De Niro being cool, calm, and collected. Hes too cool to lose his shit (most of the time). Each time I watch him in something, Im amazed at the command that he has. He doesnt need to explode to be terrifying. He just needs to exist in a room. Few actors can turn a friendly wave into a murder attempt. 
Go pick up some dresses at the store around the corner. 
Fuck. 
Joe Pesci is doing what Joe Pesci does best being fucking crazy. Pesci is obviously small in stature, but gigantic in presence. Tommy talks fast, moves fast, loves fast, kills faster. He has the emotional logic of a child, but its unbelievable how Pesci makes so much uncertainty feel real. Hes the king of gaslighting. I have to admit though that it is very satisfying to see him get what he deserves. 
Cant forget Lorraine Bracco. Karen Hill is the character in this that makes what could be a regular mob film into a tragedy. I feel like there are two points of view here. We have Henrys narration of course, but Karen is the seismic shift that happens. 
The man inside it and the woman drawn in from the outside. Ray Liotta and Bracco match each other so well and at no point is she overshadowed. She carries her own weight and does a hell of a job. 
A moment that stands out to me every time is when Henry breaks the fourth wall in the courtroom. This buildup just keeps coming and hes finally like, You know? Fuck this. Lets talk to you fuckers directly. The mob gave him purpose and excitement. Anonymity gives him nothing. He doesnt learn a lesson, but just loses the life he loved. Its his own personal purgatory. 
Thirty-five years later, Goodfellas still remains one of the best mob films of all time. I love films that are long, but dont feel long. Where youre completely and utterly sucked in entirely. 
Five stars hardly seem enough.

Going into GoodFellas, I knew its reputation and expected it to be great, but I wasnt expecting to be completely locked in it from start to finish I think my dad was really excited to watch this with me as well. What I loved most was how Scorsese puts you directly into Henry Hills world and makes you understand why this life was so appealing in the first place from his childhood experiences. The film has so much energy and confidence that I found myself getting caught up in the excitement alongside the characters, even though I knew where it was all heading. As it goes on, that excitement gradually gives way to paranoia, and I thought the way Scorsese handled that transition was masterful because as the film went on and on you could see moments where you think the film is over and then its not. The performances are phenomenal across the board, but Joe Pesci especially stood out to me. I never knew quite how good his range was because he was psychopathic in this. Ray Liotta is also fantastic as Henry, especially the narration making it easy to understand both the appeal and the cost of the life he chose.
What really cemented film for me was just how effortless everything feels. The direction, editing and cinematography all come together so naturally that I completely lost track of time while watching it, I really do think a true judge of a film at least for myself is when Im so enthralled that after the film I go away and do my research and learn about these people and thats exactly what I did for this. There are so many iconic moments, but the final act was probably my favourite part, I loved how interesting it was seeing Henrys life spiralling out of control and the frantic pace perfectly reflected that. I can see why so many people consider this one of the greatest crime films ever made. It really is an incredibly engaging character study and a showcase of a filmmaker who is so good and loves what he does. After finally watching it, I honestly think it deserves every bit of praise it gets, and its easily one of the best films Ive seen this year.

Strap in.. this first week of November Im about to go on a generational run of cinematic excellence, starting with a few films I was considering for my 1000th review. Goodfellas is one of those films, youd be shocked to know Ive never visited before and I realize now just what Ive been missing out on. 
The film is structurally a marvel, and perfectly executes the rise and fall of the two and a half decade story of Henry Hill from a starry-eyed neighborhood kid mesmerized by the mobs glamour, to a paranoid broken down informant living in the bleak reality of witness protection. The narrative glides with a hypnotic flair, propelled by Henrys witty, street-smart narration and Scorseses breathtaking technical prowess. A few minutes into the opening act and I am captivated by the allure of the mob life, it captures the seductive, intoxicating energy, perfectly juxtaposing the ensuing chaos and violence. 
Martin Scorsese and legendary cinematographer Michael Ballhaus are a match made in heaven its not just technically brilliant, but its completely in sync to the narrative and the characters emotional state, driving them forward. The long, unbroken tracking shots, the dolly zooms, the whip pans, the freeze frames, its a plethora of dynamic camera work and frantic editing no doubt in my mind Goodfellas is still a foundational piece for timeless, kinetic filmmaking.
I mean take scenes like the famous Copacabana long take, its more than just mere showmanship it establishes Henrys untouchable status whilst placing us, along with Henrys new girlfriend Karen, directly into the mesmerizing experience of Henry Hills early gangster life. We are seduced by the access, the privilege, and the effortless power he wields as he bypasses the line and is ushered through the back.
The soundtrack is outstanding. Scorsese didnt hire a composer, instead scored the film with musical genius. In choosing the songs, he set himself two rules The lyrics had to describe the scene, and the song had to have been released before the time the scene was set. Scorsese reportedly played music on set to keep the rhythm of each scene, another reason the film still moves like a living, breathing thing.
The cast of Goodfellas can only be described as one of the greatest cinematic ensembles of all time, thats largely due to Scorseses impeccable casting and direction. The success of the film lies within the core group of actors chemistry and the forever changing dynamics, their collective synergy is what makes the film feel so authentic and immersive. Each of the actors provide masterful performances I pro viably dont have to go into detail Ray Liotta, Robert De Niro, Joe Pesci.. just outstanding work really engulfing their characters. 
One thing I really enjoyed is the aging is done mostly through dramatic, psychological shifts rather than just heavy makeup, though the makeup is still subtle and extremely effective. You watch the characters change from charming, small-time criminals to paranoid, volatile killers the actors ability to convey this decades-long psychological toll, coupled with the great costume and hair design, is why the film feels like a complete epic even without the ultra-long runtimes of some other gangster films, thats a testament to the script and Scorseses style. 
My favorite character, hard call to make, but it has to be Joe Pesci as Tommy DeVito, its one of if not his career-best. A performance of raw, unpredictable terror, full of genuine and frightening moments. Tommy is a live wire, capable of passionate camaraderie one moment and horrific violence the next, that scene with Spider is truly shocking. Its his chilling delivery and unsettling intensity that helps completely nail his character, and it comes at no shock it earned him a deserved Academy Award. 
Ray Liotta also delivers what could be a career best, its such a complex performance, effortlessly balancing that outlandish radiance with that narcissistic over current, snowballing into that declined, paranoia as the characters life fell apart. His work as the narrator gives a voice to the story, not only making it easy to follow but adds authenticity and depth to the piece. I think his work during the final act is out of this world the whole helicopter following his actions is perfected through his facial expressions and high energy performance, seriously impressive. 
Also of course Samuel L Jackson is involved, his screen time is short lived but to say that hes in Goodfellas is just awesome, did not expect to see him show up at all. Talking about extras for a second, its fantastic that Scorsese hired some real-life wise guys. The first time we enter The Bamboo Lounge, we see a lot of real gangsters and in the famous Funny How? scene, Liotta and Pesci were surrounded by actual mobsters.
Talking on that funny how scene, its one of the more memorable scenes in any gangster film and I find it hilarious Joe Pesci experienced something similar in his own life making it all the more classic. I guess one day, a young Pesci complimented a mobster by calling him funny, in the sense that he was amusing. The mobster did not take the comment as a compliment and became angry, demanding to know what exactly was funny about him. Its bloody fantastic lore and the scene is made all the more fun by the Ray Liotta laugh.. man he fuckin nails that laugh every damn time. 
I think what truly elevates Goodfellas is its complete lack of filler, much like my most recent revisit of The Batman every scene, every needle drop, the soundtrack, and every structural decision is purposeful. Scorsese crafts a story that is not just about crime, but about the corrosive nature of loyalty, the illusion of power, and the terrifying speed at which the glamorous life can dissolve into paranoia and murder.
I could have posted this review hours ago before going into work, but my goodness did I need to think about it and give it the care and attention such a film deserves. Its a breathtaking gangster film with perfect execution and immaculate storytelling, the dialogue is iconic, and the performances are flawless. Its a masterclass honestly, the way its both stylish beyond measure and brutally honest, it certainly cements its place as an undeniable cinematic classic. 
If you made it this far, I appreciate you.. the film is an incredible accomplishment(so is reading this review) and Ive been foolishly to only just lay eyes on it, I suspect Ill revisit this during December.. yes its a Christmas movie, did you not see the Christmas scene with Ronettes Frosty the Snowman? so fucking peak.

A critique often hurled at Martin Scorseses work is that it glamorises the despicable and makes exciting that which should be repulsive. Its true that his films dont play out like morality plays, functioning in the same way as ancient Greek myths. The Wolf of Wall Streets Jordan Belfort certainly faces few repercussions for his excess, his exploitation, his lack of empathy and his greed. But what Scorsese understands is the alluring nature of the parallel worlds his characters inhabit. Worlds of status, exoticism, romance, but also of brutality, sadism, and indulgence.
Henry I always wanted to be a gangster Hill is pulled towards the mafia like an excitable moth to an ungovernable flame. The career criminal leads us through a portal to another dimension, or in this case the Copacabanas side door. Its a dimension where our dreams are attainable and where our every shallow want and desire is catered for. After enjoying such extravagance, how could you live like one of those goody-good people who worked shitty jobs for bum paychecks? But Hill isnt just attracted to the materialistic items his dirty money can buy his choice of occupation gives him a family. A community of likeminded individuals similarly vulnerable to the endless trappings of the gangster lifestyle.
Of course, it shouldnt be suggested that Goodfellas is a tale of Henry Hills spiritual and financial fulfilment. Like much of the acclaimed filmmakers work  reminiscent of Travis Bickles unstable vigilantism in Taxi Driver and Jake La Mottas innate self-loathing in Raging Bull - its an appraisal of male toxicity. Hill succumbs to a visceral desire to escape from societal norms, instead embracing acts of adultery, abuse and thievery with few misgivings. His vigour for such work only deteriorates because of an inclination towards powdery substances. The films cocaine-fuelled third act encapsulates this deterioration, and though the filmmaking is often exhilarating, its always expository, not celebratory.
If morality exists in Scorseses dynamic crime classic, it exists only as an abstract concept. The flimsy veneer of loyalty, respect and family inevitably shatters upon powerful forces of gluttony, distrust and self-absorption. The gangs initial unity and jubilation over the success of the Lufthansa heist quickly erodes into paranoid savagery, culminating in a series of murders which provide one of the films most iconic sequences and a typically audacious flourish from the seasoned director. This capitulation suggests Scorsese isnt placing these people on a grand pedestal hes exposing their gaudy artifice. 
Contrasting the climaxes of numerous gangster pictures, Goodfellas protagonist doesnt shuffle off this mortal coil in a triumphant hail of bullets, evoking well-worn tragedies of ambition and greed. In his eyes, Hill suffers a fate worse than death. To live the rest of his life like a schnook. Now, what is so glamourous about that?

GoodFellas is inspired by Henry Hills true story within the Mafia, from his beginnings as a petty criminal to his involvement in increasingly important and dangerous illegal activities. Based on the novel Wiseguy by Nicholas Pileggi, the film is the chronicle, not devoid of unusual black humor, of the evolution of Italian-American organized crime narrated from the perspective of an individual who has been an integral part of it for almost thirty years. This synergistic combination of action and irony deprives the story of that epic aura typical of the mafia-movies of the past, giving Martin Scorsese the opportunity to describe the brutal context of a world constantly outside the law, without ever falling into any moralism.
The narration develops in a chronologically discontinuous and fragmented way, with repeated temporal leaps and changes of perspective, giving life to a fragmented but compelling plot. The staging is very accurate, centered on a finely stylized direction that juggles between sinuous sequence shots, suggestive slow-motion and ironic still images, which is accompanied by a fast-paced editing, a skilful use of the narrative voice and a soundtrack that constitutes a real own musical treasure of the time. The film also stands out for the extraordinary skill of the cast, made up of actors of the caliber of Ray Liotta, Robert De Niro and Joe Pesci, who manage to flawlessly represent the absurdity of a harsh and violent reality, but which at the same time is permeated by bonds of friendship and solidarity, in which honor and loyalty are considered sacred values.
