Of the three most acclaimed films by Martin Scorsese (the other two being Taxi Driver and Raging Bull), Goodfellas is the one which remains the most mainstream. So many of Scorseses later works are inflected by this film (Casino, The Departed, The Wolf of Wall Street), and as well as been a key film in his career, its become a cultural landmark as an influencer on an entire subgenre. Goodfellas is a stylish film, with Nouvelle Vague inspirations, and filled with freeze-frames, zooms, long takes, popular music, and fast editing. Its style is smooth and suave, with clean camera pans and perfectly constructed complex shots. Goodfellas is a film of technical excellence, and an endlessly rewatchable experience.
The trio at the core of Goodfellas are all fascinating characters. Theres Henry (Ray Liotta), Jimmy (Robert De Niro), and Tommy (Joe Pesci), and the actors all commit to their roles commendably, although Liotta is easily the blandest and least compelling screen presence. Joe Pesci is really the scene-stealer, with his explosive character key to so many of the films most memorable scenes (funny how?, now go home and get your fucking shine box, killing Spider). Its always a little surprising to me that Robert De Niro plays just a supporting role in Goodfellas, with his character appearing unacknowledged when surrounded by the films lead character and the lively and loud Joe Pesci. But, as always, De Niro plays his role with precision and does so much with a character who appears quite enigmatic at times. Goodfellas is a film of loud, overlapping social interactions with these three characters, and even has a comedic edge to it because of that. The central performances and excitable tone allow Goodfellas to succeed even in sequences that seem superfluous (like the dinner with Tommys mother). I doubt theres been a gangster film with a more memorable central trio.
Goodfellas has a contrast at its heart, between the idolisation of gangsterdom and the grim reality of criminality. No film captures the appeal of being a gangster more than Goodfellas, with the life shown as a kind of fantasy bound to attract people. For Henry, being a gangster brings him purpose and respect. It also places him within a group that becomes family. Goodfellas is a detailed depiction of this life, with the narration providing a crash course in the reality of being a gangster. It highlights the weird principles, of family but also of murder. It also highlights how enterprising such criminality can be. These crimes are steeped in corruption and a business-like approach, which makes it all the more complicated. In the end, if this is your life, it just becomes a routine, you dont even think about it.
If the first half of Goodfellas depicts a glamorous life, the second half presents a horrible descent. Living the fantasy life becomes being nostalgic for the fantasy life. However, this fantasy life was never that great. Sure, it was a life where you could be angry and vengeful and face no consequences, but murder was an occupational hazard and you had to accept that. Besides, Goodfellas shows us the crude life lived beneath the fancy veneer, a life of domestic violence and being turned on by guns. The gangster life is quite insular, dependent only on a few close friends and family. Various sub-communities in Goodfellas - Italian, Jewish, Sicilian, Irish - interact in different ways, with conflicts drawn from not trusting people outside your little group. This is how Goodfellas ends up with Henry and his wife feeling trapped, as the gangster life ends up dangerous and with few allies who care beyond the money. This is what Goodfellas depicts in its entirely, the good and bad sides of the gangster life. There is some nasty violence in Goodfellas, almost always quite incidental in presentation, but it remains as background noise to the entire plot. As the gangster life falls apart, the second half becomes more chaotic. Goodfellas ends up being about losing the movie-star lifestyle that being a gangster provided, and having to wake up from the dream.
Goodfellas is one of Scorseses many masterworks, a rise-and-fall tale made with incredible consistency. Its a harsh look at the criminal life, but almost doting in how it shows the highs of gangsterdom. Its a film that shows both sides of things at the same time, creating an intricate and nuanced perspective of how and why people choose to live this way. Its a story of dreams and a slow-motion crash into reality.

Goodfellas is the best kind of film one which is almost impossible to turn off when youve started watching. With its exhilarating cinematography and performances it draws the viewer into a violent but somehow glamorous world. 
The movie follows three decades in the life of mobster Henry Hill, who starts as a Mafia hanger-on and slowly works his way up to truck-jacking, scams and leg-breaking. He and his friends Jimmy and Tommy live the life carefree, violent and blighted only by the risk of death or arrest. The film follows the highs and lows of the mid-level gangsters as they put food on the table through one crime after another, without the operatic style of The Godfather but with plenty of brutality.  
Scorcese enjoys protagonists who arent perceptive enough to take a wider view of their situation, and Hill is a classic example a blue-collar street hood with an unthinking acceptance of violence. Whilst he occasionally has qualms over the more murderous actions of his organization this rarely rises above mild discomfort. The emotional side of the story is deeply tied to his relationship with his wife Karen fucked up and dysfunctional though it is, its the closest thing to a moral centre he has. 
Lorraine Bracos performance is crucial to Goodfellas as she provides a rare feminine perspective on the macho world of organised crime. Karen is in many ways an equal partner in Hills lifestyle as she is seduced by his charm, money and willingness to break the rules in his favour. Her relationship with him in some ways is similar to the audience she is desensitized to his worst actions and even begins to admire his audacity noting It was like Henry was enterprising and he and the guys were making a few bucks hustling, while all the other guys were sitting on their asses waiting for handouts.
Joe Pesci and Robert De Niro complete the trio as hot tempered Tommy DeSimone and cold, calculating Jimmy Conway shakedown artists and sociopaths but a pleasure to hang out with. The films dialogue has entered movie legend apart from Joe Pescis well known rants one throwaway moment I like is a character called Pete the Killer growling I took care of that thing for ya.
Scorsese seems to understand the Mafia through the lens of an addict it gives you good times but theres a hideous price to buy your way into it, and it is ultimately likely to result in death or imprisonment. The rush created by the fast-moving cinematography is matched by devastating lows as murders, beatings and brutality take their toll and the protagonist becomes more and more haggard. 
Henrys decision to get out of the life and become an average schmuck coincides with him getting clean, breaking his dependence on both intoxicants although not his desire for them. Goodfellas is in many ways a perfectly entertaining movie, but the darker side of the life still shows through, like a stylish club built on a rotten foundation.

Hes dead. What do you think, Im gonna miss? I know how to shoot.  - Tommy DeVito
GoodFellas de Martin Scorsese, est lun des classiques incontournables. Un film qui nous saisit dès la première seconde et qui dit clairement  Bienvenue. Voilà comment ça se passe vraiment. Juste une immersion totale dans un monde où ladrénaline, largent et la loyauté dictent tout. Et franchement, des films de gangsters aussi vivants, aussi nerveux, aussi maîtrisés, il ny en a pas énormément.
Cest un film sur la mafia, évidemment. Mais surtout, cest un film sur la fascination. La fascination pour le pouvoir, pour largent facile, pour lappartenance à un clan. On suit Henry Hill, gamin dun quartier qui regarde les mafieux comme des rockstars. Et très vite, on comprend que pour lui, devenir gangster, cest devenir quelquun. Cest une ascension sociale par la violence, par la débrouille, par lillégalité. Et Scorsese montre pourquoi cest attirant. Pourquoi ça brille. Pourquoi ça fait rêver. Et ensuite, il montre les conséquences.
Ce qui frappe immédiatement, cest lénergie. La réalisation de Martin Scorsese est exceptionnelle. Les travellings sont mythiques, la narration nous met parfaitement dans la tête du personnage, le montage est solide. Tout va vite, voire trop vite. Comme la vie de ces types. Ça rit, ça boit, ça cogne, ça flingue. Cest drôle, puis ça devient glaçant en une fraction de seconde. Une blague peut se transformer en menace mortelle sans prévenir. La fameuse scène Funny how ? est lexemple parfait  on rit puis on ne rit plus du tout. La violence nest jamais stylisée. Elle est sèche, brutale, parfois absurde. Un coup de feu, et cest fini. Juste le choc. Et ça rend plus réel.
De plus, le récit montre la mafia de lintérieur, avec ses règles, sa hiérarchie, ses trahisons. Mais il montre aussi la paranoïa, la drogue, la chute. Plus le film avance, plus le rythme devient intense, presque stressant, surtout dans la dernière partie. On ressent la pression, la peur dêtre surveillé, arrêté, trahi. Ce nest pas glorieux à la fin, cest chaotique.
La musique joue un rôle énorme. Les morceaux des années 60 et 70 correspondent et accompagnent parfaitement les différentes périodes, renforçant lénergie et lévolution des personnages. Et dans le dernier acte, quand tout seffondre, le montage devient presque frénétique. Les hélicoptères, la coke, les casseroles, les allers-retours constants. On est dans la tête dHenry. On suffoque avec lui.
Si le film reste incontournable, cest grâce à des performances et à un casting extraordinaires. Robert De Niro est dun calme terrifiant. Jimmy Conway, cest le mec charmant, rassurant jusquau moment où tu comprends quil calcule tout. Derrière le sourire, il y a la paranoïa et la froideur. Il ne crie pas. Il décide. Et cest encore plus inquiétant.
Ray Liotta, en Henry Hill, est parfait dans cette trajectoire dascension puis de chute. Il a ce mélange de naïveté, dambition et de fragilité. Et ce rire particulier, presque exagéré  à la fois dérangeant et hilarant. Mais, plus le film avance, plus son regard change. À la fin, il est vidé, paranoïaque, bouffé par la coke et la peur. On ressent physiquement lépuisement.
Evidemment, Joe Pesci en Tommy DeVito est monumental et imprévisible. Il peut être hilarant, presque enfantin puis devenir une bombe à retardement. Il incarne la violence pure, lego fragile prêt à exploser pour une remarque de travers. Son énergie est électrique. Il fait peur parce quil est incapable de se contenir.
Et au milieu de tout ça il y a Karen, magnifiquement interprété par Lorraine Bracco. Son point de vue est essentiel. Elle aussi est fascinée au départ. Elle aime le pouvoir que ça lui donne, largent, lattention. Elle entre volontairement dans ce monde. Mais progressivement, la peur sinstalle. La drogue, les armes planquées dans la maison, la paranoïa. Le film montre aussi ça  la famille comme extension du crime. La maison devient un bunker. Lamour devient dépendance.
Au final, Goodfellas, ce nest pas juste un film de gangsters. Cest un film sur lillusion du rêve américain version criminelle. Sur le fait de vouloir appartenir à quelque chose de plus grand que soi. Sur ladrénaline qui devient une drogue. Et sur la chute inévitable quand le système se retourne contre eux.
Cest drôle, violent, brillant, excessif, mais surtout dune sincérité brutale. Scorsese ne juge pas, il expose. Il montre lattrait du crime, mais aussi sa réalité inéluctable. Il fait aimer ce monde puis il rappelle pourquoi il est condamné à sautodétruire.
Et quand le film se termine, il reste ce sentiment  davoir vécu trop vite, trop fort, et davoir tout perdu.
Un grand film de mafia, intense et toujours aussi efficace.

One of my favorite things about Letterboxd is this feeling that Ive discovered and am now sorta-kinda a part of a community of like-minded folks. The movie nerd table in the school cafeteria. I started really diving into this platform when I moved away from a place with a solid group of friends who shared my interests, to a much smaller town where I suddenly found myself without movie-lovers to gab with in person. 
I relate everything in my life to the movies to specific scenes, to characters, sometimes entire films. Movies are my general reference point on almost everything. Possibly to an unhealthy degree. And in my town, among my friends, Im basically the movie guy. Ive somehow become the expert (unlike on Letterboxd where, compared to many, I feel like a total novice). Almost nobody I engage with in my day-to-day life has heard of Satyajit Ray or Elaine May or Yasujirō Ozu or Kelly Reichardt or Costa-Gavras or even cinema giants like Billy Wilder or Howard Hawks, and so on. Hell, most people I know havent even heard of current best picture nominees like Anatomy of a Fall or The Zone of Interest. I imagine this is all true for a lot of the folks I follow on here - that LB provides a movie-centric oasis we dont get in our everyday lives. 
 
And the thing is, my love of movies can make me a bit of a broken record. Movies are pretty much all I want to talk about. When I really get going, I often notice a trend - the eyes of my friends slowly start to glaze over with disinterest as Ive made my 6th film reference of the evening... gosh, what you just said reminds me of a scene from this wonderful movie called Marty, ever heard of it? No? Its from the 50s and stars Ernest Borgnine. Ever heard of him? No? Oh, let me tell you all about it. I recommended Cleo From 5 to 7 to a friend recently, and he watched it and said this is one of your favorite movies? Huh... I feel like you have to watch a lot of movies to like this movie. Well, guilty as charged, my dude. 
When the people in my life are humoring me, or are sincerely trying their damndest to meet me on my level, they will ask me a question Im sure we all get asked pretty often so, what is your favorite movie? 
What a question. The snobbish prick in me sometimes wants to respond, well, asking what is your favorite movie is like asking what is your favorite color? I dont have one, Im not a child. But I dont actually ever say that, cuz that would be a nutty, overly confrontational dipshit thing to do. I also dont fully believe the above statement, either. So what I usually say is both true and not true. I pick a movie they might have heard of, something maybe a bit more mainstream, but one that I still love with all my heart. I say the movie that I consider to be the most re-watchable film of all time. Goodfellas. 
Goodfellas, for me, is like my Beatles or Radiohead. At any given moment, I might be in a John Prine phase or a Tyler the Creator phase or a Big Thief phase or a Frank Ocean phase or an Angel Olsen phase or a Nick Drake phase or a Noname phase. But I always come back to The Beatles and Radiohead. If I could only bring two records with me on a spaceship journey to the ends of the galaxy, itd be In Rainbows and Revolver. And thats how I feel about Goodfellas. Always there, always sitting right next to whatever flavor of the month is taking up space in my brain. 
Aint much I can say about this masterpiece that hasnt already been said. Henry Hill is a young Irish American boy who lives across the street from a cab stand owned by Paulie, a captain in the Lucchese crime family, one of the notorious five families of the New York arm of the Italian mafia. Henry starts running errands for them at a young age and rises through the ranks with age as a well liked associate. As a young man he is introduced to Jimmy The Gent Burke, another Irish American man who is feared and respected by everyone around him. He takes a liking to Henry and takes him under his wing. This begins the dark journey of Hill, from petty theft to drugs and one of the most infamous heists in American history.
Scorsese. Scorsese. Scorsese. Martin Scorsese. A true master of his craft, most of the films he has directed are considered masterpieces by both film buffs and casual viewers alike. Many are well over two hours long and tend to deliver the most interesting plots, usually based on true events, with some of the best camera work youll ever see. Of all of those films, I think I am in good company, and can safely make the claim that  GoodFellas  is his magnum opus. Its a product of Scorsese in his prime. Violence, underground politics, crime, the allure of the mafia, and the perfect timing of being extremely relevant to the current events of the time all come together to deliver a tremendous experience. 
The actors are the Crème de la crème of mob films. All familiar faces from previous and future Scorsese projects as well as series like  The Sopranos.  Joe Pesci, Robert De Niro, and Ray Liotta lead a tremendous cast including names like Paul Sorvino, Lorraine Bracco and Frank Vincent. Even the legendary Paulie Walnuts Tony Sirico makes an appearance. It doesnt get much better than this. 
Based on the true life story of Henry Hill, the plot is almost as good as the cast. The first two acts are brilliant. A violently interesting look into the inner workings of a crime family from the 1950s to the 1970s. I personally consider that part of the film to be flawless. However, the third act suffers from the inevitable. Something that I have branded  The Mark of Scorsese.  What that is, is a lull that almost always plagues the third act of his films. The common pattern is an excellent first two acts followed by a third that extends the film far too long and breaks everything that made the previous two so interesting. In this case we go from the excellent mafia stuff to the drug stuff. Sure its part of Henry Hills true life story but its just not as interesting or well paced. As the great Joe Bob Briggs says, its  too much plot getting in the way of the story.  Fortunately the final aspect of  The Mark of Scorsese  process kicks in just in time, and that is the ending. His endings always do their best to pick up the twenty minute slog that precedes them and it usually works out. This is no exception.
My centennial reviews tend to be reserved for excellent films that Ive seen before. Films that have a chance of receiving that rare five star rating from me.  GoodFellas  comes close. If it werent for that lull that drags down much of the third act it would be a five star banger all day. If you like films at all, this must see viewing for you. Hell, its must see material for everyone. Considering the untimely death of Ray Liotta a few days ago I think  GoodFellas  is the perfect film to review for number 1,100. Check it out.
 R.I.P RAY LIOTTA

As I near the end of the AFIs 100 Years100 Movies list, there are still a couple of big I cant believe you havent seen that films left, and Goodfellas was one of them. What can I say? Much like The Godfather and Titanic, it was such a part of the collective consciousness when I was growing upnot least through endless Sopranos referencesthat I never felt an urgent need to actually sit down and watch it. Well, a few weeks shy of the big 4-0, I am glad to have finally put that right! Better late than never, I guess.
For a film about unrepentant criminals, Goodfellas feels remarkably politeat least at first. Its Scorsese doing what he does best inviting us into the mobsters world with a sly grin and a tonne of style. He opens the door of the Copacabana with that famous tracking shot through the kitchen and enthrals with his hypnotic camera moves, pop-song montages and conspiratorial voiceovers until I felt almost complicit in the horrornot necessarily supportive, but complicit.
Ray Liottas Henry Hill narrates his rise and fall with the breezy, almost carefree energy of a man doing a podcast about his own federal indictment. The more I think about it, the more perfect his performance seems. It is just detached enough to let the horrors breathe and just naïve enough that I could pretend I might not have made the same dumb choices in his shoes. Robert De Niro oozes icy charm as Jimmy Conway, but its Joe Pesci who completely steals the show. I never quite know whether Tommy was going to crack a joke or a skulland that tension, fuelled by the films pitch-black humour, is half the fun.
Lorraine Bracco also deserves a shout-out as Karen Hill, Henrys wife and occasional partner in crime. Karen offers a gripping outsider-turned-accomplice perspective at first shes seduced by the thrills of Henrys lifestyle (who wouldnt be after that Copacabana date?), and later shes just as deep in the muck as the guys. Her own voiceover moments and fiery confrontations with Henry add a whole other dimensionwe see how the madness seeps into family life through her eyes. And Paul Sorvinos Paulie might be the most understated mob boss ever he barely needs to speak above a whisper. One disapproving look from him carries more weight than all of Tommys wild unpredictability.
The pacing is relentless, which is fitting for a story thats basically one long, spiraling comedown. In the first half, Scorsese uses all his razzle-dazzlesmooth tracking shots, freeze-frames and a wall-to-wall rock soundtrackto seduce us right along with Henry. By the second half, as Henrys life and coke habit spiral out of control, the editing and camerawork get faster and choppier, and suddenly I was as jumpy and paranoid as he wasat one point I couldve sworn I heard helicopters outside. Scorsese doesnt exactly glamorise crime, but he shows how the early glamour is always half a mirage, half a trap, and totally exhausting. Cocaine, it turns out, is not a sustainable time-management strategy.
By the end, when Henry laments having to live like a schnook, I almost felt sorry for himuntil I remembered that for Henry, living like a schnook means hes safe in witness protection with a nice house and a quiet life. Poor guy. Goodfellas never asks for forgivenessit just lays out the wreckage, and walks away.

Zum Beispiel am Cast, der mit zum Besten gehört, was jemals für nur einen Film vor der Kamera stand. Ob nun der undurchsichtige Robert De Niro, der so grenzenlose wie grauenvoll geladene Joe Pesci, Ray Liotta in der Rolle seines Lebens, die zähe wie zerbrochene Lorraine Bracco, Paul Sorvino, Frank Vincent, Imperioli, Jackson, Sirico alle klasse, alle on fire, alle so wichtig für diese filmische Gangsterwelt. 
Daneben hat mich die Kamera von Michael Ballhaus und seine sensationellen Steadicam-Fahrten beeindruckt. Und dann eben diese großartigen Momente, die Scorsese mit Ballhaus und der Besetzung erschaffen hat. Natürlich der legendäre Copacabana Shot, vorbei an der Warteschlange und durch die Küche in den Nachtclub, aber auch das allabendliche Kochfest im Knast, Braccos Aufmarsch vor Liottas Stammkneipe, die Leichen-Montage zum Outro-Part von Layla, die How funny-Eskalation oder die Spider-Situationen. 
Szenen und Leistungen, weshalb ich meine Goodfellas immer wieder in der Player geschoben habe. Und je häufiger ich den Film sah, umso mehr habe ich Scorseses Plan verstanden. Umso mehr habe ich ihn lieben und bewundern gelernt. Es ist dieses Zusammenspiel aus herkömmlicher, übergeordneter, exakter Einteilung und diesem fuck you, pay me-Vibe im Detail. 
So hat der Film zwei erklärte wie klare Ziele der unaufhaltsame Aufstieg und der unentrinnbare, qualvolle Abstieg. Doch dazwischen gibt er auf solche Dinge wie Drehbuch-Formeln, Sehgewohnheiten, Zartgefühl, Noblesse oder Normen so kontinuierlich wie beherzt einen Mittelfinger. Mit anderen Worten er ist so ungezähmt, grob, wild, brutal, beweglich, witzig, irre, rastlos, kaltschnäuzig, unvorhersehbar, gnadenlos, explosiv und heißblütig wie die Gangster, von denen er erzählt. 
Scorsese treibt die Erzählung beharrlich voran, überrascht mit Umwegen oder Momentaufnahmen, hält dabei fast durchweg ein berauschendes Tempo und wechselt immer wieder frei Schnauze Stil und Ton der Inszenierung. Diese Methode hat er danach noch in mindestens zwei Filmen angewandt und verfeinert, um sie schließlich mit einem dritten Film zu brechen. Letzterer heißt The Irishman, einer der beiden anderen heißt The Wolf of Wall Street. Und der konnte gleich mehrere Dinge belegen. 
Unter anderem, dass seine Methode auch 23 Jahre nach Goodfellas noch aufgeht dass sie kein One-Hit-Wonder war. Und dass es Scorsese auch mit 71 Jahren noch drauf hat. Dass er es immer noch schafft, die Faszination wie auch die Grausamkeit solch eines in sich geschlossenen Mikrokosmos zur dichten, direkten und triebhaften Erfahrung zu machen. Egal, ob es nun um Wolfsrudel an der Wall Street oder die Goodfellas der New Yorker Mafia geht. Und deswegen bin ich in Letztere verliebt, so weit ich mich an sie zurückerinnern kann.

This film is unrelenting in its portrayal of the horrors of war and the loss of innocence.
Grave of the Fireflies is a beautifully constructed tale that is a unique achievement in both storytelling and artistic vale. It tells a story of a brother and sister who try to survive in a world that makes no sense, where adults either abandon them or fight each other. The older brother tries to take care of his very young sister as best he can, but we are constantly reminded that he, himself, still is a child and is not ready to carry such responsibility.
We are shown from the very first scene how this film is going to end and that dramatic effect adds a stunning and deeply moving tragedy to everything that is shown to us. Make no mistake, this film is uncompromising in the depth of its tragic narrative. See, as noble as the boys actions are we already know they are pointless. He tries to make the war invisible for his sister, to hide the death around her and he succeeds in doing just that for a while. The scenes in which they are together and build up their own little world inside the bomb shelter are some of the most beautiful and heartwarming slices of cinema I have ever seen.
What makes this film work and adds strength to the drama is the fact that there is no storytelling veneer. It is told in a rather sober fashion, with outstanding pacing. If you let it get under your skin it will stay with you for a long time and that has everything to do with the fantastic characterization, the stunning visuals and the great respect for the story its telling.
I immediately fell for the little girl. The way she is drawn, her expressions, her actions and her sobering utterances just felt very real. The fact that she comes across as a real person made this film get to me. I cared. For a drawing. Rationally, that makes no sense, but there is no rationale in the essence of a child. Draw it, act it, write it, sculpt it, it doesnt matter. If you manage to capture it, it is always disarming, engrossing and in this case deeply tragic.
The animation is just absolutely amazing. The eye for detail and the use of light and dark give this film a gorgeous aesthetic. Animation is just one half, the other half is comprised of the direction. There are a couple of scenes in this film that are directed with such great skill that they leave and incredible lasting impression.
I was emotionally exhausted after watching this, but also fulfilled. See, this film does manage to show us the innocence of a child and allows it to linger and remain in a state of grace, forever playing, dancing and loving. And even though it is a small comfort, it is one I will gladly take and really need after watching this beautifully horrific masterpiece.

This is simply an unabashed descent into miserya concentrated, conscious effort of subsequent misfortunes meant solely to make us feel progressively shittier about the fates of our protagonists. This was my first Studio Ghibli film, although Ive watched tons of anime, and honestly, it didnt disappoint. But the emotional weight is what made it feel real. The story gets to you because things fall apart bit by bit. These poor kids, got separated from their mom right away. Then their house burns down. Soon, they have no safe place. Finally, they run out of hope completely. The narrative never tricks you into tearing up with dramatic music or anything. We simply see what happens and it lets us process the full impact on our own.
That makes it seem honest, and this genuine approach creates such a powerful connection with the characters. By experiencing everything alongside Setsuko, the meaning behind it becomes much more personal. She cannot understand why these countless terrible challenges continue to occur. She still wants to catch glowing insects and play and have fun, as young children usually should. Your heart breaks as she gradually understands how awful their situation really is.
Even long after finishing the movie, the sibling relationship is what sticks with you. Within this deep family bond, Seita tries his best as the big brother. He makes mistakes, being only a kid himself. But he always struggles to take care of Setsuko. He even prepares her a nice bath in one scene, which demonstrates how deeply he cares. It shows how much he wants to give her normal, happy moments, despite their world crumbling around them.

The film takes place during World War II and follows Seita and his little sister, Setsuko, as they struggle to adapt to a world transformed by war, a world that has stripped them of their sense of safety. Between the cruelty of their circumstances and the innocence of childhood, we witness Seitas attempts to protect his sister and Setsukos efforts to hold on to the little things that make her feel like a child.
The film shows us two children, but it never treats them as mere fictional characters trying to overcome their circumstances. Instead, it reveals how easily human beings can be deprived of their most basic rights because of decisions they had no part in making. To those who wage wars, they may be about maps, borders, victories, and losses. But to the children living through them, war means a home that no longer feels the same, days in which the feeling of safety never returns, and a future they can no longer clearly imagine.
The film makes you reflect on the very meaning of survival. Does survival simply mean continuing to breathe? Or does it mean having a life you can actually live, people you can turn to, and a place where you dont have to fear every new day? Because human beings need more than food and shelter to live. They need tenderness, belonging, and the feeling that their existence matters to someone else.
Through the bond between the brother and his sister, the film raises a painful question about love and responsibility what does it mean to try to protect someone you love when you are still a child yourself? How can someone who has barely had the chance to grow up be expected to face circumstances that no child should ever have to endure? And how can love be a source of strength while also reminding you of just how fragile you are in a world that shows no mercy?
In the end, the film reminds us that history often remembers wars through their beginnings and endings, through the names of leaders, the battles fought, and the outcomes that followed. But it cannot preserve every little detail lost between those beginnings and endings. It cannot give a child back the years stolen from them, make up for the home someone has lost, or give someone who is gone the chance to live the life they were supposed to have.

The film makes you realize that war does not only destroy the world we live in. Sometimes, it destroys the small world that was supposed to grow within every child.

The horrors of war are often discussed in film. Bombs are dropped, bullets fired, blood spilled, soil stained, lives lost. But wars casualties exist beyond the uniform. Every pilot has a mother, every foot soldier has a father, and every face behind a gun, every finger gracing a trigger has a family. Grave of the Fireflies doesnt concern itself with the soldiers, with the lives being lost on battlefields, in enemy waters, or in the sky, but rather the family of a soldier, whose story is just (as if not more) important to human history.
I think what I like so much about Grave of Fireflies is its unflinching resolve to keep itself grounded in reality. Miyazaki seems much more concerned with using the fantastical to explore rather bleak subject matter, but Takahata instead depicts the horrors of war and the futility of nationalism through the most human lens possible. I think my one critique lies with the films ending. Perhaps this is wishful thinking but I cant stop thinking that the ending was needlessly tragic. in english There are films that move you, and there are films that quietly destroy you  Grave of the Fireflies belongs to the latter. Isao Takahata doesnt craft a typical war drama he composes an animated elegy, a sorrowful poem about childhood abruptly ended by the cruelty of adulthood. The beauty here is paradoxical every frame feels tenderly painted, yet within that gentleness lies an unbearable ache.
The contrast between the soft watercolor visuals and the tragedy that unfolds is what makes the experience so haunting. The pastel tones, the warm glow of the night scenes  especially when the fireflies light up the darkness  evoke a fleeting sense of life and memory. Its as if the film itself is whispering that beauty exists only for a moment before fading away.
Takahatas direction is restrained, almost observational. He avoids sentimentality, instead allowing silence and subtle gestures to carry the emotion. The pacing is deliberate, the sound minimal  every quiet moment, every lost gaze, every small act of care between the siblings feels magnified. The film breathes a kind of sadness that feels inevitable, as if time itself were saying goodbye.
More than an anti-war statement, Grave of the Fireflies is a devastating portrait of innocence in ruins  a reminder that horror doesnt end when the bombs stop falling. It stands as a requiem for humanity, painted in brief lights and brief lives. One of those films you dont just watch  you endure.

The film strips away the typical heroic tropes of cinema, and we are left with nothing but the raw yet avoidable tragedy of two children falling through the cracks of a crumbling world. It serves a haunting reminded that this world is cruel and unforgiving, all she needed was food, and a place to belong.. much like todays reality for a people, that is hard to come by, this one hits heavy. 
Thats where the true cruelty of Grave of the Fireflies lies in the realization that death wasnt an inevitable casualty of a bomb it was the slow result of a world that had simply run out of empathy. So those moments where she does find joy in something so minuscule as a firefly, playing at the beach, or simply just being around her brother Seita, it transforms the film from a brutal tragedy into an indictment of the human hearts capacity to look the other way.
I say thats where the true cruelty lies, but Seita has been dealt a vicious hand the entire length of the film, its such a sad snowball of events the brutal nature of his life.. loosing everyone close to him, only to be burdened with the impossible weight of a fathers role before he had even finished being a son.

Seeing him navigate this cruel reality is a masterclass in the resilience of the human spirit, even as it serves as a heartbreaking reminder that love, no matter how pure or boundless, can not always conquer the crushing indifference of war.
The animation is classic Ghibli, its not the usual fairylike, suns and roses, its a harrowing subversion of the studios signature beauty. They use the same depth and detail as there other projects but to render the grime of a bomb shelter and the hollowed out eyes of starvation with a realism that is just as brutal, maybe even more so, than any live action film. 
The usual lush landscapes that mostly signify wonder in a Ghibli film are replaced by the suffocating glow of firebombs and the dusty, scorched earth of a nation in collapse. Its fascinating to see an animation go this truly brutal route, its as intimate and powerful as you like and proves that animation is more than just escapism, it can still be used to show the difficult truths of the human condition.
The score from Michio Mamayi was equally powerful, and still as beautiful as ever. Its the perfect harmony to partner such a beast, weaving a delicate melancholic thread through the silence that captures the fragility of the siblings world before it finally unravels, its flawlessly realized and transforms the film into a poetic requiem. 
I really think this is one of the best animated films to ever grace the medium, its a devastating war drama with an incredible amount of heart. It serves as a poignant reminder that even when the world is at its most cruel, there is a vital, aching beauty in the smallest things a shared laugh, a tin of fruit drops, or the fleeting glow of a firefly. Some spoiler talk
A brother and sister living in a small Japanese town loose their mother during an air raid, and their father is off fighting in the war.
They go live with their aunt, who starts out being nice enough, but as time goes on, she ends up being a total heartless bitch.
She complains that the children are not doing their part, but never gives them any guidance on what they could be doing to contribute. Geez lady they are kids who just lost their mom. She even cons them into selling some of their stuff to help buy more food, but then make them feel guilty for actually eating it. She keeps saying her daughter and husband are doing so much to help the war effort, and that the children were lazy. Of course this irritated the heck out of me, you dont be mad at someone without helping them figure out what you want from them.
Eventually the kids set on their own because they cant take the mental stress anymore and live on their own.
Not only is their aunt totally self absorbed, but so is the rest of the town who shows no compassion to these orphans. Why cant the darn farmer or shop keeper offer this kid a job??? Even the doctor is totally passive to the reality that the kids are starving to death. 
The best part of the film is the tender relationship between the brother and his young sister and they have several wonderful moments of joy throughout. 
The young girls final moments are especially heartbreaking since the brother finally figures out how they can get some food that will last them awhile, but it is too late.
After watching the entire film, I recommend going back at watching the first few moments of the film up until the opening title card. Having that prospective really makes the films opening even more powerful, and I kinda wish they would have repeated that sequence before the end. 
Another touching moment was when the brother hears the news of Japans surrender, and being in total shock that his father who was a leader in their Navy was defeated.
This is a Studio Ghibli production, so of course the animation is beautiful, especially all the fireflies that are featured prominently.
Thinking you are not a fan of anime is no excuse, everyone should experience all the films of studio Ghibli, because they are all masterpieces.

I get that this movie is a sacred cow for a lot of people, so let me tread carefully here.  Also, for those that havent seen the film, SPOILERS ahead.  
Given the source material, an autobiographical short story by Akiyuki Nosaka, I think the decision to have Seita die and be peacefully reconciled in the afterlife with Setsuko is deeply problematic.  Nosaka has spoken publicly about his motivations for writing the story, in which heSeita lives, as a way of atoning for the death of Setsuko, his little sister who died of starvation after the firebombing of Kobe.  He has spoken publicly about the way he allowed his own pride and selfishness to influence his actions, which he believes directly led to her death.  By changing the ending, and by presenting the film in a naturalistic manner (otherwise a commendable choice), the film presents Seita as a victim as well, rather than, as Nosaka intended in the original story, a guilty party.
Now, Im not suggesting the film needed to punish Seita for his actions, or that it should have adopted a more scolding tone.  Rather, Im accusing the film of taking the easy way out, of choosing, in the end, sentimentality over the kind of moral wrestling it otherwise invites when showing the graphic horrors of war.  In doing this, the film alters the original intent of Nosakas story, and presents a moral dichotomy (WAR BADCHILDREN GOOD) that, while having emotional resonance, is also emotionally familiar and therefore easy.  The film falls short of the complexity I think this story demands.  Yes, Seita was a child who shouldnt have been asked to make the kinds of choices he was asked to make.  War is indeed terrible.  But in making those choices he made mistakes, and those mistakes had a tragic result for Setsuko.    I wish the film, like the short story, had acknowledged this.

Reading Eberts review, I was sensitive to his commentary regarding pillow shots as quiet moments in the film that dont advance the plot, but just work as punctuating marks, little pauses so we can have a breath of off-topic humanity.
Obviously, Ebert didnt grow up with Japanese anime. I did. And in the 90s animated series, you had some peaceful moments where a character would just wash his hair or go to the bathroom. It doesnt play a part in the plot, except the most essential one making the story human and seemingly devoid of narrative manipulation. This is perhaps the most significant difference between Japanese anime and the American school, aside from the painterly backgrounds and facial shapes. And naturally, Grave of the Fireflies is the perfect incarnation of these cultural differences. This is definitely not a Disney film, and this comes from a Disney fan.
I cry at Disney films, but I couldnt with Grave of the Fireflies. There was a pain somewhere, but it was just too heavy a feeling to let it flow through tears. Grave of the Fireflies made me sad in a way I didnt expect  silent, almost peaceful. Its a sad story, theres no doubt about it. Its probably the saddest story I ever saw in a film, and I already knew that Japanese animated series could be devastating, but the film is sad because it is real and it is simple. Theres no narrative, just life, and I knew how cruel it could get.
When I saw the way Setsuko was sulking in the beginning, it immediately reminded me of my little niece, whom Im really close with. Shes 4, and she makes the same facial expressions, the same grimaces. It hit a very sensitive chord. This is no Elsa and Anna playing with snowballs this is a real teenage boy and a real little sister. The scene where they take a bath together and he catches that air bubble with a towel was enough to convince me that it was going to be a very special experience.
Moreover, it says something important its not a film about childhood in the sense that it captures the innocence of children, but simply because it shows children who feel real  playful, ingenuous, smart, naive, and lazy, just like any other child in the world. In fact, the story reveals more about the cruelty of the adult world and its devastating effects on two defenseless kids. Its precisely because theyre so limited as children that I somewhat accepted their fate.
Because the story is not about playing, its not about the grave of the fireflies (which I supposed would play a significant part of the story) its just about a boy trying to feed his sister. Theres no trick behind it, theres no childhood symbolism. Even in great films like Life Is Beautiful, you could argue that the father is not just trying to protect his sons life, but his spirit too. In Grave of the Fireflies, to hell with the spirit its about the basic need for food, survival, and if it takes bombings to drive people into shelters so Seita can steal food and clothes, so the hell with patriotism.
People invoke the motherland and patriotism, but when confronted with hunger and fraternal love, they become empty words. However, the reverse can also be true in the name of patriotism, theres no room for sentimentality. I hated the aunts character, but I loved her as a character. She wasnt heartless she would have been the most lovable person in peacetime, but because of war, pity and empathy were feelings she couldnt afford. This is why she kept pressuring Seita to earn his ration of rice and couldnt stand Setsukos cries. That was harsh, but it was also realistic.
That reminded me of the scene in Schindlers List when a kid hides in a toilet hole, only to have other kids tell him to go to another hiding place. See, there cant be a great war film that isnt an anti-war film, because war is the antithesis of humanity. Thats the tragedy of Seita and Setsuko  theyre entrapped in a world where everything must be earned. Even a little girl, the purest and most fragile creature, must earn her right to live through her brothers efforts. And while stealing is an option, it relies on luck until it runs out.
Sure, they love each other, but this is no Disney material even love cant triumph over reality. Worse, the tragedy could have been avoided  Seita could have gone back to his aunts or gone to the bank earlier. But I accept these flaws because they come from a boy whos resourceful and admirable, but who has his limitations too. Sometimes, his aunt had a point, and it seemed like he took it easy for a little while until it backfired on him. When he left his aunts house, you could tell she was hurt, but she had too much pride to tell him to stay. And we, as the audience, also figured the boy would take care of his sister, but parenting cant be improvised, and more than that, Seita was a child too. He did the best he could physically, but mentally, he wasnt ready.
Thats his tragedy. After all, we can also wonder how he ended up dying after his sister. Apparently, he couldnt even find a job, or maybe he just gave up and let himself die. I hate plot contrivances, especially when they lead to a happy ending, but when they have tragic consequences, they stop being contrived they simply illustrate the fact that life can be cruel and capricious.

Aerei che volano minacciosi nel cielo (tra cui il famigerato Enola Gay), edifici ridotti a un ammasso di macerie, un gran numero di morti e feriti. Questa é la realtà del Giappone del secondo conflitto mondiale. Isao Takahata non mostra alcun combattimento, la lotta armata viene tenuta alla massima distanza, ma quello che conta é mostrare soprattutto il dolore, la perdita della speranza e di ogni tipo di sogno, simboleggiato da una confezione di caramelle destinate inevitabilmente a finire. Ci sará una ragione se Roger Ebert abbia voluto considerare questo film animato uno dei migliori film di guerra di tutti i tempi.
Attraverso la storia di Seita e Setsuko, fratello e sorella rimasti orfani e messi in ginocchio dalla povertà, divengono i rappresentanti di una generazione perduta, effimera quanto le lucciole contenute nel titolo del film, schiacciata da una società belligerante che ha anteposto lonore e le proprie energie nello sforzo bellico fino allultimo mettendo dunque da parte pietà e spirito di comunione (lo stesso Gen di Hiroshima proveniva da una famiglia con pensieri antimilitaristi). La guerra cé e lascia le sue tracce, anche sotto la forma di spettri
Dalla devastazione bellica si passa al paesaggio verde e idilliaco in cui si rifugiano i due fratelli, locus amoenus sospeso fuori dal tempo in cui si riscoprono per poco le gioie dellinfanzia, ma che si fa invece portatore di nuove sventure. Quello che mette in scena Takahata nel titolo forse più realista, malinconico e drammatico dello Studio Ghibli é ancora una volta il male che gli uomini provocano nei confronti dei propri simili a causa di unideologia o della propria stupidità e testardaggine.
Un requiem animato nei confronti di chi ha perso la vita troppo presto, ma per cui si spera che possa trovare finalmente la pace.



Planes flying menacingly in the sky (including the infamous Enola Gay), buildings reduced to a pile of rubble, a large number of dead and injured. This is the reality of Japan during the Second World War. Isao Takahata does not show any, the armed struggle is kept at the maximum distance, but what matters is above all to show the pain, the loss of hope and of every type of dream, symbolized by a pack of sweets destined inevitably to end. There must be a reason why Roger Ebert wanted to consider this animated film one of the best war films of all time.
Through the story of Seita and Setsuko, brother and sister orphaned and brought to their knees by poverty, they become the representatives of a lost generation, as ephemeral as the fireflies contained in the films title, crushed by a belligerent society that has put honor and their energies in the war effort to the end, thus putting aside pity and a spirit of communion (Gen of Hiroshima himself came from a family with anti-militarist thoughts). The war exists and leaves its traces, even under the resemblance of ghosts
From the devastation of war we move on to the green and idyllic landscape in which the two brothers take refuge, a locus amoenus ubicated outside time itself in which the joys of childhood are briefly rediscovered, but which instead brings new misfortunes. What Takahata stages in what can be considered Studio Ghiblis most realistic, melancholy and dramatic title is once again the evil that men cause towards their fellow men due to an ideology or their own stupidity and stubbornness.
An animated requiem for those who lost their lives too soon, but for whom it is hoped that they can finally find peace.

While it is easy to view this strictly as a heartbreaking look at the innocent casualties of conflict, the films emotional weight also lies in its quiet, deeply uncomfortable observations of human nature.
The structural brilliance becomes clear from the beginning and ending of the film, starting right from the opening sequence. Watching the station workers treat a dying boy like an inconvenient obstacle, only to callously discard a rusted candy tin they pocketed from, establishes a chilling emotional detachment. It seems minor initially, but once you understand the weight of that tin, the moment transforms into a staggering gut wrenching blow. As we get more into the film this cold indifference extends to the aunt her cruelty isnt just about harsh survival, i understand trading her sisters kimonos for rice, but the deceptive way she deprives the children of what is rightfully theirs to prioritize her own family under the guise of necessity.
Ultimately, the film presents death not with grand melodrama, but as a routine, ignored background fixture of existence. The horror isnt just the environment, but the profound apathy of the surrounding world, for example when Seita swiftly averting Setsukos eyes from a beachside corpse, the doctor indifferently prescribing food to a starving child without a offering, and the police officer offering just glass of water after hearing Seita story. When those station guards toss the tin jar away at the start, they are discarding the final, fragile remnant of a childs joy. It is a brutal reminder of how easily the world forgets the vulnerable, and how quickly humanity can abandon its empathy when looking backward at the ghosts of the past.

My 4000th Review - as nominated by kiwi
4000 reviews is too many for one person to write, isnt it?
Maybe I should set up one of those Ko.Fi things that everyones doing. Except I dont like coffee. Can you get tea on them? Or an iced finger? I dont know. That will be the next thing on Letterboxd though, people doing Patreons for their thoughts on Beverly Hills Cop 2 or their list for which film Jake Gyllenhaal was the most fuckable in.
But you know, sites change and all that, and someone like me who has been here since near the start, we will always moan about change and things not being the way they used to be. I dont think Ive changed much though. I think my writing is still pretty much the same. I watch more movies these days because of the way my personal and professional life is, so my reviews are, unless its a viewing of something notable, on the whole shorter than they used to be.
I also think the way I view films is pretty much the same as well, although I have been questioning that recently, as I did on my review of Mustang. If I drag myself, like Sean Connery after his encounter with Billy Dragos Tommy gun in The Untouchables, towards a 5000th review, Im hoping that I will have viewed more stuff that challenges the way I look at films, or at least have viewed more things outside my comfort zone.
I wasnt expecting to get to 4000, or even much past 3000 as I was planning on quitting last year. If that had happened I certainly would have watched considerably fewer films this year than I have. A lot of the time now, part of the enjoyment of watching a film comes through being able to write about it afterwards. The enjoyment of writing about something that stunk can even save having sat through something awful.
Its good to have that feeling back because I lost that for quite a while last year. I do hope it stays and I am thankful that Letterboxd exists, no matter how much I may moan about it, as a place for me to write about films. Im especially glad this feeling has stuck around for me to write about Grave of the Fireflies too, a film that deserves to be written about when in a place where you feel something for writing.
Its probably not the most celebratory film, thats for sure! Especially at this time of year. But I think its quite a fitting one for a year where Ive made more of an effort to watch more Japanese animation, and in a year where I set aside a month to try and watch some films that I felt might earn a 5 star rating.
Grave of the Fireflies was actually a part of that project but I had to set it aside because I ran out of time to watch any more films in that particular project. While it may just miss out on making the full grade with me, this is clearly one of the best films Ive seen this year and one of the best animated movies Ive ever seen. Its also another that sparks off the why make this animated? debate which I find so fascinating to delve in to.
Unsurprisingly, Im not an expert on comic books or graphic novels. Even so, my understanding is that not all of them are about superheroes. Some of them are actually straightforward dramatic stories. So why do they get questioned on this front less than animation? An odd one, really. On a practical level, I think animation helps to make telling a story like this a lot easier.
It would be quite a challenge asking a very young child to provide the dramatic and tragic heft that Isao Takahata can bring to the table with his style here. I also think the upsetting but ultimately uplifting final stages of Grave of the Fireflies are lifted somewhat by the naturally lowered realism of animation. It would be a Herculean task pulling off the upbeat turn in the final scene if youd just witnessed that cremation in live action. Not impossible, but it certainly seems easier this way.
On a different note though, it had me wondering if, in the West, we see nearly enough films or media about the level of destruction and hardship that Japan suffered during the second World War. In 2018, it still feels as though we dont. I still feel as though I havent seen enough of that. Perhaps this is where Takahatas film is strongest, showing the desperate state that people find themselves in and the unsurety of everyday life.
Takahata claimed that this film wasnt anti-war. He may not have set out to explicitly make Grave of the Fireflies as such, but its pretty clearly a film that focuses on the horrors of war rather than any of the minute amount of positives that can emerge from such a conflict. Its more a film about youth finding a willingness to live and support each other even during the hardest of times, sure, but these kids would not find themselves in such a situation without it.
Takahata finds beauty and loveliness in the very bleakest of settings and scenarios, making his film just as occasionally delightful as it is bleak. An awesome achievement, thoroughly worthy of its multitude of plaudits down the years.
Oh, and thanks to everyone who continues to read this junk. If youve been around since somewhere approaching review number one, my condolences, but thanks also.

Not long after Japans unconditional surrender that marked the end of World War II, Seita, like many other children who suffered the ravages of war, dies in complete abandonment and loneliness on the floor of a train station in the face of the indifference of those who pass through. Hotaru no Haka Seita recounts what happened before that agonizing moment, the desperate struggle of two siblings abandoned by fate seeking to survive. Seita takes care of little Setsuko in an attempt to protect her from the tragedy that surrounds them, he does everything in his power to preserve her innocence and allow her to enjoy her childhood, even if only for brief moments. Everything seems to be in vain and, after his last breath in that station, Seitas spirit meets that of his little sister nothing can separate them, nothing can hurt them. 
Hotaru no Haka is a heartbreaking story about the brutality of war and how it devastates the lives of civilians, all those innocent lives subjected to diplomacy, power games and the political ambitions of governments. It is a film of an overwhelming realism because it is the bitter portrait of a lost battle, of misery and adversity that end up prevailing over the strongest will. It is inevitable to feel invaded by an absolute hopelessness and a great impotence in spite of some moments of great beauty in which all the nonsense provoked by war is momentarily absent. Fireflies symbolize that brief instant and the ephemeral hope that shines incandescent before it is definitively extinguished.
An absolutely moving drama, one of those stories that is engraved in the unconscious because of its devastating beauty.

When many people said that this film made them cry a lot, I didnt think it would be truly devastating. It is an incredibly sad and emotional story that is much deeper than it may seem. The animated film also has an interesting structure, as it begins with Setsukos death, which may be confusing, but this is done to shift the focus from the fact of death to the reasons that led to such a tragic outcome, and everything that led up to that moment is even more painful than the beginning of the film.
Its difficult to simply describe my impressions of watching this, and I dont want to write anything about the technical aspects of the film, the animation, the music, or the actors, since everything here is wonderful, but the main thing is that there are so many more emotions here. Even tears gather in your eyes when you see what is happening, and yet you can see and feel that the animation is not intentionally tear-jerking. Instead, no matter how overwhelming the madness of hell might be, no matter how much even worse news arrives or trouble happens, Setsuko and Seita encourage each other, which is both beautiful and makes you want to cry even more. There are a bunch of other undertones, but I dont want to go through them. Its horrible that this movie is still relevant, but I still want to believe that all these movies, music, and art in general can somehow change things. Grave of the Fireflies is the war trauma evil twin of My Neighbor Totoro. Both films take the theme of the loss of a parent and interpret it through the eyes of children - to whom it is a nearly incomprehensible concept. 
Both Totoro and Fireflies are rife with imagery that is definitively art, but otherwise are made to be interpreted by viewers whom are also their subjects... by children. Simply. To look deeper into the films meaning is to lose their point entirely. 
And that... is why I personally just cannot bring myself to love either Totoro or Fireflies.
On the converse side, The Wind Rises, Studio Ghiblis other take on the topic of WWII, sits high on my all time favorites list for its moral complexity and questioning of arts place within national identity. 
In all likelihood, I came to Fireflies and Totoro too late... with too much disconnect to a childs necessity of fantasy, and so without the capacity to understand these two much-beloved Ghibli works.

Dont mind me. Just picking up the millions of little pieces of my heart off the ground. Grave of the Fireflies fills you with a very particular kind of distress. Its an anguish that gets you right where it hurts, honing in on all of the little buttons needed to cut deep and going ham on the keyboard to your compassion centre. These out of the way little empathy boxes you didnt even know you had in you. Its that same numbing sadness that makes waves through your body, your heart weeping and bones stinging heavy with the pounding boulder of grief. Yet, it never has to beg for it. 
Thematically, Grave bears a lot of similarities to its Ghibli neighbour, Totoro. And like Miyazaki, Takahata never feels the need to stoop low enough to over-sentimentality or fetishisation of the siblings suffering to get his points across. Still, rotting corpses linger in full eyeshot. And death rears its ugly head around every forlorn corner. Familial bonds and neighbourly niceties exist only as nostalgic fantasy of days gone by. Typically, the emotional cruxes would be used as anchors around which the emotive core of the film would be propelled. But Takahata doesnt care to dwell. Single sentences are afforded to fragile goodbyes, before we move on. Because we have to. Because in life, you rarely have a choice.
Theres a lot to be said here about the ugly treatment of one another during turbulent times and the price tag placed on poor decisions. But mostly, I cant help but question what Id do in Seitas shoes. As an (overly) protective brother of an equally delightful little sister, its a tough question to have to ask myself if my 14 year old self wouldve known any better.

September 21, 1945... that was the night I died.
Some time after my viewing, I came across a line - by Dutch filmmaker Michael Dudok de Wit - about Grave of the Fireflies that stayed with me By and large the audience preferred to cry rather than to reflect and engage in self-reflection. This isnt meant to belittle the tears the film often provokes - tears I fully understand - but to suggest theres something deeper beneath the surface, something that demands more than just an emotional release. So yes, that line resonated with me. It matched my own experience watching the film - the sense that its not just a tearjerker, but something far more complex, more demanding. Something that stays with you in silence, long after the tears have dried.
Yes, its an anti-war film - even if director Isao Takahata, interestingly enough, explicitly denied it - but its also a story of guilt, pride, and unbearable personal loss. This burden of survival haunts every frame. Its not just the world that failed them - its also Seitas choices, his silence, his shame. A tragedy shaped by war, made devastating by human frailty. No easy answers here - only reflection.
What makes Grave of the Fireflies so devastating isnt just whats shown, but how its shown - through the layered, haunted memories of two men marked by war. The film is the creative product of two Japanese survivor-narrators who were subjected to firebombing attacks in their youth the original author of the heavily autobiographical novel, Akiyuki Nosaka, tormented with guilt over surviving his sister, and the director, Takahata, carrying his own childhood memories of wartime Japan. Both filter this story through deeply personal trauma. The result is a psychic landscape, a space where reality blurs with emotional residue. Were not watching history unfold - were witnessing the kaleidoscopic interior of trapped psyches, looping endlessly through grief, shame, and memory. Theres no distance, no escape - just the unbearable weight of a catastrophe relived from within.
Its a multilayered piece of art - an act of working through trauma. While Nosakas original story served as a means to personally confront his grief and guilt over the death of his infant sister, Takahatas adaptation expands that personal wound into a broader reflection on mourning, memorialization, and responsibility. He opens a space where trauma is not just privately endured, but collectively processed - where working through trauma and grief becomes something intergenerational. The film seems to suggest that only by remaining present - by facing this horror through silence, discomfort, and time - can any kind of healing take root. That said, Takahata himself was deeply affected by war trauma, and that unresolved intensity shapes the emotional undercurrent of the film. What emerges is a fusion of two wounded voices - the film doesnt just recount events, it re-experiences them. And in that re-experiencing, reality itself becomes a dreamlike memory - unstable, unreliable, emotionally distorted. There is no objective truth to be found. In this light, Takahatas claim that this is not an anti-war film has to be re-evaluated - because the film doesnt just argue against war, it embodies its aftermath, its weight, its haunting imprint on memory
This is where the films uncompromising tone takes shape - how deeply you connect with it depends largely on how much youre willing to accept the flawed choices Seita makes in trying to care for Setsuko. Despite the subtle moral undercurrents, the film never passes judgment. It doesnt demand your sympathy, nor does it excuse his pride or blindness. It simply presents a human being - a little boy confronted with the monstrous atrocities of wartime reality - caught in a collapsing world, making impossible decisions with limited understanding.
The film doesnt moralize - it observes. And it asks us to do the same. To absorb what we can, and to let in as much as were willing to let in. Its a hard film to watch, full of death, hunger, and quiet despair - broken only by momentary flickers of light, each as fleeting and fragile as a fireflys glow.
The cinematography is often grim and dark, making the moments of relief and light-heartedness stand out all the more, while the editing is slow, meditative - at times it almost feels too intimate and close. Shots linger, giving space for silence to settle, but at times they start to crumble beneath you. Even at under 90 minutes, the film can feel emotionally long - its near-constant fog of misery wears you down, and a creeping numbness begins to set in. But maybe that isnt a failure of feeling - its part of the experience. You stop crying not because youve stopped feeling, but because youve reached a place beyond tears. I had to work through a strange feeling of derealization. It wasnt until I realized how Id been placed in Seitas position that I could reconnect with my empathy. Grave of the Fireflies doesnt just portray trauma - it transmits it. Like all unresolved trauma, it seeps into its environment. It overwhelms you, quietly, persistently, without permission.
But what happens here isnt actual trauma dumping - its sharing, reaching out without words, without knowing. And maybe thats what makes this film so emotionally demanding. It doesnt offer healing - it only offers the chance to witness. To uncover, slowly, the possibility of empathy. The possibility of forgiveness - but not without all the weight, without the powerlessness in the face of the dehumanizing toll war takes on the land and its people.

It takes hold of you and stays. It never did fully let go of me. I couldnt quite figure it all out for some time - so yes, it took a while to process this, and even longer to write it all down.
So no, this isnt a kitschy tearjerker. This weighs as heavy as it gets. And now, perhaps, with all that said, its time to feel the pain and shed some tears.

Just like the brief happiness Seita and Setsuko manage to create for themselves, every hopeful moment feels fragile, reminding you that even the brightest light cant always overcome the darkness surrounding it.
What hurt the most wasnt only the tragedy of war it was the indifference. Watching two innocent children be ignored, judged, or left without help when even the smallest act of kindness could have changed everything was heartbreaking. Told through silence and sorrow, Grave of the Fireflies unfolds like a mournful lullaby, a delicate elegy to love and loss, tracing the fragile journey of two souls, adrift in the aftermath of devastation, bound by blood and by the persistence of hope that flickers ever fainter with each passing day. It is a film that offers itself with raw honesty and a profound stillness, allowing the gravity of what remains unspoken to settle deeply into the viewers chest, like a weight that cannot be shed. Its power lies not in grand gestures but in the hushed moments the empty landscapes heavy with absence, the glances that speak volumes and the quiet ache of everything that can no longer be touched. The film understands, with heartbreaking clarity, that grief does not end with loss. It continues as an invisible burden, one we carry within us, shaping the contours of our days. That weight lingers in every frame, in every pause, in every desperate attempt to shield someone we love from a world that no longer offers shelter.
Grave of the Fireflies feels like a final letter never sent, composed in quiet sobs and phantom embraces, a whispered goodbye that arrives too late. A devastating masterpiece, it serves as both a tender tribute to the irrevocable beauty of innocence and a brutal reminder of its vulnerability in the face of unrelenting cruelty. Some goodbyes are not spoken aloud, theyre endured, remembered, and borne silently for the rest of our lives.

Grave of the Fireflies unfolds in a series of snapshots that expand the magnitude of its tragedy with every passing moment and show the beauty of life through the cracks of a raging war. Lives turn to ash, towns to memories, and two children attempt to survive the unsurvivable while facing the loss of their childhood. 
Seita and Setsuko are brother and sister. After losing both their parents to war, they make their way out of their town into a ravaged world that has lost its compassion. For a while, they stay with an aunt who reserves her care only for those helping their nation and treats the mementos of their past life as possessions to be exchanged for food. Then, they find a shelter somewhere in the woods, and though its bliss for some time, the war will make its presence known. Seita fights with hunger, desperation, a loss of self to provide for his little sister, as Setsuko shows him the happiness in simply being alive and appreciating the small pleasures. But their living  isolated and a perpetual struggle  is no life and their will to move forward lessens every day. 
Grave of the Fireflies leads with patience. The beauty in every moment comes to life, and so does the pain. With each day they survive, Seita and Setsuko are faced with more burdens to carry, and hope continues to slip away from their grasp. There is no future here, just the present moment and dreams that die too young. When the fighting comes to an end, there is no celebration, but regret for what has been lost because what has happened can never be erased and home can only be found in memories for so many. 
The emotion evoked by Grave of the Fireflies spills over its runtime, making its way into our hearts. Even in a world of complete fantasy as animation, the tragedies of real life cant be escaped and life is as painful as it is beautiful.

If youre one of the three people in the universe that hasnt seen this film, therell be spoilers here
The Nolan Brothers are poor writers, something they prove once again with a high concept, beautifully shot but shoddily written script that overreaches its grasp at just about every turn. Christopher Nolan is a far better director than he is a writer, he really should direct something once that wasnt written by him or his brother.
Interstellar is not a bad film. Its one third fantastic, one third serviceable and one third obnoxiously annoying. Ill start with the good bits.
Nolans aesthetic throughout the film is spot on. He creates a low-tech future that feels palpable and real. I loved the look of all the spacecraft and the fact that everything had a gritty and slap dash feel to it. No frills, no bling bling, it looked the way it should look. The bots took some getting used to, but in the end I liked their design quite a bit. But what is perhaps most impressive in Interstellar is its world creation and the way it paints the universe. There are some breathtaking shots in this film and the poetic license Nolan takes with how certain things could or should look works tremendously. It is safe to say that this is Nolans best looking film to date. It also feels well researched and that is something I respect. The look of the black hole, some of the tech, it never feels as if Nolan rushed through this when conceiving his film. There are also a couple of action sequences, not usually his strongest point, that are tense and exciting. They are far and few between though, which is actually a refreshing thing to find in a film of this scope. Most of what I describe above is abundantly present in the strongest, middle segment of the film. Its in the bookends and the central thread where my problems lie.
The cast is ok. They make the most of the hollow dialogue they are given and McConaughey and Hathaway try their hardest to find the necessary emotional resonance. Unfortunately they rarely succeed, but more on that later. Even though it was filled with a lot of static, I felt the establishing opening act was fine. There are a couple of odd moments (what was up with that drone?), but it mostly sets the scene pretty well. It is when the gears start to churn into motion and the real plot starts kicking in where looming melodrama rears its ugly head. We are given a character in brush strokes with his stereotypical  family and were asked to invest in them without hesitation from the get go. It just didnt work for me, resulting in me watching what should be a pivotal and emotional scene (Dad leaving) and seeing something that should pack a punch but just doesnt. Its all superficial veneer that smothers any potentially real drama in either too loud music or Michael Caine citing poetry. The idea of an emotion is not enough, you have to do more to get something real.
And thats where we get to the central problem of the film. Now, I can nitpick this film apart completely which is a pointless exercise for any film, but whenever science fiction films jump into the ocean of paradoxes my feathers get ruffled. Why mess with time? It is the weakest solution possible in a film with as grand a scale as Interstellar. There are so many why questions while analyzing this film, so many things left unexplained. It is the same thing they did in Inception, leaving out the blanks for the audience to fill in but not giving enough to do so adequately. Why does Cooper tell himself to stay? Why doesnt he just tell himself where to go? Why doesnt NASA just go to Cooper and ask him to fly for them?  Why does Cooper feel it is necessary to fall into the black hole? In the Tesseract, why is he in a hurry? Why? Why? Why? Lots of questions with one simple answer. Because the plot needs it and there are apparently no other ways to tie up everything neatly. Still, Im not going to fall over that. Looper was riddled with paradoxes but still an enjoyable film. And, like I wrote earlier, once they get into space it is a very good film. But then Anne Hathaway gives a speech. About love. And thats when a lot of alarm bells started ringing in my head. 
Interstellars central thesis is the most arrogant imaginable. Love, a human emotion, solves everything. There was a moment, after the reveal that Caine revealed his deception and Damons character ruined everything because of his ego that I though this would head in the direction that the arrogance of mankind will eventually be its downfall. Or that the central question about Plan B would be dealt with more in depth. Do you save your species when you repopulate using embryos? Alas. It relishes in that arrogance. It starts by trying to portray us as a species of explorers, never commenting on the fact that were probably the ones that messed up the planet to begin with, sketchily touching upon the fact that the food scarcity must have led to some grim times, only to end up saying we are survivors. There is a plethora of potential here to explore, but the Nolans skip over it to get to what they really want to say. Humans are defined by the connection to their families and the love they share. A sentiment, mind you, I agree with wholeheartedly. 
I just find it astonishingly ironic that a film that purports such a lofty emotional message is so hollow in the emotions it tries to evoke. It has a lot to do with the obsessive show and tell nature of the Nolans writing. Practically every line is expository. With all the tech stuff I didnt mind that much, even though it was a bit too much at points, but when dealing with emotions, showing should be enough. Constantly rubbing our faces in it with melodrama and stunted dialogue doesnt work. Love and gravity are the only forces that travel through time. Im sorry, but that is just a bridge too far and using it as a plot device to save the day in this setting just feels preposterous to me. And and unbelievably arrogant. 
The Nolans talent for creating ideas does not seem to match their talent for fleshing them out. In search for a human connection they find so important in their film they stepped over the connection to their audiences (or, you know, just me). This film tries far too hard to be profound where it should just have focused on being very good. Ambition is commendable, knowing your limits is essential.
