There are so many extraordinary choices here, small and large decisions that make this unusually, almost painfully ambitious movie greater than the sum of all its tiny particles. Nolan seems to be after some unholy alliance of Close Encounters and Days of Heaven, an agrarian family drama vaulted into the cosmos, with a heaping portion of Cosmos. The sequence in which Dr. Mann and Cooper wrestle crosscut with Murph and Toms showdown on the farm is some of Nolans finest work everthe sheer dread and emotional clarity of that moment is a true second act climax. Hes so great at those. Every single actor is game, and wisely cast. God bless Matthew McConaughey, ever fearless with an overwritten monologue. Theres more unimpeachable moments or images like it Endurance entering the vast spherical black light of Gargantua the race after the Indian drone through the cornstalks the tidal wave surf the dust storm any time TARS walks. This is massively budgeted architecturethe scope and precision is breathtaking, built from an expansive blueprint by a filmmaker desperate to prove he can hang with Spielberg (parental abandonment wonder and its relationship to duty), Kubrick (the pitiless aloneness of life spinning spaceships), and maybe even Tarkovsky (philosophy in the wheat and anger in the dust). Still just a miracle of a movie in which Nolan found a way to merge his blockbuster scaled science-fiction imagery with personal ideas about being a father on a dying planet and how his professionaltechnical passions are directly connected to losing to time with his children, finding a way to package them both as something that contains a bit of The Right Stuff, Solaris, Close Encounters (if we stuck with the wonder-obsessed dad after he left his kids behind), and 2001 obviously. 
All crashing into each other via Nolans often cold, literal-minded precision and momentum-driven construction that attempts to turn scientific theory about time and space and very basic existential and emotional ideas of generational mortality and hope into something not just physically tangible but physically achievable. The inherent thrill of innovation and exploration reflected in space travel sequences (a blend of his usual tactile craftsmanship and attempt at black hole photography so accurate it achieves an even more abstract beauty than it would otherwise) and Zimmers astonishingly bombastic and melancholy electronic organ score never too far removed from the desolate, unforgiving reality of ecological deterioration and the grim, cynical side of our individual survival instincts.
Ultimately makes this kind of feel like watching a weird, sad robot man who knows were kind of fucked try to algorithmically process a future where the collective value of humans as deeply frail and emotional beings can overcome those things through love anyway, which is maybe dramatically misguided occasionally (and hard for actors to have to sentimentalize about out loud) but so broadly conceptually moving I cant help but get swept up in the awe of it all. Once youre a parent, youre the ghost of your childrens future.
What I continue to find so emotionally compelling here about the core conflict in Coopers relationship with Murph is the way we see both sides of his departure, both Dont let me leave like this and Dont let me leave at all, and ultimately we see how both Coopers are sort of misperceiving the essence of his own fatherdaughter relationship. First he doesnt want to leave on a sour note and second he doesnt want to have left at all, but the point about parents being the ghosts of their childrens future is that paradoxically Cooper must leave in order for Murph to grow up on her own terms. If Cooper had never left, he never could have gotten stuck behind Murphs bookcase, he never could have become her ghost.
The fantasy of every parent is to see their children grow up, but even here where Cooper gets to live an element of that fantasy, where he gets to see Murph at the other end of her life, he still doesnt actually get to see the process of her growing up, because becoming her own person is something that necessarily happens away from him. Though it is undeniably painful and sad in the moment, trapped behind the bookcase of our present perspective, forced to leave or forced to watch yourself leave, its not actually a tragedy that parents become ghosts for their children. Every parent must leave their child at some point, to some extent, in order to give their children the freedom to grow. Parents must become ghosts in order for their children to become themselves.

Talk about a film whose perception has changed almost drastically since its release. This was one of the first films whose soundtrack was hated by nearly everyone, especially the sound mix, and I remember how many people mocked it. However, all of this is immensely compensated for by what is arguably the finest technical film in Nolans filmography to date. Starting with its stunning cinematography, in which you can appreciate the immense power of celluloid with its grainy texture, which gives it such a striking quality. Best of all, however, is the production design, which is on the same level of ambition as Kubricks 2001 A Space Odyssey, whether Manns Desolate Planet or the minimalist but complex look of the Tesseract. All in all, while I would have preferred a less clichéd script, this is a film that should be seen on the biggest screen that you can find and with the best sound system you can afford to get the best immersive experience it deserves.

A Great American Novel of a movie, with a Great American Protagonist. Cooper is by turns stubborn and reckless, sentimental and curious, powered by a nuclear core of dogged belief in the human spirit, with himself (and his daughter) as its de facto avatars. Cooper is a scientist, but hes a red-blooded American, too, and hes often so beside himself that he cant resist waxing a little poetic Interstellar operates in this spirit. Theres the part of it that wants to be hard sci-fi, but its also movie about the idea of destiny, and what the idea of destiny can guide us toward. 
Cooper is someone born 40 years too early, or 40 years too late, in the middle of his life, mostly feeling that hes not going to really have the chance to do the thing he thought he was supposed to do. Hes frustrated, but hes certainly still got the spark of ambition and curiosityyou can see how much hes reinvested that energy into raising his clever daughter, Murph. (This is a movie about a having a Favorite Child). The catching the drone scene is where you first see all that power that Cooper is storing under the hooda man willing to crush ten thousand corn stalks for a chance to see a piece of historic tech in action. Hes a gifted, unusual person whos had to channel his gifts into a field he doesnt care for, but at least he has a protégé, and therefore, perhaps, a legacy. 
The idea that it turns out that its not too late for such a personthat, even after having given up, there may still be time for a cometh the hour, cometh the man momentis an irresistible fantasy come true. But it comes, of course, at a terrible price, one that any second-time viewer of the movie knows. 
The question becomes, Was it the right choice? Was it worth it? And I think Interstellar answers this question in a really interesting, ambiguous, vibrating way. Its a film about the moments where life really Asks Something of You, in a way that you really do have to answer, and about the consequences of answering. It depicts a group of people (Cooper, Brand, and the other astronauts) making the best high-stakes choices they know how to make, with the information that they haveand still making the wrong choice, over and over, and having to live with what comes of it. And it also depicts the idea that the right action in the future has the power to cast back over the past, reverberate through it, and, functionally, change it. That redemption is possible, and that if someone can change how the story ends, they can change what the story meant. 
The Millers planet sequence is a remarkably vivid parable about what it feels like to try to do the right thing, and to realize in the moment that you have made a costly mistake, and not even really through fault of your own. Nolan creates the perfect sensory environment for the shitty emotional experience Brand goes througha 200-yard wade through knee-high water in 130 gravity, whipping wind, an enormous wave coming at you in slow motion, an inability to follow through on the thing you insisted on, your coworker yelling at you the entire time, and then the cresting realization of everything youve lost, regret clanging through every cell of your body. Nolans pacing through this whole sequence is magisterial firm establishment of up-front stakes nail-biting initial blunder horrifying time-out in the middle for everyone to have it out seat-gripping escape processing the grief and regret back on the ship. I dont know how much screen time it all takes up, maybe 20 minutes, but its perhaps the storytelling coup of the Nolan brothers career it feels somehow like an ancient fable. Some of life is, inevitably, like this. Throbbing regret for a situation in which it felt like you were doing what you had to do, every step of the way. 
The fact that we compound this situation with the choice to go to Manns planet, and are there confronted with the consequences of not just human error but human cowardice, feels almost punishing the revelation about Professor Brands secret knowledge about Plan A is salt in the wound. Interstellar is not at all uncynical about people. For a movie where the main character says the stirring, trailer-ready tagline out loud (Mankind was born on earth it was never meant to die here), it spends so much of its runtime dwelling on mistakes, regret, miscalculations, deception, and human frailty. Structurally, Interstellar is very nearly tragedy. 
But running in parallel, of course, is Murphs story on earth her will, like her fathers, to press onward her willingness to set something on fire in order to save it her openness to receiving wisdom from beyond, and acting on it in the present. Nolan uses Hans Zimmers score, and an elegant, psychologically-driven cross-cutting pattern, to weave Murphs and Coopers stories together. I often find Zimmers scores unnecessarily bombastic, but throughout, the organ is the perfect tonal match we get the spaciousness and spookiness of space alternating with the thunderous, muscular, sublime sounds of the cathedral. The suspended chords and organ texture keep us vibrating back and forth between a feeling of melancholy and hope, and never let us forget that the stakes are spiritual. 
Im not going to sit here and tell you that the whole thing entirely hangs together, logically the movie is pretty much asking you, within the text, not to do that. But this is nonetheless a time travel movie that makes deep emotional sense. You can make a choice in the present that suddenly changes the next twenty years, but you can also make a choice in the present that changes the tenor of the last twenty years. I imagine most parents have thought about their own childrens deaths, hoping that theyll be surrounded by loved ones Interstellar gives Cooper this ultimate grace. The last act of the movie offers its characters a kind of circular, psychedelic, mystical redemption. Things can go wrong, very wrong, for years, but somehow be made right in the fullness of time. 
As I approach middle age, Ive developed a taste for stories about someone crossing a thresholdstories of someone walking through a door that locks behind them. Interstellar is a very adult epic, in that sense. Its about the things you cant take back. Its about becoming prepared for the moment, and then realizing that nothing could have prepared you, not really. Theres no way you could have known, and you had to choose anyway. Its about the way that a sense of destiny might kill youbut that it might save you, too. 
Theres a nice moment in the script that happens twice. Before he leaves, Coopers father-in-law Donald questions his motives
Cooper Im not gonna lie to you, heading out there is what I feel born to do and it excites me. That doesnt make it wrong.
Donald It might.
Later, Cooper repeats this dialogue when Cooper questions her motives for wanting to go to Wolf Edmunds planet
Brand Yesthe tiniest possibility of seeing Wolf again excites me. But that doesnt mean Im wrong.
Cooper Honestly, Brand... it might.
The key word here is might. It depends. The characters change their minds over whether theyve made the right or wrong choices here based on information they can only get later. But what Interstellar seems to propose is that passion may be as good a data point as any for deciding what to do. Theres so much you wont know, either way. You may be in for pain, either way. But, in an age of listlessness and learned helplessness, theres something very rousing about watching characters launch themselves at something want something love something rage against the dying of the light. A beautiful and morally serious film I wish we had many more things like it.

I wanted to experience this for the first time in the most spectacular way possible, and the closest place near me to do that was The Franklin Institute in Philly, on its giant domed IMAX screen. Unfortunately, my friend and I didnt think to get there early to acquire the best seats (which are at the very top, or at least towards it) and we were stuck near the bottom, where you have to crane your neck to see the screen correctly. Being as I have a pretty bad backneck injury due to a car accident a few years ago, this was not a very ideal situation to be in for nearly three hours.
But what Im getting at is, despite already being in a tremendous amount of pain at around the 10-minute mark, I still somehow managed to absolutely love Christopher Nolans Interstellar. Usually, an uncomfortable experience like this would almost completely ruin my first time viewing something, due to not being able to become entirely immersed in the film itself. But that was (very) fortunately not the case here. I was in complete and utter awe from the moment it started, and remained just as entranced throughout the rest of its running time. 
Despite so many different things racing through my head about this, Im not sure what to say at this point. Visually, everything about it is astonishing, and the incredible shots of space are literally breathtaking.  There wasnt a single moment where I thought, That wasnt very convincing... Instead I kept thinking Did Nolan actually film this shit in space? That crazy bastard. Because, hey, if there was a modern filmmaker to actually travel through space and wormholes to work on his latest film, it would most likely be Chris Nolan. I also found this to be Nolans most emotionally-engaging film to date. There was a true heart to the story, and it definitely shown throughout. One of my favorite scenes is quite possibly the simplest (at least, in a film involving space travel), where Cooper (Matthew McConaughey, still on a magnificent roll and not showing signs of stopping) sits down to watch messages from loved ones (dont want to ruin anything by saying more). The moment wrecked me and McConaughey was astounding.
Im still gathering my thoughts despite seeing it nearly 24 hours before writing this, and my mind is still recuperating from the fucking Nolan has dished it once again. Ill be going to the theater (a regular one) to experience this extraordinary film again, hopefully later this week or early next week, and then again once my buddy gets home from college for Thanksgiving break. Maybe by either of those times Ill have more coherent thoughts to include on here. 
But despite what some reviews are saying otherwise, I personally believe that Nolan has done it again. I may just be a sucker for his work in general, or maybe Im simply a Nolan fan-boy as Ive heard people label others who truly admirecherish his work. But to me, he has created another phenomenal film that further pushes me to regard him as one of the very best filmmakers currently around with fascinating vision, scope and originality that cinema needs these days. And, as always, I cant wait to see what hes up to next.

At the moment when humanity realizes that the planet Earth is beyond saving, will it have the ingenuity, resources, and willpower to find another home? Knowing that through its own actions humanity poisoned its only known source of food, water, and shelter, will that humanity have what is needed to start afresh? Can humanity stand upright and not go quietly into the good night?
It is impossible to absorb Christopher Nolans majestic Interstellar without dealing with the above questions. They power Nolans story, but they remain with the films audience log after the credits roll. Though, Interstellar, itself, has an answer for each question, the science fiction epics most important strength may be that it forces its audience to examine the questions and come up with its own response. That is the effect of great science fiction and great cinema. Interstellar manages to be both.
Taking place on a planet that is slowly succumbing to a blight that wrecks crops, strangles life, and decimates hope, Interstellar follows humankinds last ditch effort to save itself. Taking to the stars to chart a course through a wormhole where hospitable planets may be found, a team of astronauts leaves its old life behind to find a new life for humankind. Of course, the team finds something else entirely.
Nolans film works not only because it builds itself around important questions, but it works because of its sense of hope and humanity. It is a film about the direst of situations, but its narrative and thematic motor is fueled by the ideas that are deeply connected to hearts, minds, and souls. The need for exploration, the importance of science and discovery, the unceasing draw of love and family, and the imperative of looking beyond the horizon drive the story. These ideas make the film accessible and authentic when it could have been cold and artificial.
Outside of its narrative, Interstellar is just as excellent. Its cinematic canvas is evocatively and beautifully rendered. Its performances are textured. Its designs are fantastic yet grounded. It is meditative and thrilling it is thoughtful and visceral. 
Nolans paints his land and spacescapes as airy, naturalistic worlds that are both dangerous and inviting. Warm and cool tones combine to illustrate a human home that is nostalgic yet strange, while steely blues and ash whites meld to form alien worlds that hold promises and threats. Slipping seamlessly from vast IMAX compositions to intimate, character-centric shots, Nolan frames a film that showcases the beauty of the cosmos and the lined anguish of the human face.
With a running time of nearly thee hours, Lee Smith weaves scenes that, like the narrative, bridge space and time. His editing keeps the film sharp but allows passages to ebb and flow with both a grace and immediacy. Cutting between spacebound and earthbound sequences, the editing ties the sequences together thematically and creates a palpable energy.
The films design creates a lived-in world full of recognizable artifacts and fantastic elements. It is a world where fingerprints smudge chrome and subtly tattered fabrics adorn protagonists. Props and vehicles are both tributes to previous science fiction masterworks and fresh renderings of technological possibilities.
Nolan, as is his way, puts together a pitch-perfect cast. Here, Matthew McConaughey continues his recent run of excellence with a character that is embodies everything for which the film stands. Torn between protecting his family and saving humanity, McConaugheys Cooper is full of fear and hope. He is both the quintessential genre hero and a man willing to let his emotions be pillars on which he stands. It is a powerful performance. Jessica Chastain, Anne Hathaway, and others offer nuanced characters. They are people of logic and science, but they are tied to their humanity-generating emotions.
Christopher Nolans Interstellar is an ambitious, beautifully rendered science fiction film that finds as much hope in love as it does in science. It is a film whose ideas stick to the minds of it audience long after the piece ends it is a film whose emotions are biting and alive. Remarkable on a technical, aesthetic, and narrative level, Interstellar is an outstanding piece of work whose driving questions linger, perhaps spurring its audience to some kind of important action.

Watching Interstellar in IMAX was an unforgettable experience. The visuals were so immersive, that I felt as if I were floating in space, overwhelmed by awe, wonder, and emotion. The film took me on a journey through the cosmos and deep into human emotion, making me smile, cry, and feel everything in between.
Hans Zimmers score was exceptional, adding a unique, otherworldly depth to the film. His music perfectly captured the films vastness and emotional core, elevating every moment.
Interstellar is a film that truly shines on the big screen. Its an experience that stays with you, and I believe it deserves to be seen in IMAX to fully appreciate its greatness.

I really shouldnt even attempt to review this beast until I see it again... maybe even until I see it two more times, but oh well, Im just gonna try to pour as much out as I can and hope that it doesnt sound idiotic. Its probably going to turn out much like my Nymphomaniac review one giant, incoherent mess of a paragraph... but I suppose thats better than nothing or a sly one-liner (although sly one-liners are a lot of fun, and it wouldnt be too hard to come up with a bunch relevant to this film, haha). Overall, I loved it. I really did. There are certainly some things that I didnt love about it, and Ill get those out of the way first, but Im not going to spend too much time on them because 1) you guys know me Im an overwhelmingly positive reviewer I like to focus on the things that I adore about films rather than the problems that I have with them, and 2) going along with that, Im the type of viewer who is able to look past minor errors in films and recognize that I loved the experience as a whole, even if certain parts mightve been better than others. So here it goes - Ill just focus on two main points, in particular. First, the pacing in the first act of the film was too quick for me, but in Nolans defense, he had to have pretty rapid pacing in this film in order to get everything out of the way in 180 minutes and I also think that he knows his audience, and he knew that his audience would want to get out into space as fast as possible, haha. Which they cant be blamed for. Second, I wouldnt say that it was over explained, and I wouldnt say that it was under explained either I would just say that there was a little too MUCH exposition. Sometimes they would be speaking about abstract notions beyond my grasp, and it didnt matter how much they talked and talked and talked about them, because I was never going to understand quantum theory and concepts related to relativity from a five minute speech from Anne Hathaway anyway so those parts dragged a little bit for me. They reminded me of an AP physics course more than a cinematic experience. But those aspects aside - and a couple other minor things that honestly arent even worth mentioning because Im probably just nitpicking andor dont deal with (over?)sentimentality in blockbusters quite as well as most viewers do - this was a hell of a film. Nolans directions here is stellar he really went out of his way to craft a science fiction film that almost transcends science fiction into pure science with how much research he put into the ideas behind it. There are a lot of unbelievable things about it (and I mean that literally), especially when you near its end, but all in all, I respect how much thought went into the skeleton of this film, the screenplay, the design, the vision, the intricacy. So even if I didnt particularly enjoy some of the exposition, I always respected it. Next, the acting is amazing. Ive said it many times and Ill say it again I dont know what the fuck happened to Matthew McConaughey. I cant believe how far hes come. He now delivers incredible performance after incredible performance Killer Joe, Mud, Dallas Buyers Club, True Detective, Interstellar. Hes solidified himself as one of the finest actors of his generation, and ten years ago if one would have attempted to predict that, nobody would have believed them. But above all else, this film is visually and aurally masterful. The cinematography and editing always remains very Nolan (very reminiscent of Inception, The Prestige, etc. in its perfect flow between past and present or Earth and space), but its almost like theres a touch of MalickLubezki in here as well. Its definitely Nolans most visually stunning film yet (by far) there are certain shotssequences that will make your jaw drop if youre a fan of the Stargate sequence in 2001 A Space Odyssey, theres plenty of that here as well. And Hans Zimmer has crafted his finest score since The Thin Red Line - I was blown away by the music. Its SO beautiful. Theres nods to plenty of films in Interstellar, but for me, one of the most recognizable nods of all was to Suspiria (of all films). This nod doesnt surface till the second half of the film, but I swear, there were certain composition sequences in the second and third acts that reminded me so heavily of a Goblins score for Suspiria. Awesome stuff. Speaking of the third act, there are a number of complaints about it in reviews all across the web but I didnt have any issues with it in fact, it really made the film for me. Sure, some of the ideas behind it and some of the character realizationsepiphanies are stretches, but thats forgivable. It was (toward the end of) the second act of the film that almost brought the film down a half star for me the sequence of the film with you-know-who (Dr. Mann) was probably my least favorite part. I didnt downright dislike it, but the film started to head in a different direction than I was hoping for, so Im glad that section of the film was short-lived because then it went in EXACTLY the direction that I was hoping for, transforming into the tripped out, psychologically affected science fiction film that I was waiting for it to be throughout its entire runtime. I love the idea of playing with the intergalactic unknown through the world of cinema, whether it be black holes, wormholes, time dilation or five-dimensional reality. It takes balls and it is, above all else, just so damn COOL, especially when youre presenting to your audience visually by warping the fabric of time and space as we know it. It makes for a truly unforgettable experience its those kinds of things, those kinds of memorable images and ideas that allow me to look past any minor problems that I might have had with the film and see it as a success, an enormous achievement. So bravo, Mr. Nolan, and everyone else involved. I enjoyed this film as much as I ever could have hoped to enjoy it, and Im already dying to see it again. Oh yeah, and I really, reeeaaally want a TARS. Like really badly.

Musings on Poetry and Interstellar
A friend of mine - a former student and a budding poet, headed for an MFA in poetry program this fall  recently told me that the more he works his craft, the more he finds he wants to compress, the more he wants to replace an initial phrase with a single word or to replace a set of phrases with just one brief phrase. The idea is to create a work full of just a few potent words - words that contain multitudes, so to speak - instead of a work full of many less resonant ones.
What he wants to offer the reader, I think, is something like a seed, a latent, fertile thing that, when planted in the readers mind, germinates and expands. And his poetry, as I read each new poem he sends me, is increasing in these kinds of compression-fueled expansions. His work is, more and more, made up of compact sets of lines that feed a readers delight they puzzle at first in their bold brevity  but then, as I sit with a particular poem, letting my tongue savor the sounds and my mind mull the possibilities, a meaning will open as with a sudden blooming, and then theres another, and another meaning, until the poem fills all my thoughts and feelings  and I find I have been a participant in that deeply personal discovery that readers of poetry often feel, a discovery dependent upon that unique, intimate interaction between poem and reader.
Poets like my friend understand that poetry is not really poetry if it has no reader to even exist, it, in some sense, needs a reader, a reader willing to grasp, plant, and water those word-seeds. The poet depends on readers for the poems to live. And the reader, likewise, understands that there is very little joy in reading if the poet does not trust the reader enough to allow the reader to do the nurturing, to offer care and feeding to those seeds. 
A poem, then, might be considered not as a thing on a page but as an interaction, a relationship.  And the greater the trust and investment on both sides, the greater the love, the greater the joy.  As Jeanette Winterson writes in her essay, Imagination and Reality, Love is reciprocity, and so is art. 
But if the use of Dylan Thomass Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night, in Interstellar is any indication, I do not think Nolan understands that about poetry that latent fertility of a poets words, that need for trust between poet and reader.
And perhaps he doesnt even understand how much the visual, sensory building blocks that make up the cinematic experience can be like those potent word-seeds we find in poetry, visual and sensory things that truly bloom only when allowed to be planted in the mind and heart of the viewer.
For Nolan does not trust that Thomass words contain a potency that needs no explaining, no repetition.
Nor does he trust that his own visuals will tell the story he wants to tell.
Instead, he lectures through the mouths of his characters, telling us what to think. He harangues with a deafening, ever-present score, telling us what to feel. 
Virginia Woolf in her brilliant and provocative essay, How Should One Read a Book, writes, The impact of poetry is so hard and direct that for the moment there is no other sensation except that of the poem itself. What profound depths we visit then  how sudden and complete is our immersion! . . . Our being for the moment is centred and constricted, as in any violent shock of personal emotion. Afterwards, . . . the sensation begins to spread in wider rings through our minds remoter senses are reached these begin to sound and to comment and we are aware of echoes and reflections.
But Nolan will not let that hard, direct sensation of Dylans brilliant words or of his own visuals reach the profound depths they have the capacity to do. Instead of being centred and constricted, instead of having the joy of sensation spreading in wider rings through our minds, we have only a strident bombast, and in leaving the theater, we leave with very little that is ours. No relationship has been established, no seeds have been planted in the mind and heart and allowed to grow and delight us with their secret and expansive growth. 
And its not that every piece of writing needs to be a poem to offer satisfaction. And not every film needs to offer the subtle delight of densely resonant visuals that tell their own story, sans explicit explanation. The non-fiction essay and the pulp novel offer their own delights as does a simple genre film - a rom-com or an action flick. 
But the disappointment here is that Nolan seems to believe that any move towards complexity, away from a simple genre film, necessitates lengthy, direct explanation. We do need those lengthy explanations sometimes say, in scientific essays and political editorials. But a fiction film is neither an essay nor an editorial - and should not complexity be broached differently, so as to make full use of the unique medium of film, so as to invite the viewer into joys of the cinematic relationship? 
I try to imagine what 2001 A Space Odyssey would have been had Kubrick put explanations of the monolith into the characters mouths. Would not the thing lose its potency? As it is, that monolith sits like a provocative weight in the mind, growing in density and meaning throughout the film and in the aftermath of the film, as I sit at home or in my car and ponder.  It grows in meaning and significance exactly because its given wholly to the viewer, and the viewer must interact with it, decide what it is, what it means. And so the monolith becomes personal. Its no longer exterior to me, but it sends ever wider rings of resonance through my mind - and it has, indeed, taken on such resonance in so many minds since 1968, that it appears again and again in the film world and elsewhere - and is now a part of our cultural cache, a thing, as Yeats might put it, of the Spiritus Mundi , containing multitudes, containing both Kubrick and his ideas and ourselves. Nolan ought to know all that, for  his use of the monolith in figures of TARS and CASE gives him no excuse not to know it. The monolith needed no explanation to be powerful  in fact, it is powerful still because it lacks direct explanation.
Total ambiguity in the realm of art is, of course, frustrating  a slosh of vague symbols with no clues as to their meaning(s) and contributing to no discernible pattern can make a reader or a viewer feel betrayed. 
There is the other problem, too, that the perhaps the artist is not actually offering a complex or satisfying set of meanings and ideas, and mulling over a work from from such an artist leaves us essentially empty handed. 
My friends poems work because they do not remain, ultimately, ambiguous, and the ideas and meanings they contain, once discerned, satisfy the intellect and heart. Its worth it to invest myself in the poetry he sends me because I know, as a reader, I will be rewarded for my trust, for my belief that the poem is worth investing myself and my time in. 
Nolans film avoids ambiguity (perhaps) as it layers exposition upon exposition, assuming, apparently, that the complexity of the film is too much for the viewer, but in the end, ironically, the films central idea seems trite and unsatisfying, very little more than a shallow sentiment about love transcending time and space.
Nolan has the skill, I think, to offer something visually, viscerally arresting and resonant.  But as of yet, particularly in recent years, I am less and less rewarded as a viewer  in large part because, even if the ideas are shallow, Nolan will not give the trust to the viewer that the viewer has given to the films. There is no deeply significant interaction between filmmaker and viewer.
Winterson writes of the interaction between artist and viewer, The exchange that art offers is an exchange in kind energy for energy, intensity for intensity, vision for vision. This is seductive and threatening. And then she asks, Can we make the return? Do we want to? Our increasingly passive diversions do no equip us, mentally, emotionally, for the demands that art makes. Winterson, here, puts the pressure on us, as art-consumers, to offer ourselves to the art, to be consumed as much as we are consumed  if we want to be fully rewarded by the art. 
Does Nolans work and his level of investment in me as a viewer merit my own return? I am increasingly uncertain that the answer is, yes.

With 21st century masterpieces like Memento, Batman Begins, The Prestige, The Dark Knight  Inception already to his name, Christopher Nolan has risen exponentially through the ranks of American film industry as one of the finest directors working today and in a career that spans just over 15 years has already cemented an impressive legacy with an incredibly devoted fan following that continues to grow with every subsequent feature.
Set in a near future, Interstellar presents a world thats unable to sustain humanity. With humans having reverted to an agrarian society due to shortage of food, their last hope for survival is a recently discovered wormhole that allows the possibility of intergalactic space travel. Piloting the spacecraft to embark on an interstellar voyage in search for a potentially habitable planet is Cooper whose relationship with his daughter is the core element the story continues to revisit  explore throughout its runtime.
Brilliantly directed by Nolan who today is one of the only few filmmakers who gets to make his films his way, with complete artistic control over his projects yet with rare advantage of big-budget support from major Hollywood studios, his latest is an extremely ambitious  audacious effort that exhibits both the best  worst of his talents, for the sense of warmth he manages to invoke through those awe-inspiring moments of beauty  wonder often get nullified by the clunky  expository dialogues which unfortunately inhabit the whole picture.
The screenplay is inspired from the works of theoretical physicist Kip Thorne and was penned down by Jonathan Nolan until Chris took over the directorial duties  merged his own ideas into the script. Now when it comes to outlining a plot structure, Nolan is a master strategist yet the one aspect he tends to go overboard with is exposition as he relies too much on dialogues to spoon-feed every scene to his viewers which in a way does make his stories more accessible to mainstream audience but also diminish their overall impact.
On the technical front, Interstellar is a marvel from start to finish. The bleak future of human race on the verge of extinction is depicted in a grounded manner while events unfolding in space manage to stay within the established realms of theoretical physics for the most part. Production design work is marvellous and set pieces are meticulously detailed. Visual effects make minimum use of CGI and enhances the visual presentation by a great deal. Editing keeps the interest alive despite the 169 mins runtime and Sound Design is expertly executed as well.
Cinematography marks Nolans first collaboration with Hoyte van Hoytema who effortlessly steps into Wally Pfisters shoes  elegantly photographs the film in all its magnificence yet in a picture full of so many breathtaking visuals, its heartbreaking that the camera never lingers on those moments of dazzling beauty. Nevertheless, the divine, mesmerising score marks a welcome change from Hans Zimmer as the soundtrack is lot more intimate, personal  emotional this time around and beautifully complements the narrative.
Coming to the performances, Interstellar features a star-studded ensemble in Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, Jessica Chastain, Bill Irwin, Casey Affleck  Michael Caine while also including cameos from Matt Damon, Ellen Burstyn  Topher Grace. McConaughey makes fab use of his screen presence here but his performance is a mixed bag. Hathaway is quite bland in her role, Chastain  Mackenzie Foy are the only ones who leave a lasting impression while the artificially intelligent robot TARS (voiced by Bill Irwin) exhibits more character depth than its human counterparts.
On an overall scale, Interstellar is Christopher Nolans ode to human spaceflight and is a stellar work of science-fiction filmmaking thats worthy of praise, admiration  appreciation for its ambition alone yet what stops this space opera from realising its full potential is the lack of depth evident in its characters compared to the profundity present in its science. Not everyone is going to appreciate what Nolan attempts to do here but after the mishap that was his last film, Interstellar surfaces as a respite coz this gifted filmmaker is still capable of leaving us in a state of pure bliss.

One of the funny things about Nolans movies is how little there really is to be said about them. Everything is already right there in the text. Theres no mystery to the intent or effect, nothing to interpret, nothing that resists articulation. This is despite his films being about things like dreams, memory, magic, and entering a black hole.
He reaches for a spiritual kind of awe here but the best sequence, maybe the best thing hes ever done, is tactile and physical in the extreme a shuttle trying to dock with a spacecraft thats falling into a planet and spinning really fast. Theres no meaning to it beyond what it actually is, but you feel every ounce of desperation and g-force. Its possible that his pathological literalism is also what makes him a master of gravity, mass, and solid objects. In an era of weightless cinema there are worse things to be.

So I keep talking about how this film continues to grow on me, and how much I have grown to respect it, but I havent been able to rewatch it in quite some time. It is absolutely one of the movies that you hope Tenet can be (Or could have been for some). I saw it upon release and thoroughly enjoyed it, but I wasnt fully on board the hype train. It took a rewatch or two to get there, but even then, I still had my questions regarding the ending. Even after this viewing, Im not entirely sure if the bookcase scene works, but I respect the hell out of it. Nolan shoots for the stars (literally) here, and while it isnt as perfect as he may believe it is, there is so much to admire. I often see complaints about the structure, and how the storylines in the third act do not necessarily intertwine like your average film.
The entire concept of an A, B, and C storyline makes some look at what Interstellar does and scoff. I understand to a degree, but I dont mind Nolan trying to take that leap and think outside of that box. Filmmakers are constantly trying to change that game, and while this film hasnt necessarily made that impact on other projects, it did enough to justify why its story played out in that way. Then we dive into the why behind the concept of love being the fifth dimension. It does feel ridiculous on its surface, and I struggled with it, but rewatching this film signifies its true intentions. I used to see that moment as something meant to be literal, and obviously it cant be entirely literal, but I couldnt quite put my finger on what it meant.
Looking at Brand, Murph, and Cooper, and seeing their motivations fully play out, I see that the line was fully meant to play as love and gravity are the way to communicate across dimensions. This is even explicitly said in the film at one point, but the problem I continued to have was balancing who the bulk beings were, trying to figure out how the tesseract played in, and then grasping the fact that love is not the fifth dimension. This is Coopers way of justifying the events in his head, and the idea of time solely being that dimension (and using love and gravity to communicate through it) is much more satisfying. This is especially the case when you look at those three characters and see how each journey utilizes that idea so heavily.
Again, it isnt perfect, but I respect the film so much that it is hard to not absolutely love it. It is also just a long journey that flies by, and it is one of the most technically impressive films of all-time. Zimmers score is perfection. I will also say that it makes as much sense as 2001, and that is easily one of my favorites of all-time, yet I can forgive certain ambitious moments that dont quite make sense at first. I like the guts behind making a film like this, and everything about Coopers journey is satisfying. I just had to wait for the ending to click, and while I could still question certain elements, I am much more on board with it now. Also, on a purely scientific note, Im not sure if it entirely works, but the film establishes rules and never breaks them in my opinion. All I am worried about is what the film establishes as real, so following its own rules set up is key, and I believe it does that well.

Em outro mundo
Com o imperfeito mas sempre assombroso e por vezes magnífico Interestelar, Christopher Nolan, da trilogia Cavaleiro das Trevas, se mantém firme na liderança do time de diretores para os quais o cinema tem de sempre tentar chegar mais longe
     Não é fantasia já aconteceu antes. Nos anos 1930, no coração rural dos Estados Unidos, depois de algumas décadas de cultivo intenso de grãos no que antes haviam sido vastas pradarias, a destruição da vegetação original cobrou seu preço sem as raízes tenazes das gramíneas para segurá-la, a camada superior do solo se desprendeu e virou pó, literalmente. Gigantescas tempestades de poeira levantavam-se e varriam áreas de milhares de quilômetros, deixando atrás de si fome, miséria e desânimo. E se toda a Terra estivesse assim comprometida?, imagina Interestelar (Interstellar, Estados UnidosInglaterra, 2014). Então em pouco tempo a presença humana no planeta se tornaria inviável. Como espécie, estaríamos condenados à extinção sumária. A não ser que nos radicássemos em outro planeta de outro sistema solar ou mesmo de outra galáxia. Que encontrássemos, enfim, um meio de atravessar distâncias incalculáveis até um novo abrigo. Um meio como, por exemplo, um tipo de buraco negro chamado buraco-minhoca, ou Ponte de Einstein-Rosen  um furo no universo que ligaria dois pontos linearmente distantes entre si, permitindo viajar em velocidade superior à da luz. E não, isso também não é fantasia é uma hipótese científica que funciona muito bem no papel e é postulada, entre outros, por Kip Thorne, uma das maiores autoridades na área da física gravitacional e colaborador de Interestelar.
     É o alter ego de Thorne, vivido por Michael Caine, quem busca se aproveitar de um buraco negro surgido nas proximidades de Saturno para enviar a humanidade à sua salvação. Sua própria filha, Amelia (Anne Hathaway), e Cooper (Matthew McConaughey), um ex-piloto da Nasa, viajarão pelo buraco e decidirão qual de três planetas na outra ponta do atalho melhor serve à vida. No filme, como na ciência que se tem hoje, não existe maneira de saber como seria essa travessia, e o que haveria do lado de lá. Amelia está disposta a enfrentar a jornada por seu pai e Cooper, fazendeiro descontente e viúvo com um menino de 15 anos e uma menina de 10 de quem cuidar, o faz pelo futuro de seus filhos, e porque é incapaz de resistir ao apelo da aventura e do desconhecido.
     Um dos mais ambiciosos cineastas em atividade hoje, o anglo-americano Christopher Nolan é ele próprio um desbravador com a trilogia Cavaleiro das Trevas, reimaginou a trajetória de Batman em escala operística e rompeu uma barreira fenomenológica, criando filmes de perspectiva profundamente niilista que fizeram bilheteria bilionária, e espetáculos colossais ancorados no íntimo de um herói que é um reflexo freudiano dos vilões que combate. Interestelar é todo ele também uma fusão de opostos  começa num mundo de simplicidade agrícola e dele se descola abruptamente para uma viagem no limite teórico do conhecimento percorre planetas recobertos de gelo, ou nos quais ondas da altura de cordilheiras correm sobre um mar sem fim, impulsionado apenas pela ligação entre Cooper e sua filha, Murph (Mackenzie Foy na infância e depois Jessica Chastain, ambas excelentes) dobra o tempo, o espaço e a gravidade na tentativa de atender ao mais primordial impulso da vida, o de persistir e continuar. Depois de assombrar a plateia com o estrondo de Cavaleiro das Trevas, Nolan propõe a ela agora um ritmo introspectivo e meditativo.
     Nem sempre a conciliação entre esses extremos é pacífica. Há muita ciência difícil e altamente contraintuitiva que explicar, com o resultado de que várias das proposições soam fantasiosas embora não o sejam  e de que os atores que têm de dar voz a elas, como Anne Hathaway, parecem sobrecarregados e constantemente fora de registro. Quanto mais se chega perto do clímax, também, mais certas cenas na Terra ficam supérfluas e reiterativas, ou simplesmente sentimentais demais. Nos dois extremos tão afastados que quer unir, porém, o filme se realiza plenamente na sua inquietante viagem pelo universo e na conexão vívida, intensa, entre McConaughey e Mackenzie Foy. Na inspiração e na ambição, Interestelar é descendente direto de 2001  Uma Odisseia no Espaço. E, ainda que o filme de Stanley Kubrick permaneça o horizonte inatingível, Nolan, com seu imperfeito mas muitas vezes magnífico Interestelar, pelo menos continua a buscá-lo. A seguir, o próprio diretor explica a VEJA a gênese de seu projeto
DE VOLTA AO PONTO DE PARTIDA
O filme lida com um futuro em que a agricultura na Terra está reduzida a um único cultivo, o do milho, e mesmo este está ameaçado, em razão das enormes tempestades de poeira que varrem a superfície. O apogeu humano aqui, enfim, está nos seus últimos dias. Revertemos a uma sociedade agrária, em que a subsistência é a primeira e a maior preocupação. Em certos sentidos, é uma sociedade agradável essa, de gente da terra. Mas mais e mais se pressente que essa situação não é sustentável e vai se deteriorar até que não mais possa haver vida humana no planeta.
A CATÁSTROFE AMBIENTAL
Eu tinha na mente as imagens do Meio-Oeste americano à época da Depressão, quando se testemunhou uma das maiores catástrofes ambientais causadas pela ação humana de toda a história. Fui muito influenciado por The Dust Bowl, o documentário de Ken Burns, que contém imagens atordoantes da devastação. Outra referência foi a chamada fome da batata dos anos 1840 e 1850, quando os irlandeses, dependentes dessa colheita para sua sobrevivência, morreram ou tiveram de emigrar aos milhares ao ver suas plantações atingidas por uma praga que as dizimou. Há vários momentos na história em que comunidades se viram em situação de extrema vulnerabilidade em relação ao ambiente, e é esse o quadro que pretendo evocar.
FUTURO X PRESENTE
Na ficção científica, a concepção e a execução da tecnologia são cruciais para que a plateia acredite no que está vendo e embarque na história. Por isso, desde o início rejeitei a alternativa de imaginar um design do futuro se essa é uma sociedade que teve de regredir até suas raízes agrárias, é de supor que a ciência e a tecnologia não tenham feito grandes avanços assim, tudo o que se vê de equipamento no filme é o que seríamos capazes de construir hoje, com total obediência à função que esse equipamento deveria cumprir.
UM MUNDO PALPÁVEL
É vital fazer a plateia suspender sua descrença. Meu instinto é aderir à realidade imagens feitas e calcadas no mundo físico real, com as quais o espectador tenha relação imediata e direta. Por isso, quase todos os elementos dos meus sets são práticos  são construídos de forma operacional e podem ser usados e manipulados pelos atores. O interior da nave em que Matthew McConaughey e Anne Hathaway viajam foi feito tal e qual, e as paisagens que eles veem pelas escotilhas não são um truque digital eram o que eles viam enquanto rodávamos as cenas. Quero que a plateia sinta que pode tocar e até cheirar os ambientes. Não só a plateia, na verdade. Para os atores, esse recurso torna o trabalho muito mais fácil e convincente do que ser jogado num estúdio vazio forrado de verde. E também para mim é ao mesmo tempo libertador e inspirador dirigir dentro de um mundo concreto e palpável é num set assim que minha imaginação se solta.
O FATOR McCONAUGHEY
Cooper, o protagonista de Interestelar, tinha de ser um desses espíritos independentes do Oeste como o Chuck Yeager que Sam Shepard interpretou em Os Eleitos. Quem escolher? Bom, por acaso vi Amor Bandido, em que Matthew McConaughey se saiu com uma interpretação completamente diferente de qualquer coisa que eu esperaria dele. Ver um astro de cinema fazer algo que nunca fez antes tem o efeito de abrir seus olhos para a sedução dele e fazer com que você o redescubra. McConaughey, nesta excelente fase de sua carreira, tem uma austeridade dramática que não se suspeitava nele, e se encaixou à perfeição em Cooper.
A IMAGEM MAIS FASCINANTE
Não existe nada mais interessante no mundo do que o rosto humano. Quando você se torna cineasta porque seu interesse é visual e cinemático, mais do que dramático  e foi esse o meu caso  você quer ir para uma locação e filmar imagens impactantes. Se está chovendo, ou escureceu e você perdeu a hora de rodar uma cena, pensa mas o que então vou filmar? Pouco a pouco, descobri que estava menosprezando o elemento mais intrigante, fascinante e essencial de todos que pode haver em um filme o rosto dos meus atores. É nos atores, nas pessoas, que um filme vive ou morre. Criar outros planetas, filmar em Imax, imaginar uma travessia do universo  tudo isso só faz sentido se girar em torno do elemento humano.

ROUNDTABLE GUESTS Christopher Nolan, Matthew McConaughey, TARS (Interstellar), Darth Vader, Han Solo, C3-PO and R2-D2, Spock, Captain Kirk, Matt Damon (Interstellar), Matt Damon (The Martian), Ellen Ripley (Alien), and Hal 9000 (2001 A Space Odyssey)

I used real, physical sets and Kip Thornes exact equations for Gargantua to ground Interstellar. CHRISTOPHER NOLAN Whoa, Mr. Vader, lets keep on topic. Did you all know we built real sets, projected actual starlight onto the actors, and even grew our own corn and actually made a profit on it.

SPOCK (Eyebrow raised, hands folded behind his back) The physics of your gravitational time dilation are entirely logical. However, Dr. Brands assertion that love is a quantifiable, multi-dimensional force is highly illogical. Love is a chemical phenomenon. 
MATT DAMON (DR. MANN) Dont brink me into this, elf ears

Why do we like (love) Christopher Nolan?
Is it because he makes perfect movies?  Of course not.  His most recent attempts have all been chock full of problems.  If you are the kind of person who is taken out of an experience because of a single mistake, Ill go ahead and tell you there is a chance you wont like this movie.  If youre the kind of person looking to find one of the only major blockbuster producing sources of wonder, imagination, and risk then buy your ticket.  Interstellar is a giant, unwieldy, monster shot into space with the goal of solving humanitys biggest problems.
Its a shame this movie is nearly three hours long.  It should have been four.  I think I could have watched five hours of this.  I can only hope that Nolan will release some sort of directors cut of the film.  The first hour of the film feels SO rushed.  We all know they have to get to space eventually, thats what its about.  But they move the characters through their last moments on Earth so quickly you hardly get a chance to establish your footing.  They do sort of a poor job of explaining the drought, the food shortage, the reason for leaving.  It doesnt feel like the end of the world.  Theres a PTA meeting in the first half hour for Gods sake.  Despite it feeling like I was being hurried along I was still able to connect deeply with the character and the mood of the film, especially the character played by Mackenzie Foe, Murph. (hence, cry number one).  
I think a huge part of the emotional impact this film puts out comes from the amazing Hans Zimmer score.  Ive been a big fan of Hans stuff in the past.  This trumps everything Ive heard.  Just like the movie, this score is so imposing, so monumental.  He takes a step away from the blaring trombones (dont worry, there is still tons of bass) and steps up to the organ to give the movie a sort of Gothic, Catholic church, religious power.  The first hour moves quick, but manages to fill in a ton of mega important moments.  By the time Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) gets in his truck for the last time the score has already sunk its hook deep, and it got me (hence, cry number two).
So now we are in space and I have to admit its almost a little underwhelming.  I mean, dont get me wrong it was great.  Certain of the space scenes were especially impressive.  But the camera work by Emmanuel Lubezki on last years Gravity makes this look three years older than it actually is.  And thats not the only time youll be thinking about Gravity while watching this movie.  I dont think its any mistake either.  I wasnt counting but the word gravity is uttered about a hundred or more times.  At one point someone even says that their job is to beat gravity.  I cant imagine this was all a big coincidence.  Its a very similar movie in a lot of ways, and that extends to the painfully unsubtle dialogue and developments.  Where I think this movie falls short of being a great movie is in its subtly.  Nolan must think the average audience member has an IQ close to that of a ten year old.  Everything is so heavy handed and easy to predict.  Lines like, Its not impossible, its necessary.  The twists are expected and pretty much come from other movies.  Its not a movie that lets you fill in the gaps and that can be a bit frustrating.  But that being said, it is a still a very CHALLENGING movie in its own right.  I was not expecting Nolan to take this movie to the places he did.  He does use very conventional elements, but he also makes some extremely bold and never before seen choices.  It was sappy.  But it worked.  That score got me every time it was intended to and even when I knew it was coming I couldnt help but be overwhelmed (hence, cries number three and four). 
Its close to being Nolans masterpiece.  Its definitely the closet thing hes done to Inception and I would say it rivals that one.  It has so many problems, it almost ends up being a guilty pleasure.
I wish it were four and a half hours long, I cried four and a half times, so I think it deserves four and a half stars.
Thank you Nolan for being brave.  
Do not go gentle into that good night.  Rage, rage against the dying of the light.

Interstellar (2014) is a science fiction adventure drama movie directed by Christopher Nolan, who co-wrote the screenplay with his brother Jonathon Nolan. The movie features Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, Wes Bentley, Bill Irwin, Jessica Chastain, Casey Affleck, John Lithgow, Matt Damon, and Michael Caine.
The movie focuses on a farmer named Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) returning to his career as a NASA pilot to work with a researching team, so they can find a new planet to call home after home has became uninhabitable. However, this adventure has caused serious consequences to Joseph after he discovers the future of his family.
The story was fantastic and engaging as it has the same charm of Christopher Nolans other movies. It has an emotional weight that will make the viewers heartbroken in some scenes, surprising twists, relatable characters, and intense moments. Exploration, future, and family were key themes that the movie explores. These were shown when the researchers explore different planets in outer space in the future while Joseph Cooper continues to think about the love of his family. In my opinion, this was done by Christopher Nolans writing and directing because of his experience in film making.
The performances from the cast were phenomenal because they have developed strong emotions with strong realistic movements, which were powerful enough to make the audience relate to the characters better. Matthew McConaughey has delivered the best performance as Joseph Cooper because of his powerful emotions and energy that make him a caring father for his family. The same can be said for Anne Hathaway, who does an excellent performance as Brand.
The special effects were incredible as they resemble a real life space atmosphere by making everything realistic and accurate to the recent researches about space. They also have a great attention to detail that keep the viewers more engaged with the film. For instance, the docking station Endurance looks awesome and well designed.
Although the movie has 2 hour and 49 minute runtime, the pacing was perfect and just right because there were plenty of scenes that did not feel too slow or too fast. This helps the audience become more interested with the movie as it progresses.
The production design for this movie was impeccable. This is because the production crew have successfully brought the movie to life with the impressive set designs for the planets, accurate costume designs that connect with the story and its characters, and well designed props. In my opinion, the water-based and winter-based planets have the best production designs in the film since they appear realistically with their great lightings, creativity, and surroundings.

For example, there were establishing shots of the winter-based planet with light grey-white lighting. Christopher Nolan has wanted Hoyte van Hoytema to create these shots because he wanted the viewers to feel like they are really venturing the different planets with the characters.
Hans Zimmers music score was beautiful since it creates an emotional impact to the story, as well as a tension to build up the intense moments in the film. In conclusion, Interstellar (2014) is still an amazing movie Christopher Nolan succeeds to keep the audience engaged and feel emotional. Algo parecido me pasó con Tom, el hijo de Cooper, quien es un buen personaje pero tiene algunas cosas que no me convencieron de él, toda la trama de la granja y sus pensamientos sobre eso me cansó un poco, lo que hizo que se me haga un poco insoportable por momentos. Por último, el Dr. Mann fue un personaje interesante de ver, me parece que a la historia le hacía falta alguien así que, desesperado, busque una manera de recuperar su vida, haciendo que lo odiemos pero que se nos haga fácil de entender su actuar.
En otros aspectos destaco la banda sonora de Hans Zimmer, sin él la cinta no hubiese sido lo mismo, el trabajo que hace es uno de los mejores de la historia del cine, tiene melodías memorables y hermosas que acompañan perfectamente a las escenas, principalmente las más emotivas. Además, el apartado sonoro en general es una locura, muy inmersivo, escuchar todo en una sala de cine potenció mi experiencia de ver la película por primera vez. Por otro lado, la dirección de Christopher Nolan es magistral, hace que todo lo que vemos en la cinta luzca de maravilla y tiene planos hermosos, en cuanto a dirección no se le puede criticar nada a este hombre. También destacar los efectos, es una locura que ya pasaron diez años y se ve muchísimo mejor que muchas de las películas de hoy en día, un trabajo fantástico sin lugar a dudas. Por último, el cast que tiene es espectacular, repleto de estrellas y todos otorgando unas interpretaciones magníficas, destaco principalmente a Matthew McConaughey, Jessica Chastain y Anne Hathaway, también hay otros actores que están muy bien, pero ellos son los que más se lucen a mi parecer, con actuaciones dignas de premios.
En conclusión, una excelente película y una obra maestra del cine de ciencia ficción, pocas cintas construyen su complejidad de una forma tan buena como ésta, sin dejar de lado la emotividad de su historia para hacer que te llegue al corazón. Muy recomendada.

2001 A Space Plodyssey, more like.
As regular sufferers of my reviews will know, I dont deal well with long films. So much so that I had to make sure that I watched Interstellar on a day off work in the afternoon because I knew if I watched this in the evening, where I watch almost all films, I would have fallen asleep and  or got distracted and started betting on eastern European football instead.
So my emotions towards longer or long films tend to be a bit more exaggerated, I think. If the film is really good then I am SO thankful to the point of endless gushing. If its not so good then I get VERY angry to the point of wanting actual physical harm to come upon those who made it and on to myself for sitting through the motherfucking thing in the first goddamn place.
For a long time, my feelings toward Interstellar were ambivalent to actually quite positive. I even quite liked the first 40 minutes. The slow, thoughtful and relatively considered build-up had some good characterisation and some intriguing bits and pieces that I was quite interested in.- most notably the drone plane they end up commandeering, even if Ive no idea how they did that and they never bother explaining it. And then I realised, ahh, yes. This is a Christopher Nolan film. Not explaining stuff that I want to know more about has been his modus operandi in previous films Ive seen by him.
Then the pacing goes to shit at around the 40 minutes mark. The slow and intriguing opening gives way to ooh I found a hidden NASA bunker and a few minutes later ooh Im in space? Completely bizarre. Again, hes done this before. He and I just dont seem to be on the same wavelength as to how these things should work. Hes glossing over the bits that I want to know more about.
How exactly are they fuelling this massive trip? What are they doing for food? I dont need whacking great complex explanations for how theyre covering these points, just a bit of lip service would be enough. Its all very well harping on about gravity and the properties of a black hole for fuck knows how long, but its disproportionate to stuff that I think, in terms of creating a coherent and enjoyable story, needs at least a bit of explaining. Also, the robots? Theyre absolutely great! Brilliantly designed and fascinating - but can you tell us a bit about those, Chris? No? Well why not?
Its also littered with odd scenes that range from the completely awful to Hang on, he nicked that from Event Horizon, surely? Anne Hathaways speech about love is bad in itself but even worse when it becomes clear that Nolans having a go at trying to stick a scientific explanation on the concept of love. It was at this point where I more or less gave up on any hope the opening stretch of Interstellar had given me.
Theres also the question of why David Gyasi didnt just kill himself instead of waiting around for 23 years if he thought Hathaway and Matthew McConaughey had carked it. Plus, for a scientist, Hathaway seems to be, to borrow a quote from McConaugheys son in this, a complete dumbass. They drop down on a totally frozen wasteland of a planet, she buys Matt Damons explanation that yeah humanity could totally, like, relocate there and shit, and didnt bother once to question how the actual fuck they were going to grow anything there. How much sodding corn do they grow in Antarctica, professor?!
The odd thing is I never thought it was a slog, but once the adventure begins here its just so resolutely short of anything REALLY interesting happening and far too much stupid crap as outlined above. You get a couple of action scenes and neither of them are all that exciting, with the spinning docking scene overlaid by another unnecessarily over-dramatic Hans Zimmer score that sounded more like a church organ dirge.
Then theres the ending. The last 20 minutes of this are an absolute disaster. I dont use that word lightly. They are staggeringly, laughably dreadful. Not content with presenting us with dialogue that makes the previous 2 hours seem like a David Mamet film in comparison (He was my ghost!), Nolan manages the seemingly impossible by making almost every second that passes by, especially in the last 10 minutes, count towards making this so much worse than it already was.
An utter shambles of pathetic dialogue, sub-Star Trek clunky nonsensical science jargon and a bizarre clutter of random drivel, it then drags us back to the love  science nonsense that I was hoping was left behind what seemed like hours beforehand before going for a pointless afterthought of a final shot.
Right from the first dreadful scene with McConaughey, Hathaway really struggles to convince in her role but shes hardly the only one. McConaughey himself is a real struggle. I do really like him and hes good in bits here, mainly when hes asked to be a farmer and dad. But as an astronaut he makes a good farmer. And during the bits when hes asked to tackle science and thinking, hes hopeless. Also, all the crying just made me want to strangle myself.
That said, I do feel as though Jessica Chastain has been hardest done by here. It shows how dreadful some of the dialogue is here that it makes a wonderful actor like her look very poor indeed. Its almost like Nolan had a grudge against her or something and deliberately gave her all of the worst dialogue in this film as revenge for something. I agree to a certain extent with the theory that a truly great actor can make the worst material seem ok but I think that theory has holes - and one of those holes is Interstellar, especially when shes on about ghosts. 
Even so, and this may seem bizarre considering this is review largely resembles an evisceration, I didnt actually hate Interstellar! I didnt find myself utterly bored by it, as I feared would actually be the case before I watched it, and as I was by Inception. I was quite interested in it even through a lot of the negative stuff Ive highlighted - although Im not sure why. It could be to do with the fact that I just really like science fiction and Im more likely to tolerate utter nonsense here than in most other genres. So the rating Ive given might seem at odds with this review.
Having said all this, and as I said earlier, me and Nolan dont seem compatible at all. Ive seen all but his Batman films now and aside from Insomnia, which in itself was hardly sensational, Ive just had much the same problems with all of them. When I need him to delve deeper, he throttles back and skips over stuff. When I want him to ease off a bit and move on, he enlarges. I think Ive given up hope that he will make a film any time soon that I love as much as many people seem to love most of his films, and Im actually quite sad about that.
For although they may have done little for me, I acknowledge that Nolan deserves credit for trying to create more cerebral blockbusters and actually making huge amounts of money from them. Clearly hes doing something right with a lot of people. Im stuck with the minority left feeling rather isolated by the adulation. Im not saying I dont understand said adulation, by the way. But I certainly have many questions about it.

We used to look up in the sky and wonder at our place in the stars. Now we just look down and worry about our place in the dirt.
Interstellar is still one of the greatest movie ever made. it perfectly combines science, emotion, and breathtaking visuals into one unforgettable experience. The story is much more than a journey through space. At its core, it is about love, sacrifice, hope, and the human desire to survive. The relationship between Cooper and his daughter Murph gives the film incredible emotional depth, making every decision feel meaningful and personal.
One of the films greatest strengths is its scientific realism. With the help of physicist Kip Thorne, many of the concepts-such as black holes, time dilation, and wormholes-are based on real science. This makes the movie feel believable while still inspiring a sense of wonder. The visuals are absolutely stunning. Every planet, the black hole Gargantua, and the vastness of space are beautifully created, making us feel as if we are truly traveling through the universe.
Hans Zimmers score is another reason why Interstellar stands above other films. The powerful organ score perfectly matches the emotions of each scene, creating moments that are unforgettable and deeply moving.
Finally, Interstellar leaves us with questions about humanity, time, love, and our place in the universe. It is a film that still stays with me long after the credits roll, encouraging us to think about life from a completely different perspective.
Overall, Interstellar is not just an amazing science fiction film it is a masterpiece and, the best movie ever made.

Because my dad promised me.
I dont even know where to begin. Interstellar is the reason I downloaded Letterboxd in the first place. There will never be another movie made in my lifetime that will make me feel the way Interstellar made me feel. When it comes to movies, Ive never been the person that cried. In my mind, its just a movie, but after watching this film, it changed my perspective on movies forever. I think if a movie can bring out emotions in you, whether it be happiness, sadness or even anger it has succeeded as a movie. When I tell you I cried watching this movie, it would be an understatement. When the credits rolled, I was hyperventilating and had the most monstrous headache from how much I cried. Ive never been so emotionally connected to a group of characters and story in my life. Ive surpassed 200 movies watched on Letterbox and Im still chasing that feeling Interstellar left me with. 

Interstellar also made me fall in love with scores and showed me how important they are to the making of a film. This movie has the GREATEST score that has even been made ever. Cornfield Chase, No Time for Caution, Mountains, Dust, Day One, Stay. I could go on and on about this Hans Zimmer masterclass, but those are my favorites. Ill just play those pieces randomly and they give me chills all over my body. Ive never been so emotionally moved by any piece of music in my life. The original score is a big contribution as to why I love this film as much as I do. People love to give Christopher Nolan shit for not having emotion in his movies, so he went and made the saddest movie Ive seen. His ability to attach the audience to Murph and Coopers relationship in the first 30 minutes of the runtime is something that needs to be studied. I fell in love with them so quick, which is exactly what he intended to happen. The power of their relationship, their love for each other, is the crux of the story.
The entire movie is flawless to me, but there are a few moments in particular that are my personal favorites. First, when Cooper and the group reach Millers planet. The score (Mountains), Coopers realization of the waves, the tension, and those beautiful ass visuals. What follows is what made me realize what type of movie I was watching. After Cooper realizes he lost 23 years and 4 months to Millers planet, he sits down and experiences the life of his children literally flash before his eyes. When I first seen this, I definitely was sad, but it didnt hit me until Murph popped up on that screen. As soon as she muttered, Hey dad I started to cry like a little bitch. That is when my love for movies really started. Of course, the docking scene is a personal favorite for anybody whos watched Interstellar. Its one of the most beautiful looking scenes ever and the climax of the movie. Again, the score (No Time for Caution) is just riveting during this scene. Last, but certainly not least, is the iconic Cornfield Chase. Its mainly one of my favorites because of the score, but the cinematography is another big reason why I cherish that moment of the movie.
The final thing I want to talk about is the third act of Interstellar. To me, its the greatest third act Ive ever seen. Starting with the docking scene (peak), which I mentioned in the previous paragraph. After Cooper successfully docks, himself and Brand immediately plan on what to do as they are being pulled into Gargantua. Cooper decides to use it as a slingshot, slinging them towards Edmonds planet. When Cooper decides to sacrifice himself to ensure Plan B, the waterworks came again. I loved McConaughey and his performance as Cooper so much, the thought of him dying was extremely depressing. It doesnt help when you think he would never get to see his daughter ever again. Thankfully, this leads to him falling into the Tesseract. You were my ghost. Again, I cried from that point until the movie ended. Murph coming back to her room and taking the watch because Cooper gave it to her was perfect. Finally, the Tesseract closes as Cooper drifts off into nothingness. Hes found and he wakes up on Cooper Station, which is when he learns Murph is still alive. Their reunion is what got the most out of everything. Because my dad promised me. It will get me every time I hear it. Murph then telling Cooper to go find Dr. Brand and it revealing Edmonds planet was habitable all along was the icing on the cake. 
Love. Love is the one thing were capable of perceiving that transcends dimensions of time and space. Brands love for Edmonds, that was telling her to go to his planet, was right all along. Murphs love for her dad led her to the watch with the necessary data to save the world. Its beautiful. Im thankful everyday I was born in an era where I got to experience Interstellar. The GREATEST movie ever made.

This one took me a while to fully come around to. Its origins go back almost 20 years, developed originally by Steven Spielberg with astrophysicist (and now Nobel laureate) Kip Thorne, whod written up early wormhole concepts. Jonathan Nolan came on to write it, spent years working with Kip and Spielberg, even picked up an unofficial half-assed postgrad degree in astrophysics along the way. Then Jonathan told Spielberg if you ever bail on this, I know exactly who wants to direct it. My brother. Spielberg moved on, and Christopher folded in pieces of his own unfinished scripts on top of what was already there. What we got is this strange, brilliant merger 90s scientific ideas, by way of Spielberg and Jonathan Nolan, filtered through Christophers sensibility.
What held me back for a long time was the way it plays by two sets of rules at once... ghost story rules and hard science-fiction rules. The bookshelf at the beginning, the third-act bookshelf payoff, wrapped around a movie thats otherwise deeply rooted in real science. That bugged me for years. What got me there eventually was realizing the film establishes those rules from minute one... it ties the ghost stuff directly into gravity, and once you buy that framework, the ambiguity stops feeling like a cheat.
People love to say Nolans movies are too cerebral, not emotional enough. Watch the video-message sequence after McConaughey loses all that time with his kids and try to hold onto that opinion. Its one of the hardest gut-punches in any movie, period... and the wildest part is where it comes from. That sequence traces back to Einsteins thought experiments identical twins, one boards a train accelerating to light speed, comes back, and you just sit with the sadness of where did my twin go? Thats the exact blend that makes this movie work real research and real ideas fused with a genuine understanding of human emotion.
And then theres the pure craft side... the docking sequence is phenomenal on every level, and its not an isolated set piece. Its planted early enough to establish the emotional stakes for the entire runtime, so every scene after it carries this creeping sense of loss and cost. Even the wins cost something. Thats why the victories land as hard as they do.
Immaculate production from top to bottom, one of the best surprise cameos in movie history (Matt Damon, Scotty doesnt know), and McConaughey playing a Texan opposite this Texan reviewer doesnt hurt either. What started as somebody elses idea, passed through three different creative minds, ended up as one of Nolans most purely moving films.
