Interstellar has matured into a cinematic masterpiece that astonishes not only with magnificent scenes, but also with the depth of human emotion. From the moment the film begins, youre transported into a breathtaking universe, where every minute feels meticulously crafted. The visuals, from the gargantuan black hole to the vast, desolate planets, are an absolute ride. Each scene is a visual spectacle that remains embedded in your mind. However the movies beauty goes beyond its visuals. Its filled with pure sentiment, the untameable desire for knowledge, and even a bit of faith. The characters, especially Matthew McConaugheys portrayal of Cooper, are rich in the complexities of love, sacrifice, and survival. Não acho Interestelar o melhor filme de Christopher Nolan, mas acho que é o filme com os melhores momentos da carreira do cara. A ideia aqui é clara filmar o drama familiar de maneira bem contida e tradicional, pra contrastar a grandeza dos rostos de Cooper e Murph com Saturno ou um buraco negro. É a jornada homérica de atravessar o mundo para descobrir que as respostas te esperam em casa  como também fez via scifi James Gray no bom Ad Astra. É quando está no seio familiar, na fazenda do protagonista, que Nolan encontra esses grandes momentos. Dos planos detalhe das mãos de Cooper ensinando Murph a guiar o drone até os olhares admirados dos filhos tentando aprender sobre a vida com o pai, Nolan sabe estabelecer uma relação de amor entre aquela família quebrada. Aquele quarteto  ainda há o avô de John Lithgow e o primogênito de Timothée Chalamet  existe para contrastar o espaço e o indivíduo. O mundo tomado por desesperança e a família que se recusa a desistir de sonhar.
Nolan nos apresenta um mundo que marcha lentamente para o penhasco. Uma humanidade destruída por uma crise ambiental que aceita resignada o iminente fim. Mas a família de Cooper vai na contramão disso. Cooper é um ser humano à moda antiga, e deseja oferecer para os filhos um futuro melhor do que morrer asfixiado na poeira. Quer explorar o universo, mas pra isso precisa abandonar a família sem garantia de retorno.
Quando é o melodrama familiar clássico, Interestelar é bem bom. O problema pra mim surge mais quando o filme vai para o espaço. A preocupação em fazer as cenas espaciais parecerem um documentário da NASA não trazem força. Mas pior do que isso, me incomoda muito como o peso da ausência de Murph nunca é sentido. O filme passa tanto tempo apresentando conceitos e explicando acontecimentos que não sobra nenhum segundo para o ócio. E é no ócio que Copper deveria sentir a ausência da família. Não que precisasse ser desse jeito, mas por que não ao menos um plano de Copper olhando para o relógio? Encarando a escotilha da nave e tendo a imagem cortada por uma fração de segundo pelo sorriso da filha? Por que não sedimentar o peso dessa ausência? Murph parece só existir de novo quando Cooper a vê nas gravações, deixa de ser, por ora, uma personagem, e mais parece uma NPC.
Isso não torna Interestelar o pior filme do mundo, mas tira a força, pra mim. Se a alma do filme tá toda na relação entre Cooper e Murph, trocar isso por explicação de dilatação de tempo e buraco negro não me parece a escolha mais inteligente. Em um filme com tantos eventos, cenários e personagens, cada escolha é uma renuncia. E Nolan renuncia o drama familiar em prol do próprio encantamento pelo vazio infinito do espaço.

Being officially the first person to review this on all of Letterboxd is daunting.
Lets get a few things out of the way first.
Yes, I saw the film. Yes I got tickets to an early screening. Yes I saw it in IMAX, and yes it was 70mm film.

Interstellar is easily one of the most ambitious films Ive ever seen, and possibly one of the best blockbuster films ever. Nolans semi non-linear storytelling is back in full form, just like in his earlier films Memento and Inception. He has no problem giving his audience something to chew on while watching, which is truly great, and I am still thinking about it and running it through my mind, which is certainly a very good thing. But Ive learned that a grand scale and the attempt to reach to other universes and dimensions...... doesnt always mean its automatically a great film.
Where the film suffers the most with me is its writing. To me, nothing is more important in a film than its story. Its everything. Its the deciding factor on whether or not we care about what is happening on screen.
I love love love being challenged by films, but when things - important developments that are crucial to the audiences understanding of the film- are glossed over, I simply cant fully get on board.
The film runs at 169 minutes. Make it 200-210 minutes, and then you have an excellent film.
Believe me. You do NOT feel the run time of this film (WHICH IS AWESOME). And it would have been lightyears better with a better understanding of the situation the Earth is in, BEFORE we go out into space. The film feels like its in a RUSH, actually, and I was like WAIT NO! SLOW DOWN THIS IS IMPORTANT. And I still cant tell if all the information was there, but it was just covered so quickly..? or if the information wasnt there and youre just supposed to go with it. And believe me, you have to just accept a LOT of the information that you are told.

OK WILL, lets please for fucks sake move on to the positive!!
What a beautiful and transformative film. Its one of the most powerful and deeply felt films to hit the big screen in I dont know how long. The performances are all tremendous, specifically Mcconaughey and Mackenzie Foy. Because of the tremendous direction by Nolan, you still feel deeply for these characters because they are all richly realized and focused people. I sure did cry. No shame.
But all in all the film is juuust a bit rushed. Thats my biggest complaint. It had the potential of being semi brilliant, and I just wanted to go back into that editing room and tweak a few things. Its so rushed that when you are supposed to feel tension in these really big intense moments!!....... all you feel is the seats trembling from the roaring Hans Zimmer score. And yes there is a mindfuck that Im still thinking about. And its a beautiful and fantastic one that I cant get out of my head for the life of me.
I guess the biggest positive I can give the film is that it is ultimately about LIFE and LOVE and all of its beauty, and I commend Nolan for making that its core, because theres nothing that we as humans should care more about.

I did go a bit critical with my review, to some. But its truly how I feel. I didnt let the stunning visuals and dramatic manipulation win me over completely. On the 7th I will see it again and maybe grasp a little bit more, but for now, sit tight, and EXPERIENCE Interstellar as soon as you can.

Mankind was born on Earth. It was never meant to die here.
Theres a moment in Interstellar where Matthew McConaugheys Cooper stares at decades of video messages from his children. Children he left behind on a dying Earth to venture through the stars. 
You feel it. 
Interstellar wears its heart on its space suit. Kip Thornes real-life physics anchor the film in plausibility. We see a dusty farm in what feels like the coming end of Earth. Cooper, a former pilot and now reluctant farmer, is restless. His daughter Murph is brilliant and stubborn. Like all good sci-fi tales, the call to adventure quickly pulls them in. 
The performances are stellar (get it?!). McConaugheys natural drawl carries both grit and grief. Jessica Chastain as the grown-up Murph is filled with fire and melancholy. The visuals are breathtaking, thanks to Nolan and his cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema. This is a vast, dangerous void. 
As we dive into the final act, Nolan decides to go metaphysical and sends Cooper into a tesseract. Not quite like the one in the Avengers, but more of a fifth-dimensional library of memories. We know the central theme here. As Anne Hathaway says, Love transcends time and space. While she gets some flack for it, she sells it really well here. 
Truthfully, when you see McConaughey crying into the void and whispering across time to a young Murph through a bookshelf, it hits hard. When Murph is an old woman talking to her much younger father, its brutal. This is probably Nolans most emotionally naked film. 
And, of course, Hans Zimmer just magnifies the emotion. He gives literal church organs and turns the film into a secular hymn. It elevates each scene as only great film composers can. The docking sequence alone is an opus. 
Some critics knock the films final act for slipping into sentimentality or over-explaining itself. But, it works here. It doesnt have the precision of Inception or Tenet. Its messier and its beautiful. 
Interstellar is a space opera in the best way. Its imperfect, ambitious, and unforgettable. It might make your head hurt, but it will also make your heart ache.

First and foremost, please ignore what I said in my Memento review. Lets just say I was drunk and had no idea what I was talking about.

As like many people have agreed, Interstellar is a film like no other. Unlike many apocalyptic sci-fi films that depict advanced technology as the cause of our destruction, it instead asserts that technology will save us.
Farming became paramount, while advanced technology is deemed frivolous. Cooper (McConaughey) remains one of the few survivors who still appreciates the need for engineering. He feels like a man lost in time until he stumbles upon the NASAs headquarters, which has been operating in secret due to public disapproval. There, he meets others who realize that a return to our old ways is unsustainable and will ultimately lead to our demise. We need technology to save us. As Michael Caine, playing the brilliant (duh!) Professor Brand, eloquently tells Cooper, We were never meant to save the world. We were meant to leave it.
For a film that won an Oscar for Best Achievement in Visual Effects (deservedly so), and as a visual person myself, I have to admit that the sound stole the show. Hans Zimmer unleashed a performance that was, quite appropriately, out of this world. Rarely have I seen a film elevated so much by its score. The music literally took my breath away.
Zimmers compositions fueled every crucial scene. In every meaningful moment, his harmonies captivated viewers attention in the way of a coach commanding a locker room with a pregame speech. The music elucidated those emotional scenes, particularly ones featuring Cooper and his daughter, in a way that no words or visual ques possibly could. I sat frozen, jaw agape, with tears streaming down my face as the music completely overwhelmed my emotions. The sound penetrated my soul and reverberated through my body, flowing to my appendages, supplying me with life like a heartbeat pumping blood through my veins. The music was truly the films life force.
Yes, we all witnessed a visual triumph, a daring creative wonder. Yes, nearly every actors performance proved worthy of commendation. McConaughey is on fire. Chastain is blossoming into a star. At this point, Michael Cain exudes such knowledge and wisdom by merely appearing on screen that if he were cast as Albert Einstein, people would wonder if the role were beneath him. All this considered, and the sound still towered over everything.
Once again, I walked out of the theater believing that I had experienced something unique, something truly special. Interstellar inspires, it awes, and above all, it entertains. I cant ask for more than that.

Christopher Nolan excels again with a truly challenging, emotional and visually stunning piece of work. Interstellar is by far his most ambitious film and a fascinating journey through time and space. Its not only a film about exploring the unknown, but it also shows our unrelenting will to survive in the face of extinction. I was often completely enthralled by the mystery, visual splendor and really strong performances from its talented cast. Interstellar is packed with touching moments and everyone gives their best efforts here in order to make them feel quite endearing and genuine. In addition, there are many intriguing surprises along the way and some really thrilling situations that will leave you in a state of awe. Interstellar is one of the most astonishing sci-fi films Ive seen, being a very unique experience and a total feast for the senses.

Theres nothing like seeing a world class shot-in-IMAX movie in a top-flight IMAX theater. It turns seeing a movie into a true event. And this one is quite the event. The visual splendor. The jaw-dropping Hoyte van Hoytema cinematography. The dazzling production design. The immersive sound. Its got an involving save-the-world story that carries you along, and plenty of great individual sequences. The entire Matt Damon portion is riveting, and the docking scene at the end of it is just terrific cinema.
That said, I have to admit that this movie doesnt really land for me emotionally like it does for a lot of other people. Im not a fan of the characters or dialogue. After watching the theatrical rerelease several months ago, I was mentally comparing Interstellar to Nolans recent Oscar winner Oppenheimer. Both movies have stories where civilization faces an existential crisis and a group of people are called upon to carry out a long-shot plan to save the world. In Oppenheimer, the world-savers are emotionally stable, practical people who realize that they are  dealing with a situation that requires setting aside ones personal issues to ensure the survival of humanity. In Interstellar, the world-savers are all emotional basket cases who bring their personal dramas into the mission, and then crank them up to eleven. In Oppenheimer, Nolan allows the emotion to come from the story in Interstellar, he tries to get it with histrionics from his actors.
The worst part is that, in the end, were left wondering whether our protagonists actually did anything. Its made clear early on that an unseen They are guiding our protagonists like rats through a maze in doing what they need to do. At the end, Chastain doesnt seem to have done much since McConaughey fed her the answers she needed (transmitting data via an analog watch, yeah right). And McConaughey doesnt seem to have done much since They provided the communication channel and the means of gathering the data. And it seems fairly apparent that the ultra-advanced They could have done everything our protagonists did themselves, McConaugheys sappy platitudes about love is the equation notwithstanding.
So maybe the whole thing was a test that They were putting humanity through to determine whether we were worth saving, like so many old Star Trek episodes? Or maybe it was some sort of twisted reality show entertainment for They, where the fifth-dimensional beings watch the proceedings on their fifth-dimensional flat screens, and then they go on fifth-dimensional letterboxd and leave reviews like Well, McConaughey blubbering for three hours didnt really do much for me, but did you see how awesome that black hole looked?

Both relieved and a little disappointed to discover that I wasnt the only one to see more Shyamalan than Kubrick or Tarkovsky in this imperfect space odyssey. The clunky dialogue and thin characterizations, the undeniable formal pleasures, the secondhand Spielberg family dynamics, the gooey New Age spiritualityall feel like vintage M. Night. And the twisty climax is swing-away-Merrill ridiculous, overpowering any emotional truth with the sheer power of its absurdity. 
Im right down the middle on this one, to the extent that its a little hard for me to fathom how someone could completely love or hate it. Those calling the film a masterpiece seem to be willfully ignoring its most embarrassing momentselementsthe revelation, for example, that the U.S. educational system of this (not-so-distant?) future has been teaching kids that the moon landing was faked, or the scene of one astronaut explaining wormholes to another in simple Star Trek terms right before they pilot into a wormhole. At the same time, though, anyone who can sit stone-faced during that 23-years-of-messages scene is more of a robot than TARS. (A better movie would have shaved off the fat and circled everything around the relativity angle what I wouldnt give for an even-less-crowd-pleasing third act, one focused entirely on the reconciliation between two characters who are now the same age.)
Ultimately, I admire Interstellar more than I like it, which is about the same reaction I had to Inception. Both films are impressive for simply existing those Batman movies wrote Nolan a blank check that hes been cashing on big, flawed blockbuster passion projects. This one is almost perversely uncommercial in many respects, and I cant help but be grateful for it on principle alone, even as I wish Nolan had put more of his efforts towards creating real characters. A gushy, ambitious near-misfire like this is worth a thousand proficient Planet Of The Apes movies.

Once youre a parent, youre the ghost of your childrens future.
For a movie so deeply rooted in science and its exploration of space, its almost mind-blowing just how human and emotional the story feels. With a long runtime and slow pacing, Interstellar could seem boring or almost like a chore, yet there is something strangely perfect about the slow burn. Like a series of books, you want to sit down and connect to the characters you want to read late into the night, promising yourself itll be just one last chapter, purely because you want to know what happens next. By investing your time, you form a bond with its story, its world, until it begins to feel like a part of your life. The emotions, the heartbreak, the morals  these all stay with you. Not because you simply watched the film, but because you felt it.

Time is the ultimate sacrifice, and Cooper lost so much of it to give his children, and their children, a fuller life. I should not be able to relate to his pain or his guilt over missing out on such important moments, yet somehow, even as someone who is not a parent, my throat tightened and my heart sank. Nolan had fleshed out these characters into humans with their own motivations and traits, and the actors, especially Matthew McConaughey, gave them a soul  a realism, a rawness that let me understand the depths of their feelings. Interstellar was never just a story about planets or black holes. It is a powerful love story about a father and daughter, woven together with beautiful cinematography and an unforgettable score. A masterpiece that will be treasured for years to come.

Mal wieder Nolans 2001. Und schon wieder sitze ich da und warte. Wie Cooper auf Nachrichten seiner Kinder. Nur warte ich darauf, dass mich das interstellare wie interdimensionale Familiendrama kriegt, packt oder ergreift. Eben dann, wenn es sich am meisten dafür anstrengt. Doch es passiert abermals nicht. Egal, wie viel Mühe sich Matthew McConaughey gibt. Oder die Musik. Wo Cooper und sein Team nicht über den Ereignishorizont hinaus schauen können, kann ihre Mission meinen Emotionshorizont nicht überschreiten. 
Das ist immer noch bedauerlich. Denn ansonsten ist Interstellar für mich einfach ein Wahnsinnsfilm. In jedwedem Sinne. Der Aufwand, die Greifbarkeit der Technik, die Bilder, die irritierende Kamerawinkel, mit denen sie mitunter gefilmt werden, die Struktur, die Länge des Films, das Sounddesign, all die physikalischen Begriffe, die Botschaften und Metaphern, die Kritik an der Ausbeutung der Erde, die Warnung davor, sich nicht zu sehr von ihr zu entfremden, das Paradox, dass sich jemand so weit wie möglich von seinen Kindern entfernt, um wieder zu ihnen zurückzufinden Was Noland seinem Publikum und Film abverlangt, ist wahrlich wahnsinnig.
Und als wäre das alles nicht schon genug, erklärt er inmitten all der Expositionen zu Begriffen wie Singularität, Wurmloch oder Tessarakt mit dem gleichen Ernst die Liebe zur Naturgewalt. Damit hatte ich einstmals schon so meine Probleme. Und zusammen mit anderen Verständnisproblemen (Wieso haben die Planeten um das Schwarze Loch Sonnenlicht? Was ist Manns Motivation? Warum ruft Cooper sich selbst aus der 5. Dimension zu, dass er bleiben soll? Wieso das Wurmloch wie ein weiteres Paradox wirken lassen?) hielt sich meine Euphorie schon in Grenzen. Ich hoffe, damit war ich nicht ganz allein.
Doch was mir damals schon bewusst war, empfinde ich inzwischen noch viel mehr Die Eier, das alles so durchzuziehen, musst du auch erstmal haben. Bei aller Liebe oder verständlichen Kritik, die man an Nolan und seinen Film richten kann. Und so gehe ich inzwischen (sorry, Dr. Brand) echt gelassen in die gute Nacht. Manches habe ich mir selbst erarbeiten müssen, manches verstehe ich immer noch nicht ganz. Aber das kann ich nun besser ignorieren. Genau wie die Szenen, die so unbedingt meine Tränen wollen. Denn es gibt nun andere, die es auf die eine oder andere Art doch schaffen. Oder eben einfach zum Heulen gut sind.
Die Andock-Sequenz ist natürlich ganz vorne mit dabei. Mittlerweile kann ich auch das, was ich sehe, viel besser zu dem übertragen, was es bedeuten soll. Und was auf dem Spiel steht. Aber es ist der Moment zu Beginn der Sequenz, wenn Cooper instinktiv zum Anflug auf die rotierende Endurance ansetzt und der Score einsetzt, der meine Haut vibrieren lässt. Genau wie der Wellenberg auf Millers Planet. Oder wenn Jessica Chastain den Flüchtlings-Convoy flankiert, um dann zu ihrer Farm umzukehren. Und wenn Cooper von dort aufbricht, um ins All zu fliegen, hab ich als nun älterer Vater das, was ich als junger noch nicht hatte feuchte Augen. 
Nein, Interstellar wird niemals 2001 sein. Dafür ist er zu sehr aufs Emotionale und den Zusammenhalt der Familie verdichtet. Oder zu wenig beschäftigt mit den religiösen, philosophischen, über-existenziellen Fragen. Aber vielleicht wird er ihm eines Tages noch ebenbürtiger sein. Sein Mut, das Risiko, das er eingeht, die Visualisierung, sein Vertrauen in sein Publikum, seine dennoch zahlreichen Ideen, seine dann doch vorhandene Rätselhaftigkeit, sein Wille, zum Staunen zu bringen und dass er eben auch wie Kubrick daran erinnert, was es heißt, Mensch zu sein, sollten dazu beitragen können. 
Die finalen Worte sollen allerdings einem anderen Dirigenten gehören - eben weil ich seine Musik permanent im Kopf hatte, während ich zuletzt in Scavengers Reign abgetaucht bin Hans Zimmer, youve done a mans job, sir! Wenn es wahr ist, dass es nur diese eine Seite gab, anhand der er den Soundtrack komponierte, ist das Resultat ein kleines wie absolut passendes Wunder für mich. Und falls die von John Lennon geforderte Kathedrale für 2001 jemals gebaut wird, sollte, nein, muss S.T.A.Y. mindestens einmal am Tag darin laufen. Blicken wie zuversichtlich in die gute Nacht, dass es weiterhin solche Filme und Menschen gibt, die ihr Ding so durchziehen.

We used to look up at the sky and wonder at our place in the stars. Now we just look down, and worry about our place in the dirt.
Happy 10th anniversary to this beautiful piece of cinema! Between the breathtaking visually stunning scenes and mind bending space concepts, this has always been one of my favorite Sci-fi films. What makes Nolans Interstellar so beautiful is the deeply raw human emotion shown throughout the film uniquely fusing science fiction, emotion, and humanity all together, specifically through relationships with those we love. From start to finish, the film is a masterpiece that draws you in even if youre rewatching it. I always found the space premise of this movie to be so intriguing. Though not absolutely correct in scientific terms, how it plays with concepts like time dilation, wormholes, and black holes is simply brilliant.
Without a doubt, my favorite part about Interstellar every single time I watch the film is Zimmers iconic score. The score in this film is such an integral part of the experience, it perfectly mirrors the films emotional highs and lows. Especially during the scenes on Millers planet, as the score kicks in with mountains and the waves start rushing towards them, it is goosebump inducing every single time. Till this day, its still my favorite score that Hans Zimmer has composed. 
Overall, Interstellar is not just a film it is an experience. Breathtakingly beautiful, emotionally strong, and ambitiously epic. Its one of those types of films that will leave you thinking and emotional all at once when the credits role.

At times, it feels like the film is trying too hard to be profound, layering big concepts over each other until the emotion starts to feel forced. The science is impressive, the visuals are unforgettable, but the core message, especially about love transcending dimensions, can come off as cheesy.
I think thats why calling it overrated doesnt mean its bad, it just means the expectations around it can overshadow what it actually is.

I found myself gasping and in complete awe at the sheer spectacle of it all, whether it was the wormhole scene, the intense docking sequence, or the mind-blowing fifth dimension and closing tesseract scene. You could feel the entire theater holding its breath, collectively whispering wowww.  
Watching it on the big screen, with that immersive, thunderous sound, made it an experience beyond words, pure cinematic ecstasy.
The heart of Interstellar for me is the relationship between Cooper and Murph, the father-daughter bond that just wrecks you emotionally. Sure, everyone praises Nolan for the mind-blowing sci-fi elements the time travel, the black hole, all that cosmic stuff. And yeah, its incredible. But what really gets me, what makes this film so special, is how Nolan writes the emotions, the characters, their regrets, the way their pain feels so real it touches your soul. The agony of Coopers departure isnt just a plot beat- its a visceral gut-punch. When Murph tells him to stay, we feel the fracture of a childs trust and the weight of a parents impossible choice. Nolan condenses a lifetime of love and regret into mere minutes, making their separation feel as vast as the universe Cooper is about to venture into. The genius of the film lies in how its scientific concepts reflect its emotional core. Relativity isnt just a theory here, its a storytelling tool. When Cooper returns after spending mere hours on Millers planet, 23 years have passed in the real world. Watching him scramble to see his childrens messages, now grown, distant, and shaped by years of grief, is absolutely soul crushing. Even the tesseract sequence, often praised for its stunning visuals, is, at its core, a fathers desperate cry across time and space. Cooper isnt solving equations to save humanity, hes using Morse code to reach his daughter, turning quantum physics into a simple, heartbreaking Stay. This moment captures the films true message love isnt just an emotion, its a force, a connection powerful enough to bend time itself. Nolans real triumph isnt making us believe in interstellar travel, its making us feel the cost of Coopers journey in every frame. The science is mesmerizing, but the true weight of the film lies in the emotion. Murph waiting for her father, and Cooper, stranded lightyears away from the life he left behind. Interstellar isnt just a lesson in astrophysics, its a deeply human story about love, loss, and the hope that, somehow, it can transcend time and bring them back together.
The music, oh, that fucking music! I swear, I felt like straight-up kissing Hans Zimmers hands, no cap. Damn, its just so fucking mesmerizing, like it was made to seep into your soul.  
The first time it played during the drone chase through the cornfield, I felt like my soul just left my body. The way the rhythm builds, and the score completely takes over. One of the greatest film scores ever.
The Performances - Every actor delivers a flawless performance, but for me, the standout is the young actress who plays Murph, she was simply remarkable, she overshadowed everyone. 
Jessica Chastain, Casey Affleck, and Anne Hathaway all bring depth and authenticity to their roles, while Matthew McConaughey delivers an emotionally charged performance that will be remembered for generations.
I could talk for hours about what it felt like to watch Interstellar in a theater and still not do it justice. The experience was truly unforgettable, theres nothing quite like it.  
Christopher Nolan will always have a special place in my heart for the way he pushes the boundaries of cinema with his relentless pursuit of perfection. Interstellar is the ultimate proof of that. Its not just a film you watch-its a film you feel.

I have no idea how many times I have watched this film. This is easily my favorite Christopher Nolan film and one of my all time favorite film.
Everything about this film is perfect to me. The mind boggling screenplay by Chris and Jonathan Nolan is brilliant. The writing here is very bold and moving, the duo didnt restrain themselves from exploring many fascinating and daring ideas. The concept of this film might be crazy and highly theoretical in paper but only some wild conviction, the childlike energy, a command over his project and his deep love towards someone could have made Nolan craft something as epic and profound like Interstellar.
Interstellar does not stand so high because of its bold science concept, it plays a important part sure, but the heart and soul of this movie is its charged and layered emotions. Every scene has a heartbeat, a father wants to save the world and join his family is the underlying emotion here. And my god did it work for me every bit. The story of Cooper wanting to save the world here might sound like a typical Hollywood cliche plot device but Nolan wrote and executed those scenes masterfully. 
A film doesnt work simply because it has stunning visuals and wild concepts, you need connectable characters and strong emotions along with them in order to make it memorable and have an long lasting impact. Interstellar does that job wonderfully. The sequence where Coop leaves his daughter and his final realization of that scene broke me.
The performances here were amazing. Matthew McConaughey was absolutely terrific here, every scene the man was in he steals the show. Anne Hathaway was brilliant, one of her career best performance. Jessica Chastain was great as usual, the younger version by McKenzie Foy was amazing as well, they were the souls of this movie. Matt Damon was perfect here. Cassey Affleck made an impact with little screen time, Timothee Chalamet made an adorable debut here. Michael Caine was legendary as ever. David Gyasi and Wes Bentley were great in their respective roles. Bill Irwin and Josh Stewart did an amazing job as the voice artists to TARS and CASE.
How can I talk about this movie without raving about its outstanding score by Hans Zimmer. The score just flows through the film, it was beautiful. Every time I hear the score I get this feeling of pain and hope infused, no words can express that feeling. The cinematography by Hoyte was exceptional, every shot felt like an art. The editing was seamless. The visuals were ground breaking, every shot was a revelation. The visuals of the Black Hole and the endurance in the vast space among the stars is something I can never forget.
Calling it a masterpiece would be an understatement for me, Interstellar is life changing.

What I find most invigorating about Rian Johnsons work isnt his adept knack at subverting the status quo of the genre template, but how he finds himself lost in the mechanics of said world. Watching Brick, Looper, or even the blockbuster tendencies of The Last Jedi provides an innate understanding of what he loves as a fan of the work in question, in addition to his own thrilling developments as a storyteller. Knives Out begins as a handsomely-mounted, tantalizing murder mystery, but it soon finds itself wrapped up in the divisions of class and the falsities of the uber-rich, all while never losing sight of its traditional whodunit pleasures. Many detractors are labeling this as Online and cringe-y, but Rian Johnson has a pulse on Americas tendency, whether on social media or in the clusters of familial dynamics, to ultimately lose sight of sturdy political objectives in favor of echo chamber argumentation. At the end of the day, the rich are staying rich, and when the familys money is threatened, their party of choice falls by the wayside. The solidarity is rooted against those who will most definitely have ramifications from this presidency, and this late-stage of capitalism. Rian Johnson dissects that class disparity, that detachment from civility of real-life consequences, and has an A-game cast backing up his often magical whiplash plotting and eye for theatrics. Daniel Craig and Ana de Armas are the standouts, but they all find a place to shine, and this movie is truly a blast and a half, recoiling somewhat from Johnsons TLJ backlash but mostly barreling forward as a supreme auteur vision of acidic wit and often ingenious twists and turns. An often funny and cleverly constructed modernized throwback to classic Christie whodunit murder mysteries that Johnson seems to have unfortunately grafted his Twitter timeline onto in hopes of making it About Something. Its honestly so clearly reverse-engineered from the easy, heavy-handed talking points it wants to make about the monstrously wealthy, privileged American family vs. their kind-hearted immigrant help it becomes hard to really engage with this as anything but clockwork piece of call-and-response machinery for a lot of its runtime. Where genre fans get to enjoy the plot details playfully revealed through non-linear sleight of hand trickery, and online liberals get to hoot and holler at the references they understand  the parts where the morally good people own the bad ones. Part of the appeal is that Johnson is obviously smart and well-read and is gleefully toying with tropes and expectations (and even the small scale of his setting), and I think trying to insert class consciousness into a mainstream piece of entertainment like this is perfectly well-meaning and admirable, but the flipside of how he incorporates both is that hes incredibly self-conscious about it to a fault. Especially when he starts putting Twitter-speak caricature dialogue into his largely pretty good ensembles mouths, a few of which manage to survive it but not all. Anyway, dont get me wrong, I still had a lot of fun with this, especially with Daniel Craigs whole Foghorn Leghorn Hercule Poirot routine (almost every line delivery is a complete delight, and hes half the reason the nearly 20-minute monologue it ends on is as amusing as it is), but Rian really needs to log off.

Ein Kriminalfilm von Rian Johnson? Dem seit The Last Jedi vielfach verkannten Autorenfilmer, der einfach nicht die Finger davon lassen kann, das Bisherige zu dekonstruieren und ihm seine eigene Perspektive aufzudrücken?
Eigentlich müsste man seit seinem Erstlingsmeisterwerk Brick (2005) genau wissen, dass er Kriminalfilme beherrscht. Nur hier war das Subgenre ein anderes der klassische Film Noir - verlegt an die moderne High School!
Hier ist es das klassische Whodunnit - frei nach Agatha Christie. Ein launiges Kammerspiel der Schauspielgrößen, herausgefordert von einem genauso launigen Gentlemen-Privatdetektiv.
Und dieser Transfer in die Moderne gelingt Johnson ungleich besser als dem Kollegen Kenneth Branagh mit seiner Neuauflage vom Orient-Express. Johnson nimmt diese klassischen Verhörszenen und schneidet sie so gekonnt und pointiert zu einer Montage zusammen, wie man es wahrscheinlich noch niemals zuvor in diesem Genre gesehen hat. Schon nach 15min ein Meisterwerk für sich!
Doch Rian Johnson wäre nicht Rian Johnson, wenn er einfach nur den Regeln des Genre folgen würde. Und so sind eigentlich nur der 1. und der 3. Akt des Filmes genau das, was einen klassischen Whodunnit ausmacht.
Der längere 2. Akt wird zu einem Suspense-Thriller à la Hitchcock Der Zuschauer weiß etwas, was die meisten Figuren nicht wissen. Eine andere Art des Spannungsaufbaus.
Das einzige Problem ist nur, dass Johnson nicht Hitchcock ist. Dieser 2. Akt ist sehr unterhaltsam und eine erfrischend andere Perspektive auf Agatha Christie. Die Idee ist genial!
Nur in der Ausführung nimmt er damit auch die Spannung raus, ohne an das Suspense-Genie Hitchcock herankommen zu können. Dafür bleibt genau dieser zweite Akt auch nach dem dritten (!) Kinobesuch immer noch unterhaltsam - man könnte sogar sagen, dass der Film dabei sogar noch anzieht.
Er gewinnt an Details, Deutungsebenen und verliert nie seinen eigenen Charme.
Knives Out ist der beste Whodunnit seit den Üblichen Verdächtigen (1995), der unterhaltsamste Whodunnit seit Sir Peter Ustinovs Poirot-Filmen und zum Glück kein weiterer Versuch, ein Orient-Express-Whodunnit sein zu wollen.
Rian Johnson liebt offensichtlich Whodunnit-Filme!
Und ich werde diesen hier noch viele Male bewundern - ähnlich wie den Mord im Orient-Express. Den Klassischen!

The movie successfully creates an atmosphere of uncertainty from the beginning and is strengthened by the sufficient ambience of mystery by the musical score composed by Nathan Johnson. 
The movie additionally attaches a unique comedic tone to create something that feels very much its own, and everyone in the vast and immensely accomplished cast generates memorable and intriguing characters. Johnson captures the intrinsic and indispensable qualities of the murder mystery genre while deftly managing to avoid becoming weighed down by its more familiar tropes, and sharp comments on politics and illegal immigration are interweaved with the comedy. What good is an allegedly class conscious film if you have to already be class conscious to get it? At best, someone who isnt class conscious walks away from this thinking these rich people were mostly awful, and maybe, hopefully, they extend that to all rich people - that is, those who exploit the people and live in luxury because of it - but its not guaranteed. If this feels like an argument for hitting people over the head with a class conscious message, it absolutely is. That doesnt make this a bad movie it just makes it not the class conscious piece I kept getting told it was. Which is fine, because I suspected it wouldnt be.
My biggest problem with its class portrayal is that it still portrays wealth as a good thing, a happy ending, and it suggests that one might get rich off labor alone (in the case of Harlan and his books), which only perpetuates capitalist myths. One can argue that Harlan and Marta, especially, are metaphors for the working class owning the means of production, but in order to see that, you have to understand all of those things to begin with. And thats useless. We need to spread class consciousness, not cheerlead to those who already have it.
And of course, it doesnt remotely get the cops right. Those jackals should have been clambering to arrest Marta without a shred of evidence if this wanted to be either realistic or class conscious. Show them for what they are - lackeys of the rich people this film is revealing to be awful - rather than use them as devices to liberate the working class character(s). Arguing that Blanc was a private detective doesnt cut it arguing that the cops and Blanc were kinda absurd doesnt, either. Though they were funny.
Edit to add It also gets very hamfisted with its racial commentary, coming off as the kind of patronizing it wants to critique the more liberal-hearted rich folks for. It presents some of the more reactionary politics of the rich (especially the kid) in a way that is clearly mocking, but it never delves into the why of it - we need people to understand not just that its bad, but how it affects them, why it affects them. Its not enough to say this person is an immigrant and also not a bad person predicating solidarity with immigrants on whether or not Hollywood thinks theyre good or bad is not the right move. Its better than the average Hollywood film, playing into more hateful stereotypes, but it doesnt hit the mark.
Again, that doesnt make the movie completely bad. Just means it isnt what others have claimed.
What makes the movie good - or fun, anyway - is the dynamics of the camera. The way that thing moves is refreshing in a big budget film. Rattling about as Marta gets waylaid, slipping and sliding through the big mansion, just having a grand old time not sitting too still, it gives energy to a film living in a more static genre. Unfortunately, the color palette is a little too drained to keep up theres a way to get moody, dreary, and gloomy without sucking it dry. It also drags on a bit too much. That first half needs to be whittled down a bit the camera gives this thing life, but the plotting is at odds with that up until the last 40 minutes or so. 
Still, its a decent mystery to waste some time with.

Harlan Thrombey (Christopher Plummer) é encontrado sem vida em sua mansão. O caso, que à primeira vista parece um suicídio, rapidamente se torna alvo de uma investigação conduzida pelo detetive Benoit Blanc (Daniel Craig). Para desvendar o que realmente aconteceu na noite da tragédia, Blanc precisa interrogar a excêntrica família Thrombey e os funcionários mais próximos do falecido escritor. A partir dessa premissa, aparentemente convencional para um mistério policial, o diretor Rian Johnson se destaca ao estruturar sua narrativa de maneira pouco ortodoxa.
Em vez de guardar suas principais revelações para o clímax, como é comum no gênero, ele as entrega cedo, subvertendo as expectativas e forçando o espectador a questionar cada nova informação apresentada. Isso não significa que o filme renuncia às tradicionais reviravoltas de histórias de investigação. Pelo contrário, elas estão todas ali, mas utilizadas de maneira sagaz, sem truques baratos ou mudanças artificiais de perspectiva para confundir o público. Sabemos mais do que muitos personagens, mas isso não diminui o impacto das surpresas, tornando a experiência tão intrigante quanto divertida.
Johnson utiliza arquétipos bem definidos para apresentar rapidamente cada personagem e suas respectivas motivações, sem que isso pareça raso ou preguiçoso. O primeiro ato é especialmente eficaz ao construir essa dinâmica, servindo-se dos interrogatórios conduzidos pelos investigadores para revelar traços de personalidade e versões contraditórias dos eventos da noite fatal. Dessa forma, cada personagem é introduzido de maneira fluida e envolvente, com o espectador percebendo de imediato suas intenções ocultas e interesses velados.
Além disso, a direção explora com inteligência o casarão onde a trama se desenrola, fazendo da mansão um personagem por si só. Câmeras percorrem corredores estreitos, revelando passagens secretas e detalhes da ambientação que ampliam as possibilidades do crime, contribuindo para o clima de mistério. O roteiro, por sua vez, aproveita a rapidez da revelação inicial para brincar com as suspeitas do público, sem tornar a experiência previsível ou desinteressante. Ao utilizar entrevistas e depoimentos como se estivéssemos assistindo a um documentário, Johnson dá uma nova dinâmica à narrativa, permitindo que o filme explore diferentes perspectivas e manipule nossas expectativas de maneira inteligente.
Outro aspecto interessante é como Entre Facas e Segredos insere discussões sociais dentro da trama sem perder o tom lúdico e envolvente. A história transita por questões de classe e poder, expondo dinâmicas familiares marcadas por hipocrisia, egoísmo e ganância. O roteiro utiliza o contexto do crime para ilustrar disputas entre membros de diferentes estratos sociais, trazendo à tona tópicos como meritocracia, imigração e até mesmo polarização política, tudo isso sem soar panfletário ou deslocado. Assim, enquanto a investigação avança, o filme se aprofunda na psicologia dos personagens e nos pequenos detalhes de suas interações, revelando mais do que apenas um mistério a ser solucionado.
O grande elenco é um dos pontos fortes do filme, com atuações que intensificam ainda mais a trama. Todos os atores conseguem interpretar seus personagens de forma convincente, trazendo mais profundidade à aparente superficialidade de suas figuras. A montagem é bem feita, equilibrando os diálogos com um ritmo rápido, o que faz com que até as cenas mais longas não se tornem cansativas. Se há algum momento um pouco mais devagar, ele não afeta o resultado geral, pois a estrutura do filme mantém o interesse e a tensão em alta. Embora todos o elenco esteja excelente, é impossível não destacar Ana de Armas (como Marta). Sua personagem está constantemente assustada e inquieta, e a atriz transmite isso de maneira eficaz, mantendo o suspense e a emoção da trama. 
Ainda mantendo uma narrativa ágil, mesmo com muitos momentos de diálogo (e talvez eu deva dizer que apenas um ou outro seja um pouco mais chato, mas nada grave), Entre Facas e Segredos é uma demonstração clara do talento de Rian Johnson. O diretor consegue criar uma trama de detetive clássica, misturando elementos contemporâneos de maneira muito eficaz  algo que se fecha de forma inteligente na última cena, consolidando a visão do cineasta sobre os temas que explora. 
Além disso, ele cria personagens interessantes e autênticos. O filme resgata a atração por uma narrativa que, ao invés de se apoiar na profundidade dos personagens, se destaca pela engenhosidade da trama. Ela mantém o espectador envolvido em um labirinto de possibilidades, que revela ambiguidades morais e verdades ocultas sob a fina camada de civilidade. Com uma trama repleta de reviravoltas e um desenvolvimento empolgante e divertido, Entre Facas e Segredos se mostra uma ótima surpresa, sendo perfeito para quem gosta de filmes investigativos com um tom mais leve.

Knives Out is a wonderfully witty, brilliantly biting, and magnificently manic murder mystery, elevated immensely by its extravagant ensemble cast who deliciously deliver the dialogue present in Rian Johnsons stupendous screenplay, in which he once again demonstrates his strong grasp on subverting expectations all while stealthily sneaking in some scathing social commentary.
Within the first 10 minutes of Knives Out, its clear that youre in the hands of a master. Rian Johnson isnt simply an overly ardent fan of murder mysteries - hes an auteur capable of authentically and audaciously applying his affection to his work and lovingly paying homage to the tense tales of times past while simultaneously imbuing his story with courageous creativity and a mordant, modern edge. As Lakeith Stanfields Detective Lieutenant Elliot and Noah Segans Trooper Wagner begin interrogating the Thrombeys in rapid-fire succession - with each interview interwoven and edited to perfection by Bob Ducsay - you find yourself uncontrollably enthralled with the waltz of Johnsons words, hypnotized by every seemingly insignificant detail and each comedically caustic quip. However, just as you begin to settle into a raucous rhythm with these continually charming character interactions, Johnson promptly pulls the rug out from beneath you, subverting the traditional structure of stories like this and relaying a major revelation only at the close of the first act. From then on, you may be wondering where else this plot could possibly go yet, little do you know, Johnson has a surplus of secrets left up his sleeve.
Yes, writer-director Rian Johnson continues his signature expectation subversion tactics with Knives Out, but with this original feature - which is unbeholden to the obligations of fervent franchise fare - hes allowed significantly more fearless freedom to do as he pleases. Its difficult to classify this as a traditional murder mystery by any means, but those elements are certainly front and center, and Johnson gleefully rearranges his puzzle pieces until the films final frame, continuously and cleverly contorting our calculations. While this twisty tale is certainly a terrific treat simply taken at face value, its the powerfully potent political commentary that truly caught me off guard (in the best way). Johnson is understandably aggressive with his opinions on wealth inequality and cultural divides, but he is strikingly subtle when it comes to integrating these ideas into his story. His social critiques never overwhelm or overshadow his core character development or primary plot progression by any means instead, these observations exponentially enhance the narrative at hand, taking what couldve been a diverting yet easily dismissible drama and twisting it into something far more sinister and directly significant to our world today.
Though the oft-advertised ensemble at the center of this story may not be as front and center as one would initially imagine, each actor is utilized perfectly and in satisfying amounts. From Jamie Lee Curtiss icy real estate mogul Linda to Don Johnsons philandering Richard to Michael Shannons wily publishing CEO Walt to Toni Collettes flighty lifestyle guru Joni to Katherine Langfords SJW-inspired liberal arts student Meg, every single member of this commendably captivating cast gets their moment to shine in the spotlight and play a part in this wild web. However, it is Ana de Armas, Daniel Craig, and Chris Evans who stand out the most amongst this stacked showcase of stars. Evans is a devious delight as the roguish Ransom, the black sheep of the Thrombey family with a bone to pick with each and every one of his relatives. Craig too turns in a crackerjack performance as the droll Detective Benoit Blanc, but Ms. Ana de Armas may actually walk away with the film with her effortlessly endearing execution in the role of Marta, the immigrant nurse to the murdered Harlan Thrombey who finds herself embroiled in a complicated controversy far outside of her expertise. Its wholly openhearted and earnest work, and she deserves considerable kudos for anchoring this whole production with her infectious innocence alone.
Id be remiss if I didnt to place some more praise at the feet of the films purposeful production design, which ominously and bewitchingly draws you in to the towering Thrombey Manor from the first frame. Furthermore, Johnsons direction proves just as deft as his writing, capturing the claustrophobia of the manor to intense effect. The film may lose a bit of its urgency as we leave this central location in the second act, but Johnson manages to regain that intensity fairly quickly, and its never lost from there on out.
Knives Out is exactly the kind of brilliantly bold and ravishingly risky filmmaking I adore. It reminds me of why I fell in love with the medium in the first place, and it gives me hope for further freshness from the future. With an utterly enchanting ensemble and a sharp, stellar screenplay, this murder mystery is a mighty marvel.

This is a twisted web, and we are not finished untangling it, not yet.
Crackling with a spirited originality made all the more pleasurable by the utter adoration for the narratives influences, Rian Johnsons Knives Out is a whodunit for the ages an irresistible, topical, and devilishly entertaining stroke of taut brilliance whose Christie-inspired roots find themselves simultaneously revered and rejuvenated with equal shades of Hitchcock, Columbo, and the filmmakers genre-melding aptitude. The grasp on the assorted threads in play and their achievement by means of both frame and talent is genuinely extraordinary, making this mysterious matter of murder as tireless as it is faultless. 
Johnsons expertise on the page and through the lens cannot be understated, abilities only bolstered by David Cranks jaw-dropping production design, the immaculate compositions of cinematographer Steve Yedlin, Bob Ducsays tight editing, and an expectedly essential score from Nathan Johnson. Yet one mustnt forget the superb cast at the core of the thorny yarn itself. Daniel Craig delivers a potentially career-best turn as the Poirot-esque gentleman of Southern hospitality and unrivaled deductive genius, Detective Benoit Blanc. Accompanying the renowned private investigator is a cavalcade of unsuspecting unfortunates and apparent asshats, the outstanding likes of which include Ana de Armas, Chris Evans, Jamie Lee Curtis, Don Johnson, Toni Collette, Michael Shannon, and Christopher Plummer. Every performer absolutely revels in the vibrant material at hand, and each are dressed to a T thanks to Jenny Eagans costuming .
Knives Out brims with an evident precision and sincerity indicative of the masterful artists at work. The film is yet another exceptional chapter for Rian Johnson, one that may be his most accomplished feat to date. Its a nimble, dynamic balancing act that managed to exceed every one of my already astronomical expectations. An assured gem of the genre and quite possibly the best slice of the silver screen that Ive seen all year. Suspenseful, swift, uproarious, and razor-sharp.

To my surprise the killer is revealed fairly early into the plot so instead of a Who did it? it turns into a How are they gonna get away with it? exemplifying Benoit Blancs whole thesis about this case


It was a strange case from the start. A case with a hole at its center. A doughnut.
The same could be said about The Thrombeys, they may not be killers but they sure are a group of people with a hole at the center of their beings, blinded by the commodity of their own privilege since birth. They may pretend to care about the less fortunate but its only until the tables are turned on them, the best example being the latina nurse of their late fathergrandfather whom most of them couldnt even bother to learn which country she comes from. Its social and political commentary was one of its most unexpected qualities yet its also probably my favorite (well, that and the comedy), they never out right name drop him but theres something poetically ironic about a scene where multiple characters are discussing Trmps mantra about inmigrants and were STILL having these exact same conversations almost 7 YEARS after its release .

This cast is STACKED, all bringing their A game despite most of them being relegated to just side characters although, they all felt super well developed and fleshed out. The MVP for me will always be my queen Toni Collette playing a vapid, performative influencer, girl boss mother , honestly a lot of comedic moments came from just her performance and line delivery. One thing that i love is that since this is a whodunnit youd think wed follow the detective for most of the runtime right? But no, Rian Johnson turns that expectation on its head and instead we follow this random character named Marta, as a mexican woman it wasnt hard for me to relate to her position and its very easy to empathize with her situation since from the beginning it is VERY CLEAR that shes at the mercy of this rich family. I also love that her values and demeanor is the exact opposite of The Thrombeys and that her actions throughout are the reason why the ending is as poignant and satisfying as it is (although i cant discuss why here as it would veer into spoiler territory).
I hadnt seen Ana de Armas anywhere prior to this film and truth to be told, i havent seen her much anywhere else afterwards (still need to watch Blade Runner 2049 and Ballerina ) so this is my favorite performance of hers. Likewise i know Daniel Craig got his breakthrough playing James Bond in the modern 007 movies but me personally, Benoit Blanc is my favorite character of his . Even though we dont really learn much about him in this first installment and he essentially works as a secondary protagonist in his own story you really get the sense that hes a VERY good detective (mainly during the last 30 minutes) and it doesnt take long before you start warming up to him since hes not afraid to be a little goofy, i love his accent , it almost feels like a combination of Craigs own british accent and a southern one for me. Also peep Chris Evans in one of his few good roles post MCUEndgame . 
Another thing i dont see people talk about often enough is that Rian Johnson was able to come back from the disaster that was The Last Jedi, a movie that shouldve (and probably wouldve) ruined his career had he not came back with a bang just 2 years later and delivered us this Oscar worthy script . I could go on and on about my love for this first entree for days, about how it has a lot of rewatch value, theres SO MANY details you dont notice upon first viewing with my favorite being Richard throwing Harlans baseball out the window being the sole reason why Linda eventually finds out about his affair when thats the only thing he was trying to hide from her and everyone else .

This is one of those rare cases where im glad an original idea spawned sequels, while i wouldve been satisfied had Benoit Blancs story ended here i do think there was more room to expand upon this universe so im glad we live in a timeline where we get more of this movies fairly regularly although i dont think this next installment is as strong as this one...

I forget just how insanely good Knives Out is, the way it operates as a meta whodunnit is brilliant. Johnson takes the deep familiarity with the mystery genre and uses that knowledge against us, and him showing the supposed truth of the killing within the first act, always tricks me. Its genius honestly, and the tension immediately shifts from who, to will she be caught? Freeing up the rest of the film to focus on character, class commentary, and a second, deeper mystery. 
Johnson still populates the film with exaggerated, recognizable tropes the suspicious family, the reading of the will, the eccentric detective, the dark mansion. But by centering the story on the genuinely kind and moral Marta Cabrera(the good immigrant nurse who cannot lie without spewing her guts), he replaces the cold, calculated detective logic with a messy, yet extremely human empathy. Its this shift that truly gives it a freshness, unbelievable work honestly.
The script structure is meticulously crafted with it essentially acting as a double-sided sword of plotting. Theres an outstanding balance to the narrative layers first seeing the night of Harlans death through the familys unreliable testimonies, then through Martas accurate but incomplete perspective, and finally through the perspective of Benoit Blanc piecing together the true, third layer of events. Its extremely rewarding and never falters when it comes to entertainment and keeping me engaged bell to bell. Not only that but the script manages to hide crucial information in plain sight without ever deceiving the audience, but rather just cleverly misdirecting our attention, its truly impressive screenwriting.
The commentary isnt just in the plot either, it embodies itself within the characters. The entire Thrombey family serves as a satire on generational wealth and entitlement, its honestly hilarious how they navigate the death of their late father and the change of will. The acting from the ensemble is incredible, the family dynamics were nailed and they create some wow moments throughout. The level of acting, when you look at the cast list, is to be expected, its still outstanding though.  
Especially that climax, with around 30 minutes to go I particularly lock in. That three-way dynamic between spoiler, Benoit Blanc, and Marta, is in my eyes the films best moments. Its not only Daniel Craig acting his heart out, but its a ridiculous narrative payoff that really does floor me every time, not to mention its absolutely hilarious when Marta chucks up last nights dinner, comedy gold. 
Daniel Craig as Benoit Blanc is as close to perfection as character casting can get, you can tell he loves the role. The American Southern twang is cherry on top, and not only is he stylish and well dressed at all times, but he carries a flamboyant, humorous, and delightfully eccentric manner to his highly theatricality and keenly observant character. 
Really enjoy the work of Ana de Armas in this film aswell, she has a purity and serves as the glue so well, her best role. This may be the only role post Cap that Chris Evans has actually sold me on, the rest of his work post MCU has been fairly dire. 
The Thrombey estate is such a stunning location and perfect setting for such a mystery. It acts as a character in itself, perfectly embodying the films themes. Its richly detailed with the house becoming a labyrinthine a cluttered museum of wealth, full of unsettling artifacts, taxidermy, and secret passages.
Its full of depth in terms of props and lush furniture, meticulously arranged and beautifully gathered to best appease the viewers, it manages to always have outstanding blocking and perfect framing, really a well shot film. Like that final image Marta standing on the balcony, serenely sipping from Harlans mug, looking down at the defeated and entitled Thrombey family outside, is such clever imagery, its the ultimate poetic justice. 
Its been a couple of years since I last visited Knives Out but its certainly a film that rewards intellectual engagement without sacrificing entertainment, making it a truly enjoyable rewatch. As even 6 maybe 7 viewings later Im still surprised by the twists and turns, a piece of cinematic gold that looks good, flows beautifully and maintains a high level of acting across the board, such an enjoyable film.

Knives Out may rely on every Agatha Christie-esque cliche in the book, but how it utilises those cliches is what makes it stand out.

Às vésperas de se aposentar como 007, Daniel Craig enche Entre Facas e Segredos de sabor e diversão, no papel clássico do detetive que desvenda qualquer mistério
Enquanto os dois policiais interrogam os familiares do morto, o detetive particular Benoit Blanc se mantém em silêncio, oculto nas sombras  mas, no exato momento em que a história do depoente atinge o que Benoit julga ser uma mentira crucial, ele soa uma nota aguda no piano ao seu lado. Para cada interrogado, uma única nota, econômica e precisa, em perfeito contraste com os modos e o fraseado floridos com que Benoit então se apresenta, tendo já tirado o rebolado à filha mandona (Jamie Lee Curtis) do falecido, ao marido dela (Don Johnson), à nora viúva (Toni Collette) e ao filho incompetente (Michael Shannon). Só não passam pelo ritual o neto Ransom (Chris Evans), porque ele é temperamental e não quis dar as caras, e Marta (Ana de Armas), a tímida e meiga enfermeira do finado autor de mistério Harlan Thrombey (Christopher Plummer), porque é sabido que ela sofre de uma aflição peculiar se uma mentira passa pela boca de Marta, esta é imediatamente seguida pelo conteúdo do estômago da jovem. A morte de Thrombey foi declarada suicídio, mas Benoit tem lá suas dúvidas sobre o veredicto do legista  mais ainda porque o escritor era milionário e seus parentes são, sem exceção, bajuladores e aproveitadores. Não pode haver ferramenta melhor para um investigador do que uma pessoa como Marta, fisiologicamente incapaz de dizer inverdades, e Benoit pretende tirar tanto partido dela quanto possível.
Tirar todo o partido de uma boa oportunidade é também o que faz Daniel Craig em Entre Facas e Segredos (Knives Out, Estados Unidos, 2019). A alguns meses de estrelar sua derradeira aventura no papel de James Bond em 007  Sem Tempo para Morrer, o ator inglês aproveita para lembrar ao público que nem de longe está em fim de carreira. Ao contrário, pode muito bem estar no começo de uma nova parceria com um personagem excelente. Craig compõe Benoit Blanc como a sua própria e colorida versão de um cavalheiro sulista tão arguto que nem se incomoda em ser subestimado, e que usa os ternos afetados de tweed e o sotaque rebuscado (um ótimo truque, já que Craig não tem grande ouvido para falas regionais) para criar a imagem de alguém que se acha mais do que é e assim induzir os adversários a baixar a guarda. Saboroso, divertido e repleto de notas calorosas, seu desempenho além disso se casa à perfeição com o da cubana Ana de Armas, de Bata Antes de Entrar e Blade Runner 2049  e, mais ao ponto, também de Sem Tempo para Morrer, em que ela voltará a contracenar com Craig como o primeiro nome feminino do elenco.
O verdadeiro engenho por trás das reviravoltas precisas de Facas e Segredos, entretanto, é o do diretor e roteirista Rian Johnson, que, às vésperas da estreia do capítulo final de Star Wars, troca as impressões dúbias deixadas por seu comando do episódio anterior da saga por um novo e convidativo cartão de visita. Em sua ainda enxuta carreira, Johnson se dividiu entre o crime ou o noir (A Ponta de um Crime, de 2005, e Vigaristas, de 2008) e a ficção com ação (Looper  Assassinos do Futuro, de 2012, e Star Wars Os Últimos Jedi, de 2017). Aqui, porém, ele para de flertar com gêneros para investir tudo no whodunit (quem matou) à moda de Agatha Christie. Parte homenagem, parte sátira respeitosa mas inteligente, o filme é inteiro um acerto.

Knives Out is a mystery film written, co-produced and directed by Rian Johnson. Its the 1st installment in the Knives Out film series.
This is one of those movies where everything comes together perfectly Every line of dialogue is smart and layered. Every actor is perfectly cast and an utter delight to watch. Every gag is hilarious and hits its target. Every little detail is important and clever.
Knives Out is a masterfully, meticulously and beautifully constructed old-school murder mystery, with layers upon layers of conflicting viewpoints the audience can peel away gleefully while watching. Since every detail matters, watching it only once wont be enough - you just have to rewatch the movie when you finally know the real story, and you will be just as amazed how Johnson crafted this ingenious masterpiece.
Knives Out is also incredibly funny and features biting satire, never loses momentum and never stops to be entertaining, with the next twist always just around the corner. Just like a classic Agatha Christie whodunit, it features an illustrious ensemble cast of suspects, which includes Chris Evans, Jamie Lee Curtis, Don Johnson, Toni Collette, Michael Shannon, and more, all delivering amazing performances.
Then, theres Daniel Craigs debonaire super sleuth Benoit Blanc, a wonderful creation, and you can see just how much fun Craig has with bringing this character to life. And yet, at the end of the day, this is foremost Ana de Armas movie, who delivers a standout performance - no small feat with a stellar cast like this all around her.
In conclusion, Knives Out is a hilarious, flawless and old-fashioned whodunit which both honors and spoofs genre tropes, meticulously and masterfully constructed, with a smart and clever screenplay, as well as stellar performances by its brillant cast.

Rian Johnsons Knives Out (2019) is proof that the whodunit genre can be done with excellence. Clearly, he did his research. Knives Out is like the best Agatha Christie films rebooted for a new generation. The production team found a Mansion in Massachusetts, assembled an A-list cast, and chose Daniel Craig as Benoit Blanc (The modern PoirotDetective). With the aforementioned formula and a 40 million budget, Knives Out Worldwide Gross was 311,605,581. 
The cinematography by Steve Yedlin (who is Rian Johnsons regular DP) served as the eyes that eventually revealed the true series of events that lead to the murder of Harlan Thrombey (Christopher Plummer, RIP). However, this is an editors film and Bob Ducsay assembled the footage with precision and accuracy. 
Daniel Craigs accent was hilarious yet, effective and Ana de Armas as Marta Cabrera were the perfect match for the suspect and the detective. Frank Oz had a great cameo as the Thrombeys Will and Probate attorney. Nathan Johnsons score keeps the tensionsuspense exactly in the zone until the big reveal. We are excited for the release of Knives Out 2 and 3. Rian Johnson has a Midas touch when it comes to writing who-dun-it scripts and scripts in general.

Johnson revives the Agatha Christie spirit but updates it with a whip-smart script, political satire, and a cast clearly having the time of their lives. The film is the proof that cleverness doesnt have to come at the cost of entertainment.
Daniel Craigs Benoit Blanc becomes instantly iconic, a detective as theatrical as he is brilliant, deploying monologues with a Foghorn-Leghorn drawl that shouldnt work but absolutely does. 
Ana de Armas is the emotional anchor, delivering warmth and sincerity that grounds the absurdity swirling around her.
Johnson and cinematographer Steve Yedlin craft a modern film that feels classic  mahogany-soaked rooms, dramatic shadows, and a mansion filled with eccentric props (including that unforgettable knife wheel) create instant atmosphere. 
What truly makes Knives Out stand out is Johnsons narrative confidence. Instead of a traditional reveal at the end, he rearranges the genre showing us how the murder supposedly happened early on, then turning the rest of the movie into a twisty, character-driven unraveling.

I gotta be careful writing this. Yesterday I told Sebastian that I expected to like the movie more than Raymond and less than everybody else, and now I have to explain why that ended up being the case without losing anyones respect.
I love a good whodunnit. Ill eat up any whodunnit movie or tv show or random episode of a sitcom that crosses my path (except for s4e7 of Its Always Sunny, which is just bad). That said, I dont go out of my way to consume whodunnits. Ive only read one Agatha Christie novel, and Im sure you can guess which one it is. Even looking back at Scooby Doo, my memory fails to emphasize the actual structure of the mysteries and instead opts to remind me how spooky Zombie Island was or how cool the Hex Girls were or how appetizing those fucking sandwiches looked. Im digressing. My point isnt that I like Scooby Doo (though I do), its that Im no whodunnit aficionado, so do with that credibility what you will.
Knives Out I think is mostly successful on a narrative level. Theres something about the reveal in all these stories that seems to cover up all your potential discrepancies with the truth of the crime, to the point where you cant even remember them anymore and feel like youd be nitpicking if you went back to try and find them. After all, if theyre not important enough to remember, how detrimental could they be? In this case, however, some big ones poked through, namely a certain convenience regarding Martas digestive system that a surprising amount of the story hinges on. Its the sort of thing where you can rationalize that its one thing and shouldnt bring down the story, but then you realize how pivotal it is to the events playing out the way they do, and you dont really know what to think anymore.
Regarding the Rian Johnson-ism of the film, there is certainly something to be said for a wishy-washiness of subversion, that while on one hand you think youre getting a new type of story in a genre that seems tired, on the other hand in order to deliver something narratively satisfying the film then has to revert to genre staples, but I dont think its the sacrilegious practice others may feel it is. At the very least, it made for a story that never lost my interest, but I feel like whodunnits more so than other genres have a quality that stales each story the more one consumes, and the fun I had with this film is more a testament to my lack of whodunnit experience. Though, seeing that written down, it doesnt seem like such a bad thing.
What felt a little more wishy-washy was the look of the film, often attempting to capture the beautiful pastiche of the genre while simultaneously providing something sleek and sharp. Id go so far as to say it looks perhaps too sharp. DP Steve Yedlin knows more about image processing than I ever will and I admire his ideas and innovations, but this film looks so processed by cutting-edge technology that the whacky whodunnit zooms and stretches with such a digital finish give the aesthetic a sense of parody rather than subversion or elevation. Maybe its for this specific reason that other elements of the story then felt parodical, or maybe its just the farcical nature of the genre. Again, thats not my area of expertise. I do selfishly wish deep down that this film had the look of an Anna Biller film, but I cant fault anyone for that.
I guess what probably bothered me the most about this film, which I should remind you I like, is the commentary, which I found to be a bit too on-the-nose and surface-level. I think a plot beat in which most of the characters become hypocrites is supposed to suggest another layer to their personalities, but when they nearly all change behavior in the same way, it feels one-note and doesnt leave much room for nuance within their hypocrisy. Little did I know the one-off Hamilton reference Immigrants! We get the job done! would cover half the thematic ground this movie treads.
But maybe Im missing something. Maybe my third eye isnt quite open and further viewings will yield more to chew on. At the very least, I think they would further provide me a fun 2 hours, but I wish I could say a little more. Maybe Im being too hard on the film so as to analytically keep up with people I respect, but theres no way for me to distance myself from myself to confirm or deny that. I guess the note Ill leave this on is that most of the performances are solid and Ana de Armas is my favorite. Favorite what, you ask? I dont know, but shes my favorite.

The main attraction here isnt necessarily the central mystery - its certainly admirable how many elements Johnson manages to juggle in that regard, but in the end, it doesnt really subvert as many expectations as it thinks it does. It wraps up in fairly predictable fashion, in my opinion. The main attraction is, as expected, the incredible cast, which tears into the material with aplomb and hams it up like theres no tomorrow. Shannon is the early star, but Craig slowly but surely takes over the film with his silly accent, Bond suaveness, and eccentric comedic edge. He and de Armas are great foils for each other, and their dynamic develops in an incredibly entertaining way. Honestly, everyone in the cast deserves a shoutout in some regard. 
Occasionally the film struggles to keep things moving, as it has to consistently utilize flashbacks, shift gears, and explain things to the audience. But like any good whodunit, it makes up for some of those issues with a distinct visual style and an understanding that being over the top isnt necessarily a bad thing. Johnson brings technique, talent, and even a distinctly political energy behind the camera, and he lets the cast and production design play off of each other until youre drawn into his world. Its a lot of fun, but also a really lovely production and a great excuse to get all these actors in the same room to be assholes to each other. Its nice to know that we can still not take ourselves too seriously during Fall Prestige Movie Season.

The atmosphere of Mamma Mia does not just serve as a backdrop, it is a character in its own right . The film is bathed in a festive vibe and sunny nostalgia. The joy of life is so contagious. The emotional heart does not lie so much in the quest for the father or the upcoming wedding, but in the relationship between Donna and her friends, as well as between Donna and her daughter. The direction refuses to isolate the women it frames them together, often in constant motion, whether they are running on the docks or jumping on the beds. 
Donna is trapped by her past choices and the management of her crumbling hotel. The establishment itself is a metaphor for her state of mind charming but in ruins, in need of repairs 
The plot moves forward through the music. The dialogues serve as transitions, often short and light, to bring on the next song. While Sophies quest for identity serves as a common thread, the script shines above all in its ability to deal with deep themes such as aging, regrets, and lost youth love.
Meryl Streep is so incredible, as always. The script is a bit light, but that is not important in itself. The songs are not mere interludes, they express the unspoken thoughts of the characters, and the choice of tracks resonates perfectly with the narrative arcs. in english A musical that feels like popping champagne in the middle of summer light, fizzy, and impossible to take seriously  which, ironically, is exactly what makes it so irresistible. Phyllida Lloyd embraces kitsch with near-religious devotion and crafts something rare cinema that isnt afraid to be purely, unapologetically joyful. Nothing here tries to be cool, restrained, or tasteful. Its all about excess, glitter, sun-drenched choreography, and, of course, ABBA  lots of ABBA.
Whats most impressive is how this orchestrated chaos never falls apart. Theres a genuine emotional thread running through the musical numbers  a tenderness in how the film confronts aging, revisiting the past, and reimagining what family can be. And it does all this without ever missing a beat.
Sure, the vocals falter at times, and the melodrama stumbles in others, but it would be heresy to ask for perfection from a film whose greatest strength is inviting us to let go. Mamma Mia! is pop catharsis  ridiculous, freeing, and all the more authentic because of it.

Phyllida Lloyd abraça o kitsch com uma devoção quase religiosa e cria algo raro um cinema que não tem vergonha de ser puramente feliz. Nada aqui tenta ser cool, contido ou bem comportado. É tudo sobre exagero, glitter, coreografias ensolaradas e, claro, ABBA  muito ABBA.
O mais impressionante é que esse caos orquestrado não desmorona. Há um fio emocional sincero costurando os números musicais, uma ternura na maneira como o filme encara envelhecer, revisitar o passado e redefinir família. E tudo isso sem jamais perder o ritmo da festa. É como se o Mediterrâneo inteiro estivesse dançando com você.
Sim, a voz falha em alguns momentos, o melodrama escorrega em outros, mas seria uma heresia exigir perfeição de um filme cuja maior qualidade é justamente nos convidar a baixar a guarda. Mamma Mia! é cinema como catarse pop  ridículo, libertador, e por isso mesmo profundamente autêntico.
