Midsommar is a 2019 cult horror film written and directed by Ari Aster and starring Florence Pugh, Jack Reynor, William Jackson Harper, Vilhelm Blomgren, Ellora Torchia, Archie Madekwe, and Will Poulter. Midsommar has a certified fresh score of 83 on Rotten Tomatoes and grossed 47.90 million worldwide on a 9 million budget. The story follows a group of friends who travel to Sweden for a once in 90 year festival however as they arrive they soon find themselves in the midst of a pagan cult group. 
Midsommar is an admirably strange film, that thematically muddled me while still leaving me curious throughout and is from the talented filmmaker Ari Aster who allows his ambitions to take over and engage the audience with the beautiful arthouse look of the film while unfortunately leaving other qualities of the film lacking. Aster has concocted a weird mixture of dread and humour that leaves the audience on the edge of their seat while also leaving you in shock and confused at what youd just seen occur. Asters script for Midsommar is at times both horrible and beautiful which I dug at times and didnt at others. The art direction is phenomenal in providing a floral, candy coloured, nightmare world that mixes with the music incredibly well. 
Shot by shot Ari Aster constructs a film that is top notch in terms of visuals yet sadly lacks in many other areas. Im unsure whether the twists the storyline takes were meant to surprise me but I managed to predict many of them straight away, this took quite a lot out of the movie for me as I wanted to be surprised by the movie and ultimately many of the twists and turns didnt surprise me and left me quite disappointed. This is undoubtedly the style that modern day horror movies are trying to achieve with its great cinematography and beautiful bright scenery but yet, it doesnt work that well for me compared to other horror movies from the past. The horror element is extremely lacking as Midsommar is an eerie film but it just isnt a scary film as theres not a single horrifying moment for me. I hate to bash films like this because I get what he was going for and I respect that, Midsommar does truly have stunning cinematography but whilst I did enjoy certain moments, on the whole it just felt far to slow for me to enjoy a lot as it was very drawn out and lacked substance especially in the first hour. However, after the first hour the film does pick up a bit and does become slightly more enjoyable for the proceeding hour and a half, but for me, that doesnt make the first painfully slow hour any better unfortunately. 
The cast all give good enough performances, Florence Pugh is mostly a joy to watch and gives a great performance as Dani and Jack Reynor has a great screen presence throughout and again gives a great performance. The rest of the cast all do a good enough job as well but theres nothing phenomenal about them but they all are uniquely interesting on their own terms and do provide some good moments throughout. I dont quite know how to describe my experience of watching this film, Midsommar worked in certain aspects but ultimately failed in others. Unfortunaly it didnt quite pull me in as much as I thought it would and therefore left me slightly disappointed by the final theatrical cut, lets hope when I eventually watch the directors cut Ill enjoy this more. Midsommar is a film I feel would have been better suited to having a shorter runtime as it just feels too drawn out at times and didnt engage me as much as I wanted it too. 
Midsommar is Ari Asters strange, audacious attempt at creating a uniquely styled horror movie, whilst it does fall flat at times for me, I can appreciate the audacity it must have took to create something like this. Whilst it this film isnt exactly my cup of tea, I can see why others might love it whilst also seeing how people can hate it. Its weird and wonderfully created, eerily shocking and extravagant in its storytelling and a uniquely strange movie that both repelled me and drew me further into it the more I watched. Whilst I didnt love it, I cant exactly say I hated it either as it left me with a very mixed viewing experience. By all means this is a good film. Just not for me.

Through the mid to late 2010s, one of the juiciest topics of discourse in horror circles was centered around a trio of filmmakers crowned by many as the contemporary masters of horror Robert Eggers, Jordan Peele and the reason Im here right now, Ari Aster. While less regarded in 2026 (happy almost new years!) strictly as a horror auteur, especially with my personal favorite film of this year, Eddington, having helped change the way Aster is viewed as an artist, Id been rather guiltily missing the only other outright horror flick in his brief filmography, 2019s Midsommar. 
Surprise, I absolutely adore it. 
As is the standard now when Im engaging with an Aster production (even Beau is Afraid to some degree) there are just so many beautiful filmmaking touchstones to marvel and gawk at. Every shot feels careful, and methodical. Multiple bleak, yet clever storytelling devices are at play. Each character works. Everything feels so carefully laid out, its so easy to fall into its hypnotic and psychedelic world. 
Seemingly a companion film to Hereditary,  family trauma, grief, and psychological dread through slow-burn tension and violent, unsettling imagery lead as Midsommars primary horror devices. But while Hereditary is a dark and claustrophobic journey, Midsommars is a brightly lit, daytime horror whose landscape is as much of a character as any living being. And just as much tense terror was conjured up in me. Good lord the gravity of that opening was straight up horrific. 
Slathered on top of Midsommars visual heights, its score works perfectly to prop up an intoxicating atmosphere. Tonally opposing and even barren through some of its most brutal horror sequences, the overall sound design is yet another layer of a unique horror film that has me head over heels. 
Ari Aster may be as divisive a director working today, but dammit. Im all in again.

Midsommar. 2019. Directed by Ari Aster.
Midsommar (2019) is a multigenre (drama, horror, mystery, thriller) A24 produced masterclass in filmmaking. We wouldnt expect anything less from horror screenplay master Ari Aster. Every chapter hits the correct notes and this folk horror film that plays like a perfect symphony of distress that meets the highest levels of anxiety. As the films bounces back and forth between drama and suspense like a professional tennis match, the audience may begin to feel that this isnt the average graduate student trip to Sweden. This is our third viewing of the film and our second viewing of the directors cut and it is just as visceral as the first time. 
Dani (Florence Pugh) and Christian (Jack Reynor) are taking a trip to Sweden so Christian can make a concrete decision on his thesis topic. Their trip happens to be taking place during midsummer which corresponds with a Scandinavian pagan cults Midsommar festival which occurs every 90 years. Although they are joined by several others, the film primarily revolves around Dani and Christians strained relationship. Dani has lost her family due to her sisters psychotic murder-suicide of Danis entire family. So, this puts a great deal of stress on Christian and his fellow graduate student friends. In fact, a great deal of melodrama unfolds. Dani and the groups lack of awareness of the Hårga and its rituals leads to a multitude of surprises and gasps. As Ari displays many elder Futhark runes with deep and complex meanings (just as The Northman (2022)), the cult is well aware of their ancient rituals and are in need of new genetics to prevent inbreeding. 
With regard to screenplay, direction, composition, and cinematography, this film is top tier. Midsommar had a 9 million dollar budget and grossed 47 million dollars worldwide. This is a testament to the aforementioned talent. The screenplay is multilayered and weaves like a well oiled machine in and out of many genres making it attractive to a larger demographic. In other words, it isnt just a gore filled horror film. Nevertheless, it is filled with horrific scenes. Asters direction is unparalleled in this world. Many films like The Shining (1980) directed by Stanley Kubrick exhibit the same level of horror felt by a family that travels to a strange state and hotel. The Haxan Cloak composed the score that highlighted the folk cult nature and showcased the murder suicide with such tragic mastery. In addition, many other rituals are elevated by their subtle yet profound vocals and instrumentals. The cinematography by Pawel Pogorzelski (Hereditary, Midsommar, and Nobody) can be tight depending on the scene. For example, the murder suicide relies on a tracking zoom whereas the outdoor ritual scenes involve panning zooms and booms. 
Overall, Midsommar left us with a sense of closure and despair. This was our third viewing and we were just as in awe of Asters skills as we were the first time. Midsommar is not for everyone but, apparently millions have seen it. Just like the classic The Wicker Man (1973), Midsommar takes the audience blindly into a cult dominated world while concurrently taking us on a journey in which many characters will not return.

Going into this completely blind and only knowing the basic premise based off of trailers, Midsommar at first didnt feel like it would do anything for me. Combine the overdone happy secluded medieval cult trope with the director Ari Aster, who last made the movie Hereditary which I didnt think that much about - and I was convinced this would be just another attempt at a Wicker Man, but with more modern and mature themes. Boy, was I in for a shock. Much like how the video game The Last of Us takes a cliched background plot, but turns it into something special based entirely on how its told - Midsommar for me does the same thing but for movies - except instead of a zombie apocalypse, weve got a cult. And damn, is it a frightening one. Sex, gore, screaming, chanting, drugs, it has it all - and doesnt shy away from being graphic and disturbing.

This movie not only explores the ideas surrounding a cult in a visual way Ive never seen before - including many fantastically clever shots with mirrors and how certain characters only seem to act a certain way when visibly standing in them, or how whenever some characters start being spiked with hallucinogenic drug water, the entire screen starts coming to life with waving trees and disgusting breathing flowers - but the journey that our main character Dani takes from the start to the horrifically morbid ending is a level of tragedy I was surprised to see. This film isnt about the sickening cult that is being studied by Danis boyfriends mates, as much as it is about how easy it is to indoctrinate vulnerable people into ideologies that - given enough positive meaning and drug-fuelled violence - almost start to make sense. For her entire life, Dani has essentially been subconsciously conditioned to the lifestyle of a cult, leading to a smooth and uncomfortable build up of her eventually falling victim to the worst kind of cult of all - which unfortunately, is the only one that has given her any positivity and love for many years. She starts off in this movie with her bipolar sister believing that suicide and parental murder is something she must do to save them (cultish), following on to her mentally abusive and manipulative boyfriend that is to cowardly to leave her, yet constantly treats her like shit for the promise of sex and security (cultish), and by the end, shes stranded in a foreign country with a group of insane zealots that put her on a pedestal, slowly kill everything she thought she loved, and eventually convert her as she gets convinced that burning alive the true evil of the world was a logical and justifiable thing to do (obviously, cultish).

Dani is a brilliant and sympathetic character expertly played by Florence Pugh who carries the movie alone as it is, but the supporting cast are equally believable and brilliantly acted, especially when it comes to reacting to whats going on around them. The cinematography captures the pure isolation yet natural beauty of the environment perfectly. The villagers are all demented and unsettling, yet welcoming and warm. The amount of show-dont-tell details surrounding the belief systems of the cult and the implied backstories of all the people that are a part of it are fantastic (women being separated and put to work, while being spoken to last in a group and having their names forgotten like Dani when she first arrives, or how most of the people there seem to have broken family backgrounds and never seem 100 happy to be stuck there for fear of death). The score is unnerving and compliments the trippy visuals brilliantly. Midsommar really caught me off guard.

The only things I can really knock it for are the fact that it is ultimately an overdone setting and premise with nothing new being added to how the cult operates or what they do to new arrivals, making it slightly predictable, and to be honest I didnt really understand the significance placed on the scenes involving The Oracle. Sure, I understand his place in the cult, but those brief scenes focusing on him made me feel like he was more important that what was being let on.....and I couldnt find any meaning in it. I dont think he added anything for how often hes brought up.

Either way, Midsommar is ace. It unnerved me, saddened me, fucked with my brain, and I will never look at the maypole dancing I did in primary school ever again.

Em 2018, Ari Aster escreveu e dirigiu Hereditário, uma obra que trazia um drama familiar envolto em uma seita satânica. Em Midsommar, a ideia se assemelha. Dani, interpretada muito bem por Florence Pugh, é uma garota depressiva e que tem constantes ataques de pânico, muitos deles ocasionados por mensagens suicidas de sua irmã. Seu namorado, Christian, não aguenta mais ela, mas também não a liberta. Ele não a apoia, não lhe entende, não lhe dá suporte e ainda fala mal dela para seus amigos Pelle, Mark e Josh. 
Um dia sua irmã mata os pais e se mata, abalando completamente Dani e deixando por um fio o resto que lhe sobra de sanidade. Christian a convida para uma viagem a Suécia, a convite de Pelle, que os convida para visitar sua comunidade isolada cheia de pessoas excêntricas. A cada 90 anos eles realizam um festival para celebrar o solstício de verão. 
Se Hereditário utilizava do luto e até de doenças mentais em suas analogias, Midsommar em partes também explora o luto da protagonista, mas principalmente sua dependência emocional e a depressão que a atinge. É impressionante como a seita do filme, que eles chamam de Harga, serve de pano de fundo para fazer as metáforas para os problemas de Dani, onde tudo o que ela busca é acolhimento e tudo que a seita lhe oferece é exatamente isso. Desde que os personagens chegam ao lugar, lhe são oferecidos substâncias alucinógenos, tudo para manipular a mente das pessoas, e isso pode ser subentendido como um relacionamento abusivo pode ser silencioso onde as coisas vão acontecendo e você mal percebe, na maioria das vezes tenta buscar justificativas plausíveis para aquilo  a comunidade tem hábitos incomuns, como achar que a vida só vai até os 72, e messe momento, esses mais velhos escolhem voluntariamente se sacrificar. Eles tentam explicar isso como cultural, fazendo com que os visitantes normalizem isso. 
O fato de todo mundo estar sob efeitos de substâncias alucinógenas ajudam a confundir o telespectador também, até porque adentramos naquela viagem dos personagens, que em vários momentos se pensa estão fazendo porque querem ou por estarem chapados?. Mas isso também é responsável por evidenciar a vulnerabilidade de seus sentimentos e também deixar eles ainda mais vulneráveis as condutas da seita. 
É um desenvolvimento extremamente lento, com uma construção demasiadamente demorada que quer construir tijolo por tijolo,m. Fica o questionamento, precisava? Se parar para pensar tem muita cena que não fazia a menor diferença ou cenas que demoram muito tempo e que não mudaria nada se tivessem um tempo menor. Ele explora todos os detalhes daquela comunidade e cada desenho que aparece dá pistas sobre os hábitos da seita, mas dificilmente dá para captar isso vendo o filme uma vez, sendo isso muito interessante e bem pensando no roteiro.
Apesar da longa duração, prende a atenção pela sensação de não saber o que está acontecendo. O gore aqui é diferente por causa da áurea do filme todo colorido, todo mundo usando roupas brancas, tudo acontecendo durante o dia. 
O final carrega muitos simbolismos, trazendo a libertação de Dani, seja dos seus traumas ou seja do seu namoro tóxico, sua nova identidade dentro daquela comunidade que a acolheu, dando fim em seu passado doloroso.

I wasnt a huge fan of Hereditary, which struck me as a mishmash of at least three or four better horror films, but Midsommar is a step up for director Ari Aster in just about every way. For starters, it only obviously rips off just one horror classic The Wicker Man. Midsommar is a flawed film for sure but it reaches heights that few recent horror films have.
I appreciate the glacial pace of Midsommar and the restraint to have just a few truly horrific moments, which Aster maximises well. Ari Aster knows how to terrify the audience but I often wonder why he makes horror films as he never really unifies the themes and the horror within his films. Hereditary was about grief and spiritual horror, but they remained distinct. Midsommar is about problematic relationships and folk horror, but one doesnt necessarily compliment the other. What about pagan rituals reflects the relationship within the film? Hes made two different films within both his projects, a horror film and a drama, and the connecting tissue lacks. Midsommar succeeds more than Hereditary however, because Aster keeps both aspects present and together from the beginning. Though its redeemed somewhat by its sadly limited number of striking fantasy sequences, it saddens me to have to be the one to point out that Pans Labyrinths portrayals of its twin themes of childhood and human cruelty are about as nuanced and insightful as Crashs portrayal of racism.
Truthfully, Im in disbelief that I didnt love this. Its almost impossible for me to feel relatively indifferent to such an original cinematic concoction, especially when its loaded to the brim with gorgeous cinematography and astoundingly creative and well-acted otherworldly creatures, and yet thats how much the lack of depth bothers me.
As usual, Guillermo del Toro the directors brilliance is undone by the fact that Guillermo del Toro the writer has absolutely no idea how to write a character that feels remotely real. All of these characters, while reasonably well acted, exist and do what they do in service of the plot and its shallow themes, not because they are believable human beings. Two obvious examples - when Ofelia dangerously disregards Pans warning for no particular reason and when a character is left scarred but alive when he could have easily been dealt with once and for all - strike me as being particularly necessitated by plot rather than character motivation. But the problem is deeper than that as both of the main characters fundamentally ring false
1) Captain Vidal is a caricature of evil who exhibits none of the complexity and pain that would inevitably factor into the formation of such a man. He is neither a flawed but eminently human villain like Daniel Plainview or a mythically exaggerated one like Anton Chigurh. Instead he is a shallow thematic and plot device showing heinous act after heinous act in such an unfiltered way in a film about a child provides the illusion that the movie has something to say about humanitys darkest depths, while simultaneously setting up the cathartic release when he inevitably gets whats coming to him and Ofelia prevails (sort of).
2) Frankly, Im amazed that this movie was supposedly inspired by The Spirit Of The Beehive, a movie that understands completely what it is like to be a child, because Del Toros superficial portrayal of childhood here is the complete opposite. Ofelia as written (this is no knock on the performance) talks and behaves nothing like a real child - she repeatedly shows little to no fear in horrifying fantasy situations, she displays no personality traits of note, and she tells stories that couldnt possibly sound more like the words and ideas of Guillermo del Toro rather than those of a child
Many, many years ago in a sad, faraway land, there was an enormous mountain made of rough, black stone. At sunset, on top of that mountain, a magic rose blossomed every night that made whoever plucked it immortal. But no one dared go near it because its thorns were full of poison. Men talked amongst themselves about their fear of death, and pain, but never about the promise of eternal life. And every day, the rose wilted, unable to bequeath its gift to anyone... forgotten and lost at the top of that cold, dark mountain, forever alone, until the end of time.
By the way, beyond not being true to the character in question, can anyone tell me the thematic purpose of the above tale? Is the rose supposed to represent the importance of childlike wonder and innocence that we all unfortunately lose as we mature and become too burdened by lifes difficulties and horrors?
Which brings me to another issue - in general, this movies metaphor is executed far more messily than Id like. If it is a movie about a child using her imagination to avoid having to face atrocity, then A) why is it made so obvious that what she is seeing is real and not merely a fantastical means of escape - for instance, when magic is used to temporarily cure her mother or when she is able to use chalk to access places that she would otherwise not be able to gain access to? Additionally, B) why do the horrors that have ostensibly caused her to retreat into this fantasy world seem so tangential to her own narrative until near the end of the movie? The horrible actions of Vidal and his compatriots go largely unseen by Ofelia while she focuses on the fantasy world for most of the movie, implying that her entry into that world has little to do with any tragedy she has witnessed at that point only at the end of the movie does her situation become so horrible that it feels she is using fantasy to escape.
Life Of Pi is an example of a (unfortunately somewhat maligned) movie that executes a similar theme better, simply because it avoids both of these issues - its both entirely possible that the story takes place completely in Pis imagination and entirely possible given the terrible things that Pi has suffered that he would construct such a fantasy to escape.
Admittedly, Del Toro is a director whose other (Hollywood) movies consist of superhero franchises and robots punching giant lizards, but its still deeply unfortunate that such a visually robust movie with such a unique and potentially profound concept - a dark fairy tale set in the midst of a nation at war - manages to execute its themes and, especially, its human characters so poorly. With deeper characterization and plotting, this could easily have been one of the most interesting and touching movies Ive ever seen.

The girl who dies. Pans Labyrinth is Guillermo del Toros most perfect movie. As usual its a work about monsters both literally and figuratively, set within a dark corner of human history. It is a fairy tale set in a world unsafe for children. Youth does not protect someone from evil or from witnessing evil. However Pans Labyrinth goes beyond being a fiction set in oppressive times featuring an escapist fantasy. Fascism is real and relevant to those who cannot escape such things. It is audacious for any movie to centre on the killing of a young girl, yet Pans Labyrinth uses that premise to drive home how merciless fascism can be. It is the story of a girl who died to protect the innocent, and depending on your outlook, its either very Catholic and about her resurrection as reward for sacrifice, or its very cynical and set within the dreams of a dying girl. Likely it is both.
Captain Vidal is the greatest cinematic villain, a pure embodiment of the single-minded, ruthless evil of authoritarian fascist rule. He is a man insecure and paranoid, yet completely confident in his own masculine purity. His patriarchal worldview roots his fascism, believing in the value of strong men and preserving his bloodline. Hence why his swift, unapologetic death scene is the perfect end, as his dream of raising a son is taken away by people with no respect for him or his worldview. Hes a cruel man, toying with the people he tortures and kills, so such an ending is cathartic, but that doesnt mean it isnt tragic from his point of view. Vidal is a man who expects to be followed absolutely, as choice is something fascism wants to take away from us. Only fascists can obey without questioning. To choose to be good, to choose to believe in something else and not just follow orders, that is the heart of Pans Labyrinth and hence the reason that choice becomes the final challenge for our heroine.
Lead character Ofelia is young and kind, born into a cruel world devastated by war. The fantasy world she encounters is a dream where the past and future are not so cruel. Yet it exists beneath our own, forgotten and ruined. Mankind has lost its way, producing adults unable to see and appreciate the world of fantasy. They live in their own, human pain. There is the kind king of the underworld and the cruel king of the human world, the fascist world. Religion becomes a friend of fascists, as seen in a dinner scene with the Captain and various guests. Belief in fighting for good has been lost. Yet Ofelia is an affront to that, a child with love from beyond this world, a love for the real and the fantastical, the dead and the unborn. Pans Labyrinth is a testament to bravery, to doing the right thing in a challenging world. Both Ofelia and the rebels stand against fascism, one through love and one through violence. But Ofelia is just a child, fallible and able to make mistakes. Pans Labyrinth is about the children who died under fascism, the generations not born free.
I am fairly confident that Pans Labyrinth is the finest film made in my lifetime. It works on every conceivable level. Del Toros story is brutal and bloody, making its fairy tale qualities all the more stark. It has such a bold and original set of fantasy creations, though inspired by so much mythology and folklore. The films political themes are adult and serious, yet it takes us back to the innocence of childhood even as we witness it in a particularly harsh time. Its a complete artistic work, where every element of cinema comes together perfectly to tell a powerful, important, heartfelt story. Its so dark and yet it is also so beautiful. There are no words to describe how perfect I find Pans Labyrinth to be.

No extraordinário O Labirinto do Fauno, uma menina entra nos subterrâneos da imaginação
           	O diretor mexicano Guillermo del Toro, de 42 anos, diz que tem atravessado a vida tentando se recuperar dos primeiros dez  passados em companhia de uma avó fanática religiosa (que advogava inclusive a mortificação da carne) e de outras criaturas monstruosas (estas produto de sua imaginação). Pois Del Toro que perdoe o egoísmo fazem-se aqui votos de que ele não consiga espantar seus fantasmas, os quais serviram de matéria-prima a vários filmes interessantes, como Cronos, A Espinha do Diabo e Hellboy, e agora a um trabalho verdadeiramente extraordinário. Em O Labirinto do Fauno (El Laberinto del Fauno, MéxicoEspanhaEstados Unidos, 2006), a menina Ofelia (Ivana Baquero), de 11 anos, é levada para dentro da toca do lobo um posto avançado do Exército do caudilho Francisco Franco, no norte da Espanha, onde um capitão assassino (Sergi López, exalando ameaça) tenta esmagar focos de resistência republicana. O capitão acabou de se casar com a mãe de Ofelia e já produziu nela um herdeiro. O que está dentro de sua mãe é, para Ofelia, um mistério. Pode ser alguém como ela própria  um inocente  ou então alguém como o padrasto.
           	Rodeada de medo e brutalidade, a garota acha uma saída. Adentra um labirinto, nos fundos da propriedade, e então se vê num mundo subterrâneo, encenado em cores e detalhes tão vívidos que, desde o início, ele é que parece ser o mais real. Lá, um fauno antiqüíssimo informa Ofelia de que ela é a princesa desse reino. Se cumprir três tarefas, poderá retornar a ele. As tarefas seguem as regras clássicas dos contos de fadas, com sapos, portas misteriosas, chaves e proibições  como a de nunca, jamais, provar de algum alimento quando se está numa dimensão mágica. (Regra que Ofelia, aliás, quebra, despertando um homem pálido, com olhos na palma das mãos, onde ficam os estigmas de Cristo.) Del Toro conhece as convenções dos contos de fadas de trás para a frente, e devolve a elas seu sentido tradicional o de símbolos que servem para ao mesmo tempo simplificar e codificar os grandes temores da existência. De posse deles, Ofelia consegue lidar com a realidade esmagadora à sua volta. Mais consegue dominá-la. Del Toro sabe que o fascismo não tem inimigos piores do que a pureza e a imaginação  a mais desobediente das qualidades, como definiu o diretor em entrevista a VEJA. Ofelia possui ambas as coisas, e por causa delas se transformará num adversário formidável para o padrasto.
           	O Labirinto é desses casos únicos em que a narrativa e a alegoria não só convivem bem como multiplicam o efeito uma da outra. O mundo da imaginação de Ofelia é poderoso em si mesmo, porque Del Toro acredita nos símbolos que está usando e na força que eles contêm. E é igualmente eficiente como representação do século singular que a Espanha atravessou. Ofelia rouba o irmão recém-nascido e permite, assim, que ele venha a crescer sem saber o nome nefasto de seu pai. É a Espanha da resistência dando à luz a Espanha inquieta e criativa que ressurgiu dos subterrâneos com o fim da ditadura franquista. Mais do que qualquer outra coisa, porém, O Labirinto é uma promessa  de um diretor original, que dá indícios de conter outros tantos filmes magníficos dentro de si.

What lingers with me after watching Pans Labyrinth are the vibrant colors that envelop Princess Ofelia as she steps into the magical world, along with the achingly beautiful score that accompanies her journey. 
The film features unforgettable monstrous creations that twist my stomach, as well as benign forest creatures that are equally imaginative and enchanting.
The Faun is a fascinating character can we really trust him? I thought the root under the bed would harm the mother, but she ultimately sealed her fate by throwing it into the fireplace.
The haunting image of the root, contorting and screaming in agony, evokes a sense of deep sadness. It vividly depicts an innocent, magical being suffering in the harsh reality of the world.
The scene featuring the Pale Man in the banquet hall, surrounded by unnatural-looking food, terrifies me to this day. 
Doug Jones physical performance, the meticulous design of this nightmarish creature, and the horrific sounds it makes while stumbling around in an attempt to end the Princesss life all contribute to a moment that captures the true essence of a fairy tale. 
I love the scene where the pages of the ancient book begin to turn an ominous shade of red, followed by the pregnant mother collapsing in a puddle of blood, sending a wave of horror through the narrative. 
Dont let the magical realism fool you, this is a horror film at heart.
Pans Labyrinth is Guillermo Del Toros finest film because the human drama is as engaging as the fantastical story. You genuinely empathize with Ofelia and her sick mother, the resistance fighters, the kind doctor, and the maid Mercedes, who is the true hero of the story. 
Even the fascist villain is portrayed with compelling character traits, without justifying his monstrous actions. Indeed, this is one of those films where the true monsters are the humans. 
There are many parallels between this film and The Devils Backbone, an earlier Del Toro film. Both feature magical realism set against the backdrop of wartime Spain, with an innocent child protagonist. I remember being deeply affected by that film, which is worth seeking out.
Pans Labyrinth serves as the perfect introduction to Spanish horror, despite the fact that the director is Mexican. Spanish horror narratives frequently balance sadness and eeriness, merging gothic melancholy with romantic elements. This clash of beauty and bleakness is utterly irresistible to me. 
Pans Labyrinth is a strong contender for the most visually stunning movie of the 21st century. Its rich production design, vibrant colors, and tasteful special effects are grounded in reality by soulful performances, a gripping script, and all-too-real human tragedy.
The film is a glorious feast where you can eat all the grapes your heart desires. Guillermo Del Toro is more generous than the Pale Man, after all.

This film has been compared to lots of fantasies, from The Chronicles of Narnia and Bridge to Terabithia to Lord of the Rings. Ebert  Roeper once called it a well told adult fairy tale. And I understand that. After all, there is a fantasy world, a brave mission to accomplish, and danger lurks at every turn. But this film is so much more grounded in reality than that to me, it is a tragic war movie that just happens to have a very imaginative sub-plot.
To be specific, I never felt like crying while watching Narnia or the LOTR trilogy, but this got to me to the point of tears. Harsh truths. Innocence lost. Inhuman cruelty. Scenes of torture and bloody attempts at healing. Unlike those fantasy films, this isnt an escapist vehicle at all. Instead, it carries us into the deepest, darkest recesses of the soul and forces us to lament every misstep we ever made on the labyrinthine journey to adulthood. 
Of course, the cinematography is outstanding. Despite how scary it can be, it is a singularly beautiful piece of filmmaking. Excellent acting is delivered, too, by Ivana Baquero as the bookish girl Ofelia who dreams of being a princess and by Ariadna Gil as her pregnant mother Carmen. Maribel Verdú is also noteworthy in her performance as the conflicted housekeeper Mercedes, and Doug Jones is peerless under all the make-up that turned him into the giant Faun and the freakish Pale Man.
For me, however, it was Sergi López playing the pitiless Captain Vidal that brought this film to a higher level. His ruthlessness gives new meaning to the term cold-blooded. I understand that theaters in Spain had to post warnings so that parents would think twice before bringing their children to see this fairy tale.
I also read that immediately after the film was first shown at Cannes, it received a 22-minute standing ovation. This was repeated at its North American debut in Toronto. If I had been in either audience, I certainly would have been on my feet cheering, even as tears ran down my face. It is a masterful production.

O Labirinto do Fauno se passa em 1944, quando o regime nacionalista de Franco já se estabeleceu, enfrentando apenas algumas resistências isoladas de pequenos grupos republicanos. Ofélia (Ivana Baquero), uma jovem que viaja com sua mãe grávida (Ariadna Gil) para um posto militar no Norte da Espanha, sabe que terá que conviver com seu novo padrasto, o cruel Capitão Vidal (Sergi López), com quem sua mãe se casou em busca de maior segurança em um país marcado pela incerteza. Enquanto o capitão se dedica à captura de rebeldes locais, Ofélia explora a região e descobre um labirinto, no centro do qual encontra um Fauno (Doug Jones) que acredita ser a reencarnação de uma princesa perdida do Mundo Subterrâneo. O Fauno desafia a menina a cumprir três perigosas tarefas, cuja realização provará seu valor e dignidade.
A obra se afasta bastante daquilo em que se tornaram os contos de fada, apresentando personagens bondosos que não se mostram tão amigáveis com Ofélia. O fauno, uma criatura híbrida de homem, árvore e bode, se comporta de maneira muito mais rude e agressiva do que se espera. Quando Ofélia falha na sua segunda missão, o Fauno a repreende de forma severa. A criatura é bruta, representando a força da natureza, e coloca Ofélia em contato com uma ancestralidade que é central para a história do filme. O cinema é uma excelente maneira de mostrar diferentes níveis de realidade dentro de uma mesma obra, permitindo que o público se mova entre eles. O cinema pode ser visto como uma ponte, nos convidando a atravessar de uma realidade para outra, às vezes de forma suave, outras vezes de forma mais brusca. Documentários, por exemplo, parecem dar uma visão objetiva do mundo, enquanto filmes de ficção criam mundos totalmente imaginários. No entanto, ambos os tipos de filme misturam de maneira complexa a ficção com a realidade.
Embora isso aconteça em todos os filmes, em alguns, essa mistura é feita de forma intencional, sendo uma parte importante da proposta do filme. É essencial notar que quase todos os personagens do filme são silenciados pelos franquistas, desde o médico da aldeia até a mãe de Ofélia. Aqueles que se recusam a se calar são eliminados, como evidenciam as cenas de violência extrema que permeiam a obra. A fantasia, assim, surge como a única forma que a protagonista encontra para resistir à brutalidade de seu entorno. Não é por acaso que seja uma criança, um ser que preserva a essência mais pura da humanidade, a responsável por descobrir o mundo mágico e ancestral, com um poder arquetípico capaz de confrontar o mal absoluto que dominou o mundo dos adultos.
As atuações em O Labirinto do Fauno são muito marcantes. Ivana Baquero, como Ofélia, faz um trabalho incrível ao mostrar a mistura de inocência e coragem da personagem. Seu olhar e a maneira natural de atuar fazem com que o público se conecte com ela e entenda sua luta. Sergi López, como Capitão Vidal, é realmente assustador. Ele interpreta o vilão de forma fria e implacável, sem exageros, o que o torna ainda mais ameaçador. Ele transmite uma obsessão pelo controle, e sua calma é tão assustadora quanto sua violência. A interação entre esses dois personagens destaca a diferença entre o mundo de fantasia de Ofélia e a realidade brutal de Vidal, a imaginação contra a tirania, a sensibilidade contra a brutalidade.
O filme alterna entre dois mundos visuais bem distintos. O mundo real, dominado pelo fascismo e pela guerra, é fotografado com tons frios, azulados e acinzentados. Essas cores reforçam a frieza e a brutalidade do ambiente, tornando-o opressor e sem vida. O quartel do Capitão Vidal, por exemplo, é sempre iluminado de forma dura, com sombras bem definidas que acentuam a rigidez e a violência da narrativa. No mundo fantástico, as cores são mais quentes e douradas, principalmente nas cenas dentro do labirinto e quando Ofélia encontra o Fauno. A luz é mais suave, e as sombras não são tão marcadas, o que dá uma sensação de sonho e mistério. Isso cria um forte contraste com a realidade sombria e faz o espectador sentir que aquele lugar pertence a outra dimensão, sendo mágico, mas também ameaçador.
O Labirinto do Fauno é um filme denso e cheio de camadas desde o começo. Ele lida com uma questão política forte, bem fundamentada e histórica, enquanto sua mensagem está sempre presente nos contrastes. Essa palavra talvez seja a que melhor define o filme contrastes. Durante toda a história, somos confrontados com o equilíbrio entre os opostos, o caos das nossas vidas e a tentativa de sobreviver e ser feliz em meio a tudo isso, sem cair em um ceticismo pesado. Algumas pessoas podem achar que tudo aquilo é apenas uma fábula na cabeça de Ofélia, uma forma dela escapar da realidade e lidar com o que acontece ao seu redor (e essa ideia psicológica faz sentido). Porém, o filme não nos diz que isso não é real. De algum modo, entramos na mente da protagonista e começamos a acreditar que aquela outra realidade é real, mas de um jeito que se conecta diretamente à nossa.

What I think now is that the scene where Mercedes says she used to believe in all sorts of things and no longer does is why the movie just suddenly started hitting me like a ton of bricks. When you become a parent, you suddenly are reminded of all of the things you did not know once upon a time, and to watch your child grow is to see a series of possibilities for how the world might be die right in front of them. First, it is the things we can all accept are not true. There are no fairies or fauns or monsters under the bed. But then, as you age, the world encourages you to let the parts of yourself that believe in a better, more equitable world die because its more convenient to the people who hold imagination on the tightest of reins. Pans Labyrinth argues that ceasing to believe in fairies and ceasing to believe in the possibility of some better world are the same thing and that anything good carries with it some whiff of the fantastical. But so does anything evil. What is Vidal but yet another monster under the bed? 
Anyway, the other day I had to tell my child ghosts arent real because I could tell she was vaguely scared of them in that way you get when you are that young, when you know enough to be scared but not yet enough to know why. Pans Labyrinth will always hold a special place in my heart. A couple of years ago, I chose this movie for my final oral presentation in my Spanish Film class, and that deep dive changed the way I see it forever. By analyzing it closely, I started noticing details that had slipped past me on earlier viewings. Visual cues, thematic threads, and subtle design choices are details that made me appreciate this movie on an entirely different level. Its one thing to watch Pans Labyrinth and be moved by its story its another to study it and realize just how meticulously crafted it really is.
One of the elements that stood out to me most was the design of Captain Vidals lair. The mechanical, almost sterile structure of his space reinforces the idea that he is cold, robotic, and emotionally detached, unfit to support a Spanish society still reeling from poverty and war. The strict orderliness of his surroundings mirrors his own personality disciplined, severe, and obsessed with appearances. Even the clock-like symbols that decorate his lair highlight his dependency on time as a form of control. Vidal is defined by time, whether through the broken pocket watch passed down by his father, or simply by how much of his existence is tied to keeping order and precision. I believe his obsession with time stems from the fact that he never truly had it with his father. His fathers death marked him, and his anger and desperation later in the movie can be read as his frantic attempt to live up to an image of authority and legacy he was never able to reconcile.
Another layer of his characterization comes through sound and objects. The Captain listens to music on his gramophone, which is a form of luxury in a time of scarcity. While others suffer, he indulges without a second thought, a clear sign of class conflict. The Republicans share and support one another with what little they have, but Vidal, like the Fascists, hoards his resources and wields them as symbols of power. The music he listens to has the cadence of patriotic propaganda, a further reinforcement of his devotion to authoritarian tradition. Even his grooming ritual speaks volumes. The razor he uses is not just an everyday object but a weapon-like tool. Razors carry connotations of bravery and violence, and in his hands, it becomes an extension of his brutality. Its as if Vidal actively cultivates an unsettling image for himself, shaping his persona after the sinister trappings of fascist leaders of the time. Through these details, del Toro shows how Vidal isnt just a villain, but a man desperately clinging to symbols of control, tradition, and violence to validate his existence.
Color in Pans Labyrinth is another dimension of its storytelling brilliance. Guillermo del Toro uses color not simply as an aesthetic choice but as an emotional language. The real world of post-Civil War Spain is steeped in greys, blues, and greens. These tones feel cold, harsh, and uninviting, a reflection of its hostility and oppression. The intermediate world, like the mossy green of the labyrinth itself, hints at life and renewal, standing in contrast to the bleakness outside it. Then theres the fantasy world that is bathed in gold and red, organic, and warm. As the movie progresses, these worlds begin to blur. The golden hues of fantasy bleeding into the cold palette of reality, culminating in a clash where boundaries collapse. Through this use of color, del Toro makes us feel which world is worth yearning for, even as we know the real one is inescapable.
Pans Labyrinth is the kind of movie I could analyze to death. There are so many layers to unravel, like how the Pale Man embodies not just the evil in individuals, but the monstrous hunger of entire empires devouring innocence, consuming resources, and leaving nothing behind. Or how fantasy isnt limited to Ofelias personal refuge, but also extends to the Republicans, who in their struggle against fascism carried their own dreams of a better, freer world. This movie makes you feel that fantasy is not just about escapism, but about survival, hope, and resistance in the face of cruelty. Every viewing brings something new to notice, whether its a detail in the set design, the way colors shift between worlds, or how silence is used as power. I think the balance is what makes it so remarkable it is both a storybook and a tragedy, both enchanting and devastating. For me, Pans Labyrinth will always stand as one of the most beautiful yet haunting pieces of art my eyes have ever laid on and a movie that feels timeless in its message and unforgettable in its imagery.

Last night a fairy visited me.
That fairy first visited me years ago, when my dad first showed me this. I was very little. Some scenes horrified me, but I was still under the spell of this. Yes, little me had found her new favorite movie. Its a fairy tale. Dark, cold, painful, magical, full of secrets. Its like a fairy tale you know, but something else. Both a surreal fantasy and the harsh reality itself. Pan, fairies, magic labyrinth. Fascism, anarchy, war. Although the story seems to be in two parts, these two parts belong to a whole. They complement each other. I used to watch this so much when I was little. Every time I watched it, I would notice different details. Even though I knew everything that was going to happen, my eyes would still fill with tears. I also wanted to be the princess of the underworld and meet Pan. I havent watched it in a long time. Now I feel like a little girl again. 
There are two important characters in this Captain Vidal and Mercedes. Captain is fascist authority. He expects obedience from everyone. He is suspicious, he cannot tolerate a single dissent. He is wild, merciless. He has no mercy, and his heart has long since darkened. Mercedes is anarchy, freedom. Brave, warrior, intelligent. Big hearted, compassionate, motherly. Its impossible not to feel safe around her. She is right in the middle of danger, still always she is the safety. She is an ideal, just like the saviors in fairy tales. While the captain is the bad wolf, the old witch, and the scary queen Mercedes is the good-hearted hunter, the old sage, and the prince. They are the black and white in Ofelias life. The contrast in fairy tales, clash of ideals. 
In Pans Labyrinth, the worst are humans. The 3 tasks Pan gives to Ofelia are for this reason. Because humans, selfish wretches, cannot do these tasks. In order for Ofelia back to her utopia, she must prove that she has not become human.
Task One Frog Exploit 
A huge frog has settled into the root of an old tree and is exploiting the tree. He is taking what tree has and feeding only himself. Just like the authorities who exploit the places they rule by intimidating. In this task, Ofelia actually fights not only the frog but also this authority. 
Task Two Feast Greed
All Ofelia has to do is get the fairies inside the room. But most importantly, she cant eat anything on the table. But how is that possible when the table is so appetizing? And theres no one to stop her. Ofelia is alone with her desires. She should not act like human without will and eat from the table. Greed is a completely human characteristic, despicable feeling. Like those who always want more, who always want what belongs to someone else. Like those who enter the lands they want and steal from the people there. Ofelia must fight with this human inside her. 
Task Three Brother Sacrifice
In last task, Ofelia must do the most difficult thing. She must fight with herself, she must give up on herself first. She must protect her innocent brother and give her own blood. Sacrifice requires sublime emotions love, devotion, courage. And one last time, Ofelia must prove that she has not yet lost her golden heart. Just like those who sacrificed their lives to protect a noble ideal. 
Ofelia never does any of the tasks completely by following the rules. She goes her own way to the end. She does not show strict obedience, she is not limited by orders. Like a rebel against fascism, a free spirit. Despite the promised beauty, she still did not obey. Because to reach the real beauty, she had to do what was right. What she believed in. A complete fairy tale. Dark black bad characters, pure white good characters. A soft-hearted, honorable princess. And the virtuous messages the fairy tale gives us. 
If you havent watched this, please do. Im sure youll be impressed. Youll feel like a child again and at the same time, youll feel things that are tough for even an adult.

El laberinto del fauno (The Labyrinth of the Faun) or better known as Pans Labyrinth is a 2006 Spanish-Mexican dark fantasy film written and directed by Guillermo del Toro and stars Ivana Baquero, Sergi López, Maribel Verdú, Doug Jones, and Ariadna Gil. 
After the disappointment of not writing a review for last weeks Film Club pick Jesus Christ Superstar (sorry Michael!) i decided to move onto our newest Film Club pick the foreign language film Pans Labyrinth suggested by Quintin. Being a great admirer of dark fantasy films like this its rather embarrassing I never found the time to watch it until now. 
The story of Pans Labyrinth takes place in Spain 1944, a few years after The Civil War, which ended in 1939 when General Franco emerged victorious and began taking over as Dictator of Spain. Amidst this time setting, the narrative of the film takes place and intertwines the real world with a mythical world centered on an overgrown abandoned labyrinth and a mysterious faun creature. 
Undoubtedly Guillermo del Toro is the unrivalled master at showcasing these weird wacky yet incredibly wonderful creatures and thats what he does best within this. These creatures, most important the faun and the Pale Man have become icons in todays cinema as the subtle horror-esque feeling they emit to the audience is truly creepy to watch at times as, this being my first watch, they often took the story to darker, stranger places than I would have ever predicted whilst also allowing it to feel realistic with the soldiers storyline and fantastic ending. Guillermo del Toros, El laberinto del fauno won 3 Oscars (direction, cinematography and makeup) and its clear to see why. The films cinematography is breathtaking throughout, the make up is of course completely stunning and del Toros direction is flawless. 
El laberinto del fauno is unlike any movie Ive ever seen before, the brothers Grim tales always work for me. Its a haunting mix of horror, history and fantasy that all work simultaneously on nearly every level. However, like 99 of films, this film isnt perfect. At times Pans Labyrinth can be utterly predictable and that did cause the storyline to have less effect as the story moves in a manner where you can anticipate what will occur next and sadly, that did slightly disappoint me. Yet, although its slightly predictable for the first two acts, the ending knocked it out of the park and blew me away. The sadness that comes from her final smile, how everyone around her looked and the way the storyline plays out in its final moments are all truly mesmerising as the performances from Ivana Baquero, Sergi López and Maribel Verdú and all phenomenal in those closing moments. 
At the end of the day, upon first watch its clear to me that Pans Labyrinth is a special, more meaningful film. Although the young girls fantasy world juxtaposes her harsh real world, the film makes a point in sayings its not just mere escapism, its more than that, its a way for her to take control of her life, feel like shes special and ultimately, of course, escape the harsh reality of the current world around her. Whilst not every aspect is as flawless as they first may seem, it does very little to downgrade the overall film. For me this was an amazing watch and its one Im thankful I can now say Ive seen.

This has quickly skyrocketed into one of my favourite films. I love films filled with allegory, symbolism, and multiple interpretations, and this is absolutely rife with them. It feels like such an original fantasy, with visceral characters and a layered narrative that juxtaposes fairytale elements against the brutality of guerrilla warfare after the Spanish Civil War. The visuals are beyond stunning. I especially loved how the three tasks tie directly into the story and what they represent. Im going to structure this around them, because they parallel both the war narrative and Ofelias journey remarkably well.
The first task, where Ofelia enters the ancient fig tree, strongly resembles the reproductive system the trunk like a uterus, the branches like fallopian tubes. It ties into the films exploration of fertility and her transition toward maturity. Within the tree, therein lies the giant toad, who can be read as her unborn brother, the thing draining her mother from within, directly paralleling her mothers deteriorating pregnancy, though only slowly at this point in the story. Theres also a clear thread of disobedience versus blind obedience, one of the films core ideas executed to perfection by del Toro. By muddying up her dress and returning late, she challenges rigid authority and rejects the superficial expectations imposed on her by Vidal and reinforced or expected by her mother. You could even stretch this further into a metaphor for fascism itself, something rotting Spains identity from within, though Im not too knowledgeable about the Spanish Civil War so I wont really go into this.
The second task, with the Pale Man, directly mirrors what we see unfolding in the real world of the film. Fascist control, rationing, and the hoarding of resources are reflected in the image of a creature sitting before a feast it doesnt need or eat. This comes just as Ofelia is punished and denied food, sent to bed without any, making the parallel even clearer. Vidal mirrors the Pale Man hes a figure of authority who consumes, or has too much to consume, while others have little to none, and are left to suffer. It also becomes a lesson about temptation. Ofelia gives in, and that failure reflects her struggle to navigate temptation. I know theres plenty possible meanings here, but I dont think her failure is entirely negative shes acting on her own desire rather than blindly obeying rules set out to her, but in this act she also learns of consequences, in the form of the death of those two fairies. Still her disobedience here feels less like failure and more like a step toward rejecting that imposed obedience, but also to maturing for her final task.
Speaking of, the final task completes that arc of maturity. Ofelia chooses a selfless act, refusing to spill innocent blood, and, in doing so, brings life in the form of the blooming white flower as the film ends. Its the culmination of everything the film has been building. This choice directly mirrors the resistance, particularly Mercedes and the rebels, who defy authority through action rather than submission. Ofelias refusal ties back to the films core idea of rejecting blind obedience, especially under fascism, where violence is justified in the name of control. Vidal embodies a willingness to sacrifice others without hesitation. In contrast, Ofelias refusal to sacrifice her brother becomes a moral victory, completing her journey and showing her selflessness, while also reflecting the rebellions resistance and disobedience to that same brutal system.
Her death at the end is especially devastating. Her innocence and belief in fantasy simply cannot survive in a world defined and shaped by violence and control. There is no physical escape for her, mirroring the reality for children in such conflicts, trapped between forces beyond their understanding or control. For them, imagination becomes their only form of escapism. Theres an ambiguity with whether the fantasy is real or imagined, and you could find evidence for either, but I like how this was done. Both interpretations lead to the same end. She was searching for escape, whether through imagination or something genuinely magical, but either way she was still consumed by the world around her.
Theres a real sense of completeness to the story as well. The ending lands perfectly, with ambiguity that is intentional and meaningful rather than just unclear. The tasks reflect her internal journey as much as her external one, eventually showing her resolve and her refusal to give in to fear or temptation. Its such thoughtful writing that gets better the more you think about it. The film feels meticulously crafted to allow for so many interpretations while remaining emotionally grounded and provocative no matter which way you interpret things. One of my favourites now for its pure originality, its fairytale framing, and just its unflinching portrayal of brutality, and how seamlessly these narratives parallel each other to explore morality, resistance, and growing up.

The characters are all well developed, and the symbolism, though subtle, is so exquisite that it makes me want more with the thought of it. The dialogue is natural and authentic, and he handles the film expertly to convey that timeless feel even with some of the films harsher moments. The final scene is also a true mountain, with a killer of a send-off line and an ambiguous ending, which still fuels debates to this day. Pans Labyrinth leads us through parallel stories and themes without once losing its internal consistency.  Innocence and brutality, fantasy and reality, together in a beautiful fairy tale about the power of magic in dark times. This is one of my favorite fantasy films of all time.

In 1944 Spain, at the end of the Civil War, ten-year-old Ofelia (Ivana Baquero) accompanies her pregnant mother to meet her new stepfather, Captain Vidal (Sergi López), who has been assigned to hunt down resistance fighters in the mountains. One night, a fairy leads Ofelia to a nearby labyrinth, where she meets a Faun, who reveals to the girl she has to pass a series of three tests ...
El laberinto del fauno (The Labyrinth of the Faun) is a dark fantasy horror film written and directed by Guillermo del Toro. It won three Academy Awards (Best Cinematography, Best Art Direction, and Best Makeup).
Del Toros movie is his absolute masterpiece and his magnum opus. It received widespread critical acclaim, received many awards, and has been regarded as one of the greatest fantasy films ever made, as well as one of the greatest films of all time. It also still holds the record of the longest standing ovation at Cannes.
Considered by del Toro to be a companion piece of El espinazo del diablo (my review), which also takes place at the end of the war and with which it shares a few themes, its also influenced by Alice in Wonderland and many other works. This isnt a movie for children, however, since del Toro doesnt hold back with displays of graphic violence.
El laberinto del fauno marks del Toros third collaboration with the great Doug Jones, who portrays two of the creatues appearing in the film, and no one couldve done it better. The 11-year-old Ivana Baquero is wonderful in the lead role, while Sergi Lópezs brutal and sadistic Captain Vidal is yet another very well-developed villain by del Toro.
Creature design, makeup and art direction are all imaginative and gorgeous, with beautifully realized creatures, almost exclusively achieved with practical effects. The movie also features an achingly sad, utterly beautiful film score by Javier Navarrete.
And yet, the genius of the movie lies in the fact you can decide yourself whether the storys fantastic elements are true or just the result of a young girls imagination. There are hints supporting both, and its up to you to decide which works better for you. I like to think its all Ofelias imagination because this makes it much more impactful and sad.
In conclusion, El laberinto del fauno is filmmaker del Toros greatest achievement, a dark and visually stunning fantasy tale which is deeply grounded in a war story, engrossing and captivating, imaginative and emotional, poetic and sad, a truly unforgettable experience with a perfect ending.
This film is on my list of All-time Favorite Movies, and I added it to my Liked Films - the movies I enjoy the most, regardless of their rating. Also, the films score made my list of Favorite Film Scores.

The story is about a little girl named Ofelia and her pregnant mother Carmen, who travel to the country side to be with Carmens new husband who is the ruthless army Captain Vidal. The Captain and his men are working to kill the remaining forces of the opposition following the Spanish Civil War.

Pans Labyrinth is an excellent film from Director Guillermo del Toro on every level, and while I admire his style I have yet to see a film of his that I really blew me away. Since I did enjoy this more on a re watch, I am now more eager to check out his films Cronos and Devils Backbone.

Many creative minds have left their touch upon the fantasy genre, but never in the way that Guillermo del Toro has offered his very own in Pans Labyrinth. Revolving around the concept of imagination and what it does to us as we grow older, what we are left with is not only one of the greatest fantasy films to have come out in the 21st century, but also one of the most creative projects of its own kind. Its already one to admire the imagination of a man like Guillermo del Toro, but when watching Pans Labyrinth, youre seeing everything put at its very fullest. He tells a tale that clearly is so personal to him, and the evidence is clear when you pick up on its influences, no matter what they range from fairy tales, Victor Erices The Spirit of the Beehive, the hardships encountered in childhood all forming something so magnificent in Pans Labyrinth.
Set after the Spanish Civil War, Pans Labyrinth tells a story that blends together reality and fantasy through the eyes of Ofelia, a curious 10-year-old girl who faces the horrors of the reality which she is living in through interacting with a faun whom she discovered inside of a decaying labyrinth near her stepfathers home. The faun sees Ofelia as the reborn spirit of a princess who had died inside of a fairy tale, whose father had awaited her return. With the films setting inside of a Francoist era Spain, it adds more to the wonder that is created by the storytelling that Guillermo del Toro has provided in Pans Labyrinth, in a manner that the fantasy works as a way to balance out the sanity of a human being especially upon facing the harsh reality as Ofelia begins to find comfort inside of the world that the faun had introduced her to.
The building blocks for Pans Labyrinth carry many different references to what is so recognizable inside of fairy tales, but in such a mystifying sense that pulls one in. For one, we have the evil stepparent in Captain Vidal, the lost princess, and the means of escaping from reality. It is clear from here that we have one method of looking at how Guillermo del Toros film is operating, it is operating like a fairy tale, which is only a small fraction of where the beauty has come out. Yet unlike most fairy tales, Pans Labyrinth is not a story that is meant for very young children, but the structural resemblance adds more to the effect to which such a film leaves behind.
Coming down to the role of Ofelia, it is mystifying just to witness how Guillermo del Toro is capturing the terrifying world of Francoist Spain from the eyes of a young child - but at the same time it also adds more to the wonder Pans Labyrinth creates. Ofelia, a girl at the brink of puberty, resorts to these fairy tales as a means of keeping herself in comfort, but it is also these fairy tales that help her in growing up from the moment she first wanders into the labyrinth. This labyrinth is not just merely a piece only for comfort, but also a place for discovery. It is a place for discovery in the sense that not only is it a new world that she found, but it is also fueling a challenge in order to find out whom she really is. One can draw back to Hayao Miyazakis Spirited Away in the sense that both films establish a young protagonist discovering the challenges of coming of age through the use of a world beyond the real, but in Guillermo del Toros case, something else altogether has been presented. In her debut performance, Ivana Baquero carries one factor that is crucial to the films success inside of herself, carrying a convincing array of emotion that draws back to Ana Torrent inside of The Spirit of the Beehive.
One of the most crucial elements to Pans Labyrinth is the power of choice. The young Ofelia had been warned by Mercedes to be wary of fauns but the image that the faun presents for her is another factor that helps what Guillermo del Toro had been forming with the films unconventional coming-of-age narrative. Since I do not wish to spoil the details of the film, it is such a critical aspect to Ofelias coming of age, as the faun presents her with a series of tasks which he promises will grant her a return to her father. The image of the faun at first is frightening, but Ofelia obeys when the faun notes how he does not mean harm upon her. The faun carries good and evil inside of it, but he is not offering either to Ofelia, and instead it is the choice between them. Said theme is crucial in defining Ofelias quest because, ultimately, she is given the choice to decide whether or not she should discover what she will need to face inside of her life, without any aid from peers.
From the set pieces that capture such an era, it is where Guillermo del Toro also works around another way of looking into Pans Labyrinth as a horror film. In its detailing of the time period, Guillermo del Toro never holds back in order to establish the harshness of the real. The Captain, who is devilishly portrayed by Sergi Lopez, is a menacing, sadistic figure who looms all throughout the film, in which he is a man who only wants things to go by his way, no matter how impossible it is. As subplots come in, whether they revolve around Captain Vidal or the housemaid Mercedes, the tapestry which is established is nothing short of beautiful. Captain Vidal claims he is a man of choice, but his actions show otherwise - and those against him are people who define the power of choice, with where it takes them inside of a tragic reality.
Visually, Pans Labyrinth still remains among the most gorgeous cinematic creations to have come out in the 21st century. It is not only from the set pieces which Guillermo del Toro puts together for both the fantasy and the real, nor is it the astounding special effects when it comes to creating the many creatures of the fantasy world, but it is all Guillermo del Toros imagination that ultimately fuels Pans Labyrinth, given as it is also a vital aspect to what keeps a film so tightly put together. All of the small details to the worlds which Guillermo del Toro creates are necessary in letting his imagination flow, but then we also have creatures like the faun and the Pale Man (both of whom are magnificently portrayed by Doug Jones) that also express more creativity at hand. Together with the eye of Guillermo del Toro going behind the camera, everything fits so perfectly into place as he continues to let these visuals define the piece.
Pans Labyrinth is a film that works in so many ways whether it be as a fairy tale, a coming-of-age story, or a horror film. There are few films that I have ever seen that carry the sort of imagination which Guillermo del Toro laces Pans Labyrinth with, but at its core, something so resonant comes about. It is a film about the power of choice, and how it helps us in finding our identity inside of the harsh reality which we live in. And in that sense, Guillermo del Toro has let himself out to the very fullest inside of Pans Labyrinth for he finds a manner of bringing together the imagination of a child with the brutal horrors of the adult world, but he also creates a means of encountering what sort of conflict it would present in ones life.

The real world story of the film, about Francoist soldiers hunting down the remnants of republican guerrilla resistance after the end of the Spanish civil war, was deeply affecting for me. It features viscerally realistic battle scenes and a sustained but not overbearing sense of place. Sergei Lopez, who plays the monsterous Captain Vidal, is a living embodiment of Fascism in all its self-mythologizing machismo. Also, credit sound effects editor Roland Thai for smartly emphasizing the most sinister noise of the 20th century the creak of leather jackboots and a Sam Browne belt.
Unfortunately, the fairy tale that is interspersed throughout the civil war story, in which a young girl (the Captains stepdaughter) must complete dangerous tasks in order to prove her identity to an ancient tree-creature, doesnt have the same impact. The fantasy set pieces sit awkwardly next to the realism, and the supposedly magical elements, the faeries, the giant toads, that dude with eyes in his hands from the cover of Fangoria, are rendered and presented in an oddly matter-of-fact way. The director, Guillermo Del Toro, rushes through his introduction of the fantasy elements, mythic creatures appearing before the eyes of the girl, pages of a book writing themselves, in an oddly off-hand fashion. When Pan, the tree-legged faun, first comes onto the screen, the camera doesnt linger over this supposedly fantastic creature in wonderment. Hes almost instantly taken for granted. Coupled with the blank expression on the face of lead actress Ivana Baquero, this flat presentation undercuts any attempt to infuse the film with child-like awe or majesty. When Baquero does set off to complete her missions, they are brief, one-dimensional and generally suspense free, except for some scares courtesty of the Fangoria cover boy that feel rather contrived.
The two stories co-exist uneasily together for most of the movie, until Del Toro brings them together for a climax which makes the point that righteous choices will long outlive the unjust, petty rule of tyrants. The fairy tale provides some moving symbolism for this theme, but its undercut by the general thinness of the fantasy world Del Toro attempts to create. The movie suggests a magical fantasy realm just beyond our sight, but doesnt flesh it out beyond the merest sketches for the majority of the film. So, when viewer finally gets to see a larger swath of this underworld at the end of the movie, instead of feeling moved, I was left thinking, where the hell did all these people come from?

Up until now Ive only seen Guillermo del Toro at his kitschiest his brilliantly entertaining B-movie of Pacific Rim and his ridiculously fun and creative Hellboy films. So while I do admire him quite a bit, I still never felt like I understood why exactly people praised him so much as an acclaimed visionary and I figured I wouldnt until I saw his more serious films.
Pans Labyrinth basically confirms both what I already knew (that the man truly does have an eye for dark fantasy thats sorely lacking in the film industry) and what I gleaned from others (that he really is an astounding director and deserves the renown hes built-up). Theres a vivid synthesis of the harsh realities of a fascist war-state and a childlike playfulness, a type of genre- and tone-blending that Ive only really found as masterfully done with directors like Bong Joon-ho and at this point indicative of a real auteur to me considering how defiantly difficult it is to label such works.
Youre getting older, and youll see that life isnt like your fairy tales. The world is a cruel place. And youll learn that, even if it hurts.
And thats the real impressive nature of the work, is how it takes an amalgamate of themes and imagery from its inspirations and predecessors and still executes it so well. Perhaps the biggest fault I can find with it is that I wish it delved more into its creation, its surreal and bizarre world it teases. I think thats indication enough of its prestige.

Guillermo del Toro tells the horror of 1944 Spain through the innocent eyes of a little girl, his Pans Labyrinth is a dark fairy tale that manages to be so sweetly charming and so tremendously brutal
Carmen, a young widow, has married the captain of the army Vidal, directly responsible for breaking down the last resistance groups in defense of their country. The little Ofelia, her daughter, experiences every day the evil and wickedness of the Franco regime, suffering enormously for the influence of the rigid and arrogant stepfather and especially for the difficult conditions of the mother struggling with a troubled pregnancy.
The world of fairy tales and her imagination become a necessary refuge, a faun and some small fairies reveal to her the existence of a fantastic underworld of which she is the princess, in order to reach it she must complete three dangerous tasks 
An extraordinary narrative style constantly shifts the focus of the story from moments of harsh reality to the fantastic parallel events involving Ofelia in a perfect mix of reality and fantasy that, although seemingly so distant, collaborate in creating a single big picture.
The director shows the devastating effect of abuse and the immense power of imagination and innocence, the other world becomes a vital expression of the need to find that peace that is impossible to reach in reality, without giving up that natural coming-of age journey which is a fundamental part of growth.
The heart-breaking ending is extraordinary in its ambivalence, according to the essence of the whole work it stages a really bitter conclusion by combining it delicately with the typical sweetness of fairy tales
The cinematography of Pans Labyrinth is absolutely gorgeous, the skilful use of lights and colors gives life to an evocative setting in which every single shot could be a perfect freeze frame.
The design and practical realization of the fantastic creatures is really effective and perfectly embodies the tones of the horror fairy tale, from the mysterious and charming Faun to the disturbing Tenome.
The general technical level is excellent, from del Toros direction to the quality  performances of the actors.
Ivana Baquero is perfect with her sweet and brave Ofelia, as well as Maribel Verdú who, in the role of Mercedes, gives life to an extraordinary female character.
Everyone does his job well but Sergi López is really impressive in the complex role of captain Vidal, a wicked villain that goes far beyond the limits of tolerability
I loved Pans Labyrinth and its ability to tell the horror through fairy tales and childhood innocence, while still maintaining all its raw realism. Guillermo del Toro is successful in a really complex combination, also managing to stage it with extraordinary power and an enchanting aesthetic

Now I understand why this is my best friends favorite movie. Pans Labyrinth truly is a masterpiece, Guillermo del Toro was operating at the height of his powers here.
This film feels like a major evolution in del Toros work. Much like in The Devils Backbone, he uses horror not just to frighten, but to explore something deeper about human nature our capacity for cruelty, for resistance, for hope. But here, he elevates those ideas even further, transforming horror into something lyrical and heartbreaking. It becomes poetry made of monsters and fairy tales. His script carries a profound humanism, the kind of emotional depth and moral clarity that reminds me of Bayonas The Orphanage or even Hideo Nakatas Dark Water, films where the supernatural is a vessel for something deeply human.
Del Toro masterfully blends fantasy and horror to tell a story that is both rooted in the specific trauma of the Spanish Civil War and completely universal. You dont need to know the history or the context of Fascism to understand whats at stake, because he shapes those elements into something mythic and symbolic. The film becomes a haunting meditation on man-made evil, how it takes root, and how its resisted.
This film its absolutely breathtaking. The cinematography by Guillermo Navarro is stunning (the lighting, the colors, the framing), its all meticulously composed and often painterly, pulling us into a world where reality and fantasy bleed into each other. The practical effects, creature design, and makeup work are out of this world. Everything feels tactile and real, even in the most surreal moments. And Javier Navarretes score is absolutely gorgeous. Its melancholic, sweeping, and perfectly attuned to the emotional rhythm of the story.
Ivana Baquero gives an incredible performance as Ofelia, so much depth and maturity in such a young actress. And Maribel Verdú is just as compelling as Mercedes, quietly commanding and heartbreaking in equal measure. The supporting cast is also excellent, especially Sergi López, whose performance as Captain Vidal is one of the most chilling portrayals of cruelty Ive seen. Every actor is doing remarkable work, grounded and deeply affecting.
This is one of those films that lingers. Its beautiful and brutal, tender and terrifying, and utterly unforgettable.
