El laberinto del fauno is a rare film that blends fantasy and harsh reality in a way that feels both magical and deeply tragic. Set in post-Civil War Spain, the story follows Ofelia, a young girl who escapes into a mysterious, mythical world while the brutal rule of her stepfather, Captain Vidal, unfolds around her.
The film is visually stunning, filled with breathtaking imagery and hauntingly beautiful set pieces. From the eerie faun who guides Ofelia to the nightmarish Pale Man, every creature feels like it belongs in an old, forgotten fairy tale-one that is far darker than the ones were used to. The practical effects and CGI blend seamlessly, creating a world that is both believable and surreal.
At its core, Pans Labyrinth is a story about innocence and resistance in the face of cruelty. Ivana Baquero gives a heartfelt performance as Ofelia, perfectly capturing a childs wonder and determination. Sergi López is terrifying as Captain Vidal, embodying cold, ruthless authority. The contrast between his brutality and Ofelias escapism is what makes the film so powerful.
The story is both heartbreaking and mesmerizing, leaving you with a sense of wonder and sadness long after the credits roll. Del Toro masterfully weaves fantasy and history together, making Pans Labyrinth not just a fairy tale, but a meditation on war, sacrifice, and the power of imagination. Its a film that stays with you, haunting and beautiful in equal measure.

Rewatching Pans Labyrinth after so many years felt strangely different, almost like the film had shifted while I wasnt looking. The fantasy that once felt magical now reads like something sadder  a world Ofelia builds for herself because the real one is just too brutal to face. The violence around her isnt abstract anymore its constant, suffocating, and completely indifferent to her.
What struck me this time is how her imagination isnt an escape in a whimsical sense  its more like a shield. Each creature, each task, feels like her mind trying to make sense of the cruelty in front of her. Its her way of surviving a world that keeps taking things from her.
And that ending it still hits hard, but for different reasons now. Less fairy tale, more tragedy. A child trying to hold onto a story because its the only place she has any control. The way the film cuts between her inner world and the cold, merciless reality outside makes it almost unbearable, but also incredibly beautiful in its own way.

The film itself is a narrative labyrinth due to the absence of a solid boundary between fantasy and reality, family friendly until someone gets smashed in the face by a glass bottle, still remember the shock on my face when I first watched this. Pans Labyrinth is a fairytale unlike anything Ive ever seen, a combination of impeccable storytelling and spellbinding visuals, del Toros ingenious masterpiece. (Gave up directing Narnia, turned down offers by Hollywood producers, wrote the subtitles and did all the designs, both monsters and set, himself, all totally worth it. Magnum opus? Magnum opus.)

Fantastik bir kurgu izleyeceğimi düşünerek açtım, film bana savaşın ortasında çocukluk travması bıraktı.
Beni en çok şaşırtan tarafı fantastik dünyayı filmin merkezine koymak yerine onu gerçek dünyanın acımasızlığının yanına yerleştirmesi oldu. Ben açıkçası daha çok yaratıklar, görevler, masallar ve garip bir fantastik evren bekliyordum. Bunların hepsi var ama filmin asıl ağırlığı bambaşka bir yerde. Bir noktadan sonra dışarıdaki gerçek dünyanın, Ofelianın karşılaştığı yaratıklardan çok daha korkunç olduğunu fark ediyorsun. Fantastik dünya ne kadar karanlık ve ürkütücü görünürse görünsün, insanların birbirine yaptıklarının yanında neredeyse güvenli hissetmeye başlıyor.
Ofelianın bütün bu korkunç gerçekliğin içinde kendisine başka bir dünya yaratması da çok hoşuma gitti. Fantastik tarafın gerçekten var olup olmaması benim için bir noktadan sonra çok da önemli değildi açıkçası. Gerçekten başka bir dünyanın parçası olabilir, yaşadıklarından kaçabilmek için zihninde bunların hepsini yaratıyor da olabilir. İki yorumda da aynı yere çıkıyorum yaşadığı dünyaya dayanabilmek için bir masala ihtiyacı var. Çocukken korktuğumuz şeyler genelde canavarlar olurken burada insan büyüdükçe asıl korkulması gereken şeyin bazen insanın kendisi olduğunu izlemek bayağı üzücüydü.
Filmin ruh ile bedeni birbirinden ayrı ele alması ise üzerine en çok düşündüğüm şeylerden biri oldu. Beden fiziksel dünyanın kurallarına bağlı yaralanabiliyor, acı çekiyor, öldürülebiliyor. Ama ruh için aynı kurallar geçerli değilmiş gibi davranılıyor. Bir insanın bedenini yok edebilirsin ama onun kim olduğunu, neye inandığını veya zihninde kurduğu dünyayı aynı şekilde yok edemiyorsun.
SPOILER
Özellikle finali bu yüzden çok sevdim. Fiziksel olarak baktığında ortada korkunç derecede üzücü bir son var. Ofelianın bedeni kurtulamıyor. Fakat film aynı anda onun ruhunun başka bir yere geçtiği ihtimalini de önümüze koyuyor. Yani gerçek dünyanın içinde kaybediyor ama kendi masalının içinde kazanıyor.
Burada filmin kesin olarak bu dünya gerçektir ya da bunların hepsi Ofelianın hayalidir dememesi bence olayı daha da güzel yapıyor. Eğer fantastik dünya gerçekten varsa Ofelia sonunda ait olduğu yere dönüyor. Eğer yoksa bile son anlarında bütün o şiddetin ve acının içinden zihnen kaçıp kendisine huzurlu bir son yaratıyor. İki ihtimal de bir şekilde ruhun, bedenin başına gelenlerden bağımsız olarak kurtulabilmesi fikrine bağlanıyor.
Sanırım beni en çok üzen şey de bu oldu. Filmin bize sunduğu mutlu sonun gerçekten mutlu olabilmesi için önce hangi gerçekliğe inanacağımıza karar vermemiz gerekiyor.
Ben fantastik bir macera izlemeye gelmiştim, film bana faşizm, ölüm, çocukluk, kaçış, ruh ve beden üzerine düşündürüp gönderdi.
Gerçekten çok güzeldi ama hiç beklediğim türden bir güzellik değildi.

Tatli bi masal filmi beklerken bu kadar trajedi dolu bi hikaye olmasi beni cok sasirtti. 
Ofelia babasinin olumunden sonra annesiyle beraber uvey babasi olan Captain Vidalin yanina tasinir. Daha sonra ormanda Pan ile karsilasir ve Pan, Ofeliaya yer alti kralliginin kayip prensesi oldugunu ve tahti kazanmasi icin 3 gorevi basarmasi gerektigini soyler. 
Film boyunca Ofelianin masalinin yani sira bize o donemin ispanyasinda yasanan fasist duzen de gosteriliyor. Yapilan eziyetlerin, catismalarin icinde Ofelia kendi masalina odaklaniyor ve bu 3 gorevi tamamlamaya calisiyor. Bu gorevlerin de aslinda bi metafor oldugunu farkediyoruz. Mesela ilk gorevdeki agactaki kurbagaac gozluluk, kendini kaybetmis olan iktidar. Curuyen agac bozulmakta olan dunya. Ama her seye ragmen Ofelia curumeye baslamis olan dunyada masumiyetini kirletmemeyi basarabiliyor. 
İkinci gorevdeki Ofelianin yememesi gereken meyveler mesela onlar birer yasak ama bazen masum kalabilmek icin itaati reddetmek gerekebiliyor. Ofelianin yaptigi da buydu.
Filmin sonunda Pan, Ofeliadan masum birinin kanini akitmasini istiyor ve Ofelia buna karsi cikiyor. Boylece aslinda farketmeden testi gecmis oluyor ve kralligina geri donuyor.  Peki Ofelianin inandigi masal aslinda gercek miydi? Bu soru sanirim Del Toronun bizi ikilemde birakmak istemesi sonucunda kesin olarak yanitlanamiyor. Yani Ofelia gerceklerden kacmak icin kendince boyle bi masal uydurmus ya da inandigi masal dunyasi gercekten var olmus olabilir.

What a Wonderful World Challenge Film 8
Roughly a year ago, I celebrated the start of a weekend by doing one of my absolute favorite things making a Blu Ray purchase. With any other type of shopping, I prepare a strategy in advance that will get me in and out of a store in the shortest amount of time imaginable. Life is too short to spend it grocery or clothes shopping, but adding a movie to my collection? That is simply the bees knees. I could spend hours wandering the aisles of a store containing a vast amount of Blu Ray options and I will enjoy every second of it. On this particular day, I ended up leaving that store with Guillermo del Toros Pans Labyrinth in my hand, a blind buy made with faith that I would cherish a film so highly regarded, and I couldnt wait to get home and give it the debut spin.
That night, Pans Labyrinth began and all was well for about 15 minutes until something forced my finger to press down on the stop button and call it a night. Annoying, sure, but no big deal really. I would get back to this magical cinematic world the next day and finally understand what so many people had fallen in love with over the years. The strange thing though is, I didnt get back to it the next day...or the next day, or the next week, or the next month after that and so on. It wasnt that the film did anything wrong during those brief 15 minutes I had witnessed, in fact it had already enchanted me throughout the early moments, but instead it was merely a case of being distracted by other new and shiny options laid out before me. So many brilliant films to see, and seeing as how I now owned Pans Labyrinth I could get back to it anytime I wanted. No rush.
Finally tonight was the night, and after witnessing this exquisite film a part of me is angry that it took so long to delve back into it. The other part of me is trying to focus on a bright side to this story, the side that recognizes how much I have grown with my appreciation for film during that year which possibly allowed me to look at Pans Labyrinth with a different frame of mind than I would have then. A few months ago I witnessed the masterpiece The Spirit of the Beehive, a film I loved immediately during my initial viewing and my admiration for it continues to grow daily as the imagery and themes of that work linger in my mind and occasionally invade my thoughts. The first 15 minutes of Pans felt like a completely different experience this time around, as I noticed the striking similarities between Spirit of the Beehive and this film and my appreciation for Del Toro and his ability to embrace the art that inspired him soared to new heights. 
Pans Labyrinth tells the story of a young girl named Ofelia as she enters a new world she wants no part of, a move to a different home and a different life due to her pregnant mothers marriage to the cold and ruthless Captain. It is a time of Spanish civil war and Ofelia is surrounded by conflict, both between the men on the battlefield and also her desire to escape this new situation which she recognizes is poisonous, much to her mothers dismay. Ofelia finds comfort in a fantasy world escape from reality after a fairy points her in the direction of a labyrinth that resides nearby, and it is here that she first meets a Faun that recognizes her as royalty and sets her on a quest to leave this all too real nightmare behind forever.
Every second of this perfectly crafted beauty fascinated me, but the aspect that most impressed me was the way Del Toro so perfectly balanced telling two completely different stories at the same time and yet tonal shifts are never felt, confusion never sets in and while the separation between fantasy and reality is clearly defined, they both manage to enhance the other, as if both a civil war between everyday men and encounters with mythical creatures in impossible locations were needed to form a complete cinematic vision. At times hauntingly beautiful and yet at other times just plain haunting, Pans Labyrinth is an absolute master class in the glory of cinema, completely engrossing and enjoyable as surface level entertainment and yet so thematically rich and profound underneath, an allegory of the highest order. 
I am both humbled and inspired by this film. I am both concerned about the potential for nightmares derived by its imagery and yet excited about the possibility of visiting an imaginative dream world thanks to Del Toro tapping into my subconscious. I love so many films, but rarely does one impact me the way Pans Labyrinth did.

Pans Labyrinth is a coming-of-age story about a young girl who must navigate the dangers of adulthood and find her place in the world. The film is a stunning work of art that blends fantasy and reality in a way that is both mesmerizing and thought-provoking. 
Pans Labyrinth is a film that delves into complex themes such as childhood innocence, morality, and power. The story is told through the eyes of Ofelia, a young girl who is coping with her mothers pregnancy and the presence of her mothers new husband, the fascist captain Vidal, who is tasked with crushing the Spanish resistance. The film uses the fantastical elements of the labyrinth and the creatures that inhabit it to represent the magical and imaginative aspects of childhood, while the brutal realities of the fascist regime represent the harsh and cruel world that adults must navigate.
The film is a masterful blend of fairy tale and historical fiction, and del Toros direction is impeccable. The visuals are stunning, and the special effects are seamlessly integrated into the story. The use of practical effects and makeup is particularly impressive, especially in the design of the films creatures, which are both grotesque and beautiful. The films visual style is a feast for the eyes, with intricate and elaborate sets, costumes, and makeup that transport the viewer to a world that is both familiar and otherworldly. Del Toros use of lighting and color is particularly noteworthy, with warm, natural tones used to represent the world outside of the labyrinth and cool, otherworldly blues and greens used to represent the realm of the faun and the magical creatures.
One of the most interesting aspects of Pans Labyrinth is its use of fairy tale tropes to explore the real-life horrors of Francos Spain. The film juxtaposes the magical elements of the fairy tale world with the brutal violence of the real world, drawing parallels between the two. The faun is not the benevolent figure one might expect from a fairy tale instead, he is a morally ambiguous character who is willing to sacrifice innocent lives in order to achieve his goals. This subversion of traditional fairy tale archetypes adds to the films overall sense of unease.
The character of Captain Vidal is also a notable element of the film. He is a brutal and sadistic figure who embodies the worst aspects of Francos regime. His obsession with power and control is contrasted with Ofelias innocence and imagination, highlighting the destructive effects of authoritarianism on the human spirit. The film also explores the theme of patriarchy, as Vidals toxic masculinity is contrasted with the nurturing, maternal figure of Ofelias mother.
The performances in the film are outstanding, particularly that of Ivana Baquero, who plays Ofelia. Baqueros portrayal of the young girl is both vulnerable and strong-willed, and she carries the films emotional weight on her shoulders. The supporting cast is equally impressive, especially Sergi López, who plays the fascist captain Vidal, and Doug Jones, who portrays the faun.
One of the films strengths is its ability to blend the fantastical with the brutal realities of war. The film is unflinching in its depiction of the violence and atrocities committed by Vidal and his soldiers, and this juxtaposition creates a sense of unease that lingers throughout the film. The fantastical elements, such as the faun and the labyrinth, serve to emphasize the horrors of the real world rather than detract from them.
At its core, Pans Labyrinth is a meditation on the power of imagination and the resilience of the human spirit in the face of adversity. Ofelias ability to hold onto her imagination, even in the face of Captain Vidals brutality, gives her the strength to face the challenges of both the real and magical worlds. The film also explores themes of sacrifice and redemption, as Ofelias quest to complete the fauns tasks.
Another strength of the film is its use of ambiguity. The viewer is left to question whether the events of the film are real or simply the product of Ofelias imagination. It is worth noting the films ending, which is left open to interpretation. The final scene shows Ofelia lying motionless on the ground, surrounded by her fairy tale companions. It is unclear whether she has died and been reborn in the magical realm, or if this is simply a manifestation of her imagination in her final moments. This ambiguity adds to the films sense of mystery and leaves the viewer to ponder the deeper meaning of the story. The film presents both possibilities, and the viewer is free to interpret the film in whichever way they see fit. 
The films score, composed by Javier Navarrete, is also a standout feature. The haunting melodies and choral arrangements add to the films otherworldly atmosphere, while also underscoring the emotional weight of the story, providing a haunting and ethereal score that perfectly complements the films visual and emotional elements. The use of traditional Spanish instruments such as the guitar and the accordion adds to the films authentic feel and its connection to Spanish history and culture. And the use of lullabies and nursery rhymes in the score also adds to the fairy tale-like quality of the film.
Overall, Pans Labyrinth is a stunning work of art. Its blending of fairy tale and historical fiction, its outstanding performances, and its ability to create a sense of unease make it a must-see film. Guillermo del Toros direction is masterful, and the film is a testament to his ability to create visually stunning and emotionally resonant works of art.

Anyone who spends a significant amount of time with me finds me disagreeable.
Gluttony
He has taken on too much. Det. David Mills (Brad Pitt), deliberately uprooting his wife, Tracy (Gwyneth Paltrow), from upstate and dragging her to this lurid hellhole, all out of a naïve desire to save the world. So much ambition, he nearly chokes on it. So much chatter, he sucks all the air from the room.
Det. William Somerset (Morgan Freeman) long ago saw his passion wither. He is one week from retirement, too exhausted to keep pace with the horrible goings-on around him. Like his spiritual descendant, Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) in No Country for Old Men, he sees the world as a cruel and ugly place, one which he cannot wait to leave behind. Away from all the incessant noise, the aural clutter of traffic and shouting and delinquent activity outside his windows. Off to a place where it doesnt rain every day. A place of peace and quiet, where he can hear himself think.
But Somersets intelligence gets the best of him. He cannot deny itit is what makes him such a gifted detective, even if it annoys the cocky Mills (and seemingly everyone else on the force). Somerset knows a personally motivated work-in-progress when he sees one. Being force-fed to death is such a psychologically invasive way to die. It is a crime of passion and of patience. The corpulent corpse rotting in its disgusting apartment, its skin a spiderweb of veins, is only the beginning of something complicated and grotesque, something epitomizing Somersets desire to wash his hands of this grey, grimy city.
Greed
Somersets recusal is of no matter to Mills. More for him, he thinks. A shocking crime, ready-made for the front page, and all to himself. And where better to hoard acclaim than in an opulent high-rise law office, a tower to mammon, a place that exists chiefly to be looked upon and showered with prestige and lucrative billable hours.
Bills are not usually paid in pounds of flesh outside of Shakespeare (Merchant of Venice. Didnt see it.), but then again invoices arent usually so explicit about their avaricious impulse. Blood on the floor neatly arranged in Roman letters has a way of attracting attentionit is not the calling card of a wallflower.
Somerset is erudite and wise. He sees a pattern developing and heads for Chaucer, Dante, Aquinas, immersing himself in a sea of ghostly green lamps. The books illustrations offer a reminder that, despite the detectives growing despair, evil is not new under the sun. And now the seven deadly sins, played out in intricate and horrifying detail, each a condemnation of self-idolatry referenced with the darkly ironic purpose of idolizing the man play-acting them. 
Mills, by contrast, is cloddish and dim, straining over photographs in his apartment. He is aimless where Somerset is methodical. He is loved by his wife where Somerset is alone.
Sloth
A quiet evening at the Mills apartment. Tracy, more perceptive than her husband would like to admit, senses an opportunity to bond with someone in her new city, to help Mills forge an alliance with a useful partner. Dinner and wine, a loving couple teasing each other and a self-deprecating older man. The train rumbling past breaks down defenses while threatening the china. The realtor failed to mention it. Sloth is not mere laziness, it is the failure to do right by ones obligations.
That has never been our killers problem. He is thrifty and organized and always committed to his plan. His mission is warped, but he executes it with vigor. Fingerprints on a wall spelling out a mournful plea. Making use of each and every part of the animala mindful butcher.
It leads in the direction of a drug-dealing pederast, a direction Somerset spots as too convenient. This molester is not reading the Divine Comedy, nor has he any interest in the morbidly obese. All pieces must fit, but this one is jagged. No, the molester has been tied to his bed, locked awayas he should have been long agoslowly, almost lovingly, starved to near death. Desiccated and rife with sores, he can no more remember his name than Mills can recall the name of his former partner shot down his rookie year. Life is disposable. Sloth is not mere indolence, it is the flourishing of evil under the unwatchful eye of good yet diffident and forgetful men.
Lust
David Finchers films specialize in the fetishization of filthhe gives life to the notion of beauty as residing in the eye of the beholder. The dark, dank rooms lit only by carefully placed beams of light recall Spielbergs favorite awe-inspiring ploy only to pervert it in favor of something uglyor, at least, something that should be ugly. But Fincher, with his muted color palette and his careful, elegant compositionsably assisted by cinematographer Darius Khondjihas a way of finding the grandeur in the mundane and the elegance in the grotesque. If Se7ens progeny are the annoyingly interchangeable ocean of serial killer films and television procedurals that followed its success, Fincher makes sure that the cost was worth it by painstakingly crafting a pitiless-yet-beguiling universe. A world drenched in the baser impulses, inciting unspeakable desires pulsating just beneath the surface.
Those impulses, when properly channeled, lead the species to propagate. But even for a beautiful young woman married to a beautiful young man, procreation is daunting. Without friends or family nearby, without a job to distract from the degeneracy on every corner, bringing a child into the world can seem not just intimidating but foolish and wrong. Even lust put to Gods good ends bows under the weight of so much sorrow. At least its better than death by improvised SM device, a bloodletting as scarring for the man forced at gunpoint to pathologize his lust as for the woman on the receiving end of John Does (Kevin Spacey) lesson in chastity.
Pride
And who is John Doe? He is Gods messenger, and he is ever so proud of his work. His apartment is less a home than a shrine to the scourge of casual sinfulness to which he must bear daily witness. There is, as they say, a method to his raging madness. He will get the world to take stock of its wrongdoing, and in the most memorable possible way.
Of course, we all know which way pride goeth, whether its a models choice to go permanently to sleep rather than awaken to a reconfigured face or a madmans symphonic diatribe against modern callousness. Doe sees the world much as Somerset doesneither can stand living in a place that encourages apathy as a virtue. But prideself-regard mutated into contempt and hatred of otherspushes Does despair into action, even into an endgame which Doe by design cannot survive.
Envy
The talent onscreen is nothing short of brilliant, particularly Freeman, whose effortlessness must make most actors seethe with jealousy. Lending his innate gravitas to the stock role of the older, wiser half of a mismatched pairing, Freeman imbues Se7en with a world weariness that makes his desire to quit seem like good sense rather than cowardice. Pitt uses his jittery 1990s energy productively as the overeager, inexperienced half of the duo, a man whose admirable goals are undone by his hotheadedness and inattention to detail. And Spacey brings a chilling intelligence to Doe, a bright, well-bred, educated, moneyed lunatic who, thanks to a perversion of the American dream of being a white male, is afforded the opportunity to play out his messianic dreams as a piece of anti-moral-degradation performance art. Spaceys icy stillness plays off of Pitts over-caffeinated hyperactivity beautifully, with Freemans composure keeping everything in balance. Together they make what could be an interminably long car-ride conversation dynamic and fleet. A casting director would kill for such a team.
Figuratively, that is. But others truly do kill for similar reasons. They pass beyond the understandable feeling of discontent at seeing ones own shortcomings implicitly highlighted by anothers strengths. They covet. Anothers blessing must be undonethe only cure for ones envy is anothers deprivation.
Wrath
Outside of the city, it is no longer overcast. Rain no longer pummels the weary traveler. For the first time, the sun shines down. But industrial totems are never far away, not with a web of power lines slicing the sky into pieces.
The sunshine should allow for clearer sight, but darkness is not all that obscures Mills vision. The problem, he thinks, is a handful of crazies, the periodic lunatic flailing about and wreaking havoc. The sense of otherness is disturbing in its unknowability, but comforting in its false sense of security. If the problem is more endemic, more fundamentalas both Doe and Somerset believethen comfort is a scarce resource indeed.
Hence Somersets repeated admonition that Mills not dismiss Doe or his ilk as just loonies. Their madness both grows out of and infiltrates the world around them, impacting one in ways one couldnt imagine. Best to be prepared for what iseventuallyto come.
Finchers camera knows this, cross-cutting between the helicopters vantage and low angles of Does hectoring and medium shots of Somersets thoughts playing across his face. The cutting and close-ups increasing in frequency, in step with the heart rate, mirroring the rising emotions. One can never truly inure oneself to deep, pitiless cruelty, but acknowledgement of its existence can cushion the blow. Somerset has spent years preparing for thishis pragmatism is his saving grace. But Mills is too scattered and impulsive not to be blindsided by the evil that men do. With no prefabricated outlet, his wide-eyed fondness for justice gives way to explosive anger. So much pain and suffering, as much as anyone you could encounterand still Hell to look forward to.

about an hour into this movie morgan freeman takes brad pitt to bribe an fbi agent for information about library reading.
is that even legal? pitt asks.
freeman literally waves his hand at the question. legal? illegal? these things dont apply. then explains that because they cant use it as evidence its fine, its just a guide.
this payoff leads them directly to the perpetrators door and a shootoutchase. internalized justifications of unscrupulous law violations are common to all kinds of movies about the police. the ends justify the means. i shouldnt exactly expect this movie to be different. but the precise language showing a through-line from these early computing days of privacy violation to the current widespread surveillance state we find ourselves in now upsets me.
this scene is just one specific example of sevens rampant conservatism, though. its a film that sees urbanity as a literal hell of irrational violence. crime is everywhere, its monstrous, and nothing can be done to stop it.
at one point paltrow tells freeman that where they used to live she was a school teacher, and that shes been looking into it and becoming disheartened, because the schools are so bad here.
have you tried looking into private schools? freeman asks.
this movie is white flight the movie. the only answer people can come up with is running away. because crime is a disease. it has nothing to do with systems, or power relations, or income inequality. its a cancer that is spreading and worsening and terminal.
and in the way it glorifies spaceys killer, this movie validates this position. he is not what crime is. hes smart, rational, committed, thorough, patient, comprehensible, not crazy. all the anecdotes about crime that make up the digressive dialogue of this movie focus on how incomprehensible they are. their motives make no sense. pitt repeatedly projects onto spacey the stereotypes of insanity and freeman repeatedly chastises him for it. spacey isnt crazy. hes travis bickle if bickle were smart. fed up with the dirt of the city, distrustful of societys ability to handle these problems itself, and consumed by a religious self-righteousness.

The sloth victim SWAT raid twist is still one of the most upsetting in serial killercop procedural history (the image of him waking up fucked me up so bad as a teen, as did the Polaroid of the improvised, bladed strap-on during the interrogation scene). And even the writing manages to really sing via these well-cast central performances. When Mills drunkenly confronts Somerset about his apathetic worldview in the face of all this horror, Pitts gradual delivery of I wont agree with you... I do not... I cant from confident to shaky is so expressive and revealing, as is Freemans incredibly resigned Were collecting all the evidence, taking all the pictures and samples, writing everything down, noting the times things happen... However, its also telling that despite how horrifying and miserable this gets that Fincher still makes time for people... On rewatch, I always find myself drawn to the quiet scenes of camaraderie, conversation or introspection that play as interludes to the horror, like all the scenes of characters sitting around, driving, eating food, sleeping on the couch, doing the grunt work, and talking about life, philosophy, and literature. I have been thinking long and hard about it and the only flaw I can find in this film is the way the title is written. It makes no sense and is annoying.
The rest? Sheer perfection.
It is always difficult to determine when you are allowed to call a film a classic or a masterpiece. To avoid that discussion lets use a term I think we can all agree on. Masterclass.
Each and every aspect of this film is executed with such a degree of perfection and dedication that it is nigh impossible to call it anything else. This is filmmaking at the highest level, a level that has not been equalled or surpassed often in the genre. 
It all starts with an idea, a story. There had never been, nor has there been since, a plot like the one in Seven (I refuse to write it any other way!!). Exploring the nature of evil has been done before, but never quite like this and never as firmly rooted in the zeitgeist in which it was made. It is disturbing and intelligently so. While pulling no punches it is never concerned with outsmarting its audience, but rather captivate and entertain them in this escalating spiral of violence and depravity in which its main protagonists live with a false sense of control, only to be propelled towards a certain doom. Whether you saw it coming or not, the impact of the full extent of John Does plan is absolutely devastating. A good script is a necessity for a great film, a superb script a guarantee.
While the cast is excellent in every way, the true star here is David Fincher. He has created an aesthetic that has been copied so many times, but has never really been equalled. He added a disturbing degree of realism to the gore and practical effects and made the world the characters inhabit a dark and bleak place with little to no room for levity. And that is what creates this films staying power. It is a completely submersive experience, one that is hard to escape from and one that stays with you for a while afterwards. All Finchers qualities he so often displayed with later efforts serve this film perfectly. Its meticulously made, beautifully paced and creatively shot. 
Reading this all back Im going to say to hell with it.
Its a classic and a masterpiece.

Empecé a repasar toda la filmografía de David Fincher para hacer su respectivo video que, como me suele pasar, quizás no lo termine nunca. O quizás si. Ya vi su ópera prima, Alien 3, película que no quisiera ver nunca más en la vida. Y ahora sigo con lo que REALMENTE es su primera película 
    Esta es una de las tantas películas que mi mamá no me dejaba ver porque era demasiado violenta (la película, no ella) Se basaba en una suposición que sacó viendo el trailer de Telefe que te mostraba al gordo que aparece muerto al principio y para ella eso era motivo suficiente como para considerar que no era algo apto para un niñato de once años.    Me acuerdo de otra noche que yo estaba en mi pieza viendo Batman (la serie animada) y el narrador anuncia el capítulo que se venía Profecía Satánica. Mi mamá desde su pieza escuchó el título y vino corriendo a cambiarme de canal. Nunca pude ver ese capítulo hasta hoy que lo vi antes de escribir esto y la verdad no era para tanto. 
    Todo un esfuerzo inútil de mi mamá para evitar que viera escenas no aptas para mi edad pero no pudo evitar que vea la película que más me traumó en la vida Cementerio De Animales. La vi a los siete u ocho años y ahí si me hubiese venido bien que me hagan cerrar los ojos cuando aparece el colorado con toda la cabeza destruida, o cuando la empleada se suicida, o como cuando atropellan al bebé, o como cuando aparece la Tía Zelda. Por Dios la Tía Zelda, que cosa tan espantosa y tan bien hecha. 
   Pude ver Pecados Capitales (así le pusieron en Latinoamérica) ya en la época que Blockbuster desembarcó en la ciudad de La Plata. Me acuerdo perfectamente la primera vez que fui y como no podía creer la CANTIDAD de películas que había bajo un mismo techo. Más teniendo en cuenta que el videoclub de mi barrio tenía apenas una décima parte y casi la mitad eran películas porno. 
    Ir a Blockbuster a recorrer las estanterías era, para mi, una salida en sí misma aunque no alquilara nada. Generalmente me iba con las manos vacías porque, como le pasaba al Asistente de Los Simuladores, yo no tenía DVD. Igual no me importaba, ya con pasear por el local y conocer la existencia de nuevas películas me conformaba. 
    Esa primera vez fui con un amigo (Juan) que sí tenía reproductor de dvd. Su familia estaba mejor económicamente que la mía. Por lejos. Cuando a mi recién me pudieron comprar el Sega, Juan ya tenía Playstation. Mientras que en mi casa se desayunaba con pepas, en la suya había Oreos. En mi casa se tomaba agua o jugo Carioca, en la suya Coca Cola. Tan imponente era su poder adquisitivo que tenía uno de los juguetes más deseados por los niños de los noventa un Megazord gigante que se podía desarmar para tener todos los Dinozords individuales. ¿Qué tiene que ver esto con Se7en? Nada. 
    Esa primera vez alquilamos Volver Al Futuro. Obviamente ya la habíamos visto un millón de veces pero nunca en tan buena calidad. Aunque el verdadero atractivo de esta alquilada era que el disco venía con escenas eliminadas. Vimos al Doc sobornar al policía que le reclama el permiso para tener un aparato meteorológico, vimos la escena completa de Marty disfrazado de Darth Vader asustando a George, y vimos la escena entera de Johnny B. Good (en el corte final no está completa) 
    Un par de años después alquilé, finalmente, Pecados Capitales. Ya para esa época mi papá se dignó a comprar un reproductor de DVD por insistencia de mi mamá que estaba harta de perderse películas que toda la ciudad veía. La alquilé, la vi y no me pareció la gran cosa. Hay que tener en cuenta que las expectativas que tenía eran altísimas. Era LA PELÍCULA CENSURADA, esa película que yo NO PODÍA VER PORQUE ERA MUY CHICO. Viéndola de adolescente no me pareció para tanto. 
    La vi muchísimas veces a lo largo de mi vida y en cada visionado la apreciaba un poco más hasta que llegó el momento de considerarla una obra de arte. Se7en no se aprecia solo por la investigación en sí o por las escenas explícitas que espantaban tanto a mi mamá (que al final no resultaron ser tan explícitas porque parte de la magia es que uno termine de construir el horror) sino por como David Fincher construye desde lo visual y lo argumental toda una atmósfera oscura e infernal por donde los personajes viajan intentando encontrar al asesino. No hay ni una escena donde se respire un poco de tranquilidad. Ni en las que transcurren en interiores, porque son todos espacios reducidos, laberínticos, oscuros, sucios y desprolijos. Ni en las que transcurren en exteriores porque siempre está nublado y lloviendo. Ni siquiera nos podemos relajar en la escena donde Morgan Freeman, Brad Pitt y Gwyneth Paltrow se juntan a comer porque hay un subte que cada tanto pasa por abajo haciendo que tiemble la casa. Todo esto contrastado con la escena final donde por fin podemos ver el sol y el cielo despejado.
    Los protagonistas también están construidos con esta estética pesimista como si fuesen una versión oscura de Martin Riggs y Roger Murtaugh (los de Arma Mortal) Por un lado el Detective Somerset, el experimentado que está al borde de la jubilación y que se resignó a vivir en un mundo hostil. Por el otro el Detective Mills, el novato con un poco más de esperanza en la humanidad pero invadido por una ira asesina. Y además con un dolor de espalda que lo acompaña a todos lados (Como a mi. Soy ese) 
    Se7en es una joya del cine que hay que ver más de una vez para poder valorar todo lo que David Fincher nos quiere contar.  Imposible de apreciar teniendo once años  y viéndola en una canal de televisión donde seguramente le cortaban un montón de escenas tanto como para eliminar la violencia como para ajustarla en una programación. Habrá que ver si su siguiente película (The Game) está a la altura.

Original, disturbing, grim, brutal, shocking  emotionally devastating, David Finchers breakthrough feature is a haunting masterpiece that today is widely  rightly ranked amongst the greatest examples of its genre(s), and is also notable for kickstarting an impressive directorial career that has only continued to strengthen with each new entry.
Se7en follows two homicide detectives who become deeply involved in the latest case of appalling crimes relating to the seven deadly sins and desperately try to hunt down the sadistic serial killer before he accomplishes his mission. The plot also covers their initial friction with each other and the contrast in their working methods.
Impeccably directed by Fincher, the picture is a work of perfection from start to finish in which even the tiniest details end up contributing to the entire experience, plus the dark narrative itself feels like something that came right out of the abyss. Andrew Kevin Walkers screenplay is also meticulously structured with each event, character, motivation  purpose properly weighed before they make their way into the final draft.
Coming to the technical aspects, production design team does a stellar job in creating the decaying  dismal environment the plot takes place in and it is further heightened by the bleak photography that adds to the nihilistic tone  inhospitable look the story was aiming for. Editing makes sure every scene is relevant to the plot and expertly paces the unfolding drama. And Howard Shores score gradually elevates the nerve-jangling tension to an almost unbearable level.
As for the performances, the film features a dependable cast in Morgan Freeman, Brad Pitt, Gwyneth Paltrow  more but what makes the picture sing is the terrific chemistry between Freeman  Pitt as veteran  rookie respectively. Freeman plays his character in a calm  composed fashion and contributes with a measured showcase. Pitt goes slightly overboard in few scenes but his input still stays within the realms of his characters dimensions.
However, it is actually our serial killer who ends up stealing the show from the moment he reveals himself to the audience to the very twisted, bone-chilling  unforgettable finale thats powerful enough to scar its viewers for a long time. Also, the opening credits sequence alone is a masterwork in itself, for the sense of eeriness it evokes only serves as a forewarning for the horrors that lie ahead. And the film as a whole works immensely well as a fascinating meditation on evil.
On an overall scale, Se7en is one of the darkest, creepiest  finest examples of psychological horrors that remains as effective today as it was back at its time of release. The extent to which it tries to delve into the mind of a serial killer is rather unsettling yet the uncompromising approach the director took in envisioning a sinister script on the screen makes it all the more admirable. A dark, brooding  unrelenting terror of devilish proportions, Finchers darkest masterpiece is in my eyes one of the greatest films ever made.

This is the darkest blockbuster of the 90s, and its hard to believe this movie made 328 million. I believe David Fincher softened his filmmaking style after Fight Club. 
His earlier films tend to be grim, with low lighting and an incredibly nihilistic philosophy. If you want to see what a less skilled filmmaker does with a dark Andrew Kevin Walker script, just look at the bizarre calamity 8MM. 
The film serves as a musing on the death penalty. The dilemma faced by Brad Pitts character reflects the laws struggle with vengeance. 
John Doe is incredibly influential. The ongoing interest in true crime today, along with the glorification of the genius philosophical serial killer, can be traced back to films like Seven. I dont share this view on serial killers when it comes to real-life examples, and I think Fincher feels the same way. 
Consider John Carroll Lynchs character in Zodiac. The killer is depicted as a despicable moron, living in a filthy trailer filled with live squirrels in cages and frozen rodents in the freezer, consuming these animals. 
He incriminates himself in various ways during his interrogation. The letters he sends to the newspapers are poorly written. His clumsy use of language, along with the insecurity and frail ego reflected in these letters, make it clear that he is both dim-witted and pathetic. 
Real serial killers are nothing like John Doe. While they may attract a following and fascinate true-crime enthusiasts, the reason they evade law enforcement is that catching criminals is incredibly difficult. The odds are against the police. 
Criminals lack the intriguing philosophies of the seven deadly sins any manifesto they produce is merely the ramblings of a madman. 
Seven is genuinely an intoxicating film. The shoe-leather scenes are made thrilling through the Hitchcock-esque score, Morgan Freemans haunted and world-weary performance, masterful use of creepy insert shots, and the intelligent way the breadcrumb trail is laid out. 
Its impressive how scenes are illuminated only by flashlight beams, making us feel suffocated by the oppressive darkness. 
The best scenes in the movie feature Gwyneth Paltrow, particularly the breakfast scene where she discusses her pregnancy and the challenges of bringing a baby into this cursed world (with Freeman). 
The dinner scene is also vital we need to care deeply for her in a very short amount of time for the ending to hit with the force of a freight train. The dinner scene provides a moment of levity, charm, and humor, allowing the audience to breathe freely for a moment. Its like a cool drink of water on a hot summer day.
The film features only one pure action sequence (when John Doe unexpectedly arrives at his apartment). Fincher crafts this chase with remarkable precision and a clear vision, resulting in a scene so tense that I almost stop breathing. This moment showcases the screenplay taking bold shortcuts in the investigation that shock the audience. 
Consider the thrill of witnessing John Doe walk into the police station with bloody fingertips. His surrender dramatically raises the stakes in the final half houranything can happen. This unpredictability intensifies the horror, as it makes the audience feel unsafe.
Fincher is working in an emotionally cold mode, when compared to the heavy emotions The Silence of the Lambs evokes in me. 
Jonathan Demme is a different type of filmmaker he finds humanity and empathy in the darkest corners of the serial killer genre, while Fincher executes his dark vision of life without any compromise to his nihilism. 
This makes Seven more of a one-dimensional musing on vicious crimes, albeit a very viscerally affecting one. 
However, since turning 30, I have grown less interested in the films misanthropy as my views on life have mellowed.

Se7en remains David Finchers greatest film and has one of the greatest scripts ever thrown around Hollywood. It is so incredibly precise and well thought out. It is a high concept crime thriller, elevated by its genius twists and ever-building pace. Se7en is never a fast and flashy movie, it starts off grimly contemplative and just gradually builds into an intense psychological war. Four of the titular seven deaths occur only in the final forty-five minutes. Se7en is a film to grind down your soul, moving faster and faster until it suddenly stops, with a bang.
Se7en is a nihilist depiction of a rotten world. It exists in state of urban moral decay. The unnamed city is a creation never bettered in Hollywood, besides some sci-fi cities. The city is depicted through Finchers carefully constructed, rarely moving camerawork. He paints scenes in the dark, with little light and only depressing colours. Everything is dilapidated, damp, and rotting. The desaturated colour scheme creates somewhere lifeless, a world without hope. There is not one ounce of joy in the entirety of Se7en. Instead there exists only a sinful, disgusting world, and a puritanical morality derived surely from madness. Se7en is a meditation on evil and the society of apathy we inhabit. It has to exist in a fictional place, because we would never sleep well if this were real.
The city in Se7en is evil, yet there are two kinds of people those who want to stay and those who want to leave. Part of that is embodied by the two detectives, who are fundamentally good people, but drawn with such well-defined and different personalities. One is mature and cerebral, wanting to leave this life behind. The other is short-tempered, impatient, and idealistic, willing to move to a city so awful. They are confronted with some of the most disturbing murders in cinema. Se7en is a truly gruesome film, and one scene (the sloth) terrifies me to this day. It has one of the most effective jump scares ever, but the sheer concept of its evil is beyond comprehension.
Se7en remains the highest bar for this type of dark detective film. It is scary and nasty, yet drawn deeply from human darkness rather than supernatural depravity. Every second delivers, with a stellar script, expert direction, and a fantastic cast. Its the stuff of nightmares and the most depressing thing I could ever call entertaining.

If David Fincher isnt a great director, hes pretty damn close. The Social Network and Zodiac are classics, and Gone Girl just might be, too. One thing I feel pretty strongly, though, is that for all of the technical skill apparent in Finchers earlier films, it was occasionally put to use in the service of broadly drawn characters and gotcha! conceits.
Brad Pitts character in Seven is written as a foil to Morgan Freemans weathered, cynical, but mature Detective Somerset. Just so we dont miss the fact that Detective Mills is, in essence, Dennis the Menace with a handgun, he delivers zingers like, Who?! Stinky man?! and This is retarded! After the killer has executed four meticulously planned murders, Mills describes him as, Dancing around in his girlfriends panties, rubbing peanut butter all over himself. We also get not one but two montages of Detective Somerset in the library, poring over the pages of Paradise Lost and Dantes Inferno, while Detective Mills shoves the Cliffs Notes of said texts into Somersets now former desk.
In order to build anticipation for Kevin Spaceys Evil Genius character, we have THE MURDER SCENES. While I guess theyre a production designers wet dream, the look of this film is so Its Always Raining in Murderdelphia and The Dim and Dimmer Interior Lighting Company... It all looks a bit cartoonish and over the top. 
Spoiler-ish, but the twist to this film is tied to one of the most meme-ified lines in film history, so youre probably good. When Kevin Spacey, the OOOOOH HE SO CRAAAAZY! killer shows up at the precinct, drenched in blood and self-satisfaction, we begin to understand why Fincher felt like he had to go so overboard in establishing Brad Pitt as Detective McLovin. He has to be the perfect mark for John Doe!s master scheme. A mature Mills would have made for Six Deadly Sins and no Whats in the boooooooooxxxxxxx!?
So while this film is well done, and sufficiently nihilistic, I dont think it comes close to Finchers recent work. In the past, Finchers meticulous visuals and dark sensibility seemed to serve circuitous, Fight Club-y plots more than its characters. But when I think about how much the characters in Social Network, Gone Girl, and Zodiac pop, I get really excited for what Fincher might do with Mank later this year.

Every time I watch Finchers version of The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo, I like it more. Not sure if itll ever reach the level of those three, though.

After enjoying Zodiac so much I thought it was time to revisit Seven, another one of Finchers best and where Zodiac is a closer more focused look at the frustrations of the hunt, Seven is more structured in approach with a steady progression towards a climax. I think both movies are amazing in their own right, Zodiac will probably shine with multiple viewings but theres no doubt the first time watch of Seven is greater than that of Zodiac purely down to that god tier ending. 
Its funny the ending of Seven is so fucking awesome the studio wanted to change it as it was too gruesome. You gotta be kidding me, about suggesting if they should use Mills dogs head instead of what we actually got. So, good on Pitt for fighting to keep the original ending as its one of the greatest endings in cinema history. 
Again Finchers signature style is all over this, the visuals are both disturbing and compelling, with perfect composition and lighting executed to great heights its hard to look away from the visceral horror of events we see unfolding. A lot of the lighting is evoked from natural sources, keeping its dark and claustrophobic tone, whilst subtly highlighting the details in the shadows. He worked hands on with the lead cinematographer and the piece definitely benefited from two extremely well versed cinema heads working together. 
Darius Khondji does terrific work as the lead cinematographer evoking a terrifying and captivating world, not only elevating the narrative visually but metaphorically with his use of different techniques. You can be sure this is a reference piece and something many aspiring filmmakers take inspiration from.
The film is very well acted, Morgan Freeman and Brad Pitt have great chemistry and absorb me from the opening scene. Both contrasting but complementary performances with Freeman being the veteran detective on his last legs soon to retire, whereas Pitt is the rookie with a small fuse. Their chemistry adds depth and interest to the story, both delivering magnificent performances and it may be a top 35 Brad Pitt performance, especially for that ending scene. 
The visual tone is Fincher level of outstanding, I expect nothing less. Hes a genius at drawing the viewers into every scene, the rain soaked city landscape keeps things gritty and oppressed with a certain level of morbidness, engulfing the viewers in a state of terror and unsettlement. 
The score is a masterstroke, evoking all the right emotions and adding to the atmosphere of unsettlement. Howard Shore blessed the film with over 60 minutes of original eerie music, I absolutely love what he did with the score come the final few scenes, terrific work. 
However you look at Spacey its clear he elevates that third act and puts this movie into the upper echelon. His mannerisms and dialogue push his performances as John Doe forward and he as a character is so complex, so many variables and opinions on his motives and actual plan. Most of his motives are based on the blind hypocrisy of the world, and he believes hes making the difference. His entire plan is flawed in hypocrisy as him seeking to erase evil is halted by the fact hes a sadistic narcissist, although we do see the seventh and deathly sin wrath, in full force during those ending moments. 
Brad Pitts whats in the box has to be one of my favorite scenes in cinema, an absolute all timer. His acting is at an all time high here and you can clearly see why he wanted this original ending, it was even written in his contract that it had to be this.
I do think this is Finchers best work and its quickly rising in my favorites. I want to watch more Fincher so Im gonna be watching The Killer soon, Im interested to see how Fassbender does at the hands of Fincher, and Im also on a little crime thriller binge after I adored Zodiac. Dont think many will reach the heights of Seven as this truly felt like the pinnacle of crime thrillers.

In 1996, at the young dumb age of 12, my older brother rented a movie from the local family run video store. As he started to watch it, I became curious and joined him, but my introduction into the brilliance of David Fincher was short lived as my mother would soon enter the room and announce that I wasnt old enough for such things. I didnt even try to fight her on the subject, it was useless, so I did what any good kid would do. I sat in the next room pretending to do homework, both listening to the events of the film unfold and also conjuring up a plan to be able to watch it later in secret. 
That night I snuck downstairs after everyone had reached a heavy depth of slumber and laid my eyes on this dark, brooding masterpiece. It is hard to describe how I must have felt in that moment, as the haunting concept of a serial killer and the horrific images of his work danced through my mind. Such evil was new to me, as I had screened quite a few works involving terror, brutality and death before, but they had all been works of undeniable fiction like Alien and Predator. Never before had I considered the possibility that such evil could be lurking in the darkness in the form of a person like myself. I understand why my mother would want to hide this side of the world from me, as I probably was too young to truly understand the level of fear that came with the knowledge that real, pure evil actually existed. The ironic thing is, before I experienced Se7en, I never fully appreciated why it was so important that I didnt talk to strangers.
18 years after I first observed the ominous, rain soaked streets walked by Mills and Somerset as they hunted the killer portraying his depraved artistry as a representation of the seven deadly sins, I not only love this film, I consider it to be one of the great works of cinema. Practically every frame makes me uneasy, but in the best possible way. I have so many viewings of Se7en under my belt I lost count a long time ago, yet I still get chills from some of the most unsettling sequences of the film. Im not much of a gore guy, so it isnt some insatiable craving for the graphic nature of these scenes that brings a smile to my face. It is the incredible craftsmanship by a filmmaker with a vision that I cannot get enough of. 
As my passion for gritty, disturbing noir cinema continues to flourish, I will always look back at Se7en as the film that started it all. I will never forget, I watched this on a Sunday night when I had school the next morning, and when I returned to class on Monday my teacher asked us individually what we had done over the weekend. For some reason I felt like being honest when it was my time to shine, so I said I had watched a movie called Seven. The smile left her face immediately, and she moved on to the remaining others without responding. As the end of the day neared, she asked me to stay after school to talk about the movie I had watched. After 5 to 10 minutes of listening to the typical youre too young, its not good for you rhetoric, she sent me on my way. 
The funny thing is, I probably failed to absorb 90 percent of the shit she had taught me that year. Hell, I dont even remember her name at the moment, but one question I had answered for me on that Sunday night will be ingrained in my mind forever.

By the act of immersing the viewer into place full of sin, Fincher  Walker, just like Virgil, provide Dantesque journey through circles of hell (reference to Dantes Inferno).
Many other filmmakers tried to imitate Fincheresque style  most of them failed the director of Zodiac is the one who influenced parents of all these cheesy, silly monsters, like Saw, I Saw the Devil or Shutter Island. One of the genius elements of Se7en is its intense violence achieved without throwing cheap meat in viewers face Fincher shows only corpses, not the killing processes its thoughtful decision that stimulates our consciousness  imagination we generate this violence in our heads. 
The whole movie definitely wouldnt be so compelling if the chemistry between Morgan Freeman  Brad Pitt wasnt so great their characters are complete opposites that complement each other perfectly. William Somerset is sophisticated, almost retired old hand whos representative of high culture he symbolizes ethical heart of the film. David Mills is inexperienced, younger  way more idealistic, impulsive detective. Wilderesque topos, i.e. social dualism is most present in this incredible sequence (best moment in the movie) it flawlessly, eloquently describes two main characters by showing them working calm Somerset looks for answers in literature (incl. This thoughtful, thrilling  transgressive criminal intrigue skillfully leaves the viewer with impression that its some kind of prophetic, profound allegory, but there is actually no such thing here. The world is a fine place and worth fighting for. I agree with the second part.  Ernest Hemingways quote crowned with Williams thought precedes end credits of the film. So many freaks out there doin their little evil deeds they dont wanna do The voices made me do it. My dog made me do it. Jodie Foster told me to do it says Brad Pitt to Morgan Freeman at one point. Although it may seem like a simple casual hint, the reference to Foster actually hides a precise meaning, considering that the actress embodies the very essence of the two masterpieces that inspire this story. On the one hand, The Silence of the Lambs, which consolidated the serial killer thriller genre, and on the other,  Taxi Driver, from which the film inherits the vision of a world crushed by the presence of evil.
Se7en is a painful journey into a degraded, oppressive and violent city, in which an incessant rain accompanies the dramatic hunt of two detectives for a serial killer, responsible for a chain of brutal murders inspired by the seven deadly sins. A journey through an unidentifiable urban space, in a metropolis which - intentionally lacking a name and defined geographical references - assumes the function of a moral metaphor, a metaphysical microcosm through which to explore the dark nature of humanity. David Finchers direction is an excellent example of creative control and technical mastery, capable of perfectly rendering the films disturbing atmosphere. Substantial contributors to this effect are Darius Khondjis very gloomy cinematography, Arthur Maxs sets, and Andrew Kevin Walkers solid screenplay. The director carefully avoids portraying violence explicitly, preferring to focus on its effects and consequences, so as to create a sense of inevitability and helplessness around it. Through this choice, Fincher highlights our inability to face a world out of control, forcing us to reflect on human fragility in the face of malevolent and destructive forces, and leaving us with a bitter feeling of inadequacy with respect to an impenetrable reality.

David Fincher is one of a kind. Seven was way ahead of his time and I consider it to be one of his best, if not his best, film. On this rainy day, I thought we could use a little more rain. With Seven, its always rain...and decay...and apathy. 
Detective Somerset, played by Morgan Freeman, has seen a lot of shit. Hes burnt out from seeing way too many corpses and not nearly enough justice. Detective Mills, played by Brad Pitt, is hot-headed and eager to get done what needs done. Its your typical police drama pair-up. Theyre investigating a series of grotesque murders themed after one of the seven deadly sins. 
I consider this film to be peak 90s grit. Films in this era just had a ruined and decaying ambience to them. In his direction, Fincher and his cinematographer Darius Khondji paint the film in browns and greens, shadows and smog, barely any sunlight bleeding through. You feel the hopelessness throughout like a real-life depiction of Dantes inferno. 
The killings are grotesque, but not really gratuitous. Seven has often been stated as being the inspiration for Saw. Whether thats true or not, I dont think so, but Im sure there was plenty of inspiration from various films. Each killing has a message to it and is rather performative, much like the traps in the Saw franchise. The horror isnt in the gore, but more the ideology. Although the knife dildo is pretty fucking gnarly. 
The pairing of Freeman and Pitt is a stroke of genius. This is one of Freemans most understated performances. He knows the ship is going down around him, but he continues to fix it. Pitt contrasts with brash passion and then helplessness. Its just compelling from start to finish. 
John Doe, played by Kevin Spacey (vomits...), is someone condemning society for its disgusting nature. He sees the apathy and the stagnation of everything around him. He wants to be felt as this overarching presence. 
Frames are never wasted and the dialogue is filled with tension. This could have been a film that drags and drags, but Seven doesnt give us any room to breathe. Its always encompassing and theres always something lurking in the corner. Its not a perfect film, but its pretty damn close. 
Then, the final act just suffocates you. Its not just a plot twist, but a statement. Did John Doe win? Its as quotable now as it was 30 years ago. Whats in the box?! 
David Fincher directed the hell out of this film. And, weve been awestruck in the silence ever since.

The film follows detectives Somerset and Mills as they begin investigating a series of strange and disturbing murders. As the investigation progresses, they realize that these crimes are not random at all, but are connected to the concept of the seven deadly sins. The killer carefully constructs each crime as if he wants to turn every murder into a message, forcing the detectives, and society itself, to confront the darker side of human nature.
Somersets character especially stood out to me because he has such a different view of life. He has witnessed so much evil that he has started to see the world through a pessimistic lens, but at the same time, he still tries to remain rational and hold on to his humanity. Mills, on the other hand, is more impulsive and passionate, and he has a stronger belief that he can actually change things. Their contrast makes the investigation more interesting because they represent two completely different ways of dealing with a world filled with violence and corruption.
To me, the film isnt just about the seven deadly sins. Its about hopelessness, and about living in a world where you see so much evil that you start questioning whether goodness is really enough to change anything. This is especially clear through Somerset, who spends the entire film trying to deal with a world he has almost completely lost hope in.
The film also makes the seven deadly sins more than just a concept behind the murders. Each sin is connected to a different part of human nature, and the killer uses them to justify what he does. This raises questions that go beyond the crimes themselves where is the line between justice and revenge? Where is the line between punishing evil and forcing your own beliefs onto other people?
Because the film doesnt just make you ask, Why does this person kill? It makes you ask something much deeper How does someone reach the point where they believe committing evil is the only way to fight evil?
The killer has a terrifying belief that the world has become so full of sin that people have stopped even noticing it. Greed has become normal, lust has become normal, indifference has become normal, and people have learned to live surrounded by all this darkness as if it were simply a normal part of life. So he decides that he is going to force people to look at the things they have become accustomed to ignoring.
And in the end, Se7en isnt just a film about detectives hunting down a serial killer. To me, its a film about sin, hopelessness, justice, revenge, and the limits a person can cross once they become convinced that they have a greater reason.

Excelente película, una de las obras maestras de David Fincher.
Se7en es uno de los mejores thrillers de la historia del cine, su trama es magnífica y construye un misterio de una forma espectacular, con algunos giros buenísimos y personajes fascinantes, todo esto con visuales bellísimas en la que vemos una ciudad en decadencia que queda perfecto con el tono que maneja la trama y la cinta en general.
Sinopsis Somerset es un solitario y veterano detective a punto de retirarse que se encuentra con Mills, un joven impulsivo. Ambos investigan un particular asesinato. Es este el primero de una serie de crímenes que aluden los siete pecados capitales.
La historia es maravillosa, muy atrapante e inmersiva. Una de las cosas que más me gusta de su trama es cómo se construye el misterio principal, sintiéndonos como uno más de los detectives e intentando descifrar el caso junto a ellos, lo que la vuelve una cinta demasiado inmersiva. Todo esto a través de una trama que nunca deja de sorprender, tomando algunas decisiones inesperadas y teniendo giros excelentes. Además, nunca deja de ser entretenida por lo atrapante que es desde su inicio, ya el simple hecho de tener que resolver un caso me engancha completamente por lo mucho que amo este género en el cine. Encima acá está muy bien hecho y tiene el factor original de que el asesino va realizando asesinatos relacionados a los pecados capitales, algo que la diferencia de otro tipo de películas parecidas. Esto nos da algunas escenas del crimen espléndidas que nos hacen pensar muchas cosas sobre la humanidad me quedo con la ejecución de los últimos dos pecados capitales, simplemente desgarrador. Por otro lado, la ambientación es fantástica, la ciudad se siente un personaje más y me encantó cómo la presentaron en la película, viendo como la lluvia está casi siempre presente, sumándole algo de misterio y oscuridad a la trama. Otra cosa a destacar es alguna que otra escena de acción que tiene, con una tensión bastante presente que te mantiene al borde del asiento. Por último, el final es espectacular y memorable, de los mejores que hay en el cine a mi parecer, tiene un suspenso buenísimo y te deja completamente shockeado, pensando algunas cosas sobre lo injusta que es la vida y la ley en algunas circunstancias. También destacar la locación en la que se sitúa el final de la historia, a pesar de ser un descampado te da una sensación completamente contraria, sintiéndote incómodo y acorralado por lo que está pasando.
En cuanto a los personajes, estos son excelentes. Los detectives Mills y Somerset son geniales, tanto individualmente que como dupla, ambos tienen su respectivo desarrollo y se profundiza un poco en sus vidas, haciendo que conozcamos más sobre ellos y que podamos empatizar fácilmente. Además, la química que tienen es formidable, me gustó mucho poder ver el desarrollo que tiene su relación, siendo algo mas distante al comienzo y teniendo algunos problemas, para después ser más cercanos hasta el punto que Somerset tiene algo de relación con la familia de Mills. Por otro lado, también conocemos a la esposa del joven Mills Tracy, quien no tiene mucho tiempo en pantalla pero juega un papel fundamental en la historia, por momentos parece que su personaje no va a aportar tanto, pero al final es todo lo contrario. Por último, el asesino es fascinante, una mente maestra que tiene todo planeado a la perfección y encima sabe como salirse con la suya siempre, es sumamente inteligente y hasta aterrador por la locura que maneja, parece que te va a sorprender con algo en cualquier momento.
En otros aspectos destaco la dirección de David Fincher, uno de mis directores favoritos que a mi parecer el género de thriller le queda perfecto, me encanta cómo maneja el misterio en sus películas y lo hermosas que son visualmente, ésta particularmente me pareció de las mejores en todo lo visual. Por otro lado, las actuaciones son brillantes, principalmente las de Brad Pitt, Morgan Freeman y Kevin Spacey, quienes hacen unas interpretaciones memorables y de las mejores de sus extensas carreras, no veo a otros actores haciendo de estos personajes, les quedan perfectos. Por último, la banda sonora de Howard Shore es sensacional, me parece que acompaña muy bien a las escenas de suspenso y misterio.
En conclusión, una excelente película que había visto una vez hace años e increíblemente no me había gustado, por suerte pude ir a verla al cine y disfrutar de lo perfecta que es. Gloria a Fincher y a su maravillosa filmografía, de mis directores favoritos sin dudas. Muy recomendada.

David Finchers Se7en  is a psychological thriller of rare intensity, where evil is taken to its extreme. Far from being a simple detective story, this film explores the darkest corners of the human psyche through a gripping investigation led by two detectives who are worlds apart.
Morgan Freeman portrays a seasoned, weary, and disillusioned investigator, marked by decades of gruesome crimes. Opposite him, Brad Pitt plays a young, idealistic, and fiery cop, convinced that justice can prevail. Their forced collaboration leads to electric exchanges, where the clash of generations and philosophies fuels constant tension.
The serial killer, methodical and ruthless, draws inspiration from the seven deadly sins to orchestrate his murders with surgical precision. Each crime is a puzzle, a piece of a macabre jigsaw that the two men must solve. The films atmosphere is heavy and suffocating the incessant rain, dark interiors, and the sordid streets of a decaying city symbolize the moral corruption that permeates every scene.
David Fincher delivers a masterful direction here. Darius Khondjis cinematography, dark and high-contrast, heightens the growing anxiety that builds to a crescendo as the investigation unfolds. The pacing is relentless the audience is kept on the edge of their seats, forced to follow every clue, every detail, to try and guess what comes next. The dialogue is sharp, the actors performances, exceptional.
But its the films ending that leaves a lasting impression. Without revealing the details, the conclusion is daring and utterly bleak. It offers no escape, no glimmer of hope, no redemption. It is this brutal and unforgettable ending that makes Se7en a major work, a reflection on evil, justice, and the absurdity of existence.
A cult film, that redefined the codes of the psychological thriller. A unique cinematic experience, both captivating and deeply disturbing, proving that cinema can be both entertainment and an exploration of the depths of the human soul.

Se7en. 1995. Directed by David Fincher.
Se7en (1995) is a gem in the oeuvre of David Fincher. David Finchers films have entertained us and we have been enamored by his style since his music video (Madonna, Iggy Pop, and George Michael) days. After Se7en, we were hooked. The world of noir has been a favorite genre of ours as well. In HitchcockTruffaut (2015), Fincher explains his obsession with the (book) Hitchcock Truffaut (1984) and how it was a definitive source (like a film makers Bible) to him. 
With this in mind, Se7ens screenplay by Andrew Kevin Walker embodies the world of an existential examination of two investigators portrayed by Morgan Freeman (Somerset) and Brad Pitt (Mills). Mills is considered a neophyte in Somersets world as he has a hot temper and lack of patience. Somerset is weary and was about to step into retirement. Unfortunately, an enigmatic, intelligent serial killer delays Somersets retirement. In fact, the killer is using the seven deadly sins to target specific victims that fit the seven deadly sins definitions. Mills is idealistic and encourages Somerset that he can handle the case by himself. Somerset lies awake at night and worries and frankly disagrees that Mills has it under control. So, Somerset finds himself bound to this case and Mills. Moreover, Walkers script adds layers and Mills has a wife who is pregnant. She is portrayed by Gwyneth Paltrow (Tracy). In the noir universe, a female such as Tracy grounds the movie. She serves as a guiding light for Mills, Somerset and the audience. Will Finchers serial killer get away with his crimes? In the world or neo-noir, and in Finchers world inspired heavily by Hitchcock, how will this play out? 
The aforementioned questions keep the audience guessing and on the edge of their seats. Fincher is a master. He honed his craft by making music videos first. This allowed him to establish a style for his films. Se7en is quite possibly one of Finchers most stylized films aside from Fight Club (1999). Pitt and Freeman were superstar celebrities by the time Se7en came around. Fincher had established himself as the new Hitchcock with more creative narratives, more creative scripts. This is not to say that Hitchcock is not among our favorites. We also adore Truffaut, Chabrol, Houston, Lynch, and Ray. Fincher has his niche and Se7en, Fight Club, Zodiac, and Gone Girl are masterpieces of neo-noir. More recently, we watched Decision to Leave by neo-noir master Park Chan-wook and I needed a neo-noir to warm up with so I viewed Se7en. 
Se7en is ranked number 91 out of 250 on LBs Official Top 250 Narrative Feature Films. On IMDBs Top 250 Films list Se7en is ranked number 19. Either way it made the top 100 in both lists. In our opinion, it is a fine example of neo-noir entertainment and one of David Finchers best. Furthermore, I would be remiss if I did not mention that Shafts (1971) Richard Roundtree was District Attorney Martin Talbot.
