Se7en is one of a handful of movies Ive called my all-time favourite. It came right after Fight Club for me, at a time when my taste was continuing to mature. Of course, a film like Se7en would feel very grown-up to a 14-year-old. My username when I first got online was TheEighthDeadlySin as a neat little reference (which is, still, Im sure youll agree, very badass). 
So it was and possibly still is my most watched movie ever. I used to watch it twice a week on my old Sony PSP, usually for the mood and the thrills, sometimes only for the opening credits. It was just me and a six-inch screen glowing in my face. Even though I know the movie by heart, it was a cherished experience to see Se7en now for the IMAX re-release.
Of course, when you have an opportunity like this, you tend to pay more attention and notice details you hadnt before. Theres not much more this movie can do for me at this point, I was mostly there for the vibes in a full theater, but I felt myself putting together a lot of the little details this time and understanding their connection a lot more as well as figuring out why this movie in particular is one I can endlessly revisit. 
For one, it has to be said how it owes a big debt to Jaws and The Silence of the Lambs in the way it operates in close-ups and lives in the imagination. Even if you do the sin of telling instead of showing, you can expand the world-building when you leave exposition to Oscar-calibre actors. The framework and archetypes are familiar, so itll always be boxed in as a Hollywood movie, but its how all these elements (writing, craft, acting) come together that make it a special one.
I think Ive always known that its the relationship between Somerset and Mills that makes the movie, rather than its seven murders gimmick. This is a movie that understands male friendships, but Ive realized its the lynchpin to the films entire social commentary. No matter how many times I watch it, I always go through the whole journey with the two that intolerable friction they start from, then the shared interest that bonds them, the sense of mentorship and trust that strengthens, and the care that comes along the way. 
You share jokes, you share memories, you share thoughts, you share feelings. Eventually, the walls fall, you get more honest, and you become invaluable to each other. Most crucially you now have someone to lose that you didnt have before.
Its a clever way that Se7en builds its stakes throughout and it does it entirely without sentiment. Their relationship is built incrementally, through gestures, through opportunities for intimacy, through Tracy greasing the wheels. We begin firmly in Somersets headspace and Mills is eventually recruited alongside us. Every time I watch it, my investment in the case and its results grows as the film goes along with them. 
Some examples of the details I love from the writing that depict their gradual growth are Somerset letting Mills interview Goulds wife, their whispers when investigating the fingerprints, Mills insecurity at the pizza place when theyre getting closer, their communal silence in the interrogation rooms deep in the same thought, and most importantly, the way they continue to aggravate each other in the second half but always stick together, almost as if theyre brothers. 
Yeah, a lot can happen in a week. Its corny but its true in the way that people who seem to be completely different can learn a lot from each other and come to be close friends. We never reach that on a societal level. Were too removed from each other. And theres truth in the general sense of apathy that Se7en raises as a significant problem. How do we deal with it?
Most of us would agree that in a big enough city, theres some fucked up shit going on behind closed doors. Well disagree on what and who, but we all dont abide it either. That feeds into conservative ideology that big cities are scary places to avoid, though that misunderstands the laws of averages where, for example, violent crime is inevitable in a big city, but its astronomically unlikely to happen to you personally. Most times people wont care about a societal issue until it does.
Even with Se7ens bleak outlook and horrific tragedy at every grisly aftermath in each iconic setpiece, what keeps you going and also keeps me returning to the film is that little shred of light. Yeah, Somerset and Mills start off like oil and water, but they begin Sunday with Somerset ready to continue the investigation with Mills. Does he want to find out what happens or does he not what to lose what he gained? 
Maybe well continue to pass judgment on strangers, if not passing punishment like John Doe, and maybe well continue to avoid them at all costs. How can I trust you to help me instead of hurt me when were all in it for ourselves? The world may never feel like a fine enough place to bring in the next generation, but what is worth fighting for are the personal relationships we make to keep us safe and surviving in our small communities even when all else appears to be lost.

David Finchers Se7en is a brooding, ominous and phenomenally suspenseful neo noir thriller, which I personally rank as the finest of all his collective works (yes, I even love it more than Fight Club). 
Atmospheric and rain-drenched, it starrs Morgan Freeman as William Somerset a soon-to-be-retired detective who pairs up with the young and temperamental David Mills (a superlative Brad Pitt), after being assigned a murder case, which leads them on a staggering hunt for a serial killer, who is claiming victims in accordance with the seven deadly sins. 
Following the puzzle trail, they are pushed to their psychological limits, as each new homicide presents increasingly disturbing and stomach-churning atrocities. The type of nightmarish imagery, that once it has been seen, cannot be unseen. A haunting segment in particular, which I never seem able to shake off, concerns a corpse found on a bed, which then - in a sudden, terrifying twist - turns out to be still alive giving whole new meaning to the phrase starved to within an inch of his life. 
It isnt a very fast-moving story, yet never for a moment dreary or slackened in its intrigues. Carefully and meticulously, it heat things up to a steady boil - resulting in a mood and suspense that reminds me of Hitchcock at his most effective. As much a brilliant character study as it is a heart-racing whodunit piece. For while the seven cardinal sins may be the central theme of the plot, it boasts at least as many virtues, in all areas of its making. The screenplay by Andrew Kevin Walker is one of the most intelligent Ive ever come across, which in symbiosis with the performances and Richard Francis-Bruces impeccable editing, amounts to an experience of fine-tuned perfection. 
Above all else though, I just love the great interactions between the two lead detectives. One cocky, unruly and governed by emotional impulse. The other serving as the voice of reason with his skillfully deductive methods. As the films antagonist, the mysterious John Doe, we also find a peak-performing Kevin Spacey, in a very chilling and provocative turn, that despite his late appearance in the film, makes an incredibly strong and memorable impression.
Then last, but not least, theres Finchers directing subtle, magnificent and visually unhinged. Flawlessly executed for its entire 2-hour run right up until the shocking finale, which offers a gut-wrenching, curveball of a twist and Brad Pitt at his visceral best. An achievement, which in turn, leads me to my personal definition of what constitutes a masterpiece. 
For in my eyes, the signature of a chef doeuvre, is a film you keep coming back to, even though youre well-aware of the outcome and how everything plays out. Where some films are just great the first time around, Se7en is the rare example of a movie that continues to fascinate, despite the mileage on its existence. A thinking mans thriller, whose superior dominance of the genre remains extraordinarily intact.
Watch it, feel it, let it break through the barriers of your mind. For whichever way you enter this ingenious magnum opus, I can assure you itll dig itself in, whether you want it to or not.

Disillusioned police detective William Somerset (Morgan Freeman) is one week away from retirement, so hes partnered with young, hot-tempered detective David Mills (Brad Pitt), whos preparing to take over from Somerset. Then, a murder victim is found, with the word Gluttony written on a nearby wall. Somerset soon realizes theyre dealing with a serial killer who picks his victims according to the seven deadly sins ...
Se7en (also known as Seven) is a crime thriller film directed by David Fincher.
For my 2,000th Letterboxd review I picked a really great movie, Finchers masterpiece, which I actually hadnt seen in quite some time.
After Finchers first feature film, Alien 3 (my review), became a miserable experience for him, it took Fincher three years to return to feature film making, and in the process, he created one of the most influential crime thrillers in cinematic history, a seminal entry in the genre.
It became a sleeper hit, one of the most successful films of 1995, and has since been widely regarded as one of the greatest movies ever made. It established Pitt as a serious actor and made Fincher a household name.
Its aestethics alone are remarkable, even though the filmmakers certainly watched The Silence of the Lambs (my review) once or twice. The beautiful and creepy title sequence lead to a renaissance for elaborate opening titles, and the style and looks of Se7en inspired countless films and TV series to follow.
Taking place in an unnamed city overrun with crime and violence where it seemingly always rains, Finchers film is thematically rich and invites the audience to analyze and study it. Its also one of the greatest examples in film of two diametrically opposed cops having to work with each other, and Freeman and Pitt are terrific together.
Despite its bleak look, pessimistic outlook and washed-out style, its beautifully filmed and wonderful to watch. Its art direction is outstanding, and Howard Shores musical score atmospheric and eerie, one of his best.
Something the countless imitations would oftentimes forget, but Fincher knew very well is the fact that nothing he could depict would top what his audience would imagine in their heads, so in Se7en, the violence is mostly implied. Still, even if youre used to horror and gore, the killers victims rank among the most shocking ever put on screen (or, as I said, not put on screen) - which, back then, actually made it hard to find actors and even crew to work on Se7en.
Despite this, the cast, which also includes Gwyneth Paltrow, and R. Lee Ermey, as well as Leland Orser in a small but memorable role, is outstanding. The mysterious killer, however, isnt revealed for a long time, and when it happens, its a surprise in more than one regard, and upends all our expectations how a crime thriller should unfold.
Finally, theres the twist ending, one of the most shocking, most unforgettable and most famous in cinema history. While the studio wanted something more optimistic, Fincher wisely insisted on the bleak original ending, or otherwise, we might not praise it as high as we do today.
In conclusion, Se7en is a landmark serial killer movie, smart, incredibly tense, unsettling and utterly engrossing, which defies and subverts expectations while leaving a lasting influence at the same time, an outstanding masterpiece by David Fincher.

It rivals The Silence of the Lambs for the top spot as my favourite psychological crime thriller of all time! They just dont make them like this anymore. 
I wont spend too much time on plot. Its been 30 years! Its one of the greatest films ever made. If you dont already know the plot by now, do yourself a favour! However, briefly,  for the uninitiated, the film follows two detectives who are on the hunt for a sadistic serial killer who has been carrying out murders based on the seven deadly sins. Detective Somerset is played by Morgan Freeman, an experienced older detective on the eve of retirement and Mills played by Brad Pitt, is the younger more impulsive detective who wants to kick doors down and be in the middle of the action. The rest is history!
Seven defys genre! It stands out on its own as a singular piece of work that doesnt fit the ususal genre conventions. While it is a psychological crime thriller, it also leans into horror. Fincher himself said The movie is a horror movie. The movie is about utter and total loss of control. What makes Seven so scary is the fact that it feels so realistic. Much like Silence of the Lambs, its not supernatural or science fiction, it taps into human nature and the idea that this could actually happen. The audience can recognise and maybe even relate to the themes and aspects of society depicted in the film. At a very basic level, it also taps into our primal human curiosity. We all love a good serial killer documentary or miniseries. Every time Netflix drops a new one, its an event!
Andrew Kevin Walkers perfectly paced script is soaked in themes of moral degradation, apathy and societal decline. His narrative delves into the darkest parts of the psyche to disturb and disgust with an engaging and intellectual plot. Walker writes with an unflinching approach to the twisted and dark psychology of human nature creating a sweeping sense of discomfort and dread throughout the film. Despite a heavy use of dialogue, Walker still maintains total edge of your seat levels of tension. 
Walker also gently reminds the audience of the good that is still trying to shine through the bleakness of the world of the film. The script is riddled with small humanising insights through some of the main characters quieter conversations. Mainly, David and Tracey Mills. Humour and tenderness is often found in these scenes too, putting focus on the goodness in these people. While also lending more and more emotional weight to the films gut wrenching conclusion...
Mills also has a more optimistic perception of the world, we see this as his relationship with Somerset develops. Even though Somerset seems like the ever pessimist, his years of experience have given him a very different world view and he gently tries to warn Mills how the city will break him. However, Mills (like the audience) holds on to hope in humanity. Even if misplaced, its admirable when he tells Somerset
I dont think youre quitting because you believe these things you say. I dont. I think you want to believe them, because youre quitting. I wont say that. I dont agree with you. I do not. I cant.
Fincher masterfully builds tension with his unique and visually meticulous style of storytelling. Combined with Darius Khondjis incredible cinematography, the film generates a haunting sense of dread in the unnamed city. Using locations and settings soaked with a gothic noir atmosphere, the film provides an unwavering depiction of a corrupt and decaying city that is rampant with crime. Khondjis use of shadow heightens the constant sense of danger that ominously looms over ever frame. The relentless rain also feels like a constant reminder of perpetual gloom!
Most of the film is underlit with a gritty 90s edge. The exterior shots of the industrial gothic architecture give the film a timeless and nihilistic metropolitan aesthetic. Even the interiors, including the homes of the main characters, have a grimy and bleak feel.
That said, while the film may feel thematically dark and murky, it isnt visually void of colour. There is a highly stylised use of light and colour contrasting that adds a certain vibrancy more in keeping with neo-noir. This really pops in the latest 4k restoration of the film. The cinematography is stunning and meticulously crafted. 
Think about this! You dont actually see any of the actual murders in the film take place. Fincher and Walker leave that entirely up to audiences imagination. The powerful use of suggestion and implication is enough. The film does contain violent imagery, however, the acts of murder themselves, while deeply disturbing in nature, are left for the viewer to visualise in their own minds (with the exception of Victor - Sloth). Again, the film is cleverly tapping into that primal human curiosity. Fincher is relying on our imaginations to come up with much worse than he could ever show! Consider the infamous box scene, you never actually see whats inside. We dont need to see it. The disturbing psychological suggestion does all the horrifying work! Would it have been as effective if Fincher decided to show the contents? I dont think so. Ill come back to THAT scene later.
Seven is elevated by a superior cast of performances. Morgan Freeman is perfectly cast as the seasoned and somewhat weary Somerset. His understated and methodical performance, quietly highlights Somersets methodical and obsessive compulsive nature.
Brad Pitt is great as the wreckless and impulsive Mills. The polar opposite of Somerset, hes not built for the intricate approach. He is the hard charging and hungry for action kind of cop. While this character arc can be seen as a generic and tired routine, having the old cop team up with the hot head cop, it actually pays off here. 
Gwyneth Paltrow has a miminal but vital role in the film. Her portrayal of lonliness and alienation is extremely effective and heavily felt. Her conversation with Somerset in the cafe when she reveals she is pregnant is some of the most heartbreaking acting Ive ever seen with such minimal dialogue. She is very impressive in the film.
Enter, Kevin Spacey. Regardless of his social standing today, his creepy and methodical performance as John Doe is utterly chilling. For a character with such limited screen time, I have so much to say about him. Spacey is brilliant in this. John Doe is deviously intelligent and meticulous. He is a self-loathing lunatic with a disdain for humanity. Spacey gets this across perfectly by simply speaking.
Maybe Im reaching here, but whats really interesting about John Doe is that he seems to be a shadow version of Somerset. Walker has written Doe to cleverly mirror aspects of Somersets personality. Hes obsessive compulsive, methodical, well educated and studied. They are almost two halfs of the same person. The only difference being their mental state. Doe is the perfect antagonist to Somersets protagonist because they are almost completely alike.
Fincher and Walker tread a fine line with John Does contention with society to justify his horrific actions and allow him an almost sympathetic edge. The narrative toys with the disturbing idea that there isnt much distinction between what Doe believes and what the detectives (and even the audience) believe. Its very sleek writing that gets under the skin, embedding the disconcerting notion that we might actually understand him. I am sure I am not the only one who has repeatedly said Whats in the box? like a maniac every time I see a box. Se7en is one of the most culturally significant and highly influential films ever made. Many people have said that director David Fincher barely ever misses, and I have to admit they are absolutely right. 
Gluttony, Greed, Sloth, Lust, Pride, Envy, and Wrath. Those are the seven deadly sins, but the brilliance of the story does not lie in the crimes themselves, but how they connect to one anotherand who they really affect. They also serve as a way of reminding us how horrible the world is, as the characters often mention. For example, some do not want to bring children into this terrible world, while others, like John Doe, argue that society has become so accustomed to human misery that ordinary sins have become part of every day life. 
Those sins are also highlighted within William Somerset and David Mills, our two detectives. One could argue that Somersets apathy and spirituality represent Sloth, as he repeatedly points out that the cityand the countryare beyond saving. Mills, on the other hand, represents both Pride and Wrath he is prone to aggression and sometimes even dismisses the psychological and philosophical weight of the case. The film makes them wrestle with those sins, and in the end, it is only a matter of time before they either overcome them or succumb to the very sins they investigate. 
It is one of those films that are included on every beginners must-watch list, so just like Interstellar, everyone and their mother has either watched or at least heard about it. Undoubtedly one of the best and most successful thrillers ever made, it that makes you question the extent of ones ability to remain in total controlor whether we are all capable of becoming sinners, or perhaps both.

So I thought as a birthday treat, Id revisit the movie of a famous actor also born on 1st June. There was Tom Holland, but uhhhhh I have made my unpopular opinions on his movies more than clear on this app. There was Amy Schumer, but Wikipedia tells me she is an actor and I am yet to find proof of this. 
And then theres everyones favorite weed smoking caramel voice of God Morgan Freeman! Lucky me for sharing a birthday with God, right?! So do I rewatch Lean On Me? Glory? Bruce Almighty? Million Dollar Baby? Invictus? Dark Knight Trilogy? Hell Id rewatch Driving Miss Daisy just to see if I can feel something other than cringe! Smart answer would be Shawshank.but eventually it just had to be my favorite movie of all time Se7en! 

Its my mission on earth to give Detective Somerset all his flowers as one of the least appreciated David Fincher characters! I think people get caught up in Se7ens grim aesthetics and Does philosophy. At best, they only mention Freemans deep silky voice. I love how minimalist he plays Somerset. I love how he carries himself.  Hes like the complete opposite of everyone in this unnamed city! Hes kind, well-mannered, cultured, patient, wise, considerate.....its not a showy performance, its one of composure combined with world-weariness.

In many ways, Zodiac could be read as a twisted prequel to Se7en! Both Somerset and Gyllenhaals Graysmith are outcasts in their departments, consumed by their work both men practically throw away the chance of being with a wife and kids! I like to imagine Graysmith as a younger Somerset not yet jaded, not nearly enough experience with human ugliness he doesnt smoke, doesnt swear, doesnt party, and just sincerely concentrates on his work, just like Somerset. They really are the same soul!

All this talk about how Matt Reeves recreated Se7en for The Batman, and yet its only feels like a flattering imitation. Sure Reeves and cinematographer Fraser makes his Gotham all rainy and dour like how Fincher and cinematographer Khondji shot it, but Se7en to me is about the moments of levity between Somerset and Mills that brilliant discussion about apathy both men shaving their chests and having a laugh about workers comp how oversized Mills clothes are, highlighting his petulant character....how revealing it is when Mills gives Somerset wine in a beer glass....or Tracy telling Somerset about her pregnancy.....or even Somerset just reading in the library. Fincher spaces things out well enough, and he lets you believe these characters have lives and aspirations outside the John Doe killings. With The Batman, its almost trying too hard to impress - even if it is in fact impressive! Se7en isnt one constant mood running through for 3 hours. Theres variety in feelings, and you understand why the characters hate living in this unnamed city! Dont get me wrong, I like that Jeffrey Wrights Gordon is on the case with Bats, solving shit together. Gordons like the comic relief in the movie. But again, I feel like I dont know him like whats his family life like? Why is he still continuing to be a good cop? He seems to only exist to walk Batman into crime scenes and thats it! Anyways, rant over!

You wanna watch a genuine partnership blossom? Fincher starts Somerset and Mills as opposites clearly not too thrilled being in the others company. Then he slowly inches both characters frame after frame. When Tracey calls Somerset to dinner when Mills and Somerset sleep on each other in the waiting room, all of it builds this understated fatherson dynamic. But when Mills gives into WRATH and shoots Doe, he looks one way and Somerset looks the opposite direction. The friendship has been irrevocably damaged! Fincher indeed learned from Marty that cinema is a matter of whats in the frame and whats out!

Can you believe they were actually planning something different for the now iconic opening credits? But they ran out of budget so they ended up making something dark, gritty, urban, raw, explicit, graphic, and unnerving. Way ahead of its time and duplicated to death since 1995, Kyle Coopers intro is like an industrialgrunge hybrid nightmare, but upscale. 
Funny fact, all Does notebooks were actually written by one man. All the books would be used in the intro, but instead they were all put in the background when they search Does apartment. Funny to me.

The SLOTH victim, true to his sin, took the most time to perfect for both Doe and the film crew! I can imagine this murder scene spoke directly to slackers in the 90s. Prior to Se7en, the actor who played the still alive corpse had starred as a mummy, a gargoyle, and a.sleepwalker! Probably Finchers sick sense of humour at play here! Huge props to Rob Bottin  the makeup artist behind The Thing, RoboCop and Total Recall to name a few! It was a grueling 14-hour process of covering the actors in gelatin sores! They wrapped him in rubber, paint and scars, even giving the actor overgrown fingernails. On top of all this, he had to lay perfectly still for 4 more hours  Fincher being the master dictator he is, would direct him to hold his breath for extended periods so as to not have his stomach rising and falling. It gets better, the actor kept sweating, so the crew would sprinkle cold water on him to induce shivers! That cough was not expected  the reaction youre watching from everyone is humans forgetting they are on a film set and genuinely scared shitless! Apparently Freeman was freaked out when he first saw SLOTH and then jokingly said to the actor, You dont look too good!  I love Morgan Freeman, man!

A thing I dont see brought up much is how the PRIDE murder is kinda just skimmed over! Its almost as if at that point, the futility of catching Doe is really hitting our characters! This particular victim was asked to choose between her life and her vanity - a prototype to the Saw movies a classic Jigsaw setup!
You get the real sense that this world has gone insane, there is no order, and our worst impulses will get the better of us! Incredible movie with a simple message the world is a fucked up place filled with fucked up people. But its worth fighting for, despite all that. It argues people must abandon apathy as a private solution to the problem of pandemic human suffering.



Se7en remains beautifully grainy like a renaissance painting of something awful! We dont talk enough about how this bleak, nihilistic serial killer tragedy made 330 mil at the box office! Man, what was happening in 1995 to have made this resonate so much with audiences then?! I bet it was the OJ Simpson verdict, wasnt it!
Gwyneth Paltrows head gives a better performance in this than she does with her whole body in Shakespeare in love. Im not (s)e7en kidding.

Seven is probably the film that made me fall in love with serial killers stories, I remember watching it when I was quite young and that strange feeling between fascination and horror. 
David Fincher combines and reworks classic elements of thriller, noir and detective fiction, staging a story that is both close to and far from the typical cliches
What makes Seven so special is undoubtedly its staging and the construction of the atmosphere, the constant tension and cinematography characterized by dark tones work perfectly to immerse the viewer in a dirty story. 
An endless rain that oppresses a chaotic and noisy city, the closed and claustrophobic places, the suffocating darkness illuminated only by artificial lights, each element contributes to increase a general sense of anxiety that remains alive for the entire duration
The detectives Somerset and Mills, in charge of the case, initially appear in line with the classic stereotypes on one side the old detective near retirement, lonely and grumpy and on the other the arrogant young man, willing and unconcerned about the rules.
Starting from here, Fincher enriches his characters with different aspects, such as well-defined personalities, past stories and current lives, giving them substance and depth. Men with their inner torments and their reflections on life, different in age and experiences, the hope of Mills youth and the disillusionment of Somerset.
Both of them fit perfectly into the films pessimistic and dramatic vision, within a empty and selfish social context, so inured to horrors and brutality to consider them normal
Continuing along these lines, the film comes to a wonderful ending, harrowing and bitter, which overturns the expectations of the viewer and the classics of the genre, while remaining faithful to its pessimistic nature
Ernest Hemingway once wrote, The world is a fine place and worth fighting for. I agree with the second part.
No hero, kind of victory or happy ending, what remains is the same sense of desolation that dominates the whole work.
It was really interesting to see the storyboard of the never made alternative ending (in this case fortunately), which is enormously weaker and classic in its development
The direction of Fincher is excellent, as always technically perfect, the film takes the time necessary to build the atmosphere of tension, also thanks to shades of horror in the scenes of murders, but the result is still that of a work that flies by, keeping the viewer glued to the screen.
Morgan Freeman and Brad Pitt stage extraordinary performances, supported by excellent writing, they manage to convey a vital realism to their characters, a detective couple that works exactly for their differences.
Kevin Spacey in the role of John Doe gives life to one of the most fascinating and famous villains of this genre even with a reduced screentime, an intelligent, calculating and patient killer who acts convinced to be a tool of God. 
His crazy mission, entrusted to him by a higher power, finds fulfillment just when everything appears resolved, as the most perverse and cruel part of a general scheme
If we catch John Doe and he turns out to be the devil, I mean if hes Satan himself, that might live up to our expectations, but hes not the devil. Hes just a man.
Seven deserves all its fame, it overturns and reinterprets the eternal conflict between good and evil through a cynical and realistic solution that reflects on the drift of society. 
I dont know if its objectively a masterpiece, but it is without doubt one of my favorite thrillers and one of the best works born from the talent of David Fincher

O ótimo desenho Shrek consegue o que parecia impossível desafiar a primazia da Disney
           	Para os executivos da Disney, ele é uma criatura de pesadelo. E não só por causa de sua pele verde, de sua pança exagerada ou de seus hábitos repugnantes  como o de comer rato tostado no espeto ou o de fazer velas com a cera guardada no ouvido. Para o estúdio do Mickey, o ogro Shrek é aterrorizante justamente por ser irresistível. Há quase um mês o estupendo desenho animado que leva seu nome se mantém no topo da bilheteria americana, na qual já acumulou extraordinários 182 milhões de dólares e colheu elogios rasgados da crítica. Desde O Rei Leão ou, no máximo, desde os dois Toy Story produzidos em parceria com a empresa Pixar, a Disney não desfruta tal unanimidade. O duro é que todos esses louros são recebidos por um concorrente  palavra que nem sequer constava do vocabulário da empresa quando o assunto era animação. Shrek (Estados Unidos, 2001) é uma produção da DreamWorks, o estúdio fundado por Steven Spielberg, Jeffrey Katzenberg e David Geffen. Sua vitória é ainda mais dolorosa porque Shrek satiriza, da primeira à última cena, as produções da Disney. E o faz com conhecimento de causa. Katzenberg foi alto executivo do estúdio e até sair de lá  às turras  supervisionou a realização de nada menos que A Pequena Sereia, A Bela e a Fera, Aladdin e O Rei Leão.
           	Não que Shrek lembre esses filmes. Para começar, não há nenhum príncipe encantado à vista. Não bastasse seu bafo de onça, o ogro Shrek (que na versão nacional é dublado pelo humorista Bussunda) exibe uma singular falta de graças sociais. Mora sozinho num pântano, não sabe conversar e não tem o menor interesse em fazer amigos. Só aceita a ajuda do Burro, um quadrúpede expansivo e tagarela, por força das circunstâncias. O despótico Lorde Farquaad expulsou da vizinhança todas as figuras de contos de fadas. Assim, Branca de Neve, os sete anões, os três porquinhos, Cinderela e o Lobo-Mau (entre outros personagens que já freqüentaram desenhos da Disney) invadem o pântano de Shrek em busca de asilo político. Para livrar-se deles, o ogro faz um trato com Farquaad. Ele libertará a linda princesa Fiona de sua torre, para que o nobre possa casar-se com ela. Em troca, o malvado cuidará de devolver a paz ao pântano de Shrek. O problema é que o ogro tem um coração que não é exatamente imune aos encantos de Fiona.
           	A exemplo de outros desenhos feitos em computação gráfica, como Toy Story e Dinossauro, Shrek é um assombro do ponto de vista técnico. Seus protagonistas têm até 900 músculos capazes de responder aos comandos dos desenhistas. Só a princesa Fiona exigiu o trabalho de 25 dos 275 animadores envolvidos no projeto. Eles se debruçaram sobre detalhes tão mínimos quanto os trejeitos das suas pálpebras ou a relação entre seu peso, por assim dizer, e seus movimentos corporais  seu andar é verossímil, sem aqueles saltitos das heroínas de desenho. Mas é sintomático que esses avanços tecnológicos não tenham merecido mais do que comentários passageiros nas resenhas do filme. O vanguardismo de Shrek reside na irreverência de seu roteiro.
           	É preciso topete para fazer troça de personagens que são adorados há gerações  por exemplo, colocar Branca de Neve e Cinderela para trocar tapas. Também é novidade que um herói seja celebrado por sua feiúra e conte com um ajudante de intelecto muito superior ao seu  ainda que ele se chame Burro. Tampouco Fiona é uma princesa como as outras. É desbocada, disputa concursos de arrotos e, numa cena que a plateia costuma aplaudir, derrota o bando de Robin Hood com golpes de kung fu tirados do filme Matrix. Numa paródia a Cinderela, Fiona faz um dueto com um passarinho gorjeante  e o leva à morte com seus agudos ensurdecedores. Noutra seqüência, Shrek e o Burro descobrem que o castelo de Farquaad é um parque temático que anda às moscas, numa referência bem clara às dificuldades enfrentadas ultimamente por esse setor da corporação Disney. O lorde Farquaad tem semblante de príncipe encantado, exceto por alguns detalhes vive de barba por fazer, é covarde, estúpido e cafona. Não há nada no filme que pretenda ser mesquinho ou desabonador em relação à tradição da Disney, jura Katzenberg. Acredite nessa afirmação quem quiser. Mas não custa esclarecer que o sócio da DreamWorks ganhou uma quantia vultosa no processo que moveu contra seu antigo patrão.
           	Shrek não é a primeira investida de um estúdio contra a hegemonia da Disney no desenho animado. A Fox, por exemplo, tentou abalroar o campeão com Anastasia e Titan. Esse último foi um fracasso tão grande que culminou no fechamento da divisão de animação do estúdio. A Warner também desanimou depois que O Gigante de Ferro, muito elogiado pela crítica, recolheu uns meros caraminguás na bilheteria. Só a DreamWorks se mantém firme no propósito. Começou com o enfadonho O Príncipe do Egito, ousou com Formiguinhaz (considerado mais divertido para os adultos que para as crianças) e se saiu muito bem com A Fuga das Galinhas  feito em parceria com a produtora inglesa Aardman. Shrek is one such film, a brilliant piece of animated that, beneath its humor and adventure, carries a deep and subversive critique of societal norms and prejudices.  
Lord Farquaad, the films antagonist, is not just a tyrant obsessed with perfection, he embodies the authoritarian impulse to eliminate difference. His campaign to deport all magical creatures from Duloc is a blatant metaphor for xenophobia and the systematic oppression of those who do not conform to a rigid, idealized, and overwhelmingly white standard. These fairy tale beings, much like real-world marginalized communities, are labeled as undesirable simply because they disrupt the status quo. From the very first scene, Shrek establishes themes of prejudice and social exclusion, portraying how fear and hatred toward the unknown can overshadow even the most basic notions of fairness and justice. The towns immediate hostility toward Shrek is not based on anything he has done but rather on the mere fact of who he is an ogre, an outsider, a figure that does not fit within their sanitized and homogenous world.  
Beyond its thematic depth, this film stands as one of the greatest in history, revolutionary not only in its technical achievements but also in its very essence. The movie dismantles fairy tale tropes that had long been taken for granted, mocking the sanitized, formulaic narratives that glorify conventional beauty, heroism, and romance. By doing so, Shrek redefined what an animated film could be, proving that childrens movies could be just as socially and politically incisive as they were entertaining.

You know the scene where Dragon cuddles Donkey and then Shrek crashes the party and Dragon ends up kissing Shreks ass? Now, thats what Shrek threw smack in the face of the American movie industry by simply existing. The setup gets even more sublime in Shrek 2, with Far Far Away symbolizing Hollywood and all the muck under the (Prince) Charming glitter. But... well leave Shrek 2 for another time. Back to Shrek.
I always tell people who still listen to my rants about this film that it is Dantes Divina Commedia but flipped inside out. Youre about to read a literary analysis of me comparing Dantes magnum opus with Shrek. I can picture your face now, dear reader. Rest assured, your reaction is perfectly natural, and I smiled at you smiling, so all is well. So... why is Shrek the inverse of Divina Commedia?
Firstly, both works are spiritually transcendent but differ in the nature of their ascension. In Shrek, true love is both the means and the goal of transcendence, whereas with Dante, love is merely the incentive to reach Gods literal realm. The relationship between Dante and his muse Beatrice is never truly direct as their love is not the ultimate destination in Dantes life but merely the means by which he acquires Gods grace. Dante refers to Beatrice as his salvation, but she barely appears in Inferno, has a brief role in Purgatorio, and only takes on a more meaningful one in Paradiso, where she substitutes Virgil as Dantes guide. While Dante and Beatrices love takes a tangible shape and is undoubtedly real, the true relationship in Dantes work is between him and God.
Shrek, on the other hand, crosses the literal bridge that leads to hells realm but ascends to the highest room of the tallest tower to embrace the only spirituality he knows that has nothing to do with God in his eyes true love. It is then doubly sublime that upon hearing the iconic song Hallelujah, we as viewers transcend the mortal confines of love and behold the true rays of heaven, ruled not by God but by love. It is just the cherry on top that Hells master in Shrek (Dragon) is also the inverse of Dantes Satan as seen in the Centre of Hell. In colloquial language, shes a good lad, whereas Satan is not.           
That brings us to the 3rd difference the characters themselves. They are total opposites. Dantes compassion is directed outwards to the suffering souls in the Nine Circles of Hell Shreks empathy is oriented inwards, focusing on the self and accepting himself for who he is. Virgil is Dantes guide and represents wisdom and reason Donkeys name is in itself symbolic, signifying that hes not the brightest of the bunch but still a faithful companion to Shrek. Furthermore, the two guides shape their protagonists fates differently Virgil is wise but keeps a distance he is the isolated sage who aids Dante in his spiritual journey but who never embraces it through feeling himself  remember, he was a Roman poet and not of the Christian faith. Therefore, he helps Dante reach his spiritual destination, but he himself never partakes of it.
Donkey, on the other hand, believes with all his heart in the ultimate destiny that shifts from God to love in Shrek. He experiences it first-hand through his romance with Dragon, and his simple candour in giving advice to Shrek has a more immediate effect on the latter. Remember, it was solely thanks to Donkeys persuasion that Shrek went to stop the wedding in the first place left to himself, hed have continued his lonely outcast life in the swamp and would never have reunited with Fiona. Both Virgil and Donkey are invaluable in the protagonists journeys but in completely different ways and with different goals in sight. God or love take your pick.

Shrek - What an All-Star!
Shrek (2001) is an animated fantasy adventure comedy movie directed by Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson, and written by Joe Stillman, Roger S. H. Schulman, Ted Elliot and Terry Rossio. The movie features the voice talents of Mike Myers, Eddie Murphy, Cameron Diaz, and John Lithgow.
The movie centers on an ogre named Shrek (Mike Myers) discovering that his swamp home has been taken over by fairy tale creatures, who were banished by the evil Lord Farquaad (John Lithgow)! After he meets Donkey (Eddie Murphy), Shrek negotiates a deal with Farquaad that involves Shrek and Donkey going on an adventure to rescue the beautiful Princess Fiona (Cameron Diaz), so Shrek can get his swamp back!
The story was fantastic because it has a shocking twist of a fairy tale creature rescuing a princess instead of a knight, as well as offering memorable characters, perfect fast pacing, a well-written screenplay, and hilarious moments to entertain the viewers! The movie explores the themes of friendship, love, and acceptance because Shrek learns about the importance of friendship by understanding the feelings of Donkey and Fiona during his adventure! This has led the movie to become the first movie to win an Oscar for Best Animated Feature at the 74th Academy Awards!
The movie is the home to some of the most iconic, likeable, and memorable characters, who have been well developed! For example, Shrek started off as a grumpy ogre who wanted to live alone and found Donkey and the fairy tale creatures annoying. However, as he got to know Donkey and Fiona better on their adventure, he becomes more sociable with others and is willing to accept companionship.
The voice acting is outstanding since the cast have used entertaining methods to use their emotive language to deliver their lines! Mike Myers does an amazing job as the voice of Shrek with his iconic Scottish accent, which was hilarious to listen to throughout the film!
For 2001, the animation was spectacular as it has realistic fairy tale backgrounds and appealing character designs, which holds up well to todays standards!
Harry Gregson-Williams and John Powells music score was incredible and heartwarming as it has a perfect mixture of a relaxing tone and an exciting tone, making the audience feel calm and thrilled at the same time!
The movies target audience are children and families because of the movies magically and lighthearted tone alongside the important messages. However, there is some adult humour that only the parents would understand, which makes it enjoyable watch for the family!
In conclusion, Shrek (2001) remains a childhood classic that holds up very well with its memorable story and hilarious characters! It is certainly worth the watch! It is amazing!

Shrek is probably the DreamWorks movie Ive seen the most times aside from the first HTTYD. One could argue that its the film that put the studio on the map and put other animation studios on notice. It was also the first movie to win the Best Animated Feature award at the Oscars back in 02. Although it is still very much a fairy tale movie, Shrek takes a familiar concept, turns it on its head and gets pretty creative with it. Think of it as an odd, but hilarious spin on Beauty and the Beast. 
I love that they set out to differentiate this one from Disney or similar studios. One of the best kinds of animated films to me are the ones that have humor and jokes that fly right over kids heads and can be thoroughly enjoyed by adults. There were quite a few things that went over my head as a child like Farquaads name or him getting a boner in bed, but younger me thought he was just shy about not wearing a shirt. The magic mirrors face said it all. Mike Myers, Cameron Diaz and John Lithgow provided solid voice work, but its Eddie Murphy that easily steals the spotlight as Donkey. Theres a couple things leading up to the final act that Im not a fan of like the hearing a conversation at the wrong time that causes friction trope or how the dragon just magically appears near the swamp somehow only to give Shrek and Donkey a quick way to get  to the wedding. Contos de fadas são histórias com elementos fantásticos e mágicos que, geralmente, contam sobre princesas, feiticeiros, objetos encantados, animais falantes e outros. Estima-se que estes surgiram há milhares de anos, quando eram contados de forma oral. Porém, os contos de fadas como conhecemos hoje  isto é, como gênero literário e com uma estrutura narrativa sólida  consolidaram-se no final do século XVII, com Charles Perrault. Os Irmãos Grimm, por sua vez, ao reunirem diversas histórias de diferentes culturas (principalmente a alemã) e as adaptarem para a forma literária, definiram as referências modernas dessas histórias e se tornaram o maior nome do gênero.
Lançado em 2001 pela DreamWorks Animation, Shrek narra a história de um ogro de mesmo nome que, após ter seu pântano tomado por personagens dos contos de fadas, precisa resgatar uma princesa trancada em uma torre para trocá-la com o governante do reino pela expulsão das criaturas. Em Shrek, os diretores Andrew Adamsone e Vicky Jenson fazem bom uso das referências aos contos de fadas, entre elas o espelho de Branca de Neve e clássicos personagens, como Pinóquio e Peter Pan. Essas referências, contudo, não possuem fins narrativos práticos, porém são fundamentais para definir o tom cômico e a ambientação do filme.
Percebe-se, também, que, ao satirizar de modo inteligente os contos de fadas, o filme prioriza uma inspiração clara nas versões desenhadas nos clássicos da Disney. Há debates sobre o porquê dessa escolha. Esta, por sua vez, pode ser justificada pelo fato de que Jeffrey Katzenberg, produtor do filme e um dos fundadores da DreamWorks, foi demitido de forma conturbada da Disney. No entanto, esse fato torna as piadas ainda mais engraçadas.
É interessante notar que Shrek, na verdade, mesmo satirizando, segue a estrutura clássica de um conto de fadas. Um herói, Shrek (Mike Myers), tenta resgatar uma princesa presa em uma torre, Fiona (Cameron Diaz), junto de um animal falante, Burro (Eddie Murphy). Aqui também temos um vilão vaidoso, uma importante lição sobre beleza e um final feliz. Com isso, Shrek até consegue (e muito bem) ironizar os contos de fadas, mas não deixa de ser um deles, fazendo com que tudo isso seja de um brilhantismo inusitado e divertido.
Além dos poucos secundários, como o Biscoito e a cativante dragoa, todos os acontecimentos giram em torno de quatro personagens Shrek, Fiona, Burro e Lord Farquaad (John Lithgow). Ao longo de 90 minutos, o filme desenvolve temas complexos, mas de jeitos simples para todos eles. Shrek, por ter se isolado a vida toda, acaba se tornando um sujeito pouco seguro, evidenciando isso quando, ao ser questionado se seria ele o verdadeiro amor da princesa, ridiculariza a si próprio. Já Fiona, pressionada para ser salva e ter a vida perfeita com um belo cavalheiro, acredita que até Shrek, alguém de aspecto semelhante, julgará sua aparência. Enquanto o Burro, que inicialmente se recusa a falar para não ser vendido, passa o restante do filme falando sem parar. Por fim, para compensar a baixa estatura, Farquaad constrói o que seria um Empire State da época medieval.
Se, por um lado, a DreamWorks satirizava os contos de fadas em Shrek, por outro, a Pixar, com Monstros S.A., apresentava o mundo atrás do armário. Derrotando a pioneira na animação 3D, Shrek ganhou o primeiro Oscar de Melhor Animação da história. Considerando a qualidade técnica, a Pixar, que criou um software especial para simular os movimentos de cada pelo de Sullivan, certamente acaba sendo superior. Porém, a produção da DreamWorks conta com planos realmente bonitos devido a um trabalho de cores bem feito e movimentos de câmera dinâmicos e imersivos. Com isso, Shrek, mesmo não querendo, mostra-se um inusitado e prazeroso conto de fadas o qual os Irmãos Grimm jamais imaginaram existir.

As a tribute to one of my favourite art forms and visual mediums, going to do a challenge for fun to watch as much animated media as I can in May. Can be anything so long as its animated whether its a movie, tv show or anthology short. Figured where better to start than possibly the most iconic animated film ever made. 
Shrek is an absolute classic, its impact on culture and the fact that its an hour and a half long meme is hard to understate. I mean, I dont know any other movies with such a devoted following that they have an equivalent to Shrek Retold, which alone is a testament to how beloved Shrek is. The movie is essentially a deconstruction of fairy tale tropes, with the hero being an monstrous ogre instead of a hansome prince, one whose mainly acting out of self interest rather than any selfless goal of saving a princess. Shreks lonely abode becomes the dumping ground for all the fairy tale creatures Farquad has outlawed, and goes on a quest with his trusty steed Donkey to save a princess for Farquad to get him to make them leave. Its through that the movie tells a pretty touching story about breaking out of ones shell, learning to trust others, and not judging eachother for appearances. Shrek is lonely because everyone around him thinks of him as a monster, so he wears it on his sleeve and adopts the monstrous persona, and becomes comfortable in his loneliness. It makes him irritable with others and he needs to learn how to be more selfless and caring about what they want. A major theme of the film is not to judge people by their looks but by their deeds and character, with both Shrek and Fiona and with how they and others perceive them. Their love story is touching and plays with tropes of the classic knight in shining armour fantasy as they start off not liking eachother and learn to love each other as they share their journey, and question what they wanted before. Its a classic story of timeless themes, which have helped the movie stay so rewatchable and remain so beloved. I cant say I love the whole miscommunication near the end, where Shrek overhears Fiona and Donkey out of context and almost ruins everything for them, it feels cheap and contrived rather than character driven. I think it could have been played better if it played more off both of their insecurities rather than this awkward conflict, but its not a huge issue and still leads to a satisfying end.
The movies animation is solid as youd expect from Dreamworks, but where Shrek really shines is its style and humour. I dont know how you even come up with this stuff, an ogre and a talking donkey becoming friends on a fantasy adventure to rescue a princess sounds unhinged as hell as a premise, and yet it works. I know it is based on a book, but no idea how close this is as an adaptation. The movie is a fun adventure, thematic family movie and funny comedy all in one. The movie is still really funny, with humour for kids and adults, with much of it having become a meme literally from the opening credits onwards. Part of that is the fact Shrek is played by the Canadian legend Mike Myers, whose performance is just iconic. Hes both hilarious and adds some nice heart to the more emotional side of Shrek when he opens up to Donkey and Fiona, played by Eddie Murphy and Cameron Diaz respectively and they both do a great job. Shreks scene opening up to Donkey about how he keeps everyone away out of the fear of being feared is great, a highlight for sure and Shrek overcoming his insecurities is nice to see. Eddie Murphy does a lot to add to the comedy, and could have easily been a really annoying character but his friendship with Shrek is great and really well built up and helps make him so endearing. Fiona is great, a further subversion of fairy tale tropes being both a princess whose a badass fighter and one whose happy to choose being a monstrous ogre to be with the man she loves. Fiona and Shrek learn to appreciate themselves through their relationship with eachother which is why it works so well across all the movies. John Lithgow as Farquad is just fantastic, hilarious villain performance (SOME OF YOU MAY DIEBUT IT IS A SACRIFICE I AM WILLING TO MAKE Is sooo good). Its a great cast of unconventional yet loveable characters who form a endearing friendship and romance over the course of the story. 
Overall, its Shrek. Its an iconic classic thats a perfect comfort film and fun for the whole family. A story with such an outwardly bizarre premise manages to stand the test of time and be beloved by millions thanks to some great comedic style, well rounded characters, great voice acting, a banger soundtrack (someBODY once told me), and solid animation. Even with some bunoy story beats, its movie thats already timeless and a cultural phenomenon. Most of you have probably seen it, but Shrek gets my highest recommendation anyway! And as a bonus, its of the rare movies where the sequel is actually better

On the eve of what felt like the end of a mixed bag of a year, I thought I should go back in time to a comfort movie of my childhood, a movie that I constantly rewatched from a tape my neighbours recorded for me because we couldnt afford to buy DVDs then. And just to relive through the joy of listening to the iconic All Stars opening again, I chose to rewatch the original Shrek duology to mark my shift to 2026, the movies that instantly catapulted DreamWorks as the main competition to Disney and has since become an important part of pop and internet meme culture to date. 
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Once upon a time there was a lovely princess. But she had an enchantment upon her of a fearful sort, which could only be broken by loves first kiss. She was locked away in a castle guarded by a terrible fire-breathing dragon. Many brave knights had attempted to free her from this dreadful prison, but none prevailed. She waited in the dragons keep, in the highest room of the tallest tower, for her true love and true loves first kiss.
Ive never noticed how weirdly gross a lot of the introduction sequence was as a kid, seeing Shrek pull out his ear wax for his dinner table candle or the daily bathing scene in the hot muddy field of his swamp. But thats just the beauty of the opening that sets up two important cornerstones of this movies themes - to set up Shreks daily life to understand why he would go extreme lengths to protect this life in isolation and to understand how the dark humor dissectsparodies the cliches of Disney princess movies. And what stood out the most from the very beginning is how the narrative structure is well structured, conventional in how it presents the characters before diving into the central conflict and world buckskin, and yet the way they organically pull it off is just so efficient at maintaining the perfect pacing. By setting decent introductions to Shrek and Donkey before reaching the quest to free Princess Fiona, the story perfectly sets the parody of the knight and his noble steed without forcing the comical nature, slowly pulling both characters through Lord Farquaads wish to become the noble king of Duloc through a marriage with the cursed princess.
Ogres are like onions!
And while the story still lands a decent dynamic between Shrek, Donkey and Fiona, what stuck me rewatching as an adult is the exploration of the life that Shrek purposefully keeps hidden from the outside world. Through the growing bond between him and Fiona, the plot focuses on Shreks ideas about closing into himself breaking down as the goal of their noble quest clashes with hid growing affection for the princess. Even though the story follows a very telenovela-ish circumstance based conflict between the two to drive the urgency of the final act, how Shreks insecurities and those of Fionas challenge each others perceptions is what becomes the biggest strength of the narrative. Breaking apart the standards of the Beauty and the Beast trope, the mutual acceptance of each others ogre still remains as a memorable ending to a beautifully unconventional romance, even if  the story does still depend on the dated beauty in the eyes of the beholder idea.
Donkey - Hi, Princess!
Fiona - It talks!
Shrek - Yeah, its getting him to shut up thats the trick!
Besides the forced circumstances of the conflict that lead to the drastically hastened urgency of the marriage, the movie does fall slightly short in its comedy. Of course the movie aces in its jabs at the princess genre cliches and the abundance of pop culture references are still enjoyable. And the fact that the phony appearance of Duloc and the iconic childrens song pop-up art sequence was supposed to be a parody of Disneyland only dawned on me on this rewatch. But while I do enjoy a little dark humor from time to time, it did feel like the little person jokes on Farquaad ran out of steam by the midpoint and they still kept pushing unnecessarily. I get the urgency of the situation when Fiona pushes for a marriage before the arrival of sunset, but the tension between Shrek and Donkey does dissipate faster than I remembered. And last but not the least, the whole Robin Hood sequence isnt exactly necessary given how we dont get to see Fionas fighting skills until the third movie (thats probably why I didnt remember this one scene at all).
Fiona - And my groom-to-be Lord Farquaad, whats he like? 
Shrek - Well, let me put it this way, men of his stature are in short supply. 
Donkey - Yeah! Though there are those who think little of him!
I can appreciate the tidings that Shrek made in the field of animation for how it pushed the limits of performance driven animation, but the style definitely shows its age at this point. The way the highly expressive faces work against the rigid body models are definitely noticeable now, but its not something that affected my experience. As a matter of fact, the visuals in this movie were gorgeous for its many stellar landscape shots, capturing the intricate 3D worlds that the team painstakingly created to immerse us in Shreks world. Despite being a movie that came before the revolutionary water physics many games from the 2000s used to flaunt a lot, Shrek featured many moments like Farquaads contest for the champion scene where the particle effects and fluid movement on the wed ground is remarkable for its time. The groundbreaking use of popular licensed songs not only breaks Disneys monopoly on musicals, but also sticks with the narrative approach of breaking apart the old cliches. But Ill admit that the movie is a little over reliant on these songs after a point, even the Hallelujah cover is still one of my favorites of all time. Mike Myers, Cameron Diaz and John Lithgow still nail their iconic roles, but Eddie Murphys voice as the chatterbox Donkey will always remain goated for his exceptional comedic timing.
Overall, while I dont think it holds the same pedestal my once 5 year old seld did, theres no denying that Shreks legacy as the radical change to the animation scene is well rooted in its balance between breaking apart from the usual cliches of fairy tales and maintaining an identity of its own. Its iconic songs, witty dark humor and visuals have been etched into my mind since childhood for all the right reasons.

Establishing DreamWorks Animation as the first real competitor to Pixar Animation Studios, Shrek is a clever, creative  comical delight that finds its creators firing on all cylinders and is a wonderfully animated  endlessly entertaining tale that works for viewers of all ages.
The story follows an ogre whose peaceful life in the swamp is disrupted when many magical creatures show up at his place. To drive them out, he strikes a deal with an evil lord for whom he must rescue a princess  bring her to him in exchange for his land, and is joined by a talking donkey on his quest.
Directed by Andrew Adamson  Vicky Jenson, Shrek comes jam-packed with gags  parodies, all incorporated into a storyline thats simple in structure, easy to follow, and features elements that are more targeted at grown-ups, thus succeeding as an adventure that has something in store for everyone.
All the set pieces  characters are cleverly imagined, expertly designed  skilfully rendered. The relevant characters exhibit sufficient depth and are easy to relate to. Voice actors bring their A-game to infuse life  soul into these animated caricatures, with Eddie Murphy effortlessly winning hearts  stealing the show as Donkey.
On an overall scale, Shrek is an end-product of clever imagination, intelligent writing  top-notch animation and though the latter aspect appears slightly dated today, the story hasnt lost much of its magical charm  hilarious wit. Taking a dig at Disney and proving its animation studio to be a worthy challenger to Pixar, Shrek is still one of DreamWorks Animations finest films to date.

Tragic news for anyone whos sick of superhero movies Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse completely reinvigorates the genre, reaffirms why its resonating with a diverse modern audience thats desperate to fight the power, and reiterates to us how these hyper-popular spandex myths are able to reinvent themselves on the fly whenever things get stale. Just when it seemed like Infinity War might be the culmination of a cultural phenomenon, that Stan Lees death could symbolize the end of an era, and that Turn Off the Dark was always going to be the silliest possible subtitle for a Spider-Man adaptation, along comes a delirious postmodern spectacle to remind us that these movies will exist for as long as people need to see themselves reflected in them. Sometimes, that can feel like a threat. Watching Into the Spider-Verse, its more like a promise.
An eye-popping and irreverent animated experience from the marvelous comic minds who brought you 21 Jump Street, The LEGO Movie, and roughly 75 percent of that misbegotten Han Solo movie, Into the Spider-Verse is somehow both the nerdiest and most inviting superhero film in a long time every single frame oozes with fan service, and yet the entire project seems optimized for people who were rooting for Thanos to snap the Avengers into oblivion and put us all out of our misery.
This is an origin story for viewers who didnt think they could stomach another origin story its an origin story about how empowering origin stories can be. However much fun it might be to watch Captain America save the world for the umpteenth time, the most basic thrill of these movies is the idea that anyone can become a superhero (an ethos that Spider-Man has always personified) and Into the Spider-Verse stretches that idea to hilarious new dimensions.

review_text:
This movie slaps every single time. Ive probably watched it over 30 times at this point, but I still find myself nodding to the music, laughing at all the jokes, and noticing new things with every go around.
The coming of age angle becomes stronger and stronger for me every time. Miles leaves his shoes untied as a fashion statement (its intentional!) because hes trying to hold onto his roots in the culture of his old inner-city school. This isnt an inherently bad or immature thing to do, but as the film goes on, it becomes clear that hes clinging to his old life and holding himself back in the process Miles foolishly trips over his untied shoelaces on numerous occasions, one of which results in shattering the goober. Ironically, Miles says the kids at his new school are elitist but his untied shoelaces are themselves representative of his desperate attempt to be different and cultured compared to his peers. He makes makes no effort to bond with his roommate (or his dad, for that matter) and intentionally holds himself back in school, too unsure of his identity to explore his full potential or express himself in fulfilling and productive ways.
The interactions with all the Spider-People(?) often strike parallels between Miles personal life, too. When the Spider-Gang bombards Miles with questions about his abilities (can you rewire a mainframe while being shot at? can you float through the air when you smell a delicious pie?) the music and editing in the sequence are the same as the initial montage of his stressful day at school. Once again, the great expectations overwhelm him, and he retreats to his uncles apartment to relieve himself from the pressure.
Miles Uncle Aaron is somewhat divergent from the usual Uncle Ben mentor archetype, because hes actually the character who embodies the immaturity that Miles will eventually learn to grow beyond. Miles clings to his Uncle Aaron as a reminder of his old life, and bonds with him because (unlike Uncle Ben) he doesnt have any interest in reminding him about his responsibilities. In fact, Aaron encourages him to abandon his schoolwork and go spray some graffiti even when he has an essay due the next day. 
(Not-so-accidentally, the graffiti painted by Miles says No Expectations which serves as the most clear-handed representation of his lack of drive or purpose.)
The revelation that Aaron is The Prowler makes total sense thematically while he may not have the superpowers that Miles does, Aaron is a similarly gifted individual who has chosen to express his gifts in a selfish and destructive way. In a sense, The Prowler is the expression of what Miles could become if he continues to limit himself and refuse any responsibility for his gifts. Aarons death and apology to Miles (I let you down, man) serve as the catalyst for Miles to move past his obsession with his cool uncle who rejects responsibility and actually embrace the mantle he needs to embrace.
Gratefully, the message of Spider-Verse is not gentrify yourself! stop expressing your personality and just conform to what society wants you to be! After all, what makes you different makes you Spider-Man, and Miles final expression of himself as a superhero still retains much of his personality and individuality...theyre just being used in more productive and fulfilling ways. Its the little things that drive the point home, like noticing that the title page for Miles finished Great Expectations essay has been stylistically doodled and colored like street art. Rather than seeing his artistic gifts as an opposition to his schoolwork, Miles infuses them together to make the best of the hand hes been dealt. And thats really what coming-of-age movies are about, right?

Its not rough around the edges or anything, but it really showcases the lack of dexterity that big-screen Spider-Man stories are seemingly always crippled with, and even with its wonderful inclusive measures, it can only feel standardized in the face of the films animation. review_text:
I love how this film manages to do everything all Marvel origin stories have done a gazillion times and manages to get away with it brilliantly. 
How?
By not giving a shit and submerging itself 100 in its own vision. See its one thing to re-tell a story and tell it well, but its another thing entirely to completely reinvent it. And that it does. 
This reiteration into the story of Spiderman revels in one thing, the character, something so many super hero films get wrong. And instead of just rehashing old ideas it instead stretches them to its limits in a flurry of creativity that only comes by every once in a while. 
Itd be too easy to ascribe all these qualities to the fact that this is an animated movie, but that would sell the collaborative efforts of writer, directors, actors and animators short. Because thats what this is, a film that is harmonious on all levels. 
The tone is set early on in the opening act, betraying a self awareness I can always appreciate. What follows is a long, never boring and at points hilarious introduction to our wonderful protagonist Miles. It is through him we experience the exquisitely paced narrative that manages to entertain, emote and make me giddy with excitement by yet another beautifully animated action sequence. 
From the talents that lend their voices to the crisp, gorgeous animation to the unbridled enthusiasm with which the story is presented, I can only come up with one word perfection. 
Plain and simple perfection.

review_text:
An all new Spiderman comes into his own as Marvel and Sony unleash the Spider-Verse!
Wow, that is one hardcore origin story kid.
The dazzling pages of a comic book come to life in this highly unique and imaginative animated film. For so long I have wanted to see a Spiderman movie that was not handcuffed to the constraints of a simple hero story and one or two villains. And Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse delivers that and much more as we get an impressive tribute to all things Spidey and one of his creators Stan Lee (RIP).
The movie is well aware that the idea of a Spiderman origin story has been run into the ground, so it has fun with that concept and tells at least 7 of them. This self referential humor carries on throughout the whole movie and had me laughing out loud several times.
I thought the first part with just Miles Morales was ok, but it really clicked in for me when a surprise alternate version of a character we know and love comes into play to reluctantly show him the webs (Instead of ropes LOL). Seeing these alternate Spider guys, girls, and Pig helped keep the plot driving forward while Miles works to come into his own as Spiderman. And that wait pays off, because the scene when Miles finally becomes his own version of Spidey gave me some serious good movie moment chills.   
I had heard the villains in this were not that great, but I would strongly disagree just based on how many of them and how entertaining they are. We get to see
- The main baddie King Pin (Who actually has a motive that ties into a back story)
- A surprise Doc Ock
- Tombstone
- Prowler
- A unique take on Scorpion and Green Goblin
You would think multiple villains and heroes would cause the story to get messy, but they managed to balance it all really well.
It is hard to describe the animation based on how dynamic it is, with its colorful blend of styles. It felt like it was trying to jump off the screen, and it was not even 3D, but it kind of looked like it was at times. One aspect that stood out to me was that much of the animation appeared to be made up by these layered dots, which reminded me a lot of what an actual comic looks like. 
The pacing is really quick, so I can easily imagine appreciating so many more of the little nuisances on a rewatch. There was an emotional moment toward the end of the second act, that I wish had been setup more so I could have really been pulled in by the heartbreak it was going for. I think my happiest moments watching a Spiderman movie are when he is web slinging in the big city, and I wish there would have been some more of that other than his big Spiderman reveal sequence heading into the climax. The web shooters in this are mechanical right???? So why does he have such a hard time using them?
Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse is hands down one of the best Spiderman movies we have ever gotten based on how much Spidey we get, and it not having to be so weighed down by Peter Parker. I think this is easily the top family movie of the Holiday season, and I want to see more of Miles in this wild animated Spiderman universe. 
Make sure to stay until the very end of the credits to get an old school Spiderman tribute.

review_text:
so heres the thing about superheroes.
i grew up with the bust and then the boom. there was a time when as far as the film world was concerned, superheroes were dead. there were some exceptions of course, perhaps the biggest being the x-men but even they had fizzled out with a lack-luster third showing. i was ten years old and i was dimly aware of comic books and yellow panels. it was 2008. no one cared about superheroes.
naturally you know the rest of the story. two movies came out and they changed the course of cinematic history.
ive always had a complicated relationship with the genre. superheroes are our american mythology and they represent the burden of all that entails. i am uneasy with vigilante justice. i do not always like their escapism or the distillation of complicated moral issues. superhero movies could make all the concessions they wanted to the real world, the one i inhabit, from UN restrictions to metaphors about civil rights. in our world, superheroes do not and cannot exist.
i think of superheroes as encapsulated in fight scenes. they kick and they punch and they fly through the air as army hordes attack and bad guys charge to meet them. they are pulp fiction, they are flashy cartoons, they are ideals and idols.
at the end of the day, i can be uneasy and skeptical of the concept all i want. 
but. 
you know what else superheroes are? they are our pure distilled heart, standing up for what is right against all the odds.
i think that element gets lost in the noise sometimes. superheroes have only gotten bigger and grander and more more of everything since 2008. there are crossovers and credit scenes and spoiler warnings and huge infinite battles stretching across mega-universes. there is the merchandise and the restaurants and the halloween masks.
knowing how vast the superhero empire has become, one lone kid getting up after they were knocked down doesnt seem like anything. in this movie however, as it is in life, its everything.
i want my life to mean something, as corny as it sounds. i want to help people. i can skip forward through the fight scenes. i dont need the adrenaline or the bruises. i dont need a costume or a theme song either (itd be nice though, not going to lie). i want to hold a kids hand who looks up to me. i want to know that the community i live in is a little safer and better because i happened to be there. i want to be proud of what ive given others. i want no regrets.
so heres the thing about superheroes. they cant exist in our world. not really. 
but you know what? that heart, that yearning to make the world a kinder place, this weird sort of idea that anyone can put on a mask and make things even a fraction a bit better. well, that will exist as long as we are human. that will exist as long as something beats behind our chest.
fairy stories are more than true. not because they tell children that dragons exist but because they tell all of us that dragons can be beaten.

Im going to say the magic words that will (hopefully) allow me to criticize this movie without being yelled at. I think this is one of the only visually interesting blockbuster films to come out in this part of the decade, even if that style has now been copy pasted to so many different other films that even Puss in Boots does the differing frame rates and cel shading now. Hell some of the jokes are even funny. 
All that said, this movie opens on the Comics Code Sticker, a Symbol of the Hayes Code-esque repression that drove so many of the original creators we love today out of the business and into paupers graves. This movie doesnt earn that symbol. Ditko is mentioned once, and the second film is on track to make millions while Peter David lies in hospice, ruined financially by insurance bills. Like Thomas Hurt in Grant Morrisons Batman The Black Glove, this movie wears a skin suit of comics to trick people into thinking that Capeshit blockbusters can be empathetic. However, the only thing Spider-Verse proved was that The Multiverse is a hidden wealth to pillage by corporations. EEAAO and Far From Home owe their profitable existence to this film, just like the resurgence of quirky animation owes itself to this movie. 
One group that doesnt owe anything to this movie is black people. If Dwayne Mcduffie were alive today, Miles never would have made it off his very first comic script. But, to Brian Michael Bendiss eternal gratitude, Mcduffie had the foresight to die 6 months before Miles first appearance, and now the Zoomer Spider-Man with a Basketball on his chest that listens to your moms favorite rap songs is the face of Black Popular Culture.  More thoughts on this in the forthcoming episode of Marvelous, Or The Death Of Cinema.

review_text:
Holy shit.
Set the superhero stuff aside for a moment. I dont think Ive ever seen a computer animated movie that looks like this that bucks the photo-realism that has defined the form in favor of Lichtenstein-esque pop art-stylings and Ditko-inspired near-psychedelic sequences. And thats before we get to the translation of familiar comic book elements like thought bubbles into things dynamic and visually arresting. If this movie only had its animation style to go for it, it would still be worth your time and attention.
As it stands, it uses those visuals to tell the compelling story of Miles Morales, heir to the Spider-Man legacy, and his struggle to live up to that legacy. Its a familiar story made distinctive by how grounded it is. Miles feels like a real 13-year-old kid from Brooklyn, situated in a real neighborhood with a distinctive culture and heritage. And the extent to which he fully breathes as a character pulls you in as a viewer makes you invested in his journey and that of his friends and family. Its foundation for everything that follows.
And what follows is great A collection of different Spider-people, including a dirtbag Peter Parker and John Mulaneys delightful Spider-Ham, all working together to stop an existential threat. Its funny, exciting, and genuinely compellingthe first superhero film in a long time to do something different and in doing so push the genre forward. Hopefully, if these films still exist in ten years, we will be talking about the immense influence this movie had on everything going forward.
