Esa persona que ayuda a los demás solo porque debe o tiene que hacerlo, y porque es lo correcto, es, sin duda, un auténtico superhéroe.
Detrás de la máscara nunca ha tenido que existir alguien perfecto. Solo alguien dispuesto a hacer lo correcto, incluso cuando tiene miedo, incluso cuando no sabe qué hacer y, sobre todo, incluso cuando sea difícil levantarse.
También creo que hay algo muy bonito en la manera en la que habla de nuestros padres. No siempre saben decirnos lo que necesitamos escuchar, ni siempre encuentran la manera correcta de demostrarnos lo que sienten, pero eso no significa que no estén intentando hacer lo mejor que pueden. A veces, lo más importante no es que tengan todas las respuestas, sino que simplemente estén ahí.
Y cuando no pueden estarlo, están nuestros amigos, quienes terminan convirtiéndose en nuestro lugar seguro cuando todo lo demás se está viniendo abajo.
Todo esto funciona porque la película nunca olvida que Spider-Man ha pertenecido a muchas generaciones. Puede ser una historia para niños, para adolescentes o para adultos, y cada uno puede encontrar algo diferente detrás de la máscara.
Visualmente, es alucinante. Parece que un cómic hubiera cobrado vida los colores vibrantes, las texturas, los trazos, las viñetas y la manera en la que la animación juega con el lenguaje del cómic hacen que cada escena se sienta viva. Es una auténtica carta de amor a la animación.
Aunque el villano no me pareció interesante y la película tiene un tono mucho más familiar y ligero que su continuación, ninguno de esos aspectos logró quitarme la emoción de la experiencia. Pero su accesibilidad es uno de sus mayores aciertos puede hablar de conceptos científicos y multiversos sin dejar de sentirse como una historia cercana.
La vi con mi papá y mi hermana, e incluso ellos, que no suelen conectar tanto con la animación, pudieron disfrutarla.
Además, pude verla en la mejor calidad que pude conseguir y creo que esta es de esas películas que merecen verse así. La animación tiene tantos detalles, colores y texturas que se disfruta aún más cuando puedes apreciarlos en todo su esplendor.
Pero al final, quizá eso sea lo más bonito de Spider-Man solo necesitas decidir que, cuando llegue el momento, vas a ayudar.
Todos podemos ser Spider-Man.
Todos podemos ser héroes.
Todos podemos usar la máscara.

Teen Miles Morales becomes the Spider-Man of his universe and must join with five spider-powered individuals from other dimensions to stop a threat for all realities.
Into the Spider-Verse gets so much right. This is not only a beautiful introduction to one of the better superheroes of this generation, and yes Im talking about Miles, but it perfectly integrates numerous Spider-people yet doesnt feel convoluted? How did this movie not fall flat on its face? The idea of why this works on the level that it does is simple, and that is the fact that there was so much passion put into this project that it just could not fail. This passion comes from all parties, from the directors to the writers, and the cast obviously plays a huge role. Moores voice will forever be tied to Miles, and Hailee Steinfeld brings Gwen to life in a magical way. The big surprise is Jake Johnson absolutely crushing Peter B Parker. Would it be strange to admit that he may be one of the best Peter Parker representations we have seen yet?
The villains, while classic, each have a twist. I remember the discussion being about how Kingpin wasnt a great villain, or that his design was strange. He may look a bit odd, but this design-choice is (at least) interesting and bold enough to catch your attention. He feels menacing due to his stature and voice, yet his main mission is a personal one. The rise of Miles may be handled just a bit quicker than it should be, as we need more time between when he leaves the group and then gets the suit. This being said, there isnt much more to complain about here, as this is a brilliant way to start (or continue) a franchise. The animation was stunning at the time, and while plenty have tried to replicate it, there is only one that looks like this. After tomorrow, there may be two, but there is something about the simplicity of an origin story.

One dimension too many. No, not the alternate dimension that disgorged Spider-Ham (though Mulaney only gets one really good line, making the character feel like a wasted opportunity). Im talking about width, about contemporary animations misguided insistence on replicating the contours of the real world. People are raving about Spider-Verse as a dazzling visual experience, and I half-concurwhenever the film gets aggressively 2-D, adding delirious motion to the multi-layered flatness of comic-book panels, its something to behold. But its baseline is standard-issue computer-generated sculpting, which basically amounts to photo-realism that signifies cartoonishness via exaggerated rounding, as if everything onscreen were made of rubber. Ive grown quite weary of this particular look, and was crushed to find it dominating the first act here add to that the scripts rather laborious setup, with its focus on Miles dad and surrogate dad, and the movie had kinda lost me by the time it finally explodes into delirium. And even then, the mundane keeps re-asserting itself, both formally and narratively. A friend who adores The Lego Movie, and was flummoxed by my finding that film a bit too hyperactive, warned me that I might have a similar response to this one if anything, the opposite is truetoo much of it is too normal, too conventional, insufficiently deranged. Its a lot of e.g. Spider-Man Noir not understanding a Rubiks Cube, and jokes about Peter B. Parkers paunch, and Peni snacking at the controls of her robot or whatever it is. Cute, but forgettable. And then of course theres the earnest life lesson, which one can still rarely escape when it comes to mainstream entertainment. (Thats the main reason why Game Night isnt my favorite film of the year.) As is often the case, Im emphasizing what didnt delight me at the expense of what did, but only because theres nearly universal consensus on the latter. Had I gone into this with low expectations, Id be expressing pleasant surprise, marveling at the unusually offbeat premise and the creative use of comic-book text and the intermittent hand-drawn dynamism. Instead, people are treating it like the Second Coming, and Im forced to don my supervillain costume yet again. Kneel before the Contrarian!

JUNIMATION
What can I say about this film that hasnt already been said? Certainly, in my second viewing after seeing it in the cinema (fun fact my first review for this film was my second review on this platform), certainly everything about it is still awesome. 
Although it clearly influenced future films, notably those made by Dreamworks, the animation still feels fresh and original. In fact, I was surprised by how little The Bad Guys and Puss in Boots 2 borrowed from this film. What makes this films animation truly remarkable is that it is not a single style but rather an amalgamation that are seamlessly and spectacularly interwoven.
Furthermore, Miles Morales is a very great character who I enjoyed following, and his relationship with this Peter Parker past his heyday is great. At first I was worried that this would be another Homecoming-style situation in which Morales is pushed to the side, but the movie does a fantastic job of making sure everyone has their moment in the spotlight without losing sight of the fact that its Miles Morales story. His bond with his father, and the way it ends, almost brought tears to my eyes. While I was amused, I never laughed out loud, and I found that many of the jokes and antics, especially those involving characters like Spider Man Noir and Spider Ham didnt have the same impact as they did the first time around.
Last but not least, the music is still a banger. Whats up, Danger? still being my second favorite Spider-Man song behind Hero. And Daniels score is similarly amazing, adding a lot of excitement to the film.
All in all, although in many ways it lost some of its initial greatness, this was still a blast of a film.

This movie takes the familiar idea of Spider-Man and presents it from a completely different perspective. The story isnt just about someone getting superpowers and deciding to become a hero its mainly about Miles himself  his fear, his hesitation, his relationship with his family, and his struggle to understand himself and figure out who he wants to be.

What? How? How is this possible?
When this movie was announced I had my doubts. A Spider-Man movie that would feature Miles Morales with a bunch of other Spider-People, created by Sony Pictures Animations. The studio that brought us the disasters known as, Open Season, Hotel Transylvania 2 and 3 and The Emoji Movie. How would they handle a Spider-Man film? I thought they might screw it up by being to safe, not taking any risk or not focusing on Miles Morales, but when I saw one of the trailers, I was sold. I was still a bit scared, but I had hopes.
The same day as I was going to see the movie, I saw that it was all the way up in number nine on Letterboxd 250, so I got pretty excited. This is the first movie, in a long time, that I have been genuinely excited to see in the cinema. I think the las movie was probably Star Wars The Force Awakens. And by God, Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse blew my expectations away. This is one of the best movies I have seen, it might even surpass The Big Lebowski in being my favorite movie of all time.
I am a huge fan of animation, and the animation style this movie used is insanely good. The movie is created in a way that it looks like youre reading a comic book. Dots and lines everywhere, I love it! The use of color is great and I loved the way they handled the focus of a shot, very creative. The soundtrack of the film fit perfectly and had an awesome song by Post Malone called Sunflower.
There were so many good characters in this movie. Shameik Moore did a pretty good job voice acting Miles Morales, but the best voice actor was Nicholas Cage. Im kind of joking here, but also kind of not. Nicholas Cage as Noir Spider-Man fit perfectly and made me laugh almost every time he was on screen. Most of the characters was well written and animated and such, only had a few gripes with some of them, but it didnt bother me too much.
This might be one of the funniest films Ive seen, at least for a while. I was laughing all the way through and some of the time I was on the verge of crying, because of emotional scenes. Its weird how emotional I got at times. The jokes landed almost every time, at least for me, and the emotional scenes didnt get cut with jokes. It was a good mix.
There were so many shots and moments that got me in awe. So many stunning and beautiful scenes, especially when Miles got his suit. That was incredible. You can really see and feel how much effort the animators, writers and everyone working on this movie, put into this movie. Even the credits were incredibly well made, and is one of the most entertaining credits Ive seen.
In my opinion, I do think this is the best Spider-Man movie that has been released. There were so many creative things they could do with the spider powers since it was animation and not live action. I dont know what to say, it was simply awesome
Overall, this might be my favorite movie of all time. Ive got to see it one more time to make up my mind, but it is pretty close. I have probably hyped up this movie more than intended, but its just because I love this movie. I suggest to go into this movie with an open mind, and not really think what everyone else thinks, make up your own opinion. But I loved this movie, and I cant wait to see it again.

That person who helps others simply because it should or must be done, and because it is the right thing to do, is indeed without a doubt, a real superhero.
You know Spider-Man was one of the biggest components to my childhood. I loved watching the shows like The Spectacular Spider-Man or even Ultimate Spider-Man, it was one of those big franchises that made up my childhood along stuff like Nintendo games, power rangers  stuff like Skylanders or Sonic. Seeing Spider-Man get the perfect (and i mean it) animated treatment, genuinely made me happy and it makes me appreciate it more reflecting on all the happy memories i received from this beloved character. Another thing that i liked about Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse, is that it makes me enjoy the animated aspects of films, see growing up and getting older im starting to lose that spark that i had with animated media  feel like its more of a virtue which younger me had to fulfil and that it doesnt give me the same vibes, and it also makes me envious to see my younger cousins or sisters genuinely enjoying animated media the way that i used to. Thats exactly why i loved My Neighbour Totoro so much, because it had the quality which a film deserves and still gave me a spark of nostalgia with the beautiful animation, and these 2 films make me glad of it. 
Honestly, i just want to appreciate the effort put into the animation and acting of the film, since i dont feel like i need to write an entire review for this beautiful piece of animated literature since im 100 sure thatll rewatch it. A lot of films, animated films truly grew out of the hidden gems that they were kept in after the release of this film such as The Mitchells vs The Machines  Puss in Boots The Last Wish, but they could never amount to the amount of effort put into Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse, basically every single frame of this film has its own secret easter egg and to share it with you guys i have compiled a list of trivia (off of IMDb) to share with you guys!!

Trivia
1) If you hit pause anytime a train goes by, because all the animators wanted to animate Stan Lee, hes in almost every single train.
2) It was Peter Ramseys idea to hold off on the visual comic language - word bubbles, panels, etc. - until Miles is bitten by the spider.
3) It was announced shortly after Stan Lees death, at age 95, that he had recorded a cameo for the film and that it would be his final voice-acting role. Phil Lord and Christopher Miller felt it was important that Lee was given a bigger moment compared to previous Marvel films because he was so integral to the spirit of this movie, and considered his role extra meaningful following his death.
4) Art directors Dean Gordon and Patrick OKeefe and their team turned to Cubism to help represent the dimensional quakes. Cubist art often presents a collection of different views all happening at the same time, so it was a natural metaphor for the multiple universes converging in Spider-Verse.
5) (at around 52 mins) The bagel text as the bagel hits the scientists head was a joke pitch that an animator took seriously and added in. They loved it.
6) The unique animation style of Spider-Verse aims to make the viewer feel as if they are in the pages of a comic book. According to Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, the film combined the latest computer-generated animation technology with hand-drawn artistry. It was very important to us that every frame of the movie was refined by the artists hand after the visuals were rendered by computers. If you freeze any part of the movie at any time, it will look like an illustration with hand drawn touches and all.
7) Completing the animation for the film required up to 180 animators, the largest crew ever used by Sony Pictures Animation for a film.
8) This film was dedicated in memory of Spider-Man co-creator Steve Ditko, who died on July 6, 2018, while this film was finishing production however, this was not the only dedication, as a month before the film was released, Stan Lee died on November 12, 2018. The film was dedicated to both of Spider-Mans creators.
9) Daniel Pemberton followed the ambitious lead of the Spider-Verse animation by developing an equally intricate score. After all the musical elements had been recorded, they were recorded onto vinyl and then re-scratched into the mix. Daniel Pemberton says, I got a DMC World Scratch champion DJ to scratch all the parts in.
10) Nicolas Cage was excited that the directors let him have fun with the role of Spider-Man Noir. Cage says, ...its no secret that I like to play with different sources. It was fun to go back in time and pull back a little of that Humphrey Bogart essence. Cage thinks that the movie will appeal both to the adults who like old movies and the kids who will want to learn more about them.
11) During the coronavirus pandemic, Jake Johnson offered to record free personalized messages as Peter B. Parker for children under quarantine.
12) Phil Lord and Christopher Miller had a goal for the movie, Inspire young people to become heroes, inspire grown-ups to help them do it, and remind us all that you dont need to be bitten by a radioactive spider to do your part. You are powerful, and we are counting on you.
13) The directors of Spider-Verse spoke with io9 about the Prowlers signature siren noise. Composer Daniel Pemberton used the sound of an elephant as the base for the noise. According to the filmmakers, they wanted the noise to be frightening, but also have a sense of sadness.

The moment Miles Morales was first shown with his black suit, oh my God. I will cherish that whole scene for the rest of my life.
Ive had my fair share of comic book collecting back in my day (which I sold because I needed money) and Ive always noticed how Marvel comics always tried to get their message across through their characters. Characters and stories that represent the LGBTQ, segregation, feminism, diversity, minorities, and everything. Ive seen it in issues of X-Men, Spider-Man, The Avengers, Captain America, Black Panther, and many more. Writers and artist from back then would do this (like Stan Lee and Steve Ditko), as well as writers and artist now. 
Most superhero movies try to slowly build upon those messages, but they all try very hard to make the story itself great, the characters great, the villains, and of course the action sequences and so on, they dont focus much on the message itself. 
Now what I loved about Into The Spider-Verse is that they took one of those messages from the comics and gave that sense that everyone can see themselves as these heroes we all know and love. This is similar to the Black Panther and Wonder Woman film, but no one wouldve thought Spider-Man, which we all knew to be Peter Parker. Now we added Miles Morales (coming from a diverse family background), Gwen Stacy (a girl) and even Peter Porker (an animal)! Now the game has changed and theres this wonderful message that was brought from the comic books and put straight onto the big screen. And if theres one thing for sure, its the fact that adults and kids watch more movies than they read comics so now that message is more alive and out there and its perfect for people to see it from a whole new perspective. Both kids and adults can be inspired, not just about being a superhero but relating to a superhero, no matter where you come from and no matter who you are.
Plus adding the comic book style to the movie gives this thing a whole fresh look on how we look at animated films and superhero films. 
This movie definitely has it all, a moving story, moving characters, great friendships and family. Then with great humor added in the mix, it makes this movie even more phenomenal.
I applaud all the creators, illustrators, designers, filmmakers behind this movie and behind all those comic books too. The world needed this and I for one, enjoyed this a lot.

Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse will always have a special place in my heart. Not only is it one of the best animated films ever made but I saw it with 18 of my closest friends at the cinema. We were the only people in the room and that experience of watching everyone be in awe of what they had just saw and chatting about it afterwards over dinner will always be special to me. This was my first rewatch since 2018 and I must say, I loved every second. 
Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse is one of the best animated movies ever made. The animation is absolutely stunning to watch with the vibrant colours and comic book style animation all working in the films favour which, when mixed with the gorgeous soundtrack, creates a brilliant experience that warrants repeat viewings. The multiple villains Kingpin, Green Goblin, Tombstone, Doctor Octopus and The Prowler, wouldnt all work in a live action format but with this being an animated film they work perfectly throughout as the film allows adequate time for our heros to interact with them and learn more about them as the film progresses. Now the team, comprised of Miles Morales, Gwen Stacy, Peter Parker, Spider-Man Noir, Peni Parker and of course Spider-Ham, are all unique, interesting and undeniably fantastic to watch as each character as their moment to shine with the drama and emotive moments that are showcased throughout all feeling earned as they develop far beyond the films premise into characters you care about and want to see more of. The use of the repetitive narrative when introducing every character is incredibly fun and when mixed with the beautiful, truly gorgeous animation and catchy soundtrack all amount to a truly stellar film.
An Ethos that Spider-Man has always personified is the idea that anyone can be a hero and thats where the film gains its most basic, but arguably greatest, thrill. Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse stretches that idea to hilarious new dimensions with wacky sequences and a story thats as heart-warming as it is daring and for me, that all amounts into a rather fantastic spectacle that always makes this a rather special film to watch. Its undeniable that this film is beautiful, Ive said it time and time again, but its also one of the best, most visually daring animated movie to have ever graced our screens. Its a film thats hard not to love. Its truly incredible!

Remember, what makes you different is what makes you Spider-Man. 
It is crazy to me that were in a year where Black Panther and Avengers Infinity War came out and this Sony animated film is the best superhero movie Ive seen in 2018. Its difficult to collect my rambling thoughts about how much I loved this film so this review wont be very analytical. 
Everything about this movie was so fresh, beautiful, and fun. The story was suprisingly mature for a movie with a younger demographic, the animation style was so ambitious and one that I hope to see more of in the future, and the characters were so well developed and fun to watch. 
Every single cast member did an amazing job. Peter and Miles dynamic was heartfelt, Gwen was a cool character who I cant wait to see more of, and Spider-Man Noir, Spider-Ham, and Peni Parker were really fun and had great designs. I dont think Ive ever related more to a movie character than the depressed Peter Parker who came from another dimension.  Miles dad is a conflicted man with a huge heart and a stubborn head and his relationship with Miles feels real and tangible, the scenes with them are very emotionally charged and showcase the difficulties in raising a child who you begin to lose a connection with. 
The villains were pretty fantastic too, with a fantastic take on The Prowler from Mahershala Ali and Liev Schriebers brutal but ultimately sympathetic Kingpin. Doc Oc, Scorpion, and other tertiary antagonists were well designed, well acted, and fun to watch. 
The Stan Lee cameo made me tear up a little bit. And the end credits sequence is wonderful. The music was great, with a tense and powerful score and a catchy soundtrack. The film is funny and so sharply written, which isnt surprising considering Phil Lords hand in the screenplay. 
I loved the world of the movie, how the universe was familiar but slightly different. The scenes in Times Square emphasized this so well with minor changes from our world like Chance the Rappers hat on a billboard having a number 4 instead of a number 3 on it. 
The animation style is the star of this film without a doubt, its so refreshing and cool. Ive never seen a two dimensional style like what youd see in a comic book realized so wonderfully in three dimensions. Every frame was gorgeous and full of color and style. I will be highly disappointed if it isnt Best Animated Feature this year at the Oscars 
This movie is one of the best Ive seen all year, and honestly one of the best superhero films Ive ever see. Please go see it so we can get many more of these.
Thank you Stan Lee. Thank you Steve Ditko. Your work has made a huge impact and its inspired fans, filmmakers, actors, comic book artists, authors, and so many more.

review_text:
Okay, lets do this one last time. I dont like superheroes.
Obviously, this isnt the first time Ive said this in one way or another, and it wont be the last time. Its not a dislike that has been born out of the proliferation of superhero films weve seen over the last five or six years either, Ive not liked them for a lot longer than that.
When I was a kid I watched the Spider-Man cartoon and the Superman cartoon and the Christopher Reeve films and the Tim Burton Batman and even the X-Men cartoon when I got a bit older. Like most people, Im sure. And I liked them! I really did. Somewhere along the line though, I stopped caring about any of this stuff.
I dont know when or where it happened. I think it might have been when I went to see the first X-Men movie. Despite having watched the cartoon for a fair while, I didnt understand half of what was going on and my two best friends, who I went to see it with, pointed out to me that I would have liked it more if Id read the comic books, like they did.
Nah, fuck that. I went to see a film. I didnt go to initiate a multimedia commitment that would be the only way to get a full handle on what was going on with these characters. And then the MCU and DCU happened and we see, what, at least two films a year from both these lot now? Maybe its more or maybe it just feels that way.
My dislike of these films is not blind and, I will admit, is occasionally embellished for comedy effect. I recognise that many of these films have been critically acclaimed and have meant a lot to many different people in many different ways. Especially so in the case of Black Panther, Wonder Woman and the upcoming Captain Marvel. Even Im not that blinkered.
But I am genuinely concerned at how much these films are dominating blockbuster filmmaking. It sits uncomfortably with me that two super-franchises, the likes of which have never been seen on this scale in the history of cinema, so utterly dominate big budget filmmaking and cinema releases these days. Its making it increasingly difficult for standalone films, tentpole titles and franchise startup hopefuls to get a word in edgeways.
Theres also this notion of universes that bothers me. These two labels are now so far down the road of their shared narratives that for those who havent been a part of it all from somewhere near the start, it must be a daunting prospect to get into it at this comparatively late stage. You then factor in the fact there are TV series and animated series and the obvious comic book links, and its completely overwhelming to me.
I did delve into it briefly just over a year ago when I watched Deadpool after somebody said to me that I would like this one because it wasnt really like all the other superhero films. This one is self-mocking and doesnt take itself seriously and youll like it, honest! But outside of the inside jokes, it was just the same as any other superhero film. Superheroes and supervillains twatting each other about for ages, just with more swearing. 
It fascinated me that this was the superhero film that was supposed to be cleverer than the rest, the one that didnt take things seriously. Yet all I got was a film that actually lacked the self-awareness that it was claimed it had. I took away from it the realisation that these films dont even know how to mock themselves properly. It wasnt a good film at all for all of Ryan Reynolds admirable energy and commitment to the character and movies.
The appearance of Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse on the horizon elicited a groan from me. I assumed it was another way for Marvel to tighten their grip on the multiplexes, only this way they were doing it with animation, perhaps as the start of a two-tiered assault on dominating the blockbuster market. It was also another title where people were insisting that I should see it because its different and hey, you said you wanted to sample more animation and stuff out of your comfort zone in 2019! which frankly was a low blow, you bastards.
So along came the trailer and some admiring glances from my daughter and, Ill admit, a raised eyebrow from me regarding the involvement of Lord and Miller. Again, another low blow. Plus there was the fact that the trailer was pretty fantastic but I actually didnt pay that much attention because I dont think that sort of thing can ever be truly relied upon.
Then theres the fact that its the Christmas holidays and I will quite often find myself dragged to see stuff half-reluctantly by my daughters that I sometimes really dont want to see. I say half-reluctantly because it keeps them quiet for a couple of hours and occasionally the film were seeing turns out far better than expected. Last year that was the case with Jumanji Welcome to the Jungle and only last week I was unexpectedly charmed by Bumblebee.
This was a different kettle of fish though. Even the kids are not normally bothered by the whole superhero thing, unless its the Caped Crusader in Lego form. And that goes for me too. Obviously. This was a giant leap to say the least.
I wish I could say that Im so confused right now by how great I found this film to be but Im actually not. You know, if I were to ever want to have an entry point into the whole Spider-Man story, this would be it. Because what they have done here is craft a film that probes the origins of Spider-Man while also finding the time to spin an entirely different story, bring in new characters, and leave the door open for a multitude of opportunities without the kind of To Be Continued ending that has been problematic not just (apparently) in superhero films of late, but in big budget filmmaking for even longer.
It takes the time to introduce us, at a sprightly pace, to who Peter Parker(s) is  are. Even I didnt feel that was wholly necessary because even those of us who arent comic book nerds know all about the whole radioactive spider thing. Come on guys, give us some credit! But in transitioning away from the original Parker it doesnt then ignore his background and comes up with in-depth characterisation that made me interested in everyone here.
Most importantly of all - I didnt feel lost! I was concerned by one or two reviews suggesting this would be a comic book nerds heaven but it does that thing that ALL these films should be doing. It gives fans of the characters and stories plenty to be getting on with but its also accessible to ignoramuses like me. Im sure its not easy to find that balance, but it can be done, and on this occasion its made to look as though it really wasnt difficult at all - as Dredd also did
Sure, it maybe rushes through one or two things, which is understandable when youre covering so much ground and trying to keep the running time under two hours. But it is at least in keeping with its scintillating pace and in that way it makes some sense. Its story is terrific, though, really thoughtful and it included a trope that I REALLY like in an action film of introducing a villain with a motive.
Kingpins backstory is one that I hope they develop further in the future. Its something that is done so infrequently but it reminded me of Ed Harris in The Rock of a villain with principles who, despite clearly being a madman, isnt just another bastard intent on destroying the world for the usual old reasons. It adds a resonance and layer to the ending that prevents it from being the usual superhero film of climax of superhumans battering each other endlessly.
The strength of character is, I think, perhaps why this film worked so well for me. The odd bunch of heroes are a balance of comedy and individuality as well as collective strength, and they all have their time in the sun as well as their own universes that would each all make for enjoyable stories and films in their own right. As an old school crime and noir fan, Spider-Man Noirs story holds particular interest for me.
The pleasing development of the relationship between Miles and Gwen into a friendship was great too. You know, Im here for the argument that modern day films could get carried away with not focusing on romantic couplings between a pair of leads as was traditional. You can have too much of a good thing. However, in this case it works for a number of reasons, not least that there are bigger things going on in their young lives, such as the fact that they have the burden of saving their respective worlds.
Theres a sharpness of humour and self-reference here that also brings me back to Deadpool. With that film, it never felt as though what was going on was ever really at all serious or a threat. It really weakened the characters and the story that it spent so much of its time mocking it all. Yet here, it keeps its silliness and its deeper subjects more or less separate, but not in such a way that it felt aggressively divided. This is a very funny film indeed but not at the expense of going somewhere tangible.
Oh yeah, the animation. Look, Im pretty hyperbolic when it comes to my reviews, something Ive never apologised for, but Im still quite guarded with some things that I say. But Ive never seen a better animated film than this. Ever. Its one of those wonderful occasions where I cant possibly fathom how they did this, any of this. There are so many styles in the offshoots and subplots here, as well as the neat comic book style inserts and sound effects text even before I get to the main strand here.
Imagination is limitless, but the ability to transfer that into visuals is far from it. Yet on a few occasions here, especially during the breathtaking dimension-melding visuals of the last 20 minutes here, it felt like the gap between the two was at the very least mininal. Like with all things that mesmerise me on the big screen, I dont want to know how they did it, Im just glad that they did.
There you have it. Phew. The finest animation Ive ever seen and one of the better films of any kind Ive ever seen, full s

Hands down one of the finest films of 2018, definitely the best Spider-Man feature since Spider-Man 2, and inarguably the greatest comic-book entry of the entire decade, which is no mere feat considering that 2010s is filled to the brim with superhero pictures.
Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse is a jaw-dropping feat of originality, imagination  top-tier storytelling. Every frame is a throwback, every scene sets up the next, every moment is accounted for, every aspect is neatly executed, and all the elements work in pure, perfect harmony.
Add to that, its distinct, unique  groundbreaking animation is achieved by not striving for perfection but by simply embracing the imperfections of those comic book prints when translating it to the film canvas, which in turn gives its images a cinematic look that feels both fresh  familiar.
In short, Into the Spider-Verse is clever, creative  confident piece of filmmaking throughout. Animation is the best medium to explore the universe of comic books to their full potential, and this instant classic proves why. Easily the best big screen experience Ive had in a long, long time.

So a few days ago, before my friend and I went to go watch the spectacle that was Demon Slayer Infinity Castle, we stopped at this second-hand shop that sells video games, consoles, and most importantlyDVDs and Blu-rays. Now, the reason this matters is because physical media is dying, and its nearly impossible to find without paying an arm and a leg.
As I was scanning through the new stock (the owner lets me see it early because Im his best friend... he just doesnt know it yet), I stumbled upon SPIDER-MAN INTO THE SPIDER-VERSE!!! I gasped and went, Bro, what the heck!? How did you get this!? He just shrugged and said, Its what I do. I snatched that bad boy up instantly. (Also grabbed War for the Planet of the Apes while I was at it.)
So tonight, I decided to watch Spider-Verse for what feels like the 10,000th time. But before I hit play, an option popped up Play Alternate Universe Mode. I was like, huh? I flipped the Blu-ray box over and it said Discover alternate scenes, plotlines, characters, and more with the filmmakers as your guide. My eyes lit up like a 5 year old at a carnival.
THE WHOLE FILM IS DIFFERENT. LIKE WHAT IS GOING ON?! Its almost like a directors cut. There are so many deleted scenes that wouldve completely changed the narrative. Dont get me wrong, I still adore the final version, but this alternate one adds so much.
The biggest takeaway for me was the stronger relationship between Miles and Ganke. Their friendship is front and center here! Just two 13 year olds, one suddenly a superhero, figuring out what to do with all that power. review_text:
It took me a little while to get used to Into The Spider-Verses busy, hyper-kinetic style, but once onboard these flourishes make way for a story with a genuine emotional core underneath, combining heart with a bold visual approach that allows for the best of both worlds (or universes) in a fresh spin on the classic Spider-Man story. 
This does a great job in bringing a strong comic book sensibility to the screen, often splitting scenes into panels and threading classic visual devices like onomatopoeia in to really enhance the larger than life feel in the moment the CGI itself used to render this isnt as strong when it comes to characters faces (which dont always look the best), but really comes into its own for the peerless action sequences, each incredibly entertaining and breathtaking to watch play out as lots of different techniques are brilliantly used together over the runtime (pioneering in a way that presumably played a major part in netting this an Oscar for Best Animated Feature). 
Theres quite a lot going on here in terms of narrative, which in establishing and juggling each of new elements runs the risk of this story becoming overstuffed, but the through line is always in the characters and their relationships, whether that be Miles and his dads sweet (and very believable) dynamic, or Jake Johnsons brilliant turn as a dishevelledwashed up alternate universe Peter Parker discovering his mojo again after being suddenly thrown into the role of reluctant mentor. 
This sense of heart at the centre of it all makes for a great fusion of spectacle and substance, though I think the film perhaps packs a few too many character arcs and story threads in to entirely work all the time. Still, even if a little overcrowded, the film is hugely entertaining, a reminder of just how creative comic book movies can be when put to screen in such an inventive way.

Homem-Aranha no Aranhaverso é uma experiência que prefiro avaliar pelo impacto que causou do que por uma nota. Foi um daqueles filmes que mudaram a forma como a indústria enxerga a animação e provaram que ainda era possível reinventar o Homem-Aranha.
Miles Morales conquista rapidamente porque sua história é simples e sincera. Ele erra, aprende e cresce sem parecer apressado. Peter B. Parker funciona como um mentor cheio de defeitos, bem diferente da imagem tradicional do herói. Gwen Stacy, Noir, Peni Parker e Porco-Aranha entram pouco em cena, mas todos conseguem ter personalidade própria.
O maior destaque está na direção de Bob Persichetti, Peter Ramsey e Rodney Rothman. A animação mistura quadrinhos, grafite, texturas impressas e diferentes estilos visuais de um jeito que nunca tinha visto no cinema. Cada universo possui sua própria identidade, e tudo isso é acompanhado por uma trilha sonora excelente que combina perfeitamente com Miles e sua cultura.
O filme venceu o Oscar de Melhor Filme de Animação, além do BAFTA, Globo de Ouro e diversos Annie Awards. O reconhecimento veio porque a qualidade técnica realmente era diferente de tudo que existia naquele momento. Não foi apenas um sucesso de público, mas uma produção que influenciou inúmeras animações lançadas depois.
Poucas obras conseguem mudar uma indústria inteira. Homem-Aranha no Aranhaverso fez exatamente isso. É um filme que continua moderno, divertido e visualmente impressionante anos depois do lançamento. Sempre que penso nas melhores adaptações do Homem-Aranha, ele está entre elas, independentemente de ser animação.
  I dont rate animated films with stars. 
Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse is something I prefer to judge by its impact rather than a numerical score. It changed the way the industry looked at animation and proved there was still room to reinvent Spider-Man.
Miles Morales quickly becomes an engaging protagonist because his journey feels honest. He makes mistakes, learns, and grows at a natural pace. Peter B. Parker works perfectly as a flawed mentor, offering a refreshing contrast to the traditional Spider-Man. Gwen Stacy, Spider-Man Noir, Peni Parker, and Spider-Ham all have limited screen time, yet each one leaves a lasting impression.
Bob Persichetti, Peter Ramsey, and Rodney Rothman deserve enormous credit for the direction. The animation blends comic-book art, graffiti, print textures, and multiple visual styles in a way cinema had never seen before. Every universe has its own identity, supported by an outstanding soundtrack that perfectly matches Miles and his world.
The film won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, along with the BAFTA, Golden Globe, and numerous Annie Awards. Those honours recognised a film whose technical quality genuinely stood apart from everything else released at the time. It became both a critical success and a major influence on modern animation.
Very few films reshape an entire medium. Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse did exactly that. It still feels fresh, entertaining, and visually stunning years later. Whenever I think about the greatest Spider-Man adaptations, this one is always part of the conversation.

In a banner year for comic book adaptations, Spider-Verse comes to plant its flag near the top of the competition. This is a movie that can stand next to the best of Pixar and Disneys classics. .𖥔    A film made to go down in history... and it deservedly did. 
I remember seeing this movie in theaters, and it was funny how there were only about... twelve of us in the room. There wasnt much of a buzz when it was released, but it deservedly became a modern classic that did a 180 in how animation is made and seen. After watching it and No Way Home back to back, i reinforced an idea ive always had in my head This movie is what it is because its animated. And so it elevates animation as one of the most sophisticated art forms, deserving of greater respect. More respect that it gets!  If Into the Spiderverse were a live-action film, it would probably be considered mid. Its solutions are similar to those of No Way Home, but one seems smart and creative, while the other seems... goofy. And thats precisely because animation brings a different flavor to things. A kind of freedom that live-action simply cant have due to budget.
Its delightful to watch. Its really cool to see this old and tired version of Peter Parker. A modern, arachnid Gwen. The weight of legacy.
Ive tried reading Miles Morales comics several times, but honestly, you need a lot of patience to connect with this character. He seems pointless and kind of... more of the same? Sure, he has different powers that honestly dont even make sense... invisibility and electricity? In a Spider-Man? What a stupid choice, only Michael Bendis goofy ass could come up with something like that! But while in the comics he seems like Peter Parkers crumbs-eater, just reheating OGs nachos over and over and over, cinematically HE WORKS VERY WELL. And there are characters who are just like that! Example i dislike Tony Stark in the comics, but adapted to the movies, he worked perfectly well. By that i mean that Miles journey here is very fluid and moving. Great protagonist. 
The action scenes are good and creative, the soundtrack is perfect, the villains are perfect, the vibrant colors are a feast for the eyes. Its honestly a film made to go down in history... and it deservedly did.

Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse redefines what a Spider-Man story can be, proving that even the most familiar characters can still surprise and delight. Directed by Bob Persichetti, Peter Ramsey, and Rodney Rothman, with the creative touch of Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, this film shatters superhero conventions with a story thats smart, hilarious, and visually groundbreaking.
This time, the hero is Miles Morales, a bright but uncertain teen far from the classic Peter Parker nerd archetype. Struggling with his identity in a prestigious boarding school and a police officer father, Miles becomes a modern, relatable Spider-Man after a bite from a genetically altered spider.
The film pushes the boundaries of animation with a vibrant, ever-shifting style that adapts to each character and universe like a living comic book page. The nods to fans and the very energetic soundtrack add to its joyful yet heartfelt tone.
The true strength of Into the Spider-Verse lies in its universal and inclusive message Spider-Man isnt confined to a single face. By exploring six distinct versions of the hero, the film celebrates diversity in all its forms and reminds us that the Spider-Man spirit, defined by resilience, humility, and hope, an live in anyone, regardless of age, gender, or universe.
While the plot sometimes follows familiar beats, the visual and narrative originality more than makes up for it. And as always with Marvel, the post-credits scene is a must-watch, just like the urge to revisit this one-of-a-kind film.

Although I have seen Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse a dozen times, and everyone has already pointed out what makes this film so special, I still wanted to give my two cents. While this may not be the best animated film of all time, it is by far the best looking animated film of all time in my opinion. Everything jumps off the screen at you and feels like a comic book has come to life. I love how the film adds in the sound effects of film to the screen, exactly like it is in the comics. These little attentions to detail are what elevate this above most films. The films colors are vibrant and feel like they are something out of a psychedelic experience at times. Every single voice actor in the film is perfectly cast for their character. Their performances are boosted by the fact that every character in the film is given unique character traits and adequate screen time. Shameik Moore as Miles Morales is one of the best protagonist in any superhero film.
Miles goes through an emotional roller coaster of a journey, that, by the end of the film, has us, the audience, fully bought in on Miles taking that leap of faith. Jake Johnson as Peter B. Parker cracks me up everytime I watch this film. His Peter consistently brings heart and laughs for the audience while also providing Miles the guidance he needs in his life in wake of the death of his universes Spider-Man, and later the death of his Uncle Aaron. Brian Tyree Henrys Jefferson Davis, Hailee Steinfelds Gwen Stacy, and John Mulaneys Spider-Ham are a few of the others doing standout voice work, but everyone is on their a game and fit in well with the film. A lot of people have a problem with the villain, Lie Schriebers Kingpin. While kris backstory isnt given a lot of screen time, it is drawn out enough to understand where he is coming from and this film is doing so much that I think having a more bare bones villain is of benefit. Spider-Verses script has so many touching moments, its unreal. So many emotional lines throughout the film that you are almost left in tears, such as the talk Miles dad gives him outside his dormroom or the leap of faith Peter B. Parker takes back to his universe. Going along with what I said about the characters in the film, a lot of the reason as to why all of the characters work is due to the script introducing everyone of importance in a concise manner that never misses a beat in its pacing When I was watching this with my girlfriend over the weekend, she said that she really enjoyed the film but thought that the action in the film wasnt very exciting and I couldnt disagree any more. The action is fast paced and again gives that feeling of a comic book or a sandbox of toys is leaping into life on the screen. The ending fight with the Kingpin, along with the other array of villains hes got working for him, is one of if not my favorite action scene in any comic book movie of all time. Never would I have thought that I would be seeing multiple Spider-Men take on basically his entire rogues gallery all in one movie, but this movie did it. I honestly Though its not my favorite Spider-Man film, as Spider-Man 2 has such a nostgolic and special place in my heart that I dont think it can ever be topped, but this film came just about as close as you can get. Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse truly understands the character of Spider-Man better any film before or after it, culminating perfectly into what is the best animated film since WALL-E for me.

review_text:
When will I know when Im ready? - Miles Morales
You wont. Its a leap of faith. Thats all it is, Miles. A leap of faith. - Peter B. Parker
The worlds most recognizable  beloved superhero changed cinema for a 2nd time with the release of his 1st animated film. Its funny thinking about it in retrospect since its so obvious now but this fundamentally reshaped Hollywood animated features forever.
Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse is THE GREATEST comic book film of all time.
The craziest part is that at the time, Sony Pictures was in a terrible place when the film was greenlit. The Amazing Spider-Man duology came and went with zero fanfare due to lackluster reception and poorly constructed quality. During the infamous 2014 Sony Hack, it was hinted within those emails that notorious producer, Amy Pascal, was searching for filmmakers to create their first-ever animated Spider-Man movie.
Thankfully, they didnt have to search too far as they picked someone in-house. Phil Lord  Christopher Miller were selected to spearhead the project...but only on one condition.
It needs to be about the Spider-Verse starring Miles Morales. - Lord  Miller
Now many of you may not know this but Phil Lord is actually a Cuban Latino so the choice to make their only Spider-Man project centered on a Latino instead of Peter Parker was a bold swing. Miles was popular in the comics and fans have been rooting for his theatrical debut for years but to actually commit to it is another thing.
The script saw several drafts, one including a romantic subplot with Gwen Stacy that was eventually deleted, and just like that, the film was on its way to being officially made. Only one small problem now.
How is it going to look?
Well, at this point in time, animation was in a dry spell in terms of creative styles. Either you were going for realistic aesthetics similar to Pixar  Dreamworks Animation or your film was 2D like anime or traditional cartoons.
Lord  Miller pushed for Spider-Verse to have a resemblance to its original medium, a comic book, so the directors, writers, and the extensive team at Sony Pictures Imageworks did some soul-searching. The result...was to completely rework the animation medium forever.
Although this isnt common knowledge, Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse did not invent its art style, it simply perfected it. The origins of this art style come from EuropeanFrench animation but they lacked that extra Oomph that Spider-Verse has.
What separates the two comes down to several factors. For one, Spider-Verse implemented framerate changes that were unheard of for 3D animation. Back in the old days, hand-drawn 2D animation contained framerate changes due to budgetary constraints or stylistic choices. Looney Tunes is the greatest example of such. Sometimes Bugs Bunny or The Roadrunner are lightning fast which can last 2-3 frames...and sometimes they are expertly animated like in fluid slow motion. As for CGI animated films, this was never truly attempted.
This one layer changed Spider-Verses style completely. And to top it all off, the film uses this creative choice on a story level too. Since Miles Morales is a novice superhero, his framerate is on 2s, causing him to look more stuttery, and inexperienced. As compared to Peter B. Parker who is on 1s, his animation is fluid, showcasing expertise at being the titular hero. Truly, genius.
The second layer is the addition of 2D animated linework to amplify the comic-book aesthetic. Whether its a wrinkle, a dimple, a smirk, some Spider-Sense tingling, or rim-lighting, there is 2D drawn linework added to the animation. Outside of this film, this had only been seen once in a Disney animated short titled Paperman. However, this was the 1st project to implement it for a full animated feature. By doing this, it makes the comic book-iness pop.
The third layer is something called Benday dotslines. Now, whenever you read a traditionally printed comic book, youll notice this interesting texture on the print which consists of millions of tiny circlesscratches. Sometimes the circleslines are the color of the characters skin, hair, and clothing. Sometimes the circleslines are used for the shading. As for Spider-Verse, this has never been used in animation before because the need to do so is insane  unnecessary. But, because this is going for a comic-book look, it continues the trend of making this film look bold  unique.
But thats fine and all. Style, animation, and aesthetics can only get you so far. And while the animated film is truly one of the most breathtaking films Ive ever seen, at the end of the day, it always comes down to the story.
Look, sometimes... people drift apart, Miles. And I dont want that to happen to us, okay? Look, I know I dont always do what you need me to do or say what you need me to say, but I... I see this... this spark in you, its amazing, its why I push you. But its yours, and whatever you choose to do with it, youll be great. - Jefferson Davis
Miles Morales goes through an emotional journey of self-worth  faith. While the idea of believing in yourself is NOT new to animation, the way it is used for this specific Spider-Man story is.
Because Miles is the 1 and only Spider-Man...in his universe. Outside of that...he is 1 of billions. How can someone find individuality in an ocean of sameness?
On top of that, there is this feeling of inadequacy since Miles is inexperienced as Spider-Man. He has never fought anyone, thwipped web, or even jumped across rooftop buildings. How can he even compare himself to the likes of Spider-Man Noir, SPY-DR, or Spider-Woman?
This is also commentary on raceethnicityheritage. As a mixed-race Latino, Miless uniqueness stands out from others in a beautiful way. To find comfortsecurity in your heritage is something that is consistently put to the test every day in America and for Miles to be confident in that is amazing. What helps is that one of the Co-directors is black, with a script written by a Latino, starring a black American. As a Latino myself, to see this type of representation on screen is extremely impactful, and for it to be done in such a loving way is beautiful.
But like all things in life, the risk is part of the journey. Life is never easy and while loss is around every corner, its about taking a leap of faith that maybe things will be right in the end.
And this all culminates in a story about loss.
Miles loses a family member just like every Spider-Man loses their Uncle Ben. Kingpin loses his family due to greed, anger, and abuse. Peter B. Parker loses the love of his life because he fears hes too inadequate to be a father.

You wont. - Miles
Right. - Peter B. Parker
Its a leap of faith. - Miles

Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse, with all its style, gorgeous animation, heartfelt story, and emotional journeys, might never be topped by any other comic-book film...and you know what? Thats ok.
No need to compare yourself to anything and anyone.

Youve got 24 hours.
Day 4  Day 365 
I keep writing these late in the night, Im not sure why but I think its getting to be a bad habit with school starting up again  But today I was very conflicted on what to watch, although there was one film that is highly praised and made by an amazing director that I had in mind, I decided maybe at a later time or tomorrow since its a bit lengthy as well. But I wanted to go back to a nice little rewatch, and that was this, Spider-Man  Into the Spider-Verse.
This will always be an outstanding film to me, one that pops out and one that will always look stunning no matter how well future animated films look. This is the film that really changed the game for animation, one that has inspired many other animated films and one that proves to everyone that animated films are NOT just for kids. Its a film that appeals to everyone, its Spider-Man and I dont think theres one person on this earth who will hate on one of the greatest heros of all time, except for J Jonah Jameson of course. But this film is most visual appealing thing you can watch, its beautifully made and has the literal feel of a comic book solidifying it as one of the best comic book films of all time, and one of the best Spider-Man stories that is being told as its not completed yet.
No matter how many times I watch this, the film never gets boring, it always finds a way to keep me interested whether its the visuals, the fast pace, or the incredible story and characters, but it never bores me in any way. A story about Miles Morales trying to live up to the previous Spider-Man, as he tries to embrace and follow in Peters foot steps, later realizing that he needs to make his own path to being Spider-Man. Its a spectacular film about personal growth and perseverance, while also connecting the fact that you are not alone in the entire universe, or in fact multiverse. But I think my favorite part about this film is that it proves to everyone that Miles Morales IS Spider-Man.
Its truly disappointing to see many still argue about this, but if this film proves anything, it is that Miles is Spider-Man. Its honestly insane how people watch this film and dont realize that anyone can wear the mask, no matter what race, what gender, or where they come from. Ive seen many online say how Miles can never be Spider-Man and its so saddening to see when hes truly one of my favorite iterations after these films came out. I was never fully invested into comics and only knew about the basic films, so seeing this for the first time made me truly explore Spider-Man and understand the character. But to see the debate and hate online about this is truly annoying to see and makes those that say that not understand Spider-Man at all.

Shifting more focus towards the film, I love the amount of detail and work that is put into them. There are so many small things to miss and parallels that reflect change of Miles that you dont notice on a first watch. All the hints of foreshadowing about the true origins about the spider that bit him, the green and purple spider sense changing to red and blue to symbolize Miles destiny changing from becoming the prowler to being Spider-Man. Then theres the opposite parallels of his first leap of faith attempt and his true leap of faith moment, with him being in his own suit rather than merch of Spider-Man, and his screams going up rather than down to showcase the rise of his character. Its incredible how much thought was put into these films and thats honestly my favorite part about animated films and these films in general. Theres so many details to still find and that are still being found despite this film being around 7 years old, and thats why I love going back to rewatch it, I always find something new.
Something smaller that I like to point out is the characters in this film, I really love how they brought lesser known (at the time at least) villains in this film who have never been brought onto the big screen such as Miles (obviously), Prowler, Tombstone, Scorpion, Spider-Man Noir (I cant wait for the show btw), Peni Parker, and Peter Porker of course. I love that it didnt stick to older and more popular characters for a story line and let less popular characters take the spotlight which is awesome.
Also I will say, I AM PRAYING THERE IS A REFERENCE TO THE HAMMER SPIDER-HAM GIVES TO MILES IN THE BEYOND THE SPIDER-VERSE, IF THERE IS, INSTANT 10.
But this is a film I will always cherish, its got everything you could possibly ask for in a comic book film, and its even crazier that the second film does almost everything even better. Im not sure if Ill watch the second film tomorrow, but Im so glad I gave this one a rewatch as its been needing it and its a reminder that no matter how hard things get, you are never alone and that you should always get back up.

Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse ist einer der wenigen Animationsfilme, denen ich auf Anhieb fünf Sterne gegeben habe, und er hat diese Bewertung auch nach erneutem Ansehen mehr als verdient. Ohne Zweifel ist dies mein liebster Spider-Man-Film und ich freue mich schon auf die Fortsetzung.
Der Film hat mich von Anfang an mit seinem einzigartigen visuellen Design und dem innovativen Animationsstil in seinen Bann gezogen. Die Kombination aus traditioneller Comic-Panel-Ästhetik und modernster CGI-Technologie schafft ein atemberaubendes visuelles Erlebnis. Jedes Bild scheint direkt aus einem Comic zum Leben erweckt worden zu sein, und die dynamische Darstellung von Bewegungen und Actionszenen ist einfach atemberaubend.
Neben der hervorragenden Animation ist auch die Handlung sehr gut gelungen. Das Drehbuch ist intelligent, fesselnd und voller Humor. Die Geschichte von Miles Morales Aufstieg zu Spider-Man und die Begegnung mit anderen Versionen des kultigen Helden aus verschiedenen Dimensionen ist spannend und fantasievoll. Auch ernste Themen wie Verantwortung, Identität und Selbstakzeptanz werden angesprochen und verleihen dem Film eine bemerkenswerte Tiefe.
Die Figuren sind liebevoll ausgearbeitet und haben individuelle Persönlichkeiten, die sie zu glaubwürdigen und sympathischen Helden machen. Miles Morales ist ein fesselnder Protagonist, der mit seinen Ängsten und Unsicherheiten kämpft, aber letztendlich seine eigene Stärke findet. Auch die anderen Spider-Persönlichkeiten bringen eine einzigartige Dynamik in die Geschichte und sorgen für wunderbare Interaktionen.
Auch der Soundtrack gefällt mir sehr gut, und die Auswahl der Lieder ist perfekt auf die einzelnen Szenen abgestimmt. Die Mischung aus Originalsongs und Klassikern schafft eine mitreißende Atmosphäre.
Fazit
Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse konnte mich einmal mehr mit seiner innovativen visuellen Gestaltung, der fesselnden Handlung und den charismatischen Charakteren begeistern. Es ist ein Film für Kinder und Erwachsene, der das Wesen von Spider-Man auf einzigartige Weise perfekt einfängt. Ich freue mich schon darauf, wieder in diese faszinierende Welt einzutauchen und hoffe sehr, dass die Fortsetzung mindestens genauso gut wird.
 E N G L I S H 
Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse is one of the few animated films that I gave five stars right off the bat, and it more than deserves that rating even after watching it again. Without a doubt, this is my favorite Spider-Man movie and Im already looking forward to the sequel.
The film captivated me from the start with its unique visual design and innovative animation style. The combination of traditional comic book panel aesthetics and cutting edge CGI technology creates a stunning visual experience. Each image seems to have been brought to life straight out of a comic book, and the dynamic rendering of movements and action scenes is simply breathtaking.
In addition to the excellent animation, the plot is also very well done. The script is intelligent, captivating and full of humor. The story of Miles Morales rise to become Spider-Man and meeting other versions of the iconic hero from different dimensions is exciting and imaginative. Serious themes of responsibility, identity and self-acceptance are also addressed, giving the film remarkable depth.
The characters are lovingly fleshed out and have individual personalities that make them believable and sympathetic heroes. Miles Morales is a compelling protagonist who struggles with his fears and insecurities, but ultimately finds his own strength. The other Spider personalities also bring a unique dynamic to the story and make for wonderful interactions.
I also really like the soundtrack, and the song choices are perfectly suited to each scene. The mix of original songs and classics creates a rousing atmosphere.
Conclusion
Spider-Man Into the Spider-Verse was once again able to thrill me with its innovative visual design, captivating plot and charismatic characters. Its a film for kids and adults that perfectly captures the essence of Spider-Man in a unique way. Im really looking forward to diving into this fascinating world again and I really hope that the sequel will be at least as good.

This is Miyazaki at his best. I sometimes forget how slow this movie is. He allows time for Chihiro and the audience to see the beauty of the world. As opposed to Howls Moving Castle which has a lot crammed in, this film will take time to watch her wash a stink spirit, or take a train ride.
It functions much like The Odyssey, where our main character meets a series of different and smaller challenges to form a larger narrative. This is one of the oldest form of story, dating back to Ancient Greece, and I think there is something about the format that can form an instant classic. Modern examples include Wizard of Oz, Shawshank Redemption, The Hobbit, 2001, and the aforementioned Alice in Wonderland. Theres something about this format that is able to address humanity. A marvel of originality, a standard of cinematic vision  a stunning work of art, Hayao Miyazakis Spirited Away presents the master storyteller revelling at the prime of his filmmaking career by blending together all the ingredients of his previous works into one mystically magical adventure thatll have its viewers intrigued, transfixed  transported to a whole new different world from start to finish.
Spirited Away is a coming-of-age drama, adventure, comedy, romance  fantasy, all merged into one, and concerns Chihiro a 10-year old girl who, while moving to a new neighbourhood with her parents, gets stuck in the world of gods, witches  monsters. After her parents are turned into pigs by the witch Yubaba, Chihiro takes up a job at the witchs bathhouse in order to free herself  her parents from the magic spell and return to the human world.
After setting an animation benchmark with Princess Mononoke, writer-director Hayao Miyazaki comes out of his self-imposed retirement to set another standard  delivers the most artistic work of his glorious career. The film is abundant with his trademarks, recurrent themes, allegories  fascinating characters yet it retains the innocence  childlike sense of wonder to eventually deliver a truly spellbinding experience.
There isnt a single scene in the film that doesnt display the wonderful craftsmanship of the people working at Studio Ghibli, the themes of environmental pollution, greed  the passage to adulthood is carefully portrayed plus the 2D animation is simply astonishing. The plot is nicely structured  finely paced while the characters make the drama more compelling  are cleverly fleshed-out in the script. And Joe Hisaishis score adds even more richness to an already amazing story.
On an overall scale, Spirited Away is a masterpiece of bold, creative  fearless imagination that takes its genre to a whole new level and despite its complexity, it can be enjoyed by viewers of all ages. Many hail this anime as Miyazakis magnum opus  even though I dont share the same view, I can see why its called so. One of Miyazakis most ambitious features, one of Studio Ghiblis greatest accomplishments  one of world cinemas highly treasured gems, Spirited Away is magical enough to take your breath away. As I grow older my appreciation for Spirited Away grows larger. It is so obviously a masterpiece, yet its charms grow ever more endearing. It is not Hayao Miyazakis best movie, neither is it the best of Studio Ghiblis output, but I struggle to think of a better film for children. Miyazakis protagonists are always so well-rounded, with kindness and strength yet also allowed to be children and allowed to cry. He creates leads who are reassuring to us all. The pains of childhood can be outgrown and defeated. Watching Spirited Away the world feels safer. Not because there is no danger, but because it feels possible to survive what life throws at us.
After Princess Mononoke, the pinnacle of Miyazakis filmography, his return in Spirited Away became a culmination of his entire career. Princess Mononoke exists as a separate entity in his canon, a cynical work with dark touches. By contrast Spirited Away is lighter and less nasty. It returns Miyazaki to the formula of My Neighbour Totoro and Kikis Delivery Service, but now perfected with the mature sophistication his work gained in the 90s. Spirited Away is another episodic adventure about a young girl caught in a fantasy world within our reality, a world where the fantasy exists within the confines of human psychology. In Spirited Away, the creatures are motivated by greed or loneliness or selfishness. They are no better or worse than us. The parents of lead character Chihiro most represent the modern world, with their consumerist goods and gluttonous appetites. Our world has fallen to decadence and destruction, our planet ruined by pollution and dried-up rivers, two plot points that continue Miyazakis environmentalist themes established in earlier works.
In many ways the most important element of Spirited Away is its story of a child gaining responsibility and discovering within themselves what they are truly capable of. Centering on a young girl moving house, Spirited Away is a film about change and learning to meet the challenges which change presents us. Chihiro has her name taken from her and is thrust into adulthood through an expectation that she must work to survive. The film becomes about Chihiros search for identity, between her two names and her two lives, the one before she entered fantasy and the one within it. Similarly the entire world is caught between the real and fantastical, the modern and the traditional, the Eastern and the Western. The films pairs Japanese folklore with the encroaching global homogeneity of consumerist greed. The world has changed and it is not just children who need to realise that. The parents in Spirited Away come from the generation that experienced the boom of the 1980s Japanese economy followed by the economic stagnation of the 1990s, yet that generation did not relent on their materialist desires. They gained the soul of pigs, greedy and shallow.
Spirited Away is near flawless. Miyazakis incredible imagination makes every moment special. It is fast paced but, unlike Howls Moving Castle, there is a simplicity to the story and universality to the themes that stop the movie becoming a sprawling mess. There are a few contrived plot elements, but otherwise Spirited Away is a perfect movie. It is so lovable in spirit, so rich in themes, and so entertaining as a story. It has real drama and a strong sense of style. From the surface level visuals down to its soul, Spirited Away is an absolutely beautiful movie that I cannot help but love. Its mere existence makes the world a better place to live.

Define what it is that makes the greatest animated film in your eyes. It can come from anywhere, it can be about anything, or it can just do anything. When Im faced with this question, three Hayao Miyazaki films come to mind Spirited Away, Princess Mononoke, and My Neighbor Totoro. But if I had to pick a singular one from all of them, then said film is none other than Spirited Away. For how captivating the beauty of Princess Mononoke can be or how touchingly innocent My Neighbor Totoro is, my heart goes out to Spirited Away - for as cliche an answer it may be when asked about Hayao Miyazakis greatest achievement, it is not only my favourite of his films, but to this day it also remains my favourite animated film of all time.
All of the wonder of Spirited Away starts at the Alice in Wonderland-esque story in which we have the young Chihiro and her parents stopping by what appears to be an abandoned site that turns out to be the outer shell of a magical underworld. Her father insists that they explore the world, and soon enough Chihiro finds herself wandering off into a whole different area in which humans are transformed into animals. It flows with such a beautiful feeling of simplicity, but in such a captivating manner that can be absorbed by children and adults alike - just as the very best of Hayao Miyazakis fare have done so. With the grand scale of Princess Mononoke and the innocence of My Neighbor Totoro, we have something else in Spirited Away, which renders itself the most wonderful.
Where all the beauty of Spirited Away begins to start comes about with how it handles a coming-of-age story within Chihiros character arc. When the ten-year-old Chihiro first appears on the screen, one impression comes to mind when we hear of how she is moving to a new school. It is a clever hint already for what is set to come before Chihiro enters this other world where she is unready to confront what already must come up. She is still trapped inside of one world of her own, but as shown from what happened as a result of her parents transformation into pigs, she is not one to confront her own problems and she instead runs away from them. Yet with her progression all throughout Spirited Away from the moment she enters this realm, her growth becomes more apparent and it adds more to what forms such a brilliant work all throughout, perhaps the best of its own sort.
When I looked at Chihiro as her arc develops from a sheltered child to a girl who found herself, there were clear hints laced all throughout that resembled that of a child confronting a barrier. The allegory that Hayao Miyazaki presents in Spirited Away, ultimately, is a key factor as to why the work is as enchanting as it presents itself to be. There are many personal beats to which it can hit upon and that ultimately is a key to the power of the very best films that Hayao Miyazaki has made. In Spirited Away, we are not looking at Chihiro as any animated child taking up the screen but soon afterwards she becomes more than just such, for she is a reflection of oneself growing up to find whom they really are. It is hinted already from the moment in which her name has been taken away and reduced to Sen by the antagonist Yubaba, a figure who represents a stage in confrontation.
What exactly is there to confront, to be exact? All throughout, we can see that the workers at the bathhouse have one goal on mind, it is the hard work that they put in all to collect gold. But why do they want all of this gold? What good is it going to do for them? It adds more to the brilliance of Hayao Miyazakis commentary, that being how greed has consumed these souls to become what they are. Chihiros parents, the moment in which they first explore the spirit world, are eventually transformed into pigs as a result of their greed, for they stuffed themselves with food they just find out of the blue just like pigs eating at a trough. How exactly has it affected Chihiro? It was clear from there onward it was a state of her being neglected by her parents in favour of pleasure. I reflect back soon enough about those times my parents have taken me on trips and I was just alienated on my whole go, theres a brilliant parallel to be found right in Spirited Away.
Just as all of the best fantasy films would, Hayao Miyazaki is never afraid to explore every nook and cranny of this universe which he created in Spirited Away, which is something that made Princess Mononoke and My Neighbor Totoro work for the atmospheres that they carry, whether it be a complex tale of war between man and earth or simply, a recollection of innocence. In Spirited Away, the dreamlike atmosphere only enhances the experience all the more when one looks upon how Miyazaki draws every last image on the screen and gets down to the bare bones of the world which he has formed. Every design so beautiful, and in turn, so hypnotic. When I think of the very highest points that animation can ever achieve, it is with how much Hayao Miyazaki mixes in just to form Spirited Away where I can find myself sure Im watching the very best of the best.
I grew up on Studio Ghibli for the longest while already, and my journey with Spirited Away is still one of the most life-changing of them all. I still remember the first day in which I ever saw it, and on the many times I come back I reflect upon my life back in those days and the progress that has led me into what I am now. In a sense, that is what Spirited Away is. Hayao Miyazakis animated films are never just animated films, but instead they are meaningful creations that speak so much even to the real world maybe in more subtle ways than one would ever imagine on the spot. But that alone is only one of my reasons for seeing it as my favourite animated film of all time. Everything about Spirited Away just hits so perfectly, from the exploration of its universe down to the details within the drawing, mixed together with some of the most beautiful pieces of music to associate with the mood, Spirited Away is not only the greatest animated film of all time in my eyes. It is truly one an experience that leaves me in a state of reflection in regards to where I want to lead myself. Yet an English translation of the final song, Itsumo Nando Demo (a piece of music which still has never left my head from day one) has said it all even in the closing memories, there are always whispers that cannot be forgotten even on the shattered mirror shards, a new scenery is reflected.
