Mas é importante não confundir enredo simples, um mero gatilho narrativo, por assim dizer, com história vazia e rasa. Não é o que acontece aqui. Os contornos da expansão de crescimento e amadurecimento estão todos lá e Chihiro realmente lida com seu próprio rito de passagem, começando como uma menininha assustada e agarrada à barra da saia da mãe e chegando a uma jovem capaz de atos de coragem para fazer o que acha que é certo, sem jamais deixar que sua personalidade meiga, inteligente e curiosa funcione como ímã para as mais improváveis amizades. A trama é espetacular e, recomendada tanto para crianças quanto para adultos. Não bastasse isso, a película também conta com uma animação espetacular, superior a qualquer produção americana não 3D. De fato, é provavelmente a animação convencional de melhor qualidade de todos os tempos, um tributo ao enorme talento dos animadores do Studio Ghibli (do próprio Miyazaki), que se superam a cada nova investida. Em suma, A Viagem de Chihiro continua sendo uma jornada cinematográfica como poucas que desafia os limites da imaginação, mais uma vez coroando Miyazaki como um dos reis da arte da animação cinematográfica.

I remember the first time I watched this when I was little. I was hypnotized, the brilliance of the movie immediately drew me in. I remember wanting to be Chihiro for a few days. I remember wanting to never come back, to stay with Haku, maybe work in a bathhouse and serve the spirits. I showed it to every friend who came to my house. I watched it over and over again, and I dont think there could have been a better choice to end the year. Miyazakis films dont have the kind of sharp lines we often see in Western animations. Just because a character is bad doesnt mean he will never do good just like in real life, there is bad in good and good in bad. In other words, it is from life. I think this is what makes his films ageless. I felt the same way when I watched them as a child.
The reason why Miyazaki is so legendary and loved by everyone is his unique style as well as his presentation of Japanese culture and lifestyle to us with all its naivety. While art is generally human-centered in Hollywood movies, Japanese movies is universe and nature-centered. In one, person is glorified, in the other, nature is glorified and person is seen as merely a part of nature. Thats why Miyazaki gives more importance to the life and spirit of the scene he depicts than to the physical form that can be seen with the eye. Because, according to him, even the most insignificant thing has a life and spirit as long as it is a part of the universe.
Hayao Miyazaki, like all his films, made this film to entertain while also writing a story that conveys his deep concerns about human issues. For this reason, the Spirited Away film is seen one step ahead of his other films because in this production, he skillfully uses the Japanese kanji seen in the background like a magician to find and create new meanings. He criticizes every situation that humanity is in through a ten-year-old petulant girl and defends the superiority of his own utopia. By creating a universe where people take the place of spirits and spirits take the place of people, he has ensured that the audience is in an empathic state. In these contexts, Spirited Away is a gentle story of the escape of Spirits from humans.
The film begins in a way that suits the beginning of many Miyazaki films, namely with a journey. Chihiro and her family are moving to a new city. However, it is not that easy for Chihiro to break away from her ties and migrate to a brand new world. She tries to keep her past alive with a small farewell card and a bouquet of flowers that she carries with her throughout the journey. Chihiro and her family take a wrong turn on the way to their new life and find themselves in front of a long tunnel. And this tunnel is the beginning of a chain of events that changes both Chihiros and my life. This movie is very personal to me. Because I feel like I really experienced the adventures Chihiro went through. I really felt them. I dont know, it touched me that a movie that affected me when I was 10 had the same effect on me when I was 20.
No matter what happens to Chihiro, she is so kind-hearted that she helps everyone she sees and is rewarded for her good deeds. She even helps No Face, who has been the character Ive been most interested in since I was little. Although he seems relatively weird and scarier than the others, I think hes one of the most important characters in the movie. The mysterious No Face character, from whom we do not know where he comes from and where he wants to go, is one of the deepest lines of the film. No Face, whose lack of belonging, loneliness, and lack of communication are combined with the image of a ghost, has a different feeling compared to all the characters. This spirit, which wanders around as a calm, silent, faint ghost, cannot even communicate with its surroundings without swallowing someone and possessing their voice and speaking. We get the chance to observe a great character evolution in his scenes, just like Chihiros, as he transforms from such a profile into a ball of ego trying to buy happiness and love with money. Chihiro heals and improves not only herself but also those around her. She is not just a 10-year-old girl, she has a bigger heart.
And one of my first crushes is Haku (one of my 2025 goals find your own Haku) Jokes aside, Haku is very strong and he is also a mysterious character. The film does not highlight the possible love theme - despite all its availability - in order to easily attract attention. Every character is treated equally, as is the relationship between Haku and Chihiro. Long before Haku and Chihiro met at Yubabas bathhouse, the moments when Chihiro met Chihiro as a child at the river she fell into, do not turn into a great love story from the scene where they realize this situation later in the movie, and remain as an innocent memory. This meeting helps Haku to escape the world he is trapped in by remembering his real name and identity, and it completes Chihiros mission to return to her old life with her family, lighting the way home for everyone.
In this tale where every soul is purified and a happy ending is somehow achieved, what is important is not the ending but the experiences and feelings that come while reaching the end. I was very happy to take a break from studying for exams on the last day of the year and enter the new year with Chihiro. If you havent watched this yet, I think this should be your first goal this year. Happy New Year to everyone

This film barely missed out on my Top 30 of all-time, but theres a definite possibility it could slip its way in there at some point. While it isnt my personal favorite animated film of all-time, I think Im ready to say that I believe its the best. Spirited Away combines fantastical elements, gorgeous animation, fleshed out characters, cute and quirky creatures, and absolutely terrifying moments to create an experience unlike any other. While I have seen most Studio Ghibli films, I need to see them all again before I can rate them (coming soon). They are mostly great, but Spirited Away is the one I have went back to revisit the most. A lot of it has to do with its themes, and how it has managed to age so well as a narrative. The basic premise revolves around Chihiro. Chihiro is the perfect way to introduce us to this world she is just as terrifiedunaware as we are.
During her familys move to the suburbs, a sullen 10-year-old girl wanders into a world ruled by gods, witches, and spirits, and where humans are changed into beasts. Characters like Yubaba and Zeniba encapsulate fear, yet manage to give us some of the more tender moments in the film. Haku swoops in like a superhero, and the mystery of his presence adds an extra level of depth to the overall story (loved that resolution). Kamaji is this horrifying being, but you embrace the fact that he makes decisions out of love (and he is really good at his job). The journey hits every level of emotion as you follow our title character. I wasnt fortunate enough to see this as a pre-teen, but I imagine kids going on this adventure for the first time having nightmares afterwords. The striking creature design, the pig scenes, the witches, and anything to do with No-Face probably would have scarred me for life.
Its scary enough as an adult, but it is also a movie full of hope. As the adventure progresses, we see even the least likely characters making decisions to help Chihiro. We see growth from almost all of them (good or bad). How did she get here? How long were they there? What is the true meaning of this place? Many of these questions are subtlety answered, but its a film that requires multiple watches to grasp. The story itself is simple, but the nuances may take a while to soak in. There isnt a scene out of place, or a moment that is too on the nose. The lack of exposition is astonishing. We obviously get a bit, but nowhere near the level of most other anime films. They show us with this story instead of telling us, and thats the sign of a concrete narrative. Its rock-solid from top to bottom, and the perfect visualsmusic cues are icing on the cake. The word to use here is haunting, but its done in the most beautiful way. Spirited Away is a masterpiece.

A viagem de Miyazaki
O Disney japonês mistura o real ao surreal no deslumbrante A Viagem de Chihiro

Cinco meninas de 10 anos, filhas de amigos seus, que costumam passar o verão em seu chalé nas montanhas foi delas, segundo o diretor japonês Hayao Miyazaki, que veio sua ideia para A Viagem de Chihiro (Spirited Away, Japão, 2002). Ao ler alguns quadrinhos que as garotas haviam deixado para trás, Miyazaki surpreendeu-se com as histórias  nada além de romances baratos. Em resposta à pobreza dessa dieta, o diretor decidiu criar um desenho em que a protagonista fosse uma menina comum, também na faixa dos 10 anos  a Chihiro do título , que se vê num lugar aparentemente hostil, e que vai descobrindo os pontos fortes de seu caráter à medida que enfrenta os obstáculos. É só até esse ponto, o da sinopse mais resumida, que A Viagem de Chihiro guarda alguma semelhança com as animações americanas a que o público está habituado. Miyazaki, de 62 anos, é chamado de o Disney japonês (um apelido que ele detesta).
Mas o que ele e o criador do Mickey têm em comum é apenas a excelência da animação e o enorme sucesso obtido com ela  Chihiro bateu o outro recordista de Miyazaki, Princesa Mononoke, e é hoje a maior bilheteria da história do Japão. Ao contrário dos desenhos da Disney, os de Miyazaki não têm nada de reconfortante, e as questões morais de que eles tratam são duras e complexas. Veja-se, por exemplo, o enredo de seu filme mais infantil, Meu Amigo Totoro duas irmãs mudam-se para o campo para ficar perto da mãe, que está à morte num hospital, e têm de lidar com todos os sentimentos de negação, fuga e descoberta que a situação implica. Que a plateia não espere dos filmes de Miyazaki alguma lição bem amarrada sobre o valor da amizade  a vida não é fácil, pensa o diretor, e seus personagens não devem imaginar que haja soluções simples para ela.
Não bastassem essas diferenças, só à base de alucinógenos um estúdio como a Disney (que distribui Chihiro internacionalmente) teria bolado algo como esse filme. Chihiro está de mudança para uma nova cidade, e não se sente feliz com a ideia. Quando seu pai erra o caminho e vai dar no que parece ser um parque temático abandonado, a menina se enche de medo. Os pais comem de um jantar servido num restaurante deserto, mas ela não quer nem saber de provar da comida. Com razão ao voltar de um passeio por ali, a garota descobre que seus pais se empanturraram até virar porcos. Chihiro tem então de ficar naquele lugar  na verdade, uma casa de banhos que atende deuses e divindades, gerenciada pela feiticeira Yubaba , arrumar trabalho e achar um meio de libertar seus pais. A animação de Miyazaki é invariavelmente deslumbrante, mas mistura o lírico e o horrível, o real e o surreal, de uma forma impensável na tradição ocidental.
As cenas em que Chihiro corre entre flores, ou navega no mar que se formou à volta da casa de banhos, são de uma beleza singular. Ao mesmo tempo, as criaturas que povoam o filme são no mínimo perturbadoras  como o homem cheio de braços que maneja as caldeiras, ou o Deus Fedido, que carrega em seu corpo todos os detritos de um rio poluído.
Miyazaki diz que tentou imaginar o que uma garota como as filhas de seus amigos sentiria se tivesse de ir trabalhar no Studio Ghibli, sua produtora, que ele fundou em meados dos anos 80. Para ele, o Ghibli é uma segunda casa. Para uma dessas meninas, ele poderia parecer um lugar estranho e labiríntico, repleto de pessoas mal-humoradas. Quem se une a uma organização tem de procurar forças ignoradas dentro de si para achar seu lugar e ser reconhecido. É isso que significa juntar-se à sociedade, diz Miyazaki. Com Chihiro, ele quis estimular suas jovens amigas a se pôr à altura do desafio. O resultado, porém, não tem limite de idade para ser apreciado.

Once youve met someone, you never really forget them. It just takes a while for your memories to return.
I was 10 years old in October 2002. My family had just moved a few states away from Georgia to Spring, Texas. In addition to dealing with trauma stemmed behavioral problems from a messy adoption that made us move to Georgia in the first place, I was having a hard time adjusting to our new environment. A new school, new house, new kids on the street who thought I was weird. One weekend, after spending the day getting sunburned at our new neighborhood pool, my brother and I asked our dad if we could rent a movie. Video on Demand was on the come up and really found its bearings in our game room. Without any trailer, any information other than it was an Oscar nominee, my dad randomly rented Spirited Away from Hayao Miyazaki.  
I had no idea that Spirited Away would be one of the biggest films in Japanese history or the only hand drawn anime film to win an Academy Award. All I knew was that I had never seen anything like it before. Chihiros journey was spiritually familiar. Its a confusing descent into the unknown, a psychedelic exploration of identity, fear, and growing up before you feel ready to. Hayao Miyazaki is famous for his obsession with detail and is known as a powerhouse writer, director and animator. Without his personal attention into the world building, I dont know if I would have ever had the switch flip for me. The next year, I found another foothold into the world of Japanese animation when Chrono Crusade was released in the U.S. The following year, my brother and I started reading XxXholic from our local library, and the year after that, Naruto was officially airing on Toonami and Cartoon Network. Thats what really blew the floodgates open for me and Ive been obsessed with anime, manga, and Japanese horror ever since!  
Imagine Alice in Wonderland but with Japanese themed mythology. I love showing Spirited Away to people for the first time and seeing which characters theyre drawn to, because this world is brimming with imaginative yokai. But this movie isnt just about spirits and creatures. Its a fairy tale about confronting human evils, just without a clear-cut villain like youd get in a traditional Disney movie. Through the different characters Chihiro encounters like Yubaba, No-Face, and Aogaeru, shes really facing things like greed, exploitation, and manipulation. What I love is that none of its spelled out for you like a childrens book trying to teach you a lesson. Hayao Miyazaki trusts the viewer enough to sit with it, to interpret it, to connect the dots on their own. But at the same time, he leaves just enough of a blueprint there that youre never lost, youre just discovering it at your own pace. 
Theres a saying thats been floating around on the internet for about a decade Disney movies touch the heart, Studio Ghibli touches the soul. Even though Hayao Miyazaki famously denies it, he argues that when you give something enough heart, it gains a soul. Spirited Away touched mine at a time when I needed it and gave me a bridge to a new world at the same time. Every re-watch feels like slipping into a familiarly strange, terrifying, and beautiful dream. This isnt just a comfort movie, its a world that youll keep wanting to return to again and again. Absolute masterpiece.

Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli once again apprehend the curiosity of unmitigated imagination and remarkable magnificence with the spellbinding Spirited Away. The characters, set designs and the world that is created are rendered with some extraordinary animation and theres a beautiful musical score to assist the richly creative layering indicated in the complicated framework which is apparent even in the tiniest of moments, and its feasible to discover something new with every rewatch.
The film promotes a fantastical and mythical storyline with one unusual and extraordinary incident after another, remarking on topics such as labour relations and environmental conservation along the way before unravelling to an imaginative conclusion. Spirited Away is an extraordinary film and a complete pleasure to watch, with many thoughtful considerations implemented into the overall storytelling with a remarkable realm of creatures and is steeped in Japanese mythology and Shinto beliefs.

Its incredible to me that after just a couple years of becoming more acquainted with the genre of anime, I still find myself fascinated the most with Spirited Away, arguably one of the greatest examples of Hayao Miyazakis creative ingenuity. Its fantastical world, fraught with danger and intrigue for our young heroine Chihiro, is never short of extraordinary characters, always managing to outdo the last mystical creature we are shown with another more deviously bizarre creation.
Chihiro is by far the best developed character in any given Miyazaki work. Her personal journey from her terrifying beginning to her daunting finale can be felt in its progress each step of the way, with the storys own memorable hallmarks making clear their impact on how it shapes her into a different person. Shes not just another ordinary child whisked away into a majestic spiritual world with all the help in the world- you can feel her epic struggle as she tries to find her way back home amidst overwhelming adversity. Theres a kind of intricacy found in most of Miyazakis works that is, more often than not, missing from mainstream American animation- from the astounding hand-drawn frames that seep with his heartfelt artistry, to the palpable character weaving and progressions that make us feel as though we could actually be watching real people in real scenarios, amidst the magical moments rooted in mysticism.
I was surprised when I began to realize that there are many structural parallels that can be drawn between Spirited Away and Howls Moving Castle- one of the most divisive entries in Miyazakis filmography. Both, of course, deal with a central theme of love and how it is used to overcome a seemingly impossible obstacle. But more so, the two films have some similarly crafted characters that make me wonder if Miyazaki was drawing some hasty inspiration from here to complete his next film. We have a young character who is suddenly tossed into an adventure accompanied with an animal and a small magical creature. Two villain-type characters who resemble witches and experience a transformation (to them or to the one closest to them) in some way or another. Perhaps drawing comparisons is vapid, and realizing similarities doesnt really make me dislike Howl any less but the correlations still leave questions in my mind.
Spirited Away is a stroke of genius- often considered to be one of the greatest animated films ever made. Its cavalcade of masterfully designed characters, brought to life in a fully realized world of fantasy and gorgeous artistic talent, make this the apex of Miyazakis unadulterated craftsmanship. He builds up a protagonist whose progression can be felt and appreciated with each crescendo of successive energy, in arguably one of the best realized protagonists in animated history. Spirited Away is a film to be marveled for its technical and artistic merit, and revered for its characteristic brilliance.

Spirited Away is a descent into the symbolic unconscious and a confrontation with the repressed traumas of dislocation, individuation, and capitalist oppression. Beneath its folkloric surface is a dialectic between selfhood and the systems that seek to reshape it. The spirit world Chihiro enters can be seen as a microcosmic capitalist society ruled by a bourgeois elite that commodifies labor, bodies, and identity. It is a liminal space allegorical of the real world, where value is determined by transaction, and the sacred is rendered profitable.
Chihiros journey begins with the stripping of her name through contractual bondage. In Lacanian terms, she loses her position in the symbolic order, and her subjectivity is overwritten by her use-value. Chihiro (千尋) becomes Sen (千), meaning a thousand, reducing her to a number, a unit of labor, stripped of her identity. In Marxist terms, this is proletarian alienation. The more a worker forgets their real name (i.e., their roots, history, self), the easier they are to control. To survive, Chihiro must become legible to capital by contributing to the bathhouse economy, which is a place teeming with spirits yet governed by extractive logic.
The bathhouse itself is a theater of commodified ritual, where even the sacred must pay to be purified. Spirits line up not for renewal, but as clients in a luxury service economy. Labor in the bathhouse is unceasing, joyless, and devoid of meaning. The soot sprites toil without end, reduced to mechanical function, embodying the dehumanized workforce. The head of this system is Yubaba, the grotesque capitalist matriarch, whose maternal facade masks a regime of surveillance, exploitation, and control. In Freudian terms, she mirrors the superego of capital, which is the internalized voice of discipline and debt. From a Jungian lens, she embodies the dark side of the maternal archetypeone that consumes rather than nurtures, keeping the child dependent. Yubabas twin, Zeniba, offers a counterpoint. She is a maternal figure who trusts, empowers, and gives without domination. Positioned between these two figures, Chihiros journey becomes a symbolic navigation of the tension between dependence and independence. Her reclamation of her name signifies resistance to systemic erasure and a rejection of commodified identity. The bathhouse, then, is more than just a workplace. Its a crucible of economic and psychic subjugation, where the machinery of capitalism feeds on spirit, and the devouring mother disguises institutional authority as care.
This dehumanizing logic reaches its most grotesque form in the transformation of Chihiros parents into pigs. It is the films most explicit political allegory and a literalization of capitalist gluttony. Their fate demonstrates how unlimited consumption (or chasing endless desires) results in self-destruction and the erosion of identity. By indulging in food not meant for them, they become what they consume. The pig symbolizes both a moral and an ontological state driven by greed, and as long as Chihiro forgets who they were, they remain trapped. This symbolizes how memory and recognition are essential to resisting capitalist enchantment.
No-Face, meanwhile, is both a victim and a product of the system. When immersed in the bathhouse economy, he consumes food, gold, and attention, growing grotesque with each indulgence. He is commodity fetishism made flesh, hungry not for validation through consumption. He mirrors the logic of unchecked capital, offering wealth, status, and admiration only to consume others in return. In Jungian terms, No-Face is the shadow the disowned part of the self that becomes monstrous when denied integration. His grotesqueness is not innate but inherited from the system. Only when removed from the bathhouse (away from capital) can he return to a state of quiet receptivity. Both Chihiro and No-Face undergo a sort of reintegration, but where Chihiro retains her selfhood within the system, No-Face must be taken out of it to rediscover his capacity for genuine connection. Their contrasting paths reveal two responses to commodification and affirm that healing begins by learning how to relate without the need for transaction.
Boh, the massive baby, represents Chihiros infantilized self, swaddled in privilege, fear, and immaturity. Like Chihiro at the start, Boh is overly protected by a system that prevents him from growing. His world reflects Chihiros psychic prison, a place of comfort and isolation where meaningful development doesnt happen. Similar to the capitalist elite, Boh is untouched by labor, feels entitled to endless comfort, and fears anything that disrupts his bubblebe it germs, contamination, or the outside world. Bohs growth through Chihiros influence represents the potential for change even in the most sheltered parts of the self. His maturity offers hope that protected aspects of ones psyche can unlearn fear and develop empathy. Bohs growth is another part of Chihiros journey, showing that the self, when faced with transformation, can evolve from immaturity to understanding.
Haku, once a river spirit, is a ghost of ecological loss and capitalist destruction. His broken memory reflects Chihiros own erasure. In this sense, Haku represents an unconscious part of Chihiros psyche that she must reintegrate to fully understand herself. Their reunion is a shared act of recovery a Freudian return of the repressed, a Jungian integration of the lost self, and a Marxist re-rooting of value beyond utility. It is a restoration of memory and identity repressed by commodification.
When Chihiro finally leaves the bathhouse, she carries no gold or status, but only her name. She has not overthrown the system, nor escaped its reach. But in remembering her name and all it signifies, she reclaims something the system cannot fully consume. Unlike in the similarly dreamlike The Boy and the Heron, where there is a grand resistance to imperialism and capitalism, Spirited Away offers a call to remember. Through Chihiros labor and her refusal to forget those she loves, the film suggests that even in worlds that commodify us, we can retain our essence. Our identities may be rewritten, but the journey of remembering is the journey of becoming. Identity is forged in memory, in the courage to care, and in the quiet defiance of staying true to ourselves. Though our paths may be shaped by forgetting, we must never cease to remember who we are and who we were.

A imaginative yet subtle animated epic masterpiece.
I took time to revisit Spirited Away since it was playing at the movies as part of The 2017 Studio Ghibli Fest. This was my first Hayao Miyazaki film which I saw for the first time couple years ago, and this year I finally went and watched most of his other popular classics with my kids.
Spirited Away is a little slower paced than I remember it being, likely because this hyper creative new world that is introduced seems more familiar upon repeated viewings.
But seeing this on the big screen gave the unique opportunity to notice some of the smaller nuances. For example in the final shot of the film when we see Chihiros profile for the last time, you can clearly see the purple hair tie that was made for her in the spirit world, and this hints that this whole thing was not just a dream. In the famous quiet moments on the train Miyazaki brilliant shows Chihiro reflection in the window behind her, hinting that not only is she finally being given a moment to rest, but she may also be reflecting on this wild journey and her own personal growth.
Finally the gorgeous animation on the big screen seemed flushed out even more in small details like the amazingly colorful flowering bushes that fill the screen in a couple of scenes.
If I had to have a complaint about the film it would be Haku. I think he fades from the story to allow Chihiro to shine on her own and let us get to know the other supporting characters, but I wish he was more present during the middle of the film. But him stealing the token from the sister witch is the essential plot device that propels the film to its climax and actually gives Chihiro a reason to leave the Bath house.
There are so many great themes in Spirited Away that make it a wonderful film for kids. It is obvious to see over indulgence when the parents eat themselves into becoming pigs. We also have the scene where No Face turns into a crazy monster eating everything in site before spewing it all over the place.
The theme of a coming of age story gives Chihiro and almost perfect character arc. At first she is timid, clumsy, and whiny ... and by the end she is confident, determined, and hard working. I hope kids can get inspired by this as they watch the film.
There a lot of things that dont make much sense like the giant baby, the three green heads, the stink spirit actually being a dragon. But these are simple small elements that make this dream like world seem more real. And the long run time perfectly immerses in this experience. 
But one thing still has be thinking... why does Chihiro starts calling the mean witch Granny just like what the nice witch said to call her at the end of the film?? 
I love how the beautiful score is highlighted in so many places with out sounding repetitive, and the main themes featuring the piano are so effective when they come back around and give me those awesome movie chills.
This is an excellent film for the whole family to see. It is weird and intense at points, but thats what makes it so well rounded and timeless!

so unfair how a film is so objectively amazing. I mean you cannot even argue that this film is bad in any sort of way, Spirited Away is a visual-spectacle of animationfantasy...and youd be lying if you said this was anything below a 4 and giving it a 4 feels like a terrible atrocity. 
before I explain my rating, ill explain the importance and symbolism of the film--through my interpretation. Spirited Away is a fantastical creation delving into the themes of self-discovery, the ugliness of society, and the struggle to fit in. from the start, Chihiro isnt adamant on moving to a new house, city, andor location...her fears seem to materialize into reality as she steps into the spirit haven that is Spirit Realms bathhouse shes surrounded and austracized by bizarre groups of spirits or creatures --showing Chihiros viewpoint of feeling alienated in a new environment--hence the struggle to blend inconform to the spirits rules, and work.
as the film progresses with its constant vibrancy and stunning art-work, Chihiro lives amongst a greedy and materialistic crowd of sometimes ugly entities. No Face is the only spirit that seems to stand out from the conformity, much like her No Face mirrors and seemingly exaggerates his surrounding - transforming into a gluttonous monster - much like the gold-hungry, slave-workers, of the bathhouse. this bathhouse community is strongly representative of society, and its transition towards a hoggish-like culture. 
finally, as the film reaches its conclusions, Chihiro is seen to discover herself. she is no longer the person she was at the start - a fearsome little girl, burying herself in her knees - she becomes a young-woman, taking on responsibilities and tackling foul predicaments. through her many acts of bravery she finds her inner-strength, which she didnt know she posessed. all of these points come together wonderfully as she remembers her identity symbolizing her adaptation to the spirit world (or the ravenous society that she returns to) as she stays connected to who she truly is, becoming in-tune with her values and personal convictions. 
Chihiros journey in Spirited Away teaches viewers that personal growth comes from facing challenges, stepping out of comfort zones, and staying true to oneself. Her transformation shows that resilience, compassion, and courage are key to discovering ones potential and navigating lifes uncertainties. 
I found the film very visually captivating. but it cant solely carry the film - animation is a very impressive feat to master and direct so I can grandly applaud Hayao Miyazaki for his artistry. I found the ending to be a little too-surface leveled, the remaining 40-30 minutes wasnt what I was expecting it to be and I found myself craving something more. maybe it was the massive amounts of craftsmanship that fed into this hunger, along with the enthralling world-building...but I felt like I missed out on something, and it made the ending slightly disenchanting. 
that being said though, this film is ABSOLUTELY AMAZING. its everything I expected, AND MORE?! I mean I was honestly just expecting a cute-little ghost story from the art Ive seen of this film prior...but not a whole journey into a representative realm? a super awesome concept that was excellently executed through its animation design.

so i understand that feeling a little better now. chihiro is so small, and yet from the moment her parents turn into pigs, everything is on her. she has to find a job, learn the rules, figure out who to trust, keep herself alive, and get her parents back too. she just has to do it (
her parents make me especially sad now. theyre careless with her fear from the very beginning, and then, once they become pigs, she has to carry the consequences of their stupidity all by herself. chihiro has to go through this whole journey to get them back, only for them to.. never even remember any of it..? gosh, my poor girl!! they get their daughter back, never knowing what she went through for them, how much was put on her, how much she had to handle all A.L.O.N.E!
and then, of course, my first ever fictional crush haku. 
will we meet again sometime?
sure we will.
promise?

25 years jubilee open air screening on the cinema rooftop. 
Original language with subtitles. 
Never get bored watching Spirited Away all over again and I think it is also the third time I watched it on a cinema screen. 
I would even call it my favorite modern fairytale. 
This film has this perfect structure. 
Chihiro finds with her parents the entrance to this secret place, experiences a most fantastic adventure that is so afar from all that classic fantasy concepts, and her journey ends where everything begun. 
Just happier, lighter and grown like a whole lifetime. 
I love all this many fantasy creatures. 
Overblown in creativity. 
The bathhouse is busy with the sweetest and oddest characters. 
I also love Yubaba. She is so oddly funny. 
She is also not that complete bad witchy character. She does a lot of good things for the community. 
Her twin sister Zeniba is of course the much sweeter version. 
That scene at her home is always so cute and cozy. 
Chihiro is just a wonderful character. 
It is a bit an Alice in Wonderland adventure but her character has much more varieties. 
I always have to giggle about the hamster and the fly. Such a cool team!
The dust bunnies (Susuwatari) are also favorites, they already appeared in Totoro. 
Kamajis heating cellar is always a pleasant place. 
The No-Face (Kaonashi) is one of the most unique fantasy creations. 
A character that is even difficult to explain, he just is what he is. But most, he is just lonely.  Sympathy without greed and company makes him a pleasant comrade. 
That special bathing guest is always a highlight. With that plop at last, I always have to imagine where all this stuff came from. 
And of course the story between Chihiro and Haku. What a beautiful dragon!
I have to think a bit of Fuchur. 
I love everything about this movie. 
I realized there is a scrolling technique I think I have seen only in this film. When they run through the flowers, the middle is scrolling with a radiate depth-effect. 
When the train runs through the water, there is also a very special water scrolling effect. 
The animation is still on the highest level for 2D animation. 
A perfect movie, extremely fantastic, humane, humorous, gripping, tensing, divine. 
Best ever composer Joe Hisaishi, he is a melodic magician. So soft and sweet. 
I always forgot about that song at the credits that comes so different to the movie. 
When Youmi Kimura is singing so happy - lalalala lalala and huhuhuhu huhuhu it always makes me smile. 
Of course a 5 star all time favorite. 
It feels strange that I still keep it at 5 in my Miyazaki ranking but they are all so close together. 
Each film has something for its own. 
Now I hope they will also bring Nausicaä back to the cinema. My biggest wish to see this film on a big screen!

One of the most beautiful films ever made.. I remember my sister and I watching Spirited Away for the first time as kids, and we were absolutely terrified by it. The idea of moving to a new foreign place, parents being turned into pigs, a faceless monster devouring people, and having to rely entirely on yourself for the first time. 
But it makes sense that it would scare us as kids, because in many ways Spirited Away is a story of a child learning to face their fears. Traveling far away from home, getting a taste of life outside of their parents guidance, confronting things they dont fully understand, and ultimately gaining a sense of Independence from it. 
I love that about Miyazakis films, that they are stories that both adults and children can connect with and gain something from, regardless of age.

La mayor obra del maestro Miyazaki y del Studio Ghibli( junto con  tumba de las luciérnagas).
El viaje de Chihiro es una película mágica. De principio a fin.
Su lista de logros es interminable nombrada la cuarta mejor película de lo que llevamos de siglo por la BBC, en el top 50 de múltiples portales de todo lo que se ha rodado en la historia, ganadora del Óscar a la mejor película de animación, entre múltiples premios. La respuesta a todas esas preguntas es la misma la ambición. Es la naturaleza de nuestros deseos lo que nos dice quiénes somos. El viaje de Chihiro trata de la identidad, por supuesto, pero Miyazaki usa la narración para colocar a la ambición como elemento que más esculpe nuestra identidad.

¿Qué es la ambición?
Los personajes de una historia son uno de sus elementos más importantes.
Y dichos personajes nunca serán lo bastante interesantes ni complejos si no desean con todo su corazón, si no quieren algo y luchan por conseguirlo, ya sea para sí mismos o para los demás.
Frodo quiere destruir el anillo.
Luke Skywalker quiere derrotar al lado oscuro.
Silvestre quiere comerse a Piolín.
Bueno, creo que me entiendes ya.
El caso es que una historia no funcionará si no nos cuenta del modo correcto acerca de la ambición de sus personajes. Y El viaje de Chihiro no solo hace eso. No habla únicamente de la ambición concreta de sus actores. Sino que habla al mismo.
La ambición es lo que se quiere, lo que se busca, el deseo que quiere realizarse. Es algo que orienta tus acciones y tu motivación.
Tipos de ambición
Sin embargo, no todos los tipos de ambición son iguales.
No es lo mismo desear la paz mundial que querer alimentarte únicamente a base de postres y no engordar.
Podemos clasificar los distintos tipos de deseos que puede tener el ser humano. Y una de estas categorizaciones nos la da Robert Fisher en El Caballero de la armadura oxidada

La ambición que procede de la mente te puede servir para conseguir bonitos castillos y buenos caballos. Sin embargo, solo la ambición que proviene del corazón puede darte, además, la felicidad.
En este fantástico libro, que no debería existir ser humano que no lo haya leído, se nos dan dos tipos de ambición
Ambición de la mente. Es la que nos mueve a conseguir mejorar nuestro estilo de vida, nuestro poder, nuestro orgullo.
Ambición del corazón. Es cuando deseamos aquello que busca el bien propio o el de los demás.
Y ahora, sabiendo de estos dos tipos, podemos hablar sobre la ambición de los personajes de la obra de Hayao Miyazaki.
Chihiro ambiciosa como pocas
Estoy seguro de que nadie definiría a Chihiro como ambiciosa. Y es que siempre pensamos en ambición como el deseo chungo de acumular riqueza o poder, la ambición de la mente.
Pero ahora que sabes lo que es la ambición del corazón, quizá quieras replanteártelo.
Chihiro es una niña caprichosa que, desde el principio, nos muestra una faceta egocéntrica y asustadiza. No para de quejarse en el coche por la mudanza, en el parque temático pide una y otra vez que vuelvan, se enfada y no quiere comer nada Incluso cuando sus padres se han transformado en cerdos, su primer impulso es huir de allí dejando todo (y a todos) atrás.
Pero entonces se encuentra con que el riachuelo se ha transformado en un mar y no puede volver. Y es ahí, tras una oportuna intervención de Haku, cuando Chihiro toma la determinación de ayudar a sus padres a toda costa.
En ese momento, Chihiro sale de su egocentrismo infantil (Piaget estaría orgulloso) y empieza a preocuparse por las necesidades de los demás. Antes incluso que por las suyas.
Y con esto, sin pretenderlo, cambia el mundo que la rodea para siempre.
O mejor dicho cambia a quienes la rodean.
Kamaji y Lin
Antes de conocer a Chihiro
Kamaji y Lin son dos prisioneros. Él lo menciona al presentarse como esclavo de las calderas, y ella lo dice textualmente cuando confiesa que lo único que quiere es escapar de allí.
Ambos son una representación de los trabajadores de la Casa de Baños individuos que no recuerdan sus nombres y que, por lo tanto, no pueden escapar de Yubaba. Sin embargo, trabajan duro para ser libres algún día.
¡Pero del modo equivocado!
En un primer momento, tanto Kamaji como Lin se muestran distantes y tensos con Chihiro. Y podemos suponer que ese es su comportamiento habitual con el resto de miembros de la casa de baños. Incluso entre ellos no se ayudan a menos que consigan algo a cambio (recordemos que Lin le dice a Kamaji que se acueste cuando este le pide que lleve a la niña ante Yubaba).
Después de conocer a Chihiro
Kamaji, que al principio no quiere saber nada de nadie, termina mintiendo por Chihiro (diciendo que es su nieta) y dándole a Lin un tritón asado, algo muy valioso en ese mundo para que la ayude.
Esta nueva dimensión más altruista de Kamaji se sigue desarrollando hasta completar acciones más puras como cuidar de Haku durante su convalecencia o regalar a Chihiro los míticos tickets del tren.
Con Lin pasa algo semejante. De borde y condescendiente pasa a amable y protectora. Lin cuida de Chihiro, es comprensiva cuando se pone mala, le da comida, la lleva navegando hasta la estación en ese mortero gigante
Dos ejemplos similares de personas individualistas que, poco a poco, van saliendo de sí mismos y pensando más en otros. Y ambos, a raíz de conocer a Chihiro.
Sin cara  Kaonashi la tentación de Chihiro
El Kaonashi es el personaje más enigmático de la película.
Aparece al principio siempre alrededor de Chihiro. La ayuda a conseguir una tarjeta, y parece que busca su compañía (¿es otra alma errante buscando la manera de recuperar su identidad?). Y para conseguir su atención, le intenta dar decenas de tarjetas más.
Pero ella las rechaza.
¿Por qué?
Porque solo necesita una.
Esto es importante.
El Sin Cara es una representación, una metáfora en sí mismo, de la ambición humana. Engorda y crece más cuanto más tiene, cuanta más atención recibe, cuando consigue que las personas con las que se cruza se dejen llevar por su ambición de la mente.
Por eso soborna a Chihiro en distintas ocasiones, porque ella es la ambición del corazón.
La primera vez es con las tarjetas de baño. Y ella solo acepta la que necesita (que no es ni siquiera para ella).
Después de que Chihiro salve al dios del río, los empleados se abalanzan sobre el oro que deja en el suelo. En ese momento, el Sin Cara aparece en una esquina, observando, y se mira la mano, como en un primer intento de crear eso que la gente tanto ansía.
Y aunque Sen es la única que no le pide nada, es a ella a quien le ofrece una montaña de oro de agarrarse los machos.
Y ella lo rechaza otra vez.
¿Por qué?
De nuevo porque no lo necesita. Solo quiere salvar a Haku
La escena clave es cuando Yubaba obliga a Chihiro a ir a ver al Sin Cara para sacarle dinero. Y él se lo ofrece. Más aún, le pregunta que qué es lo que más desea, pero ella responde que no puede ayudarla con lo que quiere.
Y ojo en este momento.
Porque ella, en un acto de infinito altruismo, le ofrece el pastel que tenía guardado para sus padres y que pensaba que podía salvarles. Y se lo da a él, que no es bueno, ni es su amigo. Pero Chihiro descubre que lo necesita, así que se lo da. Ambición del corazón en su máximo exponente.
Y ¿qué ocurre en ese preciso instante? Que el Sin Cara, que engorda con lo material (comida, dinero) y se alimenta de la ambición personal de otros, empieza a desinflarse. Y de una forma un tanto asquerosa, por cierto.
Después de vomitar a la gente y de sacar de su interior la suciedad que había acumulado sigue a Chihiro y se vuelve bueno de nuevo.

I have a long history with this film throughout my entire life which is pretty crazy considering I watched it fully for the first time this week.

My idiotic mind thought he was talking about that animated horse movie called Spirit so I was pumped to watch horses prancing in the fields. 
The movie starts and I dont notice anything wrong. I dont remember humans entering an empty village but maybe the horses are in a stable there or something. They approach a table with food and instead of turning into horses, the parents turned into pigs. I was terrified. This wasnt horses galloping, this was a nightmare. I jumped off the couch and had my uncle change the movie. Unfortunately for me, that brief encounter was enough. 
For years after that I would have nightmares of my parents turning into pigs. The visual of the father pig turning his head sideways and letting out a screech is imprinted in my dreams for years. I forgot all about the movie, I only remembered the scene. That soon changed. 
I am about 15 years old at this point and I was hanging out with an old girlfriend. She said she wanted to watch her favorite film of all time Spirited Away. I didnt recognize the name anymore since its been eight years but we throw the film on and I instantly got a weird feeling. It wasnt until I saw the family approach the table of food when I realized it was the film from my nightmare. I jump off the couch and told the girl to turn it off. 
The next three years I stopped having the nightmare. I was completely past that experience and started to fall in love with the reality show Survivor. I was a huge fan of the show when I was 18 and even bought some of the buffs. For those that dont know, the Survivor buffs are pieces of cloths that have the shows logo and can be worn in different ways. 
Anyways, I was seeing a new girl at the age of 18 and wouldnt you know it, her favorite film was Spirited Away as well. I knew the film this time so I was ready to face my demons. Every character is doing their own thing, on their own agenda, and they couldnt care less what the main character does because unlike most movies the world doesnt revolve around her here.
This is going to be quite the stretch, but its for this exact reason why I love FromSoft games like Dark Souls and Bloodborne. You just get lost in this wonderful, weird world, and even though youre the main character youre just a tiny part of this vast machine that marches on regardless of what you do. Spirited Away is one of the odd few movies that taps into that same feeling.

Miyazaki does so much in so little time to show us that while Chihiro is a lovable young kid, shes also immature, naive, and a bit spoiled. She complains in the back of the car, shes instantaneously overwhelmed by the new, strange world, and she cries several times when she feels hope is lost. While we need to feel emotionally invested in Chihiros journey, we also need to see her evolve from a lost, dependent child to a decisive, confident girl.
And then theres the beauty of Miyazakis world

-the dilapidated amusement park with bright but faded colors, games with no one to play them.
-a parade of creatures visiting the bath house, their bright colors and kooky sounds juxtaposed with No-Faces black and white mask and soft uuuuhhhs.
-Chihiros precisely pre-adolescent body movements her lanky knob-kneed legs flipping over when she face plants the GAAAAHHH!! face she makes when something scary comes out of nowhere, her eyes huge, her hair spiking out, and her teeth maniacally gritted.
-Kamaji the many-armed boiler man and his chirpy dust mites (?) carrying coal on their heads to throw into the fire. (Miyazakis animation personification is amazing)
-The gargantuan polluted river spirit that Chihiro must bathe, looking like Jabba the Hut if he hoarded too many internal organs and fell into a tar pit. 
-The stunning animation work of Hakus beautiful-to-begin-with dragon becoming even more beautiful with each new physical transformation.
-The. Score. 

Ive never seen an animated film that was a 1010 in both aesthetics and story. In the first half of the film, Miyazaki consistently emphasizes Chihiros vulnerability by placing her in a frame with huge creatures, or showing a wide shot of the new strange land. As Chihiro gains strength and confidence, she literally drains some creatures of their size, and her passivity turns to action, by land and by air.
Every time I see Spirited Away, I notice something new. So exciting to hear that Miyazaki has a new film coming out!

somehow every rewatch makes me feel like im discovering it for the first time. there is something about spirited away that feels almost impossible to explain. its technically a childrens movie, but every time i come back to it i find something in it that feels a little more grown-up than i remembered. maybe thats why it means so much to me. i think i keep growing up alongside chihiro. cause when i first watched this i mostly saw the magic of it. the spirits, the bathhouse, the train floating through the water, no-face, haku, all these strange little creatures and places that felt like they came straight out of a dream. and i still see all of that, obviously, because this movie is just ridiculously beautiful, but now i think about how much of the story is really about growing up and trying not to lose yourself while youre doing it.
chihiro starts the movie as this scared little girl who doesnt want anything to change. she doesnt want to move, she doesnt want to leave what she knows, and then suddenly shes forced into a completely unfamiliar world where she has no idea what shes supposed to do. and she has to figure it out anyway. i love that she doesnt suddenly become fearless either, shes still just a scared kid, she just learns that being scared doesnt mean she cant keep going. and the whole thing with her name makes me so emotional ) yubaba taking her name and turning her into sen has always felt so much bigger to me than just part of the fantasy. its like the world is slowly trying to tell her who she is, and she has to remember her own name so she doesnt forget herself completely. haku has forgotten his name too, and thats why chihiro being the one who remembers him feels so important. and she doesnt save him by fighting some huge battle or something, she saves him by remembering who he is.. i think thats such a beautiful idea ୧      ෆ
maybe thats what this film is really about to me. remembering yourself.
because there are sooo many things in this world that can make you forget who you are. expectations, work, money, other peoples opinions, wanting to belong, wanting to be liked, wanting things you dont even really need. the bathhouse is full of people constantly working and consuming and wanting more and more, and no-face becomes this perfect example of it. everyone suddenly loves him when he starts giving them gold, but theyre not really interested in him. theyre interested in what he can give them. and he absorbs all of that until he doesnt even seem to know himself anymore. i actually find no-face kind of heartbreaking. hes so lonely. and because he doesnt really know who he is, he becomes whatever the people around him are. when hes surrounded by greed, he becomes greedy. when hes around chihiro, who doesnt want anything from him, he becomes quiet again. she gives him kindness without asking for anything back, and somehow that means more than all the gold in the world 
and then theres haku, who is literally a river spirit that humans have forgotten because the river was destroyed. i love how casually the movie tells us something so sad. he isnt just some mysterious boy who happens to help chihiro, hes something that was forgotten and his entire identity is tied to a place that no longer exists. the polluted river spirit makes that even more obvious. everyone looks at it and sees something disgusting, but chihiro looks closer and realizes that there is something beautiful underneath all that dirt and waste. it feels like miyazaki quietly asking us how often we mistake something damaged for something worthless.
i also cant stop thinking about chihiros parents becoming pigs. its almost funny because its so absurd, but its actually kind of terrifying when you think about it  they see all this food and immediately start eating because they assume they can have whatever they want. they dont even question where it came from or whether theyre allowed to take it. and suddenly theyre completely consumed by their own appetite. it feels like another warning about greed and excess, except its told through the strangest possible fairytale logic. and somehow despite everything around her, chihiro doesnt become like them. she doesnt take no-faces gold. she doesnt become obsessed with the bathhouse. she doesnt forget haku. she doesnt forget her own name. she keeps choosing people over things, and maybe thats what ultimately gets her home.
i think thats also why the ending makes me so emotional. chihiro has changed, but she doesnt get to stay in the spirit world forever. she has to leave and go back to the ordinary world even though shes experienced something that can never really be explained to anyone else. and i love that the movie doesnt give her some huge dramatic goodbye where everything is perfectly resolved, she just has to trust herself and keep walking . theres something so bittersweet about that. sometimes you enter a place, or meet someone, or experience something that changes you completely, and then you have to leave it behind. it doesnt mean it wasnt real. it doesnt mean it didnt matter. you just cant stay there forever..
maybe thats why i love this film more every time i watch it. it feels different depending on where i am in my own life. as when i was younger i wanted to live in the spirit world because it looked magical, but now i think i understand that the magic isnt really the point the point is that chihiro goes into this strange, frightening world and comes out knowing herself a little better. and maybe growing up is exactly that. not becoming someone completely different, but remembering who you are while everything around you keeps changing.
ill probably watch this another hundred times and still find something new to love.

It was less than three years ago that Todd Phillips mid-budget but mega-successful Joker threateningly pointed toward a future in which superhero movies of all sizes would become so endemic to modern cinema that they no longer had to be superhero movies at all. With Matt Reeves The Batman  a sprawling, 176-minute latex procedural that often appears to have more in common with serial killer sagas like Se7en and Zodiac than it does anything in the Snyderverse or the MCU  that future has arrived with shuddering force, for better or worse. Mostly better.
This isnt Captain America The Winter Soldier posturing as a 1970s conspiracy thriller or Logan half-committing to its Western heart, nor is it a simple throwback to Christopher Nolans Bush-era take on the Dark Knight, which grounded Bruce Wayne in a tactile Gotham while still broadly adhering to the storylines and spectacles expected of its genre. No, the better part of this Batman belongs to another genre altogether, as Reeves stubbornly eschews the usual razzmatazz in favor of a hard-boiled murder-mystery in which The Worlds Greatest Detective just happens to be a (very) tortured billionaire with an unexplained hard-on for bats.
Which isnt to suggest that people will confuse this mirthlessly dark Bat-noir for a Raymond Chandler adaptation, or even any of the David Fincher movies that lent The Batman its grim style or haunted air of fear  not with Colin Farrell playing Oswald Cobblepot under 50 pounds of Jake LaMotta cosplay, Paul Danos Riddler drawing foam question marks in his lattes, and a glowering Robert Pattinson karate-chopping street gangs while entombed inside a rubber Batsuit thicker than the tires of a monster truck. But its those brief (and very rare) dashes of action that best illustrate the films defiantly anti-blockbuster approach, as Reeves designs them with a much greater emphasis on close-up emotion than big screen excitement.
The combat is shot in silhouette, the sole Batmobile sequence is framed tighter than Locke, and the setpieces double down on Greig Frasers bonfire cinematography  his Stygian color palette extending Bruces personal hell across the whole of Gotham  to a degree that makes them seem like a scorched-earth rebuttal to the candied aesthetic of most other superhero movies (and a serious crisis for any corporate multiplex that doesnt regularly change its projector bulbs). Even this films relatively familiar, broadly Nolan-esque Batman tries to save the city climax is discomforting for the way it stages all the usual POWs! and BAMs! against a recognizable backdrop of real-world horror.
And there is plenty to be afraid of in this Gotham, as The Batman makes clear by opening with a Halloween-night home invasion that unfolds like a chapter from the Book of Saw (a fitting prelude to a film whose Riddler is equal parts Joker and Jigsaw). The mayor is murdered by a serial killer just days before his potential re-election, leaving behind the first of several mangled bodies and taunting clues.
What it doesnt leave behind is a power vacuum. If the mayors vacated office is certain to be awarded to the inspirational young Black woman who was challenging him for it (Jayme Lawson as the wonderfully named Bella Reál), that foregone conclusion allows Reeves to shift his attention towards the rats nest of festering white men who are ominously unconcerned with the outcome of the vote. Gotham has been controlled from inside Falcones nightclub for longer than Bella has been alive, and the rot has grown deep enough to keep things from changing.
That stagnation bleeds through the films retro-modern production design, as Koch-era taxi cabs and MS-DOS coexist alongside Trumpian identity politics and viral livestreams, all of them housed together in a Gotham that seamlessly blends parts of London, New York, and Chicago into a single mega-city buried under a mountain of violent grime (the films immaculate CGI is largely invisible and pointed towards world-building instead of than spectacle). The past is always coming back to haunt people in The Batman, though some are determined to prove that it never really went away.

Its funny, whenever a new Batman reboot is announced, I think to myself, do we really need another fucking version of Batman? And then Im there, opening night, having a total blast. WB knows how to do right with this character. Matt Reeves latest film earns its stripes pretty much right away. What an engrossing slow-burn. Gotham City is so well-realized and its quite immersive. This is about as close to the Arkham games as well probably see theatrically. A vision of perpetual rain and grime, head-to-toe corruption, sinister serial killers, big shot mob bosses, and damaged family legacies. Matt Reeves packs in two movies worth of material here, but it doesnt feel nearly as arduous as youd expect. This detective mystery is attempting the elusive thrills of Fincher and Pakula films, while still supplying the necessary superhero highlights. It mostly works, although I cant deny that I felt a little fatigued by the end. Robert Pattinson absolutely rules as Batman. The voice, costuming, everything. Hes perfect. It feels iconic and different, fresh and new. Even better is his vampiric Bruce Wayne. A portrait of a young man so committed to lurking in the shadows that whenever he emerges as Bruce in the daytime, he looks like an emo nosferatu stumbling out of an ancient coffin. 
The ensemble cast, from Zoë Kravitz to Paul Dano, Colin Farrell and John Turturro, is uniformly excellent, with the stand-out supporting role being Jeffrey Wright as Commissioner Gordon. Seeing him and Pattinson working together is so good. It helps that to tie everything together, the movie is as gorgeous as can be. DP Greig Fraser continues to be a major show-off, and basically every frame here is rich and detailed, shrouded in orange and red hues, lingering in inky shadows that are just the right level of under-lit. The Batman is a beautifully photographed movie, and a unique vision that (mostly) side-steps a few rough patches in its plotting.

over and over again throughout the years, ive heard batman fans and comic heads say yeah bro, some batman movies are good, but wheres the WORLDS GREATEST DETECTIVE? hes never the savvy detective, hes always using computers and shit, weve never gotten the gritty street-level batman film!, and given that the role of batman has basically become the caped-equivalent of james bond, we were fated to inevitably receive this sleuth-oriented iteration in fact, we got three-fucking-hours worth of that damnable detective, and i cant say its particularly interesting.
on the positive this isnt the constipated nolan batman that strives at every turn to make you take it seriously. the batman is more than happy to embrace the sheer visual goofiness of the character, with robert pattinson stomping around in thick-heeled boots like a walking action figure, his bangs artfully-swept across his eyes when hes in the bruce wayne guise. this movie isnt afraid to make batman out to be a weird socially-stunted loser instead of a super-cool playboy-cum-pugilist. reeves captures pattinsons physicality well on the whole, the film strikes a good character balance between keatons reclusive psycho and afflecks affable burnout. 
on the negative i love that this tries to bring back the gothic extravagance that tim burtons films had now gotham actually looks like GOTHAM, not like chicago. it takes a huge visual influence from the batman arkham games, with seemingly endless torrential rain and orange-tinted cobblestone. the problem is that reeves really embraces a penchant for shallow focus here, so you end up not actually seeing a while lot of the obviously-detailed environments, and for a movie thats more interested in a morose tone than the most propulsive storyline, that lack of texture means that a great deal of this feels like a shallow videogame world instead of an actual gritty city.
that would be more than forgivable, however, if it wasnt for this abomination of a script its no exaggeration to say that this probably has the worst script out of any batman film, definitely the worst dialogue, with nothing memorable exiting the mouths of some very fine performers. every bit of the mysterys clues are spelled-out miles in advance, anxious to make sure the viewer isnt confused by indelible puzzles like how does the spanish language work?, and the actual crimes at the heart of the story are weirdly tame and bloodless even by the standards of a PG-13 blockbuster. paul danos riddler feels like an afterthought to his own crimes, an aesthetic character slapped onto a story that never bothers to really make him seem like anything but a dorky tryhard. hes just not an adequate nemesis while colin farrell and john turturro give admirable villain performances, you really end up wishing that one of them was at the center of this tale instead of this forgettable mad-bomber. farrell in particular is enjoying playing one of the bats scummier foes, and could have easily held this film in his fat-suited fist if given the opportunity. 
to say that the batman feels undercooked is to admit that, despite its admirable pretensions towards noir in its first 23rds, the structure of the modern superhero formula demands that the third act becomes a big punch-up with rapidly escalating stakes, and one immediately understands that the director isnt really interested in that sort of thing. the batman relishes its many moments of quiet musing and brooding, so when it gets loud and explosive, the illusion of noir is broken, and the dark knight ditches playing dour detective in order to appease the inattentive appetites of studio executives and general audiences.

By virtue of being the 7th live-action iteration of Batman in such a short span of time, it cant help but feel like a bit of a derivative remix of so much of whats come before. How many times can we see these same characters and situations molded to wrestle with the same ideas what is an individuals power in the face of overwhelming large, corrupt institutions? Is fear a useful tool? Is it a political one? Can real heroism or justice still be that when accompanied by violent revenge? After over 3 decades it feels like weve stripped all the meat off the bone on this stuff. However, that being said, look, Im not gonna pretend that even coming too late that this version of this specific character isnt something I was basically in the bag for and that Ive wanted to see since I was a teenager listening to 90s alt-rock and devouring The Long Halloween, Year One, all the Scott Snyder runs, etc and its a testament to Reeves skill as a for-hire style engineer that despite finding some of the writing here a bit rudimentary that most of my qualms with it were pretty much pounded into submission by the pure, sustained brooding tone.
Unlike so many comic book adaptations that play coy dress-up with their influences while not actually taking on any of their formal elements this movie frequently and genuinely feels like the dour conspiratorial procedurals, gangster crime sagas, and serial killer noirs its indebted to. It has legitimate cynicism and voyeurism built into it, and the mournful, downbeat register is consistently alluring rather than dull. Its very wet, slow and seedy, and eschews quite a few of the commercial demands made on previous entries to make this character into an action blockbuster hero in order to really savor the time spent on the grimy streets of Gotham observing the imposing gothic architecture and beautiful, ominous skies as our paranoid, watchful protector rummages through filthy alleys and night clubs following up the various leads that leak out of the gruesome crime scenes and jigsaw traps set for him around the city. Theres a lot of subjective perspective to the compositions and I appreciated the incredibly cinematic focus on eyes, screens and shadowy, low-light locales intruded by rain-smeared lenses and glaringly bright headlightsflares.
Pattinson excels at this kind of wounded, awkward, hunched, almost ghostly physicality and his hard-boiled pulp diary narration funneled through emo-angst philosophizing was exactly what I was hoping for. (Havent seen this much antisocial silence out of a protagonist since basically any performance in a Refn movie.) Almost every periphery performance bouncing around him is a total blast. Farrell and Dano seem to be getting the most attention for the cartoon fun theyre having but Kravitz upstages them both (nearly destabilizing the power dynamics with Pattinson with just the way she looks and moves in a scene), and I was especially impressed by Turturro and Sarsgaard who reliably slime things up. 
So despite the fact that I do think the structure isnt perfect and it doesnt have what I would describe as the... Firmest grasp on all its threads that try to update some of the thornier elements of the material, it is the most stylistically engrossing and faithfully grim depiction of this insanely silly character. A character that could never in a million years be used as a tool to provide coherent, ethical solutions to poverty, crime, corruption, etc (which makes it even funnier that the movie even tries) because that stuff has only ever simply been an effectively ugly backdrop to an angry, grieving rich kid who tries to solve his internal moral conflicts by externally staging them as an act of sheer violent might barely pumping some blood back into a suffering city thats been a mud-caked corpse for most of his life and probably long before that. Say what you will of that image in all its reactionary dumb-guy pretension its a striking one that lends itself well to gloomy genre exercise, and I think Reeves just got the closest to it.

Im all in favor of scrapping the charismatic philanthropist aspect of the Bruce Wayne dichotomy and just making him a weird little freak. Every other Batman is just a competent guy under the mask, when he meets with Gordon its like meeting with a fellow project manager at an engineering firm. This Batman feels like a dog thats run inside with a dead squirrel in its mouth. If other iterations of Gordon found out Batman was Bruce Wayne (as weve already seen), theyd having nothing but noble respect for the humility of Bruce living this double life, but I think if this Gordon found out who Batman was, it would actually put him off. Like yeah man its actually kinda weird that youre doing this and I dont feel comfortable talking to you anymore. I think that dynamic makes a better case for Bruces reliance on Batman than any other live action movie.
Im contending with some major qualms here, but for now Ill just say that every time there was a riddle, Batman shouldve paused and looked into the camera for thirty seconds because he was shouting out the answers before I could even process what the riddle was asking. Its fucked up.

Batmans coolest new gadget in The Batman is also one of his smallest. Without spoiling the specifics, its a high-tech camera that allows him to sift through crime scene clues or surveil a suspect without them ever realizing theyre being watched. While gadgetry is a crucial part of every Batman movie, this camera is doubly effective because it ties directly into The Batmans most important theme The question of who is seen and who goes unseen in a society, and how problems that are willfully ignored  if not intentionally buried  can metastasize from the shadows.
The shadows are also where youll mostly find Batman in this movie, although in his case, its by choice. In an early voiceover, Robert Pattinsons Caped Crusader notes that Gotham Citys criminal element think Im hiding in the shadows. But I am the shadows. Boy is he ever.

When the Riddler, a sadistic serial killer, begins murdering key political figures in Gotham, Batman is forced to investigate the citys hidden corruption and question his familys involvement.
We have finally arrived. This is my most anticipated movie in quite some time. Matt Reeves behind the camera, Robert Pattinson wearing the cowl, and small nuggets of Giacchinos score are just a few of the ingredients that have been getting me excited for this one. The film opens (no spoilers, dont worry) in a way that we have never seen a Batman movie open, and I knew we were in for something special. Not only is this a three hour murder mystery, with a hint of a classic noir film, and a touch of a detective Thriller, but this film genuinely embodies the Batman that I know from the comics. We will make our way to Bruce Wayne, but lets talk about how good is Pattinson is when he is wearing the mask. The level of enthusiasm from Bruce feels three times stronger when he is decked out in costume because that is who he is. In this film, his face is his mask, and his mask is his face. The only form of happiness he is able find comes from his time in the suit. Not even Alfred can change his mentality, even though he tries. Speaking of Alfred, Serkis is great as the character, but he is the only one that feels underserved in this film. There is an important arc that comes from their relationship, but the movie leaves a lot on the table.
Beyond this, the script does an excellent job of balancing all of these characters and multiple crime bosses. Farrell embodies the Penguin in a physical way, but he also uses every bit of enthusiasm to play this character. Turturro plays a surprisingly massive role in the film as Falcone, and his straightforward nature is refreshing. Paul Dano crushes this unstable character and gives a difficult performance because he plays such a shady figure for most of the film. There is a choice made with his personality that I enjoyed quite a bit. Kravitz plays Catwoman with ease, and her chemistry with Pattinson works so well. Batman is the embodiment of fear in this movie. Criminals fear him at all times in the night, even when they know he isnt there. To deliver a film that makes us feel as scared as the criminals is impressive, but it also places us in the shoes (boots) of our main hero. The closeups that Reeves uses to capture the varying emotions of our characters is just one example of the many brilliant filmmaking choices that he goes for here. On a technical level, the film is gorgeous. It is definitely dark, but every now and then there is a pop of color that catches your eye. The darkness is the perfect way to capture the proper tone, even if it may be too much for some.
My main complaints include the lack of Alfred and time spent in the bat-cave itself. The film also makes the third act much bigger than the first two. The ending isnt bad by any means, but I cant say that it ended as strongly as it started. That being said, the opening few scenes of this film may go down as the best hero introduction we have ever seen in a comic book movie. Another talking point will be the fact that there is less action than many anticipated, but the strength of this film is its dialogue, and we get so much brilliant dialogue as Gordon is helping Batman solve these riddles. These two are essentially the dynamic duo of this movie, and Gordon gets a ton of screen-time. It is the best pairing of these two characters we have seen yet, animated or live-action. There are so many elements of this movie that I could say are the best we have seen in a Batman movie because we have yet to see a Batman movie like this. The focus is on the worlds greatest detective being a detective, and Riddler is treated like the Zodiac killer. There are shades of other great Thrillers such as Seven (as expected) and Prisoners (Dano is great in both). Pattinson is absolutely awesome as Batman. Reeves has created a force of nature, as this franchise has the potential to do so much in the television and movie space. As long as WB maintains this dark tone and gothic feel, I am salivating for more.

A staggering feat of franchise filmmaking, The Batman is one of the most immersive and uncompromised superhero films. It is three hours dedicated not to cameos and action scenes, but instead something focused on character and style. It is complex, it has a vision, and it walks the line between smart and silly without being pretentious. The film isnt flawless, but it stands above most of its blockbuster contemporaries. Films on this budget are rarely so interesting and intricate. The Batman is a stunning achievement.
The prospect of yet another dark, edgy Batman movie did not seem appealing, but The Batman finds a new approach and it totally won me over. It doesnt play as an endless action movie and theres no big half hour action sequence, as you often find in many superhero movies. Instead The Batman is mostly a detective movie, like a noir at times, with shadowy streets, nihilist themes, and even some voiceover. It is paced very slowly and carefully, going for a slow-burn approach that is very rewarding. The plot has shades of Se7en and High and Low, which gives this a different set of inspirations than other comicbook adaptations. The atmosphere resembles a horror film at times, built on tension and disturbing reveals. Mostly The Batman is a small stakes serial killer movie, without global consequences or a whole universe to deal with. Yet The Batman is also not going for realism. It is clearly set in a fantasy world, one of an exaggerated Gotham that exists as a disgusting, grimy harbour of all that is corrupt and broken. There are contrivances and coincidences that defy logic, but thats how superhero movies work. The Batman plays with both what is established and what hasnt been seen in this kind of movie. Its incredibly distinct.
The Batman is a feat of craftsmanship, a showcase of almost impeccable technique. Almost every shot and edit works perfectly. There are times when the film does seem to get lost, such as during a chaotic car chase, but the momentum of the narrative and personal stakes in the story pull it through. This is a film which really explores Batman. It doesnt have an origin story or rely on an established setup, it just presents Gotham and Batman as fully formed. The film also doesnt rehash the death of Waynes, instead investigating the headspace of Bruce Wayne independent of one childhood event. Here Batman is unrestrained, above the law and so close to breaking his own rules. Hes an addict, able only to think as the Bat and not able to find peace away from that. The film asks what it is that Batman inspires and the journey of the film is Batman trying to find purpose, to find a way to make a difference. He exists in a symbiotic relationship with his city, depending on them as they depend on him. With the extended runtime The Batman is able to introduce many characters and create a city of people, not fodder to be killed. Yet the film also examines and critiques Gotham, looking at its corruption and wealth inequality. The Batman not a politically radical or progressive work, but it understands only a privileged few could ever fulfil a Batman fantasy. Batman may be a symbol of hope and heroics, but hes also the symptom of a very broken society.
The Batman shocked and amazed me. I was enraptured all the way through and there wasnt a single second where I didnt feel immersed in the experience. Matt Reeves has now fully established himself as the greatest franchise filmmaker working. He has constructed a symphony of darkness and superheroism that I have only respect for. Yet it also has the right amount of humour, enough to not make this a totally dour film. The Batman is not depressing, it is ultimately uplifting. The mesmerising style and detailed world-building are then just the finishing touches that elevate this even more. The Batman is a real gem of a blockbuster and one of the finest superhero films I have ever seen.
