Unforgettable imagesthe coned, fiery blue flames of the Batmobile, bodies thrashing, enveloped in shadows, the brailed scars crawling across Robert Pattinsons muscled backconverge in Matt Reeves three-hour, noir-infused epic The Batman. Ever since Bob Kane and Bill Finger created him in 1939, the philanthropist playboy by day, Caped Crusader by night, has signified isolation, grief, trauma  vengeance. Over the decades, television and cinematic incarnations, projected through the personalities of the actors whove portrayed him, have amplified those traits through both campy and brooding means. But Pattinsons Dark Knight, more vicious, more forlorn, and less worldly, hampered by his privilege rather than aided, is not only different from every version before him. Inspired and enthralling, this detective story veers far away from the current homogenous superhero landscape.
This superhero film isnt reliant on the tired narrative repetitions of the genre. This superhero film moves with a cinematic spirit. The robust ensemble avoids hollow theatrics. It approaches these larger-than-life characters through every shade of melancholy. All Batman movies take their identity from the state of Gotham this new iteration overlooks a weary city of broken social contracts income disparity, tattered safety nets, supposedly outsider politicians promising change and delivering nothing. This cynical city is tired of believing its best days are just around the corner. And those generational disappointments weigh heavy on each character in different and profound ways.    
In Reeves rusty, carbon-colored Gotham, Bruce Wayne (Pattinson), the citys proverbial once and future prince, lives reclusively in the bowels of Wayne tower as a moody, emo-ridden loner, cared for by his dutiful butler Alfred (a rugged Andy Serkis). In a voiceover, the audibly demoralized Bruce explains how its been twenty years since an unknown gunman assassinated his parents  for a change, their deaths are rendered offscreen  during his fathers mayoral run. And two years since he first donned the cowl and cape. He feels cursed.
While the very visage of the bat signal in the sky strikes fear in every criminal, actionable change from his form of vigilante justice remains elusive The dream of the Wayne Renewal Program, a project begun by his father, promising to help the lower and middle class, catches no one. An opioid crisis is sweeping across the city. Gangsters like the unflappable Carmine Falcone (John Turturro) and The Penguin (Colin Farrell) rule the streets. Perhaps these obstacles could be surmounted if James Gordon (Jeffrey Wright) wasnt the only trustworthy cop. Or if every public servant werent on the take. But its a new, brutal serial killer, The Riddler (Paul Dano), who, to the strains of Ave Maria, opens the film by spying on Mayor Don Mitchell (Rupert Penry-Jones)  savagely murdering him  which most concerns Batman.  full review via The Playlist

O mais interessante do Coringa e desse filme do Reeves é que, apesar de serem trabalhos focados nesse aspecto psicológico, eles não buscam uma relação tão verossímil com o mundo. Todo o espaço que os personagens percorrem soa mais como uma projeção amaldiçoada da realidade do que a realidade propriamente.
Inclusive a ambientação possui aspectos anacrônicos nesse sentido. É difícil definir um tempo preciso, já que elementos de épocas diferentes parecem coexistir de modo muito natural.
O Bruce Wayne literalmente mora no castelo do Drácula, tem uma maquiagem de gótico dos anos 80 e possui os gadgets do James Bond da última década. São trabalhos que, nesse sentido, encontram um meio cinematográfico que reflete com maior fidelidade um imaginário universal dos quadrinhos.
Não estão preocupados em ser fiel a uma ideia narrativa ou dramática muito específica dos quadrinhos, mas se apropriam, justamente, do que de mais cinematográfico eles possuem a interação entre os personagens e o espaço que eles habitam. O modo como essa interação, mesmo visualmente falando, responde a uma definição muito maleável e possibilitadora de mundo real.
Muito da atitude dos heróis é definida através dessa sua perspectiva da realidade, dessa visão do mundo a sua volta. Enquanto alguns voam indiscriminadamente, o Batman possui uma dimensão muito mais terrena e maldita.
O filme do Reeves parte muito bem dessa ideia pra situar o personagem, inclusive, em um nível abaixo da civilização - o que me parece uma ideia muito boa no sentido de uma refundação da imagem dele no cinema, já que rejeita a ideia de uma superioridade cool que os filmes do Nolan estabelecem e dialoga com questões que já fazem parte da gênese nos quadrinhos.
O fato do rato ser uma figura recorrente reforça essa ideia. Quando o Batman e o Gordon conversam sobre a relação dos enigmas do Charada com ratos, o Gordon até diz algo como parece que esse é o tema dele.
A ideia de um rato voador, que se torna central no filme, também enfatiza essa imagem do morcego como um animal indigno (é confundido com uma pomba na resolução do enigma). Um animal que, mesmo voando, não possui qualquer graciosidade.
Mesmo o fato do Reeves deixar, quase sempre, os personagens em uma espécie de segundo plano nas composições dos enquadramentos reitera essa perspectiva de um mundo que é caracterizado mais como um pesadelo de formas e figuras do que um lugar fiel à realidade. 
As composições abusam de elementos e objetos na frente da câmera - vidros sujos, elementos desfocados, luzes remodelando a fisionomia dos personagens e por aí vai. O modo como usa a baixa profundidade de campo, principalmente nas cenas em que o Charada está matando alguém, concebe, igualmente, uma abordagem quase abstrata do espaço.
Até os closes e planos médios nunca são limpos. Sempre existe uma luz ou uma área muito desfocada antagonizando com as figuras humanas. 
É ótimo como o Reeves consegue propor esses elementos ultra estilizados sem fazer do filme um mero exercício maneirista. Assim como no Let Me In e nos melhores momentos dos filmes do Planeta dos Macacos, ele equilibra muito bem essa ideia de distorção dos espaços e de fascinação por elementos externos (como luz e chuva) com a presença dramática dos personagens.
Consegue fazer com que isso funcione, também, nas cenas de ação. As cenas em que o Batman entra na boate e a perseguição com o Pinguim dialogam diretamente com algumas das sequências de filmes contemporâneos que melhor sintetizam essa ideia cinematográfica de filme de gibi John Wick e Mad Max. 
São cenas austeras no sentido de não abusarem de modo tão óbvio de efeitos digitais, mas que também recusam uma encenação totalmente realista e assumem uma ideia de espetáculo visual oportuno.
Me parece que o erro do Nolan, de modo geral, foi ignorar esse potencial, digamos, pulp dos quadrinhos e reimaginar toda aquela dimensão dentro de uma ação policial realista-estilosa à Michael Mann.
Com certeza tem seus momentos, mas é algo que nunca explora possibilidades mais fantasiosas - não num sentido clássico de elementos fantásticos, mas de sugestões alegóricas que podem surgir daquela figura e daquele mundo - da premissa que tem em mãos.
O Reeves, pelo contrário, faz o que pode pra fazer um filme dramático que ainda dialoga diretamente com essas ideias. Além do possível imaginário psicanalítico que se concretiza em elementos de cena e dessa maleabilidade com a representação da realidade, toda a base que remete a questões de filme noir ou de literatura hardboiled é outra clara tentativa de buscar essa essência pulp.
Em um momento ou outro, acho que ele exagera um pouco nessa sobreposição dos espaços e cenários para suprir algo que não consegue tirar do elenco (o Pattinson me parece até subaproveitado em certas sequências), mas no geral é inegável que encontra uma harmonia muito poderosa entre as fantasias e patologias do personagem e a sua busca por uma humanidade e dignidade perdida.

Im not what youd call an avid comic book reader, but Ive read a few, practically all of them being Batman, including the massive anniversary book that barely features any Batman. Hes my favorite superhero, hands down. Not simply because he feels the most relatable in many ways, not because I will ever be like him (at least some filthy rich guy wants to make me filthy rich), but because many of his intricacies and issues feel more like a civilian to which I can connect the most. Additionally, as Ive stated numerous times, Im a fan of detective films, television series, and books.
Something that immediately stands out about this Batman is not so much his brooding nature as it is the fact that, at least in live action, he feels the most like a detective. A violent, broken, emo version of Philip Marlowe. Even while the references to films like Se7en were not subtle, the film noir components that permeate the whole picture are. Furthermore, the film has a strong horror film atmosphere to it, not only because of the character of Riddler and the way Reeves directs certain moments such as the opening sequence and the scene with a man in a car, but also that Giacchinos score reinforces this with a soundtrack consisting of low notes, shrieking noises, and a mournful choir that contributes to the overall feeling of doom and dread. Frasers cinematography, of course, is equally superb, capturing the 90s serial killer vibe of Se7en but also paying homage to the film noir genre.
Everyones performances are top-notch. Dano comes off as a frightening force of sheer lunacy who treads the narrow line between the films grounded nature and Jim CarreysFrank Gorshins campy, over-the-top attitude. This combination makes him a threatening yet amusing character (seriously that prison scene had me both shaking out of fear and bursting on laughter). Colin vanishes as The Penguin, a much amusing version of Tony Montana. Zoe Kravitz is without a doubt my favorite catwoman because she embodies both the sensuality and the fierce attitude of the character. Even though I still like Oldman, Wright is fantastic as Gordon in this film and his chemistry with Batman was top notch. Lastly, our Robert Pattinson has completed his transformation from gothic vampire to bat emo. But, seriously, Robert is terrific, and while I may need to see the film again, I feel very confident in declaring that Pattinson is my favorite Batman. Again, he conveys the moody, fractured essence of Batman, but he also comes off as quite genuine and engaging in his role as a detective.
All in all, though I maintain The Dark Knight is slightly superior and remains in first position, this is unquestionably my second favorite Batman picture. The final act may have been improved and shortened here and there, but this was still an enjoyable picture overall.

Matt Reeves é desses diretores que ainda me encantam frente a uma indústria que tende a padronização do estilo com o fim da padronização do gosto. É notório que o diretor, ainda que sob uma estrutura padrão, tenha realizado em seus filmes algumas escolhas pouco convencionais  vide o inventivo plano e contra-plano entre Bruce Wayne (Robert Pattinson) e Selina (Zöe Kravtiz) no televisor  quando em comparação com aqueles que os grandes estúdios empurram ao espectador com frequência, filmes sem memória, que são logo esquecidos em razão de sua mesmice.
O autor já havia feito um excelente trabalho em seus dois filmes da saga Planeta dos Macacos. Ainda que, como dito, sua estrutura não fuja do comum, a velha jornada de fácil aderência possibilitada pela padronização do seu uso, em Batman há um aspecto mais performático e intuitivo de seu personagem que uma extravagância espetaculosa.
	Sem curvas, o filme carrega uma atmosfera muito mais investigativa do que as adaptações anteriores. O herói carrega consigo um ofício que o aproxima de um braço da polícia, um detetive particular à espreita, atuando nas sombras. Contudo, o mais interessante é que ao passo que todo esse processo investigativo externo, referente a busca do crime, da corrupção e do próprio Charada (Paul Dano) seja um artifício inventivo para uma investigação moral e psicológica do personagem chave. Não de Bruce Wayne, mas do Batman.
	Conforme avança em sua investigação, mais próximo de dar luz ao que há de mais escuro no sombrio personagem. Um caminho curioso a se seguir, na medida que traz Batman para fora de onde costumeiramente espreita. Sair das sombras, dar luz aos seus medos. Em tal caso, como se toda sua jornada investigativa à Gotham fosse uma espécie de terapia psicanalítica, a medida que mais profundamente adentra no inconsciente da cidade, mais próximo fica de sua própria condição. Charada é um vilão que, acima de tudo, faz revelar as sombras do sombrio personagem, faz ser o homem morcego cúmplice psicológico da existência de Gotham e sua tormenta. Nesse lugar, há uma compreensão bastante profícua do personagem em questão, onde sua existência está associada justamente ao medo, a perda e a dúvida.
	Interessante que esse caminho adotado por Matt Reeves faça com que haja uma mudança significativa do filme de maneira progressiva. Os primeiros minutos expõem um Batman amedrontador, que caminha pelos ambientes com passos lentos ao som legível de seu coturno sob o chão. Uma figura fantasmagórica que expõe em sua persona um ser que visivelmente contém uma violência e que, caso haja necessidade, não medirá esforços em usá-la  ainda que o amedrontamento em si já faça que essa violência por vezes nem precise ser usada. 
	A progressão do personagem, porém, vai em direção a esse desmascaramento do Batman. Não o revelar de Bruce Wayne, mas do inconsciente do próprio homem morcego. À medida que Charada intensifica a missão investigativa do herói, aproxima-o psicologicamente dos problemas da cidade, fragilizando o personagem que pouco a pouco vai perdendo sua persona fantasmagórica, ganhando contornos trágicos e até mesmo melodramáticos.
	Particularmente, meu filme favorito do personagem em questão. Ainda que ainda sob a égide de um realismo intrínseco ao que a indústria comumente vem realizando, o filme opta por caminhos menos estéreis, sensibilizando e expondo seu personagem a uma posição menos confortável e, principalmente, permitindo ao espectador uma experiência menos passiva.

I dont like the vast majority of superhero films. I cohost a podcast where I bitch and moan my way through countless score of them. Frankly theres a lot not to like studio greed, rampant anti intellectualism, insufferable fandom, the list goes on. But one thing thats never been an issue to me is the fact that they are comic book movies, and I dont think a lot of people share this sentiment.
Theres an unspoken sentiment in film criticism circles that the entire genre is an infection from a lesser medium and in purging this infection will cinema finally be made whole once again. When Reeves cites films like Klute (1971) or the works of Wong Kar Wai the obvious response is no you didnt, you made a Batman film. The idea of any common ground is flat out rejected, based solely on the fact that these carry the same logos that are associated with walls of funko pops and bad taste. 
Obviously, people can find enjoyment with a work for good and bad reasons. Not everyone in an auditorium full of people seeing Pulp Fiction are there to witness a well crafted tale of human greed and violence set against the back drop of a post racial Los Angeles, some people simply want to watch Uma Thurman in pain. But when I watch the capeshit they revile against Im right there with them, because they are poor films and awful adaptations. Most go for a xerox approach where lossy elements are poorly transcribed to film and then honed into edgeless spheres by committee. Others try to imitate a story panel for panel. Neither attempt to adapt to the medium. When I see Reeves describe using Hitchcock inspired thoughts on Voyeurism in film to create a text like sense of knowing what every character thinks of at any moment, I see adaptation. And unlike Joker which simply grafts a character onto an existing film archetype, The Batman never feels derivative of its peers in a Star Wars like sense of genre ancestry.

Because Reeves actually conceived Gotham as place and not a CGI abstraction, theres a sense people do live in it which give the movie some stakes. Most of the stuff with the Riddler is pretty bad annoying pseudo trendy stuff, but Farrell is very fun. The movie is more functional than the grand thing Reeves seems to hope for, but in its own modest ways it is far above average for the genre.

Wasnt fully prepared to be thinking about Sidney Lumets dirty cop opus PRINCE OF THE CITY throughout a good chunk of a Batman movies runtime, yet here we are. A sprawling, overly ambitious pop epic that tackles similar themes regarding corruption, privilege, rage against institutions, and notions of moral relativity, all wrapped up in a muscular, rain slicked beast of a motion picture that repurposes Gotham City into a nightmare metropolis not too far removed from Finchers SEVEN or Scotts BLADE RUNNER.
Speaking of SEVEN, yes this is a serial killer thriller. Its also a tech noir investigative procedural. Its also an amped up underworld melodrama where John Turturro gets to vamp as a sunglass-adorned mob boss, Colin Farrell goes New Yawk Undercover via mounds of DICK TRACY-esque latex, and Jeffrey Wrights Jim Gordon is one bad motherfucker, floating in a river full of ethically compromised piranha. In short, its a lot of movie. Maybe too much (the second act definitely drags a bit). But its also hard to knock something that seems to be flexing a different muscle every fifteen minutes. Hell, it practically becomes De Palmas MISSION IMPOSSIBLE at one point. 
The performances are uniformly idiosyncratic. Pattinsons Batman is a legit detective while his Bruce Wayne is...different, this odd mix of Gerard Way and Howard Hughes. Zoe Kravitz gets the most comic-booky dialogue (cmon Vengeance, lets get into some trouble...) but also gets some meaty drama to chew on, becoming a human stand-in for the films entire tone this cartoonish take on gritty realism thatd almost be subversive if it wasnt taking itself so seriously. Danos the one who spins off into an alternate universe, his version of The Riddler acting like this giggly Brundlefly hybrid of John Doe and Tyler Durden as Michael Giacchinos thunderous score repurposes Ave Maria into his literal theme song, leaving Frank Gorshin and Jim Carrey in the dust of media history as THE BATMAN becomes a story of dueling Rorschachs, possibly only differentiated by their respective lots in life. 
If anything, Matt Reeves again proves himself to be a master stylist. Is it too long? Sure. Does it bite off more than it can chew? Probably. But honestly, in an era where an IP event like NO WAY HOME requires almost 150 minutes to tell a story of several Spider-Men paling around the Multiverse, and folks will commit to 8 hours of Hawkeye on Disney Plus just because its there, its nice to just have a Capital M Movie arrive in this arena for a change. Will definitely take more viewings to fully unpack the thorny political avenues it decides to navigate during the final third, but I feel confident saying this version of THE BATMAN might actually be in contention for best of the franchise, ranking right up there with Chris Nolans Mann-aping masterpiece, THE DARK KNIGHT. More words to come, thats for damn sure.

Round two with friends. Lots of thoughts and even some issues (Paul Danos performance post-unmasking, underdeveloped Riddler army idea, not enough Selina Kyle). But overall I really dug it. This has the theatrics, noir sensibility, and detective work I have long yearned for in a Batman flick. A fun time at the movies, baby!

Batman comienza en un Halloween lluvioso. 
En la noche en la que todos se enmascaran, el Acertijo comete su primer asesinato, que persigue como objetivo final desenmascar a la cadena de criminales y corruptos que lideran Ciudad Gótica, entre los cuales se encontraría también Bruce Wayne. 
Hago mención de la lluvia porque forma parte esencial de la escenografía. Cuesta imaginar la presentación de Batman desde las sombras sin su presencia. Una presentación cuya pelea ante vándalos de tiendas recuerda en espíritu al caos final del Joker, con los jóvenes tomando armas. La aparición final de este personaje ayuda a confirmar dicha búsqueda. 
A su vez, otro elemento natural pero opuesto, como el fuego, adquiere una importancia similar. La misma puede verse acompañada por la enorme cantidad de escenas iluminadas por un naranja cálido que quema la imagen. Asimismo, caben recordar los disparos de metralletas en la oscuridad antes de que Batman lidie con Falcone, como así también la subjetiva del Pingüino dentro del auto derribado, con Batman emergiendo desde el fuego, cual Ave Fénix, teniendo su primer renacimiento. 
Sobre el climax, el Acertijo, luego de hacer caer en la trampa a Bruce Wayne (Lo llevaste hasta la luz) de la misma forma que John Doe utiliza la ira de David Mills haciéndolo parte de su sinfonía, desea ahora transformar todo en pedazos y pasar a la historia.
Este plan maestro consta de hacer detonar bombas en distintos sitios estratégicos, para posteriormente provocar una inundación en Ciudad Gótica que barrerá con todo. Es decir, planea unir aquellos dos componentes históricamente opuestos, como lo son el fuego y el agua, pero en este caso en función del mal. Acaso toda la película rondará sobre esta idea de componentes que se suponen opuestos, pero que al final no lo son tanto, como sucede con Batman y el Acertijo.
Sin embargo, existe algo que los distancia mientras a Acertijo sólo le queda la venganza como vínculo, Bruce Wayne construyó su vida e identidad en función de Ciudad Gótica, casi como si la propia Gotham se hubiera hecho cargo de él tras la muerte de sus padres. 
De esta manera es que nace el nuevo día cero bajo el agua. No sólo con el superhéroe, yendo contra viento y marea, para salvar a la población (al mismo tiempo que adopta a la ciudad que lo crió), sino también con Batman, en modo jesuítico, extendiéndole su mano de esperanza a dos personajes que anteriormente se había cruzado en la iglesia Un joven huérfano, que vendría a ser un reflejo de sí mismo, y una mujer que dice representar al cambio real.

A dark, gripping  grounded portrait that digs into the lifelong trauma of Bruce Wayne in ways previous iterations never bothered before, The Batman is one of the most thrilling  refreshing entries in the comic-book film genre that borrows elements from many well-known examples yet has its very own identity thats firmly rooted in the character lore. Rendered on screen with deft care  attention to detail, featuring first-rate work in most filmmaking aspects and anchored by a thoroughly compelling lead showcase, this film delivers the goods  then some.
Co-written  directed by Matt Reeves, the opening monologue from the masked vigilante is an instant classic sequence in itself as it right away acquaints the viewers with the films grim tone, noirish feel  brooding atmosphere and when coupled with the gritty camerawork  foreboding score, it not only makes for an ideal introduction to Batman but also serves as a welcome insight into Gotham on brink of tearing itself apart. That scene is a masterclass in storytelling, for it instantly gets us into the caped crusaders state of mind while also creating intrigue, excitement  anticipation for what lies ahead.
Reeves puts as much effort into the visual language, cinematic flair  technical craftsmanship here as he does in the narrative aspects, thus resulting in a superhero film that has an organic, fleshed out and fully formed quality to it which is becoming a rarity in the genre of lately. The film offers ample breathing space to its plot  characters but its pacing couldve been further improved as one does start to feel its 176 mins runtime, especially during the second half. The quietly unnerving  gradually escalating slow-burn approach has its merits but then it also doesnt always work out in the films favour.
Greig Frasers cinematography expertly balances the colours, textures  lighting to elevate the rich set pieces and makes Gotham look way more realised, immersive  engrossing than ever before. Michael Giacchino also contributes with a great score that captures  amplifies the mood Reeves was going for. But the real highlight is Robert Pattinson who delivers an excellent performance both in n out of the suit and navigates the emotional crevices  complexities of the eponymous vigilante with finesse. Paul Dano brings a certain creepiness to his role but also hams every now n then. Zoë Kravitz is sensual  slick throughout while Jeffrey Wright chips in with a measured act.
Overall, The Batman is a bold  ambitious undertaking that finds Matt Reeves in prime form, is crafted with passion  panache, comes enveloped with an eerie vibe  menacing aura, delivers the entertaining goods with terrific action set pieces, puts more emphasis on Batmans investigative mind  detective skillset, unravels like a psychological thriller, and makes for an invigorating reboot that journeys into Bruce Waynes psyche further than earlier iterations. While it isnt without its shortcomings, given its overlong runtime  underwhelming third act, the positives far outweighs the negatives and the film as a whole remains an interesting  engaging ride for the most part if not all the way.

Matt Reeves The Batman is the epitome of a movie made for the theater. One batshit insane car chase sequence, a booming score, masterful sound design, a rich darkly lit atmosphere and crisp cinematography instantly sell that. Exceptional performances from every member of the cast and effective mystery allow for this to greatly exceed your typical blockbuster. And although it doesnt achieve the depth of the Christopher Nolan Batman films and has some underwritten character motivations, its a technical marvel of a slow burn crime thriller that earns its three hour runtime. 
Batman (Robert Pattinson) digs deep into the corruption of the city of Gotham that may have caused his parents death. Along the way, he faces the likes of The Riddler (Paul Dano), a serial killer who has been targeting men in positions of power. 
With the Batman taking up the vast majority of screen time compared to Bruce Wayne, it was essential for Robert Pattinson to nail the portrayal of the vigilante. He did exactly that. His quieter and even more physically demanding version of the Batman is stunning. Hes able to convince you that the man in a bat suit is genuinely intimidating with his properly lowered voice and brutally physical performance. Pattinson also manages to express more emotion than you would expect from the masked character. This is most notable during scenes with his potential love interest, the devious Catwoman (Zoë Kravitz). Kravitz was made for the role. Her talented non verbal acting fully expresses the characters underlying sadness and her line deliveries are silky smooth. Her and Pattinson also have a very natural romantic chemistry. 
The writers (Matt Reeves and Peter Craig) choice to make the Batman come out to play for about 85 of the time compared to Bruce Wayne is a choice that Im sure most fans of the caped character will love. But I found myself wanting more characterization of Bruce Wayne as a result. Even Pattinsons great performance never let me truly understand what makes Bruce Wayne tick. The writing needed to do that. Sure we find out about his parents but why does he really want to stop crime? Wanting to get deeper inside of Bruce Waynes head was my biggest issue with Matt Reeves reboot. I felt like I better understood Selina Kyle (Catwoman) at times even. 
But its easy to move past that with how well all three of Batmans villains fit into the story. Paul Danos version of The Riddler feels uncomfortably real, with his edgy charisma. And the characters enragement from being left out of society is fully realized by the time we witness a fantastic interrogation sequence. Danos breathy line deliveries, raspy yells and awkward pauses make for a captivating few minutes there. But I might be in the minority in saying that my favorite performance in the entire film was John Turturro as the harsh natured mob boss, Carmine Falcone. The few scenes with him are unforgettably tense thanks to his controlled and menacing cadence. His moments with The Penguin (Colin Farrell) are also exciting to watch. But did anyone who hadnt read the cast list even know that is Colin Farrell? The makeup is absurdly great and his acting is top notch. Farrell fully transforms into the witty character. 
Jeffrey Wright as Lieutenant James Gordon assisting Batman was also excellent. He brings in some of the very few appropriate moments of humor to the story and has lovable chemistry with Pattinson. The same exact thing can be said for Andy Serkis portrayal of Bruce Waynes butler, Alfred. But I have to point out that Alfreds only in a tiny portion of the film. Him being seemingly cut out of the runtime further emphasizes how prioritized Batmans screen time was in the writing. But, as a whole, I honestly find The Batman to be worthy of a SAG Ensemble nomination at the very least. The entire cast excels and brings unending believability into the story. 
That plausibility is also successful due to remarkably gritty and dark visuals that youd expect from a crime ridden city like Gotham. Greig Fraser (Dune, Rogue One) was the director of photography for The Batman and it shows. Its mesmerizing to watch with his countless wide shots of action sequences, yellowy red color palette over the shadows and gorgeous tracking shots of vehicles. And those higher stakes action scenes have seamless editing and what has to be the best sound design of the year (I dont even think its that bold to call it this early in the year either). And Michael Giacchinos score proves why hes one of the biggest names in the industry. Talk about elevating scenes with the depth of the sound that he reaches. I adored how often he uses the original music and how long each song is. Although I know its a very American media thing to need music every two seconds, it simply works here. 
The conclusion is even more sullen and cynical than The Dark Knights and I find that to work. Its very representative of the times we are living in today and fits neatly alongside the overall cynicism in cinema post 911. However, something happens in the early half of the third act that makes you feel like the movie has already ended, yet theres still 40 minutes left. Thats a more minor problem with pacing than the characterization of Bruce Wayne but it is still somewhat jarring. However, thats the only pacing problem I noticed and I found the three hour runtime to surprisingly not feel overlong. 
What an experience this was. The Batman doesnt quite have a flawless screenplay but it does have a lineup of acting titans and unreal technical prowess. Its a film you should be required to see in a theater. The initial widespread praise and inevitable sequel tease all but confirms that this is going to be one hell of a trilogy. And, without a doubt, I am all for that.

Si hay algo que me interesa de películas de superhéroes o cercanas al genero como Logan, Joker o The Batman es que su base parte de otros géneros del cine y no de su propia autosuficiencia en relación a otras películas de un universo mayor. Me explico Logan bebe del western, Joker bebe de Taxi Driver y el Rey de la Comedia y The Batman esta claramente ligada al cine detectivesco que inició su era moderna con la aparición de David Fincher. Esto las diferencia de sus compañeras contemporáneas porque su búsqueda nace a partir del cine mismo y desde allí se construye su mirada personal y no sobre una maraña de personajes y referencias que necesitan imperiosamente tener todo conectado para que funcione. En definitiva hay un entendimiento del cine como punto de origen de las historias y no desde otro lado.
Sin embargo, The Batman tiene un problema que la hace perder por bastante diferencia con respecto a las otras dos propone un punto de partida, el cine de Fincher y luego lo tira a la basura cuando no desea ir mas allá. Casi como si el director o los guionistas tuvieran miedo de dar el paso final para pertenecer a la obra en la que se están basando. Esto no ocurría en Logan, ya que Mangold al releer Shane de George Stevens, comprende que la historia del final de un nuevo oeste tiene que estar acompañada por una muerte como punto final del camino. Incluso podemos pensar que Mangold lleva esta idea a las últimas consecuencias su Shane, Logan, muere literalmente a diferencia del vaquero que tenía una muerte simbólica al alejarse del Oeste pero manteniendo su ser físico en la tierra. Pensemos en Joker y como su Travis Bickle es coronado héroe pero, primero, por un grupo de indeseados que lo toman como bandera y segundo, dentro de una prisión literal, a diferencia de la prisión de Travis dentro de su propia cabeza.
The Batman no da ese paso mas. Son muchas las oportunidades donde la película amaga a tirarse para el final de Se7en y lo descarta rápidamente por miedo al que dirán. Por nombrar algunas que Thomas Wayne era un hombre corrupto como el resto de los políticos y empresarios de Gotham es explicado por Carmine Falcone en una escena e inmediatamente en la siguiente es descartado por Alfred en un discurso solemne. Luego hay dos en el clímax, primero, cuando la película quiere hacer su final de Se7en y el whats in the box de John Doe con el último atentado del Acertijo pero como todo no puede terminar tan mal, Batman debe cumplir su rol una vez mas y salvar el día (en un clímax bastante plano, la verdad). Y segunda, la mas grave de todas, es esa aparición tan pero tan berreta del Joker porque la película se acuerda de que debe comenzar a formar un universo para seguir haciendo películas. Quizás nos podríamos preguntar, lo cual estuve meditando desde que la termine de ver hace un rato ¿Pueden dos escenas arruinar toda la concepción del mundo de una película? No necesariamente pero aquí, en The Batman, no puedo dejar de sentirme engañado por haber visto una película de tres horas (con un buen ritmo, pero son tres horas al fin y al cabo) que sienta unas bases y un desarrollo que no termina de concretar porque hay pudor por poner el clavo final en el ataúd que diferencie a la película del resto de sus contemporáneas (en especial todo lo relacionado a la factoría Marvel).
A favor de Reeves, la acción se entiende y hay algunas ideas interesantes (por citar una rápidamente, las pantallas del acertijo y como la última confrontación entre él y Batman es en una pantalla de vidrio como la de la cárcel, las simetrías con el agua, etc). Ya con eso, como mínimo, me parece mas interesante de ver que la trilogía de Nolan. Se nota una mayor preocupación por la puesta y no una desesperada atención a la banda sonora o a la fotografía para ocultar otros errores. En definitiva, me termino quedando con lo que podría haber sido con ese paso mas, aunque en el camino se hayan quedado las buenas intenciones.

Isnt it funny that true classics can stand up to decades of close scrutiny and critical analysis, yet still retain their standing among the greatest films of all time...but a deluge of completely obvious flaws in todays so-called masterpieces are immediately evident upon first viewing?
Lets begin this review by asking a question what does it mean for a film to be intelligent or mature? These types of words are frequently kicked around like a ten-cent hacky sack when people discuss films such as this, but what do they mean? In what context do these adjectives apply? I would like to find out. 
Ill begin at the top and work my way down, starting with the best aspects of this film and concluding with the worst. Please note that this will not be a leizurely stroll down a grassy hill with a pail of water, but more like a step out of an airplane in turbulance at 40,000ft. No parachutes will be provided. 
Heath Ledger, your performance is far too good to be in a movie this poor. 
And now, the rest. 
As good as the performance as the Joker is, its really all for nothing. The Joker is such a dumb character - meaning, he does incredibly dumb things for one of two possible reasons to appear cool and dark and awesome, or because the plot calls for it. There are too many glaring examples of this, from the holiptal scene to the ferry boats to pretty much every scene he appears in. The hospital, for example...Joker is able to simply walk into the hospital, wire the entire structure with several thousand kilos of explosives, and walk out without anyone noticing...just because he was wearing a nurses outfit? Im not sure if I can believe that. Not even in a movie where a ninja billionaire plays after-dark vigilante in a rubber bat costume. Perhaps it was his league of henchmen, who, seemingly overnight, grew from a small gang of random dudes to a sizeable organization capable of operating rapidly and without flaw - a group were told is made up primarily of schizos and psychopaths from Askham Asylum. Were they all released in a sudden mass exodus? And the Joker is really lucky that they all decided to become hyper-obedient and hyper-competent criminals, robbers, terrorists and explosive experts. Yeah, right. As if running a criminal empire made up of Arkham inmates would be an easy task in any way whatsoever. I think it would be a lot more entertaining and intelligent to see the Joker having to deal with insane and imperfect henchmen to inject a little conflict and doubt into his side of the story - will Joker be able to do what he wants to do? Sadly, this is not the case. At all. Joker simply surfs on the action, survives all kinds of explosions and automobile crashes, and moves around the city as if Gotham was butter and he was a hot knife. Yawn.
And while were still on the terrorist threat at the hospital, why was everyone evacuated...except Harvey Dent? You know, the District Attorney whos been all over the news? The guy for whom you are doing the evacuation?! 
How about the ferry boats...nobody seemed to notice the thousands of gallons of flammable liquid in the engine rooms? Is there a deleted scene on the blu-ray where Joker robs a small middle-eastern country of their entire oil reserve, by chance? And what was with that scene with all the people on the boats, anyway? Its a huge departure from the main action to a bunch of random, unknown characters late in the story that served no previous purpose and ended just as quick as it began. Where did that come from? What was the point of that? Id rather see what the main characters were up to at the climax of the film, not a bunch of anonymous strangers. 
I know the writers were trying to set Joker up as a dangerous villain who was capable of anything, but the problem with that is the notion of being capable of anything completely defies the mature and intelligent tone the film was desperately trying to strike. Joker never faces any obstacles - he plants bombs anywhere he wants, as if everyone in Gotham simply allowed him to do so! There is no realism in that. That type of writing is the exact opposite of mature and intelligent. And hell - Batman never seems to have a difficult time doing anything, either. He pulls technological rabbits out of a hat seemingly at will. Way to struggle, Bruce.
Moving on to Batman himself, Christian Bane of Cinemas Existence Bale once again proves to be the most over-rated actor in the history of the medium. He brings his trademark painted-stick charisma and shit-savoring, sub-70 IQ dumbass grin back again, along with a new and improved Marge Simpson impression. Theres a pointless sub-plot where some random guy on TV says he knows who Batman really is, but that goes absolutely nowhere and has nothing to do with the rest of the movie. Come on, random guy, how difficult is it to discern that it would take a man of great wealth to afford his own personal state of the art custom tank? The people in Gotham are humans, right? They have brains like us, right? They have the same form of currency as we do in real American, right? I assume they do, as evidenced by yet another entirely extraneous scene where Batman galavants to Hong Kong to kidnap yet another random guy who has no other critical function in the movie. What purpose do these characters serve in an already over-long film? They are superfluous - get them out of here. They are making an already bad movie even worse.
And that dumb cell-phone gag was ridiculous, unbelievable, and felt completely out of place, both thematically and in comparison to the attempted realism that the film was striving for oh so very desperately. It may be the most far-fetched idea Ive ever seen in a movie. Sure, its a comic book movie, but when you take great pains to show the audience how serious youre trying to be, it comes off as convincing as a 12-year-old smoking a cigarette to get people to think hes cool. Fucking absurd. 
So, what is Batmans motive? What does he want? Sure, he wants to stop Joker and all that, but what about all the other conflicts going on with his character, like his relationship with Rachel? Does he love her or doesnt he? Where is the scene that shows us that he loves her? There is none. Where is the scene that shows us he doesnt love her? Again, there is none. So...whats going on, Bruce? Why not clue us in a little bit. Where is the scene that tells us why he believes he must put down the cape and stop being Batman? He does this, but we dont know why. Does he want to live a normal life? We dont know. Why did he believe his only hope for no longer having to be Batman rested in Harvey? And why did he feel all hope was lost for his goal of no longer being Batman when Harvey vanished from the hospital to become a psychotic killer? We have no idea. His actions make no sense and were left to assume his motives - not a good thing.
Theres the letter to Bruce from Rachel, but that comes after her death, which is too late to serve the function of telling us there was a great romantic bond between them that necessitated Bruce stopping his crusade as Batman so they could be together. Plus, it only tells us her feelings, not Bruces. Because the scene is done the way it is, it is impossible to tell if Batman is amping his assault because of Rachel, or Harvey, or the threat of their imminent death. Once again, we are left to assume. If that is indeed the scene that tells us Bruce is deeply in love with Rachel, it is handled very badly to the point that it is virtually non-existent and comes far too late in the story to function at all. We should have known long before this that Bruce was deeply in love with Rachel, and that his crusade as Batman was preventing him from being with Rachel...but there is no such scene that tells us this. 
Is that a hallmark of maturity and intelligence in screenwriting? Not in any way.
Why is Rachel even in this movie? She seems to act only as a device to pit Harvey and Bruce against one another without having anything to do the rest of the time except play the part of a schoolgirl with a crush. At least Katie Holmess Rachel Dawes was a strong willed lawyer that fought for whats right. Maggies Rachel Dawes needs to grow up and find some better priorities. I suppose the only positive thing that can be said of her is that she fits in perfectly with the rest of the non-developed, off-the-shelf, one-dimensional cardboard characters in this movie - and the movie is littered with them, each one taking away valuable screen-time from the hero. For a film called The Dark Knight, there is a very significant lack of Batman doing things. 
The movie tries to be realistic, but logic has no place anywhere. It tries to be dramatic, but the drama is manufactured, out of place, and doesnt build up from anything. Lots of poor philosophical monologues going nowhere - and for all the pseudo-intellectual monologues and faux-philosophical rambling, it all just ended up with someone getting punched or shot. 
Gordon getting shot was the worst of all. It was all part of a grand scheme to get the Joker to chase Dent to get him out in the open so he can be caught...but the problem with that is, in order for the plan to succeed, they needed to know the mayor was going to be shot at from the ground and who was going to do the shooting in order for Gordon to jump in front of the bullet. If they knew that much about the Jokers plan, why not just stop him? I am frankly sick and fucking tired of this movie and the dichotomy it has created within the film community. I attended this really wonderful lecture on superheroes and the War on Terror, and how a number of very important comics post-911 became self-critical in their examination of states of emergency and exceptional politics, and the autoimmune system that leads to the violent pursuit of order becoming the greatest source of chaos. Because superheroes respond to emergency situations and operate within a non-legal or extra-legal capacity to inflict sovereign violence on the enemy (the enemy itself prone to slippage e.g. bin Laden, Hussein), they serve as the perfect analogy for global politics in our world which for 15 years has been in a permanent State of Emergency (and so one where illegal, extra-legal (exceptional) violence is now expected, as well as (exceptional) surveillance). This brings us to the figure of Batman who Frank Miller outed as a fascist in The Dark Knight Returns as well as the sole cause of the Jokers existence (a weirdly prescient analogy for the War on Terror that was not lost on Obama). The Dark Knight is descended directly from this Miller-ish scepticism of Batmans usefulness, with Alfred and Lucius saying throughout yeah its kind of your fault for declaring a with us or against us crisis situation, and the film being structured as a series of decision-moments in which this debate can play out. Before long however Nolan weighs in and closes it off. The its your faults become somebody had to do its and things get worse before they get betters, and Nolan contrives a situation in which Batman has to turn surveillance in on the citizens of Gotham in order to save them, which of course he does. After this there is a thing about popular opinion and myth-making and fall-guys, which of course is supposed to be analogous to the Obama Hope campaign, and the villainy associated with Bush (this being 2008). Such is the wonder of reader-response that we can read this in any way we want to, but chances are we will either see it as a criticism of the War on Terror (a sort of horror film in which Batman is the villain, exercising the Patriot Act at every turn), or a love-letter to the Bush administration as the non-heroic man we needed (justification of his actions Whatever the Cost). There is no right or wrong way to read the text, nor is there a right or wrong way to view the situation, but fwiw I find it hard to agree with the former reading in light of Nolans classism in the Dark Knight Rises and bro-science anti-environmentalism in Interstellar. The conflicts and conversations are only there because they have to be (a rare case of comic-lore stifling an individuals creativity for something better than if heshe were allowed free rein).
A piece of right-wing propaganda which kisses Bush on the cheek and says dont worry, we know who the real hero is and insists that we proceed down the path we have taken before things get better (a tragi-comically misguided statement 8 years on), could still make for this horror film reading, or at least provide the viewer with thrills in its with us or against us mindset, as many jingoist guilty pleasures have over the years. My issue with Nolan is not his worldview however much I despise it, but his films themselves, maybe as exemplified by The Dark Knight. I genuinely cannot see what people get from his films, and I cannot see what interest he has in making them either. He does not seem interested in humans or emotions, which is fine, but he does not seem interested in the sensorial experiences that films can provide either. Michael Bay for example discards human poetry for effects fetishisation and action formalism- he gleefully explores the filmic language of editing or at least enjoys blowing shit up. Nolan in the Dark Knight conservatively cues talking points for exposition which establish action bits. His characters speak dryly and functionally with occasional Bad Ass one-liners fit for movie trailers and desktop wallpapers. The people who are not Important are instead anonymous (panicked man on boat, horrified party guest 3) which can be expected in superhero films (and as I have already pointed out Nolan is not interested in people), but that does not mean that his worlds have to be so lifeless either. Its this anonymity, these predictable 21st century Dark visuals (my gut tells me that we have Nolan to thank for this, but its probably Fincher), and the nature of Gotham as solely existing as (non)context for Batman and Joker Doing Things. Kubrick was a misanthrope who built unforgettable worlds and atmospheres, films like The Matrix are 90 exposition for the function of worldbuilding and not just talking (and the Wachowskis directed the shit out of every conversation any way), and even the much maligned Warcraft which flows biblically also wants badly to exist outside of its processes (and had surplus heart and humanity, but whatever). Green Room, shaved down to a stage for ultraviolent encounters, feels more alive than any of Nolans films, and Saulnier would probably resent that too. As far as violent encounters go, Nolan seems just as disinterested in action as he does humans, emotions, worlds, and cinematic languages. As mentioned before, Michael Bay who can seem just as cynical as Nolan w.r.t. human emotion, tends to break from meat-space logic for cinematic thrills and experiments. A more conventional director might consider humans as bodies (rather than feeling things or narrative devices) in spaces, and so focus on ways to explore bodies against bodies, and bodies in environments. A lesser director might only consider these bodies, and not filmic environments. Nolan does not care for the immediate space of a scene, and breaks from them so regularly with geographical and temporal jumps that there are no stakes because there are no bodies in the spaces, only flashes of contact, and either the choreography of said bodies or their editing severs them from simple cause and effect. I suppose that this really is horror cinema for the Age of Emergency because there are no bodies, there are no environments, there is no time, and there is no reason. Its action formatted to the logic of a 21st century news channel, and just as propagandic.
Still I am unable to divorce the film from the director and his filmography. I wonder again a) what anybody sees in his films and b) what his motivation is for making them. He cannot tell a story visually (or verbally either, but thats another matter), he does not care about stories, and he does not care about the things that anyone would expect him to, having freed himself from the confines of narrative and human emotion. I suppose that his cinema is a cinema of ideas, e.g. the one with the Joker, the one about the War on Terror, (or gleefully thrown around back when his trilogy began) its Batman but its really dark, and not of film or film experiences. I thought I could enjoy this as an idea- as the horror film that Nolan never intended it to be, but it insults just about everything I care about in narrative and visual media in the blandest, most grandiose way possible. Perhaps I will lose my respectable arthouse-lover credentials for this, but I side with the IMDb crowd and the supposed film bros The Dark Knight is a masterpiece. Not only is it a masterpiece, it is a cultural landmark we are foolish to downplay. It is the Star Wars or Godfather of the internet era, a smash-hit film that gained undeniable classic status very quickly. It remains probably the only 21st century film to have that status with the general audience and not just us film nerds (who are fawning over Mulholland Drive, In the Mood for Love, and Boyhood instead, although shocker The Dark Knight is superior to all three of those). The Dark Knight transcends the traditional limitations of superhero adaptations. It is a visionary film. The Dark Knight is the Hamlet of popcorn cinema, a profound, popular tragedy deeply engrained in our culture and morally unanswerable.
The Dark Knight is sadistic, grim, and bleak. There is always more humour than you remember, but this is radically dark for a story of heroism. Christopher Nolans command of technique is impeccable, as every moment coils in ever-rising tension. Structurally The Dark Knight is bold, with about seven different climaxes as each set-piece tops the previous. Every watch reveals dialogue and subtleties you didnt spot before. It is just so perfectly constructed and well thought out, with layers of complexity few films have. The opening heist would be a perfect short film - its self-contained, mysterious, twist-filled - and yet from this opening, the film proliferates out a sprawling chaos, all whilst Nolan maintains complete control. Every shot is framed beautifully, every throbbing music beat suits the tension, every action scene is made with a clarity and realism. Then, beneath Nolans direction, is a script so well put together, balancing many moving pieces whilst weaving now-iconic quotes easily into the dialogue. Unlike The Dark Knight Rises (still a great film despite the era of CinemaSins nitpicking it to death), The Dark Knight is never overwhelmed by its deep discussions. Instead, like everything else, its planned to perfection.
The Dark Knight is about chaos as a facet of human civilisation. Batman, intent on destroying all crime, strives for order. The Dark Knight opens with order reaching Gotham because of Batmans actions and the Joker subsequently attempting to ensure chaos reigns eternal. This is the fight for the soul of a city. Superheroes, as above-the-law übermensch, are inherently fascistic. Nolan may not be a liberal, but he plays with the ethical limits of superheroism. Bruce Wayne monitors people, an authoritarian impulse, and Batman breaks society with the order he imposes. Crime networks already kept order through corrupt allegiances and Batman destroys them, allowing chaos to rise. Order may be Batmans ideal but this isnt what he ends up with, eventually he compromises, destroying his monitoring technology and allowing himself to be seen as a symbol of chaos. In the arc of Batman, The Dark Knight is about the rejection of total power, crafting order through inspiring self-sacrifice and not violent supremacy.
If things go to plan, we never notice. Order is ignored. Society falls apart when faced with chaos, and people easily turn on what they trust (Batman, Harvey Dent, the status quo). In a time of chaos (terrorism), people will accept security over freedom, as seen during the Bush years. People claim they want freedom (chaos) but actually they want order. By creating a city in chaos, the Joker is trying to show people their hypocrisy. Batman does not defeat the Joker in The Dark Knight, instead he just believes in the goodness of people. Citizens rejecting the Jokers final twisted proposition is his defeat, proof that in a chaotic world people arent inherently bad. However, in an even more twisted way the Joker still wins. The true evil in the world is the crushing of idealism (you either die a hero or live long enough to see yourself become the villain), a revelation the Jokers plan reveals to all. The only way for Batman to win is to accept that mantra and become the villain, letting Harvey Dent die a hero. This is the end of true order, a naïve victory. The truth is chaos as reality proves, but lying to create a narrative that inspires all, thats order. So, Batman chooses to make the citizens happy rather than tell them the truth. He creates an ordered city as he always wanted, but at the cost of learning that its a lie and chaos rules subconsciously. Its a hollow utopia, one that modern society is built upon. Happiness vs truth is a dichotomy that defines all morality, and people will always choose the lies that help them sleep at night.
The Joker is not a character but a catalyst, a constant for all other events to swirl around. He is truly psychotic, just an agent of chaos, and nothing else. Heath Ledgers performance is mesmeric, going beyond acting to be a work of art by itself, his performance entrenched in his physicality. The Joker needs Batman, as an opposite and equal. It takes both of them to shape the world, one of constant conflict between order and chaos. Harvey Dent represents a pure force, the same side as Batman but able to show his face. He needs to be a hero and the fact that he isnt shows the victory as being the Jokers. Batman is just a symbol and not a true hero. Batman may defeat chaos but he loses all that he values - his love, his belief in order, his symbolism of hope. Bruce Wayne wants to be Harvey, but knows that he doesnt have the character to be. He will never be the citys white knight. The Joker says that in their last moments people reveal who they really are. Harvey Dent, as it turns out, is a villain. In the final scene, the three prongs of law enforcement are purely defined. Harvey Dent is the ruined idealist. Commissioner Gordon is the hardworking pragmatist. As for Batman, hes the soulless abyss of vigilantism, a symbol to fear yet yearn for, and the malleable byproduct of a diseased, chaotic world. He shouldnt be a hero, he shouldnt be admired, and learning that, thats how the people save their city.

Nolan believing that lying is necessary to preserve liberal order was far more telling than I think he ever realized, haha.  This actually does have its fair share of interesting ideas and is very well put together, but its most fascinating as a key relic in the crossover between the Bush era and the Obama era.  Its too easy to merely write off Nolan as a conservative - at worst hes just ideologically incoherent, though its easy to forget that what passes as Nolans apparent conservatism now were standard mainstream liberal talking points a mere decade ago.  Which in a way tells on itself, but hes really the ultimate American (even though hes British) liberal.  
And TDK is really the ultimate liberal movie, with specific signifiers tossed out the window for vague generalities about chaos and order - though of course the broadness of those generalities open the door to clarity in purpose.  Where it becomes muddled is when what is essentially Nolans modernization of Platos Republic comes into contact with modernity itself, or at least the world of 2008.  The Dark Knight is essentially a defend the Republic epic, except its never quite clear why were defending the Republic.  But its very clear what were defending, and its telling in how all reactionary it all looks twelve years later.  The weird part is that even Nolan can perceive it as corrupt, yet chooses to continue sustaining that same system.  Also - Nolans fondness for Kubrick becomes more blatantly apparent starting with Inception, but here a shared misanthropy is often evident as well - which, no problem with that.  Its not unjustified cynicism in this area, where every member of society does exactly what youd expect them too, but its also why elements of the films ending doesnt quite work - the ferry sequence seems like a left-field cop-out if not complete deus-ex machina given what weve seen throughout the rest of the film - which is the Jokerchaos figure being constantly proven right.  And he essentially wins given Harveys turn and Batmans villianizing at the climax.  But I guess that also plays into Nolans whole But you HAVE to lie! thing, I suppose.  Who knows.
Still, theres a considerable amount to admire here in how patiently and rather marvellously constructed this all is, with Nolans attempt to draw the fabric of a city by ultimately honing in on political and media figures, crafting a sort of comic book simulacra of normality, honing in on those two specifics in order to identify the weaker planks of a system.  Its essentially why the film is effective, because (and even though TDKR arguably goes even farther in this regard) when the Jokerchaos figure creates ruptures it only really shatters the cities illusion of stability, and because of the films focus on those prior figures, we can identify the source of the problem.  A comparison I dont believe has ever been made, but Nolan can be like Zhang Yimou in this regard - hes more or less for the system, but he also shows you the inner workings of it, whether intentionally or not.

They said it couldnt be done, they said it couldnt be watched once youre no longer a teenager Anyway, first watch in at least 10 years just cause I had seen it so many times between 2008-2012 I never really felt the need to actually logreview. But here we are! And its good! 
I do feel like this is remembered as a masterpiece simply for being the movie where Nolan figured out how to effectively merge his logical, clockwork formal precision and the sadder, more severe and tortured tone (of say MementoThe Prestige) with broad, blunt-force blockbuster momentum that he never turned back from. And to be fair, the cold steely engineering of the IMAX set pieces here still absolutely rips the bank heist, Batman going Bond mode in Hong Kong, the truck flip, the hospital explosion, etc, and go a long way to further and better developing the mission he (and Goyer) started with Begins to give an inherently silly character his most thorough and grounded explanation both in terms of psychology and real-world practicality. Here he complicates that reality by incorporating some grim, incoherent zeitgeist-bait about Batmans role in a Gotham tormented by police corruption, terrorism, and our post-911 security statePatriot act, that wherever you stand on it nowretrospective critiques of it as a conflicted, paradoxical Bush-era liberal power fantasy arent unfairit certainly proved a cathartic Rorschach test for an American viewing audience 15 years ago. 
A huge part of that was Nolans taste for crafting and structuring a modern hit crime-thriller this cribs quite blatantly from Se7ens gruesomesadistic criminal mastermind angst-noir (similarly structured like were a rat in their trap alongside the protagonists) and Heats more grandiose, tragic, and philosophical cat-and-mouse between copsrobbers, predatorprey. Theres a bit too much clumsy exposition and dorky, literal-minded screenwriter-isms inherent to a PG-13 variation on subject matter like this to completely earn those comparisons, and it truly is a bit thematically stupidstrained if you stop and think about it but the true Jokers Trick of this movie is that you dont! Even just casually throwing on in the background on the 4K disc youre absorbed in the pain, weight and rage of the characters (good casting helps a lot with this) and the vice-like single-minded thriller momentum from frame one. Like a dog chasing cars it moves, pummels and overwhelms with a bleaker intensity than was common for the genre at the time, and certainly is more (even if just superficiallytonally) concerned with ambiguity and consequences. 
The horror-adjacent Zimmer soundscape helps a lot with this, as does Ledgers performance which is a rare example of genuine raw nerve live-wire energy in the Nolan catalog frequently unpredictable and frightening despite being ingested into the norm for the following decade and counting. So yeah, idk that Nolan is actually saying anything about symbolic Greater Good pragmatism or compromising moralsidealism in an indecent, unfair cruel political world by the end or if he is just wearing all these ideas as easy genre shorthand for somber drama, but also the fact that more people remember it not for any of that but for it being sick and awesome and filled with tactile, analog FX and impeccable movement and tonemood makes perfect sense to me. Stylish bozo depth is a perfectly admirable space to operate in, and some of our finest genre movies were born from it.

I always loved the whole Wanna know where I got these scars? thing about him because its adds complexity to his character while also keeping the mystery by having each story be a load of bullshit. The subtle transformation he goes through before the end of the film is just so brilliant. He starts out as a man on top of the world and then when he loses everything he loves, he loses his morals along with his mind and its just so fascinating and tragic to watch his character from beginning to end and Eackhart is just outstanding. Katie Holmes as Rachel Dawes is replaced by Maggie Gyllenhal who does a really great job in the role and is a massive improvement from Holmes.
Batman Begins put story and characters before action while this film balances it all hand in hand and it really works. The opening of Dark Knight is legendary for a reason. It is the perfect match of spectacle, playfulness and ingenuity. It is heightened and a touch contrived, but it is lean and slick and subversive. It is a dynamite heist scene that promises a style of film that Nolan never delivers.
As I articulated in my review of Batman Begins, that film is very cleanly (even if unsubtly) about something. It has a very cogent central theme and uses it as a catalyst for characters and character growth. The Dark Knight is a thematic mess, full of troubling ideological posturing and scale over substance as it escalates out of control. The constant motivation of but what is cool? outweighing but what makes sense?
Batman Begins fits its cleverly structured narrative around the growth of Batman. Its not just a clever title. This film, well it is just a clever title. Batman may the eponymous hero but this film is a Joker film, and - despite a fascinating performance - this doesnt really work. Joker here is chaos, he is part of the films hackneyed (and deeply suspect) world view its classic post 911 stuff where the Western world is suddenly obsessed with the idea of chaos, nihilism and moral maelstroms. I cite 911 with care, but the films approach to torture and interventionism are uncomfortable markers for its overall politics. 
This film takes the view that Batman, who can be sensibly read as a symbol of American interventionism - the American ideal coming to save the day, has created prosperity for some but has also led to opportunism. His actions have led to a new breed of terrorism cue the Joker. This is a very interesting viewpoint, with an obvious real world parallel, but it isnt the end point. Batman is still the hero, and thats the issue.
This logic belongs to a film where Batman does step away, or has to act differently - or has to actually self sacrifice. Instead he adapts. Instead he follows the actual arc of America and stays the positioned hero of the film. The films fears turn towards random acts of terrorism and threats on state officials and the police, it highlights this concern a lot. This pushes it towards legitimising the need for excessive force arm the police and militarise.
Batman is the extended symbol of all of this. Whereas in Begins he is an agile, stealthy figure, here he is burlier, stronger and constantly using advanced military tech. The most controversial point is the third act manoeuvre, where the writers concoct a plot in which a deeply unethical piece of tech is invented but needs to be used. This film believes that the lines have been blurred and now, some good men need to cross them. Batman even makes the point that Freemans Fox must use the deeply unethical spying tech, because what we need is a compassionate surveillance state. You know, good guys with their fingers on the button.
To build up to these points, the film engages several straw men (one even being Scarecrow). The Harvey Dent arc, a bad performance from Eckhart (but seemingly due to direction), is awful. His first scene is atrocious as he showboats in court, disarms a gun toting goon and then punches him in the face before promoting American manufacturing - all in the court room. And its not a joke. He then becomes an awkward symbol for something, in a very unclear way - more on this later.
The issue is that, as mentioned, the narrative structure matches Joker in the same way the structure matched Batman in the first. It makes sense that Joker is an enigma at the films heart. He is chaotic and unknowable. But he needs to be foiled to work. The fragmented structure apes his chaotic energy, as the ever moving (irritatingly so) camera keeps us on our toes. This pace eschews characterisation, necessary for Joker but a hindrance for all others.
Dent and Dawes (now Maggie Gyllenhaal) have no chemistry. I dont know who they are. Dent never seems legitimate and I dont trust his motivations (and I dont know if Im supposed to or not). Pushing in the rise of Two-Face in the Joker film just over stuffs it. His rise is secondary and unbalanced. The film as a whole just pushes in too many arcs and the structure, with its love of cutting better viewpoints, doesnt let any develop. Again, the film is too in concert with Joker, pushing him in a way that tears down the film around him.
This makes for rushed plotting regressive sacrificing of the only proper female character to create a narrative for two men, and a host of moments that dont really make sense. Too much is built around what looks cool and a belief in nihilism (as oxymoronic as that sounds). But then the film doesnt even sell that. It ends in such a forced way, with a ludicrous set piece that presents a moral at odds with everything else in the film. And while I always support earned humanism in films, this film does it inauthentically. It establishes a world with a clear ideology (which Im against but it is mostly coherent) and then it undercuts it.
We end with an armed siege that legitimises the weaponry of the state. Dent was a symbol, a clumsy one, of hope and order - of compassionate power, of a fairer justice system that works for the people. And the film shows that as an impossibility. What we need is a strong state, a militarised state, a surveillance state. A state that works heroically in the dark. Secret ops and special ops.
We need the Dark Knight to fight the battles, to fight for the people. To save us from ourselves. We need to go dark to get good.
And I hate all of this, and I hate it more because of how forced it seems. I hate how unnatural the character growth is. How empty and forced the dichotomies are. How every line of dialogue is empty philosophising and portentous nonsense. And I hate how the film constantly links facial disfigurement with evil.
And I hate the film the most at the very end. Where it promotes the need for shadowy operations, for doing dark things to keep society running, while we keep our empty figureheads to placate the people.

As I fully intend to watch The Dark Knight Rises, I felt it necessary to re-watch its predecessor. I liked it better the first time.
 Technically good 
This is technically a very good film. I still like the look and feel of it, building forth on the style of Batman Begins. Nolan manages to conjure up a Gotham City that feels both real and plausible. The practical and special effects, the make up, costume and production design are all very good and much to my liking. There were some fantastically choreographed action sequences that were high tension and very enjoyable.
 The Joker
I think the main reason I liked it so much the first time was because of Heath Ledgers performance. His sparkling insanity made me turn a blind eye towards any possible flaws the first time round. Upon second viewing his performance doesnt loose any of its impact. He manages to walk that tiniest of tightropes between convincingly insane and overacting evil really well. He still plays a comic book villain, but does so with a grounded realism.
Comic book or reality? 
We should not forget one important thing. The source of this film. This is still a comic book adaptation. If we look at it any other way, it will fail miserably. Many people heralded this film as the second coming in actioncrime films, well, it isnt. I dont believe in the term  super hero movie, but I do believe in the comic book adaptation genre, that is a big difference. The problem is that this film doesnt decide what it sees itself as. It tries to explore the nature of good and evil. It does so by choosing for a gritty aesthetic. And heres where the trouble starts. The Dark Knight loses sight of where it comes from. It doesnt wholeheartedly see itself as a comic book adaptation, nor as an actionadventure film based in reality. Sure, the graphic novel it is based on is dark as hell, thats inherent to the nature of the vigilante character of batman. It is still a comic, though, it never tries to be real. The concept of the unambiguously evil Joker and the ambiguously good Batman is a concept that would work in a real world setting and it is what this film focusses on. The way the action and violence is portrayed, the gadgets and the inclusion of Harvey Dent belong to the realms of the comic book. For me this film unhinges because of this imbalance.
The plot thickens
Christopher Nolan always tends to walk a fine line between complicated plot and dense narrative. He often manages to pull this off, but here he doesnt. The plot here is simple, but the narrative is unnecessarily complicated and convoluted.  It is such a shame that the only way to portray the Joker as a mastermind criminal was to have him turned into someone who can somehow predict and foresee just about anything that is going to happen. I find this type of storytelling to be completely unbelievable as it is simply impossible to predict human behaviour to such a degree. There are so many other, better ways to do this. This type of narrative simply leaves too many  What ifs? Normally I wouldnt mind so much, but here, due to the imbalance mentioned earlier I do. 
In Batman Begins I felt I was watching an almost perfect blend of plot and narrative set in a comic book world I actually never really liked. The Dark Knight (2008) is a superhero movie directed by Christopher Nolan, who also wrote the screenplay with his brother Jonathon Nolan. and based on the DC Comics superhero Batman. The movie features Christian Bale, Heath Ledger, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Aaron Eckhart, Gary Oldman, Michael Caine, Cillian Murphy, and Morgan Freeman.
Serving as the second entry in The Dark Knight Trilogy (2005 - 2012) and the sequel to Batman Begins (2005), the movie follows Bruce Wayne (Chrstian Bale) continuing to defeat crime as Batman in the dark streets of Gotham City. Suddenly, a new crime organisation led by a dangerous clown-like mastermind called The Joker (Heath Ledger), who plans on corrupt Gotham City. With the support from Police Commissioner James Gordon (Gary Oldman) and Gothams district attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart), will Batman stop The Joker and his organisation from causing more harm to the city?
The story was fantastic and was so much better than its predecessor. It offers a darker tone, slow pacing to make room for splendid character development, thrilling moments, iconic scenes, and realistic elements that make it stand out from most superhero movies. What makes the story so special is that it explores the strong themes of corruption, judgements, and rules and order, as it adds more realism into a superhero movie and was well-executed by Christopher Nolans amazing directing skills.
The performances from the cast were phenomenal as they make the characters move and feel realistic by using strong body language and emotive language that suits the characters personalities. This will keep the viewers engaged and excited about how intense the actors perform because this is how they wanted the Batman characters from the comics to be visualled in a dark toned film. Heath Ledger was the main actor who steals the show since he has delivered a sinister performance as The Joker by making him menacing and terrifying. In my opinion, his version of the iconic supervillain is my favourite movie Joker.
The Nolan brothers writing skills for the screenplay were outstanding since most of the dialogue was well-written and how it creates a strong impact on the characters and the storys dark tone. The best lines include Why so serious?, How about a magic trick?, and Hit Me!.
The production design for this movie was magnificent. This is because it offers realistic set designs for the different buildings within Gotham City (both interior and exterior), disturbing make up and costume designs that suit the characters roles, and great lightings that stay true to Christopher Nolans dark vision for the film. The Jokers make up and costume designs were the greatest elements of the production design because they stay true to the iconic villains appearance from the comics while having some creepy elements that make him stand out from the other Jokers.
The action sequences were extraordinary to watch since each one was well-edited by Lee Smith, well-choreographed and have an amazing balance of special effects and practical effects. In my opinion, the best action scene was the car chase as it was intense yet thrilling to witness, which has kept me curious as to how Batman will catch up with his arch enemy.
Wally Pfisters cinematography skills was amazing. The reason being is that he came up with awesome camera shots and dark colour saturations that perfectly visual the movies gritty mood and capture the important details of Gotham Citys atmosphere. An important aspect in the cinematography to point out is that Wally Pfister has improved on the camera movements from Batman Begins (2005), as it feels less shaky, which makes it easier for the audience to see what is happening in the movie. For example, there is a over the shoulder shot of Batman interrogating The Joker in the interrogation room. This shows the audience that Batman has all the power and that they are on his side about wanting answers from The Joker.
Hans Zimmers music score was spectacular and unforgettable as it fits the movies mood perfectly by having tensions to build up the presence of The Joker and the action sequences. This will make the audience feel unsettled about the main antagonist because of his menacing backgrounds and making the atmosphere darker.
The movies target audience are people who enjoy watching superhero movies with a dark tone. This is because the movie has a disturbing story with realistic aspects and gritty moments that are unsettling for younger viewers. Also, the movie appeals to older Batman fans as they have been waiting for a long time to see a true Batman movie with a really dark tone that follows the comics well, in addition to the fans wanting to continue the movies legacy by passing it on to a new generation of Batman, DC, and superhero fans.
In conclusion, The Dark Knight (2008) is still a remarkable superhero movie that develops its impressive themes by having a great story that was well-directed by Christopher Nolan. It also has memorable characters, an iconic film score, and magnificent cinematography. In my opinion, this is certainly worth the watch. This is now my all time favourite superhero movie.
