Criminals arent complicated says Bruce Wayne and for the most part, hes right. At their core, most criminals, especially of the organized variety, are nothing more than supremely unscrupulous businessmen. As such, when The Dark Knight begins, the Caped Crusaders war on crime that began in 2005s Batman Begins has reached an equilibrium of sorts the gang bosses try to extract as much money from Gotham through drugs and racketeering as they can, and Batman tries to stop them, with both sides battling for the souls of the citys police officers, judges and politicians. The question will these bureaucrats be corrupted by the mobs money, or inspired by Batmans unyielding crusade? Its a straightforward, rule-bound dynamic, almost...boring. At least thats what a greasepainted, costumed freak calling himself The Joker thinks. Hes not interested in anything as banal as money he wants to upend every system of belief and code of behavior adhered to by Gothamites of all stripes, from city fathers to godfathers. Robbery, murder, arson, he commits these crimes with gusto, but they are not ends to themselves. No, the Joker wants to strip the veneer of civilization from the Gotham citizenry and enjoy the show as they tear themselves, and all of their illusions of decency, to pieces.

How do you respond to a malevolence such as this? Thats the central question of Christopher Nolans film, easily the best movie every made about the usually farcical or dull world of costumed superheroes. Like the best film of 2007, No Country For Old Men, The Dark Knight explores how people choose to engage with an absurd universe ruled by random chance and casual cruelty.
Bruce Wayne deals with the guilt, pain and fear that accompany such an existence by creating the Batman, a heavily armored crimefighter without guilt, fear or pain. He escapes from the powerlessness of life by embodying omnipotence. He escapes from the meaningless of life by dedicating himself to one cause with total focus justice and the meting out of said. In the short term, this means jumping from rooftops and striking fear into the Gotham criminal element through the liberal application of fists, batarangs, and keen detective work. In the long term, this means inspiring the citizens of Gotham through his example to live honestly within the system they profess to uphold. If cops would stop taking bribes and start taking down gangsters, Batman would be able to ride off into the sunset...if he could bear it. In the meantime, Batman can work out his demons by tuning up the demimonde. The cost of all this power and purpose is alienation and unresolvable internal conflict. Batman fights to defend the system, but he breaks the law with every ride in the Batmobile (no way is that thing street legal). His most important goal is to make Gothams criminal justice bureaucrats honest guardians of the public trust, but his liaison with the Gotham Police Department requires Lt. Jim Gordon to ignore the law by failing to apprehend him. This conflict, coupled with the oppressive secret that Bruce Wayne must carry with him every day, make him utterly isolated from the system and the city he loves. It also keeps him from the woman he loves, Assistant District Attorney Rachel Dawes, forcefully played by Maggie Gyllenhaal, who knows his secret identity, and who refuses to be with him as long as Bruce Wayne, the man she loves, is merely a front for the Batman.
When non-caped crusader District Attorney Harvey Dent takes office (and starts dating Rachel), with a promise to clean up Gotham using proper legal channels, Bruce Wayne sees the chance to retire his cowl for good. But not if the Joker has anything to say about it.
Most of the time in films, comic book villains seem to wear silly costumes for no more reason than...thats what villains in comic books DO. Heath Ledgers Joker is a different breed. Every sinister giggle, every guttural snarl, every nauseating lick of the lips, show the audience what the face paint and motley mean. For the Joker, every concept of humane behavior, from love to honor to dignity, and every human institution, is a fraud, a hideous joke people play on each other and on themselves. But nobody acknowledges this, and the Jokers mission is to let as many people in on the joke as he can. Ledger channels the manic nihilism of the character through a live-wire intensity and a parade of textured tics and vocal mannerisms, transforming him from a mere symbol of anarchy into a nightmare made flesh. The Joker is made even more compelling by the fact that he has a good point. Who among us hasnt been sickened by societys smug hypocrisy? Theres a perverse pleasure in watching him torment pillars of righteousness like Dent, Gordon and Batman, using their principles as weapons against them, forcing them to reconcile the essential paradoxes of their natures through the gleeful application of savagery.
All of this angst and moral ambiguity plays out through a dizzying action plot that features some of the most purely entertaining and unnerving sequences in the Batman canon. the intensely focused performances of Ledger, Christian Bale and Aaron Eckhart as Dent are matched by a dread-soaked atmosphere, propulsive direction, and a canny editing choices. Crucial events happen offscreen, forcing the audience to piece things together as they go. It enhances the Jokers seeming omnipresence and the sense that Gotham is slowly succumbing to chaos. A prominent feature of the films score is a unbroken, atonal note that sings in the background whenever the Joker is about the strike. Its deliciously unsettling, and it reflects the nature of the movie as a whole its one long, sustained note of heightened tension and fear, with no prospect of release, even as the credits role. Similarly, the movie channels anxieties about terrorism and the ethical response to it without offering the comfort of resolution or pat answers. Its all accumulated tension, the only catharsis available in the amazing action scenes, with the knotty philosophical and personal questions left unanswered.

You either die a hero or you live long enough to see yourself become the villain. 
No matter how many times I watch this film, I am always in complete awe of Heath Ledgers Joker. It is insane. Its a performance so singular and so electric that it rewrote how movie villains can be. 
It is at the center of what makes The Dark Knight so incredible. There is no doubt about it. 
His Joker is a whirlwind of menace and dark humor or as he says, an unpredictable agent of chaos. Where Batman Begins was all about Bruce Wayne finding a philosophy or an ideal to uphold, the Joker here does the same thing and its what makes him so much more terrifying. That deep down, people are as ugly and as selfish as he is. All it takes to reveal it is the right push. 
Even though his performance is mainly what we remember, The Dark Knight has plenty of other aspects that make it an incredible ride. You almost forget it features a man dressed as a bat. 
I stand by my statement that Christian Bale is the best Bruce Wayne. Hes a man that is constantly pulled between the life he wants and the life hes chosen. A hero who learns that victory sometimes demands sacrifice and that heroism can mean being hated for doing the right thing. 
His battle is as much against his own limitations as it is against crime. Juggling these moral compromises that Gotham forces upon him constantly. 
Bruce Wayne wants to retire the Batman, hand over the city to Harvey Dent and finally be with Rachel. Nolan, however, twists the knife. The closer that Batman gets to his goal, the more the Joker forces him into impossible choices. 
The action itself is fantastic. The Batpod roaring down the streets. An eighteen-wheeler flipping end over end. The chaos of the set pieces mirrors the unraveling morality of Gotham itself. Yet, for all of its explosions and chases, The Dark Knights most intense moments are quiet ones. A simple coin flip or a boat full of frightened people holding detonators. Or, a Joker in a nurses outfit casually strolling away from an exploding hospital. 
There really is just so much to appreciate here. Between Wally Pfisters cinematography turning Gotham into a battlefield or Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howards score giving unbearable tension to every scene. Goosebumps. 
The Dark Knight is about order vs. chaos, but more importantly, it discusses how both forces live within every person. Harvey Dents arc is obviously the clearest showing of this. 
Five stars, without hesitation. Not because its flawless, but because it proved that a superhero movie could be as thoughtful and resonant as any prestige drama. 
Even after 17 years of the MCU and countless DC attempts, The Dark Knight still remains one of the best superhero films of the 21st century.

The movie quote heard around the world... WHY SO SERIOUS? ... Lets put a smile on that face.
So here we  go......
Even calling The Dark Knight a game changer when it comes to modern super hero movies is under selling it. Director Christopher Nolan did a great job of reintroducing us to Batman, but he completely out did himself with the level of realism and morale conflict he incorporated into this sequel. And to make a comic book story line like Batman vs the Joker work in an action movie reminiscent of Michael Manns Heat, is a towering achievement. But what really makes it all come together was Heath Ledgers iconic Oscar winning performance as the Joker. And he may have gotten too lost in the role, since he died not long after making the film. 
Its simple. We, uh, kill the Batman.
Nolan starts the film with an amazing setup for this character with the opening bank heist scene. It works so well to quickly show how brutal he is, as we see each one of these meaningless henchmen get picked of one by one as they talk about the Jokers growing reputation. 
Some men just want to watch the world burn.
Real world fears give the Joker some actual weight as a villain. He commits acts of terrorism like blowing up a hospital, and scare tactics like making a hostage torture video similar to those created by middle eastern terror groups. His look is so unsettling with the smeared clown makeup, greasy green hair, and puffy lips with those signature smiling scare marks. It was such a clever touch to further enhance that sense of unease, with him constantly licking his lips like a cat. 
He is a truly terrifying on screen presence with how spontaneous he is, like in the opening scene with the other gangsters when your heart skips a beat when he slams one of their heads into a pencil. But the most tense and disturbing moments are when we see how much of a unreliable narrator he is, while putting his knife into the mouths of victims and telling them various stories about how he got his scares.
Do you want to know why I use a knife? Guns are too quick. You cant savor all the... little emotions.
So is Ledgers Joker better than Jack Nicholsons performance in the original? Well yes, but it is not fair to compare based on how drastically different their approaches to the character are.
It is so heartbreaking to see the Jokers final moments on screen when he tells Batman that they will forever repeat this cycle of Batman stopping but not killing him .... since everyone knew Ledger had died when the movie was released. So we knew the Jokers final statement would never come true in terms of seeing Ledgers genius take on the Joker ever again.  
I dont want to kill you! What would I do without you? Go back to ripping off mob dealers? No, no, NO! No. You... you... complete me.
The performance is so great that it totally over shadows how great a job Aaron Eckhart did as Harvey Two-Face Dent.   
The hazy comic book feel of Batman Begins has been whipped away in The Dark Knight in favor of showing Gotham as a vast real life city, which is actually Chicago. You could also interrupt this visual change as a way of showing that Batman has eliminated much of the crime in the city, thus giving the city a more polished look. This cinematography from Wally Pfister is simply gorgeous. There is such a strong use of the color blue throughout, and it especially looks great in that iconic shot of Batman with his cape flapping in the wind, while he is reflecting at the site of a building explosion. I also love the depth they give to long rooms by shooting them wide and from a distance, like the Wayne Enterprises board room and Batmans lair in he city. BTW, that lair was a brilliant touch to show how Batman could realistic respond to crime in downtown Gotham.
Hans Zimmer continued to fine tune the score he created for Batman Begins, by added even more percussion and electrical sounding rhythms to amp up the tension, that can be heard right from the start during the opening bank heist scene. From those opening moments only you can tell that they took extra care in crafting the sound design to really emphasize noises like shattering glass, and grappling hooks being fired. But my favorite is how you can hear the strong sound of Batmans wings flapping in the wind, while he is flying thru the sky in Hong Kong.  
A really interesting touch I noticed this time around is how there is no score in the opening of the scene where Joker is attacking the armored car, and Batman comes in with the Tumbler Batmobile again. I think this works great in two ways, first no music gives the scene a more realistic feel. Second, we saw an action scene involving the Batmobile like this in the previous film, so you will notice the score finally does kick in when the new Bat-Pod motorcycle was revealed. I really admire how in each film Nolan cranked up the coolness factor by introducing new Bat vehicles into his arsenal. Speaking of the Bat-Pod, that sequence where he flips the semi-truck might be one of the most bad ass moments in any Batman film, which is then immediately followed up by how cool it is to see the Bat-Pod turn around by running up a wall.
For a superhero movie, The Dark Knight is extremely heavy when it comes to the story, so it was nice to get a solid action scene early on to see Batman take out his familiar foe the Scare Crow and couple of goons, by perfectly timing his jump down on their van in a parking garage. Everyone rags on Bales over the top gruff voice, but now I see that it works best in just short bursts. When he uses it during moments of extended dialogue with commissioner Gordon, he starts sounding like he has a frog in his throat.
Spoilers...
The final action set piece comes during the first of the movies two climaxes, one for each villain. In order to track the joker down, Bruce constructs this sonar tracking system that functions off the waves omitted from cell phones. This again calls back to the political environment we were in when this film came out, when politicians were debating about how ethical Government monitoring of communications was to track crime, but at the same time be sensitive to the right citizens have for privacy. But the tool pays off big time for creating some outstanding visuals for the sequence where he takes down the Joker. The great visuals we get show Batman having blue x-ray vision like in a video game, where he can see the locations of all the bad guys in the building.            
Writer and director Christopher Nolan layers in some big themes to add weight to the narrative including chance, good versus evil, and fallen figure heads. Chance speaks for itself since it becomes Two Faces obsession once he emerges, and starts seeking vengeance on everyone responsible for Rachels death. 
I think the plot thread that does make the story a bit clunky is with Rachel writing the letter to Bruce about deciding to marry Harvey. But then Alfred decides it would be better to let Bruce live with the notion that she would return to him, once he no longer has to be Batman. It does tie up Rachels story line nicely, but I find it to be the least compelling part of the story. Ultimately this all ties in with how Commissioner Gordon and Batman were hoping to make Harvey become an unstoppable District Attorney and eliminate organized crime for good, which gets torn down by the Jokers plan. It was such a brilliant little touch to have the Joker wear a Dent campaign sticker when he comes to confront him in the Hospital. It is a real slap in the face based on Dents downfall, but he is way too infuriated to care.       
You either die a hero or you live long enough to see yourself become the villain.
Despite being cliche, the good versus evil theme is what really elevates the Jokers role in the story. After multiple watches I have begun to pick on how he was able to corrupt cops in Gordons department in order to pull off his plan. And this can be as innocent as one of the cops confessing they accepted getting paid off, in order to help pay for some medical bills. I used to think the final pay off for this theme with the boats was a bit cheesy, but this time I found myself getting way more immersed in the situation. During the Jokers final fight with Batman, you can tell that he thinks those people will lose their humanity and blow the other boat up, in order to save their own lives. There are some touching moments on the boats involving these people who we have just been introduced to, dealing with this dilemma which helps us feel the same pressure of making this choice. Is a convicts life less valuable than the average person? ... and who are we to make such a decision?         
The first couple times I saw The Dark Knight, I thought the plot did drag some in the third act. But now I see how all the emphasis on the politics of showing how Joker made Harvey fall from grace, is what makes the tragic part of Batman having to become an anti-hero by being involved in the cover up to protect Harveys legacy work. This in turn elevates this epic super hero film not only into the definitive Batman movie, but also arguably into Christopher Nolans cinematic masterpiece.  
Because hes not our hero. Hes a silent guardian. A watchful protector. A Dark Knight.

The Dark Knight is a turning point, a cinematic awakening to me. It was the movie that made me fall in love with cinema, the one that showed me how powerful, devastating, and exhilarating a story could feel on screen. Whenever I return to it, it feels personal, like revisiting a moment in my life when everything changed. For years, it has held its place as my second favorite film (number one is LOTR of course) of all time, and that says something about how deep it runs in my veins. 
And at the heart of that impact is Heath Ledger. What a performance! Watching him as the Joker moves me. Its a great loss for the world that we wont get to see more of him. His Joker isnt just a simple villain he is chaos incarnate, a court jester, messenger of chaos cloaked in grease paint and anarchy. Ledgers transformation is the kind of thing you only witness a handful of times in cinema history, the same kind of raw, devastating brilliance he gave us with Ennis Del Mar in Brokeback Mountain. With these two roles alone, he cemented himself as one of the greatest actors of all time. 
Joker isnt a cartoonish trickster. Hes something far more terrifying, unpredictable, gleeful in destruction, and philosophically profound in the most disturbing ways. He slithers through Gotham, dismantling order with a grin and a matchstick, whispering lines that linger long after the credits roll. Why so serious? is a thesis for his entire existence, a challenge to morality, to structure, to us. Introduce a little anarchy. Upset the established order, and everything becomes chaos. Thats not just a villain talking, thats a prophet of doom, a man who wants to prove that everyone, no matter how righteous, is just one bad day away from becoming like him. And my favorite? Im like a dog chasing cars. I wouldnt know what to do with one if I caught it. That line is genius because it strips away the romanticism of villainy, he doesnt want power he wants the world to burn, simply because he can. Every scene of his is adrenaline-filled enough to get me out of my seat, but I think the magic trick scene is my second favorite. 
Ledgers Joker steals the film. Every scene with him feels electric, almost dangerous, like the movie could detonate at any moment. Thats why The Dark Knight is a crime saga dipped in nihilism, a meditation on chaos and order, and it dares to go places most blockbusters never dream of. Its ruthless, characters die, ideals crumble, and no one feels safe. The film has the courage to burn its own heroes, to show that the line between savior and monster is terrifyingly thin. That brutal honesty makes it timeless.
And lets not forget one of the most chilling things the Joker doeshe doesnt just cause chaos he creates it in others. He takes Gothams White Knight, Harvey Dent, the man who was supposed to save the city, and twists him into Two-Face. That transformation is brutal and heartbreaking because it feels so earned like the Joker didnt just break a man, he broke an ideal. Turning hope into horror with just a push, he proves his point anyone can fall. Thats what makes him terrifying, he doesnt destroy buildings, he destroys souls.
And then theres Hans Zimmer. God, what a genius. His score is pure adrenaline, pure emotion. That razor-sharp Joker theme, that sinister string that feels like a blade against your nerves, its genius in its simplicity. And then those massive, crashing crescendos during the chase scenes? Zimmer makes me feel like Gothams fate is my fate. When the music soars, my chest tightens when it drops into silence, Im holding my breath. Even though Ive watched it dozens of times, this is the first time the music has touched me so deeply. I think watching it on a big screen with a massive sound system had an impact. 
I wish I were a girl who saw Batman Begins in the cinema and waited with insane excitement for The Dark Knight, who participated in conversations about how Heath Ledger would portray the Joker, and who got the best seat at the cinema on the day it first came out, instead of being a snotty 4-year-old child in 2008. Do you have a time machine or something? If so, Im in a hurry! 
Even if Gotham doesnt need The Dark Knight anymore, I will always need him.

Ever since I first watched The Dark Knight, its always been a favourite of mine, and four watches later it remains that way. Ive always been in between 4.5 or 5 but I think this watch certifies its position as a four and a half star film. There are some little flaws throughout but not enough to stop this from being one of the greatest comic book movies ever made.
Living up to the incredible origin story of Batman in Batman Begins was a very difficult task but Christopher Nolan, as usual, smashed it out the park. He took everything which made Batman Begins great, and made it even greater, with deeper themes, bigger and better action sequences and more memorable characters. Nolan went from creating one of the best introductions to a trilogy to one of the greatest sequels in a trilogy.
Of course I cant write a review about The Dark Knight without mentioning Heath Ledgers portrayal as the Joker. And Im going to write a paragraph about him, because he deserves it. Its honestly such a shame he passed away because he was incredibly talented and unfortunately very young. Such a deserved Oscar win for him, because he didnt act as The Joker, he became him. Heath transformed himself into this psychopathic anarchist and criminal mastermind, an agent of chaos. 
There is obviously a theory about the Joker being the hero of the film, which I do see more in every rewatch, but I still like to see him as the villain. He is without doubt the greatest antagonist in film, alongside Darth Vader. Not only is he in awesome villain, but he is an exceptional character to study. His motives and manipulation of others is genius and his colourful clothing mixed with smeared clown makeup just makes him look stylish yet sick.
Not only does The Dark Knight have the greatest antagonist but it also obviously has the greatest protagonist in Batman. Alongside Samwise Gamgee and Gollum from The Lord Of The Rings, Batman is my favourite character in film, whether its Bales portrayal, Pattinsons portrayal or even a Lego batman. I love almost everything about him. His costume, his mask, the way in which he fights crimes, how he stays in the shadows, and the fact that he became Batman because of his fear. Does that mean because I have a massive fear of spiders that I can become Spiderman, Im not too sure.
Although I adore Christian Bale as an actor and a person, he is quite easily one of my favourite actors of all time, his voice as Batman is something I really dislike. It feels so goofy and unnatural and to me, it seems like he tries to hard with it. Similar to Batman Begins though, he is such a good Bruce Wayne. 
The other performances in The Dark Knight are also really good. I personally prefer Maggie Gylenhaal to Katie Holmes as Rachel, mainly because I just think her performance seems more natural and she suits the character more. Aaron Eckhart is often overshadowed by Heath because his performance as Harvey Dent and Two Face is exceptional and really underrated in my opinion. He plays both a district attorney and a complicated and mentally destroyed villain to near perfection.
The Dark Knight is non stop fun and entertainment for its entire runtime. Right from the opening second, its immersive and captivating due to the instant heist and twisted story. That scene definitely took inspiration from another favourite of mine, Heat. It is the perfect introduction to the Joker, as it shows both the dark and the comedic side to him.
My personal favourite scene is probably the interrogation scene. It is the first opportunity that Batman gets to have an extended conversation with the Joker. The writing here is genius, perfectly illustrating why they have such a great rivalry. This is also the scene where Heath is at his absolutely best. His laughing, facial expressions and the constant licking of his lips is just so good to watch. 
Other unbelievable scenes include the Why So Serious, the Joker crashing the party, the car chase underground, the blowing up of the hospital and the final thought-provoking sequence on the boats. All of these scenes listed above could honestly be in like my top fifty favourite scenes ever, theyre just so damn good in their own ways and I will never get bored of watching them.
Also another important factor of Nolans masterpiece is the deeper themes. These include justice and judgement, the impact of defeat, principles and order. It is also a tale about the duality of good and evil, as you cannot have good without evil, or evil without good. This duality is not just about the Joker and Batman, but also Batman and Bruce Wayne due to him living two lives and also arguably Harvey and Rachel.
The cinematography is also outstanding, beautifully showing the high scale buildings and the dark surroundings. Also the use of colour is exceptional, particularly the colours blue and orange. The blue showcasing the police and Batman, as well as emotion, and orange depicting the distrust and caution created by the Joker. Finally, the score is intense, the action is cool and the editing, although a little choppy in places, is really good too.
All in all, The Dark Knight, fifteen years on from its release, remains as one of the greatest superhero movies of all time. Not only because of the iconic performances, but due to the fact that it is more than just a superhero film. It does unfortunately drop in rating but it will always be a favourite of mine, for providing me so much entertainment but also for getting me into film in the first place.

Now that were just (kind of) starting to move on from this realm of never-ending superhero fatigue, its getting easier and easier to recall a period when a big-budget superhero film actually meant something of critical worth to general audience members, not by promising to swindle them by jingling keys with their favorite characters and calling it a day, but by actually dishing out an enthralling experience well worth a few hours of their time and their eager handful of some meager 7 bucks. And as the single highest-rated film of its genre on Letterboxd, I was heading into The Dark Knight with marginally higher expectations over the promising contents of its maniacally alluring giftbox, and sure enough, I found myself to have been pleasantly surprised by it, even if I didnt seem to enjoy it quite as much as most people did.

If we were to talk about both sides of the same coin, those being technical and thematic, then this film can simply leave a lot to be desired, often inconsistently the cinematography here is unremarkable for the most part, being more so utilitarian and boilerplate in contrast to the comic-book aspirations of the narrative in which its applied over. That abnormally shoehorned side plot involving some wannabe Italian mobsters, a vaguely Eastern European macho-man and a Hong Kong tycoon feels surprisingly undercooked (although I cant tell from which cuisine that would be). Harvey Dents formidable transition into Two-Face lacks in dramatic weight due to it just being the pitiful byproduct of some tragic accident rather than a deliberate unraveling of his decaying psyche and troubled philosophy. And finally, that bittersweet ending concerning Batmans legacy to the people of Gotham feels marginally forced and unearned, as if the stakes of the story suddenly became inflated just to half-engineer the vague premise of a potential sequel, rather than setting up what could have been a logically organic resolution to the dramatic events that are exclusive to this entry in particular.

But Ill be damned how, despite my general burst of critiques, I still enjoyed the overall viewing experience that is, once taking into consideration its unprecedented ambitions for your average superhero flick. I loved those sweeping aerial shots of the city shown from up above, punctuating not only a physical scale of verticality but also this unearthed magnitude of the gravity of the story depicted. That saturated yet desolate color palette renders Gotham into this minuscule playground ideal for pandemonium abrewing, with some top-tier action and suspense that lands its fully intended blow, leading the viewer cautiously anxious regarding where the Joker could be sharply concealed from the ruling eyes of the law, and what type of lunatic horseplay he was predetermined to bring to fruition next, almost as if he were this universal harbinger of chaos rather than a singularly clad man of devilishly fickle motives. And need I say anything about Heath Ledgers performance? You already know how impeccable it is.

So dont get me wrong The Dark Knight is ultimately a great motion picture by execution alone, although I wouldnt go as far as to consider it this untouchable grand tour of the superhero genre as others would. Its couple of flaws are rather bothersome and ever-present, yet they are just sufficiently eclipsed by the lofty entertainment value of those immense cinematic highs that manage to overshadow them. But to be honest, for my 9 bucks, I much prefer Matt Reeves version of the black-caped crusader.

Like most of Christopher Nolans filmography, The Dark Knight banks heavily on the appearance of intelligence. Nolan is not a lazy director, and he knows how to hold the audiences attention, as well as how to weave deep themes into big, stupid blockbusters. His unique visual style, coupled with the interesting concepts he deals with, has led many moviegoers to name him the second coming of Kubrick (despite never having seen any of the latters films). But Nolans films are rarely deep. He applies a thin veneer of thematic weight to his stories, neglecting his characters and actors in the process, and his smoke-and-mirrors approach to filmmaking does not hold up under close examination.
Take, for instance, the negotiation scene in The Dark Knight, where a blackmailer tries to scam Morgan Freemans character out of millions of dollars by asserting (correctly) that Wayne Enterprises is building technology for Batman. The blackmailer makes no mention of Batmans identity-- his sole claim is that the company is secretly funding Batmans crime-fighting endeavors. Freemans character then jumps to the conclusion that the blackmailer has discovered Batmans identity, and inadvertently reveals Bruce Waynes double life to the blackmailer in an attempt to scare him straight. And for some reason, this seems to work. The audience cheers. Fuck yeah! Morgan Freeman sure showed him!
This is one of many examples in which this movies internal logic does not cohere at all. The motivations of the characters, and the decisions they arrive at, dont make a lick of sense. Lets look at another scene-- a man holds a gun to the head of the psychopath who killed his fiancée and burned half his face off. He has every motivation to pull the trigger. Instead, he leaves it up to chance. The flip of a coin, to be precise. The Joker wins that particular coin toss, and lives to fight another day, all while Two-Face decides to go after the REAL villains-- the innocent children of a police officer. This is a person who (we are expected to believe) was an upstanding citizen, a white knight of the law, mere days before. Perhaps he wasnt too great of a guy after all.
Nolan apologists will tell us that this character has suffered a mental breakdown, gone insane, and that he is no longer capable of thinking rationally-- even of thinking in terms of his own interests. To anyone who cares about well-written characters, this is not only unrealistic, its uninteresting too. When your villains are motivated solely by primal instincts of revenge and chaos, it makes for a very simplistic movie. The Joker may be an unstoppable force, yes but thats all he is, nothing more. If he werent supported by such an astonishingly great performance, hed be a very boring character indeed (Jared Leto, anyone?). 
When people discuss the acting in The Dark Knight, and in Nolans films in general, they tend to focus solely on Heath Ledgers performance. They ignore the wooden Christian Bale, the obnoxious Maggie Gyllenhaal, and Aaron Eckharts horribly rushed and silly character arc. I agree wholeheartedly that Ledger is fantastic in this movie, but there is nothing holding him up. In fact, he overshadows the storys hero to the point that he almost detracts from the film as a whole. We come to dread the scenes in which he is absent (which is most of the film), and are instead treated to a boring crime syndicate subplot that ultimately contributes very little to the films story. I can recall with 90 accuracy the scene in which the Joker sticks his head out the window of a moving car, howling like a mad dog. But the ten-minute sequence with Batman in Hong Kong? I had to look this film up on Wikipedia just to confirm that it was, indeed, Hong Kong. A solid half-hour could easily be shaved off of this movie, and it wouldnt lose much. 
A lot of people whose opinions I respect love this movie. I accept that. At the same time, I cant bring myself to even call it mediocre. Its horribly paced, the characters arent written particularly well, and the acting (aside from Ledger) adds nothing to the film. Nolans a fine visual director, but as always, my judgement has to come down to story and characters, and this movie doesnt excel in either department. The only character I felt any emotional attachment to was the Joker, and that was only through a sort of grim fascination. Sorry, Nolan fans. But even when I first saw this movie, back when I was going through my all-superhero-movies-are-awesome phase, I didnt care much for it. If it werent for Ledger, this thing would be truly dismal.

This movie is my first love. It was my first discovery of the importance of cinema within me. When I first watched it years ago, I thought this is the best movie ever made. Years, rewatches, and hundreds of movies Ive watched havent changed that. Nolans magnum opus. I know every scene, every line by heart. That chilling music has been echoing in my ears for years. I was a high school girl when I first watched it, and it was my first crush. Thats when I realized that boys dont mean much to me, movies are better. THIS IS MY MOVIE! And I finally saw it in theater. Oh my god, I almost sobbed. 
After the first film, The Dark Knight does something new. Batman Begins was a heros self-discovery, his first blow to evil. Now, as he tries to avoid drowning in the complex waters of heroism, he encounters the joker, unknowable face of evil. Stylish, tough, epic. Gothams dark streets, rainy, gloomy weather, neon police sirens, skyscrapers, guns, and a black-cloaked knight. The vibe is delicious. Even though Gotham may seem like a broken city in the grip of despair, plagued by crime, I want to live there. Theres something about this city that draws me in. I love all its hustle and bustle, its shadows.
Because hes the hero Gotham deserves, but not the one it needs right now. So well hunt him. Because he can take it. Because hes not our hero. Hes a silent guardian, a watchful protector. A dark knight.
Gotham now has a new knight Harvey Dent. The polar opposite of Batmans darkness, mystery, and harshness. He relies on the law, not his powerful weapons. Hes all eyes on him, open. Hes a romantic lover, with a heart that beats with warmth. Hes the hero Gotham needs, the white knight. He radiates hope. Thats what laws are for. To act as a scale that promises equal treatment for everyone. To show that no one will get away with evil and crime. Unfortunately, just as in society, laws are not enough in Gotham. We need law enforcement officers brave enough to enforce them transparently. Thats why Harvey Dent is important as Batman. While Harvey may seem perfect, what makes him two-face doesnt happen overnight. He was brave enough to sacrifice himself, but he was also too fragile to bear the pain of a loved one. Hes not a symbol like Batman, because hes human. Batman is all about principles, Harvey is all about emotions. Harvey, like us, breaks down, makes mistakes, fears, loves, hates, goes mad. He may be the White Knight, but he can never be the Dark Knight. Because hes human, but Batman is a hero. Its clear that Harvey and Bruces love for Rachel isnt just for drama. Shes their way out, the light at end of the tunnel. The relief theyll find when they achieve their ideals. And when Rachels gone, so is their hope. Rachel must go, because a hero is all alone. Because his broken heart, broken bones, exclusion, hatrednothing can stand in the way of his ideals. This is what sets Nolans Batman apart from the cliched superhero. He didnt create a superpowered, muscular, monster-fighting guy. He depicted the transformation of a person into an idea. Batman isnt an avenger who dons batsuit and kicks bad guys. Hes the idea of justice over crime. The power that comes only from the law (which, ironically, he constantly breaks). Batman, The Dark Knight, my hero.

Some men just want to watch the world burn
and Nolan lets us feel the heat.
Theres a certain kind of film that doesnt just transcend its genre it rewrites the expectations around it. The Dark Knight is exactly that. 
Nolan didnt make a superhero film. He made a heat-lamp held over the moral circuitry of a city until the wiring melted and then asked whose fault it was.
Nolan directs with a kind of austere grandeur, favoring practical spectacle over digital excess. The IMAX sequences particularly the now-iconic truck flip arent just technical achievements they ground the films operatic stakes in physical reality. 
The ferry scene, the interrogation, the hospital explosioneach one feels like the final test, yet the film keeps going, as if refusing to give the audience relief.
Wally Pfister shoots Gotham with a stark, almost documentary-like clarity, making the chaos feel immediate and inescapable. Meanwhile, Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard craft a score that pulses like a tightening vice, especially in the Jokers signature two-note motif, which feels less like music and more like a warning.
I believe, whatever doesnt kill you, simply makes you... stranger. 
The idea here is chaos as a philosophical argument. The Joker and Heath Ledgers performance has only calcified into something more extraordinary with time, a piece of committed physical poetry that makes method acting look timid doesnt want money. He doesnt want power. He wants to demonstrate something. His thesis  scratch the civilised surface and every person will choose themselves when the cost is high enough.

Opposite him, Bruce Wayne played by Christian Bale is increasingly peripheral in his own narrative, and thats by design. Batman here is not the answer hes a question. How far can one man bend the rules before he becomes indistinguishable from the chaos he fights?
You either die a hero, or you live long enough to see yourself become the villain.
The films great, underappreciated gamble is Harvey Dent. Aaron Eckhart carries the legitimate weight of the films tragedy. A man who believed in systems and institutions so completely that their failure didnt just wound him, it split him down the middle. Two-Face is not a supervillain origin story. He is what happens when hope is used against you. Thats not a genre beat. Thats a broken society.
The night is darkest just before the dawn. And I promise you, the dawn is coming.
By the time Batman chooses to become the villain in the public eye, it doesnt feel triumphant, it feels inevitable. A necessary lie to preserve a crumbling truth. The film closes not on victory, but on compromise, which somehow hits harder.
Most superhero films ask what power can do. The Dark Knight asks what it costs.
Because hes not our hero. Hes a silent guardian, a watchful protector a Dark Knight.
 Christopher Nolan  The Architect of Time

Do you renounce Satan? I do renounce him. And all his works? I do renounce them. And all his promises? I do renounce them. 
In Italy, for 30 years under the Borgias, they had warfare, terror, murder, and bloodshed. But they produced Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci, and the Renaissance. In Switzerland, they had brotherly love500 years of democracy and peace. And what did they produce? The cuckoo clock.
In America, they had the criminal underground. Decades of organized crime punctuated by violence. Victimless crimesso long as the victims were kept out of sight and thus out of mind. And what did that produce? A fortune. For the heads of the five families, yes, but also for the undertaker. Death is, was, and always will be lucrative. No wonder the undertaker believes in America.
From the outset, Francis Ford Coppolas The Godfather immerses its audience in a world of darkness. The iconic themehaunting, vaguely ethnic, vaguely mournfulsegues to a blackened roomminimal lighting, dark wood paneling, spotty amber pools of illumination. It is a world of back-room bargaining and illicit dealings, but it is also a world of family and ritual and tradition. Power and the American dream and the legacy one leaves for ones children and the lengths to which one will go to preserve ones familythey are age-old themes, the subject of countless artistic works. But Coppola weaves them together so deftly, his nearly three-hour film flies by in an instant. The grand, Shakespearean motifs are subsumed by a rich, detailed portrait of a specific way of life for a specific set of characters, granting those motifs inestimably more weight.
Structure is key to Coppolas sprawling epic. While he and co-screenwriter Mario Puzo survey a decade in the Corleone familys life, covering disparate events in disparate locales, they are deceptively discursive but are careful never to become shambolic. Instead, they design The Godfather as a series of short films, perfectly constructed miniatures that add up to even more than the sum of their exquisite parts.
But these pieces are not like the gears of the insipid cuckoo clock. As with his Italian forebears, Coppola made his masterpiece amid the constant threat of destruction. The studio, Paramount, had a standby director on hand for Coppolas imminent firing. Paramount did not want the film set in New York, did not want it set in the postwar period, did not want Marlon Brando, did not want Al Pacino, did not appreciate Gordon Willis stunning cinematography. Everything upon which Coppola insisted, they hated. Warfare, terror, murder, bloodshed. And yet they produced the Renaissancethe highest-grossing picture of all-time for a spell, and one of the towering works of American cinema. If great art can only come from great suffering, then Coppola must have suffered indeed, yielding a textured, spellbinding film of novelistic depth and breadth.
Consider the opening scene. Connie Corleone (Talia Shire), the only daughter of Don Vito Corleone (Brando), is getting married. It is a grand celebration, and one steeped in tradition, with the Don bound to grant any reasonable request. And so we meet the undertaker, Bonasera (Salvatore Corsitto), who seeks vengeance on the boys who attacked his daughter. It is a riveting opening, a soliloquy begun in tight close-up, pulling back ever so slowly to reveal the listener, the Don. As Don Vito plays idly with a cat in his lap, we get a sense of who he iscalm, reasonable, thoughtful, but accepting of violence as a cost of doing businessand of the sphere in which he operatesone in which supplication is the price of admission. The Don may be a kind and reasonable gangster, but he is a gangster nonetheless.
As Coppolas camera roams throughout the wedding celebration, chronicling the party, the food, the dancing, the laughing outside, and the goings-on, the favors being granted, the barrage of negotiations inside, we are given a sense of all of the major players and their roles within this universe. Sonny (James Caan), the eldest son, is a hothead and a womanizera big dick with a big dick. Tom Hagen (Robert Duvall), the familys adopted foundling, is quiet and reserved and logical. The Dons caporegimes, Clemenza (Richard Castellano) and Tessio (Abe Vigoda), are a Laurel and Hardy pairthe former a fat and gregarious galoot, the latter much milder and more observant. Fredo (John Cazale), the middle son, is the proverbial fifth wheel, dim and powerless. Paulie (John Martino), one of the familys underlings, is young and impressionable and susceptible to being bought as he eyes the cash in Connies purse. Luca Brasi (Lenny Montana), a Corleone enforcer, is a sweet, slow-witted oaf, loyal to a fault but awkward. And youngest son Michael (Pacino) is on the straight and narrow, a war hero, reluctant to be involved with his family. He is the smart one, the one with a legitimate future, the one whowith his bright and bubbly girlfriend, Kay Adams (Diane Keaton)does not belong in this world.
What appears to be an informal, unstructured slice of life serves as invisible, carefully choreographed table setting. Small details, never underlined, establish the personalities and the relationships. Sonny smashes a camera and tosses money on the groundhe is volatile and reckless, and the family is rich. The Don refuses to take the family wedding picture until Michael arrivesfamily is important above all else, and Michael is the favorite. It is sublime storytelling of the sort rarely achieved, such that by the weddings end, we feel we know the Corleones and have known them for some time.
It would be a remarkable one-time feat, yet Coppola manages to reproduce it throughout the film with his succession of short stories. Any of these scenes, so beautifully shot and richly developed, could be plucked from the film and work on its own. Tom flying to California to confront Jack Woltz (John Marley), a movie mogul denying the Dons godson, Johnny Fontane (Al Martino), a part in a big upcoming picture. The confrontation at the movie studio, the languid tour around Woltzs estate (including the stables), Woltzs ultimate refusal to bend to the Dons wishes over a grudge styled as romantic but much more about objectification and ownership. And finally, the dissolves from the courtyard to the house to Woltzs bedroom, revealing the price of his intractability. The scene begins with California sunshine and swanky music, setting it apart from the Mafia netherworld of New Yorkbut the swinging tunes give way to the famous Godfather theme as Woltz discovers what is underneath his bedsheets. It is a violation that in some ways makes no logical sense (unless perhaps Woltz was drugged), but its logistical plausibility is of little consequence. It is a profoundly unsettling intrusion, and one that demonstrates the Corleones power (and the lengths to which they will go to bring that power to bear), while directing their ire at a man who could charitably be described as unsavory.
This romanticized point of view is crucial to The Godfathers success, which is concerned with the goings-on within this family and this business as a metaphor for capitalism and the American dream in all its avaricious, destructive glory. Immortal for its contribution to cinema  one of the prime examples of filmmaking art, The Godfather is a remarkable inside-out look at the life of a mafia family that also paints an astounding portrait of organised crime. Scoring full marks in all aspects of filmmaking, be it direction, screenplay, acting, cinematography, editing or music, this crime drama immerses viewers into its world from the very beginning and narrates its story with such strong magnetic grip for the next three hours that its impossible to not be impressed  amazed by it. Even after so many viewings, there is nothing to complain about this classic, there is no weakness to exploit and with each view, the respect for this motion picture masterpiece only gets higher.
Based on the novel of the same name by Mario Puzo, The Godfather tells the story of the Corleone family, a respectable  powerful family having major underworld influences which are overseen by Don Vito Corleone, who is termed as Godfather by his peers as a token of respect. But when Don Corleone refuses to enter the drug business, a series of events are set in motion which results in an assassination attempt on the Don, increasing rivalries among the mafia families, and paves way for Dons youngest son to rise  take up his fathers job in order to protect his family and to settle all disputes. The film revolves around Michael Corleone (Dons youngest son) and even the main plot of the story is the evolution of Michael from a doe-eyed outsider, who didnt want to get into the family business, into a ruthless boss later in the story.
The direction by Francis Ford Coppola is no short of amazement. The way he filmed most of the scenes from the very beginning to the end, the casting decisions he made, the chosen locations for shooting, the remarkable screenplay  memorable quotes co-written with Mario Puzo and the overall style of narration  look of the film, its all brilliantly done. Cinematography is carried out beautifully and the decision to shoot in Technicolor print pays off enormously well for it provided this film a vintage look that wonderfully matched the timeline it represented and also added an artistic flair to the whole medium. Editing is very precisely done with each character getting enough time on-screen without robbing its expertly controlled pace. Nino Rotas score opens the film with a sad, almost funeral-like theme music, and boasts tracks which sound very unusual for a crime drama but then it also fits the films ambience remarkably well. The overall work by the entire technical crew is as much responsible for this films success as the direction, writing  performances.
As far as performances go, The Godfather features a cast of incredibly gifted actors in Marlon Brando, James Caan, Al Pacino, Robert Duvall, John Cazale, Diane Keaton, Richard S. Castellano, Talia Shire, Al Lettieri  many more, and every one of them is in top-notch form. Marlon Brando makes Don Corleone truly his own, giving his character a set of unique look  traits and delivers, possibly, the greatest performance of all time which also immortalised the character of Don Corleone in cinema forever and permanently engraved Brandos status as one of worlds finest actors. Al Pacino also makes his mark on the big stage and delivers the next great performance as Michael Corleone, plus his rise to power from a reluctant outsider into a ruthless mafia boss remains one of the most spectacular character arcs ever exhibited on film canvas. James Caan stars as Sonny Corleone, Dons hot-headed eldest son, and I dont recall Caan delivering any other performance of this calibre and same goes for Richard S. Castellano who plays Clemenza, a caporegime for the Corleone family. Other notable works include Robert Duvall as Tom Hagen, Diane Keaton as Kay Adams, Talia Shire as Connie Corleone, Abe Vigoda as Tessio  Al Lettieri as Virgil Sollozzo. All in all, there are no complains in this department either.
Telling a tale that spans ten years of the Corleone family in three hours, while also reflecting the world of organised crime with immense character depth  complexity unlike anything before it, and ingeniously blending it with impressive direction, sturdy writing, impeccable performances, striking quotes, innovative storytelling  a mesmerizing score, The Godfather is an exceptionally well-made motion picture and certainly the one with the best cast. Ever since its release, it has become the benchmark by which all the great masterpieces are measured and its influence on cinema, especially gangster genre, is unprecedented. On an overall scale, The Godfather is universally accepted as one of world cinemas finest films, arguably the greatest ever, and the performances by Marlon Brando  Al Pacino alone are the stuff of legends. Plus, this films also marks a significant moment in cinema, in my opinion, in which the baton was passed from Marlon Brando, the finest actor of his generation, to Al Pacino who later became the finest actor of the subsequent era. The film doesnt need my recommendation because its a must watch for every cinema lover. There are very few movies which are unanimously hailed as a great one from critics, filmmakers  viewers all around the world and The Godfather is unquestionably one of those classics and, in my opinion, the only one that deserves the top spot. A cinematic treasure you should neither refuse nor ignore, The Godfather is genre filmmaking at its most perfect, genuine, complete, crystalline  pure. One hundred percent recommended.

Cinema has value because of films like The Godfather. This artform, pictures at twenty four frames per second, can tell the most wonderful stories, and this is one of the best. The least controversial opinion in the world is that The Godfather is a masterpiece. Time moves forward, the seasons change, The Godfather will outlast us all.
The very first lines of The Godfather give praise to America. To these immigrants who have made a fortune, the streets are truly made of gold. To succeed, they have bought power. The iconic theme for The Godfather series may as well be the song of American Exceptionalism, or at least for a special form of American corruption. This is the story of a man, a war hero in uniform, who gets corrupted from that Americana and becomes a criminal overlord. Yet his path arises through inheritance and market forces. This is a film of gangsters who reject communism, so commit grubby deals to maintain their monopoly. The Godfather is not the story of criminals, it is the story of men in suits. A façade of respectability and you can get away with murder.
At the centre of The Godfathers fantastic ensemble is Michael Corleone, whose descent into darkness comes from a place not so evil. He starts by just wanting to protect his family, then begins to justify actions against crooked cops and vicious mobsters. That slippery slope, that corruption of purity, its a tale as old as time, the original sin if you will. The Godfather tells this over an extended time period. It is not a film of constant movement, it is one of set pieces with huge jumps in between. Every moment counts. Every shot is among the greatest of all time. Every scene avoids patronising or insulting the audience. It is all excellent.
The Godfather presents a world of crude, cruel men, and does so openly. While not an innovation, it signifies the changing mood of 70s Hollywood. Here is a gangster film that was not genre fodder. It probes the complexity and psychological depths of a gangster, examining the contradictions of a family man who could shoot somebody else. The awful violence is brief, as mostly this is a film of leadership and those who give the orders. This new kind of American cinema pushed boundaries, adopting an innovative, European style. The colours alone are noteworthy, moving from dark and textured interiors to flat outdoor realities. The real power is decided inside these rooms, the rest of the world is a less significant extension of it all.
There are two weddings in The Godfather. One extravagent and for business, one passionate and for love. A third is never shown, such is its irrelevance to the emotional power-play at hand. Which is ideal for the finale, an acceptance of the lies we have to tell ourselves. The lie that only others can be crooked. The lie that fragile masculine egos can withstand pressure. The lie that we are telling ourselves the truth. A new man has been born into power, and all it took was lies and gunshots. Its the perfect ending. The cycle continues.

While Id still choose the second film by a landslide, Pauline Kaels assertion of this being a perfect merger of commerce and art is absolutely correct - this is arguably the blueprint for the ideal form of popular narrative cinema.  Structurally magnificent - constantly astonishing in how the film doesnt follow A-B plot mechanics at all (if not traditional plot devices period) and is actually almost devoid of subtext two things were often told (whether it be teachers or producers) should not work!  Instead it derives its propulsive narrative drive (as well as flawless pacing) almost entirely via character dynamics and moments.  Aesthetically, its directly influenced by the merging of Classical Hollywood technique and 60s European Modernism of Bertoluccis The Conformist - something that should be obvious to anyone who has seen the two films even if Coppola hadnt admitted it himself.  This aesthetic is arguably the most influential thing about this movie (and by extension, both films) but at the same time aesthetics can date and often do.  The style is only one portion of this movies impact and influence, the fact that it still works today is for a myriad of additional reasons.  Theres hardly any action in this thing - instead the spectacle is in the details between characters, alliances and betrayals, universalities about family, life and death.  Coppolas own statements at the time about the film being about American business holds true - except its better explicated in the sequel, and this film works for different reasons.  Theres almost no good reason to write about Godfather 1 because it has been justly acclaimed through the years, and it remains a pillar of narrative storytelling in cinema-form.  If anything, the subtext only really comes into effect following Vitos death in the garden - itself one of the most sublime moments in cinema history.  Its here where Michaels brilliant, classical and tragic arc comes into full effect - he takes full control of the family business after running from it, he accepts the cultural specifics of his heritage after running from it, he becomes his father after running from it.  Coppola rightly saw this as the main hook which to develop the sequel with, but many of that films ideas are already here in simpler, primordial form.  The films own equivalency with gangsterism and business becomes more pronounced - before, we see Coppola have the Corelone family continue their daily lives as everyone else, as if their main source of income is the olive oil business they run as a front.  Michael accelerates this detachment plotting the murder of Barzini at his own fathers funeral - as if the time to mourn has come and gone - and most importantly the crosscutting of the murder of the Five Families with his nephews baptism. The Godfather is inserted, in its own way, in that nostalgic vein widely frequented by New Hollywood filmmakers, within which the classic genres are reworked and revitalized, according to a very explicit language, distant from previous stylistic and content conventions. The subject - the world of immigrants dedicated to crime - has in fact already been the basis of many films in the past, but thanks to the extraordinary talent of Francis Ford Coppola and Mario Puzo, and the superproduction characteristics of the project, the film can enjoy an unprecedented epic breath. The director reinvents the boundaries of the gangster-movie, placing them in the context of a majestic choral portrait that embraces more than one generation and which, narrating the story of a New York mafia family, reflects on the evils of American society, in which good and evil increasingly merge and confuse.
The Godfather is the most powerful and tragic family melodrama in the history of cinema. A film of family ceremonies (weddings, baptisms, funerals) that mix with a humanity made up of deceptions, betrayals and ferocity. Coppola masterfully emphasizes this moral ambiguity, for which on the one hand values such as a sense of honor and attachment to the family are defended, and on the other violence and murder are used to pursue ones ends. The wonderful protagonists (a successful amalgam of past stars and brilliant newcomers) are offered the space and time necessary to gradually give depth to their respective characterizations. Among these, it is impossible not to mention the monumental performance by Marlon Brando, who takes possession of the authoritative and feared mafia patriarch, giving him an absolutely unforgettable, tragic and painful consistency. No less important is the performance of Al Pacino, which expresses himself by well underlining the repressed fire and the inner restlessness of his character. At the end of the movie, the old and wise Vito Corleone will give way to his favorite son, just like the great star Brando will pass the baton to the young Pacino, an emerging star of a Cinema that will no longer be the same after The Godfather.

 In English Few films carry a mythological weight as immense as The Godfather. Its very name resonates like a cinematic entity, an unquestionable monument of the seventh art. Revisiting Francis Ford Coppolas epic is to witness a work that not only shaped modern cinema but also transcended its own fictional nature, merging into popular imagination in an almost biblical way.
The mafia has always been a fascinating theme in cinema, but what The Godfather does is humanize this criminal structure without romanticizing it. The narrative immerses us in the Corleone family with an intimacy almost documentary-like, following the decline of the patriarch and the inevitable rise of his sona man who begins as an outsider to the family legacy, only to be consumed by the fate he so desperately tried to avoid.
What makes The Godfather so timeless is its operatic approach to violence and power. Death is never gratuitous each murder carries dramatic weight and reverberates as an irreversible blow to the soul of its characters. The restaurant scene, where the son fires his first shots and crosses the threshold into criminality, is one of the most electrifying moments in film history. No music, no rushjust the sound of a passing train and a suffocating silence before the inevitable.
Moreover, Coppola imprints a near-liturgical rhythm to the narrative, with cinematography reminiscent of Renaissance paintingsdeep shadows and amber tones that envelop the characters in an aura of classical tragedy. The film does not move hastily, yet every scene is essential, every glance carries weight, every silence speaks louder than a thousand words.
And it is impossible to discuss The Godfather without praising its performances. The patriarch, with his hoarse voice and calculated gestures, becomes a father figure as fearsome as he is melancholic. But the true heart of the film is his son. His journey from idealistic outsider to ruthless warlord is built so subtly and meticulously that, by the time we reach the final scenethe door closing on his wifewe feel an overwhelming sense of loss.
The greatness of The Godfather lies in the fact that it is not just a film about gangsters, but about family, legacy, and the inevitable corruption of power. An epic that echoes like a Greek tragedy, where the pursuit of absolute control ironically results in the loss of ones own humanity. More than 50 years later, its influence remains unshaken. Some offers, simply, cannot be refused.

Following the unfortunate American tradition of not giving the full recognition that outstanding geniuses deserve in their particular era, the capacity of Francis Ford Coppola of portraying a powerful crime manifesto from a partially American style came slightly unnoticed. However, this capacity would be finally recognized until the release of the highly competitive sequel The Godfather Part II (1974). The Godfather is quite possibly the best American film ever made, ranking along the superiority of Orson Welles Citizen Kane (1941), a task that already constitutes a nearly unsurpassable and considerably expert achievement. It is a film released at the exact right time that literally changed, perhaps permanently, the perspective that the audiences of the 70s, a decade that was barely starting regarding cinema, had towards the art of filmmaking. The film has changed lives and has created fans around the world, transforming Francis Ford Coppola into one of the best directors in America that completely caused a sudden filmic boom, including Steven Spielberg (The Sugarland Express 1974, Jaws 1975), George Lucas (American Graffiti 1973, Star Wars 1977) and Martin Scorsese (Mean Streets 1973, Alice Doesnt Live Here Anymore 1974), an Italian director. It has also redefined the crime genre once more, just like Elia Kazans On the Waterfront (1954) and Arthur Penns Bonnie and Clyde (1967) did during their respective decades, especially regarding the nowadays prolific gangster branch.
The Godfather is the first part of a crime trilogy, focusing on the aging don Vito Corleone and his Corleone Mafia Family that represents a very big part of the organized crime within the city of New York. The film opens with the overseeing of his daughters wedding and introduces Michael Corleone, his beloved son who has recently returned from the Second World War and who does not have the slightest interest in belonging to his fathers business. A rival of Corleone named Virgil Sollozzo seeks Vito Corleone and asks him for protection while offering a payment of drug money however, the morality of Vito does not allow him to accept the payment, an event that will eventually release a sequence of violence, death, destruction and betrayal on the Corleone family and a brutal war between different parts of the organized crime. The film received 11 Academy Award nominations for Best Costume Design, Best Film Editing, Best Music, Original Dramatic Score, Best Sound, Best Director, three nominations for Best Actor in a Supporting Role, Best Actor in a Leading Role, Best Writing, Screenplay Based on Material from Another Medium and Best Picture, winning only the last three Oscars and blasphemously losing most of the rest against the popular musical Cabaret (1972), directed by Bob Fosse, including the award for Best Director.
Francis Ford Coppolas particular approach towards the organized crime inevitably results in a cataclysmic explosion of unparalleled cinematographic brilliance. Every single talented element has been put together into a 3-hour timeless crime American masterpiece. The musical score composed by master Nino Rota has become a cinema icon, being endless times referenced throughout the upcoming decades and creating that very peculiar nostalgic and memorable feeling that makes the viewer to instantly remember the specific movie, just like Psycho (1960), 2001 A Space Odyssey (1968), The Exorcist (1973), Jaws (1975) and Star Wars (1977) managed to do, for mentioning famous examples of American filmmaking. Basically, every performance is extraordinary, forming fully developed, identifiable and even empathetic characters in the process. Marlon Brando, on the other hand, managed to portray one of the most powerful, multiphacetic and memorable film characters ever brought to the big screen, turning the appearance of a mad bulldog into a cold-blooded, fearless and loyal head of a mafia family. These talents are deliciously enlightened by a remarkable cinematography of Gordon Willis, atmospherically shooting the disciplined functioning of the underworld and capturing both the colonial beauties of the streets of Italy and a breathtaking old-New York art direction. The Seventh Art has been blessed.
The Godfather is, ultimately, a film rich in character. It plays homage of how a full organism is the consequent result of the sum of its parts. The film has different facets, from brutally portraying the world from the perspective that is usually hidden from the conventional members of a common, standard and stereotypical society to dramatically showing components that seem to resemble a Greek tragedy. Coppola reunited each and every one of the elements that could fully incarnate the interior structure of an operational mafia group, such as crime, betrayal, sex, violence, loyalty towards the family, competition, romance, marriage and passion, perhaps with the brilliant purpose of depicting a criminal portion of society that forcefully tries to fit in through the following of moral values and standards but escaping from the authorities when these standards are intentionally violated. The surprisingly graphic and merciless violence is compensated with the naturally irradiated beauty throughout, like witnessing an elegant and well-decorated orgy full of sin, which means that the story is shown from different points of view, not necessarily creating characters that could be interpreted as smarter and superior, but people who slowly climbed to the top of the world through the easiest and most incorrect path while possessing a distorted view towards the religion they possess.
This constant change of elements and perspectives would inevitably become an influential landmark for several future filmmakers, but whereas Martin Scorsese would add a strong dose of dark humor and a hyperactive pace, a fact that would influence the style of Quentin Tarantino (Reservoir Dogs 1992, Pulp Fiction 1994), Coppola orchestrated an opera of distinct emotions and striking vibes. He also managed to smarty attract audiences with a famous cast, from an eternal legend (Marlon Brando) to talented ones (Al Pacino). Characters are shown from their most human sides. Vito Corleones most relevant priorities are loyalty towards the family and the protection of the youth since it represents the future of a successful America. This argument is contradictory in its most literal sense, but it served the purpose of being a wonderfully stylish psychological complement. Vito Corleone is a young man who is unwillingly included into his own fate, experiencing a brutal change of personality while witnessing the cruelness of the world. The rest of the characters are just puppets who mindlessly feel that their obvious obligation is to obey the commands of their own Fuhrer. Their respective backgrounds remain mostly unclear, a fact that adds too much mysteriousness to the possible motives of their actions. Nevertheless, this would be one of the principal tasks held by the sequel to reveal pasts and to bring the demons to their doom.
Criminals have disguised themselves as common citizens. A film has disguised itself as a true work of art. The Godfather is much more than a merely influential and revolutionary gangster testament it is one of the best films ever made. An extraordinarily developed screenplay by one of the most passionate and stylish crime novellas ever written allowed a filmic plot to explosively unravel in front of the possibly unprepared audience. It is an epic of criminal proportions and a direct attack to the senses and cathartic emotions that may irremediably ensue. Nowadays, Coppola has got the credit that we, as faithful fans, had since the beginning, but that does not even seem to be enough. It is a towering achievement which vision will be hardly top in the future generations to come.

Adapted from Mario Puzos novel, this film is a cornerstone of American filmmaking, presenting a profound and immersive storyline.

Themes of The Godfather
Family Loyalty The movie emphasizes the importance of family loyalty. The Corleones stick together and protect each other no matter what. This loyalty is both a strength and a weakness, as it leads them into dangerous situations.
Power and Corruption The Godfather explores how power can corrupt people. Michael starts as an innocent war hero but becomes a ruthless mafia boss, showing how power changes him.
The American Dream The film also touches on the idea of the American Dream. The Corleone family, immigrants from Italy, achieve great wealth and power, but at a high moral cost.

Al Pacino is remarkable as Michael Corleone, capturing the characters evolution from a outsider to a great leader. Marlon Brando delivers an unforgettable performance as Vito Corleone who is both a loving father and a ruthless crime lord. I am absolutely speechless. What a breathtaking 3 hours. The Godfather did not disappoint and I am so unbelievably excited to watch Part II when I get the chance to. I have been holding off from watching these films because I have not seen the full trilogy be on at the same time on streaming services so when I saw last month that Netflix has added all 3 Godfather movies to their catalogue, I knew I had to watch them this November after my spooky season marathon. It is going to be tough to unpack my thoughts onto here after watching the credits roll, but I will try my best.
The poor movie I watch after this is going to only get compared to this unbelievably immersive experience Ive just had. Both Marlon Brando and Al Pacino give one-of-a-kind performances and I was honestly thinking after the movie finished I wish this was even longer. Do you know how rare that is for me? Thank the lord there is a second part, I just need to free up like half my day for it. 
Music and clever dialogue play a deceptively major role in movies that I think isnt recognised quite nearly enough. I was stunned when 1 hour 40 minutes into the film I paused it and realised how quickly the time has went by and then started to think how for a 3 hour film, this is a wonderfully entertaining watch. The beautiful music that plays throughout has such a romantic tinge to it that it makes me feel like Im in love with the film itself. The dialogue alongside the performances makes this 3 hour crime drama an enthralling story that hooks you in and keeps you there. 
However, I dont want to downplay the visuals of this film by gushing on about the analog sound design of characters speaking or mentioning the iconic and memorable soundtrack. I dont know what it is about films from the 70s (or pretty much any film that isnt shot on digital) but the warm and grainy texture makes The Godfather feel so alive!! A genuinely perfectly shot film with every scene holding weight to it - I wouldnt cut a single minute out of this movie. Every scene is like an actual painting, and I aint no artist but I can definitely tell why this movie is so timeless. I mean the use of these dark colours really sets the mood appropriately and it never once feels like fiction (even if it is) because quite frankly the cinematographer was a genius when working on this movie. The music paired with the fantastic cinematography had my eyes and ears dancing while my brain was wired in to this gripping story.
Speaking of story, the character arc Michael faces in The Godfather going from an innocent and disassociated member of the Corleone family to a man of power and corrupt morality is so utterly perfect. I think I just simply love character arcs such as this one as it is so fascinating watching family men progress into family men like in Breaking Bad (my favourite show fr). I really do love the script and direction that went into this, because the deliberate pacing and pure talent on-screen had me touched by this movie in ways movies havent touched me before.
Theres films Ive watched that I consider perfect (12 Angry Men, Prisoners, The Shawshank Redemption etc. just to name a few) but this feels like the perfect film. A masterclass in storytelling and immersion. The Godfather feels incredibly timeless and for a crime drama, theres actually lot of reflection on loyalty to our family. These characters on display may be sinful but they feel more human than I could have ever imagined.
I admire this film, and if my trajectory in life was different and I chose to be a film student, then The Godfather wouldve been my inspiration. I cannot stress enough how much I loved this film. It wowd me in a way that I thought it wouldnt be able to considering the abnormal amount of people who put high expectations on this film, and I am so glad that my expectations still got beaten. Now lets see, will I find Part II better the way everyone else does? Ill be stunned if that becomes the case.
I want to praise The Godfather more but my mind has gone blank honestly, I think its time I go to bed. I am really glad Ive finally watched this.
