In the beginning, a young war hero tells his future wife how his father helped a successful crooners career by making his manager an offer he couldnt refuse, essentially threatening him at gunpoint. Through this story, he reveals a secret that shows how menacing his family is, and how different he believes himself to be. By the end, not only does he threaten his brother-in-law, but he kills him and when his wife asks if its true, he answers, no, concluding one of the most fascinating character arcs in film. What happens in between is the greatest cinematic metamorphosis, pure magic.
This is not the story of a pure soul being corrupted, but rather the story of a man whose only choice, in order to protect someone dear, was to become like his father  and in doing so to realize that the crime that defined his fathers life could not only be justified, but was ultimately the only destiny that could allow him to succeed. This is the irony of the American Dream a man who parodied capitalism in order to expose its limits, only to find that those same limits ultimately built his power. Its an irony inherited by his youngest son, who lost his soul for the sake of blood loyalty, sacrificing principles for the sake of more powerful ones.
The fact is that some principles transcend conventional ones, and if the father didnt want to be a puppet, he had to be the one pulling the strings  like presidents who dont pull the trigger, but instead are the ones to declare war. More than an iconic cinematic allegory, the strings symbolize the thin line between being a legitimate politician and a respected criminal in other words, being Vito Corleone. He is the master who offers protection in exchange for loyalty, allowing others to act while knowing that everything is under control. Thats the point with Vito, everything is under control. When he promises that the two thugs who brutalized a poor undertakers daughter will get their comeuppance, we know he will deliver. Now, the question asked at the beginning is which of his three sons will succeed this exceptional man?
The answer relies on one scene. Michael kisses his fathers hand while he lies in danger in the hospital and says respectfully, Im with you, Pop, as a tear runs down Vitos face. His son is protecting him, and for some reason, we are almost certain that his father will survive, just as with the undertaker. The only man who inspires the same level of confidence as Vito is his son Michael, who is  ironically once again  the civilian, the non-criminal. Not because the other sons were not meant to be Dons the eldest, Sonny, was hot-headed and good-hearted the other was also good-hearted but weak-minded. Both were criminals in one way or another. Michael is the one because he has to be. More than a story of succession, its a story of destiny.
The Godfather is one of the greatest achievements ever to enrich the silver screen, mainly because of a story that everyone can relate to a man who loves his family and whose only choice is to corrupt his soul in order to protect it. Its not about crime its about the very necessities that make crime not legitimate, but justifiable. Its not about crime its about its roots. Its not a crime or gangster film, but one in which the criminal setting highlights principles such as blood loyalty, friendship, and family  values that would otherwise be meaningless in a more legitimate world. This is the thought-provoking genius of The Godfather, which made it so universally appealing, because people from every culture respect values such as courage, loyalty, family, and respect itself.
The nature of the story is one of the key pillars upon which the greatness of The Godfather has built its legendary status. I focus on this aspect because the rest requires no further proof the acting, direction, music, quotes, characters, and cinematography  every analyzable element is living proof of the films near perfection. Why should I elaborate? If youre reading these lines, you already know what I mean. So lets remain reserved and avoid excessive enthusiasm. How ironic that the film was based on a pulp fiction novel How ironic that the direction, which imbued the film with such confidence, was so subtle and imperceptible.
Coppola makes us feel like part of this family, of the Corleone. They are criminals, yes, but the intimacy of the family dynamic makes us root for them. Another irony is that the direction remains present through these small details that give the film its legendary feeling. Each death has something memorable about it, from Khartoums decapitation to Sonnys ambush, from the restaurant scene to the baptism sequence, and not to forget the two strangulations that opened and closed the series of human deaths. The details are everywhere, in the script that elevated the cinematic lexicon with iconic quotes, from delightful culinary parallels to fish-related metaphors. Its a script that transcended its source material and made the film even more legendary.
When it comes to defending The Godfather, Ill turn into its most passionate fan, but I prefer to avoid an overdose of superlatives in this review. I know the film is the greatest, not because its my personal belief, but because I cant see any film topping it, no matter what cinematic category I use  story, acting, casting, writing, scoring, editing, direction... I can find a better film in each of these elements, but not in all of them. And beyond all this technicality, The Godfather is simply a film that grows on you after several viewings, one that commands cinematic respect in every frame. The greatest...

Se a ideia por trás do vídeo é a de que The Godfather foi um filme que mudou o cinema, eu me vejo obrigado a concordar com o pessoal do canal Entreplanos.
Só que eu diria, e acho que aqui é o ponto em que o pessoal do canal Entreplanos provavelmente discordaria de mim, que mudou para pior.
Mal comparando, o sucesso e a subsequente influência de The Godfather em basicamente todo o cinema comercial produzido por toda a década de 1970 e por boa parte dos 80, 90, 2000 e vá saber até quando é análogo ao que os anos 1940 e 1950 teriam sido se Gone with the Wind tivesse exercido a maior influência sobre a produção do período ao invés de, entre muitos outros, Citizen Kane, Vredens dag, Laura, To Have and Have Not, Paisà, My Darling Clementine, Out of the Past e Rope.

Além disso, para perceber os méritos do que Coppola fez basta comparar este filme aos filmes que Scorsese realizou sob a sua influência (para perceber os deméritos, basta perceber as similaridades entre esses filmes do Scorsese e o do Coppola).

IMDBs top 4 highest rated films of all time are The Godfather, The Godfather II, The Dark Knight, and Shawshank Redemption. Among these four, The Godfather is the only one I truly believe to be deserving of this status. The Godfather is in a league of its own. TDK has a weird ethics narrative insertion in the 3rd act, terrible action shooting and fight choreography, and an underwritten romance subplot. Shawshank feels tv-standard, and the overuse of narration to speak themes literally turns it into a frustrating watch. The Godfather IIs romanticization of Vito is off-theme which messed the pacing, character revelations get redundant, and the flashback scenes really meddle with the final product. My point is none of the three are even remotely close to what The Godfather is. I know I have a tendency to coin highly rated films as overrated, but The Godfather is an exception. Its true it is THAT good. Im impressed, the public consensus is actually right. 
As much as people would want to force themselves to try and wiggle their way to finding flaws in this film, I hate to break it to you, its just perfect. The opening scene alone shows you how great the film is. I think of The Godfather as a micro-version of the history of humanity, a layered and complex epic centered on the legacy of downfall. There are countless of scenes, like the wedding in the 1st act, that contain entire truths of the whole thing Vitos sham life, his failure to protect his family from himself, the inevitability of corruption, every chess piece in a position that leads the game into one big inevitable checkmate - All one scene. Its pure magic. The way the downfall is distinctly male, particular to the pressure and pain of being a man, is even more thought-provoking to me than examining the flaws and cracks in one single mans ambition. Its incredible how on-point everything is. Every minuscule detail is a miniature of the larger picture, yet it never halts to explain visual details to the audience - its driven BY visuals. 
The Godfather features the rise of Michael and the fall of Vito. The story of The Godfather is how the old-world desires a cycle which ultimately ruins generations of families in a modern setting. Its about breaking down machismo, reverence, compassion etc. The brilliance of The Godfather was that we could sympathize with someone so violent and cruel. The goal, at least in my humble opinion, was never to respect him. Of course, the performances really do elevate the characters. The Godfather is perfectly written, perfectly acted, perfectly shot. The attention to detail is phenomenal, and the direction is outstanding. Without a doubt, one of the best of all time. Truly a timeless masterpiece

Ive just witnessed cinematic perfection.
Now, Im only a budding cinephile, but Ill say this nevertheless few films can come close to The Godfather in terms of storytelling, cinematography, thematic value, direction, and of course, acting. I couldnt take my eyes off the screen until the credits began to roll.
The technical brilliance of the film is apparent in the 40s and 50s aesthetic, in the way Francis Ford Coppola sets us up to understand the true power of the Godfather, and in the tight, merciless editing. There isnt a single unnecessary moment in the film. The cinematography and music score are haunting, giving the film a truly iconic look and feel.
Marlon Brando is the best of the lot as the eponymous Godfather. Its hard to believe that he was only forty-seven during the films shooting I could have sworn that he really was as old as he looked. Don Vito Corleone never comes across as cruel or ruthless despite the fact that he commissions so many killings, making for some of the most interesting characterization Ive ever come across on film.
Al Pacino gives a career-making performance as Michael Corleone. Quiet, suave, and handsome, his progression from a reluctant bystander to the next Don Corleone is utterly fascinating. James Caan is also excellent (bada-bing!), as is Robert Duvall and the rest of the cast. In fact, nobody in the film strikes a single wrong chord.
Although Mario Puzos novel was definitely entertaining, it had none of the elegance and restraint that is characteristic of the film. The Godfather as a film rises far above Puzos mediocre prose (though it obviously takes advantage of his excellent plot) and ignores unnecessary subplots to become what it truly is a family saga with shocking bursts of violence.
The Godfather is brilliant, gripping, and fascinating, every minute of it. The long running time all but disappears as the film pulls viewers into a dark, ambiguous world where the lines between good guy and bad guy are completely blurred.
I dont fully understand why I (and millions of other viewers) became so invested in the film. Perhaps its because The Godfather is not so much about gangsters as it is about family loyalty and making the best out of a situation you never wanted to get into. And you appreciate the power of the film all the more because it is fully apparent just how much passion, talent, and love was funneled into creating The Godfather.
Brilliant. I cant wait to watch it again. And again. And again.

Ive watched The Godfather more than a dozen times now, and every single time it feels different. It just keeps hitting me in new ways, and I keep loving it more. This time though, it was special, I finally saw it on the big screen, and honestly, it felt like a bucket list moment checked off. Completely fulfilling.
This time, while watching, I started noticing how the film is divided into parts almost like chapters each with its own storytelling rhythm.
1. The Wedding
The movie begins with Connies wedding, and in those opening 26 minutes, Coppola basically gives us a whole portrait of the family. Its like an act in itself. We meet Don Vito Corleone- dignified, calm, always about family first, a man who earns respect without raising his voice. We even get little glimpses into characters with barely a few lines Sonnys wife, for example, who knows hes cheating on her but silently endures it or Luca Brasi rehearsing his speech in nervous devotion. Sonny comes across hot headed and impulsive, already reckless in his personal life. Michael feels like an outsider at this point, charming Kay with the stories, but clearly someone who wants to keep a distance from the family business. Even in subtle ways, Coppola sets the whole chessboard for whats to come.
And heres something that struck me this time when Vito tells Johnny Fontane, A man who doesnt spend time with his family can never be a real man, Sonny walks into the room right then. It feels almost pointed as if Vito, without saying it directly, is scolding his son for his infidelity and recklessness. Maybe Im reading too much into it, but it felt intentional.
2. The reach of Don Corleone 
Right after the wedding, we get Tom Hagen flying to Hollywood to help Johnny Fontane get that film role. Its short, but it perfectly shows the Dons reach. Woltz thinks hes untouchable until he wakes up with that horses head in his bed, and suddenly we understand just how far Corleone influence goes. This part cements that Vito isnt just a neighborhood figure, hes national.
3. Sollozzos Offer
By the time Sollozzo enters, the table is fully set. We know who everyone is, and now the story moves. Sollozzo represents the future- the drug trade but Vito refuses because it threatens the familys legitimacy. Here we see a contrast Sonny, impulsively, shows interest, revealing the cracks, while Vito holds firm. That rejection kicks off the chain of betrayals and violence, and then the attempt on Vitos life just flips everything.
4. Michael Steps In
This is Michaels turning point. At first, hes the clean one, the war hero, the outsider. But when Vito is in danger at the hospital, and Michael stands guard, he whispered to his father, Im with you now, you feel the shift. Its heartbreaking and powerful the son who wasnt supposed to be part of this world stepping into it. Thats when Vitos tears mean so much. And then, of course, Michael murders Sollozzo and McCluskey- one of the most iconic sequences ever. When Vito later asks Tom about Michael, and learns it was him, you can feel the fathers silent heartbreak. He wanted so much more for his youngest. That moment foreshadows his later conversation where he admits he hoped Michael would be a senator or governor.
5. Michael in Sicily
Honestly, one of my favorite stretches of the film. Michael in Sicily feels like a whole other movie inside The Godfather. Its slower, poetic we see him embracing his heritage, falling in love with Apollonia, and for a moment you think maybe hes found peace, something pure away from the corruption. But tragedy follows him- his brother Santino murdered back home, and then Apollonia killed by the bomb meant for him. Sicily becomes the place where Michael loses innocence completely.
6. The rise of Michael 
Back in New York, Vito returns to the table but only briefly. He makes peace between the families, but really, its the last act of the old Don. The scenes where Michael starts taking command show everything without needing words. That moment where he dismisses Tom from being consigliere, we see that Vito just pats him, like saying yeah, you did good, its the subtle handover of power. Michael is the head now, and you can feel how different his style is.
7. Vitos last words
One of the most beautiful scenes. Vito, old and tired, sits with Michael in the garden, talking about the familys future. He confesses how he never wanted this life for him, how he always dreamed his son would live A life of legitimacy. But in the same breath, he passes down everything he knows warnings about betrayal, lessons on survival, the weight of the family legacy. Its a quiet, intimate moment a father giving his son both love and regret, wisdom and burden, right before his death. Vito dies playing with his grandson- the quietest and most human of deaths for such a towering man.
8. The Baptism
Maybe the greatest sequence ever put on film. Michael stands as godfather in the church, renouncing Satan, while his men wipe out all the rival bosses. The parallel editing, the organ music, the way Michaels calm face is juxtaposed with brutal killings- its filmmaking perfection. Its not just the murders its the birth of the new Don.
9. The Godfather
The final transformation. Michael consolidates everything- killing Carlo, cleaning house, securing his power. Then the iconic closing Kay asks about Carlo, Michael lies, and the door shuts in her face. That door closing is everything. Michael has become what his father never wanted him to be. He is The Godfather.
This time I also got completely caught up in the cinematography on the big screen it just looks stunning. Its Foibles

It has the finest use of black in any film. It is drenched it. Cinematographer is surely the reincarnation of Edouard Manet.

The studio sent us a stuffed head from one of the Western sets. The leather was so old, the fucking thing split. Needless to say, the head arrives on the studio. Its unacceptable. Francis Ford Coppola and the art director went shopping for a head at a slaughterhouse. The horse had emphysema and was going to be killed anyway. The horse we featured in the movie wasnt the same one as the head, it was a horse that looked just like him. John Marley, the guy who played the movie producer, was a pain in the ass because he was a complainer every time he was on screen. Now, we go to shoot the famous scene. Were shooting out on Long Island on a winter day, which is cold, dark, and rainy outside. Were down at an elegant old stone mansion, and John is wearing his silk coat and his pajamas, standing by the bed. Now, four grips walk in carrying this huge metal case. He has no idea what the hells inside. Im not exaggerating, it was probably about six to eight-foot square with the latches on each corner. He stands by the bed, and they lower this thing on the floor. They take off the four latches, and he almost faints. He sees this fucking horses head with the tongue hanging out. Oh, Jesus Christ! The next thing we know, the head is on the bed, on the yellow sheets. So you know, the horses head was frozen with dry ice, so it was fucking cold. Francis figures, This is my shot to get him. They put all the phony blood. John refuses to stretch his legs out. Hes got his legs pulled in so it doesnt hit the horses head. Francis kept telling him to straighten out. His scream was blood-curdling. What you hear in the movie was not done later on. We were laughing at a certain point. We were fucking howling. He was freaking out. Original, inventive, influential, stylish  jam-packed with allegories, The Matrix is a groundbreaking feat that not only set a new benchmark for sci-fi filmmaking that still remain unsurpassed to this day but also redefined the action genre with its innovative action set pieces  pioneering visual effects. But it is the ideal balance between its in-depth philosophy, game-changing action  thought-provoking concept that makes this sci-fi actioner a breathtaking experience of the highest order.
The story follows Thomas Anderson, a software engineer whose secret life is lived in computers where he goes by the hacker alias Neo. Having always questioned his reality, he is contacted by a notorious outlaw named Morpheus who eventually awakens him to the truth that the world hes been living in is a simulated reality pulled over his eyes and that hes nothing more than a slave in a dystopian world, created  controlled by machines.
Written  directed by The Wachowskis, it appears as if they took ideas  inspirations from almost every great sci-fi film out there and put it all in their story and filled it with enough style  substance for everyone to end up devouring it for one reason or another. The research that went into the preparation of its screenplay is extensive but the manner in which it is presented on the screen is no less extraordinary either.
Cinematography has newness written all over it, be it the camera angles, fluid manoeuvres, controlled zooms, slow motion captures or even different tints used to differentiate the two worlds. Editing makes sure every single scene matters and unfolds the story at a riveting pace. The Visual Effects were pioneering for its time and its influence can still be noticed in many films today. And Don Davis background score imparts a heightened sense of emotions and seamlessly fits this dystopian world.
Coming to the performances, the ensemble cast consists of Keanu Reeves, Laurence Fishburne, Carrie-Anne Moss, Hugo Weaving, Joe Pantoliano  more. And even though everyone does a terrific job in their respective roles, its Hugo Weavings disciplined rendition of Agent Smith that leaves the most lasting impression for me. Whats even more admirable is that every character in here is neatly defined, has a set of purpose, and is far from just a filler.
On an overall scale, The Matrix is the biggest leap science-fiction genre has taken since Stanley Kubricks 2001 A Space Odyssey and just like that classic, it is immortal for its contribution to its genre  cinema as a whole. An ingenious blend of style  substance which with the help of its pioneering visual effects, imaginative vision, thematic depth  breathtaking action easily elevates itself into the league of cinemas greatest  most entertaining examples of all time, The Matrix is a bonafide masterpiece in every way, shape  form.
Also, as Morpheus said, Unfortunately no one can be told what The Matrix is. Youve to see it for yourself. And he cant be anymore right. So forget everything you know, free your mind, take the red pill, and find out for yourself just how deep the rabbit hole really goes. One of my all-time favourites. One hundred percent recommended. Multiple viewings advised.

There arent that many true gamechangers around in film, but if there ever was one that changed the face of what a true science fictionaction piece should entail, it is the Matrix. When you can speak of a pre-Matrix era, you know youre dealing with an important film.
It isnt that difficult to pinpoint the reasons why this film is so groundbreaking, but lets start with the obvious one. The technical qualities are mindblowing. I remember seeing it in the cinema 13(!) years ago, gawking at the screen like an idiot, simply not believing what I was seeing. This did not only have to do with the phenominal special effects, but also with the stunning aesthetic and the unique and vibrant way in which the action was presented to me. It was so innovatively shot that it was bound to be followed by many copycats, which, of course, it did.
But even more importantly, it is the story and the backdrop. The plot is not only original, but also multi layered and the directors manage to balance this complex narrative really well. They never lose focus and show great skill at dealing with multiple storylines. What they also do is flesh out a complete and intriguing universe. The futuristic world we are presented with is a harrowing futuristic image, but the true strength of this film lies with the inclusion of the virtual reality. A kind of collective purgatory of mankind in which a saviour needs to arise to resurrect his species. That concept alone carries the entire film.
The way this virtual afterlife is conceived and portrayed is fantastic. It, and the programs that inhabit it, are used as a critique on our species.It puts its finger on a sore spot in what we are and how we inhabit our world and it does this, opposed to its sequels, with refreshing intelligence and a soft philosophical tone.
And it wraps it all in an adrenaline fuelled rollercoaster with amazingly choreographed fight scenes and beautifully shot action sequences.
Im not hesitant to call this a classic, it is a game changer that perfectly matches brain and brawn.

Maybe love will truly conquer all, when it comes to me finally breaking down and admitting The Matrix is one of the most innovative badass actions films ever made.
Im trying to free your mind, Neo. But I can only show you the door. Youre the one that has to walk through it.
Spoilers...
I was in my Freshman year of Highschool when The Matrix came out, and everyone was talking about how awesome it was. As so soon as it came out on DVD my family had a movie night to check it out, and I remember enjoying it ... but then the ending happened. I remember thinking the whole part where Trinity says she loves Neo after he dies, and then he magically comes back to life and is more powerful than the agents, was super lame. So because of this silly moment, I have always held a grudge against this film and would often call it overrated. So this time I came in looking to take away a whole new perspective, and despite the few cheesy moments The Matrix does have, overall it is a very smart film that works on many levels.   
Lets just take a step back and think about all the things we specifically think about when it comes to The Matrix
- Sunglasses and trench coats
- Bullet time effects
- Keanu Reeves saying Wow, I know Kung Fu
- Eastern philosophy
- Alice in Wonderland metaphor
- Lots of Guns!!!
- Take the red pill!
- Mr. Anderson
- And that awesome green coding that flows down computer screens
All these moments from this action, sci-fi, horror experience the Wachowskis so thoughtfully crafted, stick in our minds because of how fresh, innovative, and entertaining they were.
Neo, sooner or later youre going to realize just as I did that theres a difference between knowing the path and walking the path.
The element that surprised me most on this rewatch was how many moments of horror are included, that help up the stakes in this futuristic dystopia where humans are being harvested to power the machine world. From the bug that is put in Neos belly button, to awakening in a fluid filled harvester pod, the agents busting through the wall to grab at the team, and the aggressive nature of sentinels attacking their ship are all very intense. 
Then you have the great Hugo Weaving who transforms into one of the best villains of all time in his role as Agent Smith. I remember really looking forward to that final fight between him and Neo in the third Matrix movie. Actually, while most people say they love the original and hate the sequels, I have always had a great time with Matrix Reloaded. Right from the onset you could tell it was trying to be a silly over the top action movie, and that worked. Meanwhile, the first one walks a fine like between wanting you to take it seriously and being a little silly. Then you have the third one that is fun, but wow does my head still hurt from how much it pounds you with that Neo being Jesus metaphor.  
Let me tell you why youre here. Youre here because you know something. What you know you cant explain, but you feel it. Youve felt it your entire life, that theres something wrong with the world. You dont know what it is, but its there, like a splinter in your mind, driving you mad.
So what do I mean by silly? While these moments are not as abundant as I remembered, you still have lines like Buckle your seatbelt Dorothy, because Kansas is going bye bye. The fact that Joe Pantolianos character turns on the team before we ever really get to know him. Keanu Reevess acting which is not bad, but its not great either. Cypher getting caught monologuing and being so surprised when Tank comes back to blast him away.   
Finally the love conquers all moment I mentioned before, and to be honest as much as I was fighting them off ... I was getting some of those good movie chills during that moment. But they kicked into overdrive when they cut back to Neo and we see him being able to see through the fabric of the Matrix for the first time, as he becomes The One, aka a Matrix super saiyan. Also so many of the team members getting killed off before we really get to know them was pretty lame. 
I didnt come here to tell you how this is going to end. I came here to tell you how its going to begin. Im going to hang up this phone, and then Im going to show these people what you dont want them to see. Im going to show them a world without you. A world without rules and controls, without borders or boundaries. A world where anything is possible.
So while the philosophy mixed into The Matrix is not very complex or groundbreaking, I think it works pretty well to add some brains to this action thriller geared toward a general audience. The sequence were Morpheus is teaching Neo to open is mind is very reminiscent of Yodas teachings from Empire, about someone not just trying and hoping to accomplish something, but instead being determined and just doing it. And that is a great lesson to live by. 
You also have all the Alice and Wonderland stuff and Neo being like Jesus, out there to easily chew on. I kind of feel like having blatant references like this in a movie geared to the average movie goer, is a good thing. Because they will become more aware of looking for references after spotting these, and then may look for some in films where they are not so obvious. You also have the Oracle telling Neo that he is not Matrix jesus, in order to take off the pressure about him being The One. I wonder if she was aggravated with Morpheus, for pounding that into his head for the whole first half of the story LOL.
Finally, we go to the action scenes, and wow did I enjoy jacking up the sound on my home theater and sitting back with smile while rewatching these. The scene where they shoot up the lobby is fantastic with all the shooting, acrobatics, and that popular music fueling it all. I chuckle every time when I see how they edited that specific shot in, of Neo grabbing that gun while doing a cartwheel and shooting. Why reload when you have so many guns LOL. Earlier in the film I loved hearing and singing along to Rob Zombies Dragula, which I had not heard in forever.
All the training scenes are great along with the wire work, and the scenes where the camera shoots all the way around the slowed down action. But by far that big moment that gave me the biggest smile, was seeing that incredible helicopter crash where the glass ripples before exploding into a huge mass of broken glass and fire. And for the most part all the effects have aged really well.
For some reason I always remembered the opening of the movie with Neo supposedly working some IT job taking forever, but with this rewatch I noticed that part was barely fleshed out at all. So what exactly are these hacker discs that people are paying him big money for? They never follow up on the building jump scene, with a moment where he can actually do that ... I guess skipping to him flying like Superman is better. There is nowhere near enough stuff in that cube for me to believe that is where he works. Wow, does his apartment and most of the buildings look dingy, which is likely due to the green hue which is everywhere in the movie, and is a clear sign that the Matrix is truly all around us. 
The Matrix does have a few small issues, but the amount of enjoyment I found with everything it does do a fantastic job at, far outweighs my small gripes that used to prevent me from truly loving it. I am hoping this realization does not cause me to enjoy Reloaded any less.

Released in 1999, this groundbreaking film merges cutting-edge visual effects with a compelling narrative that explores the nature of reality, consciousness, and human freedom. At its core, The Matrix poses a fundamental question What is real? Keanu Reeves stars as Neo, a disillusioned hacker who discovers that his reality is an elaborate simulation created by sentient machines to subjugate humanity. The films intricate plot unfolds with a masterful blend of high-concept ideas and adrenaline-pumping action sequences, creating a captivating experience that invites viewers to ponder existential themes while simultaneously being entertained.
The visual style of The Matrix is nothing short of revolutionary. The use of bullet time photography, which allows for dynamic slow-motion effects, redefined action choreography and set new standards for visual storytelling. The films iconic aesthetic, characterised by its green tint and sleek, cyberpunk design, has influenced countless works in the years since its release. Its a testament to the Wachowskis vision that even more than two decades later, the films visuals feel fresh and innovative. Thematically, The Matrix delves into concepts of choice, identity, and the nature of reality itself. The philosophical underpinnings, drawing from various influences including Platos Allegory of the Cave and cyberpunk literature, encourage viewers to question their own perceptions of reality. The films memorable charactersparticularly Morpheus (Laurence Fishburne) and Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss)embody these themes, serving as guides in Neos awakening. Moreover, the films soundtrack, featuring a mix of industrial rock and electronic music, perfectly complements its frenetic energy, making each action sequence even more exhilarating. In conclusion, The Matrix is a groundbreaking and thought-provoking masterpiece that transcends its genre. It expertly weaves together visually stunning action, deep philosophical inquiry, and a compelling narrative that resonates with audiences on multiple levels. Its influence on cinema, culture, and even technology cannot be overstated, and it remains a must-watch for anyone who appreciates the art of filmmaking. The film is not just a classic its a profound exploration of what it means to be human in an increasingly complex world.

The end of the millennium is accompanied by a mixture of anticipation and anxiety, a moment in which technology ceases to appear as simple progress and begins to emerge as a potential form of control. In this liminal climate, the 1999 release of The Matrix represented a turning point in science fiction cinema. The Wachowski sisters film combines postmodern aesthetics, revolutionary visuals, and metaphysical depth, transforming an action blockbuster into a device that reworks, in an accessible form, some of the most ancient philosophical questions about the substance of reality. A year earlier, The Truman Show had already depicted an artificial reality, built around a gigantic television set in which a single man, unaware of everything, lived within a still circumscribed and recognizable deception. In The Matrix, the illusion is total, produced by an artificial intelligence capable of subjugating the entire human race. Unlike Truman, who ultimately cracks the fiction through doubt, here that critical distance does not exist no one suspects, because everyone is convinced that that world is the only one that exists. The few who question the imposed order immediately become an anomaly to be identified and repressed. But the most radicale paradox comes when Neo, finally disconnected from the system that held him enslaved, discovers that the reality is no less unsettling than the simulation he escaped. There is no reassuring return to truth, but rather a shift between different forms of alienation. In perfect continuity with the cyberpunk canon, the film depicts a bleak dystopian vision in which freedom itself has nothing liberating about it. And it is precisely this that makes The Matrix, decades later, still so distressing not the domination of machines in itself, but the idea that beyond the prison there is no true refuge, only another prison.

In spite of wearing its own influences on its sleeve and many countless imitators that have followed, the Wachowskis The Matrix is truly a film of its own kind - one that has went on to define its own era and not without good reason. Blending the cyberpunk aesthetic with Hong Kong-inspired action set pieces, what the Wachowskis have managed to create was no ordinary action film but a film that stretches even beyond the set expectations for the genre. Yet its long-lasting appeal doesnt ever feel limited, and its easy to see why because the Wachowskis also became a household name ever since this. Its a film that bridges the gap between blockbuster cinema and philosophical cinema, from its weighty thematic content to the stunning action choreography and in the twenty years that have followed ever since it has only ever remained talked about in extensive detail. To take Morpheuss own words, The Matrix is everywhere and for all I know its influence will only continue spreading because it still finds a way into the changing cultural landscape as if there were truly any other sign that the film has only aged like fine wine.
Keanu Reeves stars as the computer hacker Neo, who is called into joining a group of resistance fighters after realizing that he has been living in a simulated reality otherwise known as the Matrix. The Matrix presents itself like the world as we knew it, nearing the end of the 20th century, but upon a wake up call, Neo realizes that it is actually the 22nd century and a war had been waged between machines and their human creators, leaving much of the human race enslaved within the system. The Wachowskis have already made a case for their impressive worldbuilding in here, but also worth noting is the political allegories and how the literary influences also come into play with allowing The Matrix to remain every bit as stunning today as it was in 1999. If there was ever a film that truly defined postmodern, this would be that film without doubt, because it only finds new ways to remain revolutionary from generation to generation.
Observing the inside of the Matrix as being an authoritarian state where humans are enslaved to feed into a corrupt system, the Wachowskis work around this template in order to create another allegory of their own. Its easy enough to note the philosophical influence that The Matrix has left upon its audiences, because it also begs the question about what would one do if they had the choice to see the world for what it really is or to continue living inside a paradise constructed to suit oneself. Yet theres also an obvious queer subtext to moments like the iconic red pill or blue pill scene, one that has only become more evident thanks to the Wachowskis both having come out as transgender women (encouraging another hint that alludes to fighting against transphobia with Agent Smith referring to Neo as Mr. Anderson akin to deadnaming a trans person). It begins simply enough, with those choosing to live a lie in order to suit higher authority amidst homophobia being the blue pill option, and the red pill being equated to coming out of the closet living ones own truth and putting up with the world around themselves no matter what the consequences may be. The many political readings dont limit itself only to this extent, but as much as many films attempted to recreate the accomplishments of the Wachowskis, nothing has matched the sense of genuineness that their film has presented.
Theres another case being made regarding how The Matrix presents gender roles onscreen (an obvious visual cue can be found near the films ending), but Trinitys arc would also present many ideals that can ring off as being progressive in todays world. Although she may appear to be your usual tough girl in an action movie embodying masculine qualities to work together with the films main hero, she is still crafted in an endearing manner. In part this is indebted to the performance of Carrie-Anne Moss, but the film also presents another idea at hand especially with how she realizes her own power through setting off on the word of the Oracle. The religious allusion also makes it clear enough in her name (Trinity akin to the Holy Trinity, with Morpheus being the Father, and Neo being the Son), but noting how she starts off as only being one among the group assembled by Morpheus to wage war to preserve the human race, theres another quest that she also finds herself a part of without ever feeling like she allows anything to control her. Its the realization of her own power that allows her arc to remain so impactful, effectively subverting the heteronormative romance that would normally be found in action films of this sort.
Despite many of the characters feeling stoic for the good lot of the film, especially in the way they present the many ideas that the Wachowskis sought to deliver to the screen, they still manage to stick inside your head. This is also a big factor as to what makes Keanu Reevess portrayal of Neo so engrossing, because he starts off as an observer trying to piece together how everything he had known about the world was an absolute lie - and the confusion is one that the Wachowskis still understood could easily get into the heads of the audiences. But for as passive as Neo may come off to be to some viewers, theres still a sense of growth to him as he goes along the familiar heros journey to save Morpheus from the system and even as he stands up to Agent Smith, declaring his own title - and even realizing what potential he has. Theres still a sense of human instinct present in him, and it starts to become even more fully realized as the film shifts over towards the direction heading into the action genre. Yet as we continue sticking around Neo, he still remains an engaging presence because of how he echoes the amazement regarding what is real and what isnt.
As the film quickly moves towards action, theres no denying that the choreography still remains impressive especially in its resemblance to Hong Kong action cinema, but it also makes a case for why it remains one of the best films of its own sort. Its a film that appears so visually 1999 yet never in a sense that its already dating itself, but in the sense that everything about it still remains so visually attractive from the special effects (one among many obvious standouts being the famous bullet time sequence) and the primarily green colour coding resembling the programmed world of whats inside the Matrix. But the way in which these sequences come together with the films philosophical undertones, especially in the more contemplative nature that the Wachowskis employ for most of the films first half already makes clear a case that a film can be both philosophical and pure escapist fun at the same time. The Wachowskis already know the very nature of what theyre handling in one film, and they utilize everything they can to allow the film to be so stimulating - just like the very best auteurs would craft such a film.
We continually ask ourselves about what truly is the Matrix, even with Morpheuss own words declaring that it is everywhere. If theres anything else that perfectly sums up what allows the very impact of The Matrix to remain so long-lasting, it has to be that one moment. Its truly a film where so many possibilities can come to be, and in the twenty years that have come since its release it still remains so heavily talked about for good reason. And even amidst its overwhelming popularity with audiences ever since its release, it also remains misunderstood even by a certain group of its own admirers. Everything that can be said about the films philosophical values to its visual aesthetic to pure entertainment factor would already have been said many more times by others, but whats also heavily underestimated are the political undertones that allow the film to stand atop many others. Of course, the queer subtext worth noting given it being a creation of the Wachowskis, but also in how it bands together people of all different sorts to start up their own revolution against an oppressive system - theres a whole lot more to a film like this than many would realize. And admittedly, it was one I had underestimated for so long. You dont often come across films like The Matrix, especially in how they define a generation the way the Wachowskis had done so.

 In English If 90s cinema had a peak of conceptual and technical ambition, that peak was The Matrix. Directed by the Wachowski sisters, the film is not just an action and sci-fi spectacle but one of the most influential works in cinematic history. It shaped the cyberpunk imagination of the late 20th century, introduced groundbreaking effects, and established a new narrative paradigm that fused philosophy, technology, and dystopian aesthetics like never before.
At its core, The Matrix is a modern retelling of Platos Allegory of the Cave we live imprisoned in an illusion, unaware of the true reality. In the film, this illusion is the Matrix, a simulation program created by artificial intelligences to keep humanity under control. The protagonist, Neo, is the chosen one who must awaken from this prison and lead the resistance. This narrative arc, inspired by messianic myths, Buddhism, and cyberpunk, is one of the screenplays greatest triumphs. His journey is not just physical but metaphysicalhe must not only fight against the Matrixs agents but also confront his own disbelief and accept his role. Morpheus serves as the archetypal mentor, a guide who introduces the protagonist to the truth, while Trinity adds an essential emotional layer to the story.
Visually, The Matrix redefined action cinema with the iconic bullet time, a technique that slowed down movements while the camera rotated around the scene. The influence of Hong Kong martial arts cinema is also evident, with impressive choreography coordinated by Yuen Woo-ping. Each fight is not just a physical spectacle but a philosophical extension of the conflict between control and freedom. The color palette, dominated by greenish tones inside the Matrix and cold blue in the real world, visually reinforces the idea of simulation and the contrast between realities. The production design and art direction, heavily inspired by cyberpunk and 90s hacker aesthetics, have become timeless.
What remains fascinating about The Matrix is how it still resonates today. In an era of artificial intelligence, the metaverse, and social networks shaping our perception of reality, the films central questionWhat is real?has never been more relevant. Cyphers dilemma, choosing to ignore the truth in favor of the comfort of illusion, mirrors contemporary debates on post-truth and information control.
More than a brilliant action film, The Matrix is a philosophical manifesto and a technical milestone that redefined sci-fi cinema. Blending existentialism, technology, and impeccable action sequences, the Wachowskis created a work that transcends time. Even decades later, Morpheuss question still echoes Have you ever had a dream, Neo, that you were so sure was real?

The idea that we are all a slave, born into bondage, resonates with how the world around us actually works. The Matrix is so novel, even though it takes so many forms of inspiration, from both philosophical and cultural sources. Its cool to have a giant action movie that also has philosophical overtones. With incredible visual effects and action, The Matrix is definitely a classic of its kind and always entertaining. Its great stuff.

That all said, Ive always had reservations with The Matrix. Despite the amazing premise, the actual story of this film is not very interesting. The plot is basically just Neo escapes the matrix, Morpheus trains him, and then Neo must rescue Morpheus who has been captured. That doesnt work as a standalone film. They have a whole imaginary world to work with, but the plot itself is so basic. Its like a TV pilot, designed to set up future instalments. If you want action and cool images, The Matrix delivers. But the actual philosophical and narrative meat is all in the sequels, however those films have their own problems. I admire a lot about The Matrix, but even as a teenager, once Morpheus is saved and Neo becomes The One, I was like, is that it? Youre ending there? Isnt there more to tell? Spending ages giving Neo a kung fu lesson or spending half an hour of screentime rescuing Morpheus is all in service of cool action moments, sure, but what is the point of these in the grand scale of things? So while I dont deny that every minute of The Matrix is entertaining, and there are a lot of great ideas here, I always feel like its a prelude that doesnt deliver the emotional satisfaction it could if the plot felt like it mattered.

Mind bending concepts were gracefully intertwined with rapidly paced action in this sci-fi classic. The Matrix is one of the most intelligent blockbusters ever made, challenging the viewer with its many philosophical and spiritual questions.
Neo (Keanu Reeves) is a computer hacker who has a life changing experience after becoming aware of the awful reality of his world. Hes been living in a simulation his entire life and his real life is only a fragment of what it once was. He must face off against an evil computer program to save whats left of the human race. 
The Matrix is one of those perfectly casted films. I cant picture anyone else playing the main four characters. I especially loved Carrie-Anne Moss as the menacing Trinity. Hugo Weaving as the villain (Agent Smith) was also perfectly casted. His robotic portrayal of a sentient computer program was spot on. Some supporting roles were equally as memorable as the main cast. The late Gloria Foster as the Oracle is unfathomably great. Her acting is incredible and elevated what I expected to be such a stereotypical character. Joe Pantoliano as the traitorous Cypher was also intriguing. If given the chance to return to an ignorant state, would you? The red pill blue pill question will forever be relevant in our society. 
Outside of the memorable cast, another aspect worth complimenting is the inconceivable action sequences. It was nothing short of revolutionary when it first released. I instantly knew I was in for something special when Trinity first stayed suspended midair. Wide shots on the hand to hand combat scenes allowed for Yuen Woo-Pings choreography to be stared at in awe. The martial arts in The Matrix is insane and deserves all the praise it gets. An iconic score from Don Davis was icing on the cake. It fit so well with the theme, thanks to its mixing of techno beats. Clubbed to Death is easily recognizable even for those that havent seen The Matrix. 
My only major issue with the film is the unnecessary romance between Neo and Trinity. It isnt pulled off successfully, as the characters have no realistic chemistry ever established. This is thankfully fixed in the Matrix Reloaded. A more minor grievance was that I wanted just a little bit more philosophical exploration of the idea of us living in a matrix. 
The Wachowskis achieved so much with this film. The standards for fight scenes and digital effects were completely reworked and lead to the incredible action films we received in the aughts. And it has some unmatchable pacing. Engaging action was seamlessly mixed with interesting exposition that wasnt over explained. The Matrix is also a gorgeous representation of Plato and René Descartes philosophy. 
Ill end with one of Descartes most famous quotes. I can doubt everything, except one thing, and that is the very fact that I doubt. Simply put - I think, therefore I am. There really is no spoon.

The CGI is inevitably showing its age a little, but The Matrix remains so visually striking that I soon stopped caring and became that awestruck teenager once again. Much like the online conspirasphere it influenced, the film invites us to pull back the curtain on a world orchestrated by, in this case, sinister machine overlords. It was this combination of techno-pessimism and existential pondering, which elevates the film beyond typical sci-fi fare into a heady rumination on identity, free will and truth, that grabbed me and countless other teenagers back in the day. Muy buena película, una cinta adelantada a su tiempo.
The Matrix fue muy importante para el mundo del cine por la revolución que fue en cuanto a efectos y todo lo visual lo cual es increíble y no hay nada que reprocharle, además de estar acompañada de una historia interesantísima y llena de elementos filosóficos, sin caer en lo ultra complejo como para marear o resultar confusa.
Sinopsis Un experto en computadoras descubre que su mundo es una simulación total creada con maliciosas intenciones por parte de la ciberinteligencia.
La historia es muy buena, muy llamativo y original todo lo que propone. Como historia de ciencia ficción es una locura, presenta muchas cosas interesantes que desde el primer momento nos atrapan y así es durante toda la trama, aunque si hay momentos (sobretodo al inicio) con un ritmo un poco lento, pero no me parece aburrida ni ahí, sabe cómo mantenerte enganchado durante más de dos horas. Otra cosa a destacar es que es compleja pero sin llegar a resultar confusa o innecesaria, si creo que hay cosas que podrían haber sido mejor explicadas, pero como pasa en todas éstas películas que abordan temas tan filosóficos, lo bueno es que no se siente innecesario o forzado. Por otro lado, la acción es una locura, si por algo es tan memorable es por algunas secuencias de acción brillantemente realizadas y con coreografías innovadoras para la época, siempre acompañadas de un CGI espectacular. Ya dejando de lado todo lo positivo que tiene, siento que el guion tiene algunas cosas no del todo pulidas, la resolución de todo se me hizo un poco conveniente y tonta en comparación a todo lo otro que se animó a presentar, casi que parecía algo de otra película.
Los personajes me encantaron, aunque hay algunos secundarios menos relevantes. ThomasNeo es un personaje buenísimo con un gran desarrollo y personalidad, me gustó toda la historia de él excepto el tema de que es El Elegido y esa parece ser la justificación a varias de las cosas que le pasan y logra sobrevivir como si nada. Igualmente también destaca por su vínculo con Morpheo y Trinity, otros dos personajes muy buenos e igual de icónicos que el protagonista. Lo malo es que los demás secundarios si que están un escalón por debajo de ellos, exceptuando Cypher y Tank que son los que más protagonismo tienen y al menos nos cuentan algo sobre ellos que los diferencia del resto. Por último, el Agente Smith como el villano me pareció excepcional y de las mejores cosas de la película, está muy bien escrito su personaje y se entienden completamente sus motivaciones.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente los increíbles efectos con los que cuenta, sin dudas una revolución en ese tiempo, una locura lo bien que se ven para que ya hayan pasado 26 años desde su estreno, envejeció mejor de lo que imaginaba. Además, también es destacable el gran trabajo de las hermanas Wachowski en guion y dirección, muy original todo lo que presentan. Algo en lo que me quedó debiendo un poco es en la banda sonora, no siento que haya sido tan memorable como esperaba, destaca más el sonido. Por último, las actuaciones son sensacionales, resaltando Keanu Reeves, Carrie-Anne Moss, Laurence Fishburne y Hugo Weaving.
En conclusión, una muy buena película llena de ideas interesantes y muy única en cuanto a todo lo que presenta y la manera en la que lo hace, me arrepiento de no haberla visto antes, se entiende por qué es todo un clásico. La recomiendo.

The Matrix offers the most exhilarating inventive action sequences to come down the pike ever. To say that it must be seen for yourself is no understatement. Id go so far as to boldly say its basically a perfect movie.

Morpheus Throughout human history we have been dependent on machines to survive. 
Fate, it seems. Is not without a sense of irony.
When rewatching Bound, the Wachowski siblings style and panache is clear to see. They had a unique vision in that film and you just knew that this was just a taste of what they could be capable of.
When The Matrix was released there was an immediate positive response from viewer and critics like. 
From the moment the film starts, seeing the Warner Brothers and Village Roadshow logos in green you can see that this is something different.
The world building here is astounding. Although this can be loosely traced back to William Gibsons 1984 novel Neuromancer. The foundational basis for The Matrix, borrows heavily the novels central concept of a pervasive, immersive virtual reality accessible through direct neural connection.
All the same this story is phenomenal and myself along with most other audience members had their mind blown by this film.
From the astounding futuristic concept of us being enslaved by machines after AI went rogue and fought against us. (I have always said AI is a bad idea!) then enslaving the human race to be used as an abundant energy source.
The stylish vision is delivered with fantastic costumes including super cool full length leather trench coats and wicked sunglasses. 
(Especially Morpheus. On set Laurence Fishburne was handed sunglasses with arms and he went back to the props department and said that they have to be like in the concept art and they had to design ones with a spring to pinch to the bridge of his nose.)
The main thing that I loved about this film was the amazing action sequences. Being a life long fan of kung fu films this ticked all the boxes for me.
Neo I know Kung Fu.
Morpheus Show me.
Fight choreographer Yuen Woo-Ping (Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon, Kill Bill) trained Keanu Reeves for 4 months and Laurence Fishburne for over a month for their fight sequence and it looks amazing. The little nods to Bruce Lee, the speed and ferocity of their combat is excellent.
Later in the film we also have the building lobby scene, a combination of kung fu, gun fu and acrobatics all combines to have Neo and Trinity take out a slew of soldiers. 
Slow motion shots of spins, bullet dodges and masonry being destroyed looks like nothing we had seen before and took us all by surprise.
As they get into the elevator, that final section of tile that falls down was not planned, it just fell and was a happy accident that looked great at the end of the shot.
I remember seeing a preview of how they shot the bullet time sequences with multiple cameras around in a loop and extracting the footage from each and stitching them together to make some unique and amazing shots that were copied, emulated and spoofed by every other film maker after the release of this film.
The stylish vision of this film cannot be denied.
The soundtrack for this film is sick, I had this on CD. 
That lobby fight is to Spybreak by the Propellerheads. 
Minefields by the Prodigy plays in the club when Neo first meets Trinity. And Clubbed to Death by Rob Dougan plays in Agent training program with the woman in the red dress. It is a rocking sound track that appropriately ends with Rage Against the Machine.
The entire album is spot on.
The story is amazing. 
Choosing and making choices play throughout this film.
You either choose to be at your desk on time, or you choose to find another job.
Choose to get on the window cleaners scaffolding or leave in their custody.
Blue pill, red pill.
Sacrificing Morpheus life or Neos. 
There is also the Jesus analogy. Before going to the club the guy collects the programmed Sony Minidisc says.
Youre my saviour man, my own personal Jesus Christ.
When he is released from the Matrix this is like a resurrection. 
Neo Am I dead.
Morphious Far from it.

Plus he rises from the dead at the end as well. 
He comes back as their saviour.
Having faith as well plays into this.
Trinity What is he doing?
Morpheus Hes starting to believe.
The casting here is great. Will Smith famously passed on the role of Neo because he didnt understand the script. I cannot image anyone else in this role other than Keanu. 
Reeves had done some action roles. Point Break, Speed, Chain Reaction and Johnny Mnemonic (which was also written by William Gibson and takes place in the same universe as Neuromancer) This film certainly put Reeves on the right path to play John Wick.
Carrie Anne Moss looks fantastic as Trinity and I am sure she was the fantasy for many teenagers. She plays this role so well, she did all her own stunts, she kicks ass in all the fight scenes and looks bad ass doing it. 
Carrie Anne Moss is a massively underrated actor in my opinion. (Best performance ever for both her and of Michael Sheen is in the criminally under seen, Unthinkable.)
Laurence Fishburne is great as the captain and mentor, Morpheus.  
Joey Pants is always good. (He appears in Momento after this, again with Carrie Anne Moss.)
But for me the stand out performance comes from Hugo Weaving as Agent Smith. 
The tenacious program stuck in the matrix in the body of an Agent. He delivers his action scenes really well. He looks like a robotic killing machine. His stilted line delivery is fantastic. 
His monologue about humans being similar to a virus and his hatred of this place. So good to watch.
I cant stand it any longer. Its the smell. If there is such a thing. I feel saturated by it. I can taste your stink. Every time I do I somehow feel like Ive been infected by it. Its repulsive, isnt it? 
Weaving has been acting since the 80s in Australia. He was fantastic in The Adventure of Priscilla Queen of the Desert and the year before this he was amazing in The Interview, a small Australian film where his is being harshly interrogated by a detective about a murder. Another great watch.
It was the antipodean productions of this trilogy along with the Lord of the Rings trilogy that made Hugo Weaving a household name.
Sydney does a great job doubling as a major American city and it is only a few scenes where you notice. (Like the helicopter scene) But at this time Sydney was becoming increasingly popular for a filming location. Mission Impossible 2 and The Phantom Menace were just a couple of examples around this time using the huge Fox Studios in Sydney for their productions.
The green tint of the whole film gives the production that computer feel, the nostalgia of the old BBC computers from the classroom and of the old monitors.
I love how the Agents all wear dark green suits and there is just lots of green used everywhere.
1999 is a great year in film. 
The Phantom Menace and Sixth Sense dominated the box-office that year but The Matrix still came in 5th place.
The legacy of this film is tarnished by the disappointing sequels. But we still have this phenomenal first film with astounding world building and fantastic face kicking action.
This film still stands up and is a great watch. 
Take the red pill and you see how deep the rabbit hole goes.

The character of Switch was originally supposed to switch genders, being a woman in the real world and a man in the matrix. But they couldnt make it work so instead cast a more androgynous actor to play the part.
Warner Brothers estimated that this film would cost them 180 million dollars for a US shoot. They relocated the entire film to Australia and made the film for 80 million. 
The actor who plays Mouse is played by Matt Doran who was in Australian soap Neighbours, so in the UK he is most famous for that. But he also tried to sell Death Sticks to Obi Wan Kenobi in another Australian production. Star Wars Episode 2.

I cant imagine him coming all the way from LA to Sydney for this production. (Cocaine is shit in Australia for a start!) so he probably produced this remotely.
In the door knob shot where you see Neo and Morpheus reflection, you can see the camera too, it has a cover over it and a green line painted down the cover to blend in with Morpheus tie. Very clever.
The original concept for human farming was not to use the humans as batteries for power but to use our minds as storage. Which, now is a much better concept but the studio heads thought that the audiences wouldnt be able to get their heads around it. (To be fair in 1999 many wouldnt because we werent used to backing up terabytes worth of stored data then.) So it was changed to humans being used for power instead.

What is the Matrix? What is real?
What if our world was not the world as we know it but a virtual reality created by Artificial Intelligence. So goes the premise of the movie known as The Matrix. When released, the series broke many boundaries for the time. Special effects, stunts, the ability to tell a complex story so that the viewer could understand it, and bringing together a stellar cast to tell that story certainly helped. 
After nearly 22 years, how does The Matrix stack up? Well, pretty damn fine, thank you very much. Keanu Reeves as Neo is  though still finding his way in the role, I couldnt help spotting him slip into his character from Bill  Teds occasionally. This did improve as the film went on. Carrie-Anne Mosss Trinity was one of the most kick-ass women on screen at the time, and even now, she is the epitome of a powerful female character. Laurence Fishburnes Morpheus is the compelling yet calm leader the group need. Hugo Weaving as Agent Smith is perfection. It is a tailor-made role for him and one that made it difficult for me to watch him in his later projects. A special mention of a familiar New Zealand actor Julian Arahanga in the role of Apoc, a member of Morpheus crew (I have to spot the Kiwi connections ) Those nightmare-inducing special effects are still hyper present The Bug, Dont speak, along with the breakthrough 360-degree bullet effect and super slow-motion martial arts-inspired fight scenes. When you see similarities in other films, you always compare them with The Matrix. The cinematography is one aspect I probably didnt pay much attention to back in the day, but the gorgeous green colour tone and use of shadows is a huge part of the overall ominous feel. And finally, the soundtrack is phenomenal with the score from Don Davis and featured songs from artists including Marilyn Manson and Rage Against the Machine. 
The Matrix is a top-class sci-fi action movie, one of the best! I loved this revisit, and I look forward watching to the next in the series.

Perhaps the defining science fiction film of the 1990s, The Wachowski siblings The Matrix is a genre marvel. With its bold aesthetic, layered narrative, and heady and classic themes and archetypes, the film is a strikingly visualized, fully imagined, and excitingly told piece of work. Combining a cerebral genre tale with an action-enhanced hero quest, The Matrix entertains, provokes, and completely engages.
Fifteen years after its original release, its story is ingrained in the pop culture canon. When a programmerhacker is targeted by the authorities, he realizes that his reality is not what it seems. Punctuated with action beats, the programmer embarks on a quest to his learn his true identity and the truth behind the Matrix. 
The Wachowskis take a Campbellian hero quest and dress it with an instantly compelling what-is-reality angle. The angle allows for the films characters to dip between two realities and engage in both a future-world plot and more contemporary story beats. It is a riveting combination made sturdier by the films classical, even philosophical themes.
The film seamlessly moves between its two worlds. In visual contrast to the icy blue, tech-imbued reality, the contemporary landscape is bathed in sickly green hues. The Wachowskis shoot in a style that celebrates the films science fiction sensibilities but revels in future noir and comic book compositions. Shadows, angles, and special effects fully realize the siblings both reverent and original vision.
The Matrix moves quickly, exploding into moments of action and quieting for thoughtful musings. Its pace is as varied and textured as its evocatively rendered visuals. The film plays with time, slowing things and speeding things for narrative and visceral impact.
The now-iconic pairing of Keanu Reeves as Neo and Laurence Fishburne as Morpheus is a stroke of great casting. Each fits his role ideally, imbuing it with distinctive personality. Carrie-Anne Moss and Hugo Weaving add class in fully-fleshed support.
Technically, visually, and narratively appealing, The Matrix is worthy of its status as a genre great. Though sometimes lacking a human warmth, the film is an outstanding, maybe groundbreaking blend of style, story, and swiftness. Entertaining and influential, it is a must-experience piece of cinema for any film fan.

La perfetta trasposizione fantascientifica del mito della caverna di Platone (bisogna avere il coraggio di guardare oltre il mondo che si conosce per raggiungere una nuova consapevolezza di sé). Il film rimane anche uno degli esempi più mirabili del lato oscuro di una tecnologia (lintelligenza artificiale) destinata a sopraffarci e a inglobarci.
Il viaggio delleroe che Thomas AndersonNeo affronta è quello di un moderno Messia che scopre lilluminazione e lequilibrio dentro di sé. Lo spettatore assiste alla sua nascita (da quella matrice sintetica, liquido amniotico artificiale, in cui sono coltivati e schiavizzati gli esseri umani) come uomo nuovo (Neo in latino significa proprio nuovo) e alla sua rinascita definitiva (Neo è anche lanagramma di One, unico, speciale). Questopera dei Wachowski è come se fosse un Cronenberg ambientato nellera dei videogame e del digitale (proprio mentre il maestro era al lavoro sulla propria versione della realtà virtuale, ossia il suo film-rompicapo ExistenZ).
Un film che racconta, dunque, del potere della mente umana che sovrasta quello apparentementelogico e razionale delle macchine, rappresentato da quellagente Smith (pronto a uniformare ciò che non è conforme alla progettazione) che riprende ironicamente il nome del protagonista di 1984 di Orwell (cosè poi The Matrix se non la rappresentazione di una feroce dittatura del futuro?). La bellezza sta dunque oltre il regolare e ripetitivo codice binario che costituisce le simulazioni di Matrix. 
Questo è, naturalmente, un film sul corpo, soggetto a stress, mutazioni e prove di forza oltre ai celebri e citati combattimenti di arti marziali si assiste anche a sequenze clamorose e, volutamente, irreali (digitali) poiché è proprio la mente deve strappare il velo di Maya, deve abituarsi ad andare oltre il possibile, ampliando perciò le percezioni di chi osserva e sperimenta il mondo che lo circonda. Pertanto, le possibilità divengono infinite.



The perfect science fiction transposition of Platos cave myth (you must have the courage to look beyond the world you know to reach a new self-awareness). The film also remains one of the most wonderful examples of the dark side of a technology (artificial intelligence) destined to overwhelm and encompass us.
The heros journey that Thomas AndersonNeo takes is that of a modern Messiah who discovers enlightenment and balance within himself. The spectator witnesses his birth (from that synthetic matrix, artificial amniotic fluid, in which human beings are cultivated and enslaved) as a new man (Neo in Latin means new) and his definitive rebirth (Neo it is also the anagram of One, unique, special). This work by the Wachowskis is as if it were a Cronenberg set in the era of video games and the digital world (just as the master was working on his own version of virtual reality, namely his puzzle film ExistenZ).
A film that tells, therefore, of the power of the human mind that surpasses the apparently logical and rational power of machines, represented by that Agent Smith (ready to standardize what does not conform to the project) who ironically takes the name of the protagonist of Orwells 1984 (what is The Matrix if not the representation of a ferocious dictatorship of the future?). Beauty therefore lies beyond the regular and repetitive binary code that constitutes the Matrix simulations.
This is, of course, a film about the body, subject to stress, mutations and tests of strength in addition to the famous and cited martial arts fights, we also witness sensational and, deliberately, unreal (digital) sequences since it is precisely the mind that must tear the veil of Maya, it must get used to going beyond what is possible, thus broadening perceptions of those who observe and experience the world around them. Therefore, the possibilities become endless.

Interesting how the greatest cultural desire right now is for the simulacrum we now replicate and imitate what we already know. This isnt inherently bad, but man is this current nostalgia bait so cheap and cynical like never before (I see you, No Way Home). So I chose to revisit my favourite simulacrum that kinda predicted a lot of our current state! You bet your ass I rewatched the most influential movie of the last 30 years!

  The first 45 minutes of The Matrix might be the greatest mystery story Ive seen. Questions upon questions fill your head 
Who are those two voices talking about a clean line?
Why do these three robotic men in suits walk like they own the place? 
How the fuck does this leather-clad woman do a crane kick and jump that high, and where did she disappear to from that phonebooth? 
Who is this informant the Agents talk about? 
Who is Morpheus and what does he want with Neo?
Who is watching Neos interrogation from those countless monitors? 
How did these men in suits glue Neos lips? 
And most importantly WHAT IS THE BLOODY MATRIX EVERYONE KEEPS YAPPING ABOUT?! 
All of this is slowly teased through seamless editing and transition shots! Its like youre being let in on some secret world and subculture youre not supposed to know about! I cannot describe the sensation that the trailers for this film left on young me! The whole world at the time was gonna watch a movie whose marketing deliberately told you nothing about it! Youll never see that again for one hot minute! 

  Diablo Cody once explained why she cast Megan Fox for Jennifers Body that Fox has the mystique of older movie stars like Ava Gardner that our social media era has made people too accessible to be rare. I definitely felt that for Carrie-Anne Moss - the embodiment of this Matrix mystery. When we first meet Trin, we have no preconceptions of her coz Moss wasnt a well known actress Is she a good guy? A bad guy? We only know she has an intense presence and can put up a hell of a fight. Theres that one moment of vulnerability where she dives through the window, draws out her double pistols, and tells herself Get up Trinity. Just get up!. Mosss eyes sell whats going through her internally. Wonderful fusion of physicality, calm and humanity!

 The Matrix sparked my love for characters becoming detached from their selves, the world around them, and others in their lives. I love characters having to come to terms with their status as an outsider, and the isolation or fear of it. Yes Neo is the Chosen One, but he is revealed later on to be a part of that very program he rages against. But Neo isnt the only character alienated from his surroundings.......theres Cypher on the Nebuchadnezzar!

Its not subtle that the dry cynical Cypher is the Judas to the Christ-like Neo its even more on-the-nose that the mustached Cyphers past name is Mr Reagan. Joe Pants has this look of.....shame....when he puffs a cigar, agreeing to betray Morpheus for Smith. Watch the film from Cyphers POV hes featured on the movies poster, yet hes usually out of frame from the crew. He doesnt even sit at the table as everyone has breakfast - or Last Supper?! Imagine spending 9 years on a ship you regret choosing, where youre the comic relief for people you dont quite get along with, and your feelings for the woman youre into isnt reciprocated.........yeaahhhh you can see why Cypher would snap and seek his own self-preservation. He wishes to be a rich actor, because he wants to feel important and loved. Subtlety is a means, not an end! The real goal is nuance.

  Few things in movies have aged better than Agent Smiths animalistic fury at being terminally online 247! His guttural IHAte this place....this zoo...this prison....this reality, whatever you wanna call it. I cant stand it any longer.....I feel saturated by it! the disgust on his face with his forehead vein popping as he breaks Morpheus his cadence sounding like someone talking down to a child....utter misanthropy! And then he drops all pretense and demands Morpheus give him Zions codes so that he can be FREE? Thats when you realize this guy hates his job, doesnt give a damn about this Man vs Machines war, and just wants to be free from his duties so that he can leave the Matrix! Weird how Neo, Cypher and Smith share a common disdain for their jobs! Never thought Id find one of the most iconic villains relatable like a work colleague! Hugo Weavings calculated performance is so Oscar worthy, but yall only think screaming dramatic lines equals great performance lol. 

The late Roger Ebert complained that he was denied a Third Act he felt this movies climax was a generic action showdown. With all due respect good sir, this is an action movie - with just enough sophistication and originality to rub shoulders with the arthouse crowd! Something about our heroes saving their leader and friend Morpheus just warms my heart for whatever reason. Sure saving Morpheus means saving Zion, but we arent yet introduced to this mythical city. Its selfless and risky, since everything weve been told about the Agents makes them formidable! I love when saving the world is accidental or not what the heroes in the story planned, yet happened to achieve along the way. 

  The Wachowskis love for graphic novels, kung fu, anime, Frank Miller, Hitchcock, Kubrick, Ridley Scott, Philip K Dick and John Woo among other things bleeds all over this green hue masterpiece. There is a sense every camera angle and character motion is exactly what was storyboarded. They were the Brothers Grimm - now the Sisters Grimm?! 
Legendary fight choreographer Yuen Wo Ping trained Reeves, Moss, Fishburne and Weaving daily from 1997 to 1998! Ankles, ribs and joints were hurt, all for our entertainment!
Production designer Owen Paterson blends retro with contemporary, mirroring how the real world is woven with the virtual one.
VFX supervisor John Gaeta gave us Bullet Time a rare moment where the right questions are being asked with the technology available for its time!

Monumental. Groundbreaking. Transcendent. 
A benchmark for other films to be disciples of! 
Giving this anything other than 5 stars doesnt make you a contrarian, cultured or cool!
