 The Silence of the Lambs  is a landmark of psychological thrillers with a twist of horror. What better film to mark my 2,100th centennial review milestone? As part of my ongoing  31 Days of Horror,  this film stands out not just as a critical and audience favorite, but as one that reshaped the genre and Ive had it pegged for today since I reviewed  Braveheart  for 2,000.
The plot centers on Clarice Starling (Jodie Foster), a young FBI cadet eager to prove herself in the field of criminal psychology. Her assignment? Interview the brilliant yet terrifying Dr. Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins), a former psychologist turned notorious serial killer and cannibal. Clarice strikes a tense tango of a deal with Lecter, using his insight to hunt down another serial killer known as Buffalo Bill (Ted Levine), who skins his female victims to satisfy his deviant psychopathic thoughts.
The brilliance of  The Silence of the Lambs  lies in both complexity of its plot, and its execution. Most of the mystery is revealed early on so we know who the killer is but not where it resides. The true tension comes from the hunt and, more importantly, the relationship between Clarice and Lecter. The interrogation scenes, where these two minds probe one another, are nothing short of excellent. The power dynamic between them is a game of chess, with Clarice trying to hold her own against Lecters cold intellect.
Anthony Hopkins delivers a masterclass performance. While he tends to always nail his roles, Hannibal Lecter is probably his crowning achievement. Hopkins portrays Lecter with an eerie calmness, making his moments of violence and manipulation all the more chilling. Jodie Foster also shines as Clarice, bringing depth and vulnerability to a character determined to overcome her personal demons. Then theres Ted Levines portrayal of Buffalo Bill, a chilling depiction of a deeply disturbed individual.
 The Silence of the Lambs  is basically a lesson in how to do a psychological serial killer flick. It builds tension through psychological warfare rather than jump scares or gore. The horror here comes from the mind games, the dark corridors of the human psyche. Its a crime thriller, yes, but its also a disturbing look at the nature of human monsters and how the mindset that drives them lurks both outside and within. Its also worth noting that  The Silence of the Lambs  achieved something rare for a horror film as it swept the Oscars, winning Best Picture, Best Director, Best Actor, Best Actress, and Best Adapted Screenplay. That kind of recognition is practically unheard of in this genre, cementing its legacy as one of the greatest films in modern times.
As I mark my 2,100th review,  The Silence of the Lambs  feels like the perfect film to celebrate this milestone. It represents everything I love about watching movies. Memorable performances, tight direction, and the ability to unsettle and provoke thought long after the credits roll. While it may be labeled a horror film, I would classify it as a crime-thriller accessible to a wide audience beyond just your standard horror hounds. If youve been living under a rock and have never seen this film you need to make it a goal. Pure Excellence.
Soon Ill have to go down the Hannibal Lecter rabbit hole which spans multiple films and a television series. Damn.

If there ever was a film genre that needed constant reinvention to maintain its appeal, its certainly horror, and at this level, The Silence of the Lambs not only reinvented it but also transcended it.
Fear is based on a simple principle the boo effect. The less we expect something to happen, the more it scares us. Psycho, by featuring a seemingly ordinary, demented villain, terrified audiences used to associating horror with vampires and exotic monsters. The Exorcist pushed realism to a level of magnificent artistry, while Jaws suggested a mysterious presence, making it even more frightening  a device later perfected by films like Alien and The Shining. All these films share an iconic significance in the evolution of thrillers, and more specifically horror films, and it seemed as though nothing could surprise a mature audience anymore
This situation worsened with the rise of slasher films and their overused, cheaply plotted formulas, which turned classic ingredients  such as those introduced by earlier masterpieces  into increasingly unreliable recipes an overdose of gore, gruesome, over-the-top special effects, and various experiments that, in the worst cases, pushed the genre down to Z-movies, and in the best, to cult-status B-movies. A masterpiece built from fresh material was clearly waiting to be made. And the cinematic gods entrusted this mission to Jonathan Demme with The Silence of the Lambs, the first horror film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture. Finally.
The Silence of the Lambs is one of the greatest cinematic achievements in the history of cinema. Every single element contributes to creating a disturbing and unique atmosphere, and I use the word unique very carefully. I highly doubt anyone had encountered a villain of the same caliber as Dr. Hannibal  aptly nicknamed the Cannibal  Lecter, masterfully portrayed by Anthony Hopkins. Likewise, its hard to recall another film in which a young, vulnerable, nonEllen Ripley-type heroine is neither a victim nor a love interest, but the central hero. Clarice Starling, an FBI trainee, is played by Jodie Foster in a performance that subtly combines feminine vulnerability with heroic tenacity. And few would have expected the film to adopt such a binary structure on the one hand, a classic serial-killer investigation on the other, a subplot involving one of the greatest villains of all time and his intense psychological interplay with the heroine.
The script is tightly constructed, patiently leading us to assemble each piece of the puzzle until the series of interactions between Clarice Starling and Hannibal Lecter approaches a disturbing truth. The relationship between the two leads is even more fascinating because it deepens their personalities and allows us to delve further into their backgrounds the wounds in Clarices past, the mystery surrounding Hannibal Lecter, and the roots of evil that inspire serial killers acts. This is where the films freshness lies in its ability to put everything into perspective and invite us to move beyond the simple good vs. evil dichotomy. The villains are no sharks, monsters, or possessing demons they are everyday men  something akin to Norman Bates, but with an added level of savagery and perverse creativity. We try to understand them in order to fight them, under the perverse irony that the investigation requires one psychopathic mind to catch another.
Speaking of psychopaths, the way Hannibal Lecter is introduced after the opening minutes is impressive and gloomy enough to make us expect the worst, and when we finally see him, standing, well-dressed and clean-cut, the impact is immediate. Jonathan Demmes meticulous direction introduces Clarice Starling in a very clever way as well she is essentially a young woman enduring intense stress and hardship while trying to overcome the limitations imposed on her in a male-dominated world. In one scene, she enters an elevator surrounded by a group of men whose imposing size emphasizes her smallness. In another, she struggles to address a room full of officers, attempting to assert a degree of authority.
Clarice Starling is endearing and compelling as a heroine driven by a desire for justice and accomplishment, earning the trust  and perhaps even the fondness  of both the Agent in Charge, Jack Crawford (Scott Glenn), and possibly Hannibal Lecter himself. The many close-ups of his face during their conversations, along with the suavity of his voice, create a disturbingly intimate connection between him and Clarice. As the investigation progresses, the extraordinary portrayal of the films true villain by the underrated Ted Levine keeps us hooked until the final confrontation.
If youve noticed, Ive mentioned every element that generally makes a great film  writing, acting, and directing. The Silence of the Lambs was indeed the third film, and the last to date, to win the five major Academy Awards, after It Happened One Night and One Flew Over the Cuckoos Nest. It had a classic feel, because it combined so many new elements that helped define the psychological thriller, before it became a trend. Its no surprise, then, that the film topped many lists from the American Film Institute 5 on AFIs 100 Thrills, Clarice Starling ranked 6 among heroes, and good old Hannibal Lecter was named the 1 movie villain  even though he isnt the films main antagonist. That says as much as his Academy Award win for less than 20 minutes of screen time. To find a character with a comparable cinematic aura, one might have to go back to Vito Corleone.
The Silence of the Lambs reinvented the horror genre as the kind of film that would have made Alfred Hitchcock proud a terrifying villain, a sympathetic hero, a script that respects our intelligence, and top-notch direction and editing  and it doesnt even need a twist ending.

While I wrote (or rather linked) earlier about how Akira Kurosawa fills his frames with information, making each shot a dense essay on experience, I was shocked to see how Jonathan Demme manages to convey so much with the opposite tactic repetitive, unwavering close ups. Id have to think on it to know for sure what the best close-ups are of all time, but this film has to be near the top of the heap. The first real scene of the film is an interview between Clarice Starling and her future bossformer professor, Jack Crawford, and its almost completely done in close ups. Crawford looks right into the camera and right at the audience, while Starlings body is angled slightly away from the camera, looking just a bit off center. Hes in a position of power, and its communicated both visually and through his acting. Foster on the other hand, is sweaty, nervous, she looks down and off camera, looking for an escape from the moment.
This is how much of this film is, claustrophobic close ups of intense emotion. Many of them of Clarice. Foster, in my opinion, was very deserving of her Oscar Demme trusts her in every scene, and she rewards him for it. Much of this movie rides on Foster, in close up, carrying the audience with her emotion by emotion. In fact, that gets at what is my favorite thematic element of this film women in a world of men. Its not a coincidence that Buffalo Bills victims are women. Or that the Senator is a woman who is publicly humiliated by Hannibal Lecter. That Frederick Chiltons first on screen comment to Clarice is to mention how pretty she is. When her and her friend are walking along the training course, every male FBI trainee looks at them, some more overtly sexually than others, but all understand that they are an anomaly.
While the film is not overtly feminist, it is about the overwhelming presence of men, how theyre allowed to make comments that women cant, about how sexual politics are forced onto the table in a way that a male boss and male subordinate doesnt usually include. About how men are not afraid of their sexuality being used as a weapon against them, but Clarice has to afraid be in almost every encounter she has. Her interactions with Lecter all center around him forcing her to let down her guard, to ignore her boundaries as a woman. In a way, hes trading her career success for a form of sex or at the very least emotional intimacy, that would never be offered if Starling didnt feel like she had to go further than anyone else to succeed.
Which leads me to my complaint. I hate Anthony Hopkins acting. I dont find him menacing, mostly I find him cartoonish. It could simply be that this film has been so influential in the serial killer genre that all serial killers carry an element of Hopkins in their performace, so it no longer seems striking or original to me. But I dont like the films portrayal of Buffalo Bill either. The whole idea of the mastermind serial killer has never truly struck a chord with me, and perhaps the encouraged lack of humanity in both of them leaves me wanting in finding a kernel of truth in their performances. Even ignoring what Buffalo Bills whole existence implies about gender fluidity (that its wrong and associated with psychosis), theres something conservative and exploitative about serial killers and popular cultures fascination with them (as Jonathan Rosenbaum argues). And of course we shouldnt ignore what Buffalo Bills goal says about the makers of this film and how they might view the trans population. But even beyond that, theres a gonzo conservatism to the fascination of mastery and violence that someone like Hannibal Lecter provides, a dark indulgence in ourselves.
Change a little about Buffalo Bill, perhaps, and replace Hopkins as Lecter and maybe tone him down a bit, and this could easily be one of my favorite movies. I rarely, if ever, see close ups used this well repeatedly. But many of the things that this film is most remembered for are what I like least. In fact, you could maybe even remove the serial killer story whatsoever and just make it about a woman trainee trying to fit in with the boys, and I might love it. As is though, I want more.

If Clarice Starling is to face all the evil of a patriarchal world then the characterization of Buffalo Bill complicates and endangers the film. Bill is coded as a transsexual, but in the text of the film Clarice and Lecter toss this aside with a cute, but rather inaccurate description of transgender people as docile and non-violent. Tell that to the cops at Stonewall. Bill has asked for sex reassignment surgery, but has been denied by many doctors for not qualifying under their guidelines, which in turn is a rather nimble way of discussing the stigma within the medical community of transgender bodies and medically necessary treatment. In the rather famous tucking sequence set to the song Goodbye Horses, Bills body is framed as something monstrous, crossing the line between femininity and masculinity despite being in alignment with true-to-life transgender bodies to a degree. Bill prances and whispers before we see his Rocky Horror lips in close up utter the morbidly hilarious line, Would you fuck me? Id fuck me. Its altogether shocking, like opening the apartment door in Blue Velvet and entering into territory that we were never supposed to see. If Bill is a trans woman then The Silence of the Lambs feminist intentions are damned to a degree, but theres something within the characterization of Bill that strikes me as sympathetic rather than truly vile. He is very obviously a monster, but he has looked for help in the only way he knew how to by seeking psychiatric counseling and gendered medical transition before being denied for both. Was he driven towards these actions by societys misunderstanding of transgender bodies or was he always evil? The film never comes to a definitive conclusion on these questions. Bill is an enigma that Ive never quite been able to figure out. Hes a curiosity with some level of hidden depth among all the bloodshed (which is only ever implied, not shown). Hes akin to Anthony Perkins in Psycho with his deep-seated secrets and confused reactionary violence rather than the blanket evil of most serial killer examinations in cinema.

Few thrillers hold up as well as The Silence of the Lambs. Jodie Fosters Clarice Starling is at the center, vulnerable but unflinchingly sharp, and every scene with Anthony Hopkinss Hannibal Lecter crackles with tension, even though hes barely on screen. Jonathan Demmes close-up framing, with characters staring straight into the lens, makes you feel as if youre being studied right alongside Clarice. Its a rare horror film that earns its dread through psychology and atmosphere rather than gore, and it still unsettles decades later.

FBI profiler Clarice Starling (Jodie Foster) seeks the help of notorious incarcerated serial killer Hannibal Lector (Anthony Hopkins) to track down another killer (Ted Levine), going to the recesses of her own psyche in the process, in Jonathan Demmes classic with Scott Glenn, Diane Baker and Anthony Heald. 
For all the homages, imitators and parodies over the years, I think whats kept Demmes iconic horror thriller ticking to this day is just how rich all the little details here are, everything down to the seemingly throwaway scenes getting a level of attention that really matches the forensic feel of the actual story. 
Even the supporting roles have a colour to them you dont usually find in the margins of these stories everyone from Healds entertainingly pompous doctor, Ted Levines compellingly off-kilter killer and even to Dan Butlers bug expert each feel like they have lives outside of the movie and just so happened to cross over to this story, all part of what Demme and screenwriter Ted  Tally do so well here. 
The pair walk a line between chilly procedural and full on Grand Guignol horror thats tricky to do, and proved hugely influential on a generation of movies that came out in its wake, but keeping these characters firmly at the centre stops some of the inherent morbidness here from completely overbalancing, Jodie Fosters Oscar-winning lead performance bringing a sort of tough, vulnerable humanity to Clarice where that sort of attention to the people behind the plotting (flaws and all) really pays off here. 
Ive never seen this one until now, and its the sort of film so iconic its a bit surreal to watch scenes in context, Demme knowing just when to ramp to those crescendos I think familiarity is a part of it, but watching in real time the hamminess of some of the bigger moments got in the way a little for me. Anthony Hopkins famously got Best Actor on  15 minutes of screentime, and makes the most of it Hannibal is his defining role for a reason, he dominates each scene, but he really chews the scenery too, a broadness that early on almost overwhelms the rest, 
At a certain point the movie itself seems like it gets hijacked by Hannibal, as if both Tally and writer Thomas Harris even at this point have got a bit overly enamoured of him, a knock-on for the rest of the story too. It even has to stop the plot for MacGyver-esque escape sequence that feels like something out of a more violent superhero movie its all maybe a bit sillier than it pretends to be really, which sometimes comes across in the plotting too, a bit of a tension between the more dour investigation side and a few of those hammier moments that can clash with the prestige-y tone here. 
That said, its a rightfully iconic performance, and both Foster and Hopkins have so many great chances to play off of each other, even stronger as they go along, and I think one of the very last ClariceLector interactions at the prison is where the dynamic between these leads feels at its best. Both are (literally) mesmerising in the odd, quasi-father daughter bond that gets explored here, the more procedural and genre sides combining here with an intensity that really feels like this is firing on all cylinders. 
Building to so many real crescendos, the whole thing feels like a director fully in control of his craft some of Demmes indie experience comes through, a left of centre approach that benefits here. For all of the compelling two handers, those show-stopping moments of tension show how comfortable he is at going small, and ramping up to really compelling full-on Gothic territory as the thriller side just builds up, an almost dark fairytale quality that always keeps some sort of (slightly twisted) light at the end of the tunnel even as it leads you further in.
I wouldnt say Silence Of The Lambs an absolute favourite its never fully going to be my thing, but its all so well done I was drawn in anyway, even when the mix didnt always land for me at times. A dark, entertaining, deceptively offbeat journey into the heads of these characters, psychopath and normal alike, theres an uneasy fascination and repulsion Demme skilfully works with here, almost a horror-tinged rollercoaster ride, knowing when to pull in and draw away enough in a way that feels expertly done all the pieces coming together and elevated by a filmmaker on top of his game, so as the credits roll you know youve just watched a classic.

Lets start with the obvious
Blah blah holy shit Hannibal Lecter blah blah cinematography blah blah atmosphere blah Clarice blah what the actual fuck blah blah crazy blah.
SPOILER ALERT
Look, Silence of the Lambs is a masterful exercise in suspense and is a landmark in the thriller horror pantheon. 
You dont need me to tell you that.
In addition to its brilliant technical aspects-- specifically the visionary use of close-ups in mise-en-scene to convey balance of power during the films many tense exchanges (driving home the feeling that our protagonist is not in command of her space), praise should also be given to the films somewhat unprecedented strong feminist stance, wherein our lead (whose small-framed vantage point we experience the story through) is faced with the challenge of subsisting within a predominantly male law-enforcement workplace, and more broadly, patriarchal society. She does this while confronting a nightmarishly misogynistic monster in Ted Levines iconic Buffalo Bill-- a man who pushes the concept of the male gaze to a shocking end by literally using the female body for his perverse fulfillment. In the process of her figurative descent into hell and triumphant resurgence, Clarice Starling comes to terms with her own screaming demons.
Add to this a few brilliant thematic elements, such as rampant patriotic symbolism, a winged motif (storage garage, Lecters hanging security guard, moths, Buffalo Bill dance scene), as well as the gender reversal of the traditionally male lawman (Starling) vs traditionally female seamstress (Bill), and youve got yourself a dense, cerebral work that has depth.
Of course, there have always been some points of contention surrounding the film, the most prominent of which are
1-- The debate revolving around Anthony Hopkins pantomime-villain depiction of Dr. Lecter, in which the actor chews (apologies for the pun) the scene in a way that only he can. Divisive to audiences since its release, youll either come away singing the actors praises over an iconic performance or youll dismiss it as heavy-handed smoke and mirrors-- it is impossible to imagine an ambivalent viewer.
2-- An argument that has been gaining traction over the years since SotLs release that I feel worth looking into, and that is... 
Transphobia. Dramatic dun dun duuuun!
(Sorry it took so long to get to the point, but, in spite of my efforts, I could not jump into this discussion without giving the film some due praise.)
Anyway, I want to begin by saying that I dont mean to invalidate or devalue anyones takeaway from this film, especially in regards to how it might reflect on their own personal experiences and gender identity.
That being said, I would like to address the claim that Harris novel, Tallys script, as well as director Demmes finished film are transphobic, as I believe that to be a surface-level reading of a much more complex work, in much the same way as an assessment of the character of Buffalo Bill as a trans person (he is not) is a misreading of a deeply frayed character-- a monster who has a twisted notion of trans identity, and is, himself, deeply confused about it.
Its important to note that while Buffalo Bill is characterized as having a pathology that is rooted in his sexuality, a large portion of his backstory was cut from the final version of the film (notably pertaining to his history of child abuse), leaving the notorious villain as little more than a cipher to the audience. We never get to experience anything more than the briefest glimpses of his frayed psyche, yet its safe to assume that there is quite a bit to unpack there-- specifically (and in keeping with the overarching theme of the film) regarding his attitude towards women. 
Ted Levine (who portrays Bill) has stated that, in doing research for the role, he set out not to play a gay man, a transvestite or a trans person, as he believed the character to bear no relation to any gender identity hes ever come across-- including those of his subjects during his extensive research into serial killers. 
The character he portrays is a tortured aberration that is not in any way based on an individual psychological profile. 
Bill, rather, is an extension of the abstract concept of the male gaze, although twisted by his deranged pathology and psychopathic predisposition. Like the concept he embodies, Bill objectifies women, and in the process, seems genuinely incapable of seeing them as anything more than objects 
(
it rubs the lotion on its skin, or else it gets the hose again.
)-- specifically objects of desire. See if you can spot a picture of a euphoric Bill and a nude (female) stripper on one of the walls in his lair-- his ecstasy in the photo seeming to be rooted in an oversimplified notion of femininity as a coveted thing, and of his own male gaze as an honest and sincere form of flattery, desire and love. To be female is to want to be coveted, possessed and objectified.
More disturbingly, there doesnt seem to be more to his notion of womanhood and gender dynamics beyond that. This perversely one-dimensional idea of femininity is all there is to Bill, and he fixates on it.
The path to his transformation, then, is the actualization of this warped notion of womanhood-- the fuckable thing. 
As such, his transformation culminates in becoming the recipient of the male gaze-- he yearns to be objectified in the way that he has always objectified women (notice how he says
Id fuck me
during that infamous scene-- as if thats the highest compliment that he can givereceive) as that is the closest thing hes ever experienced of closeness intimacy love. He is incapable of conceiving of anything beyond that dynamic.
This is why he is deemed by his analysts as not fitting the parameters of a trans person. The notion he seems fixated on is a perverted, myopic notion of femininity. His ideal, which he feels compelled to transform into, is the corrupted product of patriarchal society.
Theres more to explore here about the character of Buffalo Bill, but anything short of a dissertation wouldnt do him justice, Im afraid. But you get the point.
It should be noted that, while there was an effort on the part of the production team to steer clear of any characterization that might be misconstrued as an attack on the LGBTQIA community (there are clearly stated lines to that end, such as Lecters Billy is not a real transsexual. But he thinks he is. He tries to be. Hes tried to be a lot of things, I expect. As well as Starlings There is no correlation in the literature to transsexualism and violence. Transsexuals are very passive.), the fact remains that the film has undoubtedly caused members of the LGBTQIA community indirect harm by seemingly reinforcing stereotypes. And that is a tragedy in itself, as any work of fiction that impacts a person or a group of people negatively (regardless of what it set out to achieve) should be called out on it, and its a shame that any person or group of people should suffer for it. The mistake seems to have been in the assumption that audience members are always discerning and would not come away with a surface reading of a really complex character, but lets face it, theres always going to be some fucking idiot who looks at the character of Bill and comes away with Aha! See? I knew it! Theyre all like that, these insert phobic slur!
That is the trouble with presenting an intelligent work of art-- the risk that part of the audience might misinterpret its meaning-- or worse, that they might use its content and warp it to push their own biases. And while it might be tempting to dismiss this concern as having to cater to the lowest-common-denominator in society, theres no denying that these opinions do have consequences in the real world (see Nietzsches writing as interpreted by Nazi party). And for that, I truly feel for anyone whose personhood might have in any way been negatively impacted by this film, in spite of its noble intentions.
There. Ive gone and rambled way longer than expected. Thanks, Bill.
In summary, is Silence of the Lambs a masterpiece Yes.
Is it transphobic (in my opinion) No.
Can it be misinterpreted as transphobic Yes.
Is that a problem Unfortunately-- Yes.

The story chronicles the life of Truman Burbank whose entire existence has been nothing but a 24x7 running TV show. This comedy-satire is much more heavy hitting than I remember it being when I first watched it as a teenager. Its a commentary on entertainment, reality, and our lives.

Twitch Plays Pokémon was an internet phenomenon that started in 2014 wherein viewers are the ones controlling the game by submitting inputs into the chatroom which were then read by the game. Initially starting as just a proof of concept, it quickly went viral and reached an average viewership of over 80,000 and an estimate of 1.16 million participants in total, whole communities borne out of the single cause of crowdsourcing the playthrough of a single-player game.
In being controlled by thousands of viewers simultaneously, the player avatar finds even performing the most basic of tasks to be nigh-insurmountable. Walking in a straight line is a practical impossibility, choosing an action in battle is a total crapshoot, even opening the menu reliably is a task too much to ask. Yet, regardless of how often he runs into the same wall over and over and over again, the avatar does so unerringly because that is all he knows. He is not aware of what the Pokemon experience is supposed to resemble, he is not aware of what his life should be like, he is not aware of all the voyeurs who come to directly influence his life. He simply does as he is compelled to do as he simply accepts the reality of the world with which he is presented.
The audience, however, is aware, and they are placed in a unique position of being both viewer and controller of the player avatar. To them, the players daily life is itself a spectacle simply because the context which surrounds it has declared it to be. Why is witnessing a myriad of players controlling an avatar inherently more compelling than a single player? Simply because it is declared to be, the spectacle itself born from the idea of the spectacle and thus perpetuating itself if anyone is responsible for it, it is the audience who willingly participates and thus creates the spectacle. In accordance with this is the creation of content from nothing more than the spectacle itself, a hivemind of humans finding meaning where there is none by simply making connections between patterns that are purely accidental affectionately nicknaming a Rattata Jay Leno because twitch collectively named it JLVWNNOOOO, revering the Helix Fossil as a deity despite it being a near-useless item because twitch collectively selected it so often giving the impression the avatar was worshipping it, dubbing an event Bloody Sunday because twitch collectively (inadvertently) deleted much of their captured pokemon. These occurrences by themselves do not have a significance greater than their literal meaning, but the collective audience of Twitch Plays Pokemon has instilled a greater significance through nothing but the shared experience of watching the spectacle.
However, ultimately the player avatar is nothing more than that an image in a computer program which lacks the capacity for free will. No matter how incongruent its experiences may be, no matter how meaningless its life may be, it is unable to question. Truman is the audience avatar of The Truman Show, which is itself within The Truman Show (of which we are the audience), and though his life is similarly a simulation which is controlled and influenced by his voyeurs, he differs in being able to question. He has the capacity to exert his own self back onto the audience and take control of the spectacle, take control of his existence as spectacle. It is in doing so that he attains free will, and so becomes a true man.

I remember growing up as a kid in the early 2000s and the big debate (besides Backstreet Boys or NSync) was between who was funnier Jim Carrey or Adam Sandler. I have always been on the side of Jim Carrey and that may simply be due to his natural physical comedy or that charisma that Sandler really didnt have for me as a child. 
My opinion has since changed regarding Sandlers acting (thank you, Uncut Gems), but Jim Carrey has held a special place in my heart. I grew up with a lot of his films when he was at the peak of his career. So, it was very surprising when I first watched The Truman Show and saw this completely different side of him. Of course, he is still naturally cheerful and expressive. That doesnt go away. 
But rather than play those traits for laughs, Carrey uses them here to establish Trumans innocence. Truman is just a naturally friendly person. I thought this was the coolest story as a child. Youre always famous and youre on TV! Each time I go back to this film, I cant help but be awestruck at how relevant it now is. It is neat (and I have to commend Weir on his creativity with camera angles) to see where exactly and how exactly Truman is being watched. 
With social media and influencers, the ability to maintain privacy or not be broadcasted by someone with a camera is difficult today. Watching the film now is very prophetic to me. The brilliance of this screenplay is how it balances sci-fi, comedy, and even drama. You get to see a bit of the outside world, but Weir decides to focus solely on Trumans experience which helps us connect even more to his struggles and eventual determination to break free. 
When the spotlight falls from the sky, I feel on the same wavelength as Truman. This unease amongst the impossibly perfect background. I also find it eerie how the depiction of small towns can feel like a cage. Growing up in one and currently living in one, while the quiet life can be nice, it can also be unrelentingly lonely. But, everyone knows each other in a small town, hence the constant feeling of being watched and therefore, judged. 
Weir does a brilliant job, I think, with the structure and pacing too. Truman begins to notice the small inconsistencies, the glitches in the Matrix. He rationalizes what occurs and moves on, but Weir keeps chipping away. I also love that we as the audience know the truth almost immediately. Sometimes, I wonder how this film would be if we spent the entire time wondering if Truman is correct or not. 
But, focusing on Truman is what makes this film work. For me, when we cut to the shows audience or production crew, Im not invested. However, Im always going to be invested in Ed Harris as Christof. I think I like him because hes not this maniacal villain who takes pleasure in running someones life. He truly thinks that hes protecting Truman from all of the bullshit in the real world. 
That may seem like love, but really its possession. Truman never had the chance to choose...well, anything. More than a great performance by Jim Carrey, The Truman Show is actually an insightful film about media and surveillance. Are we ever truly by ourselves or is someone always watching or listening?

The Truman Show is about the world as you know it dissolved, leaving nothing but your paranoid delusions. It truly is the most eloquent examination of solipsism this side of the Mississippi!
It works on every level. Truman is a prophecy his existence is a harbinger of reality television. His existence is that of ethical media consumption - when does acting become prostitution? Also, is there free will if an omniscient bystander is controlling the weather, your relations and your circumstances?
The eye is a camera, but for Peter Weir, the camera is an eye. Through some feat of directorial project or accident, The Truman Show is a sign of the times, so prominent that it never, sadly, falls from relevance.

On the surface, this is a film about media overreach, but The Truman Show offers so much more besides. Our protagonist begins the movie unaware that his life is actually the subject of a mass market international TV show. The film delivers the story as Truman, the only true man in his entirely fabricated reality, comes to realise the extent of the manipulation he is facing. Peter Weirs film augments the central thesis wjth commentary from the shows creator, technical crew and various viewers sat at home watching. At all times we the audience are aware of everything Truman is not. The story could easily be seen as a mirror to real life societal systems and unwritten rules that must be obeyed. Truman of course eventually realises that his false reality encompasses literally everything he knows and that in order to beat the system, you cant use the rules of the system itself. The ending of the film is so poignant in the way the hero is forced to literally upend his own manufactured programming to ultimately find the salvation of true autonomy. One of those films that gets better the more you think about it.

The details to this movie are insane. Taking the idea of having your life be a tv show and doing every possible psychological and emotional situation with that concept is just brilliant. While there hasnt been a show or anything quite as extreme as something like the Truman show, even in the internet age, the basic concepts of broadcasting your life to the world is very relevant. But even looking at it from a psychological perspective, its actually a pretty timeless concept. The idea of being watched, the idea of being seen by people you dont know, having to act a certain way without realizing how artificial it kinda is. We all act a certain way in front of people, the actual concept of privacy shrinks more and more as the years go by. Again, I dont think well ever see the literal concept of a Truman reality show, but the ideas the movie deals with can certainly be applied. 
Even as a movie, its insanely detailed. The travel agency having numerous posters of plane accidents, the fact that the people around Truman advertise products to make money for the show, every time an irregularity happens on the set, theres always something brought up afterward to make excuses for it. I could honestly list a bajillion things more because this movie is so dense with all that sweet sweet detail. 
This has probably my favorite ending stinger in a movie. Some random viewers asking what else is on after Truman goes off the air. Truly a masterpiece of a film, Im glad this came out the year I was born. Hopefully Im not living in a TV show.

The Truman Show de Peter Weir, est un film à la fois simple dans son concept et vertigineux dans ce quil raconte. Lidée est presque absurde au départ  un homme dont toute la vie est filmée à son insu, transformée en émission mondiale. Mais derrière ce principe brillant, le film transforme ça en réflexion très profonde sur la liberté, le contrôle, le mensonge et le besoin de sortir dune illusion confortable mais pervertie, dans notre rapport au divertissement .
On commence dans une ambiance lumineuse, presque publicitaire, avec cette ville parfaite qui ressemble à un décor de catalogue, et progressivement, tout devient inquiétant. Ce basculement est ce qui rend le film aussi fort  on découvre la prison de Truman en même temps que lui.
La réalisation de Weir joue énormément sur cette dualité entre illusion et réalité. Sur la sensation de surveillance permanente, avec des plans larges très propres qui montrent un monde artificiellement parfait, puis des angles cachés, presque voyeuristes, qui rappellent constamment que tout est observé. Cette opposition entre chaleur apparente et froideur du contrôle crée une tension douce mais constante. Le film ne cherche jamais le spectaculaire, il repose sur lidée que quelque chose ne tourne pas rond, comme un rêve trop bien organisé pour être réel. Le cadre est souvent très maîtrisé, pour montrer à quel point lenvironnement de Truman est contrôlé. Plus le film avance, plus cette perfection devient étouffante.
Et au centre de tout ça, il y a la performance de Jim Carrey, qui est vraiment la clé du film. Il livre un jeu beaucoup plus nuancé, mêlant naïveté, humour et profonde détresse existentielle. Il rend Truman incroyablement attachant, sincère, presque enfantin dans sa manière de faire confiance au monde. Et cest justement cette innocence qui rend la manipulation encore plus cruelle. Tout de même, on sent sa curiosité, sa peur, puis son courage qui apparaît lentement. 
En face, Ed Harris incarne Christof, une forme de dieu réalisateur avec un calme glaçant et convaincu de faire le bien. Il ne se voit pas comme un monstre, mais comme un créateur, un protecteur, ce qui rend le conflit encore plus intéressant. Ce nest pas un affrontement classique entre un héros et un méchant, mais entre deux visions du monde  la sécurité contre la liberté. Laura Linney, quant à elle, apporte aussi une dimension troublante, jouant une épouse factice coincée entre rôle imposé et culpabilité.
Enfin, ce qui rend le film aussi actuel, cest sa manière de parler du spectacle et de limage. Il évoque le besoin de sécurité face à la peur du réel. Truman vit dans un monde sans surprise, sans danger véritable, mais aussi sans liberté. À mesure quil doute, quil observe les incohérences, quil teste les limites de son univers, le film devient une quête philosophique  vaut-il mieux vivre dans une illusion confortable ou affronter une vérité incertaine ? Cette question résonne aujourdhui, à lère des réseaux sociaux et de la mise en scène permanente de nos vies dans une société fascinée par celles des autres. Et pourtant, malgré cette critique, le film reste très humain et même assez optimiste. La dernière partie, quand Truman décide daller jusquau bout de ses doutes en gravissant les marches, cela donne au film une dimension presque symbolique  quitter un monde fictif pour entrer dans linconnu. Cest simple, mais incroyablement puissant.

As a kid, you can enjoy the comedy and the ridiculousness of the concept, but as an adult, you start noticing all the deeper stuff about freedom, control, identity, routine, and how easy it can be to stay in a life simply because its familiar. Truman has an entire world telling him who he is and what his life should be, but he eventually realizes that even an uncertain reality is better than a perfect life that isnt really his. That idea has stuck with me way more this time around.

Man, what an absolute classic!
The Truman Show is a masterpiece. Id say its a basically a perfect film, blending genres of comedy, drama and even horror to explore how a mans reality and life is controlled for the sake of viewer ratings and money. Its both a modern telling of Platos ancient Allegory of the Cave and a haunting foreshadowing of the gamification of human lives and the depths humanity will go for entertainment. The former is the idea of someone loving living in their cave so much that they fear what could be beyond the light outside which is functionally the final dilemmas of the titular Truman himself. He can stay in this fake, manufactured world and live in relative comfort for the rest of his life (eventhough he knows something is false about it), or he can uncover the lie and go into the real world. The Matrix is another movie that explores this idea. It makes for a captivating story sure to stir the mind that stars an incredibly endearing main character. 
Jim Carrey as the main character Truman Burbank is probably his greatest role, disproving any notion that he was only a goofy comedic actor and delivers one of the greatest dramatic performances ever. His slow discovery of his reality is enthralling to see, and its a perfect way to display evil corporate capitalism through things like product placement and ya know, the fabrication of his entire family and existence. An absolute crime Jim Carrey didnt get an Oscar nod for this. Ed Harris is also noteworthy as the films antagonist, whose success profiting off of the facade of Trumans life makes him have a massive ego and act as if he is the god of his own manufactured world. Its a mask he maintains to the very end, until it becomes his undoing and leads to one of the most satisfying climactic decisions and final lines in film (In case i dont see ya, good afternoon, good evening and good night!) 
The Truman Show is one of my favourite movies, a thought provoking thrill ride as you uncover the world along with the main character and cheer for him in his journey. It tells a disturbing warning about the future of entertainment and how we disregard people for the sake of money and views. Its incredibly well made by director Peter Wier, with fantastic production design, cinematography and a great screenplay that delivers both comedy and strong emotion. Jim Carreys defining dramatic role that is rightfully iconic and this is worth seeing just for that, but i think its an amazing and touching story regardless. One of the all time greats, a must see!

The movie follows Truman Burbank, a man who lives what seems to be a peaceful, ordinary life in a seemingly perfect town. He has a job, a wife, and friends, and everything in his life appears perfectly normal. But as time goes by, strange things begin to happen, making him question the reality he lives in. He starts wondering whether everything around him is really what he believes it to be, or if theres a much bigger truth being hidden from him.
My favorite thing about this movie was its original and creative concept, and the clever way it was used to build the story. The idea itself is fascinating because it makes us question the nature of the reality we live in and how much we truly know about the truth surrounding us. Its true that these kinds of questions arent entirely new, and I think most of us have wondered at some point whether life is necessarily the way we see or understand it. But what makes this movie special is how it takes that question and turns it into a complete, entertaining story that encourages the audience to look at it from a different perspective.
For me, the aspect that deserves the most attention isnt simply the idea that someone could live in a fabricated reality without knowing it, but their right to know the truth and choose their own life. Even if Trumans life appears perfect and comfortable from the outside, hes still a person who never chose the circumstances he lives in. He doesnt know the truth about the world around him, and he cant make decisions based on a genuine understanding of his reality. And thats where the most important question comes in Whats the value of a perfect life if its built on deception, and the person living it doesnt even have the freedom to choose it?
This brings us to the most disturbing aspect of the concept the people controlling Trumans life. Their selfishness is obvious to me because theyve placed entertainment above his humanity. They treat his life as a source of amusement for others rather than as the life of a human being who deserves to know the truth and decide his own fate.
Whats frightening is that an entire persons life has become something for others to consume for entertainment, while he has absolutely no idea whats happening behind his back. This is where the movie opens the door to questions about the ethics of exploiting human lives and the boundaries people are willing to cross when entertainment becomes more important to them than human rights and dignity.
Despite how much I appreciated the way the movie explored its concept, I feel it couldve gone deeper into its message and some of its philosophical aspects. Not because it failed to communicate its ideas on the contrary, I think it used its concept cleverly and presented it in a clear and entertaining way. But the subject itself leaves room for deeper discussions than the ones we got to see. The movie had more potential to explore the meaning of freedom, a persons right to know the truth, and the difference between a life that appears happy and one that a person chooses for themselves.
These arent criticisms that take away from what makes the movie special, but theyre the reason I feel its concept deserved a deeper exploration to truly reach greatness.
As for the characters, I sympathized with Truman, but I never became deeply attached to him. My interest in the concept and the questions it raised was greater than my emotional connection to the character himself. Still, I think Jim Carrey delivered a very good performance that suited the role. He portrayed Truman in a way that served the movies overall vision, and seeing him outside the comedic roles were used to was a good fit for the kind of experience the movie was trying to deliver.
The pacing was also well-balanced and enjoyable for me. I had a good time watching the movie from beginning to end without ever feeling bored or wanting to stop.
The story progresses in a way that keeps your curiosity alive, and as Trumans suspicions grow, you become increasingly interested in discovering the truth hes trying to uncover. At the same time, though, the direction of the story made the ending relatively predictable to me, so it wasnt much of a surprise when it finally arrived.
Even so, I liked the ending and thought it suited the concept the movie had built its story around. I just wish wed gotten to see what happened to Truman afterward, because leaving the world hed lived in his entire life raises so many questions about his future and the life hell face after discovering the truth.
I was curious to know how hed adapt to a world he knew nothing about after spending his entire life inside a reality that was completely different from the truth. Thats one of the things that stayed on my mind after the ending, not because I disliked the ending itself, but because the story made me want to know more about Trumans fate after his decision.
I also think that if Id watched this movie years ago, it mightve affected me more because its concept wouldve felt much newer to me. That doesnt mean the idea has lost its value, but sometimes, when we encounter concepts weve already considered similar possibilities about, they dont inspire the same sense of wonder, even when the way theyre presented is remarkable.

Admittedly, Im not the biggest Jim Carrey fan, his filmography is hit and miss for me, and truly mostly misses. The Truman Show however is the exception. Not only is it one of my favorite Carrey led films, but its one of my favorite films as a whole. The Truman Show is a highly creative, heartfelt, and campy classic that has left a lasting a legacy and helped usher in a new genreera in cinema. The Truman Show walked so films like EDtv, The Matrix, The Island, and Dont Worry Darling could run. The Truman Show is comedic paranoia at its finest, a surrealist critique of societal voyeuristic tendencies through a satirical but effective lens. 
Most of Jim Carreys roles are slapstick and over the top in nature, its his shtick and to his credit hes one of the best in the category, its just not for me. The Truman Show subverts that notion and gives us a more a serious and even-keeled Carrey, one of his best performances to date. This version of Carrey felt real, and thats what made him so good to watch.
The Truman Show, being a show within a film, is unique for its time and remains a remarkably timeless form of cinematography. The Truman Show is intentionally hammy and peak sitcom (in the worst ways) in its presentation. The sets are cookie-cutter and vibrant. The color schemes are an array of nostalgic technicolor blends that harken back to the I Love Lucy classics of yesteryear, which is what they were going for, and nailed. While at times the script is clunky and the designs a bit too on the nose, The Truman Show behind Peter Weirs direction overcome these faults with its zany but grounded cinematography and memorable performances. 
Jim Carrey. Sure he still has his trademarked quirks and eccentric mannerisms littered throughout The Truman Show, but whats really special was his more earnest and thoughtful moments in his performance. Carrey pulled off the backwards childlike persona well while also handling his emotional turmoil and apparent confusion admirably. The Truman Show for me is Jim Carreys breakout performance. The Truman Show is a diverse film that is equal parts psychological drama, dystopian comedy, and science-fiction, and somehow, despite its scattershot approach, it works. The Truman Show is a clever and thought provoking film that masterfully melds comedy and emotional heft into a compelling and now timeless classic. ¿Qué es la realidad?
La alegoría de La Caverna fue creada por el filósofo Platón, para simbolizar el conocimiento humano. Según esta teoría, el hombre sería como un prisionero en una cueva, y lo que conoce es solo un reflejo o la sombra de la realidad. Lo real está fuera de la cueva, algo es difícil de comprender cuando no hemos salido nunca de ella y nos hemos acostumbrado a utilizar y a trabajar con las sombras. En este sentido, no conocemos la existencia de lo real o nos da miedo.
Para salir de la Caverna no se precisa fuerza física, sino fuerza mental(tal como hace Truman en ese final PERFECTO). Tras pasar varios años observando una realidad en forma de sombras, llega un momento en el que el individuo tiene que hacer un ejercicio de reflexión para conseguir su libertad. Pensar críticamente, cuestionándose el sistema establecido y sospechando de la información que recibimos.
¿Cuál es nuestra caverna? El hogar familiar o el entorno en el que hemos crecido. Lo normal es que desde la infancia nos hayan inculcado una serie de valores, que van desde los religiosos a lo políticos. Al nacer en una comunidad, crecemos con unas tradiciones que nos aportan identidad. Así, muchas personas son reticentes a lo nuevo por miedo a perder esa identidad.
Como seres humanos buscadores de seguridad, habita en nosotros una cierta tendencia a acoger las costumbres conocidas que practican las personas que queremos, en este sentido ni la sociedad ni la familia nos enseñan a mirar (aunque nosotros podamos observar). No se fomenta la opinión crítica. Pocos niños tienen entornos que les estimulen para analizar, comparar y tener una opinión propia, así como practicar la autoconciencia.
El personaje principal de esta película, Truman, es un hombre que no ha podido decidir nada en su vida. Desde que nació, fue comprado por el programa de televisión del que es el propio protagonista, y todas las decisiones que toma (tener novia, casarse, comprarse una casa, trabajar) no son escogidas por él, sino que son acciones guiadas por el creador del programa (que en este caso, lo comparan con un dios).
Truman vive feliz y ajeno a todo, dentro de la enorme cúpula que le han construido como ciudad. Y cuando sospecha algo o tiene un atisbo de duda, no puede salir de ese mundo porque está controlado por los miedos e inseguridades que le han inducido en la infancia (por ejemplo, el mar y el trauma con su padre). Pero llega un momento en el que ya no puede obviar sus dudas, porque su mundo no es el de antes.
En verdad, todos somos Truman. La única opción que tenemos de ser auténticos es cuando esa chispa, ese despertar de la conciencia, se produce en nosotros. Y solo nuestra voluntad nos ayuda a superar el miedo que nos pueda suscitar el escenario que nos espere.
En El Show de Truman observamos dos sociedades. La película se centra en el mundo en el que vive Truman, el falso mundo, a través del cual se pretende despertar.Pero además del falso mundo de Truman, la trama tiene lugar de alguna manera también fuera del programa de televisión, es decir, en el mundo real. Así, a parte de la sociedad que rodea a Truman en su vida diaria, podemos analizar a la sociedad que está viendo el show.
Es esta sociedad sobre la que vamos a reflexionar a continuación, y que es oportunamente caricaturizada y criticada en la película. Una sociedad enganchada al televisor, que sigue el show de Truman como si sus propias vidas estuvieran ligadas al destino del personaje Truman. Son personas que en la película aparecen siempre mirando la pantalla de la televisión, y que ríen, sufren y lloran siguiendo a Truman.
¿Hasta qué punto son personas estos espectadores? ¿Ejercen su papel de ciudadanos activos, o por el contrario son simples espectadores sentados en un sofá? En la película se muestran una serie de personas que viven para y por el show de Truman. Es lo más importante que hacen cada día ver ese programa de televisión. Vemos dos guardias de seguridad que se olvidan de su trabajo, una madre que no presta atención a su bebé, una pareja de abuelas que no tienen nada más que hacer todos ellos han dejado a un lado el mundo real y se centran en seguir la vida de un personaje ficticio.
Estando sentado en el sofá, viendo la telenovela o escuchando a la ex-pareja de aquel torero gritarle a la amante de tal actor, el ciudadano no sólo está adoptando un papel de espectador. El individuo no sirve al sistema únicamente como observador pasivo, sino que también es convertido en un potencial consumidor. Las estrategias de publicidad encubierta son muy bien representadas en El Show de Truman, puesto que los televidentes, enganchados al show, están recibiendo continuamente mensajes que les incitan a comprar productos que, en realidad, no necesitan.
¿Por qué hay tanta publicidad? Porque hay millones de potenciales consumidores. Son millones los espectadores que, cada día, se sientan frente al televisor y se dejan desinformar y distraer. Y entre tanta distracción, sin darnos cuenta, nuestro cerebro va recibiendo mensajes muy claros Necesito esas zapatillas, ese videojuego es el mejor, tengo que beber ese refresco
Por otra parte me gustaría hablar sobre, la desinformación que se trata en esta pelicula. Desinformar es la acción de dar información insuficiente o manipulada intencionadamente, al servicio de ciertos fines. Suelen ser las grandes esferas de poder quienes están interesadas en someter a la población al engaño.
En el caso de El Show de Truman, la desinformación es en realidad el pilar fundamental sobre el que se asienta la trama Truman está completamente desinformado. No conoce el verdadero mundo real. Está engañado. No tiene información veraz para conocer la realidad que le rodea.
Una de las estrategias de la desinformación (y que hace más complicado detectarla) es conseguir que el consumidor de información crea estar bien informado. Aunque en la película Truman acaba sospechando, lo cierto es que pasa muchos años engañado, confiando en la información que recibe. En el caso de la desinformación aplicada a la otra sociedad de la película (el mundo real, donde viven los televidentes que ven el show), no podemos decir que los medios de comunicación estén desinformando directamente a la población, pero se puede inferir que los espectadores del programa de televisión están de alguna manera manipulados, ya que no atienden a los problemas reales de la vida, sino que se limitan a sentarse y a ver el Show de Truman. Un ejemplo extremo lo podemos observar en la madre que se olvida de cuidar a su bebé porque está viendo el show.
El acto de libertad más puro es pensar
Como conclusiónCuando se produce en nosotros ese despertar de la conciencia, adquirimos energía y determinación para salir de la zona de confort y de nuestro entorno, alentados por la sensación de que alejándonos veremos las cosas más claras para luego, desde nuestro interior, preguntarnos ¿Qué quiero hacer con mi vida? ¿Me siguen llenando mis creencias? ¿En qué creo o confío? ¿Cuál es mi verdad?
Tus respuestas deben tener para ti más valor que la opinión de los demás, puesto que son perfectas para ti están hechas a tu medida y no a la de otros. Es fácil pensar que no somos libres, puesto que todos tenemos responsabilidades (familia, estudios, trabajo), pero la verdad es que el acto de libertad más accesible y puro es pensar. Somos libres de pensar e imaginar lo que queramos, igual que somos libres de decidir en consecuencia a ello. A Truman también se le da la oportunidad de conocer la verdad.
Cuando nos quedamos con lo de siempre, solo con lo que nos han enseñado, impedimos que se produzca una evolución. En cambio, cuando superamos el miedo a lo desconocido y buscamos nuestro propio conocimiento, empezamos a caminar por un sendero en el que adquirimos principios, valores y creencias propios, que son más sanos y auténticos, menos disonantes. But how do you stay in such a place, fighting against yourself to feel something where theres nothing to feel, where youre surrounded but alone, used and deprived from what every human being should have - basic human relationships and decency - for the pure sake of other peoples entertainment.
Its a film that very well played with its concept and the meaning of what a happy ending truly is. And if such a thing could even exist. Its heartbreaking but hopeful in its ambiguity of how this mans life is shown and how were taught it should be. Im not as angry at James Camerons Titanic as I once was as a stupid teenager. In its expansive canvas, I find a great deal of interest in its class tension, the spectacle of modernity, the unsinkable ship in motion, with Cameron carefully stacking various narratives and propulsive melodrama in the layers of the maiden voyage. The interplay between the framing device and the titanic recreation results in graceful dissolves, thrilling crane shots, and an evolving romance doomed and kept away. Theres a lot to love about Camerons film, and I understand why it has enraptured so many (my sister saw it 12 times in its original run at my small-town one-screen theater), but it fails to fully expand on its moving parts. It chugs along, the end result being quiet desperation, inevitability, and death, but often it is too sluggish to sing as a romance in addition to the overwhelming spectacle. Cameron is still a king, though.

My favorite image in Titanic is probably the brief slow-motion shot of Kate Winslets white gown as she runs through the engine room with DiCaprio.  It pairs down the films central, very obvious rich and poor juxtaposition down to one single image - rare to find in such a total behemoth of movie.  But its obviousness doesnt mean its impact is syphoned out nor does it mean it loses its complexity, and whats most important is that it actually doesnt show class as separated as it is throughout the movie but rather suggests a fluidity between the two - and while that concept of fluidity will ultimately end in defeat by the films end, its still the films central idea and one that Cameron will continue to develop in, of all things, his two Avatar films. 
Part of Titanics appeal is that it actually barely has a plot and is more like an engine - even the movies central romance is in service to the engine.  And piece by piece Cameron hangs each section of the Titanic and its social classes and systems onto the engine so we can see them clearly and most importantly, simply.  Thats why its characters are like bots or sims - even Jack and Rose have very little characterization beyond their class positions, only carried over further because of the charm and genuine chemistry DiCaprio and Winslet bring to their respective roles.  But everyone on the Titanic is like a bot, an unthinking vessel for their class and social position.  Its only through seeing what - by way of decorum - is supposed to be inaccessible, which provokes internal revolt in these bots, and force two of them to break the rules.  The first is Jack - the obvious stand-in for Cameron himself given his own rather humble beginnings as a Northern Ontario truck driver who couldnt afford to go to film school (in fact the most unrealistic thing about the movie is that Jack dies, given that Cameron would go on to become one of the most powerful men in the American film industry) - who quickly becomes aware of the simple relationship between class and decorum he discovers fitting in is just a nice suit and table manners.  Meanwhile characters like Billy Zanes Cal and his fellow passengers sit and reflexively talk politics as though a game, with little awareness of those who reside in steerage below them.
In the same way, Titanic isnt like, a Marxist film by any means, but it understands that these same ideas make up the core contradictions of the basic societies which we live in and furthermore understands that most everybody is aware of these contradictions, whether conciously or not.  Thats why it connects with so many people, thats even why its so successful and why its the romantic aspect and not the disaster aspect that draws people back.  Its an almost perfect example of the inequalities which provoke romanticism in the first place.  And with that clear understanding of social contradictions which make up our world today, Titanic is one of the perfect examples of a true film for the masses.  People leave the theatre weeping because true love dies with not being wealthy enough to be placed on an escape boat.  
Thats also why the disaster element is so effective, and more thrilling than even suspenseful.  It doesnt inspire fear, it inspires awe, because we get to watch all these systems be destroyed in one huge swing - even the Church!  Because despite everything, the huge budget, the melodramatics, Camerons own occasional directorial clumsiness, our director is interested in truth above all.  Its a beautiful work of engineering that in a way is a work of reverse engineering of the majesty of the ship itself, and as such the social systems it upholds and facilitates.  Titanic even gets called an end of the world film - bizzare on paper yet it makes sense because we are shown the world in microcosm, and then we watch it be destroyed because maybe its not worth saving if it facilitates the division that it does.  For the same reason, its why this films grand romantic tradition is so effective, because it stands at counterpoint with the divisions, as though the romantic and the end of the world are on the same side.  Truth has always been the goal of the philosopher and the artist, while Cameron is perhaps debatable as the former, he certainly is not at the latter.

O clássico e o tecnológico em TITANIC (1997)

Memória espectral, o cinema é um luto magnífico, um trabalho de luto magnificado. E ele está pronto a se deixar impressionar por todas as memórias enlutadas, isto é, pelos momentos trágicos ou épicos da história. São então esses enlutamentos sucessivos, ligados à história e ao cinema, que, hoje, fazem caminhar as personagens mais interessantes. Os corpos enxertados desses fantasmas são a matéria mesma das intrigas do cinema.
Jacques Derrida em entrevista para a Cahiers du Cinéma (abril de 2001).

Jean-Marc Lalanne, em texto sobre Titanic (1997) para a Cahiers du Cinéma em 1998, afirma que a obra de Cameron representa um ponto de inflexão do cinema americano. Uma transição do seu maneirismo para um sonho neoclássico.
Distante das visões apocalípticas ou irônicas de diretores como Oliver Stone e Irmãos Coen, abordagens que direta e indiretamente marcaram o imaginário estadunidense noventista e, definitivamente, longe de qualquer caricaturização oitentista, Cameron procurou, em seu longa, ressuscitar uma grandiosidade atemporal, uma natureza arquetípica das histórias de amor e morte que é pedra fundamental das grandes narrativas da humanidade.
Seria Titanic o primeiro filme pós anos 80 que busca repensar uma iconografia clássica? Uma obra que rejeita a simples reverência ou reciclagem, mas parte em busca de uma reconquista pelo que é efetivamente inocente.
Ao mesmo tempo que o filme parte de uma perspectiva artesanal muito comovente nessa restituição de um sonho clássico, de uma narrativa grandiosa e tradicional, é evidente que o longa funda essa mediação sobre uma base bastante cara ao seu autor a tecnologia. 
E não estamos falando apenas da tecnologia que permitiu a reconstrução virtual do navio e de sua tragédia grandiosa, mas em como a obra assume a artificialidade na sua dinâmica dramática.
O cenário idílico é sinteticamente recriado, da sua luz falsa alaranjada  uma filiação muito pouco solar  ao tom asséptico dos ambientes de um navio novo em folha. Nas externas o que brota é essa luz inautêntica  mais artificial ainda na icônica cena do casal protagonista na ponta do navio  e nas internas, a reprodução ideal e intocável de tudo, dos objetos aos ambientes. Uma espécie de PROJAC utópico.
Cameron assume aquele espaço como um estúdio magnificado. O tempo não passou aqui. É tudo novo e fresco, conservado numa ordem de simulacro. O navio é um estúdio de cinema, um sonho clássico naufragado que o diretor tenta recriar.
Nem por isso Titanic é um obra nostálgica. Mais do que uma reverência, o que se procura é uma continuidade, uma leveza que nos aponte para aquilo que já sabemos que vai acontecer. Amor e morte se complementam a partir dessa fantasmagoria, desse espectro cinematográfico que ronda o filme, mas que nunca é exatamente impositivo em sua orientação.
Mesmo já sabendo o que vai acontecer, que a tragédia é iminente, o trabalho nos prende através da sutileza  com que Cameron leva a história. Estamos diante de uma obra grandiloquente, mas também de condução muito delicada.
Até a morte aqui é convidativa, imersa numa perspectiva de sonho, de pesadelo distante em que somos espectadores protegidos. É evidente que a tensão existe, mas o fim é guiado por uma delicadeza, um aconchego, uma tragédia contemplativa produzida para ser acolhida numa cadeira almofadada de cinema.
O naufrágio, o fato real, é muito mais mote de fantasia, de cenário disparador de efeitos lúdicos, do que contextualização crua dos eventos. O cinema testemunha, mas remodela, recompõe a realidade a partir do tema novelesco e sedutor. A imersão do espectador é natural. E a tecnologia é responsável por isso. Uma tecnologia que não se escancara ,mas que se integra ao modo sutil e elegante do diretor conduzir a narrativa.
Cameron parte de um arsenal técnico muito pesado, mas nos guia com mãos leves. As panorâmicas externas em CGI, o deslizar da steadycam, os corpos despencando em ângulos primorosos. Tudo reitera um ponto de vista onipresente que testemunha aquela situação com a devida distância, com o devido balançar harmônico das ondas.
Titanic é uma fábula em que autoria e tecnologia se unem, acima de tudo, em benefício de uma experiência de espectador. É como se tudo fosse matematicamente programado para ser o mais eficientemente assimilado, do tempo de cada olhar a iminência dramática das cenas, em uma perspectiva ao mesmo tempo hábil, afável e devastadora.
A autoria é equilibrada por essa visão tecnológica, contemporânea em suas relações com o suporte e a imagem, mas absolutamente aberta a demandas populares, articulando-se numa dimensão que ao mesmo tempo que nunca isola a visão de seu autor, compreende a eficiência do seu produto, integra-se ao seu meio e a engrenagem mercadológica dele.
Seria James Cameron de 1997 o mesmo o artesão freelancer que David Fincher é nos dias de hoje? Dois diretores em que o estilo fala mais sobre a exigência de um meandro do entretenimento do que sobre uma visão autoral pesada do trabalho, dois autores em que a tecnologia funciona, constantemente, em prol dessa reivindicação, dessa fruição do clássico que encontra a solicitação astuta contemporânea.
E se Fincher rejeita a ingenuidade de Cameron  é inegável que vivemos a era das narrativas cínicas -, se Fincher refunda o clássico com uma acidez que é característica dos nossos tempos, o cineasta, atualmente, é um dos que melhor concilia a evolução dos suportes (o uso do digital) com uma ideia de produto cinematográfico, de entregar não apenas um filme, mas um trabalho que cumpra seus desígnios industriais na cultura que pertence. Em poucas palavras a assimilação tecnológica como mote dramático atemporal
Não que Avatar (2009) não tenha dado uma continuidade digna a esse sonho neoclássico, já que ele até o deslumbra ainda mais  tanto no sentido do tecnologia como um acontecimento (o primeiro grande filme em 3d), como dessa sentença inocente do romance  mas um só filme não pode dar conta de um panorama tão extenso.
É claro que existem constantes tentativas de retomar esse ideal clássica, mas diferente de Fincher, diretores como James Gray, Christopher Nolan e Paul Thomas Anderson (para ficarmos numa tríade clássica contemporânea de intenções bastante específicas entre si) estão muito mais empenhados em uma visão individualizada e isolada, em construir uma ideia de clássico (até de blockbuster no caso de Nolan) partindo de uma inflexão autoral mais incisiva, do que em se integrar a uma demanda.
Não é por menos que os três diretores compartilham de um gosto pela produção grandiosa, mas que conserve a tecnologia em um campo muito mais limitado, prezando por um realismo, efeitos práticos e até uma vontade em perpetuar o suporte da película.
Cameron e Fincher compartilham de uma iconoclastia quase maquiavélica. São homens que acreditam que para perpetuar alguns mitos é preciso abrir certas concessões. Não existe a romantização do processo (tão cara para James Gray), mas a assimilação de uma evolução pragmática inevitável da linguagem, de uma eficiência pela fraude.
O que é Titanic se não um grande circo tecnológico encenado na impessoalidade de um estúdio? A renovação vem pelas vias de suas próprias mentiras. E em Titanic, literalmente, do seu próprio ideal de morte.
Ao magnificar esse luto, Cameron transforma a memória espectral de uma tragédia e de um cinema em um apelo atemporal, em uma luta não pelo que é novo, mas pelo que sempre pertenceu ao presente.

The romance that defined a generation, beautifully contrasted by the tragedy of the Titanic.
Im the king of the world!
I was in middle school when the world became obsessed with the love affair between Jack and Rose, which swept both box office records and the Academy Awards. And for good reason, because Writer and Director James Camerons epic romance Titanic is a Hollywood blockbuster through and through that is executed to perfection.  
I figure lifes a gift and I dont intend on wasting it. You dont know what hand youre gonna get dealt next. You learn to take life as it comes at you... to make each day count.
Having seen the other great Titanic movie A Night to Remember recently, it is interesting to see how Cameron took the most captivating elements of the tragic event in that film and expanded on them by putting us in the shoes of these two people we have grown to care about, experiencing these events first hand. Could this be a turn off to people that would prefer the historical aspect of the story placed front and center ... absolutely. For example, there is a scene where the guys watching out for icebergs get distracted by Jack and Rose kissing. Also, there is that connection between the builder of the Titanic and Rose that is used and a plot device to introduce the lifeboat shortage element. While I see these conventions, they dont bother me at all since these amazing characters give me such an emotional gateway into this experience.
But lets be honest, that amazing score from James Horner does much of the heavy lifting to make us feel the weight of this story. Plus you have the incredible Celine Dion singing such a powerful song that ties into the plot perfectly with My Heart Will Go On.
I just have to say it .... DAMN this is a beautiful movie, and it makes my heart soar!
Its been 84 years, and I can still smell the fresh paint. The china had never been used. The sheets had never been slept in. Titanic was called the Ship of Dreams, and it was. It really was...
I love how the movie takes its time in the opening showing us the actual Titanic at the bottom of the North Atlantic. And old Rose becomes this pathway back in time as she describes her experience. Sure the whole Heart of The Sea stuff and her bad guy fiance are very Hollywood, but they still work well within the context of the story and dont feel forced. Rose has grown up in an upper-class family but has a earning passion to live a more adventurous life, apart from fancy dinners with other rich people.
Jack being this super charming working-class guy contrasts Rose so well, and it is clear to see why she would be fond of him. Plus he is an artist, which she also has a passion for. I just love that scene where they go to the economy class section and dance to those very Irish sounding drums, kind of like River Dance. Kate Winslet is so charming and stunning and those scenes with her and Leo like at the front of the ship, her showing off her old ballet skills, the naked portrait session, and the car windows getting steamed up are all on point. I find it interesting how the front of the ship becomes such a focal point throughout the story as we return to it during each phase. 
As a kid I had no idea so much of the boat on the water scenes were all CGI, and they still look so convincing. The production design of the entire ship is outstanding, and I especially enjoyed how they captured the look of the water bursting into all those cabins, and those huge pistons in the engine room area of the ship. Finally, the ship going upright in the water before breaking in half and sinking is simply breathtaking.
The first few times I saw this I thought plenty of emphasis was placed on the Captain and the prideful decision to make the ship go faster. This part and the attempts to get help are covered much better in A Night to Remember, which makes these movies excellent companion pieces to each other. And I would be remiss as a musician myself, if I did not note the subplot about the small string ensemble continuing to play amongst the chaos.    
I am not sure if it was the settings on my TV or what, but I kept seeing these strong pops of red and blue during the dark nighttime scene on the water, that unfortunately really pulled me out of that moment. I noticed the same thing last year when I watched the Helms Deep scene in LOTR The Two Towers. 
But the film does do an excellent job of conveying how cold it was for all those people floating in the water, slowing freezing to death while so many lifeboats had room to spare. Could Jack have crawled up on the piece of wood too? Maybe, but he wanted to put Roses safety before his own, and was able to do so during a time of crisis when so many others acted selfishly. Now watching this as an adult, this was the first time I noticed how the pictures of Rose once she got to America reflected many of the conversations she had with Jack like being on the beach by the roller coaster, and riding a horse cowboy style.   
I grew up loving big sweeping Hollywood movies with powerful music, characters, and action. And while I have grown to also love more artsy and subtle films ... movies like Titanic are what made me fall in love with cinema and I will never turn my back on them!
Thanks for reading.
