There are two kinds of people in this world Those who consider this film to be perfect. And those who are wrong.
Winner of 11 Academy Awards including Best Picture, the highest-grossing motion picture of its time and a cultural phenomenon that arguably has no equals, Titanic is an extraordinary feat of blockbuster filmmaking that presents its gifted filmmaker at the apex of his craft as he offers a spectacle of such breathtaking cinematic ingenuity  profound emotional depth that it can still rival  demolish majority of tentpole releases of today on most fronts without breaking a sweat.
Written  directed by James Cameron (Aliens  Terminator 2), the story takes a simple premise of two star-crossed lovers from different social class who fall in love on the maiden voyage of the ill-fated vessel. It is a safe narrative framework to apply amid the backdrop of a tragedy but it is done with such warmth  sincerity that we are fully immersed  invested in the unfolding love story and are already aboard when the inevitable happens and turns this tender romance into a tense  thrilling survival tale.
Every aspect leaves an awe-inspiring impression, be it the meticulous detailing of the set pieces that summons the ship back to surface from the oceanic depths in a jaw-dropping fashion, era-appropriate costumes  props that transport us to its period setting, impeccable camerawork  lighting that photographs each moment in stunning clarity, neat editing that allows the romance to blossom at its own pace while steadily pacing the drama, and groundbreaking visual effects that set a new benchmark for the entire industry.
Despite the project marking a radical departure for Cameron when compared to his earlier efforts, he steers the production ship with sophistication and directs each scene with unfailing authority to deliver the desired goods. James Horners exquisite  evocative score is just as essential to the viewing experience, for it elevates  enriches the emotional journey by an enormous magnitude. And it doesnt end there, for the performances are just as brilliant, with Leonardo DiCaprio  Kate Winslet leading from the front with an intoxicating chemistry that just works.
The young  novice DiCaprio  Winslet make for perfect casting here as Cameron moulds them into our generations Romeo  Juliet and lets their youthful energy  passion anchor the core element of the picture. And then there is the final hour where James Cameron proves why he is a visionary with no equals as he turns the sinking of the ship into one of the most emotionally harrowing, nail-biting  nerve-wracking sequences ever conceived  attempted on the film canvas.
Overall, Titanic is an immaculately crafted  flawlessly executed Hollywood epic that expertly blends old-school melodrama with state-of-the-art visuals  first-rate craftsmanship to deliver a grand, memorable  powerfully moving delight. Establishing James Cameron as the one artist you never bet against, catapulting its leads into overnight stardom, and still retaining every bit of its magic, allure  emotional appeal after all these years, Titanic is one of the greatest achievements of its medium and is a romantic saga for the ages that engulfed  enraptured a whole generation unlike anything before or since.

a hundred things could be said of the total mastery of craft on display here witnessing the third act in a theater felt like seeing the trench run in Star Wars for the first time. this, along with LOTR, feels like it marks the end of the celluloid era of VFX innovation and experimentation the blowing up miniatures in a basement era, so to speak. more than anything, the attention to detail in the timeline of the ship sinking and sheer scope on display all feel birthed out of the wide-eyed childlike imaginations of Camerons boyhood, before any of this had ever been brought to life on a movie screen and it was all just an ominous and spectacular historical image in the public memory. everything about the third act feels like an attempt to finally translate that hazy image into reality, and its remarkable and harrowing and magnificent and terrifying and one of the greatest action movies of all time. Camerons third acts are something else. And Ill never be able to explain or understand the way that still, after all these years, my brain still thinks the ship might manage to steer away from the iceberg just in time.
more than anything Im struck again by the overtly political nature of so much of Camerons work in many ways, this movie is saying exactly what things like Snowpiercer or even Dont Look Up are trying to say, but cloaked in a far more palatable pop art romance format. the sinking of the Titanic is faithfully realized as a historical event in a vacuum, but its also strikingly prophetic to the way humans respond to impending disaster throughout all time. Cameron depicts the breadth of human reactions with elegant grace some fight for their lives, some try to buy their way out, some humbly pray to God, some are paralyzed with guilt and grief, some hold their loved ones close and wait to meet their end together. And some, even as the ship is sinking, continue to make music. I cant help but think that Cameron sees himself as that violin player, playing his heart out on the eve of the end of the world. 
The characters in Titanic are not complex, the plot is not complex, and even the social commentary is not complex in the sense of going beyond the black-and-white, but I think the commentary particularly does have more layers than people often give it credit for. We see the way that despite its claims to be the epitome of culture, the upper-class actually erases culture, or buries it in the bowels of the lower decks, where Irish jigs are still going strong. We witness the way that uncontrollable disasters always implicate and affect the most low-income populations first - in this case, because they are literally at the lowest part of a flooding ship. You couldnt come up with a more poignant parable if you tried. We watch the complete luck-of-the-draw nature of who lives and dies combined with the systemic hierarchy that does make some things go beyond luck. And of course, like much of Camerons work, one of the primary antagonists is a cop.
In the midst of all this, theres a love story so pure and saccharine and good that its impossible to resist. Some might see this as a stain on an otherwise political or harrowing historical epic, but I think Camerons instincts are good in the midst of incomprehensible loss, we need to be able to view and understand things through the lens of an individual relationship...and why not a relationship tailor-made for us to care about it? Some might call that manipulative, but I say thats what cinema is all about.

In English Titanic is an operatic spectacle, a romantic epic wrapped in James Camerons grandiose filmmaking. But above all, its a film that transcends the historical event itself to capture the heart of classic melodrama, where tragedy and love intertwine in an immortal narrative.
The films structure is ingenious, anchoring itself in the present to revisit the past with an almost mythical sense of nostalgia. Through Roses memory, the Titanic resurfaces not just as a sunken relic but as a microcosm of its eraa floating palace reflecting class disparities and the illusion of invulnerability in the pre-World War I world. Camerons film moves with the grandeur of a David Lean epic but carries the emotional sensitivity of a Douglas Sirk drama.
The relationship between Jack and Rose could have easily fallen into the stereotype of an impossible love between social classes, but Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet inject such sincerity into their roles that their connection becomes genuinely visceral. Jack is the spark of freedom and spontaneity, while Rose represents the suffocating weight of societal expectations. What could have been merely a teenage love story transforms into a cry against the chains of social oppression and the inevitability of fate.
The impact of the disaster is amplified by Camerons vision, which balances technical spectacle with an overwhelming emotional weight. Every phase of the sinking is meticulously detailed, creating a crushing sense of helplessness. The water flooding the corridors, the musicians playing until the end, the class divide persisting even in deatheverything contributes to one of the most astonishing sequences in cinema history. The tragedy of the Titanic unfolds not just as a historical event but as a meditation on the fleeting nature of life and the indifference of fate.
In the end, Titanic remains a film that defies cynics. Its technical grandeur and Hollywood aesthetics never overshadow the humanity of its story. Cameron captures beauty and horror in equal measure, proving that spectacle can be just as intimate as it is epic. And above all, that some storiesno matter how much time passesnever sink.

It of course figures that Camerons crowning achievement as an on-set tyrant and a man hell-bent on drowning at least one above-the-line actor before he dies is also (at least until The Way of Water) his most shamelessly earnest and empathetic movie. Cameron has spoken of being drawn to the project first for the technical challenge and the nerdy minutiae of the disaster itself, only to find himself more and more touched by the loss of life he read about while researching. That can be seen at every turn, whether in the first halfs extended interest in the socially isolated spheres of each cabin classs little world of spartan furnishing or unbearable splendor. Even among the rich, the film finds it cannot hate anyone not played by Billy Zane, for even though first-class had a much higher survival rate than those deemed less important, the films foreknowledge that many will find equality with their lower-placed peers in death.
Even though a lot of the CGI has inevitably dated, this remains a visual and technical marvel. Thats obviously true of the second halfs use of sinking sets and utterly terrifying rushing water, but it even applies to earlier scenes that do as much to patiently set up every significant area of the ship so you feel that much more horrified watching them obliterated later as it does building the characters. Still, every time I return to this I come away more transfixed by the little classical compositions of peoples varied responses to impending doom that are charged with so much emotion. The displays of cowardice from men who sneak onto lifeboats that you can hardly condemn. The image of an elderly couple entwining their limbs into each others in bed as the water starts to rise. And yes, even that shot of the guy bonking off the propeller as he falls to his death has a queasiness to it that belies attempts to turn it into a gag Cameron is hammering home the indignity of death, not trying to get a gallows laugh out of you. Leo spent a decade running from the heartthrob image this gave him and Winslet didnt get another part worthy of her exposure here almost until the mid-Aughts, but both have rarely been better than they are here, selling instant, life-ruining infatuation better than just about anyone who have played Romeo and Juliet.

Buenísima película, al fin vi por primera vez este clásico.
Titanic me calló la boca, me negué a verla por años con la idea de que estaba sobrevalorada y al final la vi y puedo decir que me gustó, su historia es muy linda y, a pesar de ya saber sobre casi todo, me pareció emocionante y entiendo por qué tanta gente la ama.
Sinopsis Una joven de la alta sociedad abandona a su arrogante pretendiente por un artista humilde en el trasatlántico que se hundió durante su viaje inaugural.
La historia me gusto muchísimo, se me pasó volando. La película dura poco más de tres horas y la verdad es que se me pasó rapidísimo. La historia intercala entre presente y pasado, mostrándonos a una anciana Rose contando los hechos en el Titanic. Todo esto le suma mucho a la cinta y al desarrollo de Rose, a quien vemos lo mucho que le afectó el accidente y que no olvida su historia con Jack. También, yendo hacia el pasado, vemos la historia de ellos dos, la cual me encantó y me parece que está muy bien desarrollada, lo único que se le puede criticar es que se enamoraron rápido, ya que compartieron poco tiempo juntos. Sin embargo, me parece que esto está un poco justificado por cómo Jack la ayudó a volver a ser ella. Me parece que su relación es el corazón de la película, ellos dos nos dan algunos momentos muy emotivos y memorables, sin dudas de las más icónicas del cine. Por otro lado, todo el momento del accidente me pareció increíble, está muy bien hecho para la época y tiene escenas muy tristes como la de los ancianos en la cama o los músicos tocando hasta el hundimiento. En general la representación del accidente me encantó, también destacar lo bien hecho que está el barco y todos sus interiores, tiene un gran trabajo detrás que les quedó genial. Por último, su final me pareció hermoso y emotivo, lo de que Jack se podría haber salvado es una estupidez, lo escuché toda mi vida y cuando vi la situación me parecía imposible.
En cuanto a los personajes, estos son muy buenos. La verdad se me hace difícil elegir un personaje entre Jack y Rose, ambos son excelentes y me cayeron muy bien, no entiendo las personas a las que no les gusta Rose. La manera en la que Jack la salva de la vida que tiene me encantó, como dije antes, no me convence del todo el poco tiempo que convivieron juntos, pero entiendo lo que significó Jack en su vida, ya que fue muy importante para ella y le enseñó muchas cosas en el poco tiempo que compartieron. Por otro lado, hay personajes que buscan caer mal y lo logran, como Cal y Ruth (la madre de Rose), quienes son las personas que no dejaban a Rose ser quien ella quería y vivía prisionera de una vida en la que no era feliz. Por último, hubo personajes de los que me hubiera gustado ver más, como Molly y Fabrizio, quienes me caían muy bien y no tienen tanto tiempo en pantalla como esperaba.
En otros aspectos destaco las actuaciones, principalmente las de Kate Winslet y Leonardo DiCaprio, quienes hacen las interpretaciones más icónicas de sus carreras, luciéndose y demostrando el gran talento que tienen. Por otro lado, el trabajo de James Cameron en el guion y en la dirección es excelente, me parece que supo como llevar a cabo esta triste historia real y la volvió un clásico del cine. Mi única crítica con todo lo visual son los efectos, hay momentos que no se ven del todo bien como los planos del barco desde arriba o las escenas donde se ve demasiado el cielo, se notaba mucho que era falso. Por último, la banda sonora de James Horner es magistral, creo que acompaña de maravilla a las escenas y tiene melodías muy emotivas e icónicas.
En conclusión, una gran película que es tan buena como todos dicen, su historia es sumamente emotiva y entretenida en todo momento, no tiene un solo momento aburrido a pesar de su larga duración. La recomiendo.

I dont quite know what to say. Its been years since I last saw Titanic and thus my memory of it had faded. I remembered it being good, but as a youngster it never quite hit me just how awe-inspiring and emotional it truly is. James Cameron has filled every moment with rich stories and themes of romance that pull at the heartstrings, cementing it as undoubtedly one of the greatest romantic tragedy there has ever been. Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet are magnificent throughout, their love echoes through every scene and their chemistry is wonderful, without them the film simply wouldnt work as well as it does. Yet its Camerons direction that continues to transfix me. The transitioning shots between the past and present, the scope and scale of the spectacle and the use of the score are all masterful and the brilliance of the story, how touching and heartfelt it is, is what ultimately left me reeling once it concluded. 
The real story of Titanic is a tragedy and any film depicting it had to demand greatness and thats exactly what Cameron achieved, the result is a three-plus-hour epic, an adventure that immerses the audience into a touching romance, then takes a sharp turn into action and thrills while keeping its deeply romantic feeling. Everything about it is masterful. Its simply one of the grandest, most spectacular pieces of filmmaking there has ever been. A true masterpiece if there ever was one.

Titanic is, quite simply, the last great epic of American cinema, the final stroke of a century that gave us the greatest masterpieces of the seventh art. While many remarkable films have been released in the years since, this one draws a definitive line under the golden age of grand blockbusters. It embodies everything that blockbuster cinema should be a daring spectacle born of audacious ideas, obsessive directors, hundreds of extras, and meticulously crafted sets. It is the pinnacle of cinematic mass appeal, where spectacle, love, and tragedy ascend to the very heights of Olympus.
James Cameron delivers the greatest disaster film ever made, one where the end of the world does not come from a meteor or nuclear war but from the relentless power of nature. The iceberg doesnt just sink a ship, it dismantles an entire microcosm of society that was carefully built in the films opening hour. Class oppression and inequality dont escalate they simply reveal their raw, unfiltered truths. Amid the chaos, love doesnt falter, it grows stronger and rekindles. In Titanic, the story of humanity is distilled into three unforgettable hours of cinematic brilliance

VIEWED IN 3D VIP FOR THE 25TH ANNIVERSARY SCREENING 
Since theres just so much out there to watch, its really rare I rewatch films unless theyre Christmas classics. However, I made an exception in order to bridge the gap between now and a quarter-century ago. Funny thing, I asked Spotify to play 1998 hits while I write this, and of course on comes My Heart Will Go On... too appropriate. Both the original viewing and this rewatch come during periods of related familial emotional turmoil, so its a bit of a trippy and deeply nostalgic time loop for me right now. Seriously, everyone has seen this movie at one time or another, and I would be curious to see what someone thought of any film this phenomenal then and now, with 25 years in between.
WHAT TITANIC MEANT TO ME ON FIRST VIEWING (CHRISTMAS 1997)
I was 15 going on 16 and I saw this with my best friend at the time, and her parents. It was such a big movie with such a big following, coming at a time when everything was getting so modern, high-tech and immersive. Theatres all over the country were expanding and getting fancier, with stadium seating , round-the-clock operating hours and expanded concessions instead of staggered seat multiplexes being engulfed and hidden inside of mini-malls, the new megaplexes had come to occupy huge parking lots and accompany big box outlet stores. But the movies themselves were getting SO MUCH BIGGER... watching this one in Grade 10 in the dead of winter, it was just so substantial and engrossing. In so many ways it was depicting the ship of dreams, and seeing Canadian talent (James Cameron, Celine Dion, even Victor Garber) be established as blockbuster powerhouses and earn worldwide recognition was truly something, and actually inspiring.
The Maritime provinces of Canada definitely did not dodge the TITANIC mania that ensued. Not only was the Celine Dion ballad playing non-stop on the radio here up north, but even on a class trip to Halifax we visited the graveyard of the dead passengers identified and washed ashore the grave of Jack Dawson - although having nothing or little in common with the fictionalized Romeo type- was buried under lots of new gifts and fresh flowers. Yes, in many ways it was silly since this epic adventure and romance wasnt actually based on this man, but as a tribute to the poor Everyman and working class who died as a result of such opulence and extravagance in which they could not partake, it was a fitting way to honour the Jacks of all trades and times.
Later that year I would turn 16 and be separated from my best friend, and it was finally time to get a job. As I mentioned in another review, I ended up working at a movie theatre because, in a group interview, everyone said their favourite movie was TITANIC - still the 1 film at the box office even in the late summer of 1998 - except for a handful of us who had other personal favourites. Of course I chose LADYHAWKE since it was the only non-Christmas film I had watched more than a dozen times. Only the most particular handful of us were hired, and so I started at one of the best jobs I ever had. Two of my older brothers had worked at video stores and during that experience had also fallen in love with film, and later I would work at one of the last video stores too. There are a few jobs which I would be happy to do if I werent now deemed overqualified andor after retirement, and those include working at a cinema, a videostore or as a bartender. There are some jobs so enjoyable that they just dont feel like work... its a shame they dont often pay enough to live, but thats another issue.
My oldest brother moved out while still in his teens with his first fiancée to live in her parents basement. He had the courage to ask her to marry him but as a fairly shallow and ungrateful woman she threw the ring back in his face so many times that he finally gave up and pawned it, and shortly after moved out west to try for a better life. We were always taught as kids to see the good in everyone, and that led him to trust someone out there who took him for all he was worth - well, financially at least, but still it was hard for him to remember that he was worth something after all that. Hitchhiking back across the country after such a loss, he was distraught and certainly wasnt ready to trust again. My family has always said that he and I are doormats to people who walk all over us, and its our fault for being swindled or used.
Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. My mother always used to say. So needless to say, my brother didnt want to feel the shame of being fooled a second time.
His second fiancée, and my current sister-in-law celebrating 25 years of marriage with him this year, had to propose to him and I remember my father always made fun of that fact, that somehow that proposal didnt have the same weight and sincerity as the traditional sort in which the man asked the woman.
But her favourite movie for a good two years if not more, almost watching it on a loop, was TITANIC. It was her absolute obsession. My father of course hated it because it was too violent and somehow disrespectful, and there were a couple of teenagers who giggled at some of the deaths and he took out his disgust and anger at them on the film itself. He would badmouth the film as much as she would praise it, and since after their marriage the young couple moved back into our house, she became this really resolute but firm other emotional pushing bag for my father. Mainly because she just didnt react with anything else other than conviction and commitment when my brother and I were used to cowering or conceding. She went on loving TITANIC and collecting absolutely every documentary and book she could find on its accounts and history, and she didnt give a damn if he liked it or not. At Christmas, her presents were all TITANIC memorabilia if I remember correctly.
Still, I associate this first viewing of TITANIC coming at a time when I was making new friends, gaining new family members (two of my brothers married that year, and the other a year or two before), and seeing new possibilities. In so many ways, in my mind I was riding that ship of dreams, and the wave of collective global excitement that went with it.
WHAT TITANIC MEANT TO ME TODAY (FEBRUARY 2023)
Yesterday I spoke to my oldest brother for longer than I have ever spoken with him in my entire life. Hes a dozen years older than me so we werent really close growing up, and besides which, no one was allowed to speak much at home. My brother and I were both naturally quite talkative but we had to keep silent while our father dominated each and every conversation, mainly to complain for hours. To this day, we still cant even talk to our mother if our father is in the room. Imagine how much we both bonded with people we found later in life who actually listened to us, and who spoke about stuff actually worth listening to, instead of universal badmouthing and constant criticism.
I could fill a whole book or maybe several volumes with all of the awful things my father has said about my siblings, me, my mother, every member of our extended families and every family friend or acquaintance we had... not to mention a whole bunch of art, people and activities we dared to like exclusively, in order to try to diminish the importance of any personal comfort in our life. The issue is that all of that criticism, gossip and greatly biased nastiness had a huge toll on our perceptions of each other, and caused a lot of misunderstandings, mixed feelings and years of confusion and isolation.
When my brother came to rescue me on this last fateful visit to my parents in January, we stayed at his house before heading to the train station. Just because I wanted my father to be dead to me and finally sought permanent estrangement, my father was convinced I was having a psychotic break in the same way he had convinced our family that my brother was years earlier when he was dealing with tons of unresolved trauma from our childhood.
Youre just like your father, thats why you dont get along our mother used to tell both of us, although that didnt explain our other two brothers or everyone else, nor was it objectively a fair comparison. As a result, we have done everything possible in our lives thereafter to be nothing like him, but we have to accept that shell never see that, or more accurately, never admit it. Were not our father we can now say to each other, outside of the toxicity and mindsets we had been long conditioned to. And its the truth, and we dont owe the burden of truth to anyone who wont hear our side of the story or even listen to reason.
I never realized how little credit I had given my sister-in-law, who with my brother runs a very chill, understanding and patient household, and where actual two-sided or multiple-perspective conversations are not only allowed but encouraged. Theyre a very loving and secure couple who talk things out like mature adults should, and are very much still in love, despite living in sin before their marriage and not going to church - so a very different prediction from the prognosis provided by an overzealous Catholic father.
Watching TITANIC tonight, I never realized how much Rose and Jack save each other in different ways. Yes, Rose lost her grip in the end but she went to great lengths and risked her own life and stability to save a man she knew was worth saving. She also picked the average Joe (well, Jack) with the warm and kind soul out of all of those supposedly stronger men of higher status. The romance in the film never resonated with me at the time, and I found the dialogue to be cheesy and chemistry lacking, but now I see how being watched on repeat it might have inspired some of the romance in my brothers and his wifes life together. More important than names or words, it was their actions that mattered. Thank you, M, for saving my brothe

La diferencia en la clase social en la relación entre Jake y Rose será marcado desde el momento en que se conozcan con Rose arriba (subida a la popa del Titanic para intentar suicidarse) y Jake abajo (intentando detenerla). Esa misma diferencia de alturas se irá repitiendo a lo largo de la película, cuando Rose le enseñe su mundo a Jake en aquella primera cena (él la verá desde abajo), lo mismo sucederá al revés cuando Jake le enseñe su mundo a Rose (en ese momento será ella quien deba ir a buscarlo y él aparezca entre las alturas).
A su vez, su primer encuentro será resignificado varias veces. La escena del primer beso en la proa del barco (parte delantera, porque dejaran de ocultarse sus sentimientos entre sí y a los demás). Dicha escena repetirá a Rose arriba como en aquel intento de suicidio pero esta vez Jake la sostendrá desde abajo y será su cable a tierra necesario para su nueva vida.
Luego, con el Titanic hundiéndose y pudiendo salvarse ella en los botes dejando a Jake en el barco (quien, de vuelta anticipaba su final), se repite el plano contrapicado con ella viendo desde abajo a Jake, que se irá marcando cada vez más porque la distancia entre ellos se va haciendo cada vez mayor. Entonces ella da el paso definitivo para abandonar su antigua vida saltando hacia el piso de abajo del barco, abajo donde se encuentra su amado, sellado definitivamente su destino.
Además, el arriba y el abajo incluso se repetirá hacia el final cuando Rose quede arriba de la tabla y él abajo, de nuevo sacrificandose para salvarla como aquella ocasión donde estuvo dispuesto a mentir y pasar por un asesino o al menos el intento de, con tal de no deshonrarla contando la verdad.
Por último, Rose tira el corazón del océano hacia el abajo, hacia Jake y con ella muriendo en el final se repite una vez más el plano contrapicado con Jake esperando arriba, en el otro mundo con todos los fallecidos aplaudiendolos. Sellando la historia de amor más grande de todos los tiempos.

Titanic is an epic romantic disaster film written and directed by James Cameron. It won 11 Academy Awards (among them Best Picture, Best Director, Best Cinematography, Best Visual Effects, Best Art Direction, Best Costume Design, Best Original Dramatic Score, and Best Original Song).
Camerons movie was the most expensive ever made at the time of release, and became a global phenomenon, just like the titular ship herself. Titanic also became the first film to earn more than 1 billion worldwide, as well as the most successful movie of all time (until it was surpassed by Camerons own Avatar (my review)), and won a record 11 Oscars (tied with two other movies).
In 1997 and 1998, Titanic was certainly everywhere. It was in release for almost a year, spending months at number one, and demand was so high, I remember my local cinema showed Titanic on all but one screen.
When it comes to authenticity and impact, I still slightly prefer A Night to Remember (my review), which largely eschews fictional characters and storylines. But Camerons meticulous attention to detail, with incredible special effects, beautiful costumes, props and sets - all worthy Oscar winners - is unsurpassed. Cameron also employs actual footage of the wreck he captured himself to great effect, and the framing device is inspired.
While the dialogue is the movies weak spot, making me wish Cameron had found a better writer to polish the script, it doesnt take away from it. I do miss, however, S.S. Californian - which is omitted and never mentioned - as well as the heroic efforts of RMS Carpathia which only shows up at the end.
There are inaccuracies in the movie, but none that ruin it, or couldnt be explained away. And then, when the films first half is over, we arrive at what Cameron does best, resulting in a flawless second half.
Both Leonardo di Caprio and especially Kate Winslet - perfect as a young woman longing to break free from a whole life of misery already laid out for her - are terrific. Ill also mention the wonderful Kathy Bates as Margaret Brown, as well as the movies MVP, Gloria Stuart, who, at 87, received a well-deserved Academy Award nomination for her incredible performance.
Titanic is a deeply romantic film, but not only because of its love story. It takes us back into a different, simpler era, when mankind created never before seen technological wonders - declaring itself king of the world - only to see it fail because of its own hubris.
I also like the fan theory Rose is a highly unreliable narrator - because she definitely is. She tells the story from her perspective, drawing from 80-years-old memories, and certainly from reports of events she never actually witnessed, which explains the movies inaccuracies and simplified characterizations.
The Titanic - both the ill-fated ship and the tragic disaster - always gets to me, but here, Cameron masterfully manipulates the audiences emotions. And as worn-out My Heart Will Go On is, its a brillant piece of music, and its instrumental version, which is used as the films leitmotif throughout, will always give me goosebumps, as does the rest of James Horners brillant film score. And when that ending comes around, it never fails to make me choke up.
In conclusion, with Titanic James Cameron managed the unthinkable - bring together astonishing technical aspects, an achingly romantic story about love and tragedy, high authenticity as well as grand emotions, for a spellbinding, unforgettable, touching and thrilling cinematic experience.

A couple of years ago, I was arguing about this with a friend - I was trying to poke holes in it, and I came up with two complaints that I found unanswerable. First I thought (and I still think) that they shouldnt have had sex after the drawing scene. Its impeccably-staged, the hand slapping against the steamed-up window is a top-flight piece of PG-13 synecdoche, but its a comedown from the erotic fever pitch of the earlier scene.
The other thing, which was not at all new to me in that argument, was that the 1996 framing material was just unnecessary, providing the spurious exposition that, get this, RMS Titanic sank on its maiden voyage, pretending that Bill Paxtons plot mechanism is a character and clearly designed primarily to scratch James Camerons itch to film a major motion picture on the god-danged bottom of the god-danged ocean. And to this my friend responded with unbeatable wisdom but without the framing narrative, it wouldnt have been over three hours long, and Titanic is a movie that needs to be over three hours long.
By God if that didnt shut me right up. For Titanic, indeed, is a movie that needs to be over three hours long. Is it possible to imagine improvements to make this a better movie? Absolutely. It is not, however, possible for me at least to imagine improvements that would make this a better James Camerons Titanic. It is a gorgeous sprawl of excess that has been tuned perfectly. The script, for example, is just a joy of careful, deliberate mechanics this casual, scruffy scene exactly sets up an echo or a mirror or a rhyme two hours down the road that empty line of filler dialogue is called back to create an emotional arc across the whole movie. So many little grace notes of moments that answer other moments despite the whole movie feeling like its being played loud and without a shred of nuance.
The editing, at the level of individual scenes, is airtight. The slightest insert shot comes at exactly the moment is has to to augment the explicit and implicit currents in the dialogue and acting. Every time screen direction is fucked with, it somehow happens at a crucial emotional moment - perhaps it is that the fuck-withing creates the crucial emotional moment. I am thinking of how Roses decision to keep hunting for Jack in the bowels of the waterlogged ship after she first steps into waist-deep water feels like a chapter break in the movie simply because we cut from her back to her face in a place that strict rules of continuity would prefer that we not do so.
I get that people think that screenwriting means crafting naturalistic dialogue, but thats merely (please find it in your heart to forgive me) the tip of the iceberg. The structure here is beautiful - the way it constantly, gently ratchets tighter (even in the second half, the sinking starts out slowly and casually with lots of wide-shot blocking on the sets with an inch of water on them, and only then steadily ramps up into horror movie chaos theres a particular moment of flickering light that feels precisely like Aliens), the way that it knows exactly when to leave the protagonists for the side characters, or even just the featured extras, the way that every beat in 194 minutes somehow manages to have at least one thing its building towards or paying off. Also, cheesy dialogue and all, the universe is a better place because the sentiment A womans heart is a deep ocean of secrets has been read into it.
Man, I dont know, its just so fucking watchable. Is there anybody else this side of Spielberg who makes movies that are just as legible as Cameron without ever revealing the slightest level of disrespect for the audiences intelligence? I really feel that there isnt.

One reason I should never rate anything on this site is that it only results in grief.  I can handle almost all of that, truly, yet after awhile I wonder why people focus on the negative ratings so much.
Well I know why. In matters of taste, if were basically the same, thats boring. But if were different, lets fight!
A student asked me why I rated this movie as a half-star on here.  So Ill tell you why, and its almost solely personal reasons.
Back in eighth grade, our school decided to unify the curriculum around a theme. For an entire semester, every single class would use that theme to highlight learning in a discipline.  
That theme the Titanic.
Youd go to English class, and youd write as if you were a person on the Titanic. Youd do research on certain people, then try to create their persona in writing.
Then youd go to Social Studies class and discuss everything about 1900-whatever. Then go to math class and calculate the dimensions of the Titanic while learning geometry.  Then go to gym class and simulate trying to escape a sinking ship.
Thats four months of Titanic, circa 1993, when I was 13 or so.  You cant imagine how absolutely sick of the subject I became. To this day, I wince on the inside when the word is brought up, Titanic.  Ahhhhhhhhh!  
Now fast-forward four years later, to 1997, when a major moviemaker decided to try his hand, after making 2-3 of the coolest science-fiction spectacles ever, at a classic Hollywood love-bloat story.  Every single female I knew, or so it seemed, went to see this movie seventy-five times.  Leo was hot, or so they said, but most of us thought he looked and acted like a weenie.
You must remember Im talking about a 16-year-old guy whod been Titanicked to death 3-4 years earlier.  Thats the perfect storm school makes you sick of a subject, then the subject gets coded as hyper-feminine, while you and your buddies are rocking out to Metallica and renting every Arnold, Bruce Willis, and Nic Cage testosterone-laced action flick.  
To boot, add in that Celine Dion song that has never stopped playing in my head, like the CIA torturing Gitmo inmates at night  Neeeeeeeeeeear ..... faaaaaaaaaar .... where EVVVVVVVVVVVVVVVVVVVVVer yoooou arrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrre ....
I should probably tell my therapist about this, undergo somatic therapy, go take a few sensory-deprivation-tank sessions, and see if I can heal from all this trauma caused by the Titanic, a psychological wreckage that feels as big as the crash itself.

The 25th anniversary theatrical rerelease of Titanic retooled the iconic film with a layer of the latest remastering technology and a 3-D presentation that that was wholly unnecessary for an already great film but ultimately enjoyable. The film itself is a masterpiece, one part tragic romance, one (extremely long) part epic historical disaster drama. James Cameron does what he always does, painstakingly juxtaposing innovative technology driven sci-fi against a deeply imaginative, idealistic emotional core and ended up with his first biggest movie ever.
 
The film really has a scale that is truly titanic in its own right, with sets that include a near life-size version of the ship, meticulous miniatures, period appropriate interiors, and archival costumes. The scenes in the ships boiler room were especially astonishing, with mirrors being used to create the illusion of the massive size of the ships pistons and boilers. The clarity enabled by the anniversary remaster almost did the film a disservice by allowing for some of the computer generated shots to stand out as outdated and uncanny and probably looked far more impressive upon the initial release.
 
The sinking of Titanic is an tragedy that, due in large part to this film, has been seared into the collective consciousness of modern society. As a person born in 1996, I dont have any memories from a world that didnt know the story Titanic because of the groundbreaking impact the film had on culture. Now, 25 years later, the mythic nature the real life events has taken on heightens the dramatic irony of Jack and Roses story to an emotional boiling point that had me sobbing from the beginning of the film.
 
Using the present day storyline to bookend the events of the ships sinking was extremely effective in setting up the tragedy and allowing the researchers to lay out, in detail, how the ship was breached and sank only deepened the feeling of impending disaster that I felt throughout the film.
 
I think Rose and Jacks relationship is incredibly pure and romantic thanks in such large part to the insane chemistry between Kate Winslet and Leonardo DiCaprio. This might be my favorite performance of both their careers. The hope and newfound freedom that Jack inspires in Rose is so insanely tragic to watch knowing hes about to fuckin die was so palpable and deeply sad. The photos that 100 year old Rose brings aboard the research ship which are revealed to document the prolific and full life that Rose went on to have after she was saved by Jack broke me. I was so messed up. Its so beautiful. And, at the risk of sounding even more sappy, the sunset scene on the bow of the ship fuck. Perfect. Just an amazing cinematic moment.
 
My Heart Will Go On is an all-time great film theme.

In the party scene below deck after the first class dinner, Jack dances with an 8-year-old girl named Cora until he leaves her to join Rose. Youre still my best girl, Cora he tells her. Jack seemed pretty interested in Rose at the time, but I thought maybe 25 years later Cora could still have a shot. After some quick math (Im a software developer), Im sad to report that she will never be Jacks best girl. The actress that played Cora is now 34 years old, and Jacks body sank to the bottom of the ocean. Also Leonardo DiCaprio has never dated anyone over the age of 25

Its been 84 years, and I can still smell the fresh paint. The china had never been used. The sheets had never been slept in. Titanic was called the Ship of Dreams, and it was. It really was...
Want to hear something insane? This film was an immense part of my childhood, but with good reason besides it being a masterful piece of cinema. History was my favorite subject  everything from the turn of the 20th Century  on was my favorite era to study. I would do so in my own free time  included many films such as Titanic to help me visualize  imagine what it was like to live in those times. 
So much so, I began to convince myself that perhaps I once lived in these times. Reincarnation had fascinated me from a young age  at some point I began to believe that my deep emotional connection to the events of the night of April 14th, 1912 were more than it seemed. Now, its not that I didnt have any reason to believe that, in my young mind I connected the events of the Titanic sinking, Abraham Lincolns murder  even World War 2, purely because my birthday is April 14th  I had such great feelings for these events. My mother actually brought me into the theater just a few weeks to months after I was born to see Titanic. Technically, this film was the first movie I went to the theaters to see. I didnt actually watch it, obviously, but apparently I slept peacefully through it. This was a film my mother just had to watch. 
I know, this sounds crazy, but when I was younger it was fun to speculate about past lives  whether or not reincarnation is real. I spent many nights researching what I could to even begin to understand it. When I was a child I drew the conclusion that perhaps I was Abraham Lincoln, shot on the night of April 14th, died the morning of April 15th, 1865. Reborn as a man destined to perish on the Titanic, 47 years later on the night of April 14th, early morning of April 15th, 1912. After that, I led myself to speculate that I was born again, to die in some battle, perhaps the pacific theater of World War 2. Though, I couldnt find much that happened that I felt drawn to on the date of April 14th, or the morning after, so I felt as though I reached a dead end. 
Until, I learned that Im actually related to the famous actor, Jackie Gleason. Born 1916, almost 4 years after the sinking of the Titanic. I even look like him. I act like him. We share the same mannerisms, attitude, facial and body expressions almost down to a scary similarity. My family were the ones who brought it to my attention. At first I denied it, then I realized the dates make sense. Suddenly my interest in reincarnation came flooding back. Was I Jackie Gleason in a past life? Who knows. I know it sounds silly, trust me, I think it does too. However, its fun to speculate, its fun to imagine. I truly believe reincarnation is real and there is hard truth to it. Many others have recounted past lives at a young age to an impossible degree.
When I was just a preteen, I had a really bad time period, where I felt as if I wasnt where I belonged. I continuously cried I want to go home! and other phrases of the sort. But I was already home. I was in my bed for Gods sake. My parents confused as to why I was acting in such a way. My family just felt so alien to me, this was long before I ever knew what reincarnation was or ever researched the subjects. I truly felt like I was in a time period or a place where I wasnt from. Then, as I grew older it started to click. I grew a fond interest in history  certain events that stuck out to me way more than normal. 
Perhaps this is insanity, perhaps Im wrong and all of what Ive said is just coincidence  bullshit  everything was made up in my head. I can honestly accept that, but its fun to think maybe theres more to it. This has little to do with Titanic, the film itself, but its just part of what influenced me at a very young age. If youve read to here, I want to say thank you. I truly love this film  it means way more to me than I could ever explain. Its an epic that everyone should see at least once. 
Oh, and I think Kate Winslet was my first major on screen crush. I loved her so much.

Titanic is an undeniable cinematic phenomenon that captures the grandeur and tragedy of the Titanics maiden voyage with undeniable skill. James Camerons meticulous direction and attention to historical detail recreate the ships opulence and the poignant circumstances that surrounded its ill-fated journey.
The films sprawling production design and visual effects are nothing short of awe-inspiring. The ship itself becomes a character, brought to life with remarkable authenticity. The central love story between Leonardo DiCaprios Jack and Kate Winslets Rose adds an emotional anchor, effectively encapsulating the societal constraints and human connections of the era.
While the romance occasionally leans into melodrama, Camerons storytelling prowess shines in his ability to interweave personal narratives with the overarching disaster. The attention to detail is apparent, and the technical achievements remain groundbreaking.
Yet, Titanic falls just short of perfection due to its occasionally uneven pacing and reliance on well-trodden romantic tropes. Nonetheless, it remains an iconic cinematic experience that highlights both the potential and limitations of blockbuster filmmaking.
In its breathtaking spectacle and emotional resonance, Titanic stands as a landmark film of the 1990s, skillfully capturing the heartbreak and courage of those who lived through the tragedy. Its a testament to the power of cinema to blend history, spectacle, and human emotion into a compelling narrative that continues to touch hearts across generations.

Just when you think the zombie genre is, well, dead and permanently transported to the realms of The Walking Dead, along comes this express train to zombie movie heaven.
All zombie movies are basically a variety of us against them. Train to Busan is no different. Only the really great genre films manage to find creativity in the premise, something this film does extraordinarily well for the better part of its running time.
It doesnt happen often that I actually find myself enjoying a film relishing in every single trope its genre has to offer. Theres the host of characters, the mundane anti-hero, the last stand, the inhumane bastard, the heroic sacrifice, the narrow escapes and the zombies. Bus-, ney, trainloads of them. And they run. And theyre freaky bastards.
Id say the opening act is perhaps one of the best ever in the genre. It is paced to perfection. A swift introduction to our main character and the reveal that things are not well quickly lead to the introduction of the zombies. Now, Im not a zombie purist. Whether they run or walk slowly, doesnt matter as long as theyre gnarly. Turns out Korean zombies are fast, twitchy and contorting frenzied fiends that are unpredictable and unrelenting. 
The pacing starts to wobble a bit in the middle, but it makes up for it with wonderful character moments. Even though most of them are what youd expect in a film like this, director Yeon Sang-Ho still manages to find an emotional connection to his audience through these characters, always skirting the edges of melodrama like only the Koreans can.
There is a plethora of memorable, unique and jarring moments in this train ride from hell, making it an unmissable and outstanding entry into the genre.

Zombie films have become tired and generic churn-fests over the years (save a few special ones, of course), but thankfully Train To Busan is here to change that formula. A heartfelt story with well-rounded characters and a wonderful humanist message that rises above the horror of the undead hordes. 
It really can be described in four words zombies on a train. But the concept has never been executed as efficiently or as effectively as it has here, with director Sang-ho Yeon revitalizing the often played-out zombie genre. 
Release Date 20 July 2016
Distributor Well Go USA
Using his confined locationa packed intercity trainto maximum effect, Yeon expertly ramps up the tension, the living gradually whittled down to a handful of passengers fighting for survival against the hordes of the undead.
What really shocked me is that there are almost no firearms, a bullet is rarely shot, and the blood flow is kept to a minimum... no headshots or dismemberments, which prove to be the core of most zombie flicks, and barely a few bites with minimum gore. However, the impact of the attacks is undeniable, due to Yeon Sang-Hos brilliant direction, whose ingenuity doesnt know any limits in order to orchestrate chases, escapes, and situations of great danger which flow organically without damaging the logic and realism of the premise.
Despite so many sub-plots, Train to Busan never gets confusing, and much less boring, because it continually finds new ways to create suspense about each core characters ultimate journey through the film.

Train to Busan is edge-of-your-seat thrilling, immensely entertaining, and surprisingly deep, offering some thoughtful social commentary on class warfare and personal responsibility rarely explored in this brand of movie. All in all, this is my favorite Romero-less zombie movie of all time, and another example of Korean cinema taking North American concepts and elevating them through creativity and care about the humanity of each character, no matter what theyre put through. 
If youre a fan of Korean cinema, then I suggest you add this to your watch list. Full of buckets of bloody horrorsuspense, amazing special effects, but most of all full of heart. Train to Busan is an infection-style zombie horrorthriller done correctly. After a short setup, a few choice bites create and unleash frenzied zombies crashing through windows and doors in human waves, snapping and biting while running with broken limbs bent in all directions, and even falling from the skyTrain to Busan goes from calm to total chaos in a way few films have managed as thrillingly.
28 Days Later rendered it slightly dull to have slow infecteds, refused to call them zombies, and set a new standard for how these action sequences are shot. But, at least in my view, it fell to a less serious Spanish found-footage film, REC, to master the style of kinetic chaos that is so satisfying and often hard to find.
Here is another great iteration of this model, and its one of the most successful Ive seen. The claustrophobic environment of a train leaving Seoul for Busan turns bite by rapid bite into a death trap. Battling to clear car after car in order to survive has some meaningful resemblance to films like The Raid and The Horde that are sequence after sequence of absolute mayhem.
But the emotional stakes are high here, and this makes a big difference. Embedded in all of this madness is a simple story of a father learning to be present with his daughter. Hes been working to support their life but has struggled always to be there. In this crisis setting, what story could be more basic and clear than a father readjusting his assessment of what matters in his life to be there for his daughter in a crisis? The outbreak is a setting for the film to do this emotional work.
And I have to hand it to Yeon Sang-ho this story is cleanly written and at times very touching. The film did not put too much sentiment in the way of emotional impact. It is easy to connect to these characters because they are handled well, and the bedlam surrounding it certainly brings enough escapist thrills to avoid feelingat least, for the most partheavy-handed.
Some things here dont work perfectly for me. There is a severe case of plot armor and a trail of conveniently self-sacrificing or morally compromised but noble characters who are made briefly important to the viewer only to be sacrificed to advance a plot. Honestly, this is very normal. But its also very ignorable when a story is this entertaining.
Few films bottle chaos this well, and some that do (like The Sadness) are unwatchable to mainstream audiences. This manages all the intensity while minimizing eye-rapes and blood orgies. In case you are concerned, in this case minimized means zero. 
Train to Busan is watchable, tense, thrilling, and still with feelingIts a classic for a reason. Please watch it if you havent yet! Youre likely to love it. 
Strongly recommended.

Its got a fair number of pulse-pounding set pieces and striking images, with zombies raining from the sky and crowds of zombies bursting through a glass barrier with their sheer weight. Those things, plus a solid core premise and some good character dynamics, combine to make for a fun first two acts.
The last act is a lot less successful, as things start to drag and get more cliched and repetitive. But even if the ending isnt quite as satisfying as the setup, it gets the job done, and the movie overall is one that any zombie fan can enjoy.

That, or the sun will explode or a meteor will hit, and then it wont matter. It will be done in a flash, and still, long after were dead.
The good news is, of course, that glacial death is avoidable, because of all of the things this movie believes in. Community, sacrifice, compassion, hope. Train to Busan is definitely one of the best zombie action films Ive ever seen. Actually, it would be wrong to call those infected with the epidemic zombies. The infected people are only sensitive to sound and cannot see in the dark. Throughout the film, we see transformed people who are prone to biting each other. From what I learned from my friend, these zombies are not like the slow-walking walkers in The Walking Dead. There is no image of ripped flesh, intestines and blood. The sudden changes, fast movements and running of the bitten people greatly increase the tension level of the film. Also, the zombies make-up is both realistic and scary. We all know that Asian Cinema is much more emotional than European and Hollywood. Unlike Hollywood films, which often prioritize spectacle and pace, Asian cinema weaves emotion into every frame like threads in a delicate tapestry. Each glance, each silence, carries the weight of unspoken sorrow or tender longing. There is a poetic stillness in Asian dramas, where pain is not shouted but felt, echoing quietly in the soul. In this world, tragedy is intimate, and love is a slow-burning flame subtle, aching, and deeply human. In Train to Busan, the story that seems like a zombie story is about a father and his daughter, being a family, being human, sacrifice, not being selfish. There were even many scenes that filled my eyes. 
I also like this because it focuses on the characters so much and because it makes us experience a lot of emotions in all this chaos. O destaque de Invasão Zumbi não está só no terror visual, mas na forma como transforma o horror em reflexão sobre o ser humano. Os zumbis, rápidos, violentos e imprevisíveis, não são monstros sobrenaturais e sim o próprio ser humano reduzido ao instinto. São corpos sem consciência, movidos apenas pelo medo e pela necessidade de sobreviver. Representam o que nos tornamos quando o instinto fala mais alto que a razão. O impulso de se manter vivo é natural, mas o que garantiu a sobrevivência da humanidade foi a união. Desde o início, o ser humano aprendeu que sozinho não resistiria e que a solidariedade era a única maneira de enfrentar o perigo.
Na sociedade atual, essa lógica foi invertida. O sistema de competição fez com que cada pessoa visse a outra como inimiga e a solidariedade deu lugar ao egoísmo. Invasão Zumbi mostra exatamente isso uma sociedade destruída pelo individualismo, onde o medo revela o pior de cada um. Mas o filme também mostra que ainda existe esperança, que o sentimento de empatia e união continua vivo em alguns. O que mais impressiona é como o cinema coreano consegue transformar um filme de zumbis, normalmente cheio de ação, em um drama profundamente emocionante.
As duas horas de Invasão Zumbi são frenéticas, me deixaram tenso o tempo todo e o desfecho me envolveu de um jeito inesperado, muito por causa da atuação da pequena Kim Soo-ah, que foi incrível. A frase Você já está infectado revela algo além do vírus o personagem não está tomado só pelo vírus, mas pela ganância e pelo egoísmo que o consomem. Ele vive atormentado e sem paz, como muitos que perdem o sentido da vida tentando vencer os outros. Já o pai da menina precisa passar por toda aquela tragédia para entender o que realmente importa. Ele percebe que o valor da vida está no amor e não no trabalho ou no dinheiro. Esse amor simples e gratuito, que todos podem sentir, é o que ele reencontra antes de morrer. E é por isso que, mesmo no fim, ele sorri, porque finalmente entende o que é ser humano.

Yeon Sang-hos frenetic, apocalyptic survival tale isnt a zombie film following the conventional genre trappings of over the top, effects driven gore, and decaying body-horror imagery. I scare because I care, and many times for me, the emotional weight of a well executed plot can be ten times as horrifying as any jump scare or gruesome kill can be. Ugly crying at midnight on a Sunday over zombie infection isnt my normal wiring, but dammit, Korean drama never fails to tug on my heaviest of heartstrings.
When it comes to horror, Im a practical effects fan first and foremost, and the only thing keeping me from a full 5 star rating lies in that department. The use of CG is necessary in these hyperspeed horde of undead movies, but does seem a little out of place given its grounded approach to plot development. Its easy enough to get past as well though. I finally watched Train to Busan last night!
People had been telling me this movie was incredible for years, and they werent wrong. 
In a genre full of movies with a similar flavor  outbreak, survival, chaos  this one still finds a way to feel fresh. It shows things I hadnt seen before, even after watching dozens of zombie films in a row.
Like the best of them, it has that idea running through it that mans inability to communicate and cooperate is often the real monster. But Train to Busan manages to explore that in new ways. The setting is perfect tight, kinetic, constantly moving and it gives every moment a sense of danger and inevitability. 
Some of the visuals echo World War Z with waves of bodies piling and crashing forward, but the difference is scale. In World War Z, the scope was so big it lost intimacy here, its all personal. You know who everyone is. You care about them.
Thats what makes this one so good. You get the spectacle and the emotion. Its not cynical or nihilistic, but its still brutal  your heart gets ripped out over and over again. At its core, its a classic redemption story a dad whos been too focused on work learning, in the worst possible way, what really matters. The sacrifices land, the payoffs hurt, and it never forgets the humanity inside the horror. 
For a film that couldve easily been just another zombie ride, Train to Busan turns out to be one of the best of all.

I genuinely believe Train to Busan is the blueprint for how to make a survival film work. The stakes are immediately high, the characters are easy to root for, and the emotional payoff hits harder than you expect. It shows how to do a disaster film with precision and urgency, never wasting time on anything unnecessary. I think that every scene is there for a reason, either to push the tension forward or deepen who these people are.
The film leans into familiar archetypes, the coward, the selfless hero, the pregnant woman, the young lovers, the child, the selfish opportunist. And what makes it compelling is how those archetypes dont stay fixed. As the story unfolds, the dynamics shift. Personalities evolve under pressure. Motives become clearer. Relationships deepen or fracture. We see how far each character is willing to go for survival and, more importantly, for the people they love.
The momentum itself is relentless. From the moment the infection breaks out, the film locks into a rhythm that barely lets you breathe. The confined setting of the train turns every encounter into a pressure cooker, and the action is staged with clarity and purpose. Each major sequence builds toward a climax that actually earns its emotional release, rather than just functioning as spectacle.
But I think what really elevates Train to Busan is the social commentary running beneath all the chaos. Its a film about who people become when systems collapse. The best and worst of human nature surface at the same time. Theres commentary on selfishness masked as self-preservation, on collective responsibility versus individual survival, on class tension, authority, and indifference. You see ordinary people band together, workers standing up to management, citizens losing faith in institutions, and parents forced to confront their own emotional distance.

Tenso e eximiamente executado, Invasão Zumbi reafirma o talento dos cineastas sul-coreanos para expor a derrocada das relações sociais em qualquer gênero ou contexto
          O SOBRESSALTO e a ansiedade estão na base do cinema superlativo que tem saído da Coreia do Sul na última década e meia. E se, nas mãos dos cineastas do país, essas emoções perturbam de maneira autêntica é porque em geral elas acompanham algum desastre sem mitigação. Os bons e os justos, as crianças e os cães  não há certeza de salvação para ninguém em filmes como o policialhorror O Lamento ou Invasão Zumbi (Busanhaeng, Coreia do Sul, 2016). Ainda que o título pareça autoexplicativo e a ação seja ininterrupta (além de eximiamente concebida), os mortos-vivos não são o centro do filme do diretor Sang-ho Yeon desde o momento em que a epidemia de zumbis eclode até a última cena, o que está em questão são as excessões que os personagens abrem (ou não) para si mesmos na premência de escapar da fome bestial dos metamorfoseados. Yeon vai além se sobreviver exige acovardar-se, proteger-se na indiferença ou mesmo abandonar os semelhantes, então o sobrevivente não poderá se acreditar muito mais humano que os zumbis.
          Esse é o teste a que é submetido o jovem financista Seok (Yoo Gong). Ainda no carro, rumo à estação ferroviária, ele e a filha pequena, Soo-an (Soo-an Kim), percebem uma certa agitação em Seul. Mas só dentro do trem, no trajeto até a cidade de Busan, eles se darão conta da calamidade um após o outro, passageiros e tripulantes vão se transformando e instaurando o pânico nos vagões. Seok é um pai distante trabalha muito, convive pouco e está levando Soo-an para Busan apenas para largá-la na casa da ex-mulher. O desespero faz o amor paterno aflorar com violência. Mas a menina não quer ser salva a qualquer custo quer que o pai ajude outros além dela, porque sofre a cada morte que vê e porque precisa que o pai se prove o homem que ela imagina. A aflição não dá trégua, o arrependimento é constante. E o horror, esse está não só nos mortos-vivos repugnantes, mas sobretudo na facilidade com que o medo transforma gente em bicho.

Sempre enrolei demais pra assistir Train to Busan e agora que finalmente fiz isso, estou arrependido de ter demorado tanto. Adorei a premissa e como ela própria consegue transformar o ambiente em uma ferramenta de terror. Um trem já é um espaço limitado, com corredores estreitos, vagões separados e pouquíssimas rotas de fuga. Quando você adiciona zumbis com uma velocidade absurda e uma agressividade quase animalesca, qualquer tentativa de atravessar alguns metros vira uma sequência de tensão. E o filme sabe aproveitar isso brilhantemente. Essa ideia de que um vagão pode representar segurança enquanto o próximo se transforma em um pesadelo é simples, mas funciona demais.
O filme tem personagens bem estereotipados, mas acho que existe uma diferença entre apresentar figuras que reconhecemos facilmente e desenvolver essas figuras de maneira superficial. A mulher grávida, a criança, os jovens atletas, a idosa... cada um ocupa um lugar muito específico no grupo, mas o filme usa essas diferenças para explorar como pessoas em situações completamente distintas reagem à mesma catástrofe. A Su-an, por exemplo, ainda tem uma visão muito mais inocente do mundo, enquanto os adultos precisam lidar com decisões que colocam em xeque os próprios valores. Esses dilemas são muito bem desenvolvidos, fazendo com que a gente entenda as motivações dos personagens e realmente torça por eles. Existe ainda uma discussão bem interessante sobre até onde vai a bondade do ser humano em situações extremas. E por mais cruéis que algumas decisões sejam, o filme consegue mostrar como o desespero e o instinto de sobrevivência podem levar alguém a agir daquela maneira sem que isso torne suas escolhas necessariamente justificáveis.
E eu acho que o ponto mais forte do filme está nessa maneira como ele usa o apocalipse para falar sobre o comportamento humano. A jornada do Seok-woo não se resume a escapar dos zumbis, mas envolve aprender a enxergar o mundo para além dos próprios interesses e da própria Su-an. Isso dá um peso enorme ao desfecho e, mesmo que eu já esperasse algo naquela direção, não deixou de me entristecer. É um final agridoce que combina muito com a proposta do filme, mas que ainda é extremamente cruel.

Muy buena película, de las mejores del género a mi parecer.
Train to Busan es una cinta muy tensa y con algunos momentos emotivos buenísimos, con algunas pequeñas fallas en su desarrollo pero que no hacen que deje de ser disfrutable de inicio a fin.
Sinopsis Un virus desconocido se expande por Corea del Sur, zombificando a los infectados. Los pasajeros de un tren KTX que ha partido de Seúl luchan desesperadamente por sobrevivir hasta llegar a Busan, ciudad que supuestamente se mantiene como el único lugar seguro del país.
La historia es muy buena, faltó hacerla un poco más completa y era excelente. Lo único que no me convenció del todo es que siento que se podría haber profundizado mucho más en el origen del virus y cómo afectó a las demás personas, ya que después de todo estamos viendo solo una parte de lo ocurrido. Sacando eso y algunas pequeñas conveniencias que tiene, se me hace una gran historia de zombies, con sus momentos de tensión espectaculares que están muy bien realizados para generar suspenso. Además, también tiene algo de drama que está bien plasmado dentro de la historia, sobretodo en cosas como su final que a pesar de ya haberla visto me llegó bastante. Por último, el ritmo me parece genial, arranca un poco lenta (aunque no aburre) pero después empieza lo bueno y no para exceptuando algunos momentos, las dos horas pasan muy rápido.
Los personajes me encantan, destacan más allá de los dos protagonistas. Seok-Woo junto a su hija Soo-Ahn son dos personajes con los que es muy fácil empatizar, me gusta la relación de ambos y también destacan individualmente, aunque el vínculo entre padre e hija termina siendo el corazón de la película y de las mejores cosas que presenta. Por otro lado, de los secundarios el que más destaca es Sang-Hwa, me acuerdo que cuando la vi por primera vez me había encantado éste personaje y me sigue pareciendo buenísimo, lo mismo su esposa Sung-Gyeong, ambos caen bien rápidamente.
En otros aspectos destaco principalmente las actuaciones de Gong Yoo y Kim Su-an, sobretodo la de ésta última que para lo joven que era en ese momento lo hace de maravilla también destaco a Ma Dong-seok y Jung Yu-mi. Por otro lado, el trabajo de Yeon Sang-ho en guion y dirección es grandioso, no vi otras películas de él pero lo que hace acá es realmente bueno. También hay que destacar los efectos que para tener un presupuesto algo corto se termina viendo de una gran manera. Para cerrar, la banda sonora de Jang Young-gyu funciona por momentos, sobretodo en escenas como la del final donde logra generar cierta emotividad.
En conclusión, una muy buena película que resultó tan buena como la recordaba, de lo mejor que pude ver del género, construye bien su historia y personajes y termina siendo bastante memorable. La recomiendo.

Yeon Sang-ho directs a classic genre film, enriching it with a series of elements he manages to elevate a simple plot by staging an entertaining and full of tension work
The development of events is quite linear with the protagonists moving from point A to point B pursued by hordes of infected, it is made more interesting by the setting of the train that allows some really nice narrative solutions (for example the sequence that exploits a weak point of the infected with tunnels crossed by the train)
The characters are well written and have different psychologies that develop gradually throughout the story. 
In particular the protagonist Seok-woo (who comes from the world of finance and is the expression of the logic dog-eat-dog) starts as a very negative figure expressing an egoistic and negative attitude that is also reflected in his relationship with his little daughter Soo-ahn, for him the apocalypse of the undead will become a real learning process that will unlock his more human side
Through the social differences of the characters, rendered useless by a lethal virus that makes no distinction, the director expresses a critique of his own society, also conferring to his work a political depth.
To be honest sometimes the actions of the characters are not exactly clever, although in general this does not compromise the effectiveness of a good tension and does not prevent the viewer to care for them (Sang-hwa youre my hero). 
We have the classic scenarios like the child wandering alone, characters who do not close the doors or stop in the middle of extremely dangerous situations to make important speeches, in short all the tricks to make us angry, make us die of anxiety and carry on the story
In addition to a great horror and action component that takes full advantage of the setting to create excellent sequences, the film features a strong emotional and dramatic component. 
In particular the ending is really heart-breaking, even if it is rather predictable it does not lose its great strength thanks to the magnificent performances of the actors
Train to Busan is a great film that perfectly combines drama, action and horror avoiding that one element weakens the others.
Definitely one of the best works of this genre that I have watched and that, besides a few hours of fun and quality entertainment, has gifted me one of the most hateful and detestable characters ever

This is one of the best zombie films Ive seen in years.  It follows a dad and daughter as they try to get out of Korea after zombies have infected the country.  Most of this film takes place on a train, Koreas answer to Snakes on a Plane... Zombies on a Train.  Theres some very real and decent horror moments on this and quite a few great characters as well. 
I do love how theres always that one jackass in zombie movies who wont admit that theyve been bitten and keeps it to themself.  Another life lesson is that if youre ever trapped on a zombie-infested train, its good to have an entire baseball team on board to beat the snot out of the zombies with bats.

Given how well worn this type of material is, I feel that Train to Busan plays things a little too safe to leave much of an impression. I could forgive the lack of inventiveness on concepts weve seen many times before such as quick zombies or action on transportation if the characters were strong, but theyre all so rigidly cliched that I struggled to get invested in their plight which deadened most of the emotional impact. It also doesnt help that many of the plot threads like the father learning to care more or the individual versus the collective social commentary feel overly trite. The high-concept premise providing an appreciable sense of propulsion combined with the urgent pacing and some suitably intense set pieces is what keeps things ticking along even as the character work falters. However, you can really feel the lack of emotional connection during the messy third act as it makes the conclusion come across as rather hollow.

The zombie apocalypse is a well-worn concept, and at this point most modern films try to put a different spin on it. Train to Busan however shows that going back to the roots of the genre can work brilliantly with an approach which combines thrills and genuine scares on a huge scale.
The plot is simple workaholic fund manager Seo Seok-woo is taking his daughter to Busan for her birthday via rail. Their travel is interrupted by an outbreak of disease which turns its victims into rabid, hyper-aggressive monsters, leaving the train as the only island of safety in the country. The group must travel from station to station looking for the somewhere safe to disembark, whilst being wary of the swarms of passengers who have already turned in carriages further down. 
Train to Busan feels like a modern version of a Romero zombie film with a bigger budget. This includes the social consciousness of movies like Dawn of the Dead with its chaos and massive social disruption the apocalypse resembles a twisted fantasy version of a North Korean attack and many of the subplots concern the class divisions between the train passengers. The antagonist is 1-er who is willing to sacrifice anyone below him in the social hierarchy in order to survive, whilst it is implied that the rich protagonists company is in some way responsible for the plague. 
The ensemble cast resembles nothing less than one which would appear in a Roland Emmerich film they are broadly-drawn archetypes but in a way which makes it easier to understand their relationships quickly and avoid bogging down the action of the story. Ma Dong-seok is particularly impressive as the working-class martial arts expert who serves as the secondary protagonist, and his abilities lead to some surprisingly fun fight scenes. The movie also features such standard characters as a team of jocks, a cheerleader and a selfish greedy businessman, but sticking to the basics allows the film the time to go in unexpected directions with its plot and action. 
The zombies are scary fast moving and prone to contorting their bodies in grotesque ways when attacking, although the lack of creative makeup is a bit disappointing. The crowds of transformed police and soldiers also add to the anxiety, since it feels as though the whole apparatus of the state is becoming part of the attack. The film is set in sterile and claustrophobic locations which add to the fear of the outbreak with the anxiety of being trapped in an unfamiliar environment.
Train to Busan shows that a big movie about apocalypse and national disasters can still work very well, and that zombies arent played out when approached with energy and directing skill. Its a real breath of fresh air for the living dead.

Well, Train to Busan is one hell of a ride, for sure. This is an emotional family drama disguised as a relentless zombie-apocalypse thriller, one with its own rules. I was pleasantly surprised by how well-done and slick this film was and didnt expect to get so invested in the fate of these characters as much as I did. 
Directed by South-Korean director Sang-ho Yeon, Train to Busan follows a father and his estranged little daughter who make a trip to Busan to see the mother. Meanwhile, a mysterious zombie virus breaks out in South Korea. One of the infected people manages to hop on the train at the last minute and, of course, all hell breaks loose. So you can imagine how traumatic it must be to stay alive in such a limited space.
Theres some eye-rolling movie clichés like characters exchanging meaningful looks when one of them makes a sacrifice so that the other can escape and some predictable plot points. After a while, you can tell whos going to die and whos going to survive. But those minor flaws didnt detract from how well-made and engrossing the movie was. Train to Busan is a zombie thriller that finds its dramatic pulse in the father-daughter dynamic, while also exploring the inevitable question of morality that arises out of the apocalyptic event.
In addition to excellent technical aspects like genuinely creepy zombie makeup and impressive CGI, the movie also has solid characterization that make you care fore these people and great performances, especially from Yoo Gong who plays the father and Soo-an Kim who plays the daughter. If youre a fan of zombie flicks, you really shouldnt miss this one!
