A non-stop locomotive ride that lets the fast-moving  instantly-infected zombies from Brad Pitt-starring World War Z go haywire inside a fast-moving train, this South Korean zombie apocalypse horror is a highly gripping, thoroughly entertaining  consistently engaging journey that moves at breakneck speed from start to finish and keeps ratcheting up the tension throughout its runtime.
The story of Train to Busan finds an absentee father  his young daughter boarding a train from Seoul to Busan to meet her mother. But all hell breaks loose when the train is overrun by zombies and results in death  reanimation of numerous staff members  passengers. With nowhere to run, the two team up with other surviving members to ward off the infected until the train makes it to its destination.
Directed by Yeon Sang-ho, the film borrows certain elements from Marc Forsters World War Z  Bong Joon-hos Snowpiercer but carves an original storyline thats brilliantly executed on the film canvas. Sang-hos kinetic direction keeps escalating the stakes with skilfully crafted moments of horror and slowly but steadily manages to compel the viewers to invest in the characters journey  eventual fate.
The zombies retain their vicious nature but an added weakness does allow for some suspenseful moments that are expertly carried out. While the movie makes use of CGI in the depiction of the reanimated corpses, the zombies look far more believable than the artificial mess they were in the film they are lifted from, not to mention that even the human characters exhibit an emotional core that was missing in that feature.
The dramatic portions, however, are a tad too overblown as the director is unable to pull them off with same zeal with which he carries out the action-horror segments. The technical aspects are finely executed and the film as a whole really benefits from its energetic camerawork, tight editing, excellent choreography, first-rate production design  fitting score and although a few CGI shots dont look realistic enough, it serves its purpose well.
Coming to the performances, the entire cast chips in with serviceable inputs and even though the characters they play lack an interesting persona  certain amount of depth, the actors somehow succeed in making the audience get on board with their characters predicament. While everyone does an apt job in their given roles, there really was no need to add a despicable human character when you already have a train full of zombies so that felt a bit out of place.
On an overall scale, Train to Busan still makes up for an exciting, action-packed zombie horror and boasts numerous sequences of sustained terror. The build-up is quick and once the train begins to move, it becomes all the more relentless  unstoppable. A few shortcomings like numerous stupid decisions made by a few characters does rob it of its uniqueness but there is no denying that Train to Busan delivers a healthy dose of adrenaline-filled extravaganza until the very end.

Im not even going to pussyfoot around. 
Train to Busan is one of my favorite Asian cinematography films. Its up there with the likes of Old Boy, Parasite, Ichi the Killer and Seven Samurai.  When my cousin told me to watch this, I watched the trailer and rolled my eyes. On paper it looks like Night of the Living Dead but on a train. People from different walks of life, forced to form alliances  and work together while being confined to a claustrophobic inducing environment  during a zombie outbreak. Really though, thats what this film reminds me of. Im not even 100 sure that George Romero, zombie grandpa himself, didnt go to Korea and under another pseudonym (like King did with Bachman) wrote this movie because it hits beat by beat on class and survival which is exactly what made his Dead films legendary. But heres a kicker. Some of the shots literally play out like its a Sam Raimi film as well. When one of the train attendants bites her male counterpart, a second passes and he rises like some kind of deadite (think Ed, Annies boyfriend in evil dead 2 who becomes possessed and levitates scene). Then immediately after the zombies come swarming towards our protagonist Gong Yoo in a running in a manner akin to how Wanda MaximoffScarlet witch chased  Chavez in Raimis Multiverse of Madness. 
Now I know Im throwing all these films and references at you and Im probably looking like Charley from its always sunny when he had all those red yarns connected to different boards and he was looking for Pepe Silvia. But theres some truth here I promise! Just follow the pop culture references! Theyll help I swear!
All jokes aside, this film could have just been a lackluster foreign take on zombies and just be a cheap throwaway. But the characters, Seok-woo, Sang-Hwa, Soo-An, Yong-guk with Jin-hee and pretty much all the side characters dont come across like simple zombie movie stand ins. Even two guys who we dont ever get to learn their names who youll cheer for (homeless man and train conductor). Their characters are fleshed out and humanistically flawed in application and that brings such a breath of fresh air to this zombie film that could have easily been created lifeless for cheap thrills and jumps. Even the zombies are unique. Fast, yes, like Dawn of the dead remake, but they seem almost possessed by how they reanimate after being bitten. Its done in all the spectacularly best ways which gives this film its own identity away from zombie clones. 
With great characters, an intense and gripping plot that moves like a bullet train to busan (finger guns), deaths and kills galore. It only leaves me with one questionwhy havent you watched this? And if you have, you know exactly what Ive been talking about throughout this review. Fans of George Romero will definitely be intrigued by this entry as it follows in his footsteps about making a movie not only about cannibalistic corpses that have raised from death to consume the flesh of others, but the social commentary on society, class and societal division. Even when the undead roam the earth, the real monsters are selfish human beings and we learn that throughout zombie films. If you find yourself unsure of what to view, this is my suggestion.

Train to Busan doesnt revolutionize the zombie genre in any way, but it accomplishes a rare feat in that genre, humanity.

Frischer Wind im Zombie Genre!
Ach Train to Busan. Ein Film, den ich schon so lange sehen wollte, aber irgendwie ist es nie dazu gekommen. Nun habe ich mir endlich die Bluray für die Sammlung geholt und den Film von Yeon Sang-ho sogleich in den Player geschoben. Und was soll ich sagen? Vielleicht waren nach all den Jahren meine Erwartungen etwas zu hoch, dennoch ist Train to Busan ein toller Vertreter des Genres, der mit seinem Setting frischen Wind mit sich bringt!
Seok-woo ist ein vielbeschäftigter Fondsmanager, der kaum Zeit für seine Familie findet. Da er den Geburtstag seiner Tochter Su-an mit einem doppelten Geschenk versaut, erfüllt er ihr den Wunsch, gemeinsam nach Busan zu fahren, um die Mutter von Su-an zu besuchen, von der er sich mittlerweile getrennt hat. So steigen sie am frühen Morgen in den Hochgeschwindigkeitszug KTX ein. Wenige Zeit später bricht hier aber die Hölle los. Denn im gesamten Land ist über Nacht eine Epidemie ausgebrochen. Menschen greifen sich gegenseitig an und verwandeln sich scheinbar in Zombies. Ein gebissenes Opfer hat sich dabei in den Zug geschmuggelt und lässt nun die Hölle über die Reisenden hereinbrechen
Ein Zombiefilm, der grösstenteils in einem fahrenden Zug spielt, habe ich so auch noch nicht gesehen. Dementsprechend abwechslungsreich und frisch gestaltete sich der Film für mich. Die Eskalationsstufe wird dabei ziemlich schnell hochgefahren. Was noch gemütlich beginnt, explodiert nach dem ersten Zombiebiss im Zug gewaltig. Sofort werden die Wagen überrannt und die letzten Überlebenden kämpfen um ihre Sicherheit. Genretypisch dient das beengte Setting dazu, die Figuren einzukerkern und ihre wahren Seiten nach aussen zu kehren. Train to Busan ist mal wieder eine 1A Gesellschaftskritik, die jedoch leider etwas zu sehr mit dem Holzhammer daherkommt. So wird hier die Einzelgängerschiene stark kritisiert, da die heutige Welt nur noch auf sich selbst schaut und keine Nächstenliebe mehr empfindet. Das ist grundsätzlich zwar gut analysiert, doch wird das so offen herausgetragen, dass selbst der hinterste in der Reihe diese Symbolik erkennt. Dabei entwickelt sich dann die Figur Seok-woo, der immer nur an sein eigenes Wohl denkt und seiner Tochter zu Beginn sogar beibringt, ebenso nur an sich zu denken, auch einfach zu schnell.  Hintenraus taut er dann von einem Moment auf den anderen auf, was zwar durch die Hilfe, die er angeboten bekommt, geschieht, dennoch hätte das abgestufter vorgetragen werden dürfen. Auch die typische Figur des bösen Einzelgängers, der wirklich alle ins Verderben stürzt, nur damit er davonkommt, wird hier zu schnell im Finale abgefrühstückt. Hier fehlt manchmal etwas der vielschichtige Aufbau, wenngleich der Typ dennoch fantastisch funktioniert, da man kaum eine hassenswertere Figur findet. Insgesamt ist Train to Busan etwas zu sprunghaft in seinen Figurenentwicklungen erzählt. Dafür gefallen andere Ideen umso besser.
Um den Zombies noch etwas mehr Abwechslung zu spendieren, reagieren diese stark auf Licht. Das bedeutet, dass sie im Dunkeln nahezu blind sind. Dadurch entsteht eine spannende Sequenz, in der sich einige Figuren versuchen, durch den Zug zu kämpfen und dabei die Dunkelheit von Tunnels ausnutzen. Geräusche werden insgesamt zwar wahrgenommen, doch im Allgemeinen greifen die Zombies erst bei Sichtkontakt an. Somit muss die Schleicherei hier gut getimed sein, damit man rechtzeitig aus den Waggons verschwindet, bevor das Tunnelende erreicht ist. Diese Sequenzen funktionieren besonders gut, weil hierbei drei Figuren enger zusammengeschweisst werden. Seok-woo schliesst sich dabei mit dem baldigen Familienvater Sang-hwa und einem jungen Baseballspieler namens Young-gook zusammen. Insbesondere Sang-hwa tritt dabei als sympathischer Kerl auf, der grossartig von Don Lee aka Ma Dong-seok verkörpert wird. Sein Abschied trieb mir dabei auch ein paar Tränchen ins Auge. Leider war dies der einzige Tod, der mich wirklich mitgenommen hat, denn insgesamt tritt der Film etwas arg melodramatisch auf, insbesondere was seine Musik betrifft. Was bei der Figur von Don Lee noch funktioniert hat, wirkt bei den anderen Figuren etwas zu übertrieben dramatisch. Schade ist hierbei, dass sich die letzten 30 Minuten zu schnell abspielen und ein Tod an den anderen gereiht wird, so dass die Tragik gar nicht mehr zum Atmen kommt. Darüberhinaus hätte man gerade mit Sang-hwa als Zombie noch so einiges anstellen können, was für noch mehr Tragik und Thrill gesorgt hätte. Immer wieder lässt Train to Busan etwas Potenzial vermissen, was schade ist. Ebenso schade ist der recht offensichtliche CGI Einsatz, der mich immer wieder unangenehm aus dem Film herausgerissen hat. Mir ist schon klar, dass dies wohl dem Budget geschuldet ist, aber sobald man den Zug verlässt, wirkt alles nur noch extrem künstlich. Die Massen an CGI Zombies, die sich dann manchmal über den Bildschirm ergiessen, liessen bei mir keinerlei Bedrohung aufkommen und das Finale wirkt dann in einigen Einstellungen besonders unschön. Dafür können die praktischen Effekte überzeugen. Das Make Up der Zombies sieht toll aus, insbesondere die hungrigen Augen, und Blut spritzt auch genug, wenngleich der Film nie besonders brutal oder explizit wird. Etwas absurd wird es, wenn sich die drei Figuren durch den Zug kämpfen und die Zombies teils mit blossen Fäusten zur Seite schubsen und diese keinen Anreiz zeigen, wieder anzugreifen. Spass machen diese Prügeleien zwar dennoch, logisch sind sie jedoch nicht immer, so dass man schon einmal ein Auge zudrücken muss, denn die Zombies sind immer nur so gefährlich, wie es das Drehbuch gerade vorgibt. 
Dennoch, Train to Busan weiss zu grossen Teilen wirklich zu gefallen. Gong Yoo gibt eine gute Hauptfigur ab, die noch etwas mehr Tiefe und Gesprächsstoff hätte liefern dürfen, doch das gilt beinahe für alle Figuren. Scenestealer bleibt aber Don Lee, der als sympathisches Muskelpaket immer die richtigen Worte findet und sich heldenhaft aufopfert. Un incidente in uno stabilimento biochimico dá luogo a una catastrofe nazionale in Corea del Sud, ossia una feroce aggressione da parte di orde di esseri umani infettati pronti a mietere vittime e a far scorrere sangue. In mezzo a tutto questo caos si muovono un padre e una figlia dal rapporto ormai sregolato. Le colpe del governo e delle istituzioni, una famiglia disfunzionale al centro del racconto e il conflitto sociale sono temi già comparsi nei film di Bong Joon-oh. In effetti, il film sembra ispirarsi a pellicole come The Host e Snowpiercer. La regia, grazie a un ritmo rapido e tagliente, riesce a destreggiarsi sia nelle scene dazione negli spazi angusti delle carrozze sia nei momenti in cui il lato peggiore delle persone esplode in tutta la sua violenza e follia (una simile atmosfera riporta alla mente The Mist di Darabont, dal racconto omonimo di Stephen King). Pure in tutto ciò cè spazio (che classico!) per laltruismo, leroismo e la fiducia verso il prossimo.
Alla fine quello a cui assistiamo è il percorso di maturazione di un giovane padre, prima sostenitore della legge del più forte e poi come individuo pronto a sacrificarsi per il bene della propria figlia, simbolo dellinnocenza e della volontà di proteggere gli altri in modo incondizionato.
Alla fine il film non è altro che una favola nera.


An accident at a biochemical facility leads to a national catastrophe in South Korea - a vicious onslaught by hordes of infected humans ready to kill and draw blood. In the midst of all this chaos, a father and daughter move for survival arguing with their unregulated relationship. The faults of the government and institutions, a dysfunctional family at the center of the story and social conflict are themes that have already appeared in Bong Joon-ohs films. In fact, the film seems to be inspired by films like The Host and Snowpiercer. The director, thanks to a sharp and fast pace, manages to juggle both the action scenes in the narrow spaces of the carriages and even in the moments in which the worst side of people explodes in all its violence and madness (such an atmosphere brings to mind The Mist of Darabont, from the short story of the same name by Stephen King). Even in all of this there is room (how classic!) for altruism, heroism and trust in others.
In the end what we witness is the maturation process of a young father, first a supporter of the law of the fittest and then as an individual ready to sacrifice himself for the sake of his daughter, a symbol of innocence and the will to protect others in a way unconditional.
In substance, the movie represents a dark fable.

Train to Busan was the biggest surprise of Scaretober 2021, a radical delight from end to end, bursting with urgency, terror, joy, humor, and mountains of style, a movie as thoughtful as it is eager to entertain for every moment of its runtime. So of course I picked it up on bluray and lined it up for a revisit a year later with my wife, a fellow zombie connoisseur. Zomboisseur.
Spoiler alert its just as good if not better the second time around. Heck, Id throw it on again today if a friend showed up saying theyd never seen it. Unsurprisingly, I had no fresh thoughts about the movie, so Ill direct yall to last years review, which really says it all
  
Almost twenty years after watching 28 Days Later in the movie theater, I once again felt a sense of awe watching a zombie movie. This is a true rupture in the genre, doing something fresh and vital and blisteringly entertaining with the tired old zombie trope. Its as fun as it is thoughtful, overlaid with an obvious but sharp sociopolitical framework while delivering visceral slaughter, a gripping narrative, and most of all, characters to really care about.
So here we are, kicking off Scaretober 2021 (yeah I do my own thing with my not-very-online friends every October - and this year we started early thanks to the month being so busy with work) with a rip roaring zombie adventure that doubles as a damning, funny critique of capitalism and the culture of extreme individualism it fosters. Its a fantastic example of show, dont tell we simply see how, over and over again, selfish actions of individuals lead to death and destruction not only of themselves but everyone around them. Meanwhile, the zombies, who seem to move like giant schools of fish or ant colonies, consistently gain the upper hand as an organized collective. Its simple, its effective, and it works perfectly with the well known horror mechanics of zombies.
It sounds a lot like the way zombies are portrayed in World War Z, because it is. But incredibly, Train To Busan takes that great conceptual kernel buried in a turd of a movie and breathes fresh, radical life into it. Instead of a mere visual flourish to spice up a worn trope, theres narrative and thematic resonance to the way the zombies flow with hive-like force. Its consistently astonishing how many creative scenarios the filmmakers have woven into the seemingly linear premise of zombies on a train, using their specific stylings and a series of inventive decisions on behalf of the humans. Even better, the smart writing delivers character development through action, endearing us to the dwindling folks left on the train, anxious about their survival and empathetic to their very human follies.
At the center is an investor dad who spends all his time and energy on making money to the neglect of his daughter, but weve also got a brave but hotheaded father-to-be with his smart, scared pregnant wife, a young baseball star and his surprisingly resourceful crush, a pair of elderly working class sisters, and a low wage railroad employee acting as the scab, crossing the proverbial strike line and siding with perhaps the real villain of the movie, his monstrous uber-capitalist CEO. Theyre all archetypes ripe for cliche, but miraculously the movie teases out some innate, relatable humanity in each of these characters, revealing their fears and motivations at a naturalistic pace as the action erupts around them. All around, the writing is truly upper tier genre fare, blasting out satisfying arcs, thematic cohesion, and snappy dialogue at a rollicking pace while never cutting narrative corners.
I dont know if theres any one single aspect here that I could point to as an elevating factor, what lifts Train To Busan into the upper echelon of modern horror movies for me. Its truly a confluence of skilled writing, attention to detail, obvious passion, and some incredible editing that snaps it all together airtight. Its rare for a horror movie with something more on its mind to deliver its action and its themes so tightly woven, with such seemingly effortless style. The class commentary and the violence on screen are inextricable, dovetailing into an essentially perfect final act that pays off the collective momentum of all that came before it. The ending gifts catharsis and character in equal measure, wrapping an extremely satisfying bow on the whole production.
I literally said WOW out loud when the credits hit, and my wife was smiling ear to ear. This movie is going into regular spooky season rotation and might become a household classic with repeat viewings.

Its nice to see a zombie film that takes a humanist angle and uses it to the best of its ability, one that unexpectedly took out much more tears from where it moved. Train to Busan, Yeon Sang-hos first live-action film shows another side to zombie films that I wish I could find more often, and quite quickly on that note it adds to South Koreas roll with 2016 releases - for they have been enjoying success more than anything this year in films like The Age of Shadows, The Handmaiden, Right Now, Wrong Then, and The Wailing. Train to Busan comes along the bunch.
Initially the setup comes just like any other zombie film, for we have an outbreak that affects an entire area in South Korea although a small group has remained safe. These people are all boarding the titular train to Busan, which reportedly has been noted as safe from the zombie outbreak which has spread. Of all the people whom we keep focus on, we have our eyes on the divorced Seok-Woo and his daughter Su-an, who plan to head to Busan so that they can see her mother as a birthday gift. Plans end up heading a whole other route when a zombie infection ends up spreading throughout the train and the journey to Busan soon becomes a quest for the survival of those who made it safely.
What the film does so perfectly well as a zombie film is where Train to Busan finds itself at its most thrilling. From how it keeps itself confined within a single area in order to rack up the tension, contrasting it with the moments the survivors end up heading into the outside world which is so full of danger, its always intriguing to see where Train to Busan wishes to move along with its zombie storyline because there is still a whole lot of energy present in order to keep everything in a constant motion, making all of the tension much more effective right on the spot. It showcases the zombie subgenre of horror at some of the best it has been in years, and while it lasts, it is wonderful.
Theres an interesting humanist angle coming along from the concept that we are watching the survivors recoup from their paranoia about another group, and perhaps this can come off as a detriment on some areas for it can draw too many familiar notes towards Snowpiercer, a common complaint that Ive seen. When it comes to how we look at the selfishness of one class being ahead of all the others with their refusal to let others in for they still try to fight for their own survival, theres a note that rings a tad familiar on some counts but it never takes away enough in order to make for something boring. We still care enough about these characters and their stories so that they keep our attention for the whole ride, which is what is most important.
Regardless, theres still an interesting idea to which it can raise about what will happen to the survivors because of what they have done to keep their own lives during the outbreak. Seok-Woos ark is perhaps the most compelling of the bunch, for all he wanted is to keep his daughter safe. Its nothing particularly new for the horror genre but the amount of emotion that comes from both Gong Woo and Kim Su-ans performances ultimately makes their arc rewarding - for we recognize in these survivors humanity. With the final sequence coming to mind, that is where Train to Busan hits more moving notes.
Train to Busan is a bit standard but theres always something interesting coming along at every minute, because of the incredible amount of intelligence that is laced within - making it one of the better zombie films of recent memory. Imagine World War Z had it been inside of a more confined space, but at the same time if it ever had at least twice as much tension as said film did - for thats the best way to put Train to Busan into words. For the opening half alone, youll have what anyone would want out of any zombie film and while there are many notes that ring predictable in its second half, the new angle it attempts to bring in is where it still keeps ones attention.

Beyond the potential theme of class and generational divide you could get from Train to Busan, I also enjoyed how it examines the concept of selflessness versus selfishness. Are you the kind of person that helps others or helps yourself? How conscious are you of your actions, and can you change? The action and spectacle of the film does take precedence, but Train to Busan leaves at least some room for introspection and character, and that combined with the stellar technical filmmaking makes it more than worth the time of anyone, regardless of language. Who doesnt love a good zombie film, especially when they can be this engaging?

Considering so much of the acting is this way (in Hardwickes other films as well), I have to put the blame on her.
But everything else, from the aesthetics (harsh and washed out, overly blue) to the concept seem to emulate that teenage perspective in a way that is both beautifully longing and deeply critical at the same time. While many people critique the film for encouraging women to abandon their whole lives for true love, I dont believe Hardwicke is aligned with the source text at all. In every scene in which Bella seems to be most overt about her undying love, theres always something undercutting the rationality of those feelings. Perhaps most perfectly when she attends her own prom with a broken leg. Theres very few films that can equally capture the duality of incredible and addictive love while also being open about its dangers and entropic nature.
But even if this film werent critical of the central romance, it still wouldnt deserve the level of scorn it receives. Critics and audiences alike are so accepting of teenage boy fantasies uncritically made into films why should teenage girl fantasies be any different? Weird how a film written by a woman and directed by a woman is more likely to get called out for sexism than so many written and directed by men.

First love in youth is always so mysterious, that feeling in your stomach, a glance in the moonlight, and a burning desire to fall in love. its a dangerous leap into the unknown, and like Bella, I will jump into this movies world and plan to watch all the films completely through.

Everything in this movie is so subdued. Its colors, the weather, and the entire atmosphere. Everything is very melancholically cloudy, rainy, and represents a state of darkness, that it brings out a strange feeling in me when I try to watch this masterpiece with wide eyes. It embodies everything that symbolizes coldness and isolation. At the same time, it creates such an oppressive sexual tension between the characters that you could cut it with a knife. This is threat in the mist and love in the rain. A glance that will definitely give you butterflies in your stomach as you watch it. I might have blushed a few times when Batman looked me straight in the eyes during the movie.
The relationship depicted in the movie is contradictory. It is the freedom of choice but at the same time the fulfillment of destiny. Dependent on love, a self-destructive mindset. This is an escape from the realities of everyday life. It creates a combination of danger, adrenaline, and love, echoing the age-old theory of the forbidden fruit. Love that is old-fashioned, yet somehow modern.
But in the end, the movie reminds me of something. It brings me back to a time and state of mind when life was different. It brings back memories of first love, which felt like a fantasy. This creates a tear in my heart in the way it tells its own story. The movie doesnt create anything perfect, but for me, it evokes a sense of longing. This is likely a comfort movie for many in its own way, and its no surprise that it gained such huge popularity when it was released. For me, its a memory of youth, excitement, and a way to express oneself. A cliché, unintentionally hilarious movie full of mysterious love.

American Post-911 Genre Film
American conservatism through the lens of its sexual politics
A rural American romantic melodrama. The cultural coordinates are all here the cop-dad, the red pickup truck, the move from the big city to the middle of nowhere Washington State, the descendants of Native Americans who dont go to school with you because theyre stuck out on their reservation. Enter stage left the Capulets and Montagues, or rather here the Cullens and the Quileutes and their mythical antagonism. We have our Romeo, Edward Cullen, but where is our Juliet? Bella Swan is an outsider, neither a Capulet nor a Montague, neither a Cullen nor a Quileute, although her cop-dad is friends with an elder of the Quileute tribe who has a bad habit of coming over right when Bella and Edward want to hang out, forcing Edward to leave.
But the conflict between the Cullens and the Quileutes isnt the only thing holding Bella and Edward back from being together  heck, its not even, like, the main thing. Whats really holding them back is Edward himself, or rather his received ideas about himself and how he ought to act around others, especially those hes physically attracted to. And his attraction to Bella is physical, and powerfully so he cant even sit next to her without being overwhelmed by her scent and the desire for her that it arouses in him. But hes been told that he must resist this attraction, hes been told that hes a vampire and that if he bites someone hell release venom into their body that will make them undead. He has been told that sex is evil.
Abstinence-only sex education is a controversial topic in the United States because a large portion of the country either ignores or denies the scientific evidence that it doesnt work and insists on teaching it in school instead of comprehensive sex education, usually on religious grounds. The conservative Christian right in America opposes comprehensive sex education on the ideological grounds that it promotes sex before marriage in theory, despite demonstrated evidence of the ineffectiveness of abstinence-only sex education to actually increase abstinence rates in practice. In 2017, the U.S. federal government spent 90 million dollars funding abstinence-only sex education. It is a central tenet of American culture and national identity.
Edward Cullen is laboring under the delusion of abstinence-only sex education. He cant be with Bella because he doesnt know if he can control himself,  hes afraid he wont be able to stop himself from biting with his venom. He has been taught that hes the worlds most dangerous predator, and he believes it despite being gentle with a 17-year-old girl he desperately wants to eat, despite not actually killing anyone, despite being part of a family of vegetarian vampires who dont drink human blood. Hes not literally a 108-year-old vampire, hes not actually a predator, hes just another teenage boy whos been taught that his urges are bad, are deadly, are literally monstrous, so it falls on Bella to re-educate him, because she wants him, she wants his bite, his venom.
This is what the conservative Christian right misses about abstinence-only sex education making sex taboo makes it even hotter, makes it more attractive, makes it more of an impossible object of desire. Theres an element of Catholic guilt in Edwards predicament, and while this ideological repression of sex makes it more exciting, it also does psychological damage to Edward, it makes him cold and abrasive and standoffish. But Bella is willing to fight for him, partly because, you know, hes really hot, but also because falling in love with an immortal is an appealing fantasy, it transforms Romeo and Juliets star-crossed lovers from a tragedy into a straightforward romance they still die, but in death they live together forever.
And this fantasy of a lover whos an immortal predator but also a tender little vampire pet is not only harmless but downright convincing for most of Twilights runtime. Its just a mythological vehicle for the films cornucopia of pregnant glances, longing gazes, hungry eyes. Its a genre-inflected riff on the romantic teen melodrama in all its awkward corny truth, and whether or not thats your personal cup of tea (and judging by the polarization of its reception upon the films release, there were many folks for whom this was not their cup of tea), its hard to deny that its accomplished well, at least for the first three quarters of the film. It captures that shifting-weight-from-one-leg-to-the-other awkward emotional discomfort of adolescence.
And for the most part, the film is happy to languish in this ennui without bothering to set its characters in the artificial rat-race of a plot, but then, with about thirty minutes left, it tosses in an antagonist almost literally out of left field (I think he and his vampire friends technically emerge from center field, but you get it, the baseball idiom works surprisingly well), and suddenly we have not only the artificial propulsion of a villain to run away from, we have a moral justification for Edwards predatory characterization. Suddenly hes not just a cute vampire pet, he actually is a hundred-year-old (sexual) predator, and Bella needs him to protect her from the even more dangerous predator who wants to do a lot more than bite her and fill her with venom.
With the introduction of James the tracker vampire, Bellas innocent schoolgirl fantasy of an immortal predator-boyfriend transforms into something much more sinister. For most of its runtime, it feels like Twilight is fighting its own conservative politics, with Bella re-educating Edward in order to help him find some release from his sexual repression, with the threat of Edwards vampiric violence mostly relegated to the realm of genre set-dressing for an otherwise traditional teen romance, but here its reactionary politics become necessary rather than incidental, they become the solution rather than the cause of the films conflict, and suddenly the romantic fantasy begins to feel like propaganda to smuggle in paranoid fear-fantasy.
What we have here actually isnt so different from what we find in post-911 superhero cinema. Edward is written like Americas post-traumatic incarnations of Batman, where hes a violent vigilante whos corrupting the law with his personal brand of justice, but hes a necessary violent vigilante, because (the films tell us) there are even worse evils out there from which we need him to protect ourselves. Its a fear-fantasy of omnipotent terrorists who can track us by scent and kill us in our own homes, an ideological justification for the post-911 American surveillance state. We need fascist Batman, we need the Patriot Act, we need this scary, sexy vampire-boyfriend to save us from the even worse threat, which, the movie assures us, is definitely real and not imaginary.
We pretend we dont want fascist Batman, we pretend we dont want the Patriot Act, we pretend we dont want scary, sexy vampire-boyfriend, we just want regular fun Batman, we just want good old-fashioned American patriotism, we just want the hot vampire without the predatory threat, but when James and the Joker come out to play it becomes clear that its all ideology, its all propaganda, its all an excuse when we really do want the violent dark side of our heroes, theyre an integral inextricable part of the fantasy. And the most revealing part of Twilight in particular is the way it extends this reactionary political propaganda into repressive psycho-sexual propaganda and shows how the same kernel is at the root of American ideology.
Edward Cullen isnt just an overly protective superhero figure, hes a romantic overly protective superhero figure. His violence isnt only politicized, its romanticized, its sexualized, which is doubly dangerous. The romanticization infects the politics and the politicization infects the romance. It both retroactively justifies his creepy behavior where hes showing up in her room uninvited and dating outside not only his age but his generation, and it romanticizes his violent over-protectionism. There are real bad guys out there, the film tells us, so we need the only-a-little-bad guys to keep us safe. This is American ideology at its purest the lie that we need the little-evil to protect us from the big-evil.
The big-evil is a fear-fantasy used to justify the little-evil. The little-evil is the real big-evil. We (the U.S.) are the real big-evil.

I find discomfort in the idea of engaging with a work with the objective of deriding the creators efforts and intentions as such an engagement is so often driven by a mundane cruelty or desire to confirm mass consensus (both of these with schoolyard origins). A friend convinced me to watch Twilight as its value lies not in its ability to be ridiculed, but in its individual weirdness as a piece of popular cinema. She was right. Not once does the film shoot for (and fall short of, as critics had me believe) the mystery-driven adventure of something like the Harry Potter series, nor the naivemacabre art-goth stylisations of Let the Right One In. It is for the most part committed entirely to teen girl fantasy, ever-drenched in the damp atmosphere of a shithole town, with little interest in following cinematic convention.
Prior to reading the Twilight Wikipedia page I was convinced that Catherine Hardwicke had worked as a television director before moving into cinema, and that Stephanie Meyer was home-schooled. As it transpires Hardwicke directed the much-loved films Thirteen and Lords of Dogtown before Twilight, and Meyer attended the same high school as Busy Phillips (!). Twilights depiction of the high school experience is eerily smooth, non-specific, and full of red herrings, but Hardwickes confidently loose pacing almost pulls it together in the style of an unimportant but vaguely fond memory (you might recall primary school in this way if you were not gifted but basically got by just fine waiting for holidays, weekends, and lunchtimes). Conventionally Romantic literature might have relegated the school to a background detail accounting for what Bella as a seventeen year old does during the week, and had the lovers interactions take place in evenings or even weekends, but one of the Twilight series enduring concerns is an almost egalitarian approach to what does and does not matter, offering the same screen-time to weird mundane shit as to inspired supernatural romance. The other purpose of the uncanny high school is that it defines Bellas angst in a way that is safe. She is immediately welcomed into a group of of teen archetypes when she arrives, each one standing in for a conflict that she will not have the jock ensures that she will not be bullied, the preppy one that class will not be an issue, the popular one that she will not be ostracised. Her feelings of alienation are not due to any discernable feature in her character, nor to some event or series of events actioned by anyone or anything, but by the absence of her satisfaction or even dissatisfaction for these people and what they represent.
This having but not having, this definition by way of absence, is wholly embraced by Hardwicke who paces the film like a mid-afternoon nap. I had not considered it before but there must be some correlation between high school ennui and dull television, because Twilight both feels like the experience of watching Sunday afternoon television and the Sunday afternoon television programme itself. Each scene is given the same attention and duration, whether the subject is Bella going on a field trip, a family of vampires playing baseball during a thunderstorm, or a tree-top declaration of love. This could make for a film that is jarring or worse, boring, but these (often contradictory) pieces are held together by an atmosphere of dampness and generic teen-angst which makes the film feel more like life-remembered than life-experienced. This is not to say that Twilight sets out to do Sans Soleil for teens, but its structure is effectively Bergson re-tooled for an age-group for whom nostalgia is starting to take on serious weight. The future is indeterminate and the past with all its warmth is gone forever (a theme further explored in New Moon where Bella attempts to re-live her childhood). Had I been younger and more open-minded when Twilight was released I might have learned something about the sick-stomach dizziness I had been feeling for years and didnt know how to describe. The idea that teens have been given access to something approachable before they bump into Antonioni further down the track to make them feel less alone in their sad-not-sadness warms my heart.

So I have a bizarrely specific enjoyment of the Twilight Franchise despite having no specific attraction or obsession with any of the actors or directors or writers so just go with it. 
HOW I FEEL 
I like, dare I say love, super melodramatic crazy shit and for me the Twilight series is one of the more amazing things to ever happen in film and Im not going to be judged about that. Many people dont like these movies that much and thats fine but the joyful hatred of these films... come the fuck on. Its a successful film franchise that many women liked and we all know that Americans would rather Trump be President than have women be comfortable with their lives so this got way too much shit during a hateful generation of online culture building. But Twilight is fucking wonderful, hysterical, fantasy YA melodrama and Im proud to own the Twilight Forever Blu Ray box set. I think too many people go into this film wanting to hate it instead of going into this film looking to learn about a bizarre and fun world and opening their hearts to a dopey teen romance with decent direction, score, and soundtrack... but mostly you are there for YA vampires. 
THE PLOT 
Bella Swan, a super awkward girl, moves to live with her father in Forks, Washington. While awkwardly transitioning to a new school she meets a vampire who is hot as fuck and cool and lives with his incestuous brothers and sisters in a house that children dream of living in when they grow up.  They fall in love and then people try to kill them but there are four more movies so... you know. There love is is hindered by Edwards strong desire to eat Bella, who is his own personal brand of heroin. 
PRIMARY CHARACTERS Ill get to them all eventually 
Robert Pattinson is an effective actor who fucking kills it as Edward Cullen, a crazy over the top psychic possessive vampire who is hot to trot. While he looks like he is a strapping young adult he is over a hundred years old (try not to think about it too much). His specialty is beating up suburban rape gangs, watching girls sleep, being worried about others, and smouldering. His intimidating monologue where he shows his horrible beautiful skin and tells Bella how he could kill her but wants her at the same time is the most insane shit Ive seen a vampire do and is PG-13 hotness to the max. 
He falls in love with Bella because she knows timeless things like the square root of pi and says things like Clare DeLune is great. He also cant read her mind... so that turns him on. 
Dont like Kristen Stewart in this? Okay... well no offense but I hope you go to hell because as far as Im concerned she IS fucking Bella Swan. She is so much better than the book depiction of Bella and so perfectly annoying and indecisive and ready to have a character arc. She gets rid of the gruntingmoaning problem in later films but is just fantastic in this because her being kind of annoying and boring is in some ways what makes the film so great (do you know how many boring as fuck dudes have been the center of movies). Anyways, Bella is a young, above average intelligence girl with levels of self-doubt that border on psychotic. Her strengths are hurting herself, martyrdom, sighs and weird noises, killing buzzes, and being totally over the whole high school thing. 
I also sincerely love and appreciate Billy Burke in the role of goofy and caring dad Charlie Swan. Having read the books (and by that I mean having listened to the books) I can tell you that Burkes portrayal of Charlie is kind of masterful. People will make fun of this but I think he is a really great dad character in the film and represents a well-intentioned and loving man who is just an okay father, but trying. Its a more complex role than it is given credit for. I like how hes always drinking a beer and talking about fish. 
The supporting cast in these films is actually pretty impressive including a group of regular teens highlighted by a truly fantastic supporting supporting role by Anna Kendrick, Native American wolf boy tribes and Vampire covens. I especially love how the group of regular teens lives are contrasted with the batshit crazy vampire subplots. 
WHY I LIKE IT
I think Twilight is a compelling story that is high theatrics and drama. I love movies that commit to bold and ridiculous ideas and explore broad archetypes. In addition, I think these films are hysterical and the world building is fun fantasy. I think many of the haters of this film assume people that like Twilight are too dumb to get how over the top everything is... I also think many of these haters spend most of their film money to watch people in tights fight super-villains or to rubber stamp films theyve been told are good since they started reading film reviews online. Im not stupid, I dont think these films are high art, I think they are compelling and entertaining as fuck and they embrace the ridiculous in a way that is impressive and apparently has mass appeal as this was a mid-budget (even low mid-budget) franchise that made close to 4 billion dollars worldwide.  
SPECIFIC STUFF I LOVE (spoilers) 
Im not going to lie I pretty much love every scene in this movie. Having listened to the commentaries for each one of the films I think one of the strengths of these movies is that the directors all had some sense of humor about this being an insanely over the top world. Ten favorite scenes 
(1) The baseball scene 
(2) Anna Kendrick exposition dump on the Cullens
(3) Edward shows diamond skin and hides in tree. 
(4) The prophasemetaphase meet cute
(5) Charlie and Bella eating cobbler together
(6) The Cullens dont come around here scene on La Push. 
(7) This isnt a scene but I like Jackson Rathbones I want to eat you stare
(8) Bella googling
(9) The Cullens cook Italian foodRosalie flips the fuck out
(10) Compost Tea scene... I really like that teachers hustle. 
While the film is only my second favorite in the series it is definitely the most approachable and the best single story. 
RECOMMENDED TO (1) People that are fucking awesome and down to have fun (2) Soap Opera fans (3) YA fantasy fans (4) Romance novel readers (5) People into all that drama.

Its the feeling of never wanting a dream to end, desperately trying to go back to sleep hoping that your dream would somehow pick up where it had left off.
But you know very well that it wont. First youll forget the details. What shirt you were wearing, the exact words you said or wanted to say. Her hand on your palm that felt so tangible just a few seconds ago, reduced to a cold sensation that served as nothing but a reminder of the warmth that was once there. 
Then the timeline becomes murky, sequences become knotted up -- like how mitsuhas grandmother had so wisely put it Musubi  dayo. Time is a knot. The location comes before the journey there, cause and effect all collapse in an instant.
You cant remember the weather, or the exact time of day. It felt golden, the sun may or may not be present, was her eyes sparkling because of the comet? Why yes, there was a comet slowly crawling up above, leaving a trail of sparkling dust behind like something out of a desktop wallpaper. The comet traveled all across the galaxy to arrive on earth, like how you had traveled all across the country to meet----
To meet who, again? Ah, all is lost now, absolutely irrevocable. Whats left is a lingering sadness which reason you had forgotten. A need to remember someone dear, a stroke of marker pen on your palm and a simple wish for company. How cruel it is for our dream to force itself away from us, beyond our control.

Watching my family experience this movie for the first time was nothing short of magical, and reminded me why I love it so much in the first place. Some have accused Shinkai of style over substance, but in this case, the style creates the substance. Why? Because first and foremost, this is a film that articulates and exemplifies divine beauty and indescribable feelings that only imagery and visuals can evoke. The way a meteor falling through the sky can be both beautiful and terrifying, tragic and poetic, destructive and spiritual, at the same time. The splendor and artistry of the untouched natural world, from sunsets and forests to lakes and falling leaves, that something inside us all just knows must be worthy of respect and wonderment. The impressiveness of human achievement and technology and city life. The way the two can (and should) work together to make something even better.
Its a movie about the forgotten memories and emotions you experienced when you were younger that now briefly materialize as shadows and figments in your head, like the beach-house I used to visit as a kid that Ill probably never see again, even though I still remember how the carpet smelled and the sheets on the bed felt against my pajamas. Like my great-aunt and the jokes she would tell before she died. Like the plays my dad directed that I (reluctantly) attended at age 5 and only remember fragments of now. This movie is wish-fulfillment, a beautiful fantasy about reaching out and finding those things you thought were lost into the depths of your memory and heart.
Its also about love. I must confess, for much of my life, Ive always been a little torn between two sides of my own personality in some ways, Im a total romantic, and in others, Im more of a realist. Many movies I watch sway one way or the other, which is fine. But one of the reasons I love Your Name so much is that it satisfies both sides of my head the romantic and the realist. This is, in many ways, a movie about lovers destined to be together, bound by a cord of fate and meant to find each other in the end. In a sense, theyre soul mates. And I love that. But its also a film about how, in all honesty, you can love anyone when you see what their life is like firsthand and walk around in their shoes. When you appreciate what theyve been through to become the person they are today and the struggles they still face, and see the beauty in their life that maybe even they might have missed. Maybe Mitsuha and Taki were fated to be together and fall in love from the start. Or maybe theyre just two special people who, through divine or magical intervention, saw firsthand what made the others life beautiful and had to fall for each other because of what they had been through and seen with their own eyes. The ambiguity there makes the movie that much more nuanced and transcendent for me.
As a Christian (and bear with me here), one of the things I find most beautiful about Your Name is actually the way it intertwines the Shinto religion into its subtext and meaning. The beliefs about time and the way divine spirituality transcends it, the importance of tradition and ancestors, the symbolic and spiritual significance of nature. One of the quotes that comes to mind whenever I watch this film is from CS Lewis, but its not one that many other Christians ever seem to bring up, because it makes the entire meaning of the Gospel that much more complicated. CS Lewis said in a letter from 1952, I think that every prayer which is sincerely made even to a false god, or to a very imperfectly conceived true God, is accepted by the true God and that Christ saves many who do not think they know him. For He is (dimly) present in the good side of the inferior teachers they follow. In other words, where there is Truth and Beauty, God is there too - even if people know him by a different name. If God is Love and God is Goodness and God is Peace, then wherever those things truly manifest, He manifests too. Even, perhaps, in parts of Shinto belief. I am not a universalist. I dont believe every religion ultimately points to the same God or all religions are the same or right and wrong are in the eyes of the beholder. In general, theres a lot about religion and spirituality that Im willing to admit I just dont have an answer for. But I do believe that God is present in far more places and belief systems than most western, conservative, white evangelical Christians ever give Him credit for. And Your Name is a film that gives me an appreciation for the beauty of the Shinto religion and some of the things it has that western Christianity just doesnt or at least, doesnt articulate nearly as well in todays age.
This is the most impeccable blend of animation and music Ive ever witnessed onscreen. If the animation assigns imagery to the emotional beauty, the music gives a voice to it. Never before have the two artforms complimented each other so well. If you havent watched Your Name, I highly recommend you do it on the biggest screen you have, subtitled, and with no distractions. Ask any hardcore anime fan, and theyll likely tell you that stunning animation aside, this probably isnt the greatest anime movie ever made, and has been overhyped by many. And theyre probably right. But this is undoubtedly the anime movie that means the most to me. Its the rare, beautiful experience of a film that sticks with you long after the credits roll and offers poetic meaning to daily life in a way not much else does. I love it with all my heart.

Theres no way we could possibly meet. But one thing is certain If we ever see each other, well both know that you were the one within me. That I was the one within you.
Your Name (君の名は) asks us right out of the gate if we believe in infatuation enduring long before first contact, shying away from that love at first sight thesis and metamorphosing it into a little Pandoras box, utilizing its isekai fare to bring forth a palpably transcendental romance as an aftermath. And it works wonders through the secretive whispers that are threaded along the labyrinthine lanes that help unite Mitsuha and Taki together, clairvoyant in stature by dazing our senses with the prompted allure of its story, and flustering our minds with a discouraging cataclysm that induces a much-needed scale of drama to our characters and the miraculous relationship that binds them.

Its each deliberate stroke of those pencil brushes, each carefully concocted detail in the animation that flurries that abiding twinkle in your eyes, where the unwithering glamor fixed upon the horizon cant help but pluck your heartstrings along with the unspoken mesmerism from the cosmos up above. Double lives are entangled as flustered states of consciousness become dovetailed into a mingled, consolidating knot of head-scratching quandaries autumn leaves weave and bend in service of the cursory passage of the seasons, and the Gods bellow out a wabi-sabi (侘び寂び) plea of existence that amalgamates all living creatures as one, incomposite. Past and present collide through a Möbius loop that engenders a compromised third state, hidden in its slender clefts and defined by the mutual absence of its adjacent duplicities, in a twilight bliss of existence (Tasokare 誰そ彼) where magical happenstance spirals upwards into a comely little burst of make-believe novelty.

And those duplicities arent just implanted as handy deus ex machina they are one and the same with the story those country-girl doldrums and city-slicker commotions, the fervid blithe of day and the moonlit blankets of night, the pious aspirations of faith battling against the pagan let-downs of overwrought realism, and so on. You start to accept the mundane flukes of everyday living as a means to yearn for some kind of escapist fantasy, which in this instance conjures up one wholesome yarn of soul-stirring gratification. Finally, Your Name leaves us flabbergasted with its tooth-achingly sweet conclusion, taking a gold-coated page out of what the best love stories are capable of offering us by making us reminisce over the precious moments that follow its conclusion its precisely when the cameras stop rolling (or when the last lines are drawn in place) that our minds start to race ardently with a multitude of zippy thoughts, all of pure and endearing intent, over the circumscribed destiny that bestows our leading duet of flustered beloveds.

This fits really nicely with Shinkais always perfectly articulated anxieties of irrevocable disconnection and separation, but it just crumbles under a seemingly endless, repetitive narrative when it would have seriously benefitted from the more intuitive, clipped emotional scaffolding of his earlier short stuff. Gorgeous but shouldve only been about 45 minutes long.

Makoto Shinkai, the rising Japanese animator whose heartbreaking, hyper-saturated films marry the delicate beauty of Hayao Miyazaki with the workaday wistfulness of Yasujirō Ozu, has always gravitated towards stories that take place in the space between people.
His breathtaking 22-minute breakthrough, a homemade project called Voices of a Distant Star, lucidly illustrated Shinkais preoccupation with distance and how the immediacy of modern communication has had the perverse effect of clarifying our isolation from one another. Effectively a more compelling (and much more compact) anime precursor to Interstellar, the 2002 short traces a high school crush as its stretched across the length of an intergalactic war  the boy stays on Earth and the girl goes off to fight aliens in the farthest reaches of space, but their feelings for one another are soon contorted by the cruelty of relative time.

Interweaving dreams, reality  timeline into one perfectly braided storyline, the highest grossing anime of all time is an exquisitely envisioned, elegantly composed  sumptuously animated fantasy thats crafted with care, narrated with flair and brims with endless warmth  intimacy to finish as one of the most enchanting  emotionally captivating films of 2016.
The story of Your Name follows two strangers whose lives interconnect in the most bizarre fashion. One of them is a young girl who lives in the small town of Itomori and is fed up of her countryside life while the other is a young boy in Tokyo who works at an Italian restaurant. Their normal routine is thrown out of balance when they discover that they are switching bodies when they go to sleep.
Written  directed by Makoto Shinkai, Your Name acquaints the audience with its protagonists in a sensible manner while emanating a hint of mystery simultaneously but once Shinkai lets them know what exactly is going on, he begins stepping up the gear as the story gets more n more intricate as time passes yet does so in a way that keeps the viewers interest  their emotional investment alive  undisturbed.
The narrative structure is clever, for it is always ahead of viewers at all times and takes sharp turns at the most unexpected moments to keep things unpredictable but even more impressive than that is how the characters arcs unfold and the thread connecting their destinies is unraveled to deliver an incredibly satisfying finale. The film is truly a roller-coaster ride, sending its audience on a whirlwind of emotions throughout its runtime.
The graceful quality, heartwarming beauty  remarkable simplicity of its rich, colourful animation is very much in tune with Studio Ghiblis works, and same can be said about the careful attention with which it brings every frame to life. The voice cast does an outstanding job with the characters they lend their voices to, and the films emotional impact is all the more magnified by its mesmerising  emotionally resonant soundtrack.
On an overall scale, Your Name may as well be the best Studio Ghibli film that the famed animation studio never made, for it is just as transporting as their finest works and radiates such an immense joy  intoxicating feeling that its difficult to not be swept by its magical tide. There are times when it gets confusing or overwhelming to an extent but majority of those issues are eliminated once all the dots are connected. Definitely one of the finest films of its year, Your Name comes delightfully recommended.

The fanbois will be out for your blood if you give another negative review of a Shinkai film - message from a friend
Lets talk bias. At this point it is hard for me to watch a film by Makoto Shinkai. When I watched his last film Weathering With You I wrote a review which inexplicably became popular. Since then I have posted hundreds of messages about Shinkai in comment sections, really digging into what I deem to be his strengths and weaknesses. So whenever I now watch a Shinkai film I find it hard to separate what I am actually watching from the version I created in my head from all my writing. I didnt rewatch every Shinkai film every time I posted a comment. I was constructing memories and critiquing those memories of his works. But as my reviews of Shinkais films are predominantly negative, the majority of comments other people have written on my reviews are either rebutting my criticism or expressing similar criticisms of his films. So whether I am defending my stance or standing in solidarity with others, I was always replying by talking only about the negative. This means when I now approach a Shinkai film, it is the negatives that come to mind first, before I even watch. So how can I judge or write about his films? I have a bias, shaped by experience on Letterboxd. Then again, doesnt everyone have a bias and expectation before watching anything? Am I just being silly by explaining this particular bias, and ignoring all my others? I dont really know.
People may expect me to dislike all of Shinkais films, but I actually like Your Name. I dont think its amazing, or matches the hype, but it has some good things in it and minimises a lot of Shinkais weaknesses. For starters it is rarely irritating, which is a good thing by Shinkais standards. There isnt a lot of sappy faux-deep voiceover, or anything too morally egregious. There is an emphasis on saving lives, as opposed to just selfishly acting for love, so thats a nice dynamic. The female characters are still mostly reduced to being controlled by their love for our male lead Shinkai stand-in, but there isnt creepy or paedophilic undertones like other Shinkai films. A repetitive gag about fondling boobs is still a bit unnecessary though.
The first half of Your Name still strikes me as dull and predictable. Its mostly generic body swap stuff, dragged down by clichéd characters that have no real personality. However the middle stretch of Your Name is where it really shines. It stops being about body swapping and becomes about seeking out someone you have lost a connection to. There are some clever twists and very moving moments. The final act is a bit of a mess, but to get to that involves a time travel sequence that switches animation style and is easily the best thing Shinkai has ever done. Its a beautiful little montage, of the moments that shape a life. 
The biggest thing that drags down Your Name for me, is that it insists on being a romance movie. At no point do I understand why these two leads fall in love. They never meet or really interact, they just swap bodies. But then suddenly their love is so strong that it becomes an indisputable fact and a key motivation for their actions. Why couldnt this story be about sharing a strange emotional connection? Or wanting to save someone in danger because its the right thing to do? Why does Shinkai always have to make it be that these people have the deepest, purest love and that is the reason they act how they do? Obviously Shinkai has a perpetual fantasy about the quiet, lonely guy saving the cute girl and she loves him forever, which fine, we all have our dreams. But its just such boring storytelling. No matter how many monologues and sci-fi tropes he stuffs in a movie, he never produces story depth beyond schmaltzy romance. Which works okay in Your Name, I suppose, but does leave all its other interesting ideas redundant because they must become subservient to this fantasy romance.
I feel pretty much the same about Your Name as I did when I first saw it. My rating has not changed. The film has some great moments, but also a lot of mediocre ones. The visuals are wonderful works of art and you cant criticise Shinkai in that sense. It tells the same type of flawed story as he usually does, but the less obnoxious characters and less repugnant vibe at least makes Your Name watchable. I think its mainstream nature smoothes out the quirks I most dislike in Shinkais films, so the whole thing is decently entertaining. There are a lot of individual elements to criticise, but Your Name has enough good ideas and moving moments to make for something pretty decent overall.

They begin to take notes, log moments in journals and write on their bodies what they do when they arent in their normal body just to keep the other informed. This part of the film is what I signed up for and I was having a great time. I almost had to take a breath because my heart was racing when this situation sunk in. As much as I loved the film prior to this it was nothing compared to when the story started to shift. It becomes this race against time that keeps you on the edge of your seat because this devastating situation feels inevitable. The fact that their thoughts become blurry, their ideas grow more confusing and its not as easy as it should be make for a thrilling ride. The end is beautiful. I love when a movie knows how to never let you out of its grasp and then deliver on a hard-hitting final note. Your Name lived up to the hype. It is easily one of the best animated movies I have ever seen.

SPOILERS at certain sections, but I wont mark my entire review as spoilers. I will give a proper warning before I get to them. 
Letterboxd mods Please implement this feature of marking certain sections as spoilers instead of the entire review. Even Delicious Fruit does it.
The intangibility of human bonds is the topic at hand now, how one can transcend time with a significant other. To be in the perspective of another, embrace another life and live it, literally, in the flesh, and challenge the laws of causality and space without the need of resorting to the overused topic of time-travelling. To pursue one dream and ones own identity. Thats what the film is.
Except, it turns out it isnt. A commercial product is not necessarily the enemy of quality filmmaking, quality necessarily being a subjective term however, this is Shinkais most commercial product, his most popular and renowned one, and sadly his most superficial and, at times, idiotic. The film opened the possibility for exploring the idea of becoming another person in another body, to experience a life and feel emotions you will never ble able to live for your own. We are unique individuals with a well-defined individuality, and it is this uniqueness that makes that precious, insurmountably valuable. Shinkai opens this concept with a man in a womans body touching his boobs for comedic effect. Not once. Not twice. Not even thrice. He even plays this dirty card during a dramatic moment for... comedic relief? The girl is not absent from sin as she is seen doing this with male genitalia, again, for comedic effect. If I want Rob Schneider comedy, Ill look for it (I freaking dont).
Your Name represents a thematic remake of the directors astonishing masterpiece, The Place Promised in Our Early Days (2004) (up to the point of visually replicating the iconic crater scene in this film), but with a notorious decrease in emotional maturity and psychological exploration. It becomes more an adventure against time where a romance is born, against Shinkais previously established ideology, very coincidentally. The resolution it gives during the final minutes is also a betrayal against how life goes on (and must go on) in spite of our hopeless insistence of trying to retain improbable relationships. Hes a realist, an honest one. Not here. Here, he sells the Disney World fantasy of happily ever after. This radical change is clearly appealing the sensibilities of a Western audience who receives exactly that fantasy as a satisfactory resolution. It is no surprise that his most mature works receive the least praise and are even cataloged as boring, self-indulgent and empty narrated monologues. If only directors could achieve that depth of vocabulary and stream of consciousness when it comes to treating their characters...
Not here. This film is a product of popular demand and it paid pretty well in cash but against Shinkais philosophy of lifes unpredictability and the multi-generational complexity of human relationships.
The key scene is the kuchikamizake drinking, were we are taken into a segment that basically represents experimentation in the animation department. It works because it is so radically different. With an unintended nod to Noés Enter the Void (2009), we become a cell again, forming life, witnessing birth and exploring an entire life and its challenges with a different visual style. Its stunning. Its one of the relevant revelatory moments in cinema, like the imagined, hypothetical flashback Aron Ralston has in Boyles 127 Hours (2010). It almost convinces you that the film has a deeper agenda than a rom-com with sexual humor and dramatic moments. Its indescribably gorgeous.
Credit where it is due, the second act picks up quite nicely the superficiality of the first act, describing the act of tragedy just as it is, utilizing exceptional animation and editing, and a beautiful score (with a cringe soundtrack I must add), but then stupid script decisions are made, such as
SPOILERS
-Both not being able to remember their respective names even if they lived within each others bodies and had an astral encounter!
-Both recognizing each other even if they, supposedly, had forgotten about each other, which was also inexplicable
-Him writing I LOVE YOU in her hand instead of her name, which is just a cheap and cliched stunt to extract emotions freely from the audience while not helping the plot at all (something that, hilariously, she agrees with when she reads the palm of her hand)
-Related to the previous point, not enough dramatic background is offered to justify that he LOVES her. What are his motivations for such a strong decision? Just a coincidental, sexually-related fantasy perspective?
END OF SPOILERS
It comes as clear what Shinkai used for replacing epistemological discussion body-swapping and alternate timelines. These topics are immediate attention-grabbers for audiences. Ask Nolan. He loves playing with theories on time and space, even dreams and memory. Those elements make his films almost automatically attractive to try out. Thats not bad per se, sure, until you throw out all valuable possibilities out of the window and push the plot forward with Deus-Ex-Machina decisions in the name of romance and suspense.
Characters, on the other hand, are very human. I tremendously loved the story of the grandmother and their journey to the mountain to cross the underworld and offer the kuchikamizake as a tribute. The whole journey with Mitsuha carrying her grandmother and speaking about past lives couldnt stop me from thinking of Ballad of Narayama (any version you wish). Subplots like that add a lot of value to character backstories. The film is full of little moments like this, mostly in the second act, which add the depth Shinkai is known for (and unjustifiably maligned).
The greatest deceit this film does is that it tries to convince you that the two characters have a significant and even transcendent connection, when they actually dont. And people believe they do, because of the visuals. What is the correlation there? Zero. However, it seems people are, indeed, falling for what it is supposed to represent, for what it was meant to be, and never achieved to be.
So, this is Makotos Shinkai worst, even below Children Who Chase Lost Voices (2011), so Ill have to favor the he gave me a kiss out of nowhere and therefore I am willing to risk my life and follow him to the underworld forever amidst a milkshake of random international culture references flick over the he probably touched my boobies and I touched his wee wee because we swapped bodies randomly, but we are meant to be together forever even if we inexplicably forget about each other, not necessarily meaning that we will be able to illogically recognize ourselves if we make eye contact ever again flick.
At least, we have tons and tons of trains again.

When I watched this film, I was completely blown away by a compelling storyline that transcended time and space, and was lost in this universe. This was for all but a brief moment - slight distraction from the unbearable cramped leg roomseat combo thingy present in every screen at Odeon Panton Street.

This is one of the most visually striking and beautiful films Ive ever seen. The comet shots, and the gorgeous scenery and nature especially, are absolutely breathtaking. Its all balanced with a beautiful storyline too. I love a film that plays with time in such a unique way, and the message about how love and memory can transcend it really hits the spot for me. It reminded me of Arrival in this way, how it explores love and time. Its executed just as superbly too, which is a huge compliment since thats one of my favourite films ever. I also feel like theres something to be said here about how it shows how important truly understanding someone is in love, shown through the switching of lives, alongside the idea that you cant change whats fated to happen, but you can change how you respond to it.
What a layered plot as well. Its complex enough to be genuinely thought provoking, but it balances all that intricacy and mystery with such a strong emotional core. The themes of love, memory, and fate run deep, yet it never feels confusing because everything is so meticulously put together. It really emphasises those central ideas in a way that keeps it engaging and accessible, while still being emotional and moving. Its the kind of story that invites you to think, but never at the expense of how it makes you feel, which I really liked. This is something that I think some films dealing with similar concepts fail to do, but the storytelling and sci-fi concepts are so grounded in intimate human experiences, and this balance in execution really stuck with me. Exceeded my expectations. Honestly, outside of Ghibli films, if you even count them as such, I actually havent seen, like, any anime films, so I was really pleased with how much I enjoyed this!
Mitsuha ultimately wished for a life beyond her town, only to end up connecting with Taki and fighting through time itself to save that very town. Theres something so compelling in that idea of ancestral power surfacing in a moment of crisis, working across timelines with knowledge gained before and after the disaster. And then theres the red braid, this quiet but powerful symbol that transcends time and destiny. Even when the timeline is corrected and their memories of each other are gone, that connection still endures, even unknowingly. The braid feels like a physical representation of their bond, proof that their lives remain tied together through something deeper than memory, their longing hinting at a love that cant fully fade. These are just my interpretations anyway, but theyre what made this film so remarkable for me. It has literally everything you could want from a film like this!

Tocó ir al cine a ver el reestreno de Your Name en su décimo aniversario, lo que me hizo reflexionar sobre cómo ha pasado el tiempo. No soy el mismo desde la primera vez que la vi sin embargo, me sigue emocionando como el primer día. Nunca me canso de verla y, cada vez que la miro, sigo creyendo en el amor, aunque esté más soltero que nunca . Esta vez, verla en el cine fue una experiencia llena de nostalgia, fue como si la estuviera viendo por primera vez de nuevo.
Y verla de nuevo me hace pensar que nunca he sido suficiente para nadie, que nunca he sido la primera opción de nadie y que jamás nadie se ha fijado en mí. Me da envidia saber que una historia así, como encontrar a alguien mediante el hilo rojo del destino, jamás me va a pasar a mí.
Duele ver una película de este estilo porque, aproximadamente un mes atrás, intenté volver a sentir el amor. Y digo intenté porque fue un total fracaso, esa chica me rechazó, dejándome otra vez con todo el amor que deseaba darle en las manos. Siempre es lo mismo y siempre será lo mismo, pero sé que todo fue mi culpa por pensar que esta vez sería diferente. Si al final nunca fuimos nada, nunca llegamos a ser más que dos personas que compartían conversaciones, risas y pequeños momentos que, para mí, significaban mucho más de lo que imaginaba.
Creo que mi error fue confundirlo con algo más que una amistad, porque la manera en que me trataba me hacía sentir especial. Se preocupaba por mí, me preguntaba cómo estaba, me escuchaba cuando necesitaba hablar y tenía pequeños detalles que, aunque quizás para ella eran normales, para mí significaban demasiado. No sé en qué momento empecé a sentir algo por ella, solo sé que, poco a poco, comencé a esperar sus mensajes, a sonreír cuando me hablaba y a encontrar felicidad en cosas tan simples como pasar un rato con ella. Mientras ella probablemente solo estaba siendo una buena amiga, yo comenzaba a imaginar cómo sería tener algo más.
Me ilusioné con la posibilidad de que algún día sintiera lo mismo, de que sus palabras tuvieran un significado diferente y de que, en algún momento, yo pudiera ocupar un lugar más importante en su vida. Pero nunca fue así. Ella seguía tratándome con el mismo cariño de siempre, sin saber que yo, por dentro, cada vez sentía más cosas por ella. Y no la culpo, porque nunca me prometió nada, nunca me dijo que me amaba ni me dio razones para exigirle que sintiera lo mismo. Fui yo quien se aferró a pequeños detalles, quien confundió su cariño con amor y quien terminó enamorándose de alguien que solo quería brindarme su amistad.
Lo triste es que no extraño solamente lo que sentía por ella, también extraño hablar con ella sin tener que pensar en lo que significaba cada palabra, reírme sin preguntarme si algún día podría ser algo más y disfrutar de su compañía sin sentir este cariño que ahora me cuesta tanto guardar. Porque alejarme de ella no significa que haya hecho algo malo, significa que necesito aprender a verla como ella siempre me vio a mí. Y aunque me duela aceptarlo, ella nunca me rompió el corazón intencionalmente simplemente me trató con cariño y yo terminé enamorándome de una forma de querer que nunca estuvo destinada a ser amor. Otro año mas que terminaré SOLO.
